The formulation follows the classic “time‑space” representation of railway timetabling, enriched with **speed‑selection variables** that connect travel time on a segment to the energy consumed while traversing it. All decision variables, the objective function, and every class of constraint are written explicitly, together with a short interpretation of each term. --- ## 1. Notation | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | **Sets** | | | 𝒯 = {1,…,T} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. | | 𝒮 = {1,…,S} | Ordered set of track segments (including stations). Segment *s* starts at node *vs* and ends at node *vs+1*. | | 𝒦 = {1,…,K} | Set of admissible speed‑levels (or “speed classes”) for a train on a segment. For each *k* we know a cruising speed *vk* (km/h). | | 𝔅 ⊆ 𝒮 | Subset of *blocked* segments (the segment(s) that are partially closed). | | **Parameters** | | | 𝛿t,s | Minimum dwell time (minutes) that train *t* must spend at the beginning node of segment *s* (usually a station). =0 for pure running segments. | | τs,k | Travel time (minutes) to traverse segment *s* when cruising at speed level *k*. This is pre‑computed as length(s) / vk plus an allowance for acceleration/deceleration. | | es,k | Energy consumption (MJ) of a train on segment *s* when using speed level *k*. Linear in speed‑level (or taken from a look‑up table). | | Cs | Capacity of segment *s* (maximum number of trains that can occupy it simultaneously). Usually Cs=1 for a single track, >1 for parallel tracks. | | Bs = [bs^{start}, bs^{end}] | Time window (minutes from a reference zero) during which the blocked segment *s∈𝔅* is **unavailable** (e.g., a construction crew works). | | w1, w2 | Positive weights for the two parts of the objective (delay and energy). They are chosen by the planner (e.g., w1≫w2 if punctuality is priority). | | At | Planned (original) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (or the scheduled departure from its origin). | | αt,s | Minimum head‑way (minutes) that train *t* must keep from the train that precedes it on segment *s* (safety separation). | | βt,s | Maximum allowed head‑way (minutes) on segment *s* (to avoid excessive gaps). | | M | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to dominate any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶). | | **Decision variables** | | | xt,s,k ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k*; 0 otherwise. | | yt,s ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* **uses** segment *s* (i.e., the segment is part of its route). For a fixed topology this is often 1 for all *s* on the train’s path; we keep it to model possible rerouting around the blocked area. | | ut,s ∈ {0,1} | 1 if train *t* **enters** segment *s* (i.e., the train’s time‑space node at the entrance of *s* is active). | | dt,s ∈ ℝ⁺ | **Departure time** of train *t* from the start node of segment *s* (the instant it leaves the node and enters *s*). | | at,s ∈ ℝ⁺ | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the end node of segment *s* (the instant it leaves *s*). | | zt,t′,s ∈ {0,1} | Ordering binary: 1 if train *t* precedes train *t′* on segment *s* (i.e., *t* exits before *t′*). Only defined for *t≠t′* and *tt ∈ ℝ⁺ | **Total delay** of train *t* measured at its final destination: πt = max{0 , at, S – At}. | | ξ | The **objective value** (weighted sum) – introduced for readability. | All time variables are measured in minutes; all energy quantities in megajoules (MJ). --- ## 2. Model ### 2.1 Objective \[ \boxed{ \min \; \xi \;=\; w_{1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\pi_{t} \;+\; w_{2}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} e_{s,k}\,x_{t,s,k} } \] * The first term penalises total passenger delay. * The second term adds the total energy consumption of all trains, obtained by the speed‑level choice on each segment. --- ### 2.2 Routing / Rerouting If a train is allowed to **avoid** a blocked segment, we need binary routing variables: \[ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} y_{t,s}=|\text{required‑path}| \qquad &&\forall t \\ &y_{t,s}=0 &&\forall t,\; s\in\mathcal B \text{ when } \big[\,b_{s}^{start},b_{s}^{end}\,\big]\neq\emptyset\ \text{(optional: only if the block is permanent)}\\ &y_{t,s}\ge u_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \end{aligned} \] In many practical settings the route is fixed, so the first two constraints collapse to \(y_{t,s}=1\) for all segments on the train’s standard path. --- ### 2.3 Speed‑selection coupling Each train must select **exactly one speed level** on a segment it actually traverses: \[ \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} x_{t,s,k}=u_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S \tag{1} \] If the train does **not** use segment *s* (i.e., \(u_{t,s}=0\)) then all the \(x_{t,s,k}\) become 0. --- ### 2.4 Time‑space feasibility 1. **Travel‑time link** (travel time depends on chosen speed level) \[ a_{t,s} = d_{t,s} + \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\tau_{s,k}\,x_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t,s \tag{2} \] Because only one \(x_{t,s,k}\) can be 1 (by (1)), the right‑hand side collapses to the appropriate \(\tau_{s,k}\). 2. **Dwell / minimum stop time** (only relevant at stations) \[ d_{t,s+1} \ge a_{t,s} + \delta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,\; s\in\mathcal S \tag{3} \] If \(\delta_{t,s}=0\) the constraint simply passes the time forward. 3. **Blocking‑window avoidance** – a train may *enter* a blocked segment only outside its forbidden interval: \[ d_{t,s} \le b_{s}^{start} \;+\; M\,(1-w_{t,s}) \quad\text{or}\quad d_{t,s} \ge b_{s}^{end} \;-\; M\,(w_{t,s}) \qquad\forall t,\; s\in\mathcal B \tag{4} \] where \(w_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) is an auxiliary binary that decides whether the entry happens **before** the block ( \(w_{t,s}=1\) ) or **after** it ( \(w_{t,s}=0\) ). The big‑M eliminates the irrelevant inequality. A compact, linear way is to use two constraints: \[ \begin{aligned} d_{t,s} + M\,w_{t,s} &\le b_{s}^{start} + M\\ d_{t,s} &\ge b_{s}^{end} - M\,(1-w_{t,s})\qquad\forall t, s\in\mathcal B \end{aligned} \tag{4'} \] Only one of them can be active, forcing the entry time outside the blocked interval. --- ### 2.5 Capacity & Conflict avoidance on shared track We use **ordering variables** \(z_{t,t',s}\) to guarantee that at most \(C_s\) trains occupy a segment at the same time and that the chosen order respects the required head‑ways. For any ordered pair \(t *x* – speed choice on each traversed segment.
*u* – “is the train on this segment?”.
*d*, *a* – departure / arrival times (continuous).
*z* – ordering of trains that share a segment (binary).
*π* – penalty for being late. | Captures the two‑level decision problem: (i) **where/when** a train moves, (ii) **how fast** it moves. | | **Objective** | Weighted sum of (i) total passenger delay, (ii) total energy consumption (obtained from the speed‑choice variables). Changing the weights trades punctuality against sustainability. | | **Routing constraints** | Allow or forbid a train from using a blocked segment; can model detours because the route variables *y* are binary. | | **Speed‑travel‑time coupling** (1‑2) | Guarantees that exactly one speed level is selected per segment and that the corresponding travel time appears in the time‑space diagram. | | **Dwell / minimum stop** (3) | Enforces required station stoppage times (or a minimum clearance time on a node). | | **Blockage‑window constraints** (4) | Guarantees that a train never enters a blocked segment while the block is active; the binary *w* chooses “before” or “after”. | | **Capacity & conflict avoidance** (5‑5′) | Using ordering binaries *z* the model prevents two trains from occupying the same single‑track segment simultaneously, respects safety head‑ways, and limits the total number of simultaneous occupants to the physical capacity *C_s*. | | **Delay definition** (6) | Measures how much later a train arrives at its final destination compared with its original schedule; feeds directly into the objective. | | **Big‑M** | Standard linear‑ization device that “turns off” a constraint when a binary condition is not satisfied. The value of *M* must be larger than the latest possible time (e.g., the planning horizon). | --- ## 4. How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – For every segment *s* compute the travel‑time table \(\tau_{s,k}\) and the corresponding energy table \(e_{s,k}\) for all admissible speeds *k*. 2. **Blockage specification** – Provide the start/end times \([b_{s}^{start},b_{s}^{end}]\) for each blocked segment. 3. **Safety parameters** – Set the minimum head‑way \(\alpha_{t,s}\) (often a constant, e.g., 2 min) and, if desired, the maximum head‑way \(\beta_{t,s}\). 4. **Choose weights** – Decide the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., \(w_1=1,\ w_2=0.001\) if delay is measured in minutes and energy in MJ). 5. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The output gives a feasible schedule (arrival/departure times) together with a speed plan that respects the blockage and minimizes the weighted cost. --- ### 5. Full linear formulation (compact) \[ \begin{aligned} \min\; & w_{1}\sum_{t}\pi_{t}+w_{2}\sum_{t}\sum_{s}\sum_{k} e_{s,k}x_{t,s,k}\\[4pt] \text{s.t. } & \sum_{k}x_{t,s,k}=u_{t,s} &&\forall t,s &&\text{(speed‑selection)}\\ & a_{t,s}=d_{t,s}+\sum_{k}\tau_{s,k}x_{t,s,k} &&\forall t,s &&\text{(travel time)}\\ & d_{t,s+1}\ge a_{t,s}+ \delta_{t,s} &&\forall t,s &&\text{(dwell)}\\ & d_{t,s}+M w_{t,s}\le b_{s}^{start}+M &&\forall t, s\in\mathcal B\\ & d_{t,s}\ge b_{s}^{end}-M(1-w_{t,s}) &&\forall t, s\in\mathcal B &&\text{(blockage)}\\ & a_{t,s}+ \alpha_{t,s}\le d_{t',s}+M(1-z_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t **Constraint:** \(\displaystyle\sum_{p\in P}x_{t,p}=1 \;\; \forall t\) (each train follows exactly one route). ### 2.2 Ordering on shared segments (binary) For any ordered pair of distinct trains \((t,i)\) that may occupy the **same segment** *s* (i.e. routes of *t* and *i* both contain *s*) we introduce a binary “precedence” variable \[ y_{t,i,s}\in\{0,1\}\qquad \forall t\neq i,\; s\in S \text{ with }s\in p(t)\cap p(i) \] *1* ⇒ train *t* leaves segment *s* **before** train *i* enters it. ### 2.3 Timing (continuous) \[ \begin{aligned} a_{t,s} &\ge 0 &&\text{arrival time of train } t \text{ at the *up‑stream* node of segment } s,\\[2pt] d_{t,s} &\ge 0 &&\text{departure time of train } t \text{ from the *down‑stream* node of segment } s. \end{aligned} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in p(t) \] For the first segment of a train’s route we also have a **scheduled departure** \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t,0}\) (the planned departure from the origin). ### 2.4 Speed / Energy (binary + continuous) For each train‑segment pair we decide the *speed level* that will be applied: \[ \begin{aligned} z_{t,s,k} &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{train } t \text{ uses speed level } k \text{ on segment } s,\\ \theta_{t,s,k} &\ge 0 &&\text{travel time on segment } s \text{ if speed level } k \text{ is chosen.} \end{aligned} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in p(t),\; k\in K \] Only one speed level can be selected per segment: \[ \sum_{k\in K} z_{t,s,k}=1\qquad\forall t,s . \] The **deterministic relation** between speed, length \(\ell_s\) and travel time is linear‑approximated by a set of pre‑computed constants \(\theta^{\text{base}}_{s,k}\) : \[ \theta_{t,s,k}= \theta^{\text{base}}_{s,k}\, z_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s,k . \] Similarly, energy consumption per kilometer for each speed level is given by constants \(e_{s,k}\) (in kWh/km). --- ## 3️⃣ Parameters | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|----------| | \(\ell_s\) | Length of segment *s* (km). | | \(c_s\) | **Capacity** of segment *s* (maximum number of trains that can be on it simultaneously). Usually \(c_s=1\) for single‑track, \(c_s\ge 2\) for multi‑track. | | \(w^{\text{delay}}_t\) | Weight for delay of train *t* in the objective (e.g., passenger revenue loss). | | \(w^{\text{energy}}_t\) | Weight for energy consumption of train *t*. | | \(\Delta^{\text{block}}_{s} = [\underline{t}_s,\overline{t}_s]\) | **Blockage time window** on segment *s* (if *s*∈B). Trains cannot occupy *s* during this interval. | | \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t,\mathrm{orig}}\) | Scheduled (planned) departure time of train *t* from its origin. | | \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at segment *s* (from the original timetable). | | \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶ minutes). | --- ## 4️⃣ Objective Function We minimise a **weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption**: \[ \min\quad \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_t\; \bigl( a_{t,\text{last}} - a^{\text{sched}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{Total weighted delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in p(t)}\sum_{k\in K} w^{\text{energy}}_t \; e_{s,k}\; \ell_s \; z_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Total weighted energy}} \] where \(a_{t,\text{last}}\) is the actual arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (the **last** segment of its selected route). The objective is **linear** because all terms are either binary variables multiplied by constants or continuous variables that appear linearly. --- ## 5️⃣ Constraints ### 5.1 Routing selection \[ \sum_{p\in P} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T . \] If a train uses route *p*, then every segment belonging to *p* becomes “active’’ for that train. This is enforced with the following linking constraints (using a big‑M): \[ a_{t,s} \le M\,\Bigl(\sum_{p\ni s} x_{t,p}\Bigr),\qquad d_{t,s} \le M\,\Bigl(\sum_{p\ni s} x_{t,p}\Bigr) \qquad \forall t,s . \] When the sum on the right‑hand side is 0 (segment not used) the times are forced to zero (or any feasible value), otherwise they are free. ### 5.2 Flow of time on a route (travel‑time linking) For every train *t* and each consecutive pair of segments \((s, s')\) on its chosen route: \[ a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,\; \forall (s,s')\in\text{succ}(p(t)) . \] In continuous‑time notation we can write a compact version using the selected speed level: \[ d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K} \theta_{t,s,k}\,z_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t,\; s\in p(t) . \tag{Travel‑time} \] ### 5.3 Origin departure and scheduled delay \[ d_{t,\text{origin}} \ge d^{\text{sched}}_{t,\mathrm{orig}} . \] The **delay** of a train is the difference between its actual arrival at the final node and the scheduled arrival: \[ \text{Delay}_t = a_{t,\text{last}}- a^{\text{sched}}_{t,\text{last}} \ge 0 . \] (The objective already penalises this term.) ### 5.4 Capacity of a segment Because the model uses **continuous time**, capacity is enforced via **pairwise ordering variables** for any two trains that could be on the same segment simultaneously: \[ \begin{aligned} a_{i,s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\,\bigl(1-y_{t,i,s}\bigr) &&\forall t\neq i,\; s\in p(t)\cap p(i) ,\\ a_{t,s} &\ge d_{i,s} - M\, y_{t,i,s} &&\forall t\neq i,\; s\in p(t)\cap p(i) . \end{aligned} \] If \(y_{t,i,s}=1\) then train *t* leaves before train *i* enters; if it is 0 the opposite ordering holds. The pair of constraints together guarantee **non‑overlap** of the occupancy intervals on shared track. If a segment can host up to **cₛ > 1** simultaneous trains, we replace the pairwise formulation by a **cumulative‑resource** constraint (e.g., via a time‑indexed formulation); the pairwise version is kept for simplicity. ### 5.5 Conflict avoidance on **blocked** segments A blocked segment *s*∈B cannot be occupied during its blockage window \([\underline{t}_s,\overline{t}_s]\). This is realised by forcing the ordering variables relative to the blockage interval: \[ \begin{aligned} a_{t,s} &\ge \overline{t}_s \;-\; M\bigl(1-b_{t,s}\bigr) ,\\ d_{t,s} &\le \underline{t}_s \;+\; M\,b_{t,s}, \end{aligned} \qquad \forall t,\; s\in B . \] Binary \(b_{t,s}\) indicates whether the train passes **after** the blockage ( \(b_{t,s}=1\) ) or **before** ( \(b_{t,s}=0\) ). The two inequalities force the whole occupancy interval to be completely outside the forbidden window. ### 5.6 Minimum dwell / head‑way times (optional but common) At stations (nodes that are the downstream end of a segment) we may enforce a minimum dwell time \(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\) and a minimum head‑way \(\tau^{\text{head}}_{s}\) between consecutive trains: \[ d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} , \] \[ a_{i,s} \ge d_{t,s} + \tau^{\text{head}}_{s} - M\bigl(1-y_{t,i,s}\bigr) . \] These constraints are linear when the precedence variables \(y\) are already present. ### 5.7 Speed‑level feasibility Only one speed level per segment: \[ \sum_{k\in K} z_{t,s,k}=1\qquad\forall t,s . \] Travel‑time linking (already introduced in 5.2) together with the pre‑computed \(\theta^{\text{base}}_{s,k}\) guarantees that the chosen speed level yields the correct travel time. If the railway authority imposes a **maximum allowed speed** on a segment (e.g., due to a partial blockage), we simply restrict the admissible set: \[ z_{t,s,k}=0 \qquad\forall k \text{ with } \text{speed}_k > v^{\max}_s . \] ### 5.8 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ \begin{aligned} &x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,i,s}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\\ &a_{t,s},\,d_{t,s},\,\theta_{t,s,k}\ge 0 . \end{aligned} \] --- ## 6️⃣ Full MILP Summary \[ \begin{aligned} \min\;&\sum_{t\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_t\bigl( a_{t,\text{last}}-a^{\text{sched}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr) +\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in p(t)}\sum_{k\in K} w^{\text{energy}}_t\,e_{s,k}\,\ell_s\,z_{t,s,k}\\[4pt] \text{s.t. }& \sum_{p\in P}x_{t,p}=1 &&\forall t\\ &a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s} &&\forall t,\;(s,s')\in\text{succ}(p(t))\\ &d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\theta^{\text{base}}_{s,k}\,z_{t,s,k} &&\forall t,s\\ &\sum_{k\in K}z_{t,s,k}=1 &&\forall t,s\\ &a_{t,s}\ge d^{\text{sched}}_{t,\mathrm{orig}}\; \text{ for origin}\\ &\text{(pairwise ordering constraints 5.4)}\\ &\text{(blockage constraints 5.5)}\\ &\text{(dwell/head‑way constraints 5.6, if needed)}\\ &x_{t,p},y_{t,i,s},z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\theta_{t,s,k}\ge 0 . \end{aligned} \] All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, hence the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**. --- ## 7️⃣ How to Use the Model 1. **Data preparation** * Build the segment network (lengths, capacities). * Enumerate feasible routes *p* for each train (original route + any admissible detours around the blocked segment). * Define speed levels *k* (e.g., 250 km/h, 200 km/h, 150 km/h) and compute for each segment the travel‑time constants \(\theta^{\text{base}}_{s,k}= \frac{\ell_s}{v_k}\) and the energy rates \(e_{s,k}\). * Provide the blockage time window \([\underline{t}_s,\overline{t}_s]\) for each blocked segment. 2. **Model building** * Insert the data into the MILP template above (all indices, parameters, big‑M). * If the network is large, replace the pairwise ordering variables by a **time‑indexed cumulative resource** formulation to keep the model size manageable. 3. **Solve** * Feed the model to a commercial solver (Gurobi, CPLEX) or an open‑source one (SCIP, CBC). * The solver returns: * the **chosen route** for every train (\(x_{t,p}=1\)), * the **speed level** on each segment (\(z_{t,s,k}=1\)), * the **arrival/departure schedule** (\(a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\)). 4. **Interpretation** * **Delay** of each train is directly read from the objective term. * **Energy consumption** is the sum of \(e_{s,k}\ell_s\) for the selected speed levels. * The solution automatically respects the **partial blockage** (no train occupies a blocked segment during its forbidden window) and all **capacity/conflict** constraints. --- ### Remarks & Extensions * **Robustness / Uncertainty** – If blockage times are uncertain, the model can be duplicated for several scenarios and a **min‑max** objective can be added. * **Rolling horizon** – For very long horizons, solve the MILP repeatedly on a moving time window, fixing decisions already executed. * **Multiple train types** – Different weights \(w^{\text{energy}}_t\) and speed‑level tables can be used for passenger vs. freight services. * **Dynamic energy price** – Replace the constant \(w^{\text{energy}}_t\) by a time‑dependent price \(c^{\text{energy}}(a_{t,s})\) and keep linearity by piecewise‑linear approximation. --- ### TL;DR The formulation above captures **(i) rerouting**, **(ii) sequencing on shared track**, **(iii) speed‑selection which directly determines travel time and energy**, and **(iv) the intermittent blockage** of a segment, all inside a **single mixed‑integer linear program** whose objective is a weighted sum of train delay and energy usage. Feel free to adapt the parameter values, add more speed levels, or replace the big‑M ordering with a stronger cumulative‑resource formulation – the structure stays the same. Happy modelling!

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)  
Partial‑Segment‑Blockage Case**

---

### 1.  Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **𝒯** = {1,…,T} | set of trains |
| **𝒮** = {1,…,S} | ordered set of track segments (including stations) |
| **𝒦** = {1,…,K} | admissible speed‑levels (cruising speeds vₖ) |
| **𝔅** ⊆ 𝒮 | blocked segments (partial blockage) |
| **Cₛ** | capacity of segment *s* (max. number of trains simultaneously on *s*) |
| **δₜ,ₛ** | minimum dwell time of train *t* at the start node of segment *s* (0 for pure running) |
| **τₛ,ₖ** | travel time (min) on segment *s* with speed‑level *k* (pre‑computed: length/​vₖ + accel./brake allowances) |
| **eₛ,ₖ** | energy consumption (MJ) on segment *s* with speed‑level *k* |
| **Bₛ = [bₛ^{start}, bₛ^{end}]** | time window during which blocked segment *s∈𝔅* is unavailable |

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

& δ_{t,t',s}+δ_{t',t,s}=1 &&\forall t<t',\;s\\[4pt]
& x_{t',s}\ge y_{t,s}+ (w_{t,s}+ε)u_{t,s} - M(1-δ_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t\neq t',\;s\\[4pt]
& x_{t',s_{out}} \ge y_{t,s_{in}}-M(1-ρ_{t,t',σ}) &&\forall σ,\;t<t'\\
& ρ_{t,t',σ}+ρ_{t',t,σ}=1 &&\forall σ,\;t<t'\\[4pt]
& \pi_t = y_{t,s_{last(t)}}-τ_t^{sched} &&\forall t\\
& \text{All variables non‑negative; binaries in }\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### How the model captures DTG signalling  

* **Speed‑dependent braking distance** (`B_s(t)`) replaces the fixed‑block “number‑of‑blocks” separation rule.  
* **Brake‑indication point** (`w_{t,s}`) is explicitly modelled and linked to the **minimum separation** constraint (last two lines).  
* **Switch sections** (`β_s`) allow a different authority length, reflecting the fact that ETCS L2 may grant a shorter MA at switches.  
* **Speed‑profile selection** (`p_{t,v}`) lets the optimizer choose a slower or faster speed to alleviate conflicts, a feature absent in classical fixed‑block CDR models.  

---

## 9.  Remarks for Implementation  

* The piece‑wise linear envelopes for `1/v` and the braking‑distance parabola can be generated automatically from the set of break‑points (e.g., every 10 km/h).  
* The big‑M value should be calibrated to the longest possible travel time across the network plus a safety buffer (e.g., `M = 12 h`).  
* Commercial MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress) can handle instances with a few hundred trains and a few thousand sections in a few minutes, especially when the piece‑wise linear approximations are kept modest (3–5 segments).  

---

**The formulation above provides a complete linear (MILP) description of the conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem under distance‑to‑go signalling, ready to be implemented and solved for real‑time railway traffic‑management.**

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
*Partial‑segment blockage disruption – bidirectional track sharing*  

---

## 1.  Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (including origin / destination), indexed by *s*. |
| **L** | Set of line‑segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *ℓ*. Each segment ℓ belongs to a *direction* d∈{+ , –}. |
| **B** ⊆ L | Sub‑set of **blocked segments** (partial blockage). |
| **Wℓ** | Disruption time‑window on blocked segment ℓ = \([w^{\text{start}}_{\ell},w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}]\). |
| **Δt** | Discretisation interval for time (e.g. 1 min). |
| **τmax** | Upper bound on travel time on any segment (in Δt‑units). |
| **τmin** | Lower bound on travel time on any segment (in Δt‑units). |
| **c^E_t** | Energy consumption coefficient for train *t* (kWh per Δt when moving). |
| **c^D_t** | Penalty cost for delaying train *t* (€/min). |
| **c^C_t** | Penalty cost for canceling train *t* (€/cancellation). |
| **M** | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints. |
| **α_t** | Maximum acceleration (Δt‑units per Δt). |
| **β_t** | Maximum deceleration (Δt‑units per Δt). |
| **v^{\max}_t** | Maximum admissible speed for train *t* (Δt‑units per Δt). |
| **v^{\min}_t** | Minimum admissible speed (normally 0). |
| **d_{st}** | Scheduled (pre‑disruption) departure time of train *t* from station *s* (in Δt‑units). |
| **a_{st}** | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *s* (in Δt‑units). |
| **R_t** | Set of admissible routes for train *t*. For a normal line a train has two possible routes on a blocked segment: **original** (stay on its own direction) or **reroute** (use opposite direction). |
| **π_{t,r}** | Binary indicator: 1 if train *t* uses route *r∈R_t*, 0 otherwise. |
| **γ_{t,s}** | Binary indicator: 1 if train *t* is cancelled, 0 otherwise. |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| **x_{t,s}** | integer (≥0) | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *s* (Δt‑units). |
| **y_{t,s}** | integer (≥0) | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *s* (Δt‑units). |
| **τ_{t,ℓ}** | integer (≥0) | Travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ (Δt‑units). |
| **v_{t,ℓ}** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *t* on segment ℓ (Δt‑units per Δt). |
| **e_{t,ℓ}** | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumed by train *t* while traversing ℓ. |
| **π_{t,r}** | binary | Route choice (original vs rerouted) for train *t*. |
| **γ_{t}** | binary | Cancellation decision for train *t*. |
| **z_{t,ℓ}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies segment ℓ during its travel (used for conflict avoidance). |
| **δ_{t,t',ℓ}** | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on segment ℓ (i.e. overlap in time). Used only in linearisation (see constraints). |

*All time variables are measured in multiples of Δt (e.g. minutes).*

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The integrated model simultaneously minimises **total delay**, **cancellation cost**, and **energy consumption**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{D}_{t}\,\bigl(x_{t,s}-d_{st}\bigr)^{+}}_{\text{Delay penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} c^{C}_{t}\,\gamma_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{E}_{t}\,e_{t,\ell}}_{\text{Energy consumption}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

`(·)^{+}` denotes the positive part; it can be linearised by introducing auxiliary variables  
\( \Delta_{t,s}\ge 0\) with constraints \( \Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st}\) and \( \Delta_{t,s}\ge 0\). Then the delay term becomes \(\sum_{t,s}c^{D}_t\Delta_{t,s}\).

---

## 4. Core Constraints  

### 4.1 Cancellation logic  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,s}\le M\,(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,s,\\
& y_{t,s}\le M\,(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,s,\\
& \pi_{t,r}\le 1-\gamma_{t} \qquad \forall t,r .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a train is cancelled (\(\gamma_t=1\)) all timing variables are forced to 0 (or a dummy large value) and no route is selected.

### 4.2 Route‑selection (original / reroute)  

Each train must choose exactly one admissible route (or be cancelled):

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t}\pi_{t,r}=1-\gamma_{t}\qquad\forall t .
\]

The route choice determines which direction the train uses on a blocked segment ℓ∈B:

\[
z_{t,\ell}= 
\begin{cases}
\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}} & \text{if } \ell\in B \text{ and original direction is allowed},\\
\pi_{t,r^{\text{reroute}}}& \text{if } \ell\in B \text{ and train uses opposite direction},\\
1 & \text{if } \ell\notin B .
\end{cases}
\]

In a linear model we introduce binary parameters  
\( \rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\in\{0,1\}\) ( =1 if route *r* uses segment ℓ). Then

\[
z_{t,\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\,\pi_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

### 4.3 Temporal consistency (arrival–departure)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,s}=x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell_{s-1}} \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S\setminus\{ \text{origin}\},\\
& x_{t,s}=y_{t,s}+ d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\;(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S\setminus\{ \text{destination}\},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\) is the (minimum) dwell time at station *s* (given data).

### 4.4 Travel‑time bounds (speed limits)  

For every train‑segment pair:

\[
\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\ \le\ \tau_{t,\ell}\ \le\ \tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

The bounds are derived from speed limits:

\[
\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}= \Big\lceil \frac{L_{\ell}}{v^{\max}_{t}} \Big\rceil ,\qquad
\tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}= \Big\lfloor \frac{L_{\ell}}{v^{\min}_{t}} \Big\rfloor .
\]

\(L_{\ell}\) is the length of segment ℓ (in Δt‑units of distance).

### 4.5 Speed‑energy relationship  

Assume a linear energy model: energy per segment equals a constant times speed (or travel time). A common approximation for high‑speed trains is:

\[
e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t \, v_{t,\ell}\, \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

Because \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\), the above can be linearised by introducing a new continuous variable \(q_{t,\ell}=1/\tau_{t,\ell}\) and using a piece‑wise linear approximation, or simply use the travel‑time bounds to approximate energy:

\[
e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t\left( \alpha^{\text{acc}}_t\,\tau_{t,\ell}+ \alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\right)z_{t,\ell},
\]

where \(\alpha^{\text{acc}}_t,\alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\) are calibrated coefficients (assumption). This expression is linear in τ.

### 4.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (within a segment)  

If a train changes speed between two consecutive segments ℓ and ℓ′, the difference in average speeds must respect limits:

\[
v_{t,\ell'}-v_{t,\ell}\le \alpha_t \qquad\forall t,\; (\ell,\ell')\text{ consecutive},\\
v_{t,\ell}-v_{t,\ell'}\le \beta_t \qquad\forall t,\; (\ell,\ell')\text{ consecutive}.
\]

Using \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\) we obtain a non‑linear term; we linearise by a *big‑M* formulation with binary variables that indicate whether the speed is increased/decreased, or by piece‑wise linear approximations (assumption).

### 4.7 Conflict‑avoidance on shared (bidirectional) segments  

Only one train may occupy a segment ℓ at a given time. Using the discretised time horizon **H** = {1,…,Hmax} we introduce binary occupancy variables:

\[
u_{t,\ell,h}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train }t\text{ is on segment }\ell\text{ during time slot }h,\\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall t,\ell,h .
\]

Linking τ to occupancy:

\[
\sum_{h= x_{t,s-1}+1}^{x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}= \tau_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

Conflict‑free condition (binary linear):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} u_{t,\ell,h}\le 1\qquad\forall \ell\in L,\; h\in H .
\]

When the time horizon is large, the model can be tightened by *interval‑based* conflict variables (see Section 5). For the purpose of this MILP we keep the simple time‑slot formulation.

### 4.8 Disruption‑window feasibility  

A train that uses a blocked segment ℓ must **avoid** the disruption window unless it is rerouted (i.e. uses opposite direction). This is expressed by forcing its occupancy to be outside \([w^{\text{start}}_{\ell},w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}]\) when the original direction is chosen:

\[
\sum_{h=w^{\text{start}}_{\ell}}^{w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}\le M\,(1-\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}})\qquad\forall t,\ell\in B .
\]

If the train is rerouted (\(\pi_{t,r^{\text{reroute}}}=1\)) the constraint is relaxed because the train travels on the opposite track (which is assumed to be free).

---

## 5.  Linearisation & Modeling Remarks  

1. **Positive‑part of delay** – Introduce auxiliary \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge0\) with  
   \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st}\) and \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge0\). The objective uses \(\Delta_{t,s}\).

2. **Energy‑speed linearisation** – Use a piece‑wise linear approximation of the function \(e(v)=a\,v^{2}+b\,v+c\) over the admissible speed interval. Introduce break‑points \(\{v^{k}\}\) and binary variables \(w_{t,\ell}^{k}\) to select the segment of the piece‑wise line.

3. **Acceleration constraints** – Replace the non‑linear term \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\) by a set of *SOS‑2* variables or by a discretised speed‑level set \(\mathcal{V}_t\). Let \(s_{t,\ell}^{p}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate speed level *p* (with speed value \(v^{p}\) and corresponding travel time \(\tau^{p}=L_{\ell}/v^{p}\)). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p}=z_{t,\ell},\qquad
   \tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{p}\tau^{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p},\qquad
   v_{t,\ell}= \sum_{p}v^{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p}.
   \]

   Acceleration limits become linear differences between successive speed‑level binaries.

4. **Big‑M values** – Choose \(M\) slightly larger than the planning horizon (e.g. total number of time slots).  

5. **Time‑slot granularity** – Δt can be set to 1 min for high‑resolution schedules; a coarser Δt (e.g., 5 min) reduces model size.

---

## 6.  Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{D}_{t}\,\Delta_{t,s}
      + \sum_{t\in T} c^{C}_{t}\,\gamma_{t}
      + \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{E}_{t}\,e_{t,\ell} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st} &&\forall t,s,\\
&\Delta_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{r\in R_t}\pi_{t,r}=1-\gamma_{t} &&\forall t,\\
&z_{t,\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\,\pi_{t,r} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&x_{t,s}\le M(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,s,\\
&y_{t,s}\le M(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,s,\\[4pt]
&y_{t,s}=x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell_{s-1}} &&\forall t,\; s\neq \text{origin},\\
&x_{t,s}=y_{t,s}+ d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,\; s\neq \text{destination},\\[4pt]
&\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell}\le \tau_{t,\ell}\le \tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t\Big(\alpha^{\text{acc}}_t\,\tau_{t,\ell}+ \alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\Big)z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{h= x_{t,s-1}+1}^{x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}= \tau_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&\sum_{t\in T} u_{t,\ell,h}\le 1 &&\forall \ell\in L,\; h\in H,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{h=w^{\text{start}}_{\ell}}^{w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}\le M\,(1-\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}}) &&\forall t,\ell\in B,\\[4pt]
&\text{(Acceleration / deceleration linearised constraints)}\\
&u_{t,\ell,h}\in\{0,1\},\; \pi_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; \gamma_{t}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\\
&x_{t,s},y_{t,s},\tau_{t,\ell},e_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All remaining non‑linear terms (speed‑energy, acceleration) are replaced by the linearisation techniques described in Section 5.

---

## 7.  Key Modeling Assumptions (explicitly stated)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | Time is discretised into equal intervals Δt (e.g., 1 min). |
| A2 | Each train has at most **two** admissible routes on a blocked segment: the original direction and the opposite‑track reroute. |
| A3 | Blocked segments are unavailable **only** during the given disruption window; after the window they are free. |
| A4 | Energy consumption on a segment is approximated linearly by travel time (or by a piece‑wise linear function of speed). |
| A5 | Dwell times at stations are known, deterministic, and must be respected in the rescheduled timetable. |
| A6 | Maximum/minimum speeds are constant for a given train on all segments (no speed‑limit variation along the line). |
| A7 | Acceleration and deceleration limits are enforced between consecutive segments via linearised speed‑level variables. |
| A8 | Cancellation is allowed for any train; cancelled trains incur a fixed penalty and generate no further constraints. |
| A9 | Conflict‑avoidance is modelled at the granularity of the chosen Δt; only one train may occupy a segment in any time slot. |
| A10| Big‑M values are set sufficiently large (≥ planning horizon) but not excessively large to avoid numerical instability. |

---

## 8.  Remarks on Solving the Model  

* The MILP can become large for realistic networks because of the time‑slot occupancy variables \(u_{t,\ell,h}\).  
* A **decomposition** approach (as suggested in the source text) is often employed:  
  1. **Master IP** – decides route choices \(\pi_{t,r}\), cancellations \(\gamma_t\) and a coarse “plan” (set of feasible travel‑time intervals) for each train.  
  2. **Sub‑problems** – for each train, given a selected plan, solve a small LP that yields a feasible speed‑profile (the “train plan”).  
  3. **Iterative refinement** – add missing conflict‑avoidance cuts (e.g., via Benders or local branching) until a feasible global timetable is obtained.  

* The formulation above provides the **complete** MILP that can be handed to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress). The linearisation tricks in Section 5 keep the model within the MILP class.

--- 

**End of model description**.

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| **x_{t,s}** | integer (≥0) | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *s* (Δt‑units). |
| **y_{t,s}** | integer (≥0) | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *s* (Δt‑units). |
| **τ_{t,ℓ}** | integer (≥0) | Travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ (Δt‑units). |
| **v_{t,ℓ}** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *t* on segment ℓ (Δt‑units per Δt). |
| **e_{t,ℓ}** | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumed by train *t* while traversing ℓ. |
| **π_{t,r}** | binary | Route choice (original vs rerouted) for train *t*. |
| **γ_{t}** | binary | Cancellation decision for train *t*. |
| **z_{t,ℓ}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies segment ℓ during its travel (used for conflict avoidance). |
| **δ_{t,t',ℓ}** | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on segment ℓ (i.e. overlap in time). Used only in linearisation (see constraints). |

*All time variables are measured in multiples of Δt (e.g. minutes).*

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The integrated model simultaneously minimises **total delay**, **cancellation cost**, and **energy consumption**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{D}_{t}\,\bigl(x_{t,s}-d_{st}\bigr)^{+}}_{\text{Delay penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} c^{C}_{t}\,\gamma_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \\
&+ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{E}_{t}\,e_{t,\ell}}_{\text{Energy consumption}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

`(·)^{+}` denotes the positive part; it can be linearised by introducing auxiliary variables  
\( \Delta_{t,s}\ge 0\) with constraints \( \Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st}\) and \( \Delta_{t,s}\ge 0\). Then the delay term becomes \(\sum_{t,s}c^{D}_t\Delta_{t,s}\).

---

## 4. Core Constraints  

### 4.1 Cancellation logic  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,s}\le M\,(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,s,\\
& y_{t,s}\le M\,(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,s,\\
& \pi_{t,r}\le 1-\gamma_{t} \qquad \forall t,r .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a train is cancelled (\(\gamma_t=1\)) all timing variables are forced to 0 (or a dummy large value) and no route is selected.

### 4.2 Route‑selection (original / reroute)  

Each train must choose exactly one admissible route (or be cancelled):

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t}\pi_{t,r}=1-\gamma_{t}\qquad\forall t .
\]

The route choice determines which direction the train uses on a blocked segment ℓ∈B:

\[
z_{t,\ell}= 
\begin{cases}
\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}} & \text{if } \ell\in B \text{ and original direction is allowed},\\
\pi_{t,r^{\text{reroute}}}& \text{if } \ell\in B \text{ and train uses opposite direction},\\
1 & \text{if } \ell\notin B .
\end{cases}
\]

In a linear model we introduce binary parameters  
\( \rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\in\{0,1\}\) ( =1 if route *r* uses segment ℓ). Then

\[
z_{t,\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\,\pi_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

### 4.3 Temporal consistency (arrival–departure)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,s}=x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell_{s-1}} \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S\setminus\{ \text{origin}\},\\
& x_{t,s}=y_{t,s}+ d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\;(1-\gamma_{t}) \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S\setminus\{ \text{destination}\},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\) is the (minimum) dwell time at station *s* (given data).

### 4.4 Travel‑time bounds (speed limits)  

For every train‑segment pair:

\[
\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\ \le\ \tau_{t,\ell}\ \le\ \tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

The bounds are derived from speed limits:

\[
\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}= \Big\lceil \frac{L_{\ell}}{v^{\max}_{t}} \Big\rceil ,\qquad
\tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}= \Big\lfloor \frac{L_{\ell}}{v^{\min}_{t}} \Big\rfloor .
\]

\(L_{\ell}\) is the length of segment ℓ (in Δt‑units of distance).

### 4.5 Speed‑energy relationship  

Assume a linear energy model: energy per segment equals a constant times speed (or travel time). A common approximation for high‑speed trains is:

\[
e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t \, v_{t,\ell}\, \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

Because \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\), the above can be linearised by introducing a new continuous variable \(q_{t,\ell}=1/\tau_{t,\ell}\) and using a piece‑wise linear approximation, or simply use the travel‑time bounds to approximate energy:

\[
e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t\left( \alpha^{\text{acc}}_t\,\tau_{t,\ell}+ \alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\right)z_{t,\ell},
\]

where \(\alpha^{\text{acc}}_t,\alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\) are calibrated coefficients (assumption). This expression is linear in τ.

### 4.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (within a segment)  

If a train changes speed between two consecutive segments ℓ and ℓ′, the difference in average speeds must respect limits:

\[
v_{t,\ell'}-v_{t,\ell}\le \alpha_t \qquad\forall t,\; (\ell,\ell')\text{ consecutive},\\
v_{t,\ell}-v_{t,\ell'}\le \beta_t \qquad\forall t,\; (\ell,\ell')\text{ consecutive}.
\]

Using \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\) we obtain a non‑linear term; we linearise by a *big‑M* formulation with binary variables that indicate whether the speed is increased/decreased, or by piece‑wise linear approximations (assumption).

### 4.7 Conflict‑avoidance on shared (bidirectional) segments  

Only one train may occupy a segment ℓ at a given time. Using the discretised time horizon **H** = {1,…,Hmax} we introduce binary occupancy variables:

\[
u_{t,\ell,h}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train }t\text{ is on segment }\ell\text{ during time slot }h,\\
0 & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall t,\ell,h .
\]

Linking τ to occupancy:

\[
\sum_{h= x_{t,s-1}+1}^{x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}= \tau_{t,\ell}\;z_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t,\ell .
\]

Conflict‑free condition (binary linear):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} u_{t,\ell,h}\le 1\qquad\forall \ell\in L,\; h\in H .
\]

When the time horizon is large, the model can be tightened by *interval‑based* conflict variables (see Section 5). For the purpose of this MILP we keep the simple time‑slot formulation.

### 4.8 Disruption‑window feasibility  

A train that uses a blocked segment ℓ must **avoid** the disruption window unless it is rerouted (i.e. uses opposite direction). This is expressed by forcing its occupancy to be outside \([w^{\text{start}}_{\ell},w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}]\) when the original direction is chosen:

\[
\sum_{h=w^{\text{start}}_{\ell}}^{w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}\le M\,(1-\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}})\qquad\forall t,\ell\in B .
\]

If the train is rerouted (\(\pi_{t,r^{\text{reroute}}}=1\)) the constraint is relaxed because the train travels on the opposite track (which is assumed to be free).

---

## 5.  Linearisation & Modeling Remarks  

1. **Positive‑part of delay** – Introduce auxiliary \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge0\) with  
   \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st}\) and \(\Delta_{t,s}\ge0\). The objective uses \(\Delta_{t,s}\).

2. **Energy‑speed linearisation** – Use a piece‑wise linear approximation of the function \(e(v)=a\,v^{2}+b\,v+c\) over the admissible speed interval. Introduce break‑points \(\{v^{k}\}\) and binary variables \(w_{t,\ell}^{k}\) to select the segment of the piece‑wise line.

3. **Acceleration constraints** – Replace the non‑linear term \(v_{t,\ell}=L_{\ell}/\tau_{t,\ell}\) by a set of *SOS‑2* variables or by a discretised speed‑level set \(\mathcal{V}_t\). Let \(s_{t,\ell}^{p}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate speed level *p* (with speed value \(v^{p}\) and corresponding travel time \(\tau^{p}=L_{\ell}/v^{p}\)). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p}=z_{t,\ell},\qquad
   \tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{p}\tau^{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p},\qquad
   v_{t,\ell}= \sum_{p}v^{p}s_{t,\ell}^{p}.
   \]

   Acceleration limits become linear differences between successive speed‑level binaries.

4. **Big‑M values** – Choose \(M\) slightly larger than the planning horizon (e.g. total number of time slots).  

5. **Time‑slot granularity** – Δt can be set to 1 min for high‑resolution schedules; a coarser Δt (e.g., 5 min) reduces model size.

---

## 6.  Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{D}_{t}\,\Delta_{t,s}
      + \sum_{t\in T} c^{C}_{t}\,\gamma_{t}
      + \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{E}_{t}\,e_{t,\ell} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\Delta_{t,s}\ge x_{t,s}-d_{st} &&\forall t,s,\\
&\Delta_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{r\in R_t}\pi_{t,r}=1-\gamma_{t} &&\forall t,\\
&z_{t,\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\rho_{t,\ell}^{r}\,\pi_{t,r} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&x_{t,s}\le M(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,s,\\
&y_{t,s}\le M(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,s,\\[4pt]
&y_{t,s}=x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell_{s-1}} &&\forall t,\; s\neq \text{origin},\\
&x_{t,s}=y_{t,s}+ d^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}(1-\gamma_{t}) &&\forall t,\; s\neq \text{destination},\\[4pt]
&\tau^{\min}_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell}\le \tau_{t,\ell}\le \tau^{\max}_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&e_{t,\ell}=c^{E}_t\Big(\alpha^{\text{acc}}_t\,\tau_{t,\ell}+ \alpha^{\text{cruise}}_t\Big)z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{h= x_{t,s-1}+1}^{x_{t,s-1}+ \tau_{t,\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}= \tau_{t,\ell}\,z_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\ell,\\
&\sum_{t\in T} u_{t,\ell,h}\le 1 &&\forall \ell\in L,\; h\in H,\\[4pt]
&\sum_{h=w^{\text{start}}_{\ell}}^{w^{\text{end}}_{\ell}} u_{t,\ell,h}\le M\,(1-\pi_{t,r^{\text{orig}}}) &&\forall t,\ell\in B,\\[4pt]
&\text{(Acceleration / deceleration linearised constraints)}\\
&u_{t,\ell,h}\in\{0,1\},\; \pi_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; \gamma_{t}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\\
&x_{t,s},y_{t,s},\tau_{t,\ell},e_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All remaining non‑linear terms (speed‑energy, acceleration) are replaced by the linearisation techniques described in Section 5.

---

## 7.  Key Modeling Assumptions (explicitly stated)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | Time is discretised into equal intervals Δt (e.g., 1 min). |
| A2 | Each train has at most **two** admissible routes on a blocked segment: the original direction and the opposite‑track reroute. |
| A3 | Blocked segments are unavailable **only** during the given disruption window; after the window they are free. |
| A4 | Energy consumption on a segment is approximated linearly by travel time (or by a piece‑wise linear function of speed). |
| A5 | Dwell times at stations are known, deterministic, and must be respected in the rescheduled timetable. |
| A6 | Maximum/minimum speeds are constant for a given train on all segments (no speed‑limit variation along the line). |
| A7 | Acceleration and deceleration limits are enforced between consecutive segments via linearised speed‑level variables. |
| A8 | Cancellation is allowed for any train; cancelled trains incur a fixed penalty and generate no further constraints. |
| A9 | Conflict‑avoidance is modelled at the granularity of the chosen Δt; only one train may occupy a segment in any time slot. |
| A10| Big‑M values are set sufficiently large (≥ planning horizon) but not excessively large to avoid numerical instability. |

---

## 8.  Remarks on Solving the Model  

* The MILP can become large for realistic networks because of the time‑slot occupancy variables \(u_{t,\ell,h}\).  
* A **decomposition** approach (as suggested in the source text) is often employed:  
  1. **Master IP** – decides route choices \(\pi_{t,r}\), cancellations \(\gamma_t\) and a coarse “plan” (set of feasible travel‑time intervals) for each train.  
  2. **Sub‑problems** – for each train, given a selected plan, solve a small LP that yields a feasible speed‑profile (the “train plan”).  
  3. **Iterative refinement** – add missing conflict‑avoidance cuts (e.g., via Benders or local branching) until a feasible global timetable is obtained.  

* The formulation above provides the **complete** MILP that can be handed to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress). The linearisation tricks in Section 5 keep the model within the MILP class.

--- 

**End of model description**.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
