Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **(i)   Rerouting / line‑choice** – binary variables that decide whether a train uses the original line or a detour when a segment is partially blocked.  
* **(ii)  Timing** – continuous variables for departure, arrival and intermediate passage times of each train on every track segment.  
* **(iii) Speed‑management** – discrete speed‑level variables (binary) that select a feasible speed on each segment; the selected speed determines travel time and energy consumption.

The model simultaneously **minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption** while respecting all operational, safety and physical constraints (block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed‑time dynamics, etc.).

---

## 1.   Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of track segments, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(D\\) | Set of possible **directions** on a segment (normally \\{forward, backward\\}), indexed by \\(d\\). |
| \\(V\\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g., \\{30, 50, 70, 90\\} km/h), indexed by \\(v\\). |
| \\(P\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of **partially blocked** segments (the “blocked zone”). |
| \\(R_t\\subseteq S\\) | Ordered list of segments that train \\(t\\) must traverse if it follows its **original route**. |
| \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\subseteq S\\) | Ordered list of segments for the **detour** (alternative route) that bypasses the blocked part. |
| \\(N_t\\) | Number of stations (or way‑points) that train \\(t\\) visits; we index them by \\(n=0,\dots,N_t\\) (0 = origin, \\(N_t\\) = final destination). |
| \\( \mathcal{N}_{t,n}\\) | Segment that connects station \\(n\\) to station \\(n+1\\) on the **chosen** route of train \\(t\\). (Will be defined by the binary routing variable.) |

---

## 2.   Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \\(x_{t}^{\text{det}}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses the **detour** (otherwise it follows its original route). |
| \\(a_{t,n}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at station \\(n\\). |
| \\(d_{t,n}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from station \\(n\\). |
| \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) in direction \\(d\\) **with speed level** \\(v\\). |
| \\(z_{t,s}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) **occupies** segment \\(s\\) (any direction, any speed).  (Derived from \\(y\\) variables.) |
| \\(E_{t}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Energy consumption** of train \\(t\\) (kWh). |
| \\( \Delta_t \\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Delay** of train \\(t\\) with respect to its scheduled arrival at the final destination. |

*Auxiliary definitions*  

\[
z_{t,s}= \sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

\[
\text{Travel time on segment }s\text{ at speed }v:\;\tau_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{v}\quad (\text{where }L_s\text{ is the length of }s)
\]

\[
\text{Energy per km at speed }v:\; \varepsilon_{v}\;(\text{kWh/km})\quad\Longrightarrow\; \text{energy on }s\text{ at }v = \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s
\]

---

## 3.   Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption:

\[
\min\; \underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{Delay term}} \;+\; \underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_t}_{\text{Energy term}}
\]

where  

* \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) and \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) are user‑provided positive weights (e.g., 1 €/min and 0.5 €/kWh).  

* \\( \Delta_t = a_{t,N_t} - A^{\text{sched}}_{t} \\) where \\(A^{\text{sched}}_{t}\\) is the scheduled arrival time of train \\(t\\) at its final destination (a data parameter).  

* \\(E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s \, y_{t,s,d,v}\).

Both terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

## 4.   Core Constraints  

### 4.1   Routing (detour) choice  

For each train we must decide whether it follows its original route or the detour. The chosen route determines which segment‑direction pairs are allowed.

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} = (1-x_{t}^{\text{det}})\,|R_t|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

\[
\sum_{s\in R^{\text{det}}_t}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} = x_{t}^{\text{det}}\,|R^{\text{det}}_t|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

(If a train uses the detour, it must occupy exactly the segments of the detour, otherwise the original ones.)

### 4.2   Exactly one speed level per traversed segment  

If a train traverses a segment, it must pick **one** speed level (and the corresponding direction).

\[
\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} \le 1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If the segment is not traversed, the left‑hand side is forced to 0 by the routing constraints above.

### 4.3   Time‑flow (departure/arrival)  

For every train and every consecutive pair of stations \\((n,n+1)\\) on its chosen route:

\[
a_{t,n+1} \ge d_{t,n} + \sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \tau_{s_{t,n},v}\; y_{t,s_{t,n},d,v}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n=0,\dots,N_t-1
\]

where \\(s_{t,n}\\) denotes the segment that connects station \\(n\\) to \\(n+1\\) on the **selected** route (the segment belongs either to \\(R_t\\) or \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\) depending on \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\)).  

Departure cannot be earlier than arrival plus a minimum dwell time \\( \theta_{t,n}\) (data):

\[
d_{t,n} \ge a_{t,n} + \theta_{t,n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n=0,\dots,N_t
\]

### 4.4   Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

Let \\(B_s \subseteq D\\) be the set of directions that are **blocked** on segment \\(s\in P\\). A train may only occupy a blocked direction if it uses a speed that respects the reduced capacity (e.g., lower speed). We model this by forbidding the forbidden direction‑speed pairs:

\[
y_{t,s,d,v}=0 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P,\; d\in B_s,\; v\in V\ \text{with } v>v^{\text{max}}_{s}
\]

where \\(v^{\text{max}}_{s}\\) is the maximum admissible speed on the blocked part (data).  

If the segment is not blocked, all directions/speeds are allowed.

### 4.5   Bidirectional conflict (single‑track safety)  

On a **single‑track** segment (most railway segments) two trains cannot occupy it in opposite directions at overlapping times. We linearise this with a classic “big‑M” disjunctive formulation.

Introduce binary variable \\(c_{t,t',s}\\) that decides the ordering of trains \\(t\\) and \\(t'\\) on segment \\(s\\) (only needed for pairs that could conflict). For every unordered pair \\((t,t')\\) with \\(t<t'\\) and for every segment \\(s\\) that is single‑track:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Start time of }t\text{ on }s: \; \sigma_{t,s}= d_{t,\text{pred}(t,s)} \\
&\text{Finish time of }t\text{ on }s: \; \phi_{t,s}= \sigma_{t,s}+ \sum_{d,v}\tau_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,d,v}
\end{aligned}
\]

(\\(\text{pred}(t,s)\\) is the station index just before entering segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\).)

Then for each pair \\((t,t')\\) and segment \\(s\\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{t,s} &\le \sigma_{t',s} + M\,(1-c_{t,t',s})\\
\phi_{t',s} &\le \sigma_{t,s} + M\,c_{t,t',s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S_{\text{single}}
\]

where \\(M\\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., the planning horizon). The binary \\(c_{t,t',s}\\) forces one of the two inequalities to be active, guaranteeing non‑overlap.

### 4.6   Minimum headway on the same direction  

If two trains travel **in the same direction** on the same segment, a minimum head‑way \\(h_{s}\\) (in minutes) must be respected:

\[
\sigma_{t',s} \ge \phi_{t,s} + h_{s} - M\,(1 - u_{t,t',s})\qquad\forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

where \\(u_{t,t',s}\\) is a binary that is 1 when train \\(t'\\) follows train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) (direction must be identical). The term \\(1-u\\) deactivates the constraint when the ordering does not apply.

### 4.7   Energy accounting  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s \; y_{t,s,d,v}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because \\(y\\) is binary and each train uses exactly one speed per traversed segment, the expression is linear.

### 4.8   Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_t = a_{t,N_t} - A^{\text{sched}}_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

If early arrival is allowed, we can bound \\(\Delta_t\\) below by zero:

\[
\Delta_t \ge 0\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Optionally, a penalty for early arrival can be added by allowing \\(\Delta_t\\) to be negative and using a piecewise linear penalty, but the basic model keeps it non‑negative.

### 4.9   Logical linking of routing and segment‑direction variables  

For every train and segment we must guarantee that a direction‑speed pair can be selected **only if** the segment belongs to the chosen route:

\[
y_{t,s,d,v} \le \begin{cases}
1-x_{t}^{\text{det}} & \text{if } s\in R_t\\[2pt]
x_{t}^{\text{det}}   & \text{if } s\in R^{\text{det}}_t\\[2pt]
0                     & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; d\in D,\; v\in V
\]

Thus, a train cannot “jump” onto a segment that is not part of its selected route.

---

## 5.   Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_t\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{Routing constraints (4.1)}\\
&\text{Exactly‑one‑speed per segment (4.2)}\\
&\text{Time‑flow constraints (4.3)}\\
&\text{Block‑occupancy limits (4.4)}\\
&\text{Bidirectional conflict (4.5)}\\
&\text{Same‑direction headway (4.6)}\\
&\text{Energy accounting (4.7)}\\
&\text{Delay definition (4.8)}\\
&\text{Logical linking (4.9)}\\
& x_{t}^{\text{det}}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,d,v}\in\{0,1\},\;
z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; c_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n},d_{t,n},\Delta_t,E_t\ge 0\qquad\forall t,n
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** in the decision variables, and the only integer variables are the binaries listed above, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 6.   Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it represents | Why it is needed |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Binary detour variable \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\)** | Chooses between original route and a pre‑computed detour that avoids the blocked segment. | Allows the optimizer to decide whether a train should be rerouted, which is the core of the “integrated rescheduling” part. |
| **Arrival / departure times \\(a_{t,n}, d_{t,n}\\)** | Real‑time schedule of each train at every station (or waypoint). | Enables calculation of delays, ensures dwell‑time feasibility, and links to travel times on segments. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\)** | Selects a discrete speed (and direction) for a train on a given segment. | Speed determines travel time (hence delay) and energy consumption; discretisation keeps the model linear. |
| **Occupancy binary \\(z_{t,s}\\)** | Indicates whether train \\(t\\) uses segment \\(s\\) at all. | Used in block‑occupancy and conflict constraints; derived from \\(y\\). |
| **Energy variable \\(E_t\\)** | Total energy used by train \\(t\\). | Appears in the objective; computed as a linear sum of speed‑dependent energy per km. |
| **Delay variable \\( \Delta_t \\)** | Difference between actual and scheduled arrival at the final destination. | Directly penalised in the objective; measures service quality. |
| **Block‑occupancy constraints** | Prevents a train from using a direction on a partially blocked segment at a speed higher than allowed. | Models the physical limitation caused by the blockage. |
| **Bidirectional conflict (big‑M) constraints** | Guarantees that two trains never occupy the same single‑track segment in opposite directions at the same time. | Enforces safety on single‑track sections. |
| **Headway constraints** | Guarantees a minimum time gap between successive trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment. | Reflects signalling and braking distance requirements. |
| **Routing‑to‑segment linking** | Forces the speed‑direction binaries to be active only on segments belonging to the chosen route (original or detour). | Guarantees logical consistency between the binary routing decision and the detailed segment‑level variables. |

---

## 7.   How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – For every train provide:  
   * scheduled departure/arrival times, dwell times \\(\theta_{t,n}\\), and the list of stations (so that \\(R_t\\) and \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\) are known).  
   * segment lengths \\(L_s\\) and, for blocked segments, the admissible speed limit \\(v^{\text{max}}_s\\).  
   * energy coefficients \\(\varepsilon_v\\) for each speed level.  
   * headway \\(h_s\\) and minimum block‑clearance times (big‑M).  

2. **Model building** – Encode the sets, parameters and constraints in a MILP solver (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, or open‑source CBC/GLPK).  

3. **Solve** – The solver returns the optimal values of \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\), \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\), and the timing variables.  

4. **Interpretation** –  
   * If \\(x^{\text{det}}_t=1\\) the train is rerouted; otherwise it stays on its original line.  
   * The selected speed level on each segment is given by the unique \\(v\\) for which \\(y_{t,s,d,v}=1\\).  
   * Arrival times give the realized delays \\( \Delta_t\\).  
   * Energy consumption is directly read from \\(E_t\\).  

5. **What‑if analysis** – By varying the weights \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) and \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) the planner can explore trade‑offs between punctuality and energy efficiency, or impose a hard limit on one of them (e.g., set a maximum total energy budget and minimise delay only).

---

### Final Remarks  

* The model is **linear** because all non‑linear relationships (travel time = length / speed, energy = speed‑dependent coefficient × length) have been pre‑computed for a finite set of speed levels.  
* The binary variables are limited to the number of trains × segments × directions × speed levels, which is typically tractable for medium‑size timetables (tens of trains, a few hundred segments).  
* If the problem size becomes large, classic decomposition techniques (e.g., Benders, column generation) or heuristic warm‑starts (using a fast dispatching rule) can be employed while still preserving the exact MILP formulation presented above.  

This MILP fully captures **integrated train rescheduling, routing (detour) decisions, and speed‑management** under the presence of a partially blocked track segment, while simultaneously optimising the **trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption**.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the problem you described – “integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management under a partially blocked track segment”.  
The model contains:

* **Decision variables** (continuous and binary) that describe the routing, timing and speed choices for each train on each track segment.  
* **An objective function** that is a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay (or schedule‑delay) and the total energy consumed by the trains.  
* **A set of linear constraints** that enforce feasibility of the schedule, respect the blockage, avoid head‑on conflicts on the two‑way line, and correctly compute the energy usage from the chosen speed levels.

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model, and each group of constraints is explained in plain English.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered from origin to destination) |
| **B ⊆ S** | Sub‑set of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g. due to maintenance). |
| **D** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *d* (e.g. 0 = stop, 1 = slow, …, Dmax) |
| **L_s** | Length (km) of segment *s* |
| **v_d** | Speed (km/h) associated with speed level *d* (constant for all trains) |
| **τ_d = L_s / v_d** | Travel time (h) on a segment of length *L_s* when speed level *d* is used (will be linearised later) |
| **E_d** | Energy consumption (kWh) per km when travelling at speed level *d* (given by a linear or piece‑wise linear function of speed) |
| **Δ_t** | Planned (unperturbed) departure time of train *t* from its origin |
| **α, β** | Positive weighting coefficients (α for delay, β for energy) |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g. M = 10 000 h) |
| **C_s** | Capacity of segment *s* (normally 1 train per direction, but can be >1 for multi‑track sections) |
| **dir_t ∈ {+1,‑1}** | Travel direction of train *t* (+1 = northbound, ‑1 = southbound) |
| **pred(t,s)** | The immediate predecessor train of *t* on segment *s* in the same direction (if any) |
| **conf(t,s)** | The immediate conflicting train of *t* on segment *s* travelling in the opposite direction (if any) |

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **x_{t,s} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* **uses** segment *s* (i.e. the chosen route passes through *s*). For a simple line network this will be 1 for all *s* on the path, but the binary allows a reroute around the blocked part. |
| **y_{t,s,d} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* **with speed level d**. Exactly one speed level must be chosen on a segment that the train uses. |
| **dep_{t,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from the *up‑stream* end of segment *s*. |
| **arr_{t,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the *down‑stream* end of segment *s*. |
| **delay_t ≥ 0** | continuous | Total delay of train *t* with respect to its planned departure Δ_t (i.e. dep_{t,origin} – Δ_t). |
| **energy_t ≥ 0** | continuous | Total energy (kWh) consumed by train *t* over the whole journey. |

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T} delay_t}_{\text{total schedule delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} energy_t}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

*The first term penalises late departures; the second term penalises high‑speed (energy‑intensive) operation. The weights α and β let the planner trade‑off punctuality against energy usage.*

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Routing constraints  

1. **Every train must start at its origin and finish at its destination**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}\; \mathbf{1}_{\text{origin of }t \in s}=1,\qquad
\sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}\; \mathbf{1}_{\text{destination of }t \in s}=1\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

(If the network is a simple line, these reduce to “x_{t,s}=1 for all s on the line”.)

2. **Rerouting around blocked segment** – a train may **skip** a blocked segment only if an alternative (parallel) segment exists. For a single‑track line we simply forbid using a blocked segment:

\[
x_{t,s}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in B
\]

If a bypass exists, a binary variable **r_t** can be introduced to indicate “use bypass”, and the constraint becomes  

\[
x_{t,s} \le 1-r_t \qquad \forall s\in B
\]

### 4.2 Speed‑selection constraints  

3. **Exactly one speed level on each used segment**  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}=x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S
\]

4. **Link speed to travel time** – linear travel‑time relationship (since v_d is constant):  

\[
arr_{t,s} - dep_{t,s} = \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{s,d}\; y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S
\]

where  

\[
\tau_{s,d}= \frac{L_s}{v_d}\quad (\text{in hours})
\]

Because τ_{s,d} is a known constant, the left‑hand side is linear.

### 4.3 Temporal continuity  

5. **Departure from the next segment equals arrival from the previous one**  

\[
dep_{t,s'} = arr_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route}
\]

In a linear line this can be written as  

\[
dep_{t,s+1} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1-x_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
\]

The big‑M term deactivates the constraint if segment *s* is not used.

### 4.4 Delay definition  

6. **Delay of each train**  

\[
delay_t = dep_{t,\,\text{origin}} - \Delta_t \qquad\forall t\in T
\]

If early departure is allowed, we can enforce \(delay_t \ge 0\) (already non‑negative).

### 4.5 Capacity / occupancy constraints  

7. **No more than C_s trains on a segment at the same time (same direction)**  

For every pair of trains (t, k) that travel in the same direction on the same segment:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - z_{tks})\qquad
arr_{k,s} \ge dep_{t,s} - M\,(1 - (1-z_{tks}))
\]

where **z_{tks} ∈ {0,1}** is a binary ordering variable (z=1 ⇒ train k departs after t leaves).  
To keep the model linear we can use the classic “disjunctive” formulation:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - u_{tks})\\
dep_{t,s} \ge arr_{k,s} - M\,(u_{tks})
\]

with \(u_{tks}\in\{0,1\}\). The number of such binaries grows with \(|T|^2\) but is necessary for exact sequencing.

If the segment is single‑track (C_s = 1) this ensures **head‑way** separation.

### 4.6 Opposite‑direction conflict (bidirectional line)  

8. **Only one train may occupy a single‑track segment at a time, regardless of direction**  

For any pair (t,k) with opposite directions on the same segment:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - w_{tks})\\
dep_{t,s} \ge arr_{k,s} - M\,(w_{tks})
\]

where \(w_{tks}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first. This is the same “big‑M” disjunction used above, but applied to opposite‑direction pairs.

If the segment is double‑track (capacity 2, one per direction) the constraint can be omitted.

### 4.7 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy consumed on each segment**  

\[
energy_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D} \bigl( E_d \, L_s \bigr) \; y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because \(E_d\) (kWh per km) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

### 4.8 Optional: speed‑change penalty (to avoid unrealistic acceleration)  

If the planner wants to limit the number of speed changes:

\[
\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{d'\neq d} \bigl( y_{t,s,d}\; y_{t,s+1,d'} \bigr) \le \kappa_t
\]

The product of binaries can be linearised with an auxiliary binary \(q_{t,s,d,d'}\) and constraints:

\[
q_{t,s,d,d'} \ge y_{t,s,d}+y_{t,s+1,d'}-1,\qquad
q_{t,s,d,d'} \le y_{t,s,d},\qquad
q_{t,s,d,d'} \le y_{t,s+1,d'}
\]

Then  

\[
\sum_{s,d\neq d'} q_{t,s,d,d'} \le \kappa_t
\]

where \(\kappa_t\) is a prescribed maximum number of speed changes for train *t*.

---

## 5. Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,dep,arr,delay,energy} \;& \alpha\sum_{t}delay_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t}energy_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\sum_{d} y_{t,s,d}=x_{t,s} & \forall t,s \\[4pt]
arr_{t,s}-dep_{t,s}= \sum_{d}\tau_{s,d}\,y_{t,s,d} & \forall t,s \\[4pt]
dep_{t,s+1}=arr_{t,s} \;(\text{or big‑M version}) & \forall t,s\\[4pt]
delay_t = dep_{t,origin}-\Delta_t & \forall t\\[4pt]
energy_t = \sum_{s,d}E_d L_s \, y_{t,s,d} & \forall t\\[4pt]
x_{t,s}=0 \;\; \forall s\in B & \forall t\\[4pt]
\text{capacity / ordering binaries } u_{tks},w_{tks} \text{ enforce }\\
\qquad dep_{k,s}\ge arr_{t,s}-M(1-u_{tks}),\;
dep_{t,s}\ge arr_{k,s}-M u_{tks} & \forall t<k,\; \text{same dir}\\[4pt]
\qquad dep_{k,s}\ge arr_{t,s}-M(1-w_{tks}),\;
dep_{t,s}\ge arr_{k,s}-M w_{tks} & \forall t,k,\; \text{opp. dir}\\[4pt]
x_{t,s},y_{t,s,d}\in\{0,1\},\;
dep_{t,s},arr_{t,s},delay_t,energy_t\ge0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries that decide routing, speed level, and the ordering of trains on a segment. The model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – supply the network topology (list of segments, lengths, which ones are blocked), the train set (origins, destinations, planned departure times, direction), the admissible speed levels and their associated speeds/energy rates, and the weighting coefficients α, β.  
2. **Big‑M selection** – choose M larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 h is safe).  
3. **Solve** – run the MILP solver. The optimal solution tells you for each train:
   * whether it is rerouted around the blockage (binary *x*),
   * which speed level to adopt on each segment (binary *y*),
   * the exact departure/arrival times (continuous *dep*, *arr*),
   * the resulting delay and energy consumption.  
4. **Post‑processing** – translate the binary speed decisions back into actual speed profiles, compute any additional performance indicators (e.g., passenger‑time loss), and, if needed, feed the schedule back to an operational dispatch system.

---

### Summary of model elements  

| Element | Role in the MILP |
|--------|------------------|
| **Binary routing variables** `x_{t,s}` | Allow a train to avoid a blocked segment (partial blockage) or to take an alternative bypass. |
| **Binary speed‑level variables** `y_{t,s,d}` | Choose a discrete speed on each traversed segment; makes the problem linear while capturing the speed‑energy trade‑off. |
| **Continuous timing variables** `dep_{t,s}, arr_{t,s}` | Record the exact schedule; linked to speed through travel‑time equations. |
| **Delay variables** `delay_t` | Measure deviation from the original timetable; appear in the objective. |
| **Energy variables** `energy_t` | Accumulate segment‑wise energy use; appear in the objective. |
| **Ordering binaries** `u_{tks}, w_{tks}` | Enforce that two trains (same or opposite direction) do not occupy a single‑track segment simultaneously – the classic disjunctive (big‑M) formulation for head‑way safety. |
| **Objective** `α·∑delay + β·∑energy` | Linear weighted sum that the planner can tune to prioritize punctuality vs. sustainability. |
| **Capacity / blockage constraints** | Guarantee that blocked segments are not used (or only via a bypass) and that segment capacities are respected. |
| **Continuity constraints** | Ensure a feasible train path (departure of the next segment follows arrival of the previous one). |
| **Energy calculation** | Linear expression because speed levels are discrete and energy per km is known for each level. |

The formulation above is **complete, linear, and ready for implementation** in any standard MILP solver. Adjust the sets, parameters, or add extra constraints (e.g., crew‑working‑time limits, minimum dwell times at stations) as needed for your specific railway operation.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary for reroute decision, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed dynamics, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **(i)   Rerouting / line‑choice** – binary variables that decide whether a train uses the original line or a detour when a segment is partially blocked.  
* **(ii)  Timing** – continuous variables for departure, arrival and intermediate passage times of each train on every track segment.  
* **(iii) Speed‑management** – discrete speed‑level variables (binary) that select a feasible speed on each segment; the selected speed determines travel time and energy consumption.

The model simultaneously **minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption** while respecting all operational, safety and physical constraints (block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed‑time dynamics, etc.).

---

## 1.   Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of track segments, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(D\\) | Set of possible **directions** on a segment (normally \\{forward, backward\\}), indexed by \\(d\\). |
| \\(V\\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g., \\{30, 50, 70, 90\\} km/h), indexed by \\(v\\). |
| \\(P\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of **partially blocked** segments (the “blocked zone”). |
| \\(R_t\\subseteq S\\) | Ordered list of segments that train \\(t\\) must traverse if it follows its **original route**. |
| \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\subseteq S\\) | Ordered list of segments for the **detour** (alternative route) that bypasses the blocked part. |
| \\(N_t\\) | Number of stations (or way‑points) that train \\(t\\) visits; we index them by \\(n=0,\dots,N_t\\) (0 = origin, \\(N_t\\) = final destination). |
| \\( \mathcal{N}_{t,n}\\) | Segment that connects station \\(n\\) to station \\(n+1\\) on the **chosen** route of train \\(t\\). (Will be defined by the binary routing variable.) |

---

## 2.   Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \\(x_{t}^{\text{det}}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses the **detour** (otherwise it follows its original route). |
| \\(a_{t,n}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at station \\(n\\). |
| \\(d_{t,n}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from station \\(n\\). |
| \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) in direction \\(d\\) **with speed level** \\(v\\). |
| \\(z_{t,s}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) **occupies** segment \\(s\\) (any direction, any speed).  (Derived from \\(y\\) variables.) |
| \\(E_{t}\\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Energy consumption** of train \\(t\\) (kWh). |
| \\( \Delta_t \\) | continuous, \\( \ge 0\\) | **Delay** of train \\(t\\) with respect to its scheduled arrival at the final destination. |

*Auxiliary definitions*  

\[
z_{t,s}= \sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

\[
\text{Travel time on segment }s\text{ at speed }v:\;\tau_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{v}\quad (\text{where }L_s\text{ is the length of }s)
\]

\[
\text{Energy per km at speed }v:\; \varepsilon_{v}\;(\text{kWh/km})\quad\Longrightarrow\; \text{energy on }s\text{ at }v = \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s
\]

---

## 3.   Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption:

\[
\min\; \underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{Delay term}} \;+\; \underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_t}_{\text{Energy term}}
\]

where  

* \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) and \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) are user‑provided positive weights (e.g., 1 €/min and 0.5 €/kWh).  

* \\( \Delta_t = a_{t,N_t} - A^{\text{sched}}_{t} \\) where \\(A^{\text{sched}}_{t}\\) is the scheduled arrival time of train \\(t\\) at its final destination (a data parameter).  

* \\(E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s \, y_{t,s,d,v}\).

Both terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

## 4.   Core Constraints  

### 4.1   Routing (detour) choice  

For each train we must decide whether it follows its original route or the detour. The chosen route determines which segment‑direction pairs are allowed.

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} = (1-x_{t}^{\text{det}})\,|R_t|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

\[
\sum_{s\in R^{\text{det}}_t}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} = x_{t}^{\text{det}}\,|R^{\text{det}}_t|\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

(If a train uses the detour, it must occupy exactly the segments of the detour, otherwise the original ones.)

### 4.2   Exactly one speed level per traversed segment  

If a train traverses a segment, it must pick **one** speed level (and the corresponding direction).

\[
\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,d,v} \le 1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If the segment is not traversed, the left‑hand side is forced to 0 by the routing constraints above.

### 4.3   Time‑flow (departure/arrival)  

For every train and every consecutive pair of stations \\((n,n+1)\\) on its chosen route:

\[
a_{t,n+1} \ge d_{t,n} + \sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \tau_{s_{t,n},v}\; y_{t,s_{t,n},d,v}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n=0,\dots,N_t-1
\]

where \\(s_{t,n}\\) denotes the segment that connects station \\(n\\) to \\(n+1\\) on the **selected** route (the segment belongs either to \\(R_t\\) or \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\) depending on \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\)).  

Departure cannot be earlier than arrival plus a minimum dwell time \\( \theta_{t,n}\) (data):

\[
d_{t,n} \ge a_{t,n} + \theta_{t,n}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; n=0,\dots,N_t
\]

### 4.4   Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

Let \\(B_s \subseteq D\\) be the set of directions that are **blocked** on segment \\(s\in P\\). A train may only occupy a blocked direction if it uses a speed that respects the reduced capacity (e.g., lower speed). We model this by forbidding the forbidden direction‑speed pairs:

\[
y_{t,s,d,v}=0 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P,\; d\in B_s,\; v\in V\ \text{with } v>v^{\text{max}}_{s}
\]

where \\(v^{\text{max}}_{s}\\) is the maximum admissible speed on the blocked part (data).  

If the segment is not blocked, all directions/speeds are allowed.

### 4.5   Bidirectional conflict (single‑track safety)  

On a **single‑track** segment (most railway segments) two trains cannot occupy it in opposite directions at overlapping times. We linearise this with a classic “big‑M” disjunctive formulation.

Introduce binary variable \\(c_{t,t',s}\\) that decides the ordering of trains \\(t\\) and \\(t'\\) on segment \\(s\\) (only needed for pairs that could conflict). For every unordered pair \\((t,t')\\) with \\(t<t'\\) and for every segment \\(s\\) that is single‑track:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Start time of }t\text{ on }s: \; \sigma_{t,s}= d_{t,\text{pred}(t,s)} \\
&\text{Finish time of }t\text{ on }s: \; \phi_{t,s}= \sigma_{t,s}+ \sum_{d,v}\tau_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,d,v}
\end{aligned}
\]

(\\(\text{pred}(t,s)\\) is the station index just before entering segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\).)

Then for each pair \\((t,t')\\) and segment \\(s\\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi_{t,s} &\le \sigma_{t',s} + M\,(1-c_{t,t',s})\\
\phi_{t',s} &\le \sigma_{t,s} + M\,c_{t,t',s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S_{\text{single}}
\]

where \\(M\\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., the planning horizon). The binary \\(c_{t,t',s}\\) forces one of the two inequalities to be active, guaranteeing non‑overlap.

### 4.6   Minimum headway on the same direction  

If two trains travel **in the same direction** on the same segment, a minimum head‑way \\(h_{s}\\) (in minutes) must be respected:

\[
\sigma_{t',s} \ge \phi_{t,s} + h_{s} - M\,(1 - u_{t,t',s})\qquad\forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

where \\(u_{t,t',s}\\) is a binary that is 1 when train \\(t'\\) follows train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) (direction must be identical). The term \\(1-u\\) deactivates the constraint when the ordering does not apply.

### 4.7   Energy accounting  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{v\in V} \varepsilon_{v}\,L_s \; y_{t,s,d,v}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because \\(y\\) is binary and each train uses exactly one speed per traversed segment, the expression is linear.

### 4.8   Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_t = a_{t,N_t} - A^{\text{sched}}_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

If early arrival is allowed, we can bound \\(\Delta_t\\) below by zero:

\[
\Delta_t \ge 0\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Optionally, a penalty for early arrival can be added by allowing \\(\Delta_t\\) to be negative and using a piecewise linear penalty, but the basic model keeps it non‑negative.

### 4.9   Logical linking of routing and segment‑direction variables  

For every train and segment we must guarantee that a direction‑speed pair can be selected **only if** the segment belongs to the chosen route:

\[
y_{t,s,d,v} \le \begin{cases}
1-x_{t}^{\text{det}} & \text{if } s\in R_t\\[2pt]
x_{t}^{\text{det}}   & \text{if } s\in R^{\text{det}}_t\\[2pt]
0                     & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; d\in D,\; v\in V
\]

Thus, a train cannot “jump” onto a segment that is not part of its selected route.

---

## 5.   Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}E_t\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{Routing constraints (4.1)}\\
&\text{Exactly‑one‑speed per segment (4.2)}\\
&\text{Time‑flow constraints (4.3)}\\
&\text{Block‑occupancy limits (4.4)}\\
&\text{Bidirectional conflict (4.5)}\\
&\text{Same‑direction headway (4.6)}\\
&\text{Energy accounting (4.7)}\\
&\text{Delay definition (4.8)}\\
&\text{Logical linking (4.9)}\\
& x_{t}^{\text{det}}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,d,v}\in\{0,1\},\;
z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; c_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,n},d_{t,n},\Delta_t,E_t\ge 0\qquad\forall t,n
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** in the decision variables, and the only integer variables are the binaries listed above, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 6.   Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it represents | Why it is needed |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| **Binary detour variable \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\)** | Chooses between original route and a pre‑computed detour that avoids the blocked segment. | Allows the optimizer to decide whether a train should be rerouted, which is the core of the “integrated rescheduling” part. |
| **Arrival / departure times \\(a_{t,n}, d_{t,n}\\)** | Real‑time schedule of each train at every station (or waypoint). | Enables calculation of delays, ensures dwell‑time feasibility, and links to travel times on segments. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\)** | Selects a discrete speed (and direction) for a train on a given segment. | Speed determines travel time (hence delay) and energy consumption; discretisation keeps the model linear. |
| **Occupancy binary \\(z_{t,s}\\)** | Indicates whether train \\(t\\) uses segment \\(s\\) at all. | Used in block‑occupancy and conflict constraints; derived from \\(y\\). |
| **Energy variable \\(E_t\\)** | Total energy used by train \\(t\\). | Appears in the objective; computed as a linear sum of speed‑dependent energy per km. |
| **Delay variable \\( \Delta_t \\)** | Difference between actual and scheduled arrival at the final destination. | Directly penalised in the objective; measures service quality. |
| **Block‑occupancy constraints** | Prevents a train from using a direction on a partially blocked segment at a speed higher than allowed. | Models the physical limitation caused by the blockage. |
| **Bidirectional conflict (big‑M) constraints** | Guarantees that two trains never occupy the same single‑track segment in opposite directions at the same time. | Enforces safety on single‑track sections. |
| **Headway constraints** | Guarantees a minimum time gap between successive trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment. | Reflects signalling and braking distance requirements. |
| **Routing‑to‑segment linking** | Forces the speed‑direction binaries to be active only on segments belonging to the chosen route (original or detour). | Guarantees logical consistency between the binary routing decision and the detailed segment‑level variables. |

---

## 7.   How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – For every train provide:  
   * scheduled departure/arrival times, dwell times \\(\theta_{t,n}\\), and the list of stations (so that \\(R_t\\) and \\(R^{\text{det}}_t\\) are known).  
   * segment lengths \\(L_s\\) and, for blocked segments, the admissible speed limit \\(v^{\text{max}}_s\\).  
   * energy coefficients \\(\varepsilon_v\\) for each speed level.  
   * headway \\(h_s\\) and minimum block‑clearance times (big‑M).  

2. **Model building** – Encode the sets, parameters and constraints in a MILP solver (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, or open‑source CBC/GLPK).  

3. **Solve** – The solver returns the optimal values of \\(x^{\text{det}}_t\\), \\(y_{t,s,d,v}\\), and the timing variables.  

4. **Interpretation** –  
   * If \\(x^{\text{det}}_t=1\\) the train is rerouted; otherwise it stays on its original line.  
   * The selected speed level on each segment is given by the unique \\(v\\) for which \\(y_{t,s,d,v}=1\\).  
   * Arrival times give the realized delays \\( \Delta_t\\).  
   * Energy consumption is directly read from \\(E_t\\).  

5. **What‑if analysis** – By varying the weights \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) and \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) the planner can explore trade‑offs between punctuality and energy efficiency, or impose a hard limit on one of them (e.g., set a maximum total energy budget and minimise delay only).

---

### Final Remarks  

* The model is **linear** because all non‑linear relationships (travel time = length / speed, energy = speed‑dependent coefficient × length) have been pre‑computed for a finite set of speed levels.  
* The binary variables are limited to the number of trains × segments × directions × speed levels, which is typically tractable for medium‑size timetables (tens of trains, a few hundred segments).  
* If the problem size becomes large, classic decomposition techniques (e.g., Benders, column generation) or heuristic warm‑starts (using a fast dispatching rule) can be employed while still preserving the exact MILP formulation presented above.  

This MILP fully captures **integrated train rescheduling, routing (detour) decisions, and speed‑management** under the presence of a partially blocked track segment, while simultaneously optimising the **trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption**.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary for reroute decision, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed dynamics, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the problem you described – “integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management under a partially blocked track segment”.  
The model contains:

* **Decision variables** (continuous and binary) that describe the routing, timing and speed choices for each train on each track segment.  
* **An objective function** that is a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay (or schedule‑delay) and the total energy consumed by the trains.  
* **A set of linear constraints** that enforce feasibility of the schedule, respect the blockage, avoid head‑on conflicts on the two‑way line, and correctly compute the energy usage from the chosen speed levels.

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model, and each group of constraints is explained in plain English.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered from origin to destination) |
| **B ⊆ S** | Sub‑set of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g. due to maintenance). |
| **D** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *d* (e.g. 0 = stop, 1 = slow, …, Dmax) |
| **L_s** | Length (km) of segment *s* |
| **v_d** | Speed (km/h) associated with speed level *d* (constant for all trains) |
| **τ_d = L_s / v_d** | Travel time (h) on a segment of length *L_s* when speed level *d* is used (will be linearised later) |
| **E_d** | Energy consumption (kWh) per km when travelling at speed level *d* (given by a linear or piece‑wise linear function of speed) |
| **Δ_t** | Planned (unperturbed) departure time of train *t* from its origin |
| **α, β** | Positive weighting coefficients (α for delay, β for energy) |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g. M = 10 000 h) |
| **C_s** | Capacity of segment *s* (normally 1 train per direction, but can be >1 for multi‑track sections) |
| **dir_t ∈ {+1,‑1}** | Travel direction of train *t* (+1 = northbound, ‑1 = southbound) |
| **pred(t,s)** | The immediate predecessor train of *t* on segment *s* in the same direction (if any) |
| **conf(t,s)** | The immediate conflicting train of *t* on segment *s* travelling in the opposite direction (if any) |

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **x_{t,s} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* **uses** segment *s* (i.e. the chosen route passes through *s*). For a simple line network this will be 1 for all *s* on the path, but the binary allows a reroute around the blocked part. |
| **y_{t,s,d} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* **with speed level d**. Exactly one speed level must be chosen on a segment that the train uses. |
| **dep_{t,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from the *up‑stream* end of segment *s*. |
| **arr_{t,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the *down‑stream* end of segment *s*. |
| **delay_t ≥ 0** | continuous | Total delay of train *t* with respect to its planned departure Δ_t (i.e. dep_{t,origin} – Δ_t). |
| **energy_t ≥ 0** | continuous | Total energy (kWh) consumed by train *t* over the whole journey. |

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T} delay_t}_{\text{total schedule delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} energy_t}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

*The first term penalises late departures; the second term penalises high‑speed (energy‑intensive) operation. The weights α and β let the planner trade‑off punctuality against energy usage.*

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Routing constraints  

1. **Every train must start at its origin and finish at its destination**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}\; \mathbf{1}_{\text{origin of }t \in s}=1,\qquad
\sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}\; \mathbf{1}_{\text{destination of }t \in s}=1\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

(If the network is a simple line, these reduce to “x_{t,s}=1 for all s on the line”.)

2. **Rerouting around blocked segment** – a train may **skip** a blocked segment only if an alternative (parallel) segment exists. For a single‑track line we simply forbid using a blocked segment:

\[
x_{t,s}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in B
\]

If a bypass exists, a binary variable **r_t** can be introduced to indicate “use bypass”, and the constraint becomes  

\[
x_{t,s} \le 1-r_t \qquad \forall s\in B
\]

### 4.2 Speed‑selection constraints  

3. **Exactly one speed level on each used segment**  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} y_{t,s,d}=x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S
\]

4. **Link speed to travel time** – linear travel‑time relationship (since v_d is constant):  

\[
arr_{t,s} - dep_{t,s} = \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{s,d}\; y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S
\]

where  

\[
\tau_{s,d}= \frac{L_s}{v_d}\quad (\text{in hours})
\]

Because τ_{s,d} is a known constant, the left‑hand side is linear.

### 4.3 Temporal continuity  

5. **Departure from the next segment equals arrival from the previous one**  

\[
dep_{t,s'} = arr_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route}
\]

In a linear line this can be written as  

\[
dep_{t,s+1} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1-x_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
\]

The big‑M term deactivates the constraint if segment *s* is not used.

### 4.4 Delay definition  

6. **Delay of each train**  

\[
delay_t = dep_{t,\,\text{origin}} - \Delta_t \qquad\forall t\in T
\]

If early departure is allowed, we can enforce \(delay_t \ge 0\) (already non‑negative).

### 4.5 Capacity / occupancy constraints  

7. **No more than C_s trains on a segment at the same time (same direction)**  

For every pair of trains (t, k) that travel in the same direction on the same segment:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - z_{tks})\qquad
arr_{k,s} \ge dep_{t,s} - M\,(1 - (1-z_{tks}))
\]

where **z_{tks} ∈ {0,1}** is a binary ordering variable (z=1 ⇒ train k departs after t leaves).  
To keep the model linear we can use the classic “disjunctive” formulation:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - u_{tks})\\
dep_{t,s} \ge arr_{k,s} - M\,(u_{tks})
\]

with \(u_{tks}\in\{0,1\}\). The number of such binaries grows with \(|T|^2\) but is necessary for exact sequencing.

If the segment is single‑track (C_s = 1) this ensures **head‑way** separation.

### 4.6 Opposite‑direction conflict (bidirectional line)  

8. **Only one train may occupy a single‑track segment at a time, regardless of direction**  

For any pair (t,k) with opposite directions on the same segment:

\[
dep_{k,s} \ge arr_{t,s} - M\,(1 - w_{tks})\\
dep_{t,s} \ge arr_{k,s} - M\,(w_{tks})
\]

where \(w_{tks}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first. This is the same “big‑M” disjunction used above, but applied to opposite‑direction pairs.

If the segment is double‑track (capacity 2, one per direction) the constraint can be omitted.

### 4.7 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy consumed on each segment**  

\[
energy_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D} \bigl( E_d \, L_s \bigr) \; y_{t,s,d}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because \(E_d\) (kWh per km) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

### 4.8 Optional: speed‑change penalty (to avoid unrealistic acceleration)  

If the planner wants to limit the number of speed changes:

\[
\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{d\in D}\sum_{d'\neq d} \bigl( y_{t,s,d}\; y_{t,s+1,d'} \bigr) \le \kappa_t
\]

The product of binaries can be linearised with an auxiliary binary \(q_{t,s,d,d'}\) and constraints:

\[
q_{t,s,d,d'} \ge y_{t,s,d}+y_{t,s+1,d'}-1,\qquad
q_{t,s,d,d'} \le y_{t,s,d},\qquad
q_{t,s,d,d'} \le y_{t,s+1,d'}
\]

Then  

\[
\sum_{s,d\neq d'} q_{t,s,d,d'} \le \kappa_t
\]

where \(\kappa_t\) is a prescribed maximum number of speed changes for train *t*.

---

## 5. Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,dep,arr,delay,energy} \;& \alpha\sum_{t}delay_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t}energy_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\sum_{d} y_{t,s,d}=x_{t,s} & \forall t,s \\[4pt]
arr_{t,s}-dep_{t,s}= \sum_{d}\tau_{s,d}\,y_{t,s,d} & \forall t,s \\[4pt]
dep_{t,s+1}=arr_{t,s} \;(\text{or big‑M version}) & \forall t,s\\[4pt]
delay_t = dep_{t,origin}-\Delta_t & \forall t\\[4pt]
energy_t = \sum_{s,d}E_d L_s \, y_{t,s,d} & \forall t\\[4pt]
x_{t,s}=0 \;\; \forall s\in B & \forall t\\[4pt]
\text{capacity / ordering binaries } u_{tks},w_{tks} \text{ enforce }\\
\qquad dep_{k,s}\ge arr_{t,s}-M(1-u_{tks}),\;
dep_{t,s}\ge arr_{k,s}-M u_{tks} & \forall t<k,\; \text{same dir}\\[4pt]
\qquad dep_{k,s}\ge arr_{t,s}-M(1-w_{tks}),\;
dep_{t,s}\ge arr_{k,s}-M w_{tks} & \forall t,k,\; \text{opp. dir}\\[4pt]
x_{t,s},y_{t,s,d}\in\{0,1\},\;
dep_{t,s},arr_{t,s},delay_t,energy_t\ge0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries that decide routing, speed level, and the ordering of trains on a segment. The model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – supply the network topology (list of segments, lengths, which ones are blocked), the train set (origins, destinations, planned departure times, direction), the admissible speed levels and their associated speeds/energy rates, and the weighting coefficients α, β.  
2. **Big‑M selection** – choose M larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 h is safe).  
3. **Solve** – run the MILP solver. The optimal solution tells you for each train:
   * whether it is rerouted around the blockage (binary *x*),
   * which speed level to adopt on each segment (binary *y*),
   * the exact departure/arrival times (continuous *dep*, *arr*),
   * the resulting delay and energy consumption.  
4. **Post‑processing** – translate the binary speed decisions back into actual speed profiles, compute any additional performance indicators (e.g., passenger‑time loss), and, if needed, feed the schedule back to an operational dispatch system.

---

### Summary of model elements  

| Element | Role in the MILP |
|--------|------------------|
| **Binary routing variables** `x_{t,s}` | Allow a train to avoid a blocked segment (partial blockage) or to take an alternative bypass. |
| **Binary speed‑level variables** `y_{t,s,d}` | Choose a discrete speed on each traversed segment; makes the problem linear while capturing the speed‑energy trade‑off. |
| **Continuous timing variables** `dep_{t,s}, arr_{t,s}` | Record the exact schedule; linked to speed through travel‑time equations. |
| **Delay variables** `delay_t` | Measure deviation from the original timetable; appear in the objective. |
| **Energy variables** `energy_t` | Accumulate segment‑wise energy use; appear in the objective. |
| **Ordering binaries** `u_{tks}, w_{tks}` | Enforce that two trains (same or opposite direction) do not occupy a single‑track segment simultaneously – the classic disjunctive (big‑M) formulation for head‑way safety. |
| **Objective** `α·∑delay + β·∑energy` | Linear weighted sum that the planner can tune to prioritize punctuality vs. sustainability. |
| **Capacity / blockage constraints** | Guarantee that blocked segments are not used (or only via a bypass) and that segment capacities are respected. |
| **Continuity constraints** | Ensure a feasible train path (departure of the next segment follows arrival of the previous one). |
| **Energy calculation** | Linear expression because speed levels are discrete and energy per km is known for each level. |

The formulation above is **complete, linear, and ready for implementation** in any standard MILP solver. Adjust the sets, parameters, or add extra constraints (e.g., crew‑working‑time limits, minimum dwell times at stations) as needed for your specific railway operation.

The MILP should be described completely with equations and assumptions. Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
