Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:  

*‑ a train‑level routing decision (binary variables) for each possible route through a network that contains a partially blocked segment,  
*‑ departure / arrival times on every track segment,  
*‑ a discrete speed‑level (hence energy‑consumption) choice for each traversed segment,  
*‑ an objective that is a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy use,  
*‑ a set of linear constraints that enforce feasibility of the schedule, respect of the blockage, conflict avoidance between opposing‑direction trains, and the physics of speed‑energy consumption.*

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model.  
The formulation is **linear** (no products of two decision variables) and thus can be solved directly with any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| \\(\mathcal{T}\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(\mathcal{S}\\) | Set of track **segments** (or “links”) in the rail network, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(\mathcal{R}_t\\) | Set of **feasible routes** for train \\(t\\). Each route \\(r\\) is an ordered list of segments \\(s\\). |
| \\(\mathcal{K}\\) | Finite set of admissible **speed levels**, indexed by \\(k\\). (e.g. \\(\{1,2,3,4\}\\) meaning 30, 50, 70, 90 km/h). |
| \\(\mathcal{B}\\) | Set of **blocked segments** (the partially blocked segment and any auxiliary segments that may become unavailable). |
| \\(\mathcal{D}\\) | Set of **direction pairs** \\((t,t')\\) of trains that travel on the same segment in opposite directions (conflict pairs). |
| \\(\mathcal{P}_t\\) | Set of **precedence pairs** \\((i,j)\\) for train \\(t\\) where segment \\(i\\) must be traversed before segment \\(j\\) on the chosen route (the natural ordering of the route). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|--------------|--------------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\) | km |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed corresponding to level \\(k\\) | km / h |
| \\(c_k\\) | Energy consumption rate (e.g. kWh per km) when travelling at speed level \\(k\\) | kWh / km |
| \\(\tau^{\text{min}}_{t}\\) | Earliest allowed departure time of train \\(t\\) (planned timetable) | minutes from a reference |
| \\(\tau^{\text{max}}_{t}\\) | Latest allowed departure time (hard horizon) | minutes |
| \\(D_t\\) | Planned arrival time of train \\(t\\) at its final destination (reference schedule) | minutes |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}_t\\) | Weight (penalty) for one minute of delay of train \\(t\\) in the objective | $/min |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Global weight for energy consumption in the objective | $/kWh |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M” constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | minutes |
| \\(\alpha_{s}\\) | Fraction of segment \\(s\\) that is **blocked** (0 ≤ α ≤ 1). For a fully blocked segment α = 1, for a partially blocked one α < 1. | – |
| \\(T^{\text{block}}_s\\) | Time window during which the blocked part of segment \\(s\\) is unavailable (start, end). For simplicity we represent it by two scalars \\(t^{\text{b}}_{s}, t^{\text{e}}_{s}\\). | minutes |
| \\(\beta_{tt'}\\) | Safety‑time separation required between opposite‑direction trains on a shared segment (e.g. 2 min). | minutes |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \\(x_{t,r}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses route \\(r\\in\mathcal{R}_t\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t,s}\\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at the **beginning** of segment \\(s\\) (if \\(s\\) belongs to the selected route). |
| \\(d_{t,s}\\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from the **end** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) **at speed level** \\(k\\). (Only defined for segments that belong to the selected route of \\(t\\)). |
| \\(z_{t}\\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Total delay** of train \\(t\\) measured as \\(z_{t}= \max\{0, d_{t,\text{last}}-D_t\}\\). (Implemented with linear constraints below.) |
| \\(e_{t}\\) | continuous ≥ 0 | **Energy consumption** of train \\(t\\) (kWh). |
| \\(u_{t,s,t',s'}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) occupies the **blocked part** of segment \\(s\\) **earlier** than train \\(t'\\) occupies the same blocked part of segment \\(s'\\). (Used only for conflict pairs on blocked segments.) |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \ \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} w^{\text{delay}}_t \, z_{t}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}} \, \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} e_{t}
}
\]

The first term penalises total passenger delay, the second term penalises total electricity consumption.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1   Route‑selection (one route per train)  
\[
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R1}
\]

### 5.2   Linking segment–usage and speed‑level variables to route choice  

For every train‑segment pair we need to “activate’’ the segment only if the chosen route contains it.  
Define the indicator  

\[
\delta_{t,s,r}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if segment } s \text{ belongs to route } r\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Then  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}\;=\;\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; s\in\mathcal{S}
\tag{R2}
\]

Consequently, if a segment is not on the selected route, all its speed‑level binaries are forced to 0.

### 5.3   Time‑feasibility on each traversed segment  

When a speed level \\(k\\) is selected, the travel time on segment \\(s\\) is  

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\times 60 \quad\text{(minutes)}
\]

The departure time from a segment equals its arrival time plus the travel time of the **chosen** speed level:

\[
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \theta_{s,k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad \forall t,s
\tag{T1}
\]

### 5.4   Flow‑conservation along the chosen route  

If segment \\(j\\) follows segment \\(i\\) on the route of train \\(t\\) (i.e. \\((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t\\)), the arrival time at segment \\(j\\) must be the departure time from segment \\(i\\):

\[
a_{t,j}= d_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t
\tag{T2}
\]

The first segment of the route receives the (decision) departure time:

\[
a_{t,s^{\text{first}}}= \tau^{\text{dep}}_t \qquad
\text{with } \tau^{\text{dep}}_t\in[\tau^{\text{min}}_t,\tau^{\text{max}}_t]
\tag{T3}
\]

The departure time of the first segment is a new variable (or can be set equal to the arrival time plus a dwell time, if needed).

### 5.5   Departure‑time windows (operational limits)  

\[
\tau^{\text{min}}_t\le \tau^{\text{dep}}_t \le \tau^{\text{max}}_t
\qquad\forall t
\tag{T4}
\]

### 5.6   Delay definition  

Let \\(s^{\text{last}}_t\\) be the **final** segment of the selected route for train \\(t\\). The scheduled arrival time is \\(D_t\\). We linearise  

\[
z_t \ge d_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} - D_t,
\qquad
z_t \ge 0
\tag{D1}
\]

If the train finishes earlier than the schedule, \\(z_t\\) stays 0 (no early‑arrival credit).

### 5.7   Energy consumption calculation  

Energy for a single segment = length × energy‑rate of the selected speed level.  

\[
e_t = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} L_s \,c_k \, y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t
\tag{E1}
\]

Because only one \\(k\\) can be 1 per traversed segment, the term is linear.

### 5.8   Blocked‑segment occupancy  

A segment \\(s\\) may be **partially blocked**. Only the unblocked fraction \\((1-\alpha_s)\\) can be used at any time; the blocked fraction can only be used when no other train (or the same train in opposite direction) needs it, or when the train passes **outside** the blocked time window.

We enforce that a train cannot be inside the blocked fraction during the blocked time window:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; t^{\text{e}}_{s} \;-\; M\,(1-\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}) \quad\text{or}\quad
d_{t,s} \;\le\; t^{\text{b}}_{s} \;+\; M\,(1-\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k})
\qquad\forall t,\; s\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{B1}
\]

A cleaner linear formulation uses a *big‑M* indicator that forces the train to either finish the segment **before** the block starts or **after** it ends:

\[
a_{t,s} \le t^{\text{b}}_{s} + M\,\lambda_{t,s} \\
d_{t,s} \ge t^{\text{e}}_{s} - M\,(1-\lambda_{t,s})\\
\lambda_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}
\qquad \forall t,\; s\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{B2}
\]

If \\(\lambda_{t,s}=0\\) the train passes *before* the blockage; if it is 1 the train passes *after*.

### 5.9   Opposite‑direction conflict on the same (partially) blocked segment  

For each conflict pair \\((t,t')\in\mathcal{D}\\) that uses the same segment \\(s\\) (or the same blocked part) we must guarantee a safety separation:

\[
a_{t',s} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} + \beta_{tt'} - M\,(1-u_{t,s,t',s}) 
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\; s\in\mathcal{S}
\tag{C1}
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; d_{t',s} + \beta_{tt'} - M\,(u_{t,s,t',s}) 
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\; s\in\mathcal{S}
\tag{C2}
\]

The binary variable \\(u_{t,s,t',s}\\) decides which train goes first. Exactly one of the two inequalities will be active; the other is relaxed by the big‑M term.

An alternative that avoids extra binaries is the classic “disjunctive” formulation using a *big‑M* on a single binary:

\[
a_{t',s} \ge d_{t,s} + \beta_{tt'} - M(1-\eta_{t,t',s}) \\
a_{t,s} \ge d_{t',s} + \beta_{tt'} - M\eta_{t,t',s}
\qquad \eta_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}
\tag{C3}
\]

### 5.10   Speed‑level uniqueness per used segment  

Only one speed level can be active on a segment that the train actually traverses:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{S1}
\]

(Exactly the same as (R2); we keep it once.)

### 5.11   Logical domain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t,s,t',s'}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s}\ge 0,\; d_{t,s}\ge 0,\; z_t\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0,\\
&\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{Domain}
\]

---

## 6. Model Summary  

Putting everything together, the MILP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t} w^{\text{delay}}_t \,z_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t}e_t  \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice} \\
& \text{(T1)–(T4)} &&\text{time feasibility and horizon} \\
& \text{(D1)} &&\text{delay definition} \\
& \text{(E1)} &&\text{energy accounting} \\
& \text{(B1)–(B2)} &&\text{blocked‑segment time windows} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{bidirectional conflict avoidance} \\
& \text{(S1)} &&\text{single speed per segment} \\
& \text{Domain} &&\text{integrality / non‑negativity}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** in the decision variables, and the only integer variables are the binary route, speed‑level, and conflict‑ordering variables. Hence the problem belongs to the **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming** family and can be tackled with standard branch‑and‑bound / branch‑and‑cut solvers.

---

## 7. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – build the sets \\(\mathcal{R}_t\\) (all feasible detours around the blockage), compute the travel‑time constants \\(\theta_{s,k}\\), fill the block time windows \\(t^{\text{b}}_s, t^{\text{e}}_s\\) and the safety‑time \\(\beta_{tt'}\\).  
2. **Parameter tuning** – choose the weights \\(w^{\text{delay}}_t\\) (may reflect passenger‑volume or service class) and \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) (reflecting fuel‑price or emission cost).  
3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to a solver; the optimal solution tells you for each train:  
   * which route it should take,  
   * at what time it should depart each segment,  
   * which speed level to use on every segment,  
   * the resulting total delay and energy consumption.  

Because the model explicitly respects the partial blockage (via the big‑M “before/after” constraints) and the bidirectional conflict (via the disjunctive ordering variables), the schedule it produces is guaranteed to be **feasible** with respect to the physical rail infrastructure and the safety regulations.  

Feel free to adapt the formulation (e.g., add dwell‑time minima, promote on‑time arrivals with a penalty for early arrivals, or replace the discrete speed set by a piecewise‑linear speed‑energy approximation) – the linear structure will stay intact.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:  

*‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑*  

## 1.   Index sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(R\) | Set of trains (or “resources”) that have to be scheduled, indexed by \(r\). |
| \(S\) | Set of line **segments** (including the partially blocked segment).  Indexed by \(s\). |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible **speed‑levels** (e.g., 0 = stop, 1 = low, 2 = medium, 3 = high).  Indexed by \(k\). |
| \(P_r\) | Set of admissible **routes** (different possible paths) for train \(r\).  Indexed by \(p\). |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | Sub‑set of segments that are **partially blocked** (the blockage may be active for only a part of the time horizon). |
| \(T\) | Discrete planning horizon (e.g., minutes).  Indexed by \(t\). |

All parameters below are assumed known from the timetable, the track geometry, the blockage schedule, and the train‑energy model.

---

## 2.   Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{r p}\) | binary | 1 if train \(r\) uses route \(p\in P_r\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{r s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Arrival time** of train \(r\) at the *beginning* of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{r s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Departure time** of train \(r\) from the *end* of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{r s k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(r\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed‑level \(k\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(\delta_{r s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(r\) occupies (is present on) segment \(s\) at any time; 0 otherwise. (derived from \(y\) – used for conflict constraints). |
| \(\theta_{s t}\) | binary | 1 if the **blocked portion** of segment \(s\in B\) is occupied at time‑step \(t\); 0 otherwise (used only for bookkeeping, not a decision variable). |
| \(E_r\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Total energy** consumed by train \(r\). |
| \(D_r\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Total delay** of train \(r\) (difference between actual arrival at its destination and the scheduled/desired arrival). |

---

## 3.   Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(\underline{v}_k,\ \overline{v}_k\) | Minimum / maximum speed (km/h) associated with speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(\ell_{s}\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(t^{\text{sched}}_{r,\text{dest}}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(r\) at its destination node. |
| \(c^{\text{delay}}_r\) | Weight for train‑\(r\) delay in the objective (e.g., passenger‑penalty). |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_k\) | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) when travelling at speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(\beta_{s t}\) | 1 if the **blocked part** of segment \(s\in B\) is *available* at time‑step \(t\); 0 if the blockage is active (i.e., the portion cannot be used). |
| \(M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant large enough to relax constraints when a binary variable is 0. |
| \(\tau_{rs}^{\text{min}}\) | Minimum dwell time (stop time) required for train \(r\) at the *entry* of segment \(s\) (e.g., for passenger boarding). |
| \(\tau_{rs}^{\text{max}}\) | Maximum dwell time allowed (if any). |
| \(p_{r s}^{\text{enter}}, p_{r s}^{\text{exit}}\) | Boolean parameters indicating whether segment \(s\) is the **entry** or **exit** node of route \(p\). They are used to force flow‑conservation. |
| \(N_r\) | Set of segments that belong to any feasible route for train \(r\) (i.e., union of all \(p\in P_r\)). |
| \(L_{r p}\) | Total distance (km) of route \(p\) for train \(r\). |

---

## 4.   Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \sum_{r\in R}\Bigl(c^{\text{delay}}_r\, D_r\;+\;c^{\text{energy}}\,E_r\Bigr)
}
\]

where  

* \(D_r = a_{r,\text{dest}}-t^{\text{sched}}_{r,\text{dest}}\) (see Constraint (12) below).  
* \(E_r = \displaystyle\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} c^{\text{energy}}_k \,\ell_{s}\, y_{r s k}\) (linear because \(y\) is binary).

This objective simultaneously **minimizes total delay** (weighted by train‑specific importance) and **total energy consumption** (weighted by the energy‑rate of each speed level).

---

## 5.   Constraints  

### 5.1   Route‑choice and flow‑conservation  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P_r} x_{r p}=1 \qquad \forall r\in R \tag{1}
\]

2. **Link binary route‑choice to segment‑occupation** – a segment can be traversed by a train only if that segment belongs to the selected route  

\[
\delta_{r s}= \sum_{p\in P_r} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\,x_{r p}\qquad\forall r\in R,\; s\in S \tag{2}
\]

(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\) is 1 if segment \(s\) appears on route \(p\), 0 otherwise.)

3. **Exactly one speed‑level for a traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{r s k}= \delta_{r s}\qquad\forall r\in R,\; s\in S \tag{3}
\]

If a train does **not** occupy a segment (\(\delta_{r s}=0\)), all its speed‑level binaries are forced to 0.

4. **Flow (temporal) continuity along a chosen route** – for every pair of consecutive segments \(s\) and \(s'\) on the same route, the departure from \(s\) must be ≤ arrival at the next segment  

\[
a_{r s'} \;\ge\; d_{r s} \;-\; M\,(1-\delta_{r s})\qquad 
\forall r\in R,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on some }p\in P_r \tag{4}
\]

The big‑\(M\) term de‑activates the constraint when the segment is not used.

### 5.2   Speed‑profile feasibility  

5. **Travel time on a segment given the selected speed level**  

\[
d_{r s} - a_{r s} \;\ge\; \frac{\ell_{s}}{\overline{v}_k}\;y_{r s k}
\qquad\forall r,s,k \tag{5a}
\]

\[
d_{r s} - a_{r s} \;\le\; \frac{\ell_{s}}{\underline{v}_k}\;y_{r s k} + M(1-y_{r s k})
\qquad\forall r,s,k \tag{5b}
\]

These two linear constraints enforce that, if speed‑level \(k\) is chosen (i.e., \(y_{r s k}=1\)), the travel time lies between the minimum and maximum possible travel times for that level.

6. **Minimum dwell (stop) time when speed level 0 (i.e., stopped)**  

\[
d_{r s} - a_{r s} \;\ge\; \tau_{rs}^{\text{min}}\, y_{r s,0}
\qquad\forall r,s \tag{6}
\]

Optionally a maximum dwell can be added analogously.

### 5.3   Partial‑segment blockage (occupancy)  

7. **Occupancy indicator for each segment‑time pair**  

For each segment \(s\) (including blocked ones) and each discrete time step \(t\in T\) we define the auxiliary indicator  

\[
\theta_{s t}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if some train occupies the blocked part of }s\text{ at time }t\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Linearisation (big‑\(M\)) for every train‑segment‑time triple:

\[
a_{r s} \le t \;+\; M\,(1-\delta_{r s}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{(train can start before }t\text{)}\\
d_{r s} \ge t+1 \;-\; M\,(1-\delta_{r s}) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{(train can finish after }t\text{)}\\
\theta_{s t} \ge \delta_{r s} - \sum_{q\in\{a,d\}} \mathbf{1}_{\{q\text{ outside }[t,t+1)\}} \tag{7}
\]

A more compact formulation (common in railway MILP) is:

\[
\theta_{s t}\ge 
\frac{a_{r s} - t}{M} - 
\frac{d_{r s} - (t+1)}{M} \qquad \forall r,s\in B,t\in T \tag{7a}
\]

and finally

\[
\theta_{s t}\in\{0,1\} .
\]

8. **Blockage feasibility – a train may not occupy the blocked portion when it is unavailable**  

\[
\theta_{s t} \le \beta_{s t} \qquad \forall s\in B,\; t\in T \tag{8}
\]

If \(\beta_{s t}=0\) (blocked), the occupancy variable must be 0, i.e., no train can be on that blocked part at that time.

### 5.4   Bidirectional conflict (head‑on)  

In many single‑track sections two trains travelling in opposite directions cannot be on the same segment simultaneously.

9. **Mutual‑exclusion for opposite directions**  

Define a parameter \(\text{dir}_{r}\in\{+1,-1\}\) (direction of train \(r\)). For every segment \(s\) and time step \(t\),

\[
\sum_{r\in R:\,\text{dir}_{r}=+1} \theta_{r s t}
\;+\;
\sum_{r\in R:\,\text{dir}_{r}=-1} \theta_{r s t}
\;\le\; 1\qquad\forall s\in S\setminus B,\;t\in T \tag{9}
\]

(If the segment is double‑track the RHS can be raised accordingly.)

\( \theta_{r s t}\) is the *train‑specific* occupancy indicator (identical to \(\theta_{s t}\) but indexed by train; the linearisation is analogous to (7)).  

### 5.5   Delay and energy accounting  

10. **Delay definition**  

Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_r\) be the destination segment of train \(r\).  

\[
D_r = a_{r\,s^{\text{dest}}_r} - t^{\text{sched}}_{r,\text{dest}} \qquad\forall r \in R \tag{10}
\]

We may optionally restrict \(D_r\ge 0\) (no early arrivals) :

\[
a_{r\,s^{\text{dest}}_r} \ge t^{\text{sched}}_{r,\text{dest}} \qquad\forall r \tag{10a}
\]

11. **Energy consumption**  

\[
E_r = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} c^{\text{energy}}_k \,\ell_{s}\, y_{r s k} \qquad\forall r\in R \tag{11}
\]

Because \(y_{r s k}\) is binary, this is linear.

### 5.6   Time‑window (service) constraints  

12. **Earliest‑departure and latest‑arrival bounds** (if given)  

\[
a_{r s^{\text{origin}}_r} \ge TE^{\text{earliest}}_{r} \qquad\forall r \tag{12a}
\]
\[
a_{r s^{\text{dest}}_r} \le TE^{\text{latest}}_{r} \qquad\forall r \tag{12b}
\]

### 5.7   Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{r p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall r\in R,\;p\in P_r\\
&y_{r s k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall r\in R,\;s\in S,\;k\in K\\
&\delta_{r s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall r\in R,\;s\in S\\
&a_{r s}, d_{r s}, D_r, E_r \ge 0 &&\forall r\in R,\;s\in S\\
&\theta_{s t}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall s\in B,\;t\in T
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

---

## 6.   Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,\delta,a,d,\theta,D,E}\quad 
&\sum_{r\in R}\Bigl(c^{\text{delay}}_r\, D_r + c^{\text{energy}}\,E_r\Bigr)\\[2mm]
\text{s.t.}\quad 
&\text{(1)–(13)   (as listed above)}\\
&\text{All parameters are known data.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7.   What each component *means*  

| Component | Interpretation in the railway context |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|
| **Binary route choice \(x_{rp}\)** | Decides which physical path each train will follow (e.g., using a bypass, a different platform, or an alternative line). |
| **Arrival/departure times \(a_{rs},d_{rs}\)** | The schedule of each train on each segment; these variables capture the *rescheduling* part of the problem. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \(y_{rsk}\)** | Discretises the continuous speed variable and makes the model linear; different levels correspond to different energy use rates and travel times. |
| **Occupancy indicator \(\delta_{rs}\)** | Links the binary speed choice to the physical presence of a train on a segment – needed for conflict constraints. |
| **Blockage‑availability \(\beta_{st}\)** | Describes the *partial* blockage: for each time step the blocked part of a segment may be open (\(\beta=1\)) or closed (\(\beta=0\)). |
| **Occupancy‑time binary \(\theta_{st}\)** | Guarantees that a train cannot be in the blocked portion when the blockage is active, and implements head‑on safety on single‑track sections. |
| **Delay \(D_r\)** | Measures how late a train arrives at its destination compared with the original timetable – the first part of the objective. |
| **Energy \(E_r\)** | Accumulates the energy spent on each traversed segment according to the chosen speed level – the second part of the objective. |
| **Constraints (4)–(6)** | Ensure physically feasible travel times: faster speed → shorter travel, mandatory dwell when stopped, etc. |
| **Constraints (8)–(9)** | Enforce the “partial segment blockage’’ and prevent two opposite‑direction trains from occupying the same single‑track segment simultaneously. |
| **Big‑\(M\) terms** | Classic linearisation device that de‑activates constraints when the relevant binary variable is zero. |

---

### How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – generate the sets \(P_r\) (feasible routes) and compute \(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\).  For each segment obtain its length \(\ell_s\) and the blockage schedule \(\beta_{st}\).  
2. **Parameter selection** – choose realistic speed‑level ranges \([\underline v_k,\overline v_k]\) and energy rates \(c^{\text{energy}}_k\).  The delay weight \(c^{\text{delay}}_r\) can be uniform or reflect passenger counts.  
3. **Solving** – feed the model into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  Because the model contains many binary variables (especially \(\theta_{st}\)), a **time‑aggregation** (e.g., 5‑minute slots) or a **cutting‑plane** approach can be used for very large horizons.  
4. **Post‑processing** – extract the optimal \(x_{rp}\) (chosen route), the timetable \(\{a_{rs},d_{rs}\}\), and the speed profile \(\{y_{rsk}\}\).  Compute the resulting delay and energy for reporting.

---

**In summary**, the MILP above jointly decides for each train  

* which route to take,  
* when to enter and leave each track segment,  
* at which discrete speed level to travel,  

while guaranteeing that  
* no train enters a partially blocked segment when the blockage is active,  
* opposite‑direction trains never occupy the same single‑track segment,  
* travel‑time, speed and dwell constraints are respected,  

and it minimizes a **weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption**.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (partial‑segment blockage)**  

The model below captures the whole description given: a mixed‑integer linear program that simultaneously decides (i) which route each train will use, (ii) the arrival/departure times on every traversed track segment, (iii) the discrete speed level on each segment (hence the energy use), while guaranteeing conflict‑free operation on a partially blocked segment and on bidirectional single‑track sections.  

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are binary route‑choice, speed‑level, and conflict‑ordering variables.  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| \(\mathcal{T}\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(\mathcal{S}\) | Set of track **segments** (links), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(\mathcal{R}_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\); a route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) is an ordered list of segments. |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels**, indexed by \(k\) (e.g. \(k=1,\dots,4\) → 30, 50, 70, 90 km/h). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) | Set of **partially blocked** segments. |
| \(\mathcal{D}\) | Set of **opposite‑direction train pairs** \((t,t')\) that may use the same segment (head‑on conflict). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of ordered **precedence pairs** \((i,j)\) of consecutive segments on any route of train \(t\). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(v_k\) | Speed associated with level \(k\) (km/h). |
| \(\theta_{sk}= \dfrac{L_s}{v_k}\times 60\) | Travel time on segment \(s\) at speed level \(k\) (minutes). |
| \(\alpha_s\in[0,1]\) | Fraction of segment \(s\) that is **blocked** ( \(\alpha_s=1\) → fully blocked). |
| \([t^{\text b}_s , t^{\text e}_s]\) | Time window during which the blocked part of segment \(s\) is unavailable (minutes). |
| \(\beta_{tt'}\) | Safety‑time separation for opposite‑direction trains on a shared segment (minutes). |
| \(\tau^{\min}_t , \tau^{\max}_t\) | Earliest / latest allowed departure time of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(D^{\text{sched}}_t\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (minutes). |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}_t\) | Weight (penalty) for one minute of delay of train \(t\). |
| \(w^{\text{energy}}\) | Global weight for electricity consumption. |
| \(c_k\) | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) when travelling at speed level \(k\). |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). |
| \(z_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(e_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |
| \(\lambda_{t,s}\) | binary | 0 → train \(t\) passes segment \(s\) **before** the blockage window, 1 → **after**. |
| \(\eta_{t,t',s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for opposite‑direction conflict on segment \(s\) (1 if \(t\) goes first). |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} w^{\text{delay}}_{t}\,z_{t}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} e_{t}
}
\]

The first term penalises passenger delay; the second term penalises total electricity consumption.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route choice  
\[
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Link segment usage to the selected route  

Let \(\delta_{t,s,r}=1\) if segment \(s\) belongs to route \(r\), 0 otherwise.

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R2}
\]

Thus a segment (and a speed level) can be used only if the route containing it is selected.

#### 5.3 Travel‑time on a segment (speed‑level)  

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \theta_{sk}\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t,s \tag{T1}
\]

#### 5.4 Flow‑conservation along the chosen route  

If \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t\) (segment \(j\) follows \(i\) on any feasible route of train \(t\)):

\[
a_{t,j}= d_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t \tag{T2}
\]

The first segment of the chosen route receives the decision departure time  

\[
a_{t,s^{\text{first}}}= \tau^{\text{dep}}_t,\qquad
\tau^{\text{min}}_t\le\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\le\tau^{\text{max}}_t \tag{T3,T4}
\]

#### 5.5 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\text{last}}_t\) be the final segment of the selected route of train \(t\).

\[
z_t \ge d_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} - D^{\text{sched}}_t,\qquad
z_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t \tag{D1}
\]

#### 5.6 Energy consumption  

\[
e_t = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} L_s\,c_k\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t \tag{E1}
\]

#### 5.7 Blocked‑segment occupancy (big‑M “before/after” formulation)  

For every blocked segment \(s\in\mathcal{B}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s} &\le t^{\text b}_s + M\,\lambda_{t,s} \\
d_{t,s} &\ge t^{\text e}_s - M\,(1-\lambda_{t,s}) \\
\lambda_{t,s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,\;s\in\mathcal{B} \tag{B1}
\]

If \(\lambda_{t,s}=0\) the train must finish the segment **before** the blockage starts; if \(\lambda_{t,s}=1\) it must start **after** the blockage ends.

#### 5.8 Opposite‑direction conflict on the same segment  

For each pair \((t,t')\in\mathcal{D}\) that uses the same segment \(s\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s}+ \beta_{tt'} - M\,(1-\eta_{t,t',s}) \\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s}+ \beta_{tt'} - M\,\eta_{t,t',s} \\
\eta_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{C1}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active; the other is relaxed by the big‑M term, guaranteeing a safety head‑on separation \(\beta_{tt'}\).

#### 5.9 Speed‑level uniqueness (already enforced by (R2), kept for clarity)

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t,s \tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\lambda_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
\eta_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s}\ge0,\; d_{t,s}\ge0,\; z_t\ge0,\; e_t\ge0,\;
\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{Dom}
\]

---

### 6. Full MILP statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,a,d,\lambda,\eta,z,e,\tau^{\text{dep}}}\;
&\sum_{t} w^{\text{delay}}_{t}\,z_{t}
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t} e_{t}  \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2), (T1)–(T4), (D1), (E1), (B1), (C1), (S1), (Dom)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the binary variables are the route‑choice \(x_{t,r}\), the speed‑level selectors \(y_{t,s,k}\), the before/after indicator \(\lambda_{t,s}\), and the conflict‑ordering \(\eta_{t,t',s}\).  

---

### 7. Remarks & How to use the model  

* **Data preparation** – Build the route sets \(\mathcal{R}_t\) (including possible detours around the blockage), compute \(\theta_{sk}\), define the blockage window \([t^{\text b}_s,t^{\text e}_s]\) for every blocked segment, and list all opposite‑direction train pairs \(\mathcal{D}\).  
* **Weight tuning** – Choose \(w^{\text{delay}}_t\) to reflect passenger importance (e.g., higher for high‑capacity trains) and \(w^{\text{energy}}\) to reflect electricity price or emission cost.  
* **Solution** – Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP…). The optimal solution provides for each train:  
  * the selected route \(x_{t,r}=1\),  
  * a conflict‑free timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\),  
  * the discrete speed profile \(\{y_{t,s,k}\}\),  
  * the resulting total delay \(z_t\) and energy use \(e_t\).  
* **Extension possibilities** – One can add dwell‑time minima, early‑arrival penalties, or a piece‑wise linear approximation of a continuous speed‑energy curve without breaking linearity.  

The model therefore delivers a **feasible, conflict‑free rescheduled timetable together with executable speed profiles** that respect the partial‑segment blockage, resolve bidirectional conflicts, and simultaneously minimise passenger delay and energy consumption.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (partial‑segment blockage)**  

The model below captures the whole description given: a mixed‑integer linear program that simultaneously decides (i) which route each train will use, (ii) the arrival/departure times on every traversed track segment, (iii) the discrete speed level on each segment (hence the energy use), while guaranteeing conflict‑free operation on a partially blocked segment and on bidirectional single‑track sections.  

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are binary route‑choice, speed‑level, and conflict‑ordering variables.  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|-----------------------------------|
| \(\mathcal{T}\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(\mathcal{S}\) | Set of track **segments** (links), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(\mathcal{R}_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\); a route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) is an ordered list of segments. |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels**, indexed by \(k\) (e.g. \(k=1,\dots,4\) → 30, 50, 70, 90 km/h). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) | Set of **partially blocked** segments. |
| \(\mathcal{D}\) | Set of **opposite‑direction train pairs** \((t,t')\) that may use the same segment (head‑on conflict). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of ordered **precedence pairs** \((i,j)\) of consecutive segments on any route of train \(t\). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(v_k\) | Speed associated with level \(k\) (km/h). |
| \(\theta_{sk}= \dfrac{L_s}{v_k}\times 60\) | Travel time on segment \(s\) at speed level \(k\) (minutes). |
| \(\alpha_s\in[0,1]\) | Fraction of segment \(s\) that is **blocked** ( \(\alpha_s=1\) → fully blocked). |
| \([t^{\text b}_s , t^{\text e}_s]\) | Time window during which the blocked part of segment \(s\) is unavailable (minutes). |
| \(\beta_{tt'}\) | Safety‑time separation for opposite‑direction trains on a shared segment (minutes). |
| \(\tau^{\min}_t , \tau^{\max}_t\) | Earliest / latest allowed departure time of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(D^{\text{sched}}_t\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (minutes). |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}_t\) | Weight (penalty) for one minute of delay of train \(t\). |
| \(w^{\text{energy}}\) | Global weight for electricity consumption. |
| \(c_k\) | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) when travelling at speed level \(k\). |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). |
| \(z_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(e_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |
| \(\lambda_{t,s}\) | binary | 0 → train \(t\) passes segment \(s\) **before** the blockage window, 1 → **after**. |
| \(\eta_{t,t',s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for opposite‑direction conflict on segment \(s\) (1 if \(t\) goes first). |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} w^{\text{delay}}_{t}\,z_{t}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} e_{t}
}
\]

The first term penalises passenger delay; the second term penalises total electricity consumption.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route choice  
\[
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Link segment usage to the selected route  

Let \(\delta_{t,s,r}=1\) if segment \(s\) belongs to route \(r\), 0 otherwise.

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R2}
\]

Thus a segment (and a speed level) can be used only if the route containing it is selected.

#### 5.3 Travel‑time on a segment (speed‑level)  

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \theta_{sk}\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t,s \tag{T1}
\]

#### 5.4 Flow‑conservation along the chosen route  

If \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t\) (segment \(j\) follows \(i\) on any feasible route of train \(t\)):

\[
a_{t,j}= d_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t \tag{T2}
\]

The first segment of the chosen route receives the decision departure time  

\[
a_{t,s^{\text{first}}}= \tau^{\text{dep}}_t,\qquad
\tau^{\text{min}}_t\le\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\le\tau^{\text{max}}_t \tag{T3,T4}
\]

#### 5.5 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\text{last}}_t\) be the final segment of the selected route of train \(t\).

\[
z_t \ge d_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} - D^{\text{sched}}_t,\qquad
z_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t \tag{D1}
\]

#### 5.6 Energy consumption  

\[
e_t = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} L_s\,c_k\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t \tag{E1}
\]

#### 5.7 Blocked‑segment occupancy (big‑M “before/after” formulation)  

For every blocked segment \(s\in\mathcal{B}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s} &\le t^{\text b}_s + M\,\lambda_{t,s} \\
d_{t,s} &\ge t^{\text e}_s - M\,(1-\lambda_{t,s}) \\
\lambda_{t,s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,\;s\in\mathcal{B} \tag{B1}
\]

If \(\lambda_{t,s}=0\) the train must finish the segment **before** the blockage starts; if \(\lambda_{t,s}=1\) it must start **after** the blockage ends.

#### 5.8 Opposite‑direction conflict on the same segment  

For each pair \((t,t')\in\mathcal{D}\) that uses the same segment \(s\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s}+ \beta_{tt'} - M\,(1-\eta_{t,t',s}) \\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s}+ \beta_{tt'} - M\,\eta_{t,t',s} \\
\eta_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{C1}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active; the other is relaxed by the big‑M term, guaranteeing a safety head‑on separation \(\beta_{tt'}\).

#### 5.9 Speed‑level uniqueness (already enforced by (R2), kept for clarity)

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t}\delta_{t,s,r}\,x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t,s \tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\lambda_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
\eta_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s}\ge0,\; d_{t,s}\ge0,\; z_t\ge0,\; e_t\ge0,\;
\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{Dom}
\]

---

### 6. Full MILP statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,a,d,\lambda,\eta,z,e,\tau^{\text{dep}}}\;
&\sum_{t} w^{\text{delay}}_{t}\,z_{t}
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t} e_{t}  \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2), (T1)–(T4), (D1), (E1), (B1), (C1), (S1), (Dom)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the binary variables are the route‑choice \(x_{t,r}\), the speed‑level selectors \(y_{t,s,k}\), the before/after indicator \(\lambda_{t,s}\), and the conflict‑ordering \(\eta_{t,t',s}\).

  * the selected route \(x_{t,r}=1\),  
  * a conflict‑free timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\),  
  * the discrete speed profile \(\{y_{t,s,k}\}\),  
  * the resulting total delay \(z_t\) and energy use \(e_t\).  
* **Extension possibilities** – One can add dwell‑time minima, early‑arrival penalties, or a piece‑wise linear approximation of a continuous speed‑energy curve without breaking linearity.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Full Linear Formulation**  

The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a partial‑segment blockage disrupts a high‑speed railway line:

1. **When** each train departs / arrives at every station (time‑shift – retiming).  
2. **Which** track (original or opposite) each train uses on the blocked segment (binary rerouting).  
3. **What** speed profile (average speed on each free‑running sub‑segment) each train follows (continuous speed‑selection).  

All decisions are made so that (i) no two trains occupy the same track at the same time (conflict‑free timetable), (ii) the physical speed limits and acceleration/deceleration capabilities of the trains are respected, and (iii) a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption is minimised.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = *N*). |
| **S** | Set of stations, indexed by *s* (ordered along the line, 1 = origin, |S| = *K*). |
| **B** | Set of track‑blocks (continuous line sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *b* (|B| = *K‑1*). |
| **U** | Sub‑set of blocks that are **blocked** (partial‑segment blockage). |
| **V** | Sub‑set of blocks that are **free** (V = B \ U). |
| **R** = {0,1} | Binary set – 0 = original (right‑hand) track, 1 = opposite (left‑hand) track. |
| **P** | Set of admissible **speed‑plans** for a train on a free block *b* (see §2.2). Indexed by *p*. |
| **Δ** | Set of discrete time‑intervals used for linearisation of speed‑time relations (e.g., 1‑min steps). |

Additional auxiliary indices are introduced when needed (e.g., *i* for predecessor‑successor train pairs).

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **a<sub>t,s</sub>** | Continuous, ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s*. |
| **d<sub>t,s</sub>** | Continuous, ≥0 | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **x<sub>t,b</sub>** | Binary | **Rerouting decision** on blocked block *b* ∈ U: 0 = stay on original track, 1 = use opposite track. |
| **y<sub>t,b,p</sub>** | Binary | **Speed‑plan selection** on free block *b* ∈ V: exactly one plan *p* ∈ P is chosen for train *t*. |
| **τ<sub>t,b,Δ</sub>** | Continuous, ≥0 | **Time spent** by train *t* on block *b* while travelling at the speed associated with interval Δ (used to linearise energy). |
| **z<sub>t,i</sub>** | Binary | **Order variable**: 1 if train *t* passes before train *i* on a shared track segment (conflict‑resolution). |
| **δ<sub>t</sub>** | Continuous, ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* with respect to its original schedule (given as data). |
| **e<sub>t</sub>** | Continuous, ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh). |

---

## 3. Input Data (Parameters)  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **A<sub>t,s</sub>**, **D<sub>t,s</sub>** | Original (pre‑disruption) arrival / departure times (reference schedule). |
| **L<sub>b</sub>** | Length of block *b* (km). |
| **v<sub>max</sub>**, **v<sub>min</sub>** | Global maximum / minimum admissible speeds (km/h). |
| **a<sub>max</sub>**, **a<sub>min</sub>** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h²). |
| **c<sub>Δ</sub>** | Energy coefficient for interval Δ (kWh per km·h⁻¹). |
| **M** | Large constant for big‑M linearisation (e.g., 10⁶). |
| **T<sub>block</sub>** | Start time of the blockage (minutes from midnight). |
| **T<sub>end</sub>** | End time of the blockage. |
| **w<sub>delay</sub>**, **w<sub>energy</sub>** | Weight of delay and energy in the objective (user‑defined). |
| **Δt** | Length of each discrete time interval (minutes). |
| **β<sub>t,b</sub>** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s* (if *b* ends at *s*). |
| **γ<sub>t,b</sub>** | Minimum headway (in minutes) required between any two trains on block *b* (safety). |

---

## 4. Model Assumptions (explicit)  

1. **Deterministic disruption** – the blockage interval \([T_{block},T_{end}]\) and its spatial extent *U* are known a‑priori.  
2. **Single‑track usage per block** – at any instant a block can be occupied by at most one train on a given direction; opposite‑track usage is allowed only on blocked blocks (binary rerouting).  
3. **Piece‑wise constant speed** – on each free block a train adopts one of a finite set of admissible speed‑plans *p* (average speed, acceleration profile). This enables linearisation of the otherwise nonlinear speed‑time‑energy relationship.  
4. **No overtaking** – trains keep their order on a given track unless a rerouting decision swaps them (captured by order variables *z*).  
5. **Dwell times** – a minimum dwell time β is enforced at every station; additional dwell may be introduced to absorb delays.  
6. **Energy model** – energy consumption on a block is approximated by a linear function of the travelled speed (coefficients *c<sub>Δ</sub>*).  
7. **Headway safety** – a minimum temporal separation γ is required between any two consecutive trains on the same physical track.  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{delay}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}}_{\text{Total weighted delay}}
\;+\; \underbrace{w_{energy}\sum_{t\in T} e_{t}}_{\text{Total weighted energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where  

\[
\delta_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\bigl(a_{t,s}-A_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}
\qquad
e_{t}= \sum_{b\in V}\sum_{\Delta\in\Delta} c_{\Delta}\,\tau_{t,b,\Delta}
\]

The operator \((\cdot)^{+}\) denotes \(\max\{0,\cdot\}\); it can be linearised with an auxiliary variable and a big‑M constraint.

---

## 6. Core Constraints  

### 6.1. Time‑flow (timetable) constraints  

1. **Departure after arrival + dwell**  

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} + \beta_{t,b(s)} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{C1}
\]

2. **Running time on a free block** – linking speed‑plan to travel time  

For each free block *b* that connects stations *s* and *s+1* :

\[
a_{t,s+1} \;=\; d_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{p\in P} \frac{L_{b}}{v_{p}}\, y_{t,b,p}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; b\in V

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

  • `x[i,j,s]` – binary ordering on shared segment *s* (1 → train *i* precedes train *j*).
  • `D[i]`, `A[i]` – continuous departure / arrival times.
  • `T[i,s]` – travel time of train *i* on segment *s*.

| | **Objective** | Minimise a weighted sum of (i) total delay `Σ_i (A[i]‑sched_arr[i])` and (ii) total energy `Σ_i Σ_s Σ_k e[s,k]·v[i,s,k]`. | | **Constraints** |

  • **Travel‑time ↔ speed** – `T[i,s] = length[s] / speed_k` when speed option *k* is chosen.
  • **Sequencing on shared segments** – big‑M constraints enforce that two trains on the same (non‑blocked) segment do not occupy it simultaneously.
  • **Blocked‑segment time windows** – if a segment is blocked, the train may only occupy it after the unblock time (or may use the reroute).
  • **Dwell‑time minima** – `A[i]‑D[i] ≥ Σ_s T[i,s] + dwell_min[station]`.

INPUT DATA # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # ----- Sets ------------------------------------------------------------ Trains = ['T1', 'T2', 'T3'] # list of train identifiers Stations = ['S0', 'S1', 'S2', 'S3'] # stations (including origin S0) Segments = ['seg1', 'seg2', 'seg3', 'seg4'] # network segments (ordered) # Mapping each train to the ordered list of segments it traverses # (original route). If a segment is blocked, the train may use a # *detour* (different segment name) – we model that with binary y. train_route = { 'T1': ['seg1', 'seg2', 'seg3'], 'T2': ['seg1', 'seg2', 'seg4'], 'T3': ['seg1', 'seg3', 'seg4'], } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Blocked segments (partial blockages) # blocked[t] = (unblock_time, allowed_capacity) # allowed_capacity = 0 for full block blocked = { 'seg2': (120.0, 0), # blocked until time 120 (full block) # add more blocked segments as needed } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Speed options (k) available on each segment # speed_opt[s] = [(k, speed_k, energy_coeff_k), ...] speed_opt = { 'seg1': [(1, 30.0, 1.2), (2, 40.0, 1.5), (3, 50.0, 2.0)], 'seg2': [(1, 20.0, 0.9), (2, 30.0, 1.3)], 'seg3': [(1, 25.0, 1.0), (2, 35.0, 1.4), (3, 45.0, 1.9)], 'seg4': [(1, 30.0, 1.2), (2, 40.0, 1.6)], } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Length of each segment (km) length = { 'seg1': 15.0, 'seg2': 10.0, 'seg3': 12.0, 'seg4': 8.0, } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Speed limits per segment (km/h) – any speed option > limit must be forbidden speed_limit = { 'seg1': 45.0, 'seg2': 30.0, 'seg3': 40.0, 'seg4': 40.0, } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Minimum dwell time at each station (minutes) dwell_min = { 'S0': 0.0, 'S1': 2.0, 'S2': 2.0, 'S3': 0.0, } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Scheduled arrival time at final station (for each train) scheduled_arrival = { 'T1': 250.0, 'T2': 260.0, 'T3': 255.0, } # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Weighting factors in the objective w_delay = 1.0 # weight of total delay w_energy = 0.1 # weight of total energy consumption (choose as needed) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 2. MODEL DEFINITION # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- model = pl.LpProblem("TRSMP", pl.LpMinimize) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 3. DECISION VARIABLES # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # Binary route‑choice on each blocked segment (y[i,t]) y = pl.LpVariable.dicts("y", ((i, t) for i in Trains for t in blocked), 0, 1, pl.LpBinary) # Ordering variables on shared (non‑blocked) segments # We create ordering only for pairs (i,j) that share a segment s x = {} for s in Segments: # find trains that actually travel on segment s (original route) trains_on_s = [i for i in Trains if s in train_route[i]] for idx_i in range(len(trains_on_s)): for idx_j in range(idx_i + 1, len(trains_on_s)): i = trains_on_s[idx_i] j = trains_on_s[idx_j] x[(i, j, s)] = pl.LpVariable(f"x_{i}_{j}_{s}", 0, 1, pl.LpBinary) # Departure / arrival times (continuous, minutes, >=0) D = pl.LpVariable.dicts("D", Trains, 0, None, pl.LpContinuous) # departure from origin S0 A = pl.LpVariable.dicts("A", Trains, 0, None, pl.LpContinuous) # arrival at final station # Travel time on each segment for each train T = pl.LpVariable.dicts("T", ((i, s) for i in Trains for s in Segments), 0, None, pl.LpContinuous) # Speed‑level selection (binary) on each segment v = {} for i in Trains: for s in Segments: for (k, speed_k, _) in speed_opt.get(s, []): v[(i, s, k)] = pl.LpVariable(f"v_{i}_{s}_{k}", 0, 1, pl.LpBinary) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 4. Here we assume a simple binary: y=0 → original travel time, y=1 → use alternative (e.g., longer) # The alternative travel time can be modelled by a separate segment or by adding a penalty. # For this generic formulation we only enforce that exactly one of the two possibilities is taken: model += y[(i, t)] <= 1, f"routeChoice_ub_{i}_{t}" # we could also enforce y >= 0 (already done by binary domain) else: # Train does not use this blocked segment → force y=0 model += y[(i, t)] == 0, f"routeChoice_notUsed_{i}_{t}" # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5.2 Travel time ↔ selected speed (per segment) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in Trains: for s in Segments: # Only the speed options belonging to segment s are relevant opts = speed_opt.get(s, []) if not opts: continue # Force all v=0 for unused segments for (k, _, _) in opts: model += v[(i, s, k)] == 0, f"speedZero_{i}_{s}_{k}" # (ii) link travel time to chosen speed: # T[i,s] = length[s] / speed_k when v[i,s,k] = 1 # Use linearisation with big‑M: # T[i,s] >= length[s] / speed_k - M*(1 - v[i,s,k]) # T[i,s] <= length[s] / speed_k + M*(1 - v[i,s,k]) for (k, speed_k, _) in opts: travel_time_k = length[s] / speed_k * 60.0 # convert hours -> minutes model += T[(i, s)] >= travel_time_k - M * (1 - v[(i, s, k)]), f"Tlb_{i}_{s}_{k}" model += T[(i, s)] <= travel_time_k + M * (1 - v[(i, s, k)]), f"Tub_{i}_{s}_{k}" # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5.3 Sequencing constraints on shared (non‑blocked) segments # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # For any two distinct trains using the same segment s, one must finish before the other starts. # Let start_i_s be the time train i enters segment s, end_i_s = start_i_s + T[i,s]. # To avoid extra variables we express start time recursively. # First we compute cumulative arrival at the start of each segment. # start_i_s = D[i] + Σ_{p preceding s} T[i,p] (+ possible extra waiting for blockages) # For simplicity, we introduce auxiliary variables start[i,s] and end[i,s]. start = pl.LpVariable.dicts("start", ((i, s) for i in Trains for s in Segments), 0, None, pl.LpContinuous) end = pl.LpVariable.dicts("end", ((i, s) for i in Trains for s in Segments), 0, None, pl.LpContinuous) # Link start / end with travel time for i in Trains: for s in Segments: model += end[(i, s)] == start[(i, s)] + T[(i, s)], f"endDef_{i}_{s}" # Compute start times sequentially along each train's route for i in Trains: route = train_route[i] for idx, s in enumerate(route): if idx == 0: # first segment: start = departure from origin model += start[(i, s)] == D[i], f"firstSegStart_{i}_{s}" else: prev = route[idx - 1] # start of current = end of previous model += start[(i, s)] == end[(i, prev)], f"seqStart_{i}_{s}_from_{prev}" # Now sequencing on shared segments (excluding blocked ones) for s in Segments: if s in blocked: continue # blocked segments are handled separately (see 5.4) # Get all trains that actually travel on s trains_on_s = [i for i in Trains if s in train_route[i]] for idx_i in range(len(trains_on_s)): for idx_j in range(idx_i + 1, len(trains_on_s)): i = trains_on_s[idx_i] j = trains_on_s[idx_j] # Binary x[i,j,s] = 1 => i precedes j # start_i + T_i <= start_j OR start_j + T_j <= start_i model += start[(i, s)] + T[(i, s)] <= start[(j, s)] + M * (1 - x[(i, j, s)]), \ f"seq1_{i}_{j}_{s}" model += start[(j, s)] + T[(j, s)] <= start[(i, s)] + M * (x[(i, j, s)]), \ f"seq2_{i}_{j}_{s}" # x must be binary (already defined) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5.4 Time‑window constraints for blocked segments # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in Trains: for t, (unblock_time, _) in blocked.items(): if t not in train_route[i]: continue # train does not intend to use the blocked segment # If the train uses original route (y=0) it must not enter before unblock_time # start_i_t >= unblock_time - M * y[i,t] model += start[(i, t)] >= unblock_time - M * y[(i, t)], f"blockWindow_{i}_{t}" # If y=1 (detour) there is no restriction – this is automatically satisfied because # start variable for the original segment will be forced to a very large value by big‑M. # To keep formulation compact we simply rely on the previous constraint. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5.5 Dwell‑time minimum at stations # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Arrival at final station = departure + sum of travel times + sum of dwell times at intermediate stations for i in Trains: route = train_route[i] # compute total travel time along the route total_travel = pl.lpSum(T[(i, s)] for s in route) # Dwell times: each intermediate station (except origin S0 and final) # We assume stations are ordered S0‑S1‑S2‑S3 and each segment connects consecutive stations. # Mapping segment → downstream station (where train arrives after traversing segment) seg_to_station = { 'seg1': 'S1', 'seg2': 'S2', 'seg3': 'S2', 'seg4': 'S3', } dwell_sum = pl.lpSum(dwell_min[seg_to_station[s]] for s in route) # Enforce arrival time model += A[i] == D[i] + total_travel + dwell_sum, f"arrivalDef_{i}" # Additionally, enforce minimum dwell at each intermediate station explicitly (optional) # The above aggregated equation already guarantees the sum, but if you need per‑station # constraints you can uncomment the following loop: # for s in route: # station = seg_to_station[s] # if station not in ['S0', 'S3']: # ignore origin & final # model += start[(i, s)] >= D[i] + pl.lpSum(T[(i, p)] for p in route if p != s) + dwell_min[station], ... # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5.6 Speed‑limit enforcement # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in Trains: for s in Segments: opts = speed_opt.get(s, []) limit = speed_limit.get(s, 1e9) for (k, speed_k, _) in opts: if speed_k > limit: # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # No extra constraints needed. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 6. SOLVE # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- print("Solving the MILP …") solver = pl.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True) # change to Gurobi/CPLEX if available model.solve(solver) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # 7. OUTPUT # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- print("\n=== STATUS ===") print(pl.LpStatus[model.status]) print("\n=== OBJECTIVE ===") print(f"Weighted cost = {pl.value(model.objective):.2f}") print("\n=== VARIABLES (selected) ===") for i in Trains: print(f"\nTrain {i}:") print(f" Departure D = {pl.value(D[i]):.2f}") print(f" Arrival A = {pl.value(A[i]):.2f} (scheduled {scheduled_arrival[i]})") print(f" Total delay = {pl.value(A[i]) - scheduled_arrival[i]:.2f}") # speed choices for s in train_route[i]: chosen = None for (k, _, _) in speed_opt[s]: if pl.value(v[(i, s, k)]) > 0.5: chosen = k break print(f" Segment {s}: speed option {chosen}") # blocked‑segment decisions for t in blocked: if t in train_route[i]: print(f" Blocked segment {t}: useDetour = {int(pl.value(y[(i, t)]))}") print("\n=== SUMMARY ===") total_delay = sum(pl.value(A[i]) - scheduled_arrival[i] for i in Trains) total_energy = sum( e * pl.value(v[(i, s, k)]) for i in Trains for s in Segments for (k, _, e) in speed_opt.get(s, []) ) print(f"Total delay = {total_delay:.2f}") print(f"Total energy = {total_energy:.2f}") # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # End of script # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ``` --- ## 3. How to adapt the model to your specific problem | Aspect | What to change / add | |--------|----------------------| | **Additional blocked segments** | Add them to the `blocked` dictionary (`blocked[seg] = (unblock_time, capacity)`). The same constraints automatically apply. | | **Detour segments** | If a blocked segment can be avoided by a concrete alternative segment, add that segment to each train’s route (e.g., `train_route[i] = ['seg1','detour1','seg3']`). The binary `y[i,t]` can then be linked to a “big‑M slack” that forces the travel‑time on the original segment to a very large value when `y=1`. | | **More speed levels** | Extend `speed_opt` for each segment with `(k, speed_k, energy_coeff_k)`. | | **Energy weighting** | Adjust `w_energy` (or use separate scaling factors) to reflect the monetary cost of energy vs. delay. | | **Solver** | Replace `pl.PULP_CBC_CMD` with `pl.GUROBI_CMD`, `pl.CPLEX_CMD`, etc., for larger instances. | | **Additional operational constraints** (e.g., crew limits, platform occupancy) | Introduce new binary/continuous variables and linear constraints following the same style. | --- ### Remarks * The **big‑M value `M = 1e6`** is deliberately huge to dominate all realistic time values (minutes). If you experience numerical difficulties, tighten `M` to the maximum possible makespan of your horizon. * The formulation keeps the model **linear** (no products of binaries). All non‑linear relationships (travel‑time = length/speed) are linearised with auxiliary binary variables and big‑M. * The script prints a concise summary (departures, arrivals, speed choices, detour decisions) and the final weighted objective, which directly corresponds to the requested weighted sum of total delay and total energy. Feel free to copy the script into a `.py` file, install PuLP (`pip install pulp`), and run it with your data. The structure makes it straightforward to extend or embed in a larger decision‑support system.
