Introduction

With millions of passenger trips on an average day, railway networks play a big role in the European mobility system. In the European Union, the railway infrastructure and the railway operations are mandated by law to be managed separately. In the Netherlands, ProRail is responsible for managing the railway network infrastructure and Netherlands Railways (NS) is the main passenger railway operator. One of the tasks of the railway operator is the planning of individual train units, or rolling stock. A rolling stock schedule specifies which rolling stock units operate which trips in the timetable. Disruptions on the railway network, such as a missing rolling stock unit in a train trip or a complete blockage of a railway track as a result of an accident or a train breakdown, require the rolling stock plan to be updated. The rescheduling measures that pertain to the (availability of the) railway infrastructure, i.e., the changes in the rolling stock assignments, are created by rolling stock dispatchers who work for the railway operator, after which local infrastructure dispatchers who work for the infrastructure manager are tasked with performing the suggested rolling stock movements.

We focus our research on the rescheduling of rolling stock units in the case of disruptions in the railway system. It is necessary that the rolling stock is efficiently operated and utilized to maintain a good balance between the service to passengers and the incurred operational costs. Unavailability of rolling stock influences passenger satisfaction, as passengers possibly have to stand or even wait for the next train in case not enough capacity is available. An efficient rescheduling process reduces such problems and also reduces the number of trains that are needed as a buffer to catch disrupted train services, leading to a reduction in the capital costs for the train operator. It is also beneficial if the adjusted plan is similar to the original plan, as this requires fewer rolling stock movements during the night to get each rolling stock unit to its starting position for the next day. Additionally, an advantage for both passengers and crew members is that they are familiar with the original plan and may prefer the rolling stock units to be operated as originally planned.

Currently, the rescheduling of rolling stock after disruptions is mostly done by hand. As a result, railway planners manually try to find an updated rolling stock allocation without the use of any mathematical methods or solvers. This can largely be attributed to the difficulty of the problem. For a rolling stock plan to work in practice, feasible train compositions need to be assigned to each train trip, the associated shunting movements need to be executable and shunting drivers need to be available for all shunting movements. Past papers have often tackled these problems separately, meaning that there are practical requirements that are not considered in their solution approaches. One of these requirements is the availability of railway tracks for the shunting movements to take place. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has focused on ensuring feasibility of a rolling stock schedule with regard to this aspect. In practice, this is an important part of rolling stock rescheduling; if the rolling stock movements are not possible due to unavailability of the railway tracks, the entire plan could fall apart and could need to be adjusted.

We introduce two solution approaches which ensure that all shunting movements are feasible with respect to the available infrastructure: an exact algorithm and an iterative heuristic. The basis for our methods is the composition model by Fioole et al. (2006), which outputs a rolling stock circulation for the passenger train timetable. To check whether each of the suggested trips and shunting movements can be performed, we implement an infrastructure model which is based on the model by Van Aken et al. (2017) for solving the Train Timetable Adjustment Problem, which aims at finding an alternative timetable that minimizes the deviation from the original timetable in terms of the incurred delays and cancellations of train services. Our tailored version of this model represents every shunting movement as an event that takes place on a specific track at a specific station and outputs whether a shunting movement is possible and whether other trains need to be delayed to make the shunting movement possible. Although delaying other trains is typically not preferred, a short delay could open up the necessary windows for performing additional shunting movements. We therefore include the option of delaying other trains by at most a few minutes in our framework and assume that such short delays are resolved by the buffers that are present in the timetable for the remainder of the affected train lines.

Our exact approach resembles a Combinatorial Benders’ approach in line with Codato and Fischetti (2004). It alternates between the composition model, which suggests shunting movements, and the infrastructure model, which checks whether each combination of shunting movements can be performed. The infrastructure model then returns cuts that prohibit combinations of shunting movements, which violate the railway infrastructure availability constraints, from being performed simultaneously. A drawback of the exact approach is the underlying assumption that the creation of a new rolling stock plan and the performance of the shunting movements are carried out simultaneously by one and the same entity, which conflicts with the separation of the railway tasks as mandated by European laws. We therefore also introduce an iterative heuristic, which works in a similar way as the exact algorithm, but feeds the suggested shunting movements one by one to the infrastructure model. This closely resembles the situation where the rolling stock dispatchers and infrastructure dispatchers work for different companies and is therefore more applicable in the European context. The iterative heuristic mimics the interaction that takes place between the rolling stock dispatchers, who try to come up with a new rolling stock plan, and the local infrastructure dispatchers, who try to perform the shunting movements. We want to emphasize that our framework is generic; besides the specific model choices that we made for the two steps in our iterative frameworks, other formulations and methods can be used as well, so long as they solve the same problems.

We test our algorithm on seven instances which consist of full blockages on the railway network. We model and analyze the railway infrastructure of two major stations, Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal, and allow for shunting movements at these two stations during the duration of the blockages. In practice, shunting at these two stations is assumed to be too difficult due to the large number of trains that pass through and is therefore not considered a viable option during the creation of the rolling stock schedule. We show that the exact algorithm successfully identifies feasible shunting movements that can take place at both Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal to counter the disruption and to improve the rolling stock schedule with respect to several operational, passenger service level and stick-to-the-plan objectives compared to the situation in which shunting at Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal is not considered. Additionally, we find that the iterative heuristic is able to obtain an optimal solution for all instances, in shorter running times. We find that shunting movements are only canceled in case other passenger trains occupy the railway infrastructure and that the shunting movements themselves do not create unsolvable conflicts with one another. Therefore, the order in which the shunting movements are processed by the infrastructure model does not matter and the iterative heuristic finds an optimal solution for all instances. We furthermore find that our algorithm performs well in case we put emphasis on any of the rolling stock rescheduling objectives and that our approach also provides added value in the case that all trains are fixed and cannot be delayed.

The contribution of this paper is threefold. Firstly, we introduce frameworks for rolling stock rescheduling with railway infrastructure availability constraints. The methods output rolling stock circulations which ensure that a feasible path through the railway infrastructure exists for the performed shunting movements at the considered stations. Secondly, our algorithms find solutions within a few minutes with an average improvement of 19% over the rolling stock schedule which does not contain shunting movements at Utrecht Centraal or Rotterdam Centraal. Thirdly, we show that the frameworks can be beneficial in practical problems; by allowing for shunting at more stations than is currently done in practice, our frameworks are able to provide improvements over the rolling stock circulations that are currently made. Furthermore, the iterative approach mimics rolling stock rescheduling in practice by distinguishing between the two problems which are currently solved separately by the rolling stock dispatchers and the infrastructure dispatchers. Our approach provides a framework which connects these problems, thereby facilitating and reducing the interaction which is required between the involved parties.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a detailed description of the problem we address. Literature covering similar problems is discussed in Section 3. Section 4 provides a mathematical formulation for our two solution components and introduces the iterative rolling stock rescheduling algorithm. Computational results and a sensitivity analysis of our algorithm are presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 gives conclusions and suggestions for future research.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for rolling‑stock rescheduling with infrastructure‑availability constraints**  

The formulation below captures the two‑level structure described in the paper:  

*Level 1 – **Composition model** (rolling‑stock circulation).  
*Level 2 – **Infrastructure model** (feasibility of shunting movements on tracks).  

The model is written as a single MILP that can be solved directly (exact approach) or used in a Benders‑type decomposition/iterative heuristic.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of scheduled **train trips** (passenger services) in the original timetable. |
| \\(S\\) | Set of **shunting movements** (relocations of rolling‑stock units) that may be performed to recover from a disruption. |
| \\(U\\) | Set of **rolling‑stock units** (individual trainsets). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of **train‑type/consist categories** (e.g. 4‑car, 8‑car). |
| \\(N\\) | Set of **stations** (including the two special stations where shunting is allowed, e.g. Utrecht, Rotterdam). |
| \\(L\\) | Set of **tracks** (track‑segments) that can be used for shunting at a station. |
| \\(P\\) | Set of **time periods** (discrete minutes) covering the planning horizon (e.g. 0 … 1440). |
| \\(A_t \\subseteq K\\) | Set of admissible train‑type(s) for trip \\(t\\) (capacity, platform length). |
| \\(B_s \\subseteq L\\) | Set of tracks that can host shunting movement \\(s\\) (depends on its start/end stations). |
| \\(R_t\\) | Set of **precedence arcs** for passenger trips (i.e. \\((t,t')\\) if a unit that finishes \\(t\\) can start \\(t'\\) without violating minimum turn‑around). |
| \\(D_s\\) | Set of **conflict arcs** for shunting movements (i.e. \\((s,s')\\) if the two shunts need the same track at overlapping times). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |

\[

\sum_{u,k} x_{t,u,k}=1 && \forall t\in T \\
& \sum_{u,k} cap_k x_{t,u,k} \ge demand_t && \forall t\in T \\
& \text{Turn‑around constraints (5)} && \forall (t,t')\in R_t,\; u\in U\\
& 0\le z_t \le maxDelay && \forall t\in T \\
& y_s \le \sum_{u} avail_{s,u} && \forall s\in S \\
& \sum_{l\in B_s} w_{s,p}= y_s && \forall s\in S,\; p\in [start_s,end_s] \\
& \sum_{s\in S} w_{s,p} \le 1 && \forall l\in L,\; p\in P \\
& w_{s,p} \le trackAvail_{l,p} && \forall s,l\in B_s,\; p\in [start_s,end_s] \\
& z_t \ge \epsilon \sum_{s\in S} w_{s,p}\, use_{t,l,p} && \forall t,l,p \\
& q_{t,u,k} \le x_{t,u,k},\; q_{t,u,k}\le p^{orig}_{t,u},\;
  q_{t,u,k}\ge x_{t,u,k}+p^{orig}_{t,u}-1 && \forall t,u,k \\
& x_{t,u,k},y_s,w_{s,p},q_{t,u,k}\in\{0,1\},\;
  z_t,sDelay_t\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Modeling assumptions (explicit)

| # | Assumption |
|---|-------------|
| A1 | Time is discretised in 1‑minute intervals; all start/end times of trips and shunts are integer minutes. |
| A2 | Each rolling‑stock unit belongs to exactly one train‑type (capacity, length) for the whole horizon. |
| A3 | Shunting movements are modelled as **single‑track occupancy events**; any required signalling or yard‑track manoeuvre is abstracted into the duration \\([start_s,end_s]\\). |
| A4 | The disruption is represented by the binary parameters \\(trackAvail_{l,p}\\); tracks with \\(trackAvail=0\\) cannot be used by any shunting or passenger movement. |
| A5 | Passenger‑train schedules are allowed to be delayed by at most \\(maxDelay\\) minutes; a small additional delay (≤ \\(maxShDelay\\)) may be imposed to create a window for a shunting movement. |
| A6 | The cost of a shunting movement is independent of which unit performs it (the model only decides *whether* to execute it). |
| A7 | The “similarity’’ objective uses a linear penalty for each deviation from the original unit‑trip assignment; more sophisticated measures (e.g., number of changed units) can be added but are omitted for brevity. |
| A8 | In the Benders decomposition, the infrastructure sub‑problem is a pure feasibility check (no objective) that returns a minimal infeasible set of shunting movements; the corresponding cut is added to the master. |
| A9 | All parameters (costs, capacities, turn‑around times, etc.) are assumed known and deterministic. |
| A10| The model can be solved directly (exact approach) or used inside the iterative heuristic described in the paper; the only difference is whether cuts are added globally (exact) or shunting movements are fed one‑by‑one (heuristic). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8. How the model fits the paper’s framework  

* **Composition level** – variables \\(x_{t,u,k}\\), \\(y_s\\), \\(z_t\\) generate a rolling‑stock circulation and decide which shunting movements are to be performed.  
* **Infrastructure level** – variables \\(w_{s,p}\\) together with the track‑availability constraints guarantee that the selected shunting movements can be executed on the real railway network (including the two stations Utrecht and Rotterdam).  
* **Iterative / Benders coupling** – infeasible shunting combinations are cut out by the constraints (5)–(7) or by explicit Benders cuts, reproducing the exact algorithm; feeding shunting movements one‑by‑one reproduces the heuristic.  

The MILP therefore provides a **complete, linear, and implementable description** of the rolling‑stock rescheduling problem with infrastructure‑availability constraints, ready for use with commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or for inclusion in a decomposition/heuristic framework.

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. As transport capacity directly impacts passenger flows, further research is required to improve passenger satisfaction by including transport capacity as a decision variable.

Another direction for train scheduling problems addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing transport capacity explicitly. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. Pu and Zhan (2021) developed a two-step approach in which the first step determines the nominal line plan and the second step adjusts the time plan based on the actual measured passenger demands. Instead of changing the departure frequency, which would significantly affect the schedule, recently, many researchers have focused on optimizing the composition of the train (Ying et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023). Pan et al. (2023) developed a column-generation-based approach to optimize the timetable, train composition, and rolling stock circulation plan of an urban rail transit line. Their paper concludes that flexible train composition can provide additional adaptability to better match time-varying passenger demands. Wang et al. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. Yang et al. (2024) investigated the train scheduling problem with flexible train composition for an urban rail transit line, and they applied an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm to solve the resulting integer programming problem. As the inclusion of train composition optimization and rolling stock circulation planning introduces additional integer variables, the above studies indicate that the online computational complexity is the main challenge of incorporating flexible train composition into the real-time train scheduling problem.

MPC for real-time train scheduling

Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). The train scheduling problem is a typical constrained control problem, and many studies have applied MPC for real-time train scheduling. De Schutter et al. (2002) first applied MPC in the train scheduling problem to minimize train delays by adjusting transfer connections. Caimi et al. (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. (2022) proposed an MPC approach for train rescheduling during disruptions and delays, where in each step the resulting MILP problem is solved by combining bi-level heuristics and distributed optimization. The above studies only handle operator-related factors, leaving an open gap in including passenger demands in real-time train scheduling problems to improve the service quality of urban rail transit systems.

In recent years, several studies have focused on MPC for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. Based on a state-space model, Li et al. (2016) developed a robust MPC approach to minimize the upper bound of the timetable deviation from the nominal timetable under uncertain disturbances. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. Liu et al. (2023a) explicitly incorporated time-varying passenger demands and train capacity limitations into the real-time train scheduling problem. In Liu et al. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. The main challenge of applying MPC in real time is the online computational burden. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. (2020) applied a deep learning approach to an energy-efficient timetable rescheduling problem, where a long short-term memory (LSTM) network is trained to select the optimal operation mode. Šemrov et al. (2016) applied Q-learning in the train rescheduling problem to reduce delays caused by disturbances and disruptions, and they illustrated their method on a single-lane track with three trains. Yin et al. (2016) proposed an approximate dynamic programming approach to address train rescheduling problems, aiming to reduce passenger delays, total travel time, and train energy consumption. In Yin et al. (2016), the states include disturbance information, train arrival times, the number of boarding passengers, and the number of waiting passengers, while the actions include rescheduling the dwell times and running times. Khadilkar (2019) applied RL to determine track allocations and timetables of bidirectional railway lines to minimize the priority-weighted delay. Ying et al. (2021) developed a proximal policy optimization approach for the train scheduling problem in an urban rail transit line, considering flexible train composition. In Ying et al. (2021), the control policy and the value function are parameterized by artificial neural networks, and scheduling constraints are handled by a devised mask scheme. Simulation results show that this approach reduces the computational burden and improves solution quality compared to the genetic algorithm and differential evolution. Nguyen and Chow (2023) introduced an adaptive rollout surrogate approximate dynamic programming (ADP) framework for rail transit network operations, where the value function is approximated by a surrogate function, and the solution is obtained via a cross-entropy-based search, encompassing decisions related to service operations and flexible train unit deployment. Ying et al. (2024) proposed a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approach for disruption management with short-turning operations in a service corridor, enabling adaptive rescheduling under time-varying passenger demand. Wang et al. (2025) formulated adaptive network dispatching as a partially observable Markov decision process and applied a deep recurrent Q network to derive dispatching policies with flexible fleet deployment. These recent studies have shown that learning-based frameworks can support train scheduling and may incorporate time-varying passenger demands in rail networks. However, explicitly modeling time-varying passenger demands in the train scheduling problem further tightens the coupling among timetable adjustments, capacity allocation via flexible train composition, and rolling-stock circulation. This coupling enlarges the discrete decision space and increases online computational complexity, while operational feasibility still needs to be guaranteed for real-world implementation. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.

In the above studies, scalability and constraint satisfaction are the main challenges in developing learning-based train scheduling approaches. The train scheduling problem is typically formulated as an MILP or MINLP problem, and the computational complexity increases rapidly as the number of integer variables increases. In recent years, some research has combined learning-based and optimization-based approaches for MILP or MINLP problems by using learning-based approaches to obtain the integer variables (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023; da Silva et al., 2025). Having the integer variables fixed, the continuous variables are then obtained by solving a linear or nonlinear programming problem. This idea aims to combine the advantages of both learning-based and optimization-based approaches, i.e., the online computational efficiency of learning-based approaches and the feasibility guarantees of constrained optimization (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023). The promising results of learning-based train scheduling and the recent learning-based approaches for mixed integer programming problems have inspired us to develop an optimization-driven learning-based framework for passenger-oriented real-time train scheduling.

Paper contributions and structure

The studies introduced in Sections 1.1–1.3 are summarized in Table 1 , categorized by network details, train composition, train order, rolling stock circulation, passenger demands, and solution method. From the above literature review, it can be found that flexible train composition combined with rolling stock circulation planning is an effective approach to balance operational costs and service quality. Shorter trains can be deployed during off-peak hours and longer trains during peak hours, thereby balancing operational costs and passenger waiting times. The passenger-oriented train scheduling problem is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming problem. Various approaches can be applied to solve the resulting scheduling problem. Among them, optimization-based methods often encounter computational challenges for large-scale networks, necessitating additional efforts such as heuristics, two-step frameworks, and distributed approaches to reduce the computational burden. Learning-based methods are considered promising for addressing computational complexity. However, developing learning-based methods that are both scalable and constraint-satisfying for real-time passenger-oriented scheduling remains challenging, especially when time-varying passenger demands are explicitly considered when optimizing flexible train composition and rolling-stock circulation in network settings.

The current paper, therefore, addresses the learning-based train rescheduling problem in rail networks, considering time-varying passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. Unlike existing train rescheduling methods in the literature, the proposed approach integrates optimization and deep learning to combine the constraint satisfaction advantages of optimization-based methods with the fast online computation advantages of learning-based approaches. The main contributions of the paper are listed as follows: A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals. Four presolve techniques are developed to streamline optimization processes by pruning a subset of integer decision variables. After implementing the presolve techniques, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are applied to obtain the remaining integer variables with reduced dimensions. A deep-learning-based MPC approach is developed for real-time train rescheduling. To improve the online computational efficiency of MPC, the learning-based approach is applied to obtain integer variables, while the detailed timetable is obtained by solving a constrained optimization problem with the fixed integer variables. The remaining part of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides the problem description and general explanations. Section 3 introduces the passenger-oriented train rescheduling model. In Section 4, the problem formulation and the MINLP-based MPC approach are presented. In Section 5, we propose a learning-based MPC approach for real-time train rescheduling. Section 6 provides an illustrative case study. Section 7 concludes the paper.

A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals.

A deep-learning-based MPC approach is developed for real-time train rescheduling. To improve the online computational efficiency of MPC, the learning-based approach is applied to obtain integer variables, while the detailed timetable is obtained by solving a constrained optimization problem with the fixed integer variables.

response.content:
**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  
The formulation below follows the description in the prompt and adds the missing quantitative details (assumptions are explicitly marked). It is a *mixed‑integer linear program* that can be solved at every MPC step on a rolling prediction horizon.  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning (index) | Description / Assumption |
|--------|----------------|------------------------|
| **\(T\)** | set of trains, \(t\in T\) | All trains that may be dispatched during the planning horizon (including those already on‑track). |
| **\(S\)** | set of stations, \(s\in S\) | Ordered from the line origin (1) to the terminal (|S|). |
| **\(I\)** | set of time intervals in the prediction horizon, \(i\in I\) | Horizon \(H\) is divided into equal‑length intervals \(\Delta\) (e.g. 5 min).  \(|I|=H/\Delta\). |
| **\(K\)** | set of train‑type (composition) options, \(k\in K\) | Each type \(k\) has a fixed passenger capacity \(C_k\) and a fixed number of cars. |
| **\(R\)** | set of rolling‑stock units (trainsets), \(r\in R\) | A physical vehicle that can be assigned to a train‑type. |
| **\(d_{s,i}\)** | passenger demand (persons) at station \(s\) during interval \(i\) | *Assumption*: piecewise‑constant demand, obtained from forecast. |
| **\(\tau_{s,s'}\)** | nominal travel time (min) from station \(s\) to \(s'\) (adjacent) | Based on timetable or speed profile. |
| **\(c^{run}_k\)** | running‑cost per minute for type \(k\) (energy, crew, etc.) | Linear cost. |
| **\(c^{turn}_k\)** | turnaround cost for type \(k\) (crew change, cleaning) when a train terminates. |
| **\(c^{stock}_r\)** | fixed cost of using rolling‑stock unit \(r\) (depreciation, maintenance). |
| **\(M\)** | big‑M constant (e.g. 10⁶) used for logical constraints. |
| **\(L_{max}\)** | maximum allowed headway (min) between two consecutive trains at any station (safety). |
| **\(L_{min}\)** | minimum allowed headway (min) (signalling). |
| **\(P^{max}\)** | maximum allowed passenger waiting time (min) – optional soft bound. |
| **\(\alpha\)** | weight for passenger waiting time in the objective (tunable). |
| **\(\beta\)** | weight for operational cost in the objective (tunable). |

*All parameters are assumed known at the beginning of each MPC step.*

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_{t,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is **departing** from its origin station during interval *i* (i.e. the departure decision). |
| **\(y_{t,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **arrives** at its terminal station during interval *i*. |
| **\(z_{t,k}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned composition type *k*. |
| **\(w_{t,r}\)** | binary | 1 if rolling‑stock unit *r* is used for train *t*. |
| **\(a_{t,s,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **stops** at station *s* during interval *i* (stop‑plan). |
| **\(d_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Dwell time (min) of train *t* at station *s* during interval *i*. |
| **\(p_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Number of **boarding** passengers on train *t* at station *s* during interval *i*. |
| **\(q_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Number of **waiting** passengers left at station *s* after interval *i*. |
| **\(h_{s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Headway (min) between the two consecutive departures that serve station *s* in interval *i* (derived). |
| **\(u_{t,s,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **passes** station *s* (i.e. traverses without stopping) during interval *i*. (optional, can be expressed via \(a_{t,s,i}\)). |

All binary variables make the model mixed‑integer; all continuous variables are linear.

---

## 3. Model Equations  

### 3.1. Train‑type assignment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{t,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{1}
\]

Each train receives exactly one composition.

### 3.2. Rolling‑stock assignment  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} w_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{2}
\]

Each train uses one physical unit.

### 3.3. Compatibility between train‑type and rolling‑stock  

If a rolling‑stock unit cannot support a given type, a parameter \(\gamma_{r,k}\in\{0,1\}\) is defined (1 = feasible).  

\[
z_{t,k}+w_{t,r}\le 1+\gamma_{r,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;k\in K,\;r\in R \tag{3}
\]

### 3.4. Departure / Arrival linking  

Let \(s^{\text{orig}}_t\) and \(s^{\text{term}}_t\) be origin/terminal stations of train *t* (known).  

\[
x_{t,i}\le a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_t,i}\qquad\forall t,i \tag{4}
\]

\[
y_{t,i}\le a_{t,s^{\text{term}}_t,i}\qquad\forall t,i \tag{5}
\]

A train can only depart/arrive if it actually stops at the corresponding station.

### 3.5. Temporal feasibility (travel‑time propagation)  

For any two consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s^{+}\) (next downstream) and any interval \(i\):

\[
a_{t,s^{+},i'} \ge a_{t,s,i} - M\,(1-u_{t,s,i}) \quad\forall t,s,i,i' \text{ with } i' = i + \lceil \tau_{s,s^{+}}/\Delta\rceil \tag{6}
\]

If train *t* stops at *s* in interval *i* (i.e. \(a_{t,s,i}=1\)), then it must be present at the next station after the travel time. The binary \(u_{t,s,i}\) forces the logical link; \(M\) is a big‑M.

### 3.6. Headway constraints  

Define the departure time of train *t* at station *s* as the earliest interval where \(a_{t,s,i}=1\) and \(x_{t,i}=1\) (origin) or simply use the departure binary. For each station *s* and each pair of distinct trains \((t,\ell)\) that serve *s*:

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} - \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{\ell,i} \ge L_{min}\, \theta_{t\ell s} - M(1-\theta_{t\ell s}) \tag{7}
\]

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} - \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{\ell,i} \le L_{max}\, \theta_{t\ell s} + M(1-\theta_{t\ell s}) \tag{8}
\]

\[
\theta_{t\ell s}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t<\ell,\;s\in S \tag{9}
\]

\(\theta_{t\ell s}=1\) only if both trains stop at station *s* (enforced by linking constraints). This linearizes headway limits.

### 3.7. Capacity and passenger flow  

The number of boarding passengers cannot exceed the free seats on the train:

\[
p_{t,s,i} \le C_{k}\,z_{t,k} - \sum_{s'<s}\,p_{t,s',i} \qquad\forall t,s,i,k\in K \tag{10}
\]

Cumulative boardings up to station *s* must be ≤ capacity.  

Passenger waiting dynamics at each station:

\[
q_{t,s,i+1}= q_{t,s,i}+d_{s,i} - p_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i\in I\setminus\{|I|\} \tag{11}
\]

Initial waiting \(q_{t,s,1}=0\) (or given).  

Total waiting passengers at the end of the horizon (to be penalized):

\[
Q = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I} q_{t,s,i} \tag{12}
\]

### 3.8. Dwell‑time limits  

A minimum dwell time is required for boarding, proportional to the number of boarding passengers (assumption: 0.02 min per passenger) and a fixed safety time \(\delta^{min}\).

\[
d_{t,s,i} \ge \delta^{min} a_{t,s,i}+ \rho\, p_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{13}
\]

\(\rho\) is the boarding‑time coefficient (e.g., 0.02 min/passenger).

Upper bound on dwell time (platform capacity):

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le \delta^{max} a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{14}
\]

### 3.9. Stop‑plan (binary) linking  

If a train does not stop at a station, dwell time and boarding must be zero:

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le M\, a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{15}
\]

\[
p_{t,s,i} \le M\, a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{16}
\]

### 3.10. Rolling‑stock circulation (circular assignment)  

To guarantee that a physical unit returns to a depot after completing its service, we add a simple balance:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} = \sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} \quad\text{(trivial)} \tag{17}
\]

In practice, a *circulation* constraint can be added (e.g., each unit can be used at most once per horizon):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} \le 1 \qquad\forall r\in R \tag{18}
\]

If multiple trips per unit are allowed, a flow‑balance model would be introduced (omitted for brevity).

---

## 4. Objective Function  

A weighted sum of **operational cost** and **passenger waiting penalty**:

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\beta\Bigg[ \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} c^{run}_{k}\,z_{t,k}\, \Delta \;+\; \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} c^{turn}_{k}\, y_{t,i}\;+\;\sum_{r\in R}c^{stock}_{r}\,\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r}\Bigg]}_{\text{(A) Operational cost}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\alpha \; Q}_{\text{(B) Passenger waiting penalty}} \tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(\Delta\) is the length of a time interval (minutes).  

- **Term (A)** captures running cost proportional to the time a train of type *k* is in service, turnaround cost for each train that finishes its trip, and a fixed cost for each rolling‑stock unit used.  
- **Term (B)** penalizes the total number of passengers left waiting at the end of the horizon (or can be summed over all intervals).

The weights \(\alpha,\beta\) are tuned to reflect the relative importance of service quality vs. cost.

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,z,w,a,d,p,q,\theta} \;& \text{OBJ} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(18)} \\
& x_{t,i},y_{t,i},z_{t,k},w_{t,r},a_{t,s,i},\theta_{t\ell s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& d_{t,s,i},p_{t,s,i},q_{t,s,i}\ge 0 \\
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (e.g., product \(C_k z_{t,k}\) in (10)) are handled by standard linearization because \(C_k\) is a constant parameter.

---

## 6. Remarks & Modeling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption (explicit) |
|---|------------------------|
| A1 | Passenger demand is known *a priori* for each interval (forecast). |
| A2 | Travel times between adjacent stations are constant within the horizon (no disturbances). |
| A3 | Dwell time is linearly related to the number of boarding passengers (coefficient \(\rho\)). |
| A4 | Each train has a *single* composition throughout the horizon (no mid‑trip re‑configuration). |

**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  
The formulation below follows the description in the prompt and adds the missing quantitative details (assumptions are explicitly marked). It is a *mixed‑integer linear program* that can be solved at every MPC step on a rolling prediction horizon.  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning (index) | Description / Assumption |
|--------|----------------|------------------------|
| **\(T\)** | set of trains, \(t\in T\) | All trains that may be dispatched during the planning horizon (including those already on‑track). |
| **\(S\)** | set of stations, \(s\in S\) | Ordered from the line origin (1) to the terminal (|S|). |
| **\(I\)** | set of time intervals in the prediction horizon, \(i\in I\) | Horizon \(H\) is divided into equal‑length intervals \(\Delta\) (e.g. 5 min).  \(|I|=H/\Delta\). |
| **\(K\)** | set of train‑type (composition) options, \(k\in K\) | Each type \(k\) has a fixed passenger capacity \(C_k\) and a fixed number of cars. |
| **\(R\)** | set of rolling‑stock units (trainsets), \(r\in R\) | A physical vehicle that can be assigned to a train‑type. |
| **\(d_{s,i}\)** | passenger demand (persons) at station \(s\) during interval \(i\) | *Assumption*: piecewise‑constant demand, obtained from forecast. |
| **\(\tau_{s,s'}\)** | nominal travel time (min) from station \(s\) to \(s'\) (adjacent) | Based on timetable or speed profile. |
| **\(c^{run}_k\)** | running‑cost per minute for type \(k\) (energy, crew, etc.) | Linear cost. |
| **\(c^{turn}_k\)** | turnaround cost for type \(k\) (crew change, cleaning) when a train terminates. |
| **\(c^{stock}_r\)** | fixed cost of using rolling‑stock unit \(r\) (depreciation, maintenance). |
| **\(M\)** | big‑M constant (e.g. 10⁶) used for logical constraints. |
| **\(L_{max}\)** | maximum allowed headway (min) between two consecutive trains at any station (safety). |
| **\(L_{min}\)** | minimum allowed headway (min) (signalling). |
| **\(P^{max}\)** | maximum allowed passenger waiting time (min) – optional soft bound. |
| **\(\alpha\)** | weight for passenger waiting time in the objective (tunable). |
| **\(\beta\)** | weight for operational cost in the objective (tunable). |

*All parameters are assumed known at the beginning of each MPC step.*

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_{t,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is **departing** from its origin station during interval *i* (i.e. the departure decision). |
| **\(y_{t,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **arrives** at its terminal station during interval *i*. |
| **\(z_{t,k}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned composition type *k*. |
| **\(w_{t,r}\)** | binary | 1 if rolling‑stock unit *r* is used for train *t*. |
| **\(a_{t,s,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **stops** at station *s* during interval *i* (stop‑plan). |
| **\(d_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Dwell time (min) of train *t* at station *s* during interval *i*. |
| **\(p_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Number of **boarding** passengers on train *t* at station *s* during interval *i*. |
| **\(q_{t,s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Number of **waiting** passengers left at station *s* after interval *i*. |
| **\(h_{s,i}\)** | continuous \(\ge 0\) | Headway (min) between the two consecutive departures that serve station *s* in interval *i* (derived). |
| **\(u_{t,s,i}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* **passes** station *s* (i.e. traverses without stopping) during interval *i*. (optional, can be expressed via \(a_{t,s,i}\)). |

All binary variables make the model mixed‑integer; all continuous variables are linear.

---

## 3. Model Equations  

### 3.1. Train‑type assignment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{t,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{1}
\]

Each train receives exactly one composition.

### 3.2. Rolling‑stock assignment  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} w_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{2}
\]

Each train uses one physical unit.

### 3.3. Compatibility between train‑type and rolling‑stock  

If a rolling‑stock unit cannot support a given type, a parameter \(\gamma_{r,k}\in\{0,1\}\) is defined (1 = feasible).  

\[
z_{t,k}+w_{t,r}\le 1+\gamma_{r,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;k\in K,\;r\in R \tag{3}
\]

### 3.4. Departure / Arrival linking  

Let \(s^{\text{orig}}_t\) and \(s^{\text{term}}_t\) be origin/terminal stations of train *t* (known).  

\[
x_{t,i}\le a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_t,i}\qquad\forall t,i \tag{4}
\]

\[
y_{t,i}\le a_{t,s^{\text{term}}_t,i}\qquad\forall t,i \tag{5}
\]

A train can only depart/arrive if it actually stops at the corresponding station.

### 3.5. Temporal feasibility (travel‑time propagation)  

For any two consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s^{+}\) (next downstream) and any interval \(i\):

\[
a_{t,s^{+},i'} \ge a_{t,s,i} - M\,(1-u_{t,s,i}) \quad\forall t,s,i,i' \text{ with } i' = i + \lceil \tau_{s,s^{+}}/\Delta\rceil \tag{6}
\]

If train *t* stops at *s* in interval *i* (i.e. \(a_{t,s,i}=1\)), then it must be present at the next station after the travel time. The binary \(u_{t,s,i}\) forces the logical link; \(M\) is a big‑M.

### 3.6. Headway constraints  

Define the departure time of train *t* at station *s* as the earliest interval where \(a_{t,s,i}=1\) and \(x_{t,i}=1\) (origin) or simply use the departure binary. For each station *s* and each pair of distinct trains \((t,\ell)\) that serve *s*:

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} - \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{\ell,i} \ge L_{min}\, \theta_{t\ell s} - M(1-\theta_{t\ell s}) \tag{7}
\]

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} - \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{\ell,i} \le L_{max}\, \theta_{t\ell s} + M(1-\theta_{t\ell s}) \tag{8}
\]

\[
\theta_{t\ell s}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t<\ell,\;s\in S \tag{9}
\]

\(\theta_{t\ell s}=1\) only if both trains stop at station *s* (enforced by linking constraints). This linearizes headway limits.

### 3.7. Capacity and passenger flow  

The number of boarding passengers cannot exceed the free seats on the train:

\[
p_{t,s,i} \le C_{k}\,z_{t,k} - \sum_{s'<s}\,p_{t,s',i} \qquad\forall t,s,i,k\in K \tag{10}
\]

Cumulative boardings up to station *s* must be ≤ capacity.  

Passenger waiting dynamics at each station:

\[
q_{t,s,i+1}= q_{t,s,i}+d_{s,i} - p_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i\in I\setminus\{|I|\} \tag{11}
\]

Initial waiting \(q_{t,s,1}=0\) (or given).  

Total waiting passengers at the end of the horizon (to be penalized):

\[
Q = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I} q_{t,s,i} \tag{12}
\]

### 3.8. Dwell‑time limits  

A minimum dwell time is required for boarding, proportional to the number of boarding passengers (assumption: 0.02 min per passenger) and a fixed safety time \(\delta^{min}\).

\[
d_{t,s,i} \ge \delta^{min} a_{t,s,i}+ \rho\, p_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{13}
\]

\(\rho\) is the boarding‑time coefficient (e.g., 0.02 min/passenger).

Upper bound on dwell time (platform capacity):

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le \delta^{max} a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{14}
\]

### 3.9. Stop‑plan (binary) linking  

If a train does not stop at a station, dwell time and boarding must be zero:

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le M\, a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{15}
\]

\[
p_{t,s,i} \le M\, a_{t,s,i} \qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{16}
\]

### 3.10. Rolling‑stock circulation (circular assignment)  

To guarantee that a physical unit returns to a depot after completing its service, we add a simple balance:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} = \sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} \quad\text{(trivial)} \tag{17}
\]

In practice, a *circulation* constraint can be added (e.g., each unit can be used at most once per horizon):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r} \le 1 \qquad\forall r\in R \tag{18}
\]

If multiple trips per unit are allowed, a flow‑balance model would be introduced (omitted for brevity).

---

## 4. Objective Function  

A weighted sum of **operational cost** and **passenger waiting penalty**:

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\beta\Bigg[ \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} c^{run}_{k}\,z_{t,k}\, \Delta \;+\; \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} c^{turn}_{k}\, y_{t,i}\;+\;\sum_{r\in R}c^{stock}_{r}\,\sum_{t\in T} w_{t,r}\Bigg]}_{\text{(A) Operational cost}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\alpha \; Q}_{\text{(B) Passenger waiting penalty}} \tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(\Delta\) is the length of a time interval (minutes).  

- **Term (A)** captures running cost proportional to the time a train of type *k* is in service, turnaround cost for each train that finishes its trip, and a fixed cost for each rolling‑stock unit used.  
- **Term (B)** penalizes the total number of passengers left waiting at the end of the horizon (or can be summed over all intervals).

The weights \(\alpha,\beta\) are tuned to reflect the relative importance of service quality vs. cost.

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,z,w,a,d,p,q,\theta} \;& \text{OBJ} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(18)} \\
& x_{t,i},y_{t,i},z_{t,k},w_{t,r},a_{t,s,i},\theta_{t\ell s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& d_{t,s,i},p_{t,s,i},q_{t,s,i}\ge 0 \\
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (e.g., product \(C_k z_{t,k}\) in (10)) are handled by standard linearization because \(C_k\) is a constant parameter.

| A2 | Travel times between adjacent stations are constant within the horizon (no disturbances). |

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. As transport capacity directly impacts passenger flows, further research is required to improve passenger satisfaction by including transport capacity as a decision variable.

Another direction for train scheduling problems addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing transport capacity explicitly. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. Pu and Zhan (2021) developed a two-step approach in which the first step determines the nominal line plan and the second step adjusts the time plan based on the actual measured passenger demands. Instead of changing the departure frequency, which would significantly affect the schedule, recently, many researchers have focused on optimizing the composition of the train (Ying et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023). Pan et al. (2023) developed a column-generation-based approach to optimize the timetable, train composition, and rolling stock circulation plan of an urban rail transit line. Their paper concludes that flexible train composition can provide additional adaptability to better match time-varying passenger demands. Wang et al. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. Yang et al. (2024) investigated the train scheduling problem with flexible train composition for an urban rail transit line, and they applied an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm to solve the resulting integer programming problem. As the inclusion of train composition optimization and rolling stock circulation planning introduces additional integer variables, the above studies indicate that the online computational complexity is the main challenge of incorporating flexible train composition into the real-time train scheduling problem.

MPC for real-time train scheduling

Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). The train scheduling problem is a typical constrained control problem, and many studies have applied MPC for real-time train scheduling. De Schutter et al. (2002) first applied MPC in the train scheduling problem to minimize train delays by adjusting transfer connections. Caimi et al. (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. (2022) proposed an MPC approach for train rescheduling during disruptions and delays, where in each step the resulting MILP problem is solved by combining bi-level heuristics and distributed optimization. The above studies only handle operator-related factors, leaving an open gap in including passenger demands in real-time train scheduling problems to improve the service quality of urban rail transit systems.

In recent years, several studies have focused on MPC for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. Based on a state-space model, Li et al. (2016) developed a robust MPC approach to minimize the upper bound of the timetable deviation from the nominal timetable under uncertain disturbances. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. Liu et al. (2023a) explicitly incorporated time-varying passenger demands and train capacity limitations into the real-time train scheduling problem. In Liu et al. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. The main challenge of applying MPC in real time is the online computational burden. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. (2020) applied a deep learning approach to an energy-efficient timetable rescheduling problem, where a long short-term memory (LSTM) network is trained to select the optimal operation mode. Šemrov et al. (2016) applied Q-learning in the train rescheduling problem to reduce delays caused by disturbances and disruptions, and they illustrated their method on a single-lane track with three trains. Yin et al. (2016) proposed an approximate dynamic programming approach to address train rescheduling problems, aiming to reduce passenger delays, total travel time, and train energy consumption. In Yin et al. (2016), the states include disturbance information, train arrival times, the number of boarding passengers, and the number of waiting passengers, while the actions include rescheduling the dwell times and running times. Khadilkar (2019) applied RL to determine track allocations and timetables of bidirectional railway lines to minimize the priority-weighted delay. Ying et al. (2021) developed a proximal policy optimization approach for the train scheduling problem in an urban rail transit line, considering flexible train composition. In Ying et al. (2021), the control policy and the value function are parameterized by artificial neural networks, and scheduling constraints are handled by a devised mask scheme. Simulation results show that this approach reduces the computational burden and improves solution quality compared to the genetic algorithm and differential evolution. Nguyen and Chow (2023) introduced an adaptive rollout surrogate approximate dynamic programming (ADP) framework for rail transit network operations, where the value function is approximated by a surrogate function, and the solution is obtained via a cross-entropy-based search, encompassing decisions related to service operations and flexible train unit deployment. Ying et al. (2024) proposed a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approach for disruption management with short-turning operations in a service corridor, enabling adaptive rescheduling under time-varying passenger demand. Wang et al. (2025) formulated adaptive network dispatching as a partially observable Markov decision process and applied a deep recurrent Q network to derive dispatching policies with flexible fleet deployment. These recent studies have shown that learning-based frameworks can support train scheduling and may incorporate time-varying passenger demands in rail networks. However, explicitly modeling time-varying passenger demands in the train scheduling problem further tightens the coupling among timetable adjustments, capacity allocation via flexible train composition, and rolling-stock circulation. This coupling enlarges the discrete decision space and increases online computational complexity, while operational feasibility still needs to be guaranteed for real-world implementation. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.

In the above studies, scalability and constraint satisfaction are the main challenges in developing learning-based train scheduling approaches. The train scheduling problem is typically formulated as an MILP or MINLP problem, and the computational complexity increases rapidly as the number of integer variables increases. In recent years, some research has combined learning-based and optimization-based approaches for MILP or MINLP problems by using learning-based approaches to obtain the integer variables (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023; da Silva et al., 2025). Having the integer variables fixed, the continuous variables are then obtained by solving a linear or nonlinear programming problem. This idea aims to combine the advantages of both learning-based and optimization-based approaches, i.e., the online computational efficiency of learning-based approaches and the feasibility guarantees of constrained optimization (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023). The promising results of learning-based train scheduling and the recent learning-based approaches for mixed integer programming problems have inspired us to develop an optimization-driven learning-based framework for passenger-oriented real-time train scheduling.

Paper contributions and structure

The studies introduced in Sections 1.1–1.3 are summarized in Table 1 , categorized by network details, train composition, train order, rolling stock circulation, passenger demands, and solution method. From the above literature review, it can be found that flexible train composition combined with rolling stock circulation planning is an effective approach to balance operational costs and service quality. Shorter trains can be deployed during off-peak hours and longer trains during peak hours, thereby balancing operational costs and passenger waiting times. The passenger-oriented train scheduling problem is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming problem. Various approaches can be applied to solve the resulting scheduling problem. Among them, optimization-based methods often encounter computational challenges for large-scale networks, necessitating additional efforts such as heuristics, two-step frameworks, and distributed approaches to reduce the computational burden. Learning-based methods are considered promising for addressing computational complexity. However, developing learning-based methods that are both scalable and constraint-satisfying for real-time passenger-oriented scheduling remains challenging, especially when time-varying passenger demands are explicitly considered when optimizing flexible train composition and rolling-stock circulation in network settings.

The current paper, therefore, addresses the learning-based train rescheduling problem in rail networks, considering time-varying passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. Unlike existing train rescheduling methods in the literature, the proposed approach integrates optimization and deep learning to combine the constraint satisfaction advantages of optimization-based methods with the fast online computation advantages of learning-based approaches. The main contributions of the paper are listed as follows: A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals. | Symbol | Description | Typical value / assumption |

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |

\[

   \[

   \]

   (Here \(u_{t-1,s}^{p}\) is the number left waiting after the previous train; for the first train we set it to zero.)

    \[
    w_{s}^{p} = \Delta t \; \Bigl( d_{s}^{p} - \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} q_{t,s}^{p} \Bigr) \qquad\forall s,p .
    \]

    This follows from the fact that each passenger that is not boarded during interval \(p\) waits an additional \(\Delta t\) seconds.

11. **If a train is not dispatched, it cannot be present**  

    \[
    a_{t,s}^{p} \le \sum_{p'\le p} x_{t}^{p'} \qquad\forall t,s,p .
    \]

12. **Train must visit stations in order** (simple linear order for a single line). Let \( \sigma(s)\) be the index of station \(s\) along the line (1 = first). Then  

    \[
    a_{t,s}^{p} \le a_{t,s-1}^{p'}\quad\forall t,\; s>1,\; p'\le p .
    \]

    This ensures that a train can be at station \(s\) only after it has visited the previous station.

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t}^{p},y_{t,k},z_{t,r},a_{t,s}^{p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,p,s,k,r,\\
& d_{t,s},w_{s}^{p},h_{t}^{p},q_{t,s}^{p},u_{t,s}^{p}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s,p .
\end{aligned}
\]

* **Whether** a train is launched (\(x_{t}^{p}\)).  
* **Which composition** is used (\(y_{t,k}\)).  
* **Which rolling‑stock unit** operates the train (\(z_{t,r}\)).  
* **How long** the train dwells at each station (\(d_{t,s}\)).  
* **How many passengers** board each train (\(q_{t,s}^{p}\)) and how many remain waiting (\(u_{t,s}^{p}\)).  

The objective minimises a weighted sum of operating cost (linked to composition) and accumulated passenger waiting time.  All railway‑operational restrictions (headway, dwell‑time, track‑segment capacity, rolling‑stock availability) are expressed as linear constraints, making the problem amenable to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) inside an MPC horizon.

---

## 7. Embedding in an MPC Loop (high‑level description)

1. **At each control step** \(t_{c}\) (e.g., every 5 min) obtain the latest passenger‑demand forecasts \(d_{s}^{p}\) for the next \(P\) intervals.  
2. **Solve the MILP** above with the current system state (remaining rolling‑stock availability, trains already on‑track).  
3. **Implement the first interval’s decisions** (dispatch the trains whose \(x_{t}^{p}=1\) for the current interval, set dwell times \(d_{t,s}\) accordingly).  
4. **Shift the horizon** one interval forward, update the state (remove departed trains, update rolling‑stock availability) and repeat.

After presolve, a trained **LSTM** can predict the remaining binary variables, fixing them and leaving only the continuous part (dwell times, passenger flows) to be solved as a linear program – dramatically reducing online computation while preserving feasibility.

--- 

### End of Model  

*All equations are linear; any non‑linear terms from the original literature have been linearised by standard big‑M or piece‑wise‑constant approximations, as indicated.*

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. (2024) investigated the train scheduling problem with flexible train composition for an urban rail transit line, and they applied an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm to solve the resulting integer programming problem. Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). The train scheduling problem is a typical constrained control problem, and many studies have applied MPC for real-time train scheduling. De Schutter et al. (2002) first applied MPC in the train scheduling problem to minimize train delays by adjusting transfer connections. Caimi et al. (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. (2022) proposed an MPC approach for train rescheduling during disruptions and delays, where in each step the resulting MILP problem is solved by combining bi-level heuristics and distributed optimization. The above studies only handle operator-related factors, leaving an open gap in including passenger demands in real-time train scheduling problems to improve the service quality of urban rail transit systems.

In recent years, several studies have focused on MPC for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. Based on a state-space model, Li et al. (2016) developed a robust MPC approach to minimize the upper bound of the timetable deviation from the nominal timetable under uncertain disturbances. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.
