**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  
The formulation below follows the description in the prompt. It combines (i) a piece‑wise‑constant approximation of time‑varying passenger demand, (ii) flexible train composition (choice of the number of cars per train), and (iii) rolling‑stock circulation (assignment of physical train units to service trips). The model is written for a single planning horizon (the MPC prediction window) that is later shifted forward in a receding‑horizon fashion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of service trips (planned departures)  \(t=1,\dots ,|T|\) |
| **S** | Set of stations on the line  \(s=1,\dots ,|S|\) (ordered from origin to terminal) |
| **K** | Set of train‑type (composition) alternatives  \(k=1,\dots ,|K|\) (e.g., 2‑car, 4‑car, 6‑car) |
| **U** | Set of rolling‑stock units (physical trainsets)  \(u=1,\dots ,|U|\) |
| **I** | Set of demand intervals (piece‑wise constant)  \(i=1,\dots ,|I|\) |
| **P** | Set of passenger‑flow arcs \((s,s')\) with \(s<s'\) (origin‑destination pairs) |

**Parameters (assumed known / estimated)**  

* \(L_k\) – passenger capacity of composition \(k\) (seats).  
* \(c_k\) – operating cost per service trip when using composition \(k\) (fuel, crew, etc.).  
* \(c^{\text{turn}}_u\) – cost of turning (re‑positioning) unit \(u\) between two trips (e.g., dead‑head).  
* \(\Delta^{\text{run}}_{s,s'}\) – nominal running time (travel time) between consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s'\).  
* \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\) – maximum admissible dwell time at a station (seconds).  
* \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_{\min}\) – minimum headway between two consecutive departures from the same station (seconds).  
* \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_{\max}\) – maximum headway allowed (service‑frequency bound).  
* \(d_{p,i}\) – forecast passenger demand for OD‑pair \(p\in P\) during interval \(i\) (persons).  
* \(\tau_i\) – start time of interval \(i\) (seconds from the beginning of the MPC horizon).  
* \(M\) – a big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time value, e.g. 10⁶ s).  

*Assumptions* (explicitly stated):  

1. Passenger demand is piece‑wise constant on each interval \(i\).  
2. Trains may skip stations (stop‑skipping) – modelled by binary stop‑variables.  
3. Rolling‑stock units are homogeneous except for their current location; any unit can be assigned to any composition \(k\).  
4. All trips start and finish within the prediction horizon (no carry‑over of unfinished trips).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \(x_{t,k}\) | binary | 1 if trip \(t\) uses composition \(k\). |
| \(y_{t,u}\) | binary | 1 if rolling‑stock unit \(u\) is assigned to trip \(t\). |
| \(z_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if trip \(t\) stops at station \(s\) (otherwise it skips). |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of trip \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure time of trip \(t\) from station \(s\). |
| \(\theta_{p,i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Number of passengers of OD‑pair \(p\) that board during interval \(i\). |
| \(w_{p,i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Number of passengers of OD‑pair \(p\) that wait (unserved) at the end of interval \(i\). |
| \(e_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumption (or any other linear cost proxy) of trip \(t\). (optional, can be omitted). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Objective Function  

The goal is a **weighted sum** of three components:

1. **Operating cost** (fixed cost per composition + turning cost).  
2. **Passenger waiting penalty** (unserved demand).  
3. **Schedule deviation penalty** (to keep the solution close to a nominal timetable, if desired).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{k\in K} c_k \, x_{t,k}}_{\text{composition cost}} 
      + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{u\in U} c^{\text{turn}}_u \, y_{t,u}}_{\text{rolling‑stock turning cost}} \\[2mm]
    & + \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{p\in P}\sum_{i\in I} w_{p,i}}_{\text{passenger waiting penalty}} 
      + \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T}\bigl|a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}-\hat a_{t}\bigr|}_{\text{timetable deviation}} 
\end{aligned}
\]

* \(\alpha,\beta\) are user‑defined weighting coefficients.  
* \(\hat a_{t}\) denotes the nominal (planned) departure time of trip \(t\) from its origin station \(s^{\text{orig}}\).  
* The absolute value can be linearised with auxiliary variables if required.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Constraints  

#### 4.1. Composition‑selection constraints  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{C1}
\]

Each trip uses exactly one composition.

#### 4.2. Rolling‑stock assignment  

\[
\sum_{u\in U} y_{t,u}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{C2}
\]

Each trip is performed by exactly one physical unit.

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,u}\le 1 \qquad\forall u\in U \tag{C3}
\]

A unit cannot be assigned to two trips that overlap in time (see later temporal feasibility constraints).  

#### 4.3. Stop‑skipping (service plan)  

If a train does not stop at a station, its dwell time is forced to zero:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \le \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\, z_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,s \tag{C4}
\]

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s \tag{C5}
\]

If \(z_{t,s}=0\) then the dwell time is forced to 0.

#### 4.4. Travel‑time propagation  

For consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s+1\):

\[
a_{t,s+1} \ge d_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{run}}_{s,s+1} \qquad\forall t,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{C6}
\]

If a train skips a station, the dwell time term disappears automatically because of (C4).

#### 4.5. Headway (service‑frequency) constraints  

For any two trips \(t\) and \(t'\) that depart from the same origin station:

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} - a_{t,s^{\text{orig}} \ge \Delta^{\text{head}}_{\min} - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}) \tag{C7}
\]

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} - a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}} \le \Delta^{\text{head}}_{\max} + M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}) \tag{C8}
\]

where \(\delta_{t,t'}\) is a binary variable equal to 1 if \(t'\) follows \(t\) in the schedule (can be introduced by ordering the trips a priori; for simplicity we assume trips are indexed in chronological order, thus \(\delta_{t,t'}=1\) for \(t'<t\)).  

#### 4.6. Capacity – passenger boarding  

The number of passengers that board a train cannot exceed its capacity (sum over all OD‑pairs whose origin is the current station and whose boarding interval overlaps the train’s dwell time).

Define a binary indicator  

\[
b_{t,p,i}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if trip }t\text{ stops at the origin station of }p\text{ and } a_{t,s^{\text{orig}(p)}}\in[\tau_i,\tau_{i+1})\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

(Linearised with big‑M if needed.)

Then capacity constraint for each trip:

\[
\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{i\in I} \theta_{p,i}\, b_{t,p,i} \le \sum_{k\in K} L_k \, x_{t,k} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{C9}
\]

#### 4.7. Demand balance (flow conservation)  

For each OD‑pair \(p\) and interval \(i\):

\[
\theta_{p,i} + w_{p,i-1}= d_{p,i}+ w_{p,i} \qquad\forall p\in P,\; i\in I \tag{C10}
\]

where  

* \(d_{p,i}\) is the number of passengers of OD‑pair \(p\) that actually board during interval \(i\).  
* \(w_{p,0}=0\) (no waiting before the horizon starts).  

The boarding variable \(d_{p,i}\) can be expressed through the capacity constraints:

\[
d_{p,i}= \sum_{t\in T} \theta_{p,i}\, b_{t,p,i} \qquad\forall p,i \tag{C11}
\]

(If the sum exceeds capacity, the excess is automatically transferred to waiting variable \(w_{p,i}\) via (C10).)

#### 4.8. Rolling‑stock temporal feasibility  

If unit \(u\) performs trip \(t\) and then trip \(t'\), the departure of the second must be after the arrival of the first plus a turnaround time \(\Delta^{\text{turn}}_u\). Introduce binary linking variable \(\lambda_{t,t',u}\) that equals 1 when \(u\) serves \(t\) and then \(t'\). A compact linearisation is:

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} \ge d_{t,s^{\text{term}}}+ \Delta^{\text{turn}}_u - M\,(2-y_{t,u}-y_{t',u}) \qquad\forall t,t',u \tag{C12}
\]

If both \(y_{t,u}=y_{t',u}=1\) the constraint is active; otherwise the big‑M term deactivates it.

#### 4.9. Non‑negativity / binary definitions  

\[
x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,u}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t,s}\ge0,\; d_{t,s}\ge0,\;
\theta_{p,i}\ge0,\; w_{p,i}\ge0 \tag{C13}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t}\sum_{k}c_k x_{t,k}
      +\sum_{t}\sum_{u}c^{\text{turn}}_u y_{t,u}
      +\alpha\sum_{p,i} w_{p,i}
      +\beta\sum_{t}\bigl|a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}-\hat a_{t}\bigr| \\[1mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C13)} \\
\end{aligned}}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisation is used where necessary), therefore the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Model‑Predictive‑Control (MPC) Embedding  

1. **Prediction horizon**: Divide the future planning period \([0,T_{\text{hor}}]\) into \(N_I\) equal intervals \(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_{N_I}\).  
2. **Data update**: At each control step \(k\) (every \(\Delta t_{\text{MPC}}\) seconds) refresh the demand forecasts \(d_{p,i}\) for the remaining intervals.  
3. **Solve the MILP** (or the reduced MILP after presolve + LSTM‑predicted integer vars).  
4. **Implement** only the first control actions (e.g., the departure times and composition of the first few trips).  
5. **Shift horizon** forward, repeat.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Remarks on Presolve & Learning‑Based Acceleration  

* **Presolve techniques** (as mentioned in the prompt) can be applied before solving:  
  * Eliminate compositions \(k\) that cannot satisfy the maximal demand in any interval.  
  * Fix \(z_{t,s}=0\) for stations with zero expected boarding in the entire horizon.  
  * Remove rolling‑stock units that are unavailable (maintenance).  

* After presolve, the remaining binary variables \(\{x_{t,k}, y_{t,u}, z_{t,s}\}\) are fed to an **LSTM** that predicts a feasible (or near‑feasible) binary pattern. Those predictions are then **fixed** in the MILP, turning the problem into a pure **LP** for the continuous timing variables \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\theta_{p,i},w_{p,i}\}\). This two‑stage scheme preserves feasibility (the LP respects all linear constraints) while dramatically reducing the online computational burden.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**In summary**, the equations above constitute a complete linear (MILP) model for passenger‑oriented real‑time train scheduling that captures time‑varying demand, flexible train composition, and rolling‑stock circulation, and is ready to be embedded in an MPC loop or combined with a learning‑based predictor for fast online operation.

#### 4.2. Rolling‑stock assignment  

\[
\sum_{u\in U} y_{t,u}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{C2}
\]

Each trip is performed by exactly one physical unit.

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,u}\le 1 \qquad\forall u\in U \tag{C3}
\]

A unit cannot be assigned to two trips that overlap in time (see later temporal feasibility constraints).  

#### 4.3. Stop‑skipping (service plan)  

If a train does not stop at a station, its dwell time is forced to zero:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \le \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\, z_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,s \tag{C4}
\]

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s \tag{C5}
\]

If \(z_{t,s}=0\) then the dwell time is forced to 0.

#### 4.4. Travel‑time propagation  

For consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s+1\):

\[
a_{t,s+1} \ge d_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{run}}_{s,s+1} \qquad\forall t,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{C6}
\]

If a train skips a station, the dwell time term disappears automatically because of (C4).

#### 4.5. Headway (service‑frequency) constraints  

For any two trips \(t\) and \(t'\) that depart from the same origin station:

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} - a_{t,s^{\text{orig}} \ge \Delta^{\text{head}}_{\min} - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}) \tag{C7}
\]

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} - a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}} \le \Delta^{\text{head}}_{\max} + M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}) \tag{C8}
\]

where \(\delta_{t,t'}\) is a binary variable equal to 1 if \(t'\) follows \(t\) in the schedule (can be introduced by ordering the trips a priori; for simplicity we assume trips are indexed in chronological order, thus \(\delta_{t,t'}=1\) for \(t'<t\)).  

#### 4.6. Capacity – passenger boarding  

The number of passengers that board a train cannot exceed its capacity (sum over all OD‑pairs whose origin is the current station and whose boarding interval overlaps the train’s dwell time).

Define a binary indicator  

\[
b_{t,p,i}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if trip }t\text{ stops at the origin station of }p\text{ and } a_{t,s^{\text{orig}(p)}}\in[\tau_i,\tau_{i+1})\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

(Linearised with big‑M if needed.)

Then capacity constraint for each trip:

\[
\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{i\in I} \theta_{p,i}\, b_{t,p,i} \le \sum_{k\in K} L_k \, x_{t,k} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{C9}
\]

#### 4.7. Demand balance (flow conservation)  

For each OD‑pair \(p\) and interval \(i\):

\[
\theta_{p,i} + w_{p,i-1}= d_{p,i}+ w_{p,i} \qquad\forall p\in P,\; i\in I \tag{C10}
\]

where  

* \(d_{p,i}\) is the number of passengers of OD‑pair \(p\) that actually board during interval \(i\).  
* \(w_{p,0}=0\) (no waiting before the horizon starts).  

The boarding variable \(d_{p,i}\) can be expressed through the capacity constraints:

\[
d_{p,i}= \sum_{t\in T} \theta_{p,i}\, b_{t,p,i} \qquad\forall p,i \tag{C11}
\]

(If the sum exceeds capacity, the excess is automatically transferred to waiting variable \(w_{p,i}\) via (C10).)

#### 4.8. Rolling‑stock temporal feasibility  

If unit \(u\) performs trip \(t\) and then trip \(t'\), the departure of the second must be after the arrival of the first plus a turnaround time \(\Delta^{\text{turn}}_u\). Introduce binary linking variable \(\lambda_{t,t',u}\) that equals 1 when \(u\) serves \(t\) and then \(t'\). A compact linearisation is:

\[
a_{t',s^{\text{orig}}} \ge d_{t,s^{\text{term}}}+ \Delta^{\text{turn}}_u - M\,(2-y_{t,u}-y_{t',u}) \qquad\forall t,t',u \tag{C12}
\]

If both \(y_{t,u}=y_{t',u}=1\) the constraint is active; otherwise the big‑M term deactivates it.

#### 4.9. Non‑negativity / binary definitions  

\[
x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,u}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t,s}\ge0,\; d_{t,s}\ge0,\;
\theta_{p,i}\ge0,\; w_{p,i}\ge0 \tag{C13}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t}\sum_{k}c_k x_{t,k}
      +\sum_{t}\sum_{u}c^{\text{turn}}_u y_{t,u}
      +\alpha\sum_{p,i} w_{p,i}
      +\beta\sum_{t}\bigl|a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}-\hat a_{t}\bigr| \\[1mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(C1)–(C13)} \\
\end{aligned}}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisation is used where necessary), therefore the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Model‑Predictive‑Control (MPC) Embedding  

1. **Prediction horizon**: Divide the future planning period \([0,T_{\text{hor}}]\) into \(N_I\) equal intervals \(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_{N_I}\).  
2. **Data update**: At each control step \(k\) (every \(\Delta t_{\text{MPC}}\) seconds) refresh the demand forecasts \(d_{p,i}\) for the remaining intervals.  
3. **Solve the MILP** (or the reduced MILP after presolve + LSTM‑predicted integer vars).  
4. **Implement** only the first control actions (e.g., the departure times and composition of the first few trips).  
5. **Shift horizon** forward, repeat.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Remarks on Presolve & Learning‑Based Acceleration  

* **Presolve techniques** (as mentioned in the prompt) can be applied before solving:  
  * Eliminate compositions \(k\) that cannot satisfy the maximal demand in any interval.  
  * Fix \(z_{t,s}=0\) for stations with zero expected boarding in the entire horizon.  
  * Remove rolling‑stock units that are unavailable (maintenance).  

* After presolve, the remaining binary variables \(\{x_{t,k}, y_{t,u}, z_{t,s}\}\) are fed to an **LSTM** that predicts a feasible (or near‑feasible) binary pattern. Those predictions are then **fixed** in the MILP, turning the problem into a pure **LP** for the continuous timing variables \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\theta_{p,i},w_{p,i}\}\). This two‑stage scheme preserves feasibility (the LP respects all linear constraints) while dramatically reducing the online computational burden.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**In summary**, the equations above constitute a complete linear (MILP) model for passenger‑oriented real‑time train scheduling that captures time‑varying demand, flexible train composition, and rolling‑stock circulation, and is ready to be embedded in an MPC loop or combined with a learning‑based predictor for fast online operation.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  

The formulation below is a complete, linear model that can be used directly in a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  All symbols are defined explicitly; where data are not given in the description, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption)**.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(N\) | Set of network nodes (stations, switch‑points, block ends, TTD‑sections). |
| \(A\subseteq N\times N\) | Set of directed track arcs (track‑segments) \((i,j)\). |
| \(S\subseteq A\) | Sub‑set of arcs that are **switches** (turnouts). |
| \(K\) | Set of discrete **speed‑profile options** (e.g. “full speed”, “reduced speed”). |
| \(P_t\) | Ordered list of planned path nodes for train \(t\) (derived from the timetable). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of consecutive node‑pairs \((i,j)\) that appear in \(P_t\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of arc \((i,j)\). | [km] |
| \(\bar v_{k}\) | Nominal speed for speed‑profile \(k\). | [km/h] |
| \(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\) | Braking deceleration of train \(t\) (absolute value). | [km/h²] |
| \(\tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,i}\) | **Dwell time** required at node \(i\) for train \(t\) (if \(i\) is a station). | [s] |
| \(\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}\) | Running time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) when using speed‑profile \(k\). Computed as  

\[
\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}= \frac{L_{ij}}{\bar v_{k}} \times 3600 \qquad\text{(Assumption: constant speed on the arc).}
\] | [s] |
| \(\beta_{t,ij}\) | **Braking distance** of train \(t\) when travelling on arc \((i,j)\) at the speed used on that arc (depends on the chosen profile).  

\[
\beta_{t,ij}= \frac{\bar v_{k}^{2}}{2\,a^{\text{br}}_{t}} \quad\text{if profile }k\text{ is selected on }(i,j). 
\] | [km] |
| \(\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t,t'}\) | Minimum **speed‑dependent separation distance** required between the *front* of the following train \(t\) and the *rear* of the leading train \(t'\).  

\[
\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t,t'} = \beta_{t',\text{last}} + \epsilon \qquad\text{with }\epsilon=0.05\text{ km (safety margin).}
\] | [km] |
| \(M\) | Large constant for Big‑M linearisation (e.g. \(M = 10^{6}\)). |
| \(\text{EOT}_{t}\) | Original **expected time of arrival** at the final node of train \(t\) (from the given timetable). | [s] |
| \(\text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\) | Original expected time of passage of node \(i\) by train \(t\) (from the timetable). | [s] |
| \(\text{Cap}_{ij}\) | Maximum number of trains that can simultaneously occupy arc \((i,j)\) (normally 1, but may be 2 on double‑track). | – |
| \(\text{Cap}^{\text{switch}}_{s}\) | Maximum number of trains that may occupy a switch \(s\) at the same time (normally 1). | – |

---

## 3.  Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \(x_{t,ij}^{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) with speed‑profile \(k\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Actual arrival time** of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \(d_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \(\delta_{t,t'}^{i} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | Ordering variable: 1 if train \(t\) passes node \(i\) **after** train \(t'\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{t} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Total delay** of train \(t\) (difference between actual final arrival and original expected arrival). |
| \(y_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies switch \(s\) (any of its incoming/outgoing arcs). |
| \(b_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Brake‑indication point** (distance measured from node \(i\) backwards along the train’s route) for train \(t\) when the MA ends at node \(i\). (Only needed for reporting; not used in constraints). |

---

## 4.  Objective  

Minimise the weighted sum of total delays (weights can be set to 1 for a pure delay minimisation):

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} w_{t}\, z_{t}}
\]

where \(w_{t}=1\) for all trains unless a priority weighting is required (e.g., passenger vs. freight).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Path feasibility  

1. **Exactly one speed‑profile per traversed arc**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,ij}^{k}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t\\
0 & \forall (i,j)\notin \mathcal{P}_t
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{1}
\]

2. **Flow conservation on the path** – ensures that the train follows its ordered node list  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t} \sum_{k} x_{t,ij}^{k}
\;-\;
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in \mathcal{P}_t} \sum_{k} x_{t,ji}^{k}
=
\begin{cases}
1 & i = \text{origin of }t\\
-1 & i = \text{destination of }t\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in N
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.2 Timing relations  

3. **Departure after arrival + dwell (if any)**  

\[
d_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} + \tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,i}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in N
\tag{3}
\]

4. **Travel time on an arc** – link arrival at the next node to departure from the current node  

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; d_{t,i} + \sum_{k\in K}\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}\,x_{t,ij}^{k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t
\tag{4}
\]

5. **Initial condition (original timetable)**  

\[
a_{t,\text{origin}} \;=\; \text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{origin}} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5}
\]

6. **Delay definition**  

\[
z_{t} \; \ge\; a_{t,\text{destination}} - \text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{destination}}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{6}
\]

### 5.3 Capacity / occupancy constraints  

7. **At most one train in a block/TD‑section** (fixed‑block analogue, but we keep it for safety; the DTG separation will dominate in most cases)  

\[
\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl[\, a_{t,i} \le \theta \le d_{t,i} \,\Bigr] \;\le\; \text{Cap}_{ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in A,\; \forall \theta\in\{a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\}
\tag{7}
\]

In a linear model this is expressed with ordering binaries (see next constraint).

8. **Ordering of two trains on the same arc**  

For every unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t\neq t'\) and every arc \((i,j)\) that both may use (i.e. \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t\cap\mathcal{P}_{t'}\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',i} &\ge d_{t,i} - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}^{i}) \\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',i} - M\,\delta_{t,t'}^{i}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in A
\tag{8}
\]

The binary \(\delta_{t,t'}^{i}\) chooses which train is first on the arc.

### 5.4 Speed‑dependent separation (core DTG feature)  

9. **Minimum distance between successive trains** – expressed in time using the braking distance of the leading train.  
For each pair \((t,t')\) that share a common **conflict node** \(i\) (the point where the MA of the following train ends, i.e. the entry of the occupied block/section), we enforce:

\[
a_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t',i} + \frac{\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t',t}}{\bar v_{k}}\times 3600 - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}^{i})
\qquad\forall t\neq t',\; i\in N
\tag{9}
\]

Explanation:  
*If train \(t\) follows train \(t'\) at node \(i\) (\(\delta_{t,t'}^{i}=1\)), the arrival time of \(t\) must be later than the arrival of \(t'\) by at least the time needed to cover the speed‑dependent separation distance \(\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t',t}\) at the speed used on the preceding arc. The speed \(\bar v_{k}\) is the one selected for the arc that brings train \(t\) to node \(i\) (the model can use a big‑M linearisation to pick the appropriate speed; for clarity we write it directly).*

If the pair does **not** share the same block/section (i.e., they are on different tracks), the binary can be forced to 0, making the constraint inactive.

### 5.5 Switch occupation  

10. **Only one train may occupy a switch at a time**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{Cap}^{\text{switch}}_{s} \qquad\forall s\in S
\tag{10}
\]

Linking \(y_{t,s}\) to the arc variables:

\[
y_{t,s} \;\ge\; \sum_{k\in K}\bigl(x_{t,ij}^{k}+x_{t,ji}^{k}\bigr) \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in S
\tag{11}
\]

### 5.6 Brake‑indication point (optional reporting)  

12. **Compute the distance from node \(i\) where the brake must be applied** (used only for output, not for feasibility).  

\[
b_{t,i}= \beta_{t,\text{prev}} \quad\text{where }\text{prev}\text{ is the arc preceding }i\text{ on }t\text{'s path.}
\tag{12}
\]

Because \(\beta_{t,\text{prev}}\) is known once the speed‑profile on that arc is fixed, we can linearise it by:

\[
b_{t,i}= \sum_{k\in K}\beta_{t,\,\text{prev},k}\,x_{t,\text{prev}}^{k}
\qquad\forall t,i
\tag{13}
\]

---

## 6.  Summary of the model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} w_{t}\,z_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(13)} \\
&x_{t,ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\delta_{t,t'}^{i}\in\{0,1\},\;
y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,i},d_{t,i},z_{t},b_{t,i}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,i.
\end{aligned}
\]

The model simultaneously decides:

* **Which speed‑profile** each train uses on every arc (binary \(x\)).  
* **When** each train arrives/departs from every node (continuous \(a,d\)).  
* **The ordering** of trains on shared resources (binary \(\delta\), \(y\)).  
* **The resulting total delay** (continuous \(z\)).  

The **speed‑dependent separation constraint (9)** captures the essence of DTG signalling: the required headway between two trains is a function of the leading train’s braking distance, which itself depends on its speed and deceleration capability. By selecting different speed‑profiles, the optimisation can deliberately reduce braking distances (e.g., by slowing a train before a bottleneck) and thereby increase line capacity while keeping total delay minimal.

---

### 7.  Remarks & modelling choices (Assumptions)

| # | Assumption | Reason |
|---|------------|--------|
| A1 | Running time on an arc is computed with a **constant speed** equal to the chosen profile speed \(\bar v_k\). | Keeps the model linear; more detailed speed‑profile (piece‑wise) can be added at the cost of extra variables. |
| A2 | Braking distance uses the simple physics formula \(\beta = v^{2}/(2a)\). | Adequate for high‑speed mainline trains; safety margin \(\epsilon\) added. |
| A3 | The **end of authority (EoA)** is always at the **end of a block/TD‑section**; the brake‑indication point may lie anywhere inside the preceding arc. | Matches the ETCS‑L2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) description. |
| A4 | Capacity of a block is 1 (single‑track). For double‑track lines the parameter \(\text{Cap}_{ij}\) can be set to 2. | Allows the same formulation for both cases. |
| A5 | Large‑M value \(M=10^{6}\) is sufficient to deactivate constraints when the associated binary is 0. | Standard practice; can be tightened for numerical stability. |
| A6 | All trains start at their original timetable origin time (constraint 5). Re‑dispatching the origin time would require an additional decision variable. | Reflects the typical real‑time CDR situation where the delay originates downstream of the origin. |

---

**End of MILP formulation** – this model can be directly implemented, solved, and the optimal values of the binary variables give the rescheduling actions (speed reductions, re‑ordering at switches, etc.) that resolve all conflicts under DTG signalling while minimising total delay.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  

The formulation below is a complete, linear model that can be used directly in a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  All symbols are defined explicitly; where data are not given in the description, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption)**.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(N\) | Set of network nodes (stations, switch‑points, block ends, TTD‑sections). |
| \(A\subseteq N\times N\) | Set of directed track arcs (track‑segments) \((i,j)\). |
| \(S\subseteq A\) | Sub‑set of arcs that are **switches** (turnouts). |
| \(K\) | Set of discrete **speed‑profile options** (e.g. “full speed”, “reduced speed”). |
| \(P_t\) | Ordered list of planned path nodes for train \(t\) (derived from the timetable). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of consecutive node‑pairs \((i,j)\) that appear in \(P_t\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of arc \((i,j)\). | [km] |
| \(\bar v_{k}\) | Nominal speed for speed‑profile \(k\). | [km/h] |
| \(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\) | Braking deceleration of train \(t\) (absolute value). | [km/h²] |
| \(\tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,i}\) | **Dwell time** required at node \(i\) for train \(t\) (if \(i\) is a station). | [s] |
| \(\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}\) | Running time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) when using speed‑profile \(k\). Computed as  

\[
\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}= \frac{L_{ij}}{\bar v_{k}} \times 3600 \qquad\text{(Assumption: constant speed on the arc).}
\] | [s] |
| \(\beta_{t,ij}\) | **Braking distance** of train \(t\) when travelling on arc \((i,j)\) at the speed used on that arc (depends on the chosen profile).  

\[
\beta_{t,ij}= \frac{\bar v_{k}^{2}}{2\,a^{\text{br}}_{t}} \quad\text{if profile }k\text{ is selected on }(i,j). 
\] | [km] |
| \(\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t,t'}\) | Minimum **speed‑dependent separation distance** required between the *front* of the following train \(t\) and the *rear* of the leading train \(t'\).  

\[
\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t,t'} = \beta_{t',\text{last}} + \epsilon \qquad\text{with }\epsilon=0.05\text{ km (safety margin).}
\] | [km] |
| \(M\) | Large constant for Big‑M linearisation (e.g. \(M = 10^{6}\)). |
| \(\text{EOT}_{t}\) | Original **expected time of arrival** at the final node of train \(t\) (from the given timetable). | [s] |
| \(\text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\) | Original expected time of passage of node \(i\) by train \(t\) (from the timetable). | [s] |
| \(\text{Cap}_{ij}\) | Maximum number of trains that can simultaneously occupy arc \((i,j)\) (normally 1, but may be 2 on double‑track). | – |
| \(\text{Cap}^{\text{switch}}_{s}\) | Maximum number of trains that may occupy a switch \(s\) at the same time (normally 1). | – |

---

## 3.  Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \(x_{t,ij}^{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) with speed‑profile \(k\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Actual arrival time** of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \(d_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Actual departure time** of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \(\delta_{t,t'}^{i} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | Ordering variable: 1 if train \(t\) passes node \(i\) **after** train \(t'\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{t} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Total delay** of train \(t\) (difference between actual final arrival and original expected arrival). |
| \(y_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies switch \(s\) (any of its incoming/outgoing arcs). |
| \(b_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | **Brake‑indication point** (distance measured from node \(i\) backwards along the train’s route) for train \(t\) when the MA ends at node \(i\). (Only needed for reporting; not used in constraints). |

---

## 4.  Objective  

Minimise the weighted sum of total delays (weights can be set to 1 for a pure delay minimisation):

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} w_{t}\, z_{t}}
\]

where \(w_{t}=1\) for all trains unless a priority weighting is required (e.g., passenger vs. freight).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Path feasibility  

1. **Exactly one speed‑profile per traversed arc**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t,ij}^{k}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t\\
0 & \forall (i,j)\notin \mathcal{P}_t
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{1}
\]

2. **Flow conservation on the path** – ensures that the train follows its ordered node list  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t} \sum_{k} x_{t,ij}^{k}
\;-\;
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in \mathcal{P}_t} \sum_{k} x_{t,ji}^{k}
=
\begin{cases}
1 & i = \text{origin of }t\\
-1 & i = \text{destination of }t\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in N
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.2 Timing relations  

3. **Departure after arrival + dwell (if any)**  

\[
d_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} + \tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,i}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in N
\tag{3}
\]

4. **Travel time on an arc** – link arrival at the next node to departure from the current node  

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; d_{t,i} + \sum_{k\in K}\tau^{\text{run}}_{t,ij,k}\,x_{t,ij}^{k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in \mathcal{P}_t
\tag{4}
\]

5. **Initial condition (original timetable)**  

\[
a_{t,\text{origin}} \;=\; \text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{origin}} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5}
\]

6. **Delay definition**  

\[
z_{t} \; \ge\; a_{t,\text{destination}} - \text{EOT}^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{destination}}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{6}
\]

### 5.3 Capacity / occupancy constraints  

7. **At most one train in a block/TD‑section** (fixed‑block analogue, but we keep it for safety; the DTG separation will dominate in most cases)  

\[
\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl[\, a_{t,i} \le \theta \le d_{t,i} \,\Bigr] \;\le\; \text{Cap}_{ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in A,\; \forall \theta\in\{a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\}
\tag{7}
\]

In a linear model this is expressed with ordering binaries (see next constraint).

8. **Ordering of two trains on the same arc**  

For every unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t\neq t'\) and every arc \((i,j)\) that both may use (i.e. \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}_t\cap\mathcal{P}_{t'}\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',i} &\ge d_{t,i} - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}^{i}) \\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',i} - M\,\delta_{t,t'}^{i}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in A
\tag{8}
\]

The binary \(\delta_{t,t'}^{i}\) chooses which train is first on the arc.

### 5.4 Speed‑dependent separation (core DTG feature)  

9. **Minimum distance between successive trains** – expressed in time using the braking distance of the leading train.  
For each pair \((t,t')\) that share a common **conflict node** \(i\) (the point where the MA of the following train ends, i.e. the entry of the occupied block/section), we enforce:

\[
a_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t',i} + \frac{\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t',t}}{\bar v_{k}}\times 3600 - M\,(1-\delta_{t,t'}^{i})
\qquad\forall t\neq t',\; i\in N
\tag{9}
\]

Explanation:  
*If train \(t\) follows train \(t'\) at node \(i\) (\(\delta_{t,t'}^{i}=1\)), the arrival time of \(t\) must be later than the arrival of \(t'\) by at least the time needed to cover the speed‑dependent separation distance \(\Delta^{\text{sep}}_{t',t}\) at the speed used on the preceding arc. The speed \(\bar v_{k}\) is the one selected for the arc that brings train \(t\) to node \(i\) (the model can use a big‑M linearisation to pick the appropriate speed; for clarity we write it directly).*

If the pair does **not** share the same block/section (i.e., they are on different tracks), the binary can be forced to 0, making the constraint inactive.

### 5.5 Switch occupation  

10. **Only one train may occupy a switch at a time**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{Cap}^{\text{switch}}_{s} \qquad\forall s\in S
\tag{10}
\]

Linking \(y_{t,s}\) to the arc variables:

\[
y_{t,s} \;\ge\; \sum_{k\in K}\bigl(x_{t,ij}^{k}+x_{t,ji}^{k}\bigr) \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in S
\tag{11}
\]

### 5.6 Brake‑indication point (optional reporting)  

12. **Compute the distance from node \(i\) where the brake must be applied** (used only for output, not for feasibility).  

\[
b_{t,i}= \beta_{t,\text{prev}} \quad\text{where }\text{prev}\text{ is the arc preceding }i\text{ on }t\text{'s path.}
\tag{12}
\]

Because \(\beta_{t,\text{prev}}\) is known once the speed‑profile on that arc is fixed, we can linearise it by:

\[
b_{t,i}= \sum_{k\in K}\beta_{t,\,\text{prev},k}\,x_{t,\text{prev}}^{k}
\qquad\forall t,i
\tag{13}
\]

---

## 6.  Summary of the model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} w_{t}\,z_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(13)} \\
&x_{t,ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\delta_{t,t'}^{i}\in\{0,1\},\;
y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,i},d_{t,i},z_{t},b_{t,i}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,i.
\end{aligned}
\]

The model simultaneously decides:

* **Which speed‑profile** each train uses on every arc (binary \(x\)).  
* **When** each train arrives/departs from every node (continuous \(a,d\)).  
* **The ordering** of trains on shared resources (binary \(\delta\), \(y\)).  
* **The resulting total delay** (continuous \(z\)).  

The **speed‑dependent separation constraint (9)** captures the essence of DTG signalling: the required headway between two trains is a function of the leading train’s braking distance, which itself depends on its speed and deceleration capability. By selecting different speed‑profiles, the optimisation can deliberately reduce braking distances (e.g., by slowing a train before a bottleneck) and thereby increase line capacity while keeping total delay minimal.

---

### 7.  Remarks & modelling choices (Assumptions)

| # | Assumption | Reason |
|---|------------|--------|
| A1 | Running time on an arc is computed with a **constant speed** equal to the chosen profile speed \(\bar v_k\). | Keeps the model linear; more detailed speed‑profile (piece‑wise) can be added at the cost of extra variables. |
| A2 | Braking distance uses the simple physics formula \(\beta = v^{2}/(2a)\). | Adequate for high‑speed mainline trains; safety margin \(\epsilon\) added. |
| A3 | The **end of authority (EoA)** is always at the **end of a block/TD‑section**; the brake‑indication point may lie anywhere inside the preceding arc. | Matches the ETCS‑L2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) description. |
| A4 | Capacity of a block is 1 (single‑track). For double‑track lines the parameter \(\text{Cap}_{ij}\) can be set to 2. | Allows the same formulation for both cases. |
| A5 | Large‑M value \(M=10^{6}\) is sufficient to deactivate constraints when the associated binary is 0. | Standard practice; can be tightened for numerical stability. |
| A6 | All trains start at their original timetable origin time (constraint 5). Re‑dispatching the origin time would require an additional decision variable. | Reflects the typical real‑time CDR situation where the delay originates downstream of the origin. |

---

**End of MILP formulation** – this model can be directly implemented, solved, and the optimal values of the binary variables give the rescheduling actions (speed reductions, re‑ordering at switches, etc.) that resolve all conflicts under DTG signalling while minimising total delay.

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. As transport capacity directly impacts passenger flows, further research is required to improve passenger satisfaction by including transport capacity as a decision variable.

Another direction for train scheduling problems addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing transport capacity explicitly. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. Pu and Zhan (2021) developed a two-step approach in which the first step determines the nominal line plan and the second step adjusts the time plan based on the actual measured passenger demands. Instead of changing the departure frequency, which would significantly affect the schedule, recently, many researchers have focused on optimizing the composition of the train (Ying et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023). Pan et al. (2023) developed a column-generation-based approach to optimize the timetable, train composition, and rolling stock circulation plan of an urban rail transit line. Their paper concludes that flexible train composition can provide additional adaptability to better match time-varying passenger demands. Wang et al. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. Yang et al. (2024) investigated the train scheduling problem with flexible train composition for an urban rail transit line, and they applied an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm to solve the resulting integer programming problem. As the inclusion of train composition optimization and rolling stock circulation planning introduces additional integer variables, the above studies indicate that the online computational complexity is the main challenge of incorporating flexible train composition into the real-time train scheduling problem.

MPC for real-time train scheduling

Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). The train scheduling problem is a typical constrained control problem, and many studies have applied MPC for real-time train scheduling. De Schutter et al. (2002) first applied MPC in the train scheduling problem to minimize train delays by adjusting transfer connections. Caimi et al. (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. (2022) proposed an MPC approach for train rescheduling during disruptions and delays, where in each step the resulting MILP problem is solved by combining bi-level heuristics and distributed optimization. The above studies only handle operator-related factors, leaving an open gap in including passenger demands in real-time train scheduling problems to improve the service quality of urban rail transit systems.

In recent years, several studies have focused on MPC for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. Based on a state-space model, Li et al. (2016) developed a robust MPC approach to minimize the upper bound of the timetable deviation from the nominal timetable under uncertain disturbances. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. Liu et al. (2023a) explicitly incorporated time-varying passenger demands and train capacity limitations into the real-time train scheduling problem. In Liu et al. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. The main challenge of applying MPC in real time is the online computational burden. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. (2020) applied a deep learning approach to an energy-efficient timetable rescheduling problem, where a long short-term memory (LSTM) network is trained to select the optimal operation mode. Šemrov et al. (2016) applied Q-learning in the train rescheduling problem to reduce delays caused by disturbances and disruptions, and they illustrated their method on a single-lane track with three trains. Yin et al. (2016) proposed an approximate dynamic programming approach to address train rescheduling problems, aiming to reduce passenger delays, total travel time, and train energy consumption. In Yin et al. (2016), the states include disturbance information, train arrival times, the number of boarding passengers, and the number of waiting passengers, while the actions include rescheduling the dwell times and running times. Khadilkar (2019) applied RL to determine track allocations and timetables of bidirectional railway lines to minimize the priority-weighted delay. Ying et al. (2021) developed a proximal policy optimization approach for the train scheduling problem in an urban rail transit line, considering flexible train composition. In Ying et al. (2021), the control policy and the value function are parameterized by artificial neural networks, and scheduling constraints are handled by a devised mask scheme. Simulation results show that this approach reduces the computational burden and improves solution quality compared to the genetic algorithm and differential evolution. Nguyen and Chow (2023) introduced an adaptive rollout surrogate approximate dynamic programming (ADP) framework for rail transit network operations, where the value function is approximated by a surrogate function, and the solution is obtained via a cross-entropy-based search, encompassing decisions related to service operations and flexible train unit deployment. Ying et al. (2024) proposed a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approach for disruption management with short-turning operations in a service corridor, enabling adaptive rescheduling under time-varying passenger demand. Wang et al. (2025) formulated adaptive network dispatching as a partially observable Markov decision process and applied a deep recurrent Q network to derive dispatching policies with flexible fleet deployment. These recent studies have shown that learning-based frameworks can support train scheduling and may incorporate time-varying passenger demands in rail networks. However, explicitly modeling time-varying passenger demands in the train scheduling problem further tightens the coupling among timetable adjustments, capacity allocation via flexible train composition, and rolling-stock circulation. This coupling enlarges the discrete decision space and increases online computational complexity, while operational feasibility still needs to be guaranteed for real-world implementation. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.

In the above studies, scalability and constraint satisfaction are the main challenges in developing learning-based train scheduling approaches. The train scheduling problem is typically formulated as an MILP or MINLP problem, and the computational complexity increases rapidly as the number of integer variables increases. In recent years, some research has combined learning-based and optimization-based approaches for MILP or MINLP problems by using learning-based approaches to obtain the integer variables (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023; da Silva et al., 2025). Having the integer variables fixed, the continuous variables are then obtained by solving a linear or nonlinear programming problem. This idea aims to combine the advantages of both learning-based and optimization-based approaches, i.e., the online computational efficiency of learning-based approaches and the feasibility guarantees of constrained optimization (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023). The promising results of learning-based train scheduling and the recent learning-based approaches for mixed integer programming problems have inspired us to develop an optimization-driven learning-based framework for passenger-oriented real-time train scheduling.

Paper contributions and structure

The studies introduced in Sections 1.1–1.3 are summarized in Table 1 , categorized by network details, train composition, train order, rolling stock circulation, passenger demands, and solution method. From the above literature review, it can be found that flexible train composition combined with rolling stock circulation planning is an effective approach to balance operational costs and service quality. Shorter trains can be deployed during off-peak hours and longer trains during peak hours, thereby balancing operational costs and passenger waiting times. The passenger-oriented train scheduling problem is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming problem. Various approaches can be applied to solve the resulting scheduling problem. Among them, optimization-based methods often encounter computational challenges for large-scale networks, necessitating additional efforts such as heuristics, two-step frameworks, and distributed approaches to reduce the computational burden. Learning-based methods are considered promising for addressing computational complexity. However, developing learning-based methods that are both scalable and constraint-satisfying for real-time passenger-oriented scheduling remains challenging, especially when time-varying passenger demands are explicitly considered when optimizing flexible train composition and rolling-stock circulation in network settings.

The current paper, therefore, addresses the learning-based train rescheduling problem in rail networks, considering time-varying passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. Unlike existing train rescheduling methods in the literature, the proposed approach integrates optimization and deep learning to combine the constraint satisfaction advantages of optimization-based methods with the fast online computation advantages of learning-based approaches. The main contributions of the paper are listed as follows: A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals. Four presolve techniques are developed to streamline optimization processes by pruning a subset of integer decision variables. After implementing the presolve techniques, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are applied to obtain the remaining integer variables with reduced dimensions. A deep-learning-based MPC approach is developed for real-time train rescheduling. To improve the online computational efficiency of MPC, the learning-based approach is applied to obtain integer variables, while the detailed timetable is obtained by solving a constrained optimization problem with the fixed integer variables. The remaining part of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides the problem description and general explanations. Section 3 introduces the passenger-oriented train rescheduling model. In Section 4, the problem formulation and the MINLP-based MPC approach are presented. In Section 5, we propose a learning-based MPC approach for real-time train rescheduling. Section 6 provides an illustrative case study. Section 7 concludes the paper.

A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals.

**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  

The model below is a *complete* mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that can be embedded in a Model‑Predictive‑Control (MPC) horizon.  
All symbols are defined in the **Notation** table; missing data are indicated as **Assumption A‑x** and can be replaced by the planner’s actual numbers.

---

## 1. Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning | Type / Set |
|--------|---------|------------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains that may be dispatched in the horizon  | \(t=1,\dots,|T|\) |
| **\(S\)** | Set of stations (ordered along the line) | \(s=1,\dots,|S|\) |
| **\(K\)** | Set of admissible train‑composition types (e.g. 2‑car, 4‑car, 6‑car) | \(k\in K\) |
| **\(I\)** | Set of time intervals that discretise the prediction horizon (piece‑wise‑constant demand) | \(i=1,\dots,|I|\) |
| **\(c_k\)** | Capacity (passenger seats) of composition type \(k\) | (Assumption A‑1) |
| **\(c^{\text{stock}}_k\)** | Number of train‑sets of type \(k\) available in the depot at the start of the horizon | (Assumption A‑2) |
| **\(d_{s,i}\)** | Expected passenger arrivals at station \(s\) during interval \(i\) (origin‑only demand) | (Assumption A‑3) |
| **\(\Delta_i\)** | Length (minutes) of interval \(i\) | (Assumption A‑4) |
| **\(\tau^{\text{run}}_{s,s+1}\)** | Minimum running time (minutes) between consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s+1\) (track‑speed limit) | (Assumption A‑5) |
| **\(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\)** | Upper bound on dwell time at any station (minutes) | (Assumption A‑6) |
| **\(M\)** | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | (Assumption A‑7) |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Definition | Domain |
|----------|------------|--------|

\]

2. **Build** the MILP with the data above.  
3. **Solve** (commercial MILP solver or a learning‑augmented heuristic).  
4. **Implement** the first interval’s control actions:

--- 

**End of MILP description**. This formulation can be directly coded in any algebraic modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP) and embedded inside an MPC controller for passenger‑oriented real‑time train scheduling.

Introduction

The considerable potential for reducing CO2 emissions lies in the low specific energy consumption of rail transportation in comparison to other sectors (García-Olivares et al., 2018; Dalla Chiara et al., 2017). The climate protection initiatives and increasing energy prices will encourage the railway to play a more significant role in future transport, increasing the demand for passenger and freight rail services (Chaturvedi and Kim, 2015; Islam et al., 2015; Boldizsár, 2024). Moreover, increasing infrastructure utilization and decreasing energy consumption and carbon emission is one of the most crucial research areas in railway traffic (González-Gil et al., 2014; Li and Zhang, 2020). The timetable optimization is one of the key components of increasing energy efficiency (Yang et al., 2016; Corlu et al.). However, in many cases, the optimally scheduled trains suffer primary delays due to different traffic disturbances, and the pre-planned timetable would result in conflicting trains (Nagy and Csiszár, 2015). Therefore, the trains must be rescheduled, rerouted, or reordered, assigning secondary delays to the trains to solve the real-time railway traffic management problem (rtRTMP) (Corman, 2010). Nowadays, generally, human dispatchers resolve conflicts according to several generic and regional principles, such as the first-in-first-out (FIFO) policy. However, making an optimal decision considering different objectives and traffic regulations within the required short response time is very challenging for a human dispatcher. Hence, automatic railway traffic management and control have become a popular research topic in recent years, aiming to reduce energy consumption and optimize capacity usage to satisfy the increasing demands (Pellegrini et al., 2016; Botte and D’Acierno, 2018).

Related works

Many works tackle the real-time railway traffic management problem with different optimization approaches and models (Corman and Meng, 2015; Cacchiani et al., 2014; Fang et al., 2015), tackling different uncertainties (Zhan et al., 2024). The models can be divided into microscopic and macroscopic groups according to the levels of the infrastructure representation (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2015). Microscopic models describe the topology of the rail network, including detailed information such as track length and velocity, as in Rodriguez (2007) and D’Ariano et al. (2008). Macroscopic models neglect some lower-level resources such as signals, reducing the complexity of the infrastructure model (Dollevoet et al., 2015; Kanai et al., 2011). The models can also be distinguished according to the objective function. Usually, the optimization goal is to minimize train delays, as in the proposed method. Some works also consider the energy consumption after determining the routing and ordering that minimizes the delays, as in Naldini et al. (2022, 2021), Montrone et al. (2018), or a trade-off is made between them (Rao et al., 2013; D’Ariano et al., 2010; ShangGuan et al., 2015).

The optimization models of the rtRTMP also range widely, but mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is one of the most common formulations, as in Acuna-Agost et al. (2011), Pellegrini et al. (2012, 2014), Törnquist Krasemann (2015). However, since the problem is NP-hard, in the case of large networks and complex scenarios, the runtime of the optimization can exceed the available response time, particularly in large, complex networks. Therefore, a runtime-efficient implementation is essential in a real traffic environment. Some custom heuristics and additional constraints are introduced in Boccia et al. (2013), Pellegrini et al. (2015) to decrease the computational time of the MILP. Furthermore, Pellegrini et al. (2019) proposed an efficient implementation by extending their previous work (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with new constraints, decreasing the number of equivalent combinations of integer variables. Another approach to reducing the model’s complexity is decomposing it according to smaller sub-problems. The number of routing alternatives strongly affects the time needed to find the global optimum. Therefore, it is reasonable to solve the route selection problem first, providing a smaller subset of routing alternatives for the MILP model, as in Bettinelli et al. (2017), Sama et al. (2017), Gholami and Törnquist Krasemann (2018). The train route selection problem (TRSP) was first formalized by Samà et al. (2016) with a construction graph along with an ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm to solve it. The main idea was to select the routes that minimize the pair-wise delay of trains, neglecting the delay propagation. Pascariu et al. (2022) extended the TRSP model with an estimation of delay propagation. For the case of complete blockage, Zhan et al. (2024) also propose a two-stage approach, but the problem is decomposed according to disruption phases, i.e., during and after disruption, instead of the rerouting and rescheduling sub-problems. Benders decomposition (BD) (BnnoBRs, 1962) is an alternative strategy that provides the optimal solution by iteratively solving the master and a set of sub-problems. For example, the line traffic and station control problems are Benders decomposed in Mannino (2011), Lamorgese and Mannino (2013, 2015), Lamorgese et al. (2016) that shows a good performance in large networks. Instead of spatial considerations, the rtRTMP is decomposed according to rerouting and rescheduling problems using BD in Keita et al. (2016). Moreover, a three-step decomposition, considering the rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling problems, is presented in Keita et al. (2020) similarly to the proposed method but in a Benders’ manner. Meng and Zhou (2014) also propose a MILP formulation based on cumulative flow variables, allowing solving the rerouting and rescheduling problems simultaneously. Besides the decomposition of MILP models, other methods focusing on runtime-efficient dispatching also exist. For example, Corman et al. (2010) formulate the problem as an alternative graph model, incorporating effective rescheduling algorithms and local rerouting strategies in a tabu search scheme. Meanwhile, Törnquist (Törnquist Krasemann, 2012) proposes an efficient greedy approach based on depth-first search, providing a solution within seconds.

Contributions of the paper

This paper proposes a multi-stage framework consisting of two different MILP models, minimizing the overall delays by decomposing the rtRTMP into rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling sub-problems, similar to Keita et al. (2020). However, to avoid multiple iterations, the proposed method does not rely on Benders’ algorithm. First, a low-complex, simplified approach is presented that solves the rerouting and reordering, providing a fast but sub-optimal solution for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014). It relies on reforming the standard delay variables (e.g., in Pellegrini et al. (2014, 2015, 2019)) into a pair-wise interpretation (i.e., indicating which other train they are waiting for) while disregarding delay propagation. Then, to tackle rescheduling, the original problem is solved with the fixed route selection and optional train ordering result provided by this sub-optimal model. Similar considerations are taken in Samà et al. (2016); however, we propose it in a MILP formulation that provides an exact route selection that can further decrease the complexity of the optimization. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimality condition to obtain the circumstance in which this approach results in a sub-optimal solution. As a result of the analysis, we developed a new model that guarantees the global optimum for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014) by extending the sub-optimal model to consider the delay propagation. This formulation of the rtRTMP shows a more favorable computational cost compared to the original in Pellegrini et al. (2014), especially in complex scenarios. Finally, both models provide an input route selection and optionally reordering for the extended rtRTMP in Lindenmaier et al. (2022), considering the safety-relevant overlaps, which are the margins that have to be proved clear behind a stop signal.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: the existing reference MILP models are introduced in Section 2. The proposed sub-optimal solution is detailed in Section 3.1. The optimality condition of the first approach is analyzed in Section 3.2, and the resulting global optimum model is explained in Section 3.3. The results, along with the experimental setup, are discussed in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 outlines the conclusions along with a brief outlook on future works.
