Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the description you gave – an integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem when a railway segment is partially blocked.  
The model contains

* a set of **binary routing / conflict variables**,  
* continuous **departure / arrival / passage times**,  
* continuous **speed‑level variables** (linearised via break‑points), and  
* a **linear objective** that is a weighted sum of total passenger (or operational) delay and the estimated energy consumption.

All constraints are written in a linear form, so the model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP,…).

---  

## 1️⃣ Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* |
| **D** | Set of directions (e.g. `↑` for north‑bound, `↓` for south‑bound), indexed by *d* |
| **P** | Set of admissible speed‑levels (break‑points) for any segment, indexed by *p* |
| **B** | Set of time periods that belong to the blockage window on the partially blocked segment (see §4) |
| **δ<sub>t</sub>** | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* (reference schedule) |
| **τ<sub>t,s</sub>** | Nominal travel time of train *t* through segment *s* at the **maximum** allowed speed (used for big‑M calculations) |
| **L<sub>s</sub>** | Length of segment *s* (km) |
| **v<sub>p</sub>** | Speed value associated with level *p* (km h⁻¹) |
| **a<sub>max</sub>, a<sub>min</sub>** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻²) that can be applied between two consecutive speed‑levels |
| **E<sub>p</sub>** | Energy coefficient (kWh per km) that corresponds to travelling at speed‑level *p* (obtained from a piece‑wise linear energy‑vs‑speed curve) |
| **w<sub>d</sub>, w<sub>e</sub>** | Positive weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective function |
| **M** | A big‑M constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. horizon length) |
| **Cap<sub>s,d</sub>** | Track capacity of segment *s* in direction *d* (normally = 1 train per direction, but may be >1 for multi‑track) |
| **β<sub>t,s</sub>** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at the start of segment *s* (if the train stops there) |
| **γ<sub>t,s</sub>** | Minimum passing time of train *t* through segment *s* when travelling at the *maximum* speed ( = L<sub>s</sub> / v<sub>max</sub>) |

---

## 2️⃣ Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Interpretation |
|----------|------|----------------|
| **x<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | = 1 if train *t* uses segment *s* (i.e. the planned route passes through *s*), 0 otherwise |
| **y<sub>t,s,d</sub>** | binary | = 1 if train *t* occupies segment *s* in direction *d* (needed for capacity constraints) |
| **τ<sub>t,s</sub>⁽⁰⁾** | continuous ≥0 | **Entry time** of train *t* into segment *s* (time when the head of the train reaches the upstream node) |
| **τ<sub>t,s</sub>⁽¹⁾** | continuous ≥0 | **Exit time** of train *t* from segment *s* (time when the tail of the train clears the downstream node) |
| **z<sub>t,s,p</sub>** | binary | = 1 if train *t* travels through segment *s* with speed‑level *p* (only one level may be chosen per segment) |
| **Δ<sub>t</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* measured at its final destination (or a reference event) |
| **E<sub>t</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | **Estimated energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh) |
| **c<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | = 1 if train *t* conflicts with the blocked portion of segment *s* (used to enforce the block window) |
| **b<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | = 1 if train *t* passes the blocked sub‑segment **before** the blockage window starts, 0 otherwise (used together with `c`) |

---

## 3️⃣ Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{d}\,\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{e}\,\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

The two terms can be scaled (by changing `w_d`, `w_e`) to reflect the strategic importance that the railway operator gives to punctuality vs. energy efficiency.

---

## 4️⃣ Constraints  

### 4.1 Routing – ensure the binary `x` variables respect the pre‑defined route for each train  

If a train’s route is already known (e.g., from a timetable), `x_{t,s}` can be fixed to 1/0.  
If routing is part of the decision, we need a routing network (node‑arc incidence) – omitted here for brevity; the model simply assumes that the set of feasible `(t,s)` pairs is known.

### 4.2 Speed‑level selection per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{p\in P} z_{t,s,p}=x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S
\tag{1}
\]

Only one speed‑level can be chosen *if* train *t* actually uses segment *s*.

### 4.3 Time feasibility along a route  

#### 4.3.1 Entry‑to‑exit relationship (travel time depends on chosen speed)

\[
\tau_{t,s}^{(1)}-\tau_{t,s}^{(0)} \;=\;
\sum_{p\in P}\frac{L_{s}}{v_{p}}\,z_{t,s,p}
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{2}
\]

(If a linearisation of the reciprocal speed is needed, introduce additional variables; the above is already linear because `v_p` are constants.)

#### 4.3.2 Linking successive segments (minimum dwell & travel continuity)

For every train *t* and for each ordered pair of consecutive segments *(s, s′)* on its route:

\[
\tau_{t,s'}^{(0)} \;\ge\; \tau_{t,s}^{(1)} + \beta_{t,s'} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{t,s'})
\qquad\forall t,\;(s,s')\ \text{consecutive}
\tag{3}
\]

If the train does **not** traverse segment *s′* (`x_{t,s'}=0`) the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

#### 4.3.3 Departure‑time anchoring (initial delay definition)

\[
\Delta_{t}\; \ge\; \tau_{t,s_\text{last}}^{(1)} - \bigl(\delta_{t}+ \sum_{s\in S}\beta_{t,s}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{4}
\]

`s_last` is the final segment of train *t*; the RHS is the “planned arrival time”. The constraint forces `Δ_t` to be at least the actual lateness (it may be larger if we wish to penalise early arrivals, but the model usually sets the RHS to 0 for early arrivals).

### 4.4 Blockage‑window handling (partial segment blockage)

Assume a particular segment `s* ∈ S` is partially blocked during the time interval `[T_block_start, T_block_end]`. The blocked sub‑portion can be traversed only **outside** that window.

We introduce a binary variable `c_{t,s*}` that is 1 if train *t* **conflicts** with the blockage (i.e., its passage interval overlaps the blocked interval). The classic “overlap” linearisation gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{t,s*}^{(0)} &\ge T_{\text{block\_end}} \;-\; M\,c_{t,s*}\\
\tau_{t,s*}^{(1)} &\le T_{\text{block\_start}} \;+\; M\,(1-c_{t,s*})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t \text{ with } x_{t,s*}=1
\tag{5}
\]

If `c_{t,s*}=0`, the train must finish crossing before the block starts; if `c_{t,s*}=1`, it must start after the block ends.  

Optionally, we may permit **re‑routing** around the blocked portion; in that case `c` is only forced to 1 when the train cannot avoid the segment (modelled by extra routing constraints).

### 4.5 Track‑capacity (at most one train per direction on a shared track)

For every segment *s* and direction *d*:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,d} \le \text{Cap}_{s,d}
\qquad\forall s\in S,\;d\in D
\tag{6}
\]

The linking between `y` and the time variables is achieved by a **time‑window disjunction** (classic “single‑machine scheduling” big‑M). For any ordered pair of trains *(t, t′)* that travel in the same direction on the same segment we impose:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{t,s}^{(1)} &\le \tau_{t',s}^{(0)} + M(1 - \theta_{t,t',s})\\
\tau_{t',s}^{(1)} &\le \tau_{t,s}^{(0)} + M \,\theta_{t,t',s}\\
y_{t,s,d} &= 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \theta_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall s,d,\;t\neq t'
\tag{7}
\]

`θ_{t,t',s}` decides which of the two trains goes first. When `Cap_{s,d}=1`, constraint (6) together with (7) guarantees that no two trains occupy the segment simultaneously.

### 4.6 Acceleration / Deceleration limits between consecutive speed‑levels  

If a train changes speed between two successive segments *(s, s′)*, the speed‑difference must be feasible:

\[
\sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,z_{t,s,p}
\;-\;
\sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,z_{t,s',p}
\;\le\;
a_{\max}\,\bigl(\tau_{t,s'}^{(0)}-\tau_{t,s}^{(1)}\bigr)
\tag{8}
\]

\[
\sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,z_{t,s',p}
\;-\;
\sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,z_{t,s,p}
\;\le\;
|a_{\min}|\,
\bigl(\tau_{t,s'}^{(0)}-\tau_{t,s}^{(1)}\bigr)
\tag{9}
\]

The left‑hand sides are the speed change; the right‑hand side is the maximum attainable change given the time gap (which itself is the dwell + possible waiting time). When the gap is zero, the constraints enforce that the speed cannot change, i.e., the train must keep the same speed level.

### 4.7 Energy consumption linearisation  

Energy for a train is the sum over all traversed segments of (energy coefficient × travel time at that speed). Because the coefficient is per km, we multiply by the segment length:

\[
E_{t} \;=\; \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{p\in P} E_{p}\,L_{s}\;z_{t,s,p}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{10}
\]

If a more accurate piece‑wise linear relationship between speed and power is required, we can introduce extra break‑points and use the standard “SOS‑2” or additional binaries; the expression above already stays linear.

### 4.8 Logical linking of binary variables  

*Link route usage to direction occupancy*  

\[
y_{t,s,d}\;\le\;x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,s,d
\tag{11}
\]

If a train does not travel on segment *s*, it cannot occupy it in any direction.

*Link conflict variable `c` to the route*  

\[
c_{t,s*}\;\le\;x_{t,s*}\qquad\forall t
\tag{12}
\]

If a train never reaches the blocked segment, the conflict variable is forced to 0.

---

## 5️⃣ Full MILP Summary  

**Decision variables**  

* \(x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – route‑choice (pre‑defined or decision)  
* \(y_{t,s,d}\in\{0,1\}\) – segment‑occupancy per direction  
* \(\tau_{t,s}^{(0)},\tau_{t,s}^{(1)}\ge 0\) – entry/exit times  
* \(z_{t,s,p}\in\{0,1\}\) – speed‑level on segment  
* \(\Delta_{t}\ge0\) – total delay  
* \(E_{t}\ge0\) – energy consumption  
* \(c_{t,s*},b_{t,s*}\in\{0,1\}\) – block‑window conflict helpers  
* \(\theta_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\) – ordering of trains on a segment  

**Objective**  

\[
\displaystyle \min\; w_{d}\sum_{t}\Delta_{t}\;+\;w_{e}\sum_{t}E_{t}
\]

**Subject to**  

* (1) – (12)  (the constraints listed above)  

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, so the formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.

---

## 6️⃣ How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – supply the sets `T, S, D, P`, the segment lengths `L_s`, the speed‑breakpoints `v_p`, energy coefficients `E_p`, the original schedule `δ_t`, the blockage interval `[T_block_start, T_block_end]` and the big‑M value (e.g., the planning horizon).  
2. **Modeling software** – write the formulation in a MILP‑friendly language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, OPL …).  
3. **Solve** – give the model to a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver; the solution returns the selected routes (`x`), the speed profile (`z`), the adjusted timetable (`τ`) and the derived delay/energy values.  
4. **Interpretation** –  
   * `Δ_t` tells you how much each train is late (or early).  
   * `z_{t,s,p}` shows the speed‑level that has been assigned to each segment, which can be translated into exact speed‑set‑points for the train‑control system.  
   * `y_{t,s,d}` together with the ordering variables `θ` provides a feasible **conflict‑free schedule** respecting the capacity of the blocked segment.  

Because the model is linear, you can also run **what‑if analyses** (different blockage durations, different weightings `w_d/w_e`, additional trains) quickly, or embed it in a rolling‑horizon real‑time rescheduling tool.

---  

### TL;DR  

The MILP consists of

* **Variables** – binary routing, direction occupancy, speed‑level choice; continuous entry/exit times, delay, energy.  
* **Objective** – minimise weighted sum of total delay and total energy.  
* **Constraints** – (i) one speed level per traversed segment, (ii) travel‑time consistency, (iii) precedence and dwell‑time linking, (iv) blockage‑window enforcement, (v) single‑train‑per‑direction capacity, (vi) acceleration limits, (vii) linear energy calculation, (viii) logical linking of binaries.

All pieces together give a tractable MILP that a railway operator can hand to a commercial solver to obtain an optimal rescheduling and speed‑management plan under a partial segment blockage.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the main ingredients of the problem you described:

* **Integrated train rescheduling** – we decide when each train departs from its origin, when it arrives at each intermediate station and at its final destination.  
* **Speed‑management** – for every train and every track segment we choose a discrete speed level (e.g. “slow”, “normal”, “fast”).  
* **Partial segment blockage** – a given time window blocks a part of a segment; trains may only traverse the free part or wait.  
* **Track‑capacity** – at most one train may occupy a given direction of a shared track at the same time.  
* **Energy consumption** – a linear approximation of the energy needed for each speed level.  

The model uses binary and continuous variables, a linear objective that is a weighted sum of total delay and total energy, and a set of linear constraints that enforce feasibility.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track **segments** (including blocked ones), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(N_s\) | Ordered list of **nodes** (stations or block‑end points) that belong to segment \(s\). Index inside the list by \(i\). |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g. \(k=1\) = slow, \(k=2\) = normal, \(k=3\) = fast). |
| \(D_t\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(L_{t}\) | Planned arrival time (timetable) of train \(t\) at its final destination. |
| \(\underline{v}_k, \overline{v}_k\) | Minimum / maximum speed (km/h) that corresponds to speed level \(k\). |
| \(\tau_{s,i}^{\text{len}}\) | Physical length (km) of the elementary sub‑segment that connects node \(i\) to node \(i+1\) on segment \(s\). |
| \(\beta_{s}^{\text{blk}} = [\underline{b}_{s},\overline{b}_{s}]\) | **Blockage window** on segment \(s\): no train may occupy the blocked part during \([\underline{b}_{s},\overline{b}_{s}]\). If a segment is not blocked, set \(\underline{b}_{s}= \overline{b}_{s}=0\). |
| \(e_k\) | **Energy coefficient** (kWh per km) for speed level \(k\) (higher speeds consume more energy). |
| \(\alpha^{\text{acc}}, \alpha^{\text{dec}}\) | Maximum **acceleration / deceleration** (km/h²) that can be applied when changing speed levels between consecutive elementary sub‑segments. |
| \(M\) | A sufficiently large constant (Big‑M) used for linking binary and continuous variables. |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weights chosen by the planner for the two parts of the objective (e.g. \(w^{\text{delay}} = 0.7\), \(w^{\text{energy}} = 0.3\)). |

For each train we know the *ordered* list of elementary sub‑segments it has to traverse, i.e. a path  
\[
\mathcal{P}_t = \{(s,i) \mid \text{train } t \text{ travels from node } i \text{ to } i+1 \text{ on segment } s\}.
\]

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s,i}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at node \(i+1\) of segment \(s\) (the moment it finishes the elementary sub‑segment \((s,i)\)). |
| \(a_{t,s,i}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from node \(i\) of segment \(s\) (the moment it starts the sub‑segment). Note: for interior nodes we have \(a_{t,s,i}=x_{t,s,i-1}\) unless the train is forced to wait. |
| \(y_{t,s,i,k}\) | Binary | **Speed‑level selection**: \(y_{t,s,i,k}=1\) iff train \(t\) traverses sub‑segment \((s,i)\) with speed level \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,t',s,i}\) | Binary | **Conflict variable**: \(z_{t,t',s,i}=1\) if train \(t\) occupies sub‑segment \((s,i)\) **before** train \(t'\); otherwise \(0\). Used to enforce the “at most one train per direction” rule. |
| \(\delta_t\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Delay** of train \(t\) at its final destination: \(\delta_t = x_{t,\text{dest}} - L_t\). |
| \(E\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Total energy consumption** (kWh) summed over all trains and sub‑segments. |

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} \delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}} \; E
}
\]

The first term penalises the sum of all final‑arrival delays, the second term penalises the total (linearised) energy use.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1. Path‑time continuity  

For every train and every elementary sub‑segment it travels:

1. **Departure–arrival relation** (travel time = length / speed).  
   For each \((s,i) \in \mathcal{P}_t\) and each speed level \(k\):
   \[
   x_{t,s,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,s,i} \;+\; \frac{\tau_{s,i}^{\text{len}}}{\overline{v}_k}\; y_{t,s,i,k}
   \qquad
   \forall k\in K .
   \tag{C1}
   \]
   The denominator \(\overline{v}_k\) is the **maximum** speed attainable in level \(k\); using the max yields a conservative (upper‑bound) travel time that is linear. If a tighter linearisation is required one can use a convex combination of \(\underline{v}_k,\overline{v}_k\).

2. **Exactly one speed level is chosen**:
   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,i,k} = 1 , \qquad \forall (s,i)\in\mathcal{P}_t .
   \tag{C2}
   \]

3. **Link arrival of one sub‑segment to departure of the next** (unless waiting is required):
   \[
   a_{t,s,i+1} \;\ge\; x_{t,s,i} .
   \tag{C3}
   \]

### 4.2. Origin departure and final delay  

*Departure cannot be earlier than the scheduled departure*:
\[
a_{t,\text{origin}} \;\ge\; D_t , \qquad \forall t\in T .
\tag{C4}
\]

*Definition of delay* (let \(\text{dest}\) be the last node of the train’s path):
\[
\delta_t \;\ge\; x_{t,\text{dest}} - L_t , \qquad \forall t\in T .
\tag{C5}
\]

### 4.3. Blockage‑avoidance  

If a segment \(s\) is partially blocked during \([\underline{b}_s,\overline{b}_s]\) we must ensure that the **time interval** during which a train traverses the **blocked part** does not intersect the window.  
A simple linear way is to require that the *departure* from the node **just before** the blocked part occurs either **before** the block starts **or** the *arrival* at the node **after** the blocked part occurs **after** the block ends. Introduce a binary variable \(u_{t,s,i}\) that indicates “cross before the block”.

For each \((s,i)\) that **covers the blocked portion** (i.e. the sub‑segment lies inside the blocked region) we add:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s,i}       &\le \underline{b}_s + M \, u_{t,s,i} ,\\
x_{t,s,i}       &\ge \overline{b}_s - M \, (1-u_{t,s,i}) ,\\
u_{t,s,i}       &\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{C6}
\]

If the sub‑segment is **outside** the blocked region, (C6) is omitted.

### 4.4. Track‑capacity (conflict) constraints  

Only one train may occupy the same **directional** elementary sub‑segment at a time. For every unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) (with \(t < t'\) to avoid duplication) that share the same sub‑segment \((s,i)\) we impose a **disjunctive ordering**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s,i}   &\ge x_{t,s,i}  - M \, (1 - z_{t,t',s,i}) ,\\
a_{t ,s,i}   &\ge x_{t',s,i} - M \, z_{t,t',s,i} ,\\
z_{t,t',s,i} &\in\{0,1\} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C7}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active, forcing the two occupation intervals to be non‑overlapping.

If the infrastructure is **bidirectional** but each direction has its own track, the set \(\mathcal{P}_t\) already distinguishes directions, so the same constraints are applied only to trains moving in the same direction.

### 4.5. Acceleration / deceleration limits  

When a train changes speed level between two consecutive sub‑segments, the speed jump must respect the physical acceleration limits. For each train and each pair of consecutive sub‑segments \((s,i)\) and \((s,i+1)\) (or across segment boundaries) we linearise the jump:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k\in K} \overline{v}_k \, y_{t,s,i,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} \underline{v}_k \, y_{t,s,i+1,k} &\le \alpha^{\text{dec}} \, \Delta t_{t,s,i} ,\\
\sum_{k\in K} \overline{v}_k \, y_{t,s,i+1,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} \underline{v}_k \, y_{t,s,i,k} &\le \alpha^{\text{acc}} \, \Delta t_{t,s,i} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C8}
\]

where \(\Delta t_{t,s,i}= a_{t,s,i+1} - x_{t,s,i}\) is the **idle time** (or zero if the train continues immediately). Because \(\Delta t\) appears linearly, the constraints are still MILP‑compatible.

If a simpler linear approximation is desired, we can impose a **maximum allowable speed‑level difference**:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} k \; y_{t,s,i,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} k \; y_{t,s,i+1,k} \;\le\; d_{\max},
\tag{C8‑simple}
\]

where \(d_{\max}\) is an integer (e.g., 1) that forbids jumps larger than one level.

### 4.6. Energy calculation  

Energy for a sub‑segment is approximated as *energy coefficient* \(\times\) *distance*. Linearisation yields:

\[
E \;=\; \sum_{t\in T}\; \sum_{(s,i)\in\mathcal{P}_t}\; \sum_{k\in K} \bigl( e_k \, \tau_{s,i}^{\text{len}} \bigr) \; y_{t,s,i,k}.
\tag{C9}
\]

Because all coefficients are constants, (C9) is a linear equality linking the decision variables to the total energy variable.

### 4.7. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{t,s,i}, a_{t,s,i}, \delta_t, E &\ge 0 \quad\text{(continuous)} ,\\
y_{t,s,i,k}, z_{t,t',s,i}, u_{t,s,i} &\in \{0,1\} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{C10}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP model (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,a,y,z,u,\delta,E}\;& w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}E\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(C1)–(C10)}\\
&\text{All indices belong to the sets defined above.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Explanation of the model elements  

| Element | Role in the problem | How it appears in the MILP |
|---------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| **Binary route‑choice / speed‑level variables \(y_{t,s,i,k}\)** | Determines which discrete speed the train adopts on each elementary sub‑segment. Because speed affects travel time and energy, the binary choice directly influences both parts of the objective. | Appears in (C1) for travel‑time calculation, (C2) for “exactly one speed”, (C8) for acceleration limits, and (C9) for energy. |
| **Departure / arrival times \(a_{t,s,i},x_{t,s,i}\)** | Primary schedule variables. By shifting these times we **reschedule** trains (delays, holding). | Linked by (C1)–(C5) to speed decisions and timetables; used in conflict constraints (C7) and blockage avoidance (C6). |
| **Conflict binaries \(z_{t,t',s,i}\)** | Enforce that two trains never occupy the same directional sub‑segment simultaneously → **track‑capacity**. | Appear only in (C7). |
| **Blockage‑avoidance binaries \(u_{t,s,i}\)** | Decide whether a train traverses a blocked sub‑segment **before** or **after** the blockage window. | Appear in (C6). |
| **Delay variables \(\delta_t\)** | Capture the lateness of each train at its destination (difference from the scheduled arrival). | Appear in objective (first term) and definition (C5). |
| **Energy variable \(E\)** | Summarises fuel/electric consumption; linearised via speed‑level coefficients. | Appears in objective (second term) and definition (C9). |
| **Objective weights \(w^{\text{delay}},w^{\text{energy}}\)** | Allow the planner to trade‑off punctuality vs. energy efficiency. | Directly multiply the two linear cost components. |
| **Big‑M constants \(M\)** | Linearise logical “either‑or” conditions (blocking, conflict ordering). Must be chosen large enough not to cut feasible solutions but not astronomically large (to keep numerics stable). | Appear in (C6) and (C7). |
| **Acceleration / deceleration limits (\(\alpha^{\text{acc}},\alpha^{\text{dec}}\))** | Physical feasibility of speed changes. | Enforced by (C8) (or the simpler (C8‑simple)). |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the set \(\mathcal{P}_t\) for each train, compute the sub‑segment lengths \(\tau_{s,i}^{\text{len}}\), and identify which sub‑segments intersect a partial blockage.  
2. **Parameter tuning** – Choose appropriate speed‑level bounds \((\underline{v}_k,\overline{v}_k)\) and energy coefficients \(e_k\). The weights \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) reflect the decision‑maker’s preference.  
3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, HiGHS) MILP solver. The solution will provide a feasible schedule (times) and a speed‑profile that respects blockage windows, capacity, and physical limits while minimising the weighted sum of delays and energy.  
4. **Post‑processing** – From the binary speed variables, extract the actual speed value (e.g. midpoint of the level) for reporting, compute the realised energy, and evaluate the achieved delay distribution.

---

**In summary**, the presented formulation captures **integrated train rescheduling and speed management** under a **partial segment blockage** while keeping everything linear (except for the binary decisions). It is directly implementable in standard MILP solvers and can be extended (e.g., adding crew constraints, platform capacities, or a richer set of speed levels) by adding the corresponding variables and linear constraints.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP  
(Partial‑Segment‑Blockage Scenario)**  

---

### 1️⃣ Sets, Indices & Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | set of trains, *t* ∈ T |
| **S** | set of track segments, *s* ∈ S |
| **D** = {↑,↓} | travel directions, *d* ∈ D |
| **P** | admissible speed‑levels, *p* ∈ P (break‑points of the speed‑vs‑energy curve) |
| **B** | set of discrete time periods that belong to the blockage window on the affected segment *ŝ* |
| **δₜ** | scheduled (original) departure time of train *t* |
| **τ̂ₜ** | scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination |
| **Lₛ** | length of segment *s* (km) |
| **vₚ** | speed value associated with level *p* (km·h⁻¹) – constants |
| **Eₚ** | energy coefficient (kWh · km⁻¹) for level *p* (linearised from the true power‑vs‑speed curve) |
| **a_max**, **a_min** | maximal acceleration / deceleration (km·h⁻²) allowed between two consecutive speed‑levels |
| **Capₛ,₍d₎** | capacity of segment *s* in direction *d* (normally 1, can be >1 for multi‑track) |
| **βₜ,ₛ** | minimum dwell time of train *t* at the upstream node of segment *s* (if it stops) |
| **γₛ** | minimum travelling time of a train through *s* when travelling at the maximal speed  v_max ( = Lₛ / v_max ) |
| **T_b^start**, **T_b^end** | start and end of the blockage window on the partially blocked segment *ŝ* |
| **M** | a sufficiently large constant (big‑M) larger than the planning horizon |
| **w_d**, **w_e** | positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |

---

### 2️⃣ Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Interpretation |
|----------|------|----------------|
| **xₜ,ₛ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses segment *s* (route‑choice variable – may be pre‑fixed) |

If the idle time between the two segments is zero, the inequalities force the speed to stay unchanged.

\]

\[

\]

If a train never traverses the blocked segment, the conflict variable is forced to 0.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

| **τ<sub>dw,t</sub>** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at a station (min) – *assumed known* |

### 1.1 Speed‑dependent separation distance  

For DTG signalling the minimum distance that must be kept between two consecutive trains *i* (leader) and *j* (follower) when the follower is travelling at speed *v* is the **braking distance** plus a safety margin:

\[
\text{sep}_{ij}(v) \;=\; \beta\;\frac{v^{2}}{2\,|b_{j}|}\qquad(\text{km})
\]

Because the MILP must be linear, we discretise the speed range of each train *j* into a small set **V<sub>j</sub>** (e.g. 0, 30, 60, 90 km/h). For each speed level *k∈V<sub>j</sub>* we pre‑compute  

\[
\text{SEP}_{jk}= \beta\;\frac{k^{2}}{2\,|b_{j}|}
\]

and introduce binary variables to select the speed level that is actually used on a section (see Section 2).

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Description |

| **x<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies section *s* (i.e. its front passes the entry of *s*) |
| **y<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | 1 if train *t* leaves section *s* (i.e. its rear passes the exit of *s*) |
| **p<sub>t,s</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Planned **arrival time** of the front of train *t* at the entry of section *s* (min) |

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial track blockages**  

The model decides (i) which physical route each train will take, (ii) the order in which trains use every common track segment, (iii) the speed level that each train will adopt on every traversed segment, and (iv) the exact arrival / departure times at all stations.  
The objective simultaneously minimises the total passenger‑delay and the total energy used by the fleet.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = { i | train *i* } | Set of trains (|T| = N). |
| **S** = { s | track segment *s* } | Set of elementary track segments (including the part that connects two consecutive stations). |
| **K_i** ⊆ K | Set of admissible **routes** *k* for train *i* (a route is a ordered list of segments). |
| **R_i^k** ⊆ S | The set of segments that belong to route *k* of train *i*. |
| **L** = { t | speed‑level *t* } | Discrete speed levels (e.g. *t = 1,2,3* ⇒ slow, normal, fast). |
| **Sta(i)** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i*. For every station *σ* let *s(σ)* be the preceding segment and *s′(σ)* the following segment. |
| **B_s** = \([B_{s}^{\text{start}},B_{s}^{\text{end}}]\) | Blocking interval on segment *s* (if a segment is partially blocked). If a segment is never blocked set the interval to \([-\infty ,+\infty]\). |

---

## 2️⃣  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| \(a_i^{0}\) | scheduled (planned) arrival time of train *i* at its final destination | min |
| \( \tau_{s,t}\) | deterministic travel time of **any** train on segment *s* when speed level *t* is chosen | min |
| \( \varepsilon_{s,t}\) | energy consumption incurred on segment *s* when speed level *t* is used | kWh |
| \(g\) | required safety‑gap (separation) between two successive trains on the **same** segment | min |
| \(d^{\text{min}}_{\sigma}\) | minimum dwell time that must be spent at station *σ* | min |
| \(M\) | a “big‑M’’ constant larger than any possible time (used for logical constraints) | min |
| \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\) | non‑negative weights that balance the two objectives | – |
| \(S_{ij}\subseteq S\) | set of **shared** segments on which trains *i* and *j* could meet (i.e. they appear together in at least one route of each). |

All data are assumed known a‑priori (timetables, speed‑time‑energy tables, blockage windows, etc.).

---

## 3️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|--------------|
| \(r_{i}^{k}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* uses route *k* (k ∈ K_i). |
| \(o_{ij}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on every shared segment (i.e. *i* gets the right‑of‑way). |
| \(a_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | arrival time of train *i* at the **up‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e. just before entering *s*). |
| \(d_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | departure time of train *i* from the **down‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e. just after leaving *s*). |
| \(v_{i,s,t}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* with speed level *t*. |
| \(e_i\) | continuous ≥0 | total energy used by train *i* over its whole route. |
| \(\alpha_{i,\sigma}\) | continuous ≥0 | arrival time of train *i* at station *σ* (derived from a‑variables). |
| \(\delta_{i,\sigma}\) | continuous ≥0 | departure time of train *i* from station *σ* (derived from d‑variables). |

*Note*: For a segment *s* that does **not** belong to the chosen route of train *i*, all associated variables are forced to zero.

---

## 4️⃣  Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \;\; 
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,\;{\rm final}}-a_i^{0}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T} e_i
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(a_{i,{\rm final}}\) is the arrival time at the last station of train *i* (i.e. the variable \(a_{i,s_{\text{last}}}\) of the final segment).

---

### 4.2 Route‑choice constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link route‑choice to segment‑activation**  
   If a segment *s* does **not** belong to the selected route, the train cannot occupy it.

\[
\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t} \;\le\; \sum_{k\in K_i\;:\;s\in R_i^k} r_{i}^{k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{R2}
\]

When the right‑hand side equals 0 the left‑hand side must be 0, otherwise the train must use exactly one speed level (see (S2) below).

---

### 4.3 Speed‑level selection (segment‑level)  

3. **Exactly one speed level on an active segment**  

\[
\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}= \sum_{k\in K_i\;:\;s\in R_i^k} r_{i}^{k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If the segment is on the chosen route the sum equals 1, otherwise it equals 0.

4. **Binary nature**  

\[
v_{i,s,t}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i,s,t
\tag{S2}
\]

---

### 4.4 Travel‑time on a segment  

5. **Deterministic travel time derived from selected speed**  

\[
d_{i,s}= a_{i,s}+\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}\,\tau_{s,t}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{TT}
\]

Because at most one speed level is active, the sum reduces to the travelled time of that level.

---

### 4.5 Energy accounting  

6. **Energy of a train**  

\[
e_i = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}\,\varepsilon_{s,t}
\qquad\forall i\in T
\tag{EN}
\]

---

### 4.6 Station dwell constraints  

For each station σ that belongs to train *i*’s route we introduce the station‑specific arrival/departure variables:

\[
\alpha_{i,\sigma}=a_{i,s_{\text{in}}(\sigma)}\qquad
\delta_{i,\sigma}=d_{i,s_{\text{out}}(\sigma)}
\tag{STA}
\]

7. **Minimum dwell time**  

\[
\delta_{i,\sigma}\;\ge\; \alpha_{i,\sigma}+d^{\text{min}}_{\sigma}
\qquad\forall i,\;\sigma\in {\rm Sta}(i)
\tag{DW}
\]

8. **Link between segments around a station** (continuity)

\[
a_{i,s_{\text{out}}(\sigma)} = \delta_{i,\sigma}
\qquad\forall i,\;\sigma\in {\rm Sta}(i)
\tag{CON}
\]

---

### 4.7 Safety / headway on shared segments  

Consider any ordered pair \((i,j)\) with \(i\neq j\) and a segment *s* that both could use (i.e. *s*∈\(S_{ij}\)).  

9. **Precedence (order) variables**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& a_{j,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,s}+g - M\,(1-o_{ij}) &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}\\
& a_{i,s}\;\ge\; d_{j,s}+g - M\,o_{ij}        &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\tag{ORD}
\]

When \(o_{ij}=1\) the first inequality forces train *j* to start after train *i* leaves the segment plus the safety gap; when \(o_{ij}=0\) the second inequality does the opposite. The big‑M term deactivates the non‑selected inequality.

10. **Consistency of order across *all* shared segments**  

To avoid contradictory orders on different shared segments, we force the same binary variable for the whole pair:

\[
o_{ij}=o_{ij}^{s}\qquad\forall s\in S_{ij}
\tag{ORD‑CONS}
\]

(Implementation: define one \(o_{ij}\) per pair; the constraints (ORD) are written for every shared segment, but they all reference the same \(o_{ij}\).)

---

### 4.8 Blockage (partial track closure) constraints  

For each segment *s* that is blocked during the interval \([B_s^{\text{start}},B_s^{\text{end}}]\):

11. **Train cannot occupy the segment inside the blockage window**

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,s} \;\ge\; B_s^{\text{end}} \;&-\; M\bigl(1-\beta_{i,s}\bigr)\\
d_{i,s} \;\le\; B_s^{\text{start}} \;&+\; M\beta_{i,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{BLK}
\]

where \(\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\) is an auxiliary binary that decides “pass before” (\(\beta_{i,s}=1\)) or “pass after” (\(\beta_{i,s}=0\)) the blockage.  
If a segment is never blocked set \(B_s^{\text{start}}=-M,\, B_s^{\text{end}}=M\) so the constraints are always satisfied.

---

### 4.9 Logical linking of order variables to arrival times (optional strengthening)  

A tighter linearisation of “\(o_{ij}=1\) iff \(a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+g\)” can be written:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\ge g - M(1-o_{ij})\\
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\le M\,o_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}
\tag{ORD‑LINK}
\]

These two constraints force the binary to adopt the correct value when the time difference is known.

---

### 4.10 Domain constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i}^{k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k\\
&o_{ij}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i<j\\
&\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s\\
&a_{i,s},d_{i,s},\alpha_{i,\sigma},\delta_{i,\sigma},e_i \ge 0 &&\forall\; \text{continuous variables}
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 5️⃣  Summary of the model  

| Block | What it enforces |
|-------|-------------------|
| **(R1)‑(R2)** | Each train follows exactly one admissible physical route; a route choice switches on the corresponding segments and speed‑level variables. |
| **(S1)‑(S2)** | On every *active* segment precisely one speed level is chosen (binary). |
| **(TT)** | Travel time on a segment equals the deterministic time of the selected speed level. |
| **(EN)** | Energy consumption is the sum of the energy weight of each selected speed level on each used segment. |
| **(DW)‑(CON)** | Minimum dwell time at stations and continuity of the timetable across station boundaries. |
| **(ORD)‑(ORD‑CONS)‑(ORD‑LINK)** | Safety‑gap headway on every segment shared by two trains; a single order variable per train‑pair guarantees a coherent precedence on all shared segments. |
| **(BLK)** | No train occupies a blocked segment during the blockage window; the binary \(\beta_{i,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **(OBJ)** | Weighted sum of total delay (difference between realised final arrival and scheduled arrival) and total energy consumption. |
| **(DOM)** | Variable domains. |

All constraints are linear (or can be linearised with the big‑M technique) and the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**: binary variables \(\{r_{i}^{k},o_{ij},v_{i,s,t},\beta_{i,s}\}\) together with continuous timing and energy variables.  

Standard MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) can be used to obtain optimal or near‑optimal schedules. The formulation is modular: additional practical features (platform capacities, crew‑assignment, variable train‑lengths, stochastic delays…) can be added by inserting further linear constraints or new binary variables while preserving the MILP structure.

(10) logical linking of route choice to order variables for bidirectional conflict. (11) domain constraints. Provide assumptions for parameters: scheduled arrival a_i^0, block window [B_s,B_e] per segment, speed levels t with known time and energy, safety gap, dwell minima, etc.

### 4.9 Logical linking of order variables to arrival times (optional strengthening)  

A tighter linearisation of “\(o_{ij}=1\) iff \(a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+g\)” can be written:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\ge g - M(1-o_{ij})\\
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\le M\,o_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}
\tag{ORD‑LINK}
\]

These two constraints force the binary to adopt the correct value when the time difference is known.

---

### 4.10 Domain constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i}^{k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k\\
&o_{ij}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i<j\\
&\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s\\
&a_{i,s},d_{i,s},\alpha_{i,\sigma},\delta_{i,\sigma},e_i \ge 0 &&\forall\; \text{continuous variables}
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 5️⃣  Summary of the model  

| Block | What it enforces |
|-------|-------------------|
| **(R1)‑(R2)** | Each train follows exactly one admissible physical route; a route choice switches on the corresponding segments and speed‑level variables. |
| **(S1)‑(S2)** | On every *active* segment precisely one speed level is chosen (binary). |
| **(TT)** | Travel time on a segment equals the deterministic time of the selected speed level. |
| **(EN)** | Energy consumption is the sum of the energy weight of each selected speed level on each used segment. |
| **(DW)‑(CON)** | Minimum dwell time at stations and continuity of the timetable across station boundaries. |
| **(ORD)‑(ORD‑CONS)‑(ORD‑LINK)** | Safety‑gap headway on every segment shared by two trains; a single order variable per train‑pair guarantees a coherent precedence on all shared segments. |
| **(BLK)** | No train occupies a blocked segment during the blockage window; the binary \(\beta_{i,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **(OBJ)** | Weighted sum of total delay (difference between realised final arrival and scheduled arrival) and total energy consumption. |
| **(DOM)** | Variable domains. |

All constraints are linear (or can be linearised with the big‑M technique) and the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**: binary variables \(\{r_{i}^{k},o_{ij},v_{i,s,t},\beta_{i,s}\}\) together with continuous timing and energy variables.  

Standard MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) can be used to obtain optimal or near‑optimal schedules. The formulation is modular: additional practical features (platform capacities, crew‑assignment, variable train‑lengths, stochastic delays…) can be added by inserting further linear constraints or new binary variables while preserving the MILP structure.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
