messages.content:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial track blockages**  

The model decides (i) which physical route each train will take, (ii) the order in which trains use every common track segment, (iii) the speed level that each train will adopt on every traversed segment, and (iv) the exact arrival / departure times at all stations.  
The objective simultaneously minimises the total passenger‑delay and the total energy used by the fleet.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = { i | train *i* } | Set of trains (|T| = N). |
| **S** = { s | track segment *s* } | Set of elementary track segments (including the part that connects two consecutive stations). |
| **K_i** ⊆ K | Set of admissible **routes** *k* for train *i* (a route is a ordered list of segments). |
| **R_i^k** ⊆ S | The set of segments that belong to route *k* of train *i*. |
| **L** = { t | speed‑level *t* } | Discrete speed levels (e.g. *t = 1,2,3* ⇒ slow, normal, fast). |
| **Sta(i)** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i*. For every station *σ* let *s(σ)* be the preceding segment and *s′(σ)* the following segment. |
| **B_s** = \([B_{s}^{\text{start}},B_{s}^{\text{end}}]\) | Blocking interval on segment *s* (if a segment is partially blocked). If a segment is never blocked set the interval to \([-\infty ,+\infty]\). |

---

## 2️⃣  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| \(a_i^{0}\) | scheduled (planned) arrival time of train *i* at its final destination | min |
| \( \tau_{s,t}\) | deterministic travel time of **any** train on segment *s* when speed level *t* is chosen | min |
| \( \varepsilon_{s,t}\) | energy consumption incurred on segment *s* when speed level *t* is used | kWh |
| \(g\) | required safety‑gap (separation) between two successive trains on the **same** segment | min |
| \(d^{\text{min}}_{\sigma}\) | minimum dwell time that must be spent at station *σ* | min |
| \(M\) | a “big‑M’’ constant larger than any possible time (used for logical constraints) | min |
| \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\) | non‑negative weights that balance the two objectives | – |
| \(S_{ij}\subseteq S\) | set of **shared** segments on which trains *i* and *j* could meet (i.e. they appear together in at least one route of each). |

All data are assumed known a‑priori (timetables, speed‑time‑energy tables, blockage windows, etc.).

---

## 3️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|--------------|
| \(r_{i}^{k}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* uses route *k* (k ∈ K_i). |
| \(o_{ij}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on every shared segment (i.e. *i* gets the right‑of‑way). |
| \(a_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | arrival time of train *i* at the **up‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e. just before entering *s*). |
| \(d_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | departure time of train *i* from the **down‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e. just after leaving *s*). |
| \(v_{i,s,t}\) | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* with speed level *t*. |
| \(e_i\) | continuous ≥0 | total energy used by train *i* over its whole route. |
| \(\alpha_{i,\sigma}\) | continuous ≥0 | arrival time of train *i* at station *σ* (derived from a‑variables). |
| \(\delta_{i,\sigma}\) | continuous ≥0 | departure time of train *i* from station *σ* (derived from d‑variables). |

*Note*: For a segment *s* that does **not** belong to the chosen route of train *i*, all associated variables are forced to zero.

---

## 4️⃣  Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \;\; 
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,\;{\rm final}}-a_i^{0}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T} e_i
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(a_{i,{\rm final}}\) is the arrival time at the last station of train *i* (i.e. the variable \(a_{i,s_{\text{last}}}\) of the final segment).

---

### 4.2 Route‑choice constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i}^{k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link route‑choice to segment‑activation**  
   If a segment *s* does **not** belong to the selected route, the train cannot occupy it.

\[
\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t} \;\le\; \sum_{k\in K_i\;:\;s\in R_i^k} r_{i}^{k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{R2}
\]

When the right‑hand side equals 0 the left‑hand side must be 0, otherwise the train must use exactly one speed level (see (S2) below).

---

### 4.3 Speed‑level selection (segment‑level)  

3. **Exactly one speed level on an active segment**  

\[
\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}= \sum_{k\in K_i\;:\;s\in R_i^k} r_{i}^{k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If the segment is on the chosen route the sum equals 1, otherwise it equals 0.

4. **Binary nature**  

\[
v_{i,s,t}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i,s,t
\tag{S2}
\]

---

### 4.4 Travel‑time on a segment  

5. **Deterministic travel time derived from selected speed**  

\[
d_{i,s}= a_{i,s}+\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}\,\tau_{s,t}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{TT}
\]

Because at most one speed level is active, the sum reduces to the travelled time of that level.

---

### 4.5 Energy accounting  

6. **Energy of a train**  

\[
e_i = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{t\in L} v_{i,s,t}\,\varepsilon_{s,t}
\qquad\forall i\in T
\tag{EN}
\]

---

### 4.6 Station dwell constraints  

For each station σ that belongs to train *i*’s route we introduce the station‑specific arrival/departure variables:

\[
\alpha_{i,\sigma}=a_{i,s_{\text{in}}(\sigma)}\qquad
\delta_{i,\sigma}=d_{i,s_{\text{out}}(\sigma)}
\tag{STA}
\]

7. **Minimum dwell time**  

\[
\delta_{i,\sigma}\;\ge\; \alpha_{i,\sigma}+d^{\text{min}}_{\sigma}
\qquad\forall i,\;\sigma\in {\rm Sta}(i)
\tag{DW}
\]

8. **Link between segments around a station** (continuity)

\[
a_{i,s_{\text{out}}(\sigma)} = \delta_{i,\sigma}
\qquad\forall i,\;\sigma\in {\rm Sta}(i)
\tag{CON}
\]

---

### 4.7 Safety / headway on shared segments  

Consider any ordered pair \((i,j)\) with \(i\neq j\) and a segment *s* that both could use (i.e. *s*∈\(S_{ij}\)).  

9. **Precedence (order) variables**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& a_{j,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,s}+g - M\,(1-o_{ij}) &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}\\
& a_{i,s}\;\ge\; d_{j,s}+g - M\,o_{ij}        &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\tag{ORD}
\]

When \(o_{ij}=1\) the first inequality forces train *j* to start after train *i* leaves the segment plus the safety gap; when \(o_{ij}=0\) the second inequality does the opposite. The big‑M term deactivates the non‑selected inequality.

10. **Consistency of order across *all* shared segments**  

To avoid contradictory orders on different shared segments, we force the same binary variable for the whole pair:

\[
o_{ij}=o_{ij}^{s}\qquad\forall s\in S_{ij}
\tag{ORD‑CONS}
\]

(Implementation: define one \(o_{ij}\) per pair; the constraints (ORD) are written for every shared segment, but they all reference the same \(o_{ij}\).)

---

### 4.8 Blockage (partial track closure) constraints  

For each segment *s* that is blocked during the interval \([B_s^{\text{start}},B_s^{\text{end}}]\):

11. **Train cannot occupy the segment inside the blockage window**

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,s} \;\ge\; B_s^{\text{end}} \;&-\; M\bigl(1-\beta_{i,s}\bigr)\\
d_{i,s} \;\le\; B_s^{\text{start}} \;&+\; M\beta_{i,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{BLK}
\]

where \(\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\) is an auxiliary binary that decides “pass before” (\(\beta_{i,s}=1\)) or “pass after” (\(\beta_{i,s}=0\)) the blockage.  
If a segment is never blocked set \(B_s^{\text{start}}=-M,\, B_s^{\text{end}}=M\) so the constraints are always satisfied.

---

### 4.9 Logical linking of order variables to arrival times (optional strengthening)  

A tighter linearisation of “\(o_{ij}=1\) iff \(a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+g\)” can be written:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\ge g - M(1-o_{ij})\\
a_{j,s} - d_{i,s} &\le M\,o_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{ij}
\tag{ORD‑LINK}
\]

These two constraints force the binary to adopt the correct value when the time difference is known.

---

### 4.10 Domain constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i}^{k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k\\
&o_{ij}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i<j\\
&\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s\\
&a_{i,s},d_{i,s},\alpha_{i,\sigma},\delta_{i,\sigma},e_i \ge 0 &&\forall\; \text{continuous variables}
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 5️⃣  Summary of the model  

| Block | What it enforces |
|-------|-------------------|
| **(R1)‑(R2)** | Each train follows exactly one admissible physical route; a route choice switches on the corresponding segments and speed‑level variables. |
| **(S1)‑(S2)** | On every *active* segment precisely one speed level is chosen (binary). |
| **(TT)** | Travel time on a segment equals the deterministic time of the selected speed level. |
| **(EN)** | Energy consumption is the sum of the energy weight of each selected speed level on each used segment. |
| **(DW)‑(CON)** | Minimum dwell time at stations and continuity of the timetable across station boundaries. |
| **(ORD)‑(ORD‑CONS)‑(ORD‑LINK)** | Safety‑gap headway on every segment shared by two trains; a single order variable per train‑pair guarantees a coherent precedence on all shared segments. |
| **(BLK)** | No train occupies a blocked segment during the blockage window; the binary \(\beta_{i,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **(OBJ)** | Weighted sum of total delay (difference between realised final arrival and scheduled arrival) and total energy consumption. |
| **(DOM)** | Variable domains. |

All constraints are linear (or can be linearised with the big‑M technique) and the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program**: binary variables \(\{r_{i}^{k},o_{ij},v_{i,s,t},\beta_{i,s}\}\) together with continuous timing and energy variables.  

Standard MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) can be used to obtain optimal or near‑optimal schedules. The formulation is modular: additional practical features (platform capacities, crew‑assignment, variable train‑lengths, stochastic delays…) can be added by inserting further linear constraints or new binary variables while preserving the MILP structure.

---

\[
a_{i,s_{\text{out}}(\sigma)}=\delta_{i,\sigma}
\qquad\forall i,\;\sigma\in{\rm Sta}(i)
\tag{CONT}
\]

---

#### 4.6 Safety / headway on shared segments  

For each unordered pair \((i,j)\) with \(i<j\) and each shared segment \(s\in S_{ij}\):

9. **Ordering constraints (big‑M linearisation)**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s}&\ge d_{i,s}+g - M\,(1-o_{ij}) &&\forall s\in S_{ij}\\
a_{i,s}&\ge d_{j,s}+g - M\,o_{ij} &&\forall s\in S_{ij}
\end{aligned}
\tag{ORD}
\]

When \(o_{ij}=1\) the first inequality forces train *j* to begin after train *i* has cleared the segment plus the safety gap; when \(o_{ij}=0\) the second inequality does the opposite. The same binary \(o_{ij}\) is used for **all** shared segments of the pair, guaranteeing a coherent precedence.

---

#### 4.7 Blocked segment constraints  

For every segment *s* that is blocked during \([B_{s}^{\text{start}},B_{s}^{\text{end}}]\):

10. **Pass before or after the blockage**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,s}&\ge B_{s}^{\text{end}} - M\,(1-\beta_{i,s})\\
d_{i,s}&\le B_{s}^{\text{start}} + M\,\beta_{i,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,s
\tag{BLK}
\]

If \(\beta_{i,s}=1\) the train must finish the segment **before** the blockage ends; if \(\beta_{i,s}=0\) it must start **after** the blockage starts. For a segment that is never blocked, set \(B_{s}^{\text{start}}=-M,\;B_{s}^{\text{end}}=M\) so the constraints are always satisfied.

---

#### 4.8 Domain constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i}^{k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k\\
&o_{ij}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i<j\\
&\beta_{i,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s\\
&a_{i,s},\,d_{i,s},\,\alpha_{i,\sigma},\,\delta_{i,\sigma},\,e_i \ge 0 &&\forall\text{continuous variables}
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

### 5️⃣ Summary and Remarks  

| Block | Purpose |
|-------|----------|
| **(R1)–(R2)** | Guarantees each train selects exactly one feasible physical route; inactive segments are forced to zero speed‑level variables. |
| **(S1)–(S2)** | Enforces a single speed level on every traversed segment (binary). |
| **(TT)** | Links arrival and departure times through the deterministic travel time of the chosen speed level. |
| **(EN)** | Calculates train‑wise energy consumption as the sum of segment‑level energy of the selected speed levels. |
| **(DW)–(CONT)** | Enforces minimum dwell times at stations and continuity of the timetable across station nodes. |
| **(ORD)** | Implements safety headway on every segment shared by two trains; a single binary per pair guarantees a consistent precedence on all such segments. |
| **(BLK)** | Avoids occupying a blocked segment during its blockage window; the binary \(\beta_{i,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **(OBJ)** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay (difference between realised final arrival and scheduled arrival) and total energy use. |
| **(DOM)** | Variable type definitions. |

All constraints are linear (or linearised with the big‑M technique); the model is therefore a **mixed‑integer linear program**. It can be fed directly to commercial MILP solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). Additional practical aspects (crew‑assignment, platform capacity, stochastic delay, variable train lengths, etc.) can be incorporated by introducing further linear constraints or binary variables while preserving the MILP structure.

| Symbol | Meaning |

---

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|--------|----------|------|

| \(\varepsilon_{s,t}\) | Energy consumption on segment *s* with speed level *t* | kWh |

#### Objective (weighted sum of total delay and total energy)

w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,N_i^{\text{final}}}-a_i^{0}\bigr)
\;+\;

\tag{OBJ}
\]

\]

\]

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the problem *“integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management under a partial segment blockage”*.  
All symbols that appear in the model are defined afterwards, and each group of constraints is explained so that you can see how the model captures the operational, safety and performance requirements of the railway system.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by **t** (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (including the origin and the terminal), indexed by **i**. |
| **I** | Set of railway **segments** (the track piece that connects two consecutive stations), indexed by **i** (segment *i* runs between station *i* and *i+1*). |
| **B ⊆ I** | Subset of **blocked** segments (the segment that suffers a partial blockage). |
| **O = {0,1}** | “Route‑choice” options for a train that must decide whether to use the original direction (value 0) or the opposite (detour) direction (value 1). |
| **P** | Set of ordered pairs of trains that share at least one common segment, i.e.  (t₁,t₂)∈P ⇔ ∃i : segment *i* is travelled by both t₁ and t₂. |

---

## 2.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| **x<sub>t</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 0 ⇒ train *t* follows its **original** timetable/route; 1 ⇒ it uses the **opposite** (detour) route. |
| **a<sub>t,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous (minutes) | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *i*. |
| **d<sub>t,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous (minutes) | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *i*. |
| **v<sub>t,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous (km/h) | **Average speed** of train *t* on segment *i* (between stations *i* and *i+1*). |
| **y<sub>t₁,t₂,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable on a **shared** segment *i*: 1 if train *t₁* passes the segment **before** train *t₂*; 0 otherwise. |
| **δ<sub>t,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 iff train *t* traverses **blocked** segment *i* during the blockage window (see Section 4). |
| **E** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total energy consumption** (kWh) – linearised from speed variables (see Section 5). |

*All other auxiliary variables that appear in linearisation (e.g. big‑M coefficients) are omitted from the notation table but are defined inside the constraints.*

---

## 3.  Parameters  

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|----------|
| **τ<sub>t,i</sub>** (minutes) | **Nominal travel time** of train *t* on segment *i* according to the original schedule (when v = v̂). |
| **v̂<sub>i</sub>** (km/h) | **Design speed** (maximum allowed speed) on segment *i*. |
| **v<sub>min,i</sub>**, **v<sub>max,i</sub>** (km/h) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment *i* (incl. speed‑restriction zones). |
| **L<sub>i</sub>** (km) | Length of segment *i*. |
| **θ<sub>i</sub>** (minutes) | **Dwell time** required at station *i* (minimum stay time for boarding/alighting). |
| **B<sub>i</sub> = [b<sub>i</sub> ^{start}, b<sub>i</sub> ^{end}]** (minutes) | **Blockage window** on segment *i*∈B – the time interval during which the segment is partially unavailable (e.g. because of works). |
| **M** (large number) | Big‑M constant, larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **w<sub>D</sub>**, **w<sub>E</sub>** | Positive weighting coefficients for **delay** and **energy** in the objective (chosen by the planner). |
| **ε** > 0 | Small positive constant used to enforce strict ordering (e.g. 0.01 min). |
| **α**, **β** | Linear‑energy coefficients (derived from a piece‑wise linearisation of the function *E = k·v²·L*; see Section 5). |
| **S<sub>t</sub>**, **T<sub>t</sub>** (minutes) | Planned **departure** from the first station (origin) and **arrival** at the last station (destination) for train *t* in the original timetable. |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{D}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,|S|} - T_{t}\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{w_{E}\;E}_{\text{Total energy consumption}} .
\]

*The first term penalises the **final‑arrival delay** of each train relative to its original scheduled arrival *T<sub>t</sub>*.  
The second term penalises the **overall energy** used; the linearised expression for *E* is given in Section 5.*

---

## 5.  Core Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑choice (detour) logic  

If a train decides to use the opposite direction, its travel times on every segment are swapped accordingly. For brevity we write the constraint in a generic way; the actual implementation uses data tables that map original → detour segments.

\[
\tau^{\text{eff}}_{t,i}= (1-x_t)\,\tau_{t,i}+x_t\,\tau^{\text{detour}}_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,i .
\]

*The effective nominal travel time is a linear combination of the original and the detour travel time.*

### 5.2  Temporal precedence (train must respect travel order)

\[
a_{t,i+1}= d_{t,i}+ \underbrace{\frac{L_i}{v_{t,i}}}_{\text{travel time on segment i}}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{1}
\]

Because the term \(L_i/v_{t,i}\) is non‑linear, we replace it by a linear approximation:

\[
\frac{L_i}{v_{t,i}} \; \approx\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{k}\,z_{t,i,k},
\]

where \(\lambda_{k}\) are pre‑computed travel‑time coefficients for a set of speed break‑points and \(z_{t,i,k}\) are binary variables that select the appropriate speed interval (standard piece‑wise linearisation). For clarity the model below writes (1) directly; the linearisation is understood.

### 5.3  Dwell‑time constraints  

\[
d_{t,i} \; \ge\; a_{t,i} + \theta_i \qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in S\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{terminal}\}.
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.4  Speed limits  

\[
v_{min,i}\; \le\; v_{t,i}\; \le\; v_{max,i}\qquad\forall t,i .
\tag{3}
\]

If a train is forced to travel slower because of the blockage, (4) will tighten the upper bound (see below).

### 5.5  Blockage‑avoidance on a partially closed segment  

A segment *i*∈B is unavailable during the interval \([b^{\text{start}}_i, b^{\text{end}}_i]\). We must guarantee that either the train passes **before** the start of the window, **after** the end of the window, or that the train does not use that segment at all (detour).  

First, define the *entry* time onto segment *i* for train *t*:

\[
\text{enter}_{t,i}= d_{t,i}.
\]

Define the *exit* time:

\[
\text{exit}_{t,i}= a_{t,i+1}.
\]

Introduce binary \(\delta_{t,i}\) that becomes 1 when the train **does** use the blocked segment (i.e. when x_t = 0 for that segment). Then enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{t,i} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i - M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) ,\\
\text{exit}_{t,i} &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) .
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,\, i\in B .
\tag{4}
\]

If \(\delta_{t,i}=1\) the constraints force the whole traversal to lie **outside** the blockage window. If the train chooses the opposite route, \(\delta_{t,i}=0\) and the constraints are de‑activated.

A simpler (and often tighter) formulation is the **disjunction**:

\[
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,\, i\in B .
\tag{4‑b}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}

d_{t_2,i} + \frac{L_i}{v_{t_2,i}} &\le a_{t_1,i+1} + My_{t_1,t_2,i} ,\\
y_{t_1,t_2,i} &\in \{0,1\},
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\; i\in I\;\text{shared}.
\tag{5}
\]

Again, the travel‑time terms are linearised with the same piece‑wise representation used in (1).

### 5.7  Energy‑consumption linearisation

\[
E_{t,i}=k_i\;v_{t,i}^{2}\;L_i .
\]

\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,i .
\]

\[

\tag{6}
\]

\tag{7}

\end{aligned}

\tag{4}

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

| **d<sub>t,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous (minutes) | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *i*. |
| **v<sub>t,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous (km/h) | **Average speed** of train *t* on segment *i* (between stations *i* and *i+1*). |
| **y<sub>t₁,t₂,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable on a **shared** segment *i*: 1 if train *t₁* passes the segment **before** train *t₂*; 0 otherwise. |
| **δ<sub>t,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 iff train *t* traverses **blocked** segment *i* during the blockage window (see Section 4). |
| **E** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total energy consumption** (kWh) – linearised from speed variables (see Section 5). |

*All other auxiliary variables that appear in linearisation (e.g. big‑M coefficients) are omitted from the notation table but are defined inside the constraints.*

---

## 3.  Parameters  

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|----------|
| **τ<sub>t,i</sub>** (minutes) | **Nominal travel time** of train *t* on segment *i* according to the original schedule (when v = v̂). |
| **v̂<sub>i</sub>** (km/h) | **Design speed** (maximum allowed speed) on segment *i*. |
| **v<sub>min,i</sub>**, **v<sub>max,i</sub>** (km/h) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment *i* (incl. speed‑restriction zones). |
| **L<sub>i</sub>** (km) | Length of segment *i*. |
| **θ<sub>i</sub>** (minutes) | **Dwell time** required at station *i* (minimum stay time for boarding/alighting). |
| **B<sub>i</sub> = [b<sub>i</sub> ^{start}, b<sub>i</sub> ^{end}]** (minutes) | **Blockage window** on segment *i*∈B – the time interval during which the segment is partially unavailable (e.g. because of works). |
| **M** (large number) | Big‑M constant, larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **w<sub>D</sub>**, **w<sub>E</sub>** | Positive weighting coefficients for **delay** and **energy** in the objective (chosen by the planner). |
| **ε** > 0 | Small positive constant used to enforce strict ordering (e.g. 0.01 min). |
| **α**, **β** | Linear‑energy coefficients (derived from a piece‑wise linearisation of the function *E = k·v²·L*; see Section 5). |
| **S<sub>t</sub>**, **T<sub>t</sub>** (minutes) | Planned **departure** from the first station (origin) and **arrival** at the last station (destination) for train *t* in the original timetable. |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{D}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,|S|} - T_{t}\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{w_{E}\;E}_{\text{Total energy consumption}} .
\]

*The first term penalises the **final‑arrival delay** of each train relative to its original scheduled arrival *T<sub>t</sub>*.  
The second term penalises the **overall energy** used; the linearised expression for *E* is given in Section 5.*

---

## 5.  Core Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑choice (detour) logic  

If a train decides to use the opposite direction, its travel times on every segment are swapped accordingly. For brevity we write the constraint in a generic way; the actual implementation uses data tables that map original → detour segments.

\[
\tau^{\text{eff}}_{t,i}= (1-x_t)\,\tau_{t,i}+x_t\,\tau^{\text{detour}}_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,i .
\]

*The effective nominal travel time is a linear combination of the original and the detour travel time.*

### 5.2  Temporal precedence (train must respect travel order)

\[
a_{t,i+1}= d_{t,i}+ \underbrace{\frac{L_i}{v_{t,i}}}_{\text{travel time on segment i}}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{1}
\]

Because the term \(L_i/v_{t,i}\) is non‑linear, we replace it by a linear approximation:

\[
\frac{L_i}{v_{t,i}} \; \approx\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{k}\,z_{t,i,k},
\]

where \(\lambda_{k}\) are pre‑computed travel‑time coefficients for a set of speed break‑points and \(z_{t,i,k}\) are binary variables that select the appropriate speed interval (standard piece‑wise linearisation). For clarity the model below writes (1) directly; the linearisation is understood.

### 5.3  Dwell‑time constraints  

\[
d_{t,i} \; \ge\; a_{t,i} + \theta_i \qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in S\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{terminal}\}.
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.4  Speed limits  

\[
v_{min,i}\; \le\; v_{t,i}\; \le\; v_{max,i}\qquad\forall t,i .
\tag{3}
\]

If a train is forced to travel slower because of the blockage, (4) will tighten the upper bound (see below).

### 5.5  Blockage‑avoidance on a partially closed segment  

A segment *i*∈B is unavailable during the interval \([b^{\text{start}}_i, b^{\text{end}}_i]\). We must guarantee that either the train passes **before** the start of the window, **after** the end of the window, or that the train does not use that segment at all (detour).  

First, define the *entry* time onto segment *i* for train *t*:

\[
\text{enter}_{t,i}= d_{t,i}.
\]

Define the *exit* time:

\[
\text{exit}_{t,i}= a_{t,i+1}.
\]

Introduce binary \(\delta_{t,i}\) that becomes 1 when the train **does** use the blocked segment (i.e. when x_t = 0 for that segment). Then enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{t,i} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i - M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) ,\\
\text{exit}_{t,i} &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) .
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,\, i\in B .
\tag{4}
\]

If \(\delta_{t,i}=1\) the constraints force the whole traversal to lie **outside** the blockage window. If the train chooses the opposite route, \(\delta_{t,i}=0\) and the constraints are de‑activated.

A simpler (and often tighter) formulation is the **disjunction**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{t,i} + \epsilon &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M (1-\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}),\\
\text{exit}_{t,i}            &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i  + \epsilon\,(1-\delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}),\\
\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}&+ \delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}+ \delta_{t,i}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,\, i\in B .
\tag{4‑b}
\]

### 5.6  Conflict‑ordering on shared segments (single‑track safety)  

If two trains **share** segment *i*, only one may occupy it at a time. The binary ordering variable \(y_{t1,t2,i}\) decides which train goes first.

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t_1,i} + \frac{L_i}{v_{t_1,i}} &\le a_{t_2,i+1} + M(1-y_{t_1,t_2,i}) ,\\
d_{t_2,i} + \frac{L_i}{v_{t_2,i}} &\le a_{t_1,i+1} + My_{t_1,t_2,i} ,\\
y_{t_1,t_2,i} &\in \{0,1\},
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\; i\in I\;\text{shared}.
\tag{5}
\]

Again, the travel‑time terms are linearised with the same piece‑wise representation used in (1).

### 5.7  Energy‑consumption linearisation  

Energy consumption on a segment can be approximated by a convex quadratic function of speed, e.g.  

\[
E_{t,i}=k_i\;v_{t,i}^{2}\;L_i .
\]

We replace it by a **piece‑wise linear** approximation with break‑points \(\{v_{i}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\). Introduce binaries \(z_{t,i,k}\) that select the interval and continuous variables \(e_{t,i,k}\) for the contribution:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,i} &= \sum_{k=1}^{K} v_{i}^{(k)} \, z_{t,i,k},\\
\sum_{k=1}^{K} z_{t,i,k}&=1 ,\qquad z_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
e_{t,i} &= \sum_{k=1}^{K} \bigl(\alpha_{i}^{(k)}\,v_{i}^{(k)} + \beta_{i}^{(k)}\bigr)\, z_{t,i,k},
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,i .
\]

Then total energy is

\[
E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} e_{t,i}.
\tag{6}
\]

The coefficients \(\alpha_{i}^{(k)},\beta_{i}^{(k)}\) are obtained from a linear fit of the quadratic curve on each interval.

### 5.8  Final‑arrival delay definition  

\[
\text{delay}_{t}= a_{t,|S|} - T_{t}\;\; \ge\;0 \qquad\forall t\in T .
\tag{7}
\]

The term \(\sum_{t}\text{delay}_{t}\) appears in the objective.

---

## 6.  Summary of the Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & w_{D}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,|S|} - T_{t}\bigr) \;+\; w_{E}\,E \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)   temporal precedence (travel‑time link)}\\
&\text{(2)   dwell‑time constraints}\\
&\text{(3)   speed limits}\\
&\text{(4)   blockage‑avoidance (or its disjunctive version)}\\
&\text{(5)   conflict ordering on shared segments}\\
&\text{(6)   linearised energy expression}\\
&\text{(7)   delay definition} \\
&\text{(8)   route‑choice linking } x_t\text{ with } \tau^{\text{eff}}_{t,i} \\
&\text{(9)   binary/continuous domain definitions for }x_t,\;y_{t_1,t_2,i},\;z_{t,i,k},\;\delta_{t,i}.\\
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** (or linearised), the only non‑continuous variables are binary, so the model is a **MILP** that can be solved with any off‑the‑shelf branch‑and‑bound/MIP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.).

---

### How the model reflects the problem description  

| Requirement | Modeling element |
|--------------|------------------|
| **Two possible routes (original / opposite)** | Binary variable **xₜ**; effective travel‑time (8). |
| **Train‑specific arrival / departure times** | Continuous variables **aₜ,i**, **dₜ,i**; precedence (1) and dwell (2). |
| **Speed decision on each segment** | Continuous **vₜ,i** with limits (3). |
| **Partial blockage** | Set **B**, window **[b_start , b_end]**, binary **δₜ,i**, constraints (4) forcing traversal outside the window. |
| **Single‑track conflict avoidance** | Ordering binaries **yₜ₁,ₜ₂,i**, constraints (5). |
| **Energy consumption** | Piece‑wise linearisation of \(k v^2 L\) → variables **z**, **e**, constraint (6). |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of total delay (first term) and total energy (second term). |
| **Linear‑MIP formulation** | All terms are linear; non‑linear relationships are replaced by standard big‑M or piece‑wise linear tricks. |

---

Feel free to adjust the weighting coefficients, the big‑M size, the number of speed break‑points (K), or add additional operational constraints (e.g., headway limits, crew‑change windows) – the structure above remains a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming model** ready for implementation.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) under a Partial Segment Blockage**

---

### 1. Sets and Indices
| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N) |
| **S** | Set of stations (including origin and terminal), indexed by *i* |
| **I** | Set of railway **segments** (piece of track between two consecutive stations), indexed by *i*  (segment *i* connects station *i* and *i+1*) |
| **B ⊆ I** | Subset of **blocked** segments (partial blockage) |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment:  (t₁,t₂)∈P ⇔ ∃i : segment *i* is traversed by both trains |

---

### 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| **xₜ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 0 → train *t* follows its original route; 1 → it uses the opposite (detour) route |
| **aₜ,i** ≥ 0 | continuous (minutes) | Arrival time of train *t* at station *i* |
| **dₜ,i** ≥ 0 | continuous (minutes) | Departure time of train *t* from station *i* |
| **vₜ,i** ≥ 0 | continuous (km/h) | Average speed of train *t* on segment *i* (between stations *i* and *i+1*) |
| **yₜ₁,ₜ₂,i** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t₁* passes segment *i* **before** train *t₂*; 0 otherwise (conflict ordering) |
| **δₜ,i** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 iff train *t* traverses blocked segment *i* during the blockage window |
| **zₜ,i,k** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Speed‑interval selector for piece‑wise linearisation of speed‑energy relation (k = 1…K) |
| **eₜ,i** ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *i* (linearised) |
| **E** ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption of the system |
| **delayₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Final‑arrival delay of train *t* (relative to original schedule) |

---

### 3. Parameters  

| Parameter | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| **τₜ,i** (min) | Nominal travel time of train *t* on segment *i* in the original timetable |
| **τₜ,i^det** (min) | Nominal travel time of train *t* on segment *i* if it uses the opposite (detour) route |
| **Lᵢ** (km) | Length of segment *i* |
| **v̂ᵢ** (km/h) | Design (maximum allowed) speed on segment *i* |
| **v_minᵢ**, **v_maxᵢ** (km/h) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment *i* |
| **θᵢ** (min) | Minimum dwell time required at station *i* |
| **Bᵢ = [b_startᵢ , b_endᵢ]** (min) | Blockage time window on segment *i*∈B |
| **M** | Large constant (≥ planning horizon, e.g., 10 000 min) |
| **ε** (min) | Small positive number to enforce strict ordering (e.g., 0.01) |
| **w_D**, **w_E** > 0 | Weights for total delay and total energy in the objective |
| **vᵢ^{(k)}**, **αᵢ^{(k)}**, **βᵢ^{(k)}** | Speed break‑points and linear energy coefficients for piece‑wise linearisation |
| **Tₜ** (min) | Original scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final station |
| **K** | Number of speed break‑points used in the linearisation (typically 3–5) |

---

### 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \;\; w_D\;\sum_{t\in T}\! delay_t \;+\; w_E\;E
\]

*The first term penalises total passenger delay; the second term penalises total energy consumption.*

---

### 5. Model Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route‑choice (detour) effect  
Effective nominal travel time on each segment:

\[
\tau^{\text{eff}}_{t,i}= (1-x_t)\,\tau_{t,i}+x_t\,\tau^{\text{det}}_{t,i}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2  Temporal precedence (arrival–departure relationship)  

Because \(\dfrac{L_i}{v_{t,i}}\) is nonlinear, a piece‑wise linearisation is used. Let the set of speed break‑points be \(\{v_i^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\) and introduce binaries \(z_{t,i,k}\). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,i} &=\sum_{k=1}^{K} v_i^{(k)}\,z_{t,i,k}\,,\\
\sum_{k=1}^{K} z_{t,i,k}&=1,\qquad z_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
\frac{L_i}{v_{t,i}} &\;\approx\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{i}^{(k)}\,z_{t,i,k},
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\lambda_{i}^{(k)}=\dfrac{L_i}{v_i^{(k)}}\) are pre‑computed travel‑time coefficients.  
Using this linearisation, the precedence constraint reads

\[
a_{t,i+1}= d_{t,i}+ \sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{i}^{(k)} z_{t,i,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{R2}
\]

#### 5.3  Dwell‑time constraints  

\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \theta_i\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in S\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{terminal}\}.
\tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4  Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min,i}\le v_{t,i}\le v_{\max,i}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{R4}
\]

#### 5.5  Blockage‑avoidance on a partially closed segment  

For every train *t* and blocked segment *i*∈B, the traversal must lie completely **outside** the blockage window. Using binary \(\delta_{t,i}\) (1 if the train actually uses the segment) we enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i - M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) ,\\
a_{t,i+1} &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) .
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in B .
\tag{R5}
\]

If the train takes the opposite route, \(\delta_{t,i}=0\) and the constraints are de‑activated.

A tighter (disjunctive) formulation may be used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i}+ \epsilon &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M (1-\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}),\\
a_{t,i+1} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i  - M (1-\delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}),\\
\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}+ \delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}+ \delta_{t,i}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,\; i\in B .
\tag{R5‑b}
\]

#### 5.6  Conflict ordering on shared segments (single‑track safety)  

For every pair (t₁,t₂)∈P that share segment *i*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t_1,i}+ \sum_{k}\lambda_{i}^{(k)}z_{t_1,i,k}&\le a_{t_2,i+1}+ M\,(1-y_{t_1,t_2,i}),\\
d_{t_2,i}+ \sum_{k}\lambda_{i}^{(k)}z_{t_2,i,k}&\le a_{t_1,i+1}+ M\,y_{t_1,t_2,i},\\
y_{t_1,t_2,i}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\; i\in I.
\tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7  Energy‑consumption linearisation  

Energy on a segment can be approximated by a convex quadratic, \(E_{t,i}=k_i\,v_{t,i}^{2}\,L_i\). Using the same speed break‑points we linearise:

\[
e_{t,i}= \sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\alpha_i^{(k)}\,v_i^{(k)}+\beta_i^{(k)}\bigr)\,z_{t,i,k}\qquad\forall t,i .
\tag{R7}
\]

Total energy:

\[
E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} e_{t,i}.
\tag{R8}
\]

#### 5.8  Delay definition  

\[
delay_t = a_{t,|S|} - T_t \;\; \ge 0 \qquad\forall t\in T .
\tag{R9}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_D\sum_{t\in T} delay_t \;+\; w_E\,E \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1) – (R9) } \\[2pt]
& x_t\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t\in T ,\\
& y_{t_1,t_2,i}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\, i\in I ,\\
& \delta_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t\in T,\, i\in B ,\\
& z_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t,i,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (or transformed into linear form by standard big‑M or piece‑wise linear techniques). Consequently, the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program** ready for solution with commercial MIP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …).

---

### 7. Remarks & Modelling Choices  

* **Route choice** – binary \(x_t\) captures the decision to stay on the original track or to detour to the opposite track when the blockage occurs.  
* **Blockage handling** – constraints (R5) guarantee that any train that still uses the blocked segment finishes its traversal completely before the blockage starts or completely after it ends.  
* **Bidirectional conflict** – ordering variables \(y_{t_1,t_2,i}\) ensure that two opposite‑direction trains never occupy the same physical track segment at the same time.  
* **Speed‑energy coupling** – the piece‑wise linearisation (variables \(z_{t,i,k}\)) couples the speed decision with the energy objective while keeping the formulation linear.  
* **Delay** – the model minimises the sum of final‑arrival delays, a standard service‑quality metric in railway timetabling.  

The formulation can be extended (e.g., inclusion of crew‑change windows, rolling‑stock constraints, or stochastic disruption scenarios) by adding further sets, variables and linear constraints, while preserving the MILP structure.

\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\lambda_{i}^{(k)}=\dfrac{L_i}{v_i^{(k)}}\) are pre‑computed travel‑time coefficients.  
Using this linearisation, the precedence constraint reads

\[
a_{t,i+1}= d_{t,i}+ \sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{i}^{(k)} z_{t,i,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{R2}
\]

#### 5.3  Dwell‑time constraints  

\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \theta_i\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in S\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{terminal}\}.
\tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4  Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min,i}\le v_{t,i}\le v_{\max,i}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I .
\tag{R4}
\]

#### 5.5  Blockage‑avoidance on a partially closed segment  

For every train *t* and blocked segment *i*∈B, the traversal must lie completely **outside** the blockage window. Using binary \(\delta_{t,i}\) (1 if the train actually uses the segment) we enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i - M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) ,\\
a_{t,i+1} &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M\,(1-\delta_{t,i}) .
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in B .
\tag{R5}
\]

If the train takes the opposite route, \(\delta_{t,i}=0\) and the constraints are de‑activated.

A tighter (disjunctive) formulation may be used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i}+ \epsilon &\le b^{\text{start}}_i + M (1-\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}),\\
a_{t,i+1} &\ge b^{\text{end}}_i  - M (1-\delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}),\\
\delta^{\text{before}}_{t,i}+ \delta^{\text{after}}_{t,i}+ \delta_{t,i}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,\; i\in B .
\tag{R5‑b}
\]

#### 5.6  Conflict ordering on shared segments (single‑track safety)  

For every pair (t₁,t₂)∈P that share segment *i*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t_1,i}+ \sum_{k}\lambda_{i}^{(k)}z_{t_1,i,k}&\le a_{t_2,i+1}+ M\,(1-y_{t_1,t_2,i}),\\
d_{t_2,i}+ \sum_{k}\lambda_{i}^{(k)}z_{t_2,i,k}&\le a_{t_1,i+1}+ M\,y_{t_1,t_2,i},\\
y_{t_1,t_2,i}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\; i\in I.
\tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7  Energy‑consumption linearisation  

Energy on a segment can be approximated by a convex quadratic, \(E_{t,i}=k_i\,v_{t,i}^{2}\,L_i\). Using the same speed break‑points we linearise:

\[
e_{t,i}= \sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\alpha_i^{(k)}\,v_i^{(k)}+\beta_i^{(k)}\bigr)\,z_{t,i,k}\qquad\forall t,i .
\tag{R7}
\]

Total energy:

\[
E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I} e_{t,i}.
\tag{R8}
\]

#### 5.8  Delay definition  

\[
delay_t = a_{t,|S|} - T_t \;\; \ge 0 \qquad\forall t\in T .
\tag{R9}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_D\sum_{t\in T} delay_t \;+\; w_E\,E \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1) – (R9) } \\[2pt]
& x_t\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t\in T ,\\
& y_{t_1,t_2,i}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P,\, i\in I ,\\
& \delta_{t,i}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t\in T,\, i\in B ,\\
& z_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\}\quad\forall t,i,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (or transformed into linear form by standard big‑M or piece‑wise linear techniques). Consequently, the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program** ready for solution with commercial MIP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …).

---

### 7. Remarks & Modelling Choices  

* **Route choice** – binary \(x_t\) captures the decision to stay on the original track or to detour to the opposite track when the blockage occurs.  
* **Blockage handling** – constraints (R5) guarantee that any train that still uses the blocked segment finishes its traversal completely before the blockage starts or completely after it ends.  
* **Bidirectional conflict** – ordering variables \(y_{t_1,t_2,i}\) ensure that two opposite‑direction trains never occupy the same physical track segment at the same time.  
* **Speed‑energy coupling** – the piece‑wise linearisation (variables \(z_{t,i,k}\)) couples the speed decision with the energy objective while keeping the formulation linear.  
* **Delay** – the model minimises the sum of final‑arrival delays, a standard service‑quality metric in railway timetabling.  

The formulation can be extended (e.g., inclusion of crew‑change windows, rolling‑stock constraints, or stochastic disruption scenarios) by adding further sets, variables and linear constraints, while preserving the MILP structure.
