Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

| **K_i** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including the origin and the final destination). Index of a station on the route of *i* is *k* (k = 0,…,|K_i|). |
| **S** | Set of railway **segments** (the physical track between two consecutive stations). |
| **S_i ⊂ S** | Set of segments traversed by train *i* (|S_i| = |K_i|‑1). |
| **B ⊂ S** | Sub‑set of **blocked segments** (only one side can be unavailable). |
| **Side(s) = {L,R}** | Two parallel “sides’’ (or tracks) of a segment *s* – left (L) and right (R). |
| **c₁ , c₂** | Positive energy‑cost coefficients (fuel/ electricity model). |
| **vᵐⁱⁿ , vᵐᵃˣ** | Global lower / upper speed limits (km h⁻¹). |
| **aᵐⁱⁿ , aᵐᵃˣ** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻¹ min⁻¹). |
| **τᵈʷₑˡˡ₍i,k₎ , τᵈʷᵉₑₗ₍i,k₎** | Minimum / maximum dwell time that train *i* must spend at station *k*. |
| **schedᵢ** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “on‑time’’ reference). |
| **T_start(s), T_end(s)** | Start and end of the disruption (blocking) on segment *s*. During this interval one side (the blocked side) cannot be used. |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to dominate any feasible time difference (e.g. M = 10⁴ min). |
| **Δt** | Small positive constant used to enforce strict ordering (Δt = 0.1 min). |

All distances of segments are known (denoted *ℓₛ*).  

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **rᵢₛᴸ , rᵢₛᴿ** | binary | 1 if train *i* traverses side **L** (resp. **R**) of blocked segment *s* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. (For non‑blocked segments the side is irrelevant – we set rᵢₛᴸ = rᵢₛᴿ = 1 automatically.) |
| **oᵢⱼₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on the *same side* of segment *s* (i.e. i exits before j enters). Defined only for pairs (i,j) that share a side of a segment. |
| **aᵢₖ** | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k* (k ∈ K_i). |
| **dᵢₖ** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **tᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | **Travel time** of train *i* on segment *s* (the time spent between the departure from the upstream station and arrival at the downstream station). |
| **vᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | **Average speed** of train *i* on segment *s* (km h⁻¹). |
| **δᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable used to linearise the product *vᵢₛ·tᵢₛ* (distance = speed × time). |
| **zᵢₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* actually **uses** segment *s* (i.e. s ∈ S_i); 0 otherwise (helps to write capacity constraints compactly). |

---

## 3. Linearised relationships  

### 3.1 Distance consistency  

For every train *i* and every traversed segment *s* ∈ S_i  

\[
\ell_s = v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ell_s \le \delta_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}),\;
\ell_s \ge \delta_{i,s} - M(1-z_{i,s}),
\]
\[
\delta_{i,s} \le v_{i,s}^{\max}\,t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s}),\;
\delta_{i,s} \ge v_{i,s}^{\min}\,t_{i,s}-M(1-z_{i,s}).
\]

Because *zᵢₛ = 1* for all real traversals, the constraints reduce to  

\[
\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s},\qquad \ell_s = \delta_{i,s}.
\]

Thus the product is linearised by the auxiliary variable **δ**.

### 3.2 Speed limits  

\[
v_{i,s}^{\min}\;z_{i,s}\;\le\; v_{i,s}\;\le\; v_{i,s}^{\max}\;z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s.
\]

If a train does not use a segment (zᵢₛ = 0) the speed is forced to 0.

### 3.3 Acceleration / deceleration between consecutive segments  

Let *s* and *s′* be two consecutive segments on train *i* (i.e. the downstream segment of *s* is the upstream segment of *s′*).  

\[
v_{i,s′} - v_{i,s} \le a^{\max}\,t_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}) + M(1-z_{i,s′}),
\]
\[
v_{i,s} - v_{i,s′} \le a^{\min}\,t_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}) + M(1-z_{i,s′}).
\]

These linear inequalities enforce that the change of speed over the travel time of the first segment does not exceed the admissible acceleration/deceleration.

### 3.4 Dwell‑time (station‑stop) constraints  

For every train *i* and every intermediate station *k* (k = 1,…,|K_i|‑1)  

\[
d_{i,k} - a_{i,k} \ge \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\text{min},i,k},
\qquad
d_{i,k} - a_{i,k} \le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\text{max},i,k}.
\]

At the origin (k = 0) we set \(d_{i,0}=a_{i,0}\) (departure equals scheduled start time, which can be fixed or left free).  
At the final station we only need the arrival variable \(a_{i,\text{last}}\).

### 3.5 Time‑feasibility (linking stations and segments)  

For each train *i* and each segment *s* that connects station *k* to station *k+1*  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\in K_i\setminus\{ \text{last}\}.
\]

Because \(t_{i,s}= \ell_s / v_{i,s}\) (linearised via δ), the above is linear.

### 3.6 Route‑choice on blocked segments  

For every blocked segment *s* ∈ B and every train *i* that traverses it  

\[
r_{i,s}^{L}+ r_{i,s}^{R}= 1\qquad\text{(exactly one side is selected)}.
\]

If a segment is **not** blocked, we simply set \(r_{i,s}^{L}=r_{i,s}^{R}=1\) (or eliminate the variables).

### 3.7 Disruption‑window feasibility  

Assume side *b(s)* ∈ {L,R} is the **blocked side** of segment *s* during \([T_{\text{start}}(s),T_{\text{end}}(s)]\).  
If a train would traverse that side and its traversal interval overlaps the window, the solution is infeasible. This is enforced by a big‑M implication:

\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge T_{\text{end}}(s) \;+\; \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} + t_{i,s} \le T_{\text{start}}(s) \;-\; \Delta t \;+\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]

where \(\overline{b(s)}\) denotes the **unblocked** side (the opposite of the blocked one).  
If the train chooses the unblocked side (\(r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}=1\)) the constraints force the traversal interval to lie completely **outside** the disruption window; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraints, allowing any timing.

A more compact formulation (using a binary “overlap’’ variable) is also possible, but the two‑inequality version above is linear and sufficient.

### 3.8 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on a shared side  

Consider any pair of distinct trains *(i,j)* that both use the **same side** *s* (i.e. \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}=r_{j,s}^{\sigma}=1\) for some σ∈{L,R}).  
Define binary order variable \(o_{i j s}\) = 1 if *i* leaves the segment before *j* enters; otherwise 0.  

\[
a_{j,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{j,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]

where  

* \(\text{up}(s)\) = upstream station of segment *s* (departure side),  
* \(\text{down}(s)\) = downstream station of segment *s* (arrival side).  

These two constraints together enforce that **exactly one** of the two possible orderings holds:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}.
\]

### 3.9 Transitivity of the order variables (consistency)  

For any three trains *i, j, k* that share the same side *s*:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\qquad
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0.
\]

These linear inequalities guarantee that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k*.

### 3.10 Capacity (at most one train on a side at any instant)  

A more direct way to guarantee capacity is to use the precedence variables defined above together with the **pairwise** constraints (3.8). Because every pair of trains that share a side must be ordered, the capacity condition is automatically satisfied (no two trains can occupy the same side simultaneously). If a weaker “no‑overlap’’ formulation is preferred, one can introduce a time‑grid and enforce that the sum of binary occupancy variables ≤ 1, but the pairwise precedence formulation is sufficient and linear.

---

## 4. Objective function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.

### 4.1 Delay term  

\[
\text{Delay}_i = a_{i,\text{last}} - \text{sched}_i \qquad (\ge 0).
\]

Total delay  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Delay} = \sum_{i\in I} \bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr).
\]

### 4.2 Energy‑consumption term  

For each traversed segment *s* the (average) energy cost is modelled as  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(c_1\,v_{i,s}^{2}+c_2/v_{i,s}\bigr)\;t_{i,s}.
\]

The product \(v_{i,s}^{2}\,t_{i,s}\) and \(t_{i,s}/v_{i,s}\) are linearised with additional auxiliary variables (standard McCormick envelopes). For brevity we write the linearised version as **Êᵢₛ**; the constraints are omitted here because they follow the same pattern as in §3.1 (introducing variables \(y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) and \(w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s}\) with convex envelopes).  

Total energy  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Energy}= \sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{s\in S_i}\; \widehat{E}_{i,s}.
\]

### 4.3 Combined objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy}}
}
\]

where **α** and **β** are user‑defined non‑negative weights that reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 5. Full MILP (compact statement)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(1)  Route choice on blocked segments: } 
      r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1 &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(2)  Travel‑time / distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)}\\
&\ell_s = \delta_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i\\
&\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s} &&\text{linearised with McCormick envelopes}\\[2pt]
&\text{(3)  Speed limits} && v^{\min}z_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max}z_{i,s} \\[2pt]
&\text{(4)  Acceleration / deceleration} \\ 
&v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s}\le a^{\max}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\
&v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'}\le a^{\min}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\[2pt]
&\text{(5)  Dwell‑time bounds} \\
&\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}
   &&\forall i,\;k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1 \\[2pt]
&\text{(6)  Time feasibility (stations ↔ segments)}\\
&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\text{ upstream of }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(7)  Disruption‑window feasibility} \\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s}\le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t+M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)
   &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(8)  Pairwise precedence on a shared side} \\
&a_{j,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(1-o_{i j s})\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(o_{i j s})\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}\\[2pt]
&\text{(9)  Transitivity of order variables} \\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(10)  Binary / non‑negative domains}\\
&r_{i,s}^{L},r_{i,s}^{R},o_{i j s}\in\{0,1\},\;
z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},\delta_{i,s}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (products of continuous variables) have been replaced by standard McCormick linearisation (δ, y, w variables). The model is therefore a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

---

## 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

1. **Fixed route topology** – each train’s sequence of stations/segments is known a‑priori; only the side on a blocked segment is a decision.  
2. **Single‑track per side** – each side of a segment can host at most one train at any instant; this is enforced by the pairwise precedence variables.  
3. **Big‑M values** – choose *M* larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). The small constant Δt (≈0.1 min) guarantees strict separation of two successive trains.  
4. **Energy linearisation** – the term \(c_1 v^2 t + c_2 t/v\) is convex for \(v>0\); McCormick envelopes on the bilinear terms \(v^2 t\) and \(t/v\) give a tight linear approximation. If a tighter piece‑wise linear approximation is required, introduce additional break‑points.  
5. **Disruption handling** – the model forces any train that selects the **unblocked** side to finish its traversal **outside** the blocked time window. Trains that would have to use the blocked side simply set the corresponding binary \(r_{i,s}^{\text{blocked}}=0\) and are forced to use the other side.  
6. **Scalability** – the number of binary variables grows with \(|I|^2\) for the order variables on each shared side. In practice one can limit the set of pairs to those whose earliest possible arrivals overlap (pre‑filtering) to keep the model tractable.  

---

### 7. How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – compute for every train the list of stations, segment lengths, scheduled arrival times, and identify which segments are blocked and which side is unavailable.  
2. **Parameter selection** – choose α, β, the energy coefficients (c₁,c₂), speed limits, acceleration limits, dwell‑time windows, and a suitable big‑M.  
3. **Implementation** – encode the MILP in any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, SCIP, HiGHS) solver.  
4. **Solution** – the optimal solution provides:  
   * the side choice \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}\) for each blocked segment,  
   * the exact departure/arrival schedule \((a_{i,k},d_{i,k})\),  
   * the speed profile \((v_{i,s})\) and travel times \((t_{i,s})\),  
   * the precedence order on each side (conflict‑free timetable).  

The objective value directly quantifies the trade‑off between **punctuality** (total delay) and **energy efficiency** (total consumption) under the given partial blockage.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Formulate a MILP for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice r_{i,s} (train i uses side s of segment), binary order o_{i,j} (train i precedes j on shared track), continuous arrival a_{i,k}, departure d_{i,k} at station k, travel time t_{i,s} on segment s, speed v_{i,s}. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (a_{i,last}- scheduled_i) and energy consumption Σ_i Σ_s (c1*v_{i,s}^2 + c2/v_{i,s}) * t_{i,s}. Constraints: (1) each train chooses one side per blocked segment; (2) precedence constraints using big-M with o_{i,j}; (3) time feasibility a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,segment}; (4) speed limits v_min ≤ v_{i,s} ≤ v_max; (5) acceleration/deceleration limits linking speeds across consecutive segments; (6) dwell time bounds; (7) disruption window: if segment blocked on side s during [T_start,T_end], then r_{i,s}=0 for trains whose traversal time overlaps; (8) binary order consistency transitivity; (9) capacity: at most one train on a track side at a time using time‑overlap constraints. Provide full linearized formulation with big-M constants and note assumptions where needed.

response.content:

All symbols that appear in the model are defined in the tables that follow the formulation.

\[
\ell_s = v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad

\]

v_{i,s} - v_{i,s′} \le a^{\min}\,t_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}) + M(1-z_{i,s′}).

\]

\[
r_{i,s}^{L}+ r_{i,s}^{R}= 1\qquad\text{(exactly one side is selected)}.
\]

\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge T_{\text{end}}(s) \;+\; \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} + t_{i,s} \le T_{\text{start}}(s) \;-\; \Delta t \;+\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]

where \(\overline{b(s)}\) denotes the **unblocked** side (the opposite of the blocked one).  
If the train chooses the unblocked side (\(r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}=1\)) the constraints force the traversal interval to lie completely **outside** the disruption window; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraints, allowing any timing.

A more compact formulation (using a binary “overlap’’ variable) is also possible, but the two‑inequality version above is linear and sufficient.

### 3.8 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on a shared side  

Consider any pair of distinct trains *(i,j)* that both use the **same side** *s* (i.e. \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}=r_{j,s}^{\sigma}=1\) for some σ∈{L,R}).  
Define binary order variable \(o_{i j s}\) = 1 if *i* leaves the segment before *j* enters; otherwise 0.  

\[
a_{j,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{j,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]

where  

* \(\text{up}(s)\) = upstream station of segment *s* (departure side),  
* \(\text{down}(s)\) = downstream station of segment *s* (arrival side).  

These two constraints together enforce that **exactly one** of the two possible orderings holds:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}.
\]

### 3.9 Transitivity of the order variables (consistency)  

For any three trains *i, j, k* that share the same side *s*:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\qquad
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0.
\]

These linear inequalities guarantee that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k*.

### 3.10 Capacity (at most one train on a side at any instant)  

A more direct way to guarantee capacity is to use the precedence variables defined above together with the **pairwise** constraints (3.8). Because every pair of trains that share a side must be ordered, the capacity condition is automatically satisfied (no two trains can occupy the same side simultaneously). If a weaker “no‑overlap’’ formulation is preferred, one can introduce a time‑grid and enforce that the sum of binary occupancy variables ≤ 1, but the pairwise precedence formulation is sufficient and linear.

---

## 4. Objective function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.

### 4.1 Delay term  

\[
\text{Delay}_i = a_{i,\text{last}} - \text{sched}_i \qquad (\ge 0).
\]

Total delay  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Delay} = \sum_{i\in I} \bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr).
\]

### 4.2 Energy‑consumption term  

For each traversed segment *s* the (average) energy cost is modelled as  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(c_1\,v_{i,s}^{2}+c_2/v_{i,s}\bigr)\;t_{i,s}.
\]

The product \(v_{i,s}^{2}\,t_{i,s}\) and \(t_{i,s}/v_{i,s}\) are linearised with additional auxiliary variables (standard McCormick envelopes). For brevity we write the linearised version as **Êᵢₛ**; the constraints are omitted here because they follow the same pattern as in §3.1 (introducing variables \(y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) and \(w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s}\) with convex envelopes).  

Total energy  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Energy}= \sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{s\in S_i}\; \widehat{E}_{i,s}.
\]

### 4.3 Combined objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy}}
}
\]

where **α** and **β** are user‑defined non‑negative weights that reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 5. Full MILP (compact statement)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(1)  Route choice on blocked segments: } 
      r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1 &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(2)  Travel‑time / distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)}\\
&\ell_s = \delta_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i\\
&\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s} &&\text{linearised with McCormick envelopes}\\[2pt]
&\text{(3)  Speed limits} && v^{\min}z_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max}z_{i,s} \\[2pt]
&\text{(4)  Acceleration / deceleration} \\ 
&v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s}\le a^{\max}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\
&v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'}\le a^{\min}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\[2pt]
&\text{(5)  Dwell‑time bounds} \\
&\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}
   &&\forall i,\;k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1 \\[2pt]
&\text{(6)  Time feasibility (stations ↔ segments)}\\
&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\text{ upstream of }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(7)  Disruption‑window feasibility} \\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s}\le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t+M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)
   &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(8)  Pairwise precedence on a shared side} \\
&a_{j,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(1-o_{i j s})\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(o_{i j s})\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}\\[2pt]
&\text{(9)  Transitivity of order variables} \\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(10)  Binary / non‑negative domains}\\
&r_{i,s}^{L},r_{i,s}^{R},o_{i j s}\in\{0,1\},\;
z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},\delta_{i,s}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (products of continuous variables) have been replaced by standard McCormick linearisation (δ, y, w variables). The model is therefore a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

---

## 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

1. **Fixed route topology** – each train’s sequence of stations/segments is known a‑priori; only the side on a blocked segment is a decision.  
2. **Single‑track per side** – each side of a segment can host at most one train at any instant; this is enforced by the pairwise precedence variables.  
3. **Big‑M values** – choose *M* larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). The small constant Δt (≈0.1 min) guarantees strict separation of two successive trains.  
4. **Energy linearisation** – the term \(c_1 v^2 t + c_2 t/v\) is convex for \(v>0\); McCormick envelopes on the bilinear terms \(v^2 t\) and \(t/v\) give a tight linear approximation. If a tighter piece‑wise linear approximation is required, introduce additional break‑points.  
5. **Disruption handling** – the model forces any train that selects the **unblocked** side to finish its traversal **outside** the blocked time window. Trains that would have to use the blocked side simply set the corresponding binary \(r_{i,s}^{\text{blocked}}=0\) and are forced to use the other side.  
6. **Scalability** – the number of binary variables grows with \(|I|^2\) for the order variables on each shared side. In practice one can limit the set of pairs to those whose earliest possible arrivals overlap (pre‑filtering) to keep the model tractable.  

---

### 7. How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – compute for every train the list of stations, segment lengths, scheduled arrival times, and identify which segments are blocked and which side is unavailable.  
2. **Parameter selection** – choose α, β, the energy coefficients (c₁,c₂), speed limits, acceleration limits, dwell‑time windows, and a suitable big‑M.  
3. **Implementation** – encode the MILP in any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, SCIP, HiGHS) solver.  
4. **Solution** – the optimal solution provides:  
   * the side choice \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}\) for each blocked segment,  
   * the exact departure/arrival schedule \((a_{i,k},d_{i,k})\),  
   * the speed profile \((v_{i,s})\) and travel times \((t_{i,s})\),  
   * the precedence order on each side (conflict‑free timetable).  

The objective value directly quantifies the trade‑off between **punctuality** (total delay) and **energy efficiency** (total consumption) under the given partial blockage.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear (mixed‑integer) formulation** of the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** when a railway segment is partially blocked (one of its two parallel “sides’’ is unavailable for a given time window).  
All symbols that appear in the model are defined in the tables that follow the formulation.  
The model is written in a **single‑commodity, time‑indexed** style – i.e. each train follows a fixed ordered list of stations/segments, but the exact departure/arrival times, the side that is used on a blocked segment and the speed that is chosen on each traversed side are decision variables.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **K_i** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including the origin and the final destination). Index of a station on the route of *i* is *k* (k = 0,…,|K_i|). |
| **S** | Set of railway **segments** (the physical track between two consecutive stations). |
| **S_i ⊂ S** | Set of segments traversed by train *i* (|S_i| = |K_i|‑1). |
| **B ⊂ S** | Sub‑set of **blocked segments** (only one side can be unavailable). |
| **Side(s) = {L,R}** | Two parallel “sides’’ (or tracks) of a segment *s* – left (L) and right (R). |
| **c₁ , c₂** | Positive energy‑cost coefficients (fuel/ electricity model). |
| **vᵐⁱⁿ , vᵐᵃˣ** | Global lower / upper speed limits (km h⁻¹). |
| **aᵐⁱⁿ , aᵐᵃˣ** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻¹ min⁻¹). |
| **τᵈʷₑˡˡ₍i,k₎ , τᵈʷᵉₑₗ₍i,k₎** | Minimum / maximum dwell time that train *i* must spend at station *k*. |
| **schedᵢ** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “on‑time’’ reference). |
| **T_start(s), T_end(s)** | Start and end of the disruption (blocking) on segment *s*. During this interval one side (the blocked side) cannot be used. |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to dominate any feasible time difference (e.g. M = 10⁴ min). |
| **Δt** | Small positive constant used to enforce strict ordering (Δt = 0.1 min). |

All distances of segments are known (denoted *ℓₛ*).  

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **rᵢₛᴸ , rᵢₛᴿ** | binary | 1 if train *i* traverses side **L** (resp. **R**) of blocked segment *s* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. (For non‑blocked segments the side is irrelevant – we set rᵢₛᴸ = rᵢₛᴿ = 1 automatically.) |
| **oᵢⱼₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on the *same side* of segment *s* (i.e. i exits before j enters). Defined only for pairs (i,j) that share a side of a segment. |
| **aᵢₖ** | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k* (k ∈ K_i). |
| **dᵢₖ** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **tᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | **Travel time** of train *i* on segment *s* (the time spent between the departure from the upstream station and arrival at the downstream station). |
| **vᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | **Average speed** of train *i* on segment *s* (km h⁻¹). |
| **δᵢₛ** | continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable used to linearise the product *vᵢₛ·tᵢₛ* (distance = speed × time). |
| **zᵢₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* actually **uses** segment *s* (i.e. s ∈ S_i); 0 otherwise (helps to write capacity constraints compactly). |

---

## 3. Linearised relationships  

### 3.1 Distance consistency  

For every train *i* and every traversed segment *s* ∈ S_i  

\[
\ell_s = v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ell_s \le \delta_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}),\;
\ell_s \ge \delta_{i,s} - M(1-z_{i,s}),
\]
\[
\delta_{i,s} \le v_{i,s}^{\max}\,t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s}),\;
\delta_{i,s} \ge v_{i,s}^{\min}\,t_{i,s}-M(1-z_{i,s}).
\]

Because *zᵢₛ = 1* for all real traversals, the constraints reduce to  

\[
\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s},\qquad \ell_s = \delta_{i,s}.
\]

Thus the product is linearised by the auxiliary variable **δ**.

### 3.2 Speed limits  

\[
v_{i,s}^{\min}\;z_{i,s}\;\le\; v_{i,s}\;\le\; v_{i,s}^{\max}\;z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s.
\]

If a train does not use a segment (zᵢₛ = 0) the speed is forced to 0.

### 3.3 Acceleration / deceleration between consecutive segments  

Let *s* and *s′* be two consecutive segments on train *i* (i.e. the downstream segment of *s* is the upstream segment of *s′*).  

\[
v_{i,s′} - v_{i,s} \le a^{\max}\,t_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}) + M(1-z_{i,s′}),
\]
\[
v_{i,s} - v_{i,s′} \le a^{\min}\,t_{i,s} + M(1-z_{i,s}) + M(1-z_{i,s′}).
\]

These linear inequalities enforce that the change of speed over the travel time of the first segment does not exceed the admissible acceleration/deceleration.

### 3.4 Dwell‑time (station‑stop) constraints  

For every train *i* and every intermediate station *k* (k = 1,…,|K_i|‑1)  

\[
d_{i,k} - a_{i,k} \ge \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\text{min},i,k},
\qquad
d_{i,k} - a_{i,k} \le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\text{max},i,k}.
\]

At the origin (k = 0) we set \(d_{i,0}=a_{i,0}\) (departure equals scheduled start time, which can be fixed or left free).  
At the final station we only need the arrival variable \(a_{i,\text{last}}\).

### 3.5 Time‑feasibility (linking stations and segments)  

For each train *i* and each segment *s* that connects station *k* to station *k+1*  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\in K_i\setminus\{ \text{last}\}.
\]

Because \(t_{i,s}= \ell_s / v_{i,s}\) (linearised via δ), the above is linear.

### 3.6 Route‑choice on blocked segments  

For every blocked segment *s* ∈ B and every train *i* that traverses it  

\[
r_{i,s}^{L}+ r_{i,s}^{R}= 1\qquad\text{(exactly one side is selected)}.
\]

If a segment is **not** blocked, we simply set \(r_{i,s}^{L}=r_{i,s}^{R}=1\) (or eliminate the variables).

### 3.7 Disruption‑window feasibility  

Assume side *b(s)* ∈ {L,R} is the **blocked side** of segment *s* during \([T_{\text{start}}(s),T_{\text{end}}(s)]\).  
If a train would traverse that side and its traversal interval overlaps the window, the solution is infeasible. This is enforced by a big‑M implication:

\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge T_{\text{end}}(s) \;+\; \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} + t_{i,s} \le T_{\text{start}}(s) \;-\; \Delta t \;+\; M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\; \overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]

where \(\overline{b(s)}\) denotes the **unblocked** side (the opposite of the blocked one).  
If the train chooses the unblocked side (\(r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}=1\)) the constraints force the traversal interval to lie completely **outside** the disruption window; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraints, allowing any timing.

A more compact formulation (using a binary “overlap’’ variable) is also possible, but the two‑inequality version above is linear and sufficient.

### 3.8 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on a shared side  

Consider any pair of distinct trains *(i,j)* that both use the **same side** *s* (i.e. \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}=r_{j,s}^{\sigma}=1\) for some σ∈{L,R}).  
Define binary order variable \(o_{i j s}\) = 1 if *i* leaves the segment before *j* enters; otherwise 0.  

\[
a_{j,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{i,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(1-o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]
\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{j,\text{down}(s)} + \Delta t \;-\; M\bigl(o_{i j s}\bigr),
\]

where  

* \(\text{up}(s)\) = upstream station of segment *s* (departure side),  
* \(\text{down}(s)\) = downstream station of segment *s* (arrival side).  

These two constraints together enforce that **exactly one** of the two possible orderings holds:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1\qquad\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}.
\]

### 3.9 Transitivity of the order variables (consistency)  

For any three trains *i, j, k* that share the same side *s*:

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\qquad
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0.
\]

These linear inequalities guarantee that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k*.

### 3.10 Capacity (at most one train on a side at any instant)  

A more direct way to guarantee capacity is to use the precedence variables defined above together with the **pairwise** constraints (3.8). Because every pair of trains that share a side must be ordered, the capacity condition is automatically satisfied (no two trains can occupy the same side simultaneously). If a weaker “no‑overlap’’ formulation is preferred, one can introduce a time‑grid and enforce that the sum of binary occupancy variables ≤ 1, but the pairwise precedence formulation is sufficient and linear.

---

## 4. Objective function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.

### 4.1 Delay term  

\[
\text{Delay}_i = a_{i,\text{last}} - \text{sched}_i \qquad (\ge 0).
\]

Total delay  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Delay} = \sum_{i\in I} \bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr).
\]

### 4.2 Energy‑consumption term  

For each traversed segment *s* the (average) energy cost is modelled as  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(c_1\,v_{i,s}^{2}+c_2/v_{i,s}\bigr)\;t_{i,s}.
\]

The product \(v_{i,s}^{2}\,t_{i,s}\) and \(t_{i,s}/v_{i,s}\) are linearised with additional auxiliary variables (standard McCormick envelopes). For brevity we write the linearised version as **Êᵢₛ**; the constraints are omitted here because they follow the same pattern as in §3.1 (introducing variables \(y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) and \(w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s}\) with convex envelopes).  

Total energy  

\[
\displaystyle \text{Energy}= \sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{s\in S_i}\; \widehat{E}_{i,s}.
\]

### 4.3 Combined objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy}}
}
\]

where **α** and **β** are user‑defined non‑negative weights that reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 5. Full MILP (compact statement)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(1)  Route choice on blocked segments: } 
      r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1 &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(2)  Travel‑time / distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)}\\
&\ell_s = \delta_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i\\
&\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}\,t_{i,s} &&\text{linearised with McCormick envelopes}\\[2pt]
&\text{(3)  Speed limits} && v^{\min}z_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max}z_{i,s} \\[2pt]
&\text{(4)  Acceleration / deceleration} \\ 
&v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s}\le a^{\max}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\
&v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'}\le a^{\min}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'})\\[2pt]
&\text{(5)  Dwell‑time bounds} \\
&\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}
   &&\forall i,\;k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1 \\[2pt]
&\text{(6)  Time feasibility (stations ↔ segments)}\\
&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\text{ upstream of }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(7)  Disruption‑window feasibility} \\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s}\le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t+M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)
   &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i \\[2pt]
&\text{(8)  Pairwise precedence on a shared side} \\
&a_{j,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(1-o_{i j s})\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(o_{i j s})\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}\\[2pt]
&\text{(9)  Transitivity of order variables} \\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0 &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(10)  Binary / non‑negative domains}\\
&r_{i,s}^{L},r_{i,s}^{R},o_{i j s}\in\{0,1\},\;
z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},\delta_{i,s}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (products of continuous variables) have been replaced by standard McCormick linearisation (δ, y, w variables). The model is therefore a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

---

## 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

1. **Fixed route topology** – each train’s sequence of stations/segments is known a‑priori; only the side on a blocked segment is a decision.  
2. **Single‑track per side** – each side of a segment can host at most one train at any instant; this is enforced by the pairwise precedence variables.  
3. **Big‑M values** – choose *M* larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). The small constant Δt (≈0.1 min) guarantees strict separation of two successive trains.  
4. **Energy linearisation** – the term \(c_1 v^2 t + c_2 t/v\) is convex for \(v>0\); McCormick envelopes on the bilinear terms \(v^2 t\) and \(t/v\) give a tight linear approximation. If a tighter piece‑wise linear approximation is required, introduce additional break‑points.  
5. **Disruption handling** – the model forces any train that selects the **unblocked** side to finish its traversal **outside** the blocked time window. Trains that would have to use the blocked side simply set the corresponding binary \(r_{i,s}^{\text{blocked}}=0\) and are forced to use the other side.  
6. **Scalability** – the number of binary variables grows with \(|I|^2\) for the order variables on each shared side. In practice one can limit the set of pairs to those whose earliest possible arrivals overlap (pre‑filtering) to keep the model tractable.  

---

### 7. How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – compute for every train the list of stations, segment lengths, scheduled arrival times, and identify which segments are blocked and which side is unavailable.  
2. **Parameter selection** – choose α, β, the energy coefficients (c₁,c₂), speed limits, acceleration limits, dwell‑time windows, and a suitable big‑M.  
3. **Implementation** – encode the MILP in any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, SCIP, HiGHS) solver.  
4. **Solution** – the optimal solution provides:  
   * the side choice \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}\) for each blocked segment,  
   * the exact departure/arrival schedule \((a_{i,k},d_{i,k})\),  
   * the speed profile \((v_{i,s})\) and travel times \((t_{i,s})\),  
   * the precedence order on each side (conflict‑free timetable).  

The objective value directly quantifies the trade‑off between **punctuality** (total delay) and **energy efficiency** (total consumption) under the given partial blockage.

### 1. Sets, parameters and data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **Kᵢ** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including origin 0 and destination *last*). |
| **S** | Set of railway segments (track between two consecutive stations). |
| **Sᵢ ⊂ S** | Segments traversed by train *i* (|Sᵢ| = |Kᵢ|‑1). |
| **B ⊂ S** | Segments that are **partially blocked** (only one side unavailable). |
| **Side(s) = {L,R}** | Two parallel sides (left/right) of a segment *s*. |
| **ℓₛ** | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| **c₁ , c₂** | Positive energy‑cost coefficients. |
| **vᵐᵢⁿ , vᵐᵃˣ** | Global speed limits (km h⁻¹). |
| **aᵐᵢⁿ , aᵐᵃˣ** | Max. deceleration / acceleration (km h⁻¹ min⁻¹). |
| **τᵈʷ₍i,k₎⁽ᵐⁱⁿ⁾ , τᵈʷ₍i,k₎⁽ᵐᵃˣ⁾** | Minimum / maximum dwell time of train *i* at station *k*. |

| **T_start(s), T_end(s)** | Start / end of the disruption on segment *s* (the blocked side cannot be used in this interval). |
| **M** | Big‑M constant (≥ maximal feasible time, e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **Δt** | Small positive constant to enforce strict ordering (Δt = 0.1 min). |
| **α , β ≥ 0** | Decision‑maker weights for delay and energy, respectively. |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **rᵢₛᴸ , rᵢₛᴿ** | binary | 1 if train *i* uses side **L** (resp. **R**) of blocked segment *s* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. |
| **oᵢⱼₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* precedes train *j* on the **same side** of segment *s* (i.e. *i* exits before *j* enters). |
| **aᵢₖ** | ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k* ∈ Kᵢ. |
| **dᵢₖ** | ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k* ∈ Kᵢ. |
| **tᵢₛ** | ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *s* ∈ Sᵢ. |
| **vᵢₛ** | ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment *s* (km h⁻¹). |
| **δᵢₛ** | ≥0 | Linearisation variable for the product *vᵢₛ·tᵢₛ* (so that ℓₛ = δᵢₛ). |
| **zᵢₛ** | binary | 1 if train *i* actually traverses segment *s* (zᵢₛ = 1 for all *s* ∈ Sᵢ). |
| **yᵢₛ , wᵢₛ** | ≥0 | Auxiliary variables for the quadratic and reciprocal terms in the energy expression (see §4). |

---

### 3. Linearised relationships  

#### 3.1 Distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)  
For every *i* and *s* ∈ Sᵢ  

\[
\ell_s = \delta_{i,s},\qquad
\delta_{i,s} \le v_{i,s}^{\max} t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s}),\;
\delta_{i,s} \ge v_{i,s}^{\min} t_{i,s}-M(1-z_{i,s}).
\]

Because *zᵢₛ = 1* for all traversed segments, the constraints enforce  
\(\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) and \(\ell_s = v_{i,s}t_{i,s}\).

#### 3.2 Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min} z_{i,s} \le v_{i,s} \le v^{\max} z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s.
\]

#### 3.3 Acceleration / deceleration between consecutive segments  

If *s* and *s′* are consecutive on train *i*  

\[
v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s} \le a^{\max} t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'}),\\
v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'} \le a^{\min} t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'}).
\]

#### 3.4 Dwell‑time bounds  

For every intermediate station *k* (k = 1,…,|Kᵢ|‑1)  

\[
\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}.
\]

#### 3.5 Time feasibility (link stations and segments)  

For each segment *s* that connects station *k* to *k+1* on train *i*  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+t_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; s\in S_i.
\]

#### 3.6 Route choice on blocked segments  

For every blocked segment *s* ∈ B traversed by train *i*  

\[
r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1.
\]

If *s* is not blocked, the two binaries are fixed to 1 (or omitted).

#### 3.7 Disruption‑window feasibility  

Let side **b(s)** be the **blocked** side of *s* during \([T_{\text{start}}(s),T_{\text{end}}(s)]\).  
The unblocked side is \(\overline{b(s)}\).  

\[
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t
      -M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),\\
a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s} \le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t
      +M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]

where \(\text{up}(s)\) is the upstream station of *s*.  
If the train chooses the **unblocked** side (\(r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}=1\)) the traversal interval must lie completely **outside** the disruption window; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraints.

#### 3.8 Pairwise precedence on a shared side  

Consider any two distinct trains *i* and *j* that both use the **same side** σ of segment *s* (i.e. \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}=r_{j,s}^{\sigma}=1\)).  

\[
a_{j,\text{up}(s)} \ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-o_{i j s}\bigr),\\
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M\bigl(o_{i j s}\bigr),\\
o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1.
\]

Thus exactly one ordering holds.

#### 3.9 Transitivity of order variables (consistency)  

For any three trains *i, j, k* sharing the same side of *s*  

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\qquad
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0.
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent total order on each side.

#### 3.10 Energy‑term linearisation  

Energy on segment *s* for train *i* is modelled as  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(c_1 v_{i,s}^{2}+c_2/v_{i,s}\bigr)\,t_{i,s}.
\]

Introduce auxiliary variables  

\[
y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2},\qquad w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s},
\]

and linearise the bilinear products \(y_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) and \(w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) with standard McCormick envelopes (bounds derived from \(v^{\min},v^{\max}\)).  
Then  

\[
\widehat{E}_{i,s}=c_1\,\tilde{y}_{i,s}+c_2\,\tilde{w}_{i,s},
\]

where \(\tilde{y}_{i,s}\) and \(\tilde{w}_{i,s}\) are the linearised representations of \(y_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) and \(w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\).

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\alpha\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
}
\]

*α* and *β* are user‑defined weights reflecting the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}\\[4pt]

&\text{(1) Route choice on blocked segments: } 
      r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1 &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i\\[2pt]
&\text{(2) Distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)}\\
&\ell_s = \delta_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i\\
&\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}t_{i,s}\;\;(\text{McCormick})\\[2pt]
&\text{(3) Speed limits} && v^{\min}z_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max}z_{i,s}\\[2pt]
&\text{(4) Acceleration / deceleration constraints}\\
&v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s}\le a^{\max}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'}),\\
&v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'}\le a^{\min}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'});\\[2pt]
&\text{(5) Dwell‑time bounds}\\
&\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}
   &&\forall i,\;k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1\\[2pt]
&\text{(6) Time feasibility (stations ↔ segments)}\\
&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\text{ upstream of }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(7) Disruption‑window feasibility}\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s}\le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t+M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)
   &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i\\[2pt]
&\text{(8) Pairwise precedence on a shared side}\\
&a_{j,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(1-o_{i j s}),\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(o_{i j s}),\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}\\[2pt]
&\text{(9) Transitivity of order variables}\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0
   &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(10) Energy linearisation (McCormick)}\\
&y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2},\; w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s},\;
\tilde{y}_{i,s}=y_{i,s}t_{i,s},\;
\tilde{w}_{i,s}=w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\\
&\widehat{E}_{i,s}=c_1\tilde{y}_{i,s}+c_2\tilde{w}_{i,s}\\[2pt]
&\text{(11) Variable domains}\\
&r_{i,s}^{L},r_{i,s}^{R},o_{i j s},z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\

\]

### 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions

a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t
      -M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),\\
a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s} \le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t
      +M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),
\]

where \(\text{up}(s)\) is the upstream station of *s*.  
If the train chooses the **unblocked** side (\(r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}=1\)) the traversal interval must lie completely **outside** the disruption window; otherwise the big‑M term relaxes the constraints.

#### 3.8 Pairwise precedence on a shared side  

Consider any two distinct trains *i* and *j* that both use the **same side** σ of segment *s* (i.e. \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}=r_{j,s}^{\sigma}=1\)).  

\[
a_{j,\text{up}(s)} \ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-o_{i j s}\bigr),\\
a_{i,\text{up}(s)} \ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M\bigl(o_{i j s}\bigr),\\
o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1.
\]

Thus exactly one ordering holds.

#### 3.9 Transitivity of order variables (consistency)  

For any three trains *i, j, k* sharing the same side of *s*  

\[
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\qquad
o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0.
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent total order on each side.

#### 3.10 Energy‑term linearisation  

Energy on segment *s* for train *i* is modelled as  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(c_1 v_{i,s}^{2}+c_2/v_{i,s}\bigr)\,t_{i,s}.
\]

Introduce auxiliary variables  

\[
y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2},\qquad w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s},
\]

and linearise the bilinear products \(y_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) and \(w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) with standard McCormick envelopes (bounds derived from \(v^{\min},v^{\max}\)).  
Then  

\[
\widehat{E}_{i,s}=c_1\,\tilde{y}_{i,s}+c_2\,\tilde{w}_{i,s},
\]

where \(\tilde{y}_{i,s}\) and \(\tilde{w}_{i,s}\) are the linearised representations of \(y_{i,s}t_{i,s}\) and \(w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\).

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\alpha\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
}
\]

*α* and *β* are user‑defined weights reflecting the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

### 5. Complete MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\widehat{E}_{i,s}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(1) Route choice on blocked segments: } 
      r_{i,s}^{L}+r_{i,s}^{R}=1 &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i\\[2pt]
&\text{(2) Distance consistency (δ‑linearisation)}\\
&\ell_s = \delta_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i\\
&\delta_{i,s}=v_{i,s}t_{i,s}\;\;(\text{McCormick})\\[2pt]
&\text{(3) Speed limits} && v^{\min}z_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max}z_{i,s}\\[2pt]
&\text{(4) Acceleration / deceleration constraints}\\
&v_{i,s'}-v_{i,s}\le a^{\max}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'}),\\
&v_{i,s}-v_{i,s'}\le a^{\min}t_{i,s}+M(1-z_{i,s})+M(1-z_{i,s'});\\[2pt]
&\text{(5) Dwell‑time bounds}\\
&\tau^{\text{dw}}_{\min,i,k}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le \tau^{\text{dw}}_{\max,i,k}
   &&\forall i,\;k=1,\dots,|K_i|-1\\[2pt]
&\text{(6) Time feasibility (stations ↔ segments)}\\
&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s\in S_i,\; k\text{ upstream of }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(7) Disruption‑window feasibility}\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge T_{\text{end}}(s)+\Delta t-M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr),\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}+t_{i,s}\le T_{\text{start}}(s)-\Delta t+M\bigl(1-r_{i,s}^{\overline{b(s)}}\bigr)
   &&\forall i,\; s\in B\cap S_i\\[2pt]
&\text{(8) Pairwise precedence on a shared side}\\
&a_{j,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(1-o_{i j s}),\\
&a_{i,\text{up}(s)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(s)}+\Delta t-M(o_{i j s}),\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j i s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\text{ shared}\\[2pt]
&\text{(9) Transitivity of order variables}\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\le 1,\\
&o_{i j s}+o_{j k s}-o_{i k s}\ge 0
   &&\forall i,j,k\text{ sharing side }s\\[2pt]
&\text{(10) Energy linearisation (McCormick)}\\
&y_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2},\; w_{i,s}=1/v_{i,s},\;
\tilde{y}_{i,s}=y_{i,s}t_{i,s},\;
\tilde{w}_{i,s}=w_{i,s}t_{i,s}\\
&\widehat{E}_{i,s}=c_1\tilde{y}_{i,s}+c_2\tilde{w}_{i,s}\\[2pt]
&\text{(11) Variable domains}\\
&r_{i,s}^{L},r_{i,s}^{R},o_{i j s},z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},\delta_{i,s},y_{i,s},w_{i,s}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linear products have been replaced by the auxiliary variables and McCormick envelopes, yielding a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)**.

---

### 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

1. **Fixed route topology** – the sequence of stations for each train is known; only the side on a blocked segment is a decision.  
2. **Single‑track per side** – each side can host at most one train at any instant; enforced by the pairwise precedence variables.  
3. **Big‑M** – choose *M* larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 min).  
4. **Energy linearisation** – McCormick envelopes give a tight convex approximation of the quadratic and reciprocal terms; additional break‑points can be added for higher accuracy.  
5. **Disruption handling** – a train that selects the **unblocked** side must finish its traversal outside the blocked time window; trains forced onto the blocked side are simply prohibited (binary set to 0).  
6. **Scalability** – the number of binary order variables grows with the number of train pairs sharing a side; in practice, pairs whose earliest possible arrivals do not overlap can be omitted to reduce model size.  

---

### 7. How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – for each train compute its station list, segment lengths, scheduled arrival times, and identify blocked segments and the side that is unavailable.  
2. **Parameter selection** – set α, β, energy coefficients (c₁,c₂), speed/acceleration limits, dwell‑time windows, and a suitable big‑M.  
3. **Implementation** – encode the MILP in any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, etc.).  
4. **Solution interpretation** – the optimal solution provides:  
   * side choice \(r_{i,s}^{\sigma}\) for each blocked segment,  
   * conflict‑free timetable \((a_{i,k},d_{i,k})\),  
   * feasible speed profile \((v_{i,s})\) and travel times \((t_{i,s})\),  
   * precedence order on each side \((o_{i j s})\).  

The objective value directly quantifies the trade‑off between **total passenger delay** and **energy consumption** under the given partial blockage scenario.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
