final_answer:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model)*  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains  \(t\in T\) (|T| = *n*). |
| **S** | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD‑sections)  \(s\in S\). |
| **N(s)** | Set of neighbour sections of *s* (immediate upstream/down‑stream sections). |
| **\( \mathcal{P}_t\subseteq S\)** | Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (the route). |
| **\(L_s\)** | Physical length of section *s* (km). |
| **\(v^{\max}_{t,s}\)** | Maximum admissible speed of train *t* in section *s* (km/h). |
| **\(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\)** | Service‑braking deceleration of train *t* (km/h²). |
| **\(a^{\text{acc}}_{t}\)** | Maximum acceleration of train *t* (km/h²). |
| **\(d^{\text{stop}}_{t,s}\)** | Minimum braking distance (in km) required for train *t* to stop from speed \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\) (computed from \(a^{\text{br}}_{t}\)). |
| **\( \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\)** | Minimum dwell (station‑stop) time of train *t* in section *s* (minutes). |
| **\( \Delta^{\text{max}}_{t}\)** | Upper bound on admissible delay for train *t* (minutes). |
| **\(M\)** | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation (e.g. 10⁶). |
| **\( \beta\)** | Weight for secondary objective (e.g. number of re‑orderings). |

*Assumptions* (explicitly stated)

1. **Deterministic timetable** – the original (unperturbed) arrival/departure times at the entry of each section are known and denoted by \(\bar a_{t,s},\;\bar d_{t,s}\).  
2. **Single‑track sections** – at most one train can occupy a section at a given instant (conflict definition).  
3. **DTG separation** – the safety distance between two consecutive trains *i* (ahead) and *j* (behind) in the same section is the **braking distance of the rear train** computed from its current speed (speed‑dependent).  
4. **Continuous speed profile is approximated by a piece‑wise constant speed equal to the section‑wise speed limit \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\).** This yields a linear expression for the braking distance.  
5. **Switches** are modelled as separate sections with possibly different speed limits.  
6. **Rescheduling actions** allowed: (i) **retiming** (add delay to a train at any section), (ii) **reordering** (swap the order of two trains that would otherwise conflict), (iii) **local rerouting** (choose an alternative parallel route; modelled by a binary variable that activates a different route set \(\mathcal{P}^{\text{alt}}_{t}\)). For brevity only (i) and (ii) are fully modelled; (iii) is indicated as an optional extension.  

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Actual arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of section *s*. |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Actual departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of section *s*. |
| \(\delta_{t}\) | continuous \(\ge 0\) | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual final arrival and scheduled final arrival). |
| \(x_{i,j,s}\) | binary | **Ordering variable**: 1 if train *i* is scheduled **ahead of** train *j* in section *s* (i.e. *i* leaves the section before *j* enters). |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | **Brake‑indication activation**: 1 if a brake‑indication point for train *t* lies **inside** section *s* (i.e. the train must start braking already in *s*). |
| \(z_{t}\) | binary | **Re‑ordering flag**: 1 if train *t* participates in at least one ordering change (used for secondary objective). |
| *(optional)* \(r_{t,k}\) | binary | Route‑selection variable: 1 if train *t* uses alternative route *k* (for local rerouting). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The primary aim is to **minimise total passenger/operational delay**; a secondary aim is to keep the number of re‑orderings low (to avoid massive timetable disruption).  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\; \beta\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}_{\text{Number of reordered trains}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*If a third objective (e.g., minimise total energy consumption) is required, it can be added linearly with an appropriate weight.*

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1. Timing propagation (travel time)  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of sections \((s,s')\) on its route (\(s'\) is the downstream neighbour of *s* in \(\mathcal{P}_t\)):

\[
d_{t,s} + \frac{L_s}{v^{\max}_{t,s}} \;\le\; a_{t,s'} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t\setminus\{ \text{last}\}
\tag{1}
\]

If a dwell is required (station section), we enforce a minimum dwell time:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_t\text{ where } \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}>0
\tag{2}
\]

The departure time cannot be earlier than the arrival time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,s
\tag{3}
\]

### 4.2. Delay definition  

Let \(\bar a_{t}^{\text{final}}\) be the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (last section *s\_f*).  

\[
\delta_{t} \;=\; a_{t,s_f} - \bar a_{t}^{\text{final}} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{4}
\]

Upper bound on admissible delay (to keep the model bounded):

\[
\delta_{t} \;\le\; \Delta^{\text{max}}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5}
\]

### 4.3. DTG‑based separation (speed‑dependent safety distance)  

For any two trains *i* and *j* that share a section *s* (i.e. \(s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j\)), the **rear train must not enter the section before the front train has progressed at least its braking distance**.  
Let the **braking distance** of train *j* when travelling at its section speed limit be  

\[
B_{j,s}= \frac{(v^{\max}_{j,s})^{2}}{2\,a^{\text{br}}_{j}} \quad\text{(in km)} .
\tag{6}
\]

The time needed to travel this distance at speed \(v^{\max}_{j,s}\) is  

\[
\theta_{j,s}= \frac{B_{j,s}}{v^{\max}_{j,s}} \quad\text{(in minutes)} .
\tag{7}
\]

The ordering binary \(x_{i,j,s}\) decides which train is ahead:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} \; &\ge\; d_{i,s} + \theta_{j,s} - M(1-x_{i,j,s}) \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j \\
a_{i,s} \; &\ge\; d_{j,s} + \theta_{i,s} - M x_{i,j,s} \qquad\forall i\neq j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

Only one of the two inequalities is active; the big‑M term deactivates the non‑selected one.

### 4.4. Consistency of ordering variables  

For any pair of trains sharing a section, exactly one ordering must hold:

\[
x_{i,j,s}+x_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\tag{9}
\]

If the original timetable already defines a precedence, we can *force* that ordering (optional, used to penalise re‑ordering):

\[
x_{i,j,s}= \bar x_{i,j,s} \quad\text{if re‑ordering not allowed for this pair}
\tag{10}
\]

where \(\bar x_{i,j,s}\) is 1 if train *i* is scheduled ahead of *j* in the baseline timetable.

### 4.5. Brake‑indication point (binary \(y_{t,s}\))  

A brake‑indication may be required inside a section when the distance to the **end‑of‑authority (EoA)** is less than the braking distance. Let \(E_{t,s}\) be the distance from the upstream end of *s* to the EoA (known from the signalling layout). The condition  

\[
E_{t,s} \le B_{t,s}
\]

is linearised with a binary:

\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{t,s} - B_{t,s} &\le M y_{t,s} \\
E_{t,s} - B_{t,s} &\ge \epsilon - M (1-y_{t,s}) \qquad (\epsilon>0\text{ small})
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]

If \(y_{t,s}=1\) the train must start braking **inside** section *s*. This is enforced by tightening the departure time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\le\; a_{t,s} + \theta_{t,s} \qquad\text{if } y_{t,s}=1
\tag{12}
\]

which can be linearised as  

\[
d_{t,s} \le a_{t,s} + \theta_{t,s} + M(1-y_{t,s})
\tag{13}
\]

### 4.6. Linking re‑ordering flag  

If a train participates in at least one ordering change, set \(z_t=1\):

\[
z_{t} \;\ge\; x_{i,j,s} - \bar x_{i,j,s} \qquad \forall i\neq t,\; \forall j,\; \forall s\in\mathcal{P}_i\cap\mathcal{P}_j
\tag{14}
\]

(Any positive deviation from the baseline ordering forces \(z_t=1\).)

### 4.7. Optional: Local rerouting  

If alternative routes are available, a binary \(r_{t,k}\) selects one:

\[
\sum_{k\in K_t} r_{t,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{15}
\]

All timing constraints (1)–(3) are then written using the selected route \(\mathcal{P}_{t}^{(k)}\). This extension does **not** affect the core model presented above.

---

## 5. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}z_{t} \\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(1)–(5)} &&\text{(time propagation, dwell, delay)}\\
&\text{(6)–(9)} &&\text{(DTG speed‑dependent separation and ordering)}\\
&\text{(10) (optional)} &&\text{baseline ordering fixation}\\
&\text{(11)–(13)} &&\text{brake‑indication activation}\\
&\text{(14)} &&\text{link to re‑ordering flag}\\
&\text{(15) (optional)} &&\text{route selection}\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
& x_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t}\in\{0,1\},\; r_{t,k}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Remarks on Linearisation  

* The product of a binary and a continuous variable (e.g., \(x_{i,j,s}\theta_{j,s}\)) is avoided because \(\theta_{j,s}\) is a **parameter** (pre‑computed from speed limits).  
* Big‑M values should be chosen tight:  
  * For ordering constraints (8), \(M\) can be set to the horizon length (e.g., total schedule horizon in minutes).  
  * For brake‑indication linearisation (11)–(13), \(M\) can be the maximum possible travel time of a section.  

---

## 7. How the Model Captures DTG Features  

| DTG feature | How it appears in the MILP |
|-------------|---------------------------|
| **Speed‑dependent separation** | Braking distance \(B_{t,s}\) and corresponding time \(\theta_{t,s}\) depend on the section speed limit \(v^{\max}_{t,s}\). Constraint (8) enforces that the trailing train cannot enter until the leading train has progressed at least \(\theta\) minutes, i.e., the physical braking distance. |
| **Brake‑indication point inside a section** | Binary \(y_{t,s}\) indicates that the distance to the EoA is smaller than the braking distance, forcing the departure time to respect the braking curve (13). |
| **Distinction between switches and regular track** | Switches are modelled as separate sections with their own \(L_s\) and speed limits; the same constraints apply, allowing different braking distances on switches. |
| **Retiming, reordering, optional rerouting** | Retiming is achieved by the continuous arrival/departure variables; reordering is modelled by the binary ordering variables \(x_{i,j,s}\) and penalised via \(z_t\); optional rerouting is captured by route‑selection binaries \(r_{t,k}\). |
| **Integration with existing RECIFE‑MILP** | All constraints are linear extensions of the classic RECIFE‐MILP (which uses fixed‑block separation). The only modification is the replacement of a constant block‑based headway by the speed‑dependent \(\theta\) term. |

---

### 8. Possible Extensions  

* **Multiple speed profiles** – introduce binary variables to select among a set of admissible speed profiles per section, adding extra constraints for acceleration/deceleration limits.  
* **Moving‑block / virtual‑block** – replace the fixed EoA distance \(E_{t,s}\) by a dynamic safety margin behind the rear of the preceding train (requires additional binary linking).  
* **Stochastic delays** – replace deterministic \(\Delta^{\max}_t\) by scenario‑based variables and minimise expected delay.  

---

**The formulation above provides a complete, linear (mixed‑integer) description of the conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem for railway operations under distance‑to‑go signalling, ready to be implemented in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).**

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The formulation below captures (i) the binary decisions needed to reschedule/re‑route trains when a partial‑track blockage occurs, (ii) the continuous decisions that define a feasible speed profile for every train on every track segment, and (iii) the trade‑off between service quality (delay) and energy consumption.  All sets, parameters, variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable placeholders are introduced and flagged as **assumptions**.  

---

### 1.   Index Sets and Basic Data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run in the planning horizon. |
| **S** = {1,…, |S|} | Set of stations (including the depot) visited by the trains. |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of directed track **segments** (i→j) that can be traversed. |
| **B** ⊆ E | Subset of segments that are **blocked** for a given disruption (partial‑track blockage). |
| **K** = {1,…, Kmax} | Set of **speed‑profile intervals** (time‑distance discretisation) used to describe a feasible speed/acceleration pattern on a segment. |
| **P** = {1,…, Pmax} | Set of **pre‑computed feasible plans** for each train (a plan = a combination of departure/arrival times, route choice and a feasible speed‑profile on every traversed segment).  (Generated in a preprocessing step.) |
| **Ω** = {(t,p) | t∈T , p∈P } | Set of all train‑plan pairs. |

**Assumption 1 – Discretisation.**  
Every segment (i→j) is divided into Kmax equally‑spaced “position‑time” intervals.  Within each interval the train either **cruises**, **accelerates**, or **decelerates** at a constant rate.  The physical limits (max speed v̂, max acceleration â⁺, max deceleration â⁻) are enforced by linear inequalities on the interval variables (see §4.2).

**Assumption 2 – Pre‑computed Plans.**  
For each train *t* a (large but finite) catalogue of feasible plans *p*∈P is generated by a separate speed‑profile generation routine (e.g., using a piecewise‑linear approximation of the optimal control problem).  Each plan already satisfies all train‑dynamics constraints on unrestricted segments; only the **conflict‑avoidance** constraints (track‑capacity & bidirectional usage) are left to the MILP.

---

### 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{tp}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* adopts plan *p*; 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{e}^{t}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* (i→j) in the direction indicated by *e*; 0 otherwise. |
| \(u_{e}^{t}\) | binary | =1 if train *t* traverses the **opposite** direction on the same physical track (i←j) (i.e. uses the opposite track of a bidirectional line). |
| \(c_{e}^{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Entry time** of train *t* onto segment *e* (the time at which the front of the train reaches the upstream node of *e*). |
| \(d_{e}^{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Exit time** of train *t* from segment *e* (the time at which the rear of the train clears the downstream node of *e*). |
| \(w_{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at its final destination and the original scheduled arrival). |
| \(e_{t}\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of interval‑wise energy use, see §4.3). |

---

### 3. Parameters  

| Parameter | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| \(T_{t}^{\text{sched}}\) | Original scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (baseline). |
| \(R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\) ⊆ E | Set of segments traversed by train *t* under plan *p*. |
| \(a_{tp}^{\text{enter}}(e)\) | Planned **entry time** onto segment *e* in plan *p* (continuous). |
| \(a_{tp}^{\text{exit}}(e)\) | Planned **exit time** from segment *e* in plan *p*. |
| \(E_{tp}\) | Planned **energy** (kWh) of train *t* under plan *p* (computed from the speed‑profile). |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for typical “if‑then” linearisation (e.g., 10⁶ s). |
| \(\Delta\) | Minimum **headway** (seconds) required between two successive trains using the same physical track in the same direction. |
| \(\Delta^{\text{opp}}\) | Minimum **headway** for opposite‑direction trains on a shared single‑track segment (e.g., safety margin). |
| \(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\) | Weighting coefficients for the two objectives (delay and energy). |
| \(\tau^{\text{block}}_{e} = [\underline{t}_{e},\overline{t}_{e}]\) | **Blocking time window** for segment *e*∈B (no train may occupy the blocked side during this interval). |
| \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment *e*. |
| \(v_{\max}\) , \(a_{\max}^{+}\) , \(a_{\max}^{-}\) | Physical limits on speed, acceleration and deceleration (used in the preprocessing of plans). |

---

### 4.   Model Formulation  

#### 4.1   Plan‑Selection Constraints  

1. **Exactly one plan per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{1}
   \]

2. **Link plan choice to segment usage**  
   For every train *t* and every segment *e*:  
   \[
   z_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{e\in R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\}} \qquad 
   u_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{ \text{opposite direction of }e\in R_{tp}^{\text{route}}\}}
   \tag{2}
   \]
   (Here \(\mathbf{1}_{\{\cdot\}}\) is 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.)

3. **Derive entry/exit times from the selected plan**  
   \[
   c_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; a_{tp}^{\text{enter}}(e) \qquad
   d_{e}^{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; a_{tp}^{\text{exit}}(e) \qquad \forall t,e
   \tag{3}
   \]

4. **Delay definition** (final‑destination segment is denoted by \(e^{\text{dest}}_{t}\))  
   \[
   w_{t}= d_{e^{\text{dest}}_{t}}^{\,t}- T_{t}^{\text{sched}} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{4}
   \]
   (If a train is cancelled we may set \(w_{t}=M\) and enforce a special “cancellation” plan; omitted here for brevity.)

5. **Energy aggregation**  
   \[
   e_{t}= \sum_{p\in P} x_{tp}\; E_{tp} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{5}
   \]

#### 4.2   Conflict‑Avoidance (Track‑Capacity) Constraints  

All constraints below are linearised using big‑M.  They guarantee that at any instant the physical track capacity is not exceeded and that a blocked side cannot be used.

1. **Headway for trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical track**  

   For any ordered pair of distinct trains \((t_{1},t_{2})\) and any segment *e* (direction i→j):  
   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{2}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{1}} + \Delta - M\bigl(1 - z_{e}^{t_{1}} - z_{e}^{t_{2}} + y_{t_{1}t_{2}e}\bigr)
   \tag{6a}
   \]
   \[
   c_{e}^{t_{1}} \ge d_{e}^{t_{2}} + \Delta - M\bigl(1 - z_{e}^{t_{1}} - z_{e}^{t_{2}} + (1-y_{t_{1}t_{2}e})\bigr)
   \tag{6b}
   \]

\end{aligned}
\]

* the **total expected delay** and **energy consumption**, allowing the decision maker to evaluate the disruption‑recovery performance.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

|----------|------|----------|
| **x_{t,r}** | binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned to route *r* (i.e., rerouted), 0 otherwise. |
| **d_t** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from its origin (minutes). |
| **a_{t,s}** | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (i.e., when it enters *s*). |
| **b_{t,s}** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s* (i.e., when it leaves *s*). |
| **y_{t,s,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| **e_t** | continuous, ≥0 | Energy consumed by train *t* over the whole trip (kWh). |

*Note:* For a train that does **not** use a segment (because the segment is not on its chosen route), the corresponding variables are forced to zero by constraints.

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T}\bigl(d_t-\tau_t^0\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

* The first term penalises any departure later than the originally planned time (positive delay).  
* The second term penalises the total energy consumption, which is a linear function of the speed‑level choices (see the definition of *e_t* below).

Both weights can be tuned to reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑usage variables**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R}\delta_{t,r,s}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

The left‑hand side is 1 if the train traverses *s* (with some speed level) and 0 otherwise; the right‑hand side is 1 exactly when the chosen route contains *s*.

### 4.2 Speed‑level selection (mutual exclusivity)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

A train can use at most one speed level on a given segment (or none if the segment is not on its route).

### 4.3 Time‑flow (travel‑time) constraints  

For every train *t* and every segment *s* that it traverses (i.e., \(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=1\)):

\[
b_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{t,s,k}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

Because the denominator is a linear expression (only one *y* can be 1), the fraction can be linearised with a big‑M:

\[
b_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} - M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

\[
b_{t,s} \le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} + M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

Thus, when \(y_{t,s,k}=1\) the travel‑time on *s* equals \(L_s/v_k\); otherwise the constraint is relaxed.

### 4.4 Continuity between consecutive segments  

Let \(\text{next}(s)\) denote the downstream neighbour of segment *s* on the chosen route (if any). For each train:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \ge b_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a downstream neighbour}
\]

If a train does **not** use segment *s*, the corresponding variables are forced to zero by (4.2) and the inequality becomes non‑binding.

### 4.5 Origin and destination dwell times  

\[
d_t \ge \tau_t^0 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{origin release}
\]

\[
a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{enter first segment}
\]

\[
b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}\ge d_t + p_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{origin dwell}
\]

\[
b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}+ q_t \le \text{Horizon\_end} \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{arrival within horizon}
\]

(If the origin/destination stations are modelled as zero‑length “segments”, the same constraints apply.)

### 4.6 Partial‑blockage capacity constraints  

Only a fraction \(\gamma_s\) of a blocked segment *s* can be occupied at any instant. A simple way to enforce this in a MILP is to limit the **simultaneous** number of trains on the segment. Let \(z_{t,s}\) be a binary indicator that the train *t* is on segment *s* at a given time slice; we avoid time‑indexing by using **pairwise head‑way** constraints (next section). The capacity constraint becomes:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} \le \bigl\lceil \gamma_s \cdot C_s \bigr\rceil \qquad \forall s\in B
\]

where \(C_s\) is the nominal (full) capacity of segment *s* (e.g., number of trains that could fit side‑by‑side). For a single‑track line \(C_s=1\), so the right‑hand side reduces to 0 or 1 depending on \(\gamma_s\).

### 4.7 Bidirectional conflict (head‑way) constraints  

If the line is single‑track and trains may travel in opposite directions, we must guarantee a safe separation. For any unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) that both use segment *s* (i.e., \(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=1\) and \(\sum_k y_{t',s,k}=1\)):

\[
a_{t',s} \ge b_{t,s} + \Delta_{s,s'} \;-\; M\bigl(2- \sum_{k}y_{t,s,k} - \sum_{k}y_{t',s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
\]

and the symmetric version with *t* and *t'* swapped. The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when at least one of the two trains does **not** occupy the segment.

### 4.8 Energy‑consumption definition  

Energy for a train is the sum over all traversed segments of (segment length) × (energy rate of the chosen speed level):

\[
e_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s \, c_k \, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

Because each \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary and at most one per segment, this expression is linear.

### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K\\
&d_t,\; a_{t,s},\; b_{t,s},\; e_t \ge 0, &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. How the model works (plain‑English explanation)

1. **Route choice** – The binary variable \(x_{t,r}\) decides whether train *t* follows its nominal route or a detour that avoids the blocked part of the network. Exactly one route must be selected.

2. **Speed choice per segment** – For every segment that a train actually traverses, the model picks one speed level \(k\) (binary \(y_{t,s,k}\)). Higher speeds reduce travel time but increase the energy term \(c_k\).

3. **Timing** –  
   * The departure time \(d_t\) cannot be earlier than the original schedule \(\tau_t^0\).  
   * Once a train enters a segment, its exit time \(b_{t,s}\) is the entry time \(a_{t,s}\) plus the travel time \(L_s/v_k\) dictated by the chosen speed.  
   * The entry time of the next segment must be at least the exit time of the previous one, guaranteeing a feasible trajectory.

4. **Partial blockage** – If a segment is partially blocked, only a fraction \(\gamma_s\) of its normal capacity may be used. This is enforced by a simple capacity inequality (4.6). In practice, for a single‑track line \(\gamma_s<1\) forces at most one train on the segment at a time.

5. **Bidirectional conflict** – When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same segment, a safety head‑way \(\Delta_{s,s'}\) is required. The big‑M formulation (4.7) activates the separation constraint only when both trains actually occupy the segment.

6. **Energy accounting** – The total energy for a train is the sum of segment lengths multiplied by the energy‑rate of the selected speed level. Because the speed level is binary, the expression stays linear.

7. **Objective** – The model simultaneously minimises (i) the total delay of all trains (weighted by \(\alpha\)) and (ii) the total energy consumption (weighted by \(\beta\)). By adjusting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can prioritize punctuality, sustainability, or a balanced trade‑off.

---

## 6. Remarks on implementation

* **Big‑M value** – Choose \(M\) larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min) so that the logical constraints are never inadvertently binding.
* **Scalability** – The number of binary variables grows with \(|T|\times|S|\times|K|\) and \(|T|\times|R|\). In practice, one can prune infeasible routes beforehand or aggregate consecutive short segments to keep the model tractable.
* **Solver** – Any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, etc.) can handle the formulation directly. If the problem size is very large, a decomposition (e.g., Benders) or a heuristic (column generation for routes) may be employed.
* **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with (i) train‑specific energy‑efficiency curves, (ii) crew‑working‑time limits, (iii) passenger‑penalty terms, or (iv) stochastic blockage durations (via scenario‑based robust MILP).

---

### Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t}(d_t-\tau_t^0)+\beta\sum_{t}e_t\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. }&
\sum_{r}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r}\delta_{t,r,s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}\le 1 &&\forall t,s\\
&b_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k}-M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k\\
&b_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k}+M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k\\
&a_{t,\text{next}(s)}\ge b_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\text{ with next}\\
&d_t\ge \tau_t^0 &&\forall t\\
&a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t &&\forall t\\
&b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}+q_t\le \text{Horizon\_end} &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{t}\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}\le \lceil\gamma_s C_s\rceil &&\forall s\in B\\
&a_{t',s}\ge b_{t,s}+ \Delta_{s,s'}-M\bigl(2-\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}-\sum_{k}y_{t',s,k}\bigr) &&\forall t<t',s\\
&e_t =\sum_{s}\sum_{k} L_s c_k y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t\\
&x_{t,r},y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; d_t,a_{t,s},b_{t,s},e_t\ge 0 &&\forall t,r,s,k
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation captures **all** the requested elements—binary rerouting decisions, continuous timing variables, discrete speed‑level choices, partial‑segment blockage, bidirectional conflict, and a weighted delay‑plus‑energy objective—while remaining a **linear** mixed‑integer program that can be handed to any standard MILP solver.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the description you gave:  

*integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management under a partially blocked track segment*.  

The model is written in a **compact, “text‑book” style** so that you can copy‑paste it directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, CBC) after translating the sets, parameters and data into the appropriate format (Python‑Pyomo, AMPL, GAMS, …).  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**   | Set of track segments (ordered from origin to destination), indexed by *s* |
| **K**   | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete), indexed by *k* |
| **B**   | Set of blocked sub‑segments (a subset of **S**) – the part of a segment that is unavailable |
| **P**   | Set of possible reroute paths for a train (normally *P = {0,1}* where 0 = stay on original line, 1 = use detour) |

For each train *t* we also define a **route** as an ordered list of segments  
\(\mathcal{R}_t \subseteq S\) (original line) and a possible **detour route** \(\mathcal{D}_t \subseteq S\) (used when the binary reroute variable is 1).  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment *s* (km) | km |
| \(v^{\max}_k\) | Speed associated with speed level *k* (km/h) | km/h |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_k\) | Energy consumption per km when travelling at speed level *k* (kWh/km) | kWh/km |
| \(c^{\text{delay}}\) | Penalty cost per hour of delay (monetary) | $/h |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}\) | Penalty cost per kWh of energy (monetary) | $/kWh |
| \(a_t\) | Planned (scheduled) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (h) | h |
| \(d^{\text{min}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at the entry of segment *s* (h) (e.g. for boarding, safety) | h |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 h) | h |
| \(\tau^{\text{block}}_{s}\) | Time window during which sub‑segment *B* of segment *s* is blocked (start, end) – we store as two scalars \(\tau^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{start}}\) and \(\tau^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{end}}\) | h |
| \(g_{s,s'}\) | 1 if segments *s* and *s'* are **opposite‑direction** (i.e., a head‑on conflict can occur), 0 otherwise | – |
| \(R_t\) | 1 if train *t* is a **high‑priority** train (e.g., passenger), 0 otherwise | – |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight on delay in the objective (0 ≤ α ≤ 1) | – |
| \(\beta = 1-\alpha\) | Weight on energy in the objective | – |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data, and the blockage forecast.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,p}\) | Binary | Reroute decision for train *t*: 0 = stay on original route \(\mathcal{R}_t\), 1 = use detour \(\mathcal{D}_t\) |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\) | Binary | Speed‑level assignment: 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k* (only defined for segments that belong to the chosen route) |
| \(u_{t,s}\) | Continuous, ≥ 0 | **Departure time** of train *t* from the *start* of segment *s* (i.e., the time it *leaves* the entry node of *s*) |
| \(v_{t,s}\) | Continuous, ≥ 0 | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the *end* of segment *s* (i.e., the time it *enters* the next segment) |
| \(z_{t,s}\) | Binary | 1 if train *t* **occupies** (any part of) segment *s* (used for conflict constraints) |
| \(e_{t}\) | Continuous, ≥ 0 | **Total delay** of train *t* at its final destination: \(e_t = \max\{0, v_{t,\text{last}} - a_t\}\) (linearized) |
| \(E_{t}\) | Continuous, ≥ 0 | **Total energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh) |
| \(w_{t,s,s'}\) | Binary | Ordering variable for opposite‑direction conflict: 1 if train *t* traverses *s* **before** train *t'* traverses *s'* (used only when \(g_{s,s'}=1\)) |

---

## 4. Linearization of Non‑linear Elements  

### 4.1 Delay  
Introduce an auxiliary variable \(e_t\) and a binary \(\delta_t\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
e_t &\ge v_{t,\text{last}} - a_t \\
e_t &\ge 0 \\
e_t &\le M \, \delta_t \\
v_{t,\text{last}} - a_t &\le M (1-\delta_t)
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(e_t = \max\{0, v_{t,\text{last}}-a_t\}\).

### 4.2 Energy  
Energy is additive over segments and speed levels:

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} \bigl( L_s \, c^{\text{energy}}_k \bigr) \, y_{t,s,k}
\]

Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary and each segment is traversed exactly once (see constraints), the expression is linear.

### 4.3 Occupancy binary \(z_{t,s}\)  

\[
z_{t,s} \ge \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s
\]

(and the reverse inequality can be omitted because the left‑hand side will be 0 if the sum is 0).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

A weighted sum of total delay (monetised) and total energy (monetised):

\[
\min \; \alpha \, c^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; \beta \, c^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T} E_t
\]

If you want to give higher priority to passenger trains, you can replace the first term by  

\[
\alpha \, c^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} \bigl( 1 + \lambda R_t \bigr) e_t
\]

with a small \(\lambda>0\).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1 Route‑selection (binary reroute)  

For each train *t* we must decide which set of segments it may use:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} = 0 \quad &&\forall s \notin \mathcal{R}_t \cup \mathcal{D}_t \\
&\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} = (1-x_{t,1}) \quad &&\forall s \in \mathcal{R}_t \setminus \mathcal{D}_t \\
&\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} = x_{t,1} \quad &&\forall s \in \mathcal{D}_t \setminus \mathcal{R}_t \\
&\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} = 1 \quad &&\forall s \in \mathcal{R}_t \cap \mathcal{D}_t
\end{aligned}
\]

In words: a segment that belongs **only** to the original line can be used only if the train does **not** reroute; a segment that belongs only to the detour can be used only if the train **does** reroute; a segment common to both is always traversed.

### 6.2 Exactly one speed level per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} = z_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If a train does not occupy segment *s* (\(z_{t,s}=0\)), all \(y_{t,s,k}=0\).

### 6.3 Travel‑time relationship  

If speed level *k* is chosen on segment *s*, the travel time equals length / speed:

\[
v_{t,s} \;-\; u_{t,s} \;=\; \sum_{k\in K} \frac{L_s}{v^{\max}_k}\; y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s
\]

All times are in **hours**; \(L_s\) in km, \(v^{\max}_k\) in km/h.

### 6.4 Continuity of the schedule along the route  

For every train *t* and every **consecutive** pair of segments \((s, s^{+})\) on the chosen route (the “next” segment after *s*):

\[
u_{t,s^{+}} \;=\; v_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,\; s\in \text{predecessor}(s^{+})
\]

If the route is a simple line, this reduces to  

\[
u_{t,s+1}=v_{t,s}\quad\forall s
\]

### 6.5 Minimum dwell / safety time at segment entry  

\[
u_{t,s} \;-\; v_{t,s-1} \;\ge\; d^{\text{min}}_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,\; s\neq \text{first segment}
\]

(If the first segment has a scheduled departure time, you can fix \(u_{t,\text{first}} =\) scheduled departure.)

### 6.6 Blockage avoidance  

A train may **not** occupy a blocked sub‑segment during the blockage window. Because the blockage is only a part of the segment, we enforce that the **entry time** into the segment is either before the block starts **or** after it ends:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{t,s} \;+\; \epsilon &\le \tau^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{start}} \;+\; M (1 - z_{t,s}) \\
u_{t,s} \;&\ge \tau^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{end}} \;-\; M (1 - z_{t,s})
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t,\; s\in B
\]

Here \(\epsilon\) is a tiny positive constant (e.g., 0.001 h) to avoid equality. The big‑M terms deactivate the constraint when the train does not use the blocked segment (\(z_{t,s}=0\)).

### 6.7 Bidirectional (head‑on) conflict avoidance  

If two trains travel on opposite directions on the **same physical track** (segments *s* and *s'* that are opposite), they cannot be in the segment at the same time. A classic linear ordering formulation uses binary variables \(w_{t,t',s}\):

For every unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) and every pair of opposite segments \((s,s')\) with \(g_{s,s'}=1\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{t',s'} \;&\ge\; v_{t,s} \;-\; M \bigl(1 - w_{t,t',s}\bigr) \\
u_{t,s} \;&\ge\; v_{t',s'} \;-\; M \, w_{t,t',s} \\
w_{t,t',s} &\in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(w_{t,t',s}=1\) the model forces train *t* to finish segment *s* before train *t'* enters its opposite segment *s'*. If \(w_{t,t',s}=0\) the opposite ordering is enforced. The constraints are activated only when both trains actually occupy the respective segments:

\[
w_{t,t',s} \le z_{t,s},\qquad w_{t,t',s} \le z_{t',s'}
\]

and similarly for the complement.

### 6.8 Single‑track capacity (optional)  

If a segment can hold **only one train at a time** (even in the same direction), we can use a disjunctive formulation similar to the head‑on case, but without the opposite‑direction flag:

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{t',s} &\ge v_{t,s} - M (1 - q_{t,t',s})\\
u_{t,s} &\ge v_{t',s} - M q_{t,t',s}\\
q_{t,t',s} &\in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
\end{aligned}
\]

Again, the constraints are only needed when both trains use the segment: \(q_{t,t',s} \le z_{t,s},\; q_{t,t',s} \le z_{t',s}\).

### 6.9 Speed‑level feasibility  

If certain speed levels are prohibited on a segment (e.g., due to curvature), introduce a binary feasibility parameter \(\phi_{s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) and enforce:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le \phi_{s,k} \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

### 6.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{t,p} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,p\\
y_{t,s,k} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
z_{t,s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s\\
w_{t,t',s} , q_{t,t',s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall\text{pairs}\\
u_{t,s},v_{t,s},e_t,E_t &\ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha \, c^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; \beta \, c^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T} E_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(Route‑selection constraints)} &&\eqref{route1}–\eqref{route4}\\
&\text{(Exactly one speed per traversed segment)} &&\eqref{speed1}\\
&\text{(Travel‑time definition)} &&\eqref{travel}\\
&\text{(Schedule continuity)} &&\eqref{cont}\\
&\text{(Minimum dwell)} &&\eqref{dwell}\\
&\text{(Blockage avoidance)} &&\eqref{block1},\eqref{block2}\\
&\text{(Bidirectional conflict)} &&\eqref{conflict1},\eqref{conflict2}\\
&\text{(Optional single‑track capacity)} &&\eqref{single1},\eqref{single2}\\
&\text{(Speed feasibility)} &&\eqref{feas}\\
&\text{(Delay linearisation)} &&\eqref{delay1}–\eqref{delay4}\\
&\text{(Energy definition)} &&\eqref{energy}\\
&\text{(Variable domains)} &&\eqref{domains}
\end{aligned}
\]

*(The equation numbers \eqref{...} refer to the numbered constraints given in the sections above.)*

---

## 8. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets **T**, **S**, **K**, the original and detour routes for each train, the blockage windows, and the parameters (segment lengths, speed‑level speeds, energy rates, scheduled arrival times, etc.).  

2. **Choose the big‑M** – A safe value is the horizon of the planning horizon (e.g., the latest scheduled arrival plus a generous slack).  

3. **Solver** – Feed the model to any MILP solver. Because the model contains many binary variables (especially the pairwise conflict variables), the problem size grows **quadratically** with the number of trains that share a segment. For large instances you may:
   * use a **time‑indexed** formulation (discretise time) instead of pairwise ordering,  
   * apply **cut‑generation** (conflict‑graph cuts),  
   * or use a **decomposition** (Benders, column generation) that treats each train as a sub‑problem.  

4. **Interpretation of the solution** –  
   * \(x_{t,1}=1\) → train *t* is rerouted onto its detour.  
   * The selected speed level on each segment is given by the unique \(k\) with \(y_{t,s,k}=1\).  
   * \(u_{t,s}\) and \(v_{t,s}\) give the exact departure/arrival schedule that respects the blockage and conflict constraints.  
   * The objective value tells you the **trade‑off** between total delay and total energy consumption as dictated by the weight \(\alpha\).  

---

### Quick Example (tiny instance)

| Train | Original route | Detour route | Scheduled arrival (h) |
|-------|----------------|-------------|----------------------|
| 1     | 1‑2‑3‑4        | 1‑5‑6‑4     | 10.0 |
| 2     | 4‑3‑2‑1        | –           | 10.5 |

Segment lengths: \(L_1=5\), \(L_2=8\), … (km).  
Blocked segment: \(s=3\) blocked from 4.0 h to 6.0 h.  

Running the MILP will decide whether train 1 should take the detour (binary \(x_{1,1}\)), which speed level to use on each traversed segment, and the exact departure/arrival times that keep both trains out of the blocked part of segment 3 and avoid a head‑on conflict on segment 2.

---

**That completes the full MILP formulation** – variables, objective, and every constraint needed to model integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partially blocked track segment. Feel free to adapt the sets, parameters, or add extra practical constraints (e.g., crew‑change windows, rolling‑stock availability) as required by your specific railway planning environment.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary for reroute decision, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed dynamics, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route and when it departs/arrives)  
* **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level on each track segment)  
* **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable because of an incident, maintenance, etc.)

The model is written in a **canonical linear form** – a linear objective function and a set of linear equality/inequality constraints – with a mixture of **continuous** and **binary** decision variables.  After the mathematical statement, each component is explained in plain English.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and data

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* |
| **R** | Set of admissible routes (ordered list of segments) for each train, indexed by *r* |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete), indexed by *k* |
| **B ⊆ S** | Subset of *blocked* segments (segments that are partially unavailable) |
| **L_s** | Physical length of segment *s* (km) |
| **v_k** | Speed associated with speed level *k* (km/h) – assumed constant on a segment |
| **c_k** | Energy consumption rate (e.g. kWh per km) when travelling at speed level *k* |
| **Δt** | Length of the planning horizon discretisation (e.g. 1 min) |
| **τ_t^0** | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* (minutes from horizon start) |
| **α** | Weight on total delay in the objective (≥0) |
| **β** | Weight on total energy consumption in the objective (≥0) |
| **M** | Large constant (“big‑M”) used for logical constraints |
| **γ_s** | Fraction of segment *s* that remains usable (0 < γ_s ≤ 1). For unblocked segments γ_s = 1. |
| **p_t** | Minimum dwell time (minutes) required at the origin station of train *t* |
| **q_t** | Minimum dwell time (minutes) required at the destination station of train *t* |
| **Δ_{s,s'}** | Minimum head‑way time (minutes) required between two trains that occupy the same segment *s* in opposite directions (bidirectional conflict). |
| **δ_{t,r,s}** | Indicator = 1 if segment *s* belongs to route *r* for train *t*, 0 otherwise. (Pre‑computed from the network topology.) |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, network geometry and the incident report.

---

## 2. Decision variables

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **x_{t,r}** | binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned to route *r* (i.e., rerouted), 0 otherwise. |
| **d_t** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from its origin (minutes). |
| **a_{t,s}** | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (i.e., when it enters *s*). |
| **b_{t,s}** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s* (i.e., when it leaves *s*). |
| **y_{t,s,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed level *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| **e_t** | continuous, ≥0 | Energy consumed by train *t* over the whole trip (kWh). |

*Note:* For a train that does **not** use a segment (because the segment is not on its chosen route), the corresponding variables are forced to zero by constraints.

---

## 3. Objective function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T}\bigl(d_t-\tau_t^0\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

* The first term penalises any departure later than the originally planned time (positive delay).  
* The second term penalises the total energy consumption, which is a linear function of the speed‑level choices (see the definition of *e_t* below).

Both weights can be tuned to reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑usage variables**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R}\delta_{t,r,s}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

The left‑hand side is 1 if the train traverses *s* (with some speed level) and 0 otherwise; the right‑hand side is 1 exactly when the chosen route contains *s*.

### 4.2 Speed‑level selection (mutual exclusivity)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

A train can use at most one speed level on a given segment (or none if the segment is not on its route).

### 4.3 Time‑flow (travel‑time) constraints  

For every train *t* and every segment *s* that it traverses (i.e., \(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=1\)):

\[
b_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{t,s,k}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

Because the denominator is a linear expression (only one *y* can be 1), the fraction can be linearised with a big‑M:

\[
b_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} - M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

\[
b_{t,s} \le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k} + M\bigl(1-y_{t,s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

Thus, when \(y_{t,s,k}=1\) the travel‑time on *s* equals \(L_s/v_k\); otherwise the constraint is relaxed.

### 4.4 Continuity between consecutive segments  

Let \(\text{next}(s)\) denote the downstream neighbour of segment *s* on the chosen route (if any). For each train:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \ge b_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a downstream neighbour}
\]

If a train does **not** use segment *s*, the corresponding variables are forced to zero by (4.2) and the inequality becomes non‑binding.

### 4.5 Origin and destination dwell times  

\[
d_t \ge \tau_t^0 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{origin release}
\]

\[
a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{enter first segment}
\]

\[
b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}\ge d_t + p_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{origin dwell}
\]

\[
b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}+ q_t \le \text{Horizon\_end} \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{arrival within horizon}
\]

(If the origin/destination stations are modelled as zero‑length “segments”, the same constraints apply.)

### 4.6 Partial‑blockage capacity constraints  

Only a fraction \(\gamma_s\) of a blocked segment *s* can be occupied at any instant. A simple way to enforce this in a MILP is to limit the **simultaneous** number of trains on the segment. Let \(z_{t,s}\) be a binary indicator that the train *t* is on segment *s* at a given time slice; we avoid time‑indexing by using **pairwise head‑way** constraints (next section). The capacity constraint becomes:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} \le \bigl\lceil \gamma_s \cdot C_s \bigr\rceil \qquad \forall s\in B
\]

where \(C_s\) is the nominal (full) capacity of segment *s* (e.g., number of trains that could fit side‑by‑side). For a single‑track line \(C_s=1\), so the right‑hand side reduces to 0 or 1 depending on \(\gamma_s\).

### 4.7 Bidirectional conflict (head‑way) constraints  

If the line is single‑track and trains may travel in opposite directions, we must guarantee a safe separation. For any unordered pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) that both use segment *s* (i.e., \(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=1\) and \(\sum_k y_{t',s,k}=1\)):

\[
a_{t',s} \ge b_{t,s} + \Delta_{s,s'} \;-\; M\bigl(2- \sum_{k}y_{t,s,k} - \sum_{k}y_{t',s,k}\bigr) \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
\]

and the symmetric version with *t* and *t'* swapped. The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when at least one of the two trains does **not** occupy the segment.

### 4.8 Energy‑consumption definition  

Energy for a train is the sum over all traversed segments of (segment length) × (energy rate of the chosen speed level):

\[
e_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s \, c_k \, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

Because each \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary and at most one per segment, this expression is linear.

### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K\\
&d_t,\; a_{t,s},\; b_{t,s},\; e_t \ge 0, &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. How the model works (plain‑English explanation)

1. **Route choice** – The binary variable \(x_{t,r}\) decides whether train *t* follows its nominal route or a detour that avoids the blocked part of the network. Exactly one route must be selected.

2. **Speed choice per segment** – For every segment that a train actually traverses, the model picks one speed level \(k\) (binary \(y_{t,s,k}\)). Higher speeds reduce travel time but increase the energy term \(c_k\).

3. **Timing** –  
   * The departure time \(d_t\) cannot be earlier than the original schedule \(\tau_t^0\).  
   * Once a train enters a segment, its exit time \(b_{t,s}\) is the entry time \(a_{t,s}\) plus the travel time \(L_s/v_k\) dictated by the chosen speed.  
   * The entry time of the next segment must be at least the exit time of the previous one, guaranteeing a feasible trajectory.

4. **Partial blockage** – If a segment is partially blocked, only a fraction \(\gamma_s\) of its normal capacity may be used. This is enforced by a simple capacity inequality (4.6). In practice, for a single‑track line \(\gamma_s<1\) forces at most one train on the segment at a time.

5. **Bidirectional conflict** – When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same segment, a safety head‑way \(\Delta_{s,s'}\) is required. The big‑M formulation (4.7) activates the separation constraint only when both trains actually occupy the segment.

6. **Energy accounting** – The total energy for a train is the sum of segment lengths multiplied by the energy‑rate of the selected speed level. Because the speed level is binary, the expression stays linear.

7. **Objective** – The model simultaneously minimises (i) the total delay of all trains (weighted by \(\alpha\)) and (ii) the total energy consumption (weighted by \(\beta\)). By adjusting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can prioritize punctuality, sustainability, or a balanced trade‑off.

---

## 6. Remarks on implementation

* **Big‑M value** – Choose \(M\) larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min) so that the logical constraints are never inadvertently binding.
* **Scalability** – The number of binary variables grows with \(|T|\times|S|\times|K|\) and \(|T|\times|R|\). In practice, one can prune infeasible routes beforehand or aggregate consecutive short segments to keep the model tractable.
* **Solver** – Any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, etc.) can handle the formulation directly. If the problem size is very large, a decomposition (e.g., Benders) or a heuristic (column generation for routes) may be employed.
* **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with (i) train‑specific energy‑efficiency curves, (ii) crew‑working‑time limits, (iii) passenger‑penalty terms, or (iv) stochastic blockage durations (via scenario‑based robust MILP).

---

### Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t}(d_t-\tau_t^0)+\beta\sum_{t}e_t\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. }&
\sum_{r}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r}\delta_{t,r,s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}\le 1 &&\forall t,s\\
&b_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k}-M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k\\
&b_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v_k}+M(1-y_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k\\
&a_{t,\text{next}(s)}\ge b_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\text{ with next}\\
&d_t\ge \tau_t^0 &&\forall t\\
&a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}=d_t &&\forall t\\
&b_{t,s_{\text{dest}}}+q_t\le \text{Horizon\_end} &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{t}\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}\le \lceil\gamma_s C_s\rceil &&\forall s\in B\\
&a_{t',s}\ge b_{t,s}+ \Delta_{s,s'}-M\bigl(2-\sum_{k}y_{t,s,k}-\sum_{k}y_{t',s,k}\bigr) &&\forall t<t',s\\
&e_t =\sum_{s}\sum_{k} L_s c_k y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t\\
&x_{t,r},y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; d_t,a_{t,s},b_{t,s},e_t\ge 0 &&\forall t,r,s,k
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation captures **all** the requested elements—binary rerouting decisions, continuous timing variables, discrete speed‑level choices, partial‑segment blockage, bidirectional conflict, and a weighted delay‑plus‑energy objective—while remaining a **linear** mixed‑integer program that can be handed to any standard MILP solver.
