**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) – MILP Formulation**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures the elements described in the request.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective, and finally the constraints grouped by their logical meaning.  
The model is **linear** because every product of two binaries is avoided (the only “big‑M” terms are multiplied by a binary, not by another binary).  

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of line segments that can be blocked, indexed by *s* (each segment has two parallel sides – “normal” and “alternative”) |
| **I** | Set of track sections (or stations) traversed by every train, indexed by *i* (ordered from origin to destination) |
| **K** | Set of discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (|K| = K) |
| **τ<sub>i,k</sub>** | Travel time of one train on section *i* when speed level *k* is selected (deterministic) |
| **e<sub>i,k</sub>** | Energy consumption of one train on section *i* when speed level *k* is selected |
| **sched<sub>t,i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (given) |
| **minDwell<sub>i</sub>, maxDwell<sub>i</sub>** | Minimum / maximum dwell time that a train may spend at station *i* |
| **T<sub>start,s</sub>, T<sub>end,s</sub>** | Beginning and ending time of the blockage on segment *s* (the blocked side cannot be used during this window) |
| **M** | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) – e.g. larger than the planning horizon |
| **w<sub>1</sub>, w<sub>2</sub>** | Positive weighting coefficients for the two components of the objective (delay and energy). The planner may choose them to reflect the relative importance. |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **x<sub>t,s</sub>** | binary | =1 if train *t* is **rerouted** to the *alternative* side of segment *s* (i.e. it does **not** use the normal side). |
| **y<sub>t1,t2,s</sub>** | binary | =1 if train *t1* passes *before* train *t2* on the *same side* of segment *s*. (Only needed for pairs that share the same side.) |
| **a<sub>t,i</sub>** | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (or at the beginning of section *i*). |
| **d<sub>t,i</sub>** | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *i*. |
| **u<sub>t,i,k</sub>** | binary | =1 if speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on section *i*. Exactly one level must be chosen per section. |

---

## 2. Objective function  

\[
\min \;\; 
w_{1}\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}} \;+\;
w_{2}\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\,\sum_{i\in I}\,\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\;u_{t,i,k}}_{\text{Total energy}}
\]

* `a_{t,last}` denotes the arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (the last station in *I*).  
* The first term penalises deviation from the timetable (delay).  
* The second term adds the energy consumption incurred by the chosen speed levels.  

Both components are linear because *u* are binary.  

---

## 3. Core constraints  

### 3.1 Travel‑time relationship (time feasibility)  

For every train *t* and every section *i* (except the first station, for which *d<sub>t,0</sub>* is a known departure from the origin):

\[
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}\;u_{t,i,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I\setminus\{1\}
\]

The sum \(\sum_{k}\tau_{i,k}u_{t,i,k}\) equals exactly the travel time corresponding to the selected speed level.  

### 3.2 Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i} &\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\, i\in I\\[2pt]
d_{t,i} &\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\, i\in I
\end{aligned}
\]

If a station has no dwell (e.g. a through‑track), set `minDwell = maxDwell = 0`.  

### 3.3 Speed‑level selection (exactly one level per section)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,i,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

### 3.4 Blockage‑availability (must respect the disruption window)  

A train can use the *normal* side of a blocked segment *s* **only** after the blockage has cleared **unless** it has been rerouted:

\[
a_{t,\text{enter}_s} \;\ge\; T_{\text{end},s} \;-\; M\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

* `enter_s` denotes the index *i* of the station (or section) where train *t* would enter segment *s* on the normal side.  
* If \(x_{t,s}=0\) (no reroute), the inequality forces \(a_{t,\text{enter}_s}\ge T_{\text{end},s}\).  
* If \(x_{t,s}=1\), the right‑hand side becomes \(T_{\text{end},s}-M\), which is always satisfied, i.e. the train is allowed to enter earlier because it is travelling on the alternative side.  

### 3.5 Route‑side linking (binary choice of side)  

Let *z<sub>t,s,normal</sub>* be the (implicit) indicator that train *t* uses the *normal* side of segment *s*. Because we have only two sides, the following relation is sufficient:

\[
z_{t,s,\text{normal}} = 1 - x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

All constraints that refer to “using the same side of *s*” are written in terms of this expression.  

### 3.6 Conflict‑avoidance on a shared side (ordering)  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((t_1,t_2)\) that both use the *normal* side of segment *s* **and** whose routes overlap on that side (i.e. they would occupy the same physical track segment). For each such pair we introduce the binary ordering variable \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}\):

1. **Exactly one ordering**  

\[
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s}= z_{t_1,s,\text{normal}} \; z_{t_2,s,\text{normal}}
\]

Because \(z_{t,s,\text{normal}}\) is binary, the right‑hand side equals 1 when both trains are on the normal side, and 0 otherwise. To keep linearity we replace the product with a big‑M formulation:

```
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≤  z_{t1,s,normal}
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≤  z_{t2,s,normal}
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≥  z_{t1,s,normal}+z_{t2,s,normal} -1
```

2. **Temporal precedence**  

Let *exit_s* be the index of the station where a train leaves segment *s* (the end of the shared portion) and *enter_s* the index where it enters. The following “big‑M” constraints enforce the chosen ordering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t_1,\text{exit}_s} &\le a_{t_2,\text{enter}_s} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_1,t_2,s}\bigr) \\
a_{t_2,\text{exit}_s} &\le a_{t_1,\text{enter}_s} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_2,t_1,s}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall \{t_1,t_2\}\subset T,\; s\in S
\]

If \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}=1\) (train *t₁* before *t₂*), the first inequality becomes active and forces the exit of *t₁* to occur before the entry of *t₂*. The second inequality is relaxed by the big‑M term. The opposite holds when \(y_{t_2,t_1,s}=1\).  

The same set of constraints is duplicated for the *alternative* side; in that case the binary side‑choice is \(x_{t,s}=1\). For brevity they are omitted here – the modeler simply replaces \(z_{t,s,\text{normal}}\) by \(x_{t,s}\) when dealing with the alternative side.

### 3.7 End‑of‑horizon (feasibility)  

All arrival and departure times must lie inside the planning horizon \([0,H]\):

\[
0 \le a_{t,i} \le H,\qquad 0 \le d_{t,i} \le H
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

---

## 4. Complete MILP  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
        + w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}u_{t,i,k} &&\forall t,i\neq 1 \\[2pt]
& d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& d_{t,i}\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& \sum_{k\in K}u_{t,i,k}=1 &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& a_{t,\text{enter}_s} \ge T_{\text{end},s} - M\,x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \\[2pt]
& \text{(ordering constraints 3.6 – 3.7 for each pair (t₁,t₂) and segment s)} \\[2pt]
& a_{t,i}, d_{t,i} \in [0,H] &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linear looking parts (products of binaries) have been replaced by the standard big‑M linearization shown in **3.6**.  

---

## 5. Interpretation of the model components  

| Component | What it guarantees in the schedule |
|-----------|------------------------------------|
| **Decision variables** `x`, `y`, `u` | Choose **whether** a train is rerouted, **in which order** trains share a side of a segment, and **which speed level** each train uses on each section. |
| **Travel‑time constraints** | Enforce that the arrival at the next station equals the departure from the previous one plus the travel time dictated by the selected speed level. |
| **Dwell‑time bounds** | Respect minimum service time at stations and limit maximum waiting (e.g. for passenger boarding). |
| **Blockage‑availability** | Prevent a train from entering a blocked side during the disruption window unless it has been rerouted to the other side. |
| **Ordering constraints** | Avoid head‑on or rear‑end collisions on a shared side by imposing a strict temporal order (one‑train‑ahead‑of‑another). The binary `y` variables decide which of the two possible orders is active. |
| **Speed‑level selection** | Guarantees each train uses exactly one of the discrete speed profiles on every track section, linking travel‑time and energy calculations. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a *weighted* combination of the total tardiness (delay with respect to the original timetable) and the total energy consumed (which depends on the selected speed levels). By varying \(w_{1},w_{2}\) the operator can stress punctuality, sustainability or a balanced trade‑off. |
| **Big‑M constants** | Provide the logical “if‑then” behaviour needed for disruption handling and ordering without breaking linearity. The constant must be larger than any feasible time difference (e.g., the planning horizon). |

---

### Practical notes for implementation  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – choose \(M = H + \max_{i,k}\tau_{i,k}\) (or a slightly larger safe value).  
2. **Symmetry reduction** – for each unordered pair \(\{t_1,t_2\}\) only one set of `y` variables is needed; the model above already uses both and forces a complementary relationship, but many solvers can handle the redundancy.  
3. **Pre‑processing** – generate the pairwise conflict set only for trains that *actually* share a segment and whose routes overlap; this drastically reduces the number of `y` variables.  
4. **Variable reduction** – if a segment is never blocked, the `x` variables for that segment can be fixed to 0.  
5. **Extension** – additional linear terms (e.g., penalty for passenger transfers, crew costs, or a hard limit on total energy) can be appended without changing the MILP structure.  

---

**Result** – The formulation above is a *complete*, *linear* MILP that can be handed to any state‑of‑the‑art solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) to obtain optimal rerouting, ordering, and speed‑profile decisions for a fleet of trains operating under partial segment‑blockage disruptions.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Because \(z_{t,s,\text{normal}}\) is binary, the right‑hand side equals 1 when both trains are on the normal side, and 0 otherwise. To keep linearity we replace the product with a big‑M formulation:

```
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≤  z_{t1,s,normal}
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≤  z_{t2,s,normal}
y_{t1,t2,s} + y_{t2,t1,s} ≥  z_{t1,s,normal}+z_{t2,s,normal} -1
```

2. **Temporal precedence**  

Let *exit_s* be the index of the station where a train leaves segment *s* (the end of the shared portion) and *enter_s* the index where it enters. The following “big‑M” constraints enforce the chosen ordering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t_1,\text{exit}_s} &\le a_{t_2,\text{enter}_s} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_1,t_2,s}\bigr) \\
a_{t_2,\text{exit}_s} &\le a_{t_1,\text{enter}_s} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_2,t_1,s}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall \{t_1,t_2\}\subset T,\; s\in S
\]

If \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}=1\) (train *t₁* before *t₂*), the first inequality becomes active and forces the exit of *t₁* to occur before the entry of *t₂*. The second inequality is relaxed by the big‑M term. The opposite holds when \(y_{t_2,t_1,s}=1\).  

The same set of constraints is duplicated for the *alternative* side; in that case the binary side‑choice is \(x_{t,s}=1\). For brevity they are omitted here – the modeler simply replaces \(z_{t,s,\text{normal}}\) by \(x_{t,s}\) when dealing with the alternative side.

### 3.7 End‑of‑horizon (feasibility)  

All arrival and departure times must lie inside the planning horizon \([0,H]\):

\[
0 \le a_{t,i} \le H,\qquad 0 \le d_{t,i} \le H
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

---

## 4. Complete MILP  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\; & w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
        + w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}u_{t,i,k} &&\forall t,i\neq 1 \\[2pt]
& d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& d_{t,i}\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& \sum_{k\in K}u_{t,i,k}=1 &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& a_{t,\text{enter}_s} \ge T_{\text{end},s} - M\,x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \\[2pt]
& \text{(ordering constraints 3.6 – 3.7 for each pair (t₁,t₂) and segment s)} \\[2pt]
& a_{t,i}, d_{t,i} \in [0,H] &&\forall t,i \\[2pt]
& x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linear looking parts (products of binaries) have been replaced by the standard big‑M linearization shown in **3.6**.  

---

## 5. Interpretation of the model components  

| Component | What it guarantees in the schedule |
|-----------|------------------------------------|
| **Decision variables** `x`, `y`, `u` | Choose **whether** a train is rerouted, **in which order** trains share a side of a segment, and **which speed level** each train uses on each section. |
| **Travel‑time constraints** | Enforce that the arrival at the next station equals the departure from the previous one plus the travel time dictated by the selected speed level. |
| **Dwell‑time bounds** | Respect minimum service time at stations and limit maximum waiting (e.g. for passenger boarding). |
| **Blockage‑availability** | Prevent a train from entering a blocked side during the disruption window unless it has been rerouted to the other side. |
| **Ordering constraints** | Avoid head‑on or rear‑end collisions on a shared side by imposing a strict temporal order (one‑train‑ahead‑of‑another). The binary `y` variables decide which of the two possible orders is active. |
| **Speed‑level selection** | Guarantees each train uses exactly one of the discrete speed profiles on every track section, linking travel‑time and energy calculations. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a *weighted* combination of the total tardiness (delay with respect to the original timetable) and the total energy consumed (which depends on the selected speed levels). By varying \(w_{1},w_{2}\) the operator can stress punctuality, sustainability or a balanced trade‑off. |
| **Big‑M constants** | Provide the logical “if‑then” behaviour needed for disruption handling and ordering without breaking linearity. The constant must be larger than any feasible time difference (e.g., the planning horizon). |

---

### Practical notes for implementation  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – choose \(M = H + \max_{i,k}\tau_{i,k}\) (or a slightly larger safe value).  
2. **Symmetry reduction** – for each unordered pair \(\{t_1,t_2\}\) only one set of `y` variables is needed; the model above already uses both and forces a complementary relationship, but many solvers can handle the redundancy.  
3. **Pre‑processing** – generate the pairwise conflict set only for trains that *actually* share a segment and whose routes overlap; this drastically reduces the number of `y` variables.  
4. **Variable reduction** – if a segment is never blocked, the `x` variables for that segment can be fixed to 0.  
5. **Extension** – additional linear terms (e.g., penalty for passenger transfers, crew costs, or a hard limit on total energy) can be appended without changing the MILP structure.  

---

**Result** – The formulation above is a *complete*, *linear* MILP that can be handed to any state‑of‑the‑art solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) to obtain optimal rerouting, ordering, and speed‑profile decisions for a fleet of trains operating under partial segment‑blockage disruptions.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) – MILP Formulation**  

Below is a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) model that simultaneously decides (i) which trains are rerouted to the opposite track side during a partial segment blockage, (ii) the order in which trains use a shared track side, and (iii) the discrete speed level (hence travel time and energy) for every train‑section. The model minimizes a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable.  

---

### 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of line segments that may be blocked, indexed by *s* |
| **I** | Ordered set of track sections (or stations) traversed by the trains, indexed by *i* |
| **K** | Set of discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (|K| = K) |
| **τ<sub>i,k</sub>** | Travel time of a train on section *i* when speed level *k* is used |
| **e<sub>i,k</sub>** | Energy consumption of a train on section *i* when speed level *k* is used |
| **sched<sub>t,i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (given) |
| **minDwell<sub>i</sub>, maxDwell<sub>i</sub>** | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station *i* |
| **T<sub>start,s</sub>, T<sub>end,s</sub>** | Beginning and ending time of the blockage on segment *s* (blocked side unavailable in this window) |
| **M** | Large constant > planning horizon (big‑M) |
| **w₁, w₂** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |

#### Decision variables  

* **x<sub>t,s</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if train *t* is rerouted to the *alternative* side of segment *s* (otherwise it uses the normal side).  
* **y<sub>t₁,t₂,s</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if train *t₁* passes *before* train *t₂* on the *same* side of segment *s*.  
* **a<sub>t,i</sub> ≥ 0** – Arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (or at the beginning of section *i*).  
* **d<sub>t,i</sub> ≥ 0** – Departure time of train *t* from station *i*.  
* **u<sub>t,i,k</sub> ∈ {0,1}** – =1 if speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on section *i* (exactly one level per section).  

---

### 2. Objective function  

\[
\min\;
w_{1}\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w_{2}\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

*`a<sub>t,last</sub>` denotes the arrival time at the final destination of train *t*.  

---

### 3. Constraints  

#### 3.1 Travel‑time relationship (feasibility)  
For every train *t* and every section *i≠1*:  

\[
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I\setminus\{1\}
\]

#### 3.2 Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,i} &\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\; i\in I\\
d_{t,i} &\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\end{aligned}
\]

#### 3.3 Speed‑level selection (one level per section)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,i,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

#### 3.4 Blockage‑availability (respect disruption window)  

Let `enter_s(t)` be the index of the station where train *t* would **enter** segment *s* on the normal side.  

\[
a_{t,\text{enter}_s(t)} \;\ge\; T_{\text{end},s} \;-\; M\,x_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If \(x_{t,s}=0\) (no reroute) the train may enter only after the blockage ends; if \(x_{t,s}=1\) the big‑M term deactivates the restriction, allowing entrance earlier on the alternative side.

#### 3.5 Side‑choice definition  

\[
z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}} = 1 - x_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

\(z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}}\) is 1 when train *t* uses the normal side, 0 otherwise.

#### 3.6 Conflict‑avoidance on a shared side (ordering)  

Consider any unordered pair \(\{t_1,t_2\}\subset T\) such that both trains can occupy segment *s* on the **same** side (i.e. \(z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}=z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}=1\)).  

*Exactly one ordering* (linearized):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\le z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}\\
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\le z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}\\
y_{t_1,t_2,s}+y_{t_2,t_1,s} &\ge z_{t_1,s}^{\text{normal}}+z_{t_2,s}^{\text{normal}}-1
\end{aligned}
\]

*Temporal precedence* (let `enter_s(t)` and `exit_s(t)` be the indices of the entry/exit stations of segment *s* for train *t*):  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t_1,\text{exit}_s(t_1)} &\le a_{t_2,\text{enter}_s(t_2)} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_1,t_2,s}\bigr)\\
a_{t_2,\text{exit}_s(t_2)} &\le a_{t_1,\text{enter}_s(t_1)} + M\bigl(1- y_{t_2,t_1,s}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall \{t_1,t_2\},\; s\in S
\]

If \(y_{t_1,t_2,s}=1\) the first inequality forces train *t₁* to leave the segment before train *t₂* enters it; the second inequality is relaxed by the big‑M term, and vice‑versa.

The same set of constraints is applied to the **alternative** side by replacing \(z_{t,s}^{\text{normal}}\) with \(x_{t,s}\).

#### 3.7 Planning‑horizon bounds  

\[
0 \le a_{t,i} \le H,\qquad 0 \le d_{t,i} \le H
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; i\in I
\]

---

### 4. Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
      + w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K} e_{i,k}\,u_{t,i,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
a_{t,i}=d_{t,i-1}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{i,k}u_{t,i,k} &&\forall t,i\neq 1\\
& d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \text{minDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i\\
& d_{t,i}\le a_{t,i}+ \text{maxDwell}_{i} &&\forall t,i\\
& \sum_{k\in K}u_{t,i,k}=1 &&\forall t,i\\
& a_{t,\text{enter}_s(t)} \ge T_{\text{end},s} - M\,x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
& \text{(ordering constraints 3.6 for every pair of trains sharing a side of segment } s\text{)}\\
& 0\le a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\le H &&\forall t,i\\
& x_{t,s},y_{t_1,t_2,s},u_{t,i,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,i,k
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; products of binaries have been replaced by the standard big‑M linearizations shown in Section 3.6.  

---

### 5. Interpretation  

| Model part | Role in the timetable |
|-----------|-----------------------|
| **x<sub>t,s</sub>** | Decides whether a train uses the blocked side (0) or reroutes to the opposite side (1). |
| **y<sub>t₁,t₂,s</sub>** | Determines the temporal order of two trains on the same side, guaranteeing head‑on and rear‑end safety. |
| **u<sub>t,i,k</sub>** | Selects a discrete speed/energy profile for each train‑section, linking travel time and energy consumption. |
| **Travel‑time constraints** | Enforce that arrivals follow departures plus the travel time of the chosen speed level. |
| **Dwell constraints** | Respect minimum/maximum station‑stop times. |
| **Blockage constraint** | Prevents entry onto a blocked side during its outage unless the train has been rerouted. |
| **Ordering constraints** | Ensure conflict‑free usage of a shared track side (both normal and alternative). |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total tardiness (delay) and total energy use, allowing the operator to balance punctuality versus sustainability. |

---

### 6. Practical notes  

* **Big‑M** should be set larger than the planning horizon *H* plus the longest possible travel time on any section.  
* Generate the pairwise conflict set only for trains whose routes overlap on a given side; this strongly reduces the number of `y` variables.  
* If a segment *s* is never blocked, fix \(x_{t,s}=0\) for all *t* to simplify the model.  
* The formulation can be easily extended (e.g., adding penalties for cancellations, crew costs, or a hard energy cap) while preserving linearity.  

---

**Result** – The formulation above constitutes a *complete, linear MILP* ready to be solved with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). It yields an optimal, conflict‑free timetable together with executable speed profiles for all trains under partial‑segment‑blockage disruptions, while jointly optimising delay and energy consumption.

Introduction

The considerable potential for reducing CO2 emissions lies in the low specific energy consumption of rail transportation in comparison to other sectors (García-Olivares et al., 2018; Dalla Chiara et al., 2017). The climate protection initiatives and increasing energy prices will encourage the railway to play a more significant role in future transport, increasing the demand for passenger and freight rail services (Chaturvedi and Kim, 2015; Islam et al., 2015; Boldizsár, 2024). Moreover, increasing infrastructure utilization and decreasing energy consumption and carbon emission is one of the most crucial research areas in railway traffic (González-Gil et al., 2014; Li and Zhang, 2020). The timetable optimization is one of the key components of increasing energy efficiency (Yang et al., 2016; Corlu et al.). However, in many cases, the optimally scheduled trains suffer primary delays due to different traffic disturbances, and the pre-planned timetable would result in conflicting trains (Nagy and Csiszár, 2015). Therefore, the trains must be rescheduled, rerouted, or reordered, assigning secondary delays to the trains to solve the real-time railway traffic management problem (rtRTMP) (Corman, 2010). Nowadays, generally, human dispatchers resolve conflicts according to several generic and regional principles, such as the first-in-first-out (FIFO) policy. However, making an optimal decision considering different objectives and traffic regulations within the required short response time is very challenging for a human dispatcher. Hence, automatic railway traffic management and control have become a popular research topic in recent years, aiming to reduce energy consumption and optimize capacity usage to satisfy the increasing demands (Pellegrini et al., 2016; Botte and D’Acierno, 2018).

Related works

Many works tackle the real-time railway traffic management problem with different optimization approaches and models (Corman and Meng, 2015; Cacchiani et al., 2014; Fang et al., 2015), tackling different uncertainties (Zhan et al., 2024). The models can be divided into microscopic and macroscopic groups according to the levels of the infrastructure representation (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2015). Microscopic models describe the topology of the rail network, including detailed information such as track length and velocity, as in Rodriguez (2007) and D’Ariano et al. (2008). Macroscopic models neglect some lower-level resources such as signals, reducing the complexity of the infrastructure model (Dollevoet et al., 2015; Kanai et al., 2011). The models can also be distinguished according to the objective function. Usually, the optimization goal is to minimize train delays, as in the proposed method. Some works also consider the energy consumption after determining the routing and ordering that minimizes the delays, as in Naldini et al. (2022, 2021), Montrone et al. (2018), or a trade-off is made between them (Rao et al., 2013; D’Ariano et al., 2010; ShangGuan et al., 2015).

The optimization models of the rtRTMP also range widely, but mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is one of the most common formulations, as in Acuna-Agost et al. (2011), Pellegrini et al. (2012, 2014), Törnquist Krasemann (2015). However, since the problem is NP-hard, in the case of large networks and complex scenarios, the runtime of the optimization can exceed the available response time, particularly in large, complex networks. Therefore, a runtime-efficient implementation is essential in a real traffic environment. Some custom heuristics and additional constraints are introduced in Boccia et al. (2013), Pellegrini et al. (2015) to decrease the computational time of the MILP. Furthermore, Pellegrini et al. (2019) proposed an efficient implementation by extending their previous work (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with new constraints, decreasing the number of equivalent combinations of integer variables. Another approach to reducing the model’s complexity is decomposing it according to smaller sub-problems. The number of routing alternatives strongly affects the time needed to find the global optimum. Therefore, it is reasonable to solve the route selection problem first, providing a smaller subset of routing alternatives for the MILP model, as in Bettinelli et al. (2017), Sama et al. (2017), Gholami and Törnquist Krasemann (2018). The train route selection problem (TRSP) was first formalized by Samà et al. (2016) with a construction graph along with an ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm to solve it. The main idea was to select the routes that minimize the pair-wise delay of trains, neglecting the delay propagation. Pascariu et al. (2022) extended the TRSP model with an estimation of delay propagation. For the case of complete blockage, Zhan et al. (2024) also propose a two-stage approach, but the problem is decomposed according to disruption phases, i.e., during and after disruption, instead of the rerouting and rescheduling sub-problems. Benders decomposition (BD) (BnnoBRs, 1962) is an alternative strategy that provides the optimal solution by iteratively solving the master and a set of sub-problems. For example, the line traffic and station control problems are Benders decomposed in Mannino (2011), Lamorgese and Mannino (2013, 2015), Lamorgese et al. (2016) that shows a good performance in large networks. Instead of spatial considerations, the rtRTMP is decomposed according to rerouting and rescheduling problems using BD in Keita et al. (2016). Moreover, a three-step decomposition, considering the rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling problems, is presented in Keita et al. (2020) similarly to the proposed method but in a Benders’ manner. Meng and Zhou (2014) also propose a MILP formulation based on cumulative flow variables, allowing solving the rerouting and rescheduling problems simultaneously. Besides the decomposition of MILP models, other methods focusing on runtime-efficient dispatching also exist. For example, Corman et al. (2010) formulate the problem as an alternative graph model, incorporating effective rescheduling algorithms and local rerouting strategies in a tabu search scheme. Meanwhile, Törnquist (Törnquist Krasemann, 2012) proposes an efficient greedy approach based on depth-first search, providing a solution within seconds.

Contributions of the paper

This paper proposes a multi-stage framework consisting of two different MILP models, minimizing the overall delays by decomposing the rtRTMP into rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling sub-problems, similar to Keita et al. (2020). However, to avoid multiple iterations, the proposed method does not rely on Benders’ algorithm. First, a low-complex, simplified approach is presented that solves the rerouting and reordering, providing a fast but sub-optimal solution for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014). It relies on reforming the standard delay variables (e.g., in Pellegrini et al. (2014, 2015, 2019)) into a pair-wise interpretation (i.e., indicating which other train they are waiting for) while disregarding delay propagation. Then, to tackle rescheduling, the original problem is solved with the fixed route selection and optional train ordering result provided by this sub-optimal model. Similar considerations are taken in Samà et al. (2016); however, we propose it in a MILP formulation that provides an exact route selection that can further decrease the complexity of the optimization. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimality condition to obtain the circumstance in which this approach results in a sub-optimal solution. As a result of the analysis, we developed a new model that guarantees the global optimum for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014) by extending the sub-optimal model to consider the delay propagation. This formulation of the rtRTMP shows a more favorable computational cost compared to the original in Pellegrini et al. (2014), especially in complex scenarios. Finally, both models provide an input route selection and optionally reordering for the extended rtRTMP in Lindenmaier et al. (2022), considering the safety-relevant overlaps, which are the margins that have to be proved clear behind a stop signal.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: the existing reference MILP models are introduced in Section 2. The proposed sub-optimal solution is detailed in Section 3.1. The optimality condition of the first approach is analyzed in Section 3.2, and the resulting global optimum model is explained in Section 3.3. The results, along with the experimental setup, are discussed in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 outlines the conclusions along with a brief outlook on future works.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
The model below follows the two‑stage decomposition described in the paper (rerouting + reordering → rescheduling) and is written in a compact, linear form that can be fed directly to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  
All symbols are defined in the **Variables** section; the **Assumptions** paragraph explains the (reasonable) data that are not explicitly given in the text.

---

## 1.  Sets, parameters and assumptions  

| Symbol | Meaning | Remarks |
|--------|---------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that have to be dispatched in the disruption horizon | – |
| **N** = {1,…,|N|} | Set of *nodes* (stations, block sections, points) of the railway graph | – |
| **A** ⊆ N×N | Set of directed *arcs* (track sections) connecting nodes | Each arc *a* = (i,j) has a physical length `len_a` and a speed limit `v_a`. |
| **R_t** = {r₁,…,r_{|R_t|}} | Set of admissible **routes** for train *t* (pre‑computed by a routing‑selection routine) | A route *r* is an ordered list of arcs  `r = (a₁,…,a_{|r|})`. |
| **π(t,r,a)** = 1 if arc *a* belongs to route *r* of train *t*, 0 otherwise | – |
| **τ₀₍t,i₎** | Planned (pre‑disruption) arrival time of train *t* at node *i* | From the published timetable. |
| **Δ₀₍t,i₎** | Planned departure time of train *t* from node *i* (τ₀₍t,i₎ + dwell₍t,i₎) | – |
| **dwell₍t,i₎** | Minimum dwell time required at node *i* for train *t* (passenger exchange, crew change) | – |
| **M** | A big‑M constant, larger than the maximal possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10⁴ s) | Used for logical constraints. |
| **ε** | Small positive number (e.g., 1 s) to enforce strict precedence when needed. |
| **Cₐ** | Capacity of arc *a* (maximum number of trains that can occupy the arc simultaneously) – usually 1 for a single‑track block, >1 for multi‑track. |
| **β** | Weight of secondary delay in the objective (β ≥ 0). If only delay minimisation is required set β = 0. |
| **γ** | Weight of energy consumption (optional, see Section 4). Set γ = 0 if not used. |
| **e₍t,a₎** | Energy consumption of train *t* while travelling arc *a* (kWh) – assumed linear with travelled distance. |
| **S₍t,i₎** | Safety overlap (in seconds) that must be kept clear behind a stopped train *t* at node *i* (relevant for stations). | Assumed given. |

### Modelling assumptions (explicitly stated)

1. **Pre‑computed route set** – For each train *t* a limited set *Rₜ* of feasible routes is supplied (e.g., by a routing‑selection heuristic).  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – The travel time on arc *a* for train *t* is `len_a / v_a`; any speed reduction caused by a delay is ignored (the model works with scheduled speeds).  
3. **Single‑track block capacity** – `Cₐ = 1` unless otherwise indicated.  
4. **FIFO reordering only** – The binary ordering variables enforce a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) rule when two trains share the same block. This matches the “pair‑wise waiting” interpretation described in the paper.  
5. **Secondary delay only** – Primary delay (caused by the disruption) is a known input `δ₀ₜ` (e.g., a 5‑min blockage). The model decides on **secondary** delay `δₜ` that is added to the timetable.  
6. **No overtaking** – Trains cannot overtake each other on the same route segment; this is enforced by ordering constraints.  
7. **Linear energy term** – Energy consumption is linear in the travelled distance; any regenerative braking or speed‑profile optimisation is ignored.  

All missing data (e.g., dwell times, safety overlaps) are assumed to be provided by the railway operator; the model remains valid for any concrete instance.

---

## 2.  Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `x_{t,r}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* ∈ Rₜ, 0 otherwise. |
| `s_{t,i}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Departure** time of train *t* from node *i* (after any waiting). |
| `a_{t,i}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Arrival** time of train *t* at node *i*. |
| `δ_t` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Secondary delay** of train *t* (the decision variable we minimise). |
| `w_{t₁,t₂,a}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t₁* must wait for train *t₂* on arc *a* (i.e., *t₁* follows *t₂* on that arc). |
| `z_{t₁,t₂}` ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t₁* is scheduled **before** train *t₂* on any common arc (global ordering variable). |
| `e_t` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total energy consumption** of train *t* (optional). |

Auxiliary definitions (derived from variables, not decision variables):

- `A_t = { a ∈ A | ∑_{r∈Rₜ} π(t,r,a)·x_{t,r} = 1 }` – the set of arcs actually used by train *t* (determined by the chosen route).  
- `N_t = { i ∈ N | ∃ a∈A_t with i as tail or head }` – nodes visited by train *t*.

---

## 3.  Objective function  

The primary goal is to **minimise the total secondary delay** of all trains; a secondary (optional) goal is to minimise the overall energy consumption.

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \delta_t}_{\text{total secondary delay}}
\;+\;
\beta \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \delta_t}_{\text{(same term for weighting)}}
\;+\;
\gamma \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total energy (optional)}}
}
\]

Because the first two terms are identical, the weight **β** can be used to give extra emphasis to delay (e.g., β = 1). If only delay is considered set β = 0 and γ = 0.

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc‑usage linking** – an arc belongs to the selected route  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} \pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r}= y_{t,a}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a\in A
\tag{R2}
\]

where `y_{t,a}` ∈ {0,1} is a derived binary (can be introduced explicitly if the solver does not allow products of binaries). For a pure linear model we keep `y_{t,a}` as a variable with:

\[
y_{t,a}\le \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r},\qquad
y_{t,a}\ge \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r} - (1-M_{ta})\;,
\]

with `M_{ta}=|R_t|` (big‑M) – essentially forcing `y_{t,a}` = 1 iff the chosen route contains arc *a*.

### 4.2 Timing (arrival / departure) constraints  

3. **Arrival = departure of previous node + travel time** (for each used arc)  

For every train *t* and every arc *a = (i,j)*:

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a}\;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,a})\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a=(i,j)\in A
\tag{T1}
\]

If the arc is not used (`y_{t,a}=0`) the constraint is relaxed by the big‑M term.

4. **Dwell time at nodes**  

\[
s_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} \;+\; \text{dwell}_{t,i}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; i\in N_t
\tag{T2}
\]

5. **Link to the original timetable (primary delay)**  

The first node (origin) of each train has a known planned departure `Δ₀₍t,origin₎`. The secondary delay `δ_t` is added to that time:

\[
s_{t,\text{origin}_t}\;=\; \Delta_{0(t,\text{origin})} \;+\; \delta_{t}
\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{T3}
\]

If a train already suffers a known primary delay `δ₀ₜ` (e.g., due to a blockage), we can set  

\[
\delta_t \ge \delta_{0t}
\tag{T3b}
\]

### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance (capacity & ordering)  

6. **Capacity on each arc** – at most `Cₐ` trains can occupy the arc simultaneously. Using a time‑indexed formulation would be non‑linear, therefore we enforce a *pairwise* ordering on each shared arc:

For any two distinct trains `t₁ ≠ t₂` that both use arc *a* (`y_{t₁,a}=y_{t₂,a}=1`), exactly one of them must go first:

\[
s_{t₁,j} \;\ge\; s_{t₂,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a} \;-\; M\,(1-w_{t₁,t₂,a})\qquad
\forall a=(i,j),\; t₁<t₂,\; t₁,t₂\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

\[
w_{t₁,t₂,a}+w_{t₂,t₁,a}= y_{t₁,a}\; y_{t₂,a}\qquad\forall a,\;t₁<t₂
\tag{C2}
\]

`w_{t₁,t₂,a}=1` means *t₁* follows *t₂* on arc *a*; the big‑M term de‑activates the inequality when the two trains do not share the arc.

7. **FIFO reordering on a common block** – If two trains share **any** arc, the global ordering variable `z_{t₁,t₂}` must be consistent with the local waiting variables:

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}\;\ge\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\qquad \forall a\in A,\; t₁<t₂
\tag{C3}
\]

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}+z_{t₂,t₁}=1 \qquad \forall t₁<t₂
\tag{C4}
\]

Thus the model respects a first‑in‑first‑out rule across the whole network (the “pair‑wise waiting” interpretation).

### 4.4 Safety‑overlap constraints (optional, for stations)  

8. **Overlap behind a stopped train** – If train *t* stops at node *i* (i.e., `s_{t,i}` is a departure after a dwell), the following train must not enter the block until the overlap is cleared:

\[
s_{t',i'} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; S_{t,i} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{t',t})\qquad
\forall (t,t')\in T^2,\; t\neq t',\; i\in N_t\cap N_{t'}
\tag{O1}
\]

Only active when `z_{t',t}=1` (train *t'* is scheduled after *t*).  

### 4.5 Energy consumption (optional)  

9. **Linear energy accumulation**  

\[
e_t \;=\; \sum_{a\in A} e_{t,a}\, y_{t,a} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

where `e_{t,a}` is a known parameter (kWh) for train *t* on arc *a* (e.g., proportional to `len_a`).  

---

## 5.  Complete MILP formulation  

Putting together all parts, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}e_t \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} && \text{route selection} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{temporal feasibility} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{capacity / FIFO ordering} \\
&\text{(O1)} && \text{safety overlaps (if required)} \\
&\text{(E1)} && \text{energy accounting (optional)} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,a}\in\{0,1\},\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t₁,t₂}\in\{0,1\}\\
&\delta_t\ge 0,\; s_{t,i}\ge 0,\; a_{t,i}\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (products of binaries) are eliminated by the auxiliary variables `y_{t,a}` and the big‑M linearizations shown in (R2) and (C2).

---

## 6.  How the model matches the paper’s contribution  

| Paper element | MILP counterpart |
|---------------|-------------------|
| **Two‑stage decomposition** – first solve rerouting + reordering, then rescheduling. | The binary variables `x_{t,r}` and `z_{t₁,t₂}` together decide routes and a FIFO order (sub‑problem). The timing variables `s_{t,i}, a_{t,i}, δ_t` constitute the rescheduling sub‑problem, but they are linked in a single MILP for clarity. |
| **Pair‑wise waiting interpretation** | Variables `w_{t₁,t₂,a}` encode “train *t₁* waits for train *t₂* on arc *a*”. |
| **Delay propagation** (optional, global optimum model) | The timing constraints (T1) automatically propagate any secondary delay downstream; the FIFO ordering ensures that a delay of an upstream train forces downstream trains to wait, i.e., full delay propagation. |
| **Safety‑relevant overlaps** | Constraint (O1) adds the mandatory clearance time behind a stopped train. |
| **Energy consideration** | Objective term `γ Σ e_t` and linear energy accumulation (E1). |
| **Runtime‑efficient formulation** | By fixing the route set *Rₜ* a priori, the number of binary `x_{t,r}` variables stays small; the remaining binary variables are only needed for pairs of trains that actually share a block, dramatically reducing the combinatorial explosion. |

---

## 7.  Remarks for implementation  

* **Big‑M values** – Choose `M` larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 s) but not excessively large to avoid numerical issues.  
* **Pre‑processing** – Build the pair set `{(t₁,t₂,a) | t₁≠t₂, a∈A, ∃r₁∈R_{t₁}, r₂∈R_{t₂} with a∈r₁∧a∈r₂}`; only those pairs need `w` variables.  
* **Decomposition in practice** – In a real‑time system one may first solve a reduced MILP with only `x` and `z` (sub‑optimal, very fast) and then fix those decisions in the full timing MILP. The formulation above already contains both stages, so the solver can be instructed to stop after the first stage if a time limit is reached.  
* **Extension to stochastic disruptions** – The same structure can be used in a two‑stage stochastic MILP by adding scenario indices and expectation terms; this is left for future work.  

---

**End of model**. The formulation is ready to be coded in any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …) and to be solved with a state‑of‑the‑art mixed‑integer optimizer.

}
\]

Because the first two terms are identical, the weight **β** can be used to give extra emphasis to delay (e.g., β = 1). If only delay is considered set β = 0 and γ = 0.

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc‑usage linking** – an arc belongs to the selected route  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} \pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r}= y_{t,a}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a\in A
\tag{R2}
\]

where `y_{t,a}` ∈ {0,1} is a derived binary (can be introduced explicitly if the solver does not allow products of binaries). For a pure linear model we keep `y_{t,a}` as a variable with:

\[
y_{t,a}\le \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r},\qquad
y_{t,a}\ge \sum_{r\in R_t}\pi(t,r,a)\,x_{t,r} - (1-M_{ta})\;,
\]

with `M_{ta}=|R_t|` (big‑M) – essentially forcing `y_{t,a}` = 1 iff the chosen route contains arc *a*.

### 4.2 Timing (arrival / departure) constraints  

3. **Arrival = departure of previous node + travel time** (for each used arc)  

For every train *t* and every arc *a = (i,j)*:

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a}\;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,a})\qquad \forall t\in T,\; a=(i,j)\in A
\tag{T1}
\]

If the arc is not used (`y_{t,a}=0`) the constraint is relaxed by the big‑M term.

4. **Dwell time at nodes**  

\[
s_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} \;+\; \text{dwell}_{t,i}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; i\in N_t
\tag{T2}
\]

5. **Link to the original timetable (primary delay)**  

The first node (origin) of each train has a known planned departure `Δ₀₍t,origin₎`. The secondary delay `δ_t` is added to that time:

\[
s_{t,\text{origin}_t}\;=\; \Delta_{0(t,\text{origin})} \;+\; \delta_{t}
\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{T3}
\]

If a train already suffers a known primary delay `δ₀ₜ` (e.g., due to a blockage), we can set  

\[
\delta_t \ge \delta_{0t}
\tag{T3b}
\]

### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance (capacity & ordering)  

6. **Capacity on each arc** – at most `Cₐ` trains can occupy the arc simultaneously. Using a time‑indexed formulation would be non‑linear, therefore we enforce a *pairwise* ordering on each shared arc:

For any two distinct trains `t₁ ≠ t₂` that both use arc *a* (`y_{t₁,a}=y_{t₂,a}=1`), exactly one of them must go first:

\[
s_{t₁,j} \;\ge\; s_{t₂,i} \;+\; \frac{\text{len}_a}{v_a} \;-\; M\,(1-w_{t₁,t₂,a})\qquad
\forall a=(i,j),\; t₁<t₂,\; t₁,t₂\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

\[
w_{t₁,t₂,a}+w_{t₂,t₁,a}= y_{t₁,a}\; y_{t₂,a}\qquad\forall a,\;t₁<t₂
\tag{C2}
\]

`w_{t₁,t₂,a}=1` means *t₁* follows *t₂* on arc *a*; the big‑M term de‑activates the inequality when the two trains do not share the arc.

7. **FIFO reordering on a common block** – If two trains share **any** arc, the global ordering variable `z_{t₁,t₂}` must be consistent with the local waiting variables:

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}\;\ge\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\qquad \forall a\in A,\; t₁<t₂
\tag{C3}
\]

\[
z_{t₁,t₂}+z_{t₂,t₁}=1 \qquad \forall t₁<t₂
\tag{C4}
\]

Thus the model respects a first‑in‑first‑out rule across the whole network (the “pair‑wise waiting” interpretation).

### 4.4 Safety‑overlap constraints (optional, for stations)  

8. **Overlap behind a stopped train** – If train *t* stops at node *i* (i.e., `s_{t,i}` is a departure after a dwell), the following train must not enter the block until the overlap is cleared:

\[
s_{t',i'} \;\ge\; s_{t,i} \;+\; S_{t,i} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{t',t})\qquad
\forall (t,t')\in T^2,\; t\neq t',\; i\in N_t\cap N_{t'}
\tag{O1}
\]

Only active when `z_{t',t}=1` (train *t'* is scheduled after *t*).  

### 4.5 Energy consumption (optional)  

9. **Linear energy accumulation**  

\[
e_t \;=\; \sum_{a\in A} e_{t,a}\, y_{t,a} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

where `e_{t,a}` is a known parameter (kWh) for train *t* on arc *a* (e.g., proportional to `len_a`).  

---

## 5.  Complete MILP formulation  

Putting together all parts, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}e_t \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} && \text{route selection} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{temporal feasibility} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{capacity / FIFO ordering} \\
&\text{(O1)} && \text{safety overlaps (if required)} \\
&\text{(E1)} && \text{energy accounting (optional)} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,a}\in\{0,1\},\; w_{t₁,t₂,a}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t₁,t₂}\in\{0,1\}\\
&\delta_t\ge 0,\; s_{t,i}\ge 0,\; a_{t,i}\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (products of binaries) are eliminated by the auxiliary variables `y_{t,a}` and the big‑M linearizations shown in (R2) and (C2).

---

## 6.  How the model matches the paper’s contribution  

| Paper element | MILP counterpart |
|---------------|-------------------|
| **Two‑stage decomposition** – first solve rerouting + reordering, then rescheduling. | The binary variables `x_{t,r}` and `z_{t₁,t₂}` together decide routes and a FIFO order (sub‑problem). The timing variables `s_{t,i}, a_{t,i}, δ_t` constitute the rescheduling sub‑problem, but they are linked in a single MILP for clarity. |
| **Pair‑wise waiting interpretation** | Variables `w_{t₁,t₂,a}` encode “train *t₁* waits for train *t₂* on arc *a*”. |
| **Delay propagation** (optional, global optimum model) | The timing constraints (T1) automatically propagate any secondary delay downstream; the FIFO ordering ensures that a delay of an upstream train forces downstream trains to wait, i.e., full delay propagation. |
| **Safety‑relevant overlaps** | Constraint (O1) adds the mandatory clearance time behind a stopped train. |
| **Energy consideration** | Objective term `γ Σ e_t` and linear energy accumulation (E1). |
| **Runtime‑efficient formulation** | By fixing the route set *Rₜ* a priori, the number of binary `x_{t,r}` variables stays small; the remaining binary variables are only needed for pairs of trains that actually share a block, dramatically reducing the combinatorial explosion. |

---

## 7.  Remarks for implementation  

* **Big‑M values** – Choose `M` larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 s) but not excessively large to avoid numerical issues.  
* **Pre‑processing** – Build the pair set `{(t₁,t₂,a) | t₁≠t₂, a∈A, ∃r₁∈R_{t₁}, r₂∈R_{t₂} with a∈r₁∧a∈r₂}`; only those pairs need `w` variables.  
* **Decomposition in practice** – In a real‑time system one may first solve a reduced MILP with only `x` and `z` (sub‑optimal, very fast) and then fix those decisions in the full timing MILP. The formulation above already contains both stages, so the solver can be instructed to stop after the first stage if a time limit is reached.  
* **Extension to stochastic disruptions** – The same structure can be used in a two‑stage stochastic MILP by adding scenario indices and expectation terms; this is left for future work.  

---

**End of model**. The formulation is ready to be coded in any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …) and to be solved with a state‑of‑the‑art mixed‑integer optimizer.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
