Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model simultaneously decides  

* **which side of a partially blocked track segment each train will use,**  
* **the order in which trains occupy a shared (un‑blocked) track,**  
* **the exact arrival / departure times at every station,**  
* **the speed profile of each train in each discretised time interval,**  

so that total passenger delay and the energy spent for traction are minimised while respecting safety, capacity and physical‑dynamic constraints.

Below the complete linear (mixed‑integer) formulation is presented together with a short explanation of every set, parameter, variable and constraint block.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(\mathcal I\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\). |
| \\(\mathcal K\\) | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train), indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(\mathcal S\\) | Set of **track sides** for each segment (normally \\(\{L,R\}\\) = left/right). For a segment that is blocked on side \\(s^{*}\\) we will later force \\(r_{i,s^{*}}=0\\). |
| \\(\mathcal T\\) | Set of **time‑interval indices** used for speed‑profile discretisation, indexed by \\(t\\). The length of an interval is \\(\Delta t\\). |
| \\(\mathcal P\\) | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common track portion (potential conflict). Each element is a pair \\((i,j)\\) with \\(i\neq j\\). |
| \\(\mathcal B\\) | Set of **blocked side‑time windows**. Each element is a triple \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(L_{i,k}\\) | Distance (km) that train \\(i\\) must travel between station \\(k\\) and \\(k+1\\). |
| \\(v^{\min},v^{\max}\\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed (km/h). |
| \\(a^{\max}, d^{\max}\\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h²). |
| \\(t^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k}\\) | Minimum dwell (stop) time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\) (minutes). |
| \\(\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \\(i\\) at its final destination (minutes from a common zero). |
| \\(c^{\text{delay}}_i\\) | Weight for the delay of train \\(i\\) in the objective (e.g., passenger‑minutes). |
| \\(c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\) | Energy‑cost coefficients:  
  * \\(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}\\) multiplies the quadratic speed term (a proxy for aerodynamic drag).  
  * \\(c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\) multiplies the absolute speed‑change term (proxy for traction/braking energy). |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). |
| \\(N\\) | A “big‑N’’ constant larger than any feasible speed change (e.g., 500 km/h). |

All parameters are assumed to be known from the timetable, infrastructure data and train characteristics.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(r_{i,s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) uses side \\(s\\) of a segment that has two parallel sides; 0 otherwise. |
| \\(o_{i,j}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is scheduled **before** train \\(j\\) on a shared (single‑track) portion; 0 otherwise. (For each unordered pair we enforce \\(o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1\\).) |
| \\(a_{i,k}\\) | Continuous (≥0) | Arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\). |
| \\(d_{i,k}\\) | Continuous (≥0) | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(k\\). |
| \\(v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous (≥0) | Speed of train \\(i\\) during time interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(\Delta v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous (≥0) | **Absolute** speed change between two consecutive intervals: \\(\Delta v_{i,t}=|v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}|\\). Linearised with auxiliary binaries (see constraints). |
| \\(\alpha_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) **accelerates** in interval \\(t\\) (i.e., \\(v_{i,t+1}>v_{i,t}\\)). |
| \\(\beta_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) **decelerates** in interval \\(t\\) (i.e., \\(v_{i,t+1}<v_{i,t}\\)). |
| \\(y_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is **present** on a blocked side \\(s^{*}\\) during interval \\(t\\) (used to enforce the blockage). |

All speed‑related variables are defined for every interval that lies inside the travel time of the train; intervals outside the train’s horizon are forced to zero by additional linking constraints (not shown for brevity).

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min\; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
\Bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}\,v_{i,t}^{2}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\,\Delta v_{i,t}\Bigr)}_{\text{Approximate energy consumption}}
\]

*The first term penalises the lateness of each train at its final destination.*  
*The second term is a common linear‑quadratic proxy for traction energy: the \(v^{2}\) term captures aerodynamic drag, the \(|\Delta v|\) term captures the energy needed for acceleration/deceleration.*

Because the quadratic term \(v_{i,t}^{2}\) is not linear, it can be linearised with standard piece‑wise‑linear approximations (e.g., SOS2 variables) – the formulation below keeps it symbolic; in a pure MILP one would replace it by a set of linear segments.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Route‑choice – blockage handling  

For every blocked side‑time window \((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\in\mathcal B\) and for every train \(i\):

\[
\boxed{ r_{i,s^{*}} = 0 }\qquad\text{if the train would have to occupy the blocked side during the window.}
\]

A more flexible formulation lets the train stay on the blocked side **only after** the window has cleared:

\[
y_{i,t}\le r_{i,s^{*}}\quad\forall t\notin[T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}],\qquad
y_{i,t}=0\quad\forall t\in[T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}].
\]

If a train is forced to use the other side, the travel time on the segment must be long enough to “wait out’’ the blockage:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{\text{seg}}} \Delta t \; \ge \; T^{\text{end}}-T^{\text{start}} \;\;\;\;\text{whenever } r_{i,s^{*}}=0.
\]

(Here \(\mathcal T_{\text{seg}}\) are the intervals that cover the segment.)

### 5.2. Precedence on a single‑track portion  

For every conflicting pair \((i,j)\in\mathcal P\) that share a single‑track part of length \(L_{ij}\):

\[
\boxed{ d_{i,\text{exit}} + \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}} \le a_{j,\text{enter}} + M\,(1-o_{i,j}) }
\]
\[
\boxed{ d_{j,\text{exit}} + \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}} \le a_{i,\text{enter}} + M\,(o_{i,j}) }
\]

The binary \(o_{i,j}\) decides which train passes first; the big‑\(M\) term deactivates the opposite inequality.

Additionally we enforce a **total ordering**:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P .
\]

### 5.3. Time‑flow (arrival / departure)  

For every train \(i\) and every successive station pair \((k,k+1)\):

\[
\boxed{ a_{i,k+1} \ge d_{i,k} + \frac{L_{i,k}}{v^{\max}} } \tag{travel‑lower‑bound}
\]

The actual travel time is computed from the speed profile (see Section 5.5). A tighter equality can be written using the sum of interval lengths in which the train is moving:

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ \sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{i,k}} \Delta t \; .
\]

Dwell‑time constraints:

\[
\boxed{ d_{i,k} \ge a_{i,k}+ t^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k} } \qquad\forall i,k .
\]

### 5.4. Speed dynamics  

**Speed limits**

\[
v^{\min}\,z_{i,t} \le v_{i,t} \le v^{\max}\,z_{i,t}\qquad\forall i,t,
\]

where \(z_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether train \(i\) is present in interval \(t\) (linked to arrival/departure times).

**Acceleration / deceleration limits** (linearised with binaries \(\alpha_{i,t},\beta_{i,t}\))

\[
v_{i,t+1} - v_{i,t} \le a^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),
\]
\[
v_{i,t} - v_{i,t+1} \le d^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),
\]
\[
\alpha_{i,t}+ \beta_{i,t} \le 1 \qquad\forall i,t,
\]
\[
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t+1} - v_{i,t},
\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge -(v_{i,t+1} - v_{i,t}),
\]
\[
\Delta v_{i,t} \le N\,( \alpha_{i,t}+ \beta_{i,t} ).
\]

These constraints force \(\Delta v_{i,t}=|v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}|\) while respecting the maximal allowable acceleration/deceleration.

### 5.5. Travel‑time expressed through speeds  

For each train \(i\) and each segment between stations \(k\) and \(k+1\) we must have

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T_{i,k}} v_{i,t}\,\Delta t = L_{i,k},
\]

i.e. the **distance covered** by the speed profile over the intervals belonging to that segment equals the physical length of the segment. The set \(\mathcal T_{i,k}\) is defined implicitly by the arrival/departure times:

\[
z_{i,t}=1 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; a_{i,k} \le (t\!\!-\!\!0.5)\Delta t \le d_{i,k} \text{ for some }k .
\]

A common linear implementation introduces auxiliary binary variables that map each interval to a specific track‑section; the details are omitted here for brevity.

### 5.6. Linking route‑choice and precedence  

If two trains use the **same side** of a segment that is single‑track, they must respect a precedence order:

\[
o_{i,j} \le r_{i,s} + r_{j,s} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\; s\in\mathcal S .
\]

If the trains are on opposite sides (different \(s\)), the precedence variable can be forced to 0 (they can travel simultaneously).

### 5.7. Domain definitions  

\[
r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
\alpha_{i,t},\beta_{i,t}\in\{0,1\},
\]
\[
a_{i,k},d_{i,k},v_{i,t},\Delta v_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\]

---

## 6. How the model works (short narrative)

1. **Route choice** – binary variables \(r_{i,s}\) decide whether a train can occupy the blocked side of a segment. If the side is blocked during a given time window, the model forces \(r_{i,s}=0\) (or forces the train to wait until the window ends).

2. **Conflict resolution** – for every pair of trains that share a single‑track portion, the binary \(o_{i,j}\) decides which one passes first. The big‑\(M\) constraints turn the “first‑train” condition into a linear inequality linking the departure time of the leading train with the arrival time of the following one.

3. **Timing** – arrival and departure times are linked by minimum dwell times and by the travel time required to cover each inter‑station distance. Travel time is computed from the speed profile (constraint 5.5).

4. **Speed profile** – within each discretised time interval the model chooses a speed \(v_{i,t}\). Acceleration/deceleration limits are enforced with binaries \(\alpha_{i,t},\beta_{i,t}\); the absolute speed change \(\Delta v_{i,t}\) is linearised and appears in the objective to capture energy usage.

5. **Objective** – the first part penalises the lateness of every train (weighted by \(c^{\text{delay}}_i\)). The second part penalises the energy proxy, encouraging the optimizer to keep speeds moderate and avoid unnecessary accelerations.

6. **Result** – solving the MILP yields, for each train, (i) which side of each segment it will use, (ii) a feasible order on every shared track piece, (iii) a timetable (arrival/departure times) and (iv) a speed trajectory that together minimise the weighted sum of delay and energy while respecting all safety and physical constraints.

---

### Remarks for a practical implementation  

* **Piece‑wise linearisation of \(v^{2}\).** The quadratic term in the objective can be replaced by a set of linear segments using SOS2 or additional binaries; this restores pure MILP structure.  
* **Time‑interval length \(\Delta t\).** A typical choice for high‑speed rail is 30 s – 1 min; smaller intervals give a finer speed profile but increase model size.  
* **Big‑M values.** Choose the smallest values that still dominate the feasible region (e.g., \(M =\) maximal possible schedule horizon).  
* **Scalability.** For large networks the number of binary precedence variables grows quadratically with the number of trains that share a segment; a common reduction is to use a *time‑indexed* formulation or to apply a rolling‑horizon decomposition.  

The formulation above captures all the requested elements—binary route‑choice, binary precedence, continuous timing and speed variables, a weighted‑sum objective, and the key safety and physical constraints—so it can be handed over to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) after the usual linearisation of the quadratic terms.

Model 2:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) model that captures the description you supplied.  
All symbols are defined first, then the decision‑variable sets, the objective function and finally every constraint class.  
The model is written in a “canonical” MILP form – every non‑linear term that appears in the description (e.g. \(v^{2}\) or \(|\Delta v|\)) is linearised by auxiliary variables and big‑\(M\) constructions, so the final formulation is a pure MILP that can be handed to any commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).

---

## 1. Index Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal I = \{1,\dots ,I\}\) | Set of trains (indexed by \(i\)). |
| \(\mathcal S = \{1,2\}\) | Two possible **sides** of a segment (e.g. left/right track). |
| \(\mathcal K_i = \{k_{i,1},\dots ,k_{i,|K_i|}\}\) | Ordered list of stations that train \(i\) must visit. |
| \(\mathcal T = \{1,\dots ,T\}\) | Discrete time‑intervals for speed decisions (e.g. 1‑min slots). |
| \(\mathcal P = \{(i,j): i<j\}\) | Pairs of distinct trains (used for precedence variables). |
| \(\mathcal B \subseteq \mathcal S\) | Side(s) that are **blocked** (partial blockage). |
| \(\mathcal L\) | Set of track‑segments (each segment may have two sides). |
| \(\mathcal L_i \subseteq \mathcal L\) | Segments traversed by train \(i\) (in order). |
| \(\mathcal L_{i}^{s}\) | Segment‑side pair \((\ell ,s)\) used by train \(i\) (if \(r_{i,s}=1\)). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| \(\text{sched}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(k)\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(k\). | [s] |
| \(\text{sched}_{i}^{\text{dep}}(k)\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(i\) at station \(k\). | [s] |
| \(d_{\ell}\) | Physical length of segment \(\ell\). | [km] |
| \(v_{\min},\,v_{\max}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any segment. | [km/h] |
| \(a_{\max},\,d_{\max}\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers). | [km/h²] |
| \(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{\min}(i,k)\) | Minimum dwell (stop) time of train \(i\) at station \(k\). | [s] |
| \(T_{\text{start}},\,T_{\text{end}}\) | Start / end of the blockage window (absolute time). | [s] |
| \(c_{1},c_{2}\) | Energy‑cost coefficients (see objective). | – |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M” constant larger than any feasible time or speed value. | – |
| \(\Delta t\) | Length of a speed‑interval \(t\) (e.g. 60 s). | [s] |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(r_{i,s}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \(i\) uses **side** \(s\) of every segment that it traverses. (Only one side can be chosen: \(\sum_{s} r_{i,s}=1\)). |
| \(o_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \(i\) **precedes** train \(j\) on every common segment (i.e. \(i\) gets the right‑of‑way). |
| \(a_{i,k}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual **arrival** time of train \(i\) at station \(k\). |
| \(d_{i,k}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual **departure** time of train \(i\) from station \(k\). |
| \(v_{i,t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Speed of train \(i\) during time‑interval \(t\) (assumed constant inside the interval). |
| \(\delta^{+}_{i,t},\;\delta^{-}_{i,t}\) | binary | \(\delta^{+}_{i,t}=1\) if train \(i\) **accelerates** in interval \(t\); \(\delta^{-}_{i,t}=1\) if it **decelerates**. (Both cannot be 1 simultaneously). |
| \(e_{i,t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Auxiliary variable that linearises the quadratic energy term \(v_{i,t}^{2}\). |
| \(\phi_{i,t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Auxiliary variable that linearises \(|\Delta v_{i,t}| = |v_{i,t}-v_{i,t-1}|\). |
| \(z_{i,\ell}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \(i\) traverses segment \(\ell\) (used to link precedence). |

---

## 4. Linearisation of Non‑linear Terms  

1. **Quadratic speed term**  
   \[
   e_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t}^{2},\qquad
   e_{i,t} \ge 0
   \]  
   This is linearised with a **piece‑wise linear** (or SOS‑2) approximation of the convex function \(v^{2}\). In a pure MILP we replace it by a set of linear constraints over break‑points \(\{v^{(p)}\}\) and auxiliary λ‑variables (standard technique).  

2. **Absolute speed change**  
   \[
   \phi_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t} - v_{i,t-1},\qquad
   \phi_{i,t} \ge -(v_{i,t} - v_{i,t-1}),\qquad
   \phi_{i,t}\ge 0 .
   \]  

3. **Acceleration / deceleration binary linking**  
   \[
   v_{i,t} - v_{i,t-1} \le a_{\max}\,\Delta t + M(1-\delta^{+}_{i,t}) ,\\
   v_{i,t-1} - v_{i,t} \le d_{\max}\,\Delta t + M(1-\delta^{-}_{i,t}) ,\\
   \delta^{+}_{i,t} + \delta^{-}_{i,t} \le 1 .
   \]  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

The planner wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption**:

\[
\min\; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(a_{i,k^{\text{last}}}-\text{sched}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(k^{\text{last}})\bigr)}_{\displaystyle\text{Total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\alpha\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\Bigl(c_{1}\,e_{i,t}+c_{2}\,\phi_{i,t}\Bigr)}_{\displaystyle\text{Energy consumption (quadratic speed + speed‑change)}}
\]

where \(k^{\text{last}}\) denotes the final station of train \(i\) and \(\alpha\ge 0\) is a user‑chosen trade‑off weight.

All terms are linear because \(e_{i,t}\) and \(\phi_{i,t}\) are linearised auxiliary variables.

---

## 6. Model Constraints  

### 6.1. Route‑choice (side) selection  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{R1}
\]

If a side is blocked, the corresponding binary must be forced to zero for the trains that would otherwise use it (see §6.4).

### 6.2. Precedence on shared tracks  

For every pair of trains \((i,j)\in\mathcal P\) that share at least one segment (i.e. \(\exists \ell\) with \(z_{i,\ell}=z_{j,\ell}=1\)) we enforce a **either‑or** ordering:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P \tag{P1}
\]

If \(o_{i,j}=1\) (train \(i\) precedes \(j\)), then on every common segment the **departure** of \(i\) must happen before the **arrival** of \(j\):

\[
d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} \;+\; \frac{d_{\ell}}{v_{\max}} \;\le\; a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} \;+\; M\,(1-o_{i,j}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j \tag{P2}
\]

\(d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}\) and \(a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}}\) are the actual exit/enter times of the segment; they are expressed through the station‑time variables (see §6.5). The big‑\(M\) term de‑activates the constraint when \(o_{i,j}=0\).

### 6.3. Blockage handling  

A side \(s^{*}\) may be blocked during \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\). Two possibilities are allowed:

* **Avoid the blocked side**:  

  \[
  r_{i,s^{*}}\;=\;0 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I\;\text{if the train would otherwise need that side.}
  \]  

* **Traverse the side after the blockage**: the travel time on any segment that uses the blocked side must be scheduled **after** the blockage window:

  \[
  a_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} \;\ge\; T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\,(1-r_{i,s^{*}}) \qquad\forall i,\;\forall \ell\text{ on side }s^{*}. \tag{B1}
  \]

If the side is not chosen (\(r_{i,s^{*}}=0\)) the constraint is automatically satisfied.

### 6.4. Speed‑time – travel‑time coupling  

For each train \(i\) and each segment \(\ell\in\mathcal L_i\) (assume the segment is traversed in a single speed interval for simplicity; a more detailed version would split the segment across several \(t\)s):

\[
a_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \frac{d_{\ell}}{v_{i,\ell}} = d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} \tag{S1}
\]

where \(v_{i,\ell}\) is the **average** speed on that segment. Because \(v_{i,\ell}\) must be one of the interval speeds \(v_{i,t}\), we introduce linking binaries:

\[
v_{i,\ell}= \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} v_{i,t}\,\beta_{i,\ell,t},\qquad
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta_{i,\ell,t}=1,\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\}.
\]

If a finer resolution is required, the travel time can be expressed as the sum of the durations of the intervals used, each with its own speed.

**Speed limits**

\[
v_{\min}\le v_{i,t}\le v_{\max}\qquad\forall i,t. \tag{S2}
\]

**Acceleration / deceleration limits** (already linearised in §4)

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t} - v_{i,t-1} &\le a_{\max}\,\Delta t + M(1-\delta^{+}_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t-1} - v_{i,t} &\le d_{\max}\,\Delta t + M(1-\delta^{-}_{i,t}),\\
\delta^{+}_{i,t}+\delta^{-}_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned} \tag{S3}
\]

### 6.5. Station‑time logic (arrival / departure)  

* **Dwell time**  

  \[
  d_{i,k} - a_{i,k} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{\min}(i,k) \qquad\forall i,\;k\in\mathcal K_i. \tag{D1}
  \]

* **Travel between consecutive stations**  

  Let \(\ell(i,k)\) be the segment that connects station \(k\) to station \(k+1\) for train \(i\). Then

  \[
  a_{i,k+1} \;=\; d_{i,k} \;+\; \frac{d_{\ell(i,k)}}{v_{i,\ell(i,k)}}. \tag{D2}
  \]

  Using the same linking variables as in (S1) we keep the model linear.

* **Schedule‑adherence (optional soft constraint)**  

  If we want to penalise early arrivals we can add  

  \[
  a_{i,k}\;\ge\;\text{sched}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(k) \qquad\forall i,k,
  \]  

  but early arrivals are usually allowed (no penalty).

### 6.6. Linking route choice to segment‑side usage  

For each segment \(\ell\) we know which side \(s\) it belongs to. If train \(i\) chooses side \(s\), it must set the corresponding \(z_{i,\ell}=1\); otherwise \(z_{i,\ell}=0\):

\[
z_{i,\ell}\;\le\; r_{i,s(\ell)}\qquad\forall i,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i. \tag{L1}
\]

Conversely, if a train traverses a segment it must have selected *some* side:

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,s}\; \ge\; z_{i,\ell}\qquad\forall i,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i. \tag{L2}
\]

These constraints guarantee that the precedence variables \(o_{i,j}\) are only active on segments that are actually used by both trains.

### 6.7. Domain definitions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\quad o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\quad \beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\},\quad \delta^{+}_{i,t},\delta^{-}_{i,t}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k}, d_{i,k}, v_{i,t}, e_{i,t}, \phi_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(a_{i,k^{\text{last}}}-\text{sched}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(k^{\text{last}})\bigr)
      +\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\bigl(c_{1}e_{i,t}+c_{2}\phi_{i,t}\bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)} &&\sum_{s} r_{i,s}=1 &&\forall i,\\[2pt]
&\text{(P1)} &&o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\\[2pt]
&\text{(P2)} &&d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}+\frac{d_{\ell}}{v_{\max}}\le a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}}+M(1-o_{i,j}) &&\forall (i,j),\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j,\\[2pt]
&\text{(B1)} &&a_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}}\ge T_{\text{end}}-M(1-r_{i,s^{*}}) &&\forall i,\;\forall \ell\text{ on blocked side }s^{*},\\[2pt]
&\text{(S1)} &&a_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}}+\frac{d_{\ell}}{v_{i,\ell}}=d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} &&\forall i,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i,\\[2pt]
&\text{(S2)} &&v_{\min}\le v_{i,t}\le v_{\max} &&\forall i,t,\\[2pt]
&\text{(S3)} &&\begin{cases}
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t-1}\le a_{\max}\Delta t+M(1-\delta^{+}_{i,t})\\
v_{i,t-1}-v_{i,t}\le d_{\max}\Delta t+M(1-\delta^{-}_{i,t})\\
\delta^{+}_{i,t}+\delta^{-}_{i,t}\le 1
\end{cases} &&\forall i,t,\\[2pt]
&\text{(D1)} &&d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\ge \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{\min}(i,k) &&\forall i,k,\\[2pt]
&\text{(D2)} &&a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+\frac{d_{\ell(i,k)}}{v_{i,\ell(i,k)}} &&\forall i,k,\\[2pt]
&\text{(L1)} &&z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} &&\forall i,\ell,\\[2pt]
&\text{(L2)} &&\sum_{s} r_{i,s}\ge z_{i,\ell} &&\forall i,\ell,\\[2pt]
&\text{(Linearisation)} &&e_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t}^{2}\;(PW\text{-linear}),\;
\phi_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t}-v_{i,t-1},\;
\phi_{i,t}\ge -(v_{i,t}-v_{i,t-1}) &&\forall i,t,\\[2pt]
&\text{Domain} && r_{i,s},o_{i,j},\beta_{i,\ell,t},\delta^{+}_{i,t},\delta^{-}_{i,t}\in\{0,1\},\\
&&& a_{i,k},d_{i,k},v_{i,t},e_{i,t},\phi_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

## 8. How the Model Works (Explanation)

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Route‑choice (R1)** | Forces each train to pick exactly one side of every segment it will use. |
| **Precedence (P1‑P2)** | Guarantees a conflict‑free ordering on any segment shared by two trains. The binary \(o_{i,j}\) decides who goes first; the big‑\(M\) de‑activates the inequality when the opposite ordering is chosen. |
| **Blockage (B1)** | Implements the partial blockage: a train may still travel on the blocked side **only after** the blockage window, otherwise it must avoid that side (by setting \(r_{i,s^{*}}=0\)). |
| **Speed‑travel coupling (S1‑S3)** | Links the continuous speed variables to the actual travel time on each segment, while respecting speed limits and acceleration/deceleration capabilities. The auxiliary binaries \(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\) map a segment to a speed‑interval. |
| **Station logic (D1‑D2)** | Enforces minimum dwell times at stations and computes the arrival time at the next station from the departure time and the travel time on the connecting segment. |
| **Linking side to segment (L1‑L2)** | Makes sure that a train can only claim a segment if it has selected the side that contains that segment. |
| **Energy linearisation** | The quadratic term \(v^{2}\) (proportional to aerodynamic drag) and the absolute speed‑change term (representing acceleration energy) are replaced by linear approximations using auxiliary variables \(e_{i,t}\) and \(\phi_{i,t}\). |
| **Objective** | The first part minimises total passenger delay (difference between actual and scheduled arrival at the final destination). The second part penalises energy consumption through the two linearised terms, weighted by \(\alpha\). By varying \(\alpha\) the planner can trade‑off punctuality against energy use. |

---

### Practical notes for implementation  

* **Big‑\(M\)** should be chosen as a tight upper bound on any feasible time (e.g. the horizon length plus the longest possible travel time).  
* **Piece‑wise linearisation of \(v^{2}\)**: select a modest number of break‑points (e.g. every 10 km/h) and use SOS‑2 variables; this preserves MILP structure.  
* **Time‑interval discretisation**: if a segment is long relative to \(\Delta t\), you may need to split it into several consecutive intervals and impose flow‑conservation constraints on the \(\beta\) variables.  
* **Scalability**: the number of precedence binaries grows as \(O(I^{2})\). In large networks one can pre‑process to keep only pairs that actually share a segment, dramatically reducing model size.  

---

**Result** – The formulation above is a *complete linear MILP* that can be fed directly to a solver. It simultaneously decides (i) which side of each segment each train will use, (ii) the temporal order of competing trains, (iii) the exact arrival/departure schedule at every station, and (iv) a speed profile that respects acceleration limits while minimising a weighted combination of delay and energy consumption.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model simultaneously decides  

* which side of a partially blocked track segment each train will use,  
* the order in which trains occupy a shared (single‑track) portion,  
* the exact arrival / departure times at every station,  
* the speed profile of each train in each discretised time interval,  

so that total passenger delay and the energy spent for traction are minimised while respecting safety, capacity and physical‑dynamic constraints.  

All symbols, variables, objective and constraints are given below; the formulation is a pure mixed‑integer linear program (any non‑linear term is linearised with auxiliary variables and big‑M constructions).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(\mathcal I\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\). |
| \\(\mathcal K_i\\) | Ordered list of stations visited by train \\(i\\); index \\(k\\). |
| \\(\mathcal S=\{L,R\}\\) | Two possible **track sides** (left / right) of a segment. |
| \\(\mathcal L\\) | Set of track segments; each segment may have two sides. |
| \\(\mathcal L_i\subseteq\mathcal L\\) | Segments traversed by train \\(i\\) (in order). |
| \\(\mathcal T\\) | Set of discrete time‑intervals for speed decisions, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(\mathcal P\\) | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one segment, i.e. \\((i,j)\in\mathcal P\\) iff \\(\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j\neq\emptyset\\). |
| \\(\mathcal B\\) | Set of blocked side‑time windows, each element \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \\(d_{\ell}\\) | Length of segment \\(\ell\\). | km |
| \\(v^{\min},v^{\max}\\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed. | km/h |
| \\(a^{\max},d^{\max}\\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration. | km/h² |
| \\(\Delta t\\) | Length of a speed‑interval \\(t\\). | h |
| \\(\tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k}\\) | Minimum dwell time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\). | h |
| \\(\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \\(i\\) at its final destination. | h |
| \\(c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\\) | Weight for the delay of train \\(i\\) in the objective. | – |
| \\(c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\) | Energy‑cost coefficients (quadratic speed term and absolute speed‑change term). | – |
| \\(M\\) | Big‑M constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 h). | – |
| \\(N\\) | Big‑N constant larger than any feasible speed change (e.g. 500 km/h). | – |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data and train characteristics.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(r_{i,s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) uses side \\(s\\) of a two‑sided segment; exactly one side must be chosen. |
| \\(o_{i,j}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is scheduled **before** train \\(j\\) on every common segment; for each pair \\(o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1\\). |
| \\(a_{i,k}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(k\\). |
| \\(d_{i,k}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(k\\). |
| \\(v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Speed of train \\(i\\) during interval \\(t\\) (assumed constant inside the interval). |
| \\(\\Delta v_{i,t}\\) | Continuous, \\(\\ge 0\\) | Absolute speed change between intervals \\(t\\) and \\(t+1\\); linearised (see §4). |
| \\(\\alpha_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) accelerates in interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(\\beta_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) decelerates in interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(z_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is present on the track during interval \\(t\\) (links speed variables to the timetable). |
| \\(y_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) occupies a **blocked** side during interval \\(t\\) (used to enforce blockage). |

---

## 4. Linearisation of non‑linear terms  

*Absolute speed change*  

\[
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\]

*Acceleration / deceleration limits*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The quadratic energy term \\(v_{i,t}^{2}\\) is replaced by a piece‑wise‑linear (PW‑L) approximation using SOS2 variables; the resulting linear auxiliary variable is denoted by \\(e_{i,t}\\) (the formulation below keeps the term symbolic – in a real implementation it is linearised).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
\Bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}\,e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\,\Delta v_{i,t}\Bigr)}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

The first term penalises lateness at the final destination; the second term is a standard linear‑quadratic proxy for traction energy (quadratic speed term + absolute speed‑change term).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Route‑choice (side) selection  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I . \tag{R1}
\]

### 6.2. Blockage handling  

For each blocked side‑time window \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\in\mathcal B\\) and each train \\(i\\):

*If the train would occupy the blocked side during the window it is forbidden:*  

\[
y_{i,t}=0 \qquad\forall t\text{ with }t\Delta t\in[T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]. \tag{B1}
\]

*If the train uses the blocked side it must start **after** the window:*  

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} y_{i,t}\,\Delta t \;\ge\; T^{\text{end}}-T^{\text{start}} \;-\; M\,(1-r_{i,s^{*}}) . \tag{B2}
\]

The binary \\(y_{i,t}\\) is linked to the side‑choice:

\[
y_{i,t}\le r_{i,s^{*}} \qquad\forall i,t,s^{*}\in\mathcal S . \tag{B3}
\]

### 6.3. Precedence on shared (single‑track) portions  

For every pair \\((i,j)\in\mathcal P\\) that share at least one segment:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P . \tag{P1}
\]

If \\(o_{i,j}=1\\) (train \\(i\\) precedes \\(j\\)) then, for each common segment \\(\ell\\in\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j\\),

\[
d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} + \frac{d_{\ell}}{v^{\max}} \le a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,(1-o_{i,j}) . \tag{P2}
\]

The exit/enter times of a segment are expressed through the station times (see §6.5).  

### 6.4. Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min}\,z_{i,t} \le v_{i,t} \le v^{\max}\,z_{i,t} \qquad\forall i,t . \tag{S1}
\]

### 6.5. Station‑time logic (arrival / departure)  

*Dwell time*  

\[
d_{i,k} \ge a_{i,k} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in\mathcal K_i . \tag{D1}
\]

*Travel between consecutive stations*  

Let \\(\ell(i,k)\\) be the segment linking station \\(k\\) to \\(k+1\\) for train \\(i\\). Then

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k} + \frac{d_{\ell(i,k)}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} v_{i,t}\,\beta_{i,\ell(i,k),t}} . \tag{D2}
\]

The binary \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) selects the speed interval used on segment \\(\ell\\):

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta_{i,\ell,t}=1,\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\le z_{i,t},\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\}\;\;\forall i,\ell,t . \tag{D3}
\]

### 6.6. Linking side choice to segment usage  

If a segment \\(\ell\\) belongs to side \\(s(\ell)\\),

\[
z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} \qquad\forall i,\ell . \tag{L1}
\]

where \\(z_{i,\ell}\\) is a binary indicating that train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(\ell\\) (derived from the \\(\beta\\) variables).  

### 6.7. Acceleration / deceleration linearisation (already given in §4)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned} \tag{A1}
\]

### 6.8. Domain definitions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i,s},\,o_{i,j},\,\alpha_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,t},\,z_{i,t},\,y_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},\,d_{i,k},\,v_{i,t},\,\Delta v_{i,t},\,e_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Complete MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)
      +\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
        \bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\Delta v_{i,t}\bigr)\\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)} &&\sum_{s} r_{i,s}=1 &&\forall i,\\
&\text{(B1)–(B3)} &&\text{blockage constraints} &&\forall i,t,s^{*},\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{precedence on shared tracks} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\\
&\text{(S1)} &&v^{\min}z_{i,t}\le v_{i,t}\le v^{\max}z_{i,t} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(A1)} &&\text{acceleration / deceleration limits} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(D1)–(D3)} &&\text{arrival / departure and segment‑speed linking} &&\forall i,k,\ell,\\
&\text{(L1)} &&z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} &&\forall i,\ell,\\
&\text{(Linearisation)} &&\Delta v_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\;
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\\
&&&e_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t}^{2}\;\text{(PW‑L)} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{Domain} &&\text{binary / non‑negative variables as listed.}
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

### How the model works  

* **Route choice** (R1) forces each train to pick a side of every two‑sided segment.  
* **Blockage constraints** (B1‑B3) either forbid the blocked side during the disruption window or force the train to start using it only after the window has ended.  
* **Precedence variables** \\(o_{i,j}\\) guarantee a conflict‑free ordering on any single‑track portion (P1‑P2).  
* **Speed variables** \\(v_{i,t}\\) together with binaries \\(z_{i,t}\\) and \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) describe the speed profile and link it to the travel time between stations (D2).  
* **Acceleration / deceleration limits** (A1) and the linearised absolute speed‑change variables \\(\Delta v_{i,t}\\) capture realistic train dynamics and appear in the energy part of the objective.  
* **Arrival / departure times** obey minimum dwell times (D1) and are computed from the speed‑derived travel times (D2‑D3).  
* The **objective** minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and the energy proxy, allowing the planner to trade‑off punctuality against energy consumption via the coefficients \\(c^{\text{delay}}_{i},c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\).

The formulation is ready to be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). By adjusting the big‑M/N values, the granularity of the time‑interval \\(\Delta t\\) and the piece‑wise‑linear approximation of the quadratic speed term, the model can be scaled to realistic high‑speed railway instances while preserving the exact coupling between train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockages.

| \\(\\beta_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) decelerates in interval \\(t\\). |
| \\(z_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) is present on the track during interval \\(t\\) (links speed variables to the timetable). |
| \\(y_{i,t}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) occupies a **blocked** side during interval \\(t\\) (used to enforce blockage). |

---

## 4. Linearisation of non‑linear terms  

*Absolute speed change*  

\[
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t} \ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\qquad
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\]

*Acceleration / deceleration limits*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\,\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The quadratic energy term \\(v_{i,t}^{2}\\) is replaced by a piece‑wise‑linear (PW‑L) approximation using SOS2 variables; the resulting linear auxiliary variable is denoted by \\(e_{i,t}\\) (the formulation below keeps the term symbolic – in a real implementation it is linearised).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
\Bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}\,e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\,\Delta v_{i,t}\Bigr)}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

The first term penalises lateness at the final destination; the second term is a standard linear‑quadratic proxy for traction energy (quadratic speed term + absolute speed‑change term).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Route‑choice (side) selection  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I . \tag{R1}
\]

### 6.2. Blockage handling  

For each blocked side‑time window \\((s^{*},T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}})\\in\mathcal B\\) and each train \\(i\\):

*If the train would occupy the blocked side during the window it is forbidden:*  

\[
y_{i,t}=0 \qquad\forall t\text{ with }t\Delta t\in[T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]. \tag{B1}
\]

*If the train uses the blocked side it must start **after** the window:*  

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} y_{i,t}\,\Delta t \;\ge\; T^{\text{end}}-T^{\text{start}} \;-\; M\,(1-r_{i,s^{*}}) . \tag{B2}
\]

The binary \\(y_{i,t}\\) is linked to the side‑choice:

\[
y_{i,t}\le r_{i,s^{*}} \qquad\forall i,t,s^{*}\in\mathcal S . \tag{B3}
\]

### 6.3. Precedence on shared (single‑track) portions  

For every pair \\((i,j)\in\mathcal P\\) that share at least one segment:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P . \tag{P1}
\]

If \\(o_{i,j}=1\\) (train \\(i\\) precedes \\(j\\)) then, for each common segment \\(\ell\\in\mathcal L_i\cap\mathcal L_j\\),

\[
d_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}} + \frac{d_{\ell}}{v^{\max}} \le a_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,(1-o_{i,j}) . \tag{P2}
\]

The exit/enter times of a segment are expressed through the station times (see §6.5).  

### 6.4. Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min}\,z_{i,t} \le v_{i,t} \le v^{\max}\,z_{i,t} \qquad\forall i,t . \tag{S1}
\]

### 6.5. Station‑time logic (arrival / departure)  

*Dwell time*  

\[
d_{i,k} \ge a_{i,k} + \tau^{\text{dwell}}_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in\mathcal K_i . \tag{D1}
\]

*Travel between consecutive stations*  

Let \\(\ell(i,k)\\) be the segment linking station \\(k\\) to \\(k+1\\) for train \\(i\\). Then

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k} + \frac{d_{\ell(i,k)}}{\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} v_{i,t}\,\beta_{i,\ell(i,k),t}} . \tag{D2}
\]

The binary \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) selects the speed interval used on segment \\(\ell\\):

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\beta_{i,\ell,t}=1,\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\le z_{i,t},\qquad
\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\}\;\;\forall i,\ell,t . \tag{D3}
\]

### 6.6. Linking side choice to segment usage  

If a segment \\(\ell\\) belongs to side \\(s(\ell)\\),

\[
z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} \qquad\forall i,\ell . \tag{L1}
\]

where \\(z_{i,\ell}\\) is a binary indicating that train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(\ell\\) (derived from the \\(\beta\\) variables).  

### 6.7. Acceleration / deceleration linearisation (already given in §4)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t} &\le a^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\alpha_{i,t}),\\
v_{i,t}-v_{i,t+1} &\le d^{\max}\Delta t + N\,(1-\beta_{i,t}),\\
\alpha_{i,t}+\beta_{i,t} &\le 1 .
\end{aligned} \tag{A1}
\]

### 6.8. Domain definitions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{i,s},\,o_{i,j},\,\alpha_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,t},\,z_{i,t},\,y_{i,t},\,\beta_{i,\ell,t}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,k},\,d_{i,k},\,v_{i,t},\,\Delta v_{i,t},\,e_{i,t}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Complete MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}c^{\text{delay}}_{i}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\tau^{\text{sched}}_{i}\bigr)
      +\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}
        \bigl(c^{\text{energy}}_{1}e_{i,t}+c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\Delta v_{i,t}\bigr)\\
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)} &&\sum_{s} r_{i,s}=1 &&\forall i,\\
&\text{(B1)–(B3)} &&\text{blockage constraints} &&\forall i,t,s^{*},\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{precedence on shared tracks} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal P,\\
&\text{(S1)} &&v^{\min}z_{i,t}\le v_{i,t}\le v^{\max}z_{i,t} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(A1)} &&\text{acceleration / deceleration limits} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{(D1)–(D3)} &&\text{arrival / departure and segment‑speed linking} &&\forall i,k,\ell,\\
&\text{(L1)} &&z_{i,\ell}\le r_{i,s(\ell)} &&\forall i,\ell,\\
&\text{(Linearisation)} &&\Delta v_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t},\;
\Delta v_{i,t}\ge -(v_{i,t+1}-v_{i,t}),\\
&&&e_{i,t}\ge v_{i,t}^{2}\;\text{(PW‑L)} &&\forall i,t,\\
&\text{Domain} &&\text{binary / non‑negative variables as listed.}
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

### How the model works  

* **Route choice** (R1) forces each train to pick a side of every two‑sided segment.  
* **Blockage constraints** (B1‑B3) either forbid the blocked side during the disruption window or force the train to start using it only after the window has ended.  
* **Precedence variables** \\(o_{i,j}\\) guarantee a conflict‑free ordering on any single‑track portion (P1‑P2).  
* **Speed variables** \\(v_{i,t}\\) together with binaries \\(z_{i,t}\\) and \\(\beta_{i,\ell,t}\\) describe the speed profile and link it to the travel time between stations (D2).  
* **Acceleration / deceleration limits** (A1) and the linearised absolute speed‑change variables \\(\Delta v_{i,t}\\) capture realistic train dynamics and appear in the energy part of the objective.  
* **Arrival / departure times** obey minimum dwell times (D1) and are computed from the speed‑derived travel times (D2‑D3).  
* The **objective** minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and the energy proxy, allowing the planner to trade‑off punctuality against energy consumption via the coefficients \\(c^{\text{delay}}_{i},c^{\text{energy}}_{1},c^{\text{energy}}_{2}\\).

The formulation is ready to be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). By adjusting the big‑M/N values, the granularity of the time‑interval \\(\Delta t\\) and the piece‑wise‑linear approximation of the quadratic speed term, the model can be scaled to realistic high‑speed railway instances while preserving the exact coupling between train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockages.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1: Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the key decisions required for **integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked**. The model is written in a **compact, linear‑algebraic form** (suitable for a solver such as CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) together with a short narrative that explains every set, parameter, decision variable, the objective function and each group of constraints. --- ## 1. Sets and Indices | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|----------| | **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* | | **S** | Set of line‑segments (track sections) that a train may traverse, indexed by *s* | | **D** | Set of directions on a segment: `d = 1` (original/original direction), `d = 2` (opposite direction) | | **B ⊆ S** | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (the blockage window is known) | | **P** | Set of ordered train‑pairs that could conflict on a shared segment (i.e., pairs of trains that may occupy the same segment in opposite directions). Each element is a tuple *(t, t′, s)*. | --- ## 2. Parameters | Symbol | Description | Units | |--------|-------------|-------| | `L_s` | Length of segment *s* | km | | `Vmax_{s,d}` | Maximum admissible speed on segment *s* in direction *d* | km/h | | `Vmin_{s,d}` | Minimum admissible speed on segment *s* in direction *d* | km/h | | `Δt_acc` | Minimum time needed to accelerate from `Vmin` to `Vmax` (or decelerate) on any segment | h | | `Δt_dwell_t` | Minimum dwell (station‑stop) time for train *t* (if it stops on segment *s*) | h | | `E_{s,d}` | Energy cost coefficient for travelling segment *s* in direction *d* at speed `v` (linearised, see §4) | $/h | | `W_delay` | Weight of total delay in the objective | $/h | | `W_energy` | Weight of total energy consumption in the objective | $/h | | `t0_t` | Planned (unperturbed) departure time of train *t* from its origin | h | | `t_deadline_t` | Latest acceptable arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (service‑level constraint) | h | | `β_{s}` | Binary indicator of whether segment *s* is **blocked** (`β_s = 1` if blocked, 0 otherwise) | | `τ^{start}_s , τ^{end}_s` | Start and end of the blockage time window on segment *s* (only defined if `β_s = 1`) | h | | `γ_{t,s}` | 1 if train *t* **must** traverse segment *s* (its route passes through *s*), 0 otherwise | – | | `σ_{t,s}` | 1 if train *t* **stops** on segment *s* (i.e., a station is located on *s*), 0 otherwise | – | --- ## 3. Decision Variables | Variable | Type | Meaning | |----------|------|----------| | `x_{t,s,d} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | **Route‑choice**: 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* in direction *d* (original direction = 1, opposite = 2). For a given *(t,s)* exactly one direction can be chosen if `γ_{t,s}=1`. | | `z_{t,t′,s} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | **Conflict‑ordering** on shared segment *s*: 1 if train *t* passes segment *s* **before** train *t′* (when they travel in opposite directions). | | `a_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** (entry) node of segment *s*. | | `d_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** (exit) node of segment *s*. | | `v_{t,s,d} ≥ 0` | continuous | **Average speed** of train *t* on segment *s* when it uses direction *d`. | | `Δ_{t}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total delay** of train *t*: `Δ_t = a_{t,last} – (t0_t + Σ travel‑time on nominal schedule)` (linearised later). | | `e_{t}` ≥ 0 | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of segment‑wise energy terms). | *Notation*: `last` denotes the final segment of train *t*’s route. --- ## 4. Linearisation of the non‑linear speed/energy terms Both travel‑time and energy are naturally `time = distance / speed`. To keep the model linear we introduce a **piece‑wise constant speed set** `K = {k_1,…,k_K}` (e.g., 30, 60, 90 km/h). For each admissible speed `k ∈ K` we create a binary variable ``` y_{t,s,d,k} ∈ {0,1} (train t uses speed k on segment s in direction d) ``` with ``` ∑_{k∈K} y_{t,s,d,k} = x_{t,s,d} (exactly one speed if the segment is used) v_{t,s,d} = ∑_{k∈K} k·y_{t,s,d,k} ``` Travel time on segment *s* becomes a linear expression ``` τ_{t,s,d} = L_s / k when y_{t,s,d,k}=1 ``` Hence we can write ``` d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} = ∑_{k∈K} (L_s / k)· y_{t,s,d,k} for the chosen direction d ``` Energy consumption is also linearised with a coefficient `e_{s,d,k}` (energy per hour at speed *k*) : ``` e_t = ∑_{s,d,k} e_{s,d,k} · y_{t,s,d,k} ``` All remaining constraints use only linear expressions of the above variables. --- ## 5. Objective Function \[ \min \; \underbrace{W_{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} \Delta_t}_{\text{total delay penalty}} + \underbrace{W_{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{energy consumption penalty}} \] The two weighted terms allow the planner to trade‑off punctuality against energy usage. --- ## 6. Constraints ### 6.1 Route‑choice and direction consistency 1. **Exactly one direction per traversed segment** \[ \sum_{d\in D} x_{t,s,d} = \gamma_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \] If a train does not need segment *s* (`γ_{t,s}=0`) both binaries are forced to 0. 2. **Speed‑selection coupling** \[ \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,d,k}=x_{t,s,d}\qquad \forall t,s,d \] 3. **Speed bounds** (implicitly satisfied by the choice of the set *K*; if a continuous speed variable is kept, add) \[ V_{\min_{s,d}}\,x_{t,s,d}\le v_{t,s,d}\le V_{\max_{s,d}}\,x_{t,s,d} \] ### 6.2 Temporal feasibility (travel‑time definition) For every train‑segment pair that is used: \[ d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s}{k}\; y_{t,s,d,k}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; d\in D \] ### 6.3 Dwell‑time (if a station is on the segment) \[ d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}\ge \Delta t^{\text{dwell}}_{t}\; \sigma_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \] ### 6.4 Acceleration / deceleration limits (minimum time to change speed) If a train changes speed between two consecutive segments *s* and *s′*: \[ a_{t,s′} - d_{t,s} \ge \Delta t_{\text{acc}} \; \bigl|v_{t,s,d} - v_{t,s′,d′}\bigr| \] Because the absolute value is non‑linear, we use a big‑M linearisation with binary “change‑direction” variables (omitted here for brevity). In many practical instances a **minimum headway** `h_min` is sufficient: \[ a_{t,s′} - d_{t,s} \ge h_{\min}\qquad \forall (t,s,s′)\text{ consecutive} \] ### 6.5 Blockage‑window feasibility If segment *s* is blocked (`β_s = 1`), a train may occupy it **only outside** the blockage window: \[ a_{t,s} \ge \tau^{\text{end}}_s \; \text{ or } \; d_{t,s} \le \tau^{\text{start}}_s \] Linearised with a binary indicator `b_{t,s}` : \[ \begin{aligned} a_{t,s} &\ge \tau^{\text{end}}_s - M\,(1-b_{t,s})\\ d_{t,s} &\le \tau^{\text{start}}_s + M\,b_{t,s}\\ b_{t,s} &\in \{0,1\} \end{aligned} \qquad\forall t,\; s\in B \] If the train does **not** use the blocked segment (`x_{t,s,d}=0`) the constraints are automatically satisfied (big‑M `M` larger than the planning horizon). ### 6.6 Track‑capacity (single‑track conflict ordering) Only one train may occupy a **shared** segment at a time, irrespective of direction. For each conflict triple *(t, t′, s)∈P* we enforce a **disjunctive ordering**: \[ \begin{aligned} a_{t′,s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\,(1-z_{t,t′,s})\\ a_{t,s} &\ge d_{t′,s} - M\,z_{t,t′,s}\\ z_{t,t′,s} &\in \{0,1\} \end{aligned} \qquad\forall (t,t′,s)\in P \] If `z=1` train *t* goes first; if `z=0` train *t′* goes first. The big‑M constant must be larger than the planning horizon. ### 6.7 Service‑level time windows 1. **Release time at origin** \[ a_{t,\,\text{origin}_t}\ge t0_t\qquad \forall t \] 2. **Final‑arrival deadline** \[ a_{t,\,\text{last}_t}\le t_{\text{deadline},t}\qquad \forall t \] 3. **Delay definition** Let `T^{nom}_t` be the scheduled (reference) travel time of train *t* from origin to destination. Then \[ \Delta_t \ge a_{t,\,\text{last}_t} - (t0_t + T^{\text{nom}}_t)\qquad \Delta_t \ge 0 \] (The objective will minimise `Δ_t`, so the inequality becomes equality at optimality.) ### 6.8 Energy accounting \[ e_t = \sum_{s,d,k} e_{s,d,k}\; y_{t,s,d,k}\qquad \forall t\in T \] where `e_{s,d,k}` is pre‑computed (e.g., from a train‑performance model) as the **energy cost per hour** when travelling at speed *k* on segment *s* in direction *d*. --- ## 7. Summary of the Model | Component | Linear formulation | |-----------|--------------------| | **Decision variables** | Binary route‑choice `x`, binary conflict ordering `z`, binary speed‑selection `y`; continuous times `a`, `d`, delays `Δ`, energy `e`. | | **Objective** | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay (∑Δ) and total energy (∑e). | | **Key constraints** |
  • Direction selection (one per segment).
  • Travel‑time = distance / selected speed (piece‑wise linear).
  • Minimum dwell and acceleration headways.
  • Blockage‑window exclusion (big‑M).
  • Single‑track capacity via ordering binaries.
  • Service‑time windows (release, deadline, delay definition).
  • Energy accounting.
| All constraints are **linear** in the variables, and the only integer (binary) variables are `x`, `z`, `y`, and the auxiliary big‑M binaries (`b`). Hence the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed directly to a commercial or open‑source MILP solver. --- ### How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets `T`, `S`, `P`, compute distances `L_s`, speed limits, blockage windows, dwell‑time flags, and the piece‑wise speed set `K` together with the coefficients `L_s/k` and `e_{s,d,k}`. 2. **Choose weights** – `W_delay` and `W_energy` reflect the railway operator’s preference (e.g., punctuality is usually more important, so `W_delay` may be set an order of magnitude larger). 3. **Solve** – Feed the model to a MILP solver. The optimal solution provides for each train: (i) which direction to take on every segment, (ii) the exact speed class, (iii) the scheduled arrival/departure times, (iv) the conflict ordering on shared tracks, and (v) the resulting total delay and energy consumption. 4. **Interpretation** – The binary `x` variables indicate whether a train must be rerouted onto the opposite track to avoid the blocked portion. The `z` variables give a feasible timetable that respects the single‑track capacity. The continuous times `a`/`d` can be directly used for dispatching. --- **That completes the MILP formulation together with a clear description of each element.** Model 2: **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP** *(partial segment blockage – one‑track corridor, two possible routes: original direction or opposite‑track detour)* --- ## 1. Sets, parameters and data | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. | | **S** = {1,…, |S|} | Set of track‑segments (including the blocked segment **b**). | | **D** = {1,2} | Direction index: 1 = original (north‑bound), 2 = opposite (south‑bound). | | **δ(s)** | Length (km) of segment *s*. | | **v̂_min , v̂_max** | Global admissible speed limits (km/h). | | **v̂_min⁽s⁾ , v̂_max⁽s⁾** | Speed limits that are specific to segment *s* (e.g., due to curvature). | | **a_max , d_max** | Max acceleration / deceleration (km/h²). | | **τ_dwell** | Minimum dwell time at a station (minutes). | | **τ_block_start , τ_block_end** | Start / end time of the blockage on the critical segment *b*. | | **w_delay , w_energy** | Weights in the objective (relative importance of delay vs. energy). | | **E(v)** | Energy consumption function for a given speed (convex, e.g.  αv³ ). | | **π(i)** | Planned (original) departure time of train *i* (reference schedule). | | **dir⁰_i ∈ D** | Planned travel direction of train *i* (normally 1). | | **O(i)** | Set of trains that share at least one common segment with train *i* (potential conflict set). | | **B** | The blocked segment (single element of **S**). | --- ## 2. Decision variables | Variable | Type | Meaning | |----------|------|---------| | **xᵢᴰ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇒ train *i* uses **direction D** (D=1 original, D=2 opposite). | | **yᵢˢ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇒ train *i* traverses segment *s* (only the segments belonging to the chosen route are active). | | **zᵢⱼ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable for a pair (i,j) that share a segment: 1 ⇒ train *i* passes the common segment **before** train *j*. | | **tᵢᵒᵘᵗ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Actual **departure** time of train *i* from its origin node. | | **tᵢˢᵉᵍ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *i* at the **entering** node of segment *s* (only defined if yᵢˢ = 1). | | **tᵢˢˡᵉᵃᵥ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *i* from the **leaving** node of segment *s*. | | **vᵢˢ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Average speed of train *i* while traversing segment *s* (km/h). | | **Δᵢ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *i*: Δᵢ = tᵢᵒᵘᵗ – π(i). | | **eᵢ** ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumed by train *i* (sum of segment‑wise energy). | --- ## 3. Objective function \[ \min \; \underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_i}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T} e_i}_{\text{total energy}} . \] The two terms are linearized as described in the constraints (energy uses a piece‑wise linear approximation of the convex function *E(v)*). --- ## 4. Core constraints ### 4.1 Route‑choice consistency 1. **Exactly one direction is chosen** \[ x_{i1}+x_{i2}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T . \] 2. **Segment activation follows the chosen route** (A pre‑computed binary matrix **R(s,D)** = 1 if segment *s* belongs to the route for direction *D*.) \[ y_{is}\;=\;\sum_{D\in D} R(s,D)\,x_{iD} \qquad \forall i\in T,\; s\in S . \] Thus *yᵢˢ* becomes 1 only for the segments that belong to the selected direction. ### 4.2 Time‑flow on a segment For every train *i* and segment *s* with \(y_{is}=1\): 3. **Travel‑time = distance / speed** \[ t_{i\text{leave}}^{s} - t_{i\text{enter}}^{s} \;=\; \frac{ \delta(s)}{v_{is}} \qquad \forall i,s . \] 4. **Speed limits** \[ v_{\min}^{(s)} \, y_{is} \;\le\; v_{is} \;\le\; v_{\max}^{(s)} \, y_{is} \qquad \forall i,s . \] 5. **Acceleration / deceleration between successive segments** Let \(s'\) be the predecessor of *s* on train *i*’s route (if it exists). \[ v_{is} - v_{is'} \;\le\; a_{\max}\, \bigl(t_{i\text{enter}}^{s} - t_{i\text{leave}}^{s'}\bigr) \\ v_{is'} - v_{is} \;\le\; d_{\max}\, \bigl(t_{i\text{enter}}^{s} - t_{i\text{leave}}^{s'}\bigr) . \] If a predecessor does not exist (origin node) the constraints are omitted. ### 4.3 Dwell‑time at stations For each station segment *s* that is a **stop** for train *i* (pre‑computed set **St(i)**): \[ t_{i\text{leave}}^{s} - t_{i\text{enter}}^{s} \;\ge\; \tau_{\text{dwell}} \, y_{is} \qquad \forall i,\; s\in \text{St}(i). \] ### 4.4 Blockage window (partial segment closure) The blocked segment **B** can be used only outside the blockage interval: \[ t_{i\text{enter}}^{B} \;\ge\; \tau_{\text{block\_end}} \; \text{or}\; t_{i\text{leave}}^{B} \;\le\; \tau_{\text{block\_start}} \qquad \forall i . \] This logical “or” is linearized with a big‑M formulation. Introduce binary \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\): \[ t_{i\text{enter}}^{B} \ge \tau_{\text{block\_end}} - M\,b_i,\\ t_{i\text{leave}}^{B} \le \tau_{\text{block\_start}} + M\,(1-b_i),\\ b_i \in \{0,1\}. \] If \(b_i=0\) the train passes **before** the block opens; if \(b_i=1\) it passes **after** it closes. ### 4.5 Single‑track capacity (conflict ordering) For any pair \((i,j)\) that share at least one common segment (i.e. \(\exists s\) with \(y_{is}=y_{js}=1\)), we enforce that at most one train occupies the segment at a given time. The classic disjunctive (ordering) constraints are: \[ t_{i\text{enter}}^{s} \ge t_{j\text{leave}}^{s} - M\,(1-z_{ij}) \qquad \forall s\in S,\; (i,j)\in O(i)\\ t_{j\text{enter}}^{s} \ge t_{i\text{leave}}^{s} - M\,(z_{ij}) \qquad \forall s\in S,\; (i,j)\in O(i) \] where * \(z_{ij}=1\) ⇒ train *i* goes **before** train *j* on the shared segment, * \(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., horizon length). Only one of the two inequalities is active because \(z_{ij}\) is binary. ### 4.6 Delay definition \[ \Delta_i = t_{i}^{\text{out}} - \pi(i) \qquad \forall i . \] The departure time from the origin must be consistent with the first segment: \[ t_{i}^{\text{out}} = t_{i\text{enter}}^{s_{\text{origin}}} \qquad \forall i . \] ### 4.7 Energy calculation (piece‑wise linear) Assume we approximate \(E(v)=\alpha v^{3}\) by *K* linear segments \((\underline{v}_k,\overline{v}_k,\,c_k)\) where \[ c_k = \alpha \, \frac{\overline{v}_k^{3}-\underline{v}_k^{3}}{\overline{v}_k-\underline{v}_k} \] Introduce auxiliary variables \(u_{ik}^{s}\) (fraction of segment *s* of train *i* that uses speed interval *k*). \[ v_{is}= \sum_{k=1}^{K} \underline{v}_k\, u_{ik}^{s} + \sum_{k=1}^{K} (\overline{v}_k-\underline{v}_k)\, w_{ik}^{s},\\ \sum_{k=1}^{K} u_{ik}^{s}= y_{is},\qquad 0\le u_{ik}^{s}\le y_{is}. \] Energy on segment *s*: \[ e_{is}= \frac{\delta(s)}{v_{is}} \; \sum_{k=1}^{K} c_k \, u_{ik}^{s}. \] Total energy for train *i*: \[ e_i = \sum_{s\in S} e_{is}. \] (If a simpler linear approximation is acceptable, replace the above by a single linear term \(e_i = \sum_{s} \beta_s v_{is}\).) ### 4.8 Variable domains \[ \begin{aligned} &x_{iD}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{is}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{ij}\in\{0,1\},\; b_i\in\{0,1\},\\ &t_{i}^{\text{out}},\,t_{i\text{enter}}^{s},\,t_{i\text{leave}}^{s},\,\Delta_i,\,e_i \ge 0,\\ &v_{\min}\,y_{is}\le v_{is}\le v_{\max}\,y_{is}. \end{aligned} \] --- ## 5. Model summary | Component | What it does | |-----------|--------------| | **Binary route choice** (`x_{iD}`) | Allows each train to stay on its original line or to detour onto the opposite track (the only feasible alternative when a segment is blocked). | | **Segment activation** (`y_{is}`) | Links the binary route decision to the continuous variables that describe the train’s motion on each segment. | | **Ordering variables** (`z_{ij}`) | Resolve bidirectional conflicts on the shared (single‑track) portion; guarantee that at most one train occupies a segment at a time. | | **Time‑flow constraints** (`t_{i\text{enter}}^{s}, t_{i\text{leave}}^{s}`) | Ensure causality (enter → travel → leave) and respect the physical relationship between speed, distance and travel time. | | **Speed limits & acceleration** (`v_{is}`) | Keep speeds inside segment‑specific bounds and limit how fast a train can speed up or slow down between consecutive segments. | | **Blockage‑window constraints** (`b_i`) | Enforce that the blocked segment is used only before it is closed or after it re‑opens. | | **Dwell‑time constraints** | Guarantee a minimum stop time at stations (important for passenger service). | | **Delay definition** (`Δ_i`) | Provides the quantity that is penalised in the objective. | | **Energy approximation** (`e_i`) | Adds a realistic (convex) cost for higher speeds; linearised through a piece‑wise representation. | | **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption, producing a compromise schedule that respects the blockage and the single‑track capacity. | --- ### How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Build the route‑segment incidence matrix **R(s,D)**, the conflict set **O(i)**, and the segment‑specific speed limits. 2. **Choose a big‑M** – Typically a horizon of a few hours (e.g., 10 000 min) is safe. 3. **Energy linearisation** – Select *K* (e.g., 3‑5) speed intervals that give a good fit to the cubic energy law. 4. **Solve** – The resulting MILP can be handed to any modern solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP). Because the model is linear (binary + continuous), optimal solutions are guaranteed. The formulation above captures **integrated rescheduling (departure‑time shifts & route changes)** together with **speed‑management (continuous speed variables, acceleration limits, energy cost)** while respecting **partial segment blockage** and **single‑track capacity** – exactly the requirements described in the problem statement.
