Introduction

The considerable potential for reducing CO2 emissions lies in the low specific energy consumption of rail transportation in comparison to other sectors (García-Olivares et al., 2018; Dalla Chiara et al., 2017). The climate protection initiatives and increasing energy prices will encourage the railway to play a more significant role in future transport, increasing the demand for passenger and freight rail services (Chaturvedi and Kim, 2015; Islam et al., 2015; Boldizsár, 2024). Moreover, increasing infrastructure utilization and decreasing energy consumption and carbon emission is one of the most crucial research areas in railway traffic (González-Gil et al., 2014; Li and Zhang, 2020). The timetable optimization is one of the key components of increasing energy efficiency (Yang et al., 2016; Corlu et al.). However, in many cases, the optimally scheduled trains suffer primary delays due to different traffic disturbances, and the pre-planned timetable would result in conflicting trains (Nagy and Csiszár, 2015). Therefore, the trains must be rescheduled, rerouted, or reordered, assigning secondary delays to the trains to solve the real-time railway traffic management problem (rtRTMP) (Corman, 2010). Nowadays, generally, human dispatchers resolve conflicts according to several generic and regional principles, such as the first-in-first-out (FIFO) policy. However, making an optimal decision considering different objectives and traffic regulations within the required short response time is very challenging for a human dispatcher. Hence, automatic railway traffic management and control have become a popular research topic in recent years, aiming to reduce energy consumption and optimize capacity usage to satisfy the increasing demands (Pellegrini et al., 2016; Botte and D’Acierno, 2018).

Related works

Many works tackle the real-time railway traffic management problem with different optimization approaches and models (Corman and Meng, 2015; Cacchiani et al., 2014; Fang et al., 2015), tackling different uncertainties (Zhan et al., 2024). The models can be divided into microscopic and macroscopic groups according to the levels of the infrastructure representation (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2015). Microscopic models describe the topology of the rail network, including detailed information such as track length and velocity, as in Rodriguez (2007) and D’Ariano et al. (2008). Macroscopic models neglect some lower-level resources such as signals, reducing the complexity of the infrastructure model (Dollevoet et al., 2015; Kanai et al., 2011). The models can also be distinguished according to the objective function. Usually, the optimization goal is to minimize train delays, as in the proposed method. Some works also consider the energy consumption after determining the routing and ordering that minimizes the delays, as in Naldini et al. (2022, 2021), Montrone et al. (2018), or a trade-off is made between them (Rao et al., 2013; D’Ariano et al., 2010; ShangGuan et al., 2015).

The optimization models of the rtRTMP also range widely, but mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is one of the most common formulations, as in Acuna-Agost et al. (2011), Pellegrini et al. (2012, 2014), Törnquist Krasemann (2015). However, since the problem is NP-hard, in the case of large networks and complex scenarios, the runtime of the optimization can exceed the available response time, particularly in large, complex networks. Therefore, a runtime-efficient implementation is essential in a real traffic environment. Some custom heuristics and additional constraints are introduced in Boccia et al. (2013), Pellegrini et al. (2015) to decrease the computational time of the MILP. Furthermore, Pellegrini et al. (2019) proposed an efficient implementation by extending their previous work (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with new constraints, decreasing the number of equivalent combinations of integer variables. Another approach to reducing the model’s complexity is decomposing it according to smaller sub-problems. The number of routing alternatives strongly affects the time needed to find the global optimum. Therefore, it is reasonable to solve the route selection problem first, providing a smaller subset of routing alternatives for the MILP model, as in Bettinelli et al. (2017), Sama et al. (2017), Gholami and Törnquist Krasemann (2018). The train route selection problem (TRSP) was first formalized by Samà et al. (2016) with a construction graph along with an ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm to solve it. The main idea was to select the routes that minimize the pair-wise delay of trains, neglecting the delay propagation. Pascariu et al. (2022) extended the TRSP model with an estimation of delay propagation. For the case of complete blockage, Zhan et al. (2024) also propose a two-stage approach, but the problem is decomposed according to disruption phases, i.e., during and after disruption, instead of the rerouting and rescheduling sub-problems. Benders decomposition (BD) (BnnoBRs, 1962) is an alternative strategy that provides the optimal solution by iteratively solving the master and a set of sub-problems. For example, the line traffic and station control problems are Benders decomposed in Mannino (2011), Lamorgese and Mannino (2013, 2015), Lamorgese et al. (2016) that shows a good performance in large networks. Instead of spatial considerations, the rtRTMP is decomposed according to rerouting and rescheduling problems using BD in Keita et al. (2016). Moreover, a three-step decomposition, considering the rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling problems, is presented in Keita et al. (2020) similarly to the proposed method but in a Benders’ manner. Meng and Zhou (2014) also propose a MILP formulation based on cumulative flow variables, allowing solving the rerouting and rescheduling problems simultaneously. ---

## 1.  Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |

| **Sets** | |
| 𝒯 | Set of trains that have to be scheduled (|𝒯| = *T*). |
| 𝒩 | Set of nodes (stations or junctions) of the railway network. |

---

## 2.  Objective function  

The primary goal is to **minimize the total secondary delay** (the delay that the dispatcher may add to resolve conflicts). A secondary term penalises the use of many alternative routes, encouraging the original timetable when possible.

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  \;  \underbrace{ \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}  r_t }_{\text{total secondary delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{ \lambda \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} (1-\mathbf{1}_{p=p^{\text{orig}}})\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{route‑change penalty}}

\]

*λ* is a small positive weight (default = 0.1).  
*𝟙*<sub>p=p^{orig}</sub> equals 1 if *p* is the originally planned route; otherwise 0.

---

## 3.  Constraints  

### 3.1  Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall\,t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc‑usage linking** – an arc is traversed iff it belongs to the selected route  

\[
y_{t,a}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t:\; a\in p} x_{t,p} \qquad \forall\,t\in\mathcal{T},\; a\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{R2}
\]

3. **Entry time on the first arc**  

Let *a₀(t)* be the first arc of the chosen route. The train cannot start before its (primary‑delayed) departure:

\[
\tau_{t,a_0(t)} \ge \hat d_t + s_t \qquad \forall\,t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{T1}
\]

4. **Propagation of entry/exit times along the route**  

For any two consecutive arcs *a = (i,j)* and *a' = (j,k)* that belong to the same route of train *t*:

\[
\tau_{t,a'} \ge \tau'_{t,a} \qquad \forall\,t,\; a,a' \text{ consecutive on the selected route}
\tag{T2}
\]

\[
\tau'_{t,a}= \tau_{t,a}+ \theta_{t,a}\qquad \forall\,t,\;a\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{T3}
\]

6. **Arrival deadline (service‑level)**  

Let *a\* (t)* be the last arc of train *t*’s route. The final exit time must respect the latest admissible arrival:

\[
\tau'_{t,a^{*}(t)} \le U_t \qquad \forall\,t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{T4}
\]

For every conflict pair *(t,t′) ∈ 𝒞* that share an arc *a* (i.e., *y_{t,a}=y_{t′,a}=1*) we enforce a **mutual‑exclusion** using the binary variable *z<sub>t,t′,a</sub>* :

\[

\tag{C1}
\]

\[

\tag{C2}
\]

\[

\tag{C3}

where the sum denotes the scheduled (undelayed) travel time up to arc *a*. This guarantees that *r_t* is at least the longest additional waiting time; the objective minimises it, thus it will be equal to the maximum.

10. **Overlap enforcement**  

\[
\tau_{t',a} \ge \tau'_{t,a}+ \Delta \;-\; M\,(1-o_{t,a}) \qquad 
\forall\,t\neq t',\; a\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{O1}
\]

11. **Coupling of overlap activation with arc usage**  

\[
o_{t,a} \le y_{t,a} \qquad \forall\,t,a
\tag{O2}
\]

If a train does not occupy arc *a*, the overlap variable is forced to 0.

### 3.5  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\quad y_{t,a}\in\{0,1\},\quad z_{t,t′,a}\in\{0,1\},\quad o_{t,a}\in\{0,1\}\\
&r_t,\;s_t,\;\tau_{t,a},\;\tau'_{t,a}\ge 0\qquad\forall\,t,a
\end{aligned}
\tag{V}
\]

---

## 4.  Model summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} r_t \;+\; \lambda\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\!\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}(1-\mathbf{1}_{p=p^{\text{orig}}})x_{t,p}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T4)} &&\text{travel‑time propagation and service limits}\\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{pair‑wise conflict avoidance, secondary delay}\\
&\text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{optional safety‑overlap (if used)}\\
&\text{(V)} &&\text{binary / non‑negative domains.}
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable and a continuous variable, which is allowed in MILP) and can be handed to any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  

---

## 5.  Remarks on the decomposition  

1. **Stage 1 – Rerouting & Reordering (sub‑optimal model)**  
   - Solve the MILP **without** the secondary‑delay variables *r_t* (set *r_t = 0*) and without constraints (C3).

2. **Stage 2 – Rescheduling (optimal model)**  
   - Fix the route decisions *x_{t,p}* (and optionally the ordering *z*) obtained from Stage 1.

   - This yields the minimum total secondary delay while respecting the chosen routes and ordering.  

3. **Global‑optimal extension**  
   - If the optimality condition of Section 3.2 of the paper is violated (i.e., a train that waits on one arc later creates a new conflict on a downstream arc), the overlap constraints (O1)–(O2) together with (C3) guarantee that the model accounts for **delay propagation** and therefore returns the true optimum for the original rtRTMP.

---

## 6.  Possible model extensions (not required for the core formulation)

| Extension | How to incorporate |
|-----------|--------------------|
| Multi‑track arcs (capacity > 1) | Add a capacity parameter *cap_a* and a cumulative flow variable; replace (C1) with a capacity‑sum ≤ *cap_a*. |
| Energy‑consumption objective | Introduce a linear term *α·θ_{t,a}·y_{t,a}* (energy proportional to travel time) and add it to the objective with weight α. |
| Stochastic disturbances | Replace deterministic *θ_{t,a}* by its expected value and add robust‑optimization cuts (e.g., using scenario‑based binary variables). |
| Passenger‑service level (penalise late arrivals) | Add a penalty *β·max(0, τ'_{t,a^{*}} – U_t)* via an auxiliary slack variable. |

---

**End of model description**.  
All equations are linear, the binary variables capture routing, ordering, and safety‑overlap decisions, while the continuous variables represent timing and delays. The model follows directly from the narrative of the paper and can be used as a stand‑alone MILP formulation for the real‑time railway traffic management problem.

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **stand‑alone Pyomo implementation** of the mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) that captures the description you gave:

* **Binary route‑choice variables** – `r[i,t]` (train *i* uses its original route on period *t*) and `rr[i,t]` (train *i* is rerouted).  
* **Binary ordering variables** – `y[i,j,s]` tells which train is allowed to occupy shared segment *s* first when both trains use it.  
* **Continuous time, travel‑time, speed and energy variables** – departure/arrival times (`d[i]`, `a[i]`), travel time on each segment (`tt[i,s]`), speed on each segment (`v[i,s]`) and segment‑wise energy (`E[i,s]`).  

The model minimizes a **weighted sum of total delay** and **total energy consumption** while respecting:

* schedule propagation,
* speed limits that depend on the chosen route,
* physical relationship  `tt = length / speed`,
* safety‐time separation on every shared segment,
* capacity of a segment (only one train at a time),
* logical linking of rerouting to the disruption window.

You can copy‑paste the code into a Python file (e.g. `train_rescheduling.py`) and run it with any MILP solver supported by Pyomo (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, …).

---

## 1.  Imports & Data ---------------------------------------------------------

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Pyomo model for integrated train rescheduling & speed management
#   (partial segment blockage)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
from pyomo.environ import (
    ConcreteModel, Set, Param, Var, NonNegativeReals,
    Binary, Reals, Objective, Constraint, summation, minimize,
    SolverFactory
)
import pandas as pd
```

### Example data structures (replace with your real data)

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Sets
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model = ConcreteModel()

# Trains
model.T = Set(initialize=['T1', 'T2', 'T3'])               # add all train IDs

# Segments (track pieces)
model.S = Set(initialize=['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'S4'])        # all segments in the network

# Original route of each train (list of segments)
orig_route = {
    'T1': ['S1', 'S2', 'S3'],
    'T2': ['S1', 'S2', 'S4'],
    'T3': ['S1', 'S3', 'S4']
}
# Rerouted alternative (if any) – can be empty list if no alternative exists
reroute = {
    'T1': ['S1', 'S4'],          # example alt route for T1
    'T2': [],                    # T2 cannot be rerouted
    'T3': ['S2', 'S4']
}

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Parameters
# --------------------------------------------------------------

# Length of each segment (km)
seg_len = {'S1': 10, 'S2': 8, 'S3': 12, 'S4': 7}
model.L = Param(model.S, initialize=seg_len)

# Speed limits (km/h) for original and rerouted routes
# (if a train travels a segment on its original route, use v0,
#  on a rerouted route use v1 – normally v1 ≤ v0)
v0 = {('T1','S1'):120, ('T1','S2'):110, ('T1','S3'):100,
      ('T2','S1'):120, ('T2','S2'):110, ('T2','S4'):105,
      ('T3','S1'):120, ('T3','S3'):115, ('T3','S4'):105}
v1 = {('T1','S1'):110, ('T1','S4'):95,
      ('T3','S2'):100, ('T3','S4'):95}
model.v_max0 = Param(model.T, model.S, initialize=lambda m,i,s: v0.get((i,s), 0))
model.v_max1 = Param(model.T, model.S, initialize=lambda m,i,s: v1.get((i,s), 0))

# Minimum and maximum speed allowed on any segment (km/h)
model.v_min = Param(initialize=40)   # common lower bound
model.v_max = Param(initialize=130)  # common upper bound

# Dwell time at stations (minutes) – you may have a train‑specific table
dwell = {'T1':5, 'T2':4, 'T3':6}
model.Dwell = Param(model.T, initialize=dwell)

# Scheduled arrival time at the final station (minutes from time 0)
sched_arr = {'T1':120, 'T2':115, 'T3':130}
model.t_sched = Param(model.T, initialize=sched_arr)

# Safety separation time on a segment (minutes)
model.Safety = Param(initialize=3)

# Disruption window on a blocked segment (start, end) – same for all trains
# Example: segment S2 is blocked between 30 and 70 minutes.
model.blocked_seg = Param(initialize='S2')
model.block_start = Param(initialize=30)
model.block_end   = Param(initialize=70)

# Energy model parameters (α, β) – same for all trains/segments
model.alpha = Param(initialize=0.02)   # [kWh/(km·(km/h)²)]  — scaling factor
model.beta  = Param(initialize=0.5)    # [kWh/km]                — baseline consumption

# Weights in the objective
model.w_delay = Param(initialize=1.0)   # weight of total delay
model.w_energy = Param(initialize=0.01) # weight of total energy
```

---

## 2.  Decision variables -----------------------------------------------------

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Binary route‑choice variables
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# r[i] = 1  → train i follows its original route
# rr[i] = 1 → train i uses the rerouted alternative (if any)
model.r = Var(model.T, within=Binary)
model.rr = Var(model.T, within=Binary)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Ordering variables on shared segments (only defined for i<j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
def ordering_index_rule(m):
    lst = []
    for s in m.S:
        for i in m.T:
            for j in m.T:
                if i < j:                     # avoid duplicates
                    lst.append((i, j, s))
    return lst
model.Y_index = Set(initialize=ordering_index_rule, dimen=3)
model.y = Var(model.Y_index, within=Binary)   # y[i,j,s]=1 → i before j on s

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Time variables (minutes)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.d = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # departure from first station
model.a = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # arrival at last station

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Travel‑time on each segment (minutes) and speed (km/h)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.tt = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)   # travel time
model.v  = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Reals)            # speed

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Energy consumption on each segment (kWh)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.E = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)
```

---

## 3.  Model constraints -----------------------------------------------------

### 3.1  Route‑choice logic  

```python
def route_choice_rule(m, i):
    # either original or reroute (or none if no alternative)
    return m.r[i] + m.rr[i] == 1
model.RouteChoice = Constraint(model.T, rule=route_choice_rule)
```

### 3.2  Speed limits depending on the chosen route  

For each train‑segment pair we enforce the correct upper bound:

```python
def speed_ub_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment belongs to the original route → use v_max0
    # If it belongs to the rerouted route → use v_max1
    # Otherwise the segment is not traversed → speed = 0 (will be forced later)
    orig = 1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0
    rer  = 1 if s in reroute[i] else 0
    # Upper bound = orig*v_max0 + rer*v_max1  (both terms zero if not used)
    ub = orig * m.v_max0[i, s] + rer * m.v_max1[i, s]
    # If ub = 0 (segment not on any feasible route) force speed = 0
    return m.v[i, s] <= ub
model.SpeedUB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_ub_rule)
```

```python
def speed_lb_rule(m, i, s):
    # Speed cannot be positive if the train never uses this segment.
    # Use a big‑M (here 1e4) to turn on the lower bound only when segment is used.
    M = 1e4
    used = 0
    if s in orig_route[i]:
        used = 1
    elif s in reroute[i]:
        used = 1
    return m.v[i, s] >= m.v_min * used - M * (1 - used)
model.SpeedLB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_lb_rule)
```

### 3.3  Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship  

`tt = length / speed`  (linearised by cross‑multiplying, because `v` is a variable).

```python
def travel_time_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment is not used, enforce tt = 0.
    # Use binary indicator u[i,s] = 1 if segment s belongs to chosen route.
    # Instead of a new binary we reuse the speed bounds: speed = 0 ⇒ tt = 0.
    return m.tt[i, s] * m.v[i, s] == m.L[s] * 60   # convert km/h → km/min
model.TravelTime = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=travel_time_rule)
```

*(The product `tt * v` is bilinear.  To keep the model MILP we linearise it with
McCormick envelopes – see the next block.)*

#### McCormick linearisation of `tt * v = const`

```python
M_tt = 200   # upper bound on travel time (minutes) – choose a safe big‑M
M_v  = model.v_max.value
const = { (i,s): model.L[s]*60 for i in model.T for s in model.S }

def mc_tt_lower(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] >= const[(i,s)]/M_v - (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
def mc_tt_upper(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] <= const[(i,s)]/M_v + (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
model.McLower = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_lower)
model.McUpper = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_upper)
```

*(If you have a commercial solver that supports bilinear terms you can skip the above and keep the exact equality.)*

### 3.4  Time propagation (departure → arrival)

```python
def arrival_rule(m, i):
    # Sum of travel times on all segments used + dwell at intermediate stations
    # For simplicity we assume dwell only at the start (d[i]) + final dwell.
    travel_sum = sum(m.tt[i,s] for s in m.S)
    return m.a[i] == m.d[i] + travel_sum + m.Dwell[i]
model.Arrival = Constraint(model.T, rule=arrival_rule)
```

### 3.5  Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments  

If two trains both occupy the same segment **s**, the ordering binary `y[i,j,s]`
decides who goes first.

```python
def conflict_rule_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + (1 - m.y[i,j,s])*M_tt
def conflict_rule_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + m.y[i,j,s]*M_tt
def segment_used(m, i, s):
    # 1 if train i traverses segment s, 0 otherwise
    return 1 if (s in orig_route[i] and m.r[i].value==1) or \
                (s in reroute[i] and m.rr[i].value==1) else 0
```

We need to activate the conflict constraints only when **both** trains use the
segment.  This is achieved with a big‑M multiplied by the complement of the
usage indicators (`u_i_s`, `u_j_s`).  To stay within pure linear form we create
auxiliary binary usage variables.

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Auxiliary binary: u[i,s] = 1  ⇔ train i traverses segment s
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.u = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Binary)

def use_original_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0)
def use_reroute_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
def use_upper_rule(m, i, s):
    # cannot be larger than sum of the two possibilities
    return m.u[i,s] <= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0) + \
                     m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
model.UseOrig = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_original_rule)
model.UseRer  = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_reroute_rule)
model.UseUpper= Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_upper_rule)
```

Now the disjunction:

```python
def conflict_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + \
           (1 - m.y[i,j,s]) * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
def conflict_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + \
           m.y[i,j,s] * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
model.Conflict1 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_1)
model.Conflict2 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_2)
```

The term `(2 - u_i_s - u_j_s) * M_tt` de‑activates the constraint when at least
one of the trains does **not** use the segment (value ≥ M_tt).

### 3.6  Rerouting only allowed inside the disruption window  

```python
def reroute_window_rule(m, i):
    # If train i is rerouted, its departure must be after the block starts
    # and before the block ends (simple approximation).
    return m.d[i] >= m.block_start * m.rr[i]
model.RerouteStart = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_window_rule)

def reroute_end_rule(m, i):
    return m.d[i] <= m.block_end + (1 - m.rr[i]) * 1e4
model.RerouteEnd = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_end_rule)
```

### 3.7  Energy consumption on each segment  

Energy on segment *s* for train *i* :  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(\alpha v_{i,s}^{2} + \beta \bigr) \; t_{i,s}
\]

Again the product `v² * tt` is bilinear, we linearise with McCormick envelopes
by introducing an auxiliary variable `z[i,s] = v[i,s]²`.

```python
# auxiliary variable for v²
model.z = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)

def v_squared_def(m, i, s):
    return m.z[i,s] >= m.v[i,s] * m.v[i,s]
model.VSqDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=v_squared_def)

def energy_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.E[i,s] == (m.alpha * m.z[i,s] + m.beta) * m.tt[i,s]
model.EnergyDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=energy_rule)
```

(If your solver handles quadratic terms you can drop the auxiliary variable
and keep the exact expression.)

### 3.8  Total delay definition (used in objective)

```python
def delay_expr(m, i):
    return m.a[i] - m.t_sched[i]
model.Delay = Expression(model.T, rule=delay_expr)
```

---

## 4.  Objective ------------------------------------------------------------

```python
def obj_rule(m):
    total_delay  = sum(m.Delay[i] for i in m.T)
    total_energy = sum(m.E[i,s] for i in m.T for s in m.S)
    return m.w_delay * total_delay + m.w_energy * total_energy
model.Obj = Objective(rule=obj_rule, sense=minimize)
```

---

## 5.  Solve the model -------------------------------------------------------

```python
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Choose a solver that you have installed (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, GLPK, …)
    solver = SolverFactory('gurobi')          # <-- replace if needed
    results = solver.solve(model, tee=True)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   Reporting
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\n=== SOLUTION SUMMARY ===")
    for i in model.T:
        print(f"Train {i}:")
        print(f"  departure = {model.d[i]():.2f}  arrival = {model.a[i]():.2f}")
        print(f"  route choice – original: {model.r[i]():.0f}, reroute: {model.rr[i]():.0f}")
        for s in model.S:
            if model.u[i,s]():
                print(f"       segment {s}: speed = {model.v[i,s]():.1f} km/h, "
                      f"travel = {model.tt[i,s]():.2f} min, energy = {model.E[i,s]():.2f} kWh")
    print("\nTotal weighted objective =", model.Obj())
```

---

### What you need to adapt

| Item | What to change |
|------|----------------|
| **Sets** (`model.T`, `model.S`) | Fill with your actual train IDs and segments. |
| **Routes** (`orig_route`, `reroute`) | Provide the list of segments belonging to the original and any feasible alternate routes for each train. |
| **Lengths, speed limits, dwell times, scheduled arrivals** | Populate with the real network data. |
| **Disruption window** (`blocked_seg`, `block_start`, `block_end`) | Set to the segment that is partially blocked and the time interval of the blockage. |
| **Big‑M values** (`M_tt`, `M_v`, etc.) | Make them large enough for your instance but not excessively huge (helps solver performance). |
| **Solver** | Replace `'gurobi'` with the name of the MILP solver you have (e.g., `'cplex'`, `'cbc'`). |

The model is now a **pure MILP** (except for the optional quadratic tricks that can be kept if you use a solver with quadratic support). Running the script will give you the optimal set of departure times, speed profiles, route selections and the corresponding delay + energy trade‑off. Happy optimisation!

### Example data structures (replace with your real data)

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Sets
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model = ConcreteModel()

# Trains
model.T = Set(initialize=['T1', 'T2', 'T3'])               # add all train IDs

# Segments (track pieces)
model.S = Set(initialize=['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'S4'])        # all segments in the network

# Original route of each train (list of segments)
orig_route = {
    'T1': ['S1', 'S2', 'S3'],
    'T2': ['S1', 'S2', 'S4'],
    'T3': ['S1', 'S3', 'S4']
}
# Rerouted alternative (if any) – can be empty list if no alternative exists
reroute = {
    'T1': ['S1', 'S4'],          # example alt route for T1
    'T2': [],                    # T2 cannot be rerouted
    'T3': ['S2', 'S4']
}

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Parameters
# --------------------------------------------------------------

# Length of each segment (km)
seg_len = {'S1': 10, 'S2': 8, 'S3': 12, 'S4': 7}
model.L = Param(model.S, initialize=seg_len)

# Speed limits (km/h) for original and rerouted routes
# (if a train travels a segment on its original route, use v0,
#  on a rerouted route use v1 – normally v1 ≤ v0)
v0 = {('T1','S1'):120, ('T1','S2'):110, ('T1','S3'):100,
      ('T2','S1'):120, ('T2','S2'):110, ('T2','S4'):105,
      ('T3','S1'):120, ('T3','S3'):115, ('T3','S4'):105}
v1 = {('T1','S1'):110, ('T1','S4'):95,
      ('T3','S2'):100, ('T3','S4'):95}
model.v_max0 = Param(model.T, model.S, initialize=lambda m,i,s: v0.get((i,s), 0))
model.v_max1 = Param(model.T, model.S, initialize=lambda m,i,s: v1.get((i,s), 0))

# Minimum and maximum speed allowed on any segment (km/h)
model.v_min = Param(initialize=40)   # common lower bound
model.v_max = Param(initialize=130)  # common upper bound

# Dwell time at stations (minutes) – you may have a train‑specific table
dwell = {'T1':5, 'T2':4, 'T3':6}
model.Dwell = Param(model.T, initialize=dwell)

# Scheduled arrival time at the final station (minutes from time 0)
sched_arr = {'T1':120, 'T2':115, 'T3':130}
model.t_sched = Param(model.T, initialize=sched_arr)

# Safety separation time on a segment (minutes)
model.Safety = Param(initialize=3)

# Disruption window on a blocked segment (start, end) – same for all trains
# Example: segment S2 is blocked between 30 and 70 minutes.
model.blocked_seg = Param(initialize='S2')
model.block_start = Param(initialize=30)
model.block_end   = Param(initialize=70)

# Energy model parameters (α, β) – same for all trains/segments
model.alpha = Param(initialize=0.02)   # [kWh/(km·(km/h)²)]  — scaling factor
model.beta  = Param(initialize=0.5)    # [kWh/km]                — baseline consumption

# Weights in the objective
model.w_delay = Param(initialize=1.0)   # weight of total delay
model.w_energy = Param(initialize=0.01) # weight of total energy
```

---

## 2.  Decision variables -----------------------------------------------------

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Binary route‑choice variables
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# r[i] = 1  → train i follows its original route
# rr[i] = 1 → train i uses the rerouted alternative (if any)
model.r = Var(model.T, within=Binary)
model.rr = Var(model.T, within=Binary)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Ordering variables on shared segments (only defined for i<j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
def ordering_index_rule(m):
    lst = []
    for s in m.S:
        for i in m.T:
            for j in m.T:
                if i < j:                     # avoid duplicates
                    lst.append((i, j, s))
    return lst
model.Y_index = Set(initialize=ordering_index_rule, dimen=3)
model.y = Var(model.Y_index, within=Binary)   # y[i,j,s]=1 → i before j on s

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Time variables (minutes)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.d = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # departure from first station
model.a = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # arrival at last station

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Travel‑time on each segment (minutes) and speed (km/h)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.tt = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)   # travel time
model.v  = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Reals)            # speed

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Energy consumption on each segment (kWh)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.E = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)
```

---

## 3.  Model constraints -----------------------------------------------------

### 3.1  Route‑choice logic  

```python
def route_choice_rule(m, i):
    # either original or reroute (or none if no alternative)
    return m.r[i] + m.rr[i] == 1
model.RouteChoice = Constraint(model.T, rule=route_choice_rule)
```

### 3.2  Speed limits depending on the chosen route  

For each train‑segment pair we enforce the correct upper bound:

```python
def speed_ub_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment belongs to the original route → use v_max0
    # If it belongs to the rerouted route → use v_max1
    # Otherwise the segment is not traversed → speed = 0 (will be forced later)
    orig = 1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0
    rer  = 1 if s in reroute[i] else 0
    # Upper bound = orig*v_max0 + rer*v_max1  (both terms zero if not used)
    ub = orig * m.v_max0[i, s] + rer * m.v_max1[i, s]
    # If ub = 0 (segment not on any feasible route) force speed = 0
    return m.v[i, s] <= ub
model.SpeedUB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_ub_rule)
```

```python
def speed_lb_rule(m, i, s):
    # Speed cannot be positive if the train never uses this segment.
    # Use a big‑M (here 1e4) to turn on the lower bound only when segment is used.
    M = 1e4
    used = 0
    if s in orig_route[i]:
        used = 1
    elif s in reroute[i]:
        used = 1
    return m.v[i, s] >= m.v_min * used - M * (1 - used)
model.SpeedLB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_lb_rule)
```

### 3.3  Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship  

`tt = length / speed`  (linearised by cross‑multiplying, because `v` is a variable).

```python
def travel_time_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment is not used, enforce tt = 0.
    # Use binary indicator u[i,s] = 1 if segment s belongs to chosen route.
    # Instead of a new binary we reuse the speed bounds: speed = 0 ⇒ tt = 0.
    return m.tt[i, s] * m.v[i, s] == m.L[s] * 60   # convert km/h → km/min
model.TravelTime = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=travel_time_rule)
```

*(The product `tt * v` is bilinear.  To keep the model MILP we linearise it with
McCormick envelopes – see the next block.)*

#### McCormick linearisation of `tt * v = const`

```python
M_tt = 200   # upper bound on travel time (minutes) – choose a safe big‑M
M_v  = model.v_max.value
const = { (i,s): model.L[s]*60 for i in model.T for s in model.S }

def mc_tt_lower(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] >= const[(i,s)]/M_v - (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
def mc_tt_upper(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] <= const[(i,s)]/M_v + (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
model.McLower = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_lower)
model.McUpper = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_upper)
```

*(If you have a commercial solver that supports bilinear terms you can skip the above and keep the exact equality.)*

### 3.4  Time propagation (departure → arrival)

```python
def arrival_rule(m, i):
    # Sum of travel times on all segments used + dwell at intermediate stations
    # For simplicity we assume dwell only at the start (d[i]) + final dwell.
    travel_sum = sum(m.tt[i,s] for s in m.S)
    return m.a[i] == m.d[i] + travel_sum + m.Dwell[i]
model.Arrival = Constraint(model.T, rule=arrival_rule)
```

### 3.5  Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments  

If two trains both occupy the same segment **s**, the ordering binary `y[i,j,s]`
decides who goes first.

```python
def conflict_rule_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + (1 - m.y[i,j,s])*M_tt
def conflict_rule_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + m.y[i,j,s]*M_tt
def segment_used(m, i, s):
    # 1 if train i traverses segment s, 0 otherwise
    return 1 if (s in orig_route[i] and m.r[i].value==1) or \
                (s in reroute[i] and m.rr[i].value==1) else 0
```

We need to activate the conflict constraints only when **both** trains use the
segment.  This is achieved with a big‑M multiplied by the complement of the
usage indicators (`u_i_s`, `u_j_s`).  To stay within pure linear form we create
auxiliary binary usage variables.

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Auxiliary binary: u[i,s] = 1  ⇔ train i traverses segment s
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.u = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Binary)

def use_original_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0)
def use_reroute_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
def use_upper_rule(m, i, s):
    # cannot be larger than sum of the two possibilities
    return m.u[i,s] <= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0) + \
                     m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
model.UseOrig = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_original_rule)
model.UseRer  = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_reroute_rule)
model.UseUpper= Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_upper_rule)
```

Now the disjunction:

```python
def conflict_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + \
           (1 - m.y[i,j,s]) * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
def conflict_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + \
           m.y[i,j,s] * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
model.Conflict1 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_1)
model.Conflict2 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_2)
```

The term `(2 - u_i_s - u_j_s) * M_tt` de‑activates the constraint when at least
one of the trains does **not** use the segment (value ≥ M_tt).

### 3.6  Rerouting only allowed inside the disruption window  

```python
def reroute_window_rule(m, i):
    # If train i is rerouted, its departure must be after the block starts
    # and before the block ends (simple approximation).
    return m.d[i] >= m.block_start * m.rr[i]
model.RerouteStart = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_window_rule)

def reroute_end_rule(m, i):
    return m.d[i] <= m.block_end + (1 - m.rr[i]) * 1e4
model.RerouteEnd = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_end_rule)
```

### 3.7  Energy consumption on each segment  

Energy on segment *s* for train *i* :  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(\alpha v_{i,s}^{2} + \beta \bigr) \; t_{i,s}
\]

Again the product `v² * tt` is bilinear, we linearise with McCormick envelopes
by introducing an auxiliary variable `z[i,s] = v[i,s]²`.

```python
# auxiliary variable for v²
model.z = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)

def v_squared_def(m, i, s):
    return m.z[i,s] >= m.v[i,s] * m.v[i,s]
model.VSqDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=v_squared_def)

def energy_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.E[i,s] == (m.alpha * m.z[i,s] + m.beta) * m.tt[i,s]
model.EnergyDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=energy_rule)
```

(If your solver handles quadratic terms you can drop the auxiliary variable
and keep the exact expression.)

### 3.8  Total delay definition (used in objective)

```python
def delay_expr(m, i):
    return m.a[i] - m.t_sched[i]
model.Delay = Expression(model.T, rule=delay_expr)
```

---

## 4.  Objective ------------------------------------------------------------

```python
def obj_rule(m):
    total_delay  = sum(m.Delay[i] for i in m.T)
    total_energy = sum(m.E[i,s] for i in m.T for s in m.S)
    return m.w_delay * total_delay + m.w_energy * total_energy
model.Obj = Objective(rule=obj_rule, sense=minimize)
```

---

## 5.  Solve the model -------------------------------------------------------

```python
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Choose a solver that you have installed (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, GLPK, …)
    solver = SolverFactory('gurobi')          # <-- replace if needed
    results = solver.solve(model, tee=True)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   Reporting
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\n=== SOLUTION SUMMARY ===")
    for i in model.T:
        print(f"Train {i}:")
        print(f"  departure = {model.d[i]():.2f}  arrival = {model.a[i]():.2f}")
        print(f"  route choice – original: {model.r[i]():.0f}, reroute: {model.rr[i]():.0f}")
        for s in model.S:
            if model.u[i,s]():
                print(f"       segment {s}: speed = {model.v[i,s]():.1f} km/h, "
                      f"travel = {model.tt[i,s]():.2f} min, energy = {model.E[i,s]():.2f} kWh")
    print("\nTotal weighted objective =", model.Obj())
```

---

### What you need to adapt

| Item | What to change |
|------|----------------|
| **Sets** (`model.T`, `model.S`) | Fill with your actual train IDs and segments. |
| **Routes** (`orig_route`, `reroute`) | Provide the list of segments belonging to the original and any feasible alternate routes for each train. |
| **Lengths, speed limits, dwell times, scheduled arrivals** | Populate with the real network data. |
| **Disruption window** (`blocked_seg`, `block_start`, `block_end`) | Set to the segment that is partially blocked and the time interval of the blockage. |
| **Big‑M values** (`M_tt`, `M_v`, etc.) | Make them large enough for your instance but not excessively huge (helps solver performance). |
| **Solver** | Replace `'gurobi'` with the name of the MILP solver you have (e.g., `'cplex'`, `'cbc'`). |

The model is now a **pure MILP** (except for the optional quadratic tricks that can be kept if you use a solver with quadratic support). Running the script will give you the optimal set of departure times, speed profiles, route selections and the corresponding delay + energy trade‑off. Happy optimisation!

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

* **Binary ordering variables** – `y[i,j,s]` tells which train is allowed to occupy shared segment *s* first when both trains use it.

The model minimizes a **weighted sum of total delay** and **total energy consumption** while respecting:

* schedule propagation,
* speed limits that depend on the chosen route,
* physical relationship  `tt = length / speed`,
* safety‐time separation on every shared segment,
* capacity of a segment (only one train at a time),
* logical linking of rerouting to the disruption window.

# Minimum and maximum speed allowed on any segment (km/h)
model.v_min = Param(initialize=40)   # common lower bound
model.v_max = Param(initialize=130)  # common upper bound

# Dwell time at stations (minutes) – you may have a train‑specific table
dwell = {'T1':5, 'T2':4, 'T3':6}
model.Dwell = Param(model.T, initialize=dwell)

# Scheduled arrival time at the final station (minutes from time 0)
sched_arr = {'T1':120, 'T2':115, 'T3':130}
model.t_sched = Param(model.T, initialize=sched_arr)

# Safety separation time on a segment (minutes)
model.Safety = Param(initialize=3)

# Disruption window on a blocked segment (start, end) – same for all trains
# Example: segment S2 is blocked between 30 and 70 minutes.
model.blocked_seg = Param(initialize='S2')
model.block_start = Param(initialize=30)
model.block_end   = Param(initialize=70)

# Energy model parameters (α, β) – same for all trains/segments
model.alpha = Param(initialize=0.02)   # [kWh/(km·(km/h)²)]  — scaling factor
model.beta  = Param(initialize=0.5)    # [kWh/km]                — baseline consumption

# Weights in the objective
model.w_delay = Param(initialize=1.0)   # weight of total delay
model.w_energy = Param(initialize=0.01) # weight of total energy
```

---

## 2.  Decision variables -----------------------------------------------------

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Binary route‑choice variables
# --------------------------------------------------------------
# r[i] = 1  → train i follows its original route
# rr[i] = 1 → train i uses the rerouted alternative (if any)
model.r = Var(model.T, within=Binary)
model.rr = Var(model.T, within=Binary)

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Ordering variables on shared segments (only defined for i<j)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
def ordering_index_rule(m):
    lst = []
    for s in m.S:
        for i in m.T:
            for j in m.T:
                if i < j:                     # avoid duplicates
                    lst.append((i, j, s))
    return lst
model.Y_index = Set(initialize=ordering_index_rule, dimen=3)
model.y = Var(model.Y_index, within=Binary)   # y[i,j,s]=1 → i before j on s

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Time variables (minutes)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.d = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # departure from first station
model.a = Var(model.T, within=NonNegativeReals)   # arrival at last station

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Travel‑time on each segment (minutes) and speed (km/h)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.tt = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)   # travel time
model.v  = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Reals)            # speed

# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Energy consumption on each segment (kWh)
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.E = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)
```

---

## 3.  Model constraints -----------------------------------------------------

### 3.1  Route‑choice logic  

```python
def route_choice_rule(m, i):
    # either original or reroute (or none if no alternative)
    return m.r[i] + m.rr[i] == 1
model.RouteChoice = Constraint(model.T, rule=route_choice_rule)
```

### 3.2  Speed limits depending on the chosen route  

For each train‑segment pair we enforce the correct upper bound:

```python
def speed_ub_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment belongs to the original route → use v_max0
    # If it belongs to the rerouted route → use v_max1
    # Otherwise the segment is not traversed → speed = 0 (will be forced later)
    orig = 1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0
    rer  = 1 if s in reroute[i] else 0
    # Upper bound = orig*v_max0 + rer*v_max1  (both terms zero if not used)
    ub = orig * m.v_max0[i, s] + rer * m.v_max1[i, s]
    # If ub = 0 (segment not on any feasible route) force speed = 0
    return m.v[i, s] <= ub
model.SpeedUB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_ub_rule)
```

```python
def speed_lb_rule(m, i, s):
    # Speed cannot be positive if the train never uses this segment.
    # Use a big‑M (here 1e4) to turn on the lower bound only when segment is used.
    M = 1e4
    used = 0
    if s in orig_route[i]:
        used = 1
    elif s in reroute[i]:
        used = 1
    return m.v[i, s] >= m.v_min * used - M * (1 - used)
model.SpeedLB = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=speed_lb_rule)
```

### 3.3  Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship  

`tt = length / speed`  (linearised by cross‑multiplying, because `v` is a variable).

```python
def travel_time_rule(m, i, s):
    # If the segment is not used, enforce tt = 0.
    # Use binary indicator u[i,s] = 1 if segment s belongs to chosen route.
    # Instead of a new binary we reuse the speed bounds: speed = 0 ⇒ tt = 0.
    return m.tt[i, s] * m.v[i, s] == m.L[s] * 60   # convert km/h → km/min
model.TravelTime = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=travel_time_rule)
```

*(The product `tt * v` is bilinear.  To keep the model MILP we linearise it with
McCormick envelopes – see the next block.)*

#### McCormick linearisation of `tt * v = const`

```python
M_tt = 200   # upper bound on travel time (minutes) – choose a safe big‑M
M_v  = model.v_max.value
const = { (i,s): model.L[s]*60 for i in model.T for s in model.S }

def mc_tt_lower(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] >= const[(i,s)]/M_v - (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
def mc_tt_upper(m, i, s):
    return m.tt[i,s] <= const[(i,s)]/M_v + (M_tt - m.tt[i,s]) * (M_v - m.v[i,s]) / M_v
model.McLower = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_lower)
model.McUpper = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=mc_tt_upper)
```

*(If you have a commercial solver that supports bilinear terms you can skip the above and keep the exact equality.)*

### 3.4  Time propagation (departure → arrival)

```python
def arrival_rule(m, i):
    # Sum of travel times on all segments used + dwell at intermediate stations
    # For simplicity we assume dwell only at the start (d[i]) + final dwell.
    travel_sum = sum(m.tt[i,s] for s in m.S)
    return m.a[i] == m.d[i] + travel_sum + m.Dwell[i]
model.Arrival = Constraint(model.T, rule=arrival_rule)
```

### 3.5  Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments  

If two trains both occupy the same segment **s**, the ordering binary `y[i,j,s]`
decides who goes first.

```python
def conflict_rule_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + (1 - m.y[i,j,s])*M_tt
def conflict_rule_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + m.y[i,j,s]*M_tt
def segment_used(m, i, s):
    # 1 if train i traverses segment s, 0 otherwise
    return 1 if (s in orig_route[i] and m.r[i].value==1) or \
                (s in reroute[i] and m.rr[i].value==1) else 0
```

We need to activate the conflict constraints only when **both** trains use the
segment.  This is achieved with a big‑M multiplied by the complement of the
usage indicators (`u_i_s`, `u_j_s`).  To stay within pure linear form we create
auxiliary binary usage variables.

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#   Auxiliary binary: u[i,s] = 1  ⇔ train i traverses segment s
# --------------------------------------------------------------
model.u = Var(model.T, model.S, within=Binary)

def use_original_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0)
def use_reroute_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.u[i,s] >= m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
def use_upper_rule(m, i, s):
    # cannot be larger than sum of the two possibilities
    return m.u[i,s] <= m.r[i] * (1 if s in orig_route[i] else 0) + \
                     m.rr[i] * (1 if s in reroute[i] else 0)
model.UseOrig = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_original_rule)
model.UseRer  = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_reroute_rule)
model.UseUpper= Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=use_upper_rule)
```

Now the disjunction:

```python
def conflict_1(m, i, j, s):
    # i before j  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[i] + m.tt[i,s] <= m.d[j] - m.Safety + \
           (1 - m.y[i,j,s]) * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
def conflict_2(m, i, j, s):
    # j before i  (only if both use s)
    return m.d[j] + m.tt[j,s] <= m.d[i] - m.Safety + \
           m.y[i,j,s] * M_tt + (2 - m.u[i,s] - m.u[j,s]) * M_tt
model.Conflict1 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_1)
model.Conflict2 = Constraint(model.Y_index, rule=conflict_2)
```

The term `(2 - u_i_s - u_j_s) * M_tt` de‑activates the constraint when at least
one of the trains does **not** use the segment (value ≥ M_tt).

### 3.6  Rerouting only allowed inside the disruption window  

```python
def reroute_window_rule(m, i):
    # If train i is rerouted, its departure must be after the block starts
    # and before the block ends (simple approximation).
    return m.d[i] >= m.block_start * m.rr[i]
model.RerouteStart = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_window_rule)

def reroute_end_rule(m, i):
    return m.d[i] <= m.block_end + (1 - m.rr[i]) * 1e4
model.RerouteEnd = Constraint(model.T, rule=reroute_end_rule)
```

### 3.7  Energy consumption on each segment  

Energy on segment *s* for train *i* :  

\[
E_{i,s}= \bigl(\alpha v_{i,s}^{2} + \beta \bigr) \; t_{i,s}
\]

Again the product `v² * tt` is bilinear, we linearise with McCormick envelopes
by introducing an auxiliary variable `z[i,s] = v[i,s]²`.

```python
# auxiliary variable for v²
model.z = Var(model.T, model.S, within=NonNegativeReals)

def v_squared_def(m, i, s):
    return m.z[i,s] >= m.v[i,s] * m.v[i,s]
model.VSqDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=v_squared_def)

def energy_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.E[i,s] == (m.alpha * m.z[i,s] + m.beta) * m.tt[i,s]
model.EnergyDef = Constraint(model.T, model.S, rule=energy_rule)
```

(If your solver handles quadratic terms you can drop the auxiliary variable
and keep the exact expression.)

### 3.8  Total delay definition (used in objective)

```python
def delay_expr(m, i):
    return m.a[i] - m.t_sched[i]
model.Delay = Expression(model.T, rule=delay_expr)
```

---

## 4.  Objective ------------------------------------------------------------

```python
def obj_rule(m):
    total_delay  = sum(m.Delay[i] for i in m.T)
    total_energy = sum(m.E[i,s] for i in m.T for s in m.S)
    return m.w_delay * total_delay + m.w_energy * total_energy
model.Obj = Objective(rule=obj_rule, sense=minimize)
```

---

## 5.  Solve the model -------------------------------------------------------

```python
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Choose a solver that you have installed (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, GLPK, …)
    solver = SolverFactory('gurobi')          # <-- replace if needed
    results = solver.solve(model, tee=True)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    #   Reporting
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\n=== SOLUTION SUMMARY ===")
    for i in model.T:
        print(f"Train {i}:")
        print(f"  departure = {model.d[i]():.2f}  arrival = {model.a[i]():.2f}")
        print(f"  route choice – original: {model.r[i]():.0f}, reroute: {model.rr[i]():.0f}")
        for s in model.S:
            if model.u[i,s]():
                print(f"       segment {s}: speed = {model.v[i,s]():.1f} km/h, "
                      f"travel = {model.tt[i,s]():.2f} min, energy = {model.E[i,s]():.2f} kWh")
    print("\nTotal weighted objective =", model.Obj())
```

---

### What you need to adapt

| Item | What to change |
|------|----------------|
| **Sets** (`model.T`, `model.S`) | Fill with your actual train IDs and segments. |
| **Routes** (`orig_route`, `reroute`) | Provide the list of segments belonging to the original and any feasible alternate routes for each train. |
| **Lengths, speed limits, dwell times, scheduled arrivals** | Populate with the real network data. |
| **Disruption window** (`blocked_seg`, `block_start`, `block_end`) | Set to the segment that is partially blocked and the time interval of the blockage. |
| **Big‑M values** (`M_tt`, `M_v`, etc.) | Make them large enough for your instance but not excessively huge (helps solver performance). |
| **Solver** | Replace `'gurobi'` with the name of the MILP solver you have (e.g., `'cplex'`, `'cbc'`). |

The model is now a **pure MILP** (except for the optional quadratic tricks that can be kept if you use a solver with quadratic support). Running the script will give you the optimal set of departure times, speed profiles, route selections and the corresponding delay + energy trade‑off. Happy optimisation!

description.description: A description of the MILP to implement.

response.content:
**Variables**

| Symbol | Description | Type |
|--------|-------------|------|
| \(r_i\) | 1 if train \(i\) follows its original route, 0 otherwise | binary |
| \(\overline r_i\) | 1 if train \(i\) uses the rerouted (alternative) route, 0 otherwise | binary |
| \(u_{i,s}\) | 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(s\) (according to the selected route), 0 otherwise | binary |
| \(y_{i,j,s}\) | 1 if, on shared segment \(s\), train \(i\) is scheduled before train \(j\); 0 otherwise (only for \(i<j\)) | binary |
| \(d_i\) | departure time of train \(i\) from its origin (minutes) | continuous \(\ge 0\) |
| \(a_i\) | arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (minutes) | continuous \(\ge 0\) |
| \(tt_{i,s}\) | travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) (minutes) | continuous \(\ge 0\) |
| \(v_{i,s}\) | average speed of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) (km/h) | continuous |
| \(z_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^2\) | auxiliary variable for the square of the speed | continuous \(\ge 0\) |
| \(E_{i,s}\) | energy consumption of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) (kWh) | continuous \(\ge 0\) |

**Parameters**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal T\) | set of trains |
| \(\mathcal S\) | set of track segments |
| \(\mathcal R_i\) | ordered list of segments of train \(i\)’s original route |
| \(\overline{\mathcal R}_i\) | ordered list of segments of train \(i\)’s feasible reroute (may be empty) |
| \(L_s\) | length of segment \(s\) (km) |
| \(v_{i,s}^{\max,0}\) | speed limit for train \(i\) on segment \(s\) when the original route is used (km/h) |
| \(v_{i,s}^{\max,1}\) | speed limit for train \(i\) on segment \(s\) when the reroute is used (km/h) |
| \(v^{\min}\) | global minimum admissible speed (km/h) |
| \(v^{\max}\) | global maximum admissible speed (km/h) |
| \(D_i\) | dwell time of train \(i\) at intermediate stations (minutes) |
| \(\tau_i^{\text{sched}}\) | scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (minutes) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{safe}}\) | safety separation time on any shared segment (minutes) |
| \(s^{\text{blk}}\) | the segment that is partially blocked |
| \([T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\) | disruption time window on \(s^{\text{blk}}\) |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | energy‑model coefficients (kWh/(km·(km/h)²) and kWh/km) |
| \(w^{\text{delay}},w^{\text{energy}}\) | weights in the objective (non‑negative) |
| \(M\) | sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for linearisation |

**Objective function**

\[
\min \; w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\bigl(a_i-\tau_i^{\text{sched}}\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}E_{i,s}
\]

The first term penalises total passenger delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption.

**Constraints**

1. **Route‑choice exclusivity**  
   \[
   r_i+\overline r_i = 1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal T
   \]

2. **Segment usage linkage**  
   \[
   u_{i,s} \ge r_i\; \mathbf 1_{s\in \mathcal R_i}\,,\qquad 
   u_{i,s} \ge \overline r_i\; \mathbf 1_{s\in \overline{\mathcal R}_i}\,,\qquad 
   u_{i,s}\le r_i\; \mathbf 1_{s\in \mathcal R_i}+ \overline r_i\; \mathbf 1_{s\in \overline{\mathcal R}_i}
   \qquad \forall i,s
   \]

3. **Speed limits**  
   \[
   v^{\min} u_{i,s}\le v_{i,s}\le
   \bigl(v_{i,s}^{\max,0} r_i\mathbf 1_{s\in\mathcal R_i}
        + v_{i,s}^{\max,1}\overline r_i\mathbf 1_{s\in\overline{\mathcal R}_i}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i,s
   \]

4. **Travel‑time–speed coupling (McCormick linearisation)**  

   Introduce \(z_{i,s}\) and enforce
   \[
   z_{i,s}\ge v_{i,s}^2,\qquad
   tt_{i,s}\,v_{i,s}= 60\,L_s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   \begin{aligned}
   &tt_{i,s} \ge \frac{60L_s}{v^{\max}} -\frac{M_{tt}}{v^{\max}}(v^{\max}-v_{i,s})\\
   &tt_{i,s} \le \frac{60L_s}{v^{\min}} +\frac{M_{tt}}{v^{\min}}(v_{i,s}-v^{\min})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall i,s
   \]

5. **Time propagation for each train**  
   \[
   a_i = d_i + \sum_{s\in\mathcal S}tt_{i,s} + D_i \qquad \forall i
   \]

6. **Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments**  

   For every unordered pair \((i,j)\) and every segment \(s\):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &d_i + tt_{i,s} \le d_j -\Delta^{\text{safe}} + M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,s}+2-u_{i,s}-u_{j,s}\bigr)\\
   &d_j + tt_{j,s} \le d_i -\Delta^{\text{safe}} + M\bigl(y_{i,j,s}+2-u_{i,s}-u_{j,s}\bigr)
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S
   \]
   The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints if at least one of the trains does not use segment \(s\).

7. **Rerouting only allowed inside the disruption window**  
   \[
   d_i \ge T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}}\;\overline r_i,\qquad
   d_i \le T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} + M(1-\overline r_i)\qquad\forall i
   \]

8. **Energy consumption definition**  
   \[
   E_{i,s}= (\alpha z_{i,s}+ \beta)\;tt_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s
   \]

9. **Non‑negativity / binary restrictions** (as stated in the variable table).

---

### Remarks / Assumptions (explicit)

* The model assumes a single‑track line; bidirectional trains share the same physical segment, hence the ordering variables \(y_{i,j,s}\).  
* If a train does not traverse a segment, its speed and travel time are forced to zero by the usage linking constraints.  
* The product \(tt_{i,s}\,v_{i,s}=60L_s\) (conversion from km/h to km/min) is linearised with McCormick envelopes; a commercial solver capable of bilinear terms could keep the exact equality.  
* Energy is approximated as a quadratic function of speed (common in railway literature).  
* The disruption is modelled as a time window on a single segment \(s^{\text{blk}}\); trains may only be rerouted if they start after the block begins and before it ends (a simplifying but commonly used assumption).  
* Big‑M values must be chosen large enough to dominate all feasible quantities but not excessively large to avoid numerical difficulties.  

The presented MILP fully captures the integrated **train rescheduling and speed management** problem under a partial‑segment blockage, simultaneously minimising total delay and energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable.
