5. **Time propagation for each train**  
   \[
   a_i = d_i + \sum_{s\in\mathcal S}tt_{i,s} + D_i \qquad \forall i
   \]

6. **Conflict‑avoidance on shared segments**  

   For every unordered pair \((i,j)\) and every segment \(s\):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &d_i + tt_{i,s} \le d_j -\Delta^{\text{safe}} + M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,s}+2-u_{i,s}-u_{j,s}\bigr)\\
   &d_j + tt_{j,s} \le d_i -\Delta^{\text{safe}} + M\bigl(y_{i,j,s}+2-u_{i,s}-u_{j,s}\bigr)
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad\forall i<j,\;s\in\mathcal S
   \]
   The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints if at least one of the trains does not use segment \(s\).

7. **Rerouting only allowed inside the disruption window**  
   \[
   d_i \ge T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}}\;\overline r_i,\qquad
   d_i \le T^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} + M(1-\overline r_i)\qquad\forall i
   \]

8. **Energy consumption definition**  
   \[
   E_{i,s}= (\alpha z_{i,s}+ \beta)\;tt_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,s
   \]

9. **Non‑negativity / binary restrictions** (as stated in the variable table).

---

### Remarks / Assumptions (explicit)

* The model assumes a single‑track line; bidirectional trains share the same physical segment, hence the ordering variables \(y_{i,j,s}\).  
* If a train does not traverse a segment, its speed and travel time are forced to zero by the usage linking constraints.  
* The product \(tt_{i,s}\,v_{i,s}=60L_s\) (conversion from km/h to km/min) is linearised with McCormick envelopes; a commercial solver capable of bilinear terms could keep the exact equality.  
* Energy is approximated as a quadratic function of speed (common in railway literature).  
* The disruption is modelled as a time window on a single segment \(s^{\text{blk}}\); trains may only be rerouted if they start after the block begins and before it ends (a simplifying but commonly used assumption).  
* Big‑M values must be chosen large enough to dominate all feasible quantities but not excessively large to avoid numerical difficulties.  

The presented MILP fully captures the integrated **train rescheduling and speed management** problem under a partial‑segment blockage, simultaneously minimising total delay and energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable.

Introduction

With millions of passenger trips on an average day, railway networks play a big role in the European mobility system. In the European Union, the railway infrastructure and the railway operations are mandated by law to be managed separately. In the Netherlands, ProRail is responsible for managing the railway network infrastructure and Netherlands Railways (NS) is the main passenger railway operator. One of the tasks of the railway operator is the planning of individual train units, or rolling stock. A rolling stock schedule specifies which rolling stock units operate which trips in the timetable. Disruptions on the railway network, such as a missing rolling stock unit in a train trip or a complete blockage of a railway track as a result of an accident or a train breakdown, require the rolling stock plan to be updated. The rescheduling measures that pertain to the (availability of the) railway infrastructure, i.e., the changes in the rolling stock assignments, are created by rolling stock dispatchers who work for the railway operator, after which local infrastructure dispatchers who work for the infrastructure manager are tasked with performing the suggested rolling stock movements.

We focus our research on the rescheduling of rolling stock units in the case of disruptions in the railway system. It is necessary that the rolling stock is efficiently operated and utilized to maintain a good balance between the service to passengers and the incurred operational costs. Unavailability of rolling stock influences passenger satisfaction, as passengers possibly have to stand or even wait for the next train in case not enough capacity is available. An efficient rescheduling process reduces such problems and also reduces the number of trains that are needed as a buffer to catch disrupted train services, leading to a reduction in the capital costs for the train operator. It is also beneficial if the adjusted plan is similar to the original plan, as this requires fewer rolling stock movements during the night to get each rolling stock unit to its starting position for the next day. Additionally, an advantage for both passengers and crew members is that they are familiar with the original plan and may prefer the rolling stock units to be operated as originally planned.

Currently, the rescheduling of rolling stock after disruptions is mostly done by hand. As a result, railway planners manually try to find an updated rolling stock allocation without the use of any mathematical methods or solvers. This can largely be attributed to the difficulty of the problem. For a rolling stock plan to work in practice, feasible train compositions need to be assigned to each train trip, the associated shunting movements need to be executable and shunting drivers need to be available for all shunting movements. Past papers have often tackled these problems separately, meaning that there are practical requirements that are not considered in their solution approaches. One of these requirements is the availability of railway tracks for the shunting movements to take place. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has focused on ensuring feasibility of a rolling stock schedule with regard to this aspect. In practice, this is an important part of rolling stock rescheduling; if the rolling stock movements are not possible due to unavailability of the railway tracks, the entire plan could fall apart and could need to be adjusted.

We introduce two solution approaches which ensure that all shunting movements are feasible with respect to the available infrastructure: an exact algorithm and an iterative heuristic. The basis for our methods is the composition model by Fioole et al. (2006), which outputs a rolling stock circulation for the passenger train timetable. To check whether each of the suggested trips and shunting movements can be performed, we implement an infrastructure model which is based on the model by Van Aken et al. (2017) for solving the Train Timetable Adjustment Problem, which aims at finding an alternative timetable that minimizes the deviation from the original timetable in terms of the incurred delays and cancellations of train services. Our tailored version of this model represents every shunting movement as an event that takes place on a specific track at a specific station and outputs whether a shunting movement is possible and whether other trains need to be delayed to make the shunting movement possible. Although delaying other trains is typically not preferred, a short delay could open up the necessary windows for performing additional shunting movements. We therefore include the option of delaying other trains by at most a few minutes in our framework and assume that such short delays are resolved by the buffers that are present in the timetable for the remainder of the affected train lines.

Our exact approach resembles a Combinatorial Benders’ approach in line with Codato and Fischetti (2004). It alternates between the composition model, which suggests shunting movements, and the infrastructure model, which checks whether each combination of shunting movements can be performed. The infrastructure model then returns cuts that prohibit combinations of shunting movements, which violate the railway infrastructure availability constraints, from being performed simultaneously. A drawback of the exact approach is the underlying assumption that the creation of a new rolling stock plan and the performance of the shunting movements are carried out simultaneously by one and the same entity, which conflicts with the separation of the railway tasks as mandated by European laws. We therefore also introduce an iterative heuristic, which works in a similar way as the exact algorithm, but feeds the suggested shunting movements one by one to the infrastructure model. This closely resembles the situation where the rolling stock dispatchers and infrastructure dispatchers work for different companies and is therefore more applicable in the European context. The iterative heuristic mimics the interaction that takes place between the rolling stock dispatchers, who try to come up with a new rolling stock plan, and the local infrastructure dispatchers, who try to perform the shunting movements. We want to emphasize that our framework is generic; besides the specific model choices that we made for the two steps in our iterative frameworks, other formulations and methods can be used as well, so long as they solve the same problems.

We test our algorithm on seven instances which consist of full blockages on the railway network. We model and analyze the railway infrastructure of two major stations, Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal, and allow for shunting movements at these two stations during the duration of the blockages. In practice, shunting at these two stations is assumed to be too difficult due to the large number of trains that pass through and is therefore not considered a viable option during the creation of the rolling stock schedule. We show that the exact algorithm successfully identifies feasible shunting movements that can take place at both Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal to counter the disruption and to improve the rolling stock schedule with respect to several operational, passenger service level and stick-to-the-plan objectives compared to the situation in which shunting at Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal is not considered. Additionally, we find that the iterative heuristic is able to obtain an optimal solution for all instances, in shorter running times. We find that shunting movements are only canceled in case other passenger trains occupy the railway infrastructure and that the shunting movements themselves do not create unsolvable conflicts with one another. Therefore, the order in which the shunting movements are processed by the infrastructure model does not matter and the iterative heuristic finds an optimal solution for all instances. We furthermore find that our algorithm performs well in case we put emphasis on any of the rolling stock rescheduling objectives and that our approach also provides added value in the case that all trains are fixed and cannot be delayed.

The contribution of this paper is threefold. Firstly, we introduce frameworks for rolling stock rescheduling with railway infrastructure availability constraints. The methods output rolling stock circulations which ensure that a feasible path through the railway infrastructure exists for the performed shunting movements at the considered stations. Secondly, our algorithms find solutions within a few minutes with an average improvement of 19% over the rolling stock schedule which does not contain shunting movements at Utrecht Centraal or Rotterdam Centraal. Thirdly, we show that the frameworks can be beneficial in practical problems; by allowing for shunting at more stations than is currently done in practice, our frameworks are able to provide improvements over the rolling stock circulations that are currently made. Furthermore, the iterative approach mimics rolling stock rescheduling in practice by distinguishing between the two problems which are currently solved separately by the rolling stock dispatchers and the infrastructure dispatchers. Our approach provides a framework which connects these problems, thereby facilitating and reducing the interaction which is required between the involved parties.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a detailed description of the problem we address. Literature covering similar problems is discussed in Section 3. Section 4 provides a mathematical formulation for our two solution components and introduces the iterative rolling stock rescheduling algorithm. Computational results and a sensitivity analysis of our algorithm are presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 gives conclusions and suggestions for future research.

**Mathematical MILP Model for Rolling‑Stock Rescheduling with Infrastructure‑Availability Constraints**  

The model integrates two sub‑problems that are solved iteratively (or in a Benders‑type exact scheme):

1. **Composition model** – decides which rolling‑stock unit (RSU) is assigned to each passenger train trip and which shunting movements are performed.  
2. **Infrastructure model** – checks whether the selected shunting movements can be executed on the available tracks at the stations (Utrecht C and Rotterdam C) and, if necessary, introduces short delays for other trains.

Below a **single‑stage mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP)** formulation is presented that captures both aspects simultaneously.  The formulation is generic; wherever data are missing, reasonable assumptions are explicitly stated (marked **[Assumption]**).

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of passenger train trips in the original timetable (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(S\) | Set of shunting movements that may be performed (indexed by \(s\)). |
| \(U\) | Set of rolling‑stock units (RSUs) owned by the operator (indexed by \(u\)). |
| \(K\) | Set of stations where shunting is allowed (here \(K=\{Utrecht, Rotterdam\}\)). |
| \(L\) | Set of tracks at a station (indexed by \(\ell\)). |
| \(P\) | Set of time periods (discrete minutes) covering the planning horizon (indexed by \(p\)). |
| \(C\) | Set of crew‑driver teams (indexed by \(c\)). |
| \(B\) | Set of binary “big‑M” values (used only for linearisation, see constraints). |

Additional derived sets (used only for readability):

* \(T_u = \{t\in T \mid\) trip \(t\) can be served by RSU \(u\}\).  
* \(S_k = \{s\in S \mid\) shunting movement \(s\) takes place at station \(k\in K\}\).  
* \(S_{u} = \{s\in S \mid\) RSU \(u\) is the vehicle that will perform shunting \(s\}\).

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical values / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \(a_t\) | Planned departure time of trip \(t\) (minutes from midnight). | Timetable |
| \(b_t\) | Planned arrival time of trip \(t\). | Timetable |
| \(\hat a_t, \hat b_t\) | Latest allowable departure / arrival (buffer). | Timetable buffers |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum admissible delay for any passenger trip (minutes). | **[Assumption]** 5 min |
| \(cap_u\) | Capacity (seats) of RSU \(u\). | Fleet data |
| \(demand_t\) | Passenger demand (seats) on trip \(t\). | Forecast |
| \(len_s\) | Duration (minutes) of shunting movement \(s\). | Engineering data |
| \(win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s\) | Time window in which shunting \(s\) may be performed (e.g., night‑time). | Operational rules |
| \(track_{k\ell}\) | Binary indicator: track \(\ell\) exists at station \(k\). | Infrastructure layout |
| \(M\) | Large constant for “big‑M” constraints (e.g., 10 000). | **[Assumption]** |
| \(cost^{delay}_t\) | Penalty per minute of delay for trip \(t\). | Revenue impact |
| \(cost^{shunt}_s\) | Cost of performing shunting \(s\) (crew, energy). | Operational cost |
| \(cost^{reassign}_t\) | Penalty for assigning a different RSU to trip \(t\) than originally planned. | **[Assumption]** |
| \(cost^{canc}_s\) | Penalty for cancelling shunting movement \(s\). | **[Assumption]** |
| \(crew_{c,s}\) | Binary: crew \(c\) can operate shunting \(s\) (qualification). | Crew‑skill matrix |
| \(avail_{c,p}\) | Binary: crew \(c\) available at period \(p\). | Shift schedule |
| \(trackOcc_{k\ell,p}\) | Indicator whether track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) is occupied by a regular passenger train at period \(p\) (taken from original timetable). | **[Assumption]** Pre‑computed |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,u}\) | Binary | 1 if RSU \(u\) is assigned to trip \(t\). |
| \(\delta_t\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay (minutes) applied to departure/arrival of trip \(t\). |
| \(y_{s}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting movement \(s\) is **performed**. |
| \(z_{s,k\ell,p}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting \(s\) occupies track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) during period \(p\). |
| \(w_{c,s}\) | Binary | 1 if crew \(c\) is assigned to shunting \(s\). |
| \(\theta_{s}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting \(s\) is **cancelled** (i.e., not performed). |
| \(\beta_{t,p}\) | Binary | 1 if trip \(t\) (including any delay) occupies any track at period \(p\). Used to protect shunting windows. |
| \(\gamma_{k\ell,p}\) | Binary | 1 if track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) is **reserved** for a shunting movement at period \(p\). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The objective minimises a weighted sum of three competing goals:

1. **Passenger‑service quality** – minimise total delay and penalise RSU changes.  
2. **Operational cost** – cost of performing shunting movements and crew utilisation.  
3. **Plan‑stability** – penalise cancellations of shunting movements (to keep the plan close to the original suggestion).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} cost^{delay}_t \, \delta_t}_{\text{(i) Delay penalty}} 
      + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{u\in U} cost^{reassign}_t \, x_{t,u}}_{\text{(ii) RSU change}} \\
      & + \underbrace{\sum_{s\in S} cost^{shunt}_s \, y_{s}}_{\text{(iii) Shunting cost}} 
      + \underbrace{\sum_{c\in C}\sum_{s\in S} cost^{crew}_c \, w_{c,s}}_{\text{(iv) Crew cost}} \\
      & + \underbrace{\sum_{s\in S} cost^{canc}_s \, \theta_{s}}_{\text{(v) Cancellation penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All cost coefficients are non‑negative.  The relative importance of the three groups can be tuned by scaling the coefficients.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Assignment and Capacity  

1. **Exactly one RSU per trip**  

\[
\sum_{u\in U} x_{t,u}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

2. **Compatibility** – an RSU can serve a trip only if it has sufficient capacity  

\[
x_{t,u}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; u\in U\; \text{with } cap_u < demand_t .
\]

3. **Flow conservation of RSUs (circulation)** – each RSU that finishes a trip must start the next feasible trip (or a shunting movement).  
Let \(next(t)\) be the set of trips that can follow \(t\) (same RSU, respecting minimum turnaround time \(\tau\)).  

\[
\sum_{t'\in next(t)} x_{t',u} \; \ge \; x_{t,u} \qquad \forall u\in U,\; t\in T .
\]

*(If a RSU ends its day, a dummy “depot” trip can be added.)*

### 5.2 Delays  

4. **Delay limits**  

\[
0 \le \delta_t \le d^{\max} \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

5. **Temporal feasibility with delays** – a trip occupying a track at period \(p\) if it is scheduled (including delay).  

\[
\beta_{t,p} \ge 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a_t+\delta_t \le p \le b_t+\delta_t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; p\in P .
\]

*Linearisation:*  

\[
\beta_{t,p} \ge \frac{p-a_t}{M} - \frac{\delta_t}{M},\qquad
\beta_{t,p} \ge \frac{b_t-p}{M} + \frac{\delta_t}{M},\qquad
\beta_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}.
\]

### 5.3 Shunting Decision  

6. **Shunting performed or cancelled**  

\[
y_{s} + \theta_{s}=1 \qquad \forall s\in S .
\]

7. **RSU must be available for its shunting**  

\[
y_{s} \le \sum_{u\in U} x_{t(u),u} \qquad \forall s\in S,
\]

where \(t(u)\) is the trip that ends (or starts) at the moment the RSU would need to perform shunting \(s\).  
*If the RSU is not in service at the required time, the shunting cannot be performed.*

8. **Crew assignment**  

\[
\sum_{c\in C} w_{c,s}= y_{s} \qquad \forall s\in S .
\]

9. **Crew qualification**  

\[
w_{c,s} \le crew_{c,s} \qquad \forall c\in C,\; s\in S .
\]

10. **Crew availability (no overlapping shunting)**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S: p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s]} w_{c,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall c\in C,\; p\in P .
\]

### 5.4 Track‑Occupancy (Infrastructure Feasibility)  

11. **Shunting occupies exactly one track at each minute of its window**  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{s,k\ell,p}= y_{s}\qquad 
\forall s\in S_k,\; p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s] .
\]

12. **Track reservation conflicts – a track cannot be used simultaneously by a passenger train and a shunting movement**  

\[
\beta_{t,p} + z_{s,k\ell,p} \le 1 \qquad 
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

13. **Existing occupancy (blocked tracks)** – if a track is already occupied by a non‑delayable train (e.g., a freight train that cannot be shifted), shunting cannot use it.  

\[
z_{s,k\ell,p} \le 1- trackOcc_{k\ell,p} \qquad 
\forall s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

14. **Track existence**  

\[
z_{s,k\ell,p} \le track_{k\ell} \qquad \forall s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

### 5.5 Interaction Between Delay and Shunting  

15. **If a shunting is performed, the RSU must be free (no passenger trip) during the whole shunting window**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T_u} \beta_{t,p}\; \le\; 1- y_{s} \qquad 
\forall u\in U,\; s\in S_u,\; p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s] .
\]

*(If the RSU is already scheduled for a passenger trip at any minute of the shunting window, the shunting must be cancelled.)*

### 5.6 Benders‑style Cuts (optional, for exact algorithm)  

When the infrastructure model finds an infeasible combination of shunting movements, a cut of the form  

\[
\sum_{s\in \mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}} y_{s} \le |\mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}}|-1
\]

is added to the master (composition) problem, where \(\mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}}\) is the set of shunting movements that cannot coexist on the given tracks.  

*In the monolithic MILP above, this is automatically enforced by constraints (12)–(15).*

---

## 6. Summary of the Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \sum_{t} cost^{delay}_t \, \delta_t 
      + \sum_{t,u} cost^{reassign}_t \, x_{t,u}
      + \sum_{s} cost^{shunt}_s \, y_{s}
      + \sum_{c,s} cost^{crew}_c \, w_{c,s}
      + \sum_{s} cost^{canc}_s \, \theta_{s} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(15) listed above} \\[2pt]
& x_{t,u}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{s},\theta_{s},z_{s,k\ell,p},
   w_{c,s},\beta_{t,p},\gamma_{k\ell,p}\in\{0,1\},\\
& \delta_t\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **linear** (all products are either binary–binary or binary–continuous with a big‑M linearisation) and can be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 7. Remarks & Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Reasoning |
|---|------------|-----------|
| A1 | Time is discretised in 1‑minute intervals (\(P\)). | Provides a tractable horizon while preserving typical railway granularity. |
| A2 | Maximum admissible passenger‑trip delay \(d^{\max}=5\) min. | Reflects realistic buffer allowances; can be changed. |
| A3 | Shunting duration \(len_s\) is known and deterministic. | Engineering data are normally fixed. |
| A4 | Crew availability \(avail_{c,p}\) and qualification matrix \(crew_{c,s}\) are pre‑computed. | Standard crew‑planning input. |
| A5 | Track occupancy by non‑shiftable trains (\(trackOcc_{k\ell,p}\)) is known from the original timetable. | Required to guarantee feasibility of shunting windows. |
| A6 | Cost coefficients are linear (e.g., delay penalty per minute). | Common practice; non‑linear penalties can be approximated by piecewise linear functions if needed. |
| A7 | Each shunting movement uses exactly one track for its whole duration. | Simplifies the model; extensions can allow multi‑track manoeuvres. |
| A8 | RSU circulation is modelled with a simple “next‑trip” set; minimum turnaround time \(\tau\) is embedded in the definition of \(next(t)\). | Captures the essential flow of rolling stock without a full time‑expanded network. |
| A9 | The big‑M constant \(M\) is set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min). | Guarantees correct linearisation. |
| A10 | The model can be solved either as a **single MILP** (monolithic) or in a **Benders/Combinatorial Benders** decomposition where the master problem handles variables \((x,\delta,y,\theta)\) and the sub‑problem checks constraints (12)–(15) and returns feasibility cuts. | Mirrors the exact algorithm described in the paper. |

---

## 8. How the Model Relates to the Paper  

* **Composition model** – captured by variables \(x_{t,u},\delta_t\) and constraints (1)–(5).  
* **Infrastructure model** – captured by variables \(y_s, z_{s,k\ell,p},\gamma_{k\ell,p}\) and constraints (11)–(15).  
* **Iterative heuristic** – can be implemented by solving the master (composition) first, fixing a candidate set of shunting movements \(\{y_s=1\}\), solving the infrastructure sub‑problem, and, if infeasible, fixing the offending \(y_s\) to 0 (cancellation) and re‑optimising.  
* **Exact Benders approach** – the same master problem plus the addition of feasibility cuts (see section 5.6).  

The formulation therefore provides a **complete linear model** that can be used directly for computational experiments, sensitivity analyses (e.g., varying \(d^{\max}\) or the cost weights), and for integration into the iterative or exact solution frameworks described in the article.

| \(trackOcc_{k\ell,p}\) | Indicator whether track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) is occupied by a regular passenger train at period \(p\) (taken from original timetable). | **[Assumption]** Pre‑computed |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,u}\) | Binary | 1 if RSU \(u\) is assigned to trip \(t\). |
| \(\delta_t\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay (minutes) applied to departure/arrival of trip \(t\). |
| \(y_{s}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting movement \(s\) is **performed**. |
| \(z_{s,k\ell,p}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting \(s\) occupies track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) during period \(p\). |
| \(w_{c,s}\) | Binary | 1 if crew \(c\) is assigned to shunting \(s\). |
| \(\theta_{s}\) | Binary | 1 if shunting \(s\) is **cancelled** (i.e., not performed). |
| \(\beta_{t,p}\) | Binary | 1 if trip \(t\) (including any delay) occupies any track at period \(p\). Used to protect shunting windows. |
| \(\gamma_{k\ell,p}\) | Binary | 1 if track \(\ell\) at station \(k\) is **reserved** for a shunting movement at period \(p\). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The objective minimises a weighted sum of three competing goals:

1. **Passenger‑service quality** – minimise total delay and penalise RSU changes.  
2. **Operational cost** – cost of performing shunting movements and crew utilisation.  
3. **Plan‑stability** – penalise cancellations of shunting movements (to keep the plan close to the original suggestion).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} cost^{delay}_t \, \delta_t}_{\text{(i) Delay penalty}} 
      + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{u\in U} cost^{reassign}_t \, x_{t,u}}_{\text{(ii) RSU change}} \\
      & + \underbrace{\sum_{s\in S} cost^{shunt}_s \, y_{s}}_{\text{(iii) Shunting cost}} 
      + \underbrace{\sum_{c\in C}\sum_{s\in S} cost^{crew}_c \, w_{c,s}}_{\text{(iv) Crew cost}} \\
      & + \underbrace{\sum_{s\in S} cost^{canc}_s \, \theta_{s}}_{\text{(v) Cancellation penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All cost coefficients are non‑negative.  The relative importance of the three groups can be tuned by scaling the coefficients.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Assignment and Capacity  

1. **Exactly one RSU per trip**  

\[
\sum_{u\in U} x_{t,u}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

2. **Compatibility** – an RSU can serve a trip only if it has sufficient capacity  

\[
x_{t,u}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; u\in U\; \text{with } cap_u < demand_t .
\]

3. **Flow conservation of RSUs (circulation)** – each RSU that finishes a trip must start the next feasible trip (or a shunting movement).  
Let \(next(t)\) be the set of trips that can follow \(t\) (same RSU, respecting minimum turnaround time \(\tau\)).  

\[
\sum_{t'\in next(t)} x_{t',u} \; \ge \; x_{t,u} \qquad \forall u\in U,\; t\in T .
\]

*(If a RSU ends its day, a dummy “depot” trip can be added.)*

### 5.2 Delays  

4. **Delay limits**  

\[
0 \le \delta_t \le d^{\max} \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

5. **Temporal feasibility with delays** – a trip occupying a track at period \(p\) if it is scheduled (including delay).  

\[
\beta_{t,p} \ge 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a_t+\delta_t \le p \le b_t+\delta_t,\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; p\in P .
\]

*Linearisation:*  

\[
\beta_{t,p} \ge \frac{p-a_t}{M} - \frac{\delta_t}{M},\qquad
\beta_{t,p} \ge \frac{b_t-p}{M} + \frac{\delta_t}{M},\qquad
\beta_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}.
\]

### 5.3 Shunting Decision  

6. **Shunting performed or cancelled**  

\[
y_{s} + \theta_{s}=1 \qquad \forall s\in S .
\]

7. **RSU must be available for its shunting**  

\[
y_{s} \le \sum_{u\in U} x_{t(u),u} \qquad \forall s\in S,
\]

where \(t(u)\) is the trip that ends (or starts) at the moment the RSU would need to perform shunting \(s\).  
*If the RSU is not in service at the required time, the shunting cannot be performed.*

8. **Crew assignment**  

\[
\sum_{c\in C} w_{c,s}= y_{s} \qquad \forall s\in S .
\]

9. **Crew qualification**  

\[
w_{c,s} \le crew_{c,s} \qquad \forall c\in C,\; s\in S .
\]

10. **Crew availability (no overlapping shunting)**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S: p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s]} w_{c,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall c\in C,\; p\in P .
\]

### 5.4 Track‑Occupancy (Infrastructure Feasibility)  

11. **Shunting occupies exactly one track at each minute of its window**  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{s,k\ell,p}= y_{s}\qquad 
\forall s\in S_k,\; p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s] .
\]

12. **Track reservation conflicts – a track cannot be used simultaneously by a passenger train and a shunting movement**  

\[
\beta_{t,p} + z_{s,k\ell,p} \le 1 \qquad 
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

13. **Existing occupancy (blocked tracks)** – if a track is already occupied by a non‑delayable train (e.g., a freight train that cannot be shifted), shunting cannot use it.  

\[
z_{s,k\ell,p} \le 1- trackOcc_{k\ell,p} \qquad 
\forall s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

14. **Track existence**  

\[
z_{s,k\ell,p} \le track_{k\ell} \qquad \forall s\in S_k,\; \ell\in L,\; p\in P .
\]

### 5.5 Interaction Between Delay and Shunting  

15. **If a shunting is performed, the RSU must be free (no passenger trip) during the whole shunting window**  

\[
\sum_{t\in T_u} \beta_{t,p}\; \le\; 1- y_{s} \qquad 
\forall u\in U,\; s\in S_u,\; p\in [win^{start}_s, win^{end}_s] .
\]

*(If the RSU is already scheduled for a passenger trip at any minute of the shunting window, the shunting must be cancelled.)*

### 5.6 Benders‑style Cuts (optional, for exact algorithm)  

When the infrastructure model finds an infeasible combination of shunting movements, a cut of the form  

\[
\sum_{s\in \mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}} y_{s} \le |\mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}}|-1
\]

is added to the master (composition) problem, where \(\mathcal{S}^{\text{conflict}}\) is the set of shunting movements that cannot coexist on the given tracks.  

*In the monolithic MILP above, this is automatically enforced by constraints (12)–(15).*

---

## 6. Summary of the Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \sum_{t} cost^{delay}_t \, \delta_t 
      + \sum_{t,u} cost^{reassign}_t \, x_{t,u}
      + \sum_{s} cost^{shunt}_s \, y_{s}
      + \sum_{c,s} cost^{crew}_c \, w_{c,s}
      + \sum_{s} cost^{canc}_s \, \theta_{s} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(15) listed above} \\[2pt]
& x_{t,u}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{s},\theta_{s},z_{s,k\ell,p},
   w_{c,s},\beta_{t,p},\gamma_{k\ell,p}\in\{0,1\},\\
& \delta_t\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **linear** (all products are either binary–binary or binary–continuous with a big‑M linearisation) and can be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 7. Remarks & Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Reasoning |
|---|------------|-----------|
| A1 | Time is discretised in 1‑minute intervals (\(P\)). | Provides a tractable horizon while preserving typical railway granularity. |
| A2 | Maximum admissible passenger‑trip delay \(d^{\max}=5\) min. | Reflects realistic buffer allowances; can be changed. |
| A3 | Shunting duration \(len_s\) is known and deterministic. | Engineering data are normally fixed. |
| A4 | Crew availability \(avail_{c,p}\) and qualification matrix \(crew_{c,s}\) are pre‑computed. | Standard crew‑planning input. |
| A5 | Track occupancy by non‑shiftable trains (\(trackOcc_{k\ell,p}\)) is known from the original timetable. | Required to guarantee feasibility of shunting windows. |
| A6 | Cost coefficients are linear (e.g., delay penalty per minute). | Common practice; non‑linear penalties can be approximated by piecewise linear functions if needed. |
| A7 | Each shunting movement uses exactly one track for its whole duration. | Simplifies the model; extensions can allow multi‑track manoeuvres. |
| A8 | RSU circulation is modelled with a simple “next‑trip” set; minimum turnaround time \(\tau\) is embedded in the definition of \(next(t)\). | Captures the essential flow of rolling stock without a full time‑expanded network. |
| A9 | The big‑M constant \(M\) is set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min). | Guarantees correct linearisation. |
| A10 | The model can be solved either as a **single MILP** (monolithic) or in a **Benders/Combinatorial Benders** decomposition where the master problem handles variables \((x,\delta,y,\theta)\) and the sub‑problem checks constraints (12)–(15) and returns feasibility cuts. | Mirrors the exact algorithm described in the paper. |

---

## 8. How the Model Relates to the Paper  

* **Composition model** – captured by variables \(x_{t,u},\delta_t\) and constraints (1)–(5).  
* **Infrastructure model** – captured by variables \(y_s, z_{s,k\ell,p},\gamma_{k\ell,p}\) and constraints (11)–(15).  
* **Iterative heuristic** – can be implemented by solving the master (composition) first, fixing a candidate set of shunting movements \(\{y_s=1\}\), solving the infrastructure sub‑problem, and, if infeasible, fixing the offending \(y_s\) to 0 (cancellation) and re‑optimising.  
* **Exact Benders approach** – the same master problem plus the addition of feasibility cuts (see section 5.6).  

The formulation therefore provides a **complete linear model** that can be used directly for computational experiments, sensitivity analyses (e.g., varying \(d^{\max}\) or the cost weights), and for integration into the iterative or exact solution frameworks described in the article.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)** on a high‑speed railway with a partially blocked segment.  

The model contains:

* **Sets** – trains, stations, track‑segments, time‑periods, speed‑levels.  
* **Parameters** – travel‑time, energy‑cost, block‑availability, capacity, acceleration limits, etc.  
* **Decision variables** – binary routing choices, continuous departure/arrival times, binary speed‑level selections.  
* **Objective** – a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.  
* **Constraints** – feasibility of timing, block occupancy, single‑track capacity, speed limits, acceleration/deceleration, flow‑conservation, and binary routing.

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binary routing and speed‑level variables, so the model is a **MILP**.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(\mathcal{T} = \{1,\dots,T\}\) | Set of trains (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(\mathcal{N} = \{0,1,\dots,N\}\) | Set of stations (node 0 = origin depot, node \(N\) = terminal). |
| \(\mathcal{S} = \{(i,j) \mid i,j\in\mathcal{N}, i<j\}\) | Set of directed track‑segments (arcs) from station \(i\) to station \(j\). |
| \(\mathcal{K} = \{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of admissible speed‑levels (e.g., “slow”, “normal”, “fast”). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance). |
| \(\mathcal{P}\) | Set of discrete time points used for block‑occupancy checks (e.g., every minute). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from station \(i\). | min |
| \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(i\). | min |
| \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i}\) | Minimum dwell time required at station \(i\) (boarding/alighting). | min |
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of segment \((i,j)\). | km |
| \(v^{\max}_{k}\) | Maximum admissible speed for speed‑level \(k\). | km/h |
| \(v^{\min}_{k}\) | Minimum admissible speed for speed‑level \(k\). | km/h |
| \(\alpha\) | Acceleration (or deceleration) limit (absolute value). | km/h² |
| \(E_{k}\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed‑level \(k\). | kWh/km |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of energy in the objective (relative to delay). | – |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\) | Penalty weight for delay of train \(t\) at station \(i\). | – |
| \(C\) | Capacity of a single‑track segment (normally 1 train at a time). | trains |
| \(B_{ij}(p)\) | Binary indicator: **1** if segment \((i,j)\) is blocked at discrete time \(p\); **0** otherwise. | – |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶). | min |
| \(R_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Origin station of train \(t\). | node index |
| \(R_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) | Destination station of train \(t\). | node index |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \(x_{t,ij} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | **Routing**: 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \((i,j)\), 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{t,ij}^{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | **Speed‑level selection**: 1 if train \(t\) uses speed level \(k\) on segment \((i,j)\). |
| \(d_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Actual **departure time** of train \(t\) from station \(i\). |
| \(a_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Actual **arrival time** of train \(t\) at station \(i\). |
| \(\delta_{t,ij} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \((i,j)\). |
| \(\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | Occupancy indicator: 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \((i,j)\) at discrete time \(p\). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,
\bigl( d_{t,i}- d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\bigr)_{+}}_{\text{Total weighted passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
E_{k}\,L_{ij}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}}
\]

*The “\((\cdot)_{+}\)” can be linearised by introducing auxiliary non‑negative variables*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{delay}_{t,i} &\ge d_{t,i} - d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i} ,\\
\text{delay}_{t,i} &\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then the first term becomes \(\sum_{t,i} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,\text{delay}_{t,i}\).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Flow (routing) conservation  

For every train \(t\) and every intermediate station \(i\) (except origin/destination):

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ij}
\;-\;
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ji}
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } i = R^{\text{orig}}_{t},\\
 -1 & \text{if } i = R^{\text{dest}}_{t},\\
  0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{F1}
\]

Thus each train leaves its origin once, arrives at its destination once, and the number of incoming arcs equals outgoing arcs at all other stations.

### 5.2. Speed‑level linking  

A train can choose **exactly one** speed level on a segment it actually traverses:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,ij}^{k}=x_{t,ij},
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F2}
\]

### 5.3. Travel‑time definition (linearised using speed bounds)  

If speed level \(k\) is selected, the travel time on \((i,j)\) is bounded by the inverse of the speed limits:

\[
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}_{k}}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}
\;\le\;
\delta_{t,ij}
\;\le\;
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\min}_{k}}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}
\qquad\forall t,(i,j),k.
\tag{F3}
\]

Because only one \(k\) can be 1 (by (F2)), the inequalities collapse to the appropriate bound.

### 5.4. Acceleration / deceleration limits between successive segments  

Let a train leave station \(i\) on segment \((i,j)\) with speed level \(k\) and later enter segment \((j,\ell)\) with speed level \(k'\). The change in speed must respect the acceleration limit \(\alpha\). Using the fact that speed = distance / travel‑time, we obtain a linear inequality after cross‑multiplication and using big‑M:

\[
\Bigl|\frac{L_{ij}}{\delta_{t,ij}} - \frac{L_{j\ell}}{\delta_{t,j\ell}}\Bigr|
\;\le\;
\alpha \, \bigl( d_{t,j} - a_{t,j} \bigr) + M\,(2 - x_{t,ij} - x_{t,j\ell})
\qquad\forall t,\, (i,j),(j,\ell)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F4}
\]

When either of the two arcs is not used (\(x=0\)), the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

### 5.5. Dwell‑time feasibility at stations  

If a train arrives at station \(i\), it must stay at least the minimum dwell time before departing:

\[
d_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} + \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i} - M\,(1-\!\!\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ij}) ,
\qquad\forall t,i.
\tag{F5}
\]

The big‑M term removes the constraint for stations where the train does not stop (i.e., when the outgoing sum is 0).

### 5.6. Time‑consistency between successive arcs  

If train \(t\) uses arc \((i,j)\) then the departure from \(i\) plus travel time equals the arrival at \(j\):

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; d_{t,i} + \delta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-x_{t,ij}),
\qquad\forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F6}
\]

The reverse inequality is not needed because the model minimizes delay; the above ensures a feasible schedule.

### 5.7. Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

A train may occupy a blocked segment only when the block is **not active** at the time of occupation. First we link the continuous time variables to the discrete occupancy variables:

\[
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \le x_{t,ij}, \qquad
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \in \{0,1\},
\quad \forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F7a}
\]

If the train traverses \((i,j)\) then for each discrete time point \(p\) that lies inside its travel window we must set \(\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}=1\). This can be linearised with “big‑M’’ intervals; a compact version is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,i} + \epsilon &\le p \;\;+\; M\,(1-\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}),\\
p &\le a_{t,i} + \delta_{t,ij} - \epsilon \;+\; M\,(1-\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}),
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P},
\tag{F7b}
\]

where \(\epsilon\) is a small positive number (e.g., 0.1 min) to avoid equality issues.

Now enforce that no blocked time is used:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \;\le\; 1 - B_{ij}(p),
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F7c}
\]

If \(B_{ij}(p)=1\) (segment blocked at time \(p\)), the right‑hand side becomes 0, preventing any train from occupying the segment at that time.

### 5.8. Single‑track capacity (unblocked segments)  

Even on free segments only one train may be present at a given time (single‑track assumption). Using the same occupancy variables for **all** segments:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \;\le\; 1,
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{S},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F8}
\]

If a segment is double‑track in practice, the RHS could be set to the number of tracks.

### 5.9. Non‑negativity and domain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& d_{t,i}, a_{t,i}, \delta_{t,ij} \ge 0,\\
& x_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}\in\{0,1\},\\
& \text{delay}_{t,i}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F9}
\]

---

## 6. Model Summary  

Putting everything together, the MILP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t,i} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,\text{delay}_{t,i}
      \;+\; \beta \sum_{t,(i,j)}\sum_{k} E_{k}\,L_{ij}\,y_{t,ij}^{k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(F1)}\; \text{flow conservation} \\ 
& \text{(F2)}\; \text{speed‑level linking} \\
& \text{(F3)}\; \text{travel‑time bounds} \\
& \text{(F4)}\; \text{acceleration limits} \\
& \text{(F5)}\; \text{minimum dwell time} \\
& \text{(F6)}\; \text{time consistency across arcs} \\
& \text{(F7a–c)}\; \text{block‑occupancy constraints} \\
& \text{(F8)}\; \text{single‑track capacity} \\
& \text{(F9)}\; \text{variable domains} \\
& \text{(delay linearisation)}\;
\begin{cases}
\text{delay}_{t,i}\ge d_{t,i}-d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\\
\text{delay}_{t,i}\ge 0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear) and contains **binary** variables \(x, y, \zeta\); therefore it is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.  

A commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) can be used to obtain the optimal rescheduling, routing, and speed‑level decisions that minimise the weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption while respecting all operational and safety constraints imposed by the partially blocked railway segment.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** on a high‑speed railway line that suffers a **partial blockage of some track segments**.  

The model contains  

* **Decision variables** (continuous times, continuous speeds, binary routing/occupancy decisions)  
* A **linear objective** that is a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption  
* **Linear constraints** that enforce feasibility of the schedule, respect the blocked portion of the line, guarantee single‑track capacity, obey speed‑limits, acceleration/deceleration limits, and preserve flow (routing) consistency.  

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model, and a short “interpretation” of each block of constraints is given after the formulation.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(\mathcal{T}= \{1,\dots,T\}\\) | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| \\(\mathcal{S}= \{1,\dots,S\}\\) | Set of **track segments** (ordered from origin to destination). Segment \\(s\\) connects node \\(n_{s}\\) to node \\(n_{s+1}\\). |
| \\(\mathcal{K}= \{1,\dots,K\}\\) | Set of **allowable speed‑levels** (e.g., 200 km/h, 250 km/h, 300 km/h). The speed value of level \\(k\\) is \\(v_k\) (km/h). |
| \\(\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{S}\\) | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (the blockage occupies a known sub‑length of the segment). |
| \\(\mathcal{L}_s\\) | Set of **possible routes** (i.e., alternative line‑paths) that train \\(i\\) may take through segment \\(s\). For a simple line‑graph \\(\mathcal{L}_s=\{1\}\\); for a network with parallel tracks, \\(|\mathcal{L}_s|>1\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical units |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| \\(d_i\\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \\(i\\) at its origin node. | minutes |
| \\(a_i^{\text{orig}}\\) | Planned arrival time of train \\(i\\) at its final destination (without disruption). | minutes |
| \\(L_s\\) | Physical length of segment \\(s\\). | km |
| \\(L_s^{\text{free}}\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\) that remains **usable** (i.e., not blocked). For unblocked segments \\(L_s^{\text{free}}=L_s\\). | km |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed associated with speed‑level \\(k\\). | km/h |
| \\(c_k\\) | Energy consumption rate (e.g., kWh per km) when traveling at speed \\(v_k\\). | kWh/km |
| \\(\alpha_i\\) | Weight for the delay of train \\(i\\) (e.g., passenger‑hour weight). | – |
| \\(\beta_i\\) | Weight for the energy of train \\(i\\). | – |
| \\(\Delta^{\max}_{\text{acc}}\\) | Maximum admissible **acceleration** (km/h per minute). | km/h·min⁻¹ |
| \\(\Delta^{\max}_{\text{dec}}\\) | Maximum admissible **deceleration** (km/h per minute). | km/h·min⁻¹ |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). | minutes |
| \\(C\\) | Minimum headway (time separation) required between two trains occupying the **same** segment on a single‑track line. | minutes |
| \\(p_i\\) | Penalty (or revenue) associated with **rerouting** train \\(i\\) to an alternative line (if applicable). | monetary units |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{i,s} \in \{0,1\}\\) | binary | **Occupancy**: 1 if train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(s\\); 0 otherwise. (Enforces routing.) |
| \\(r_{i,s,\ell} \in \{0,1\}\\) | binary | **Routing choice**: 1 if train \\(i\\) uses route \\(\ell\in\mathcal{L}_s\\) on segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s} \ge 0\\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train \\(i\\) from the upstream node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s} \ge 0\\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train \\(i\\) at the downstream node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(y_{i,s,k} \in \{0,1\}\\) | binary | **Speed‑level selection**: 1 if train \\(i\\) travels segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\). |
| \\(\delta_i \ge 0\\) | continuous | **Total delay** of train \\(i\\) (difference between actual arrival at final node and the original schedule). |
| \\(E_i \ge 0\\) | continuous | **Total energy** consumed by train \\(i\\) over the whole route. |

*Note*: The product \\(x_{i,s} y_{i,s,k}\\) is linearised using standard big‑M or additional binary variables if needed; however, because \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) can be forced to 0 when \\(x_{i,s}=0\\) (see constraints), no product appears in the final model.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Bigl[ \alpha_i \, \delta_i \;+\; \beta_i \, E_i \;+\; p_i \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_s} r_{i,s,\ell}\Bigr]
}
\]

*The first term penalises passenger delay, the second term penalises energy consumption, and the third term (optional) penalises the use of non‑preferred routes.*

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Routing consistency  

1. **Exactly one route per traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_s} r_{i,s,\ell}=x_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S}
\tag{R1}
\]

If a segment is not used (\\(x_{i,s}=0\\)), all route‑choice binaries are forced to 0.

2. **Flow conservation (train continuity)**  

For every interior node (i.e., between segment \\(s\\) and \\(s+1\\)):

\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{s}} r_{i,s,\ell}= \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{s+1}} r_{i,s+1,\ell}\qquad
\forall i\in\mathcal{T},\; s=1,\dots,S-1
\tag{R2}
\]

At the origin and destination:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{1}} r_{i,1,\ell}=1,\qquad 
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{S}} r_{i,S,\ell}=1\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R3}
\]

(If multiple entry/exit tracks exist, the first/last segment choice can be relaxed.)

### 5.2. Speed‑level selection  

3. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s,k}=x_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in\mathcal{S}
\tag{S1}
\]

If the segment is not used, all speed‑level binaries are 0.

### 5.3. Time‑propagation (travel time on a segment)  

4. **Travel‑time equation**  

\[
t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \frac{L_s^{\text{free}}}{v_k}\; y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i,s
\tag{T1}
\]

Because only one \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) can be 1, the right‑hand side reduces to the travel time at the chosen speed. The length used is the **free length** \\(L_s^{\text{free}}\\); the blocked part is simply not traversable.

5. **Linking departure of next segment**  

\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s+1}\ge t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; s=1,\dots,S-1
\tag{T2}
\]

(If a dwell time at stations is required, add a constant \\(d^{\text{stop}}_{i,s}\\) to the RHS.)

### 5.4. Acceleration / Deceleration limits  

6. **Speed‑change feasibility between consecutive segments**  

Let \\(v_{i,s}= \sum_{k} v_k\, y_{i,s,k}\\) be the actual speed on segment \\(s\\). Then

\[
v_{i,s+1} - v_{i,s} \le \Delta^{\max}_{\text{acc}}\; (t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s+1}-t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s}) \qquad\forall i,s
\tag{A1}
\]
\[
v_{i,s} - v_{i,s+1} \le \Delta^{\max}_{\text{dec}}\; (t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s+1}-t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s}) \qquad\forall i,s
\tag{A2}
\]

These linear constraints enforce that the **average acceleration** between two successive segments does not exceed the admissible limits. Because \\(v_{i,s}\\) is a linear combination of binaries, the constraints stay linear.

### 5.5. Single‑track capacity (headway)  

7. **Mutual exclusion on the same segment**  

For any two distinct trains \\(i\neq j\\) that both occupy segment \\(s\\):

\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s} \ge t^{\text{arr}}_{j,s}+C - M(1-z_{i,j,s})\qquad\forall i<j,\;s
\tag{H1}
\]
\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{j,s} \ge t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s}+C - M z_{i,j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\;s
\tag{H2}
\]

where \\(z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}\\) is a binary ordering variable (train \\(i\\) passes after train \\(j\\) on segment \\(s\\)). The big‑M term disables the constraint when the pair does not share the segment (i.e., when \\(x_{i,s}x_{j,s}=0\\)). To keep the model linear we add the following linking constraints:

\[
z_{i,j,s} \le x_{i,s},\qquad z_{i,j,s} \le x_{j,s},\qquad 
z_{i,j,s} \ge x_{i,s}+x_{j,s}-1 \qquad\forall i<j,s
\tag{H3}
\]

If the railway line has **parallel tracks** on segment \\(s\\), the headway can be relaxed by allowing two trains to occupy the segment simultaneously; this is captured by the route‑choice variable \\(r_{i,s,\ell}\\) that distinguishes the physical track.

### 5.6. Blockage feasibility  

8. **Trains cannot use the blocked portion** – already handled by the reduced length \\(L_s^{\text{free}}\\). However, if a segment is *completely* blocked for a time window \\([B_s^{\text{start}}, B_s^{\text{end}}]\\), we must prevent occupancy during that window:

\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s} \ge B_s^{\text{end}} \; \text{or}\; t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s} \le B_s^{\text{start}} \qquad\forall i,s\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{B1}
\]

Linearisation uses a binary \\(w_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\\):

\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s} \ge B_s^{\text{end}} - M w_{i,s}
\]
\[
t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s} \le B_s^{\text{start}} + M (1-w_{i,s})
\]
\[
w_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i, s\in\mathcal{B}
\]

If the blockage is only **partial** (i.e., a lane of a double‑track line is closed), the routing variables \\(r_{i,s,\ell}\\) can be used to force the train onto the remaining usable lane.

### 5.7. Delay and Energy accounting  

9. **Delay definition**  

\[
\delta_i = t^{\text{arr}}_{i,S} - a_i^{\text{orig}} \qquad\forall i
\tag{D1}
\]

If a train departs later than its original departure, the model automatically captures the extra time because the first segment departure time \\(t^{\text{dep}}_{i,1}\\) is a decision variable; we may also enforce a **no‑earlier‑departure** rule:

\[
t^{\text{dep}}_{i,1} \ge d_i \qquad\forall i
\tag{D2}
\]

10. **Energy consumption**  

\[
E_i = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c_k \, L_s^{\text{free}} \, y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i
\tag{E1}
\]

Since only one speed level per segment is active, the expression reduces to the sum of energy rates multiplied by the traversed distance.

### 5.8. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}, \; r_{i,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\}, \; y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\}, \; z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}, \; w_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
&t^{\text{dep}}_{i,s},\, t^{\text{arr}}_{i,s},\, \delta_i,\, E_i \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,j,s,\ell,k
\tag{V}
\]

---

## 6. Model Interpretation (what each block does)

| Block | Physical meaning |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Routing (R1‑R3)** | Guarantees that each train follows a **continuous path** from origin to destination, possibly choosing among parallel tracks (different routes) while respecting the blockage (unavailable routes can be forced to 0). |
| **Speed selection (S1)** | Couples the binary occupancy variable with a **single admissible speed level** on each traversed segment. |
| **Travel‑time (T1‑T2)** | Translates the chosen speed into a **deterministic travel time** (distance / speed) and links successive segments so that a train cannot leave a segment before it has arrived. |
| **Acceleration limits (A1‑A2)** | Enforce realistic **kinematic constraints**: a train cannot change speed between two adjacent segments faster than the allowed acceleration/deceleration. |
| **Headway (H1‑H3)** | Implements the **single‑track capacity** rule: two trains on the same physical track must be separated by at least a safety headway \\(C\\). The ordering binary \\(z_{i,j,s}\\) decides which train passes first. |
| **Blockage handling (B1)** | Prevents any train from occupying a **temporally blocked segment** during the forbidden time window, or forces it onto the remaining open lane using the routing variables. |
| **Delay definition (D1‑D2)** | Computes the **total lateness** of each train with respect to its original schedule, while forbidding early departures. |
| **Energy accounting (E1)** | Calculates the **total energy** spent, using the speed‑dependent consumption rates. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a **weighted sum** of passenger delay, energy consumption, and (optionally) route‑change penalties, thus balancing service quality and operational cost. |

---

## 7. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\substack{x,r,y,z,w\\ t^{\text{dep}},t^{\text{arr}},\delta,E}} \;& 
\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Bigl[ \alpha_i \,\delta_i \;+\; \beta_i \,E_i \;+\; p_i \!\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\!\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_s} r_{i,s,\ell}\Bigr] \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{Routing constraints } (R1)-(R3),\\
& \text{Speed‑level constraints } (S1),\\
& \text{Travel‑time constraints } (T1)-(T2),\\
& \text{Acceleration limits } (A1)-(A2),\\
& \text{Headway constraints } (H1)-(H3),\\
& \text{Blockage constraints } (B1),\\
& \text{Delay definition } (D1)-(D2),\\
& \text{Energy definition } (E1),\\
& \text{Variable domains } (V). 
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is a **linear mixed‑integer program** (MILP) because all constraints are linear in the continuous variables and the binary variables appear only linearly (or through standard big‑M linearisation). It can be handed directly to any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) to obtain an optimal integrated schedule that respects the partial blockage, respects physical train dynamics, and balances delay against energy use.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) for high-speed railway with partial segment blockage. Variables: binary routing decisions, train departure/arrival times, speed segment decisions. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, single track capacity, speed limits, acceleration/deceleration, flow conservation, binary routing.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)** on a high‑speed railway with a partially blocked segment.  

The model contains:

* **Sets** – trains, stations, track‑segments, time‑periods, speed‑levels.  
* **Parameters** – travel‑time, energy‑cost, block‑availability, capacity, acceleration limits, etc.  
* **Decision variables** – binary routing choices, continuous departure/arrival times, binary speed‑level selections.  
* **Objective** – a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.  
* **Constraints** – feasibility of timing, block occupancy, single‑track capacity, speed limits, acceleration/deceleration, flow‑conservation, and binary routing.

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binary routing and speed‑level variables, so the model is a **MILP**.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(\mathcal{T} = \{1,\dots,T\}\) | Set of trains (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(\mathcal{N} = \{0,1,\dots,N\}\) | Set of stations (node 0 = origin depot, node \(N\) = terminal). |
| \(\mathcal{S} = \{(i,j) \mid i,j\in\mathcal{N}, i<j\}\) | Set of directed track‑segments (arcs) from station \(i\) to station \(j\). |
| \(\mathcal{K} = \{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of admissible speed‑levels (e.g., “slow”, “normal”, “fast”). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\) | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance). |
| \(\mathcal{P}\) | Set of discrete time points used for block‑occupancy checks (e.g., every minute). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from station \(i\). | min |
| \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(i\). | min |
| \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i}\) | Minimum dwell time required at station \(i\) (boarding/alighting). | min |
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of segment \((i,j)\). | km |
| \(v^{\max}_{k}\) | Maximum admissible speed for speed‑level \(k\). | km/h |
| \(v^{\min}_{k}\) | Minimum admissible speed for speed‑level \(k\). | km/h |
| \(\alpha\) | Acceleration (or deceleration) limit (absolute value). | km/h² |
| \(E_{k}\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed‑level \(k\). | kWh/km |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of energy in the objective (relative to delay). | – |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\) | Penalty weight for delay of train \(t\) at station \(i\). | – |
| \(C\) | Capacity of a single‑track segment (normally 1 train at a time). | trains |
| \(B_{ij}(p)\) | Binary indicator: **1** if segment \((i,j)\) is blocked at discrete time \(p\); **0** otherwise. | – |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶). | min |
| \(R_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Origin station of train \(t\). | node index |
| \(R_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) | Destination station of train \(t\). | node index |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \(x_{t,ij} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | **Routing**: 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \((i,j)\), 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{t,ij}^{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | **Speed‑level selection**: 1 if train \(t\) uses speed level \(k\) on segment \((i,j)\). |
| \(d_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Actual **departure time** of train \(t\) from station \(i\). |
| \(a_{t,i} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Actual **arrival time** of train \(t\) at station \(i\). |
| \(\delta_{t,ij} \ge 0\) | Continuous | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \((i,j)\). |
| \(\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \in \{0,1\}\) | Binary | Occupancy indicator: 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \((i,j)\) at discrete time \(p\). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,
\bigl( d_{t,i}- d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\bigr)_{+}}_{\text{Total weighted passenger delay}}
\;+\;
\beta\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
E_{k}\,L_{ij}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}}
\]

*The “\((\cdot)_{+}\)” can be linearised by introducing auxiliary non‑negative variables*  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{delay}_{t,i} &\ge d_{t,i} - d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i} ,\\
\text{delay}_{t,i} &\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then the first term becomes \(\sum_{t,i} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,\text{delay}_{t,i}\).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Flow (routing) conservation  

For every train \(t\) and every intermediate station \(i\) (except origin/destination):

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ij}
\;-\;
\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ji}
\;=\;
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } i = R^{\text{orig}}_{t},\\
 -1 & \text{if } i = R^{\text{dest}}_{t},\\
  0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{F1}
\]

Thus each train leaves its origin once, arrives at its destination once, and the number of incoming arcs equals outgoing arcs at all other stations.

### 5.2. Speed‑level linking  

A train can choose **exactly one** speed level on a segment it actually traverses:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{t,ij}^{k}=x_{t,ij},
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F2}
\]

### 5.3. Travel‑time definition (linearised using speed bounds)  

If speed level \(k\) is selected, the travel time on \((i,j)\) is bounded by the inverse of the speed limits:

\[
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}_{k}}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}
\;\le\;
\delta_{t,ij}
\;\le\;
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\min}_{k}}\, y_{t,ij}^{k}
\qquad\forall t,(i,j),k.
\tag{F3}
\]

Because only one \(k\) can be 1 (by (F2)), the inequalities collapse to the appropriate bound.

### 5.4. Acceleration / deceleration limits between successive segments  

Let a train leave station \(i\) on segment \((i,j)\) with speed level \(k\) and later enter segment \((j,\ell)\) with speed level \(k'\). The change in speed must respect the acceleration limit \(\alpha\). Using the fact that speed = distance / travel‑time, we obtain a linear inequality after cross‑multiplication and using big‑M:

\[
\Bigl|\frac{L_{ij}}{\delta_{t,ij}} - \frac{L_{j\ell}}{\delta_{t,j\ell}}\Bigr|
\;\le\;
\alpha \, \bigl( d_{t,j} - a_{t,j} \bigr) + M\,(2 - x_{t,ij} - x_{t,j\ell})
\qquad\forall t,\, (i,j),(j,\ell)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F4}
\]

When either of the two arcs is not used (\(x=0\)), the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

### 5.5. Dwell‑time feasibility at stations  

If a train arrives at station \(i\), it must stay at least the minimum dwell time before departing:

\[
d_{t,i} \;\ge\; a_{t,i} + \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i} - M\,(1-\!\!\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}} x_{t,ij}) ,
\qquad\forall t,i.
\tag{F5}
\]

The big‑M term removes the constraint for stations where the train does not stop (i.e., when the outgoing sum is 0).

### 5.6. Time‑consistency between successive arcs  

If train \(t\) uses arc \((i,j)\) then the departure from \(i\) plus travel time equals the arrival at \(j\):

\[
a_{t,j} \;\ge\; d_{t,i} + \delta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-x_{t,ij}),
\qquad\forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}.
\tag{F6}
\]

The reverse inequality is not needed because the model minimizes delay; the above ensures a feasible schedule.

### 5.7. Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

A train may occupy a blocked segment only when the block is **not active** at the time of occupation. First we link the continuous time variables to the discrete occupancy variables:

\[
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \le x_{t,ij}, \qquad
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \in \{0,1\},
\quad \forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F7a}
\]

If the train traverses \((i,j)\) then for each discrete time point \(p\) that lies inside its travel window we must set \(\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}=1\). This can be linearised with “big‑M’’ intervals; a compact version is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,i} + \epsilon &\le p \;\;+\; M\,(1-\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}),\\
p &\le a_{t,i} + \delta_{t,ij} - \epsilon \;+\; M\,(1-\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}),
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P},
\tag{F7b}
\]

where \(\epsilon\) is a small positive number (e.g., 0.1 min) to avoid equality issues.

Now enforce that no blocked time is used:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \;\le\; 1 - B_{ij}(p),
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F7c}
\]

If \(B_{ij}(p)=1\) (segment blocked at time \(p\)), the right‑hand side becomes 0, preventing any train from occupying the segment at that time.

### 5.8. Single‑track capacity (unblocked segments)  

Even on free segments only one train may be present at a given time (single‑track assumption). Using the same occupancy variables for **all** segments:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \zeta_{t,ij}^{p} \;\le\; 1,
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{S},\,p\in\mathcal{P}.
\tag{F8}
\]

If a segment is double‑track in practice, the RHS could be set to the number of tracks.

### 5.9. Non‑negativity and domain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& d_{t,i}, a_{t,i}, \delta_{t,ij} \ge 0,\\
& x_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,ij}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\;
\zeta_{t,ij}^{p}\in\{0,1\},\\
& \text{delay}_{t,i}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F9}
\]

---

## 6. Model Summary  

Putting everything together, the MILP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{t,i} w^{\text{delay}}_{t,i}\,\text{delay}_{t,i}
      \;+\; \beta \sum_{t,(i,j)}\sum_{k} E_{k}\,L_{ij}\,y_{t,ij}^{k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(F1)}\; \text{flow conservation} \\ 
& \text{(F2)}\; \text{speed‑level linking} \\
& \text{(F3)}\; \text{travel‑time bounds} \\
& \text{(F4)}\; \text{acceleration limits} \\
& \text{(F5)}\; \text{minimum dwell time} \\
& \text{(F6)}\; \text{time consistency across arcs} \\
& \text{(F7a–c)}\; \text{block‑occupancy constraints} \\
& \text{(F8)}\; \text{single‑track capacity} \\
& \text{(F9)}\; \text{variable domains} \\
& \text{(delay linearisation)}\;
\begin{cases}
\text{delay}_{t,i}\ge d_{t,i}-d^{\text{sched}}_{t,i}\\
\text{delay}_{t,i}\ge 0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear) and contains **binary** variables \(x, y, \zeta\); therefore it is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.  

A commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) can be used to obtain the optimal rescheduling, routing, and speed‑level decisions that minimise the weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption while respecting all operational and safety constraints imposed by the partially blocked railway segment.
