MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-acceleration limits, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:  

*integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked.*  

The model contains  

* **decision variables** (continuous and binary),  
* a **linear objective function** that is a weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption, and  
* a set of **linear constraints** that enforce time feasibility, block‑occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed‑acceleration limits and the linearised energy‑calculation.  

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the formulation, and a short narrative explains each group of constraints.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of line segments (track sections) between two consecutive nodes, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete), indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(R_t\\) | Set of feasible routes for train \\(t\\) (each route is a sequence of segments). |
| \\(B\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of segments that are *partially blocked* (e.g., a work site). |
| \\(D\\) | Set of directed pairs of trains that travel in opposite directions on the same segment (bidirectional conflict set). |

Additional derived sets (used only in constraints)  

* \\(S_t^r\\) – the ordered list of segments traversed by train \\(t\\) when it follows route \\(r\\).  
* \\(P_{s}\\) – the set of trains that may occupy segment \\(s\\) (i.e., all \\(t\\) such that \\(s\in S_t^r\\) for some \\(r\\)).  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Physical length of segment \\(s\\). | km |
| \\(v^{\max}_k\\) | Speed corresponding to speed level \\(k\\). | km/h |
| \\(a^{\max}\\) | Maximum allowable acceleration (positive). | km/h² |
| \\(d^{\max}\\) | Maximum allowable deceleration (positive). | km/h² |
| \\(E_k\\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed level \\(k\\). | kWh/km |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) | Weight for total delay in the objective. | – |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Weight for total energy in the objective. | – |
| \\(T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) | Planned (scheduled) departure time of train \\(t\\) from its origin node. | minutes |
| \\(T^{\text{max}}\\) | Upper bound on the horizon (large enough to contain all feasible schedules). | minutes |
| \\(B^{\text{cap}}_s\\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy the blocked part of segment \\(s\\) simultaneously (normally 1). | trains |
| \\(c^{\text{block}}_{s}\\) | Length of the *blocked* sub‑portion of segment \\(s\\) (0 if not blocked). | km |
| \\(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two opposite‑direction trains on the same segment (safety margin). | minutes |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data and the work‑site description.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{t,r}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) is assigned to route \\(r\\in R_t\\), 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(t\\) from the **down‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(v_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual speed (km/h) of train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\). (Will be forced to one of the \\(v^{\max}_k\\) by the binary \\(y\\) variables.) |
| \\(e_{t}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumed by train \\(t\\) over the whole trip. |
| \\(z_{t}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Delay of train \\(t\\) relative to its planned departure time (i.e., \\(z_t = a_{t,s_0} - T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) where \\(s_0\\) is the first segment). |

---

## 4. Linearised Relationships  

### 4.1 Route‑selection linking  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

### 4.2 Speed‑level activation  

For each train‑segment pair, exactly one speed level must be chosen **if** the segment is traversed (the segment is traversed only when the selected route contains it).

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R_t: s\in S_t^r} x_{t,r} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

### 4.3 Speed‑value definition  

\[
v_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R3}
\]

Because \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) are binary and sum to 0 or 1, \\(v_{t,s}\\) will be forced to one of the admissible speeds.

### 4.4 Energy accumulation  

Energy on a segment = length × energy‑per‑km at the chosen speed.  

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s\,E_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R4}
\]

### 4.5 Delay definition  

Let \\(s_0(t)\\) be the first segment of the selected route for train \\(t\\). Using the route‑selection variables we can write a linear expression for the departure time from the origin node:

\[
a_{t,s_0}= T^{\text{plan}}_t + z_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R5}
\]

(Alternatively, enforce \\(z_t = a_{t,s_0} - T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) directly.)

---

## 5. Temporal Feasibility Constraints  

### 5.1 Travel‑time on a segment  

Travel time on segment \\(s\\) equals length divided by speed (linearised by multiplying both sides by speed). Because speed is a decision variable, the following linear relationship works:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} = \frac{L_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{T1}
\]

To keep the model linear, we pre‑compute the **travel‑time constant** for each admissible speed level:

\[
\tau_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v^{\max}_k} \quad (\text{minutes})
\]

Then enforce:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{T1'}
\]

### 5.2 Connection between consecutive segments  

If segment \\(s\\) is immediately followed by segment \\(s'\\) on the chosen route, the departure time from \\(s\\) must equal the arrival time at \\(s'\\):

\[
a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on some }r\in R_t \tag{T2}
\]

This can be linearised with big‑M using the route‑selection variables, but a cleaner way is to write for every ordered pair \\((s,s')\\) that can appear consecutively:

\[
a_{t,s'} - d_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1- \sum_{r\in R_t: (s,s')\in S_t^r} x_{t,r}\bigr) \tag{T2a}
\]
\[
a_{t,s'} - d_{t,s} \ge -M\bigl(1- \sum_{r\in R_t: (s,s')\in S_t^r} x_{t,r}\bigr) \tag{T2b}
\]

where \\(M\\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., \\(T^{\text{max}}\\)).

### 5.3 Horizon limits  

\[
0 \le a_{t,s} \le T^{\text{max}},\qquad 0 \le d_{t,s} \le T^{\text{max}} \qquad\forall t,s \tag{T3}
\]

---

## 6. Block‑Occupancy Constraints (Partial Segment Blockage)  

Only a limited number of trains may be inside the *blocked* sub‑portion of a segment at the same time.

Define the **entry time into the blocked part** of segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\) as  

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= a_{t,s} + \frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall s\in B
\]

and the **exit time from the blocked part** as  

\[
d^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= d_{t,s} - \frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall s\in B
\]

Again we linearise using the pre‑computed travel‑time constants for each speed level:

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]
\[
d^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= d_{t,s}- \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]

Now enforce a **capacity‑at‑any‑time** constraint by a classic time‑indexed formulation (or, more compactly, a pairwise non‑overlap constraint when the capacity is 1). Assuming capacity 1 for simplicity:

For every pair of distinct trains \\(t_1,t_2\\) that may use the same blocked segment \\(s\\):

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} \ge d^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \;\; \text{or} \;\; a^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \ge d^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s}
\]

Linearised with binary ordering variables \\(u_{t_1,t_2,s}\\in\{0,1\}\\):

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \ge -M\,u_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{B1}
\]
\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} \ge -M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{B2}
\]

If the blocked capacity is larger than 1, a time‑indexed cumulative formulation can be used, but the pairwise version suffices for the typical “single‑track work zone”.

---

## 7. Bidirectional Conflict Constraints  

When two trains travel in opposite directions on the **same physical segment**, a safety head‑way time \\(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\\) must separate them.

Let \\(D_{t,s}\\) be the *interval* \\([a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}]\\). For each unordered pair \\((t_1,t_2)\\in D\\) that are opposite‑direction on segment \\(s\\):

\[
a_{t_1,s} \ge d_{t_2,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} \quad\text{or}\quad a_{t_2,s} \ge d_{t_1,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}}
\]

Again linearised with a binary ordering variable \\(w_{t_1,t_2,s}\\in\{0,1\}\\):

\[
a_{t_1,s} - d_{t_2,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,w_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{C1}
\]
\[
a_{t_2,s} - d_{t_1,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,(1-w_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{C2}
\]

Only pairs that actually use segment \\(s\\) (i.e., both have \\(y_{t,s,k}=1\\) for some \\(k\\)) need the constraints; this can be enforced with a big‑M term multiplied by the product of the corresponding \\(y\\) variables (or by activating the constraints only when the pair is present via a preprocessing step).

---

## 8. Acceleration / Deceleration Limits  

The speed change between two consecutive segments for the same train cannot exceed the physical limits.

For a train \\(t\\) that traverses segment \\(s\\) followed by \\(s'\\):

\[
v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\,\frac{d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}}{60} \tag{A1}
\]
\[
v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\,\frac{d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}}{60} \tag{A2}
\]

Because the travel time on segment \\(s\\) is already expressed as a linear combination of the binary speed‑level variables (see (T1’)), the right‑hand sides become linear constants. Substituting the travel‑time expression:

\[
v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\,\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \tag{A1'}
\]
\[
v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\,\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \tag{A2'}
\]

These constraints are applied only when both segments are part of the chosen route (again using big‑M if needed).

---

## 9. Objective Function  

The planner wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy**:

\[
\min\; 
w^{\text{delay}} \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_t}_{\text{total delay (minutes)}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}} \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total energy (kWh)}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Both terms are linear in the decision variables because \\(z_t\\) and \\(e_t\\) are defined linearly above.

---

## 10. Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimise } & \; w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t} z_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t} e_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R5)} && \text{route‑selection and speed‑level linking} \\
& \text{(T1')–(T3)} && \text{travel‑time and horizon constraints} \\
& \text{(B1)–(B2)} && \text{blocked‑portion capacity (pairwise non‑overlap)} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C2)} && \text{bidirectional head‑way safety} \\
& \text{(A1')–(A2')} && \text{acceleration / deceleration limits} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t_1,t_2,s},w_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},v_{t,s},e_t,z_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only integer (binary) variables are the route‑choice, speed‑level, and ordering variables. Consequently the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 11. How each part reflects the description  

| Description element | Model component |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Binary route choice** | \\(x_{t,r}\\) with (R1). |
| **Departure/arrival times** | \\(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\\) with (T1')–(T3). |
| **Speed levels per segment** | \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) with (R2)–(R3) and travel‑time (T1'). |
| **Weighted sum of delay & energy** | Objective (OBJ). |
| **Time feasibility** | (T1')–(T3) guarantee that travel times match chosen speeds and that connections are respected. |
| **Block occupancy** | (B1)–(B2) enforce that at most the allowed number of trains are inside the blocked sub‑portion simultaneously. |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | (C1)–(C2) guarantee a safety head‑way between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment. |
| **Speed‑acceleration limits** | (A1')–(A2') bound the speed change between consecutive segments according to \\(a^{\max}\\) and \\(d^{\max}\\). |
| **Energy calculation** | (R4) computes the total energy as a linear function of the selected speed levels. |

---

### Remarks for implementation  

* The “big‑M” constant can safely be set to the planning horizon \\(T^{\text{max}}\\) (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes).  
* If the blocked capacity \\(B^{\text{cap}}_s\\) is larger than 1, replace the pairwise non‑overlap constraints with a **cumulative** (time‑indexed) formulation or a **resource‑constrained** formulation using integer variables that count the number of trains inside the blocked part at any time.  
* The set of conflict pairs \\(D\\) and blocked‑segment pairs can be generated in a preprocessing step to keep the model size manageable.  
* If a finer granularity of speed (continuous) is required, the binary speed‑level variables can be replaced by a piecewise‑linear approximation of the speed‑energy curve, still keeping the model linear.

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures all the requested features—route choice, timing, speed management, blockage handling, safety conflicts, acceleration limits, and a dual‑objective of delay‑plus‑energy—within a single linear mixed‑integer program ready for solution with commercial or open‑source MILP solvers.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-acceleration limits, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (choice of route, departure/arrival times)  
* **Speed‑management** on each track segment (discrete speed levels)  
* **Partial blockage** of some segments (only a part of the track is unavailable)  
* **Bidirectional conflict** when two trains travel opposite directions on the same segment  
* **Energy consumption** that depends on the chosen speed level  

The model is written in a **single‑commodity, time‑indexed** form that can be fed directly to a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are defined explicitly, and a short explanation of each element follows the formulation.

---

## 1. Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| **\(S\)** | Set of track segments, indexed by \(s\). |
| **\(V_s\)** | Set of admissible speed levels on segment \(s\) (e.g., \(\{1,2,3\}\) corresponding to 30 km/h, 50 km/h, 80 km/h). |
| **\(R_t\)** | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\). A route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of segments \((s_1,\dots ,s_{|r|})\). |
| **\(B_s\subseteq [0,L_s]\)** | Length of the blocked part of segment \(s\) measured from the upstream end (0 m) to the downstream end \(L_s\) (full length). If segment is not blocked, \(B_s=\emptyset\). |
| **\(L_s\)** | Physical length of segment \(s\). |
| **\(d^{\text{orig}}_t\)** | Original (planned) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin node. |
| **\(a^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\)** | Original (planned) arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (if the train uses that segment). |
| **\(c^{\text{delay}}_t\)** | Weight (cost) for one unit of delay of train \(t\). |
| **\(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\)** | Energy cost (e.g., kWh) incurred when a train traverses segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\). |
| **\(M\)** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time value (e.g., 10 000 s). |
| **\(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\)** | Minimum travel time on segment \(s\) when accelerating from the preceding speed to the next speed (linearized, see later). |
| **\(\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\)** | Minimum travel time on segment \(s\) when decelerating (similar). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) (implied by the chosen route). |
| \(v_{t,s}\in V_s\) | integer (discrete) | Speed level chosen for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (only defined if \(y_{t,s}=1\)). |
| \(dep_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(arr_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (if \(y_{t,s}=1\)). |
| \(exit_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual exit time of train \(t\) from segment \(s\) (i.e., arrival at downstream node). |
| \(\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (difference between actual and original arrival at its destination). |
| \(e_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumed by train \(t\) on segment \(s\). |
| \(z_{t,s}^{\text{up}}\), \(z_{t,s}^{\text{down}}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies the **up‑stream** (first) part of segment \(s\) (i.e., before the blocked part) and 0 otherwise. Similarly for the downstream part. These are needed to enforce that a train never enters a blocked portion. |
| \(b_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \(s\) (used for bidirectional conflict). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

We minimize a weighted sum of **total delay** and **total energy consumption**:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{t\in T} c^{\text{delay}}_t \, \delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}
      \;+\;
      \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{\text{energy}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}} \, y_{t,s}
}
\]

*The first term penalises late arrivals; the second term adds the energy cost that depends on the chosen speed level.*

Because \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\) is a constant for each speed level, the term is linear once the speed‑level variable \(v_{t,s}\) is integer‑valued.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage**  

   For each train‑segment pair, let \(\alpha_{r,s}=1\) if route \(r\) contains segment \(s\) (otherwise 0).  

   \[
   y_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R_t} \alpha_{r,s}\,x_{t,r}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   Hence \(y_{t,s}\) becomes binary automatically.

### 4.2 Timing feasibility  

3. **Departure cannot be earlier than the original schedule**  

   \[
   dep_{t}\ge d^{\text{orig}}_{t}\qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

4. **First segment arrival equals departure + travel time on first segment**  

   Let \(s^{(t)}_1\) be the first segment of the chosen route (implicit via \(y_{t,s}\)).  
   Travel time on a segment is the **segment length divided by the speed** associated with the chosen speed level.  
   Define a parameter  

   \[
   \tau_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{\text{speed}(v)}\qquad\forall s\in S,\;v\in V_s
   \]

   (speed(v) is the physical speed in m/s for level \(v\)).  

   Then for every train‑segment pair:

   \[
   arr_{t,s}\;\ge\; dep_{t}+ \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \qquad\forall t,s
   \]

   The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when the segment is not used.

5. **Link arrival of a segment to exit of the previous segment**  

   If segment \(s'\) precedes \(s\) on the chosen route of train \(t\), denote \(\text{pred}_t(s)=s'\). Then

   \[
   arr_{t,s}\;\ge\; exit_{t,\text{pred}_t(s)} - M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

6. **Exit time = arrival + travel time**  

   \[
   exit_{t,s}\;\ge\; arr_{t,s}+ \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

7. **Total delay definition**  

   Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment (i.e., the segment that leads to the destination node).  

   \[
   \delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\;=\; exit_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\qquad\forall t
   \]

   (If the original schedule gives a destination arrival time, we use that; otherwise we can use the original departure plus planned travel time.)

### 4.2 Blockage constraints (partial segment blockage)  

8. **A train may not occupy the blocked part**  

   For each segment \(s\) that has a blocked interval \(B_s=[b^{\text{low}}_s, b^{\text{high}}_s]\) (if empty the constraint is inactive).  
   We split the segment into two “virtual’’ sub‑segments:  

   * upstream (0 → \(b^{\text{low}}_s\)) – variable \(z^{\text{up}}_{t,s}\)  
   * downstream (\(b^{\text{high}}_s\) → \(L_s\)) – variable \(z^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\)  

   The train must occupy **only** the allowed part(s). A simple linear way is to enforce that the **travel time** on the blocked part is zero:

   \[
   \tau^{\text{blocked}}_{s,v}= \frac{b^{\text{high}}_s-b^{\text{low}}_s}{\text{speed}(v)}\qquad\forall s,v
   \]

   Then:

   \[
   exit_{t,s}\;-\;arr_{t,s}\; \ge\; \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - \tau^{\text{blocked}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}} \;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

   The term \(\tau^{\text{blocked}}\) is subtracted, effectively forcing the train to “skip’’ the blocked distance; the remaining travel time corresponds to the free portion.  
   In a tighter formulation we can introduce binary variables that decide whether the train enters the upstream part **or** the downstream part and enforce that the blocked interval is never entered; for brevity we keep the above linear approximation.

### 4.3 Bidirectional conflict on the same segment  

9. **Only one direction at a time** – For any unordered pair of trains \((t,t')\) that could be on the same segment \(s\) but travel in opposite directions, we introduce a binary ordering variable \(b_{t,t',s}\) :

   \[
   exit_{t,s} \le arr_{t',s} + M\,b_{t,t',s}\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   exit_{t',s} \le arr_{t,s} + M\,(1-b_{t,t',s})\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   The two constraints together force **either** train \(t\) finishes the segment before train \(t'\) enters, **or** the opposite, thus avoiding simultaneous opposite‑direction occupancy.

   (If the pair cannot be on the same segment due to routes, the corresponding constraints can be omitted.)

### 4.4 Speed‑acceleration / deceleration limits  

10. **Speed change between consecutive segments must respect acceleration capability**  

    Let \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\) be the minimum extra travel time required when the speed on segment \(s\) is **higher** than on the preceding segment (i.e., acceleration). Similarly \(\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) for deceleration.  

    For each train and each pair of consecutive segments \((s',s)\) on its route:

    \[
    v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
    \]

    The linearization of the time penalty:

    \[
    arr_{t,s} \ge exit_{t,s'} + \Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\,\max\{0, v_{t,s}-v_{t,s'}\}
                     + \Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\,\max\{0, v_{t,s'}-v_{t,s}\}
                     - M\,(1-y_{t,s})
    \]

    To keep the model linear we introduce auxiliary binaries  

    * \(a^{\text{up}}_{t,s}\) = 1 if \(v_{t,s}>v_{t,s'}\) (acceleration)  
    * \(a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\) = 1 if \(v_{t,s}<v_{t,s'}\) (deceleration)  

    and enforce  

    \[
    v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le M\,a^{\text{up}}_{t,s},\qquad
    v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le M\,a^{\text{down}}_{t,s},
    \]

    \[
    a^{\text{up}}_{t,s} + a^{\text{down}}_{t,s} \le 1,
    \]

    \[
    arr_{t,s} \ge exit_{t,s'} + \Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\,a^{\text{up}}_{t,s}
                               + \Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\,a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}
                               - M\,(1-y_{t,s}) .
    \]

    The parameters \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s},\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) are computed from the physical acceleration/deceleration limits (e.g., \(a_{\max}=0.5\;{\rm m/s^2}\)) and the length of the segment.

### 4.5 Energy calculation  

11. **Energy consumption matches the chosen speed level**  

    \[
    e_{t,s}= c^{\text{energy}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}}\,y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,s
    \]

    (Because \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\) is a known constant, this is linear.)

### 4.6 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{t,s}\in V_s,\; b_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a^{\text{up}}_{t,s},a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& dep_{t},\,arr_{t,s},\,exit_{t,s},\,\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t},\,e_{t,s}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the context of the problem |
|---------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Route‑choice binaries \(x_{t,r}\)** | Allow each train to select one feasible path through the network (different detours may avoid blocked segments). |
| **Segment‑usage binaries \(y_{t,s}\)** | Indicate whether a train actually traverses a given segment; they are linked to the chosen route. |
| **Speed level \(v_{t,s}\)** | Discrete speed choices (e.g., low/medium/high). The speed determines travel time \(\tau_{s,v}\) and energy consumption \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\). |
| **Departure/arrival/exit times** | Capture the temporal schedule of each train on every segment, enabling delay calculation and feasibility checks. |
| **Delay variable \(\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\)** | Measures how late a train arrives at its destination compared with the original timetable. |
| **Energy variable \(e_{t,s}\)** | Accumulates the energy cost for the selected speed on each segment. |
| **Blockage handling (\(z^{\text{up}}_{t,s},z^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\) or the “skip‑blocked‑length’’ formulation)** | Guarantees that a train never travels through the physically blocked portion of a segment. The model simply reduces the usable length of that segment. |
| **Bidirectional conflict binaries \(b_{t,t',s}\)** | Ensure that two trains moving in opposite directions cannot occupy the same segment at overlapping times (a classic head‑on safety constraint). |
| **Acceleration/deceleration binaries (\(a^{\text{up}},a^{\text{down}}\))** | Enforce realistic speed transitions between adjacent segments; they add a small extra travel time when the train speeds up or slows down. |
| **Objective (weighted sum of delay + energy)** | Provides a trade‑off: the planner can give a high weight to punctuality (large \(c^{\text{delay}}_t\)) or to sustainability (large \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\)). The model will automatically pick routes and speeds that best balance the two criteria while respecting all constraints. |
| **Big‑M constants** | Used to deactivate constraints when a segment is not used (i.e., when the corresponding binary is 0). The value must be larger than any feasible time difference in the problem. |

---

## 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the set of feasible routes \(R_t\) for each train (e.g., via a shortest‑path algorithm that respects the blocked portions).  
   * Define the discrete speed levels \(V_s\) and compute the corresponding travel times \(\tau_{s,v}\) and energy costs \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\).  
   * Determine the blocked interval \(B_s\) for every segment (if any).  
   * Compute the acceleration/deceleration penalties \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s},\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) from physical limits.  

2. **Model implementation**  
   * Write the formulation in a MILP modeling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
   * Feed the data, choose appropriate big‑M values (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s).  

3. **Solution**  
   * Run a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.  
   * The optimal solution provides for each train: the selected route, the departure time, the speed level on every traversed segment, and the resulting schedule (arrival/exit times).  

4. **Post‑processing**  
   * Compute the realized total delay and total energy consumption.  
   * If the solution is too costly in terms of computation time, consider:  
     - Reducing the number of candidate routes (column generation).  
     - Aggregating speed levels (fewer \(V_s\)).  
     - Using a decomposition (Benders or Lagrangian) that separates routing from timing.  

---

### Summary  

The MILP above captures **integrated train rescheduling and speed management** under **partial segment blockage**.  It simultaneously decides:

* **Which route** each train will take (binary variables).  
* **When** the train will depart, arrive at, and leave each segment (continuous time variables).  
* **How fast** it will travel on each segment (discrete speed level variables).  

All operational safety and physical constraints (blockage avoidance, bidirectional conflict, acceleration limits) are expressed linearly, while the objective balances **punctuality** and **energy efficiency**.  The model is ready for implementation in any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:  

*integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked.*  

The model contains  

* **decision variables** (continuous and binary),  
* a **linear objective function** that is a weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption, and  
* a set of **linear constraints** that enforce time feasibility, block‑occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed‑acceleration limits and the linearised energy‑calculation.  

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the formulation, and a short narrative explains each group of constraints.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of line segments (track sections) between two consecutive nodes, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete), indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(R_t\\) | Set of feasible routes for train \\(t\\) (each route is a sequence of segments). |
| \\(B\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of segments that are *partially blocked* (e.g., a work site). |
| \\(D\\) | Set of directed pairs of trains that travel in opposite directions on the same segment (bidirectional conflict set). |

Additional derived sets (used only in constraints)  

* \\(S_t^r\\) – the ordered list of segments traversed by train \\(t\\) when it follows route \\(r\\).  
* \\(P_{s}\\) – the set of trains that may occupy segment \\(s\\) (i.e., all \\(t\\) such that \\(s\in S_t^r\\) for some \\(r\\)).  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Physical length of segment \\(s\\). | km |
| \\(v^{\max}_k\\) | Speed corresponding to speed level \\(k\\). | km/h |
| \\(a^{\max}\\) | Maximum allowable acceleration (positive). | km/h² |
| \\(d^{\max}\\) | Maximum allowable deceleration (positive). | km/h² |
| \\(E_k\\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed level \\(k\\). | kWh/km |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) | Weight for total delay in the objective. | – |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Weight for total energy in the objective. | – |
| \\(T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) | Planned (scheduled) departure time of train \\(t\\) from its origin node. | minutes |
| \\(T^{\text{max}}\\) | Upper bound on the horizon (large enough to contain all feasible schedules). | minutes |
| \\(B^{\text{cap}}_s\\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy the blocked part of segment \\(s\\) simultaneously (normally 1). | trains |
| \\(c^{\text{block}}_{s}\\) | Length of the *blocked* sub‑portion of segment \\(s\\) (0 if not blocked). | km |
| \\(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two opposite‑direction trains on the same segment (safety margin). | minutes |

All parameters are assumed known from the timetable, infrastructure data and the work‑site description.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{t,r}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) is assigned to route \\(r\\in R_t\\), 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(t\\) from the **down‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(v_{t,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual speed (km/h) of train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\). (Will be forced to one of the \\(v^{\max}_k\\) by the binary \\(y\\) variables.) |
| \\(e_{t}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumed by train \\(t\\) over the whole trip. |
| \\(z_{t}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Delay of train \\(t\\) relative to its planned departure time (i.e., \\(z_t = a_{t,s_0} - T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) where \\(s_0\\) is the first segment). |

---

## 4. Linearised Relationships  

### 4.1 Route‑selection linking  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

### 4.2 Speed‑level activation  

For each train‑segment pair, exactly one speed level must be chosen **if** the segment is traversed (the segment is traversed only when the selected route contains it).

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R_t: s\in S_t^r} x_{t,r} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

### 4.3 Speed‑value definition  

\[
v_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R3}
\]

Because \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) are binary and sum to 0 or 1, \\(v_{t,s}\\) will be forced to one of the admissible speeds.

### 4.4 Energy accumulation  

Energy on a segment = length × energy‑per‑km at the chosen speed.  

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s\,E_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R4}
\]

### 4.5 Delay definition  

Let \\(s_0(t)\\) be the first segment of the selected route for train \\(t\\). Using the route‑selection variables we can write a linear expression for the departure time from the origin node:

\[
a_{t,s_0}= T^{\text{plan}}_t + z_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R5}
\]

(Alternatively, enforce \\(z_t = a_{t,s_0} - T^{\text{plan}}_t\\) directly.)

---

## 5. Temporal Feasibility Constraints  

### 5.1 Travel‑time on a segment  

Travel time on segment \\(s\\) equals length divided by speed (linearised by multiplying both sides by speed). Because speed is a decision variable, the following linear relationship works:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} = \frac{L_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{T1}
\]

To keep the model linear, we pre‑compute the **travel‑time constant** for each admissible speed level:

\[
\tau_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v^{\max}_k} \quad (\text{minutes})
\]

Then enforce:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{T1'}
\]

### 5.2 Connection between consecutive segments  

If segment \\(s\\) is immediately followed by segment \\(s'\\) on the chosen route, the departure time from \\(s\\) must equal the arrival time at \\(s'\\):

\[
a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on some }r\in R_t \tag{T2}
\]

This can be linearised with big‑M using the route‑selection variables, but a cleaner way is to write for every ordered pair \\((s,s')\\) that can appear consecutively:

\[
a_{t,s'} - d_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1- \sum_{r\in R_t: (s,s')\in S_t^r} x_{t,r}\bigr) \tag{T2a}
\]
\[
a_{t,s'} - d_{t,s} \ge -M\bigl(1- \sum_{r\in R_t: (s,s')\in S_t^r} x_{t,r}\bigr) \tag{T2b}
\]

where \\(M\\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., \\(T^{\text{max}}\\)).

### 5.3 Horizon limits  

\[
0 \le a_{t,s} \le T^{\text{max}},\qquad 0 \le d_{t,s} \le T^{\text{max}} \qquad\forall t,s \tag{T3}
\]

---

## 6. Block‑Occupancy Constraints (Partial Segment Blockage)  

Only a limited number of trains may be inside the *blocked* sub‑portion of a segment at the same time.

Define the **entry time into the blocked part** of segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\) as  

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= a_{t,s} + \frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall s\in B
\]

and the **exit time from the blocked part** as  

\[
d^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= d_{t,s} - \frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall s\in B
\]

Again we linearise using the pre‑computed travel‑time constants for each speed level:

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]
\[
d^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= d_{t,s}- \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]

Now enforce a **capacity‑at‑any‑time** constraint by a classic time‑indexed formulation (or, more compactly, a pairwise non‑overlap constraint when the capacity is 1). Assuming capacity 1 for simplicity:

For every pair of distinct trains \\(t_1,t_2\\) that may use the same blocked segment \\(s\\):

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} \ge d^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \;\; \text{or} \;\; a^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \ge d^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s}
\]

Linearised with binary ordering variables \\(u_{t_1,t_2,s}\\in\{0,1\}\\):

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \ge -M\,u_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{B1}
\]
\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} \ge -M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{B2}
\]

If the blocked capacity is larger than 1, a time‑indexed cumulative formulation can be used, but the pairwise version suffices for the typical “single‑track work zone”.

---

## 7. Bidirectional Conflict Constraints  

When two trains travel in opposite directions on the **same physical segment**, a safety head‑way time \\(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\\) must separate them.

Let \\(D_{t,s}\\) be the *interval* \\([a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}]\\). For each unordered pair \\((t_1,t_2)\\in D\\) that are opposite‑direction on segment \\(s\\):

\[
a_{t_1,s} \ge d_{t_2,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} \quad\text{or}\quad a_{t_2,s} \ge d_{t_1,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}}
\]

Again linearised with a binary ordering variable \\(w_{t_1,t_2,s}\\in\{0,1\}\\):

\[
a_{t_1,s} - d_{t_2,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,w_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{C1}
\]
\[
a_{t_2,s} - d_{t_1,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,(1-w_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{C2}
\]

Only pairs that actually use segment \\(s\\) (i.e., both have \\(y_{t,s,k}=1\\) for some \\(k\\)) need the constraints; this can be enforced with a big‑M term multiplied by the product of the corresponding \\(y\\) variables (or by activating the constraints only when the pair is present via a preprocessing step).

---

## 8. Acceleration / Deceleration Limits  

The speed change between two consecutive segments for the same train cannot exceed the physical limits.

For a train \\(t\\) that traverses segment \\(s\\) followed by \\(s'\\):

\[
v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\,\frac{d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}}{60} \tag{A1}
\]
\[
v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\,\frac{d_{t,s} - a_{t,s}}{60} \tag{A2}
\]

Because the travel time on segment \\(s\\) is already expressed as a linear combination of the binary speed‑level variables (see (T1’)), the right‑hand sides become linear constants. Substituting the travel‑time expression:

\[
v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\,\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \tag{A1'}
\]
\[
v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\,\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \tag{A2'}
\]

These constraints are applied only when both segments are part of the chosen route (again using big‑M if needed).

---

## 9. Objective Function  

The planner wants to **minimise a weighted sum of total delay and total energy**:

\[
\min\; 
w^{\text{delay}} \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_t}_{\text{total delay (minutes)}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}} \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} e_t}_{\text{total energy (kWh)}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Both terms are linear in the decision variables because \\(z_t\\) and \\(e_t\\) are defined linearly above.

---

## 10. Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{minimise } & \; w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t} z_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t} e_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R5)} && \text{route‑selection and speed‑level linking} \\
& \text{(T1')–(T3)} && \text{travel‑time and horizon constraints} \\
& \text{(B1)–(B2)} && \text{blocked‑portion capacity (pairwise non‑overlap)} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C2)} && \text{bidirectional head‑way safety} \\
& \text{(A1')–(A2')} && \text{acceleration / deceleration limits} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t_1,t_2,s},w_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},v_{t,s},e_t,z_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only integer (binary) variables are the route‑choice, speed‑level, and ordering variables. Consequently the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

## 11. How each part reflects the description  

| Description element | Model component |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Binary route choice** | \\(x_{t,r}\\) with (R1). |
| **Departure/arrival times** | \\(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\\) with (T1')–(T3). |
| **Speed levels per segment** | \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) with (R2)–(R3) and travel‑time (T1'). |
| **Weighted sum of delay & energy** | Objective (OBJ). |
| **Time feasibility** | (T1')–(T3) guarantee that travel times match chosen speeds and that connections are respected. |
| **Block occupancy** | (B1)–(B2) enforce that at most the allowed number of trains are inside the blocked sub‑portion simultaneously. |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | (C1)–(C2) guarantee a safety head‑way between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment. |
| **Speed‑acceleration limits** | (A1')–(A2') bound the speed change between consecutive segments according to \\(a^{\max}\\) and \\(d^{\max}\\). |
| **Energy calculation** | (R4) computes the total energy as a linear function of the selected speed levels. |

---

### Remarks for implementation  

* The “big‑M” constant can safely be set to the planning horizon \\(T^{\text{max}}\\) (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes).  
* If the blocked capacity \\(B^{\text{cap}}_s\\) is larger than 1, replace the pairwise non‑overlap constraints with a **cumulative** (time‑indexed) formulation or a **resource‑constrained** formulation using integer variables that count the number of trains inside the blocked part at any time.  
* The set of conflict pairs \\(D\\) and blocked‑segment pairs can be generated in a preprocessing step to keep the model size manageable.  
* If a finer granularity of speed (continuous) is required, the binary speed‑level variables can be replaced by a piecewise‑linear approximation of the speed‑energy curve, still keeping the model linear.

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures all the requested features—route choice, timing, speed management, blockage handling, safety conflicts, acceleration limits, and a dual‑objective of delay‑plus‑energy—within a single linear mixed‑integer program ready for solution with commercial or open‑source MILP solvers.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (choice of route, departure/arrival times)  
* **Speed‑management** on each track segment (discrete speed levels)  
* **Partial blockage** of some segments (only a part of the track is unavailable)  
* **Bidirectional conflict** when two trains travel opposite directions on the same segment  
* **Energy consumption** that depends on the chosen speed level  

The model is written in a **single‑commodity, time‑indexed** form that can be fed directly to a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are defined explicitly, and a short explanation of each element follows the formulation.

---

## 1. Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| **\(S\)** | Set of track segments, indexed by \(s\). |
| **\(V_s\)** | Set of admissible speed levels on segment \(s\) (e.g., \(\{1,2,3\}\) corresponding to 30 km/h, 50 km/h, 80 km/h). |
| **\(R_t\)** | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\). A route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of segments \((s_1,\dots ,s_{|r|})\). |
| **\(B_s\subseteq [0,L_s]\)** | Length of the blocked part of segment \(s\) measured from the upstream end (0 m) to the downstream end \(L_s\) (full length). If segment is not blocked, \(B_s=\emptyset\). |
| **\(L_s\)** | Physical length of segment \(s\). |
| **\(d^{\text{orig}}_t\)** | Original (planned) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin node. |
| **\(a^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\)** | Original (planned) arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (if the train uses that segment). |
| **\(c^{\text{delay}}_t\)** | Weight (cost) for one unit of delay of train \(t\). |
| **\(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\)** | Energy cost (e.g., kWh) incurred when a train traverses segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\). |
| **\(M\)** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time value (e.g., 10 000 s). |
| **\(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\)** | Minimum travel time on segment \(s\) when accelerating from the preceding speed to the next speed (linearized, see later). |
| **\(\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\)** | Minimum travel time on segment \(s\) when decelerating (similar). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) (implied by the chosen route). |
| \(v_{t,s}\in V_s\) | integer (discrete) | Speed level chosen for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (only defined if \(y_{t,s}=1\)). |
| \(dep_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(arr_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (if \(y_{t,s}=1\)). |
| \(exit_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual exit time of train \(t\) from segment \(s\) (i.e., arrival at downstream node). |
| \(\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (difference between actual and original arrival at its destination). |
| \(e_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumed by train \(t\) on segment \(s\). |
| \(z_{t,s}^{\text{up}}\), \(z_{t,s}^{\text{down}}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies the **up‑stream** (first) part of segment \(s\) (i.e., before the blocked part) and 0 otherwise. Similarly for the downstream part. These are needed to enforce that a train never enters a blocked portion. |
| \(b_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \(s\) (used for bidirectional conflict). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

We minimize a weighted sum of **total delay** and **total energy consumption**:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{t\in T} c^{\text{delay}}_t \, \delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}
      \;+\;
      \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c^{\text{energy}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}} \, y_{t,s}
}
\]

*The first term penalises late arrivals; the second term adds the energy cost that depends on the chosen speed level.*

Because \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\) is a constant for each speed level, the term is linear once the speed‑level variable \(v_{t,s}\) is integer‑valued.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage**  

   For each train‑segment pair, let \(\alpha_{r,s}=1\) if route \(r\) contains segment \(s\) (otherwise 0).  

   \[
   y_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R_t} \alpha_{r,s}\,x_{t,r}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   Hence \(y_{t,s}\) becomes binary automatically.

### 4.2 Timing feasibility  

3. **Departure cannot be earlier than the original schedule**  

   \[
   dep_{t}\ge d^{\text{orig}}_{t}\qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

4. **First segment arrival equals departure + travel time on first segment**  

   Let \(s^{(t)}_1\) be the first segment of the chosen route (implicit via \(y_{t,s}\)).  
   Travel time on a segment is the **segment length divided by the speed** associated with the chosen speed level.  
   Define a parameter  

   \[
   \tau_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{\text{speed}(v)}\qquad\forall s\in S,\;v\in V_s
   \]

   (speed(v) is the physical speed in m/s for level \(v\)).  

   Then for every train‑segment pair:

   \[
   arr_{t,s}\;\ge\; dep_{t}+ \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \qquad\forall t,s
   \]

   The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when the segment is not used.

5. **Link arrival of a segment to exit of the previous segment**  

   If segment \(s'\) precedes \(s\) on the chosen route of train \(t\), denote \(\text{pred}_t(s)=s'\). Then

   \[
   arr_{t,s}\;\ge\; exit_{t,\text{pred}_t(s)} - M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

6. **Exit time = arrival + travel time**  

   \[
   exit_{t,s}\;\ge\; arr_{t,s}+ \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

7. **Total delay definition**  

   Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment (i.e., the segment that leads to the destination node).  

   \[
   \delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\;=\; exit_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\qquad\forall t
   \]

   (If the original schedule gives a destination arrival time, we use that; otherwise we can use the original departure plus planned travel time.)

### 4.2 Blockage constraints (partial segment blockage)  

8. **A train may not occupy the blocked part**  

   For each segment \(s\) that has a blocked interval \(B_s=[b^{\text{low}}_s, b^{\text{high}}_s]\) (if empty the constraint is inactive).  
   We split the segment into two “virtual’’ sub‑segments:  

   * upstream (0 → \(b^{\text{low}}_s\)) – variable \(z^{\text{up}}_{t,s}\)  
   * downstream (\(b^{\text{high}}_s\) → \(L_s\)) – variable \(z^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\)  

   The train must occupy **only** the allowed part(s). A simple linear way is to enforce that the **travel time** on the blocked part is zero:

   \[
   \tau^{\text{blocked}}_{s,v}= \frac{b^{\text{high}}_s-b^{\text{low}}_s}{\text{speed}(v)}\qquad\forall s,v
   \]

   Then:

   \[
   exit_{t,s}\;-\;arr_{t,s}\; \ge\; \tau_{s,\,v_{t,s}} - \tau^{\text{blocked}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}} \;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
   \]

   The term \(\tau^{\text{blocked}}\) is subtracted, effectively forcing the train to “skip’’ the blocked distance; the remaining travel time corresponds to the free portion.  
   In a tighter formulation we can introduce binary variables that decide whether the train enters the upstream part **or** the downstream part and enforce that the blocked interval is never entered; for brevity we keep the above linear approximation.

### 4.3 Bidirectional conflict on the same segment  

9. **Only one direction at a time** – For any unordered pair of trains \((t,t')\) that could be on the same segment \(s\) but travel in opposite directions, we introduce a binary ordering variable \(b_{t,t',s}\) :

   \[
   exit_{t,s} \le arr_{t',s} + M\,b_{t,t',s}\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   exit_{t',s} \le arr_{t,s} + M\,(1-b_{t,t',s})\qquad\forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   The two constraints together force **either** train \(t\) finishes the segment before train \(t'\) enters, **or** the opposite, thus avoiding simultaneous opposite‑direction occupancy.

   (If the pair cannot be on the same segment due to routes, the corresponding constraints can be omitted.)

### 4.4 Speed‑acceleration / deceleration limits  

10. **Speed change between consecutive segments must respect acceleration capability**  

    Let \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\) be the minimum extra travel time required when the speed on segment \(s\) is **higher** than on the preceding segment (i.e., acceleration). Similarly \(\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) for deceleration.  

    For each train and each pair of consecutive segments \((s',s)\) on its route:

    \[
    v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le M\,(1-y_{t,s})\qquad\forall t,s
    \]

    The linearization of the time penalty:

    \[
    arr_{t,s} \ge exit_{t,s'} + \Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\,\max\{0, v_{t,s}-v_{t,s'}\}
                     + \Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\,\max\{0, v_{t,s'}-v_{t,s}\}
                     - M\,(1-y_{t,s})
    \]

    To keep the model linear we introduce auxiliary binaries  

    * \(a^{\text{up}}_{t,s}\) = 1 if \(v_{t,s}>v_{t,s'}\) (acceleration)  
    * \(a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\) = 1 if \(v_{t,s}<v_{t,s'}\) (deceleration)  

    and enforce  

    \[
    v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le M\,a^{\text{up}}_{t,s},\qquad
    v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le M\,a^{\text{down}}_{t,s},
    \]

    \[
    a^{\text{up}}_{t,s} + a^{\text{down}}_{t,s} \le 1,
    \]

    \[
    arr_{t,s} \ge exit_{t,s'} + \Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s}\,a^{\text{up}}_{t,s}
                               + \Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\,a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}
                               - M\,(1-y_{t,s}) .
    \]

    The parameters \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s},\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) are computed from the physical acceleration/deceleration limits (e.g., \(a_{\max}=0.5\;{\rm m/s^2}\)) and the length of the segment.

### 4.5 Energy calculation  

11. **Energy consumption matches the chosen speed level**  

    \[
    e_{t,s}= c^{\text{energy}}_{s,\,v_{t,s}}\,y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,s
    \]

    (Because \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\) is a known constant, this is linear.)

### 4.6 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{t,s}\in V_s,\; b_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a^{\text{up}}_{t,s},a^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& dep_{t},\,arr_{t,s},\,exit_{t,s},\,\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t},\,e_{t,s}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the context of the problem |
|---------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Route‑choice binaries \(x_{t,r}\)** | Allow each train to select one feasible path through the network (different detours may avoid blocked segments). |
| **Segment‑usage binaries \(y_{t,s}\)** | Indicate whether a train actually traverses a given segment; they are linked to the chosen route. |
| **Speed level \(v_{t,s}\)** | Discrete speed choices (e.g., low/medium/high). The speed determines travel time \(\tau_{s,v}\) and energy consumption \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\). |
| **Departure/arrival/exit times** | Capture the temporal schedule of each train on every segment, enabling delay calculation and feasibility checks. |
| **Delay variable \(\delta^{\text{delay}}_{t}\)** | Measures how late a train arrives at its destination compared with the original timetable. |
| **Energy variable \(e_{t,s}\)** | Accumulates the energy cost for the selected speed on each segment. |
| **Blockage handling (\(z^{\text{up}}_{t,s},z^{\text{down}}_{t,s}\) or the “skip‑blocked‑length’’ formulation)** | Guarantees that a train never travels through the physically blocked portion of a segment. The model simply reduces the usable length of that segment. |
| **Bidirectional conflict binaries \(b_{t,t',s}\)** | Ensure that two trains moving in opposite directions cannot occupy the same segment at overlapping times (a classic head‑on safety constraint). |
| **Acceleration/deceleration binaries (\(a^{\text{up}},a^{\text{down}}\))** | Enforce realistic speed transitions between adjacent segments; they add a small extra travel time when the train speeds up or slows down. |
| **Objective (weighted sum of delay + energy)** | Provides a trade‑off: the planner can give a high weight to punctuality (large \(c^{\text{delay}}_t\)) or to sustainability (large \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\)). The model will automatically pick routes and speeds that best balance the two criteria while respecting all constraints. |
| **Big‑M constants** | Used to deactivate constraints when a segment is not used (i.e., when the corresponding binary is 0). The value must be larger than any feasible time difference in the problem. |

---

## 6. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the set of feasible routes \(R_t\) for each train (e.g., via a shortest‑path algorithm that respects the blocked portions).  
   * Define the discrete speed levels \(V_s\) and compute the corresponding travel times \(\tau_{s,v}\) and energy costs \(c^{\text{energy}}_{s,v}\).  
   * Determine the blocked interval \(B_s\) for every segment (if any).  
   * Compute the acceleration/deceleration penalties \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{s},\Delta^{\text{dec}}_{s}\) from physical limits.  

2. **Model implementation**  
   * Write the formulation in a MILP modeling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
   * Feed the data, choose appropriate big‑M values (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s).  

3. **Solution**  
   * Run a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.  
   * The optimal solution provides for each train: the selected route, the departure time, the speed level on every traversed segment, and the resulting schedule (arrival/exit times).  

4. **Post‑processing**  
   * Compute the realized total delay and total energy consumption.  
   * If the solution is too costly in terms of computation time, consider:  
     - Reducing the number of candidate routes (column generation).  
     - Aggregating speed levels (fewer \(V_s\)).  
     - Using a decomposition (Benders or Lagrangian) that separates routing from timing.  

---

### Summary  

The MILP above captures **integrated train rescheduling and speed management** under **partial segment blockage**.  It simultaneously decides:

* **Which route** each train will take (binary variables).  
* **When** the train will depart, arrive at, and leave each segment (continuous time variables).  
* **How fast** it will travel on each segment (discrete speed level variables).  

All operational safety and physical constraints (blockage avoidance, bidirectional conflict, acceleration limits) are expressed linearly, while the objective balances **punctuality** and **energy efficiency**.  The model is ready for implementation in any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Blockage Scenario)**  

The formulation below captures all elements described in the prompt: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, discrete speed levels per segment, block‑occupancy, bidirectional conflict, acceleration limits, and a weighted objective that balances total delay with total energy consumption.  

All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model; any missing data are indicated as *assumptions* that can be filled from the timetable, infrastructure data, or engineering specifications.  

---  

### 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments (between two consecutive nodes), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by \(k\). |
| \(R_t\) | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\); a route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of segments. |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | Sub‑set of *partially blocked* segments. |
| \(D\) | Set of ordered train pairs \((t_1,t_2)\) that travel in opposite directions on the same physical segment (bidirectional‑conflict set). |

---  

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\). | km |
| \(v^{\max}_k\) | Physical speed belonging to speed level \(k\). | km h\(^{-1}\) |
| \(\tau_{s,k}=L_s/v^{\max}_k\) | Travel time on segment \(s\) at speed level \(k\). | min |
| \(E_k\) | Energy consumption per kilometre at speed level \(k\). | kWh km\(^{-1}\) |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Maximum acceleration (positive). | km h\(^{-2}\) |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum deceleration (positive). | km h\(^{-2}\) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\) | Minimum head‑way time between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment. | min |
| \(c^{\text{delay}}\) | Weight of one minute of delay in the objective. | – |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}\) | Weight of one kWh of energy in the objective. | – |
| \(T^{\text{plan}}_t\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\). | min |
| \(T^{\max}\) | Upper bound on the planning horizon (large enough for all feasible schedules). | min |
| \(c^{\text{block}}_s\) | Length of the *blocked* part of segment \(s\) (0 if not blocked). | km |
| \(M\) | Big‑\(M\) constant, e.g. \(M=T^{\max}\). | min |

*Assumption*: the blocked part of a segment is a single contiguous sub‑segment; if the blockage is on the whole segment set \(c^{\text{block}}_s=L_s\).  

---  

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from the downstream node of segment \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,s}\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Actual speed of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (forced to a level in \(K\)). |
| \(z_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Delay of train \(t\) w.r.t. its planned departure time. |
| \(e_t\) | continuous \(\ge0\) | Total energy consumed by train \(t\). |
| \(u_{t_1,t_2,s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for opposite‑direction trains on segment \(s\) (used in (C1)–(C2)). |
| \(w_{t_1,t_2,s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for blocked‑portion non‑overlap (used in (B1)–(B2)). |

---  

### 4. Model Formulation  

#### 4.1 Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

#### 4.2 Speed‑level activation  

For every train‑segment pair, exactly one speed level is chosen **iff** the segment belongs to the selected route:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in r} x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{R2}
\]

#### 4.3 Speed definition  

\[
v_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} v^{\max}_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{R3}
\]

#### 4.4 Energy calculation  

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s\,E_k\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R4}
\]

#### 4.5 Delay definition  

\[
z_t = a_{t,s_0(t)}-T^{\text{plan}}_t \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R5}
\]

where \(s_0(t)\) is the first segment of the route selected for train \(t\) (implicit via the \(x\)‑variables).

#### 4.6 Travel‑time on a segment  

\[
d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{T1}
\]

#### 4.7 Consecutive‑segment linking  

If segment \(s'\) follows \(s\) on a feasible route of train \(t\), the departure from \(s\) equals the arrival at \(s'\). Using a big‑\(M\) to activate only when the pair appears in the chosen route:

\[
a_{t,s'}-d_{t,s}\le M\Bigl(1-\sum_{r\in R_t:\;(s,s')\in r}x_{t,r}\Bigr) \tag{T2a}
\]
\[
a_{t,s'}-d_{t,s}\ge -M\Bigl(1-\sum_{r\in R_t:\;(s,s')\in r}x_{t,r}\Bigr) \tag{T2b}
\]

#### 4.8 Horizon limits  

\[
0\le a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\le T^{\max}\qquad\forall t,s \tag{T3}
\]

#### 4.9 Block‑occupancy (partial blockage)  

Define the **entry** and **exit** times of the blocked sub‑portion of segment \(s\in B\):

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]
\[
d^{\text{blk}}_{t,s}= d_{t,s}- \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s-c^{\text{block}}_s}{v^{\max}_k}\,y_{t,s,k}
\]

Pairwise non‑overlap (capacity = 1) for every unordered pair of trains that may use the same blocked segment:

\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} \ge -M\,w_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{B1}
\]
\[
a^{\text{blk}}_{t_2,s} - d^{\text{blk}}_{t_1,s} \ge -M\,(1-w_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{B2}
\]

If the blocked capacity is larger than 1, a cumulative formulation can replace the pairwise constraints.

#### 4.10 Bidirectional conflict on the same segment  

For each unordered opposite‑direction pair \((t_1,t_2)\in D\) on segment \(s\):

\[
a_{t_1,s} - d_{t_2,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,u_{t_1,t_2,s} \tag{C1}
\]
\[
a_{t_2,s} - d_{t_1,s} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,s}) \tag{C2}
\]

#### 4.11 Acceleration / deceleration limits  

Let the travel time on segment \(s\) when using speed level \(k\) be \(\tau_{s,k}\) (already defined). For two consecutive segments \(s\) and \(s'\) on the same train:

\[
v_{t,s'}-v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\,\tau_{s,k}\quad\text{if }y_{t,s,k}=1 \tag{A1}
\]
\[
v_{t,s}-v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\,\tau_{s,k}\quad\text{if }y_{t,s,k}=1 \tag{A2}
\]

Linearising with the binary speed‑level variables gives

\[
v_{t,s'}-v_{t,s} \le a^{\max}\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\,y_{t,s,k} \tag{A1'}
\]
\[
v_{t,s}-v_{t,s'} \le d^{\max}\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\,y_{t,s,k} \tag{A2'}
\]

#### 4.12 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{t_1,t_2,s},w_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},v_{t,s},z_t,e_t\ge0\qquad\forall t,s,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

---  

### 5. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{\min\; 
c^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T} z_t \;+\;
c^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T} e_t }
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The first term penalises total minutes of delay; the second term penalises total energy (kWh). By adjusting the weights the decision‑maker can trade punctuality against sustainability.

---  

### 6. How the Model Reflects the Problem Statement  

| Problem element | Model component |
|-----------------|-----------------|
| **Binary route choice** | \(x_{t,r}\) with (R1). |
| **Departure/arrival times** | \(a_{t,s},d_{t,s},z_t\) with (R5) and (T1)–(T3). |
| **Speed level per segment** | \(y_{t,s,k}\) with (R2)–(R3) and travel‑time (T1). |
| **Partial blockage** | Block‑occupancy constraints (B1)–(B2) using the reduced travel‑time inside the blocked sub‑portion. |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | Ordering variables \(u_{t_1,t_2,s}\) with (C1)–(C2). |
| **Acceleration / deceleration limits** | (A1')–(A2'). |
| **Energy‑delay trade‑off** | Objective (OBJ). |
| **All constraints are linear** → the model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** ready for CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, etc. |

---  

### 7. Remarks & Practical Implementation  

* **Big‑\(M\) selection** – set \(M = T^{\max}\) (or a larger safe value).  
* **Speed‑level discretisation** – typical high‑speed rail choices: 250 km h\(^{-1}\), 200 km h\(^{-1}\), 150 km h\(^{-1}\).  
* **Blocked‑capacity > 1** – replace pairwise (B1)–(B2) with a cumulative (time‑indexed) formulation if more than one train may occupy the blocked sub‑portion simultaneously.  
* **Decomposition** – for very large instances the model can be decomposed into a master IP (route‑choice) and sub‑problems (single‑train timing) as described in the paper; the MILP above is the *full* integrated version.  

---  

**Result** – Solving the MILP yields, for every train, a feasible route, a conflict‑free timetable, a concrete speed level on each traversed segment, and the associated energy consumption, while minimising the weighted sum of total delay and total energy. This model directly implements the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockages as described in the introductory text.
