**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures (i) the selection of a feasible timetable (arrival / departure times, train order and possible rerouting) and (ii) the generation of admissible speed‑profile decisions for every train‑segment pair.  All variables, parameters and sets are defined first, followed by the objective function and the complete set of linear constraints.  Wherever data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are explicitly indicated (marked **Assumption**).

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\) |
| \(S\) | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train), indexed by \(s\) |
| \(E\) | Set of track‑segments (directed edges) between consecutive stations, indexed by \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) |
| \(D\) | Set of disruption time windows, indexed by \(d\) (each \(d\) is a pair \((\tau^{\text{start}}_d,\tau^{\text{end}}_d)\)) |
| \(\mathcal{R}_t\) | Set of admissible routes for train \(t\) (original route + possible reroute(s)) |
| \(\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\) | Set of pre‑computed *speed‑plans* for train \(t\) on route \(r\) (see § 4) |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of discrete time‑intervals used for linearisation of speed‑profiles (e.g. 1‑min slots) |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \(L_e\) | Length of segment \(e\) (km) | Infrastructure data |
| \(\underline{v}_e,\ \overline{v}_e\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(e\) (km/h) | Safety / line‑capacity limits |
| \(\underline{a},\ \overline{a}\) | Minimum (braking) / maximum (acceleration) longitudinal acceleration (km/h² per min) | Train performance curves |
| \(\tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (min) | Operational rules |
| \(c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\) | Energy consumption (kWh) of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) when using speed‑interval \(k\) | Obtained from a linearised energy‑speed model |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | e.g. 10⁶ |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of the energy term in the objective (dimensionless) | Decision‑maker preference |
| \(\gamma\) | Penalty weight for train cancellation (if allowed) | Large positive number |
| \(\delta\) | Penalty weight for deviation from original schedule (delay) | Positive number |
| \(\theta_{t,s}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\phi_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\psi_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original planned arrival time of train \(t\) at its terminal (min) | Timetable data |
| \(\lambda_{e,d}\) | Binary indicator = 1 if segment \(e\) is blocked during disruption window \(d\) (otherwise 0) | Disruption description |
| \(\sigma_{t}^{\text{orig}}\) | Original route identifier of train \(t\) (used for rerouting cost) | Timetable data |

*Assumption 1*: Energy consumption is linearised by discretising the speed range on each segment into a finite set of speed‑intervals \(\mathcal{K}\). The coefficient \(c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\) is pre‑computed from the train’s traction‑braking characteristic.

*Assumption 2*: All trains have the same acceleration limits \(\underline{a},\overline{a}\). If train‑specific limits exist, replace by \(\underline{a}_{t},\overline{a}_{t}\).

*Assumption 3*: The disruption may affect only one direction of a double‑track line; the opposite direction remains usable (hence the possibility of rerouting to the opposite track).

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) (original or rerouted) |
| \(y_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if speed‑plan \(p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\) is selected for train \(t\) (the plan implicitly determines the route \(r\)) |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (minutes from a reference epoch) |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) |
| \(z_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if on segment \(e\) train \(t\) travels with speed‑interval \(k\) (i.e. uses the corresponding part of the selected speed‑plan) |
| \(c_t\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) is cancelled (no service) |
| \(u_{t_1,t_2,e}\in\{0,1\}\) | Binary | 1 if trains \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) **conflict** on segment \(e\) (i.e. occupy the same track at overlapping times) – used for conflict‑avoidance constraints |
| \(\eta_{t}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (difference between new and original arrival at terminal) |
| \(\epsilon_{t}\) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumption of train \(t\) (sum over selected speed‑intervals) |

---

## 4. Speed‑Plan Construction (pre‑processing)  

For each train \(t\) and each admissible route \(r\in\mathcal{R}_t\) we generate a *finite* set of feasible speed‑plans \(\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\).  
A speed‑plan \(p\) is a vector \(\{k_{e}^{p}\}_{e\in E(r)}\) that assigns to every traversed segment a speed‑interval index \(k\in\mathcal{K}\) satisfying:

* **Travel‑time feasibility**  
  \[
  \tau^{p}_{e}= \frac{L_e}{v_{k}} \quad\forall e\in E(r)
  \]
  where \(v_{k}\) is the representative speed of interval \(k\).  

* **Acceleration / deceleration feasibility** between consecutive segments \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) and \(e'=(s_j,s_{j+1})\):  
  \[
  v_{k_{e'}}-v_{k_{e}} \le \overline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e},\qquad
  v_{k_{e}}-v_{k_{e'}} \le -\underline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e}.
  \]

* **Blockage feasibility** – if segment \(e\) is blocked during the disruption window \(d\), the plan must avoid using the blocked direction:  
  \[
  \lambda_{e,d}=1 \;\Longrightarrow\; k_{e}\notin\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}} .
  \]

All feasible plans are enumerated (or generated by a column‑generation sub‑routine). The MILP only selects one plan per train (variable \(y_{t,p}\)).

*Assumption 4*: The number of plans per train is kept moderate (e.g., ≤ 30) by limiting the granularity of speed‑intervals and by discarding dominated plans (higher energy for same travel time).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

The decision maker wants a timetable that (i) respects the disruption, (ii) minimises total energy consumption, (iii) limits passenger delay, and (iv) penalises cancellations. A weighted linear objective is:

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}}_{\text{Energy}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}}_{\text{Passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} .
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where  

\[
\epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k},
\qquad
\eta_{t}= \bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}}\bigr)\,(1-c_{t}),
\]
\(s^{\text{term}}\) being the terminal station of train \(t\).

---

## 6. Core Constraints  

### 6.1 Route‑selection and plan‑selection  

1. **Exactly one route (or cancellation) per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r} + c_{t}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Exactly one speed‑plan consistent with the chosen route**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}} y_{t,p}= x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in\mathcal{R}_t. \tag{R2}
   \]

3. **Link plan to segment‑speed‑interval variables**  
   For each train‑segment‑plan triple, we enforce  
   \[
   z_{t,e,k}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\;:\;k_{e}^{p}=k} y_{t,p}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; k\in\mathcal{K}. \tag{R3}
   \]

   (If a segment does not belong to route \(r\), the corresponding sum is zero.)

### 6.2 Timing consistency  

4. **Travel‑time from departure at upstream station to arrival at downstream station**  
   For every train \(t\) and every traversed segment \(e=(s_i,s_j)\):
   \[
   a_{t,s_j}= d_{t,s_i}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E(t). \tag{T1}
   \]

5. **Minimum dwell time at stations**  
   \[
   d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\;(1-c_{t}) \qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; s\in S(t). \tag{T2}
   \]

6. **Origin and terminal time windows (optional service‑level constraints)**  
   \[
   d_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}\ge \phi_{t}^{\text{orig}}(1-c_{t}),\qquad
   a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}\le \psi_{t}^{\text{orig}}+U(1-c_{t}) . \tag{T3}
   \]
   where \(U\) is a large upper bound on permissible delay.

### 6.3 Disruption feasibility  

7. **Blocked‑segment prohibition** – a train may not occupy a segment during its blockage window. Using a time‑index formulation with the discretised horizon \(\mathcal{K}\) we enforce:
   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}}_{e,d}} z_{t,e,k}\le M\,(1-\lambda_{e,d})\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; d\in D. \tag{D1}
   \]
   (If \(\lambda_{e,d}=1\) the RHS becomes 0, forbidding any blocked‑direction speed‑interval.)

### 6.4 Bidirectional conflict avoidance  

Because after a reroute trains may share the same physical track in opposite directions, we must guarantee **headway** on each segment.

8. **Binary conflict indicator** – for any ordered pair of trains \((t_1,t_2)\) that use the same segment \(e\):
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k} - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C1}
   \]
   \[
   a_{t_1,s_j} \ge d_{t_2,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_2,e,k} - M\,(u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C2}
   \]
   Exactly one of the two orderings must hold:
   \[
   u_{t_1,t_2,e}+u_{t_2,t_1,e}=1 \qquad\forall t_1<t_2,\; e\in E \text{ used by both}. \tag{C3}
   \]

   The big‑M value is chosen larger than the maximal possible travel time on any segment (e.g., 10 × max\(\frac{L_e}{\underline{v}_e}\)).

9. **Safety headway** – a minimal time gap \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) (minutes) is required between successive trains on the same track:
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i}+ \sum_{k}\frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_e - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) . \tag{C4}
   \]

### 6.5 Delay and energy accounting  

10. **Delay definition** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \eta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}} \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{D2}
    \]

11. **Energy aggregation** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{E1}
    \]

### 6.6 Logical linking with cancellation  

12. **If a train is cancelled, all timing and speed variables are forced to zero**  
    \[
    a_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t}),\quad d_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t})\qquad\forall t,s. \tag{L1}
    \]
    \[
    z_{t,e,k}\le 1-c_{t}\qquad\forall t,e,k. \tag{L2}
    \]

---

## 7. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}
      +\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}
      +\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} && \text{Route / plan selection} \\
& \text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{Timing consistency} \\
& \text{(D1)–(D2)} && \text{Disruption feasibility} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{Bidirectional conflict avoidance} \\
& \text{(E1)} && \text{Energy accounting} \\
& \text{(L1)–(L2)} && \text{Cancellation logic} \\
& x_{t,r},y_{t,p},z_{t,e,k},u_{t_1,t_2,e},c_t\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\eta_t,\epsilon_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks & Modelling Choices  

| Issue | Modelling choice (and why) |
|-------|----------------------------|
| **Discrete speed representation** | Linearisation via a finite set of speed‑intervals \(\mathcal{K}\) makes the energy term linear and keeps the model MILP. |
| **Rerouting** | Each alternative route is treated as a separate binary variable \(x_{t,r}\). Rerouting is only allowed on the opposite track of the blocked direction, which is captured by the blockage indicator \(\lambda_{e,d}\). |
| **Bidirectional conflicts** | The pairwise ordering variables \(u_{t_1,t_2,e}\) guarantee a conflict‑free schedule on a shared track. The headway \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) can be set per segment (e.g., 2 min for high‑speed lines). |
| **Energy vs. Delay trade‑off** | The weights \(\beta\) and \(\delta\) let the planner emphasise either energy savings (e.g., for sustainability targets) or passenger service quality (delay reduction). |
| **Scalability** | The model can be decomposed as described in the paper (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems). In the MILP presented here, the plan‑selection variables \(y_{t,p}\) already embody that decomposition. |
| **Cancellation** | Optional; if the operator never cancels trains, set \(\gamma\) to a very large number or fix \(c_t=0\). |

---

## 9. Possible Extensions (not part of the core MILP)  

1. **Crew‑resource constraints** – add binary variables linking trains to crew blocks.  
2. **Platform capacity** – enforce that at any station the number of simultaneous dwellings does not exceed the number of available platforms.  
3. **Dynamic disruption update** – introduce scenario indices and a two‑stage stochastic version.  
4. **Non‑linear energy model** – replace the linearised coefficients by piecewise‑linear approximations (still MILP).  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential elements described in the introductory text: (i) selection of a feasible timetable under a partial‑track blockage, (ii) optional rerouting to the opposite track, (iii) conflict‑free bidirectional usage of the shared track, (iv) generation of executable speed‑profiles, and (v) a bi‑objective (energy + delay) linear objective suitable for a mixed‑integer linear programming solver.

* **Acceleration / deceleration feasibility** between consecutive segments \(e=(s_i,s_j)\) and \(e'=(s_j,s_{j+1})\):  
  \[
  v_{k_{e'}}-v_{k_{e}} \le \overline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e},\qquad
  v_{k_{e}}-v_{k_{e'}} \le -\underline{a}\,\tau^{p}_{e}.
  \]

* **Blockage feasibility** – if segment \(e\) is blocked during the disruption window \(d\), the plan must avoid using the blocked direction:  
  \[
  \lambda_{e,d}=1 \;\Longrightarrow\; k_{e}\notin\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}} .
  \]

All feasible plans are enumerated (or generated by a column‑generation sub‑routine). The MILP only selects one plan per train (variable \(y_{t,p}\)).

*Assumption 4*: The number of plans per train is kept moderate (e.g., ≤ 30) by limiting the granularity of speed‑intervals and by discarding dominated plans (higher energy for same travel time).

---

## 5. Objective Function  

The decision maker wants a timetable that (i) respects the disruption, (ii) minimises total energy consumption, (iii) limits passenger delay, and (iv) penalises cancellations. A weighted linear objective is:

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}}_{\text{Energy}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}}_{\text{Passenger delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t}}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} .
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where  

\[
\epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k},
\qquad
\eta_{t}= \bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}}\bigr)\,(1-c_{t}),
\]
\(s^{\text{term}}\) being the terminal station of train \(t\).

---

## 6. Core Constraints  

### 6.1 Route‑selection and plan‑selection  

1. **Exactly one route (or cancellation) per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_t} x_{t,r} + c_{t}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Exactly one speed‑plan consistent with the chosen route**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}} y_{t,p}= x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in\mathcal{R}_t. \tag{R2}
   \]

3. **Link plan to segment‑speed‑interval variables**  
   For each train‑segment‑plan triple, we enforce  
   \[
   z_{t,e,k}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{t,r}\;:\;k_{e}^{p}=k} y_{t,p}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; k\in\mathcal{K}. \tag{R3}
   \]

   (If a segment does not belong to route \(r\), the corresponding sum is zero.)

### 6.2 Timing consistency  

4. **Travel‑time from departure at upstream station to arrival at downstream station**  
   For every train \(t\) and every traversed segment \(e=(s_i,s_j)\):
   \[
   a_{t,s_j}= d_{t,s_i}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E(t). \tag{T1}
   \]

5. **Minimum dwell time at stations**  
   \[
   d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \tau^{\text{dw}}_{t,s}\;(1-c_{t}) \qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; s\in S(t). \tag{T2}
   \]

6. **Origin and terminal time windows (optional service‑level constraints)**  
   \[
   d_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}\ge \phi_{t}^{\text{orig}}(1-c_{t}),\qquad
   a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}\le \psi_{t}^{\text{orig}}+U(1-c_{t}) . \tag{T3}
   \]
   where \(U\) is a large upper bound on permissible delay.

### 6.3 Disruption feasibility  

7. **Blocked‑segment prohibition** – a train may not occupy a segment during its blockage window. Using a time‑index formulation with the discretised horizon \(\mathcal{K}\) we enforce:
   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}^{\text{blocked}}_{e,d}} z_{t,e,k}\le M\,(1-\lambda_{e,d})\qquad
   \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; d\in D. \tag{D1}
   \]
   (If \(\lambda_{e,d}=1\) the RHS becomes 0, forbidding any blocked‑direction speed‑interval.)

### 6.4 Bidirectional conflict avoidance  

Because after a reroute trains may share the same physical track in opposite directions, we must guarantee **headway** on each segment.

8. **Binary conflict indicator** – for any ordered pair of trains \((t_1,t_2)\) that use the same segment \(e\):
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k} - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C1}
   \]
   \[
   a_{t_1,s_j} \ge d_{t_2,s_i} + \sum_{k} \frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_2,e,k} - M\,(u_{t_1,t_2,e}) \tag{C2}
   \]
   Exactly one of the two orderings must hold:
   \[
   u_{t_1,t_2,e}+u_{t_2,t_1,e}=1 \qquad\forall t_1<t_2,\; e\in E \text{ used by both}. \tag{C3}
   \]

   The big‑M value is chosen larger than the maximal possible travel time on any segment (e.g., 10 × max\(\frac{L_e}{\underline{v}_e}\)).

9. **Safety headway** – a minimal time gap \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) (minutes) is required between successive trains on the same track:
   \[
   a_{t_2,s_j} \ge d_{t_1,s_i}+ \sum_{k}\frac{L_e}{v_k}\,z_{t_1,e,k}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_e - M\,(1-u_{t_1,t_2,e}) . \tag{C4}
   \]

### 6.5 Delay and energy accounting  

10. **Delay definition** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \eta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{term}}}-\theta_{t}^{\text{orig}} \qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{D2}
    \]

11. **Energy aggregation** (already used in the objective)  
    \[
    \epsilon_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} c^{\text{energy}}_{t,e,k}\,z_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T. \tag{E1}
    \]

### 6.6 Logical linking with cancellation  

12. **If a train is cancelled, all timing and speed variables are forced to zero**  
    \[
    a_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t}),\quad d_{t,s}\le M\,(1-c_{t})\qquad\forall t,s. \tag{L1}
    \]
    \[
    z_{t,e,k}\le 1-c_{t}\qquad\forall t,e,k. \tag{L2}
    \]

---

## 7. Complete MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \beta\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_{t}
      +\delta\sum_{t\in T}\eta_{t}
      +\gamma\sum_{t\in T}c_{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} && \text{Route / plan selection} \\
& \text{(T1)–(T3)} && \text{Timing consistency} \\
& \text{(D1)–(D2)} && \text{Disruption feasibility} \\
& \text{(C1)–(C4)} && \text{Bidirectional conflict avoidance} \\
& \text{(E1)} && \text{Energy accounting} \\
& \text{(L1)–(L2)} && \text{Cancellation logic} \\
& x_{t,r},y_{t,p},z_{t,e,k},u_{t_1,t_2,e},c_t\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\eta_t,\epsilon_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks & Modelling Choices  

| Issue | Modelling choice (and why) |
|-------|----------------------------|
| **Discrete speed representation** | Linearisation via a finite set of speed‑intervals \(\mathcal{K}\) makes the energy term linear and keeps the model MILP. |
| **Rerouting** | Each alternative route is treated as a separate binary variable \(x_{t,r}\). Rerouting is only allowed on the opposite track of the blocked direction, which is captured by the blockage indicator \(\lambda_{e,d}\). |
| **Bidirectional conflicts** | The pairwise ordering variables \(u_{t_1,t_2,e}\) guarantee a conflict‑free schedule on a shared track. The headway \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_e\) can be set per segment (e.g., 2 min for high‑speed lines). |
| **Energy vs. Delay trade‑off** | The weights \(\beta\) and \(\delta\) let the planner emphasise either energy savings (e.g., for sustainability targets) or passenger service quality (delay reduction). |
| **Scalability** | The model can be decomposed as described in the paper (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems). In the MILP presented here, the plan‑selection variables \(y_{t,p}\) already embody that decomposition. |
| **Cancellation** | Optional; if the operator never cancels trains, set \(\gamma\) to a very large number or fix \(c_t=0\). |

---

## 9. Possible Extensions (not part of the core MILP)  

1. **Crew‑resource constraints** – add binary variables linking trains to crew blocks.  
2. **Platform capacity** – enforce that at any station the number of simultaneous dwellings does not exceed the number of available platforms.  
3. **Dynamic disruption update** – introduce scenario indices and a two‑stage stochastic version.  
4. **Non‑linear energy model** – replace the linearised coefficients by piecewise‑linear approximations (still MILP).  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential elements described in the introductory text: (i) selection of a feasible timetable under a partial‑track blockage, (ii) optional rerouting to the opposite track, (iii) conflict‑free bidirectional usage of the shared track, (iv) generation of executable speed‑profiles, and (v) a bi‑objective (energy + delay) linear objective suitable for a mixed‑integer linear programming solver.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

response.content:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model – Pellegrini et al., 2015)*  

---

## 1. Sets, indices and basic data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**   | Set of *track sections* (blocks or TTD‑sections). A section *s* is characterised by a start node *n⁻(s)* and an end node *n⁺(s)*. |
| **N**   | Set of network nodes (stations, switches, block boundaries). |
| **K**   | Set of *speed‑profile options* (e.g. “cruise‑high”, “cruise‑low”, “stop‑and‑go”). |
| **P**   | Set of *precedence pairs*  \((t,i) \in P\) meaning train *t* may be scheduled **after** train *i* on at least one common section (used for re‑ordering). |
| **Δt**  | Length of the planning horizon discretisation (e.g. 1 s).  (Assumption A1 – the timetable is discretised in uniform time steps.) |
| **τ₀ₜ** | Original (planned) departure time of train *t* from its origin node. |
| **vₘₐₓₜ** | Maximum allowed speed of train *t* (km/h). |
| **Lₛ** | Physical length of section *s* (km). |
| **bₛ** | Braking distance required to stop **exactly** at the end of section *s* when travelling at the speed that will be present at the entry of *s*.  (Assumption A2 – braking distance is a linear function of speed, see Eq. (2).) |
| **cₛ** | Capacity of section *s* (normally 1, i.e. at most one train can occupy the section at a time). |
| **M**   | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. |
| **ε**   | Small positive number (e.g. 10⁻⁶) to enforce strict inequalities when required. |

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **xₜₛᵏ** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses section *s* using speed‑profile *k*; 0 otherwise. |
| **aₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Arrival time* of train *t* at the **beginning** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁻(s)*). |
| **dₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Departure time* of train *t* from the **end** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁺(s)*). |
| **δₜᵢ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is scheduled **after** train *i* on every common section (i.e. *t* follows *i*); 0 otherwise. |
| **zₜ**   | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train *t* (difference between actual and original departure from origin). |
| **yₜₛ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is *blocked* on section *s* (i.e. occupies the section at any instant). Used to enforce capacity constraints. |
| **bipₜₛ**| continuous, ≥0 | *Brake‑Indication Point* of train *t* measured **up‑stream** from the end of section *s* (distance, km).  (Assumption A3 – brake‑indication point is a linear function of the selected speed profile.) |

---

## 3. Parameters derived from the speed‑profile set  

For each speed‑profile *k* we define:

* **vₖ** – cruising speed (km/h) associated with profile *k*.  
* **τₖ** – travel time to cross a unit‑length section at speed *vₖ*:  

\[
\tau_{k}= \frac{1}{v_{k}}\;\; \text{[h·km⁻¹]} .
\]

* **βₖ** – *braking‑distance factor* (km per km/h) for profile *k* (obtained from the train‑braking curve). Then the braking distance for a section entered at speed *vₖ* is  

\[
b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k}\, v_{k}\qquad\text{(km)} .
\]

These parameters are assumed known (Assumption A4).

---

## 4. Objective function  

Minimise the **total network delay** (or any weighted version). The basic formulation is  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}
\]

where  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t} .
\]

If a weighted objective is required (e.g. passenger‑weighted delay) replace the sum with \(\sum_{t} w_{t}z_{t}\).

---

## 5. Core constraints  

### 5.1. Path selection – each train must choose exactly one speed profile on each traversed section  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}= y_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{1}
\]

where \(S_{t}\subseteq S\) is the set of sections that belong to the *planned* route of train *t* (assumed known from the timetable).

\[
\sum_{s\in S_{t}} y_{t s}=|S_{t}| \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.2. Timing propagation along the route  

For every train *t* and consecutive sections \(s\) and \(s'\) (i.e. \(n^{+}(s)=n^{-}(s')\)) :

\[
a_{t s'} \ge d_{t s} + \epsilon \qquad\forall t,\; \forall (s,s')\text{ consecutive}
\tag{3}
\]

Departure from a section equals arrival plus traversal time (including dwell time if the node is a station). Traversal time depends on the chosen speed profile:

\[
d_{t s}= a_{t s}+ \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\,\bigl( \tau_{k}\,L_{s} \bigr) + \theta_{t s}
\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{4}
\]

\(\theta_{t s}\) is the *dwell time* at the end node of section *s* (zero for pure track sections, positive for stations).  

### 5.3. Brake‑indication point – speed‑dependent separation  

For every pair of trains \((t,i)\) that share a common section *s* (i.e. both traverse *s*), the **minimum safe headway** is the braking distance of the *following* train plus a safety margin *γ* (km). Using the binary precedence variable \(\delta_{ti}\) we enforce:

\[
a_{t s} \ge d_{i s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} + \gamma \;-\; M\,(1-\delta_{ti}) \qquad\forall t,i\in T,\; t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i},\; \forall k\in K
\tag{5}
\]

where \(b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k} v_{k}\) is the braking distance of train *t* when it uses profile *k* on section *s*. The term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) converts the distance into a **time** (seconds) needed for the following train to travel its own braking distance after the leading train has cleared the section.  

The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when \(\delta_{ti}=0\) (i.e. train *t* does **not** follow *i*).  

To guarantee a consistent ordering on each shared section we add:

\[
\delta_{ti} + \delta_{it}= y_{t s}\, y_{i s} \qquad\forall t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i}
\tag{6}
\]

(If both trains occupy the section, exactly one of the two precedence binaries must be 1.)

### 5.4. Section capacity (single‑track occupation)  

Because DTG allows *continuous* braking supervision, the **effective occupancy** of a section ends at the *brake‑indication point* of the following train, not necessarily at the physical end. We linearise this by ensuring that at any time instant the number of trains whose **brake‑indication point** lies inside a section does not exceed its capacity:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \Bigl[ a_{t s} \le \tau \le d_{t s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} \Bigr] \le c_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; \forall \tau\in\{0,\Delta t,2\Delta t,\dots\}
\tag{7}
\]

In practice (MILP) we replace the time‑indexation by a *pairwise* condition similar to (5). The result is that the precedence constraints already guarantee capacity, so (7) can be omitted if (5)–(6) are enforced for **all** common sections.

### 5.5. Origin‑departure delay definition  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{8}
\]

### 5.6. Re‑ordering (optional)  

If the dispatcher is allowed to **re‑order** trains on a shared corridor, we introduce binary variables \(r_{ti}\) that indicate that train *t* is placed **ahead** of train *i* in the new timetable (even if originally behind). The model already contains \(\delta_{ti}\) which serves this purpose; we simply allow \(\delta_{ti}\) to be 0 or 1 regardless of the original order, thus enabling re‑ordering.

### 5.7. Logical linking of brake‑indication point to speed profile  

\[
bip_{t s}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\, b_{s}^{k}\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{9}
\]

The *brake‑indication point* measured upstream from the end of section *s* equals the braking distance associated with the selected speed profile.

---

## 6. Additional practical constraints (assumptions)  

| # | Constraint | Reason / Assumption |
|---|------------|----------------------|
| A5 | **Maximum speed limit**: \(\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k} v_{k}\le v_{\max t}\) for all *t,s* | Guarantees that the chosen profile never exceeds the train’s technical limit. |
| A6 | **Minimum dwell time at stations**: \(\theta_{t s}\ge \theta^{\min}_{s}\) if node *n⁺(s)* is a station. | Reflects passenger boarding/alighting requirements. |
| A7 | **Switch‑specific sections**: For sections that contain a switch, a dedicated set \(S^{\text{sw}}\subseteq S\) may have a larger safety margin \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}>\gamma\). | Switches are critical points; extra headway is required. |
| A8 | **Binary linearisation**: \(y_{t s}= \min\{1,\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k}\}\) is enforced by (1) and (2). | Guarantees consistency between “section used” and “profile selected”. |
| A9 | **Big‑M value**: \(M\) must be larger than the maximal possible time difference between any two trains on a common section (e.g., horizon length). | Standard linearisation practice. |

---

## 7. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} z_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(9)} && \text{core model}\\
&\text{(A5)–(A9)} && \text{practical safety / operational limits}\\
& x_{t s}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t s}\in\{0,1\},\; \delta_{ti}\in\{0,1\} && \forall t,i,s,k\\
& a_{t s}, d_{t s}, z_{t}, bip_{t s}\ge 0 && \forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on linearity  

* All constraints are linear except the **pairwise ordering** (6) which contains a product of binaries \(y_{t s} y_{i s}\). This product can be linearised by introducing an auxiliary binary \(w_{ti s}= y_{t s} y_{i s}\) and the standard three constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{ti s} &\le y_{t s}\\
w_{ti s} &\le y_{i s}\\
w_{ti s} &\ge y_{t s}+ y_{i s}-1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then (6) becomes \(\delta_{ti}+ \delta_{it}= w_{ti s}\).  

* The conversion of braking distance into a time (Eq. 5) uses the known speed \(v_{k}\); the term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) is a constant for each \((k,s)\) pair, thus preserving linearity.

* The model contains **O(|T|·|S|·|K|)** binary variables and **O(|T|·|S|)** continuous variables, which is comparable to the original RECIFE‑MILP size and solvable with modern MILP solvers for realistic regional networks (hundreds of trains, few thousand sections).

---

1. **Speed‑dependent braking distance** – introduced via the parameters \(b_{s}^{k}\) and the brake‑indication point variable \(bip_{t s}\).  
2. **Dynamic headway** – Eq. (5) enforces that the following train may only start its movement after the leading train has cleared the *brake‑indication* distance, not merely the physical block.  
3. **Distinction between switches and regular track** – safety margin \(\gamma\) can be replaced by \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}\) on the subset \(S^{\text{sw}}\).  
4. **Re‑ordering / retiming** – the precedence binaries \(\delta_{ti}\) are free decision variables, allowing the optimizer to change the order of trains on a shared corridor when it reduces total delay.  
5. **Continuous speed‑profile choice** – the set \(K\) permits the optimizer to select a slower or faster cruising speed on each section, thereby influencing both travel time and required braking distance.

---

### End of formulation  

The presented MILP fully describes a **conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem for railways equipped with distance‑to‑go signalling**, integrating the speed‑dependent separation distances that are the hallmark of DTG systems while preserving the linear structure required for exact optimisation.

*(enhanced version of the RECIFE‑MILP model – Pellegrini et al., 2015)*  

---

## 1. Sets, indices and basic data  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**   | Set of *track sections* (blocks or TTD‑sections). A section *s* is characterised by a start node *n⁻(s)* and an end node *n⁺(s)*. |
| **N**   | Set of network nodes (stations, switches, block boundaries). |
| **K**   | Set of *speed‑profile options* (e.g. “cruise‑high”, “cruise‑low”, “stop‑and‑go”). |
| **P**   | Set of *precedence pairs*  \((t,i) \in P\) meaning train *t* may be scheduled **after** train *i* on at least one common section (used for re‑ordering). |
| **Δt**  | Length of the planning horizon discretisation (e.g. 1 s).  (Assumption A1 – the timetable is discretised in uniform time steps.) |
| **τ₀ₜ** | Original (planned) departure time of train *t* from its origin node. |
| **vₘₐₓₜ** | Maximum allowed speed of train *t* (km/h). |
| **Lₛ** | Physical length of section *s* (km). |
| **bₛ** | Braking distance required to stop **exactly** at the end of section *s* when travelling at the speed that will be present at the entry of *s*.  (Assumption A2 – braking distance is a linear function of speed, see Eq. (2).) |
| **cₛ** | Capacity of section *s* (normally 1, i.e. at most one train can occupy the section at a time). |
| **M**   | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. |
| **ε**   | Small positive number (e.g. 10⁻⁶) to enforce strict inequalities when required. |

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **xₜₛᵏ** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses section *s* using speed‑profile *k*; 0 otherwise. |
| **aₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Arrival time* of train *t* at the **beginning** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁻(s)*). |
| **dₜₛ**  | continuous, ≥0 | *Departure time* of train *t* from the **end** of section *s* (i.e. at node *n⁺(s)*). |
| **δₜᵢ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is scheduled **after** train *i* on every common section (i.e. *t* follows *i*); 0 otherwise. |
| **zₜ**   | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train *t* (difference between actual and original departure from origin). |
| **yₜₛ** | binary | 1 if train *t* is *blocked* on section *s* (i.e. occupies the section at any instant). Used to enforce capacity constraints. |
| **bipₜₛ**| continuous, ≥0 | *Brake‑Indication Point* of train *t* measured **up‑stream** from the end of section *s* (distance, km).  (Assumption A3 – brake‑indication point is a linear function of the selected speed profile.) |

---

## 3. Parameters derived from the speed‑profile set  

For each speed‑profile *k* we define:

* **vₖ** – cruising speed (km/h) associated with profile *k*.  
* **τₖ** – travel time to cross a unit‑length section at speed *vₖ*:  

\[
\tau_{k}= \frac{1}{v_{k}}\;\; \text{[h·km⁻¹]} .
\]

* **βₖ** – *braking‑distance factor* (km per km/h) for profile *k* (obtained from the train‑braking curve). Then the braking distance for a section entered at speed *vₖ* is  

\[
b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k}\, v_{k}\qquad\text{(km)} .
\]

These parameters are assumed known (Assumption A4).

---

## 4. Objective function  

Minimise the **total network delay** (or any weighted version). The basic formulation is  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}
\]

where  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t} .
\]

If a weighted objective is required (e.g. passenger‑weighted delay) replace the sum with \(\sum_{t} w_{t}z_{t}\).

---

## 5. Core constraints  

### 5.1. Path selection – each train must choose exactly one speed profile on each traversed section  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}= y_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{1}
\]

where \(S_{t}\subseteq S\) is the set of sections that belong to the *planned* route of train *t* (assumed known from the timetable).

\[
\sum_{s\in S_{t}} y_{t s}=|S_{t}| \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{2}
\]

### 5.2. Timing propagation along the route  

For every train *t* and consecutive sections \(s\) and \(s'\) (i.e. \(n^{+}(s)=n^{-}(s')\)) :

\[
a_{t s'} \ge d_{t s} + \epsilon \qquad\forall t,\; \forall (s,s')\text{ consecutive}
\tag{3}
\]

Departure from a section equals arrival plus traversal time (including dwell time if the node is a station). Traversal time depends on the chosen speed profile:

\[
d_{t s}= a_{t s}+ \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\,\bigl( \tau_{k}\,L_{s} \bigr) + \theta_{t s}
\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{4}
\]

\(\theta_{t s}\) is the *dwell time* at the end node of section *s* (zero for pure track sections, positive for stations).  

### 5.3. Brake‑indication point – speed‑dependent separation  

For every pair of trains \((t,i)\) that share a common section *s* (i.e. both traverse *s*), the **minimum safe headway** is the braking distance of the *following* train plus a safety margin *γ* (km). Using the binary precedence variable \(\delta_{ti}\) we enforce:

\[
a_{t s} \ge d_{i s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} + \gamma \;-\; M\,(1-\delta_{ti}) \qquad\forall t,i\in T,\; t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i},\; \forall k\in K
\tag{5}
\]

where \(b_{s}^{k}= \beta_{k} v_{k}\) is the braking distance of train *t* when it uses profile *k* on section *s*. The term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) converts the distance into a **time** (seconds) needed for the following train to travel its own braking distance after the leading train has cleared the section.  

The big‑M term de‑activates the constraint when \(\delta_{ti}=0\) (i.e. train *t* does **not** follow *i*).  

To guarantee a consistent ordering on each shared section we add:

\[
\delta_{ti} + \delta_{it}= y_{t s}\, y_{i s} \qquad\forall t\neq i,\; \forall s\in S_{t}\cap S_{i}
\tag{6}
\]

(If both trains occupy the section, exactly one of the two precedence binaries must be 1.)

### 5.4. Section capacity (single‑track occupation)  

Because DTG allows *continuous* braking supervision, the **effective occupancy** of a section ends at the *brake‑indication point* of the following train, not necessarily at the physical end. We linearise this by ensuring that at any time instant the number of trains whose **brake‑indication point** lies inside a section does not exceed its capacity:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \Bigl[ a_{t s} \le \tau \le d_{t s} + \frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}} \Bigr] \le c_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; \forall \tau\in\{0,\Delta t,2\Delta t,\dots\}
\tag{7}
\]

In practice (MILP) we replace the time‑indexation by a *pairwise* condition similar to (5). The result is that the precedence constraints already guarantee capacity, so (7) can be omitted if (5)–(6) are enforced for **all** common sections.

### 5.5. Origin‑departure delay definition  

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,\,\text{origin}(t)} - \tau_{0t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{8}
\]

### 5.6. Re‑ordering (optional)  

If the dispatcher is allowed to **re‑order** trains on a shared corridor, we introduce binary variables \(r_{ti}\) that indicate that train *t* is placed **ahead** of train *i* in the new timetable (even if originally behind). The model already contains \(\delta_{ti}\) which serves this purpose; we simply allow \(\delta_{ti}\) to be 0 or 1 regardless of the original order, thus enabling re‑ordering.

### 5.7. Logical linking of brake‑indication point to speed profile  

\[
bip_{t s}= \sum_{k\in K} x_{t s}^{k}\, b_{s}^{k}\qquad\forall t,\; \forall s\in S_{t}
\tag{9}
\]

The *brake‑indication point* measured upstream from the end of section *s* equals the braking distance associated with the selected speed profile.

---

## 6. Additional practical constraints (assumptions)  

| # | Constraint | Reason / Assumption |
|---|------------|----------------------|
| A5 | **Maximum speed limit**: \(\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k} v_{k}\le v_{\max t}\) for all *t,s* | Guarantees that the chosen profile never exceeds the train’s technical limit. |
| A6 | **Minimum dwell time at stations**: \(\theta_{t s}\ge \theta^{\min}_{s}\) if node *n⁺(s)* is a station. | Reflects passenger boarding/alighting requirements. |
| A7 | **Switch‑specific sections**: For sections that contain a switch, a dedicated set \(S^{\text{sw}}\subseteq S\) may have a larger safety margin \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}>\gamma\). | Switches are critical points; extra headway is required. |
| A8 | **Binary linearisation**: \(y_{t s}= \min\{1,\sum_{k} x_{t s}^{k}\}\) is enforced by (1) and (2). | Guarantees consistency between “section used” and “profile selected”. |
| A9 | **Big‑M value**: \(M\) must be larger than the maximal possible time difference between any two trains on a common section (e.g., horizon length). | Standard linearisation practice. |

---

## 7. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} z_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(9)} && \text{core model}\\
&\text{(A5)–(A9)} && \text{practical safety / operational limits}\\
& x_{t s}^{k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t s}\in\{0,1\},\; \delta_{ti}\in\{0,1\} && \forall t,i,s,k\\
& a_{t s}, d_{t s}, z_{t}, bip_{t s}\ge 0 && \forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on linearity  

* All constraints are linear except the **pairwise ordering** (6) which contains a product of binaries \(y_{t s} y_{i s}\). This product can be linearised by introducing an auxiliary binary \(w_{ti s}= y_{t s} y_{i s}\) and the standard three constraints  

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{ti s} &\le y_{t s}\\
w_{ti s} &\le y_{i s}\\
w_{ti s} &\ge y_{t s}+ y_{i s}-1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Then (6) becomes \(\delta_{ti}+ \delta_{it}= w_{ti s}\).  

* The conversion of braking distance into a time (Eq. 5) uses the known speed \(v_{k}\); the term \(\frac{b_{s}^{k}}{v_{k}}\) is a constant for each \((k,s)\) pair, thus preserving linearity.

* The model contains **O(|T|·|S|·|K|)** binary variables and **O(|T|·|S|)** continuous variables, which is comparable to the original RECIFE‑MILP size and solvable with modern MILP solvers for realistic regional networks (hundreds of trains, few thousand sections).

---

## 9. How the model captures DTG specifics  

1. **Speed‑dependent braking distance** – introduced via the parameters \(b_{s}^{k}\) and the brake‑indication point variable \(bip_{t s}\).  
2. **Dynamic headway** – Eq. (5) enforces that the following train may only start its movement after the leading train has cleared the *brake‑indication* distance, not merely the physical block.  
3. **Distinction between switches and regular track** – safety margin \(\gamma\) can be replaced by \(\gamma^{\text{sw}}\) on the subset \(S^{\text{sw}}\).  
4. **Re‑ordering / retiming** – the precedence binaries \(\delta_{ti}\) are free decision variables, allowing the optimizer to change the order of trains on a shared corridor when it reduces total delay.  
5. **Continuous speed‑profile choice** – the set \(K\) permits the optimizer to select a slower or faster cruising speed on each section, thereby influencing both travel time and required braking distance.

---

### End of formulation  

The presented MILP fully describes a **conflict‑detection‑and‑resolution problem for railways equipped with distance‑to‑go signalling**, integrating the speed‑dependent separation distances that are the hallmark of DTG systems while preserving the linear structure required for exact optimisation.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request:

* **train‑rescheduling** – which route (original or opposite track) each train will use, and the order in which trains occupy the (single‑track) shared segment;  
* **speed‑management** – which discrete speed level a train will travel on each link;  
* **partial segment blockage** – a known disruption window on a particular link that forbids use of the original track during that interval.

The model is written in a **linear** form (all constraints are linear; the only non‑linearity comes from the binary variables).  Piece‑wise linear approximations are used for the relationship between speed, travel time and energy consumption, which makes the whole formulation a MILP.

---

## 1.  Sets, parameters and indexing  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (including the start and end of the blocked segment), indexed by *s*. |
| **L** | Set of directed links (track sections) between consecutive stations, indexed by *ℓ*.  Each link ℓ = (s, s′). |
| **B ⊂ L** | The *blocked* link (the only link that suffers a disruption). |
| **K** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (e.g., k = 1 … K). |
| **O = {0,1}** | 0 = original (normal) track, 1 = opposite (detour) track. |
| **Δ** | Length of the planning horizon (discretised in minutes). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable = 0 (chosen as M = Δ). |

### Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| `Lℓ` | Physical length of link ℓ (km). |
| `v_k` | Speed associated with level *k* (km/min). |
| `e_k` | Energy consumption per km when travelling at speed level *k* (kWh/km). |
| `τ_k = Lℓ / v_k` | Travel time on link ℓ when speed level *k* is used (min). |
| `E_k = e_k·Lℓ` | Energy spent on link ℓ at speed level *k* (kWh). |
| `d_s^min` | Minimum dwell (stop) time at station *s* (min). |
| `a_t^0` | Planned (original) arrival time of train *t* at its first station (min). |
| `w_t` | Weight for delay in the objective (e.g., 1). |
| `γ` | Weight for energy consumption in the objective (e.g., 0.01). |
| `t_start^B , t_end^B` | Beginning and end of the disruption window on the blocked link **B** (min). |
| `C_opposite` | Capacity of the opposite track (here = 1 train at a time). |
| `M_time` | Large constant for time‑big‑M (≥ Δ). |

---

## 2. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `x_t ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Route choice of train *t*: 0 = stay on original track, 1 = use opposite track on the blocked link **B**. |
| `y_{t,i} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Ordering on the *shared* (single‑track) link **B**: `y_{t,i}=1` ⇔ train *t* passes **B** **before** train *i*. (Only defined for pairs (t,i) with t≠i.) |
| `z_{t,ℓ,k} ∈ {0,1}` | binary | Speed‑level selection: `z_{t,ℓ,k}=1` ⇔ train *t* traverses link ℓ with speed level *k*. |
| `a_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| `d_{t,s} ≥ 0` | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| `τ_{t,ℓ} ≥ 0` | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on link ℓ (derived from the chosen speed level). |
| `E_{t}` ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption of train *t* (sum over links). |

---

## 3.  Objective function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} w_t\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-a_t^{0}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

* `a_{t,last}` is the arrival time of train *t* at its final destination.  
* The first term penalises the deviation from the original schedule (delay).  
* The second term penalises energy use; the weight `γ` lets the planner trade‑off delay vs. energy.

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1  Route‑choice (exactly one track)  

For every train *t* that must cross the blocked link **B** we enforce:

\[
x_t \in \{0,1\}\qquad\forall t\in T_B
\]

where `T_B ⊆ T` is the subset of trains whose planned path contains **B**.  
If a train does **not** traverse **B**, we simply fix `x_t = 0`.

### 4.2  Speed‑level selection (one level per link)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{t,\ell,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;\forall \ell\in L
\tag{C1}
\]

### 4.3  Travel‑time definition (linearisation)  

\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_k \, z_{t,\ell,k} \qquad\forall t,\ell
\tag{C2}
\]

### 4.4  Energy definition  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\;\sum_{k\in K} E_k \, z_{t,\ell,k} \qquad\forall t
\tag{C3}
\]

### 4.5  Time‑flow (arrival = previous departure + travel)  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of stations *(s, s′)* linked by ℓ = (s,s′):

\[
a_{t,s'} \;=\; d_{t,s} \;+\; \tau_{t,\ell} \qquad\forall t,\;\forall \ell=(s,s')
\tag{C4}
\]

### 4.6  Minimum dwell time at stations  

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s}+ d_s^{\min} \qquad\forall t,\;\forall s\in S\setminus\{\text{last}\}
\tag{C5}
\]

### 4.7  Blockage window – original track cannot be used  

If a train stays on the original track (`x_t = 0`) it must **not** occupy the blocked link **B** during the disruption interval:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B} &\ge t_{\text{end}}^{B} \;-\; M\,(1-x_t) \\
d_{t,s_B} &\le t_{\text{start}}^{B} \;+\; M\,(1-x_t)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T_B
\tag{C6}
\]

where `s_B` and `s_B'` are the upstream and downstream stations of link **B**.  
If `x_t = 1` (detour), the constraints are relaxed because the big‑M term deactivates them.

### 4.8  Capacity of the opposite track (single‑train occupancy)  

When a train uses the opposite track (`x_t = 1`) it must respect the same non‑overlap rule as on the original single‑track.  We use the ordering binaries `y_{t,i}`:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B'} &\ge d_{i,s_B} - M\,(1-y_{i,t}) \\
a_{i,s_B'} &\ge d_{t,s_B} - M\,(1-y_{t,i}) \\
y_{t,i}+y_{i,t} &= 1 \qquad\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B
\end{aligned}
\tag{C7}
\]

The first two lines guarantee that either train *t* finishes before train *i* starts, or vice‑versa, depending on the value of the ordering variable.  The third line forces a strict ordering (no ties).

If the opposite track can host **C_opposite** trains simultaneously (e.g., C_opposite = 2), the big‑M formulation can be replaced by a time‑indexed capacity constraint; however, the binary ordering formulation above is sufficient for the assumed capacity = 1.

### 4.9  Big‑M for ordering on the original track (if needed)  

If the original track is also single‑track (which is typical), we need the same ordering constraints for trains that stay on the original track (`x_t = 0`).  Define a second set of ordering binaries `y^{orig}_{t,i}` and write:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s_B'} &\ge d_{i,s_B} - M\,(1-y^{orig}_{i,t}) \\
a_{i,s_B'} &\ge d_{t,s_B} - M\,(1-y^{orig}_{t,i}) \\
y^{orig}_{t,i}+y^{orig}_{i,t} &= 1 \qquad\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B
\end{aligned}
\tag{C8}
\]

Only the pair of trains that actually use the same physical track (original or opposite) need to be ordered; the model can be tightened by adding a product term `x_t·x_i` but the linear big‑M version above is sufficient.

### 4.10  Logical linking of route choice and speed level on the blocked link  

If a train uses the opposite track, the speed‑level set may be different (e.g., lower speed).  This can be enforced by de‑activating certain speed levels:

\[
z_{t,B,k} \le 1 - x_t \qquad\forall k\in K_{\text{orig}}
\tag{C9}
\]

\[
z_{t,B,k} \le x_t \qquad\forall k\in K_{\text{opp}}
\tag{C10}
\]

where `K_orig` and `K_opp` are the admissible speed‑level subsets for the original and opposite tracks, respectively.

### 4.11  Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_t \in \{0,1\},\; y_{t,i}\in\{0,1\},\; y^{orig}_{t,i}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}, \tau_{t,\ell}, E_t \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{C11}
\]

---

## 5.  Full MILP statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} w_t\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-a_t^{0}\bigr) \;+\; \gamma\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in K} z_{t,\ell,k}=1 &&\forall t,\ell \tag{C1}\\
&\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_k z_{t,\ell,k} &&\forall t,\ell \tag{C2}\\
&E_{t}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\sum_{k\in K}E_k z_{t,\ell,k} &&\forall t \tag{C3}\\
&a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s}+ \tau_{t,\ell} &&\forall t,\;\ell=(s,s') \tag{C4}\\
&d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d_s^{\min} &&\forall t,\; s\neq\text{last} \tag{C5}\\
&a_{t,s_B} \ge t_{\text{end}}^{B} - M(1-x_t) &&\forall t\in T_B \tag{C6a}\\
&d_{t,s_B} \le t_{\text{start}}^{B} + M(1-x_t) &&\forall t\in T_B \tag{C6b}\\
&a_{t,s_B'} \ge d_{i,s_B} - M(1-y_{i,t}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C7a}\\
&a_{i,s_B'} \ge d_{t,s_B} - M(1-y_{t,i}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C7b}\\
&y_{t,i}+y_{i,t}=1 &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C7c}\\
&a_{t,s_B'} \ge d_{i,s_B} - M(1-y^{orig}_{i,t}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C8a}\\
&a_{i,s_B'} \ge d_{t,s_B} - M(1-y^{orig}_{t,i}) &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C8b}\\
&y^{orig}_{t,i}+y^{orig}_{i,t}=1 &&\forall t\neq i,\; t,i\in T_B \tag{C8c}\\
&z_{t,B,k}\le 1-x_t &&\forall t\in T_B,\;k\in K_{\text{orig}} \tag{C9}\\
&z_{t,B,k}\le x_t &&\forall t\in T_B,\;k\in K_{\text{opp}} \tag{C10}\\
&x_t\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,i}\in\{0,1\},\; y^{orig}_{t,i}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\tau_{t,\ell},E_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s,\ell
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  Explanation of each component  

| Component | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-----------|--------------|------------------|
| **Binary route choice `x_t`** | Determines whether train *t* stays on the original line (0) or diverts to the opposite track (1) when crossing the blocked link **B**. | Captures the *rescheduling* decision caused by the disruption. |
| **Speed‑level binaries `z_{t,ℓ,k}`** | Selects a discrete speed level for each train on each link. | Allows the model to trade travel time against energy consumption; the piece‑wise linear relationship is linearised by these binaries. |
| **Travel‑time variable `τ_{t,ℓ}`** | Computed as a linear combination of the travel times of the selected speed levels. | Links the speed decision to the time‑flow constraints. |
| **Energy variable `E_t`** | Sum of energy spent on all links, again linear in the speed‑level binaries. | Provides the energy term in the objective. |
| **Arrival/Departure times `a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}`** | Capture the schedule of each train at every station. | Needed for precedence, dwell‑time, and blockage constraints. |
| **Ordering binaries `y_{t,i}` and `y^{orig}_{t,i}`** | Encode which of any two trains that share a single‑track segment passes first. | Guarantees *conflict‑free* use of the (original or opposite) track; without them two trains could be scheduled to occupy the same physical segment simultaneously. |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of total delay (difference between actual and planned arrival at the final destination) and total energy consumption. | Reflects the planner’s trade‑off: minimise passenger impact while also keeping energy use low. |
| **Constraint (C1)** – *exactly one speed level* | Guarantees a single speed is chosen per link. | Keeps the model linear and realistic. |
| **Constraint (C4)** – *time‑flow* | Propagates the schedule from one station to the next. | Fundamental for any timetable model. |
| **Constraint (C5)** – *minimum dwell* | Enforces a realistic stop time at stations. | Prevents infeasible “instantaneous” stops. |
| **Constraint (C6)** – *blockage window* | Forces trains that stay on the original track to avoid the disruption interval on link **B**. | Models the partial blockage. |
| **Constraints (C7) & (C8)** – *ordering on opposite / original track* | Use big‑M to enforce non‑overlap based on the ordering binaries. | Guarantees safety (no two trains on the same single‑track segment at the same time). |
| **Constraints (C9)–(C10)** – *speed‑level compatibility with route* | De‑activate speed levels that are not allowed on a given track (e.g., lower speed on the opposite track). | Captures physical limits of the detour. |
| **Big‑M constants** | `M` (or `M_time`) is chosen larger than the planning horizon, so that when a binary = 0 the corresponding inequality becomes non‑binding. | Standard linearisation technique for conditional constraints. |

---

## 7.  Remarks on implementation  

1. **Piece‑wise linear speed‑energy relationship** – If a finer granularity is required, increase the size of set **K** (more speed levels).  The model stays linear because each level is represented by a binary variable.  
2. **Scalability** – The number of ordering binaries grows as O(|T_B|²).  For large fleets one can replace the pairwise ordering formulation by a **time‑indexed** capacity constraint (e.g., a set of time slots) or use a **disjunctive‑graph** formulation with a smaller number of binary variables.  
3. **Big‑M selection** – Choose `M` ≥ the maximum possible schedule deviation (e.g., the planning horizon Δ).  A tighter M improves solver performance.  
4. **Solver** – The model is a pure MILP; any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, etc.) can handle it.  For very large instances, a decomposition (Benders, column generation) may be employed, but the formulation above is sufficient for a proof‑of‑concept or medium‑size case study.  

---

### TL;DR  

The MILP above simultaneously decides **(i)** which track each train uses on the blocked segment, **(ii)** the order in which trains occupy the single‑track sections, and **(iii)** the speed level on every link.  The objective minimises a weighted sum of passenger delay and energy consumption, while the constraints enforce route exclusivity, travel‑time consistency, dwell‑time, blockage avoidance, and safe non‑overlap of trains on the (original or opposite) track.  All relationships are linear, so the model can be solved directly with any commercial or open‑source MILP optimizer.
