Introduction

The considerable potential for reducing CO2 emissions lies in the low specific energy consumption of rail transportation in comparison to other sectors (García-Olivares et al., 2018; Dalla Chiara et al., 2017). The climate protection initiatives and increasing energy prices will encourage the railway to play a more significant role in future transport, increasing the demand for passenger and freight rail services (Chaturvedi and Kim, 2015; Islam et al., 2015; Boldizsár, 2024). Moreover, increasing infrastructure utilization and decreasing energy consumption and carbon emission is one of the most crucial research areas in railway traffic (González-Gil et al., 2014; Li and Zhang, 2020). The timetable optimization is one of the key components of increasing energy efficiency (Yang et al., 2016; Corlu et al.). However, in many cases, the optimally scheduled trains suffer primary delays due to different traffic disturbances, and the pre-planned timetable would result in conflicting trains (Nagy and Csiszár, 2015). Therefore, the trains must be rescheduled, rerouted, or reordered, assigning secondary delays to the trains to solve the real-time railway traffic management problem (rtRTMP) (Corman, 2010). Nowadays, generally, human dispatchers resolve conflicts according to several generic and regional principles, such as the first-in-first-out (FIFO) policy. However, making an optimal decision considering different objectives and traffic regulations within the required short response time is very challenging for a human dispatcher. Hence, automatic railway traffic management and control have become a popular research topic in recent years, aiming to reduce energy consumption and optimize capacity usage to satisfy the increasing demands (Pellegrini et al., 2016; Botte and D’Acierno, 2018).

Related works

Many works tackle the real-time railway traffic management problem with different optimization approaches and models (Corman and Meng, 2015; Cacchiani et al., 2014; Fang et al., 2015), tackling different uncertainties (Zhan et al., 2024). The models can be divided into microscopic and macroscopic groups according to the levels of the infrastructure representation (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2015). Microscopic models describe the topology of the rail network, including detailed information such as track length and velocity, as in Rodriguez (2007) and D’Ariano et al. (2008). Macroscopic models neglect some lower-level resources such as signals, reducing the complexity of the infrastructure model (Dollevoet et al., 2015; Kanai et al., 2011). The models can also be distinguished according to the objective function. Usually, the optimization goal is to minimize train delays, as in the proposed method. Some works also consider the energy consumption after determining the routing and ordering that minimizes the delays, as in Naldini et al. (2022, 2021), Montrone et al. (2018), or a trade-off is made between them (Rao et al., 2013; D’Ariano et al., 2010; ShangGuan et al., 2015).

The optimization models of the rtRTMP also range widely, but mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is one of the most common formulations, as in Acuna-Agost et al. (2011), Pellegrini et al. (2012, 2014), Törnquist Krasemann (2015). However, since the problem is NP-hard, in the case of large networks and complex scenarios, the runtime of the optimization can exceed the available response time, particularly in large, complex networks. Therefore, a runtime-efficient implementation is essential in a real traffic environment. Some custom heuristics and additional constraints are introduced in Boccia et al. (2013), Pellegrini et al. (2015) to decrease the computational time of the MILP. Furthermore, Pellegrini et al. (2019) proposed an efficient implementation by extending their previous work (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with new constraints, decreasing the number of equivalent combinations of integer variables. Another approach to reducing the model’s complexity is decomposing it according to smaller sub-problems. The number of routing alternatives strongly affects the time needed to find the global optimum. Therefore, it is reasonable to solve the route selection problem first, providing a smaller subset of routing alternatives for the MILP model, as in Bettinelli et al. (2017), Sama et al. (2017), Gholami and Törnquist Krasemann (2018). The train route selection problem (TRSP) was first formalized by Samà et al. (2016) with a construction graph along with an ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithm to solve it. The main idea was to select the routes that minimize the pair-wise delay of trains, neglecting the delay propagation. Pascariu et al. (2022) extended the TRSP model with an estimation of delay propagation. For the case of complete blockage, Zhan et al. (2024) also propose a two-stage approach, but the problem is decomposed according to disruption phases, i.e., during and after disruption, instead of the rerouting and rescheduling sub-problems. Benders decomposition (BD) (BnnoBRs, 1962) is an alternative strategy that provides the optimal solution by iteratively solving the master and a set of sub-problems. For example, the line traffic and station control problems are Benders decomposed in Mannino (2011), Lamorgese and Mannino (2013, 2015), Lamorgese et al. (2016) that shows a good performance in large networks. Instead of spatial considerations, the rtRTMP is decomposed according to rerouting and rescheduling problems using BD in Keita et al. (2016). Moreover, a three-step decomposition, considering the rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling problems, is presented in Keita et al. (2020) similarly to the proposed method but in a Benders’ manner. Meng and Zhou (2014) also propose a MILP formulation based on cumulative flow variables, allowing solving the rerouting and rescheduling problems simultaneously. Besides the decomposition of MILP models, other methods focusing on runtime-efficient dispatching also exist. For example, Corman et al. (2010) formulate the problem as an alternative graph model, incorporating effective rescheduling algorithms and local rerouting strategies in a tabu search scheme. Meanwhile, Törnquist (Törnquist Krasemann, 2012) proposes an efficient greedy approach based on depth-first search, providing a solution within seconds.

Contributions of the paper

This paper proposes a multi-stage framework consisting of two different MILP models, minimizing the overall delays by decomposing the rtRTMP into rerouting, reordering, and rescheduling sub-problems, similar to Keita et al. (2020). However, to avoid multiple iterations, the proposed method does not rely on Benders’ algorithm. First, a low-complex, simplified approach is presented that solves the rerouting and reordering, providing a fast but sub-optimal solution for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014). It relies on reforming the standard delay variables (e.g., in Pellegrini et al. (2014, 2015, 2019)) into a pair-wise interpretation (i.e., indicating which other train they are waiting for) while disregarding delay propagation. Then, to tackle rescheduling, the original problem is solved with the fixed route selection and optional train ordering result provided by this sub-optimal model. Similar considerations are taken in Samà et al. (2016); however, we propose it in a MILP formulation that provides an exact route selection that can further decrease the complexity of the optimization. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimality condition to obtain the circumstance in which this approach results in a sub-optimal solution. As a result of the analysis, we developed a new model that guarantees the global optimum for the original rtRTMP in Pellegrini et al. (2014) by extending the sub-optimal model to consider the delay propagation. This formulation of the rtRTMP shows a more favorable computational cost compared to the original in Pellegrini et al. (2014), especially in complex scenarios. Finally, both models provide an input route selection and optionally reordering for the extended rtRTMP in Lindenmaier et al. (2022), considering the safety-relevant overlaps, which are the margins that have to be proved clear behind a stop signal.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: the existing reference MILP models are introduced in Section 2. The proposed sub-optimal solution is detailed in Section 3.1. The optimality condition of the first approach is analyzed in Section 3.2, and the resulting global optimum model is explained in Section 3.3. The results, along with the experimental setup, are discussed in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 outlines the conclusions along with a brief outlook on future works.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the real‑time Railway Traffic Management Problem (rtRTMP)**  
The model below follows the description given in the text and adds the missing formal elements. All symbols are defined in the *Notation* section; any element that is not directly taken from the literature is marked as **(Assumption)**.

---

## 1.  Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(T\)** | Set of trains that have to be scheduled (|T| = *n*). |
| **\(N\)** | Set of nodes (stations, block‑sections, signal locations) of the rail network. |
| **\(A\subseteq N\times N\)** | Set of directed arcs (track sections) connecting nodes. |
| **\(R_t\)** | Set of admissible routes for train *t* (pre‑computed by a routing‑pre‑selection stage). |
| **\(r\in R_t\)** | One concrete route, i.e. an ordered list of arcs \((a_1,\dots ,a_{|r|})\). |
| **\(L_a\)** | Length (km) of arc *a* (Assumption: known). |
| **\(v^{\max}_a\)** | Maximum allowed speed on arc *a* (km h\(^{-1}\)). |
| **\(c_a\)** | Energy consumption coefficient of arc *a* (kWh per km) – used only if a secondary objective is added (Assumption). |
| **\(d^{\text{plan}}_{t,a}\)** | Planned (timetable) arrival time of train *t* at the **head** of arc *a* (minutes). |
| **\(M\)** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **\(S\subseteq T\times T\)** | Set of train pairs that may potentially conflict (i.e. share at least one arc). |
| **\(p_{t,a}\)** | Minimum dwell / safety time that train *t* must respect on arc *a* (minutes). |
| **\(\Delta^{\max}\)** | Maximum admissible secondary delay (Assumption). |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_{t,r}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r* (∈ R_t), 0 otherwise. |
| **\(y_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from the **tail** of arc *a*. |
| **\(z_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at the **head** of arc *a*. |
| **\(w_{t,i}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Secondary (real‑time) delay of train *t* at event *i* (departure or arrival). |
| **\(o_{t,i}^{\text{ord}}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t* is ordered **before** another train on the same resource at event *i* (used for re‑ordering). |
| **\(b_{t_1,t_2,a}\)** | binary | 1 if train *t₁* must wait for train *t₂* on arc *a* (pair‑wise waiting indicator). |
| **\(s_{t,a}\)** | continuous ≥ 0 | Slack (free time) left on arc *a* after the train has passed (used for overlap safety). |

---

## 2.  Model assumptions  

1. **Pre‑selected route set** – For each train a limited set *Rₜ* of feasible routes is given (generated by a routing‑pre‑selection heuristic).  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – Travel time on arc *a* for any train is \( \tau_a = \frac{L_a}{v^{\max}_a}\) (no stochasticity).  
3. **Single‑track sections** – When two trains share an arc they cannot occupy it simultaneously; a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) rule can be overridden by binary re‑ordering variables.  
4. **Safety headway** – After a train leaves an arc a safety margin *p* must be kept before the next train may enter (includes signal overlap).  
5. **Maximum secondary delay** – No train may be delayed more than \(\Delta^{\max}\).  
6. **Objective** – Primary objective is to minimise the sum of secondary delays (total passenger‑delay). A secondary energy‑minimisation term can be added if required.

---

## 3.  Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I_t} w_{t,i}}_{\text{Total secondary delay}}
\;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{a\in A} c_a \, L_a \, x_{t,r(a)}}_{\text{(optional) Energy consumption}}
}
\]

* \(I_t\) is the set of all events (departure/arrival) of train *t* (size = 2·|r|).  
* \(\lambda\) is a weighting factor (set to 0 if only delay is considered).  

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1 Route selection  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

\[
x_{t,r}=0 \quad \text{if arc } a\notin r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_{t,a}=z_{t,a}=0 \qquad \forall t,a,r \tag{R2}
\]

### 4.2 Time propagation along a chosen route  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of arcs \((a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}})\) on the selected route *r* :

\[
z_{t,a^{\text{out}}} + \tau_{a^{\text{out}}} \;+\; p_{t,a^{\text{out}}}
\; \le\; y_{t,a^{\text{in}}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,\; a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}} \in r \tag{T1}
\]

If the same arc is used again (loops) the constraint is applied for each occurrence.

### 4.3 Definition of secondary delay  

\[
w_{t,i} \;=\; y_{t,i} - d^{\text{plan}}_{t,i} \qquad \forall t,i \tag{D1}
\]

\[
0 \le w_{t,i} \le \Delta^{\max} \qquad \forall t,i \tag{D2}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict avoidance (pair‑wise waiting)  

For every pair \((t_1,t_2)\in S\) that share arc *a* :

\[
y_{t_1,a} \;\ge\; z_{t_2,a} + p_{t_2,a} - M\bigl(1-b_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{C1}
\]

\[
y_{t_2,a} \;\ge\; z_{t_1,a} + p_{t_1,a} - M\bigl(b_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{C2}
\]

\[
b_{t_1,t_2,a} \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in S,\; a\in A \tag{C3}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active, forcing one train to wait for the other.  

### 4.5 Re‑ordering (optional)  

If the dispatcher may change the FIFO order, binary ordering variables are introduced:

\[
o_{t_1,t_2,a} + o_{t_2,t_1,a}=1 \qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in S,\; a\in A \tag{O1}
\]

\[
y_{t_1,a} \ge z_{t_2,a}+p_{t_2,a} - M\bigl(1-o_{t_1,t_2,a}\bigr) \tag{O2}
\]

\[
y_{t_2,a} \ge z_{t_1,a}+p_{t_1,a} - M\bigl(1-o_{t_2,t_1,a}\bigr) \tag{O3}
\]

When re‑ordering is **forbidden** (e.g. FIFO policy), set \(o_{t_1,t_2,a}=0\) for all pairs.

### 4.6 Delay propagation (global‑optimal model)  

To capture the effect of a delay on downstream trains, we introduce cumulative delay variables \(\delta_{t,a}\) that are forced to propagate through the network:

\[
\delta_{t,a^{\text{in}}} \;\ge\; \delta_{t,a^{\text{out}}} + w_{t,a^{\text{out}}} \qquad \forall t,\; (a^{\text{out}},a^{\text{in}})\in r \tag{P1}
\]

\[
w_{t,a} = \delta_{t,a} \qquad \forall t,a \tag{P2}
\]

These constraints are activated only for the selected route (big‑M linearisation similar to (T1)).

### 4.7 Overlap / safety‑clearance (optional)  

\[
s_{t,a} \;\ge\; y_{t,a} - \bigl(z_{t,a}+p_{t,a}\bigr) \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl1}
\]

\[
s_{t,a} \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl2}
\]

A minimum required overlap \(\underline{s}_a\) can be imposed:

\[
s_{t,a} \ge \underline{s}_a \qquad \forall t,a \tag{Ovl3}
\]

---

## 5.  Complete MILP formulation  

Putting together the objective and all constraints we obtain the following compact model:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in I_t} w_{t,i}
\;+\;\lambda\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{a\in A} c_a L_a \Bigl(\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{t,r}\mathbf{1}_{\{a\in r\}}\Bigr) \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route selection} \\
&\text{(T1)} &&\text{time propagation on selected route} \\
&\text{(D1)–(D2)} &&\text{definition and bounds of secondary delay} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{pair‑wise conflict avoidance (waiting)}\\
&\text{(O1)–(O3)} &&\text{optional re‑ordering (if allowed)}\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{delay propagation (only in the optimal‑delay model)}\\
&\text{(Ovl1)–(Ovl3)} &&\text{overlap / safety clearance (optional)}\\
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; b_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\}\\
&y_{t,a},z_{t,a},w_{t,i},\delta_{t,a},s_{t,a}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,a,i .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on the two‑stage approach described in the paper  

1. **Stage 1 – Sub‑optimal model**  
   *Only constraints (R1)–(R2), (T1), (D1)–(D2) and the pair‑wise waiting variables **b** are kept.*  
   The model ignores (P1)–(P2) (delay propagation) and therefore yields a fast, but possibly sub‑optimal solution.

2. **Stage 2 – Full‑optimal model**  
   *All constraints above are activated, especially (P1)–(P2) that enforce delay propagation.*  
   The routes **x** are fixed to the solution of Stage 1 (or re‑optimised together), guaranteeing the global optimum for the original rtRTMP.

---

## 7.  Possible extensions  

| Extension | How to incorporate |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Energy minimisation** | Keep the term \(\lambda\sum c_a L_a x_{t,r}\) and possibly add a secondary objective using a weighted sum or a hierarchical (lexicographic) optimisation. |
| **Stochastic disturbances** | Replace deterministic travel times \(\tau_a\) by scenario‑dependent parameters \(\tau_{a}^{s}\) and add scenario‑indexed copies of the time‑propagation constraints; use a robust or chance‑constrained formulation. |
| **Multiple train classes (passenger / freight)** | Add class‑specific weighting in the objective (e.g. higher penalty for passenger‑train delays). |
| **Capacity of stations (platforms)** | Introduce additional binary variables for platform occupation and constraints that limit simultaneous occupancy. |

---

**The model above is a self‑contained MILP that captures the essential elements of the rtRTMP as described in the provided text, while filling the missing formal details with reasonable assumptions.**

&\text{(D1)–(D2)} &&\text{definition and bounds of secondary delay} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{pair‑wise conflict avoidance (waiting)}\\
&\text{(O1)–(O3)} &&\text{optional re‑ordering (if allowed)}\\
&\text{(P1)–(P2)} &&\text{delay propagation (only in the optimal‑delay model)}\\
&\text{(Ovl1)–(Ovl3)} &&\text{overlap / safety clearance (optional)}\\
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; b_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{t_1,t_2,a}\in\{0,1\}\\
&y_{t,a},z_{t,a},w_{t,i},\delta_{t,a},s_{t,a}\ge 0\qquad\forall t,a,i .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on the two‑stage approach described in the paper  

1. **Stage 1 – Sub‑optimal model**  
   *Only constraints (R1)–(R2), (T1), (D1)–(D2) and the pair‑wise waiting variables **b** are kept.*  
   The model ignores (P1)–(P2) (delay propagation) and therefore yields a fast, but possibly sub‑optimal solution.

2. **Stage 2 – Full‑optimal model**  
   *All constraints above are activated, especially (P1)–(P2) that enforce delay propagation.*  
   The routes **x** are fixed to the solution of Stage 1 (or re‑optimised together), guaranteeing the global optimum for the original rtRTMP.

---

## 7.  Possible extensions  

| Extension | How to incorporate |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Energy minimisation** | Keep the term \(\lambda\sum c_a L_a x_{t,r}\) and possibly add a secondary objective using a weighted sum or a hierarchical (lexicographic) optimisation. |
| **Stochastic disturbances** | Replace deterministic travel times \(\tau_a\) by scenario‑dependent parameters \(\tau_{a}^{s}\) and add scenario‑indexed copies of the time‑propagation constraints; use a robust or chance‑constrained formulation. |
| **Multiple train classes (passenger / freight)** | Add class‑specific weighting in the objective (e.g. higher penalty for passenger‑train delays). |
| **Capacity of stations (platforms)** | Introduce additional binary variables for platform occupation and constraints that limit simultaneous occupancy. |

---

**The model above is a self‑contained MILP that captures the essential elements of the rtRTMP as described in the provided text, while filling the missing formal details with reasonable assumptions.**

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three intertwined sub‑problems mentioned in the description  

* **(i) Train‑level routing (reroute / ordering decisions)**  
* **(ii) Speed‑profile selection on each track segment**  
* **(iii) Timing (arrival / departure) and energy consumption**  

The model is written in a **single, linear** formulation that can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  
All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model, and a short narrative explains the purpose of each set of constraints.

---

## 1.  Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Sets** | |
| 𝑇 = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| 𝑆 = {1,…, |S|} | Set of track segments (directed arcs) that can be traversed. |
| 𝑅 ⊆ 𝑆 × 𝑆 | Set of admissible **reroute pairs** (i → j) – i.e. a train may go from segment *i* to segment *j* (including the original continuation). |
| 𝑉 = {1,…, |V|} | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g. V = {low, medium, high}). |
| **Parameters** | |
| 𝑙_s  | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| 𝑏_s  | Binary flag = 1 if segment *s* is **partially blocked** during a known time window, 0 otherwise. |
| 𝑤_s  | Width of the blocked portion of *s* (fraction of the track width, 0 ≤ w_s ≤ 1). |
| 𝑡^B_s , 𝑡^E_s | Beginning and end of the blockage window on segment *s* (minutes from the planning horizon start). |
| 𝑣_{s}^{v} | Nominal speed (km/min) that can be achieved on segment *s* if speed level *v* is selected (must respect the physical speed limit of the segment). |
| 𝜏^{min}_s , 𝜏^{max}_s | Minimum / maximum **travel time** (min) that is physically feasible on segment *s* (e.g. due to acceleration/deceleration limits). |
| 𝑒^{v}_s | Energy consumption (MJ) required to traverse segment *s* at speed level *v*. |
| 𝑑^{orig}_t | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* from its origin (min). |
| 𝑎^{orig}_t | Planned (original) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (min). |
| 𝑝_t   | Penalty weight for **delay** of train *t*. |
| 𝑞      | Global weight for **energy** in the objective (can be set to 0 if only delay matters). |
| 𝑈      | A big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time, e.g. horizon length). |
| **Decision Variables** | |
| x_{t,s} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* (routing variable). |
| y_{t, (i,j)} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* uses the directed arc (i→j) (ordering / continuation variable). |
| z_{t,s,v} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* travels on segment *s* with speed level *v*. |
| 𝛼_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| 𝛽_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| 𝜏_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (𝛽 – 𝛼). |
| 𝜀_t ≥ 0 | **Delay** of train *t* (actual arrival at destination – original arrival). |
| 𝜙_t ≥ 0 | Energy consumed by train *t* (sum of e^{v}_s over all traversed segments). |

All variables are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries (x, y, z).

---

## 2.  MILP Formulation  

### 2.1 Objective  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} p_t \, \varepsilon_t}_{\text{weighted total delay}}
\;+\; \underbrace{q \, \sum_{t\in T} \phi_t}_{\text{weighted total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The two terms can be weighted to reflect the planner’s preference (e.g. give a high weight to delay, a low weight to energy).

---

### 2.2 Routing / Flow Conservation  

For every train *t* we must build a **directed path** from its origin node *o_t* to its destination node *d_t*.  
Let `inc(s)` be the set of arcs that **enter** segment *s* (i.e. (i,s) ∈ R) and `out(s)` the set that **leave** *s* (i.e. (s,j) ∈ R).

1. **Origin / destination activation**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S: o_t\in \text{upstream}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 ,\qquad
\sum_{s\in S: d_t\in \text{downstream}(s)} x_{t,s}=1
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Flow balance for interior nodes**  

\[
\sum_{(i,s)\in inc(s)} y_{t,(i,s)} \;-\; \sum_{(s,j)\in out(s)} y_{t,(s,j)} = 0,
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}
\tag{R2}
\]

3. **Link arc‑selection to segment‑selection**  

\[
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,i}, \qquad
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,s}, \qquad \forall t,\;(i,s)\in R
\tag{R3}
\]

Thus a train can only use an arc if it actually traverses both incident segments.

---

### 2.3 Speed‑profile selection  

For every traversed segment we must pick **exactly one** admissible speed level.

\[
\sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,v}= x_{t,s}, \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If a segment is not used (x=0) all associated z‑variables are forced to 0.

---

### 2.4 Travel‑time – speed coupling  

Travel time on a segment is the inverse of the chosen speed (linearised with the big‑M trick).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s} &\ge \frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}} \;-\; U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v\\
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s} &\le \frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}} \;+\; U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v
\end{aligned}
\tag{S2}
\]

Because exactly one *v* is active per traversed segment, the two inequalities collapse to  

\[
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s}= \frac{l_s}{v^{v^\*}_{s}} \quad\text{with } v^\* \text{ the selected speed level}.
\]

We also enforce the physical feasibility window:

\[
\tau^{min}_s \, x_{t,s} \;\le\; \mathsf{τ}_{t,s} \;\le\; \tau^{max}_s \, x_{t,s},
\qquad \forall t,s
\tag{S3}
\]

If a segment is not used (x=0) the bounds force τ=0.

---

### 2.5 Timing (arrival / departure)  

The arrival at the downstream end of a segment equals the departure from its upstream end plus travel time:

\[
\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \mathsf{τ}_{t,s},\qquad \forall t,s
\tag{T1}
\]

**Link successive segments** (flow continuity).  
If train *t* goes from segment *i* to segment *j* (i→j) we must have

\[
\alpha_{t,j} \ge \beta_{t,i} - U\,(1-y_{t,(i,j)}),\qquad \forall t,\;(i,j)\in R
\tag{T2}
\]

When the arc is active (y=1) the inequality becomes an equality (or a “≥” that will be tight at optimum). When the arc is not used, the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

**Origin departure** and **final arrival**:

\[
\alpha_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}= d^{\text{orig}}_t, \qquad
\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}= a^{\text{orig}}_t + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \forall t
\tag{T3}
\]

where \(s^{\text{orig}}\) and \(s^{\text{dest}}\) are the first and last segments of train *t*’s planned route.

---

### 2.6 Blockage (partial segment closure)  

A partially blocked segment *s* can only be occupied **outside** the blockage window **or** by a train that uses a speed level that fits through the remaining free width.  
We model it conservatively by forbidding any occupation during the window:

\[
\alpha_{t,s} \ge t^{E}_s \;-\; U\,(1-x_{t,s}),\qquad
\beta_{t,s} \le t^{B}_s \;+\; U\,(1-x_{t,s}),\qquad \forall t,\; s\text{ with }b_s=1
\tag{B1}
\]

The two inequalities together force **either** the whole traversal to finish before the blockage starts **or** start after it ends.  

If a more refined “partial‑width” rule is required (e.g., a train can still pass if its speed level uses a narrower track gauge), introduce a binary “allowed‑through” parameter  

\[
c_{s,v}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if speed level }v\text{ fits through the unblocked width of }s\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

and add  

\[
z_{t,s,v} \le 1-c_{s,v}+x_{t,s},\qquad \forall t,s,v\text{ with }b_s=1
\tag{B2}
\]

so that forbidden speed levels cannot be selected on a blocked segment.

---

### 2.7 Track‑capacity (bidirectional conflict)  

Assume each physical track segment can be used **by at most one train at a time**, regardless of direction. A classic disjunctive (pairwise) formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{t_1,s} \ge \beta_{t_2,s} - U\,\delta_{t_1,t_2,s} \\
\alpha_{t_2,s} \ge \beta_{t_1,s} - U\,(1-\delta_{t_1,t_2,s})
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall s\in S,\; \forall t_1<t_2
\tag{C1}
\]

where \(\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first on segment *s*.  
If the planning horizon is large, a **time‑window aggregation** can be used instead:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} x_{t,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S\text{ with }b_s=0
\tag{C2}
\]

i.e. at most one train may be assigned to a segment that is not blocked (a stronger but simpler capacity rule). Choose the version that matches the required level of detail.

---

### 2.8 Energy accounting  

Energy used by a train is the sum of the energy of the selected speed levels:

\[
\phi_t = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{v\in V} e^{v}_s \, z_{t,s,v},\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

---

### 2.9 Delay definition  

\[
\varepsilon_t = \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - a^{\text{orig}}_t ,\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

Because \(\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}\) is the actual arrival time at the final node, the difference gives the **positive** delay (the model will never make \(\varepsilon_t\) negative because the objective penalises it; if a train arrives early you may set \(\varepsilon_t\ge 0\) explicitly).

---

### 2.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,(i,j)}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,(i,j),v\\
&\alpha_{t,s},\beta_{t,s},\tau_{t,s},\varepsilon_t,\phi_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\}\quad\text{(if using pairwise capacity)} &&\forall t_1<t_2,\,s
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 3.  Explanation of Model Components  

| Block | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **Objective (OBJ)** | Minimises a weighted sum of total train delay and total energy consumption. | Captures the planner’s trade‑off between punctuality (service level) and sustainability (energy). |
| **Routing constraints (R1‑R3)** | Build a feasible path for each train through the network, allowing optional rerouting (binary y). | Guarantees that each train has a continuous sequence of segments from origin to destination and that any reroute decision is reflected in the binary variables. |
| **Speed‑selection (S1‑S3)** | Forces exactly one speed level per traversed segment, links speed to travel time, and respects physical min/max travel‑time limits. | Enables speed‑profile management while keeping the model linear (big‑M linearisation). |
| **Timing constraints (T1‑T3)** | Relates arrival, departure, and travel time; propagates timing from one segment to the next; defines delay at the final node. | Guarantees temporal feasibility (no “teleportation”) and provides the delay variable used in the objective. |
| **Blockage handling (B1‑B2)** | Keeps trains out of a segment during its blockage window, or forbids speed levels that cannot fit through the remaining free width. | Models the *partial* segment closure accurately, preventing unsafe or impossible traversals. |
| **Capacity / conflict (C1‑C2)** | Ensures that two trains never occupy the same physical track segment simultaneously (either by pairwise disjunction or by a simple “one‑train‑per‑segment” rule). | Avoids collisions and respects the limited track capacity, especially important when a blockage reduces the usable width. |
| **Energy accounting (E1)** | Sums the energy consumption of the chosen speed levels for each train. | Provides the energy term needed in the objective and any downstream reporting. |
| **Delay definition (D1)** | Computes the positive delay of each train as the difference between its actual arrival and the originally scheduled arrival. | Supplies the variable that the objective penalises. |
| **Domain definitions (DOM)** | Declares binary vs. continuous variables and sets big‑M bounds. | Required for a correct MILP formulation. |

---

## 4.  How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the network (segments *S* and admissible arcs *R*).  
   * For every segment compute length *l_s*, speed limits *v^{v}_s*, min/max travel times, energy per speed level, and blockage information (*b_s, t^B_s, t^E_s, w_s*).  
   * For each train define origin segment, destination segment, original departure/arrival times, and the delay weight *p_t*.  

2. **Choose big‑M**  
   * A safe choice is the planning horizon length (e.g., 1440 min for a 24‑h horizon).  

3. **Select capacity formulation**  
   * Use (C1) if you need a detailed ordering of trains on each segment (more variables, tighter model).  
   * Use (C2) for a coarse but much smaller model (good for large instances).  

4. **Solve**  
   * Feed the linear constraints, objective, and variable domains to any MILP solver.  
   * The optimal solution will give:  
     * **x, y** → the chosen route (including any rerouting).  
     * **z** → the speed level on every traversed segment.  
     * **α, β** → the exact schedule (arrival/departure times).  
     * **ε** → the resulting delay for each train.  
     * **φ** → the total energy consumption.  

5. **Post‑processing** (optional)  
   * Compute derived performance indicators (average delay, total energy savings vs. a baseline, utilisation of blocked segments, etc.).  

---

### 5.  Full Linear Model (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} p_t \varepsilon_t \;+\; q \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e^{v}_s\,z_{t,s,v}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s:\,o_t\in\text{up}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{s:\,d_t\in\text{down}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{(i,s)\in inc(s)} y_{t,(i,s)}-\sum_{(s,j)\in out(s)} y_{t,(s,j)} =0 &&\forall t,\;s\neq o_t,d_t\\
&y_{t,(i,s)}\le x_{t,i},\; y_{t,(i,s)}\le x_{t,s} &&\forall t,(i,s)\in R\\
&\sum_{v} z_{t,s,v}=x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\tau_{t,s}\ge\frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}}-U(1-z_{t,s,v}) &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\tau_{t,s}\le\frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}}+U(1-z_{t,s,v}) &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\tau^{min}_s x_{t,s}\le \tau_{t,s}\le \tau^{max}_s x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \tau_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\alpha_{t,j}\ge \beta_{t,i}-U(1-y_{t,(i,j)}) &&\forall t,(i,j)\in R\\
&\alpha_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}= d^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
&\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}= a^{\text{orig}}_t+\varepsilon_t &&\forall t\\
&\alpha_{t,s}\ge t^{E}_s-U(1-x_{t,s}),\; \beta_{t,s}\le t^{B}_s+U(1-x_{t,s}) &&\forall t, s\text{ with }b_s=1\\
&\text{(optional) } z_{t,s,v}\le 1-c_{s,v}+x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s,v\text{ with }b_s=1\\
&\text{(capacity) } \alpha_{t_1,s}\ge\beta_{t_2,s}-U\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\\
&\qquad\;\;\; \alpha_{t_2,s}\ge\beta_{t_1,s}-U(1-\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}) &&\forall s,\;t_1<t_2\\
&\phi_t =\sum_{s,v} e^{v}_s\,z_{t,s,v} &&\forall t\\
&\varepsilon_t = \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}-a^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
&x,y,z\in\{0,1\},\; \alpha,\beta,\tau,\varepsilon,\phi\ge 0,\; \delta\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries that encode routing, ordering, speed‑level choice, and (if used) the pairwise capacity decisions.  

---  

**That completes the MILP model** for *integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partially blocked segment*. It can be directly implemented in a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …) and solved with any state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **routing** – choose a (possibly rerouted) path for each train, respecting the blocked segment;  
* **sequencing / scheduling** – decide the order in which trains occupy a shared track (or a block) and compute arrival / departure times;  
* **speed‑profile selection** – for each train‑segment pair pick a discrete speed level (hence a travel time and an energy cost).

The model is written for a **single planning horizon** (e.g. one day) and a **deterministic** set of trains, blocks and speed levels. All relationships are linear; binary variables are used for routing, sequencing and speed‑level selection, while continuous variables are used for times, travel‑time and energy.

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \mathcal{T} \) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \( \mathcal{N} \) | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions), indexed by \(i\). |
| \( \mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{N} \) | Set of directed track‑segments (arcs), indexed by \((i,j)\). |
| \( \mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A} \) | Sub‑set of arcs that are **partially blocked** (e.g. due to work). |
| \( \mathcal{S} \) | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by \(s\). |
| \( \mathcal{P}_t \) | Set of **candidate paths** (ordered sequences of arcs) that train \(t\) may follow.  Each path \(p\in\mathcal{P}_t\) is a list \((i_1,i_2,\dots,i_{|p|})\). |
| \( \mathcal{O} \) | Set of ordered train‑pairs \((t,t')\) that could conflict on a common arc (used for sequencing). |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \hat{a}_t \) | Planned (original) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (or at a reference node). |
| \( \underline{d}_{ij} \) | Minimum dwell time (stop) required at node \(i\) before entering arc \((i,j)\). |
| \( \overline{d}_{ij} \) | Maximum allowable dwell time (optional, can be set to a large number). |
| \( \tau^{\text{free}}_{ij} \) | Free‑running travel time on arc \((i,j)\) at the highest speed level (baseline). |
| \( \alpha_{ij}^s \) | **Travel‑time factor** for speed level \(s\) on arc \((i,j)\).  Travel time = \( \alpha_{ij}^s \, \tau^{\text{free}}_{ij}\).  \(\alpha_{ij}^s\ge 1\). |
| \( \beta_{ij}^s \) | **Energy‑consumption factor** for speed level \(s\) on arc \((i,j)\).  Energy = \( \beta_{ij}^s \, e^{\text{base}}_{ij}\). |
| \( e^{\text{base}}_{ij} \) | Base energy (e.g. kWh) for traversing arc \((i,j)\) at the highest speed level. |
| \( \underline{t}_{ij} , \overline{t}_{ij}\) | Start and end of the **blocked time window** on a blocked arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal{B}\).  During \([\underline{t}_{ij},\overline{t}_{ij}]\) the capacity of the arc is reduced (e.g. only one train allowed). |
| \( C_{ij}\) | Capacity of arc \((i,j)\) (maximum number of trains simultaneously on the arc). For normal arcs \(C_{ij}=+\infty\); for blocked arcs \(C_{ij}=1\). |
| \( w^{\text{delay}} , w^{\text{energy}} \) | Positive weighting coefficients for the two components of the objective. |
| \( \gamma_{tt'}^{ij} \) | Big‑M constant for sequencing on arc \((i,j)\) (large enough to dominate any feasible time difference). Typically \( \gamma_{tt'}^{ij}= \overline{T} - \underline{T}\) where \(\overline{T}\) is the horizon end. |
| \( \pi_{t}^{p}\) | Indicator (0/1) that tells whether path \(p\) is **feasible** for train \(t\) (e.g. respects train length, direction).  Only feasible paths are kept in \(\mathcal{P}_t\). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \( x_{t}^{p} \) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows path \(p\in\mathcal{P}_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \( y_{ij}^{t,s} \) | Binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) **with speed level** \(s\). |
| \( a_{i}^{t} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \( d_{i}^{t} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \( \tau_{ij}^{t} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\). |
| \( e_{ij}^{t} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumed by train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\). |
| \( z_{tt'}^{ij} \) | Binary | Sequencing variable on arc \((i,j)\): 1 if train \(t\) goes **before** train \(t'\) on that arc, 0 otherwise. |
| \( \delta_{t} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (difference between actual arrival at its destination node and the planned arrival \(\hat{a}_t\)). |
| \( \theta_{t}^{p} \) | Continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Auxiliary variable to linearize the product \(x_t^p\) with other continuous terms (if needed).  In the formulation below we avoid products, so \(\theta\) is not required. |

---

## 4. Model Formulation

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\; \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_{t}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\; \sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}}\; e_{ij}^{t}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The first term penalises total passenger‑train delay; the second term penalises total energy consumption. By adjusting the weights the planner can trade‑off between punctuality and energy efficiency.

---

### 4.2 Routing constraints  

1. **Exactly one path per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{t}^{p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link path choice to arc‑usage** – if a path contains an arc, the corresponding arc‑usage variable must be 1; otherwise it must be 0.  
   For each train \(t\) and each arc \((i,j)\):

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t:\ (i,j)\in p} x_{t}^{p}= \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{R2}
\]

(The left‑hand side counts the selected path; the right‑hand side counts the speed‑level chosen for that arc.)

3. **Speed‑level selection – at most one speed per traversed arc**  

\[
\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{R3}
\]

If the arc is not used (\(y_{ij}^{t,s}=0\) for all \(s\)), the inequality is satisfied.

---

### 4.3 Time‑feasibility (flow) constraints  

We enforce a standard time‑expanded network flow:

4. **Departure after arrival + minimum dwell**  

\[
d_{i}^{t} \;\ge\; a_{i}^{t} + \underline{d}_{ij}\; \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{T1}
\]

If the train does not traverse \((i,j)\), the right‑hand side adds zero.

5. **Travel time definition** (link travel time to selected speed level)  

\[
\tau_{ij}^{t}= \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} \alpha_{ij}^{s}\,\tau^{\text{free}}_{ij}\; y_{ij}^{t,s}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{T2}
\]

6. **Arrival at next node**  

\[
a_{j}^{t} \;\ge\; d_{i}^{t} + \tau_{ij}^{t}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{T3}
\]

7. **Origin / destination fixing** – let \(o_t\) be the origin node of train \(t\) and \(d_t\) its destination node (both known).  

\[
a_{o_t}^{t}=0 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{T4}
\]

\[
\delta_{t}= a_{d_t}^{t} - \hat{a}_t \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{T5}
\]

If early arrival is allowed, we can replace (T5) by \(\delta_t\ge a_{d_t}^t-\hat a_t,\; \delta_t\ge 0\).

---

### 4.4 Blockage (capacity) constraints  

For each **blocked** arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal{B}\) we must guarantee that at most one train occupies it during the blocked time window, and that any train that enters the arc does so **outside** the window or respects the reduced capacity.

8. **Binary sequencing on a blocked arc**  

For every ordered pair of trains \((t,t')\in\mathcal{O}\) that could be on the same blocked arc \((i,j)\):

\[
d_{i}^{t} + \tau_{ij}^{t} \;\le\; d_{i}^{t'} + \gamma_{tt'}^{ij}\, (1- z_{tt'}^{ij})
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{O}
\tag{B1}
\]

\[
d_{i}^{t'} + \tau_{ij}^{t'} \;\le\; d_{i}^{t} + \gamma_{tt'}^{ij}\, z_{tt'}^{ij}
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{O}
\tag{B2}
\]

The big‑M \(\gamma_{tt'}^{ij}\) makes the constraint non‑binding for the “inactive” ordering. The binary variable \(z_{tt'}^{ij}=1\) means “train \(t\) passes before train \(t'\)”.

9. **Compatibility with the blocked time window** – a train may only occupy the arc if its whole traversal lies outside the forbidden interval, or the sequencing ensures that the forbidden interval is respected. A compact way is to use a **time‑window binary**:

Introduce auxiliary binary \(w_{ij}^{t}\) that equals 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) **outside** the blocked window, 0 otherwise.

\[
d_{i}^{t} + \tau_{ij}^{t} \;\le\; \underline{t}_{ij} + \gamma^{\text{M}} (1-w_{ij}^{t})
\tag{B3}
\]

\[
d_{i}^{t} \;\ge\; \overline{t}_{ij} - \gamma^{\text{M}} (1-w_{ij}^{t})
\tag{B4}
\]

\[
w_{ij}^{t} \ge \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s} \qquad \forall t,(i,j)\in\mathcal{B}
\tag{B5}
\]

If a train uses the blocked arc (\(\sum_s y_{ij}^{t,s}=1\)), then \(w_{ij}^{t}=1\) forces its traversal to be completely before \(\underline{t}_{ij}\) or after \(\overline{t}_{ij}\). If the train does **not** use the arc, the constraints are relaxed.

If the blocked segment can still be used but with reduced capacity (e.g., at most one train at a time), the sequencing constraints (B1‑B2) together with (B5) guarantee that at any moment only one train is inside the window.

---

### 4.5 Energy calculation  

10. **Energy consumption per arc**  

\[
e_{ij}^{t}= \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} \beta_{ij}^{s}\, e^{\text{base}}_{ij}\; y_{ij}^{t,s}
\qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}
\tag{E1}
\]

Because the right‑hand side is a linear combination of binary variables, \(e_{ij}^{t}\) is linear.

---

### 4.6 Additional practical constraints (optional)

| Constraint | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| **Maximum delay** | \(\delta_t \le \Delta^{\max}\) for all \(t\) (service‑level agreement). |
| **Speed‑level feasibility** | \(\alpha_{ij}^{s}\) and \(\beta_{ij}^{s}\) are pre‑computed from physics; only admissible levels are kept in \(\mathcal{S}\). |
| **Train length / headway** | If two trains share a *bidirectional* segment, we can add a head‑way binary \(h_{tt'}^{ij}\) and enforce \(d_i^{t} \ge d_i^{t'} + \text{headway}\) when they travel in opposite directions. |
| **Pre‑emptive rerouting** | If a train is forced to reroute because the blocked segment is unavailable, the model automatically selects a different path via (R1‑R2). |

---

## 5. Explanation of each component  

| Component | What it does | How it appears in the model |
|-----------|--------------|----------------------------|
| **Routing (binary \(x_t^p\))** | Chooses a feasible path for each train, allowing rerouting around the blocked segment. | Constraint (R1) forces exactly one path; (R2) couples path choice to arc‑usage variables. |
| **Speed‑profile selection (binary \(y_{ij}^{t,s}\))** | Determines the speed level on each traversed arc, thus fixing travel time and energy consumption. | (R3) guarantees at most one speed per arc; (T2) links speed to travel time; (E1) links speed to energy. |
| **Sequencing / capacity (binary \(z_{tt'}^{ij}\))** | Resolves conflicts when two trains would occupy the same blocked arc at the same time. | (B1‑B2) enforce a total order; the big‑M makes the non‑selected ordering irrelevant. |
| **Time variables (\(a_i^t, d_i^t, \tau_{ij}^t\))** | Record when a train arrives at and departs from each node and how long it spends on each arc. | (T1‑T3) propagate times along the chosen path; (T5) compute delay. |
| **Energy variables (\(e_{ij}^t\))** | Accumulate the energy used on each arc according to the selected speed level. | (E1) linear expression of binary speed‑selection variables. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption. | (OBJ) directly sums \(\delta_t\) and \(e_{ij}^t\). |
| **Blockage handling** | Guarantees that no train enters the blocked segment during the forbidden time window, or that only one train is present if the segment can still be used. | (B3‑B5) enforce that traversals are outside the window; (B1‑B2) enforce a safe ordering when the window is partially overlapped. |
| **Flow conservation** (implicit) | By linking path choice to arc usage and time propagation, the model ensures that each train’s schedule is a continuous path from origin to destination. | (R2) + (T1‑T3). |

---

## 6. Full MILP (compact form)

Putting everything together, the final MILP is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_t
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{A}} e_{ij}^t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_t^p = 1 && \forall t \tag{R1}\\
& \sum_{p:(i,j)\in p} x_t^p = \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s}
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{R2}\\
& \sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} y_{ij}^{t,s}\le 1 && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{R3}\\[2pt]
& d_i^t \ge a_i^t + \underline{d}_{ij}\sum_{s} y_{ij}^{t,s}
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{T1}\\
& \tau_{ij}^t = \sum_{s} \alpha_{ij}^s \tau_{ij}^{\text{free}}\, y_{ij}^{t,s}
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{T2}\\
& a_j^t \ge d_i^t + \tau_{ij}^t
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{T3}\\
& a_{o_t}^t = 0 && \forall t \tag{T4}\\
& \delta_t = a_{d_t}^t - \hat a_t && \forall t \tag{T5}\\[2pt]
& d_i^t + \tau_{ij}^t \le d_i^{t'} + \gamma_{tt'}^{ij}(1- z_{tt'}^{ij})
   && \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{O} \tag{B1}\\
& d_i^{t'} + \tau_{ij}^{t'} \le d_i^{t} + \gamma_{tt'}^{ij} z_{tt'}^{ij}
   && \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{B},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{O} \tag{B2}\\
& d_i^t + \tau_{ij}^t \le \underline{t}_{ij} + \Gamma(1-w_{ij}^t)
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{B} \tag{B3}\\
& d_i^t \ge \overline{t}_{ij} - \Gamma(1-w_{ij}^t)
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{B} \tag{B4}\\
& w_{ij}^t \ge \sum_{s} y_{ij}^{t,s}
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{B} \tag{B5}\\[2pt]
& e_{ij}^t = \sum_{s} \beta_{ij}^s e_{ij}^{\text{base}}\, y_{ij}^{t,s}
   && \forall t,\;(i,j)\in\mathcal{A} \tag{E1}\\[2pt]
& x_t^p ,\, y_{ij}^{t,s},\, z_{tt'}^{ij},\, w_{ij}^t \in \{0,1\} \\
& a_i^t ,\, d_i^t ,\, \tau_{ij}^t ,\, e_{ij}^t ,\, \delta_t \ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\Gamma\) (or \(\gamma^{\text{M}}\)) is a sufficiently large constant (big‑M) larger than the planning horizon.

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – enumerate all feasible paths for each train (e.g., using a k‑shortest‑paths algorithm that respects the blocked segment).  
2. **Parameter calibration** – compute \(\alpha_{ij}^s\) (travel‑time factor) and \(\beta_{ij}^s\) (energy factor) from the train dynamics (e.g., kinetic energy, aerodynamic drag).  
3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, CBC, SCIP). The solver will return:  
   * the selected path for each train (values of \(x_t^p\)),  
   * the speed level on each traversed segment (values of \(y_{ij}^{t,s}\)),  
   * a feasible schedule (arrival/departure times) that respects the blockage, and  
   * the total objective value (weighted delay + energy).  

The formulation is **linear** (all products are binary × binary or binary × constant), so it can be tackled directly by branch‑and‑bound/MIP solvers. Adjusting the weights \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) lets the planner explore the Pareto frontier between punctuality and sustainability.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary for reroute decision, order, speed segment selection; continuous for arrival/departure times, travel times, energy. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block window, track capacity (bidirectional conflict), speed-profile feasibility linking travel time to selected speed level, energy calculation, flow conservation for routing.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three intertwined sub‑problems mentioned in the description  

* **(i) Train‑level routing (reroute / ordering decisions)**  
* **(ii) Speed‑profile selection on each track segment**  
* **(iii) Timing (arrival / departure) and energy consumption**  

The model is written in a **single, linear** formulation that can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  
All symbols are defined in the tables that follow the model, and a short narrative explains the purpose of each set of constraints.

---

## 1.  Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Sets** | |
| 𝑇 = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| 𝑆 = {1,…, |S|} | Set of track segments (directed arcs) that can be traversed. |
| 𝑅 ⊆ 𝑆 × 𝑆 | Set of admissible **reroute pairs** (i → j) – i.e. a train may go from segment *i* to segment *j* (including the original continuation). |
| 𝑉 = {1,…, |V|} | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g. V = {low, medium, high}). |
| **Parameters** | |
| 𝑙_s  | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| 𝑏_s  | Binary flag = 1 if segment *s* is **partially blocked** during a known time window, 0 otherwise. |
| 𝑤_s  | Width of the blocked portion of *s* (fraction of the track width, 0 ≤ w_s ≤ 1). |
| 𝑡^B_s , 𝑡^E_s | Beginning and end of the blockage window on segment *s* (minutes from the planning horizon start). |
| 𝑣_{s}^{v} | Nominal speed (km/min) that can be achieved on segment *s* if speed level *v* is selected (must respect the physical speed limit of the segment). |
| 𝜏^{min}_s , 𝜏^{max}_s | Minimum / maximum **travel time** (min) that is physically feasible on segment *s* (e.g. due to acceleration/deceleration limits). |
| 𝑒^{v}_s | Energy consumption (MJ) required to traverse segment *s* at speed level *v*. |
| 𝑑^{orig}_t | Planned (original) departure time of train *t* from its origin (min). |
| 𝑎^{orig}_t | Planned (original) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (min). |
| 𝑝_t   | Penalty weight for **delay** of train *t*. |
| 𝑞      | Global weight for **energy** in the objective (can be set to 0 if only delay matters). |
| 𝑈      | A big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time, e.g. horizon length). |
| **Decision Variables** | |
| x_{t,s} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* (routing variable). |
| y_{t, (i,j)} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* uses the directed arc (i→j) (ordering / continuation variable). |
| z_{t,s,v} ∈ {0,1} | =1 if train *t* travels on segment *s* with speed level *v*. |
| 𝛼_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| 𝛽_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s*. |
| 𝜏_{t,s} ≥ 0 | Travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (𝛽 – 𝛼). |
| 𝜀_t ≥ 0 | **Delay** of train *t* (actual arrival at destination – original arrival). |
| 𝜙_t ≥ 0 | Energy consumed by train *t* (sum of e^{v}_s over all traversed segments). |

All variables are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries (x, y, z).

---

## 2.  MILP Formulation  

### 2.1 Objective  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} p_t \, \varepsilon_t}_{\text{weighted total delay}}
\;+\; \underbrace{q \, \sum_{t\in T} \phi_t}_{\text{weighted total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The two terms can be weighted to reflect the planner’s preference (e.g. give a high weight to delay, a low weight to energy).

---

### 2.2 Routing / Flow Conservation  

For every train *t* we must build a **directed path** from its origin node *o_t* to its destination node *d_t*.  
Let `inc(s)` be the set of arcs that **enter** segment *s* (i.e. (i,s) ∈ R) and `out(s)` the set that **leave** *s* (i.e. (s,j) ∈ R).

1. **Origin / destination activation**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S: o_t\in \text{upstream}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 ,\qquad
\sum_{s\in S: d_t\in \text{downstream}(s)} x_{t,s}=1
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Flow balance for interior nodes**  

\[
\sum_{(i,s)\in inc(s)} y_{t,(i,s)} \;-\; \sum_{(s,j)\in out(s)} y_{t,(s,j)} = 0,
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}
\tag{R2}
\]

3. **Link arc‑selection to segment‑selection**  

\[
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,i}, \qquad
y_{t,(i,s)} \le x_{t,s}, \qquad \forall t,\;(i,s)\in R
\tag{R3}
\]

Thus a train can only use an arc if it actually traverses both incident segments.

---

### 2.3 Speed‑profile selection  

For every traversed segment we must pick **exactly one** admissible speed level.

\[
\sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,v}= x_{t,s}, \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If a segment is not used (x=0) all associated z‑variables are forced to 0.

---

### 2.4 Travel‑time – speed coupling  

Travel time on a segment is the inverse of the chosen speed (linearised with the big‑M trick).

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s} &\ge \frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}} \;-\; U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v\\
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s} &\le \frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}} \;+\; U\,(1-z_{t,s,v}), &&\forall t,s,v
\end{aligned}
\tag{S2}
\]

Because exactly one *v* is active per traversed segment, the two inequalities collapse to  

\[
\mathsf{τ}_{t,s}= \frac{l_s}{v^{v^\*}_{s}} \quad\text{with } v^\* \text{ the selected speed level}.
\]

We also enforce the physical feasibility window:

\[
\tau^{min}_s \, x_{t,s} \;\le\; \mathsf{τ}_{t,s} \;\le\; \tau^{max}_s \, x_{t,s},
\qquad \forall t,s
\tag{S3}
\]

If a segment is not used (x=0) the bounds force τ=0.

---

### 2.5 Timing (arrival / departure)  

The arrival at the downstream end of a segment equals the departure from its upstream end plus travel time:

\[
\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \mathsf{τ}_{t,s},\qquad \forall t,s
\tag{T1}
\]

**Link successive segments** (flow continuity).  
If train *t* goes from segment *i* to segment *j* (i→j) we must have

\[
\alpha_{t,j} \ge \beta_{t,i} - U\,(1-y_{t,(i,j)}),\qquad \forall t,\;(i,j)\in R
\tag{T2}
\]

When the arc is active (y=1) the inequality becomes an equality (or a “≥” that will be tight at optimum). When the arc is not used, the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

**Origin departure** and **final arrival**:

\[
\alpha_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}= d^{\text{orig}}_t, \qquad
\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}= a^{\text{orig}}_t + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \forall t
\tag{T3}
\]

where \(s^{\text{orig}}\) and \(s^{\text{dest}}\) are the first and last segments of train *t*’s planned route.

---

### 2.6 Blockage (partial segment closure)  

A partially blocked segment *s* can only be occupied **outside** the blockage window **or** by a train that uses a speed level that fits through the remaining free width.  
We model it conservatively by forbidding any occupation during the window:

\[
\alpha_{t,s} \ge t^{E}_s \;-\; U\,(1-x_{t,s}),\qquad
\beta_{t,s} \le t^{B}_s \;+\; U\,(1-x_{t,s}),\qquad \forall t,\; s\text{ with }b_s=1
\tag{B1}
\]

The two inequalities together force **either** the whole traversal to finish before the blockage starts **or** start after it ends.  

If a more refined “partial‑width” rule is required (e.g., a train can still pass if its speed level uses a narrower track gauge), introduce a binary “allowed‑through” parameter  

\[
c_{s,v}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if speed level }v\text{ fits through the unblocked width of }s\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

and add  

\[
z_{t,s,v} \le 1-c_{s,v}+x_{t,s},\qquad \forall t,s,v\text{ with }b_s=1
\tag{B2}
\]

so that forbidden speed levels cannot be selected on a blocked segment.

---

### 2.7 Track‑capacity (bidirectional conflict)  

Assume each physical track segment can be used **by at most one train at a time**, regardless of direction. A classic disjunctive (pairwise) formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{t_1,s} \ge \beta_{t_2,s} - U\,\delta_{t_1,t_2,s} \\
\alpha_{t_2,s} \ge \beta_{t_1,s} - U\,(1-\delta_{t_1,t_2,s})
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall s\in S,\; \forall t_1<t_2
\tag{C1}
\]

where \(\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first on segment *s*.  
If the planning horizon is large, a **time‑window aggregation** can be used instead:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} x_{t,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S\text{ with }b_s=0
\tag{C2}
\]

i.e. at most one train may be assigned to a segment that is not blocked (a stronger but simpler capacity rule). Choose the version that matches the required level of detail.

---

### 2.8 Energy accounting  

Energy used by a train is the sum of the energy of the selected speed levels:

\[
\phi_t = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{v\in V} e^{v}_s \, z_{t,s,v},\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

---

### 2.9 Delay definition  

\[
\varepsilon_t = \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - a^{\text{orig}}_t ,\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

Because \(\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}\) is the actual arrival time at the final node, the difference gives the **positive** delay (the model will never make \(\varepsilon_t\) negative because the objective penalises it; if a train arrives early you may set \(\varepsilon_t\ge 0\) explicitly).

---

### 2.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,(i,j)}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,(i,j),v\\
&\alpha_{t,s},\beta_{t,s},\tau_{t,s},\varepsilon_t,\phi_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\in\{0,1\}\quad\text{(if using pairwise capacity)} &&\forall t_1<t_2,\,s
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 3.  Explanation of Model Components  

| Block | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **Objective (OBJ)** | Minimises a weighted sum of total train delay and total energy consumption. | Captures the planner’s trade‑off between punctuality (service level) and sustainability (energy). |
| **Routing constraints (R1‑R3)** | Build a feasible path for each train through the network, allowing optional rerouting (binary y). | Guarantees that each train has a continuous sequence of segments from origin to destination and that any reroute decision is reflected in the binary variables. |
| **Speed‑selection (S1‑S3)** | Forces exactly one speed level per traversed segment, links speed to travel time, and respects physical min/max travel‑time limits. | Enables speed‑profile management while keeping the model linear (big‑M linearisation). |
| **Timing constraints (T1‑T3)** | Relates arrival, departure, and travel time; propagates timing from one segment to the next; defines delay at the final node. | Guarantees temporal feasibility (no “teleportation”) and provides the delay variable used in the objective. |
| **Blockage handling (B1‑B2)** | Keeps trains out of a segment during its blockage window, or forbids speed levels that cannot fit through the remaining free width. | Models the *partial* segment closure accurately, preventing unsafe or impossible traversals. |
| **Capacity / conflict (C1‑C2)** | Ensures that two trains never occupy the same physical track segment simultaneously (either by pairwise disjunction or by a simple “one‑train‑per‑segment” rule). | Avoids collisions and respects the limited track capacity, especially important when a blockage reduces the usable width. |
| **Energy accounting (E1)** | Sums the energy consumption of the chosen speed levels for each train. | Provides the energy term needed in the objective and any downstream reporting. |
| **Delay definition (D1)** | Computes the positive delay of each train as the difference between its actual arrival and the originally scheduled arrival. | Supplies the variable that the objective penalises. |
| **Domain definitions (DOM)** | Declares binary vs. continuous variables and sets big‑M bounds. | Required for a correct MILP formulation. |

---

## 4.  How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the network (segments *S* and admissible arcs *R*).  
   * For every segment compute length *l_s*, speed limits *v^{v}_s*, min/max travel times, energy per speed level, and blockage information (*b_s, t^B_s, t^E_s, w_s*).  
   * For each train define origin segment, destination segment, original departure/arrival times, and the delay weight *p_t*.  

2. **Choose big‑M**  
   * A safe choice is the planning horizon length (e.g., 1440 min for a 24‑h horizon).  

3. **Select capacity formulation**  
   * Use (C1) if you need a detailed ordering of trains on each segment (more variables, tighter model).  
   * Use (C2) for a coarse but much smaller model (good for large instances).  

4. **Solve**  
   * Feed the linear constraints, objective, and variable domains to any MILP solver.  
   * The optimal solution will give:  
     * **x, y** → the chosen route (including any rerouting).  
     * **z** → the speed level on every traversed segment.  
     * **α, β** → the exact schedule (arrival/departure times).  
     * **ε** → the resulting delay for each train.  
     * **φ** → the total energy consumption.  

5. **Post‑processing** (optional)  
   * Compute derived performance indicators (average delay, total energy savings vs. a baseline, utilisation of blocked segments, etc.).  

---

### 5.  Full Linear Model (compact form)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} p_t \varepsilon_t \;+\; q \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e^{v}_s\,z_{t,s,v}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s:\,o_t\in\text{up}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{s:\,d_t\in\text{down}(s)} x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{(i,s)\in inc(s)} y_{t,(i,s)}-\sum_{(s,j)\in out(s)} y_{t,(s,j)} =0 &&\forall t,\;s\neq o_t,d_t\\
&y_{t,(i,s)}\le x_{t,i},\; y_{t,(i,s)}\le x_{t,s} &&\forall t,(i,s)\in R\\
&\sum_{v} z_{t,s,v}=x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\tau_{t,s}\ge\frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}}-U(1-z_{t,s,v}) &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\tau_{t,s}\le\frac{l_s}{v^{v}_{s}}+U(1-z_{t,s,v}) &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\tau^{min}_s x_{t,s}\le \tau_{t,s}\le \tau^{max}_s x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\beta_{t,s}= \alpha_{t,s}+ \tau_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&\alpha_{t,j}\ge \beta_{t,i}-U(1-y_{t,(i,j)}) &&\forall t,(i,j)\in R\\
&\alpha_{t,s^{\text{orig}}}= d^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
&\beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}= a^{\text{orig}}_t+\varepsilon_t &&\forall t\\
&\alpha_{t,s}\ge t^{E}_s-U(1-x_{t,s}),\; \beta_{t,s}\le t^{B}_s+U(1-x_{t,s}) &&\forall t, s\text{ with }b_s=1\\
&\text{(optional) } z_{t,s,v}\le 1-c_{s,v}+x_{t,s} &&\forall t,s,v\text{ with }b_s=1\\
&\text{(capacity) } \alpha_{t_1,s}\ge\beta_{t_2,s}-U\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}\\
&\qquad\;\;\; \alpha_{t_2,s}\ge\beta_{t_1,s}-U(1-\delta_{t_1,t_2,s}) &&\forall s,\;t_1<t_2\\
&\phi_t =\sum_{s,v} e^{v}_s\,z_{t,s,v} &&\forall t\\
&\varepsilon_t = \beta_{t,s^{\text{dest}}}-a^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
&x,y,z\in\{0,1\},\; \alpha,\beta,\tau,\varepsilon,\phi\ge 0,\; \delta\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries that encode routing, ordering, speed‑level choice, and (if used) the pairwise capacity decisions.  

---  

**That completes the MILP model** for *integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partially blocked segment*. It can be directly implemented in a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …) and solved with any state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.
