Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

{
  "description": "Based on the provided narrative, formulate a mixed-integer linear programming model for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockages. Include sets:
- T: trains, S: stations, L: track segments, B: bidirectional pairs, P: possible routes (original or rerouted), K: discrete time intervals within planning horizon.
Parameters:
- a_{t,s}: scheduled arrival time, d_{t,s}: scheduled departure time, 
- L_{p}: set of segments used by route p, 
- block_{l,k}: binary indicating if segment l is blocked during interval k, 
- dwell_{t,s}: minimum dwell time, 
- minRun_{t,l}, maxRun_{t,l}: minimum and maximum travel time for train t on segment l (derived from speed limits), 
- energy_{t,p}: energy cost coefficient for train t on route p (depends on acceleration/deceleration profile), 
- M: large constant.
Decision variables:
- x_{t,p} ∈ {0,1}: choose route p for train t (original or rerouted), 
- y_{t,s,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t arrives at station s in interval k, 
- z_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t traverses segment l in interval k, 
- w_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t uses accelerated mode on segment l in interval k, 
- u_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t uses decelerated mode on segment l in interval k, 
- C: total energy consumption.
Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption: minimize α Σ_{t,s,k} max(0, k·Δt - a_{t,s}) y_{t,s,k} + β Σ_{t,p} energy_{t,p} x_{t,p}.
Constraints:
1) Route selection: Σ_{p∈P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 ∀t.
2) Consistency of station visitation: Σ_{k} y_{t,s,k}=1 if station s lies on chosen route; else 0. 
3) Temporal ordering: if train t moves from s to s' on route p, then arrival interval at s' must follow departure from s plus travel time on intervening segments. Linearized using big-M.
4) Segment occupancy conflict for bidirectional pairs: for each bidirectional pair (l,l') sharing physical track and each interval k, Σ_{t} z_{t,l,k} + Σ_{t} z_{t,l',k} ≤ 1.
5) Blockage avoidance: z_{t,l,k} ≤ 1 - block_{l,k} ∀t,l,k.
6) Travel time bounds: Σ_{k} k·Δt·z_{t,l,k} - Σ_{k} k·Δt·z_{t,l,prev(k)} ≥ minRun_{t,l}·x_{t,p} and ≤ maxRun_{t,l}·x_{t,p}.
7) Dwell time: if y_{t,s,k}=1 and departure occurs at k', then k' - k ≥ dwell_{t,s}.
8) Acceleration/deceleration mode linking: w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k} ≤ z_{t,l,k}; energy cost depends on w and u.
9) Energy calculation: C = Σ_{t,l,k} (e_acc·w_{t,l,k}+ e_dec·u_{t,l,k}) where e_acc, e_dec are coefficients.
Assumptions: time discretized uniformly Δt (e.g., 1 minute); each train traverses each segment in exactly one interval; acceleration/deceleration decisions are binary per segment; energy coefficients approximate continuous speed profile effects.
Provide full mathematical formulation with indices, variables, objective and constraints.
"
}

messages.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockages**  

All time is discretised into equal intervals of length Δt (e.g. 1 min).  
For each train we must decide (i) which route (original or a rerouted alternative) it will follow, (ii) the exact interval in which it arrives at every station on the chosen route, (iii) the interval in which it occupies each track segment, and (iv) whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode on that segment.  
The model minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while respecting timetable, blockages, capacity on bidirectional track pairs, and travel‑time limits.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal T\) | Set of trains \(t\). |
| \(\mathcal S\) | Set of stations \(s\). |
| \(\mathcal L\) | Set of *directed* track segments \(l\). |
| \(\mathcal B\subseteq \mathcal L\times\mathcal L\) | Set of **bidirectional pairs** \((l,l')\) that share the same physical track (opposite directions). |
| \(\mathcal P(t)\) | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\).  Each route \(p\) is a ordered list of stations and of the directed segments that connect them. |
| \(\mathcal K=\{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of discrete time intervals in the planning horizon. |
| \(L_{p}\subseteq\mathcal L\) | Set of directed segments that belong to route \(p\). |
| \(\mathcal S_{p}\subseteq\mathcal S\) | Set of stations visited by route \(p\) (in the order of travel). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(\text{dwell}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time required at station \(s\) for train \(t\). | minutes |
| \(\text{minRun}_{t,l},\ \text{maxRun}_{t,l}\) | Minimum / maximum allowed travel time for train \(t\) on segment \(l\) (derived from speed limits). | minutes |
| \(\text{block}_{l,k}\) | 1 if segment \(l\) is blocked during interval \(k\), 0 otherwise. | – |
| \(\text{energy}_{t,p}\) | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per km) for train \(t\) if it follows route \(p\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **accelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **decelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | Weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| \(\Delta t\) | Duration of one time index (e.g. 1 min). | minutes |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(p\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **arrives** at station \(s\) in interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** directed segment \(l\) during interval \(k\). |
| \(w_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **accelerated** speed mode. |
| \(u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **decelerated** speed mode. |
| \(C\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption (to be linked to \(w\) & \(u\)). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}\,y_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)}\text{energy}_{t,p}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where \((\cdot)^{+}=\max\{0,\cdot\}\).  
Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, the product \(\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+} y_{t,s,k}\) equals the delay incurred if the train arrives later than the scheduled time and zero otherwise. (If the modeler prefers a fully linear term, introduce an auxiliary non‑negative variable \(\delta_{t,s}\) with constraints \(\delta_{t,s}\ge k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\) for the selected interval.)

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route‑selection  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad\forall\,t\in\mathcal T } \tag{R1}
\]

Exactly one route (original or rerouted) is chosen for each train.

#### 5.2  Station‑visitation consistency  

For every train–station pair we allow arrival only if the station belongs to the selected route; otherwise the binary variable must be zero.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} y_{t,s,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S } \tag{R2}
\]

\(\mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\) is 1 when station \(s\) lies on route \(p\), 0 otherwise.

#### 5.3  Exactly one interval for each segment (single‑occupancy per train)

A train that travels on a segment must occupy **exactly one** time interval on that segment.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} z_{t,l,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,l\in L_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; l\in\mathcal L } \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4  Temporal ordering between successive stations  

Let station \(s\) be followed by \(s'\) on route \(p\). Define the set of directed segments between them as \(\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}\). The departure interval from \(s\) must be **no later** than the arrival interval at \(s'\) minus the minimum travel time across all those segments, and **no earlier** than the arrival interval plus the maximum travel time.

Introduce auxiliary variables:
- \(A_{t,s}\) = interval index of arrival at station \(s\) (continuous, later forced integer by binary y),
- \(D_{t,s}\) = interval index of departure from station \(s\) (continuous).

These are linked to the binary \(y\) variables by standard “assignment” constraints:

\[
A_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{R4a}
\]

\[
D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+ \text{dwell}_{t,s}/\Delta t
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{R4b}
\]

Now for every ordered pair \((s,s')\) that appear consecutively on the chosen route:

\[
\boxed{ A_{t,s'}\; \ge\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{minRun}_{t,l} }{\Delta t}\;-\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; p\in\mathcal P(t),\; (s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R4c}
\]

\[
\boxed{ A_{t,s'}\; \le\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{maxRun}_{t,l} }{\Delta t}\;+\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; p\in\mathcal P(t),\; (s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R4d}
\]

The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when route \(p\) is not chosen.

#### 5.5  Bidirectional segment‑capacity (collision avoidance)

For each physical track shared by a pair of opposite‑direction segments \((l,l')\in\mathcal B\) at any interval \(k\) only one train may occupy it.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l,k}+ \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l',k}\;\le\;1
\qquad\forall (l,l')\in\mathcal B,\; k\in\mathcal K } \tag{R5}
\]

#### 5.6  Blockage avoidance  

If a segment is blocked in interval \(k\), no train may traverse it.

\[
\boxed{ z_{t,l,k}\; \le\; 1-\text{block}_{l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7  Travel‑time bounds per segment  

The *effective* travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(l\) is the difference between the interval index where it **enters** the segment and the interval where it **leaves** it. Because we assume “one interval per segment” (R3), we can use the interval index directly:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\; x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R7a}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;\le\; \frac{\text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\; x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R7b}
\]

Here \(z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}\) denotes the binary variable that the *same* train left the preceding segment (or the departure from the previous station) at interval \(k\); the model can be linearised by introducing an auxiliary “exit” variable or, more simply, by noting that because each segment occupies exactly one interval, the travel time on a segment \(l\) equals 1 Δt (if we force a 1‑interval traversal). If a finer granularity is needed, replace the left‑hand side with the sum of intervals for **all** directed arcs belonging to that segment (the same technique as in R4). For brevity we keep the compact formulation.

#### 5.8  Dwell‑time enforcement  

If a train arrives at station \(s\) in interval \(k\) (i.e. \(y_{t,s,k}=1\)), it may not depart before interval \(k+\lceil\text{dwell}_{t,s}/\Delta t\rceil\). Introduce departure binary variable \(y^{\text{dep}}_{t,s,k}\) (or reuse the same \(y\) with a shift). A compact linearisation:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k} + \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}
\;\le\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s',k} \qquad\forall t,\; s \text{ preceding } s' \text{ on chosen route }p
\tag{R8}
\]

where \(s'\) is the next station after \(s\) on the route. The big‑M version (activating only when the route containing the station pair is selected) can be written:

\[
\sum_{k}k y_{t,s',k}\;-\;\sum_{k}k y_{t,s,k}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}\;-\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,p,\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}
\tag{R8b}
\]

#### 5.9  Linking speed‑mode to segment occupation  

Only one speed mode can be active on a segment while it is occupied, and a mode can be active only if the segment is traversed.

\[
\boxed{ w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k}\;\le\; z_{t,l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R9}
\]

If a segment is traversed without a dedicated mode (e.g. cruise), both \(w\) and \(u\) can be zero.

#### 5.10  Energy‑consumption definition  

\[
\boxed{ C = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{l\in\mathcal L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\, w_{t,l,k}+ e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\, u_{t,l,k}\bigr) } \tag{R10}
\]

If the planner prefers a *single* objective term, \(C\) can be substituted directly into the objective. Otherwise, \(C\) can be reported as a separate performance indicator.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\sum_{t,s,k}\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}y_{t,s,k}
     \;+\;\beta\sum_{t,p}\text{energy}_{t,p}x_{t,p} \\
\text{s.t.}&\;\text{(R1)–(R10)}\\
& x_{t,p},y_{t,s,k},z_{t,l,k},w_{t,l,k},u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
C\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisations used where a condition depends on a binary route‑selection variable). The model simultaneously decides **which route each train should take**, **when it arrives/departs each station**, **how it traverses each possibly‑blocked segment**, and **whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode**, while minimising a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7. Practical Remarks  

| Issue | Recommended handling |
|-------|----------------------|
| **Choice of  M** | Take \(M\) larger than the maximum possible interval index (e.g. \(K+1\)). |
| **Integrality of arrival time** | Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, \(A_{t,s}= \sum k y_{t,s,k}\) is automatically integer. |
| **Multiple‑interval travel on a long segment** | If a segment may require more than one Δt, replace (R3) by \(\sum_k z_{t,l,k}= \tau_{t,l}\) where \(\tau_{t,l}\) is a known integer (derived from min/max run times). The travel‑time bounds (R7) then use the sum of occupied intervals. |
| **Energy for cruise mode** | Add a constant term \(e^{\text{cruise}}_{t,l}\) multiplied by \(z_{t,l,k}\) to (R10) if needed. |
| **Robustness to data uncertainties** | Introduce slack variables for delay, penalised heavily in the objective. |

The presented MILP is complete, linear, and ready to be implemented in any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) for the **Train Rescheduling & Speed Management Problem under partial segment blockages**.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockages**  

All time is discretised into equal intervals of length Δt (e.g. 1 min).  
For each train we must decide (i) which route (original or a rerouted alternative) it will follow, (ii) the exact interval in which it arrives at every station on the chosen route, (iii) the interval in which it occupies each track segment, and (iv) whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode on that segment.  
The model minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while respecting timetable, blockages, capacity on bidirectional track pairs, and travel‑time limits.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal T\) | Set of trains \(t\). |
| \(\mathcal S\) | Set of stations \(s\). |
| \(\mathcal L\) | Set of *directed* track segments \(l\). |
| \(\mathcal B\subseteq \mathcal L\times\mathcal L\) | Set of **bidirectional pairs** \((l,l')\) that share the same physical track (opposite directions). |
| \(\mathcal P(t)\) | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\).  Each route \(p\) is a ordered list of stations and of the directed segments that connect them. |
| \(\mathcal K=\{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of discrete time intervals in the planning horizon. |
| \(L_{p}\subseteq\mathcal L\) | Set of directed segments that belong to route \(p\). |
| \(\mathcal S_{p}\subseteq\mathcal S\) | Set of stations visited by route \(p\) (in the order of travel). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(\text{dwell}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time required at station \(s\) for train \(t\). | minutes |
| \(\text{minRun}_{t,l},\ \text{maxRun}_{t,l}\) | Minimum / maximum allowed travel time for train \(t\) on segment \(l\) (derived from speed limits). | minutes |
| \(\text{block}_{l,k}\) | 1 if segment \(l\) is blocked during interval \(k\), 0 otherwise. | – |
| \(\text{energy}_{t,p}\) | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per km) for train \(t\) if it follows route \(p\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **accelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **decelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | Weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| \(\Delta t\) | Duration of one time index (e.g. 1 min). | minutes |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(p\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **arrives** at station \(s\) in interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** directed segment \(l\) during interval \(k\). |
| \(w_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **accelerated** speed mode. |
| \(u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **decelerated** speed mode. |
| \(C\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption (to be linked to \(w\) & \(u\)). |

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}\,y_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)}\text{energy}_{t,p}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where \((\cdot)^{+}=\max\{0,\cdot\}\).  
Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, the product \(\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+} y_{t,s,k}\) equals the delay incurred if the train arrives later than the scheduled time and zero otherwise. For brevity we keep the compact formulation.

#### 5.8  Dwell‑time enforcement  

If a train arrives at station \(s\) in interval \(k\) (i.e. \(y_{t,s,k}=1\)), it may not depart before interval \(k+\lceil\text{dwell}_{t,s}/\Delta t\rceil\). Introduce departure binary variable \(y^{\text{dep}}_{t,s,k}\) (or reuse the same \(y\) with a shift). A compact linearisation:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k} + \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}
\;\le\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s',k} \qquad\forall t,\; s \text{ preceding } s' \text{ on chosen route }p
\tag{R8}
\]

where \(s'\) is the next station after \(s\) on the route. The big‑M version (activating only when the route containing the station pair is selected) can be written:

\[
\sum_{k}k y_{t,s',k}\;-\;\sum_{k}k y_{t,s,k}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}\;-\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,p,\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}
\tag{R8b}
\]

#### 5.9  Linking speed‑mode to segment occupation  

Only one speed mode can be active on a segment while it is occupied, and a mode can be active only if the segment is traversed.

\[
\boxed{ w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k}\;\le\; z_{t,l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R9}
\]

If a segment is traversed without a dedicated mode (e.g. cruise), both \(w\) and \(u\) can be zero.

#### 5.10  Energy‑consumption definition  

\[
\boxed{ C = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{l\in\mathcal L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\, w_{t,l,k}+ e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\, u_{t,l,k}\bigr) } \tag{R10}
\]

If the planner prefers a *single* objective term, \(C\) can be substituted directly into the objective. Otherwise, \(C\) can be reported as a separate performance indicator.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\sum_{t,s,k}\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}y_{t,s,k}
     \;+\;\beta\sum_{t,p}\text{energy}_{t,p}x_{t,p} \\
\text{s.t.}&\;\text{(R1)–(R10)}\\
& x_{t,p},y_{t,s,k},z_{t,l,k},w_{t,l,k},u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
C\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisations used where a condition depends on a binary route‑selection variable). The model simultaneously decides **which route each train should take**, **when it arrives/departs each station**, **how it traverses each possibly‑blocked segment**, and **whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode**, while minimising a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7. Practical Remarks  

| Issue | Recommended handling |
|-------|----------------------|
| **Choice of  M** | Take \(M\) larger than the maximum possible interval index (e.g. \(K+1\)). |
| **Integrality of arrival time** | Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, \(A_{t,s}= \sum k y_{t,s,k}\) is automatically integer. |
| **Multiple‑interval travel on a long segment** | If a segment may require more than one Δt, replace (R3) by \(\sum_k z_{t,l,k}= \tau_{t,l}\) where \(\tau_{t,l}\) is a known integer (derived from min/max run times). The travel‑time bounds (R7) then use the sum of occupied intervals. |
| **Energy for cruise mode** | Add a constant term \(e^{\text{cruise}}_{t,l}\) multiplied by \(z_{t,l,k}\) to (R10) if needed. |
| **Robustness to data uncertainties** | Introduce slack variables for delay, penalised heavily in the objective. |

The presented MILP is complete, linear, and ready to be implemented in any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) for the **Train Rescheduling & Speed Management Problem under partial segment blockages**.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

- T: trains, S: stations, L: track segments, B: bidirectional pairs, P: possible routes (original or rerouted), K: discrete time intervals within planning horizon.
Parameters:

- L_{p}: set of segments used by route p, 
- block_{l,k}: binary indicating if segment l is blocked during interval k, 
- dwell_{t,s}: minimum dwell time, 
- minRun_{t,l}, maxRun_{t,l}: minimum and maximum travel time for train t on segment l (derived from speed limits), 
- energy_{t,p}: energy cost coefficient for train t on route p (depends on acceleration/deceleration profile), 
- M: large constant.
Decision variables:
- x_{t,p} ∈ {0,1}: choose route p for train t (original or rerouted), 
- y_{t,s,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t arrives at station s in interval k, 
- z_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t traverses segment l in interval k, 
- w_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t uses accelerated mode on segment l in interval k, 
- u_{t,l,k} ∈ {0,1}: train t uses decelerated mode on segment l in interval k, 
- C: total energy consumption.
Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption: minimize α Σ_{t,s,k} max(0, k·Δt - a_{t,s}) y_{t,s,k} + β Σ_{t,p} energy_{t,p} x_{t,p}.
Constraints:
1) Route selection: Σ_{p∈P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 ∀t.
2) Consistency of station visitation: Σ_{k} y_{t,s,k}=1 if station s lies on chosen route; else 0. 
3) Temporal ordering: if train t moves from s to s' on route p, then arrival interval at s' must follow departure from s plus travel time on intervening segments. Linearized using big-M.
4) Segment occupancy conflict for bidirectional pairs: for each bidirectional pair (l,l') sharing physical track and each interval k, Σ_{t} z_{t,l,k} + Σ_{t} z_{t,l',k} ≤ 1.
5) Blockage avoidance: z_{t,l,k} ≤ 1 - block_{l,k} ∀t,l,k.
6) Travel time bounds: Σ_{k} k·Δt·z_{t,l,k} - Σ_{k} k·Δt·z_{t,l,prev(k)} ≥ minRun_{t,l}·x_{t,p} and ≤ maxRun_{t,l}·x_{t,p}.
7) Dwell time: if y_{t,s,k}=1 and departure occurs at k', then k' - k ≥ dwell_{t,s}.
8) Acceleration/deceleration mode linking: w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k} ≤ z_{t,l,k}; energy cost depends on w and u.
9) Energy calculation: C = Σ_{t,l,k} (e_acc·w_{t,l,k}+ e_dec·u_{t,l,k}) where e_acc, e_dec are coefficients.
Assumptions: time discretized uniformly Δt (e.g., 1 minute); each train traverses each segment in exactly one interval; acceleration/deceleration decisions are binary per segment; energy coefficients approximate continuous speed profile effects.
Provide full mathematical formulation with indices, variables, objective and constraints.
"

messages.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockages**  

All time is discretised into equal intervals of length Δt (e.g. 1 min).  
For each train we must decide (i) which route (original or a rerouted alternative) it will follow, (ii) the exact interval in which it arrives at every station on the chosen route, (iii) the interval in which it occupies each track segment, and (iv) whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode on that segment.  
The model minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while respecting timetable, blockages, capacity on bidirectional track pairs, and travel‑time limits.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal T\) | Set of trains \(t\). |
| \(\mathcal S\) | Set of stations \(s\). |
| \(\mathcal L\) | Set of *directed* track segments \(l\). |
| \(\mathcal B\subseteq \mathcal L\times\mathcal L\) | Set of **bidirectional pairs** \((l,l')\) that share the same physical track (opposite directions). |
| \(\mathcal P(t)\) | Set of feasible routes for train \(t\).  Each route \(p\) is a ordered list of stations and of the directed segments that connect them. |
| \(\mathcal K=\{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of discrete time intervals in the planning horizon. |
| \(L_{p}\subseteq\mathcal L\) | Set of directed segments that belong to route \(p\). |
| \(\mathcal S_{p}\subseteq\mathcal S\) | Set of stations visited by route \(p\) (in the order of travel). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \(a_{t,s}\) | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\) (continuous). | minutes |
| \(\text{dwell}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time required at station \(s\) for train \(t\). | minutes |
| \(\text{minRun}_{t,l},\ \text{maxRun}_{t,l}\) | Minimum / maximum allowed travel time for train \(t\) on segment \(l\) (derived from speed limits). | minutes |
| \(\text{block}_{l,k}\) | 1 if segment \(l\) is blocked during interval \(k\), 0 otherwise. | – |
| \(\text{energy}_{t,p}\) | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per km) for train \(t\) if it follows route \(p\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **accelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\) | Energy cost of using **decelerated** mode on segment \(l\) for train \(t\). | kWh |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | Weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| \(\Delta t\) | Duration of one time index (e.g. 1 min). | minutes |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(p\). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **arrives** at station \(s\) in interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** directed segment \(l\) during interval \(k\). |
| \(w_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **accelerated** speed mode. |
| \(u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(l\) in interval \(k\) using **decelerated** speed mode. |
| \(C\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption (to be linked to \(w\) & \(u\)). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}\,y_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)}\text{energy}_{t,p}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where \((\cdot)^{+}=\max\{0,\cdot\}\).  
Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, the product \(\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+} y_{t,s,k}\) equals the delay incurred if the train arrives later than the scheduled time and zero otherwise. (If the modeler prefers a fully linear term, introduce an auxiliary non‑negative variable \(\delta_{t,s}\) with constraints \(\delta_{t,s}\ge k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\) for the selected interval.)

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route‑selection  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad\forall\,t\in\mathcal T } \tag{R1}
\]

Exactly one route (original or rerouted) is chosen for each train.

#### 5.2  Station‑visitation consistency  

For every train–station pair we allow arrival only if the station belongs to the selected route; otherwise the binary variable must be zero.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} y_{t,s,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S } \tag{R2}
\]

\(\mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\) is 1 when station \(s\) lies on route \(p\), 0 otherwise.

#### 5.3  Exactly one interval for each segment (single‑occupancy per train)

A train that travels on a segment must occupy **exactly one** time interval on that segment.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} z_{t,l,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,l\in L_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; l\in\mathcal L } \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4  Temporal ordering between successive stations  

Let station \(s\) be followed by \(s'\) on route \(p\). Define the set of directed segments between them as \(\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}\). The departure interval from \(s\) must be **no later** than the arrival interval at \(s'\) minus the minimum travel time across all those segments, and **no earlier** than the arrival interval plus the maximum travel time.

Introduce auxiliary variables:
- \(A_{t,s}\) = interval index of arrival at station \(s\) (continuous, later forced integer by binary y),
- \(D_{t,s}\) = interval index of departure from station \(s\) (continuous).

These are linked to the binary \(y\) variables by standard “assignment” constraints:

\[
A_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{R4a}
\]

\[
D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+ \text{dwell}_{t,s}/\Delta t
\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{R4b}
\]

Now for every ordered pair \((s,s')\) that appear consecutively on the chosen route:

\[
\boxed{ A_{t,s'}\; \ge\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{minRun}_{t,l} }{\Delta t}\;-\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; p\in\mathcal P(t),\; (s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R4c}
\]

\[
\boxed{ A_{t,s'}\; \le\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{maxRun}_{t,l} }{\Delta t}\;+\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\; p\in\mathcal P(t),\; (s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R4d}
\]

The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when route \(p\) is not chosen.

#### 5.5  Bidirectional segment‑capacity (collision avoidance)

For each physical track shared by a pair of opposite‑direction segments \((l,l')\in\mathcal B\) at any interval \(k\) only one train may occupy it.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l,k}+ \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l',k}\;\le\;1
\qquad\forall (l,l')\in\mathcal B,\; k\in\mathcal K } \tag{R5}
\]

#### 5.6  Blockage avoidance  

If a segment is blocked in interval \(k\), no train may traverse it.

\[
\boxed{ z_{t,l,k}\; \le\; 1-\text{block}_{l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7  Travel‑time bounds per segment  

The *effective* travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(l\) is the difference between the interval index where it **enters** the segment and the interval where it **leaves** it. Because we assume “one interval per segment” (R3), we can use the interval index directly:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\; x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R7a}
\]

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k} \;-\; \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;\le\; \frac{\text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\; x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R7b}
\]

Here \(z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}\) denotes the binary variable that the *same* train left the preceding segment (or the departure from the previous station) at interval \(k\); the model can be linearised by introducing an auxiliary “exit” variable or, more simply, by noting that because each segment occupies exactly one interval, the travel time on a segment \(l\) equals 1 Δt (if we force a 1‑interval traversal). If a finer granularity is needed, replace the left‑hand side with the sum of intervals for **all** directed arcs belonging to that segment (the same technique as in R4). For brevity we keep the compact formulation.

#### 5.8  Dwell‑time enforcement  

If a train arrives at station \(s\) in interval \(k\) (i.e. \(y_{t,s,k}=1\)), it may not depart before interval \(k+\lceil\text{dwell}_{t,s}/\Delta t\rceil\). Introduce departure binary variable \(y^{\text{dep}}_{t,s,k}\) (or reuse the same \(y\) with a shift). A compact linearisation:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k} + \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}
\;\le\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s',k} \qquad\forall t,\; s \text{ preceding } s' \text{ on chosen route }p
\tag{R8}
\]

where \(s'\) is the next station after \(s\) on the route. The big‑M version (activating only when the route containing the station pair is selected) can be written:

\[
\sum_{k}k y_{t,s',k}\;-\;\sum_{k}k y_{t,s,k}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}\;-\;M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,p,\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}
\tag{R8b}
\]

#### 5.9  Linking speed‑mode to segment occupation  

Only one speed mode can be active on a segment while it is occupied, and a mode can be active only if the segment is traversed.

\[
\boxed{ w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k}\;\le\; z_{t,l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R9}
\]

If a segment is traversed without a dedicated mode (e.g. cruise), both \(w\) and \(u\) can be zero.

#### 5.10  Energy‑consumption definition  

\[
\boxed{ C = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{l\in\mathcal L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\, w_{t,l,k}+ e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\, u_{t,l,k}\bigr) } \tag{R10}
\]

If the planner prefers a *single* objective term, \(C\) can be substituted directly into the objective. Otherwise, \(C\) can be reported as a separate performance indicator.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\sum_{t,s,k}\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}y_{t,s,k}
     \;+\;\beta\sum_{t,p}\text{energy}_{t,p}x_{t,p} \\
\text{s.t.}&\;\text{(R1)–(R10)}\\
& x_{t,p},y_{t,s,k},z_{t,l,k},w_{t,l,k},u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
C\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisations used where a condition depends on a binary route‑selection variable). The model simultaneously decides **which route each train should take**, **when it arrives/departs each station**, **how it traverses each possibly‑blocked segment**, and **whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode**, while minimising a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7. Practical Remarks  

| Issue | Recommended handling |
|-------|----------------------|
| **Choice of  M** | Take \(M\) larger than the maximum possible interval index (e.g. \(K+1\)). |
| **Integrality of arrival time** | Because \(y_{t,s,k}\) is binary, \(A_{t,s}= \sum k y_{t,s,k}\) is automatically integer. |

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Partial Segment Blockages**  

All time is discretised into equal intervals of length Δt (e.g. 1 min).  
For each train we decide (i) which route (original or a rerouted alternative) it follows, (ii) the exact interval in which it arrives at every station on the chosen route, (iii) the interval in which it occupies each track segment, and (iv) whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode on that segment.  
The model minimises a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and total energy consumption while respecting timetable, blockages, capacity on bidirectional track pairs, and travel‑time limits.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **𝒯** | Set of trains *t*. |
| **𝒮** | Set of stations *s*. |
| **ℒ** | Set of directed track segments *l*. |
| **ℬ ⊂ ℒ×ℒ** | Set of **bidirectional pairs** \((l,l′)\) that share the same physical track (opposite directions). |
| **𝒫(t)** | Set of feasible routes for train *t* (original + possible rerouted alternatives). |
| **𝒦 = {1,…,K}** | Set of discrete time intervals in the planning horizon. |
| **Lₚ ⊆ ℒ** | Set of directed segments belonging to route *p*. |
| **𝒮ₚ ⊆ 𝒮** | Set of stations visited by route *p* (ordered). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| *aₜ,ₛ* | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at station *s* (continuous). | min |
| *dₜ,ₛ* | Scheduled departure time of train *t* from station *s*. | min |
| *dwellₜ,ₛ* | Minimum dwell time required at station *s* for train *t*. | min |
| *minRunₜ,ₗ*, *maxRunₜ,ₗ* | Minimum / maximum admissible travel time for train *t* on segment *l* (derived from speed limits). | min |
| *blockₗ,ₖ* | 1 if segment *l* is blocked during interval *k*, 0 otherwise. | – |
| *energyₜ,ₚ* | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per km) for train *t* on route *p*. | kWh |
| *eᵃᶜᶜₜ,ₗ* | Energy cost of using **accelerated** mode on segment *l* for train *t*. | kWh |
| *eᵈᵉᶜₜ,ₗ* | Energy cost of using **decelerated** mode on segment *l* for train *t*. | kWh |
| α, β | Weighting factors for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| *M* | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| Δt | Duration of one time index (e.g. 1 min). | min |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| *xₜ,ₚ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *p*. |
| *yₜ,ₛ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **arrives** at station *s* in interval *k*. |
| *zₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **occupies** directed segment *l* during interval *k*. |
| *wₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *l* in interval *k* using **accelerated** mode. |
| *uₜ,ₗ,ₖ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *l* in interval *k* using **decelerated** mode. |
| *C* ≥ 0 | continuous | Total energy consumption (linked to *w* and *u*). |

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\!\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\!\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}\,y_{t,s,k}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\!\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)}\! \text{energy}_{t,p}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

\((\cdot)^{+}=\max\{0,\cdot\}\).  
Because *y* is binary, the product equals the delay incurred if arrival is later than the scheduled time and zero otherwise. (A fully linear version can be obtained with auxiliary delay variables.)

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route selection  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad\forall\,t\in\mathcal T } \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Station‑visitation consistency  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} y_{t,s,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,s\in\mathcal S_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; s\in\mathcal S } \tag{R2}
\]

#### 5.3 Segment‑occupation consistency  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} z_{t,l,k}= 
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P(t)} \mathbf 1_{\,l\in L_{p}}\,x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal T,\; l\in\mathcal L } \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4 Arrival‑time and departure‑time variables (linearisation of *y*)  

\[
A_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s \tag{R4a}
\]
\[
D_{t,s}=A_{t,s}+ \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}\qquad\forall t,s \tag{R4b}
\]

#### 5.5 Temporal ordering between successive stations  

For every ordered pair \((s,s')\) that are consecutive on route *p*,
let \(\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}\) be the set of directed segments between them.

\[
\boxed{
A_{t,s'}\;\ge\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}
- M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\;p\in\mathcal P(t),\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R5a}
\]

\[
\boxed{
A_{t,s'}\;\le\; D_{t,s}+ \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{l\in\mathcal L_{s\to s'}^{p}} \text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}
+ M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,\;p\in\mathcal P(t),\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R5b}
\]

The big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when route *p* is not selected.

#### 5.6 Bidirectional‑track capacity (collision avoidance)  
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l,k}+ \sum_{t\in\mathcal T} z_{t,l',k}\;\le\;1
\qquad\forall (l,l')\in\mathcal B,\; k\in\mathcal K } \tag{R6}
\]

#### 5.7 Blockage avoidance  
\[
\boxed{ z_{t,l,k}\le 1-\text{block}_{l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R7}
\]

#### 5.8 Travel‑time bounds per segment  

Because each segment is traversed in exactly one interval (R3), the travel time on segment *l* equals one Δt.  
If a finer granularity is required, replace the left‑hand side by the sum of occupied intervals; the following linear bounds stay valid:

\[
\boxed{
\frac{\text{minRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\;x_{t,p}
\;\le\; 
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}
\;
\le\;
\frac{\text{maxRun}_{t,l}}{\Delta t}\;x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t,l,p\text{ with }l\in L_{p}} \tag{R8}
\]

\(z_{t,l,k}^{\text{prev}}\) is the binary variable indicating the interval when the train entered the segment (or left the previous segment); it can be introduced analogously to *y*.

#### 5.9 Dwell‑time enforcement (alternative linear form)  

For each consecutive station pair \((s,s')\) on the chosen route:

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s',k}
\;-\;
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} k\,y_{t,s,k}
\;\ge\; \frac{\text{dwell}_{t,s}}{\Delta t}
- M\bigl(1-x_{t,p}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t,p,\;(s,s')\in\mathcal S_{p}} \tag{R9}
\]

#### 5.10 Linking speed‑mode to segment occupation  

\[
\boxed{ w_{t,l,k}+u_{t,l,k}\;\le\; z_{t,l,k}
\qquad\forall t,l,k } \tag{R10}
\]

#### 5.11 Energy‑consumption definition  

\[
\boxed{ C = \sum_{t\in\mathcal T}\sum_{l\in\mathcal L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
\bigl(e^{\text{acc}}_{t,l}\,w_{t,l,k}+ e^{\text{dec}}_{t,l}\,u_{t,l,k}\bigr) } \tag{R11}
\]

If desired, the term \(C\) can be inserted directly into the objective instead of the separate energy term.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Full MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\alpha\!\sum_{t,s,k}\bigl(k\Delta t-a_{t,s}\bigr)^{+}y_{t,s,k}
      \;+\;\beta\!\sum_{t,p}\text{energy}_{t,p}x_{t,p}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t.}&\;\text{Constraints (R1)–(R11)}\\
& x_{t,p},y_{t,s,k},z_{t,l,k},w_{t,l,k},u_{t,l,k}\in\{0,1\},\;
  C\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear (big‑M linearisations are used where a condition depends on a binary route‑selection variable). The model simultaneously decides **which route each train should take**, **when it arrives/departs each station**, **how it traverses each possibly‑blocked segment**, and **whether it uses an accelerated or decelerated speed mode**, while minimising a trade‑off between passenger delay and energy consumption.

---------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7. Practical Remarks  

| Issue | Suggested handling |
|-------|--------------------|
| **Choice of M** | Set *M* larger than the maximum possible interval index (e.g., *K + 1*). |
| **Multiple‑interval travel on a long segment** | Replace (R3) by \(\sum_k z_{t,l,k}= \tau_{t,l}\) where \(\tau_{t,l}\) is the required number of intervals (derived from min/max run times). Adjust (R8) accordingly. |
| **Energy for cruise (no accel/decel)** | Add a constant term \(e^{\text{cruise}}_{t,l}\) multiplied by \(z_{t,l,k}\) in (R11). |
| **Robustness to data uncertainty** | Introduce slack variables for delay, heavily penalised in the objective. |
| **Solver** | The model is ready for CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.; typical size depends on |\𝒯|, |\𝒮|, |\ℒ|, |\𝒦|. |

The formulation above provides a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming model** for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem under partial segment blockages, matching the narrative’s key aspects (conflict‑free timetable, bidirectional track sharing, rerouting, and energy‑aware speed control).

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
