Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request  

* integrated **train‑rescheduling** (arrival / departure times, ordering on shared tracks),  
* **speed‑profile selection** on every track segment, and  
* **routing** (choice of the “left” or “right” side of a partially blocked segment).  

The model is written in a compact, index‑based notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
All symbols are defined in the “Sets & Parameters” section, the decision variables are listed next, and then the objective function and constraints follow.  
After the formulation a short “Explanation of the model elements” is given.

---

## 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N_T). |
| **S** | Set of sides of a segment that can be used when the segment is partially blocked (normally **S = {L,R}**). |
| **Seg** | Set of track segments, indexed by *g*. A segment may be *blocked* (see **B**) or *free* (see **F**). |
| **B ⊆ Seg** | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (the ones that have a partial blockage). |
| **F = Seg \ B** | Sub‑set of **free** segments (no blockage). |
| **N_t** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the origin and the final destination). Index *n* ∈ N_t. |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed profiles, indexed by *k* (e.g. k = 1 … K, where profile 1 = “slow”, K = “fast”). |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment (i.e. may conflict). An element is a tuple *(i,j)* with i ≠ j. |

Additional derived sets (used only in constraints)  

* **Seg_{t}** – set of segments traversed by train *t*.  
* **Seg_{i,j} = Seg_i ∩ Seg_j** – common segments of trains *i* and *j*.  

---

## 2. Parameters (all data are assumed known)

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| **a⁰_{t,n}** | Planned (unperturbed) arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **h_{t,n}** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **τ_{g,k}** | Travel time required to cross segment *g* when speed profile *k* is used (deterministic). | [s] |
| **e_{k}** | Energy consumption (or cost) associated with speed profile *k* (per traversal of a segment). | [kWh] |
| **L_g** | Length of segment *g* (used for feasibility of speed profiles, e.g. max speed). | [km] |
| **v^{max}_{k}, v^{min}_{k}** | Maximum / minimum admissible speed of profile *k* (used only to guarantee feasibility – see constraint (6)). | [km/h] |
| **T_start , T_end** | Beginning and end of the disruption window on every blocked segment (same for all *g*∈B, or can be indexed by *g*). | [s] |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate ordering constraints when the corresponding binary variable is 0. Typical value: 10⁴ s (larger than any possible schedule horizon). |
| **w₁ , w₂** | Positive weights for the two components of the objective (delay and energy). They can be normalised so that *w₁ + w₂ = 1*. |
| **C_{g}** | Capacity of side *s* on blocked segment *g* (normally 1 train at a time). |
| **Δ_{i,j,g}** | Minimum safety headway (in seconds) that must separate two trains on the same side of segment *g*. Usually a constant (e.g. 30 s). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of blocked segment *g* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every common segment they share; 0 otherwise. (Only defined for *(i,j)∈P*.) |
| **a_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| **d_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **τ_{t,g}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **v_{t,g,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses speed profile *k* on segment *g*; 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{t,g}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies **any** side of blocked segment *g* (used to enforce the disruption window). |
| **y_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies side *s* of blocked segment *g* (identical to r_{t,g,s} for blocked segments, but kept for clarity in some constraints). |

*Note*: For free segments (*g*∈F) the side‑choice variables are not needed; we simply set `r_{t,g,s}=0` for all *s*.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{1}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\,\text{final}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{w_{2}\;\sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\;\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\;v_{t,g,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

* `a_{t,final}` is the arrival time at the last station of train *t* (i.e. *n = last(N_t)*).  
* The first term penalises any lateness with respect to the original schedule.  
* The second term adds the energy cost of the selected speed profiles.

Both terms are linear because the variables appear only with coefficient 1 (or *e_k*).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side on each blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{R1}
\]

If a train does **not** traverse a blocked segment, the constraint is simply omitted.

### 5.2 Speed‑profile selection – exactly one profile per segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S1}
\]

### 5.3 Travel time linked to speed choice  

\[
\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\;v_{t,g,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S2}
\]

### 5.4 Time‑propagation along a train’s path  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of stations *(n, n⁺)∈N_t* (where *n⁺* is the next station after *n*) let *g(t,n)* be the segment that connects them.

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,n} & = a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t \tag{D1}\\[2mm]
a_{t,n^{+}} & = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\,g(t,n)} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t\setminus\{\text{final}\} \tag{D2}
\end{aligned}
\]

These two constraints enforce the minimum dwell time and the travel time on each segment.

### 5.5 Ordering on a **shared side** of a blocked segment  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* and any common blocked segment *g∈Seg_{i}\cap Seg_{j}\cap B*.  
Let  

* `enter_{i,g}` = the time train *i* **enters** side *s* of segment *g* (i.e. the departure time from the upstream station).  
* `exit_{i,g}` = `enter_{i,g} + τ_{i,g}`.

Because the side choice is binary, we can write the ordering constraints with a big‑M that is activated only when both trains use the **same** side:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{i,g} + \tau_{i,g} & \le  enter_{j,g} + M\bigl(1-o_{i,j}\bigr) + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) \\
enter_{j,g} + \tau_{j,g} & \le  enter_{i,g} + M\bigl(o_{i,j}\bigr)   + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) 
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\; \forall g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; \forall s\in S
\tag{O1}
\]

Explanation:  

* If both trains use side *s* (`r_{i,g,s}=r_{j,g,s}=1`), the term `M(2‑r‑r)` becomes 0 and the constraints reduce to the classic “either‑or” ordering using binary *o_{i,j}*.  
* If they use **different** sides, the term `M(2‑r‑r) = M` deactivates the constraint, allowing them to occupy the segment simultaneously.

A **safety headway** Δ can be added by replacing `τ_{i,g}` with `τ_{i,g}+Δ_{i,j,g}` in the left‑hand side.

### 5.6 Transitivity of ordering (to avoid cycles)  

For any three distinct trains *i, j, k* that share a common blocked segment (or a set of common segments) we enforce:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,k}-o_{i,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall i,j,k\in T,\; i\neq j\neq k
\tag{O2}
\]

This linear inequality guarantees that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k* (otherwise the left‑hand side would be 2 > 1).

### 5.7 Disruption‑window exclusion  

No train may occupy a blocked side during the interval \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\). Using the entry/exit times defined above:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{t,g} & \ge T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr) \\
enter_{t,g} & \le T_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{W1}
\]

where  

\[
x_{t,g}= \sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s} \qquad (\text{so }x_{t,g}=1\text{ if the train uses the blocked segment at all})
\]

If a train uses the blocked segment (`x_{t,g}=1`), the two inequalities force its entry time to lie **outside** the disruption window. If the train does not use the segment (`x_{t,g}=0`), the big‑M term relaxes the constraints.

### 5.8 Capacity of a side (at most one train at a time)  

Because the ordering constraints already guarantee non‑overlap when the same side is chosen, an explicit capacity constraint is not required. If a side can host more than one train (e.g. a double‑track), the model can be extended with a cumulative‑type constraint, but for the usual single‑track side the ordering constraints are sufficient.

### 5.9 Speed feasibility (optional – ensures that the chosen profile can be physically realised on the segment length)  

For each train‑segment pair:

\[
L_g \ge v^{min}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F1}
\]

\[
L_g \le v^{max}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F2}
\]

These linear constraints are only needed if the set of profiles *K* contains infeasible combinations for a given segment length. In most practical applications the parameters τ_{g,k} are pre‑computed to satisfy the physical limits, so (F1)–(F2) can be omitted.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,g} & \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,n,g\\
r_{t,g,s},\; o_{i,j},\; v_{t,g,k},\; x_{t,g} & \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\tag{B1}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
      \;+\; w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t} \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S1}\\
&\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\,v_{t,g,k} &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S2}\\
&d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t,\; n\in N_t \tag{D1}\\
&a_{t,n^{+}}=d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,g(t,n)} &&\forall t,\; n\neq\text{final} \tag{D2}\\
&\text{Ordering (O1) for every }(i,j)\in P,\; g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; s\in S\\
&\text{Transitivity (O2) for all distinct }i,j,k\in T\\
&\text{Disruption window (W1) for all }t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\\
&\text{(Optional) feasibility (F1)–(F2)}\\
& a,d,\tau \ge 0,\; r,o,v,x\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (products of binaries) have been eliminated by the standard big‑M linearisation shown in (O1).

---

## 7. Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Component | What it does | How it appears in the MILP |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------------|
| **Route choice (r)** | Decides whether a train uses the left or right side of a partially blocked segment. Guarantees exactly one side per blocked segment (R1). | Binary variables `r_{t,g,s}` with a sum‑to‑one constraint. |
| **Speed‑profile selection (v)** | Chooses a discrete speed level for each segment, trading travel time against energy consumption. | Binary variables `v_{t,g,k}` with a sum‑to‑one (S1) and a linear definition of travel time (S2). |
| **Arrival / departure times (a, d)** | Capture the actual schedule after rescheduling. Dwell‑time constraints (D1) enforce minimum stop times; propagation constraints (D2) link successive stations through the chosen travel times. | Continuous variables with linear equalities. |
| **Ordering (o)** | Guarantees that two trains that use the **same side** of a blocked segment do not occupy it simultaneously. The binary `o_{i,j}` decides which train goes first; the big‑M formulation (O1) activates the ordering only when both trains share the side. | Binary variables with “either‑or” linear constraints. |

Uses a binary indicator `x_{t,g}` (derived from the route‑choice variables) and big‑M to relax the constraint when the train does not use the segment. | Linear constraints with big‑M. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total delay (difference between actual and planned final arrival) and total energy (sum of profile‑specific energy costs). Both terms are linear in the decision variables. | Linear objective with weights `w₁, w₂`. |

---

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, Seg, B, S, N_t, K* and compute the parameters (original schedule `a⁰`, dwell times `h`, travel‑time per profile `τ_{g,k}`, energy per profile `e_k`, disruption window `[T_start,T_end]`).  
2. **Choose weights** – Decide how much importance to give to punctuality vs. energy (e.g. `w₁ = 0.7`, `w₂ = 0.3`).  
3. **Select a big‑M** – A safe value is `M = 10⁴` s (≈ 3 h) for most regional networks; increase if the horizon is longer.  
4. **Feed the formulation** to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …). The binary variables keep the problem size moderate; for large networks one can add *cut‑generation* or *decomposition* (Benders, column generation) but the core model is exactly as shown.  
5. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * `r_{t,g,s}=1` tells you which side each train uses on every blocked segment.  
   * `v_{t,g,k}=1` tells you the speed profile (hence travel time) chosen for each segment.  
   * `a_{t,n}` and `d_{t,n}` give the new timetable.  
   * The objective value quantifies the trade‑off between delay and energy.

* **Dynamic weighting** – The weights `w₁, w₂` can be made train‑specific (e.g. higher penalty for high‑priority passenger services).

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Formulate a MILP for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice r_{t,s} (train t uses side s of segment), binary order o_{i,j} (train i precedes j on shared track), continuous arrival times a_{t,n}, departure times d_{t,n} at stations n, continuous travel times τ_{t,seg} for each segment, binary speed level selection v_{t,seg,k} (k speed profile). Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_t (a_{t,final}-a^0_{t,final}) and energy consumption Σ_t Σ_seg Σ_k e_{k}·v_{t,seg,k}. Constraints: (1) each train chooses exactly one side per blocked segment; (2) if both trains use same side, ordering constraints enforce non-overlap: a_{i,enter}+τ_{i,seg} ≤ a_{j,enter}+M·(1-o_{i,j}); (3) dwell time limits d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+h_{t,n}; (4) travel time linked to speed choice: τ_{t,seg}= Σ_k τ_{k}·v_{t,seg,k}; (5) each segment speed choice binary sum=1; (6) speed feasibility bounds on acceleration/deceleration; (7) disruption window: trains cannot occupy blocked side during [T_start,T_end]; (8) precedence for rerouting: if train uses opposite side, must satisfy capacity; (9) binary order transitivity constraints; (10) big-M for ordering. Assumptions: fixed set of speed profiles with known travel times τ_k and energy e_k, known disruption window, known dwell times, known initial schedule a^0. Provide full MILP equations.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request  

* integrated **train‑rescheduling** (arrival / departure times, ordering on shared tracks),  
* **speed‑profile selection** on every track segment, and  
* **routing** (choice of the “left” or “right” side of a partially blocked segment).  

The model is written in a compact, index‑based notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
All symbols are defined in the “Sets & Parameters” section, the decision variables are listed next, and then the objective function and constraints follow.  
After the formulation a short “Explanation of the model elements” is given.

---

## 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N_T). |
| **S** | Set of sides of a segment that can be used when the segment is partially blocked (normally **S = {L,R}**). |
| **Seg** | Set of track segments, indexed by *g*. A segment may be *blocked* (see **B**) or *free* (see **F**). |
| **B ⊆ Seg** | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (the ones that have a partial blockage). |
| **F = Seg \ B** | Sub‑set of **free** segments (no blockage). |
| **N_t** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the origin and the final destination). Index *n* ∈ N_t. |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed profiles, indexed by *k* (e.g. k = 1 … K, where profile 1 = “slow”, K = “fast”). |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment (i.e. may conflict). An element is a tuple *(i,j)* with i ≠ j. |

Additional derived sets (used only in constraints)  

* **Seg_{t}** – set of segments traversed by train *t*.  
* **Seg_{i,j} = Seg_i ∩ Seg_j** – common segments of trains *i* and *j*.  

---

## 2. Parameters (all data are assumed known)

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| **a⁰_{t,n}** | Planned (unperturbed) arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **h_{t,n}** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **τ_{g,k}** | Travel time required to cross segment *g* when speed profile *k* is used (deterministic). | [s] |
| **e_{k}** | Energy consumption (or cost) associated with speed profile *k* (per traversal of a segment). | [kWh] |
| **L_g** | Length of segment *g* (used for feasibility of speed profiles, e.g. max speed). | [km] |
| **v^{max}_{k}, v^{min}_{k}** | Maximum / minimum admissible speed of profile *k* (used only to guarantee feasibility – see constraint (6)). | [km/h] |
| **T_start , T_end** | Beginning and end of the disruption window on every blocked segment (same for all *g*∈B, or can be indexed by *g*). | [s] |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate ordering constraints when the corresponding binary variable is 0. Typical value: 10⁴ s (larger than any possible schedule horizon). |
| **w₁ , w₂** | Positive weights for the two components of the objective (delay and energy). They can be normalised so that *w₁ + w₂ = 1*. |
| **C_{g}** | Capacity of side *s* on blocked segment *g* (normally 1 train at a time). |
| **Δ_{i,j,g}** | Minimum safety headway (in seconds) that must separate two trains on the same side of segment *g*. Usually a constant (e.g. 30 s). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of blocked segment *g* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every common segment they share; 0 otherwise. (Only defined for *(i,j)∈P*.) |
| **a_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| **d_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **τ_{t,g}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **v_{t,g,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses speed profile *k* on segment *g*; 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{t,g}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies **any** side of blocked segment *g* (used to enforce the disruption window). |
| **y_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies side *s* of blocked segment *g* (identical to r_{t,g,s} for blocked segments, but kept for clarity in some constraints). |

*Note*: For free segments (*g*∈F) the side‑choice variables are not needed; we simply set `r_{t,g,s}=0` for all *s*.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{1}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\,\text{final}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{w_{2}\;\sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\;\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\;v_{t,g,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

* `a_{t,final}` is the arrival time at the last station of train *t* (i.e. *n = last(N_t)*).  
* The first term penalises any lateness with respect to the original schedule.  
* The second term adds the energy cost of the selected speed profiles.

Both terms are linear because the variables appear only with coefficient 1 (or *e_k*).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side on each blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{R1}
\]

If a train does **not** traverse a blocked segment, the constraint is simply omitted.

### 5.2 Speed‑profile selection – exactly one profile per segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S1}
\]

### 5.3 Travel time linked to speed choice  

\[
\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\;v_{t,g,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S2}
\]

### 5.4 Time‑propagation along a train’s path  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of stations *(n, n⁺)∈N_t* (where *n⁺* is the next station after *n*) let *g(t,n)* be the segment that connects them.

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,n} & = a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t \tag{D1}\\[2mm]
a_{t,n^{+}} & = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\,g(t,n)} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t\setminus\{\text{final}\} \tag{D2}
\end{aligned}
\]

These two constraints enforce the minimum dwell time and the travel time on each segment.

### 5.5 Ordering on a **shared side** of a blocked segment  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* and any common blocked segment *g∈Seg_{i}\cap Seg_{j}\cap B*.  
Let  

* `enter_{i,g}` = the time train *i* **enters** side *s* of segment *g* (i.e. the departure time from the upstream station).  
* `exit_{i,g}` = `enter_{i,g} + τ_{i,g}`.

Because the side choice is binary, we can write the ordering constraints with a big‑M that is activated only when both trains use the **same** side:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{i,g} + \tau_{i,g} & \le  enter_{j,g} + M\bigl(1-o_{i,j}\bigr) + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) \\
enter_{j,g} + \tau_{j,g} & \le  enter_{i,g} + M\bigl(o_{i,j}\bigr)   + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) 
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\; \forall g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; \forall s\in S
\tag{O1}
\]

Explanation:  

* If both trains use side *s* (`r_{i,g,s}=r_{j,g,s}=1`), the term `M(2‑r‑r)` becomes 0 and the constraints reduce to the classic “either‑or” ordering using binary *o_{i,j}*.  
* If they use **different** sides, the term `M(2‑r‑r) = M` deactivates the constraint, allowing them to occupy the segment simultaneously.

A **safety headway** Δ can be added by replacing `τ_{i,g}` with `τ_{i,g}+Δ_{i,j,g}` in the left‑hand side.

### 5.6 Transitivity of ordering (to avoid cycles)  

For any three distinct trains *i, j, k* that share a common blocked segment (or a set of common segments) we enforce:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,k}-o_{i,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall i,j,k\in T,\; i\neq j\neq k
\tag{O2}
\]

This linear inequality guarantees that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k* (otherwise the left‑hand side would be 2 > 1).

### 5.7 Disruption‑window exclusion  

No train may occupy a blocked side during the interval \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\). Using the entry/exit times defined above:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{t,g} & \ge T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr) \\
enter_{t,g} & \le T_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{W1}
\]

where  

\[
x_{t,g}= \sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s} \qquad (\text{so }x_{t,g}=1\text{ if the train uses the blocked segment at all})
\]

If a train uses the blocked segment (`x_{t,g}=1`), the two inequalities force its entry time to lie **outside** the disruption window. If the train does not use the segment (`x_{t,g}=0`), the big‑M term relaxes the constraints.

### 5.8 Capacity of a side (at most one train at a time)  

Because the ordering constraints already guarantee non‑overlap when the same side is chosen, an explicit capacity constraint is not required. If a side can host more than one train (e.g. a double‑track), the model can be extended with a cumulative‑type constraint, but for the usual single‑track side the ordering constraints are sufficient.

### 5.9 Speed feasibility (optional – ensures that the chosen profile can be physically realised on the segment length)  

For each train‑segment pair:

\[
L_g \ge v^{min}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F1}
\]

\[
L_g \le v^{max}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F2}
\]

These linear constraints are only needed if the set of profiles *K* contains infeasible combinations for a given segment length. In most practical applications the parameters τ_{g,k} are pre‑computed to satisfy the physical limits, so (F1)–(F2) can be omitted.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,g} & \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,n,g\\
r_{t,g,s},\; o_{i,j},\; v_{t,g,k},\; x_{t,g} & \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\tag{B1}
\]

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
      \;+\; w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t} \tag{R1}\\

\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (products of binaries) have been eliminated by the standard big‑M linearisation shown in (O1).

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request  

* integrated **train‑rescheduling** (arrival / departure times, ordering on shared tracks),  
* **speed‑profile selection** on every track segment, and  
* **routing** (choice of the “left” or “right” side of a partially blocked segment).  

The model is written in a compact, index‑based notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
All symbols are defined in the “Sets & Parameters” section, the decision variables are listed next, and then the objective function and constraints follow.  
After the formulation a short “Explanation of the model elements” is given.

---

## 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N_T). |
| **S** | Set of sides of a segment that can be used when the segment is partially blocked (normally **S = {L,R}**). |
| **Seg** | Set of track segments, indexed by *g*. A segment may be *blocked* (see **B**) or *free* (see **F**). |
| **B ⊆ Seg** | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (the ones that have a partial blockage). |
| **F = Seg \ B** | Sub‑set of **free** segments (no blockage). |
| **N_t** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the origin and the final destination). Index *n* ∈ N_t. |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed profiles, indexed by *k* (e.g. k = 1 … K, where profile 1 = “slow”, K = “fast”). |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment (i.e. may conflict). An element is a tuple *(i,j)* with i ≠ j. |

Additional derived sets (used only in constraints)  

* **Seg_{t}** – set of segments traversed by train *t*.  
* **Seg_{i,j} = Seg_i ∩ Seg_j** – common segments of trains *i* and *j*.  

---

## 2. Parameters (all data are assumed known)

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| **a⁰_{t,n}** | Planned (unperturbed) arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **h_{t,n}** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n*. | [s] |
| **τ_{g,k}** | Travel time required to cross segment *g* when speed profile *k* is used (deterministic). | [s] |
| **e_{k}** | Energy consumption (or cost) associated with speed profile *k* (per traversal of a segment). | [kWh] |
| **L_g** | Length of segment *g* (used for feasibility of speed profiles, e.g. max speed). | [km] |
| **v^{max}_{k}, v^{min}_{k}** | Maximum / minimum admissible speed of profile *k* (used only to guarantee feasibility – see constraint (6)). | [km/h] |
| **T_start , T_end** | Beginning and end of the disruption window on every blocked segment (same for all *g*∈B, or can be indexed by *g*). | [s] |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate ordering constraints when the corresponding binary variable is 0. Typical value: 10⁴ s (larger than any possible schedule horizon). |
| **w₁ , w₂** | Positive weights for the two components of the objective (delay and energy). They can be normalised so that *w₁ + w₂ = 1*. |
| **C_{g}** | Capacity of side *s* on blocked segment *g* (normally 1 train at a time). |
| **Δ_{i,j,g}** | Minimum safety headway (in seconds) that must separate two trains on the same side of segment *g*. Usually a constant (e.g. 30 s). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of blocked segment *g* ∈ B; 0 otherwise. |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every common segment they share; 0 otherwise. (Only defined for *(i,j)∈P*.) |
| **a_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| **d_{t,n}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **τ_{t,g}** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **v_{t,g,k}** | binary | 1 if train *t* uses speed profile *k* on segment *g*; 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{t,g}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies **any** side of blocked segment *g* (used to enforce the disruption window). |
| **y_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies side *s* of blocked segment *g* (identical to r_{t,g,s} for blocked segments, but kept for clarity in some constraints). |

*Note*: For free segments (*g*∈F) the side‑choice variables are not needed; we simply set `r_{t,g,s}=0` for all *s*.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{1}\;\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\,\text{final}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{w_{2}\;\sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\;\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\;v_{t,g,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

* `a_{t,final}` is the arrival time at the last station of train *t* (i.e. *n = last(N_t)*).  
* The first term penalises any lateness with respect to the original schedule.  
* The second term adds the energy cost of the selected speed profiles.

Both terms are linear because the variables appear only with coefficient 1 (or *e_k*).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side on each blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{R1}
\]

If a train does **not** traverse a blocked segment, the constraint is simply omitted.

### 5.2 Speed‑profile selection – exactly one profile per segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S1}
\]

### 5.3 Travel time linked to speed choice  

\[
\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\;v_{t,g,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in Seg_{t}
\tag{S2}
\]

### 5.4 Time‑propagation along a train’s path  

For every train *t* and every consecutive pair of stations *(n, n⁺)∈N_t* (where *n⁺* is the next station after *n*) let *g(t,n)* be the segment that connects them.

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,n} & = a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t \tag{D1}\\[2mm]
a_{t,n^{+}} & = d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\,g(t,n)} &&\forall t\in T,\; \forall n\in N_t\setminus\{\text{final}\} \tag{D2}
\end{aligned}
\]

These two constraints enforce the minimum dwell time and the travel time on each segment.

### 5.5 Ordering on a **shared side** of a blocked segment  

Consider any ordered pair *(i,j)∈P* and any common blocked segment *g∈Seg_{i}\cap Seg_{j}\cap B*.  
Let  

* `enter_{i,g}` = the time train *i* **enters** side *s* of segment *g* (i.e. the departure time from the upstream station).  
* `exit_{i,g}` = `enter_{i,g} + τ_{i,g}`.

Because the side choice is binary, we can write the ordering constraints with a big‑M that is activated only when both trains use the **same** side:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{i,g} + \tau_{i,g} & \le  enter_{j,g} + M\bigl(1-o_{i,j}\bigr) + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) \\
enter_{j,g} + \tau_{j,g} & \le  enter_{i,g} + M\bigl(o_{i,j}\bigr)   + M\bigl(2- r_{i,g,s} - r_{j,g,s}\bigr) 
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\; \forall g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; \forall s\in S
\tag{O1}
\]

Explanation:  

* If both trains use side *s* (`r_{i,g,s}=r_{j,g,s}=1`), the term `M(2‑r‑r)` becomes 0 and the constraints reduce to the classic “either‑or” ordering using binary *o_{i,j}*.  
* If they use **different** sides, the term `M(2‑r‑r) = M` deactivates the constraint, allowing them to occupy the segment simultaneously.

A **safety headway** Δ can be added by replacing `τ_{i,g}` with `τ_{i,g}+Δ_{i,j,g}` in the left‑hand side.

### 5.6 Transitivity of ordering (to avoid cycles)  

For any three distinct trains *i, j, k* that share a common blocked segment (or a set of common segments) we enforce:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,k}-o_{i,k}\le 1 \qquad \forall i,j,k\in T,\; i\neq j\neq k
\tag{O2}
\]

This linear inequality guarantees that if *i* precedes *j* and *j* precedes *k*, then *i* must precede *k* (otherwise the left‑hand side would be 2 > 1).

### 5.7 Disruption‑window exclusion  

No train may occupy a blocked side during the interval \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\). Using the entry/exit times defined above:

\[
\begin{aligned}
enter_{t,g} & \ge T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr) \\
enter_{t,g} & \le T_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-x_{t,g}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}
\tag{W1}
\]

where  

\[
x_{t,g}= \sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s} \qquad (\text{so }x_{t,g}=1\text{ if the train uses the blocked segment at all})
\]

If a train uses the blocked segment (`x_{t,g}=1`), the two inequalities force its entry time to lie **outside** the disruption window. If the train does not use the segment (`x_{t,g}=0`), the big‑M term relaxes the constraints.

### 5.8 Capacity of a side (at most one train at a time)  

Because the ordering constraints already guarantee non‑overlap when the same side is chosen, an explicit capacity constraint is not required. If a side can host more than one train (e.g. a double‑track), the model can be extended with a cumulative‑type constraint, but for the usual single‑track side the ordering constraints are sufficient.

### 5.9 Speed feasibility (optional – ensures that the chosen profile can be physically realised on the segment length)  

For each train‑segment pair:

\[
L_g \ge v^{min}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F1}
\]

\[
L_g \le v^{max}_{k}\; \tau_{g,k}\; r_{t,g,s} \qquad \forall t,g,k,s
\tag{F2}
\]

These linear constraints are only needed if the set of profiles *K* contains infeasible combinations for a given segment length. In most practical applications the parameters τ_{g,k} are pre‑computed to satisfy the physical limits, so (F1)–(F2) can be omitted.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,n},\; d_{t,n},\; \tau_{t,g} & \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,n,g\\
r_{t,g,s},\; o_{i,j},\; v_{t,g,k},\; x_{t,g} & \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\tag{B1}
\]

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
      \;+\; w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t} \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,g,k}=1 &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S1}\\
&\tau_{t,g}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{g,k}\,v_{t,g,k} &&\forall t,\; g\in Seg_{t} \tag{S2}\\
&d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+h_{t,n} &&\forall t,\; n\in N_t \tag{D1}\\
&a_{t,n^{+}}=d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,g(t,n)} &&\forall t,\; n\neq\text{final} \tag{D2}\\
&\text{Ordering (O1) for every }(i,j)\in P,\; g\in Seg_{i,j}\cap B,\; s\in S\\
&\text{Transitivity (O2) for all distinct }i,j,k\in T\\
&\text{Disruption window (W1) for all }t,\; g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\\
&\text{(Optional) feasibility (F1)–(F2)}\\
& a,d,\tau \ge 0,\; r,o,v,x\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (products of binaries) have been eliminated by the standard big‑M linearisation shown in (O1).

---

## 7. Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Component | What it does | How it appears in the MILP |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------------|
| **Route choice (r)** | Decides whether a train uses the left or right side of a partially blocked segment. Guarantees exactly one side per blocked segment (R1). | Binary variables `r_{t,g,s}` with a sum‑to‑one constraint. |
| **Speed‑profile selection (v)** | Chooses a discrete speed level for each segment, trading travel time against energy consumption. | Binary variables `v_{t,g,k}` with a sum‑to‑one (S1) and a linear definition of travel time (S2). |
| **Arrival / departure times (a, d)** | Capture the actual schedule after rescheduling. Dwell‑time constraints (D1) enforce minimum stop times; propagation constraints (D2) link successive stations through the chosen travel times. | Continuous variables with linear equalities. |
| **Ordering (o)** | Guarantees that two trains that use the **same side** of a blocked segment do not occupy it simultaneously. The binary `o_{i,j}` decides which train goes first; the big‑M formulation (O1) activates the ordering only when both trains share the side. | Binary variables with “either‑or” linear constraints. |
| **Transitivity (o)** | Prevents cyclic precedence (i.e. i before j, j before k, but k before i). Enforced by linear inequality (O2). | Binary variables only; linear. |
| **Disruption‑window exclusion (W1)** | Ensures that no train enters a blocked side during the known blockage interval \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\). Uses a binary indicator `x_{t,g}` (derived from the route‑choice variables) and big‑M to relax the constraint when the train does not use the segment. | Linear constraints with big‑M. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total delay (difference between actual and planned final arrival) and total energy (sum of profile‑specific energy costs). Both terms are linear in the decision variables. | Linear objective with weights `w₁, w₂`. |
| **Big‑M (M)** | A sufficiently large constant that “turns off’’ a constraint when the associated binary variable is 0. Must be larger than any feasible schedule horizon (e.g. 10 000 s). | Appears in (O1) and (W1). |
| **Parameters (τ, e, h, …)** | Provide the data needed to compute travel times, energy, dwell times, and the disruption window. All are known a‑priori, so the model stays linear. | Appear as coefficients in constraints and the objective. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, Seg, B, S, N_t, K* and compute the parameters (original schedule `a⁰`, dwell times `h`, travel‑time per profile `τ_{g,k}`, energy per profile `e_k`, disruption window `[T_start,T_end]`).  
2. **Choose weights** – Decide how much importance to give to punctuality vs. energy (e.g. `w₁ = 0.7`, `w₂ = 0.3`).  
3. **Select a big‑M** – A safe value is `M = 10⁴` s (≈ 3 h) for most regional networks; increase if the horizon is longer.  
4. **Feed the formulation** to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …). The binary variables keep the problem size moderate; for large networks one can add *cut‑generation* or *decomposition* (Benders, column generation) but the core model is exactly as shown.  
5. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * `r_{t,g,s}=1` tells you which side each train uses on every blocked segment.  
   * `v_{t,g,k}=1` tells you the speed profile (hence travel time) chosen for each segment.  
   * `a_{t,n}` and `d_{t,n}` give the new timetable.  
   * The objective value quantifies the trade‑off between delay and energy.

---

### Remarks & Possible Extensions  

* **Multiple‑track blocked segments** – If a blocked segment has more than two usable sides, simply enlarge the set *S* and keep constraint (R1).  
* **Variable capacity** – If a side can host more than one train simultaneously (e.g. a passing loop), replace the ordering constraints (O1) with a **cumulative** (resource‑constrained) formulation using start‑times, durations (`τ_{t,g}`) and a capacity parameter `C_{g,s}`.  
* **Robustness** – To protect against uncertainty in the disruption duration, replace the hard window `[T_start,T_end]` by a **robust** interval or add a penalty for occupying the segment during the window.  
* **Dynamic weighting** – The weights `w₁, w₂` can be made train‑specific (e.g. higher penalty for high‑priority passenger services).  

---

**In summary**, the MILP above captures every element requested in the description: binary side‑choice, binary ordering, continuous arrival/departure and travel times, discrete speed‑profile selection, a weighted delay‑plus‑energy objective, and all the logical, safety, and disruption‑window constraints needed for an integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under partial segment blockage.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

---

### 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t*. |
| **S = {L,R}** | Sides of a partially blocked segment (Left / Right). |
| **Seg** | Set of track segments, indexed by *g*. |
| **B ⊆ Seg** | Blocked segments (partial blockage). |
| **F = Seg \ B** | Free segments. |
| **Nₜ** | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including origin & final). |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed profiles, indexed by *k* (k = 1 … K). |
| **P** | Set of ordered train pairs that share at least one common segment: *(i,j) ∈ P, i≠j*. |

Derived sets:  

* **Segₜ** – segments traversed by train *t*.  
* **Segᵢⱼ = Segᵢ ∩ Segⱼ** – common segments of trains *i* and *j*.  

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|--------|---------|------|
| **a⁰ₜₙ** | Planned arrival of train *t* at station *n*. | s |
| **hₜₙ** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *n*. | s |
| **τ_{g,k}** | Travel time on segment *g* when speed profile *k* is used. | s |
| **e_k** | Energy consumption of speed profile *k* (per segment). | kWh |
| **L_g** | Length of segment *g*. | km |
| **T_start , T_end** | Start / end of the disruption window on blocked segments. | s |
| **Δ** | Minimum safety headway between two trains on the same side. | s |
| **M** | Big‑M constant (≥ maximal schedule horizon, e.g. 10 000 s). |
| **w₁ , w₂** | Positive weights (w₁ + w₂ = 1) for delay and energy. |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r_{t,g,s}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* of blocked segment *g* (g∈B∩Segₜ). |
| **o_{i,j}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on any common side. |
| **a_{t,n}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *t* at station *n*. |
| **d_{t,n}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| **τ_{t,g}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **v_{t,g,k}** | binary | 1 ⇔ speed profile *k* is chosen for train *t* on segment *g*. |
| **x_{t,g}** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies any side of blocked segment *g*. (x_{t,g}=∑ₛ r_{t,g,s}) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{final}}-a^{0}_{t,\text{final}}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{g\in Seg_{t}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{k}\,v_{t,g,k}
}
\]

*First term*: total delay (difference between actual and planned final arrival).  
*Second term*: total energy consumption of the selected speed profiles.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side on each blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,g,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall g\in B\cap Seg_{t}\tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Speed‑profile selection – exactly one profile per segment  

\[

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
