6. **Secondary delay is the difference between actual arrival at the final destination and the planned arrival**  

\[
\delta_i \ge a_{i,\text{dest}(i)} - t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{dest}(i)} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

7. **Upper bound on secondary delay**  

\[
\delta_i \le d^{\max} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{D2}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance (re‑ordering) constraints  

For each pair of trains \((i,j)\in P\) that share at least one common edge or station, we enforce a **mutual‑exclusion** using the binary precedence variables \(y_{i,j}\) and \(y_{j,i}\).

8. **Exactly one precedence direction**  

\[
y_{i,j}+y_{j,i}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{C1}
\]

9. **If train \(i\) follows train \(j\), its entry time on the shared resource must be after the exit time of \(j\) plus a safety headway \(h\) (Assumption: \(h=2\) min).**  

Let \(\mathcal{S}_{ij}\subseteq E\) be the set of edges (or stations) that are common to both trains. For each such edge \((n,m)\):

\[
a_{i,m} \ge a_{j,n}+ \tau_{j,nm}^{r_j} + h - M\,(1-y_{i,j}) \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}
\tag{C2}
\]

(The big‑M de‑activates the inequality when \(y_{i,j}=0\).)

### 4.5 Delay‑propagation (optimal‑model extension)  

To capture the effect of a train waiting for another, we introduce the **pair‑wise waiting variables** \(p_{i,j}\) (1 if \(i\) waits for \(j\)). They are linked to the precedence variables:

\[
p_{i,j}\ge y_{i,j} \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P
\tag{P1}
\]

The actual secondary delay of a train equals the **maximum** of all waiting times accumulated along its route. In a linear model we use an auxiliary variable \(\Delta_i\) that upper‑bounds the sum of all waiting contributions:

\[
\Delta_i \ge \sum_{j\in T\setminus\{i\}} \gamma_{i,j}\,p_{i,j} \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{P2}
\]

where \(\gamma_{i,j}\) is the **minimum possible waiting time** on the first common resource (Assumption: equal to the headway \(h\)).  
Finally, the secondary delay variable is forced to be at least this propagated delay:

\[
\delta_i \ge \Delta_i \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{P3}
\]

### 4.6 Route‑selection consistency with re‑ordering  

10. **If two trains are ordered on a shared edge, they must be using routes that actually contain that edge.**  

\[
y_{i,j} \le \sum_{r\in R_i:\,(n,m)\in r} x_{i,r} \qquad \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}
\tag{RC1}
\]

(and analogously for \(y_{j,i}\)).

### 4.7 Optional safety‑overlap constraints (for the extended model)  

When a train stops at a signal, a **clear‑behind overlap** of length \(\ell^{\text{ov}}\) (Assumption: 300 m) must be kept free. Let \(\theta_{i,n}\) be the time needed to clear the overlap after departure from node \(n\). Then:

\[
s_{k,n} \ge a_{i,n} + \theta_{i,n} - M\,(1-z_{i,k,n}) \qquad \forall i,k\in T,\; n\in N
\tag{OV}
\]

where \(z_{i,k,n}=1\) indicates that train \(k\) would violate the overlap of train \(i\). The model forces \(z_{i,k,n}=0\) by minimising the objective, effectively preserving the overlap.

---

## 5. Full MILP Model  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha \sum_{i\in T}\delta_i \;+\; \beta \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{r\in R_i} c_{i,r}\,x_{i,r} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1 && \forall i\in T \quad\text{(R1)}\\
& a_{i,m}\ge a_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} - M(1-x_{i,r}) && \forall i,(n,m)\in E \quad\text{(R2)}\\
& s_{i,\text{origin}(i)} \ge t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{origin}(i)} && \forall i\quad\text{(T1)}\\
& a_{i,m}= s_{i,n}+ \sum_{r\in R_i}\tau_{i,nm}^{r}\,x_{i,r} && \forall i,(n,m)\in\text{chosen route} \quad\text{(T2)}\\
& s_{i,m}\ge a_{i,m} && \forall i,m\quad\text{(T3)}\\
& \delta_i \ge a_{i,\text{dest}(i)}-t^{\text{plan}}_{i,\text{dest}(i)} && \forall i\quad\text{(D1)}\\
& \delta_i \le d^{\max} && \forall i\quad\text{(D2)}\\
& y_{i,j}+y_{j,i}=1 && \forall (i,j)\in P\quad\text{(C1)}\\
& a_{i,m} \ge a_{j,n}+ \tau_{j,nm}^{r_j}+h - M(1-y_{i,j}) && \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}\quad\text{(C2)}\\
& p_{i,j}\ge y_{i,j} && \forall (i,j)\in P\quad\text{(P1)}\\
& \Delta_i \ge \sum_{j\neq i}\gamma_{i,j}\,p_{i,j} && \forall i\quad\text{(P2)}\\
& \delta_i \ge \Delta_i && \forall i\quad\text{(P3)}\\
& y_{i,j} \le \sum_{r\in R_i:(n,m)\in r} x_{i,r} && \forall (i,j)\in P,\;(n,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{ij}\quad\text{(RC1)}\\
& \text{(Optional) overlap constraints (OV)}\\
& x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; p_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,k,n}\in\{0,1\}\\
& s_{i,n},a_{i,n},\delta_i,\Delta_i\ge 0 \qquad && \forall i,n
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Remarks & Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Reason |
|---|------------|--------|
| 1 | \(\alpha=1,\;\beta=0.01\) | Gives a clear priority to delay minimisation while still penalising high‑energy routes. |
| 2 | Headway \(h=2\) min and safety‑overlap length \(\ell^{\text{ov}}=300\) m | Typical values used in European railway signalling. |
| 3 | Big‑M \(M=10\,000\) min | Guarantees de‑activation of conditional constraints. |
| 4 | Maximum secondary delay \(d^{\max}=120\) min | Reflects realistic operational limits for passenger services. |
| 5 | \(\gamma_{i,j}=h\) for all waiting pairs | Minimum waiting time equals the headway; any additional waiting will be captured by the cumulative \(\Delta_i\). |
| 6 | Energy consumption \(c_{i,r}\) is known a‑priori (e.g., from a power‑consumption model). | Required for the secondary objective term. |
| 7 | The set of admissible routes \(R_i\) is pre‑computed (e.g., by a routing heuristic). | Reduces the size of the MILP while preserving optimality for the chosen subset. |

---

### How the model works  

1. **Rerouting stage** – variables \(x_{i,r}\) choose a feasible path for each train.  
2. **Re‑ordering stage** – binary variables \(y_{i,j}\) decide which train yields to the other on each shared resource, guaranteeing conflict‑free schedules (FIFO, but the model can select any order).  
3. **Rescheduling stage** – continuous timing variables \(s_{i,n},a_{i,n}\) and delay variables \(\delta_i\) compute the actual timetable, while constraints (P1‑P3) propagate the waiting times caused by the chosen ordering.  

If the decision maker wishes to **ignore delay propagation** (sub‑optimal model), constraints (P1‑P3) can be omitted; the remaining MILP corresponds to the fast “rerouting + re‑ordering” stage described in the paper. Adding (P1‑P3) yields the **global‑optimal** formulation that accounts for secondary‑delay accumulation.

---

**End of MILP description**. The model is ready to be implemented in any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …) and to be solved within the short response times required by real‑time railway traffic management.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling‑and‑Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
*Partial‑segment‑blockage disruption, bidirectional single‑track sharing*  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains (both directions). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including fictitious origin 0 and destination |S|+1). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of track‑segments (directed arcs) that can be traversed. For a segment *e = (i,j)* the physical length is *ℓ_e* (km). |
| **B** ⊆ E | Sub‑set of segments that are *blocked* (partial blockage) during the disruption window \([τ^{start}, τ^{end}]\). |
| **D** = {1,…,|D|} | Set of *discrete speed‑profile plans* that can be assigned to a train on a given segment (see §2). |
| **K** = {1,…,|K|} | Set of *time‑intervals* used for the decomposition (e.g., 5‑min slots). |
| **dir(t)** ∈ {+1, –1} | Direction of train *t* ( +1  = “up‑track”, –1 = “down‑track”). |
| **Δt** | Length of a time‑interval (minutes). |

### Fixed parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(a^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum acceleration for train *t*. |
| \(d^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum deceleration (positive value) for train *t*. |
| \(v^{max}_t\) (m/s) | Maximum permissible speed for train *t*. |
| \(v^{min}_t\) (m/s) | Minimum operating speed (usually 0). |
| \(E^{run}_{t,e,d}\) (kWh) | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *e* when plan *d* is used (pre‑computed from physics). |
| \(T^{dwell}_{t,s}\) (min) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\) (min) | Minimum headway (separation) required between two trains *t* and *t'* on segment *e* (direction‑dependent). |
| \(τ^{start}, τ^{end}\) (min) | Beginning and end of the blockage window. |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant (large enough to deactivate constraints). |
| \(C^{delay}_t\) (\$ per minute) | Penalty cost for each minute of delay of train *t*. |
| \(C^{canc}_t\) (\$) | Penalty cost for canceling train *t*. |
| \(C^{energy}_d\) (\$/kWh) | Energy price used to convert energy consumption to cost (same for all trains). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s* (minutes from a reference zero). |
| \(y_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| \(z_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* (i.e. uses the “normal” direction), 0 otherwise (used for rerouting). |
| \(r_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses the **opposite** track on segment *e* (i.e. rerouted onto the blocked side). |
| \(p_{t,e,d}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if speed‑plan *d* is selected for train *t* on segment *e*. |
| \(c_t\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled**. |
| \(s_{t,k}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned to time‑interval *k* for the **headway‑checking** (used in the IP‑decomposition). |
| \(δ_{t,t',e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* precedes train *t'* on segment *e* (ordering variable). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum of operational cost, delay cost and energy cost** while heavily penalising cancellations.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;  & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{delay}_t \bigl( x_{t,|S|+1} - \hat{x}_{t,|S|+1} \bigr)}_{\text{Delay penalty}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{d\in D} C^{energy}_d \,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d}}_{\text{Energy cost}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{canc}_t \,c_t}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\hat{x}_{t,|S|+1}\) is the **original scheduled arrival time** at the final station (baseline).  
If a train is cancelled (\(c_t=1\)) all its timing variables are forced to zero (see constraints).

---

## 4. Core Constraints  

### 4.1 Feasibility of a train (cancellation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S\cup\{0,|S|+1\} \\
& y_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S .
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(c_t=1\) the train disappears from the schedule.

### 4.2 Logical link between arrival / departure

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,s} \ge x_{t,s} + T^{dwell}_{t,s} - M\,c_t &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.3 Travel time on a segment – coupling with speed plan  

For each traversed segment *e = (i,j)* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-z_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

- \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is the **deterministic travel time** (minutes) of plan *d* on segment *e* for train *t* (computed from acceleration/deceleration limits and speed‑limit \(v^{max}_t\)).  
- The big‑M term deactivates the constraint if the train does **not** use the segment in its normal direction.

If the train is rerouted onto the opposite track, the same constraint uses \(r_{t,e}\) instead of \(z_{t,e}\):

\[
x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) .
\]

### 4.4 Exactly one speed plan per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} p_{t,e,d}= z_{t,e}+r_{t,e} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If the segment is not used (\(z_{t,e}=r_{t,e}=0\)) all \(p_{t,e,d}=0\).

### 4.5 Rerouting feasibility (partial blockage)

A train may **only** use the opposite track on a blocked segment **during** the disruption window, and only if the segment is blocked for its original direction.

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,e} \le 1 &&\forall t, e\in B \\
& r_{t,e}=0 &&\forall t, e\notin B .
\end{aligned}
\]

Furthermore, the departure‑arrival times must respect the window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} \ge τ^{start} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B\\
& x_{t,j} \le τ^{end}+M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.6 Headway (conflict‑free) constraints – bidirectional sharing  

For any two distinct trains *t* and *t'* that occupy the **same physical track** (either both normal or one normal + one rerouted) on segment *e*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j)\\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

The binary ordering variable \(δ_{t,t',e}\) decides which train passes first.  
To guarantee a **minimum headway** \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} + T^{head}_{t,t',e} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) \\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} + T^{head}_{t',t,e} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a train is cancelled, the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0 (via big‑M).

### 4.7 Single‑track capacity (only one train at a time)

A compact alternative to the pairwise headway constraints uses the interval‑selection variables \(s_{t,k}\). For each time interval *k* and each physical segment *e*:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\bigr)\, s_{t,k} \le 1 \qquad \forall e\in E,\; k\in K .
\]

Linking \(s_{t,k}\) with actual timings:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,i} \le k\Delta t + M\,(1-s_{t,k}) \\
& y_{t,i} \ge (k-1)\Delta t - M\,(1-s_{t,k}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus a train occupies a segment only in the interval where its start‑time lies.

### 4.8 Physical speed‑profile consistency  

For each selected plan *d* on segment *e* the corresponding **average speed** must respect the train’s acceleration/deceleration limits. This is already embedded in the pre‑computed \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\); however, we enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \le v^{max}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 \\
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \ge v^{min}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is a constant for a given plan, these become simple bounds on the admissible plan set *D* (i.e., infeasible plans are removed a‑priori).

### 4.9 Route choice (normal vs opposite track)  

A train may travel on a segment either in its original direction or, if the segment is blocked, on the opposite track. The two binary variables must be **mutually exclusive**:

\[
z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If a segment is **not** blocked, the opposite‑track variable is forced to zero:

\[
r_{t,e}=0 \qquad \forall t,\; e\notin B .
\]

### 4.10 Continuity of route  

If a train uses the opposite track on a blocked segment, it must **switch back** to the normal track at the next station (no prolonged opposite‑track travel). This can be modelled by a simple “switch‑once” rule:

\[
\sum_{e\in B} r_{t,e} \le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

(If more complex multi‑segment rerouting is allowed, the constraint can be relaxed.)

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle \min\;  & \displaystyle
\sum_{t} C^{delay}_t\bigl(x_{t,|S|+1}-\hat{x}_{t,|S|+1}\bigr)
+ \sum_{t,e,d} C^{energy}_d\,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\,p_{t,e,d}
+ \sum_{t} C^{canc}_t\,c_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.} & \text{(4.1)–(4.10) listed above} \\[2pt]
            & x_{t,s},y_{t,s}\ge 0,\; \forall t,s\\
            & z_{t,e},r_{t,e},p_{t,e,d},c_t,s_{t,k},δ_{t,t',e}\in\{0,1\},\;\forall\text{indices}.
\end{array}
}
\]

All constraints are *linear* because the travel‑time values \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and energy consumptions \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\) are pre‑computed constants for each admissible speed plan. The big‑M terms guarantee logical activation/deactivation.

---

## 6. Modeling Assumptions (explicitly stated)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | **Deterministic disruption window** \([τ^{start},τ^{end}]\) is known a‑priori and does not change during optimisation. |
| A2 | **Partial blockage** affects only one side of a double‑track segment; the opposite track is usable but only during the window. |

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling‑and‑Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
*Partial‑segment‑blockage disruption, bidirectional single‑track sharing*  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains (both directions). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including fictitious origin 0 and destination |S|+1). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of track‑segments (directed arcs) that can be traversed. For a segment *e = (i,j)* the physical length is *ℓ_e* (km). |
| **B** ⊆ E | Sub‑set of segments that are *blocked* (partial blockage) during the disruption window \([τ^{start}, τ^{end}]\). |
| **D** = {1,…,|D|} | Set of *discrete speed‑profile plans* that can be assigned to a train on a given segment (see §2). |
| **K** = {1,…,|K|} | Set of *time‑intervals* used for the decomposition (e.g., 5‑min slots). |
| **dir(t)** ∈ {+1, –1} | Direction of train *t* ( +1  = “up‑track”, –1 = “down‑track”). |
| **Δt** | Length of a time‑interval (minutes). |

### Fixed parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(a^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum acceleration for train *t*. |
| \(d^{max}_t\) (m/s²) | Maximum deceleration (positive value) for train *t*. |
| \(v^{max}_t\) (m/s) | Maximum permissible speed for train *t*. |
| \(v^{min}_t\) (m/s) | Minimum operating speed (usually 0). |
| \(E^{run}_{t,e,d}\) (kWh) | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment *e* when plan *d* is used (pre‑computed from physics). |
| \(T^{dwell}_{t,s}\) (min) | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\) (min) | Minimum headway (separation) required between two trains *t* and *t'* on segment *e* (direction‑dependent). |
| \(τ^{start}, τ^{end}\) (min) | Beginning and end of the blockage window. |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant (large enough to deactivate constraints). |
| \(C^{delay}_t\) (\$ per minute) | Penalty cost for each minute of delay of train *t*. |
| \(C^{canc}_t\) (\$) | Penalty cost for canceling train *t*. |
| \(C^{energy}_d\) (\$/kWh) | Energy price used to convert energy consumption to cost (same for all trains). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s* (minutes from a reference zero). |
| \(y_{t,s}\) ≥ 0 | Continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| \(z_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *e* (i.e. uses the “normal” direction), 0 otherwise (used for rerouting). |
| \(r_{t,e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses the **opposite** track on segment *e* (i.e. rerouted onto the blocked side). |
| \(p_{t,e,d}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if speed‑plan *d* is selected for train *t* on segment *e*. |
| \(c_t\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is **canceled**. |
| \(s_{t,k}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* is assigned to time‑interval *k* for the **headway‑checking** (used in the IP‑decomposition). |
| \(δ_{t,t',e}\) ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* precedes train *t'* on segment *e* (ordering variable). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum of operational cost, delay cost and energy cost** while heavily penalising cancellations.

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;  & \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{delay}_t \bigl( x_{t,|S|+1} - \hat{x}_{t,|S|+1} \bigr)}_{\text{Delay penalty}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{d\in D} C^{energy}_d \,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d}}_{\text{Energy cost}} \\
        & + \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} C^{canc}_t \,c_t}_{\text{Cancellation penalty}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\hat{x}_{t,|S|+1}\) is the **original scheduled arrival time** at the final station (baseline).  
If a train is cancelled (\(c_t=1\)) all its timing variables are forced to zero (see constraints).

---

## 4. Core Constraints  

### 4.1 Feasibility of a train (cancellation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S\cup\{0,|S|+1\} \\
& y_{t,s} \le M\,(1-c_t) &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S .
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(c_t=1\) the train disappears from the schedule.

### 4.2 Logical link between arrival / departure

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,s} \ge x_{t,s} + T^{dwell}_{t,s} - M\,c_t &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.3 Travel time on a segment – coupling with speed plan  

For each traversed segment *e = (i,j)* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-z_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

- \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is the **deterministic travel time** (minutes) of plan *d* on segment *e* for train *t* (computed from acceleration/deceleration limits and speed‑limit \(v^{max}_t\)).  
- The big‑M term deactivates the constraint if the train does **not** use the segment in its normal direction.

If the train is rerouted onto the opposite track, the same constraint uses \(r_{t,e}\) instead of \(z_{t,e}\):

\[
x_{t,j} \ge y_{t,i} + \sum_{d\in D} \tau_{t,e,d}\, p_{t,e,d} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) .
\]

### 4.4 Exactly one speed plan per traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{d\in D} p_{t,e,d}= z_{t,e}+r_{t,e} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If the segment is not used (\(z_{t,e}=r_{t,e}=0\)) all \(p_{t,e,d}=0\).

### 4.5 Rerouting feasibility (partial blockage)

A train may **only** use the opposite track on a blocked segment **during** the disruption window, and only if the segment is blocked for its original direction.

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,e} \le 1 &&\forall t, e\in B \\
& r_{t,e}=0 &&\forall t, e\notin B .
\end{aligned}
\]

Furthermore, the departure‑arrival times must respect the window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} \ge τ^{start} - M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B\\
& x_{t,j} \le τ^{end}+M\,(1-r_{t,e}) &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in B .
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.6 Headway (conflict‑free) constraints – bidirectional sharing  

For any two distinct trains *t* and *t'* that occupy the **same physical track** (either both normal or one normal + one rerouted) on segment *e*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j)\\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) &&\forall t\neq t',\; e=(i,j) .
\end{aligned}
\]

The binary ordering variable \(δ_{t,t',e}\) decides which train passes first.  
To guarantee a **minimum headway** \(T^{head}_{t,t',e}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_{t,i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t,e,d} p_{t,e,d} + T^{head}_{t,t',e} \le x_{t',j} + M\,(1-δ_{t,t',e}) \\
& y_{t',i} + \sum_{d} \tau_{t',e,d} p_{t',e,d} + T^{head}_{t',t,e} \le x_{t,j} + M\,(δ_{t,t',e}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

If a train is cancelled, the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0 (via big‑M).

### 4.7 Single‑track capacity (only one train at a time)

A compact alternative to the pairwise headway constraints uses the interval‑selection variables \(s_{t,k}\). For each time interval *k* and each physical segment *e*:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\bigr)\, s_{t,k} \le 1 \qquad \forall e\in E,\; k\in K .
\]

Linking \(s_{t,k}\) with actual timings:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,i} \le k\Delta t + M\,(1-s_{t,k}) \\
& y_{t,i} \ge (k-1)\Delta t - M\,(1-s_{t,k}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus a train occupies a segment only in the interval where its start‑time lies.

### 4.8 Physical speed‑profile consistency  

For each selected plan *d* on segment *e* the corresponding **average speed** must respect the train’s acceleration/deceleration limits. This is already embedded in the pre‑computed \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\); however, we enforce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \le v^{max}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 \\
& \frac{\ell_e}{\tau_{t,e,d}} \ge v^{min}_t &&\forall t,e,d \text{ with } p_{t,e,d}=1 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Because \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) is a constant for a given plan, these become simple bounds on the admissible plan set *D* (i.e., infeasible plans are removed a‑priori).

### 4.9 Route choice (normal vs opposite track)  

A train may travel on a segment either in its original direction or, if the segment is blocked, on the opposite track. The two binary variables must be **mutually exclusive**:

\[
z_{t,e}+r_{t,e}\le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E .
\]

If a segment is **not** blocked, the opposite‑track variable is forced to zero:

\[
r_{t,e}=0 \qquad \forall t,\; e\notin B .
\]

### 4.10 Continuity of route  

If a train uses the opposite track on a blocked segment, it must **switch back** to the normal track at the next station (no prolonged opposite‑track travel). This can be modelled by a simple “switch‑once” rule:

\[
\sum_{e\in B} r_{t,e} \le 1 \qquad \forall t\in T .
\]

(If more complex multi‑segment rerouting is allowed, the constraint can be relaxed.)

---

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ll}

+ \sum_{t,e,d} C^{energy}_d\,E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\,p_{t,e,d}
+ \sum_{t} C^{canc}_t\,c_t \\[4pt]

\]

All constraints are *linear* because the travel‑time values \(\tau_{t,e,d}\) and energy consumptions \(E^{dwell}_{t,e,d}\) are pre‑computed constants for each admissible speed plan. The big‑M terms guarantee logical activation/deactivation.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run Pyomo model** (Python) that implements the mixed‑integer linear program described in the request.  
The code follows the notation used in the description and contains:

* sets and parameters (trains, speed‑plans, stations, segments, disruption window, etc.)  
* decision variables (`x`, `y`, `a`, `d`, `t`, `z`) with the correct domains  
* the objective function (weighted sum of total delay and total energy)  
* all required constraints (speed‑plan selection, time‑consistency, travel‑time definition, blockage handling, ordering on shared segments, opposite‑track capacity, speed‑plan feasibility, big‑M linking)  

You can copy‑paste the script into a Python file (e.g. `train_reschedule.py`) and run it with any Pyomo‑compatible MILP solver (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, …).  
Only the data‑loading part (`...`) has to be filled with your concrete instance data (CSV, Excel, dictionaries, …).

```python
# --------------------------------------------------------------
#  Integrated Train Rescheduling & Speed Management (MILP)
#  --------------------------------------------------------------
#  Author:   OpenAI ChatGPT
#  Date:     2024‑06
#  Solver:   Any MILP solver supported by Pyomo (CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX,…)
# --------------------------------------------------------------

import pyomo.environ as pyo
from pyomo.environ import *
import pandas as pd

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
#  1.  INPUT DATA  (replace the ... with your actual data loading)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# Sets -------------------------------------------------------------
Trains   = [...]               # list of train identifiers   (i ∈ I)
Plans    = [...]               # list of speed‑plan ids      (r ∈ R)
Stations = [...]               # list of stations (ordered) (n ∈ N)
Segments = [...]               # list of track segments      (s ∈ S)

# Mapping: which stations belong to a segment?
#   seg_start[s]  = first station index of segment s
#   seg_end[s]    = last  station index of segment s
seg_start = {...}   # e.g. {s1: n3, s2: n5, ...}
seg_end   = {...}

# Parameters --------------------------------------------------------
# Scheduled arrival time of train i at its final station
scheduled_arrival = {i: ... for i in Trains}

# Dwell time required at each station (could be train‑specific)
dwell = {(i, n): ... for i in Trains for n in Stations}

# Minimum / maximum travel time on segment s for speed plan r
t_min = {(i, s, r): ... for i in Trains for s in Segments for r in Plans}
t_max = {(i, s, r): ... for i in Trains for s in Segments for r in Plans}

# Energy consumption of train i when using plan r
E = {(i, r): ... for i in Trains for r in Plans}

# Safety head‑way time on a shared segment (same for all trains)
safety = ...

# Disruption window (same for all blocked segments)
T_start = ...
T_end   = ...

# Binary indicator: segment s is blocked during the disruption window?
blocked = {s: 1 if ... else 0 for s in Segments}   # 1 = blocked, 0 = free

# Capacity of the opposite track for segment s (how many trains can be rerouted)
capacity_opposite = {s: ... for s in Segments}

# Big‑M constant – should be larger than any feasible time value
M = 1e6

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  MODEL DEFINITION
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

model = ConcreteModel()

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.1 Sets
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
model.I = Set(initialize=Trains)          # trains
model.R = Set(initialize=Plans)           # speed plans
model.N = Set(initialize=Stations)       # stations (ordered)
model.S = Set(initialize=Segments)        # track segments

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.2 Parameters (indexed sets)
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
model.sched_arr = Param(model.I, initialize=scheduled_arrival)
model.dwell   = Param(model.I, model.N, initialize=dwell, default=0)

model.tmin = Param(model.I, model.S, model.R, initialize=t_min, default=0)
model.tmax = Param(model.I, model.S, model.R, initialize=t_max, default=1e5)

model.energy = Param(model.I, model.R, initialize=E, default=0)

model.safety = Param(initialize=safety)

model.Tstart = Param(initialize=T_start)
model.Tend   = Param(initialize=T_end)

model.blocked = Param(model.S, initialize=blocked, default=0)

model.cap_opp = Param(model.S, initialize=capacity_opposite, default=0)

model.M = Param(initialize=M)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.3 Decision Variables
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# x[i,r] = 1 if train i uses speed plan r
model.x = Var(model.I, model.R, domain=Binary)

# y[i,j,s] = 1 if train i precedes train j on shared segment s
model.y = Var(model.I, model.I, model.S, domain=Binary)

# a[i,n] = arrival time of train i at station n
model.a = Var(model.I, model.N, domain=NonNegativeReals)

# d[i,n] = departure time of train i from station n
model.d = Var(model.I, model.N, domain=NonNegativeReals)

# t[i,s] = travel time of train i on segment s
model.t = Var(model.I, model.S, domain=NonNegativeReals)

# z[i,s] = 1 if train i is rerouted onto the opposite track on segment s
model.z = Var(model.I, model.S, domain=Binary)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.4 Objective
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# weight for delay vs. energy (you can tune these)
w_delay  = 1.0
w_energy = 1.0

def obj_expression(m):
    total_delay = sum( m.a[i, max(m.N)] - m.sched_arr[i] for i in m.I )
    total_energy = sum( m.energy[i,r] * m.x[i,r] for i in m.I for r in m.R )
    return w_delay * total_delay + w_energy * total_energy

model.Obj = Objective(rule=obj_expression, sense=minimize)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  CONSTRAINTS
# ------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3.1 Each train selects exactly one speed plan
def one_plan_rule(m, i):
    return sum( m.x[i,r] for r in m.R ) == 1
model.OnePlan = Constraint(model.I, rule=one_plan_rule)

# 3.2 Arrival / departure consistency (dwell time)
def dwell_rule(m, i, n):
    return m.a[i,n] + m.dwell[i,n] <= m.d[i,n]
model.DwellCons = Constraint(model.I, model.N, rule=dwell_rule)

# 3.3 Travel time definition between consecutive stations
#    Assume segment s connects station n (origin) to station n+1 (destination)
#    You must provide a mapping seg_of[(i,n)] → s (the segment travelled after n)
seg_of = {...}   # e.g. {(i, n1): s1, (i, n2): s2, ...}
def travel_time_rule(m, i, n):
    s = seg_of[(i, n)]
    return m.t[i,s] == m.d[i,n] - m.a[i, n+1]
model.TravelTime = Constraint(model.I, model.N, rule=travel_time_rule)

# 3.4 Blockage handling: if segment s is blocked, train must either
#     use opposite track (z=1) OR be outside the disruption window.
def blockage_rule(m, i, s):
    if m.blocked[s] == 0:
        return Constraint.Skip
    # entry time onto segment s = departure from its upstream station
    # we need the upstream station index for segment s:
    n_up = seg_start[s]          # station before the segment
    entry = m.d[i, n_up]
    # enforce: entry ∈ [T_start, T_end] → must use opposite track
    # big‑M formulation:
    return entry <= m.Tend + m.M * (1 - m.z[i,s])
model.BlockageUpper = Constraint(model.I, model.S, rule=blockage_rule)

def blockage_lower_rule(m, i, s):
    if m.blocked[s] == 0:
        return Constraint.Skip
    n_up = seg_start[s]
    entry = m.d[i, n_up]
    return entry >= m.Tstart - m.M * (1 - m.z[i,s])
model.BlockageLower = Constraint(model.I, model.S, rule=blockage_lower_rule)

# 3.5 Opposite‑track capacity
def opp_capacity_rule(m, s):
    return sum( m.z[i,s] for i in m.I ) <= m.cap_opp[s]
model.OppCap = Constraint(model.S, rule=opp_capacity_rule)

# 3.6 Ordering on a shared segment
#   For every unordered pair (i,j) that share segment s, enforce y_ij + y_ji = 1
#   (Assume a pre‑computed set SharedPairs = {(i,j,s) | i<j, both use s})
SharedPairs = {...}   # e.g. {(i1,i2,s1), (i1,i3,s2), ...}
def ordering_sum_rule(m, i, j, s):
    if (i,j,s) not in SharedPairs:
        return Constraint.Skip
    return m.y[i,j,s] + m.y[j,i,s] == 1
model.OrderSum = Constraint(model.I, model.I, model.S, rule=ordering_sum_rule)

#   If i precedes j, enforce safety head‑way
def safety_rule(m, i, j, s):
    if (i,j,s) not in SharedPairs:
        return Constraint.Skip
    # entry time of i on segment s
    n_up_i = seg_start[s]
    entry_i = m.d[i, n_up_i]
    # entry time of j on segment s
    n_up_j = seg_start[s]
    entry_j = m.d[j, n_up_j]
    return entry_i + m.safety <= entry_j + m.M * (1 - m.y[i,j,s])
model.SafetyHeadway = Constraint(model.I, model.I, model.S, rule=safety_rule)

# 3.7 Speed‑plan feasibility: travel time must respect the bounds of the
#     selected plan. Use big‑M linking.
def travel_time_min_rule(m, i, s):
    # t[i,s] >= t_min * sum_r x[i,r]
    return m.t[i,s] >= sum( m.tmin[i,s,r] * m.x[i,r] for r in m.R )
model.TravelTimeMin = Constraint(model.I, model.S, rule=travel_time_min_rule)

def travel_time_max_rule(m, i, s):
    return m.t[i,s] <= sum( m.tmax[i,s,r] * m.x[i,r] for r in m.R )
model.TravelTimeMax = Constraint(model.I, model.S, rule=travel_time_max_rule)

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  SOLVE
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Choose a solver (CBC is open‑source; replace with 'gurobi', 'cplex', … if available)
    solver = SolverFactory('cbc')
    results = solver.solve(model, tee=True)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5.  OUTPUT
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------
    print("\n=== OBJECTIVE VALUE ===")
    print(value(model.Obj))

    print("\n=== SELECTED SPEED PLANS ===")
    for i in model.I:
        for r in model.R:
            if value(model.x[i,r]) > 0.5:
                print(f"Train {i} -> plan {r}")

    print("\n=== ARRIVAL TIMES (final stations) ===")
    last_station = max(model.N)
    for i in model.I:
        print(f"Train {i} : arrival = {value(model.a[i,last_station]):.2f}  (scheduled {model.sched_arr[i]})")

    print("\n=== REROUTED TRAINS ===")
    for i in model.I:
        for s in model.S:
            if value(model.z[i,s]) > 0.5:
                print(f"Train {i} uses opposite track on segment {s}")

    # (additional reporting – e.g., ordering, travel times – can be added)
```

### How to adapt the template to your data

| Item | What you must provide | Typical source |
|------|-----------------------|----------------|
| `Trains` | List of train IDs (e.g., `['T1','T2',...]`) | timetable file |
| `Plans` | Speed‑plan IDs (e.g., `['slow','normal','fast']`) | engineering data |
| `Stations` | Ordered list of stations (e.g., `['S1','S2',...]`) | network topology |
| `Segments` | IDs of track segments between stations | network layout |
| `seg_start / seg_end` | Mapping segment → upstream/down‑stream station indices | derived from topology |
| `scheduled_arrival[i]` | Planned arrival time of train *i* at its last station | timetable |
| `dwell[i,n]` | Minimum dwell time of train *i* at station *n* | operational rules |
| `t_min[i,s,r] , t_max[i,s,r]` | Minimum/maximum travel time on segment *s* under plan *r* | speed‑plan tables |
| `E[i,r]` | Energy consumption of train *i* for plan *r* | energy model |
| `safety` | Minimum head‑way (seconds) between two trains on the same segment | safety regulations |
| `blocked[s]` | 1 if segment *s* is blocked during the disruption window, else 0 | disruption scenario |
| `capacity_opposite[s]` | Number of trains that can simultaneously use the opposite track on *s* | infrastructure limit |
| `seg_of[(i,n)]` | Which segment a train *i* traverses after leaving station *n* | schedule‑segment mapping |
| `SharedPairs` | Set of unordered train pairs that share a segment (i<j) | compute from network data |
| `M` | A sufficiently large constant (e.g., 1 000 000) | any large number > max possible time |

Once all dictionaries/sets are filled, run the script. The solver will return the optimal train‑rescheduling plan that respects the blockage, ordering, capacity and speed‑plan constraints while minimizing the weighted sum of delay and energy consumption.

**Variables**

* \(x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\in I\) uses speed‑plan \(r\in R\), 0 otherwise.  
* \(y_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) precedes train \(j\) on shared segment \(s\in S\).  
* \(a_{i,n}\ge 0\) – arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(n\in N\).  
* \(d_{i,n}\ge 0\) – departure time of train \(i\) from station \(n\in N\).  
* \(t_{i,s}\ge 0\) – travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\in S\).  
* \(z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) is rerouted onto the opposite track on segment \(s\) during the disruption window.

**Parameters (assumed given)**  

* \(\hat a_{i}\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final station.  
* \(\text{dwell}_{i,n}\) – minimum dwell time of train \(i\) at station \(n\).  
* \(t^{\min}_{i,s,r},\; t^{\max}_{i,s,r}\) – minimum/maximum travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(s\) under speed‑plan \(r\).  
* \(E_{i,r}\) – energy consumption of train \(i\) when using plan \(r\).  
* \(\text{safety}\) – safety head‑way time required between two trains on the same segment.  
* \([T^{\text{start}},T^{\text{end}}]\) – disruption time window.  
* \(\text{blocked}_s\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if segment \(s\) is blocked during the disruption window.  
* \(\text{cap}^{\text{opp}}_s\) – capacity of the opposite track on segment \(s\).  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).  
* \(\text{seg\_start}_s,\text{seg\_end}_s\) – upstream/down‑stream stations of segment \(s\).  
* \(\text{SharedPairs}\subseteq I\times I\times S\) – unordered train pairs that share segment \(s\).  

**Objective (weighted sum of total delay and total energy)**  

\[
\min\; 
w^{\text{delay}}\!\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\!\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{r\in R} E_{i,r}\,x_{i,r}
\]

where \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train \(i\) at its final station.

**Constraints**

1. **Speed‑plan selection** (each train chooses exactly one plan)  
   \[
   \sum_{r\in R} x_{i,r}=1 \qquad \forall i\in I
   \]

2. **Dwell time consistency**  
   \[
   a_{i,n}+ \text{dwell}_{i,n}\le d_{i,n} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; n\in N
   \]

3. **Travel‑time definition** (segment \(s\) connects station \(\text{seg\_start}_s\) to \(\text{seg\_end}_s\))  
   \[
   t_{i,s}= d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}-a_{i,\text{seg\_end}_s}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

4. **Blockage handling – rerouting or avoidance**  
   For every blocked segment \(s\) (\(\text{blocked}_s=1\)):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\le T^{\text{end}} + M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \\
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\ge T^{\text{start}} - M\,(1-z_{i,s})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad \forall i\in I
   \]

5. **Opposite‑track capacity**  
   \[
   \sum_{i\in I} z_{i,s}\le \text{cap}^{\text{opp}}_s \qquad \forall s\in S
   \]

6. **Ordering on shared segments** (conflict‑free head‑way)  
   *Precedence sum*  
   \[
   y_{i,j,s}+y_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]
   *Safety head‑way*  
   \[
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}+ \text{safety}\le d_{j,\text{seg\_start}_s}+M\,(1-y_{i,j,s})
   \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]

7. **Speed‑plan feasibility for travel times** (big‑M linking)  
   \[
   t_{i,s}\ge \sum_{r\in R} t^{\min}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]
   \[
   t_{i,s}\le \sum_{r\in R} t^{\max}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

8. **Variable domains**  
   \[
   x_{i,r},\,y_{i,j,s},\,z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
   a_{i,n},\,d_{i,n},\,t_{i,s}\ge 0
   \]

**Assumptions (marked as such)**  

* The mapping of each segment to its upstream/down‑stream stations (\(\text{seg\_start}_s,\text{seg\_end}_s\)) is known.  
* Travel time on a segment is the difference between departure from the upstream station and arrival at the downstream station.  
* All trains share the same safety head‑way time.  
* The disruption affects only the specified blocked segments and the given time window.  
* Energy consumption depends only on the selected speed‑plan, not on the exact timing.  

The model above fully integrates train rescheduling (arrival/departure times, ordering, rerouting) with speed‑profile selection, ensuring a conflict‑free timetable that respects blockage constraints and minimizes a combination of passenger delay and energy use.

2. **Dwell time consistency**  
   \[
   a_{i,n}+ \text{dwell}_{i,n}\le d_{i,n} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; n\in N
   \]

3. **Travel‑time definition** (segment \(s\) connects station \(\text{seg\_start}_s\) to \(\text{seg\_end}_s\))  
   \[
   t_{i,s}= d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}-a_{i,\text{seg\_end}_s}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

4. **Blockage handling – rerouting or avoidance**  
   For every blocked segment \(s\) (\(\text{blocked}_s=1\)):
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\le T^{\text{end}} + M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \\
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s} &\ge T^{\text{start}} - M\,(1-z_{i,s})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad \forall i\in I
   \]

5. **Opposite‑track capacity**  
   \[
   \sum_{i\in I} z_{i,s}\le \text{cap}^{\text{opp}}_s \qquad \forall s\in S
   \]

6. **Ordering on shared segments** (conflict‑free head‑way)  
   *Precedence sum*  
   \[
   y_{i,j,s}+y_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]
   *Safety head‑way*  
   \[
   d_{i,\text{seg\_start}_s}+ \text{safety}\le d_{j,\text{seg\_start}_s}+M\,(1-y_{i,j,s})
   \qquad \forall (i,j,s)\in \text{SharedPairs}
   \]

7. **Speed‑plan feasibility for travel times** (big‑M linking)  
   \[
   t_{i,s}\ge \sum_{r\in R} t^{\min}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]
   \[
   t_{i,s}\le \sum_{r\in R} t^{\max}_{i,s,r}\,x_{i,r}\qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
   \]

8. **Variable domains**  
   \[
   x_{i,r},\,y_{i,j,s},\,z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad
   a_{i,n},\,d_{i,n},\,t_{i,s}\ge 0
   \]

**Assumptions (marked as such)**  

* The mapping of each segment to its upstream/down‑stream stations (\(\text{seg\_start}_s,\text{seg\_end}_s\)) is known.  
* Travel time on a segment is the difference between departure from the upstream station and arrival at the downstream station.  
* All trains share the same safety head‑way time.  
* The disruption affects only the specified blocked segments and the given time window.  
* Energy consumption depends only on the selected speed‑plan, not on the exact timing.  

The model above fully integrates train rescheduling (arrival/departure times, ordering, rerouting) with speed‑profile selection, ensuring a conflict‑free timetable that respects blockage constraints and minimizes a combination of passenger delay and energy use.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
