Usually \(\gamma_{t,r}=1\) for all feasible routes. | | \(\kappa_{s}\) | Nominal capacity of segment \(s\) (maximum number of trains that can occupy the whole segment simultaneously when there is **no** partial blockage). | | \(\delta_{t,s}\) | Direction of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (+1 for northbound, –1 for southbound). Needed for bidirectional conflict constraints. | --- ## 3. Decision Variables | Symbol | Type | Meaning | |--------|------|---------| | \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\); exactly one route per train. | | \(y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). Occupancy is defined as “the train is somewhere inside the segment at any point of interval \(i\)”. | | \(z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) in interval \(i\) **with speed level** \(v\). For each occupied interval exactly one speed level is chosen. | | \(D_t\ge 0\) | continuous | Total **delay** of train \(t\) (minutes) relative to its planned departure. | | \(C_t\ge 0\) | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train \(t\) (kWh) – sum of \(E_{s,v}\) over all traversed segment‑interval‑speed triples. | | \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\) | continuous | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). | | \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (i.e. the moment it **enters** segment \(s\)). | --- ## 4. Objective Function \[ \boxed{ \min\; \sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(\alpha\, D_t \;+\; \beta\, C_t\Bigr) } \] *The first term penalises total delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption. By adjusting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can trade‑off punctuality against energy efficiency.* --- ## 5. Constraints ### 5.1 Route‑selection (one route per train) \[ \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1} \] \[ x_{t,r}\le \gamma_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t \tag{R2} \] ### 5.2 Linking occupancy to the chosen route If a segment \(s\) does **not** belong to route \(r\), the train cannot occupy it. \[ y_{t,s,i}\le \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in r} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{R3} \] ### 5.3 Time‑feasibility (travel time = length / speed) For each train, segment, interval and speed level we must respect the physical travel relationship. First, define the **travel time** needed to cross segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\): \[ \theta_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{v}\times 60 \qquad\text{(minutes)} \tag{def1} \] Now enforce that if a train uses speed level \(v\) on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\), the **departure** from the segment occurs exactly \(\theta_{s,v}\) minutes after the **arrival** at the segment’s upstream node. \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} \;-\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} + M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T2} \] The two inequalities together force equality when \(z_{t,s,i,v}=1\). The **departure time from segment \(s\)** is the time the train leaves the segment (i.e. the time it enters the next segment). We therefore link successive segments: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s'} \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route} \tag{T3} \] ### 5.3‑a Speed‑choice consistency Exactly one speed level is selected for each occupied interval: \[ \sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,i,v}= y_{t,s,i}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{S1} \] ### 5.4 Delay definition Delay is the difference between actual and planned departure: \[ D_t \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_t - d^{\text{planned}}_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1} \] (If early departure is allowed, we could also add \(D_t\ge 0\); the model already forces non‑negativity.) ### 5.5 Energy calculation Energy is the sum of the pre‑computed energy for each segment‑speed pair: \[ C_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I_s}\sum_{v\in V} E_{s,v}\; z_{t,s,i,v}\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1} \] ### 5.6 Capacity constraints – normal (unblocked) segments The total number of trains occupying a segment at a given interval cannot exceed its nominal capacity: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le \kappa_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s \tag{C1} \] ### 5.7 Capacity constraints – **partial blockage** When a segment \(s\) is partially blocked during a time window \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) (block \(b\in B\)), only the **unblocked capacity** \(b_s\) may be used. Let \(\mathcal{I}_b\) be the set of intervals that intersect the blockage window: \[ \mathcal{I}_b = \{\, i\in I_s \mid \text{interval }i \text{ overlaps }[\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b] \,\} \] Then: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le b_s \qquad\forall b\in B,\; i\in \mathcal{I}_b \tag{C2} \] If a segment has **no** blockage, the constraint reduces to (C1) with \(\kappa_s\). ### 5.8 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance) When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same physical track, they cannot be in the segment at the same time. Using the direction indicator \(\delta_{t,s}\in\{-1,+1\}\): \[ y_{t_1,s,i}+y_{t_2,s,i}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s,\; t_1\neq t_2\text{ with }\delta_{t_1,s}=-\delta_{t_2,s} \tag{B1} \] (If the line is double‑track, the capacity \(\kappa_s\) would be >1 and the bidirectional constraint could be omitted; the model keeps it for single‑track sections.) ### 5.9 Logical linking of departure/arrival times to route choice If a train does **not** use a segment, its arrival/departure times on that segment are irrelevant. We force them to a dummy value using a big‑M: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L2} \] These constraints simply deactivate the time variables when the segment is not on the chosen route. ### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\} \qquad\forall t,r,s,i,v \] \[ D_t\ge 0,\; C_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s \] --- ## 6. Model‑element commentary | Element | What it captures | Why it is needed | |---------|-----------------|------------------| | **Binary route‑choice variables \(x_{t,r}\)** | Determines which physical path each train will follow (different possible detours around the blocked part). | Guarantees a single feasible route per train and allows the optimizer to select alternative routes when the blockage makes the original path infeasible. | | **Occupancy binaries \(y_{t,s,i}\)** | Indicates whether train \(t\) is present on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). | Enables capacity constraints (both normal and blocked) and bidirectional conflict constraints to be expressed linearly. | | **Speed‑level binaries \(z_{t,s,i,v}\)** | Chooses a discrete speed for each train‑segment‑interval pair. | Allows the model to trade‑off travel time (higher speed → less delay) against energy consumption (higher speed → higher \(E_{s,v}\)). | | **Departure/arrival continuous times \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t,\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\)** | Real‑valued schedule times that link the binary occupancy/speed decisions to actual clock time. | Needed to enforce the physics of motion (travel time = length / speed) and to compute delay. | | **Delay variable \(D_t\)** | Measures how late train \(t\) leaves its origin compared with the planned timetable. | Directly appears in the objective with weight \(\alpha\). | | **Energy variable \(C_t\)** | Sum of energy consumptions for all traversed segment‑speed choices. | Appears in the objective with weight \(\beta\). | | **Objective \(\min \sum (\alpha D_t + \beta C_t)\)** | Minimises a weighted combination of total passenger‑service delay and operational energy cost. | Provides a single scalar criterion for the MILP solver. | | **Travel‑time constraints (T1–T3)** | Enforce that if a speed level is chosen, the time spent on the segment equals the deterministic travel time \(\theta_{s,v}\). | Guarantees feasibility of the speed‑management decisions. | | **Capacity constraints (C1, C2)** | Limit the number of trains that can be simultaneously on a segment; C2 tightens the limit during a partial blockage. | Prevents oversaturation of the line and respects the reduced capacity caused by the blockage. | | **Bidirectional conflict (B1)** | For single‑track sections, forbids two opposite‑direction trains from occupying the segment at the same interval. | Avoids head‑on collisions; essential when the line is not double‑tracked. | | **Big‑M linking constraints (R3, L1, L2, T1‑T2)** | Linearise logical implications (e.g., “if a train does not use a segment, its occupancy variables must be zero”). | Standard technique to keep the model linear while handling logical conditions. | | **Energy‑calculation constraint (E1)** | Accumulates the pre‑computed energy values for the chosen speed levels. | Provides the exact energy term needed in the objective. | | **Delay definition (D1)** | Relates the decision variable \(D_t\) to the actual departure time. | Allows the optimizer to trade‑off earlier departure (less delay) against the need to wait for capacity or to travel slower for energy savings. | --- ### How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Discretise the planning horizon into intervals of length \(\Delta\) (e.g., 1 min). For each segment compute the travel‑time \(\theta_{s,v}\) and energy \(E_{s,v}\) for every admissible speed level. Identify the blocked sub‑segments and fill the sets \(B\) and \(\mathcal{I}_b\). 2. **Parameter tuning** – Choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to reflect the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., \(\alpha=1\) €/min, \(\beta=0.02\) €/kWh). 3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The solution returns: * the selected route for each train, * the departure/arrival schedule, * the speed level for each segment‑interval, * the resulting total delay and energy consumption. The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear, the only non‑continuous variables are binaries) and therefore can be tackled by state‑of‑the‑art MILP solvers even for medium‑size railway networks (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a planning horizon of a few hours). --- **End of MILP formulation**.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment interval. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-profile feasibility, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the three‑dimensional problem described in the prompt:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives)  
* **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level on each track‑segment‑time‑interval)  
* **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window, creating a capacity/occupancy conflict)

The model is written in a **canonical linear‑programming style** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints).  After the formulation each component is explained in plain English.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Set of **routes** (ordered sequences of track‑segments) that a train may follow. |
| \(E=\{1,\dots ,|E|\}\) | Set of **track‑segments** (physical pieces of line). |
| \(I_e\) | Ordered list of **intervals** (time‑slots) on segment \(e\).  For simplicity we use a uniform discretisation \(\Delta\) (e.g., 1 min).  The index \(i\in I_e\) denotes the *i‑th* interval on segment \(e\). |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,K\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g., \(k=1\) = 30 km/h, \(k=2\) = 50 km/h, …).  Each level has a known travel‑time per kilometre and an energy‑consumption coefficient. |
| \(B\subseteq E\) | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance). |
| \(U_{e,i}\subseteq [0,1]\) | Fraction of segment \(e\) that is **available** during interval \(i\).  For an unblocked segment \(U_{e,i}=1\); for a blocked segment it may be \(0.5\) (half the track is closed). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(d_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(a_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination. |
| \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment \(e\). |
| \(\tau_{k}\) | **Travel‑time factor** for speed level \(k\) (minutes per kilometre).  The actual travel time on segment \(e\) at speed \(k\) is \(\tau_{k} L_{e}\). |
| \(\epsilon_{k}\) | **Energy‑consumption coefficient** for speed level \(k\) (kWh per kilometre). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | Positive weighting factors in the objective (delay vs. energy). |
| \(c_{t,s}\) | Fixed cost (or penalty) for assigning train \(t\) to route \(s\) (e.g., if a route is longer). |
| \(p_{e,i}\) | Binary **blockage indicator**: 1 if interval \((e,i)\) is *partially* blocked, 0 otherwise. |
| \(cap_{e,i}\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy segment \(e\) during interval \(i\).  For a fully open segment \(cap_{e,i}= \infty\); for a partially blocked segment it may be 1 (single‑track) or 2 (double‑track with one lane closed). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(s\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(dep_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. |
| \(arr_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination. |
| \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses **the whole** interval \((e,i)\) with speed level \(k\).  (If a train only uses a fraction of an interval we model it by splitting the interval – the linear formulation assumes the discretisation is fine enough.) |
| \(z_{t,e,i}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(e\) during interval \(i\) (regardless of speed).  This is a helper variable used for capacity/conflict constraints. |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\). |
| \(D_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay of train \(t\) (difference between actual and planned arrival). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_{t}\;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T} E_{t}\;+\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c_{t,s}\,x_{t,s}
}
\]

*The first term penalises total passenger‑delay, the second term penalises total energy use, and the third term can capture route‑selection preferences.*

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑occupancy** – each route \(s\) is a known ordered list of segments \(\{e_{s,1},\dots ,e_{s,|s|}\}\).  For every segment that belongs to a route we force the occupancy variables to be zero unless the route is selected:

\[
\sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\; \le\; M\; x_{t,s} \qquad 
\forall t\in T,\; \forall e\in \text{segments}(s)
\]

If \(x_{t,s}=0\) the RHS is 0, thus no \(y\) can be positive.

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility (travel‑time)  

For each train, the time it spends on a segment equals the sum of the interval lengths it occupies, weighted by the chosen speed level.

First define the **duration of interval** \(i\) on segment \(e\) (normally \(\Delta\) minutes).  Because the model works with binary \(y\) that already indicates “the train uses the whole interval with speed \(k\)”, the travel‑time contributed by that interval is simply \(\Delta\).  However we must guarantee that the *total* time spent on a segment equals the travel‑time implied by the speed level.  The easiest linear way is to enforce that the number of intervals assigned to a segment equals the required number of intervals for the chosen speed.

Let  

\[
N_{e,k}= \Big\lceil \frac{\tau_{k} L_{e}}{\Delta}\Big\rceil
\]

(the minimum number of intervals needed to travel segment \(e\) at speed level \(k\)).  

Then for every train‑segment pair:

\[
\sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}= \sum_{k\in K} N_{e,k}\; \Big(\sum_{i\in I_{e}} y_{t,e,i,k}\Big) \qquad\text{(definition, automatically satisfied)}
\]

A more compact linear formulation uses a **big‑M** linking the chosen speed level to the total occupied intervals:

\[
\sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}= \sum_{k\in K} N_{e,k}\; \theta_{t,e,k}
\]

where we introduce auxiliary binaries  

\[
\theta_{t,e,k}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train }t\text{ uses speed }k\text{ on segment }e\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

and enforce  

\[
\theta_{t,e,k}\le \sum_{i\in I_{e}} y_{t,e,i,k}\le M\theta_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t,e,k
\]

and exactly one speed per segment:

\[
\sum_{k\in K}\theta_{t,e,k}= \sum_{i\in I_{e}} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall t,e
\]

(If a train never occupies segment \(e\) then the RHS is 0 and all \(\theta\) are 0.)

### 5.3 Departure / Arrival relationship  

The arrival time equals departure plus the sum of all interval durations the train actually uses:

\[
arr_{t}= dep_{t}+ \Delta\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{i\in I_{e}} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

where  

\[
z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\qquad\forall t,e,i
\]

### 5.4 Delay definition  

\[
D_{t}= arr_{t}- a_t^{\text{orig}}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

and we force non‑negativity:

\[
D_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

### 5.5 Energy consumption  

Energy on a segment is the length times the coefficient of the chosen speed level:

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in K}\epsilon_{k} L_{e}\; \theta_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

(If a train does not occupy a segment, the corresponding \(\theta\) is 0.)

### 5.6 Blockage / Capacity constraints  

For each **partially blocked** segment \(e\in B\) and each interval \(i\in I_{e}\) we limit the number of trains that may occupy the segment:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} z_{t,e,i}\; \le\; cap_{e,i}\qquad\forall e\in B,\; i\in I_{e}
\]

The capacity \(cap_{e,i}\) is derived from the available fraction \(U_{e,i}\).  For a double‑track line where one lane is closed, \(cap_{e,i}=1\); for a single‑track line with a 50 % blockage we may set \(cap_{e,i}=0\) (no train can enter) or allow a “passing window” by setting it to 1 only for certain intervals.

### 5.7 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance)  

If the line is **single‑track** (or a lane is closed) we must forbid two trains travelling in opposite directions on the same segment at the same time.  Let \(\sigma_{t,e}\in\{+1,-1\}\) be a known parameter indicating the direction of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (+1 = northbound, –1 = southbound).  Then for every segment‑interval we impose:

\[
\sum_{t\in T:\,\sigma_{t,e}=+1} z_{t,e,i}\; \le\; 1 - \sum_{t\in T:\,\sigma_{t,e}=-1} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall e\in E,\; i\in I_{e}
\]

A linear equivalent uses a **pairwise** big‑M formulation:

\[
z_{t,e,i}+z_{t',e,i}\le 1 \qquad\forall e,i,\; \forall (t,t')\text{ with }\sigma_{t,e}\neq\sigma_{t',e}
\]

Only needed when the segment is single‑track or partially blocked.

### 5.8 Speed‑profile feasibility (ramping)  

Trains cannot change speed arbitrarily between consecutive intervals on the same segment.  For each train, segment, and consecutive intervals \(i,i+1\) we limit the change in speed level:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i,k} - \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i+1,k} \le R\qquad\forall t,e,i
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i+1,k} - \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i,k} \le R\qquad\forall t,e,i
\]

where \(R\) is the maximum admissible “speed‑level jump” (e.g., 1 means you can only move to the next higher or lower discrete speed).

### 5.9 Logical linking of \(z\) and \(y\)  

\[
z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\qquad\forall t,e,i
\]

Because \(y\) are binary, this forces \(z\) to be 1 iff the train occupies the interval with *some* speed.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,e,i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,e,i}\in\{0,1\},\; \theta_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\}
\]

\[
dep_{t},\,arr_{t},\,D_{t},\,E_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t
\]

---

## 6. How the Model Works – Plain‑Language Walk‑through  

1. **Choose a route** – each train must pick exactly one of the pre‑defined routes (binary variables \(x_{t,s}\)).  
2. **Allocate time intervals** – once a route is chosen, the train is forced to occupy the corresponding track segments during a sequence of discrete time slots.  The binary variables \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) decide *which* speed level the train uses while it occupies a particular interval.  
3. **Respect blockage** – for segments that are partially closed, the capacity parameter \(cap_{e,i}\) limits how many trains can be on that segment at the same time.  This models the fact that only the free lane(s) are usable.  
4. **Avoid head‑on collisions** – on single‑track (or partially blocked) sections, the pairwise constraints forbid two trains travelling in opposite directions from occupying the same interval.  
5. **Travel‑time consistency** – the number of intervals a train spends on a segment must be at least the minimum required for the chosen speed (the \(N_{e,k}\) relationship).  Consequently the departure‑to‑arrival equation correctly accumulates the total travel time.  
6. **Delay and energy accounting** – the model computes each train’s delay (actual arrival minus the original schedule) and its energy consumption (length × energy coefficient of the selected speed).  
7. **Objective** – the solver minimizes a weighted sum of total delay and total energy, optionally adding a small penalty for using longer routes.  By changing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the railway planner can trade‑off punctuality against sustainability.  

---

## 7. Full Linear Model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t} D_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t}E_t \;+\; \sum_{t,s}c_{t,s}x_{t,s}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\sum_{s}x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{i,k} y_{t,e,i,k}\le M x_{t,s} &&\forall t,\; \forall e\in \text{segments}(s)\\
&\sum_{k}\theta_{t,e,k}= \sum_{i}z_{t,e,i} &&\forall t,e\\
&\sum_{i}z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k} N_{e,k}\,\theta_{t,e,k} &&\forall t,e\\
&z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k} y_{t,e,i,k} &&\forall t,e,i\\
&arr_t = dep_t + \Delta\sum_{e,i}z_{t,e,i} &&\forall t\\
&D_t = arr_t - a_t^{\text{orig}},\; D_t\ge 0 &&\forall t\\
&E_t = \sum_{e,k}\epsilon_k L_e \theta_{t,e,k} &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{t} z_{t,e,i}\le cap_{e,i} &&\forall e\in B,\; i\\
&z_{t,e,i}+z_{t',e,i}\le 1 &&\forall e,i,\; \forall (t,t')\text{ opposite direction}\\
&\big|\sum_{k}k\,y_{t,e,i,k} - \sum_{k}k\,y_{t,e,i+1,k}\big|\le R &&\forall t,e,i\\
&x_{t,s},y_{t,e,i,k},z_{t,e,i},\theta_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
&dep_t,arr_t,D_t,E_t\ge 0 &&\forall t
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, so the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### Remarks for a Practical Implementation  

* **Time‑discretisation** – choose \(\Delta\) small enough (e.g., 30 s or 1 min) so that the integer‑interval representation does not introduce large approximation errors.  
* **Big‑M value** – set \(M\) to a value larger than the maximum possible number of intervals a train could occupy on any route (e.g., total horizon / \(\Delta\)).  
* **Pre‑processing** – many \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) variables can be eliminated a priori because a train cannot reach a far‑away segment before a certain time; this reduces model size.  
* **Scalability** – for large networks the pairwise opposite‑direction constraints can be replaced by a **conflict‑graph** formulation with a single capacity variable per segment‑interval, which is often tighter for solvers.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential decisions (route, departure/arrival, speed level) and the operational realities of a partially blocked railway line (capacity, bidirectional conflicts, speed‑ramping).  By solving the MILP the planner obtains a schedule that simultaneously minimises passenger delay and the energy used by the fleet.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment interval. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-profile feasibility, energy calculation.

Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt: * **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives) * **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level for each train on each track‑segment‑time‑interval) * **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window, creating a capacity‑conflict that must be respected). The model is written in a **standard linear‑programming notation** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints). After the formulation a short “model‑elements” commentary explains the meaning of each part and how it relates to the description. --- ## 1. Sets | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). | | \(S\) | Set of **track segments** (ordered from origin to destination). A segment may be a single line or a block of several kilometres. | | \(I_s\) | Set of **time intervals** that intersect segment \(s\). Intervals are of equal length \(\Delta\) (e.g. 1 min). Index by \(i\). | | \(V\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (discrete). Index by \(v\). Speed level \(v\) corresponds to a constant speed \(v\) km/h on the segment. | | \(R_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\) (each route is a sequence of segments). Index by \(r\). | | \(B\) | Set of **blocked sub‑segments** (partial blockages). Each element \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b_s,\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b)\) where:
• \(s\) – the segment that is partially blocked,
• \(b_s\) – the *capacity* of the unblocked part (maximum number of trains that can occupy the segment simultaneously),
• \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) – the time window of the blockage. | --- ## 2. Parameters | Symbol | Description | |--------|-------------| | \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). | | \(\underline{v}_v,\ \overline{v}_v\) | Minimum / maximum speed (km/h) that can be represented by speed level \(v\). In a linear model we treat each level as a *single* speed value \(v\) (e.g. \(v\in\{30,50,80,120\}\) km/h). | | \(\alpha\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g. 1 €/min). | | \(\beta\) | Weight for energy consumption in the objective (e.g. 0.01 €/kWh). | | \(E_{s,v}\) | Energy (kWh) consumed by a train traversing segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\). Usually \(E_{s,v}=c_1 L_s v^2 + c_2 L_s /v\) linearised by pre‑computing the value for each discrete speed. | | \(d^{\text{planned}}_t\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes from a reference). | | \(a^{\text{planned}}_{t,s}\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at the *up‑stream* node of segment \(s\) (if the train follows its original schedule). | | \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | | \(\gamma_{t,r}\) | Indicator (0/1) whether route \(r\) is **compatible** with train \(t\) (e.g. train type, direction). Usually \(\gamma_{t,r}=1\) for all feasible routes. | | \(\kappa_{s}\) | Nominal capacity of segment \(s\) (maximum number of trains that can occupy the whole segment simultaneously when there is **no** partial blockage). | | \(\delta_{t,s}\) | Direction of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (+1 for northbound, –1 for southbound). Needed for bidirectional conflict constraints. | --- ## 3. Decision Variables | Symbol | Type | Meaning | |--------|------|---------| | \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\); exactly one route per train. | | \(y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). Occupancy is defined as “the train is somewhere inside the segment at any point of interval \(i\)”. | | \(z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) in interval \(i\) **with speed level** \(v\). For each occupied interval exactly one speed level is chosen. | | \(D_t\ge 0\) | continuous | Total **delay** of train \(t\) (minutes) relative to its planned departure. | | \(C_t\ge 0\) | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train \(t\) (kWh) – sum of \(E_{s,v}\) over all traversed segment‑interval‑speed triples. | | \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\) | continuous | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). | | \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (i.e. the moment it **enters** segment \(s\)). | --- ## 4. Objective Function \[ \boxed{ \min\; \sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(\alpha\, D_t \;+\; \beta\, C_t\Bigr) } \] *The first term penalises total delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption. By adjusting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can trade‑off punctuality against energy efficiency.* --- ## 5. Constraints ### 5.1 Route‑selection (one route per train) \[ \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1} \] \[ x_{t,r}\le \gamma_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t \tag{R2} \] ### 5.2 Linking occupancy to the chosen route If a segment \(s\) does **not** belong to route \(r\), the train cannot occupy it. \[ y_{t,s,i}\le \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in r} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{R3} \] ### 5.3 Time‑feasibility (travel time = length / speed) For each train, segment, interval and speed level we must respect the physical travel relationship. First, define the **travel time** needed to cross segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\): \[ \theta_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{v}\times 60 \qquad\text{(minutes)} \tag{def1} \] Now enforce that if a train uses speed level \(v\) on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\), the **departure** from the segment occurs exactly \(\theta_{s,v}\) minutes after the **arrival** at the segment’s upstream node. \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} \;-\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} + M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T2} \] The two inequalities together force equality when \(z_{t,s,i,v}=1\). The **departure time from segment \(s\)** is the time the train leaves the segment (i.e. the time it enters the next segment). We therefore link successive segments: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s'} \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route} \tag{T3} \] ### 5.3‑a Speed‑choice consistency Exactly one speed level is selected for each occupied interval: \[ \sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,i,v}= y_{t,s,i}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{S1} \] ### 5.4 Delay definition Delay is the difference between actual and planned departure: \[ D_t \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_t - d^{\text{planned}}_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1} \] (If early departure is allowed, we could also add \(D_t\ge 0\); the model already forces non‑negativity.) ### 5.5 Energy calculation Energy is the sum of the pre‑computed energy for each segment‑speed pair: \[ C_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I_s}\sum_{v\in V} E_{s,v}\; z_{t,s,i,v}\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1} \] ### 5.6 Capacity constraints – normal (unblocked) segments The total number of trains occupying a segment at a given interval cannot exceed its nominal capacity: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le \kappa_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s \tag{C1} \] ### 5.7 Capacity constraints – **partial blockage** When a segment \(s\) is partially blocked during a time window \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) (block \(b\in B\)), only the **unblocked capacity** \(b_s\) may be used. Let \(\mathcal{I}_b\) be the set of intervals that intersect the blockage window: \[ \mathcal{I}_b = \{\, i\in I_s \mid \text{interval }i \text{ overlaps }[\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b] \,\} \] Then: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le b_s \qquad\forall b\in B,\; i\in \mathcal{I}_b \tag{C2} \] If a segment has **no** blockage, the constraint reduces to (C1) with \(\kappa_s\). ### 5.8 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance) When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same physical track, they cannot be in the segment at the same time. Using the direction indicator \(\delta_{t,s}\in\{-1,+1\}\): \[ y_{t_1,s,i}+y_{t_2,s,i}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s,\; t_1\neq t_2\text{ with }\delta_{t_1,s}=-\delta_{t_2,s} \tag{B1} \] (If the line is double‑track, the capacity \(\kappa_s\) would be >1 and the bidirectional constraint could be omitted; the model keeps it for single‑track sections.) ### 5.9 Logical linking of departure/arrival times to route choice If a train does **not** use a segment, its arrival/departure times on that segment are irrelevant. We force them to a dummy value using a big‑M: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L2} \] These constraints simply deactivate the time variables when the segment is not on the chosen route. ### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\} \qquad\forall t,r,s,i,v \] \[ D_t\ge 0,\; C_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s \] --- ## 6. Model‑element commentary | Element | What it captures | Why it is needed | |---------|-----------------|------------------| | **Binary route‑choice variables \(x_{t,r}\)** | Determines which physical path each train will follow (different possible detours around the blocked part). | Guarantees a single feasible route per train and allows the optimizer to select alternative routes when the blockage makes the original path infeasible. | | **Occupancy binaries \(y_{t,s,i}\)** | Indicates whether train \(t\) is present on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). | Enables capacity constraints (both normal and blocked) and bidirectional conflict constraints to be expressed linearly. | | **Speed‑level binaries \(z_{t,s,i,v}\)** | Chooses a discrete speed for each train‑segment‑interval pair. | Allows the model to trade‑off travel time (higher speed → less delay) against energy consumption (higher speed → higher \(E_{s,v}\)). | | **Departure/arrival continuous times \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t,\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\)** | Real‑valued schedule times that link the binary occupancy/speed decisions to actual clock time. | Needed to enforce the physics of motion (travel time = length / speed) and to compute delay. | | **Delay variable \(D_t\)** | Measures how late train \(t\) leaves its origin compared with the planned timetable. | Directly appears in the objective with weight \(\alpha\). | | **Energy variable \(C_t\)** | Sum of energy consumptions for all traversed segment‑speed choices. | Appears in the objective with weight \(\beta\). | | **Objective \(\min \sum (\alpha D_t + \beta C_t)\)** | Minimises a weighted combination of total passenger‑service delay and operational energy cost. | Provides a single scalar criterion for the MILP solver. | | **Travel‑time constraints (T1–T3)** | Enforce that if a speed level is chosen, the time spent on the segment equals the deterministic travel time \(\theta_{s,v}\). | Guarantees feasibility of the speed‑management decisions. | | **Capacity constraints (C1, C2)** | Limit the number of trains that can be simultaneously on a segment; C2 tightens the limit during a partial blockage. | Prevents oversaturation of the line and respects the reduced capacity caused by the blockage. | | **Bidirectional conflict (B1)** | For single‑track sections, forbids two opposite‑direction trains from occupying the segment at the same interval. | Avoids head‑on collisions; essential when the line is not double‑tracked. | | **Big‑M linking constraints (R3, L1, L2, T1‑T2)** | Linearise logical implications (e.g., “if a train does not use a segment, its occupancy variables must be zero”). | Standard technique to keep the model linear while handling logical conditions. | | **Energy‑calculation constraint (E1)** | Accumulates the pre‑computed energy values for the chosen speed levels. | Provides the exact energy term needed in the objective. | | **Delay definition (D1)** | Relates the decision variable \(D_t\) to the actual departure time. | Allows the optimizer to trade‑off earlier departure (less delay) against the need to wait for capacity or to travel slower for energy savings. | --- ### How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Discretise the planning horizon into intervals of length \(\Delta\) (e.g., 1 min). For each segment compute the travel‑time \(\theta_{s,v}\) and energy \(E_{s,v}\) for every admissible speed level. Identify the blocked sub‑segments and fill the sets \(B\) and \(\mathcal{I}_b\). 2. **Parameter tuning** – Choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to reflect the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., \(\alpha=1\) €/min, \(\beta=0.02\) €/kWh). 3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The solution returns: * the selected route for each train, * the departure/arrival schedule, * the speed level for each segment‑interval, * the resulting total delay and energy consumption. The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear, the only non‑continuous variables are binaries) and therefore can be tackled by state‑of‑the‑art MILP solvers even for medium‑size railway networks (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a planning horizon of a few hours). --- **End of MILP formulation**.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1: Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the three‑dimensional problem described in the prompt: * **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives) * **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level on each track‑segment‑time‑interval) * **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window, creating a capacity/occupancy conflict) The model is written in a **canonical linear‑programming style** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints). After the formulation each component is explained in plain English. --- ## 1. Sets and Indices | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. | | \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Set of **routes** (ordered sequences of track‑segments) that a train may follow. | | \(E=\{1,\dots ,|E|\}\) | Set of **track‑segments** (physical pieces of line). | | \(I_e\) | Ordered list of **intervals** (time‑slots) on segment \(e\). For simplicity we use a uniform discretisation \(\Delta\) (e.g., 1 min). The index \(i\in I_e\) denotes the *i‑th* interval on segment \(e\). | | \(K=\{1,\dots ,K\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g., \(k=1\) = 30 km/h, \(k=2\) = 50 km/h, …). Each level has a known travel‑time per kilometre and an energy‑consumption coefficient. | | \(B\subseteq E\) | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance). | | \(U_{e,i}\subseteq [0,1]\) | Fraction of segment \(e\) that is **available** during interval \(i\). For an unblocked segment \(U_{e,i}=1\); for a blocked segment it may be \(0.5\) (half the track is closed). | --- ## 2. Parameters | Symbol | Description | |--------|-------------| | \(d_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. | | \(a_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination. | | \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment \(e\). | | \(\tau_{k}\) | **Travel‑time factor** for speed level \(k\) (minutes per kilometre). The actual travel time on segment \(e\) at speed \(k\) is \(\tau_{k} L_{e}\). | | \(\epsilon_{k}\) | **Energy‑consumption coefficient** for speed level \(k\) (kWh per kilometre). | | \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). | | \(\alpha,\beta\) | Positive weighting factors in the objective (delay vs. energy). | | \(c_{t,s}\) | Fixed cost (or penalty) for assigning train \(t\) to route \(s\) (e.g., if a route is longer). | | \(p_{e,i}\) | Binary **blockage indicator**: 1 if interval \((e,i)\) is *partially* blocked, 0 otherwise. | | \(cap_{e,i}\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy segment \(e\) during interval \(i\). For a fully open segment \(cap_{e,i}= \infty\); for a partially blocked segment it may be 1 (single‑track) or 2 (double‑track with one lane closed). | --- ## 3. Decision Variables | Variable | Type | Meaning | |----------|------|---------| | \(x_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(s\); 0 otherwise. | | \(dep_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin. | | \(arr_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination. | | \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses **the whole** interval \((e,i)\) with speed level \(k\). (If a train only uses a fraction of an interval we model it by splitting the interval – the linear formulation assumes the discretisation is fine enough.) | | \(z_{t,e,i}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(e\) during interval \(i\) (regardless of speed). This is a helper variable used for capacity/conflict constraints. | | \(E_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\). | | \(D_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay of train \(t\) (difference between actual and planned arrival). | --- ## 4. Objective Function \[ \boxed{ \min \; \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_{t}\;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T} E_{t}\;+\;\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S} c_{t,s}\,x_{t,s} } \] *The first term penalises total passenger‑delay, the second term penalises total energy use, and the third term can capture route‑selection preferences.* --- ## 5. Constraints ### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints 1. **Exactly one route per train** \[ \sum_{s\in S} x_{t,s}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T \] 2. **Link route choice to segment‑occupancy** – each route \(s\) is a known ordered list of segments \(\{e_{s,1},\dots ,e_{s,|s|}\}\). For every segment that belongs to a route we force the occupancy variables to be zero unless the route is selected: \[ \sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\; \le\; M\; x_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall e\in \text{segments}(s) \] If \(x_{t,s}=0\) the RHS is 0, thus no \(y\) can be positive. ### 5.2 Time‑feasibility (travel‑time) For each train, the time it spends on a segment equals the sum of the interval lengths it occupies, weighted by the chosen speed level. First define the **duration of interval** \(i\) on segment \(e\) (normally \(\Delta\) minutes). Because the model works with binary \(y\) that already indicates “the train uses the whole interval with speed \(k\)”, the travel‑time contributed by that interval is simply \(\Delta\). However we must guarantee that the *total* time spent on a segment equals the travel‑time implied by the speed level. The easiest linear way is to enforce that the number of intervals assigned to a segment equals the required number of intervals for the chosen speed. Let \[ N_{e,k}= \Big\lceil \frac{\tau_{k} L_{e}}{\Delta}\Big\rceil \] (the minimum number of intervals needed to travel segment \(e\) at speed level \(k\)). Then for every train‑segment pair: \[ \sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}= \sum_{k\in K} N_{e,k}\; \Big(\sum_{i\in I_{e}} y_{t,e,i,k}\Big) \qquad\text{(definition, automatically satisfied)} \] A more compact linear formulation uses a **big‑M** linking the chosen speed level to the total occupied intervals: \[ \sum_{i\in I_{e}}\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}= \sum_{k\in K} N_{e,k}\; \theta_{t,e,k} \] where we introduce auxiliary binaries \[ \theta_{t,e,k}= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if train }t\text{ uses speed }k\text{ on segment }e\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] and enforce \[ \theta_{t,e,k}\le \sum_{i\in I_{e}} y_{t,e,i,k}\le M\theta_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t,e,k \] and exactly one speed per segment: \[ \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{t,e,k}= \sum_{i\in I_{e}} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall t,e \] (If a train never occupies segment \(e\) then the RHS is 0 and all \(\theta\) are 0.) ### 5.3 Departure / Arrival relationship The arrival time equals departure plus the sum of all interval durations the train actually uses: \[ arr_{t}= dep_{t}+ \Delta\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{i\in I_{e}} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall t\in T \] where \[ z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\qquad\forall t,e,i \] ### 5.4 Delay definition \[ D_{t}= arr_{t}- a_t^{\text{orig}}\qquad\forall t\in T \] and we force non‑negativity: \[ D_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t\in T \] ### 5.5 Energy consumption Energy on a segment is the length times the coefficient of the chosen speed level: \[ E_{t}= \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in K}\epsilon_{k} L_{e}\; \theta_{t,e,k}\qquad\forall t\in T \] (If a train does not occupy a segment, the corresponding \(\theta\) is 0.) ### 5.6 Blockage / Capacity constraints For each **partially blocked** segment \(e\in B\) and each interval \(i\in I_{e}\) we limit the number of trains that may occupy the segment: \[ \sum_{t\in T} z_{t,e,i}\; \le\; cap_{e,i}\qquad\forall e\in B,\; i\in I_{e} \] The capacity \(cap_{e,i}\) is derived from the available fraction \(U_{e,i}\). For a double‑track line where one lane is closed, \(cap_{e,i}=1\); for a single‑track line with a 50 % blockage we may set \(cap_{e,i}=0\) (no train can enter) or allow a “passing window” by setting it to 1 only for certain intervals. ### 5.7 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance) If the line is **single‑track** (or a lane is closed) we must forbid two trains travelling in opposite directions on the same segment at the same time. Let \(\sigma_{t,e}\in\{+1,-1\}\) be a known parameter indicating the direction of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (+1 = northbound, –1 = southbound). Then for every segment‑interval we impose: \[ \sum_{t\in T:\,\sigma_{t,e}=+1} z_{t,e,i}\; \le\; 1 - \sum_{t\in T:\,\sigma_{t,e}=-1} z_{t,e,i}\qquad\forall e\in E,\; i\in I_{e} \] A linear equivalent uses a **pairwise** big‑M formulation: \[ z_{t,e,i}+z_{t',e,i}\le 1 \qquad\forall e,i,\; \forall (t,t')\text{ with }\sigma_{t,e}\neq\sigma_{t',e} \] Only needed when the segment is single‑track or partially blocked. ### 5.8 Speed‑profile feasibility (ramping) Trains cannot change speed arbitrarily between consecutive intervals on the same segment. For each train, segment, and consecutive intervals \(i,i+1\) we limit the change in speed level: \[ \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i,k} - \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i+1,k} \le R\qquad\forall t,e,i \] \[ \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i+1,k} - \sum_{k\in K} k\, y_{t,e,i,k} \le R\qquad\forall t,e,i \] where \(R\) is the maximum admissible “speed‑level jump” (e.g., 1 means you can only move to the next higher or lower discrete speed). ### 5.9 Logical linking of \(z\) and \(y\) \[ z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,e,i,k}\qquad\forall t,e,i \] Because \(y\) are binary, this forces \(z\) to be 1 iff the train occupies the interval with *some* speed. ### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ x_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,e,i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,e,i}\in\{0,1\},\; \theta_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\} \] \[ dep_{t},\,arr_{t},\,D_{t},\,E_{t}\ge 0\qquad\forall t \] --- ## 6. How the Model Works – Plain‑Language Walk‑through 1. **Choose a route** – each train must pick exactly one of the pre‑defined routes (binary variables \(x_{t,s}\)). 2. **Allocate time intervals** – once a route is chosen, the train is forced to occupy the corresponding track segments during a sequence of discrete time slots. The binary variables \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) decide *which* speed level the train uses while it occupies a particular interval. 3. **Respect blockage** – for segments that are partially closed, the capacity parameter \(cap_{e,i}\) limits how many trains can be on that segment at the same time. This models the fact that only the free lane(s) are usable. 4. **Avoid head‑on collisions** – on single‑track (or partially blocked) sections, the pairwise constraints forbid two trains travelling in opposite directions from occupying the same interval. 5. **Travel‑time consistency** – the number of intervals a train spends on a segment must be at least the minimum required for the chosen speed (the \(N_{e,k}\) relationship). Consequently the departure‑to‑arrival equation correctly accumulates the total travel time. 6. **Delay and energy accounting** – the model computes each train’s delay (actual arrival minus the original schedule) and its energy consumption (length × energy coefficient of the selected speed). 7. **Objective** – the solver minimizes a weighted sum of total delay and total energy, optionally adding a small penalty for using longer routes. By changing \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the railway planner can trade‑off punctuality against sustainability. --- ## 7. Full Linear Model (compact notation) \[ \begin{aligned} \min\;& \alpha\sum_{t} D_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t}E_t \;+\; \sum_{t,s}c_{t,s}x_{t,s}\\[4pt] \text{s.t. } &\sum_{s}x_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t\\ &\sum_{i,k} y_{t,e,i,k}\le M x_{t,s} &&\forall t,\; \forall e\in \text{segments}(s)\\ &\sum_{k}\theta_{t,e,k}= \sum_{i}z_{t,e,i} &&\forall t,e\\ &\sum_{i}z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k} N_{e,k}\,\theta_{t,e,k} &&\forall t,e\\ &z_{t,e,i}= \sum_{k} y_{t,e,i,k} &&\forall t,e,i\\ &arr_t = dep_t + \Delta\sum_{e,i}z_{t,e,i} &&\forall t\\ &D_t = arr_t - a_t^{\text{orig}},\; D_t\ge 0 &&\forall t\\ &E_t = \sum_{e,k}\epsilon_k L_e \theta_{t,e,k} &&\forall t\\ &\sum_{t} z_{t,e,i}\le cap_{e,i} &&\forall e\in B,\; i\\ &z_{t,e,i}+z_{t',e,i}\le 1 &&\forall e,i,\; \forall (t,t')\text{ opposite direction}\\ &\big|\sum_{k}k\,y_{t,e,i,k} - \sum_{k}k\,y_{t,e,i+1,k}\big|\le R &&\forall t,e,i\\ &x_{t,s},y_{t,e,i,k},z_{t,e,i},\theta_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\}\\ &dep_t,arr_t,D_t,E_t\ge 0 &&\forall t \end{aligned} \] All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, so the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). --- ### Remarks for a Practical Implementation * **Time‑discretisation** – choose \(\Delta\) small enough (e.g., 30 s or 1 min) so that the integer‑interval representation does not introduce large approximation errors. * **Big‑M value** – set \(M\) to a value larger than the maximum possible number of intervals a train could occupy on any route (e.g., total horizon / \(\Delta\)). * **Pre‑processing** – many \(y_{t,e,i,k}\) variables can be eliminated a priori because a train cannot reach a far‑away segment before a certain time; this reduces model size. * **Scalability** – for large networks the pairwise opposite‑direction constraints can be replaced by a **conflict‑graph** formulation with a single capacity variable per segment‑interval, which is often tighter for solvers. --- **In summary**, the formulation above captures the essential decisions (route, departure/arrival, speed level) and the operational realities of a partially blocked railway line (capacity, bidirectional conflicts, speed‑ramping). By solving the MILP the planner obtains a schedule that simultaneously minimises passenger delay and the energy used by the fleet. Model 2: Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt: * **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives) * **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level for each train on each track‑segment‑time‑interval) * **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window, creating a capacity‑conflict that must be respected). The model is written in a **standard linear‑programming notation** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints). After the formulation a short “model‑elements” commentary explains the meaning of each part and how it relates to the description. --- ## 1. Sets | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). | | \(S\) | Set of **track segments** (ordered from origin to destination). A segment may be a single line or a block of several kilometres. | | \(I_s\) | Set of **time intervals** that intersect segment \(s\). Intervals are of equal length \(\Delta\) (e.g. 1 min). Index by \(i\). | | \(V\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (discrete). Index by \(v\). Speed level \(v\) corresponds to a constant speed \(v\) km/h on the segment. | | \(R_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\) (each route is a sequence of segments). Index by \(r\). | | \(B\) | Set of **blocked sub‑segments** (partial blockages). Each element \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b_s,\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b)\) where:
• \(s\) – the segment that is partially blocked,
• \(b_s\) – the *capacity* of the unblocked part (maximum number of trains that can occupy the segment simultaneously),
• \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) – the time window of the blockage. | --- ## 2. Parameters | Symbol | Description | |--------|-------------| | \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). | | \(\underline{v}_v,\ \overline{v}_v\) | Minimum / maximum speed (km/h) that can be represented by speed level \(v\). In a linear model we treat each level as a *single* speed value \(v\) (e.g. \(v\in\{30,50,80,120\}\) km/h). | | \(\alpha\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g. 1 €/min). | | \(\beta\) | Weight for energy consumption in the objective (e.g. 0.01 €/kWh). | | \(E_{s,v}\) | Energy (kWh) consumed by a train traversing segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\). Usually \(E_{s,v}=c_1 L_s v^2 + c_2 L_s /v\) linearised by pre‑computing the value for each discrete speed. | | \(d^{\text{planned}}_t\) | Planned (original) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes from a reference). | | \(a^{\text{planned}}_{t,s}\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at the *up‑stream* node of segment \(s\) (if the train follows its original schedule). | | \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | | \(\gamma_{t,r}\) | Indicator (0/1) whether route \(r\) is **compatible** with train \(t\) (e.g. train type, direction). Usually \(\gamma_{t,r}=1\) for all feasible routes. | | \(\kappa_{s}\) | Nominal capacity of segment \(s\) (maximum number of trains that can occupy the whole segment simultaneously when there is **no** partial blockage). | | \(\delta_{t,s}\) | Direction of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (+1 for northbound, –1 for southbound). Needed for bidirectional conflict constraints. | --- ## 3. Decision Variables | Symbol | Type | Meaning | |--------|------|---------| | \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\); exactly one route per train. | | \(y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **occupies** segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). Occupancy is defined as “the train is somewhere inside the segment at any point of interval \(i\)”. | | \(z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) in interval \(i\) **with speed level** \(v\). For each occupied interval exactly one speed level is chosen. | | \(D_t\ge 0\) | continuous | Total **delay** of train \(t\) (minutes) relative to its planned departure. | | \(C_t\ge 0\) | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train \(t\) (kWh) – sum of \(E_{s,v}\) over all traversed segment‑interval‑speed triples. | | \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t\) | continuous | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). | | \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\) (i.e. the moment it **enters** segment \(s\)). | --- ## 4. Objective Function \[ \boxed{ \min\; \sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(\alpha\, D_t \;+\; \beta\, C_t\Bigr) } \] *The first term penalises total delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption. By adjusting \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) the planner can trade‑off punctuality against energy efficiency.* --- ## 5. Constraints ### 5.1 Route‑selection (one route per train) \[ \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1} \] \[ x_{t,r}\le \gamma_{t,r}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t \tag{R2} \] ### 5.2 Linking occupancy to the chosen route If a segment \(s\) does **not** belong to route \(r\), the train cannot occupy it. \[ y_{t,s,i}\le \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in r} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{R3} \] ### 5.3 Time‑feasibility (travel time = length / speed) For each train, segment, interval and speed level we must respect the physical travel relationship. First, define the **travel time** needed to cross segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\): \[ \theta_{s,v}= \frac{L_s}{v}\times 60 \qquad\text{(minutes)} \tag{def1} \] Now enforce that if a train uses speed level \(v\) on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\), the **departure** from the segment occurs exactly \(\theta_{s,v}\) minutes after the **arrival** at the segment’s upstream node. \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} \;-\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} + \theta_{s,v} + M\bigl(1-z_{t,s,i,v}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s,i,v \tag{T2} \] The two inequalities together force equality when \(z_{t,s,i,v}=1\). The **departure time from segment \(s\)** is the time the train leaves the segment (i.e. the time it enters the next segment). We therefore link successive segments: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s'} \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route} \tag{T3} \] ### 5.3‑a Speed‑choice consistency Exactly one speed level is selected for each occupied interval: \[ \sum_{v\in V} z_{t,s,i,v}= y_{t,s,i}\qquad\forall t,s,i \tag{S1} \] ### 5.4 Delay definition Delay is the difference between actual and planned departure: \[ D_t \ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_t - d^{\text{planned}}_t \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1} \] (If early departure is allowed, we could also add \(D_t\ge 0\); the model already forces non‑negativity.) ### 5.5 Energy calculation Energy is the sum of the pre‑computed energy for each segment‑speed pair: \[ C_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I_s}\sum_{v\in V} E_{s,v}\; z_{t,s,i,v}\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1} \] ### 5.6 Capacity constraints – normal (unblocked) segments The total number of trains occupying a segment at a given interval cannot exceed its nominal capacity: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le \kappa_{s}\qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s \tag{C1} \] ### 5.7 Capacity constraints – **partial blockage** When a segment \(s\) is partially blocked during a time window \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) (block \(b\in B\)), only the **unblocked capacity** \(b_s\) may be used. Let \(\mathcal{I}_b\) be the set of intervals that intersect the blockage window: \[ \mathcal{I}_b = \{\, i\in I_s \mid \text{interval }i \text{ overlaps }[\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b] \,\} \] Then: \[ \sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,i} \le b_s \qquad\forall b\in B,\; i\in \mathcal{I}_b \tag{C2} \] If a segment has **no** blockage, the constraint reduces to (C1) with \(\kappa_s\). ### 5.8 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance) When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same physical track, they cannot be in the segment at the same time. Using the direction indicator \(\delta_{t,s}\in\{-1,+1\}\): \[ y_{t_1,s,i}+y_{t_2,s,i}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; i\in I_s,\; t_1\neq t_2\text{ with }\delta_{t_1,s}=-\delta_{t_2,s} \tag{B1} \] (If the line is double‑track, the capacity \(\kappa_s\) would be >1 and the bidirectional constraint could be omitted; the model keeps it for single‑track sections.) ### 5.9 Logical linking of departure/arrival times to route choice If a train does **not** use a segment, its arrival/departure times on that segment are irrelevant. We force them to a dummy value using a big‑M: \[ \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L1} \] \[ \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \le M\bigl(1-\sum_{r:\; s\in r}x_{t,r}\bigr) \qquad\forall t,s \tag{L2} \] These constraints simply deactivate the time variables when the segment is not on the chosen route. ### 5.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,i,v}\in\{0,1\} \qquad\forall t,r,s,i,v \] \[ D_t\ge 0,\; C_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{dep}}_t\ge 0,\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\ge 0 \qquad\forall t,s \] --- ## 6. Model‑element commentary | Element | What it captures | Why it is needed | |---------|-----------------|------------------| | **Binary route‑choice variables \(x_{t,r}\)** | Determines which physical path each train will follow (different possible detours around the blocked part). | Guarantees a single feasible route per train and allows the optimizer to select alternative routes when the blockage makes the original path infeasible. | | **Occupancy binaries \(y_{t,s,i}\)** | Indicates whether train \(t\) is present on segment \(s\) during interval \(i\). | Enables capacity constraints (both normal and blocked) and bidirectional conflict constraints to be expressed linearly. | | **Speed‑level binaries \(z_{t,s,i,v}\)** | Chooses a discrete speed for each train‑segment‑interval pair. | Allows the model to trade‑off travel time (higher speed → less delay) against energy consumption (higher speed → higher \(E_{s,v}\)). | | **Departure/arrival continuous times \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_t,\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\)** | Real‑valued schedule times that link the binary occupancy/speed decisions to actual clock time. | Needed to enforce the physics of motion (travel time = length / speed) and to compute delay. | | **Delay variable \(D_t\)** | Measures how late train \(t\) leaves its origin compared with the planned timetable. | Directly appears in the objective with weight \(\alpha\). | | **Energy variable \(C_t\)** | Sum of energy consumptions for all traversed segment‑speed choices. | Appears in the objective with weight \(\beta\). | | **Objective \(\min \sum (\alpha D_t + \beta C_t)\)** | Minimises a weighted combination of total passenger‑service delay and operational energy cost. | Provides a single scalar criterion for the MILP solver. | | **Travel‑time constraints (T1–T3)** | Enforce that if a speed level is chosen, the time spent on the segment equals the deterministic travel time \(\theta_{s,v}\). | Guarantees feasibility of the speed‑management decisions. | | **Capacity constraints (C1, C2)** | Limit the number of trains that can be simultaneously on a segment; C2 tightens the limit during a partial blockage. | Prevents oversaturation of the line and respects the reduced capacity caused by the blockage. | | **Bidirectional conflict (B1)** | For single‑track sections, forbids two opposite‑direction trains from occupying the segment at the same interval. | Avoids head‑on collisions; essential when the line is not double‑tracked. | | **Big‑M linking constraints (R3, L1, L2, T1‑T2)** | Linearise logical implications (e.g., “if a train does not use a segment, its occupancy variables must be zero”). | Standard technique to keep the model linear while handling logical conditions. | | **Energy‑calculation constraint (E1)** | Accumulates the pre‑computed energy values for the chosen speed levels. | Provides the exact energy term needed in the objective. | | **Delay definition (D1)** | Relates the decision variable \(D_t\) to the actual departure time. | Allows the optimizer to trade‑off earlier departure (less delay) against the need to wait for capacity or to travel slower for energy savings. | --- ### How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Discretise the planning horizon into intervals of length \(\Delta\) (e.g., 1 min). For each segment compute the travel‑time \(\theta_{s,v}\) and energy \(E_{s,v}\) for every admissible speed level. Identify the blocked sub‑segments and fill the sets \(B\) and \(\mathcal{I}_b\). 2. **Parameter tuning** – Choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to reflect the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., \(\alpha=1\) €/min, \(\beta=0.02\) €/kWh). 3. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The solution returns: * the selected route for each train, * the departure/arrival schedule, * the speed level for each segment‑interval, * the resulting total delay and energy consumption. The model is **linear** (all constraints are linear, the only non‑continuous variables are binaries) and therefore can be tackled by state‑of‑the‑art MILP solvers even for medium‑size railway networks (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a planning horizon of a few hours). --- **End of MILP formulation**.

Sets | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). | | \(S\) | Set of track‑segments, indexed by \(s\). | | \(I_s\) | Set of equal‑length time‑intervals that intersect segment \(s\) (interval length \(\Delta\)). | | \(V\) | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by \(v\). | | \(R_t\) | Feasible routes for train \(t\); each route is an ordered list of segments. | | \(B\) | Set of **partial‑blockage** events. Each \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b_s,\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b)\) where:
• \(s\) – blocked segment,
• \(b_s\) – capacity of the unblocked lane (max. trains simultaneously),
• \([\tau^{\text{start}}_b,\tau^{\text{end}}_b]\) – blockage time window. | --- ### 2. Parameters | Symbol | Description | |--------|-------------| | \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). | | \(\theta_{s,v}= \dfrac{L_s}{v}\times 60\) | Travel time (min) to cross segment \(s\) at speed level \(v\) (km/h). | | \(E_{s,v}\) | Energy (kWh) consumed on segment \(s\) at speed \(v\) (pre‑computed). | | \(d^{\text{plan}}_t\) | Planned departure time of train \(t\) (min from reference). | | \(\alpha\) | Weight of total delay in the objective (€/min). | | \(\beta\) | Weight of total energy in the objective (€/kWh). | | \(\kappa_s\) | Nominal capacity of segment \(s\) (max. trains simultaneously when no blockage). | | \(\delta_{t,s}\in\{-1,+1\}\) | Direction of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (‑1 = southbound, +1 = northbound). | | \(M\) | Large constant (e.g., 10 000) for big‑M linearisation. | | \(\gamma_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | Feasibility indicator: 1 if route \(r\) can be used by train \(t\). | --- ### 3.
