Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the problem described in the prompt – integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked.  
The model is written in a **compact, “linear‑algebraic” notation** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints).  After the formulation a short **explanation of each element** is provided so that the model can be implemented directly in a solver such as CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**  | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**  | Set of line‑segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *s* |
| **K**  | Set of admissible speed‑levels (discrete), indexed by *k* (e.g., 0 = stop, 1 = low, …, Kmax) |
| **B ⊆ S** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the segment that is partially unavailable) |
| **P**  | Set of possible **routes** (different paths a train may take to reach its destination).  Each route *p* is a ordered list of segments.  Index *p* ∈ **P**. |
| **D**  | Set of directions on a segment: **F** (forward) and **R** (reverse).  Used for bidirectional conflict constraints. |

Additional derived sets  

* `S_t(p)` – set of segments traversed by train *t* if it follows route *p*.  
* `K_s` – admissible speed‑levels on segment *s* (normally equal to **K**, but may be reduced on blocked segments).  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| `L_s` | Length of segment *s* (km) | km |
| `τ_s^k` | Travel time on segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (deterministic, pre‑computed) | minutes |
| `e_t` | Earliest possible departure time of train *t* (schedule) | min |
| `d_t` | Desired (planned) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination | min |
| `w_delay` | Weight for total delay in the objective | $/min |
| `w_energy` | Weight for total energy consumption in the objective | $/energy‑unit |
| `E_s^k` | Energy consumption on segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (e.g., kWh) | kWh |
| `M` | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | – |
| `Cap_s` | Capacity of segment *s* (max number of trains that can occupy it simultaneously).  Usually 1 for a single‑track line. | trains |
| `Δ_s` | Maximum allowed occupancy time on a blocked segment *s* ∈ **B** (the “free window” left after the blockage). | min |
| `β_{s,d}` | Direction of travel on segment *s* for a train moving in direction *d* (F or R).  Used to forbid opposite‑direction conflict on a single‑track segment. | – |
| `γ_{t}` | Penalty factor for a train that is forced to reroute (optional). | $ |

All parameters are assumed known before solving (they can be derived from the timetable, infrastructure data, and a simple physics‑based energy model).

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| `x_{t,p}` | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *p*, 0 otherwise |
| `a_{t,s}` | continuous ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e., when it enters *s*) |
| `d_{t,s}` | continuous ≥0 | **Departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e., when it leaves *s*) |
| `y_{t,s,k}` | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed‑level *k* |
| `z_{t}` | continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at its final destination and the planned arrival `d_t`) |
| `e_{t}` | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of segment‑level energy) |
| `b_{t,s}` | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies segment *s* at any time (used for capacity/conflict constraints) |

*Note*: The model is linear because the product of a binary and a continuous variable never appears; all logical relations are expressed with big‑M constraints.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T} e_{t}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{p\in P}\gamma_{t}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{optional reroute penalty (if desired)}}
\]

The objective simultaneously **reduces passenger‑oriented delay** and **energy consumption**.  By adjusting the weights the planner can prioritize one criterion over the other.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑level variables**  

For every train *t* and segment *s*:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{p\in P:\, s\in S_t(p)} x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If a segment does **not** belong to the selected route, the RHS is 0, forcing all `y_{t,s,k}` to 0.

### 5.2 Speed‑level feasibility  

3. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= b_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

`b_{t,s}` becomes 1 when the segment is used (i.e., when any speed level is chosen).

### 5.3 Time‑propagation (travel‑time) constraints  

4. **Departure = arrival + travel time (selected speed)**  

\[
d_{t,s} \;=\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{s}^{k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

Because exactly one `y_{t,s,k}` is 1, the sum picks the appropriate travel time.

5. **Link successive segments**  

Let `next(s)` denote the downstream segment that follows *s* on the chosen route (if any). For each train *t* and each pair *(s, next(s))* that belong to the same route:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with } \text{next}(s) \text{ defined}
\]

This enforces **causality** (a train cannot start the next segment before it has finished the previous one).

6. **Release time (earliest departure)**  

\[
a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}} \;\ge\; e_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

where `s_origin` is the first segment of the selected route.

### 5.7 Delay definition  

7. **Delay at final destination**  

Let `s_last(t)` be the last segment of the selected route for train *t*. The actual arrival at the final station is `d_{t,s_last(t)}`.  

\[
z_{t} \;=\; d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)} } \;-\; d_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

If the model permits early arrival (negative delay), you may replace with a non‑negative formulation:

\[
z_{t} \ge d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)} - d_{t}, \quad
z_{t} \ge 0
\]

### 5.8 Energy calculation  

8. **Energy consumption per train**  

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K} E_{s}^{k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

### 5.9 Capacity / block‑occupancy constraints  

9. **Single‑track capacity (including blocked segments)**  

For every segment *s* and for every pair of distinct trains *(t, t')* that both use *s* (`b_{t,s}=b_{t',s}=1`), enforce a non‑overlap condition using a binary ordering variable `δ_{t,t',s}` (1 if *t* passes before *t'*).  

\[
a_{t',s} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \;-\; M\,(1-δ_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall s\in S,\; t\neq t'
\]
\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; d_{t',s} \;-\; M\,δ_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall s\in S,\; t\neq t'
\]

Only one of the two inequalities can be active; the binary `δ_{t,t',s}` decides the order.  
If the segment capacity `Cap_s` > 1, a **cumulative** (time‑indexed) formulation can be used instead, but the pairwise big‑M version works for the usual single‑track case.

10. **Partial blockage – limited occupancy window**  

For each blocked segment `s∈B` we must respect the free window `Δ_s`. Let `t_block_start` be the time at which the blockage begins (known) and `t_block_end = t_block_start + Δ_s` be the time when the segment becomes unavailable again.

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; t_{\text{block\_end}} \quad \text{or} \quad d_{t,s} \;\le\; t_{\text{block\_start}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

Linearised with a binary `θ_{t,s}`:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; t_{\text{block\_end}} - M\,θ_{t,s}
\]
\[
d_{t,s} \;\le\; t_{\text{block\_start}} + M\,(1-θ_{t,s})
\]

Thus each train either **passes before** the blockage starts (`θ_{t,s}=0`) or **passes after** it ends (`θ_{t,s}=1`).

### 5.10 Bidirectional conflict (if the line is single‑track and used in both directions)  

11. **Opposite‑direction exclusion**  

For any segment *s* that can be travelled in both directions, define binary `ρ_{t,s}` = 1 if train *t* traverses *s* in the forward direction, 0 otherwise (similarly for reverse). These can be derived from the route choice (`x_{t,p}`) and stored as parameters `β_{s,d}`. Then enforce:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} ρ_{t,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S \text{ with bidirectional use}
\]

or use the same pairwise ordering variables as in (9) but only for trains travelling opposite directions.

### 5.11 Speed‑level limits on blocked segments  

12. **Reduced admissible speeds on blocked segments**  

If a segment *s* is partially blocked, only a subset `K_s ⊂ K` may be feasible (e.g., lower speeds to stay within the free lane). Enforce:

\[
y_{t,s,k}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in B,\; k\notin K_s
\]

This can be written as a simple bound:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le \mathbf{1}_{\{k\in K_s\}} \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t} z_{t} \;+\; w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t} e_{t}
        \;+\; \sum_{t}\sum_{p}\gamma_{t}x_{t,p} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{p} x_{t,p}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{k} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{p:\,s\in S_t(p)} x_{t,p} &&\forall t,s\\
&\sum_{k} y_{t,s,k}= b_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k}\tau_{s}^{k} y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t,s\\
&a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \ge d_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\text{ with next(s)}\\
&a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}\ge e_{t} &&\forall t\\
&z_{t}\ge d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)}-d_{t},\; z_{t}\ge0 &&\forall t\\
&e_{t}= \sum_{s}\sum_{k}E_{s}^{k} y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t\\
&\text{(capacity / ordering constraints (9))} &&\forall s, t\neq t'\\
&\text{(blocked‑segment window constraints (10))} &&\forall t, s\in B\\
&\text{(bidirectional conflict (11))} &&\forall s\text{ with two directions}\\
&\text{(speed‑limit on blocked segments)} &&\forall t,s\in B, k\notin K_s: y_{t,s,k}=0\\
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; b_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
  δ_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\; θ_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}, z_{t}, e_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries.  The model therefore belongs to the class of **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programs (MILP)**.

---

## 7. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – compute `τ_s^k` (travel time for each speed level) and `E_s^k` (energy) from physics formulas or empirical tables.  
2. **Define routes** – enumerate all feasible routes for each train (normally the original timetable route plus a few detour alternatives).  
3. **Set blockage parameters** – `t_block_start`, `Δ_s`, and admissible speed set `K_s` for each blocked segment.  
4. **Choose weights** – `w_delay` and `w_energy` reflect the planner’s policy (e.g., 1 $/min` vs 0.05 $/kWh`).  
5. **Solve** – feed the model to any MILP solver.  The solution provides:  
   * which route each train should take (`x_{t,p}`),  
   * the speed level on every traversed segment (`y_{t,s,k}`),  
   * the exact schedule (`a_{t,s}`, `d_{t,s}`),  
   * the resulting total delay and energy consumption.  

6. **Post‑processing** – translate the binary speed‑level decisions back into actual speed values (e.g., 0 km/h, 30 km/h, 60 km/h, …) and generate a new timetable for the railway traffic‑control system.

---

### Remarks  

* The model is **linear** because the product of a binary (`y_{t,s,k}`) and a constant (`τ_s^k`, `E_s^k`) is allowed; no product of two decision variables appears.  
* If the number of routes *P* is huge, a **column‑generation** (branch‑and‑price) approach can be employed, but the formulation above already captures the essential logic.  
* The big‑M constant `M` should be chosen tight enough (e.g., larger than the planning horizon) to avoid numerical difficulties.  
* Extensions (e.g., crew‑assignment, rolling‑stock constraints, passenger‑connection penalties) can be added by introducing extra variables and linear constraints without breaking the MILP nature.

---  

**In short:** the presented MILP simultaneously decides *where* each train goes, *how fast* it travels on each segment, and *when* it occupies each piece of track, while respecting the partial blockage, capacity, and direction‑conflict rules, and it minimizes a weighted sum of delay and energy. This model can be directly implemented and solved with any modern MILP optimizer.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** that captures the problem described in the prompt – integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked.  
The model is written in a textbook‑style notation (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints) and each component is explained in plain English right after the formulation.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of line segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete) that a train may travel on a segment, indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(B\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (the segment that is partially unavailable). |
| \\(R_t\\) | Set of admissible **routes** for train \\(t\\) (different possible detours around the blocked segment). Each route \\(r\\in R_t\\) is a ordered list of segments. |
| \\(P\\) | Set of **pairwise conflict directions** (e.g., “same‑track opposite direction”). Used for bidirectional conflict constraints. |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical units |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\). | km |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed associated with level \\(k\\). | km/h |
| \\(e_k\\) | Energy consumption per km when travelling at speed level \\(k\\). | kWh/km |
| \\(c^{\text{delay}}_t\\) | Penalty weight for train \\(t\\)’s delay (e.g., monetary cost per hour). | $/h |
| \\(c^{\text{energy}}_t\\) | Penalty weight for train \\(t\)’s energy use (e.g., $/kWh). | $/kWh |
| \\(a^{\text{orig}}_t\\) | Original (planned) arrival time at the **final destination** of train \\(t\\). | minutes from a reference time |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). |
| \\(g_{s}^{\text{cap}}\\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy segment \\(s\\) simultaneously (normally 1 for a single‑track line). |
| \\(h_{s}^{\text{blocked}}\\) | Length of the blocked portion of segment \\(s\\) (0 if not blocked). |
| \\(p_{s}^{\text{avail}}\\) | Fraction of segment \\(s\\) that remains usable ( \\(p_{s}^{\text{avail}} = 1 - h_{s}^{\text{blocked}}/L_s\\) ). |
| \\(d_{t}^{\text{min}}\\) | Minimum dwell time (stop) at stations for train \\(t\\). | min |
| \\(d_{t}^{\text{max}}\\) | Maximum dwell time (e.g., for passenger boarding). | min |
| \\(\tau_{st}^{\text{min}}\\) | Minimum travel time for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) when travelling at the **maximum** admissible speed \\(v_{\max}\\). | min |
| \\(\tau_{st}^{\text{max}}\\) | Maximum travel time for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) when travelling at the **minimum** admissible speed \\(v_{\min}\\). | min |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{tr}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses route \\(r\\in R_t\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{t s k}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t s}\\) | Continuous ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream node** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t s}\\) | Continuous ≥0 | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from the **down‑stream node** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(z_{t s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) actually **occupies** (i.e., enters) segment \\(s\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(E_t\\) | Continuous ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train \\(t\\). |
| \\(D_t\\) | Continuous ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(t\\) (difference between actual arrival at final destination and original schedule). |

*Note*: Because a route is a predefined ordered list of segments, the binary variables \\(x_{tr}\\) together with the definition of \\(z_{ts}\\) guarantee that a train can only travel on the segments belonging to the chosen route.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{t\in T}\Bigl( c^{\text{delay}}_t \, D_t \;+\; c^{\text{energy}}_t \, E_t \Bigr)
}
\]

*Explanation*:  
- The first term penalises **total delay** (in minutes or hours) weighted by a train‑specific cost.  
- The second term penalises **energy consumption** (kWh) weighted by a cost factor.  
The model therefore seeks a trade‑off between keeping trains on time and using as little energy as possible.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{tr}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑occupancy**  

   For every train‑segment pair, let \\(\delta_{sr}=1\\) if segment \\(s\\) belongs to route \\(r\\), otherwise 0.  

   \[
   z_{ts}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\delta_{sr}\,x_{tr} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   Hence \\(z_{ts}=1\\) only if the chosen route contains segment \\(s\\).

### 5.2 Speed‑level assignment  

3. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} y_{tsk}=z_{ts} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   If a train does not occupy a segment (\\(z_{ts}=0\\)), all \\(y_{tsk}=0\\).

### 5.3 Time‑propagation (travel‑time feasibility)  

4. **Travel time on a segment**  

   The travel time on segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\) when speed level \\(k\\) is used is  

   \[
   \theta_{tsk}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\; \text{(in hours)}\times 60 \;\text{(to convert to minutes)}.
   \]

   Using a big‑M formulation we enforce the relationship between arrival, departure and speed choice:

   \[
   d_{ts} \;\ge\; a_{ts} + \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{tsk}\,y_{tsk} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{ts}) \qquad \forall t,s
   \]

   \[
   d_{ts} \;\le\; a_{ts} + \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{tsk}\,y_{tsk} \;+\; M\,(1-z_{ts}) \qquad \forall t,s
   \]

   When \\(z_{ts}=0\\) the constraints are relaxed (big‑M), otherwise they force the departure time to be exactly arrival + travel time.

5. **Dwell (station stop) time**  

   For every **station node** (i.e., the downstream end of a segment that ends at a station) we impose a minimum and maximum dwell:

   \[
   d_{t,s_{\text{station}}} - a_{t,s_{\text{station}}} \;\ge\; d_{t}^{\text{min}} \qquad \forall t
   \]

   \[
   d_{t,s_{\text{station}}} - a_{t,s_{\text{station}}} \;\le\; d_{t}^{\text{max}} \qquad \forall t
   \]

   (If a segment does not end at a station, the dwell constraints are omitted.)

### 5.4 Blockage feasibility  

6. **Reduced usable length on blocked segments**  

   When a segment \\(s\\) is partially blocked (\\(s\in B\\)), the effective length that a train can travel at the chosen speed is reduced to \\(p_s^{\text{avail}}L_s\\). To keep the model linear we pre‑compute the **maximum admissible speed** on a blocked segment:

   \[
   v^{\text{max}}_{s}= \max\{v_k \mid L_s p_s^{\text{avail}}/v_k \le \tau_{st}^{\text{max}}\}
   \]

   Then we forbid speed levels that would require the train to travel faster than the reduced capacity:

   \[
   y_{tsk}=0 \qquad \forall t,\; s\in B,\; k\in K \text{ with } v_k > v^{\text{max}}_{s}
   \]

   (Implemented as a set of binary‑variable fixing constraints.)

### 5.5 Track‑capacity (single‑track) constraints  

7. **No more than one train on a segment at the same time**  

   For every pair of trains \\((t,t')\\) and segment \\(s\\) we enforce a disjunctive ordering using binary ordering variables \\(w_{tt's}\\) (1 if \\(t\\) goes before \\(t'\\) on \\(s\\)):

   \[
   a_{t's} \;\ge\; d_{ts} \;-\; M\,(1-w_{tt's}) \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   a_{ts} \;\ge\; d_{t's} \;-\; M\,w_{tt's} \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   w_{tt's} \in \{0,1\}
   \]

   This classic “big‑M” disjunction guarantees that two trains cannot occupy the same segment simultaneously.

### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (opposite‑direction)  

8. **If the line is bidirectional, opposite‑direction trains cannot meet inside a segment**  

   Let \\(P\) be the set of unordered train pairs that travel in opposite directions on the same segment. For each \\((t,t',s)\in P\\) we reuse the same ordering variables \\(w_{tt's}\\) (or introduce a new set \\(w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\\)):

   \[
   a_{t's} \;\ge\; d_{ts} \;-\; M\,(1-w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}) \qquad \forall (t,t',s)\in P
   \]

   \[
   a_{ts} \;\ge\; d_{t's} \;-\; M\,w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's} \qquad \forall (t,t',s)\in P
   \]

   (If the line is single‑track, the constraints in §5.5 already cover this case.)

### 5.7 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy consumption of a train**  

   \[
   E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} e_k \, L_s \, y_{tsk} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

   Because \\(y_{tsk}\\) is 1 only for the speed level actually used on a traversed segment, the expression adds the energy per kilometre for that speed multiplied by the segment length.

### 5.8 Delay definition  

10. **Delay at final destination**  

    Let \\(s^{\text{last}}_t\\) be the last segment on the chosen route of train \\(t\\). The arrival time at the final destination is the departure time from that segment (or the arrival time at the downstream node, whichever is convenient). Using the route‑choice variable we can write:

    \[
    a_{t}^{\text{final}} = \sum_{s\in S} a_{ts}\,z_{ts} \quad\text{(the arrival time at the downstream node of the last occupied segment)}.
    \]

    Then

    \[
    D_t = a_{t}^{\text{final}} - a^{\text{orig}}_t \qquad \forall t\in T
    \]

    and we enforce non‑negativity (early arrival is treated as zero delay):

    \[
    D_t \ge 0 \qquad \forall t\in T
    \]

### 5.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{tr}\in\{0,1\},\qquad y_{tsk}\in\{0,1\},\qquad z_{ts}\in\{0,1\},\\
&w_{tt's},\,w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{ts},\,d_{ts},\,E_t,\,D_t \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. How the Model Works – Narrative  

1. **Route choice** – Each train decides which detour (if any) to take around the blocked segment. The binary variables \\(x_{tr}\\) enforce that exactly one route is selected.

2. **Speed selection** – Once a route is fixed, the train must decide a discrete speed level for every segment it traverses. The binary variables \\(y_{tsk}\\) guarantee that exactly one speed level is chosen on each occupied segment.

3. **Time propagation** – Arrival and departure times are linked through the travel‑time that results from the chosen speed. Dwell‑time limits at stations are respected.

4. **Partial blockage** – For a blocked segment the usable length is reduced; consequently only speed levels that can be achieved on the shortened usable portion are allowed (constraint 6). This models the fact that a train may have to slow down or even stop while the blocked part is cleared.

5. **Capacity & conflict** – The classic “single‑track” disjunction (constraints 7) makes sure that two trains never occupy the same segment at the same instant. An additional set of disjunctions (constraints 8) handles opposite‑direction conflicts on bidirectional lines.

6. **Energy accounting** – Energy consumption is a linear function of the chosen speed level and segment length (constraint 9). Faster speeds usually have higher \\(e_k\\) values, so the model can trade‑off energy against delay.

7. **Delay measurement** – The difference between the actual arrival at the final destination and the original schedule gives the delay variable \\(D_t\\). The objective penalises this delay together with the energy cost.

8. **Objective** – By minimizing the weighted sum of total delay and total energy, the optimizer finds a schedule that respects the blockage, respects safety‑critical capacity constraints, and simultaneously keeps trains as close to schedule as possible while using as little energy as feasible.

---

## 7. Remarks on Implementation  

* **Linearisation** – All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (e.g., product of binary and continuous variables) are handled by standard big‑M techniques, which keep the model within the MILP class.  
* **Scalability** – The number of binary variables grows with \\(|T|\times|R_t|\) (route choices) and \\(|T|\times|S|\times|K|\\) (speed choices). For large networks one may use column‑generation for routes or aggregate speed levels to keep the model tractable.  
* **Big‑M selection** – Choose \\(M\\) just large enough to dominate the longest possible schedule (e.g., a few hours beyond the horizon) to avoid numerical difficulties.  
* **Solver** – Any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, or the open‑source CBC/GLPK) can handle the formulation.  

---

### Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(c^{\text{delay}}_t D_t + c^{\text{energy}}_t E_t\Bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{tr}=1 &&\forall t\\
& z_{ts}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\delta_{sr}x_{tr} &&\forall t,s\\
& \sum_{k\in K}y_{tsk}=z_{ts} &&\forall t,s\\
& d_{ts}\ge a_{ts}+ \sum_{k}\theta_{tsk}y_{tsk} - M(1-z_{ts}) &&\forall t,s\\
& d_{ts}\le a_{ts}+ \sum_{k}\theta_{tsk}y_{tsk} + M(1-z_{ts}) &&\forall t,s\\
& \text{(dwell constraints)} &&\forall\text{station segments}\\
& y_{tsk}=0\;\; \text{if } s\in B \text{ and } v_k>v^{\max}_s &&\forall t,s,k\\
& a_{t's}\ge d_{ts} - M(1-w_{tt's}) &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& a_{ts}\ge d_{t's} - M w_{tt's} &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& w_{tt's}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& \text{(opposite‑direction constraints)} &&\forall (t,t',s)\in P\\
& E_t = \sum_{s}\sum_{k} e_k L_s y_{tsk} &&\forall t\\
& a^{\text{final}}_t = \sum_{s} a_{ts} z_{ts} &&\forall t\\
& D_t = a^{\text{final}}_t - a^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
& D_t\ge 0 &&\forall t\\
& x_{tr},y_{tsk},z_{ts},w_{tt's},w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{ts},d_{ts},E_t,D_t\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation is ready to be coded directly into a MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.) and solved with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, arrival/departure times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-profile feasibility, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the problem described in the prompt – integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management when a railway segment is partially blocked.  
The model is written in a **compact, “linear‑algebraic” notation** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints).  After the formulation a short **explanation of each element** is provided so that the model can be implemented directly in a solver such as CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**  | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**  | Set of line‑segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *s* |
| **K**  | Set of admissible speed‑levels (discrete), indexed by *k* (e.g., 0 = stop, 1 = low, …, Kmax) |
| **B ⊆ S** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the segment that is partially unavailable) |
| **P**  | Set of possible **routes** (different paths a train may take to reach its destination).  Each route *p* is a ordered list of segments.  Index *p* ∈ **P**. |
| **D**  | Set of directions on a segment: **F** (forward) and **R** (reverse).  Used for bidirectional conflict constraints. |

Additional derived sets  

* `S_t(p)` – set of segments traversed by train *t* if it follows route *p*.  
* `K_s` – admissible speed‑levels on segment *s* (normally equal to **K**, but may be reduced on blocked segments).  

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| `L_s` | Length of segment *s* (km) | km |
| `τ_s^k` | Travel time on segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (deterministic, pre‑computed) | minutes |
| `e_t` | Earliest possible departure time of train *t* (schedule) | min |
| `d_t` | Desired (planned) arrival time of train *t* at its final destination | min |
| `w_delay` | Weight for total delay in the objective | $/min |
| `w_energy` | Weight for total energy consumption in the objective | $/energy‑unit |
| `E_s^k` | Energy consumption on segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (e.g., kWh) | kWh |
| `M` | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints | – |
| `Cap_s` | Capacity of segment *s* (max number of trains that can occupy it simultaneously).  Usually 1 for a single‑track line. | trains |
| `Δ_s` | Maximum allowed occupancy time on a blocked segment *s* ∈ **B** (the “free window” left after the blockage). | min |
| `β_{s,d}` | Direction of travel on segment *s* for a train moving in direction *d* (F or R).  Used to forbid opposite‑direction conflict on a single‑track segment. | – |
| `γ_{t}` | Penalty factor for a train that is forced to reroute (optional). | $ |

All parameters are assumed known before solving (they can be derived from the timetable, infrastructure data, and a simple physics‑based energy model).

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| `x_{t,p}` | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *p*, 0 otherwise |
| `a_{t,s}` | continuous ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e., when it enters *s*) |
| `d_{t,s}` | continuous ≥0 | **Departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** node of segment *s* (i.e., when it leaves *s*) |
| `y_{t,s,k}` | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* with speed‑level *k* |
| `z_{t}` | continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at its final destination and the planned arrival `d_t`) |
| `e_{t}` | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (sum of segment‑level energy) |
| `b_{t,s}` | binary | 1 if train *t* occupies segment *s* at any time (used for capacity/conflict constraints) |

*Note*: The model is linear because the product of a binary and a continuous variable never appears; all logical relations are expressed with big‑M constraints.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T} e_{t}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{p\in P}\gamma_{t}\,x_{t,p}}_{\text{optional reroute penalty (if desired)}}
\]

The objective simultaneously **reduces passenger‑oriented delay** and **energy consumption**.  By adjusting the weights the planner can prioritize one criterion over the other.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑level variables**  

For every train *t* and segment *s*:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{p\in P:\, s\in S_t(p)} x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If a segment does **not** belong to the selected route, the RHS is 0, forcing all `y_{t,s,k}` to 0.

### 5.2 Speed‑level feasibility  

3. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= b_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

`b_{t,s}` becomes 1 when the segment is used (i.e., when any speed level is chosen).

### 5.3 Time‑propagation (travel‑time) constraints  

4. **Departure = arrival + travel time (selected speed)**  

\[
d_{t,s} \;=\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{s}^{k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

Because exactly one `y_{t,s,k}` is 1, the sum picks the appropriate travel time.

5. **Link successive segments**  

Let `next(s)` denote the downstream segment that follows *s* on the chosen route (if any). For each train *t* and each pair *(s, next(s))* that belong to the same route:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with } \text{next}(s) \text{ defined}
\]

This enforces **causality** (a train cannot start the next segment before it has finished the previous one).

6. **Release time (earliest departure)**  

\[
a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}} \;\ge\; e_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

where `s_origin` is the first segment of the selected route.

### 5.7 Delay definition  

7. **Delay at final destination**  

Let `s_last(t)` be the last segment of the selected route for train *t*. The actual arrival at the final station is `d_{t,s_last(t)}`.  

\[
z_{t} \;=\; d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)} } \;-\; d_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

If the model permits early arrival (negative delay), you may replace with a non‑negative formulation:

\[
z_{t} \ge d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)} - d_{t}, \quad
z_{t} \ge 0
\]

### 5.8 Energy calculation  

8. **Energy consumption per train**  

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K} E_{s}^{k}\, y_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

### 5.9 Capacity / block‑occupancy constraints  

9. **Single‑track capacity (including blocked segments)**  

For every segment *s* and for every pair of distinct trains *(t, t')* that both use *s* (`b_{t,s}=b_{t',s}=1`), enforce a non‑overlap condition using a binary ordering variable `δ_{t,t',s}` (1 if *t* passes before *t'*).  

\[
a_{t',s} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \;-\; M\,(1-δ_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall s\in S,\; t\neq t'
\]
\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; d_{t',s} \;-\; M\,δ_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall s\in S,\; t\neq t'
\]

Only one of the two inequalities can be active; the binary `δ_{t,t',s}` decides the order.  
If the segment capacity `Cap_s` > 1, a **cumulative** (time‑indexed) formulation can be used instead, but the pairwise big‑M version works for the usual single‑track case.

10. **Partial blockage – limited occupancy window**  

For each blocked segment `s∈B` we must respect the free window `Δ_s`. Let `t_block_start` be the time at which the blockage begins (known) and `t_block_end = t_block_start + Δ_s` be the time when the segment becomes unavailable again.

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; t_{\text{block\_end}} \quad \text{or} \quad d_{t,s} \;\le\; t_{\text{block\_start}} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

Linearised with a binary `θ_{t,s}`:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; t_{\text{block\_end}} - M\,θ_{t,s}
\]
\[
d_{t,s} \;\le\; t_{\text{block\_start}} + M\,(1-θ_{t,s})
\]

Thus each train either **passes before** the blockage starts (`θ_{t,s}=0`) or **passes after** it ends (`θ_{t,s}=1`).

### 5.10 Bidirectional conflict (if the line is single‑track and used in both directions)  

11. **Opposite‑direction exclusion**  

For any segment *s* that can be travelled in both directions, define binary `ρ_{t,s}` = 1 if train *t* traverses *s* in the forward direction, 0 otherwise (similarly for reverse). These can be derived from the route choice (`x_{t,p}`) and stored as parameters `β_{s,d}`. Then enforce:

\[
\sum_{t\in T} ρ_{t,s} \le 1 \qquad \forall s\in S \text{ with bidirectional use}
\]

or use the same pairwise ordering variables as in (9) but only for trains travelling opposite directions.

### 5.11 Speed‑level limits on blocked segments  

12. **Reduced admissible speeds on blocked segments**  

If a segment *s* is partially blocked, only a subset `K_s ⊂ K` may be feasible (e.g., lower speeds to stay within the free lane). Enforce:

\[
y_{t,s,k}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in B,\; k\notin K_s
\]

This can be written as a simple bound:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le \mathbf{1}_{\{k\in K_s\}} \qquad \forall t,s,k
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t} z_{t} \;+\; w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t} e_{t}
        \;+\; \sum_{t}\sum_{p}\gamma_{t}x_{t,p} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{p} x_{t,p}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{k} y_{t,s,k}= \sum_{p:\,s\in S_t(p)} x_{t,p} &&\forall t,s\\
&\sum_{k} y_{t,s,k}= b_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\\
&d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k}\tau_{s}^{k} y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t,s\\
&a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \ge d_{t,s} &&\forall t,s\text{ with next(s)}\\
&a_{t,s_{\text{origin}}}\ge e_{t} &&\forall t\\
&z_{t}\ge d_{t,s_{\text{last}}(t)}-d_{t},\; z_{t}\ge0 &&\forall t\\
&e_{t}= \sum_{s}\sum_{k}E_{s}^{k} y_{t,s,k} &&\forall t\\
&\text{(capacity / ordering constraints (9))} &&\forall s, t\neq t'\\
&\text{(blocked‑segment window constraints (10))} &&\forall t, s\in B\\
&\text{(bidirectional conflict (11))} &&\forall s\text{ with two directions}\\
&\text{(speed‑limit on blocked segments)} &&\forall t,s\in B, k\notin K_s: y_{t,s,k}=0\\
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\; b_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
  δ_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\},\; θ_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}, z_{t}, e_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries.  The model therefore belongs to the class of **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programs (MILP)**.

---

## 7. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – compute `τ_s^k` (travel time for each speed level) and `E_s^k` (energy) from physics formulas or empirical tables.  
2. **Define routes** – enumerate all feasible routes for each train (normally the original timetable route plus a few detour alternatives).  
3. **Set blockage parameters** – `t_block_start`, `Δ_s`, and admissible speed set `K_s` for each blocked segment.  
4. **Choose weights** – `w_delay` and `w_energy` reflect the planner’s policy (e.g., 1 $/min` vs 0.05 $/kWh`).  
5. **Solve** – feed the model to any MILP solver.  The solution provides:  
   * which route each train should take (`x_{t,p}`),  
   * the speed level on every traversed segment (`y_{t,s,k}`),  
   * the exact schedule (`a_{t,s}`, `d_{t,s}`),  
   * the resulting total delay and energy consumption.  

6. **Post‑processing** – translate the binary speed‑level decisions back into actual speed values (e.g., 0 km/h, 30 km/h, 60 km/h, …) and generate a new timetable for the railway traffic‑control system.

---

### Remarks  

* The model is **linear** because the product of a binary (`y_{t,s,k}`) and a constant (`τ_s^k`, `E_s^k`) is allowed; no product of two decision variables appears.  
* If the number of routes *P* is huge, a **column‑generation** (branch‑and‑price) approach can be employed, but the formulation above already captures the essential logic.  
* The big‑M constant `M` should be chosen tight enough (e.g., larger than the planning horizon) to avoid numerical difficulties.  
* Extensions (e.g., crew‑assignment, rolling‑stock constraints, passenger‑connection penalties) can be added by introducing extra variables and linear constraints without breaking the MILP nature.

---  

**In short:** the presented MILP simultaneously decides *where* each train goes, *how fast* it travels on each segment, and *when* it occupies each piece of track, while respecting the partial blockage, capacity, and direction‑conflict rules, and it minimizes a weighted sum of delay and energy. This model can be directly implemented and solved with any modern MILP optimizer.

The model is written in a textbook‑style notation (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints) and each component is explained in plain English right after the formulation.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of line segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \\(s\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete) that a train may travel on a segment, indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(B\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (the segment that is partially unavailable). |
| \\(R_t\\) | Set of admissible **routes** for train \\(t\\) (different possible detours around the blocked segment). Each route \\(r\\in R_t\\) is a ordered list of segments. |
| \\(P\\) | Set of **pairwise conflict directions** (e.g., “same‑track opposite direction”). Used for bidirectional conflict constraints. |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical units |
|--------|--------------|---------------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\). | km |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed associated with level \\(k\\). | km/h |
| \\(e_k\\) | Energy consumption per km when travelling at speed level \\(k\\). | kWh/km |
| \\(c^{\text{delay}}_t\\) | Penalty weight for train \\(t\\)’s delay (e.g., monetary cost per hour). | $/h |
| \\(c^{\text{energy}}_t\\) | Penalty weight for train \\(t\)’s energy use (e.g., $/kWh). | $/kWh |
| \\(a^{\text{orig}}_t\\) | Original (planned) arrival time at the **final destination** of train \\(t\\). | minutes from a reference time |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000 min). |
| \\(g_{s}^{\text{cap}}\\) | Maximum number of trains that can occupy segment \\(s\\) simultaneously (normally 1 for a single‑track line). |
| \\(h_{s}^{\text{blocked}}\\) | Length of the blocked portion of segment \\(s\\) (0 if not blocked). |
| \\(p_{s}^{\text{avail}}\\) | Fraction of segment \\(s\\) that remains usable ( \\(p_{s}^{\text{avail}} = 1 - h_{s}^{\text{blocked}}/L_s\\) ). |
| \\(d_{t}^{\text{min}}\\) | Minimum dwell time (stop) at stations for train \\(t\\). | min |
| \\(d_{t}^{\text{max}}\\) | Maximum dwell time (e.g., for passenger boarding). | min |
| \\(\tau_{st}^{\text{min}}\\) | Minimum travel time for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) when travelling at the **maximum** admissible speed \\(v_{\max}\\). | min |
| \\(\tau_{st}^{\text{max}}\\) | Maximum travel time for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) when travelling at the **minimum** admissible speed \\(v_{\min}\\). | min |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\(x_{tr}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) uses route \\(r\\in R_t\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{t s k}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t s}\\) | Continuous ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream node** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t s}\\) | Continuous ≥0 | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from the **down‑stream node** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(z_{t s}\\) | Binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) actually **occupies** (i.e., enters) segment \\(s\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(E_t\\) | Continuous ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train \\(t\\). |
| \\(D_t\\) | Continuous ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(t\\) (difference between actual arrival at final destination and original schedule). |

*Note*: Because a route is a predefined ordered list of segments, the binary variables \\(x_{tr}\\) together with the definition of \\(z_{ts}\\) guarantee that a train can only travel on the segments belonging to the chosen route.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \sum_{t\in T}\Bigl( c^{\text{delay}}_t \, D_t \;+\; c^{\text{energy}}_t \, E_t \Bigr)
}
\]

*Explanation*:  
- The first term penalises **total delay** (in minutes or hours) weighted by a train‑specific cost.  
- The second term penalises **energy consumption** (kWh) weighted by a cost factor.  
The model therefore seeks a trade‑off between keeping trains on time and using as little energy as possible.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{tr}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑occupancy**  

   For every train‑segment pair, let \\(\delta_{sr}=1\\) if segment \\(s\\) belongs to route \\(r\\), otherwise 0.  

   \[
   z_{ts}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\delta_{sr}\,x_{tr} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   Hence \\(z_{ts}=1\\) only if the chosen route contains segment \\(s\\).

### 5.2 Speed‑level assignment  

3. **Exactly one speed level on a traversed segment**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} y_{tsk}=z_{ts} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
   \]

   If a train does not occupy a segment (\\(z_{ts}=0\\)), all \\(y_{tsk}=0\\).

### 5.3 Time‑propagation (travel‑time feasibility)  

4. **Travel time on a segment**  

   The travel time on segment \\(s\\) for train \\(t\\) when speed level \\(k\\) is used is  

   \[
   \theta_{tsk}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\; \text{(in hours)}\times 60 \;\text{(to convert to minutes)}.
   \]

   Using a big‑M formulation we enforce the relationship between arrival, departure and speed choice:

   \[
   d_{ts} \;\ge\; a_{ts} + \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{tsk}\,y_{tsk} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{ts}) \qquad \forall t,s
   \]

   \[
   d_{ts} \;\le\; a_{ts} + \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{tsk}\,y_{tsk} \;+\; M\,(1-z_{ts}) \qquad \forall t,s
   \]

   When \\(z_{ts}=0\\) the constraints are relaxed (big‑M), otherwise they force the departure time to be exactly arrival + travel time.

5. **Dwell (station stop) time**  

   For every **station node** (i.e., the downstream end of a segment that ends at a station) we impose a minimum and maximum dwell:

   \[
   d_{t,s_{\text{station}}} - a_{t,s_{\text{station}}} \;\ge\; d_{t}^{\text{min}} \qquad \forall t
   \]

   \[
   d_{t,s_{\text{station}}} - a_{t,s_{\text{station}}} \;\le\; d_{t}^{\text{max}} \qquad \forall t
   \]

   (If a segment does not end at a station, the dwell constraints are omitted.)

### 5.4 Blockage feasibility  

6. **Reduced usable length on blocked segments**  

   When a segment \\(s\\) is partially blocked (\\(s\in B\\)), the effective length that a train can travel at the chosen speed is reduced to \\(p_s^{\text{avail}}L_s\\). To keep the model linear we pre‑compute the **maximum admissible speed** on a blocked segment:

   \[
   v^{\text{max}}_{s}= \max\{v_k \mid L_s p_s^{\text{avail}}/v_k \le \tau_{st}^{\text{max}}\}
   \]

   Then we forbid speed levels that would require the train to travel faster than the reduced capacity:

   \[
   y_{tsk}=0 \qquad \forall t,\; s\in B,\; k\in K \text{ with } v_k > v^{\text{max}}_{s}
   \]

   (Implemented as a set of binary‑variable fixing constraints.)

### 5.5 Track‑capacity (single‑track) constraints  

7. **No more than one train on a segment at the same time**  

   For every pair of trains \\((t,t')\\) and segment \\(s\\) we enforce a disjunctive ordering using binary ordering variables \\(w_{tt's}\\) (1 if \\(t\\) goes before \\(t'\\) on \\(s\\)):

   \[
   a_{t's} \;\ge\; d_{ts} \;-\; M\,(1-w_{tt's}) \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   a_{ts} \;\ge\; d_{t's} \;-\; M\,w_{tt's} \qquad \forall t<t',\; s\in S
   \]

   \[
   w_{tt's} \in \{0,1\}
   \]

   This classic “big‑M” disjunction guarantees that two trains cannot occupy the same segment simultaneously.

### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (opposite‑direction)  

8. **If the line is bidirectional, opposite‑direction trains cannot meet inside a segment**  

   Let \\(P\) be the set of unordered train pairs that travel in opposite directions on the same segment. For each \\((t,t',s)\in P\\) we reuse the same ordering variables \\(w_{tt's}\\) (or introduce a new set \\(w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\\)):

   \[
   a_{t's} \;\ge\; d_{ts} \;-\; M\,(1-w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}) \qquad \forall (t,t',s)\in P
   \]

   \[
   a_{ts} \;\ge\; d_{t's} \;-\; M\,w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's} \qquad \forall (t,t',s)\in P
   \]

   (If the line is single‑track, the constraints in §5.5 already cover this case.)

### 5.7 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy consumption of a train**  

   \[
   E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} e_k \, L_s \, y_{tsk} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \]

   Because \\(y_{tsk}\\) is 1 only for the speed level actually used on a traversed segment, the expression adds the energy per kilometre for that speed multiplied by the segment length.

### 5.8 Delay definition  

10. **Delay at final destination**  

    Let \\(s^{\text{last}}_t\\) be the last segment on the chosen route of train \\(t\\). The arrival time at the final destination is the departure time from that segment (or the arrival time at the downstream node, whichever is convenient). Using the route‑choice variable we can write:

    \[
    a_{t}^{\text{final}} = \sum_{s\in S} a_{ts}\,z_{ts} \quad\text{(the arrival time at the downstream node of the last occupied segment)}.
    \]

    Then

    \[
    D_t = a_{t}^{\text{final}} - a^{\text{orig}}_t \qquad \forall t\in T
    \]

    and we enforce non‑negativity (early arrival is treated as zero delay):

    \[
    D_t \ge 0 \qquad \forall t\in T
    \]

### 5.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{tr}\in\{0,1\},\qquad y_{tsk}\in\{0,1\},\qquad z_{ts}\in\{0,1\},\\
&w_{tt's},\,w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{ts},\,d_{ts},\,E_t,\,D_t \ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. How the Model Works – Narrative  

1. **Route choice** – Each train decides which detour (if any) to take around the blocked segment. The binary variables \\(x_{tr}\\) enforce that exactly one route is selected.

2. **Speed selection** – Once a route is fixed, the train must decide a discrete speed level for every segment it traverses. The binary variables \\(y_{tsk}\\) guarantee that exactly one speed level is chosen on each occupied segment.

3. **Time propagation** – Arrival and departure times are linked through the travel‑time that results from the chosen speed. Dwell‑time limits at stations are respected.

4. **Partial blockage** – For a blocked segment the usable length is reduced; consequently only speed levels that can be achieved on the shortened usable portion are allowed (constraint 6). This models the fact that a train may have to slow down or even stop while the blocked part is cleared.

5. **Capacity & conflict** – The classic “single‑track” disjunction (constraints 7) makes sure that two trains never occupy the same segment at the same instant. An additional set of disjunctions (constraints 8) handles opposite‑direction conflicts on bidirectional lines.

6. **Energy accounting** – Energy consumption is a linear function of the chosen speed level and segment length (constraint 9). Faster speeds usually have higher \\(e_k\\) values, so the model can trade‑off energy against delay.

7. **Delay measurement** – The difference between the actual arrival at the final destination and the original schedule gives the delay variable \\(D_t\\). The objective penalises this delay together with the energy cost.

8. **Objective** – By minimizing the weighted sum of total delay and total energy, the optimizer finds a schedule that respects the blockage, respects safety‑critical capacity constraints, and simultaneously keeps trains as close to schedule as possible while using as little energy as feasible.

---

## 7. Remarks on Implementation  

* **Linearisation** – All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (e.g., product of binary and continuous variables) are handled by standard big‑M techniques, which keep the model within the MILP class.  
* **Scalability** – The number of binary variables grows with \\(|T|\times|R_t|\) (route choices) and \\(|T|\times|S|\times|K|\\) (speed choices). For large networks one may use column‑generation for routes or aggregate speed levels to keep the model tractable.  
* **Big‑M selection** – Choose \\(M\\) just large enough to dominate the longest possible schedule (e.g., a few hours beyond the horizon) to avoid numerical difficulties.  
* **Solver** – Any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, or the open‑source CBC/GLPK) can handle the formulation.  

---

### Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(c^{\text{delay}}_t D_t + c^{\text{energy}}_t E_t\Bigr)\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{tr}=1 &&\forall t\\
& z_{ts}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\delta_{sr}x_{tr} &&\forall t,s\\
& \sum_{k\in K}y_{tsk}=z_{ts} &&\forall t,s\\
& d_{ts}\ge a_{ts}+ \sum_{k}\theta_{tsk}y_{tsk} - M(1-z_{ts}) &&\forall t,s\\
& d_{ts}\le a_{ts}+ \sum_{k}\theta_{tsk}y_{tsk} + M(1-z_{ts}) &&\forall t,s\\
& \text{(dwell constraints)} &&\forall\text{station segments}\\
& y_{tsk}=0\;\; \text{if } s\in B \text{ and } v_k>v^{\max}_s &&\forall t,s,k\\
& a_{t's}\ge d_{ts} - M(1-w_{tt's}) &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& a_{ts}\ge d_{t's} - M w_{tt's} &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& w_{tt's}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t<t',\,s\\
& \text{(opposite‑direction constraints)} &&\forall (t,t',s)\in P\\
& E_t = \sum_{s}\sum_{k} e_k L_s y_{tsk} &&\forall t\\
& a^{\text{final}}_t = \sum_{s} a_{ts} z_{ts} &&\forall t\\
& D_t = a^{\text{final}}_t - a^{\text{orig}}_t &&\forall t\\
& D_t\ge 0 &&\forall t\\
& x_{tr},y_{tsk},z_{ts},w_{tt's},w^{\text{opp}}_{tt's}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{ts},d_{ts},E_t,D_t\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation is ready to be coded directly into a MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.) and solved with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
