y) # entry >= d_upstream - M*(1 - y) # exit <= a_downstream + M*(1 - y) # exit >= a_downstream - M*(1 - y) # We therefore loop over all routes that contain j and pick the corresponding stations. # If the segment is not used (y=0) the constraints become non‑binding. for p in P[i]: if j in route_segments[i,p]: seg_idx = route_segments[i,p].index(j) sta_up = route_stations[i,p][seg_idx] # upstream station sta_dn = route_stations[i,p][seg_idx+1] # downstream station # Bind entry/exit to the schedule of this particular orientation model.addConstr(entry <= d[i, sta_up] + M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Entry_up_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(entry >= d[i, sta_up] - M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Entry_low_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ <= a[i, sta_dn] + M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Exit_up_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ >= a[i, sta_dn] - M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Exit_low_{i}_{p}_{j}') # Now enforce the window indicator if a_win[j] < b_win[j]: # only if there is a real disruption window model.addConstr(entry >= a_win[j] - M * (1 - z[i,j]), name=f'WinEntryLow_{i}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ <= b_win[j] + M * (1 - z[i,j]), name=f'WinExitUp_{i}_{j}') else: # No disruption → force z = 0 model.addConstr(z[i,j] == 0, name=f'NoWin_{i}_{j}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.7 Avoid traversing a blocked segment during its window # If a segment is blocked (a_win < b_win) then either # - the train does NOT use the segment (y=0) OR # - it traverses it completely outside the window (z=0) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in T: for j in L: if a_win[j] < b_win[j]: model.addConstr(y[i,j] - z[i,j] <= 0, name=f'BlockAvoid_{i}_{j}') # alternatively: y[i,j] <= 1 - z[i,j] (same) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.8 Capacity constraints (one train per direction at a time) # Because we have a continuous time horizon we discretise it into # small time slices Δt (e.g. 1 minute). For each slice τ we count the # number of trains occupying segment j during τ. # To keep the script short we use a *pairwise* conflict formulation: # For any two distinct trains i ≠ k that both use segment j, # their traversals must not overlap. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Create auxiliary start/finish times on each segment (already have entry/exit above) # We reuse the entry/exit variables defined in 3.6 (they are in the model scope). # Pairwise non‑overlap (big‑M) for j in L: for i1 in T: for i2 in T: if i1 >= i2: continue # binary variable w_{i1,i2,j} = 1 ⇔ i1 finishes before i2 starts on segment j w = model.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name=f'order_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') # retrieve entry/exit variables (they were created inside the loop of 3.6, # so we need to reference them by name) entry_i1 = model.getVarByName(f'entry_{i1}_{j}') exit_i1 = model.getVarByName(f'exit_{i1}_{j}') entry_i2 = model.getVarByName(f'entry_{i2}_{j}') exit_i2 = model.getVarByName(f'exit_{i2}_{j}') # If both trains use the segment (y=1) then enforce ordering: model.addConstr(entry_i2 >= exit_i1 - M * (1 - w) - M * (2 - y[i1,j] - y[i2,j]), name=f'NoOverlap1_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') model.addConstr(entry_i1 >= exit_i2 - M * w - M * (2 - y[i1,j] - y[i2,j]), name=f'NoOverlap2_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') # w can be either 0 or 1, the big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when # at least one of the trains does not use the segment. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.9 Speed limits (already set in variable definition) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # (nothing to add – v already bounded by v_min, v_max) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 4. OBJECTIVE # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Total delay = Σ_i (arrival at last station – scheduled arrival) delay = gp.quicksum( a[i, route_stations[i, P[i][0]][-1]] - scheduled_arrival[i] # last station of the *first* route (all routes share the same destination) for i in T ) # Total energy = Σ_i Σ_j e[i,j] * τ[i,j] (τ is the actual travel time on segment j) energy = gp.quicksum(e[(i,j)] * tau[i,j] for i in T for j in L if (i,j) in e) # Weighting parameters (choose according to your policy) w_delay = 1.0 w_energy = 0.1 model.setObjective(w_delay * delay + w_energy * energy, GRB.MINIMIZE) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5. SOLVE # ------------------------------------------------------------------ model.Params.TimeLimit = 300 # seconds, adjust as needed model.optimize() # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 6. DISPLAY RESULTS # ------------------------------------------------------------------ if model.Status == GRB.OPTIMAL or model.Status == GRB.TIME_LIMIT: print("\n=== OBJECTIVE ===") print(f"Total weighted cost = {model.ObjVal:.2f}") print("\n=== ROUTE SELECTION ===") for i in T: for p in P[i]: if x[i,p].X > 0.5: print(f"Train {i} uses route '{p}'") print(f" Stations : {route_stations[i,p]}") print(f" Segments : {route_segments[i,p]}") print("\n=== TIMETABLE ===") for i in T: print(f"\nTrain {i}:") # find the selected route to know the order of stations sel_route = next(p for p in P[i] if x[i,p].X > 0.5) stations = route_stations[i, sel_route] for k, sta in enumerate(stations): print(f" Station {sta}: arrival = {a[i,sta].X:.1f} departure = {d[i,sta].X:.1f}") print("\n=== SPEED & ENERGY ===") for i in T: for j in L: if y[i,j].X > 0.5: print(f"Train {i} on segment {j}: speed = {v[i,j].X:.1f} km/h, travel time = {tau[i,j].X:.2f} min, energy = {e[(i,j)]*tau[i,j].X:.2f}") else: print("No feasible solution found.") ``` --- ## 3. What the Code Does | Block | Purpose | |-------|----------| | **Data section** | Define all sets, parameters and a tiny example instance (replace with your real data). | | **Variables** | `x, y, s, a, d, z, v, tau, entry, exit, w` – exactly the variables requested in the description. | | **Constraints** |
  • **One route per train** (`OneRoute`).
  • **Link segment usage** to the chosen route (`Link_y`).

Formulate an integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP for high-speed railway disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. Sets: T trains, S stations, L track segments (bidirectional), P possible routes for each train (original or rerouted). Parameters: travel time base t_{i,j} for train i on segment j, energy consumption e_{i,j} per unit time, disruption window [a_j,b_j] for blocked segment j, capacity C_j for each segment (max one train per direction at a time). Decision variables: x_{i,p}=1 if train i chooses route p, y_{i,j}=1 if train i uses segment j, start time s_i, arrival time at station k a_{i,k}, departure time d_{i,k}, binary z_{i,j}=1 if train i traverses segment j during disruption window, continuous speed v_{i,j} on segment j. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (a_{i,last}- scheduled arrival) plus total energy Σ_i Σ_j e_{i,j} * (travel time on segment j). Constraints: each train selects exactly one route, segment usage consistency, time feasibility a_{i,k}+ dwell ≤ d_{i,k}, travel time relation d_{i,k}+ t_{i,j}= a_{i,k+1} adjusted by speed v, speed limits v_min ≤ v_{i,j} ≤ v_max, if segment j is blocked during [a_j,b_j] then z_{i,j}=1 forces either reroute (y_{i,j}=0) or speed adjustment to avoid window, capacity: sum_i y_{i,j} ≤ C_j for each time slice, binary linking y and x, and big-M for conflict avoidance between opposite directions on shared track. Provide all equations.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run Python script** that builds the mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) described in the prompt. The model is written with **Gurobi‑Python** (the free academic license works as well). If you prefer an open‑source solver you can replace the `gurobipy` objects with the equivalent `pulp`/`pyomo` constructs – the formulation (sets, parameters, variables, constraints and objective) stays exactly the same. --- ## 1. High‑level Overview | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | **T** | Set of trains `i ∈ T` | | **S** | Set of stations `k ∈ S` (ordered along each route) | | **L** | Set of track segments `j ∈ L` (bidirectional) | | **P_i** | Set of admissible routes for train *i* (original + all feasible reroutings) | | **t[i,j]** | Nominal travel time of train *i* on segment *j* (at the reference speed) | | **e[i,j]** | Energy consumption rate of train *i* on segment *j* (per unit time) | | **a_win[j], b_win[j]** | Beginning / end of the disruption window on segment *j* | | **C[j]** | Capacity of segment *j* (max. one train per direction at a time) | | **v_min, v_max** | Global admissible speed limits (can be made segment‑specific) | | **M** | A big‑M constant (larger than any feasible time) | ### Decision variables | Variable | Type | Description | |----------|------|-------------| | `x[i,p]` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses route *p* | | `y[i,j]` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* traverses segment *j* (in the direction implied by the chosen route) | | `s[i]` | continuous | scheduled start time of train *i* (departure from its origin) | | `a[i,k]` | continuous | arrival time of train *i* at station *k* (according to the selected route) | | `d[i,k]` | continuous | departure time of train *i* from station *k* | | `z[i,j]` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* traverses segment *j* **inside** the disruption window | | `v[i,j]` | continuous | speed of train *i* on segment *j` (used to stretch/shorten travel time) | --- ## 2. Python / Gurobi Implementation ```python # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Integrated Train Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP # -------------------------------------------------------------- # Author: ChatGPT (generated) # Date: 2024‑06‑xx # Solver: Gurobi (free academic licence works) # -------------------------------------------------------------- import gurobipy as gp from gurobipy import GRB # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 1. INPUT DATA (replace the toy data with your real instance) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Sets T = ['T1', 'T2'] # trains S = ['S0', 'S1', 'S2', 'S3'] # stations (ordered) L = ['J1', 'J2', 'J3'] # track segments (bidirectional) # For each train i we store a list of admissible routes. # A route is a list of stations (including origin & destination) and # the corresponding list of traversed segments (direction matters). # Example: route p = {'stations': [...], 'segments': [...]} Routes = { 'T1': { 'orig': {'stations': ['S0', 'S1', 'S2', 'S3'], 'segments': ['J1', 'J2', 'J3']}, 'reroute': {'stations': ['S0', 'S2', 'S3'], 'segments': ['J2', 'J3']} # skip J1 (blocked) }, 'T2': { 'orig': {'stations': ['S0', 'S1', 'S2', 'S3'], 'segments': ['J1', 'J2', 'J3']}, 'reroute': {'stations': ['S0', 'S1', 'S3'], 'segments': ['J1', 'J3']} # bypass J2 } } # Build the set of route identifiers P = {} for i in T: P[i] = list(Routes[i].keys()) # e.g. ['orig', 'reroute'] # Nominal travel times (minutes) – base speed t = {('T1','J1'): 5, ('T1','J2'): 7, ('T1','J3'): 6, ('T2','J1'): 5, ('T2','J2'): 7, ('T2','J3'): 6} # Energy consumption rates (kWh per minute) – at reference speed e = {('T1','J1'): 2.0, ('T1','J2'): 2.5, ('T1','J3'): 2.2, ('T2','J1'): 2.0, ('T2','J2'): 2.5, ('T2','J3'): 2.2} # Disruption windows (minutes from the planning horizon start) a_win = {'J1': 30, 'J2': 40, 'J3': 0} # J3 not blocked b_win = {'J1': 70, 'J2': 80, 'J3': 0} # Segment capacities (max 1 train per direction at a time) C = {'J1': 1, 'J2': 1, 'J3': 1} # Global speed limits (km/h – only needed for scaling, we keep them as factors) v_min = 200.0 v_max = 350.0 # Dwell time at stations (minutes) – can be made train‑specific dwell = 2.0 # Scheduled (planned) arrival time at the final station (used for delay calculation) scheduled_arrival = {'T1': 30, 'T2': 30} # Big‑M (larger than any feasible time, e.g. horizon = 500 min) M = 500.0 # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 2. MODEL # ------------------------------------------------------------------ model = gp.Model('TrainRescheduleSpeedMgmt') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 2.1 Decision variables # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # x[i,p] – route selection x = model.addVars(T, P, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name='x') # y[i,j] – segment usage (derived from route selection) y = model.addVars(T, L, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name='y') # start time of each train s = model.addVars(T, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name='s') # arrival / departure at each station (we will create them only for stations that appear in at least one route) a = model.addVars(T, S, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name='a') d = model.addVars(T, S, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name='d') # z[i,j] – traverses segment inside disruption window z = model.addVars(T, L, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name='z') # speed on each traversed segment v = model.addVars(T, L, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=v_min, ub=v_max, name='v') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 2.2 Helper dictionaries for quick lookup # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # For each train i and route p we store the ordered list of stations and segments route_stations = {(i,p): Routes[i][p]['stations'] for i in T for p in P[i]} route_segments = {(i,p): Routes[i][p]['segments'] for i in T for p in P[i]} # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3. CONSTRAINTS # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.1 Each train selects exactly one route # ------------------------------------------------------------------ model.addConstrs((gp.quicksum(x[i,p] for p in P[i]) == 1 for i in T), name='OneRoute') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.2 Link y[i,j] (segment usage) with the chosen route # y[i,j] = 1 iff the selected route contains segment j # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in T: for j in L: # sum of x over routes that contain j routes_using_j = [p for p in P[i] if j in route_segments[i,p]] model.addConstr(y[i,j] == gp.quicksum(x[i,p] for p in routes_using_j), name=f'Link_y_{i}_{j}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.3 Time feasibility at stations (arrival → dwell → departure) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in T: for k in S: model.addConstr(d[i,k] >= a[i,k] + dwell, name=f'Dwell_{i}_{k}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.4 Travel‑time relationship between consecutive stations on the chosen route # d(prev_station) + travel_time = a(next_station) # travel_time = t[i,j] * (v_ref / v[i,j]) → linearised with big‑M: # a_next >= d_prev + t[i,j] * (v_ref / v[i,j]) - M*(1 - y[i,j]) # Because v appears in denominator, we use a linear approximation: # travel_time = t[i,j] * (v_ref / v[i,j]) ≈ t[i,j] * (v_ref) * (1/v[i,j]) # For a pure MILP we replace the fraction by a new continuous variable τ[i,j] (travel time) # and enforce τ[i,j] * v[i,j] = t[i,j] * v_ref → linearised with McCormick envelopes # For simplicity in this script we assume speed is *fixed* at the reference speed, # i.e. τ[i,j] = t[i,j] (the model can be extended with the McCormick envelopes if needed). # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Here we keep the linear version: travel time = t[i,j] * (v_ref / v[i,j]) # To stay linear we treat v[i,j] as a *scaling factor* α[i,j] ∈ [v_min/v_ref, v_max/v_ref] # and write travel_time = t[i,j] / α[i,j]. This still yields a bilinear term. # For a pure MILP we therefore *fix* speed to the reference speed (v_ref) and later # you can replace the block with a piecewise‑linear approximation. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ v_ref = 300.0 # reference speed (km/h) used for the nominal travel times # Create auxiliary travel‑time variable τ[i,j] (continuous) tau = model.addVars(T, L, vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name='tau') # Relate τ to speed (linearised by big‑M, i.e. τ = t[i,j] when y=1, otherwise τ=0) for i in T: for j in L: # When segment is used (y=1) enforce τ = t[i,j] * v_ref / v[i,j] # Linearisation: τ >= t[i,j] * v_ref / v_max - M*(1-y) # τ <= t[i,j] * v_ref / v_min + M*(1-y) model.addConstr(tau[i,j] >= (t[(i,j)] * v_ref) / v_max - M * (1 - y[i,j]), name=f'tau_low_{i}_{j}') model.addConstr(tau[i,j] <= (t[(i,j)] * v_ref) / v_min + M * (1 - y[i,j]), name=f'tau_up_{i}_{j}') # Now enforce the station‑to‑station timing using τ for i in T: for p in P[i]: stations = route_stations[i,p] segments = route_segments[i,p] # The route is selected only if x[i,p]=1, otherwise the constraints are relaxed with big‑M for idx in range(len(segments)): seg = segments[idx] sta_prev = stations[idx] # station before the segment sta_next = stations[idx+1] # station after the segment # a_next >= d_prev + τ - M*(1 - x[i,p]) model.addConstr(a[i, sta_next] >= d[i, sta_prev] + tau[i, seg] - M * (1 - x[i, p]), name=f'TimeCons_{i}_{p}_{seg}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.5 Origin / start time linking # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # For each train, the first departure equals its start time s[i] for i in T: first_station = route_stations[i, P[i][0]][0] # origin station (same for all routes) model.addConstr(d[i, first_station] == s[i], name=f'Start_{i}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.6 Disruption‑window indicator z[i,j] # z = 1 ⇔ train i traverses segment j *and* the traversal interval overlaps [a_win,b_win] # We linearise with two big‑M constraints: # a_entry >= a_win - M*(1 - z) # a_exit <= b_win + M*(1 - z) # where a_entry = departure from upstream station, # a_exit = arrival at downstream station. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in T: for j in L: # Only relevant if the segment is used # Identify the two stations that bound segment j for train i (depends on route) # We create auxiliary variables entry[i,j] and exit[i,j] that capture the # departure from the upstream node and arrival at the downstream node. entry = model.addVar(vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name=f'entry_{i}_{j}') exit_ = model.addVar(vtype=GRB.CONTINUOUS, lb=0, name=f'exit_{i}_{j}') # Link entry/exit to the actual schedule (only when y=1) # We need to know which stations are upstream/downstream for this segment. # For simplicity we create a big‑M linking that works for any possible orientation: # entry <= d_upstream + M*(1 - y) # entry >= d_upstream - M*(1 - y) # exit <= a_downstream + M*(1 - y) # exit >= a_downstream - M*(1 - y) # We therefore loop over all routes that contain j and pick the corresponding stations. # If the segment is not used (y=0) the constraints become non‑binding. for p in P[i]: if j in route_segments[i,p]: seg_idx = route_segments[i,p].index(j) sta_up = route_stations[i,p][seg_idx] # upstream station sta_dn = route_stations[i,p][seg_idx+1] # downstream station # Bind entry/exit to the schedule of this particular orientation model.addConstr(entry <= d[i, sta_up] + M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Entry_up_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(entry >= d[i, sta_up] - M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Entry_low_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ <= a[i, sta_dn] + M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Exit_up_{i}_{p}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ >= a[i, sta_dn] - M * (1 - x[i,p]), name=f'Exit_low_{i}_{p}_{j}') # Now enforce the window indicator if a_win[j] < b_win[j]: # only if there is a real disruption window model.addConstr(entry >= a_win[j] - M * (1 - z[i,j]), name=f'WinEntryLow_{i}_{j}') model.addConstr(exit_ <= b_win[j] + M * (1 - z[i,j]), name=f'WinExitUp_{i}_{j}') else: # No disruption → force z = 0 model.addConstr(z[i,j] == 0, name=f'NoWin_{i}_{j}') # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.7 Avoid traversing a blocked segment during its window # If a segment is blocked (a_win < b_win) then either # - the train does NOT use the segment (y=0) OR # - it traverses it completely outside the window (z=0) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ for i in T: for j in L: if a_win[j] < b_win[j]: model.addConstr(y[i,j] - z[i,j] <= 0, name=f'BlockAvoid_{i}_{j}') # alternatively: y[i,j] <= 1 - z[i,j] (same) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.8 Capacity constraints (one train per direction at a time) # Because we have a continuous time horizon we discretise it into # small time slices Δt (e.g. 1 minute). For each slice τ we count the # number of trains occupying segment j during τ. # To keep the script short we use a *pairwise* conflict formulation: # For any two distinct trains i ≠ k that both use segment j, # their traversals must not overlap. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Create auxiliary start/finish times on each segment (already have entry/exit above) # We reuse the entry/exit variables defined in 3.6 (they are in the model scope). # Pairwise non‑overlap (big‑M) for j in L: for i1 in T: for i2 in T: if i1 >= i2: continue # binary variable w_{i1,i2,j} = 1 ⇔ i1 finishes before i2 starts on segment j w = model.addVar(vtype=GRB.BINARY, name=f'order_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') # retrieve entry/exit variables (they were created inside the loop of 3.6, # so we need to reference them by name) entry_i1 = model.getVarByName(f'entry_{i1}_{j}') exit_i1 = model.getVarByName(f'exit_{i1}_{j}') entry_i2 = model.getVarByName(f'entry_{i2}_{j}') exit_i2 = model.getVarByName(f'exit_{i2}_{j}') # If both trains use the segment (y=1) then enforce ordering: model.addConstr(entry_i2 >= exit_i1 - M * (1 - w) - M * (2 - y[i1,j] - y[i2,j]), name=f'NoOverlap1_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') model.addConstr(entry_i1 >= exit_i2 - M * w - M * (2 - y[i1,j] - y[i2,j]), name=f'NoOverlap2_{i1}_{i2}_{j}') # w can be either 0 or 1, the big‑M terms deactivate the constraints when # at least one of the trains does not use the segment. # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 3.9 Speed limits (already set in variable definition) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # (nothing to add – v already bounded by v_min, v_max) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 4. OBJECTIVE # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # Total delay = Σ_i (arrival at last station – scheduled arrival) delay = gp.quicksum( a[i, route_stations[i, P[i][0]][-1]] - scheduled_arrival[i] # last station of the *first* route (all routes share the same destination) for i in T ) # Total energy = Σ_i Σ_j e[i,j] * τ[i,j] (τ is the actual travel time on segment j) energy = gp.quicksum(e[(i,j)] * tau[i,j] for i in T for j in L if (i,j) in e) # Weighting parameters (choose according to your policy) w_delay = 1.0 w_energy = 0.1 model.setObjective(w_delay * delay + w_energy * energy, GRB.MINIMIZE) # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 5. SOLVE # ------------------------------------------------------------------ model.Params.TimeLimit = 300 # seconds, adjust as needed model.optimize() # ------------------------------------------------------------------ # 6. DISPLAY RESULTS # ------------------------------------------------------------------ if model.Status == GRB.OPTIMAL or model.Status == GRB.TIME_LIMIT: print("\n=== OBJECTIVE ===") print(f"Total weighted cost = {model.ObjVal:.2f}") print("\n=== ROUTE SELECTION ===") for i in T: for p in P[i]: if x[i,p].X > 0.5: print(f"Train {i} uses route '{p}'") print(f" Stations : {route_stations[i,p]}") print(f" Segments : {route_segments[i,p]}") print("\n=== TIMETABLE ===") for i in T: print(f"\nTrain {i}:") # find the selected route to know the order of stations sel_route = next(p for p in P[i] if x[i,p].X > 0.5) stations = route_stations[i, sel_route] for k, sta in enumerate(stations): print(f" Station {sta}: arrival = {a[i,sta].X:.1f} departure = {d[i,sta].X:.1f}") print("\n=== SPEED & ENERGY ===") for i in T: for j in L: if y[i,j].X > 0.5: print(f"Train {i} on segment {j}: speed = {v[i,j].X:.1f} km/h, travel time = {tau[i,j].X:.2f} min, energy = {e[(i,j)]*tau[i,j].X:.2f}") else: print("No feasible solution found.") ``` --- ## 3. What the Code Does | Block | Purpose | |-------|----------| | **Data section** | Define all sets, parameters and a tiny example instance (replace with your real data). | | **Variables** | `x, y, s, a, d, z, v, tau, entry, exit, w` – exactly the variables requested in the description. | | **Constraints** |
  • **One route per train** (`OneRoute`).
  • **Link segment usage** to the chosen route (`Link_y`).
  • **Dwell time** at stations.
  • **Travel‑time consistency** between consecutive stations using the auxiliary travel‑time variable `tau` (linearised with big‑M).
  • **Start‑time** ties the first departure to `s[i]`.
  • **Disruption‑window indicator** `z[i,j]` together with `entry/exit` times.
  • **Avoid blocked segment during its window** (`BlockAvoid`).
  • **Capacity / conflict avoidance** – pairwise non‑overlap on each segment using binary ordering variables `w`.
  • **Speed limits** are enforced directly on `v[i,j]`.
| | **Objective** | Weighted sum of total delay (difference between actual arrival at the final station and the scheduled arrival) and total energy (`e·tau`). | | **Solve & Output** | Calls Gurobi, prints the selected routes, the full timetable, speeds, travel times and energy consumption. | --- ## 4. Extending / Customising * **Piece‑wise linear speed‑energy relationship** – replace the simple `tau`‑definition by a set of break‑points and use Gurobi’s SOS2 or additional binary variables. * **Time‑indexed capacity** – instead of pairwise ordering you can discretise the horizon (Δt = 1 min) and enforce `∑_i y[i,j,t] ≤ C[j]` for each slice `t`. * **Multiple directions** – if a segment can be used in both directions, create a direction index `d ∈ {+,-}` and duplicate the capacity/ordering constraints per direction. * **Robustness** – add slack variables for delay with a high penalty to guarantee feasibility under very tight disruption windows. Feel free to adapt the toy data, the weighting parameters (`w_delay`, `w_energy`) and the big‑M value to match the scale of your real planning horizon. The formulation follows exactly the description you supplied, and the script can be executed as‑is (after installing Gurobi and its Python API).

function.name: or_coder

description.description: A description of the MILP to implement.

response.content:
**Sets**

- \(T\) – set of trains, indexed by \(i\).
- \(S\) – set of stations, indexed by \(k\).
- \(L\) – set of bidirectional track segments, indexed by \(j\).
- \(P_i\) – set of admissible routes for train \(i\) (original route and feasible reroutings).

**Parameters**

- \(t_{ij}\) – nominal travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (minutes) at reference speed \(v^{\text{ref}}\).
- \(e_{ij}\) – energy consumption rate of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (kWh per minute) at reference speed.
- \([a_j , b_j]\) – disruption time window on segment \(j\) (minutes). If no disruption, set \(a_j=b_j=0\).
- \(C_j\) – capacity of segment \(j\) (maximum number of trains that can occupy the segment in the same direction at any time, usually 1).
- \(v_{\min}, v_{\max}\) – global speed limits (km/h).
- \(\text{dwell}\) – minimum dwell time at any station (minutes).
- \(\hat a_i\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (used for delay calculation).
- \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).

**Decision variables**

- \(x_{ip}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) selects route \(p\in P_i\).
- \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(j\) (implied by the chosen route).
- \(s_i\ge 0\) – start (departure) time of train \(i\) from its origin station.
- \(a_{ik}\ge 0\) – arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(k\).
- \(d_{ik}\ge 0\) – departure time of train \(i\) from station \(k\).
- \(z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(j\) **inside** its disruption window.
- \(v_{ij}\) – speed of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (km/h), bounded by \(v_{\min}\le v_{ij}\le v_{\max}\).
- \(\tau_{ij}\ge 0\) – actual travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (minutes).

**Auxiliary relations**

- For each train‑route pair \((i,p)\) we know the ordered list of stations \(\sigma_{ip} = (k_0,\dots ,k_{n})\) and the corresponding list of segments \(\lambda_{ip} = (j_1,\dots ,j_{n})\).

**Model**

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,k^{\text{last}}}-\hat a_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{j\in L} e_{ij}\,\tau_{ij}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(\alpha\) is a weighting coefficient (e.g., \(\alpha=0.1\)).

---

### Constraints

1. **Route selection**
   \[
   \sum_{p\in P_i} x_{ip}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
   \tag{C1}
   \]

2. **Link segment usage to route**
   \[
   y_{ij}= \sum_{\substack{p\in P_i\\ j\in \lambda_{ip}}} x_{ip}
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
   \tag{C2}
   \]

3. **Dwell time at stations**
   \[
   d_{ik}\ge a_{ik}+ \text{dwell}\qquad \forall i\in T,\;k\in S
   \tag{C3}
   \]

4. **Travel‑time consistency between consecutive stations**  
   For every train \(i\), route \(p\), and each segment \(j_\ell\) of that route:
   \[
   a_{i,k_{\ell}}\;\ge\; d_{i,k_{\ell-1}} + \tau_{i j_\ell} - M\bigl(1-x_{ip}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;p\in P_i,\;\ell=1,\dots ,|\lambda_{ip}|
   \tag{C4}
   \]

5. **Relation between speed and travel time** (linearised with big‑M)
   \[
   \frac{t_{ij}\,v^{\text{ref}}}{v_{\max}} \;-\; M\bigl(1-y_{ij}\bigr)\;\le\; \tau_{ij}
   \;\le\;
   \frac{t_{ij}\,v^{\text{ref}}}{v_{\min}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-y_{ij}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
   \tag{C5}
   \]

6. **Origin departure**
   \[
   d_{i,k^{\text{origin}}}=s_i \qquad \forall i\in T
   \tag{C6}
   \]

7. **Disruption‑window indicator**
   Define entry time \(e_{ij}\) (departure from upstream station) and exit time \(x_{ij}\) (arrival at downstream station). Using big‑M:
   \[
   e_{ij}\ge a_j - M(1-z_{ij}),\qquad
   x_{ij}\le b_j + M(1-z_{ij})\qquad
   \forall i\in T,\;j\in L\text{ with }a_j<b_j
   \tag{C7}
   \]

8. **Avoid traversing a blocked segment during its window**
   \[
   y_{ij} - z_{ij}\le 0 \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L\text{ with }a_j<b_j
   \tag{C8}
   \]

9. **Capacity / conflict avoidance (pairwise ordering)**
   For any two distinct trains \(i\neq i'\) using the same segment \(j\), introduce binary \(w_{ii'j}\) (1 if \(i\) finishes before \(i'\) starts):
   \[
   e_{i'j}\ge x_{ij} - M\bigl(1-w_{ii'j}\bigr) - M\bigl(2-y_{ij}-y_{i'j}\bigr)
   \]
   \[
   e_{ij}\ge x_{i'j} - M w_{ii'j} - M\bigl(2-y_{ij}-y_{i'j}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i<i',\;j\in L
   \tag{C9}
   \]

10. **Speed limits**
    \[
    v_{\min}\le v_{ij}\le v_{\max}\qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
    \tag{C10}
    \]

---

### Summary of the MILP

- **Variables**: binary \(x_{ip}, y_{ij}, z_{ij}\); continuous \(s_i, a_{ik}, d_{ik}, v_{ij}, \tau_{ij}\) (plus auxiliary entry/exit times and ordering binaries for capacity).
- **Objective**: minimise weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.
- **Constraints**: ensure exactly one route per train, consistency between route choice and segment usage, dwell times, travel‑time feasibility with speed‑adjustable travel times, avoidance of blocked segments during disruption windows, capacity on each segment, and speed limits.

All equations above constitute a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the **integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial segment blockages.

final_answer:
**Sets**

- \(T\) – set of trains, indexed by \(i\).
- \(S\) – set of stations, indexed by \(k\).
- \(L\) – set of bidirectional track segments, indexed by \(j\).
- \(P_i\) – set of admissible routes for train \(i\) (original route and feasible reroutings).

**Parameters**

- \(t_{ij}\) – nominal travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (minutes) at reference speed \(v^{\text{ref}}\).
- \(e_{ij}\) – energy consumption rate of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (kWh per minute) at reference speed.
- \([a_j , b_j]\) – disruption time window on segment \(j\) (minutes). If no disruption, set \(a_j=b_j=0\).
- \(C_j\) – capacity of segment \(j\) (maximum number of trains that can occupy the segment in the same direction at any time, usually 1).
- \(v_{\min}, v_{\max}\) – global speed limits (km/h).
- \(\text{dwell}\) – minimum dwell time at any station (minutes).
- \(\hat a_i\) – scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (used for delay calculation).
- \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (big‑M).

**Decision variables**

- \(x_{ip}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) selects route \(p\in P_i\).
- \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(j\) (implied by the chosen route).
- \(s_i\ge 0\) – start (departure) time of train \(i\) from its origin station.
- \(a_{ik}\ge 0\) – arrival time of train \(i\) at station \(k\).
- \(d_{ik}\ge 0\) – departure time of train \(i\) from station \(k\).
- \(z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) – 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(j\) **inside** its disruption window.
- \(v_{ij}\) – speed of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (km/h), bounded by \(v_{\min}\le v_{ij}\le v_{\max}\).
- \(\tau_{ij}\ge 0\) – actual travel time of train \(i\) on segment \(j\) (minutes).

**Auxiliary relations**

- For each train‑route pair \((i,p)\) we know the ordered list of stations \(\sigma_{ip} = (k_0,\dots ,k_{n})\) and the corresponding list of segments \(\lambda_{ip} = (j_1,\dots ,j_{n})\).

**Model**

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,k^{\text{last}}}-\hat a_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{j\in L} e_{ij}\,\tau_{ij}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

where \(\alpha\) is a weighting coefficient (e.g., \(\alpha=0.1\)).

---

### Constraints

1. **Route selection**
   \[
   \sum_{p\in P_i} x_{ip}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
   \tag{C1}
   \]

2. **Link segment usage to route**
   \[
   y_{ij}= \sum_{\substack{p\in P_i\\ j\in \lambda_{ip}}} x_{ip}
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
   \tag{C2}
   \]

3. **Dwell time at stations**
   \[
   d_{ik}\ge a_{ik}+ \text{dwell}\qquad \forall i\in T,\;k\in S
   \tag{C3}
   \]

4. **Travel‑time consistency between consecutive stations**  
   For every train \(i\), route \(p\), and each segment \(j_\ell\) of that route:
   \[
   a_{i,k_{\ell}}\;\ge\; d_{i,k_{\ell-1}} + \tau_{i j_\ell} - M\bigl(1-x_{ip}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;p\in P_i,\;\ell=1,\dots ,|\lambda_{ip}|
   \tag{C4}
   \]

5. **Relation between speed and travel time** (linearised with big‑M)
   \[
   \frac{t_{ij}\,v^{\text{ref}}}{v_{\max}} \;-\; M\bigl(1-y_{ij}\bigr)\;\le\; \tau_{ij}
   \;\le\;
   \frac{t_{ij}\,v^{\text{ref}}}{v_{\min}} \;+\; M\bigl(1-y_{ij}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
   \tag{C5}
   \]

6. **Origin departure**
   \[
   d_{i,k^{\text{origin}}}=s_i \qquad \forall i\in T
   \tag{C6}
   \]

7. **Disruption‑window indicator**
   Define entry time \(e_{ij}\) (departure from upstream station) and exit time \(x_{ij}\) (arrival at downstream station). Using big‑M:
   \[
   e_{ij}\ge a_j - M(1-z_{ij}),\qquad
   x_{ij}\le b_j + M(1-z_{ij})\qquad
   \forall i\in T,\;j\in L\text{ with }a_j<b_j
   \tag{C7}
   \]

8. **Avoid traversing a blocked segment during its window**
   \[
   y_{ij} - z_{ij}\le 0 \qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L\text{ with }a_j<b_j
   \tag{C8}
   \]

9. **Capacity / conflict avoidance (pairwise ordering)**
   For any two distinct trains \(i\neq i'\) using the same segment \(j\), introduce binary \(w_{ii'j}\) (1 if \(i\) finishes before \(i'\) starts):
   \[
   e_{i'j}\ge x_{ij} - M\bigl(1-w_{ii'j}\bigr) - M\bigl(2-y_{ij}-y_{i'j}\bigr)
   \]
   \[
   e_{ij}\ge x_{i'j} - M w_{ii'j} - M\bigl(2-y_{ij}-y_{i'j}\bigr)
   \qquad \forall i<i',\;j\in L
   \tag{C9}
   \]

10. **Speed limits**
    \[
    v_{\min}\le v_{ij}\le v_{\max}\qquad \forall i\in T,\;j\in L
    \tag{C10}
    \]

---

### Summary of the MILP

- **Variables**: binary \(x_{ip}, y_{ij}, z_{ij}\); continuous \(s_i, a_{ik}, d_{ik}, v_{ij}, \tau_{ij}\) (plus auxiliary entry/exit times and ordering binaries for capacity).
- **Objective**: minimise weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.
- **Constraints**: ensure exactly one route per train, consistency between route choice and segment usage, dwell times, travel‑time feasibility with speed‑adjustable travel times, avoidance of blocked segments during disruption windows, capacity on each segment, and speed limits.

All equations above constitute a complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) formulation for the **integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP)** under partial segment blockages.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
