Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP**  
The model decides, for each train, whether it stays on its original route or takes a pre‑defined reroute, the exact departure/arrival times at every station, and the speed class used on each track segment.  The objective is a weighted compromise between total passenger‑delay and the energy consumed while travelling.

Below the complete linear (mixed‑integer) formulation is presented together with a short explanation of each set, parameter, decision‑variable, objective term and constraint family.  All non‑linear products have been linearised by standard big‑M / SOS‑1 techniques, so the model is a pure MILP that can be handed to any commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress …).

---

## 1. Index sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I**  | Set of trains,  *i = 1,…,|I| |
| **R**  | Set of possible routes (original * r* or reroute * r′*).  For each train *i* we have a small subset **R​i** ⊆ R (normally 2 elements). |
| **S​i**| Ordered list of stations that train *i* visits on the chosen route (including origin and destination). |
| **ℓ**  | Track segment (the directed link between two consecutive stations).  Set **L​i** = {ℓ | ℓ connects two successive stations of train *i* on its chosen route}. |
| **K**  | Set of admissible speed classes (e.g. *k = 1,…,K*).  Each class has a constant cruise speed *v_k* and a specific energy‑consumption coefficient *e_k* (kWh per hour). |
| **P**  | Set of ordered pairs of trains that conflict on a given segment (i.e. travel in opposite directions on the same physical track).  Elements are triplets *(i,j,ℓ)*. |
| **B**  | Set of blocked segments (maintenance, incident).  For each ℓ∈B we know a closed time window \([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},\,B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\). |

---

## 2. Input data (parameters)

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(t_i^{\text{sched}}\) | Scheduled arrival time at the final destination of train *i* (reference schedule). | minutes |
| \(L_{\ell}\) | Physical length of segment *ℓ*. | km |
| \(v_k\) | Cruise speed of speed class *k*. | km·min⁻¹ (or km·h⁻¹, consistent with time unit). |
| \(e_k\) | Energy consumption rate of class *k* (kWh per hour of cruising). | kWh·h⁻¹ |
| \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min},\;\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\) | Minimum/maximum dwell (station‑stop) time for any train. | minutes |
| \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\min},\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\max}\) | Minimum/maximum extra time needed to accelerate/decelerate when a speed class is changed (used to bound τ). | minutes |
| \(M\) | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints. | minutes (or large number) |
| \(\alpha,\;\beta\) | Weighting coefficients for delay and energy in the objective. | dimensionless |
| \(H\) | Planning horizon (latest permissible arrival time). | minutes |

*All times are expressed in the same unit (minutes are used in the formulation).*

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|--------|
| \(x_{i,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* uses route *r* (original or reroute), 0 otherwise. |
| \(t_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s∈S_i*. (For the origin station this is the actual departure from the depot; for the last station it equals the arrival at the destination.) |
| \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Travel time** of train *i* on segment *ℓ* (time spent while actually moving, i.e. from exiting the upstream station to entering the downstream one). |
| \(s_{i,\ell,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* travels on segment *ℓ* with speed class *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{ij\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* passes segment *ℓ* **before** train *j* (i.e. finishes before *j* enters); 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{i\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* occupies segment *ℓ* (only needed when a segment may be blocked, see Section 4.3). |
| \(\delta_{i\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* uses segment *ℓ* (derived from route choice, see Section 4.1). |

All other variables are linear combinations of the above or are auxiliary for modelling purposes.

---

## 4. Model constraints  

### 4.1. Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1\qquad \forall i\in I.
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage** – let \(\mathcal{L}_{i,r}\) be the ordered list of segments belonging to route *r* for train *i*.  

\[
\delta_{i\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_i} \mathbf{1}_{\{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{i,r}\}}\,x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

Thus \(\delta_{i\ell}=1\) only if the chosen route contains that segment.

### 4.2. Speed‑class allocation on a segment  

3. **Exactly one speed class on an occupied segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} s_{i,\ell,k}= \delta_{i\ell}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

4. **Travel time expressed by the chosen speed class**  

\[
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} \frac{L_{\ell}}{v_k}\,s_{i,\ell,k}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

(If \(\delta_{i\ell}=0\) then all \(s_{i,\ell,k}=0\) and \(\tau_{i,\ell}=0\).)

### 4.3. Time‑window (blocked‑segment) constraints  

A segment ℓ∈B is unavailable between \([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\).  If a train uses that segment, its **entry time** must lie either completely before the block or completely after it.

Define entry and exit times on ℓ:  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell}&= t_{i,\text{up}(ℓ)} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{p\in S_i:\,p\prec\text{up}(ℓ)}\tau_{i,p}}_{\text{cumulative travel on previous segments}} ,\\
\text{exit}_{i\ell}&= \text{enter}_{i\ell}+ \tau_{i,\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]

where `up(ℓ)` is the upstream station of ℓ and “≺” denotes the order along the route.

The logical condition  
\[
\text{enter}_{i\ell} \le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} \;\; \text{or}\;\; \text{enter}_{i\ell} \ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} ,
\]  
is linearised with a binary *w* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} + M\,w_{i\ell} ,\\
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} - M\,(1-w_{i\ell}) ,\\
w_{i\ell}&\in\{0,1\},\qquad
z_{i\ell}= \delta_{i\ell}\;( \text{so that constraints are activated only if the segment is used}).
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(\delta_{i\ell}=0\) the constraints are relaxed by a big‑M term (or they can be simply omitted).

### 4.4. Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) constraints on bidirectional shared tracks  

For every conflicting pair \((i,j,ℓ)\in P\) we introduce binary \(y_{ij\ell}\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\ge \text{exit}_{j\ell} - M\,y_{ij\ell},\\
\text{enter}_{j\ell} &\ge \text{exit}_{i\ell} - M\,(1-y_{ij\ell}),\\
y_{ij\ell}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is enforced, guaranteeing that the two trains are never on the same physical track segment at the same time.

### 4.5. Time‑propagation (schedule continuity)  

5. **From one station to the next** – let \(ℓ = (s,s')\) be the segment that connects station *s* to its immediate downstream station *s'*.  

\[
t_{i,s'} = t_{i,s} + \underbrace{\tau_{i,\ell}}_{\text{travel}} + d_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; \forall (s,s')\in L_i .
\]

where \(d_{i,s}\) is the dwell time at station *s*.

6. **Dwell‑time limits**  

\[
\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min} \le d_{i,s} \le \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\qquad\forall i,\; s\in S_i\setminus\{ \text{final}\}.
\]

(For the origin station dwell may be zero.)

7. **Acceleration / deceleration bounding** – if a speed class changes between two consecutive segments, an extra time penalty Δ​acc is required.  Let  

\[
u_{i,\ell,k}=s_{i,\ell,k}\;(1-\!s_{i,\ell^{-},k})\qquad(\text{linearised via SOS‑1 / extra binaries}),
\]  

where ℓ⁻ is the previous segment of train *i*. Then

\[
\sum_{k} u_{i,\ell,k}\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\min}\le 
\tau_{i,\ell}-\frac{L_{\ell}}{v_k}\le
\sum_{k} u_{i,\ell,k}\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\max}.
\]

In practice this is expressed by a pair of constraints using a big‑M and the binary \(u_{i,\ell,k}\); it ensures that whenever the speed class switches, the travel time is enlarged by at most the admissible acceleration/deceleration slack.

### 4.6. Horizon & final‑time constraints  

8. **No train may finish after the planning horizon**  

\[
t_{i,\text{final}} \le H\qquad\forall i\in I .
\]

9. **Definition of final‑time variable** (used in the objective)  

\[
t_{i,\text{final}} = t_{i,s_{\text{dest}}}\qquad\forall i,
\]

where \(s_{\text{dest}}\) is the last station of train *i* on the chosen route.

---

## 5. Objective function  

The MILP minimizes a weighted sum of (i) total passenger delay and (ii) total energy consumption.

\[
\min\;\; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{i\in I}\Bigl(t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}}\Bigr)}_{\text{Delay term}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{\ell\in L_i}\sum_{k\in K} e_k \,\tau_{i,\ell}\, s_{i,\ell,k}}_{\text{Energy term}} .
\]

*Explanation*

* **Delay term** – the quantity \((t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})\) is the realized arrival‑time deviation of train *i* from its original schedule; summing over all trains yields the total passenger‑delay (in minutes). The scalar \(\alpha\) translates minutes into the cost unit used for the optimisation (for instance € per minute).

* **Energy term** – travelling on segment ℓ with speed class *k* consumes energy at rate *e_k* for the whole travelling time \(\tau_{i,\ell}\). Because \(s_{i,\ell,k}\) is binary, the product \(\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\) is linear (it is simply \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) when the class is selected, zero otherwise). Multiplying by *e_k* gives the energy (kWh). Summation over all trains, segments and classes gives the total energy usage. The coefficient \(\beta\) converts kWh into the same monetary cost unit as the delay term.

Both terms are linear in the decision variables; the only “product” \(\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\) is handled by the definition of \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) in constraint (4) above.

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&\alpha\sum_{i}(t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})
        +\beta\sum_{i}\sum_{\ell\in L_i}\sum_{k} e_k \,\tau_{i,\ell}\, s_{i,\ell,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_i}x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\\
&\delta_{i\ell}= \sum_{r}\mathbf 1_{\ell\in\mathcal L_{i,r}}x_{i,r} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\sum_k s_{i,\ell,k}= \delta_{i\ell} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_k \frac{L_\ell}{v_k}s_{i,\ell,k} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\text{(blocked‑segment big‑M constraints)} &&\forall i,\ell\in B\\
&\text{(conflict‑avoidance precedence constraints)} &&\forall (i,j,\ell)\in P\\
& t_{i,s'} = t_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,\ell}+ d_{i,s} &&\forall i,\;(s,s')\in L_i\\
& \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min}\le d_{i,s}\le\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max} &&\forall i,s\\
& \text{(acc/dec acceleration linking constraints)} &&\forall i,\ell\\
& t_{i,\text{final}}\le H &&\forall i\\
& x_{i,r},s_{i,\ell,k},y_{ij\ell},w_{i\ell},\delta_{i\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& t_{i,s},\tau_{i,\ell},d_{i,s}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

## 7. Modeling assumptions (to be explicit)

1. **Fixed set of routes** – each train can either stay on its original route or take a pre‑computed detour; no dynamic re‑routing inside the horizon.
2. **Speed classes are piece‑wise constant** – a train travels on a segment at a single cruise speed *v_k*; acceleration/deceleration is modelled only as a time penalty (Δ​acc) that is added to the travel time of that segment.
3. **Energy consumption is proportional to cruise time only** – auxiliary energy for acceleration is absorbed into the per‑class coefficient *e_k* (or can be added as a constant per speed change if needed).
4. **Deterministic blocking** – the closed time windows of segments are known a‑priori and do not depend on the schedule.
5. **No overtaking on the same line** – the bidirectional conflict constraints guarantee a simple first‑come‑first‑served ordering on each physical track. If overtaking is allowed, additional binaries per train order would be required.
6. **Dwell time bounds are the same for all stations** – they can be made station‑specific by indexing with *s* if data are available.
7. **Big‑M values** – chosen large enough so that they never become active when the associated binary is 0, yet not excessively large to avoid numerical instability.

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – build the sets *R​i*, *L​i*, *P*, the segment lengths *Lℓ*, speed‑class table \((v_k,e_k)\) and the blocking windows.  
2. **Parameter tuning** – select the weighting factors \(\alpha,\beta\) to reflect the railway operator’s relative importance of punctuality vs. energy saving.  
3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to a solver (e.g. Gurobi `gurobi_cl`, CPLEX `cplex`).  The binary variables provide the chosen routes, speed class per segment and the conflict‑resolution ordering.  The continuous variables give the full timetable (departure times and travel times).  
4. **Post‑processing** – compute the realised delay and total energy from the solution, generate a Gantt‑type schedule for the dispatcher, and, if needed, feed the result into a simulation model for validation.

The formulation above is *complete* (all constraints needed for a feasible timetable are present) and *linear* (only linear expressions and binary decisions).  It can be extended straightforwardly to include additional operational aspects such as crew‑changing windows, rolling‑stock availability, or variable energy tariffs.

Model 2:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP**  

The mathematical program below combines (i) a binary routing decision (original route vs. a reroute), (ii) a departure‑time decision at every station, (iii) a speed‑level decision on every line‑segment, and (iv) conflict‑avoidance on single‑track sections.  
All data that are required to instantiate the model are listed in the *Parameters* section; the set‑notation is purposely kept linear so that the model can be entered directly into a commercial MILP solver (Cplex, Gurobi, Xpress, …).

---

## 1. Index sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\( \mathcal I \\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\) |
| \\( \mathcal S_i \\) | Ordered set of stations visited by train \\(i\\) on its **original** route \\(r_i\\) (including origin and destination) |
| \\( \mathcal S'_i \\) | Ordered set of stations visited by train \\(i\\) on its **reroute** \\(r'_i\\) |
| \\( \mathcal L_i \\) | Set of line‑segments traversed by train \\(i\\) on the chosen route (obtained from the station list) |
| \\( \mathcal K \\) | Set of admissible speed classes (e.g. \\(k=1,\dots,K\\) ), each class has a constant cruising speed \\(v_k\\) and energy coefficient \\(e_k\\) |
| \\( \mathcal B \\) | Set of **blocked** line‑segments (segments that are unavailable during a maintenance window) |
| \\( \mathcal P \\) | Set of **conflict pairs**: ordered pairs \\((i,j, \ell)\\) such that trains \\(i\\) and \\(j\\) travel on the same physical segment \\(\ell\\) in opposite directions (single‑track conflict) |

---

## 2. Parameters (input data)

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|--------|----------|-------|
| \\(t_i^{\text{sched}}\\) | Scheduled departure time of train \\(i\\) from its origin (reference) | [s] |
| \\(L_\ell\\) | Length of segment \\(\ell\\) | [km] |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed of class \\(k\\) (constant cruising speed) | [km/h] |
| \\(e_k\\) | Energy consumption rate (per unit time) for class \\(k\\) | [kWh/h] |
| \\(D_{i,s}^{\min }, D_{i,s}^{\max }\\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) | [s] |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. horizon length) | [s] |
| \\(B_{\ell}^{\text{start}}, B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}\\) | Start / end of the external blockage on segment \\(\ell\\) (only defined if \\(\ell\in\mathcal B\\)) | [s] |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) | Weight of delay in the objective | – |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Weight of energy in the objective | – |
| \\(T^{\text{H}}\\) | Planning horizon (latest time a train may finish) | [s] |

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \\(x_i \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) uses the **original** route \\(r_i\\); 0 ⇔ uses the **reroute** \\(r'_i\\) |
| \\(t_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(s\\) (the first station is the origin) |
| \\(\tau_{i,\ell}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Traversal time** of train \\(i\\) on segment \\(\ell\\) (time spent moving, not counting dwell) |
| \\(s_{i,\ell,k}\\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) travels on segment \\(\ell\\) with speed class \\(k\\) |
| \\(y_{ij\ell} \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary (only for \\((i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P\\)) | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) passes segment \\(\ell\\) **before** train \\(j\\) (conflict‑resolution ordering) |
| \\(z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}} \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary (only for \\(\ell\in\mathcal B\\)) | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) traverses a **blocked** segment \\(\ell\\) (used to enforce the time‑window) |

All other variables that are not listed are implicit (e.g. the arrival time at a station is simply \\(t_{i,s}+D_{i,s}\\) ).

---

## 4. Model formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\Bigl(t_{i,\text{dest}}-t_i^{\text{sched}}\Bigr)}_{\text{Total passenger‑delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
e_k \; \tau_{i,\ell}\; s_{i,\ell,k}}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
\tag{Obj}
\]

where \\(t_{i,\text{dest}}\\) is the departure time from the last station of the chosen route (identical to the arrival time at the destination because no dwell after that).

---

### 4.2 Routing choice  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i} 1 = |\mathcal L_i| = 
\begin{cases}
|\mathcal L_i^{\text{orig}}| & \text{if } x_i = 1\\[2pt]
|\mathcal L_i^{\text{rer}}| & \text{if } x_i = 0
\end{cases}
\]  

In practice, the set \\(\mathcal L_i\\) that appears in all subsequent constraints is defined **conditionally**:  

\[
\mathcal L_i = 
\begin{cases}
\mathcal L_i^{\text{orig}} & \text{if } x_i = 1\\
\mathcal L_i^{\text{rer}}  & \text{if } x_i = 0
\end{cases}
\]  

Implementation tip: create two copies of each train (orig‑copy, rer‑copy) and enforce \\(x_i\\) to select which copy is active; all other constraints are written for the *active* copy only.

---

### 4.3 Speed‑class assignment on each traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} s_{i,\ell,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{Speed‑choice}
\]

\[
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}\; s_{i,\ell,k}
\qquad \forall i,\ell \tag{Travel‑time‑definition}
\]

The term \\(\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}\\) is the **deterministic travel time** if the train maintains speed class \\(k\\) over the whole segment.  

If there are additional acceleration / deceleration limits you can tighten the big‑M for \\(\tau_{i,\ell}\\) but the basic linear relationship above already forces a link between the chosen speed class and the travel time.

---

### 4.4 Dwell‑time limits  

For every station \\(s\\) that train \\(i\\) visits (according to the chosen route):  

\[
D_{i,s}^{\min } \le  t_{i,s^{+}}- t_{i,s} \le D_{i,s}^{\max } \qquad \forall i, s\in\mathcal S_i\cup\mathcal S'_i \tag{Dwell}
\]  

where \\(s^{+}\\) denotes the **next** station on the same route. The left‑hand side guarantees the train stays at least the minimum required time; the right‑hand side prevents unnecessarily long stops.

---

### 4.5 Temporal linking of departure times and segment travel  

For each train \\(i\\) and each successive pair (station, segment):  

\[
t_{i,s^{+}} = t_{i,s}+ D_{i,s}^{\text{actual}} + \tau_{i,\ell} \qquad 
\forall i,\;\forall\ell\in\mathcal L_i,\;\text{where } \ell \text{ connects } s\rightarrow s^{+}
\]  

Here \\(D_{i,s}^{\text{actual}}\\) can be taken as any value within the dwell bounds; when the model solves it will automatically select a value that satisfies the inequality (the constraints can be expressed as two inequalities using the bounds above).

---

### 4.6 Blockage constraints (externally imposed closures)  

If segment \\(\ell\\) belongs to the blocked set \\(\mathcal B\\), the train may **not** be on the segment during the forbidden interval \\([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\\). This is enforced by a classic big‑M formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} &\ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} - M\,(1-z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}) \\
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}  &\le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} + M\,(1-z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal B
\]

where  

\[
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} = \text{departure time from the upstream station of }\ell,
\qquad
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}  = t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{i,\ell}
\]

The binary \\(z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}\\) forces the model to either schedule the train **before** the block (\\(z=0\\) → exit ≤ start) or **after** the block (\\(z=1\\) → enter ≥ end).  

If a reroute completely avoids a blocked segment, the corresponding \\(\ell\\) simply does not belong to \\(\mathcal L_i\\) for that train.

---

### 4.7 Single‑track conflict (bidirectional)  

For every ordered conflict pair \\((i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P\\) (trains traveling on the same physical segment in opposite directions) we introduce a binary ordering variable \\(y_{ij\ell}\\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{i,\ell} &\le t_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,(1-y_{ij\ell})\\
t_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{j,\ell} &\le t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,y_{ij\ell}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P
\]

When \\(y_{ij\ell}=1\\) the model forces train \\(j\\) to finish its traversal before train \\(i\\) enters; when \\(y_{ij\ell}=0\\) the opposite ordering is selected. Exactly one ordering is enforced because the two constraints are complementary.

---

### 4.8 Horizon / feasibility  

\[
t_{i,\text{dest}} \le T^{\text{H}} \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{Horizon}
\]

Additionally, a non‑negativity requirement for all time‑type variables:

\[
t_{i,s} \ge 0,\qquad \tau_{i,\ell}\ge 0 \qquad \forall i,s,\ell.
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i}(t_{i,\text{dest}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i}\sum_{k}e_k\,\tau_{i,\ell}\,s_{i,\ell,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k}s_{i,\ell,k}=1 &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C1}\\
&
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k}\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}s_{i,\ell,k} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C2}\\
&
D_{i,s}^{\min}\le t_{i,s^{+}}-t_{i,s}\le D_{i,s}^{\max} &&\forall i,s\in\text{stations of chosen route} \tag{C3}\\
&
t_{i,s^{+}} = t_{i,s}+ (t_{i,s^{+}}-t_{i,s}) + \tau_{i,\ell} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C4}\\
&
\text{Blockage constraints (big‑M)} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal B \tag{C5}\\
&
\text{Conflict constraints } y_{ij\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P \tag{C6}\\
&
t_{i,\text{dest}}\le T^{\text{H}} &&\forall i \tag{C7}\\
&
x_i\in\{0,1\},\; s_{i,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{ij\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}\in\{0,1\}\\
&
t_{i,s},\tau_{i,\ell}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,\ell .
\end{aligned}
\]

All other constraints (e.g., linking the active set of stations/segments to the routing binary \\(x_i\\)) are handled by a standard *route‑selection* modeling trick:

*Create two “copies’’ of each train*:  

* copy‑1 uses original route, all its associated variables are multiplied by \\(x_i\\);  
* copy‑2 uses reroute, all its associated variables are multiplied by \\(1-x_i\\).  

Then the constraints above are written **once** for each copy and the multiplication guarantees that only the variables of the selected copy can be non‑zero.

---

## 6. Main modelling assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Rationale / effect on MILP |
|---|------------|----------------------------|
| A1 | Travel on a segment is performed at a **single constant speed class** (no intra‑segment speed‑change). | Guarantees linear relation (C2); if finer granularity is needed a segment can be split into sub‑segments. |
| A2 | Dwell time at a station is a decision variable bounded by known minima/maxima. | Gives flexibility for recovery buffering while preserving realistic stop lengths. |
| A3 | Blockage windows are known **a priori** and are hard (cannot be entered). | Enforced by big‑M constraints (C5); rerouting is the primary way to avoid them. |
| A4 | Only **pairwise** opposite‑direction conflicts on a single‑track are considered; multiple‑train overlap is avoided implicitly through the binary ordering variables \\(y_{ij\ell}\\). | Keeps the model linear; larger blocks can be modeled by chaining binary variables. |
| A5 | Energy consumption is proportional to *time spent* in a speed class (i.e., constant power per class). | Leads to linear term \\(e_k\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\\) in the objective. |
| A6 | No explicit capacity constraints on stations (platform capacity) – if required, add binary variables for platform occupation and extra precedence constraints. |
| A7 | The planning horizon \\(T^{\text H}\\) is sufficiently large to contain any feasible schedule; otherwise the model may become infeasible. |
| A8 | Acceleration/deceleration limits are **implicit** in the choice of speed classes (slow classes can be used to model a slower‑accelerating train). If more accuracy is needed, additional linear constraints linking consecutive \\(s_{i,\ell,k}\\) can be added. |

---

## 7. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the two route alternatives for each train (list of stations, compute the derived segment list and segment lengths).  
2. **Parameter generation** – Specify \\(v_k\\), \\(e_k\\), dwell bounds, blockage windows, and the conflict‑pair set \\(\mathcal P\\).  
3. **Implementation** – Write the model in a MILP language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP). The “copy‑train’’ trick makes the routing decision linear.  
4. **Solver call** – Choose a commercial MILP solver; the model is of moderate size (variables ≈ |I|·|L|·|K| + |I|·|S| + |P|).  
5. **Post‑processing** – From the optimal solution extract for each train: (i) the chosen route (value of \\(x_i\\)), (ii) departure times at all stations, (iii) speed class per segment, (iv) the resulting delay and energy consumption.

---

### Bottom line  

The formulation above captures a **joint** decision problem: *which route should a train take?* *when should it leave each station?* *at which speed class should it travel on each line segment?* All decisions are linked through linear constraints, and the objective balances passenger delay against energy usage. The big‑M constraints and binary ordering variables guarantee feasibility with respect to external blockages and single‑track conflicts, while the binary speed‑class variables keep the travel‑time relationship linear and thus tractable for a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP: binary variables for train i using original route r_i or reroute r'_i, departure times t_{i,s} at stations, travel time variables τ_{i,ℓ} on segment ℓ, speed level binary s_{i,ℓ,k} (k speed class), objective minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (t_{i,final}-t_i^sched) and energy Σ_i Σ_ℓ Σ_k e_k * τ_{i,ℓ} * s_{i,ℓ,k}. Constraints: each train chooses one route; if segment ℓ is blocked during [B_ℓ_start,B_ℓ_end] then trains on that side cannot occupy it, enforce time windows using big-M; precedence constraints for bidirectional conflict on shared track: for any pair (i,j) on same segment opposite directions, either finish_i <= start_j or vice versa using binary y_{ijℓ}; travel time τ_{i,ℓ}= Σ_k (L_ℓ/v_k)* s_{i,ℓ,k}; sum_k s_{i,ℓ,k}=1; dwell time lower/upper bounds; acceleration/deceleration limits via linking τ to speed classes; total schedule horizon limit. response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP**  
The model decides, for each train, whether it stays on its original route or takes a pre‑defined reroute, the exact departure/arrival times at every station, and the speed class used on each track segment.  The objective is a weighted compromise between total passenger‑delay and the energy consumed while travelling.

Below the complete linear (mixed‑integer) formulation is presented together with a short explanation of each set, parameter, decision‑variable, objective term and constraint family.  All non‑linear products have been linearised by standard big‑M / SOS‑1 techniques, so the model is a pure MILP that can be handed to any commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress …).

---

## 1. Index sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I**  | Set of trains,  *i = 1,…,|I| |
| **R**  | Set of possible routes (original * r* or reroute * r′*).  For each train *i* we have a small subset **R​i** ⊆ R (normally 2 elements). |
| **S​i**| Ordered list of stations that train *i* visits on the chosen route (including origin and destination). |
| **ℓ**  | Track segment (the directed link between two consecutive stations).  Set **L​i** = {ℓ | ℓ connects two successive stations of train *i* on its chosen route}. |
| **K**  | Set of admissible speed classes (e.g. *k = 1,…,K*).  Each class has a constant cruise speed *v_k* and a specific energy‑consumption coefficient *e_k* (kWh per hour). |
| **P**  | Set of ordered pairs of trains that conflict on a given segment (i.e. travel in opposite directions on the same physical track).  Elements are triplets *(i,j,ℓ)*. |
| **B**  | Set of blocked segments (maintenance, incident).  For each ℓ∈B we know a closed time window \([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},\,B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\). |

---

## 2. Input data (parameters)

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| \(t_i^{\text{sched}}\) | Scheduled arrival time at the final destination of train *i* (reference schedule). | minutes |
| \(L_{\ell}\) | Physical length of segment *ℓ*. | km |
| \(v_k\) | Cruise speed of speed class *k*. | km·min⁻¹ (or km·h⁻¹, consistent with time unit). |
| \(e_k\) | Energy consumption rate of class *k* (kWh per hour of cruising). | kWh·h⁻¹ |
| \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min},\;\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\) | Minimum/maximum dwell (station‑stop) time for any train. | minutes |
| \(\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\min},\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\max}\) | Minimum/maximum extra time needed to accelerate/decelerate when a speed class is changed (used to bound τ). | minutes |
| \(M\) | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints. | minutes (or large number) |
| \(\alpha,\;\beta\) | Weighting coefficients for delay and energy in the objective. | dimensionless |
| \(H\) | Planning horizon (latest permissible arrival time). | minutes |

*All times are expressed in the same unit (minutes are used in the formulation).*

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|--------|
| \(x_{i,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* uses route *r* (original or reroute), 0 otherwise. |
| \(t_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s∈S_i*. (For the origin station this is the actual departure from the depot; for the last station it equals the arrival at the destination.) |
| \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Travel time** of train *i* on segment *ℓ* (time spent while actually moving, i.e. from exiting the upstream station to entering the downstream one). |
| \(s_{i,\ell,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* travels on segment *ℓ* with speed class *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| \(y_{ij\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* passes segment *ℓ* **before** train *j* (i.e. finishes before *j* enters); 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{i\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* occupies segment *ℓ* (only needed when a segment may be blocked, see Section 4.3). |
| \(\delta_{i\ell}\) | binary | 1 if train *i* uses segment *ℓ* (derived from route choice, see Section 4.1). |

All other variables are linear combinations of the above or are auxiliary for modelling purposes.

---

## 4. Model constraints  

### 4.1. Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1\qquad \forall i\in I.
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage** – let \(\mathcal{L}_{i,r}\) be the ordered list of segments belonging to route *r* for train *i*.  

\[
\delta_{i\ell}= \sum_{r\in R_i} \mathbf{1}_{\{\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{i,r}\}}\,x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

Thus \(\delta_{i\ell}=1\) only if the chosen route contains that segment.

### 4.2. Speed‑class allocation on a segment  

3. **Exactly one speed class on an occupied segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} s_{i,\ell,k}= \delta_{i\ell}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

4. **Travel time expressed by the chosen speed class**  

\[
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} \frac{L_{\ell}}{v_k}\,s_{i,\ell,k}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;\forall \ell\in L_i .
\]

(If \(\delta_{i\ell}=0\) then all \(s_{i,\ell,k}=0\) and \(\tau_{i,\ell}=0\).)

### 4.3. Time‑window (blocked‑segment) constraints  

A segment ℓ∈B is unavailable between \([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\).  If a train uses that segment, its **entry time** must lie either completely before the block or completely after it.

Define entry and exit times on ℓ:  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell}&= t_{i,\text{up}(ℓ)} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{p\in S_i:\,p\prec\text{up}(ℓ)}\tau_{i,p}}_{\text{cumulative travel on previous segments}} ,\\
\text{exit}_{i\ell}&= \text{enter}_{i\ell}+ \tau_{i,\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]

where `up(ℓ)` is the upstream station of ℓ and “≺” denotes the order along the route.

The logical condition  
\[
\text{enter}_{i\ell} \le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} \;\; \text{or}\;\; \text{enter}_{i\ell} \ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} ,
\]  
is linearised with a binary *w* :

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} + M\,w_{i\ell} ,\\
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} - M\,(1-w_{i\ell}) ,\\
w_{i\ell}&\in\{0,1\},\qquad
z_{i\ell}= \delta_{i\ell}\;( \text{so that constraints are activated only if the segment is used}).
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(\delta_{i\ell}=0\) the constraints are relaxed by a big‑M term (or they can be simply omitted).

### 4.4. Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) constraints on bidirectional shared tracks  

For every conflicting pair \((i,j,ℓ)\in P\) we introduce binary \(y_{ij\ell}\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i\ell} &\ge \text{exit}_{j\ell} - M\,y_{ij\ell},\\
\text{enter}_{j\ell} &\ge \text{exit}_{i\ell} - M\,(1-y_{ij\ell}),\\
y_{ij\ell}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is enforced, guaranteeing that the two trains are never on the same physical track segment at the same time.

### 4.5. Time‑propagation (schedule continuity)  

5. **From one station to the next** – let \(ℓ = (s,s')\) be the segment that connects station *s* to its immediate downstream station *s'*.  

\[
t_{i,s'} = t_{i,s} + \underbrace{\tau_{i,\ell}}_{\text{travel}} + d_{i,s}\qquad\forall i,\; \forall (s,s')\in L_i .
\]

where \(d_{i,s}\) is the dwell time at station *s*.

6. **Dwell‑time limits**  

\[
\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min} \le d_{i,s} \le \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max}\qquad\forall i,\; s\in S_i\setminus\{ \text{final}\}.
\]

(For the origin station dwell may be zero.)

7. **Acceleration / deceleration bounding** – if a speed class changes between two consecutive segments, an extra time penalty Δ​acc is required.  Let  

\[
u_{i,\ell,k}=s_{i,\ell,k}\;(1-\!s_{i,\ell^{-},k})\qquad(\text{linearised via SOS‑1 / extra binaries}),
\]  

where ℓ⁻ is the previous segment of train *i*. Then

\[
\sum_{k} u_{i,\ell,k}\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\min}\le 
\tau_{i,\ell}-\frac{L_{\ell}}{v_k}\le
\sum_{k} u_{i,\ell,k}\;\Delta^{\text{acc}}_{\max}.
\]

In practice this is expressed by a pair of constraints using a big‑M and the binary \(u_{i,\ell,k}\); it ensures that whenever the speed class switches, the travel time is enlarged by at most the admissible acceleration/deceleration slack.

### 4.6. Horizon & final‑time constraints  

8. **No train may finish after the planning horizon**  

\[
t_{i,\text{final}} \le H\qquad\forall i\in I .
\]

9. **Definition of final‑time variable** (used in the objective)  

\[
t_{i,\text{final}} = t_{i,s_{\text{dest}}}\qquad\forall i,
\]

where \(s_{\text{dest}}\) is the last station of train *i* on the chosen route.

---

## 5. Objective function  

The MILP minimizes a weighted sum of (i) total passenger delay and (ii) total energy consumption.

\[
\min\;\; \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{i\in I}\Bigl(t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}}\Bigr)}_{\text{Delay term}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{\ell\in L_i}\sum_{k\in K} e_k \,\tau_{i,\ell}\, s_{i,\ell,k}}_{\text{Energy term}} .
\]

*Explanation*

* **Delay term** – the quantity \((t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})\) is the realized arrival‑time deviation of train *i* from its original schedule; summing over all trains yields the total passenger‑delay (in minutes). The scalar \(\alpha\) translates minutes into the cost unit used for the optimisation (for instance € per minute).

* **Energy term** – travelling on segment ℓ with speed class *k* consumes energy at rate *e_k* for the whole travelling time \(\tau_{i,\ell}\). Because \(s_{i,\ell,k}\) is binary, the product \(\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\) is linear (it is simply \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) when the class is selected, zero otherwise). Multiplying by *e_k* gives the energy (kWh). Summation over all trains, segments and classes gives the total energy usage. The coefficient \(\beta\) converts kWh into the same monetary cost unit as the delay term.

Both terms are linear in the decision variables; the only “product” \(\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\) is handled by the definition of \(\tau_{i,\ell}\) in constraint (4) above.

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&\alpha\sum_{i}(t_{i,\text{final}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})
        +\beta\sum_{i}\sum_{\ell\in L_i}\sum_{k} e_k \,\tau_{i,\ell}\, s_{i,\ell,k}\\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_i}x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\\
&\delta_{i\ell}= \sum_{r}\mathbf 1_{\ell\in\mathcal L_{i,r}}x_{i,r} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\sum_k s_{i,\ell,k}= \delta_{i\ell} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_k \frac{L_\ell}{v_k}s_{i,\ell,k} &&\forall i,\ell\\
&\text{(blocked‑segment big‑M constraints)} &&\forall i,\ell\in B\\
&\text{(conflict‑avoidance precedence constraints)} &&\forall (i,j,\ell)\in P\\
& t_{i,s'} = t_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,\ell}+ d_{i,s} &&\forall i,\;(s,s')\in L_i\\
& \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\min}\le d_{i,s}\le\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{\max} &&\forall i,s\\
& \text{(acc/dec acceleration linking constraints)} &&\forall i,\ell\\
& t_{i,\text{final}}\le H &&\forall i\\
& x_{i,r},s_{i,\ell,k},y_{ij\ell},w_{i\ell},\delta_{i\ell}\in\{0,1\}\\
& t_{i,s},\tau_{i,\ell},d_{i,s}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\]

---

## 7. Modeling assumptions (to be explicit)

1. **Fixed set of routes** – each train can either stay on its original route or take a pre‑computed detour; no dynamic re‑routing inside the horizon.
2. **Speed classes are piece‑wise constant** – a train travels on a segment at a single cruise speed *v_k*; acceleration/deceleration is modelled only as a time penalty (Δ​acc) that is added to the travel time of that segment.
3. **Energy consumption is proportional to cruise time only** – auxiliary energy for acceleration is absorbed into the per‑class coefficient *e_k* (or can be added as a constant per speed change if needed).
4. **Deterministic blocking** – the closed time windows of segments are known a‑priori and do not depend on the schedule.
5. **No overtaking on the same line** – the bidirectional conflict constraints guarantee a simple first‑come‑first‑served ordering on each physical track. If overtaking is allowed, additional binaries per train order would be required.
6. **Dwell time bounds are the same for all stations** – they can be made station‑specific by indexing with *s* if data are available.
7. **Big‑M values** – chosen large enough so that they never become active when the associated binary is 0, yet not excessively large to avoid numerical instability.

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – build the sets *R​i*, *L​i*, *P*, the segment lengths *Lℓ*, speed‑class table \((v_k,e_k)\) and the blocking windows.  
2. **Parameter tuning** – select the weighting factors \(\alpha,\beta\) to reflect the railway operator’s relative importance of punctuality vs. energy saving.  
3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to a solver (e.g. Gurobi `gurobi_cl`, CPLEX `cplex`).  The binary variables provide the chosen routes, speed class per segment and the conflict‑resolution ordering.  The continuous variables give the full timetable (departure times and travel times).  
4. **Post‑processing** – compute the realised delay and total energy from the solution, generate a Gantt‑type schedule for the dispatcher, and, if needed, feed the result into a simulation model for validation.

The formulation above is *complete* (all constraints needed for a feasible timetable are present) and *linear* (only linear expressions and binary decisions).  It can be extended straightforwardly to include additional operational aspects such as crew‑changing windows, rolling‑stock availability, or variable energy tariffs.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP: binary variables for train i using original route r_i or reroute r'_i, departure times t_{i,s} at stations, travel time variables τ_{i,ℓ} on segment ℓ, speed level binary s_{i,ℓ,k} (k speed class), objective minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (t_{i,final}-t_i^sched) and energy Σ_i Σ_ℓ Σ_k e_k * τ_{i,ℓ} * s_{i,ℓ,k}. Constraints: each train chooses one route; if segment ℓ is blocked during [B_ℓ_start,B_ℓ_end] then trains on that side cannot occupy it, enforce time windows using big-M; precedence constraints for bidirectional conflict on shared track: for any pair (i,j) on same segment opposite directions, either finish_i <= start_j or vice versa using binary y_{ijℓ}; travel time τ_{i,ℓ}= Σ_k (L_ℓ/v_k)* s_{i,ℓ,k}; sum_k s_{i,ℓ,k}=1; dwell time lower/upper bounds; acceleration/deceleration limits via linking τ to speed classes; total schedule horizon limit. Provide assumptions.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP**  

The mathematical program below combines (i) a binary routing decision (original route vs. a reroute), (ii) a departure‑time decision at every station, (iii) a speed‑level decision on every line‑segment, and (iv) conflict‑avoidance on single‑track sections.  
All data that are required to instantiate the model are listed in the *Parameters* section; the set‑notation is purposely kept linear so that the model can be entered directly into a commercial MILP solver (Cplex, Gurobi, Xpress, …).

---

## 1. Index sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\( \mathcal I \\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\) |
| \\( \mathcal S_i \\) | Ordered set of stations visited by train \\(i\\) on its **original** route \\(r_i\\) (including origin and destination) |
| \\( \mathcal S'_i \\) | Ordered set of stations visited by train \\(i\\) on its **reroute** \\(r'_i\\) |
| \\( \mathcal L_i \\) | Set of line‑segments traversed by train \\(i\\) on the chosen route (obtained from the station list) |
| \\( \mathcal K \\) | Set of admissible speed classes (e.g. \\(k=1,\dots,K\\) ), each class has a constant cruising speed \\(v_k\\) and energy coefficient \\(e_k\\) |
| \\( \mathcal B \\) | Set of **blocked** line‑segments (segments that are unavailable during a maintenance window) |
| \\( \mathcal P \\) | Set of **conflict pairs**: ordered pairs \\((i,j, \ell)\\) such that trains \\(i\\) and \\(j\\) travel on the same physical segment \\(\ell\\) in opposite directions (single‑track conflict) |

---

## 2. Parameters (input data)

| Symbol | Meaning | Units |
|--------|----------|-------|
| \\(t_i^{\text{sched}}\\) | Scheduled departure time of train \\(i\\) from its origin (reference) | [s] |
| \\(L_\ell\\) | Length of segment \\(\ell\\) | [km] |
| \\(v_k\\) | Speed of class \\(k\\) (constant cruising speed) | [km/h] |
| \\(e_k\\) | Energy consumption rate (per unit time) for class \\(k\\) | [kWh/h] |
| \\(D_{i,s}^{\min }, D_{i,s}^{\max }\\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) | [s] |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. horizon length) | [s] |
| \\(B_{\ell}^{\text{start}}, B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}\\) | Start / end of the external blockage on segment \\(\ell\\) (only defined if \\(\ell\in\mathcal B\\)) | [s] |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) | Weight of delay in the objective | – |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Weight of energy in the objective | – |
| \\(T^{\text{H}}\\) | Planning horizon (latest time a train may finish) | [s] |

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \\(x_i \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) uses the **original** route \\(r_i\\); 0 ⇔ uses the **reroute** \\(r'_i\\) |
| \\(t_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(s\\) (the first station is the origin) |
| \\(\tau_{i,\ell}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Traversal time** of train \\(i\\) on segment \\(\ell\\) (time spent moving, not counting dwell) |
| \\(s_{i,\ell,k}\\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) travels on segment \\(\ell\\) with speed class \\(k\\) |
| \\(y_{ij\ell} \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary (only for \\((i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P\\)) | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) passes segment \\(\ell\\) **before** train \\(j\\) (conflict‑resolution ordering) |
| \\(z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}} \\in \{0,1\}\\) | binary (only for \\(\ell\in\mathcal B\\)) | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) traverses a **blocked** segment \\(\ell\\) (used to enforce the time‑window) |

All other variables that are not listed are implicit (e.g. the arrival time at a station is simply \\(t_{i,s}+D_{i,s}\\) ).

---

## 4. Model formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\Bigl(t_{i,\text{dest}}-t_i^{\text{sched}}\Bigr)}_{\text{Total passenger‑delay}} 
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}
e_k \; \tau_{i,\ell}\; s_{i,\ell,k}}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
\tag{Obj}
\]

where \\(t_{i,\text{dest}}\\) is the departure time from the last station of the chosen route (identical to the arrival time at the destination because no dwell after that).

---

### 4.2 Routing choice  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i} 1 = |\mathcal L_i| = 
\begin{cases}
|\mathcal L_i^{\text{orig}}| & \text{if } x_i = 1\\[2pt]
|\mathcal L_i^{\text{rer}}| & \text{if } x_i = 0
\end{cases}
\]  

In practice, the set \\(\mathcal L_i\\) that appears in all subsequent constraints is defined **conditionally**:  

\[
\mathcal L_i = 
\begin{cases}
\mathcal L_i^{\text{orig}} & \text{if } x_i = 1\\
\mathcal L_i^{\text{rer}}  & \text{if } x_i = 0
\end{cases}
\]  

Implementation tip: create two copies of each train (orig‑copy, rer‑copy) and enforce \\(x_i\\) to select which copy is active; all other constraints are written for the *active* copy only.

---

### 4.3 Speed‑class assignment on each traversed segment  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K} s_{i,\ell,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I,\;\forall \ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{Speed‑choice}
\]

\[
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}\; s_{i,\ell,k}
\qquad \forall i,\ell \tag{Travel‑time‑definition}
\]

The term \\(\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}\\) is the **deterministic travel time** if the train maintains speed class \\(k\\) over the whole segment.  

If there are additional acceleration / deceleration limits you can tighten the big‑M for \\(\tau_{i,\ell}\\) but the basic linear relationship above already forces a link between the chosen speed class and the travel time.

---

### 4.4 Dwell‑time limits  

For every station \\(s\\) that train \\(i\\) visits (according to the chosen route):  

\[
D_{i,s}^{\min } \le  t_{i,s^{+}}- t_{i,s} \le D_{i,s}^{\max } \qquad \forall i, s\in\mathcal S_i\cup\mathcal S'_i \tag{Dwell}
\]  

where \\(s^{+}\\) denotes the **next** station on the same route. The left‑hand side guarantees the train stays at least the minimum required time; the right‑hand side prevents unnecessarily long stops.

---

### 4.5 Temporal linking of departure times and segment travel  

For each train \\(i\\) and each successive pair (station, segment):  

\[
t_{i,s^{+}} = t_{i,s}+ D_{i,s}^{\text{actual}} + \tau_{i,\ell} \qquad 
\forall i,\;\forall\ell\in\mathcal L_i,\;\text{where } \ell \text{ connects } s\rightarrow s^{+}
\]  

Here \\(D_{i,s}^{\text{actual}}\\) can be taken as any value within the dwell bounds; when the model solves it will automatically select a value that satisfies the inequality (the constraints can be expressed as two inequalities using the bounds above).

---

### 4.6 Blockage constraints (externally imposed closures)  

If segment \\(\ell\\) belongs to the blocked set \\(\mathcal B\\), the train may **not** be on the segment during the forbidden interval \\([B_{\ell}^{\text{start}},B_{\ell}^{\text{end}}]\\). This is enforced by a classic big‑M formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} &\ge B_{\ell}^{\text{end}} - M\,(1-z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}) \\
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}  &\le B_{\ell}^{\text{start}} + M\,(1-z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal B
\]

where  

\[
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} = \text{departure time from the upstream station of }\ell,
\qquad
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{exit}}  = t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{i,\ell}
\]

The binary \\(z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}\\) forces the model to either schedule the train **before** the block (\\(z=0\\) → exit ≤ start) or **after** the block (\\(z=1\\) → enter ≥ end).  

If a reroute completely avoids a blocked segment, the corresponding \\(\ell\\) simply does not belong to \\(\mathcal L_i\\) for that train.

---

### 4.7 Single‑track conflict (bidirectional)  

For every ordered conflict pair \\((i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P\\) (trains traveling on the same physical segment in opposite directions) we introduce a binary ordering variable \\(y_{ij\ell}\\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{i,\ell} &\le t_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,(1-y_{ij\ell})\\
t_{j,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + \tau_{j,\ell} &\le t_{i,\ell}^{\text{enter}} + M\,y_{ij\ell}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P
\]

When \\(y_{ij\ell}=1\\) the model forces train \\(j\\) to finish its traversal before train \\(i\\) enters; when \\(y_{ij\ell}=0\\) the opposite ordering is selected. Exactly one ordering is enforced because the two constraints are complementary.

---

### 4.8 Horizon / feasibility  

\[
t_{i,\text{dest}} \le T^{\text{H}} \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal I \tag{Horizon}
\]

Additionally, a non‑negativity requirement for all time‑type variables:

\[
t_{i,s} \ge 0,\qquad \tau_{i,\ell}\ge 0 \qquad \forall i,s,\ell.
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i}(t_{i,\text{dest}}-t_i^{\text{sched}})
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_i}\sum_{k}e_k\,\tau_{i,\ell}\,s_{i,\ell,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k}s_{i,\ell,k}=1 &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C1}\\
&
\tau_{i,\ell}= \sum_{k}\frac{L_\ell}{v_k}s_{i,\ell,k} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C2}\\
&
D_{i,s}^{\min}\le t_{i,s^{+}}-t_{i,s}\le D_{i,s}^{\max} &&\forall i,s\in\text{stations of chosen route} \tag{C3}\\
&
t_{i,s^{+}} = t_{i,s}+ (t_{i,s^{+}}-t_{i,s}) + \tau_{i,\ell} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal L_i \tag{C4}\\
&
\text{Blockage constraints (big‑M)} &&\forall i,\ell\in\mathcal B \tag{C5}\\
&
\text{Conflict constraints } y_{ij\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j,\ell)\in\mathcal P \tag{C6}\\
&
t_{i,\text{dest}}\le T^{\text{H}} &&\forall i \tag{C7}\\
&
x_i\in\{0,1\},\; s_{i,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{ij\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,\ell}^{\text{blk}}\in\{0,1\}\\
&
t_{i,s},\tau_{i,\ell}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,\ell .
\end{aligned}
\]

All other constraints (e.g., linking the active set of stations/segments to the routing binary \\(x_i\\)) are handled by a standard *route‑selection* modeling trick:

*Create two “copies’’ of each train*:  

* copy‑1 uses original route, all its associated variables are multiplied by \\(x_i\\);  
* copy‑2 uses reroute, all its associated variables are multiplied by \\(1-x_i\\).  

Then the constraints above are written **once** for each copy and the multiplication guarantees that only the variables of the selected copy can be non‑zero.

---

## 6. Main modelling assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Rationale / effect on MILP |
|---|------------|----------------------------|
| A1 | Travel on a segment is performed at a **single constant speed class** (no intra‑segment speed‑change). | Guarantees linear relation (C2); if finer granularity is needed a segment can be split into sub‑segments. |
| A2 | Dwell time at a station is a decision variable bounded by known minima/maxima. | Gives flexibility for recovery buffering while preserving realistic stop lengths. |
| A3 | Blockage windows are known **a priori** and are hard (cannot be entered). | Enforced by big‑M constraints (C5); rerouting is the primary way to avoid them. |
| A4 | Only **pairwise** opposite‑direction conflicts on a single‑track are considered; multiple‑train overlap is avoided implicitly through the binary ordering variables \\(y_{ij\ell}\\). | Keeps the model linear; larger blocks can be modeled by chaining binary variables. |
| A5 | Energy consumption is proportional to *time spent* in a speed class (i.e., constant power per class). | Leads to linear term \\(e_k\tau_{i,\ell}s_{i,\ell,k}\\) in the objective. |
| A6 | No explicit capacity constraints on stations (platform capacity) – if required, add binary variables for platform occupation and extra precedence constraints. |
| A7 | The planning horizon \\(T^{\text H}\\) is sufficiently large to contain any feasible schedule; otherwise the model may become infeasible. |
| A8 | Acceleration/deceleration limits are **implicit** in the choice of speed classes (slow classes can be used to model a slower‑accelerating train). If more accuracy is needed, additional linear constraints linking consecutive \\(s_{i,\ell,k}\\) can be added. |

---

## 7. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the two route alternatives for each train (list of stations, compute the derived segment list and segment lengths).  
2. **Parameter generation** – Specify \\(v_k\\), \\(e_k\\), dwell bounds, blockage windows, and the conflict‑pair set \\(\mathcal P\\).  
3. **Implementation** – Write the model in a MILP language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP). The “copy‑train’’ trick makes the routing decision linear.  
4. **Solver call** – Choose a commercial MILP solver; the model is of moderate size (variables ≈ |I|·|L|·|K| + |I|·|S| + |P|).  
5. **Post‑processing** – From the optimal solution extract for each train: (i) the chosen route (value of \\(x_i\\)), (ii) departure times at all stations, (iii) speed class per segment, (iv) the resulting delay and energy consumption.

---

### Bottom line  

The formulation above captures a **joint** decision problem: *which route should a train take?* *when should it leave each station?* *at which speed class should it travel on each line segment?* All decisions are linked through linear constraints, and the objective balances passenger delay against energy usage. The big‑M constraints and binary ordering variables guarantee feasibility with respect to external blockages and single‑track conflicts, while the binary speed‑class variables keep the travel‑time relationship linear and thus tractable for a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
