response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures the description you gave.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, and finally every group of constraints together with a short explanation of what each group enforces.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of railway segments (track pieces) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \(s\). |
| \(S^{\rm blk}\subseteq S\) | Set of **blocked** segments (partial blockage). |
| \(N_s\) | Set of stations that bound segment \(s\) (normally two: upstream \(u(s)\) and downstream \(d(s)\)). |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete) for a train on a segment, indexed by \(k\). |
| \(P_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) must traverse if it stays on its *original* route (the “forward” direction). |
| \(Q_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) would traverse on the *opposite* (detour) route (e.g., using the opposite track on a two‑track line). |
| \(C_t = \{0,1\}\) | Choice set for the binary routing variable of train \(t\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(\underline{v}_k, \overline{v}_k\) | Lower / upper bound of speed for level \(k\) (km/h). |
| \(\alpha_k\) | Energy consumption coefficient for speed level \(k\) (kWh per km). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g., € per hour). |
| \(\gamma\) | Weight for total energy consumption (e.g., € per kWh). |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Maximum admissible acceleration (km/h²). |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum admissible deceleration (km/h²). |
| \(h^{\min}\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two trains on the *same* physical track (seconds). |
| \([B^{\rm start}_s, B^{\rm end}_s]\) | Time window during which segment \(s\in S^{\rm blk}\) is blocked (seconds). |
| \(\tau^{\rm min}_{t,s},\tau^{\rm max}_{t,s}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible travel time for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (derived from speed limits). |
| \(D^{\rm plan}_t\) | Planned (scheduled) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (seconds). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶ s). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \(x_t \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Routing choice**: 0 = original route (\(P_t\)), 1 = detour/or opposite track (\(Q_t\)). |
| \(y_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | Indicator that train \(t\) **uses** segment \(s\). (Enforced by routing choice.) |
| \(z_{t,t',s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Ordering** on a shared segment: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) passes segment \(s\) **before** train \(t'\). Only defined for pairs \((t,t')\) that may occupy the same physical track (same direction or opposite direction on a single‑track portion). |
| \(a_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at the upstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from the downstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,s,k} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Speed‑level selection**: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) travels on segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). (Exactly one level per used segment.) |
| \(\Delta_t \ge 0\) | continuous | **Total delay** of train \(t\) (difference between actual arrival at final destination and scheduled arrival). |
| \(e_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Energy** spent by train \(t\) on segment \(s\). (Linearized by speed‑level coefficient.) |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{Delay cost}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\;e_{t,s}}_{\text{Energy cost}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The objective is a weighted sum of total passenger/operational delay and total energy consumption.

---

### 4.2 Routing (Flow‑conservation)  

For every train \(t\) and every segment \(s\):

\[
y_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1-x_t & \text{if } s\in P_t,\\[2mm]
x_t   & \text{if } s\in Q_t,\\[2mm]
0     & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{R1}
\]

(Implemented with two linear constraints per segment, e.g.  
\(y_{t,s}\le 1-x_t\) for \(s\in P_t\); \(y_{t,s}\le x_t\) for \(s\in Q_t\); and \(y_{t,s}\ge 1-x_t\) or \(y_{t,s}\ge x_t\) as needed.)

---

### 4.3 Speed‑level selection  

For each train‑segment pair that is used:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\;s\in S .
\tag{S1}
\]

Thus exactly one speed level is chosen if the segment is traversed; otherwise all \(v_{t,s,k}=0\).

---

### 4.4 Travel‑time on a segment  

The travel time on segment \(s\) for train \(t\) is the sum of the inverse speeds of the selected level:

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K} \frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\; v_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{S2}
\]

Because the speed levels are discrete, the term \(\frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\) is a constant coefficient.  
If a more accurate linearisation of \(L_s/v\) is required, a piece‑wise linear approximation can be used; the formulation above already stays linear because the coefficients are pre‑computed.

---

### 4.5 Acceleration / Deceleration limits  

Let \(s\) and its predecessor on the chosen route be \(s^{-}\). When a train changes speed between two consecutive segments, the time difference must respect the acceleration bound:

\[
\bigl(d_{t,s^{-}}-a_{t,s}\bigr) \; \ge\; 
\frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\overline{v}_k} \;-\; \frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\underline{v}_{k'}}\;-\;a^{\max}\;(a_{t,s}-d_{t,s^{-}})
\]

A compact linear version uses “big‑M” and binary indicators for the speed level on the two segments. For brevity we write the linearised form:

\[
a_{t,s} - d_{t,s^{-}} \;\ge\; -M\,(1-\theta_{t,s})\qquad
\theta_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;\; \theta_{t,s}=1 \text{ if the speed change respects } a^{\max},d^{\max}.
\tag{ACC}
\]

(The detailed expansion is routine: introduce auxiliary binaries for each pair \((k,k')\) and enforce the corresponding time‑difference bound.)

---

### 4.6 Blockage (time‑window) constraints  

If a segment \(s\) is partially blocked, a train may only occupy it **outside** the blocked interval:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; B^{\rm end}_s \;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \quad\text{or}\quad 
d_{t,s} \;\le\; B^{\rm start}_s \;+\; M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S^{\rm blk}.
\tag{BLK}
\]

The disjunction is linearised with a binary variable \(b_{t,s}\) that decides whether the train passes **before** or **after** the blockage:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,s} &\le B^{\rm start}_s + M\,b_{t,s},\\
a_{t,s} &\ge B^{\rm end}_s   - M\,(1-b_{t,s}),\\
b_{t,s}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the train does not use the segment (\(y_{t,s}=0\)), the constraints become non‑binding because of the big‑M terms.

---

### 4.7 Head‑way (conflict) constraints on shared physical track  

Consider any pair of trains \((t,t')\) that may be on the same **physical** track portion (including opposite directions on a single‑track segment). For each such segment \(s\) we enforce a strict ordering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} + h^{\min} - M\,(1-z_{t,t',s}),\\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} + h^{\min} - M\,(z_{t,t',s}),\\
z_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\}, \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{C},\;s\in S .
\end{aligned}
\tag{HW}
\]

Here \(\mathcal{C}\) is the set of train pairs that share a segment.  
Exactly one of the two inequalities is active (the big‑M forces the other to be slack), thereby deciding which train passes first.

**Transitivity** (to avoid cycles) is added for any three trains that share the same segment:

\[
z_{t_1,t_2,s}+z_{t_2,t_3,s}-z_{t_1,t_3,s}\le 1 \qquad
\forall t_1,t_2,t_3\in\mathcal{C},\; s\in S .
\tag{TRANS}
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent ordering.

---

### 4.8 Time‑feasibility (causality)  

For every train \(t\) and every consecutive pair of segments \((s^{-},s)\) on its chosen route:

\[
a_{t,s}= d_{t,s^{-}} \qquad \forall t,\; s\neq \text{first segment of }t .
\tag{TIME}
\]

The first segment’s arrival time is fixed to the scheduled departure from the origin (or a decision variable if the schedule can be shifted).  

---

### 4.9 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\rm last}_t\) be the final segment on the selected route of train \(t\). The actual arrival at the destination is \(d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t}\). The delay variable is defined as:

\[
\Delta_t \; \ge\; d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t} - D^{\rm plan}_t ,\qquad \Delta_t \ge 0 .
\tag{DELAY}
\]

If early arrival is allowed (negative delay), the first inequality can be replaced by an equality; otherwise the model forces \(\Delta_t\) to capture only tardiness.

---

### 4.10 Energy consumption linearisation  

Energy on a segment is proportional to the distance travelled at the selected speed level:

\[
e_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \alpha_k \, L_s \, v_{t,s,k}\qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because \(\alpha_k\) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

---

### 4.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_t               &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t\in T,\\
y_{t,s}           &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t,s,\\
z_{t,t',s}        &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C},\,s,\\
v_{t,s,k}         &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t,s,k,\\
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\Delta_t,e_{t,s} &\ge 0   &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Group | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Routing variables** \(x_t, y_{t,s}\) | Choose for each train whether it stays on its original route or takes the opposite‑track detour; enforce that a train can only traverse segments belonging to the selected route. |
| **Speed‑level binaries** \(v_{t,s,k}\) | Discretise the continuous speed decision. Exactly one level is selected on a used segment, which linearises the otherwise nonlinear relation between speed and travel time / energy. |
| **Arrival / departure times** \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) | Capture the temporal schedule of each train on every segment. Equality (TIME) links consecutive segments, guaranteeing a feasible timetable. |
| **Head‑way / ordering binaries** \(z_{t,t',s}\) | Resolve conflicts on shared physical track portions. The big‑M formulation forces one train to leave at least \(h^{\min}\) seconds before the other enters. Transitivity constraints avoid cycles (i.e., contradictory orderings). |
| **Blockage constraints** (BLK) | Ensure that a train never occupies a blocked segment during its forbidden time window. The binary \(b_{t,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **Acceleration / deceleration limits** (ACC) | Enforce that speed changes between consecutive segments respect the maximum allowable acceleration/deceleration. Linearised with auxiliary binaries for each speed‑level pair. |
| **Delay definition** (DELAY) | Computes the tardiness of each train relative to its scheduled arrival; feeds directly into the objective. |
| **Energy calculation** (ENERGY) | Linear expression for the energy spent on each segment, using the speed‑level coefficient \(\alpha_k\). |
| **Objective** (OBJ) | Minimises a weighted sum of total delay (penalised by \(\beta\)) and total energy consumption (penalised by \(\gamma\)). The weights allow the railway operator to trade‑off punctuality against sustainability. |

---

### How to solve  

The model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**. It can be handed directly to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, CBC).  

Typical solution steps:

1. **Data preparation** – compute the segment lengths, speed‑level travel‑time coefficients \(\frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\), energy coefficients \(\alpha_k L_s\), and the set of conflicting train pairs \(\mathcal{C}\).  
2. **Parameter tuning** – choose realistic values for \(\beta,\gamma\) to reflect the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy.  
3. **Big‑M sizing** – set \(M\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 hours ≈ 36 000 s).  
4. **Run the MILP** – the solver will return the optimal routing choices \(x_t\), speed‑level selections \(v_{t,s,k}\), and a feasible timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\) that respects all physical and operational constraints while minimising the weighted cost.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures every element you asked for—binary routing, binary ordering on shared segments, continuous timing, discrete speed decisions, blockage windows, acceleration limits, linearised energy consumption, and a weighted objective—while remaining a pure MILP that can be solved with standard optimisation software.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) for high-speed railway with partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice (original or opposite track), binary ordering between conflicting trains on shared segment, continuous arrival/departure times at stations, continuous speed levels per track segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. response.content:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the “Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)”**  

The model simultaneously decides (i) which track a train will use on each segment (original vs. opposite track), (ii) the order in which trains traverse a shared (blocked) segment, (iii) the exact arrival/departure times at every station, and (iv) the speed level that each train will adopt on every track segment.  
All decisions are made so that the **weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption** is as small as possible while respecting safety, operational, and physical limits.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train), indexed by *s* |
| **E** | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) connecting two consecutive stations, indexed by *e = (i,j)* where *i,j ∈ S* |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed‑levels (discrete), indexed by *k* |
| **B ⊆ E** | Sub‑set of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance) |
| **C(t)** | Ordered list of segments that train *t* must travel (its route) – a subset of **E** |
| **P(e)** | Set of trains that use segment *e* (i.e. *t* with *e ∈ C(t)*) |

---

## 2.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|--------------|
| **xₜₑ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 → train *t* uses the **original** track on segment *e*; 0 → uses the **opposite** track (if available). |
| **yₜ₁ₜ₂ₑ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering on a **shared** (blocked) segment *e ∈ B*: 1 → train *t₁* passes *e* **before** train *t₂*; 0 → otherwise. |
| **aₜₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s* (if *s* belongs to *C(t)*). |
| **dₜₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **vₜₑₖ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 → train *t* travels on segment *e* with speed level *k* (speed = 𝑣ₖ). Exactly one speed level is chosen for each (t,e). |
| **eₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between its actual arrival at the final destination and its scheduled arrival). |
| **Eₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (linearized, see §4). |

---

## 3.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Lₑ** | Length of segment *e* (km). |
| **vₖ** | Physical speed (km/h) associated with speed level *k*. |
| **αₖ**, **βₖ** | Linear coefficients that map speed level *k* to **energy consumption per km** (e.g., *E = αₖ·vₖ + βₖ*). |
| **τₜₛ⁰** | Scheduled (planned) departure time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **Δₜₛ** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s* (for passenger boarding/alighting). |
| **hₘᵢₙ** | Minimum safety headway (time) required between any two consecutive trains on the **same** track. |
| **Bₑˢ**, **Bₑᵉ** | Start and end time of the blockage window on segment *e ∈ B* (no train may occupy the segment during this interval). |
| **aₘₐₓ**, **aₘᵢₙ** | Maximum / minimum admissible acceleration (km/h²) that can be applied when a train changes speed level between consecutive segments. |
| **w₁**, **w₂** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective (chosen by the planner). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time difference (used for linearizing ordering constraints). |

---

## 4.  Linearized Energy Consumption  

For each train *t* and segment *e* the energy contributed by speed level *k* is  

\[
E_{t e k}= (\alpha_k v_k + \beta_k) \, L_e .
\]

Because *vₜₑₖ* is binary and exactly one speed level is selected, the total energy of train *t* can be written linearly:

\[
E_t = \sum_{e\in C(t)}\;\sum_{k\in K} (\alpha_k v_k + \beta_k) L_e \; v_{t e k}.
\]

We will denote this linear expression simply as **Eₜ** in the model.

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \; w_1 \sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; w_2 \sum_{t\in T} E_t}
\]

The first term penalises passenger delay, the second term penalises the total energy used by all trains.

---

## 6.  Constraints  

### 6.1 Routing / Track‑Choice  

For each train *t* and each segment *e* that belongs to its path:

\[
x_{t e}=1 \;\; \Longrightarrow \;\; \text{train }t\text{ uses the original track on }e,
\]
\[
x_{t e}=0 \;\; \Longrightarrow \;\; \text{train }t\text{ uses the opposite track (if it exists).}
\]

If a segment does **not** have an opposite track, we simply fix \(x_{t e}=1\).  
(Implementation: a parameter `opp_e ∈ {0,1}` indicating the existence of an opposite track; add constraint \(x_{t e} \ge \text{opp}_e\).)

### 6.2 Speed‑Level Selection  

Exactly one speed level must be chosen for each traversed segment:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall e\in C(t).
\tag{SL‑1}
\]

### 6.3 Time‑Propagation (travel time on a segment)  

Travel time on segment *e* when speed level *k* is used:

\[
\theta_{t e k}= \frac{L_e}{v_k}\quad\text{(hours)} .
\]

Because only one speed level is active, the actual travel time is

\[
\tau_{t e}= \sum_{k\in K} \theta_{t e k}\; v_{t e k}.
\]

Link arrival and departure times:

\[
a_{t j}= d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall e=(i,j)\in C(t).
\tag{TIME‑1}
\]

### 6.4 Minimum Dwell Time  

\[
d_{t s} \ge a_{t s}+ \Delta_{t s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in C(t).
\tag{DWELL}
\]

### 6.5 Headway on the Same Physical Track  

If two trains *t₁* and *t₂* use the **same** physical track on segment *e* (i.e., they make the same routing choice), a safety headway must be respected:

\[
d_{t_1 i} + \tau_{t_1 e} + h_{\min} \le a_{t_2 j} \;+\; M\,(1 - z_{t_1 t_2 e}) \\
d_{t_2 i} + \tau_{t_2 e} + h_{\min} \le a_{t_1 j} \;+\; M\,(z_{t_1 t_2 e}) 
\qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e),\; \forall e\in E,
\tag{HEADWAY}
\]

where the auxiliary binary  

\[
z_{t_1 t_2 e}= 
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }t_1\text{ passes }e\text{ before }t_2,\\
0 &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

The big‑M term de‑activates the inequality for the non‑active ordering.

### 6.6 Blockage Window on Partially Blocked Segments  

A train may occupy a blocked segment *e ∈ B* only **outside** its blockage interval:

\[
a_{t i} \ge B_e^{e} \quad \text{or} \quad d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \le B_e^{s}
\]

Linearised with the ordering binary *y* :

\[
a_{t i} \ge B_e^{e} - M\; y_{t e} \\
d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \le B_e^{s} + M\;(1-y_{t e}) \qquad \forall t\in P(e),\; e\in B.
\tag{BLOCK}
\]

If *yₜₑ = 1* the train passes **after** the blockage; if *yₜₑ = 0* it passes **before**.

### 6.7 Speed‑Change (Acceleration/Deceleration) Limits  

When a train changes speed level between two consecutive segments *e₁ = (i,j)* and *e₂ = (j,k)*, the resulting acceleration must stay within bounds:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_2 k}\, v_k \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_1 k}\, v_k \;\le\; a_{\max}\, \Delta t_{t j}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_2 k}\, v_k \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_1 k}\, v_k \;\ge\; a_{\min}\, \Delta t_{t j}
\]

where \(\Delta t_{t j}= d_{t j}-a_{t j}\) is the dwell (or waiting) time at station *j*. Because the left‑hand side is linear in the binary speed‑level variables, the constraints are linear.

### 6.8 Delay Definition  

Let *sᶠ* be the final station of train *t* and *τₜ^{sched}* the scheduled arrival at that station. Then

\[
e_t \ge a_{t s^{f}} - \tau_{t}^{\text{sched}} \qquad \forall t\in T,
\tag{DELAY}
\]

and we force \(e_t\ge 0\). (If early arrival is allowed, the inequality can be replaced by an absolute‑value formulation; here we penalise only lateness.)

### 6.9 Binary Ordering Transitivity on a Shared Segment  

For any three distinct trains *p,q,r* that all use a blocked segment *e* :

\[
y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \le 1,
\qquad
y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \ge 0 .
\tag{TRANS}
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent total order on the segment.

### 6.10 Flow‑Conservation for Routing Choice  

If a train switches from original to opposite track on a segment, the choice must be consistent across the whole route (i.e., a train cannot “jump’’ between the two tracks in the middle of a segment). In practice this is enforced by fixing the binary *xₜₑ* for each segment according to the network layout; the model already contains the binary *xₜₑ* variables, therefore no extra constraint is required beyond the definition of *x*.

### 6.11 Variable Domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t e}\in\{0,1\},\quad y_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\},\quad v_{t e k}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t s}\ge 0,\; d_{t s}\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0,\; E_t\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,a,d,v,e,E}\; &\; w_1\sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; w_2\sum_{t\in T} \sum_{e\in C(t)}\sum_{k\in K} (\alpha_k v_k+\beta_k)L_e \, v_{t e k} \\
\text{s.t. } &\;\; \text{(SL‑1)} &&\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e k}=1 &&\forall t, e\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(TIME‑1)} && a_{t j}= d_{t i}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_e}{v_k}\,v_{t e k} &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(DWELL)} && d_{t s}\ge a_{t s}+ \Delta_{t s} &&\forall t, s\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(HEADWAY)} && d_{t_1 i}+ \tau_{t_1 e}+h_{\min}\le a_{t_2 j}+M(1-z_{t_1 t_2 e}) &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e), e\in E\\
&\;\; && d_{t_2 i}+ \tau_{t_2 e}+h_{\min}\le a_{t_1 j}+M(z_{t_1 t_2 e}) &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e), e\in E\\
&\;\; \text{(BLOCK)} && a_{t i}\ge B_e^{e}-M y_{t e} &&\forall t\in P(e), e\in B\\
&\;\; && d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e}\le B_e^{s}+M(1-y_{t e}) &&\forall t\in P(e), e\in B\\
&\;\; \text{(ACCEL)} && \sum_{k}v_{t e_2 k}v_k-\sum_{k}v_{t e_1 k}v_k \le a_{\max}\,\Delta t_{t j} &&\forall t, (e_1,e_2) \text{ consecutive}\\
&\;\; && \sum_{k}v_{t e_2 k}v_k-\sum_{k}v_{t e_1 k}v_k \ge a_{\min}\,\Delta t_{t j} &&\forall t, (e_1,e_2)\\
&\;\; \text{(DELAY)} && e_t \ge a_{t s^{f}}- \tau_{t}^{\text{sched}} &&\forall t\\
&\;\; \text{(TRANS)} && y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \le 1 &&\forall e\in B,\; p,q,r\in P(e)\\
&\;\; && y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \ge 0 &&\forall e\in B,\; p,q,r\in P(e)\\
&\;\; \text{(ROUTING)} && x_{t e}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,e\\
&\;\; \text{(ORDERING)} && y_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall (t_1,t_2), e\\
&\;\; \text{(VARIABLES)} && a_{t s}, d_{t s}, e_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries listed above. The model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### How the Model Works – Brief Interpretation  

* **Routing choice (`x`)** tells the solver whether a train stays on its nominal track or detours to the opposite track (useful when the original track is partially blocked).  
* **Speed‑level variables (`v`)** let the optimizer pick a feasible speed for each segment; the associated travel time and linear energy cost are then computed.  
* **Arrival/Departure times (`a`, `d`)** propagate through the network using the travel‑time equations, while respecting minimum dwell times at stations.  
* **Ordering binaries (`y`, `z`)** define a total order of trains on each blocked segment, guaranteeing that only one train occupies the segment at a time and that the order is consistent (no cycles).  
* **Headway constraints** enforce the mandatory safety gap between any two trains that happen to use the same physical track (original or opposite).  
* **Blockage constraints** keep every train out of the forbidden time window on a partially blocked segment.  
* **Acceleration constraints** make sure that the speed change from one segment to the next is physically realistic.  
* **Delay variables (`e`)** capture the lateness of each train relative to its schedule; the objective penalises this delay together with the total energy consumption.

By solving the MILP, the railway planner obtains a **globally optimal** combination of routing, sequencing, timing and speed that minimizes the weighted sum of passenger delay and energy use while respecting all safety and operational restrictions.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures the description you gave.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, and finally every group of constraints together with a short explanation of what each group enforces.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of railway segments (track pieces) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \(s\). |
| \(S^{\rm blk}\subseteq S\) | Set of **blocked** segments (partial blockage). |
| \(N_s\) | Set of stations that bound segment \(s\) (normally two: upstream \(u(s)\) and downstream \(d(s)\)). |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible speed levels (discrete) for a train on a segment, indexed by \(k\). |
| \(P_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) must traverse if it stays on its *original* route (the “forward” direction). |
| \(Q_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) would traverse on the *opposite* (detour) route (e.g., using the opposite track on a two‑track line). |
| \(C_t = \{0,1\}\) | Choice set for the binary routing variable of train \(t\). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(\underline{v}_k, \overline{v}_k\) | Lower / upper bound of speed for level \(k\) (km/h). |
| \(\alpha_k\) | Energy consumption coefficient for speed level \(k\) (kWh per km). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g., € per hour). |
| \(\gamma\) | Weight for total energy consumption (e.g., € per kWh). |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Maximum admissible acceleration (km/h²). |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Maximum admissible deceleration (km/h²). |
| \(h^{\min}\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two trains on the *same* physical track (seconds). |
| \([B^{\rm start}_s, B^{\rm end}_s]\) | Time window during which segment \(s\in S^{\rm blk}\) is blocked (seconds). |
| \(\tau^{\rm min}_{t,s},\tau^{\rm max}_{t,s}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible travel time for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (derived from speed limits). |
| \(D^{\rm plan}_t\) | Planned (scheduled) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (seconds). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10⁶ s). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \(x_t \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Routing choice**: 0 = original route (\(P_t\)), 1 = detour/or opposite track (\(Q_t\)). |
| \(y_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | Indicator that train \(t\) **uses** segment \(s\). (Enforced by routing choice.) |
| \(z_{t,t',s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Ordering** on a shared segment: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) passes segment \(s\) **before** train \(t'\). Only defined for pairs \((t,t')\) that may occupy the same physical track (same direction or opposite direction on a single‑track portion). |
| \(a_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at the upstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from the downstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,s,k} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Speed‑level selection**: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) travels on segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). (Exactly one level per used segment.) |
| \(\Delta_t \ge 0\) | continuous | **Total delay** of train \(t\) (difference between actual arrival at final destination and scheduled arrival). |
| \(e_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Energy** spent by train \(t\) on segment \(s\). (Linearized by speed‑level coefficient.) |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\beta\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{Delay cost}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\;e_{t,s}}_{\text{Energy cost}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The objective is a weighted sum of total passenger/operational delay and total energy consumption.

---

### 4.2 Routing (Flow‑conservation)  

For every train \(t\) and every segment \(s\):

\[
y_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1-x_t & \text{if } s\in P_t,\\[2mm]
x_t   & \text{if } s\in Q_t,\\[2mm]
0     & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{R1}
\]

(Implemented with two linear constraints per segment, e.g.  
\(y_{t,s}\le 1-x_t\) for \(s\in P_t\); \(y_{t,s}\le x_t\) for \(s\in Q_t\); and \(y_{t,s}\ge 1-x_t\) or \(y_{t,s}\ge x_t\) as needed.)

---

### 4.3 Speed‑level selection  

For each train‑segment pair that is used:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\;s\in S .
\tag{S1}
\]

Thus exactly one speed level is chosen if the segment is traversed; otherwise all \(v_{t,s,k}=0\).

---

### 4.4 Travel‑time on a segment  

The travel time on segment \(s\) for train \(t\) is the sum of the inverse speeds of the selected level:

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K} \frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\; v_{t,s,k} \qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{S2}
\]

Because the speed levels are discrete, the term \(\frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\) is a constant coefficient.  
If a more accurate linearisation of \(L_s/v\) is required, a piece‑wise linear approximation can be used; the formulation above already stays linear because the coefficients are pre‑computed.

---

### 4.5 Acceleration / Deceleration limits  

Let \(s\) and its predecessor on the chosen route be \(s^{-}\). When a train changes speed between two consecutive segments, the time difference must respect the acceleration bound:

\[
\bigl(d_{t,s^{-}}-a_{t,s}\bigr) \; \ge\; 
\frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\overline{v}_k} \;-\; \frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\underline{v}_{k'}}\;-\;a^{\max}\;(a_{t,s}-d_{t,s^{-}})
\]

A compact linear version uses “big‑M” and binary indicators for the speed level on the two segments. For brevity we write the linearised form:

\[
a_{t,s} - d_{t,s^{-}} \;\ge\; -M\,(1-\theta_{t,s})\qquad
\theta_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\;\; \theta_{t,s}=1 \text{ if the speed change respects } a^{\max},d^{\max}.
\tag{ACC}
\]

(The detailed expansion is routine: introduce auxiliary binaries for each pair \((k,k')\) and enforce the corresponding time‑difference bound.)

---

### 4.6 Blockage (time‑window) constraints  

If a segment \(s\) is partially blocked, a train may only occupy it **outside** the blocked interval:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; B^{\rm end}_s \;-\; M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \quad\text{or}\quad 
d_{t,s} \;\le\; B^{\rm start}_s \;+\; M\,(1-y_{t,s}) \qquad \forall t,\; s\in S^{\rm blk}.
\tag{BLK}
\]

The disjunction is linearised with a binary variable \(b_{t,s}\) that decides whether the train passes **before** or **after** the blockage:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,s} &\le B^{\rm start}_s + M\,b_{t,s},\\
a_{t,s} &\ge B^{\rm end}_s   - M\,(1-b_{t,s}),\\
b_{t,s}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the train does not use the segment (\(y_{t,s}=0\)), the constraints become non‑binding because of the big‑M terms.

---

### 4.7 Head‑way (conflict) constraints on shared physical track  

Consider any pair of trains \((t,t')\) that may be on the same **physical** track portion (including opposite directions on a single‑track segment). For each such segment \(s\) we enforce a strict ordering:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} + h^{\min} - M\,(1-z_{t,t',s}),\\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} + h^{\min} - M\,(z_{t,t',s}),\\
z_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\}, \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{C},\;s\in S .
\end{aligned}
\tag{HW}
\]

Here \(\mathcal{C}\) is the set of train pairs that share a segment.  
Exactly one of the two inequalities is active (the big‑M forces the other to be slack), thereby deciding which train passes first.

**Transitivity** (to avoid cycles) is added for any three trains that share the same segment:

\[
z_{t_1,t_2,s}+z_{t_2,t_3,s}-z_{t_1,t_3,s}\le 1 \qquad
\forall t_1,t_2,t_3\in\mathcal{C},\; s\in S .
\tag{TRANS}
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent ordering.

---

### 4.8 Time‑feasibility (causality)  

For every train \(t\) and every consecutive pair of segments \((s^{-},s)\) on its chosen route:

\[
a_{t,s}= d_{t,s^{-}} \qquad \forall t,\; s\neq \text{first segment of }t .
\tag{TIME}
\]

The first segment’s arrival time is fixed to the scheduled departure from the origin (or a decision variable if the schedule can be shifted).  

---

### 4.9 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\rm last}_t\) be the final segment on the selected route of train \(t\). The actual arrival at the destination is \(d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t}\). The delay variable is defined as:

\[
\Delta_t \; \ge\; d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t} - D^{\rm plan}_t ,\qquad \Delta_t \ge 0 .
\tag{DELAY}
\]

If early arrival is allowed (negative delay), the first inequality can be replaced by an equality; otherwise the model forces \(\Delta_t\) to capture only tardiness.

---

### 4.10 Energy consumption linearisation  

Energy on a segment is proportional to the distance travelled at the selected speed level:

\[
e_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \alpha_k \, L_s \, v_{t,s,k}\qquad \forall t,s .
\tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because \(\alpha_k\) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

---

### 4.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_t               &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t\in T,\\
y_{t,s}           &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t,s,\\
z_{t,t',s}        &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C},\,s,\\
v_{t,s,k}         &\in\{0,1\}               &&\forall t,s,k,\\
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\Delta_t,e_{t,s} &\ge 0   &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Group | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Routing variables** \(x_t, y_{t,s}\) | Choose for each train whether it stays on its original route or takes the opposite‑track detour; enforce that a train can only traverse segments belonging to the selected route. |
| **Speed‑level binaries** \(v_{t,s,k}\) | Discretise the continuous speed decision. Exactly one level is selected on a used segment, which linearises the otherwise nonlinear relation between speed and travel time / energy. |
| **Arrival / departure times** \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) | Capture the temporal schedule of each train on every segment. Equality (TIME) links consecutive segments, guaranteeing a feasible timetable. |
| **Head‑way / ordering binaries** \(z_{t,t',s}\) | Resolve conflicts on shared physical track portions. The big‑M formulation forces one train to leave at least \(h^{\min}\) seconds before the other enters. Transitivity constraints avoid cycles (i.e., contradictory orderings). |
| **Blockage constraints** (BLK) | Ensure that a train never occupies a blocked segment during its forbidden time window. The binary \(b_{t,s}\) decides whether the train passes before or after the blockage. |
| **Acceleration / deceleration limits** (ACC) | Enforce that speed changes between consecutive segments respect the maximum allowable acceleration/deceleration. Linearised with auxiliary binaries for each speed‑level pair. |
| **Delay definition** (DELAY) | Computes the tardiness of each train relative to its scheduled arrival; feeds directly into the objective. |
| **Energy calculation** (ENERGY) | Linear expression for the energy spent on each segment, using the speed‑level coefficient \(\alpha_k\). |
| **Objective** (OBJ) | Minimises a weighted sum of total delay (penalised by \(\beta\)) and total energy consumption (penalised by \(\gamma\)). The weights allow the railway operator to trade‑off punctuality against sustainability. |

---

### How to solve  

The model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**. It can be handed directly to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, CBC).  

Typical solution steps:

1. **Data preparation** – compute the segment lengths, speed‑level travel‑time coefficients \(\frac{L_s}{\overline{v}_k}\), energy coefficients \(\alpha_k L_s\), and the set of conflicting train pairs \(\mathcal{C}\).  
2. **Parameter tuning** – choose realistic values for \(\beta,\gamma\) to reflect the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy.  
3. **Big‑M sizing** – set \(M\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 hours ≈ 36 000 s).  
4. **Run the MILP** – the solver will return the optimal routing choices \(x_t\), speed‑level selections \(v_{t,s,k}\), and a feasible timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\) that respects all physical and operational constraints while minimising the weighted cost.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above captures every element you asked for—binary routing, binary ordering on shared segments, continuous timing, discrete speed decisions, blockage windows, acceleration limits, linearised energy consumption, and a weighted objective—while remaining a pure MILP that can be solved with standard optimisation software.

Model 2:
**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the “Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)”**  

The model simultaneously decides (i) which track a train will use on each segment (original vs. opposite track), (ii) the order in which trains traverse a shared (blocked) segment, (iii) the exact arrival/departure times at every station, and (iv) the speed level that each train will adopt on every track segment.  
All decisions are made so that the **weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption** is as small as possible while respecting safety, operational, and physical limits.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train), indexed by *s* |
| **E** | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) connecting two consecutive stations, indexed by *e = (i,j)* where *i,j ∈ S* |
| **K** | Set of admissible speed‑levels (discrete), indexed by *k* |
| **B ⊆ E** | Sub‑set of segments that are **partially blocked** (e.g., due to maintenance) |
| **C(t)** | Ordered list of segments that train *t* must travel (its route) – a subset of **E** |
| **P(e)** | Set of trains that use segment *e* (i.e. *t* with *e ∈ C(t)*) |

---

## 2.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|--------------|
| **xₜₑ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 → train *t* uses the **original** track on segment *e*; 0 → uses the **opposite** track (if available). |
| **yₜ₁ₜ₂ₑ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering on a **shared** (blocked) segment *e ∈ B*: 1 → train *t₁* passes *e* **before** train *t₂*; 0 → otherwise. |
| **aₜₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *s* (if *s* belongs to *C(t)*). |
| **dₜₛ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **vₜₑₖ** ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 → train *t* travels on segment *e* with speed level *k* (speed = 𝑣ₖ). Exactly one speed level is chosen for each (t,e). |
| **eₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between its actual arrival at the final destination and its scheduled arrival). |
| **Eₜ** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (linearized, see §4). |

---

## 3.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Lₑ** | Length of segment *e* (km). |
| **vₖ** | Physical speed (km/h) associated with speed level *k*. |
| **αₖ**, **βₖ** | Linear coefficients that map speed level *k* to **energy consumption per km** (e.g., *E = αₖ·vₖ + βₖ*). |
| **τₜₛ⁰** | Scheduled (planned) departure time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **Δₜₛ** | Minimum dwell time of train *t* at station *s* (for passenger boarding/alighting). |
| **hₘᵢₙ** | Minimum safety headway (time) required between any two consecutive trains on the **same** track. |
| **Bₑˢ**, **Bₑᵉ** | Start and end time of the blockage window on segment *e ∈ B* (no train may occupy the segment during this interval). |
| **aₘₐₓ**, **aₘᵢₙ** | Maximum / minimum admissible acceleration (km/h²) that can be applied when a train changes speed level between consecutive segments. |
| **w₁**, **w₂** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective (chosen by the planner). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time difference (used for linearizing ordering constraints). |

---

## 4.  Linearized Energy Consumption  

For each train *t* and segment *e* the energy contributed by speed level *k* is  

\[
E_{t e k}= (\alpha_k v_k + \beta_k) \, L_e .
\]

Because *vₜₑₖ* is binary and exactly one speed level is selected, the total energy of train *t* can be written linearly:

\[
E_t = \sum_{e\in C(t)}\;\sum_{k\in K} (\alpha_k v_k + \beta_k) L_e \; v_{t e k}.
\]

We will denote this linear expression simply as **Eₜ** in the model.

---

## 5.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{\min \; \; w_1 \sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; w_2 \sum_{t\in T} E_t}
\]

The first term penalises passenger delay, the second term penalises the total energy used by all trains.

---

## 6.  Constraints  

### 6.1 Routing / Track‑Choice  

For each train *t* and each segment *e* that belongs to its path:

\[
x_{t e}=1 \;\; \Longrightarrow \;\; \text{train }t\text{ uses the original track on }e,
\]
\[
x_{t e}=0 \;\; \Longrightarrow \;\; \text{train }t\text{ uses the opposite track (if it exists).}
\]

If a segment does **not** have an opposite track, we simply fix \(x_{t e}=1\).  
(Implementation: a parameter `opp_e ∈ {0,1}` indicating the existence of an opposite track; add constraint \(x_{t e} \ge \text{opp}_e\).)

### 6.2 Speed‑Level Selection  

Exactly one speed level must be chosen for each traversed segment:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall e\in C(t).
\tag{SL‑1}
\]

### 6.3 Time‑Propagation (travel time on a segment)  

Travel time on segment *e* when speed level *k* is used:

\[
\theta_{t e k}= \frac{L_e}{v_k}\quad\text{(hours)} .
\]

Because only one speed level is active, the actual travel time is

\[
\tau_{t e}= \sum_{k\in K} \theta_{t e k}\; v_{t e k}.
\]

Link arrival and departure times:

\[
a_{t j}= d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall e=(i,j)\in C(t).
\tag{TIME‑1}
\]

### 6.4 Minimum Dwell Time  

\[
d_{t s} \ge a_{t s}+ \Delta_{t s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in C(t).
\tag{DWELL}
\]

### 6.5 Headway on the Same Physical Track  

If two trains *t₁* and *t₂* use the **same** physical track on segment *e* (i.e., they make the same routing choice), a safety headway must be respected:

\[
d_{t_1 i} + \tau_{t_1 e} + h_{\min} \le a_{t_2 j} \;+\; M\,(1 - z_{t_1 t_2 e}) \\
d_{t_2 i} + \tau_{t_2 e} + h_{\min} \le a_{t_1 j} \;+\; M\,(z_{t_1 t_2 e}) 
\qquad \forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e),\; \forall e\in E,
\tag{HEADWAY}
\]

where the auxiliary binary  

\[
z_{t_1 t_2 e}= 
\begin{cases}
1 &\text{if }t_1\text{ passes }e\text{ before }t_2,\\
0 &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

The big‑M term de‑activates the inequality for the non‑active ordering.

### 6.6 Blockage Window on Partially Blocked Segments  

A train may occupy a blocked segment *e ∈ B* only **outside** its blockage interval:

\[
a_{t i} \ge B_e^{e} \quad \text{or} \quad d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \le B_e^{s}
\]

Linearised with the ordering binary *y* :

\[
a_{t i} \ge B_e^{e} - M\; y_{t e} \\
d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e} \le B_e^{s} + M\;(1-y_{t e}) \qquad \forall t\in P(e),\; e\in B.
\tag{BLOCK}
\]

If *yₜₑ = 1* the train passes **after** the blockage; if *yₜₑ = 0* it passes **before**.

### 6.7 Speed‑Change (Acceleration/Deceleration) Limits  

When a train changes speed level between two consecutive segments *e₁ = (i,j)* and *e₂ = (j,k)*, the resulting acceleration must stay within bounds:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_2 k}\, v_k \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_1 k}\, v_k \;\le\; a_{\max}\, \Delta t_{t j}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_2 k}\, v_k \;-\; \sum_{k\in K} v_{t e_1 k}\, v_k \;\ge\; a_{\min}\, \Delta t_{t j}
\]

where \(\Delta t_{t j}= d_{t j}-a_{t j}\) is the dwell (or waiting) time at station *j*. Because the left‑hand side is linear in the binary speed‑level variables, the constraints are linear.

### 6.8 Delay Definition  

Let *sᶠ* be the final station of train *t* and *τₜ^{sched}* the scheduled arrival at that station. Then

\[
e_t \ge a_{t s^{f}} - \tau_{t}^{\text{sched}} \qquad \forall t\in T,
\tag{DELAY}
\]

and we force \(e_t\ge 0\). (If early arrival is allowed, the inequality can be replaced by an absolute‑value formulation; here we penalise only lateness.)

### 6.9 Binary Ordering Transitivity on a Shared Segment  

For any three distinct trains *p,q,r* that all use a blocked segment *e* :

\[
y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \le 1,
\qquad
y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \ge 0 .
\tag{TRANS}
\]

These linear constraints guarantee a consistent total order on the segment.

### 6.10 Flow‑Conservation for Routing Choice  

If a train switches from original to opposite track on a segment, the choice must be consistent across the whole route (i.e., a train cannot “jump’’ between the two tracks in the middle of a segment). In practice this is enforced by fixing the binary *xₜₑ* for each segment according to the network layout; the model already contains the binary *xₜₑ* variables, therefore no extra constraint is required beyond the definition of *x*.

### 6.11 Variable Domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t e}\in\{0,1\},\quad y_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\},\quad v_{t e k}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t s}\ge 0,\; d_{t s}\ge 0,\; e_t\ge 0,\; E_t\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,a,d,v,e,E}\; &\; w_1\sum_{t\in T} e_t \;+\; w_2\sum_{t\in T} \sum_{e\in C(t)}\sum_{k\in K} (\alpha_k v_k+\beta_k)L_e \, v_{t e k} \\
\text{s.t. } &\;\; \text{(SL‑1)} &&\sum_{k\in K} v_{t e k}=1 &&\forall t, e\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(TIME‑1)} && a_{t j}= d_{t i}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_e}{v_k}\,v_{t e k} &&\forall t, e=(i,j)\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(DWELL)} && d_{t s}\ge a_{t s}+ \Delta_{t s} &&\forall t, s\in C(t)\\
&\;\; \text{(HEADWAY)} && d_{t_1 i}+ \tau_{t_1 e}+h_{\min}\le a_{t_2 j}+M(1-z_{t_1 t_2 e}) &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e), e\in E\\
&\;\; && d_{t_2 i}+ \tau_{t_2 e}+h_{\min}\le a_{t_1 j}+M(z_{t_1 t_2 e}) &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in P(e), e\in E\\
&\;\; \text{(BLOCK)} && a_{t i}\ge B_e^{e}-M y_{t e} &&\forall t\in P(e), e\in B\\
&\;\; && d_{t i}+ \tau_{t e}\le B_e^{s}+M(1-y_{t e}) &&\forall t\in P(e), e\in B\\
&\;\; \text{(ACCEL)} && \sum_{k}v_{t e_2 k}v_k-\sum_{k}v_{t e_1 k}v_k \le a_{\max}\,\Delta t_{t j} &&\forall t, (e_1,e_2) \text{ consecutive}\\
&\;\; && \sum_{k}v_{t e_2 k}v_k-\sum_{k}v_{t e_1 k}v_k \ge a_{\min}\,\Delta t_{t j} &&\forall t, (e_1,e_2)\\
&\;\; \text{(DELAY)} && e_t \ge a_{t s^{f}}- \tau_{t}^{\text{sched}} &&\forall t\\
&\;\; \text{(TRANS)} && y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \le 1 &&\forall e\in B,\; p,q,r\in P(e)\\
&\;\; && y_{p q e}+ y_{q r e} - y_{p r e} \ge 0 &&\forall e\in B,\; p,q,r\in P(e)\\
&\;\; \text{(ROUTING)} && x_{t e}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,e\\
&\;\; \text{(ORDERING)} && y_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t_1 t_2 e}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall (t_1,t_2), e\\
&\;\; \text{(VARIABLES)} && a_{t s}, d_{t s}, e_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are the binaries listed above. The model can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### How the Model Works – Brief Interpretation  

* **Routing choice (`x`)** tells the solver whether a train stays on its nominal track or detours to the opposite track (useful when the original track is partially blocked).  
* **Speed‑level variables (`v`)** let the optimizer pick a feasible speed for each segment; the associated travel time and linear energy cost are then computed.  
* **Arrival/Departure times (`a`, `d`)** propagate through the network using the travel‑time equations, while respecting minimum dwell times at stations.  
* **Ordering binaries (`y`, `z`)** define a total order of trains on each blocked segment, guaranteeing that only one train occupies the segment at a time and that the order is consistent (no cycles).  
* **Headway constraints** enforce the mandatory safety gap between any two trains that happen to use the same physical track (original or opposite).  
* **Blockage constraints** keep every train out of the forbidden time window on a partially blocked segment.  
* **Acceleration constraints** make sure that the speed change from one segment to the next is physically realistic.  
* **Delay variables (`e`)** capture the lateness of each train relative to its schedule; the objective penalises this delay together with the total energy consumption.

By solving the MILP, the railway planner obtains a **globally optimal** combination of routing, sequencing, timing and speed that minimizes the weighted sum of passenger delay and energy use while respecting all safety and operational restrictions.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below captures the whole description: binary routing (original vs. opposite track), binary ordering on shared (blocked) segments, continuous arrival/departure times, discrete speed‑level decisions, blockage‑time windows, acceleration limits, head‑way safety, delay definition and linear energy consumption. All constraints are linear; the formulation is a pure MILP that can be solved with any standard solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments (between two consecutive stations), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(S^{\rm blk}\subseteq S\) | Segments that are **partially blocked**. |
| \(K\) | Set of admissible speed levels, indexed by \(k\). |
| \(P_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) traverses on its **original** route. |
| \(Q_t\) | Ordered list of segments that train \(t\) would traverse on the **opposite‑track** detour. |
| \(\mathcal{C}\) | Set of unordered train pairs \((t,t')\) that may share a physical track (same direction or opposite direction on a single‑track portion). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(\underline v_k ,\overline v_k\) | Lower / upper bound of speed for level \(k\) (km/h). |
| \(\alpha_k\) | Energy coefficient for speed level \(k\) (kWh · km\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of total delay in the objective (e.g., € · h\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(\gamma\) | Weight of total energy in the objective (e.g., € · kWh\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(a^{\max}\) | Max admissible acceleration (km/h²). |
| \(d^{\max}\) | Max admissible deceleration (km/h²). |
| \(h^{\min}\) | Minimum head‑way time on a shared track (seconds). |
| \([B^{\rm start}_s , B^{\rm end}_s]\) | Blockage time window for segment \(s\in S^{\rm blk}\) (seconds). |
| \(\tau^{\min}_{t,s},\tau^{\max}_{t,s}\) | Minimum / maximum travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (derived from speed limits). |
| \(D^{\rm plan}_t\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (seconds). |
| \(M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., \(10^6\) s). |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \(x_t\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Routing: 0 → original route (\(P_t\)), 1 → detour (\(Q_t\)). |
| \(y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Indicator that train \(t\) **uses** segment \(s\). |
| \(z_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Ordering on a shared segment: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) passes **before** train \(t'\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from the downstream station of segment \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Speed‑level selection: 1 ⇔ train \(t\) travels on segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). |
| \(\Delta_t\ge0\) | continuous | Total **delay** of train \(t\). |
| \(e_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Energy spent by train \(t\) on segment \(s\). |

---

### 4. Model  

#### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
\beta\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t\;+\;
\gamma\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}e_{t,s}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption.

#### 4.2 Routing (segment‑usage)  

For every train \(t\) and segment \(s\):

\[
y_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1-x_t & \text{if } s\in P_t,\\[1mm]
x_t   & \text{if } s\in Q_t,\\[1mm]
0     & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{R1}
\]

Implemented with linear inequalities (big‑M).

#### 4.3 Speed‑level selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S .
\tag{S1}
\]

Exactly one speed level is chosen on a used segment; none otherwise.

#### 4.4 Travel time on a segment  

\[
d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s}{\overline v_k}\;v_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t,s .
\tag{S2}
\]

(The coefficient \(\frac{L_s}{\overline v_k}\) is the travel time if speed level \(k\) is used.)

#### 4.5 Acceleration / deceleration limits  

Let \(s^{-}\) be the predecessor of \(s\) on the chosen route of train \(t\).  
Define binary \(\theta_{t,s,k,k'}\) that equals 1 iff speed level \(k\) is used on \(s^{-}\) **and** level \(k'\) on \(s\).  

\[
\sum_{k,k'\in K}\theta_{t,s,k,k'} = y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,s .
\]

Then enforce

\[
\Bigl(\frac{L_s}{\underline v_{k'}}-\frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\overline v_k}\Bigr)
\le a^{\max}\bigl(a_{t,s}-d_{t,s^{-}}\bigr)+M\bigl(1-\theta_{t,s,k,k'}\bigr)
\tag{ACC1}
\]

\[
\Bigl(\frac{L_s}{\overline v_{k'}}-\frac{L_{s^{-}}}{\underline v_k}\Bigr)
\ge -d^{\max}\bigl(a_{t,s}-d_{t,s^{-}}\bigr)-M\bigl(1-\theta_{t,s,k,k'}\bigr)
\tag{ACC2}
\]

These linear constraints bound the feasible speed‑change.

#### 4.6 Blockage‑time‑window constraints  

For each blocked segment \(s\in S^{\rm blk}\) introduce binary \(b_{t,s}\) (0 → train passes **before**, 1 → **after** the blockage):

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,s}&\le B^{\rm start}_s + M\,b_{t,s},\\
a_{t,s}&\ge B^{\rm end}_s   - M\,(1-b_{t,s}),\\
b_{t,s}&\in\{0,1\},\qquad\forall t,\;s\in S^{\rm blk}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{BLK}
\]

If \(y_{t,s}=0\) the constraints are relaxed by the big‑M terms.

#### 4.7 Head‑way (conflict‑avoidance) on shared track  

For any pair \((t,t')\in\mathcal{C}\) and any segment \(s\) that both may occupy:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s}+h^{\min}-M\bigl(1-z_{t,t',s}\bigr),\\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s}+h^{\min}-M\bigl(z_{t,t',s}\bigr),\\
z_{t,t',s}&\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{HW}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities is active, fixing the order.

**Transitivity** (to avoid cycles) for any three trains on the same segment:

\[
z_{t_1,t_2,s}+z_{t_2,t_3,s}-z_{t_1,t_3,s}\le 1
\qquad\forall t_1,t_2,t_3\in\mathcal{C},\;s\in S .
\tag{TRANS}
\]

#### 4.8 Time‑feasibility (causality)  

For every train \(t\) and consecutive segments \((s^{-},s)\) on its selected route:

\[
a_{t,s}=d_{t,s^{-}}\qquad\forall t,\;s\neq\text{first segment of }t .
\tag{TIME}
\]

The first segment’s upstream arrival time can be fixed to the scheduled departure or left free.

#### 4.9 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\rm last}_t\) be the final segment of train \(t\) on the chosen route.  

\[
\Delta_t \ge d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t} - D^{\rm plan}_t ,\qquad \Delta_t\ge0 .
\tag{DELAY}
\]

Only tardiness is penalised (early arrival is allowed).

#### 4.10 Energy consumption linearisation  

\[
e_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\alpha_k\,L_s\,v_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s .
\tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because \(\alpha_k\) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

#### 4.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_t,\;y_{t,s},\;z_{t,t',s},\;v_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s},\,d_{t,s},\,\Delta_t,\,e_{t,s}\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5. Interpretation  

* **Routing variables** \(x_t\) decide whether a train stays on its original track or uses the opposite‑track detour (necessary when a segment is blocked).  
* **Segment‑usage** \(y_{t,s}\) links the routing decision to the actual set of traversed segments.  
* **Speed‑level binaries** \(v_{t,s,k}\) discretise the continuous speed choice, making travel‑time and energy linear.  
* **Arrival/Departure times** \(a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\) build a feasible timetable; equality (TIME) propagates times along the route.  
* **Ordering binaries** \(z_{t,t',s}\) resolve conflicts on any shared physical track, guaranteeing a minimum safety head‑way (HW) and a consistent total order (TRANS).  
* **Blockage constraints** (BLK) keep every train out of the forbidden time window on a partially blocked segment.  
* **Acceleration constraints** (ACC1‑ACC2) enforce realistic speed changes between consecutive segments.  
* **Delay** \(\Delta_t\) measures how late a train arrives relative to its schedule; it feeds directly into the objective.  
* **Energy** \(e_{t,s}\) is a linear function of the chosen speed level, allowing the objective to penalise energy consumption.  

---

### 6. Solving  

The complete formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program**. Supply the data (segment lengths, speed‑level tables, blockage windows, scheduled times, etc.) and feed the model to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, CBC…). The solver returns:

* the optimal routing choice \(x_t\) (original vs. detour),  
* the optimal speed level on every traversed segment \(v_{t,s,k}\),  
* a conflict‑free timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\) that respects head‑ways, blockage windows and acceleration limits,  
* the minimal weighted sum of total delay and total energy.

---

**In summary**, the MILP above fully implements the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem described in the prompt: binary routing, binary ordering on shared (blocked) tracks, continuous timing, discrete speed decisions, blockage‑time windows, acceleration limits, linearised energy consumption, and a weighted objective that balances punctuality against energy efficiency.

a_{t,s}=d_{t,s^{-}}\qquad\forall t,\;s\neq\text{first segment of }t .
\tag{TIME}
\]

The first segment’s upstream arrival time can be fixed to the scheduled departure or left free.

#### 4.9 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\rm last}_t\) be the final segment of train \(t\) on the chosen route.  

\[
\Delta_t \ge d_{t,s^{\rm last}_t} - D^{\rm plan}_t ,\qquad \Delta_t\ge0 .
\tag{DELAY}
\]

Only tardiness is penalised (early arrival is allowed).

#### 4.10 Energy consumption linearisation  

\[
e_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\alpha_k\,L_s\,v_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t,s .
\tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because \(\alpha_k\) and \(L_s\) are constants, the expression is linear.

#### 4.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_t,\;y_{t,s},\;z_{t,t',s},\;v_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,s},\,d_{t,s},\,\Delta_t,\,e_{t,s}\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 5. Interpretation  

* **Routing variables** \(x_t\) decide whether a train stays on its original track or uses the opposite‑track detour (necessary when a segment is blocked).  
* **Segment‑usage** \(y_{t,s}\) links the routing decision to the actual set of traversed segments.  
* **Speed‑level binaries** \(v_{t,s,k}\) discretise the continuous speed choice, making travel‑time and energy linear.  
* **Arrival/Departure times** \(a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\) build a feasible timetable; equality (TIME) propagates times along the route.  
* **Ordering binaries** \(z_{t,t',s}\) resolve conflicts on any shared physical track, guaranteeing a minimum safety head‑way (HW) and a consistent total order (TRANS).  
* **Blockage constraints** (BLK) keep every train out of the forbidden time window on a partially blocked segment.  
* **Acceleration constraints** (ACC1‑ACC2) enforce realistic speed changes between consecutive segments.  
* **Delay** \(\Delta_t\) measures how late a train arrives relative to its schedule; it feeds directly into the objective.  
* **Energy** \(e_{t,s}\) is a linear function of the chosen speed level, allowing the objective to penalise energy consumption.  

---

### 6. Solving  

The complete formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program**. Supply the data (segment lengths, speed‑level tables, blockage windows, scheduled times, etc.) and feed the model to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, CBC…). The solver returns:

* the optimal routing choice \(x_t\) (original vs. detour),  
* the optimal speed level on every traversed segment \(v_{t,s,k}\),  
* a conflict‑free timetable \(\{a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\}\) that respects head‑ways, blockage windows and acceleration limits,  
* the minimal weighted sum of total delay and total energy.

---

**In summary**, the MILP above fully implements the integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem described in the prompt: binary routing, binary ordering on shared (blocked) tracks, continuous timing, discrete speed decisions, blockage‑time windows, acceleration limits, linearised energy consumption, and a weighted objective that balances punctuality against energy efficiency.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
