**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model simultaneously decides (i) a feasible post‑disruption timetable (arrival/departure times, train order and possible rerouting) and (ii) a set of piece‑wise‑linear speed profiles that respect train dynamics, track‑capacity and energy‑consumption considerations.  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Set of trains (both directions). |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Set of stations (including the origin 0 and the terminal \(|S|+1\)). |
| \(L=\{(i,j)\mid i\in S,\;j\in S,\;i<j\}\) | Set of line‑segments (track sections) between two consecutive stations. |
| \(D\subseteq L\) | Sub‑set of *disruption segments* (blocked on one track side). |
| \(\mathcal{K}=\{1,\dots ,K\}\) | Set of *speed‑profile intervals* (time discretisation). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of *feasible plans* for train \(t\) (each plan contains a route, a sequence of segment‑travel times and a speed‑profile). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq T\times T\) | Set of *potential bidirectional conflicts* (pairs of trains that may occupy the same physical track at the same time). |

---

## 2. Parameters (assumptions are indicated)  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| \(a^{\max}_t\) | Maximum admissible acceleration (m s\(^{-2}\)) – **assumption** constant for each train type. |
| \(d^{\max}_t\) | Maximum admissible deceleration (positive value, m s\(^{-2}\)). |
| \(v^{\max}_{t,ij}\) | Speed limit of train \(t\) on segment \((i,j)\) (m s\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(L_{ij}\) | Length of segment \((i,j)\) (m). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) at station \(i\) (s). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{head}}_{ij}\) | Minimum headway (time separation) required between two trains travelling in the **same** direction on segment \((i,j)\) (s). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conf}}_{ij}\) | Minimum time separation required between two trains travelling in **opposite** directions on a single‑track segment \((i,j)\) (s). |
| \(E^{\text{base}}_{t,ij}\) | Energy consumption (kWh) of train \(t\) when travelling segment \((i,j)\) at the *nominal* speed (used for linearisation). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight of the energy‑minimisation term in the objective (user‑defined). |
| \(T^{\text{disr}}_{ij}=[\tau^{\text{start}}_{ij},\tau^{\text{end}}_{ij}]\) | Time window during which disruption blocks one track side of segment \((i,j)\in D\). |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints. |
| \(\gamma_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | Indicator: 1 if train \(t\) uses the *alternative* (opposite‑track) direction on disrupted segment \((i,j)\in D\); 0 otherwise – **assumption** that rerouting is limited to the opposite track only. |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

### 3.1 Timetable variables  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| \(a_{t,i}\) | Actual **arrival** time of train \(t\) at station \(i\) (continuous). |
| \(d_{t,i}\) | Actual **departure** time of train \(t\) from station \(i\) (continuous). |
| \(x_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \((i,j)\) on its *original* track, 0 otherwise (used to model rerouting). |
| \(y_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \((i,j)\) on the *alternative* track (only possible for \((i,j)\in D\)). |
| \(z_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) **cancels** service on segment \((i,j)\) (i.e., does not pass). |

### 3.2 Speed‑profile variables (piece‑wise linear)  

For each train \(t\) and each segment \((i,j)\) that it actually traverses (\(x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}=1\)) we introduce a set of interval‑based speed variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| \(\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if interval \(k\) is selected for the speed profile on segment \((i,j)\) (binary). |
| \(\tau^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \((i,j)\) **if** interval \(k\) is chosen (continuous). |
| \(v^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Average speed associated with interval \(k\) (parameter, pre‑computed from a speed‑profile library). |
| \(e^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Energy consumption associated with interval \(k\) (parameter, derived from the same library). |

The library is built beforehand by solving the continuous speed‑control problem for each segment and storing a small set of *representative* speed‑time‑energy triples \((v^{k},\tau^{k},e^{k})\). This linearises the otherwise nonlinear speed‑energy relationship.

### 3.3 Conflict‑resolution binaries  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| \(\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \((i,j)\) travelling in the **same** direction. |
| \(\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \((i,j)\) travelling in **opposite** directions (bidirectional conflict). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The model minimises a weighted sum of total delay (relative to the original schedule) and total energy consumption of the selected speed profiles.

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S}\bigl( a_{t,i}-a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr)}_{\text{Total passenger delay}} \;+\;
\beta\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,j)\in L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} e^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}} .
\]

* \(a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\) are the pre‑disruption planned arrival times (data).  
* The first term penalises any lateness; early arrivals are allowed but do not reduce the objective (they are neutral).  

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Logical linking of routing decisions  

1. **Exactly one route per segment (original / alternative / cancel)**  

\[
x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}+z_{t,ij}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

2. **Alternative track can be used only on disrupted segments**  

\[
y_{t,ij}\le \mathbf{1}_{\{(i,j)\in D\}} \qquad \forall t,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

3. **If a segment is cancelled, no speed‑profile is selected**  

\[
\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\le 1-z_{t,ij}\qquad \forall t,(i,j),k .
\]

### 5.2 Time‑flow (timetable) constraints  

4. **Departure after minimum dwell**  

\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i}\qquad \forall t,\; i\in S .
\]

5. **Travel‑time consistency with selected speed interval**  

\[
a_{t,j}= d_{t,i}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

6. **Headway for same‑direction trains**  

\[
d_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_{ij}\le a_{t',i}+M\bigl(1-\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) \qquad
\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{B},\;(i,j)\in L,\; \text{same direction}.
\]

\[
d_{t',i}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_{ij}\le a_{t,i}+M\bigl(\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) .
\]

7. **Bidirectional conflict (single‑track) constraints**  

\[
d_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{conf}}_{ij}\le a_{t',i}+M\bigl(1-\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) \qquad
\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{B},\;(i,j)\in L,\; \text{opposite directions}.
\]

\[
d_{t',i}+ \Delta^{\text{conf}}_{ij}\le a_{t,i}+M\bigl(\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) .
\]

8. **Disruption‑window feasibility** – a train using the *original* track may not occupy the blocked side during the disruption window; the alternative track is allowed.

\[
a_{t,i}\ge \tau^{\text{end}}_{ij}\;-\;M\,y_{t,ij}\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in D,\; \text{if } x_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

\[
a_{t,i}\le \tau^{\text{start}}_{ij}\;+\;M\,(1-y_{t,ij})\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in D,\; \text{if } x_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

(Using big‑M to deactivate the constraint when the alternative track is chosen.)

### 5.3 Speed‑profile feasibility  

9. **Acceleration / deceleration limits** – linearised by bounding the travel time on each segment.

\[
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}_{t,ij}} \le \sum_{k}\tau^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij} \le 
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\min}_{t,ij}} \qquad \forall t,(i,j) .
\]

where a minimum feasible speed \(v^{\min}_{t,ij}\) is derived from the deceleration limit:

\[
v^{\min}_{t,ij}= \sqrt{2\,d^{\max}_t\,L_{ij}} \quad\text{(worst‑case constant deceleration)} .
\]

10. **Exactly one speed interval per traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \theta^{k}_{t,ij}= x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}\qquad \forall t,(i,j) .
\]

### 5.4 Train‑order (reordering) variables (optional)  

If the planner allows reordering of trains on a given line, introduce binary order variables \(o_{t,t'}\in\{0,1\}\) (1 if \(t\) precedes \(t'\) on the whole line). The headway constraints above already enforce a local order; a global order can be added for consistency:

\[
o_{t,t'}+o_{t',t}=1 \qquad \forall t\neq t' .
\]

and link with the segment‑level precedence binaries:

\[
\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\le o_{t,t'}\qquad 
\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\le o_{t,t'} \qquad \forall (t,t'),(i,j).
\]

### 5.5 Cancellation (service reduction)  

If a train is cancelled on a segment, downstream times are set to a large penalty (or the train is removed from the objective). The model already forces \(z_{t,ij}=1\) → no travel time, but to keep the timetable consistent we may set:

\[
a_{t,j}=a_{t,i}\qquad \forall t,(i,j)\text{ with }z_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S}\bigl(a_{t,i}-a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr)
      \;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,j)\in L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} e^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4)–(10)   timetable flow, dwell, travel‑time}\\
&\text{(5)–(7)   headway / conflict resolution (same / opposite direction)}\\
&\text{(8)–(9)   disruption‑window feasibility}\\
&\text{(10)–(12) routing binary logic (original / alternative / cancel)}\\
&\text{(13)–(15) speed‑profile selection and dynamics limits}\\
&\text{(optional) global reordering constraints}\\
&\text{Variables: } a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+},\;
x_{t,ij},y_{t,ij},z_{t,ij},\theta^{k}_{t,ij},\delta^{\cdot}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous elements are the binary routing, conflict‑resolution and speed‑interval selection variables, making the formulation a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 7. Modeling Assumptions (explicit)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | Trains are homogeneous with respect to acceleration/deceleration limits; parameters \(a^{\max}_t,d^{\max}_t\) are known. |
| A2 | The disruption blocks **only one** of the two parallel tracks on a segment; the opposite track remains usable (hence the binary \(\gamma_{t,ij}\)). |
| A3 | Rerouting is limited to using the opposite track on the disrupted segment; no long‑detour alternative routes are considered. |
| A4 | Speed‑profile library \(\{(v^{k},\tau^{k},e^{k})\}\) is pre‑computed for each segment and train type, providing a piece‑wise‑linear approximation of the true nonlinear speed‑energy relationship. |
| A5 | Headway and conflict separation times are deterministic and constant for each segment (derived from signalling rules). |
| A6 | Early arrivals are allowed without penalty; only lateness contributes to the delay term. |
| A7 | Cancellation of a segment is modelled by a binary \(z_{t,ij}\); if a whole train is cancelled, all its \(z\)’s are set to 1 and the delay term for that train is omitted (or a large penalty can be added). |
| A8 | The big‑M constant is chosen sufficiently large to deactivate logical constraints but not so large as to cause numerical instability (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s). |
| A9 | All time variables are measured in seconds; energy in kWh; distances in meters – consistent units throughout. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – collect the original timetable \((a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i})\), segment lengths, speed limits, disruption windows, and build the speed‑profile library for each segment.  
2. **Model implementation** – encode the MILP in a solver such as Gurobi, CPLEX or SCIP.  
3. **Solution** – the optimal solution yields (i) a conflict‑free timetable (arrival/departure times, possible reordering and rerouting decisions) and (ii) a concrete speed‑profile (choice of interval \(k\) for each traversed segment) that respects acceleration limits and minimises the weighted sum of delay and energy.  
4. **Post‑processing** – translate the selected speed intervals back into detailed acceleration/deceleration curves for the train‑control system.

The presented MILP captures **all three core challenges** highlighted in the introduction: (1) bidirectional conflict resolution on a shared track, (2) coupling between rescheduling decisions (times, order, rerouting) and speed‑control decisions, and (3) a co‑optimisation of service quality (delay) and energy efficiency.

| \(z_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) **cancels** service on segment \((i,j)\) (i.e., does not pass). |

### 3.2 Speed‑profile variables (piece‑wise linear)  

For each train \(t\) and each segment \((i,j)\) that it actually traverses (\(x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}=1\)) we introduce a set of interval‑based speed variables:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| \(\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if interval \(k\) is selected for the speed profile on segment \((i,j)\) (binary). |
| \(\tau^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \((i,j)\) **if** interval \(k\) is chosen (continuous). |
| \(v^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Average speed associated with interval \(k\) (parameter, pre‑computed from a speed‑profile library). |
| \(e^{k}_{t,ij}\) | Energy consumption associated with interval \(k\) (parameter, derived from the same library). |

The library is built beforehand by solving the continuous speed‑control problem for each segment and storing a small set of *representative* speed‑time‑energy triples \((v^{k},\tau^{k},e^{k})\). This linearises the otherwise nonlinear speed‑energy relationship.

### 3.3 Conflict‑resolution binaries  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| \(\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \((i,j)\) travelling in the **same** direction. |
| \(\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \((i,j)\) travelling in **opposite** directions (bidirectional conflict). |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The model minimises a weighted sum of total delay (relative to the original schedule) and total energy consumption of the selected speed profiles.

\[
\min\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S}\bigl( a_{t,i}-a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr)}_{\text{Total passenger delay}} \;+\;
\beta\; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,j)\in L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} e^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}} .
\]

* \(a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\) are the pre‑disruption planned arrival times (data).  
* The first term penalises any lateness; early arrivals are allowed but do not reduce the objective (they are neutral).  

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Logical linking of routing decisions  

1. **Exactly one route per segment (original / alternative / cancel)**  

\[
x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}+z_{t,ij}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

2. **Alternative track can be used only on disrupted segments**  

\[
y_{t,ij}\le \mathbf{1}_{\{(i,j)\in D\}} \qquad \forall t,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

3. **If a segment is cancelled, no speed‑profile is selected**  

\[
\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\le 1-z_{t,ij}\qquad \forall t,(i,j),k .
\]

### 5.2 Time‑flow (timetable) constraints  

4. **Departure after minimum dwell**  

\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{dwell}}_{t,i}\qquad \forall t,\; i\in S .
\]

5. **Travel‑time consistency with selected speed interval**  

\[
a_{t,j}= d_{t,i}+ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in L .
\]

6. **Headway for same‑direction trains**  

\[
d_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_{ij}\le a_{t',i}+M\bigl(1-\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) \qquad
\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{B},\;(i,j)\in L,\; \text{same direction}.
\]

\[
d_{t',i}+ \Delta^{\text{head}}_{ij}\le a_{t,i}+M\bigl(\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) .
\]

7. **Bidirectional conflict (single‑track) constraints**  

\[
d_{t,i}+ \Delta^{\text{conf}}_{ij}\le a_{t',i}+M\bigl(1-\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) \qquad
\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{B},\;(i,j)\in L,\; \text{opposite directions}.
\]

\[
d_{t',i}+ \Delta^{\text{conf}}_{ij}\le a_{t,i}+M\bigl(\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\bigr) .
\]

8. **Disruption‑window feasibility** – a train using the *original* track may not occupy the blocked side during the disruption window; the alternative track is allowed.

\[
a_{t,i}\ge \tau^{\text{end}}_{ij}\;-\;M\,y_{t,ij}\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in D,\; \text{if } x_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

\[
a_{t,i}\le \tau^{\text{start}}_{ij}\;+\;M\,(1-y_{t,ij})\qquad 
\forall t,\;(i,j)\in D,\; \text{if } x_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

(Using big‑M to deactivate the constraint when the alternative track is chosen.)

### 5.3 Speed‑profile feasibility  

9. **Acceleration / deceleration limits** – linearised by bounding the travel time on each segment.

\[
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\max}_{t,ij}} \le \sum_{k}\tau^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij} \le 
\frac{L_{ij}}{v^{\min}_{t,ij}} \qquad \forall t,(i,j) .
\]

where a minimum feasible speed \(v^{\min}_{t,ij}\) is derived from the deceleration limit:

\[
v^{\min}_{t,ij}= \sqrt{2\,d^{\max}_t\,L_{ij}} \quad\text{(worst‑case constant deceleration)} .
\]

10. **Exactly one speed interval per traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \theta^{k}_{t,ij}= x_{t,ij}+y_{t,ij}\qquad \forall t,(i,j) .
\]

### 5.4 Train‑order (reordering) variables (optional)  

If the planner allows reordering of trains on a given line, introduce binary order variables \(o_{t,t'}\in\{0,1\}\) (1 if \(t\) precedes \(t'\) on the whole line). The headway constraints above already enforce a local order; a global order can be added for consistency:

\[
o_{t,t'}+o_{t',t}=1 \qquad \forall t\neq t' .
\]

and link with the segment‑level precedence binaries:

\[
\delta^{\text{same}}_{t,t',ij}\le o_{t,t'}\qquad 
\delta^{\text{opp}}_{t,t',ij}\le o_{t,t'} \qquad \forall (t,t'),(i,j).
\]

### 5.5 Cancellation (service reduction)  

If a train is cancelled on a segment, downstream times are set to a large penalty (or the train is removed from the objective). The model already forces \(z_{t,ij}=1\) → no travel time, but to keep the timetable consistent we may set:

\[
a_{t,j}=a_{t,i}\qquad \forall t,(i,j)\text{ with }z_{t,ij}=1 .
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{i\in S}\bigl(a_{t,i}-a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i}\bigr)
      \;+\;\beta\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(i,j)\in L}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} e^{k}_{t,ij}\,\theta^{k}_{t,ij}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4)–(10)   timetable flow, dwell, travel‑time}\\
&\text{(5)–(7)   headway / conflict resolution (same / opposite direction)}\\
&\text{(8)–(9)   disruption‑window feasibility}\\
&\text{(10)–(12) routing binary logic (original / alternative / cancel)}\\
&\text{(13)–(15) speed‑profile selection and dynamics limits}\\
&\text{(optional) global reordering constraints}\\
&\text{Variables: } a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+},\;
x_{t,ij},y_{t,ij},z_{t,ij},\theta^{k}_{t,ij},\delta^{\cdot}_{t,t',ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous elements are the binary routing, conflict‑resolution and speed‑interval selection variables, making the formulation a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 7. Modeling Assumptions (explicit)

| # | Assumption |
|---|------------|
| A1 | Trains are homogeneous with respect to acceleration/deceleration limits; parameters \(a^{\max}_t,d^{\max}_t\) are known. |
| A2 | The disruption blocks **only one** of the two parallel tracks on a segment; the opposite track remains usable (hence the binary \(\gamma_{t,ij}\)). |
| A3 | Rerouting is limited to using the opposite track on the disrupted segment; no long‑detour alternative routes are considered. |
| A4 | Speed‑profile library \(\{(v^{k},\tau^{k},e^{k})\}\) is pre‑computed for each segment and train type, providing a piece‑wise‑linear approximation of the true nonlinear speed‑energy relationship. |
| A5 | Headway and conflict separation times are deterministic and constant for each segment (derived from signalling rules). |
| A6 | Early arrivals are allowed without penalty; only lateness contributes to the delay term. |
| A7 | Cancellation of a segment is modelled by a binary \(z_{t,ij}\); if a whole train is cancelled, all its \(z\)’s are set to 1 and the delay term for that train is omitted (or a large penalty can be added). |
| A8 | The big‑M constant is chosen sufficiently large to deactivate logical constraints but not so large as to cause numerical instability (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s). |
| A9 | All time variables are measured in seconds; energy in kWh; distances in meters – consistent units throughout. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – collect the original timetable \((a^{\text{orig}}_{t,i})\), segment lengths, speed limits, disruption windows, and build the speed‑profile library for each segment.  
2. **Model implementation** – encode the MILP in a solver such as Gurobi, CPLEX or SCIP.  
3. **Solution** – the optimal solution yields (i) a conflict‑free timetable (arrival/departure times, possible reordering and rerouting decisions) and (ii) a concrete speed‑profile (choice of interval \(k\) for each traversed segment) that respects acceleration limits and minimises the weighted sum of delay and energy.  
4. **Post‑processing** – translate the selected speed intervals back into detailed acceleration/deceleration curves for the train‑control system.

The presented MILP captures **all three core challenges** highlighted in the introduction: (1) bidirectional conflict resolution on a shared track, (2) coupling between rescheduling decisions (times, order, rerouting) and speed‑control decisions, and (3) a co‑optimisation of service quality (delay) and energy efficiency.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) under a partial segment blockage**.  
The model is written in a compact “mathematical‑programming” style that can be copied directly into a solver such as Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine (e.g., CBC, SCIP).  

---  

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 𝑇 | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| 𝑆 | Set of track **segments** (directed elementary pieces of track), indexed by *s* |
| 𝐿 | Set of **links** (ordered pairs of consecutive segments)  \( (s,\;s')\in L\) – used for flow conservation |
| 𝐾 | Set of **speed‑bins** (piece‑wise constant speed intervals) used to linearise the speed‑time relationship, indexed by *k* |
| 𝑅ᵗ | Set of **feasible routes** for train *t*.  Each route *r∈Rᵗ* is a directed list of segments; the set contains at most two routes – the *original* direction and the *opposite* direction (if the train is allowed to reverse). |
| 𝐵 ⊆ S | Set of **blocked segments** (the side of the track that is unavailable during the blockage window). |
| 𝑉 | Set of **virtual “source/sink” nodes** that start/end each train’s route (used for flow conservation). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝑇ᵣₑₛₜ, 𝑇ₑₙd  | Planned (original) departure / arrival times of train *t* | [s] |
| 𝑑ₘᵢₙₜ   | Minimum dwell time that train *t* must spend at its scheduled stations | [s] |
| 𝑙ₛ      | Length of segment *s* | [km] |
| 𝑣ₘₐₓₛ , 𝑣ₘᵢₙₛ | Upper / lower admissible speed on segment *s* (may differ per segment) | [km/h] |
| 𝑎ₘₐₓ , 𝑑ₘₐₓ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | [km/h²] |
| 𝑤₁ , 𝑤₂ | Weight of **delay** and **energy** in the objective (𝑤₁+𝑤₂=1 is typical) | – |
| 𝐸ₖ     | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑bin *k* (e.g., kWh per km at that speed) | [kWh/km] |
| 𝑣ₖ⁽ˡᵒʷ⁾ , 𝑣ₖ⁽ᵘᵖ⁾ | Lower / upper bound of speed in bin *k* (km/h) | [km/h] |
| 𝑇ᴮˢᵗ , 𝑇ᴮᵉⁿ | Start / end of the **blockage window** (absolute time) | [s] |
| 𝑚ₛᵇ   | Binary indicator =1 if segment *s* belongs to the blocked side *B*, else 0 | – |
| 𝑝ₜ      | Penalty (or large constant) used in “big‑M” constraints for infeasible ordering | – |
| 𝑈ₜ      | Upper bound on the total travel time of train *t* (e.g., horizon) | [s] |
| 𝜏ₛₖ    | Travel time of a train on segment *s* when speed belongs to bin *k*:  \(\tau_{s,k}= \frac{l_s}{v_k}\) (pre‑computed) | [s] |

*All parameters are assumed to be known a‑priori.  If some values are not given, they can be estimated from timetable data or engineering specifications.*

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r∈Rᵗ* (original or opposite), 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* (i.e., *s* belongs to the chosen route), 0 otherwise |
| \(z_{t,(s,s')}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the directed link \((s,s')\) (i.e., passes from *s* to *s'*), 0 otherwise |
| \(o_{t,t',s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for a **conflict pair** (train *t* and *t'*) on shared segment *s*: 1 ⇒ *t* passes *s* **before** *t'*, 0 ⇒ opposite order |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream end** of segment *s* |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream end** of segment *s* (i.e., after traversing *s*) |
| \(u_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *s* with a speed that lies in bin *k*; 0 otherwise |
| \(\Delta_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Delay** of train *t* with respect to its scheduled arrival (or departure) time |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh) |

*The model is linear because the speed‑time relationship is captured by the pre‑computed travel‑time constants \(\tau_{s,k}\) and the binary bin‑selection variables \(u_{t,s,k}\).*

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
      \;+\; \underbrace{w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - T^{\text{arr}}_{t} \qquad
\text{(if the train arrives later than its scheduled arrival)} 
\]

and  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}  \;  E_{k}\; l_{s}\; u_{t,s,k}
\]

The objective simultaneously penalises late arrivals and the energy spent while travelling.

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection (binary plan)  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R^{t}} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link the route choice to segment‑usage**  

\[
y_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R^{t}} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\;x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.2}
\]

*(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\) is 1 if segment *s* belongs to route *r*, 0 otherwise.)*  

3. **Flow conservation on each train’s path** (including source/sink nodes)  

\[
\sum_{s' : (s,s')\in L} z_{t,(s,s')} \;-\; \sum_{s' : (s',s)\in L} z_{t,(s',s)} = 
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{source}}_{t}\\
 -1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{sink}}_{t}\\
  0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.3}
\]

4. **Link link‑variables to segment‑usage**  

\[
z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s},\qquad 
z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s'} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.4}
\]

### 5.2  Conflict (bidirectional) ordering on a shared segment  

For any unordered pair of trains \((t,t')\) that may occupy the same segment *s* in opposite directions (the set of such pairs is denoted \(\mathcal{C}\)):

\[
a_{t,s} + \tau_{s}^{\max} \, y_{t,s} \le a_{t',s} + p_{t}\,(1-o_{t,t',s}) \qquad\forall (t,t',s)\in \mathcal{C}
\tag{5.5a}
\]

\[
a_{t',s} + \tau_{s}^{\max} \, y_{t',s} \le a_{t,s} + p_{t}\,o_{t,t',s} \qquad\forall (t,t',s)\in \mathcal{C}
\tag{5.5b}
\]

where \(\tau_{s}^{\max}= \max_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\) is a safe upper bound on travel time on *s*.  
The binary \(o_{t,t',s}\) decides which train passes first; the big‑M constant \(p_{t}\) can be set to the planning horizon \(U_t\).

### 5.3  Time feasibility – linking arrival/departure to speed bins  

For every train *t* and segment *s* that the train traverses (\(y_{t,s}=1\)):

1. **Exactly one speed‑bin is selected**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.6a}
\]

2. **Travel time equals the bin‑specific travel time**  

\[
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\; u_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.6b}
\]

3. **Link departure of current segment to arrival of the next**  

If \((s,s')\in L\) and \(z_{t,(s,s')}=1\):

\[
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.7}
\]

4. **Dwell‑time (minimum stop) at stations** – let \(\mathcal{S}_t\subseteq S\) be the set of segments that contain a scheduled station for train *t*.  

\[
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d^{\min}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in \mathcal{S}_t
\tag{5.8}
\]

### 5.4  Blockage window – forbidden use of blocked side  

If a segment belongs to the blocked side (\(m_{s}^{b}=1\)), the train may not occupy it **during** the blockage interval \([T^{B}_{\text{st}},\,T^{B}_{\text{en}}]\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} \;\; \text{or} \;\; d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{5.9}
\]

Linearised with a binary “use‑outside‑window” variable \(w_{t,s}\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} - M\,(1-w_{t,s}) \\
d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} + M\,w_{t,s} \\
w_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

where \(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., the planning horizon).

### 5.5  Speed limits per segment  

The speed‑bin selection automatically respects the admissible speed interval of the segment because each bin *k* is defined globally, but we can tighten it:

\[

\[

The model is written in a compact “mathematical‑programming” style that can be copied directly into a solver such as Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine (e.g., CBC, SCIP).  

---  

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 𝑇 | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| 𝑆 | Set of track **segments** (directed elementary pieces of track), indexed by *s* |
| 𝐿 | Set of **links** (ordered pairs of consecutive segments)  \( (s,\;s')\in L\) – used for flow conservation |
| 𝐾 | Set of **speed‑bins** (piece‑wise constant speed intervals) used to linearise the speed‑time relationship, indexed by *k* |
| 𝑅ᵗ | Set of **feasible routes** for train *t*.  Each route *r∈Rᵗ* is a directed list of segments; the set contains at most two routes – the *original* direction and the *opposite* direction (if the train is allowed to reverse). |
| 𝐵 ⊆ S | Set of **blocked segments** (the side of the track that is unavailable during the blockage window). |
| 𝑉 | Set of **virtual “source/sink” nodes** that start/end each train’s route (used for flow conservation). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝑇ᵣₑₛₜ, 𝑇ₑₙd  | Planned (original) departure / arrival times of train *t* | [s] |
| 𝑑ₘᵢₙₜ   | Minimum dwell time that train *t* must spend at its scheduled stations | [s] |
| 𝑙ₛ      | Length of segment *s* | [km] |
| 𝑣ₘₐₓₛ , 𝑣ₘᵢₙₛ | Upper / lower admissible speed on segment *s* (may differ per segment) | [km/h] |
| 𝑎ₘₐₓ , 𝑑ₘₐₓ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | [km/h²] |
| 𝑤₁ , 𝑤₂ | Weight of **delay** and **energy** in the objective (𝑤₁+𝑤₂=1 is typical) | – |
| 𝐸ₖ     | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑bin *k* (e.g., kWh per km at that speed) | [kWh/km] |
| 𝑣ₖ⁽ˡᵒʷ⁾ , 𝑣ₖ⁽ᵘᵖ⁾ | Lower / upper bound of speed in bin *k* (km/h) | [km/h] |
| 𝑇ᴮˢᵗ , 𝑇ᴮᵉⁿ | Start / end of the **blockage window** (absolute time) | [s] |
| 𝑚ₛᵇ   | Binary indicator =1 if segment *s* belongs to the blocked side *B*, else 0 | – |
| 𝑝ₜ      | Penalty (or large constant) used in “big‑M” constraints for infeasible ordering | – |
| 𝑈ₜ      | Upper bound on the total travel time of train *t* (e.g., horizon) | [s] |
| 𝜏ₛₖ    | Travel time of a train on segment *s* when speed belongs to bin *k*:  \(\tau_{s,k}= \frac{l_s}{v_k}\) (pre‑computed) | [s] |

*All parameters are assumed to be known a‑priori.  If some values are not given, they can be estimated from timetable data or engineering specifications.*

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r∈Rᵗ* (original or opposite), 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* (i.e., *s* belongs to the chosen route), 0 otherwise |
| \(z_{t,(s,s')}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the directed link \((s,s')\) (i.e., passes from *s* to *s'*), 0 otherwise |
| \(o_{t,t',s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for a **conflict pair** (train *t* and *t'*) on shared segment *s*: 1 ⇒ *t* passes *s* **before** *t'*, 0 ⇒ opposite order |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream end** of segment *s* |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream end** of segment *s* (i.e., after traversing *s*) |
| \(u_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *s* with a speed that lies in bin *k*; 0 otherwise |
| \(\Delta_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Delay** of train *t* with respect to its scheduled arrival (or departure) time |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh) |

*The model is linear because the speed‑time relationship is captured by the pre‑computed travel‑time constants \(\tau_{s,k}\) and the binary bin‑selection variables \(u_{t,s,k}\).*

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
      \;+\; \underbrace{w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - T^{\text{arr}}_{t} \qquad
\text{(if the train arrives later than its scheduled arrival)} 
\]

and  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}  \;  E_{k}\; l_{s}\; u_{t,s,k}
\]

### 5.1  Route‑selection (binary plan)  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R^{t}} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\]

\[

\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.2}
\]

*(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\) is 1 if segment *s* belongs to route *r*, 0 otherwise.)*  

3. **Flow conservation on each train’s path** (including source/sink nodes)  

\[
\sum_{s' : (s,s')\in L} z_{t,(s,s')} \;-\; \sum_{s' : (s',s)\in L} z_{t,(s',s)} = 
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{source}}_{t}\\
 -1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{sink}}_{t}\\
  0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.3}
\]

\[

\tag{5.4}
\]

\]

\[

\]

If \((s,s')\in L\) and \(z_{t,(s,s')}=1\):

\[

\tag{5.7}
\]

\[
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d^{\min}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in \mathcal{S}_t
\tag{5.8}
\]

### 5.4  Blockage window – forbidden use of blocked side  

If a segment belongs to the blocked side (\(m_{s}^{b}=1\)), the train may not occupy it **during** the blockage interval \([T^{B}_{\text{st}},\,T^{B}_{\text{en}}]\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} \;\; \text{or} \;\; d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{5.9}
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} - M\,(1-w_{t,s}) \\
d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} + M\,w_{t,s} \\
w_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

### 5.5  Speed limits per segment

\tag{5.14}
\]

\[
0 \le a_{t,s} \le U_{t},\qquad
0 \le d_{t,s} \le U_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.15}
\]

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) under a partial segment blockage**.  
The model is written in a compact “mathematical‑programming” style that can be copied directly into a solver such as Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine (e.g., CBC, SCIP).  

---  

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 𝑇 | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| 𝑆 | Set of track **segments** (directed elementary pieces of track), indexed by *s* |
| 𝐿 | Set of **links** (ordered pairs of consecutive segments)  \( (s,\;s')\in L\) – used for flow conservation |
| 𝐾 | Set of **speed‑bins** (piece‑wise constant speed intervals) used to linearise the speed‑time relationship, indexed by *k* |
| 𝑅ᵗ | Set of **feasible routes** for train *t*.  Each route *r∈Rᵗ* is a directed list of segments; the set contains at most two routes – the *original* direction and the *opposite* direction (if the train is allowed to reverse). |
| 𝐵 ⊆ S | Set of **blocked segments** (the side of the track that is unavailable during the blockage window). |
| 𝑉 | Set of **virtual “source/sink” nodes** that start/end each train’s route (used for flow conservation). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝑇ᵣₑₛₜ, 𝑇ₑₙd  | Planned (original) departure / arrival times of train *t* | [s] |
| 𝑑ₘᵢₙₜ   | Minimum dwell time that train *t* must spend at its scheduled stations | [s] |
| 𝑙ₛ      | Length of segment *s* | [km] |
| 𝑣ₘₐₓₛ , 𝑣ₘᵢₙₛ | Upper / lower admissible speed on segment *s* (may differ per segment) | [km/h] |
| 𝑎ₘₐₓ , 𝑑ₘₐₓ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | [km/h²] |
| 𝑤₁ , 𝑤₂ | Weight of **delay** and **energy** in the objective (𝑤₁+𝑤₂=1 is typical) | – |
| 𝐸ₖ     | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑bin *k* (e.g., kWh per km at that speed) | [kWh/km] |
| 𝑣ₖ⁽ˡᵒʷ⁾ , 𝑣ₖ⁽ᵘᵖ⁾ | Lower / upper bound of speed in bin *k* (km/h) | [km/h] |
| 𝑇ᴮˢᵗ , 𝑇ᴮᵉⁿ | Start / end of the **blockage window** (absolute time) | [s] |
| 𝑚ₛᵇ   | Binary indicator =1 if segment *s* belongs to the blocked side *B*, else 0 | – |
| 𝑝ₜ      | Penalty (or large constant) used in “big‑M” constraints for infeasible ordering | – |
| 𝑈ₜ      | Upper bound on the total travel time of train *t* (e.g., horizon) | [s] |
| 𝜏ₛₖ    | Travel time of a train on segment *s* when speed belongs to bin *k*:  \(\tau_{s,k}= \frac{l_s}{v_k}\) (pre‑computed) | [s] |

*All parameters are assumed to be known a‑priori.  If some values are not given, they can be estimated from timetable data or engineering specifications.*

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses route *r∈Rᵗ* (original or opposite), 0 otherwise |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *s* (i.e., *s* belongs to the chosen route), 0 otherwise |
| \(z_{t,(s,s')}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the directed link \((s,s')\) (i.e., passes from *s* to *s'*), 0 otherwise |
| \(o_{t,t',s}\) | binary | Ordering variable for a **conflict pair** (train *t* and *t'*) on shared segment *s*: 1 ⇒ *t* passes *s* **before** *t'*, 0 ⇒ opposite order |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at the **up‑stream end** of segment *s* |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from the **down‑stream end** of segment *s* (i.e., after traversing *s*) |
| \(u_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train *t* travels on segment *s* with a speed that lies in bin *k*; 0 otherwise |
| \(\Delta_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Delay** of train *t* with respect to its scheduled arrival (or departure) time |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous ≥0 | **Energy consumption** of train *t* (kWh) |

*The model is linear because the speed‑time relationship is captured by the pre‑computed travel‑time constants \(\tau_{s,k}\) and the binary bin‑selection variables \(u_{t,s,k}\).*

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{w_{1}\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
      \;+\; \underbrace{w_{2}\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - T^{\text{arr}}_{t} \qquad
\text{(if the train arrives later than its scheduled arrival)} 
\]

and  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}  \;  E_{k}\; l_{s}\; u_{t,s,k}
\]

The objective simultaneously penalises late arrivals and the energy spent while travelling.

---

## 5.  Model Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection (binary plan)  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R^{t}} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link the route choice to segment‑usage**  

\[
y_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R^{t}} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\;x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.2}
\]

*(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\) is 1 if segment *s* belongs to route *r*, 0 otherwise.)*  

3. **Flow conservation on each train’s path** (including source/sink nodes)  

\[
\sum_{s' : (s,s')\in L} z_{t,(s,s')} \;-\; \sum_{s' : (s',s)\in L} z_{t,(s',s)} = 
\begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{source}}_{t}\\
 -1 & \text{if } s = s^{\text{sink}}_{t}\\
  0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.3}
\]

4. **Link link‑variables to segment‑usage**  

\[
z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s},\qquad 
z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s'} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.4}
\]

### 5.2  Conflict (bidirectional) ordering on a shared segment  

For any unordered pair of trains \((t,t')\) that may occupy the same segment *s* in opposite directions (the set of such pairs is denoted \(\mathcal{C}\)):

\[
a_{t,s} + \tau_{s}^{\max} \, y_{t,s} \le a_{t',s} + p_{t}\,(1-o_{t,t',s}) \qquad\forall (t,t',s)\in \mathcal{C}
\tag{5.5a}
\]

\[
a_{t',s} + \tau_{s}^{\max} \, y_{t',s} \le a_{t,s} + p_{t}\,o_{t,t',s} \qquad\forall (t,t',s)\in \mathcal{C}
\tag{5.5b}
\]

where \(\tau_{s}^{\max}= \max_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\) is a safe upper bound on travel time on *s*.  
The binary \(o_{t,t',s}\) decides which train passes first; the big‑M constant \(p_{t}\) can be set to the planning horizon \(U_t\).

### 5.3  Time feasibility – linking arrival/departure to speed bins  

For every train *t* and segment *s* that the train traverses (\(y_{t,s}=1\)):

1. **Exactly one speed‑bin is selected**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.6a}
\]

2. **Travel time equals the bin‑specific travel time**  

\[
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\; u_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.6b}
\]

3. **Link departure of current segment to arrival of the next**  

If \((s,s')\in L\) and \(z_{t,(s,s')}=1\):

\[
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.7}
\]

4. **Dwell‑time (minimum stop) at stations** – let \(\mathcal{S}_t\subseteq S\) be the set of segments that contain a scheduled station for train *t*.  

\[
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d^{\min}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in \mathcal{S}_t
\tag{5.8}
\]

### 5.4  Blockage window – forbidden use of blocked side  

If a segment belongs to the blocked side (\(m_{s}^{b}=1\)), the train may not occupy it **during** the blockage interval \([T^{B}_{\text{st}},\,T^{B}_{\text{en}}]\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} \;\; \text{or} \;\; d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{5.9}
\]

Linearised with a binary “use‑outside‑window” variable \(w_{t,s}\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{\text{en}} - M\,(1-w_{t,s}) \\
d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{\text{st}} + M\,w_{t,s} \\
w_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

where \(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g., the planning horizon).

### 5.5  Speed limits per segment  

The speed‑bin selection automatically respects the admissible speed interval of the segment because each bin *k* is defined globally, but we can tighten it:

\[
u_{t,s,k}=0 \qquad\text{if } v_{k}^{\text{up}} > v_{\max}^{s}\;\text{or}\; v_{k}^{\text{low}} < v_{\min}^{s}
\tag{5.10}
\]

(implemented by simply removing infeasible \((s,k)\) pairs from the model.)

### 5.6  Acceleration / deceleration limits (linearised)  

Let \(v_{t,s}\) be the **average speed** on segment *s* for train *t* (continuous). Because we already have binary bin variables, we can write  

\[
v_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \bar v_{k}\; u_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t\in S
\tag{5.11}
\]

where \(\bar v_{k}\) is the representative speed of bin *k* (e.g., the midpoint).  

Now enforce that the change of speed between consecutive segments respects acceleration/deceleration limits:

\[
v_{t,s'} - v_{t,s} \le a_{\max}\, \frac{l_{s}}{v_{t,s}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.12a}
\]

\[
v_{t,s} - v_{t,s'} \le d_{\max}\, \frac{l_{s}}{v_{t,s'}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in L
\tag{5.12b}
\]

Because the right‑hand sides are nonlinear, we linearise them with **big‑M** or with an additional set of auxiliary binary variables that select a pre‑computed feasible speed‑change interval. For brevity we keep the compact form; a practical implementation would replace (5.12) by a set of linear constraints derived from a piece‑wise linear approximation of the acceleration curve.

### 5.7  Definition of delay  

If the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination is \(T^{\text{arr}}_{t}\) (known), then

\[
\Delta_{t} \ge a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}} - T^{\text{arr}}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5.13}
\]

and \(\Delta_{t}\ge 0\). (If early arrival is allowed, the model can also include a penalty for earliness.)

### 5.8  Energy calculation (already used in the objective)  

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}  E_{k}\, l_{s}\, u_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{5.14}
\]

### 5.9  Horizon / big‑M bounds (to keep the model bounded)  

\[
0 \le a_{t,s} \le U_{t},\qquad
0 \le d_{t,s} \le U_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{5.15}
\]

---

## 6.  Summary of Variables  

| Variable | Type | Domain |
|----------|------|--------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(y_{t,s}\) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(z_{t,(s,s')}\) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(o_{t,t',s}\) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous | \([0,U_t]\) |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous | \([0,U_t]\) |
| \(u_{t,s,k}\) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |
| \(v_{t,s}\) | continuous | \([v_{\min}^{s},v_{\max}^{s}]\) |
| \(\Delta_{t}\) | continuous | \(\ge 0\) |
| \(E_{t}\) | continuous | \(\ge 0\) |
| \(w_{t,s}\) (block‑window) | binary | \(\{0,1\}\) |

All constraints are linear (or can be made linear by the standard piece‑wise linear approximations mentioned). The model therefore belongs to the class of **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programs (MILP)** and can be solved with any state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.

---

## 7.  Modelling Assumptions (to be documented when the model is used)

1. **Two‑directional routes only** – each train may either keep its original direction or reverse once (if allowed).  
2. **Speed is constant on a segment** – the piece‑wise linear speed‑bin approximation captures the speed‑time trade‑off.  
3. **Travel time per bin is pre‑computed** as \(\tau_{s,k}=l_s/v_k\); the effect of acceleration within a segment is captured by the acceleration constraints between successive segments.  
4. **Blockage affects only one side of a double‑track segment**; the opposite side remains usable.  
5. **Conflict pairs are enumerated in advance** (set \(\mathcal{C}\)). For large networks a separation routine can be added.  
6. **Energy consumption is approximated by a linear function of speed** (coefficients \(E_k\)). More detailed models (e.g., cubic resistance) can be linearised similarly.  
7. **Big‑M constants** (\(p_t, M\)) are chosen as the planning horizon or a safe upper bound on any feasible time difference; they must be tight enough to avoid numerical difficulties.  

---

### Ready‑to‑use MILP (compact notation)

```math
min  w_1 \sum_{t\in T} \Delta_t + w_2 \sum_{t\in T} E_t

s.t.

\sum_{r\in R^t} x_{t,r} = 1                                   \forall t
y_{t,s} = \sum_{r\in R^t} 1_{s\in r} x_{t,r}                 \forall t,s
\sum_{s'|(s,s')\in L} z_{t,(s,s')} - \sum_{s'|(s',s)\in L} z_{t,(s',s)}
   = \begin{cases} 1 & s = s^{source}_t\\ -1 & s = s^{sink}_t\\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}
                                                               \forall t,s
z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s},\; z_{t,(s,s')} \le y_{t,s'}        \forall t,(s,s')
\sum_{k\in K} u_{t,s,k}= y_{t,s}                              \forall t,s
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k} u_{t,s,k}          \forall t,s
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s} - M (1- z_{t,(s,s')})                    \forall t,(s,s')
d_{t,s} \ge a_{t,s}+ d^{min}_t \; \; \forall t,s\in \mathcal{S}_t

\text{(conflict ordering)}\;
a_{t,s}+ \tau^{max}_s y_{t,s} \le a_{t',s}+ p_t (1-o_{t,t',s})
a_{t',s}+ \tau^{max}_s y_{t',s} \le a_{t,s}+ p_t o_{t,t',s}
                                            \forall (t,t',s)\in\mathcal{C}

\text{(blocked side)}\;
a_{t,s} \ge T^{B}_{en} - M(1-w_{t,s}),\;
d_{t,s} \le T^{B}_{st} + M w_{t,s}
                                            \forall t, s\in B

v_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\bar v_k u_{t,s,k}                    \forall t,s
v_{t,s'}-v_{t,s} \le a_{max} \frac{l_s}{v_{t,s}}            \forall t,(s,s')
v_{t,s}-v_{t,s'} \le d_{max} \frac{l_s}{v_{t,s'}}          \forall t,(s,s')

\Delta_t \ge a_{t,s^{dest}} - T^{arr}_t                      \forall t
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} E_k l_s u_{t,s,k}           \forall t

0\le a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\le U_t                                 \forall t,s
x_{t,r},y_{t,s},z_{t,(s,s')},o_{t,t',s},u_{t,s,k},w_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}
\Delta_t, E_t \ge 0
```

This compact version contains all the elements described above and can be directly fed to a MILP solver after expanding the index sets and replacing the “big‑M” expressions with concrete numerical values.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) for Partial Segment Blockage**

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| \(S\) | set of directed track segments, indexed by *s* |
| \(L\subseteq S\times S\) | set of ordered links \((s,s')\) (consecutive segments) |
| \(K\) | set of speed‑bins (piece‑wise constant speed intervals) |
| \(R^{t}\) | feasible routes for train *t* (original direction and, if allowed, opposite direction) |
| \(\mathcal C\subseteq T\times T\times S\) | set of **conflict triples** – unordered train pairs that may occupy the same segment *s* in opposite directions |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | set of **blocked** segments (the side of the double‑track that is unavailable) |
| \(\mathcal S_{t}\subseteq S\) | segments that contain a scheduled station for train *t* (for dwell‑time constraints) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
|\(T^{\text{arr}}_{t}\) | scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its destination | s |
|\(d^{\min}_{t}\) | minimum dwell time at any station for train *t* | s |
|\(l_{s}\) | length of segment *s* | km |
|\(v^{\max }_{s},\,v^{\min }_{s}\) | speed limits on segment *s* | km h\(^{-1}\) |
|\(a^{\max },\,d^{\max }\) | maximal acceleration / deceleration (positive) | km h\(^{-2}\) |
|\(w_{1},w_{2}\) | weights of delay and energy in the objective ( \(w_{1}+w_{2}=1\) ) | – |
|\(E_{k}\) | energy consumption coefficient for speed‑bin *k* (kWh per km) | kWh km\(^{-1}\) |
|\(v_{k}^{\text{low}},v_{k}^{\text{up}}\) | lower/upper speed of bin *k* | km h\(^{-1}\) |

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. As transport capacity directly impacts passenger flows, further research is required to improve passenger satisfaction by including transport capacity as a decision variable.

Another direction for train scheduling problems addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing transport capacity explicitly. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. Pu and Zhan (2021) developed a two-step approach in which the first step determines the nominal line plan and the second step adjusts the time plan based on the actual measured passenger demands. Instead of changing the departure frequency, which would significantly affect the schedule, recently, many researchers have focused on optimizing the composition of the train (Ying et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023). Pan et al. (2023) developed a column-generation-based approach to optimize the timetable, train composition, and rolling stock circulation plan of an urban rail transit line. Their paper concludes that flexible train composition can provide additional adaptability to better match time-varying passenger demands. Wang et al. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. Yang et al. Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. Liu et al. (2023a) explicitly incorporated time-varying passenger demands and train capacity limitations into the real-time train scheduling problem. In Liu et al. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. The main challenge of applying MPC in real time is the online computational burden. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.
