**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  

The model below follows the description in the prompt.  
It is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** that is solved at every MPC step (prediction horizon \(H\)).  
All symbols are defined in the *Sets, Parameters, Decision Variables* section; the *Assumptions* section lists the modelling simplifications that were necessary because the source text does not give exact numerical data.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal{L}\) | Set of train lines (for a single‑line case \(\mathcal{L}=\{l\}\)). |
| \(\mathcal{S}=\{1,\dots,S\}\) | Ordered set of stations on line \(l\). |
| \(\mathcal{T}=\{1,\dots,T\}\) | Set of scheduled train trips (each trip = one physical train). |
| \(\mathcal{K}=\{1,\dots,K\}\) | Set of admissible **train composition types** (e.g. 4‑car, 6‑car, 8‑car). |
| \(\mathcal{H}=\{1,\dots,H\}\) | Set of discrete time intervals in the MPC prediction horizon (piece‑wise constant demand). |
| \(\mathcal{P}\) | Set of rolling‑stock pools (e.g. depot \(p=0\) and intermediate yards). |
| \(\mathcal{D}\subseteq \mathcal{T}\times \mathcal{T}\) | Set of feasible **precedence pairs** \((t,t')\) meaning train \(t'\) may follow train \(t\) on the same unit of rolling stock. |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical unit |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| \(d_{s,h}\) | Passenger demand (boardings) at station \(s\) during interval \(h\). | persons |
| \(\Delta_h\) | Length of interval \(h\) (seconds). | s |
| \(C_k\) | Seating capacity of composition type \(k\). | persons |
| \(c^{\text{run}}_{s,s'}\) | Nominal running time between consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s'\). | s |
| \(c^{\text{dwell}}_{s}\) | Minimum dwell time for door opening/closing at station \(s\). | s |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) for linearisation. | – |
| \(B^{\max}\) | Maximum allowed headway (seconds) between any two consecutive trains on the line. | s |
| \(B^{\min}\) | Minimum allowed headway (seconds) (safety). | s |
| \(\alpha^{\text{op}}\) | Unit operating cost of a train (fuel/energy, staff) per second. | \$/s |
| \(\beta^{\text{wait}}\) | Penalty cost per passenger‑minute of waiting. | \$/person·min |
| \(\gamma^{\text{travel}}\) | Penalty cost per passenger‑minute of in‑vehicle travel (including extra dwell). | \$/person·min |
| \(R^{\text{avail}}_p\) | Number of rolling‑stock units available in pool \(p\). | units |
| \(\tau^{\text{turn}}_p\) | Minimum turnaround time for a train returning to pool \(p\). | s |
| \(\pi_{t}\) | Planned (nominal) departure time of train \(t\) from the first station (used for deviation penalty). | s |
| \(\lambda^{\text{dev}}\) | Weight for timetable deviation in the objective. | – |

*All parameters are assumed known at the beginning of each MPC step (e.g. demand forecasts are piece‑wise constant over \(\Delta_h\)).*

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses composition type \(k\). |
| \(y_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) starts (or ends) its circulation at pool \(p\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | Actual arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\). |
| \(w_{s,h}\ge 0\) | continuous | Number of passengers waiting at station \(s\) at the *end* of interval \(h\). |
| \(u_{s,h}\ge 0\) | continuous | Number of passengers that board train(s) at station \(s\) during interval \(h\). |
| \(z_{t,t'}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t'\) is the immediate successor of train \(t\) on the same rolling‑stock unit (used for circulation constraints). |
| \(\delta_{t}\ge 0\) | continuous | Absolute deviation of the first‑departure time of train \(t\) from its nominal \(\pi_t\). |

*Only the integer variables \(\{x_{t,k},y_{t,p},z_{t,t'}\}\) are supplied by the learning module (e.g. an LSTM). The remaining variables are obtained by solving the MILP with those integers fixed.*

---

## 4. Model Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Piece‑wise constant demand** – Passenger arrivals at each station are approximated by a constant rate within each interval \(h\).  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – Nominal running times \(c^{\text{run}}_{s,s'}\) are used; any deviation is captured by the decision variables \(a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\).  
3. **Single line, unidirectional** – The formulation can be duplicated for each direction; the presented version assumes one direction only.  
4. **No overtaking** – Trains keep their order on the line; the precedence set \(\mathcal{D}\) enforces this.  
5. **Capacity is only seat capacity** – Standing passengers are ignored (or assumed to be covered by the same capacity).  
6. **Rolling‑stock pools are homogeneous** – Any composition type can be assembled at any pool, subject to availability.  
7. **Headway limits are hard constraints** – Safety‑related minimum/maximum headways must be respected for every pair of consecutive trains.  
8. **All passengers that cannot board a train wait for the next one** – No passenger loss is allowed.  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\alpha^{\text{op}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} (d_{t,s}-a_{t,s})}_{\text{operational time cost}} \\
& + \underbrace{\beta^{\text{wait}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} w_{s,h}\,\frac{\Delta_h}{60}}_{\text{passenger waiting cost (min)}}\\
& + \underbrace{\gamma^{\text{travel}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} u_{s,h}\,\frac{\Delta_h}{60}}_{\text{in‑vehicle travel (extra dwell) cost}}\\
& + \underbrace{\lambda^{\text{dev}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_{t}}_{\text{timetable deviation penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All terms are linear because \(\delta_t\) will be linearised (see constraints).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Train‑composition selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{t,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{C1}
\]

### 6.2. Rolling‑stock pool assignment  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} y_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{C2}
\]

### 6.3. Capacity feasibility (boarding ≤ capacity)  

For each station‑interval pair, the total number of boarding passengers cannot exceed the sum of capacities of the trains that actually stop there during that interval.

First define a binary **stop** indicator (derived from the timetable):

\[
\theta_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a_{t,s}\le d_{t,s} \text{ (train stops)}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Because the model is linear, we replace \(\theta_{t,s}\) by a big‑M formulation:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \ge c^{\text{dwell}}_{s}\,\theta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{C3a}
\]
\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \le M\,\theta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{C3b}
\]

Now capacity:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \theta_{t,s}\, C_{k}\,x_{t,k} \;\ge\; u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s\in\mathcal{S},\;h\in\mathcal{H} \tag{C4}
\]

### 6.4. Passenger‑flow balance  

At each station and interval, the waiting passengers evolve as:

\[
w_{s,h}= w_{s,h-1}+ d_{s,h} - u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s,\;h\ge 2 \tag{C5a}
\]
\[
w_{s,1}= d_{s,1} - u_{s,1} \qquad \forall s \tag{C5b}
\]

where \(d_{s,h}\) is the external demand arriving during interval \(h\) (given by \(d_{s,h}\) parameter).  
Thus:

\[
w_{s,h}= w_{s,h-1}+ d_{s,h} - u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s,\;h\ge 2 \tag{C5}
\]

All waiting variables must be non‑negative:

\[
w_{s,h}\ge 0 \qquad \forall s,h \tag{C6}
\]

### 6.5. Train dynamics (running‑time constraints)  

For any two consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s'\) (with \(s' = s+1\)):

\[
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s} + c^{\text{run}}_{s,s'} \qquad \forall t,\; s=1,\dots,S-1 \tag{C7}
\]

### 6.6. Headway limits  

Let \(t\) and \(t'\) be two trains that travel the same direction and are ordered (i.e. \(t\) precedes \(t'\) on the line). The headway at the first station is:

\[
B_{t,t'} = a_{t',1} - a_{t,1} \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D} \tag{C8a}
\]

Enforce bounds:

\[
B^{\min} \le B_{t,t'} \le B^{\max} \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D} \tag{C8b}
\]

### 6.7. Rolling‑stock circulation (successor linking)  

If train \(t'\) is the immediate successor of train \(t\) on the same unit, then the departure from the last station of \(t\) plus turnaround must precede the departure of \(t'\) from the first station:

\[
a_{t',1} \ge d_{t,S} + \tau^{\text{turn}}_{p}\;-\; M\,(1-z_{t,t'}) \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D},\; p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C9a}
\]

And each train can have at most one predecessor and one successor:

\[
\sum_{t' : (t,t')\in\mathcal{D}} z_{t,t'} \le 1 \qquad \forall t \tag{C9b}
\]
\[
\sum_{t : (t,t')\in\mathcal{D}} z_{t,t'} \le 1 \qquad \forall t' \tag{C9c}
\]

Link to pool assignment (if a train starts at pool \(p\) then its predecessor must end at the same pool):

\[
y_{t',p} \ge y_{t,p} - (1- z_{t,t'}) \qquad \forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\;p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C9d}
\]

Pool capacity (total number of trains simultaneously using a pool cannot exceed availability):

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} y_{t,p} \le R^{\text{avail}}_p \qquad \forall p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C10}
\]

### 6.8. Timetable deviation linearisation  

\[
\delta_t \ge a_{t,1} - \pi_t \qquad \forall t \tag{C11a}
\]
\[
\delta_t \ge \pi_t - a_{t,1} \qquad \forall t \tag{C11b}
\]

### 6.9. Variable domains  

\[
x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,t'}\in\{0,1\} \qquad \forall t,k,p,t' \tag{C12}
\]
\[
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},w_{s,h},u_{s,h},\delta_t \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,s,h \tag{C13}
\]

---

## 7. Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,z,a,d,w,u,\delta}&\; \text{Objective (Section 5)}\\
\text{s.t. } & \text{Constraints (C1)–(C13)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on the **Learning‑driven MPC**  

* At each MPC step the demand forecast \(\{d_{s,h}\}\) for the next \(H\) intervals is supplied.  
* An LSTM (or any other predictor) is trained offline to output a **reduced set of integer variables**:  
  * composition decisions \(\{x_{t,k}\}\) for the trains that are still in the planning horizon,  
  * pool‑assignment decisions \(\{y_{t,p}\}\), and  
  * successor links \(\{z_{t,t'}\}\).  
* Those integer values are **fixed** in the MILP; the remaining continuous variables \((a,d,w,u,\delta)\) are then obtained by solving the linear program defined above.  
* Because the integer block is much smaller (thanks to the four presolve techniques described in the source text), the MILP can be solved within the typical MPC sampling time (seconds to a few minutes).  

---

### 9. Potential Extensions (not in the core model)

* **Energy consumption** – add a term \(\alpha^{\text{energy}}\sum_t \sum_{s} (d_{t,s}-a_{t,s})\) with train‑specific energy coefficients.  
* **Multi‑direction lines** – duplicate the index set with a direction flag and add crossing‑conflict constraints.  
* **Stochastic demand** – replace deterministic \(d_{s,h}\) by scenarios and add chance‑constraint or robust‑optimization cuts.  

The formulation above is a **complete linear MILP** that captures the essential elements highlighted in the literature review: time‑varying passenger demand, flexible train composition, rolling‑stock circulation, and MPC‑type receding‑horizon optimisation. All missing numerical details have been introduced as reasonable assumptions and are clearly marked.

7. **Headway limits are hard constraints** – Safety‑related minimum/maximum headways must be respected for every pair of consecutive trains.  
8. **All passengers that cannot board a train wait for the next one** – No passenger loss is allowed.  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & 
\underbrace{\alpha^{\text{op}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}} (d_{t,s}-a_{t,s})}_{\text{operational time cost}} \\
& + \underbrace{\beta^{\text{wait}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} w_{s,h}\,\frac{\Delta_h}{60}}_{\text{passenger waiting cost (min)}}\\
& + \underbrace{\gamma^{\text{travel}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} u_{s,h}\,\frac{\Delta_h}{60}}_{\text{in‑vehicle travel (extra dwell) cost}}\\
& + \underbrace{\lambda^{\text{dev}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \delta_{t}}_{\text{timetable deviation penalty}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

All terms are linear because \(\delta_t\) will be linearised (see constraints).

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1. Train‑composition selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{t,k}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{C1}
\]

### 6.2. Rolling‑stock pool assignment  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} y_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in\mathcal{T} \tag{C2}
\]

### 6.3. Capacity feasibility (boarding ≤ capacity)  

For each station‑interval pair, the total number of boarding passengers cannot exceed the sum of capacities of the trains that actually stop there during that interval.

First define a binary **stop** indicator (derived from the timetable):

\[
\theta_{t,s}= 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } a_{t,s}\le d_{t,s} \text{ (train stops)}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

Because the model is linear, we replace \(\theta_{t,s}\) by a big‑M formulation:

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \ge c^{\text{dwell}}_{s}\,\theta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{C3a}
\]
\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} \le M\,\theta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s \tag{C3b}
\]

Now capacity:

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} \theta_{t,s}\, C_{k}\,x_{t,k} \;\ge\; u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s\in\mathcal{S},\;h\in\mathcal{H} \tag{C4}
\]

### 6.4. Passenger‑flow balance  

At each station and interval, the waiting passengers evolve as:

\[
w_{s,h}= w_{s,h-1}+ d_{s,h} - u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s,\;h\ge 2 \tag{C5a}
\]
\[
w_{s,1}= d_{s,1} - u_{s,1} \qquad \forall s \tag{C5b}
\]

where \(d_{s,h}\) is the external demand arriving during interval \(h\) (given by \(d_{s,h}\) parameter).  
Thus:

\[
w_{s,h}= w_{s,h-1}+ d_{s,h} - u_{s,h} \qquad \forall s,\;h\ge 2 \tag{C5}
\]

All waiting variables must be non‑negative:

\[
w_{s,h}\ge 0 \qquad \forall s,h \tag{C6}
\]

### 6.5. Train dynamics (running‑time constraints)  

For any two consecutive stations \(s\) and \(s'\) (with \(s' = s+1\)):

\[
a_{t,s'} \ge d_{t,s} + c^{\text{run}}_{s,s'} \qquad \forall t,\; s=1,\dots,S-1 \tag{C7}
\]

### 6.6. Headway limits  

Let \(t\) and \(t'\) be two trains that travel the same direction and are ordered (i.e. \(t\) precedes \(t'\) on the line). The headway at the first station is:

\[
B_{t,t'} = a_{t',1} - a_{t,1} \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D} \tag{C8a}
\]

Enforce bounds:

\[
B^{\min} \le B_{t,t'} \le B^{\max} \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D} \tag{C8b}
\]

### 6.7. Rolling‑stock circulation (successor linking)  

If train \(t'\) is the immediate successor of train \(t\) on the same unit, then the departure from the last station of \(t\) plus turnaround must precede the departure of \(t'\) from the first station:

\[
a_{t',1} \ge d_{t,S} + \tau^{\text{turn}}_{p}\;-\; M\,(1-z_{t,t'}) \qquad \forall (t,t')\in \mathcal{D},\; p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C9a}
\]

And each train can have at most one predecessor and one successor:

\[
\sum_{t' : (t,t')\in\mathcal{D}} z_{t,t'} \le 1 \qquad \forall t \tag{C9b}
\]
\[
\sum_{t : (t,t')\in\mathcal{D}} z_{t,t'} \le 1 \qquad \forall t' \tag{C9c}
\]

Link to pool assignment (if a train starts at pool \(p\) then its predecessor must end at the same pool):

\[
y_{t',p} \ge y_{t,p} - (1- z_{t,t'}) \qquad \forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{D},\;p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C9d}
\]

Pool capacity (total number of trains simultaneously using a pool cannot exceed availability):

\[
\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} y_{t,p} \le R^{\text{avail}}_p \qquad \forall p\in\mathcal{P} \tag{C10}
\]

### 6.8. Timetable deviation linearisation  

\[
\delta_t \ge a_{t,1} - \pi_t \qquad \forall t \tag{C11a}
\]
\[
\delta_t \ge \pi_t - a_{t,1} \qquad \forall t \tag{C11b}
\]

### 6.9. Variable domains  

\[
x_{t,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,t'}\in\{0,1\} \qquad \forall t,k,p,t' \tag{C12}
\]
\[
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},w_{s,h},u_{s,h},\delta_t \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,s,h \tag{C13}
\]

---

## 7. Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,z,a,d,w,u,\delta}&\; \text{Objective (Section 5)}\\
\text{s.t. } & \text{Constraints (C1)–(C13)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. Remarks on the **Learning‑driven MPC**  

* At each MPC step the demand forecast \(\{d_{s,h}\}\) for the next \(H\) intervals is supplied.  
* An LSTM (or any other predictor) is trained offline to output a **reduced set of integer variables**:  
  * composition decisions \(\{x_{t,k}\}\) for the trains that are still in the planning horizon,  
  * pool‑assignment decisions \(\{y_{t,p}\}\), and  
  * successor links \(\{z_{t,t'}\}\).  
* Those integer values are **fixed** in the MILP; the remaining continuous variables \((a,d,w,u,\delta)\) are then obtained by solving the linear program defined above.  
* Because the integer block is much smaller (thanks to the four presolve techniques described in the source text), the MILP can be solved within the typical MPC sampling time (seconds to a few minutes).  

---

### 9. Potential Extensions (not in the core model)

* **Energy consumption** – add a term \(\alpha^{\text{energy}}\sum_t \sum_{s} (d_{t,s}-a_{t,s})\) with train‑specific energy coefficients.  
* **Multi‑direction lines** – duplicate the index set with a direction flag and add crossing‑conflict constraints.  
* **Stochastic demand** – replace deterministic \(d_{s,h}\) by scenarios and add chance‑constraint or robust‑optimization cuts.  

The formulation above is a **complete linear MILP** that captures the essential elements highlighted in the literature review: time‑varying passenger demand, flexible train composition, rolling‑stock circulation, and MPC‑type receding‑horizon optimisation. All missing numerical details have been introduced as reasonable assumptions and are clearly marked.

Introduction

With millions of passenger trips on an average day, railway networks play a big role in the European mobility system. In the European Union, the railway infrastructure and the railway operations are mandated by law to be managed separately. In the Netherlands, ProRail is responsible for managing the railway network infrastructure and Netherlands Railways (NS) is the main passenger railway operator. One of the tasks of the railway operator is the planning of individual train units, or rolling stock. A rolling stock schedule specifies which rolling stock units operate which trips in the timetable. Disruptions on the railway network, such as a missing rolling stock unit in a train trip or a complete blockage of a railway track as a result of an accident or a train breakdown, require the rolling stock plan to be updated. The rescheduling measures that pertain to the (availability of the) railway infrastructure, i.e., the changes in the rolling stock assignments, are created by rolling stock dispatchers who work for the railway operator, after which local infrastructure dispatchers who work for the infrastructure manager are tasked with performing the suggested rolling stock movements.

We focus our research on the rescheduling of rolling stock units in the case of disruptions in the railway system. It is necessary that the rolling stock is efficiently operated and utilized to maintain a good balance between the service to passengers and the incurred operational costs. Unavailability of rolling stock influences passenger satisfaction, as passengers possibly have to stand or even wait for the next train in case not enough capacity is available. An efficient rescheduling process reduces such problems and also reduces the number of trains that are needed as a buffer to catch disrupted train services, leading to a reduction in the capital costs for the train operator. It is also beneficial if the adjusted plan is similar to the original plan, as this requires fewer rolling stock movements during the night to get each rolling stock unit to its starting position for the next day. Additionally, an advantage for both passengers and crew members is that they are familiar with the original plan and may prefer the rolling stock units to be operated as originally planned.

Currently, the rescheduling of rolling stock after disruptions is mostly done by hand. As a result, railway planners manually try to find an updated rolling stock allocation without the use of any mathematical methods or solvers. This can largely be attributed to the difficulty of the problem. For a rolling stock plan to work in practice, feasible train compositions need to be assigned to each train trip, the associated shunting movements need to be executable and shunting drivers need to be available for all shunting movements. Past papers have often tackled these problems separately, meaning that there are practical requirements that are not considered in their solution approaches. One of these requirements is the availability of railway tracks for the shunting movements to take place. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has focused on ensuring feasibility of a rolling stock schedule with regard to this aspect. In practice, this is an important part of rolling stock rescheduling; if the rolling stock movements are not possible due to unavailability of the railway tracks, the entire plan could fall apart and could need to be adjusted.

We introduce two solution approaches which ensure that all shunting movements are feasible with respect to the available infrastructure: an exact algorithm and an iterative heuristic. The basis for our methods is the composition model by Fioole et al. (2006), which outputs a rolling stock circulation for the passenger train timetable. To check whether each of the suggested trips and shunting movements can be performed, we implement an infrastructure model which is based on the model by Van Aken et al. (2017) for solving the Train Timetable Adjustment Problem, which aims at finding an alternative timetable that minimizes the deviation from the original timetable in terms of the incurred delays and cancellations of train services. Our tailored version of this model represents every shunting movement as an event that takes place on a specific track at a specific station and outputs whether a shunting movement is possible and whether other trains need to be delayed to make the shunting movement possible. Although delaying other trains is typically not preferred, a short delay could open up the necessary windows for performing additional shunting movements. We therefore include the option of delaying other trains by at most a few minutes in our framework and assume that such short delays are resolved by the buffers that are present in the timetable for the remainder of the affected train lines.

Our exact approach resembles a Combinatorial Benders’ approach in line with Codato and Fischetti (2004). It alternates between the composition model, which suggests shunting movements, and the infrastructure model, which checks whether each combination of shunting movements can be performed. The infrastructure model then returns cuts that prohibit combinations of shunting movements, which violate the railway infrastructure availability constraints, from being performed simultaneously. A drawback of the exact approach is the underlying assumption that the creation of a new rolling stock plan and the performance of the shunting movements are carried out simultaneously by one and the same entity, which conflicts with the separation of the railway tasks as mandated by European laws. We therefore also introduce an iterative heuristic, which works in a similar way as the exact algorithm, but feeds the suggested shunting movements one by one to the infrastructure model. This closely resembles the situation where the rolling stock dispatchers and infrastructure dispatchers work for different companies and is therefore more applicable in the European context. The iterative heuristic mimics the interaction that takes place between the rolling stock dispatchers, who try to come up with a new rolling stock plan, and the local infrastructure dispatchers, who try to perform the shunting movements. We want to emphasize that our framework is generic; besides the specific model choices that we made for the two steps in our iterative frameworks, other formulations and methods can be used as well, so long as they solve the same problems.

We test our algorithm on seven instances which consist of full blockages on the railway network. We model and analyze the railway infrastructure of two major stations, Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal, and allow for shunting movements at these two stations during the duration of the blockages. In practice, shunting at these two stations is assumed to be too difficult due to the large number of trains that pass through and is therefore not considered a viable option during the creation of the rolling stock schedule. We show that the exact algorithm successfully identifies feasible shunting movements that can take place at both Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal to counter the disruption and to improve the rolling stock schedule with respect to several operational, passenger service level and stick-to-the-plan objectives compared to the situation in which shunting at Utrecht Centraal and Rotterdam Centraal is not considered. Additionally, we find that the iterative heuristic is able to obtain an optimal solution for all instances, in shorter running times. We find that shunting movements are only canceled in case other passenger trains occupy the railway infrastructure and that the shunting movements themselves do not create unsolvable conflicts with one another. Therefore, the order in which the shunting movements are processed by the infrastructure model does not matter and the iterative heuristic finds an optimal solution for all instances. We furthermore find that our algorithm performs well in case we put emphasis on any of the rolling stock rescheduling objectives and that our approach also provides added value in the case that all trains are fixed and cannot be delayed.

The contribution of this paper is threefold. Firstly, we introduce frameworks for rolling stock rescheduling with railway infrastructure availability constraints. The methods output rolling stock circulations which ensure that a feasible path through the railway infrastructure exists for the performed shunting movements at the considered stations. Secondly, our algorithms find solutions within a few minutes with an average improvement of 19% over the rolling stock schedule which does not contain shunting movements at Utrecht Centraal or Rotterdam Centraal. Thirdly, we show that the frameworks can be beneficial in practical problems; by allowing for shunting at more stations than is currently done in practice, our frameworks are able to provide improvements over the rolling stock circulations that are currently made. Furthermore, the iterative approach mimics rolling stock rescheduling in practice by distinguishing between the two problems which are currently solved separately by the rolling stock dispatchers and the infrastructure dispatchers. Our approach provides a framework which connects these problems, thereby facilitating and reducing the interaction which is required between the involved parties.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a detailed description of the problem we address. Literature covering similar problems is discussed in Section 3. Section 4 provides a mathematical formulation for our two solution components and introduces the iterative rolling stock rescheduling algorithm. Computational results and a sensitivity analysis of our algorithm are presented in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 gives conclusions and suggestions for future research.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for rolling‑stock rescheduling with infrastructure‑availability constraints**  

The formulation below combines two sub‑models that appear in the paper description  

* **Composition sub‑model** – decides which rolling‑stock unit (RSU) is assigned to each passenger trip and which shunting movements are created.  
* **Infrastructure sub‑model** – checks whether the chosen shunting movements can be performed on the available tracks of the stations (Utrecht C and Rotterdam C) and, if necessary, introduces short delays for other passenger trains.  

The two sub‑models are linked through Benders‑type feasibility cuts (exact algorithm) or by feeding the shunting decisions one‑by‑one to the infrastructure model (iterative heuristic).  
For the purpose of a single, self‑contained MILP we embed the feasibility conditions directly as “big‑M” constraints; the same model can be used in a Benders decomposition framework.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of passenger trips (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(R\) | Set of rolling‑stock units (indexed by \(r\)). |
| \(S\) | Set of stations where shunting is allowed (here \(S=\{Utrecht, Rotterdam\}\)). |
| \(M_s\) | Set of shunting tracks at station \(s\) (indexed by \(m\)). |
| \(K\) | Set of possible shunting movements (indexed by \(k\)). Each movement \(k\) is defined by a tuple \((r,s,m,\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k)\) – the RSU that must be moved, the station, the track, and the time window in which the movement must start / finish. |
| \(P\) | Set of passenger‑train events that occupy a track at a station (indexed by \(p\)). Each event \(p\) is defined by \((s,m,\tau^{start}_p,\tau^{end}_p)\). |
| \(L\) | Set of “delay‑levels’’ that can be applied to a passenger event (e.g. 0 min, 1 min, 2 min, 3 min). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / assumption |
|--------|-------------|-----------------------------|
| \(c^{trip}_{t,r}\) | Cost (or penalty) of assigning RSU \(r\) to trip \(t\). | 0 if feasible, large \(M\) if not (e.g. RSU not compatible). |
| \(c^{sh}_{k}\) | Cost (or penalty) for performing shunting movement \(k\). | Positive (reflects driver time, fuel, wear). |
| \(c^{delay}_\ell\) | Penalty for delaying a passenger event by the amount associated with level \(\ell\). | Small (e.g. 1 €/min). |
| \(c^{dev}_t\) | Penalty for deviating from the original assignment of trip \(t\) (e.g. using a different RSU than originally planned). | Positive. |
| \(\Delta^{max}\) | Maximum admissible extra delay for any passenger event (in minutes). | 3 min (as stated). |
| \(M\) | Large constant for “big‑M’’ constraints (larger than the planning horizon, e.g. 10 000). |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight for similarity‑to‑original‑plan objective (0 ≤ α ≤ 1). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total operational cost objective (β = 1 − α). |
| \(T^{orig}_t\) | Original RSU assigned to trip \(t\) (used for similarity term). | – |
| \(start_t, end_t\) | Scheduled start / end time of trip \(t\) (fixed). | – |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if RSU \(r\) is assigned to trip \(t\). |
| \(y_k \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) is performed. |
| \(z_{p,\ell} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if passenger event \(p\) is delayed by level \(\ell\). (Only one level can be chosen.) |
| \(s_{p} \in \mathbb{R}_+\) | continuous | Actual start time of passenger event \(p\) after possible delay. |
| \(e_{p} \in \mathbb{R}_+\) | continuous | Actual end time of passenger event \(p\) after possible delay. |
| \(u_{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) **conflicts** with at least one passenger event on the same track (used for Benders cut generation). |
| \(w_{k,p} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) and passenger event \(p\) overlap on the same track (auxiliary). |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

We combine three goals:

1. **Operational cost** – assignment + shunting + delay penalties.  
2. **Similarity to the original plan** – minimise the number of trips that receive a different RSU.  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \beta\Bigg[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{r\in R} c^{trip}_{t,r}\,x_{t,r}}_{\text{trip‑assignment cost}}
          + \underbrace{\sum_{k\in K} c^{sh}_{k}\,y_{k}}_{\text{shunting cost}}
          + \underbrace{\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{delay}_\ell \,z_{p,\ell}}_{\text{delay penalty}} \Bigg] \\
        & + \alpha\Bigg[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(1-\sum_{r\in R} \mathbf{1}_{\{r=T^{orig}_t\}}\,x_{t,r}\Bigr)}_{\text{deviation from original RSU}} \Bigg]
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\mathbf{1}_{\{condition\}}\) is 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.  
If \(\alpha=0\) we only minimise costs; if \(\alpha=1\) we only maximise similarity.

---

### 4.2 Assignment constraints  

*Each trip receives exactly one RSU*  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{A1}
\]

*RSU flow balance (circulation)* – a RSU that finishes a trip must either start the next assigned trip or be used for a shunting movement. Let  

\[
\text{next}(t) = \{t' \in T \mid \text{the scheduled arrival of }t \text{ is before the departure of }t' \text{ and } r\text{ can be reused}\}
\]

For each RSU \(r\):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} x_{t,r} = \sum_{t\in T} x_{t,r} \quad\text{(trivial)} 
\]

In practice we enforce a **circulation** using a time‑expanded network; a compact way is:

\[
\sum_{t\in T: \; end_t \le H} x_{t,r} \;-\; \sum_{t\in T: \; start_t \ge 0} x_{t,r} = 0 \qquad \forall r\in R
\tag{A2}
\]

where \(H\) is the planning horizon (e.g. 24 h). This ensures that the number of departures equals the number of arrivals for each RSU.

---

### 4.3 Shunting‑movement feasibility  

A shunting movement \(k=(r,s,m,\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k)\) can be performed **only** if the RSU \(r\) is available (i.e., not assigned to a passenger trip at that time) **and** the track \(m\) at station \(s\) is free.

*Link to RSU assignment*  

\[
y_k \le \sum_{t\in T: \; r\text{ is used on }t \text{ and } [\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k]\cap [start_t,end_t]\neq\emptyset } x_{t,r} \;+\; (1 - \text{bigM}) 
\tag{S1}
\]

A more readable formulation uses an auxiliary binary \(a_{k}\) that equals 1 if RSU \(r\) is **busy** during the shunting window:

\[
a_{k} \ge x_{t,r} \quad \forall t\in T \text{ with } [\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k]\cap [start_t,end_t]\neq\emptyset
\]
\[
y_k \le 1 - a_{k}
\tag{S1‑alt}
\]

*Track‑occupancy conflicts*  

For each passenger event \(p\) that uses the same track \((s,m)\) we introduce binary overlap variable \(w_{k,p}\):

\[
w_{k,p} \ge y_k + z_{p,\ell} - 1 \qquad \forall \ell\in L,\; p\in P \text{ with } (s,m) \text{ equal}
\tag{S2}
\]

If both shunting \(k\) and passenger event \(p\) are scheduled (possibly delayed) then \(w_{k,p}=1\).

The actual time windows after delay are:

\[
s_p = start_p + \sum_{\ell\in L}\ell\;z_{p,\ell}, \qquad
e_p = end_p + \sum_{\ell\in L}\ell\;z_{p,\ell}
\tag{S3}
\]

The overlap condition (big‑M formulation) :

\[
w_{k,p} \le 
\frac{(\tau^{end}_k - s_p)}{M}
+ \frac{(e_p - \tau^{start}_k)}{M}
\tag{S4}
\]

If the intervals do **not** overlap, the RHS ≤ 0, forcing \(w_{k,p}=0\).

Finally, a shunting movement is **allowed** only if it does not overlap any passenger event on the same track:

\[
y_k \le 1 - \sum_{p\in P:(s,m)} w_{k,p} \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{S5}
\]

---

### 4.4 Delay limits  

Only one delay level per passenger event:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{p,\ell} \le 1 \qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{D1}
\]

Maximum admissible delay:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} \ell \, z_{p,\ell} \le \Delta^{max} \qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{D2}
\]

---

### 4.5 Benders‑type feasibility indicator (optional)  

If the model is used inside a Benders decomposition, we keep the auxiliary binary \(u_k\) that becomes 1 when a conflict is detected; the master problem then adds a cut  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_k \le |K|-1
\tag{B1}
\]

In the monolithic MILP we simply set \(u_k = y_k\) and enforce (S5); the cut is not needed.

---

### 4.6 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R\\
&y_k \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K\\
&z_{p,\ell} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall p\in P,\; \ell\in L\\
&s_p, e_p \in \mathbb{R}_+ &&\forall p\in P\\
&w_{k,p} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K,\; p\in P\\
&a_k \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Remarks & Modeling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption (explicitly stated) | Reason / comment |
|---|-------------------------------|------------------|
| 1 | **Discrete delay levels** – we allow only a few integer minute delays (0‑3 min). This matches the “short delay” policy described in the paper. |
| 2 | **Big‑M value** – \(M\) is chosen larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min) to safely linearise the overlap conditions. |
| 3 | **Shunting tracks are pre‑identified** – the set \(M_s\) is known for each station (Utrecht C, Rotterdam C). No capacity limit per track other than “one movement at a time”. |
| 4 | **RSU compatibility** – the cost \(c^{trip}_{t,r}\) is set to a very large value (or \(x_{t,r}=0\) forced) when the RSU cannot physically serve the trip (different class, length, power). |
| 5 | **Circulation balance** – the simplified equation (A2) assumes the planning horizon is long enough that each RSU that departs also returns; more detailed time‑expanded network can be used if needed. |
| 6 | **Objective weighting** – the user can tune \(\alpha\) (similarity) vs. \(\beta\) (cost) to reflect the “stick‑to‑the‑plan” vs. “operational cost” trade‑off discussed in the paper. |
| 7 | **Exact vs. heuristic** – the model can be solved directly (heuristic) or embedded in a Benders loop where the infrastructure model returns cuts (exact). The formulation above contains the necessary binaries to generate such cuts. |
| 8 | **No driver‑availability constraints** – the paper mentions shunting drivers; they are omitted here for brevity but can be added analogously (binary driver‑assignment variables with shift‑length limits). |
| 9 | **No explicit passenger‑capacity penalties** – the model focuses on feasibility and cost; passenger‑satisfaction (standing, waiting) could be added as extra terms using load variables, but is left out to keep the MILP concise. |

---

## 6. How the Model Captures the Paper’s Goals  

* **Feasibility of shunting** – constraints (S1)–(S5) guarantee that a shunting movement is only selected if the RSU is free and the track is free, possibly after delaying other trains within the allowed short window.  
* **Minimal disruption** – the similarity term (weighted by \(\alpha\)) penalises any change of RSU compared with the original schedule, encouraging solutions “close to the original plan”.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for rolling‑stock rescheduling with infrastructure‑availability constraints**  

The formulation below combines two sub‑models that appear in the paper description  

* **Composition sub‑model** – decides which rolling‑stock unit (RSU) is assigned to each passenger trip and which shunting movements are created.  
* **Infrastructure sub‑model** – checks whether the chosen shunting movements can be performed on the available tracks of the stations (Utrecht C and Rotterdam C) and, if necessary, introduces short delays for other passenger trains.  

The two sub‑models are linked through Benders‑type feasibility cuts (exact algorithm) or by feeding the shunting decisions one‑by‑one to the infrastructure model (iterative heuristic).  
For the purpose of a single, self‑contained MILP we embed the feasibility conditions directly as “big‑M” constraints; the same model can be used in a Benders decomposition framework.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of passenger trips (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(R\) | Set of rolling‑stock units (indexed by \(r\)). |
| \(S\) | Set of stations where shunting is allowed (here \(S=\{Utrecht, Rotterdam\}\)). |
| \(M_s\) | Set of shunting tracks at station \(s\) (indexed by \(m\)). |
| \(K\) | Set of possible shunting movements (indexed by \(k\)). Each movement \(k\) is defined by a tuple \((r,s,m,\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k)\) – the RSU that must be moved, the station, the track, and the time window in which the movement must start / finish. |
| \(P\) | Set of passenger‑train events that occupy a track at a station (indexed by \(p\)). Each event \(p\) is defined by \((s,m,\tau^{start}_p,\tau^{end}_p)\). |
| \(L\) | Set of “delay‑levels’’ that can be applied to a passenger event (e.g. 0 min, 1 min, 2 min, 3 min). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / assumption |
|--------|-------------|-----------------------------|
| \(c^{trip}_{t,r}\) | Cost (or penalty) of assigning RSU \(r\) to trip \(t\). | 0 if feasible, large \(M\) if not (e.g. RSU not compatible). |
| \(c^{sh}_{k}\) | Cost (or penalty) for performing shunting movement \(k\). | Positive (reflects driver time, fuel, wear). |
| \(c^{delay}_\ell\) | Penalty for delaying a passenger event by the amount associated with level \(\ell\). | Small (e.g. 1 €/min). |
| \(c^{dev}_t\) | Penalty for deviating from the original assignment of trip \(t\) (e.g. using a different RSU than originally planned). | Positive. |
| \(\Delta^{max}\) | Maximum admissible extra delay for any passenger event (in minutes). | 3 min (as stated). |
| \(M\) | Large constant for “big‑M’’ constraints (larger than the planning horizon, e.g. 10 000). |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight for similarity‑to‑original‑plan objective (0 ≤ α ≤ 1). |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total operational cost objective (β = 1 − α). |
| \(T^{orig}_t\) | Original RSU assigned to trip \(t\) (used for similarity term). | – |
| \(start_t, end_t\) | Scheduled start / end time of trip \(t\) (fixed). | – |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if RSU \(r\) is assigned to trip \(t\). |
| \(y_k \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) is performed. |
| \(z_{p,\ell} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if passenger event \(p\) is delayed by level \(\ell\). (Only one level can be chosen.) |
| \(s_{p} \in \mathbb{R}_+\) | continuous | Actual start time of passenger event \(p\) after possible delay. |
| \(e_{p} \in \mathbb{R}_+\) | continuous | Actual end time of passenger event \(p\) after possible delay. |
| \(u_{k} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) **conflicts** with at least one passenger event on the same track (used for Benders cut generation). |
| \(w_{k,p} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if shunting movement \(k\) and passenger event \(p\) overlap on the same track (auxiliary). |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

We combine three goals:

1. **Operational cost** – assignment + shunting + delay penalties.  
2. **Similarity to the original plan** – minimise the number of trips that receive a different RSU.  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \beta\Bigg[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{r\in R} c^{trip}_{t,r}\,x_{t,r}}_{\text{trip‑assignment cost}}
          + \underbrace{\sum_{k\in K} c^{sh}_{k}\,y_{k}}_{\text{shunting cost}}
          + \underbrace{\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{\ell\in L} c^{delay}_\ell \,z_{p,\ell}}_{\text{delay penalty}} \Bigg] \\
        & + \alpha\Bigg[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\Bigl(1-\sum_{r\in R} \mathbf{1}_{\{r=T^{orig}_t\}}\,x_{t,r}\Bigr)}_{\text{deviation from original RSU}} \Bigg]
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\mathbf{1}_{\{condition\}}\) is 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.  
If \(\alpha=0\) we only minimise costs; if \(\alpha=1\) we only maximise similarity.

---

### 4.2 Assignment constraints  

*Each trip receives exactly one RSU*  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{A1}
\]

*RSU flow balance (circulation)* – a RSU that finishes a trip must either start the next assigned trip or be used for a shunting movement. Let  

\[
\text{next}(t) = \{t' \in T \mid \text{the scheduled arrival of }t \text{ is before the departure of }t' \text{ and } r\text{ can be reused}\}
\]

For each RSU \(r\):

\[
\sum_{t\in T} x_{t,r} = \sum_{t\in T} x_{t,r} \quad\text{(trivial)} 
\]

In practice we enforce a **circulation** using a time‑expanded network; a compact way is:

\[
\sum_{t\in T: \; end_t \le H} x_{t,r} \;-\; \sum_{t\in T: \; start_t \ge 0} x_{t,r} = 0 \qquad \forall r\in R
\tag{A2}
\]

where \(H\) is the planning horizon (e.g. 24 h). This ensures that the number of departures equals the number of arrivals for each RSU.

---

### 4.3 Shunting‑movement feasibility  

A shunting movement \(k=(r,s,m,\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k)\) can be performed **only** if the RSU \(r\) is available (i.e., not assigned to a passenger trip at that time) **and** the track \(m\) at station \(s\) is free.

*Link to RSU assignment*  

\[
y_k \le \sum_{t\in T: \; r\text{ is used on }t \text{ and } [\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k]\cap [start_t,end_t]\neq\emptyset } x_{t,r} \;+\; (1 - \text{bigM}) 
\tag{S1}
\]

A more readable formulation uses an auxiliary binary \(a_{k}\) that equals 1 if RSU \(r\) is **busy** during the shunting window:

\[
a_{k} \ge x_{t,r} \quad \forall t\in T \text{ with } [\tau^{start}_k,\tau^{end}_k]\cap [start_t,end_t]\neq\emptyset
\]
\[
y_k \le 1 - a_{k}
\tag{S1‑alt}
\]

*Track‑occupancy conflicts*  

For each passenger event \(p\) that uses the same track \((s,m)\) we introduce binary overlap variable \(w_{k,p}\):

\[
w_{k,p} \ge y_k + z_{p,\ell} - 1 \qquad \forall \ell\in L,\; p\in P \text{ with } (s,m) \text{ equal}
\tag{S2}
\]

If both shunting \(k\) and passenger event \(p\) are scheduled (possibly delayed) then \(w_{k,p}=1\).

The actual time windows after delay are:

\[
s_p = start_p + \sum_{\ell\in L}\ell\;z_{p,\ell}, \qquad
e_p = end_p + \sum_{\ell\in L}\ell\;z_{p,\ell}
\tag{S3}
\]

The overlap condition (big‑M formulation) :

\[
w_{k,p} \le 
\frac{(\tau^{end}_k - s_p)}{M}
+ \frac{(e_p - \tau^{start}_k)}{M}
\tag{S4}
\]

If the intervals do **not** overlap, the RHS ≤ 0, forcing \(w_{k,p}=0\).

Finally, a shunting movement is **allowed** only if it does not overlap any passenger event on the same track:

\[
y_k \le 1 - \sum_{p\in P:(s,m)} w_{k,p} \qquad \forall k\in K
\tag{S5}
\]

---

### 4.4 Delay limits  

Only one delay level per passenger event:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{p,\ell} \le 1 \qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{D1}
\]

Maximum admissible delay:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} \ell \, z_{p,\ell} \le \Delta^{max} \qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{D2}
\]

---

### 4.5 Benders‑type feasibility indicator (optional)  

If the model is used inside a Benders decomposition, we keep the auxiliary binary \(u_k\) that becomes 1 when a conflict is detected; the master problem then adds a cut  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} u_k \le |K|-1
\tag{B1}
\]

In the monolithic MILP we simply set \(u_k = y_k\) and enforce (S5); the cut is not needed.

---

### 4.6 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R\\
&y_k \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K\\
&z_{p,\ell} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall p\in P,\; \ell\in L\\
&s_p, e_p \in \mathbb{R}_+ &&\forall p\in P\\
&w_{k,p} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K,\; p\in P\\
&a_k \in \{0,1\} &&\forall k\in K
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Remarks & Modeling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption (explicitly stated) | Reason / comment |
|---|-------------------------------|------------------|
| 1 | **Discrete delay levels** – we allow only a few integer minute delays (0‑3 min). This matches the “short delay” policy described in the paper. |
| 2 | **Big‑M value** – \(M\) is chosen larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 10 000 min) to safely linearise the overlap conditions. |
| 3 | **Shunting tracks are pre‑identified** – the set \(M_s\) is known for each station (Utrecht C, Rotterdam C). No capacity limit per track other than “one movement at a time”. |
| 4 | **RSU compatibility** – the cost \(c^{trip}_{t,r}\) is set to a very large value (or \(x_{t,r}=0\) forced) when the RSU cannot physically serve the trip (different class, length, power). |
| 5 | **Circulation balance** – the simplified equation (A2) assumes the planning horizon is long enough that each RSU that departs also returns; more detailed time‑expanded network can be used if needed. |
| 6 | **Objective weighting** – the user can tune \(\alpha\) (similarity) vs. \(\beta\) (cost) to reflect the “stick‑to‑the‑plan” vs. “operational cost” trade‑off discussed in the paper. |
| 7 | **Exact vs. heuristic** – the model can be solved directly (heuristic) or embedded in a Benders loop where the infrastructure model returns cuts (exact). The formulation above contains the necessary binaries to generate such cuts. |
| 8 | **No driver‑availability constraints** – the paper mentions shunting drivers; they are omitted here for brevity but can be added analogously (binary driver‑assignment variables with shift‑length limits). |
| 9 | **No explicit passenger‑capacity penalties** – the model focuses on feasibility and cost; passenger‑satisfaction (standing, waiting) could be added as extra terms using load variables, but is left out to keep the MILP concise. |

---

|------------|-----------|--------------|-----------------|
| 1 | A, B | A | 60–120 |
| 2 | A, B | B | 130–190 |
| 3 | A, B | A | 200–260 |

| Shunting movements \(K\) (only at Utrecht) | RSU | Track | Window (min) |
|--------------------------------------------|-----|-------|--------------|
| k1 | A | m1 | 125–130 |
| k2 | B | m1 | 115–120 |

| Passenger events \(P\) on track m1 (Utrecht) | Original interval (min) |
|--------------------------------------------|------------------------|

| p2 | 128–132 |

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below simultaneously decides (i) a conflict‑free timetable (arrival / departure times, train order and possible rerouting) and (ii) feasible speed profiles for every train on every track segment.  The formulation is linearised (mixed‑integer) by discretising time and speed, and by using big‑M techniques for logical conditions.  All symbols are defined in the *Sets & Indices* and *Parameters* sections; missing data are marked as **Assumption** and can be calibrated with real‑world values.

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Assumptions  

| Symbol | Meaning | Assumption / Comment |
|--------|----------|----------------------|
| **T** | Set of trains,  *t = 1,…,|T|* | – |
| **S** | Set of stations (including origin 0 and destination |S|+1) | – |
| **L** | Set of directed track‑segments (links)  *l = (i→j), i,j ∈ S* | – |
| **B ⊆ L** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (partial blockage) | – |
| **K** | Set of discrete speed levels (k = 1,…,K) | Speed levels are equally spaced between 0 and the maximum admissible speed *vmax* (Assumption). |
| **Δ** | Length of the time‑discretisation interval (minutes) | Typical value 1 min (Assumption). |
| **τ = {0,Δ,2Δ,…,H}** | Discrete time horizon (0 … planning horizon *H*) | H = 24 h (Assumption). |
| **P** | Set of *plan* indices for a train (see §4.3) | Each plan corresponds to a feasible combination of (route, departure‑time, speed‑profile). |
| **R ⊆ L × L** | Set of *conflict pairs* – two opposite‑direction segments that share the same physical track (bidirectional usage) | – |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|-----------------------|
| **τ⁰_t** | Original scheduled departure time of train *t* from its origin station | From the pre‑disruption timetable. |
| **τᵈ_t** | Original scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its destination | – |
| **c_t** | Energy consumption coefficient for train *t* (kWh per km·(speed level)²) | Calibrated from train characteristics (Assumption). |
| **d_l** | Length of segment *l* (km) | – |
| **v_k** | Speed corresponding to level *k* (km/h) | v₁ = 0, v_K = vmax (Assumption). |
| **α_l**, **β_l** | Minimum and maximum admissible travel time on segment *l* (Δ‑units) | α_l = ⌈d_l / v_K⌉, β_l = ⌈d_l / v_1⌉ (Assumption). |
| **M** | Large constant for Big‑M linearisation (≥ H/Δ) | – |
| **γ₁, γ₂** | Weight of timetable deviation and energy consumption in the objective | γ₁ = 1, γ₂ = 0.01 (Assumption – can be tuned). |
| **Δᵇ_l, Δᵉ_l** | Beginning and ending time of the blockage on segment *l* (Δ‑units) | 0 if *l∉B*. |
| **σ_t** | Binary flag =1 if train *t* is cancelled (service interruption) | – |
| **ρ_t** | Binary flag =1 if train *t* uses the *opposite* track (rerouting) on a blocked segment | – |
| **δ_{tt'}** | Minimum headway (Δ‑units) required between any two trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical track | Typically 2 Δ (Assumption). |
| **θ_{tt'}** | Minimum headway (Δ‑units) for opposite‑direction trains sharing a bidirectional track (conflict pair) | Typically 4 Δ (Assumption). |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **x_{t,l,k,τ} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment *l* at speed level *k* during time interval *τ*. |
| **a_{t,i} ≥ 0** | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at station *i* (Δ‑units). |
| **d_{t,i} ≥ 0** | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from station *i* (Δ‑units). |
| **z_{t,p} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | 1 if plan *p* (specific route, departure time and speed‑profile) is selected for train *t*. |
| **σ_t ∈ {0,1}** | binary | Cancellation flag (σ_t=1 → train *t* is removed from service). |
| **ρ_t ∈ {0,1}** | binary | Rerouting flag (ρ_t=1 → train *t* uses opposite track on blocked segments). |

\]
\[

\[

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. \[

\]

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[

\min\;&\sum_{t\in T} c_t \,\delta_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &\text{(1)–(13)} \\
&\delta_t \ge 0 \qquad\forall t\in T\\

Thus the presented MILP is a **complete, linear, mixed‑integer model** for conflict detection and resolution in a railway network equipped with distance‑to‑go signalling, ready to be embedded in a real‑time traffic‑management decision‑support system.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
