Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the problem described in the request.  
All symbols, sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and every constraint are written explicitly, together with a short narrative that explains the role of each element.  
The model is *linear* (no products of two decision variables); wherever a non‑linear expression would appear in a “real‑world” formulation (e.g. travel‑time = distance / speed) we use the usual linearisation by *pre‑defining* a finite set of admissible speed levels and associating a travel‑time (or equivalently a “time‑cost”) with each level. This is the standard way to keep the problem within the MILP class.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of line **segments** (track pieces) between two consecutive stations or control points, indexed by \(s\). |
| \(K=\{1,\dots,K_{\max }\}\) | Discrete **time‑interval indices** (e.g. each interval = 1 min). |
| \(L=\{1,\dots,L_{\max }\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (constant speed over a segment interval). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of feasible **paths** (routes) for train \(t\); each path \(p\) is an ordered list of segments \((s^p_1,\dots ,s^p_{|p|})\). |
| \(\mathcal{B}_s\subseteq K\) | Set of time intervals in which segment \(s\) is **blocked** on the *original* (right‑hand) track (e.g. due to an incident). |
| \(\mathcal{O}_s\) | Set of time intervals in which segment \(s\) is **blocked on the opposite (left‑hand) track** (if known). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / comment |
|---|---|---|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(v^{\ell}\) | Physical speed (km/h) of level \(\ell\). |
| \(\tau^{\ell}_s = \dfrac{L_s}{v^{\ell}}\) | **Deterministic travel time** (in minutes) needed to cross segment \(s\) at speed level \(\ell\). |
| \(e^{\ell}_s\) | **Energy consumption** (kWh) per km when traveling segment \(s\) with speed level \(\ell\). Often \(e^{\ell}_s = \alpha^{\ell} L_s\). |
| \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (in interval index). |
| \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s}\) | Scheduled *arrival* time of train \(t\) at the **up‑stream node** of segment \(s\). |
| \(\underline{D}_t\) | Minimum **dwell time** (minutes) that train \(t\) must spend at any station. |
| \(M\) | A large constant (“big‑M”) used for logical linking (e.g. \(M = K_{\max}\)). |
| \(\lambda_{\text{delay}}\), \(\lambda_{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weights in the objective (trade‑off between delay and energy). |
| \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\) | Binary coefficient = 1 if a speed change from level \(\ell\) to \(\ell'\) respects acceleration/deceleration limits, 0 otherwise (pre‑computed). |
| \(R_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | Indicator: 1 if segment \(s\) belongs to **original** (right‑hand) track for train \(t\), 0 if it is the **opposite** track. This data is known a‑priori. |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| \(x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) chooses path (routing) \(p\). Exactly one path per train. |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) **occupies** segment \(s\) during time interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(\ell\). One level per occupied segment. |
| \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) | continuous | **Arrival time** (in minutes) of train \(t\) at the upstream node of segment \(s\). |
| \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) | continuous | **Departure time** from the downstream node of segment \(s\). (For a station segment the same variable can be used.) |
| \(\delta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\) | continuous | **Total delay** of train \(t\) (difference between actual final arrival and scheduled). |
| \(w_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary (auxiliary) | Used to enforce “no‑overlap” (see constraint 5). |

*All times are measured in the same **time‑unit** as the discretisation (e.g. minutes).*

---

## 4. Model Explanation  

### 4.1 Routing (binary path)  
Each train selects **exactly one** feasible route (list of segments). If the original track of a segment is blocked, the path must contain the opposite‑track copy of that segment. This is captured by linking the path‑selection variable with the occupancy variables.

### 4.2 Speed‑profile linking  
When a train occupies a segment it must also choose a **single admissible speed level** for that segment. The travel time contributed by that segment equals the pre‑computed \(\tau^{\ell}_s\). Energy consumption is similarly known.

### 4.3 Blockage handling  
If a segment is blocked on the original track during a time interval, a train may still use the **opposite** track provided that the opposite track is not also blocked. The binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the train would be on the original track; switching to the opposite track is forced when the original is blocked.

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance (single‑track occupancy)  
The **no‑collision** requirement says that, at any time interval \(k\), at most one train may occupy the same physical piece of track (regardless of direction). This is expressed with a “sum‑≤ 1” constraint for every segment–time pair.

### 4.5 Temporal feasibility & dwell‑time  
The arrival/departure times of successive segments must respect the chosen travel times and a minimum dwell time at stations. 

### 4.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits  
A train may only change speed level from \(\ell\) on segment \(s\) to \(\ell'\) on the next segment if the pair \((\ell,\ell')\) respects the physical acceleration limits; the binary coefficient \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\) guarantees that forbidden changes are excluded.

### 4.7 Objective  
We minimise a **weighted sum** of the total passenger/operational delay and the total energy used by all trains.  

\[
\min\;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e^{\ell}_s\,z_{t,s,\ell}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP Formulation  

### 5.1 Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e^{\ell}_s\,z_{t,s,\ell}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

---

### 5.2 Routing constraints  

1. **Exactly one path per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Occupancy induced by the chosen path**  
If train \(t\) uses path \(p\), it must occupy every segment of that path, otherwise it cannot occupy it.

\[
y_{t,s,k}\ \le\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\; x_{t,p}\qquad
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{R2}
\]

(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}=1\) when segment \(s\) belongs to path \(p\), 0 otherwise.)

---

### 5.3 Speed‑level selection  

3. **One speed level per occupied segment**  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{t,s,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If a segment is not occupied (\(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=0\)) then all \(z_{t,s,\ell}=0\).

4. **Travel‑time linking**  

The departure time from the downstream node of segment \(s\) equals the arrival time at the upstream node **plus** the travel time contributed by the chosen speed level.

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}
=
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{\ell\in L} \tau^{\ell}_s \, z_{t,s,\ell}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S2}
\]

Because \(z\) is binary and exactly one level is selected, the right‑hand side reduces to the appropriate \(\tau^{\ell}_s\).

---

### 5.4 Temporal feasibility & sequencing  

5. **Continuity along a path** – for each train the arrival at the next segment must be the departure of the previous one (plus possible dwell time if the node is a station). Let \(s'\) be the *successor* of segment \(s\) on the chosen path of train \(t\); denote by \(\text{succ}_t(s)\) that segment (or “null” if \(s\) is the last one).  

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,\text{succ}_t(s)}
\;\ge\;
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a successor}
\tag{T1}
\]

6. **Minimum dwell time at stations**  

If segment \(s\) is a station (or a scheduled stop), we enforce  

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \;-\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\;\ge\; \underline{D}_t \; \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S_{\text{station}}
\tag{T2}
\]

If the segment is not a station, the RHS is zero.

7. **Initial departure**  

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_t}\;=\; d^{\text{sched}}_{t}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{T3}
\]

where \(s^{\text{orig}}_t\) is the first segment of the selected path (the origin node).

---

### 5.5 Blockage handling  

8. **Original‑track blockage forces opposite‑track use**  

If a time interval \(k\) belongs to the blockage set \(\mathcal{B}_s\) for segment \(s\), a train may occupy **only** the opposite track version of that segment. The binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the copy used under the current path is the original (value = 1) or opposite (value = 0). The constraint is:

\[
y_{t,s,k}\; \le\; 1 - R_{t,s} + \underbrace{(1 - \mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})}_{\text{0 if blocked}}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{B1}
\]

A cleaner linear form uses a big‑M:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le M\,(1-R_{t,s}) + M\,(1-\mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})
\]

If \(R_{t,s}=1\) (original track) **and** \(k\in\mathcal B_s\) then the RHS = 0, forcing \(y_{t,s,k}=0\).  

If the opposite track is also blocked (set \(\mathcal{O}_s\)), an analogous constraint is added with the opposite‑track indicator.

9. **No‑collision (single‑track occupancy)**  

For every physical segment \(s\) and every time interval \(k\),

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,k} \;\le\; 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{C1}
\]

If the line is double‑track and the two directions can be used simultaneously, the constraint can be relaxed accordingly (e.g. one per direction).

---

### 5.6 Acceleration limits  

10. **Speed‑change feasibility**  

Let \(s\) and its successor \(\text{succ}_t(s)\) be traversed by train \(t\). The pair of selected levels must satisfy the pre‑computed coefficient \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\). Using a big‑M formulation:

\[
z_{t,s,\ell} + z_{t,\text{succ}_t(s),\ell'} \le 1 + c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'} \qquad
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; \ell,\ell'\in L
\tag{A1}
\]

If the transition is not allowed (\(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}=0\)), the inequality forces at most one of the two variables to be 1, i.e. the forbidden combination cannot occur.

---

### 5.7 Delay definition  

11. **Delay of each train**  

Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment (or destination node) of the chosen path. The final arrival time of train \(t\) is \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The scheduled arrival time is \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The delay variable captures the positive difference:

\[
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t},
\qquad
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; 0
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

If early arrival is allowed, the objective will simply ignore negative values because \(\delta_t\) is forced non‑negative.

---

### 5.8 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,p\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
&z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,\ell\\[2pt]
&\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s},\;\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_t\ge 0 &&\forall t
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 6. Discussion of the Model  

| Component | What it does | Why it is linear |
|---|---|---|
| **Path‑selection variables \(x_{t,p}\)** | Choose a single feasible route (including the option to use the opposite track). | Binary, summed to 1 (constraint R1). |
| **Occupancy variables \(y_{t,s,k}\)** | Indicate whether a train occupies a concrete segment during a concrete time interval. | Binary, linked to path via (R2). |
| **Speed‑level variables \(z_{t,s,\ell}\)** | Choose one speed level per occupied segment; travel‑time and energy become linear expressions because the speed‑level set is enumerated. | Binary, exactly‑one via (S1). |
| **Time variables \(\tau^{\text{arr}} , \tau^{\text{dep}}\)** | Capture continuous timing; travel‑time added linearly because \(\tau^{\ell}_s\) are constants. | Linear equations (S2, T1‑T3). |
| **Blockage constraints (B1)** | Use big‑M (“if‑then”) logic to forbid occupancy of blocked original track; opposite‑track possibility handled through the binary matrix \(R\). | Only linear inequalities with binary coefficients. |
| **Conflict constraints (C1)** | Guarantees safety (no two trains in same physical piece at the same time). | Simple linear ≤ 1. |
| **Acceleration constraints (A1)** | Pre‑compute allowed speed‑level transitions; exclude forbidden ones by a linear inequality. | Binary variables with big‑M style logic. |
| **Delay definition (D1)** | Introduces a non‑negative variable that measures lateness; linear because the difference of a continuous variable and a constant is linear. | Linear inequality. |
| **Objective** | Weighted linear sum of delay variables and energy terms (energy per segment × binary speed‑level). | Both terms are linear in the decision variables. |

The whole formulation is **mixed‑integer linear**: all non‑linearities in a physical system (division by speed, product of binary with continuous) have been eliminated by *enumeration* (discrete speed levels) and by the usual “big‑M” linearisation technique.  

A commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) can handle instances of realistic size (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a moderate number of time intervals) after appropriate data preprocessing (generation of feasible paths \(\mathcal{P}_t\), pre‑computation of admissible speed transitions, etc.). The model can be extended with extra terms (e.g., passenger‑crowding penalties, crew‑working‑time limits) by adding further linear constraints and objective coefficients without changing its MILP nature.

### 4.1 Routing (binary path)  
Each train selects **exactly one** feasible route (list of segments). If the original track of a segment is blocked, the path must contain the opposite‑track copy of that segment. This is captured by linking the path‑selection variable with the occupancy variables.

### 4.2 Speed‑profile linking  
When a train occupies a segment it must also choose a **single admissible speed level** for that segment. The travel time contributed by that segment equals the pre‑computed \(\tau^{\ell}_s\). Energy consumption is similarly known.

### 4.3 Blockage handling  
If a segment is blocked on the original track during a time interval, a train may still use the **opposite** track provided that the opposite track is not also blocked. The binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the train would be on the original track; switching to the opposite track is forced when the original is blocked.

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance (single‑track occupancy)  
The **no‑collision** requirement says that, at any time interval \(k\), at most one train may occupy the same physical piece of track (regardless of direction). This is expressed with a “sum‑≤ 1” constraint for every segment–time pair.

### 4.5 Temporal feasibility & dwell‑time  
The arrival/departure times of successive segments must respect the chosen travel times and a minimum dwell time at stations. 

### 4.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits  
A train may only change speed level from \(\ell\) on segment \(s\) to \(\ell'\) on the next segment if the pair \((\ell,\ell')\) respects the physical acceleration limits; the binary coefficient \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\) guarantees that forbidden changes are excluded.

### 4.7 Objective  
We minimise a **weighted sum** of the total passenger/operational delay and the total energy used by all trains.  

\[
\min\;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e^{\ell}_s\,z_{t,s,\ell}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP Formulation  

### 5.1 Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_{t}
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e^{\ell}_s\,z_{t,s,\ell}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

---

### 5.2 Routing constraints  

1. **Exactly one path per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Occupancy induced by the chosen path**  
If train \(t\) uses path \(p\), it must occupy every segment of that path, otherwise it cannot occupy it.

\[
y_{t,s,k}\ \le\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}\; \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\; x_{t,p}\qquad
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{R2}
\]

(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}=1\) when segment \(s\) belongs to path \(p\), 0 otherwise.)

---

### 5.3 Speed‑level selection  

3. **One speed level per occupied segment**  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{t,s,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S1}
\]

If a segment is not occupied (\(\sum_k y_{t,s,k}=0\)) then all \(z_{t,s,\ell}=0\).

4. **Travel‑time linking**  

The departure time from the downstream node of segment \(s\) equals the arrival time at the upstream node **plus** the travel time contributed by the chosen speed level.

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}
=
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{\ell\in L} \tau^{\ell}_s \, z_{t,s,\ell}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{S2}
\]

Because \(z\) is binary and exactly one level is selected, the right‑hand side reduces to the appropriate \(\tau^{\ell}_s\).

---

### 5.4 Temporal feasibility & sequencing  

5. **Continuity along a path** – for each train the arrival at the next segment must be the departure of the previous one (plus possible dwell time if the node is a station). Let \(s'\) be the *successor* of segment \(s\) on the chosen path of train \(t\); denote by \(\text{succ}_t(s)\) that segment (or “null” if \(s\) is the last one).  

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,\text{succ}_t(s)}
\;\ge\;
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a successor}
\tag{T1}
\]

6. **Minimum dwell time at stations**  

If segment \(s\) is a station (or a scheduled stop), we enforce  

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s} \;-\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\;\ge\; \underline{D}_t \; \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S_{\text{station}}
\tag{T2}
\]

If the segment is not a station, the RHS is zero.

7. **Initial departure**  

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_t}\;=\; d^{\text{sched}}_{t}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{T3}
\]

where \(s^{\text{orig}}_t\) is the first segment of the selected path (the origin node).

---

### 5.5 Blockage handling  

8. **Original‑track blockage forces opposite‑track use**  

If a time interval \(k\) belongs to the blockage set \(\mathcal{B}_s\) for segment \(s\), a train may occupy **only** the opposite track version of that segment. The binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the copy used under the current path is the original (value = 1) or opposite (value = 0). The constraint is:

\[
y_{t,s,k}\; \le\; 1 - R_{t,s} + \underbrace{(1 - \mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})}_{\text{0 if blocked}}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{B1}
\]

A cleaner linear form uses a big‑M:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le M\,(1-R_{t,s}) + M\,(1-\mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})
\]

If \(R_{t,s}=1\) (original track) **and** \(k\in\mathcal B_s\) then the RHS = 0, forcing \(y_{t,s,k}=0\).  

If the opposite track is also blocked (set \(\mathcal{O}_s\)), an analogous constraint is added with the opposite‑track indicator.

9. **No‑collision (single‑track occupancy)**  

For every physical segment \(s\) and every time interval \(k\),

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,k} \;\le\; 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{C1}
\]

If the line is double‑track and the two directions can be used simultaneously, the constraint can be relaxed accordingly (e.g. one per direction).

---

### 5.6 Acceleration limits  

10. **Speed‑change feasibility**  

Let \(s\) and its successor \(\text{succ}_t(s)\) be traversed by train \(t\). The pair of selected levels must satisfy the pre‑computed coefficient \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\). Using a big‑M formulation:

\[
z_{t,s,\ell} + z_{t,\text{succ}_t(s),\ell'} \le 1 + c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'} \qquad
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; \ell,\ell'\in L
\tag{A1}
\]

If the transition is not allowed (\(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}=0\)), the inequality forces at most one of the two variables to be 1, i.e. the forbidden combination cannot occur.

---

### 5.7 Delay definition  

11. **Delay of each train**  

Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment (or destination node) of the chosen path. The final arrival time of train \(t\) is \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The scheduled arrival time is \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The delay variable captures the positive difference:

\[
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t},
\qquad
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; 0
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

If early arrival is allowed, the objective will simply ignore negative values because \(\delta_t\) is forced non‑negative.

---

### 5.8 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,p\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
&z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,\ell\\[2pt]
&\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s},\;\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_t\ge 0 &&\forall t
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 6. Discussion of the Model  

| Component | What it does | Why it is linear |
|---|---|---|
| **Path‑selection variables \(x_{t,p}\)** | Choose a single feasible route (including the option to use the opposite track). | Binary, summed to 1 (constraint R1). |
| **Occupancy variables \(y_{t,s,k}\)** | Indicate whether a train occupies a concrete segment during a concrete time interval. | Binary, linked to path via (R2). |
| **Speed‑level variables \(z_{t,s,\ell}\)** | Choose one speed level per occupied segment; travel‑time and energy become linear expressions because the speed‑level set is enumerated. | Binary, exactly‑one via (S1). |
| **Time variables \(\tau^{\text{arr}} , \tau^{\text{dep}}\)** | Capture continuous timing; travel‑time added linearly because \(\tau^{\ell}_s\) are constants. | Linear equations (S2, T1‑T3). |
| **Blockage constraints (B1)** | Use big‑M (“if‑then”) logic to forbid occupancy of blocked original track; opposite‑track possibility handled through the binary matrix \(R\). | Only linear inequalities with binary coefficients. |
| **Conflict constraints (C1)** | Guarantees safety (no two trains in same physical piece at the same time). | Simple linear ≤ 1. |
| **Acceleration constraints (A1)** | Pre‑compute allowed speed‑level transitions; exclude forbidden ones by a linear inequality. | Binary variables with big‑M style logic. |
| **Delay definition (D1)** | Introduces a non‑negative variable that measures lateness; linear because the difference of a continuous variable and a constant is linear. | Linear inequality. |
| **Objective** | Weighted linear sum of delay variables and energy terms (energy per segment × binary speed‑level). | Both terms are linear in the decision variables. |

The whole formulation is **mixed‑integer linear**: all non‑linearities in a physical system (division by speed, product of binary with continuous) have been eliminated by *enumeration* (discrete speed levels) and by the usual “big‑M” linearisation technique.  

A commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) can handle instances of realistic size (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a moderate number of time intervals) after appropriate data preprocessing (generation of feasible paths \(\mathcal{P}_t\), pre‑computation of admissible speed transitions, etc.). The model can be extended with extra terms (e.g., passenger‑crowding penalties, crew‑working‑time limits) by adding further linear constraints and objective coefficients without changing its MILP nature.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

The binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the copy used under the current path is the original (value = 1) or opposite (value = 0). The constraint is:

\[
y_{t,s,k}\; \le\; 1 - R_{t,s} + \underbrace{(1 - \mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})}_{\text{0 if blocked}}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{B1}
\]

A cleaner linear form uses a big‑M:

\[
y_{t,s,k} \le M\,(1-R_{t,s}) + M\,(1-\mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal B_s\}})
\]

If \(R_{t,s}=1\) (original track) **and** \(k\in\mathcal B_s\) then the RHS = 0, forcing \(y_{t,s,k}=0\).  

If the opposite track is also blocked (set \(\mathcal{O}_s\)), an analogous constraint is added with the opposite‑track indicator.

9. **No‑collision (single‑track occupancy)**  

For every physical segment \(s\) and every time interval \(k\),

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,k} \;\le\; 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; k\in K
\tag{C1}
\]

If the line is double‑track and the two directions can be used simultaneously, the constraint can be relaxed accordingly (e.g. one per direction).

---

### 5.6 Acceleration limits  

10. **Speed‑change feasibility**  

Let \(s\) and its successor \(\text{succ}_t(s)\) be traversed by train \(t\). The pair of selected levels must satisfy the pre‑computed coefficient \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\). Using a big‑M formulation:

\[
z_{t,s,\ell} + z_{t,\text{succ}_t(s),\ell'} \le 1 + c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'} \qquad
\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; \ell,\ell'\in L
\tag{A1}
\]

If the transition is not allowed (\(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}=0\)), the inequality forces at most one of the two variables to be 1, i.e. the forbidden combination cannot occur.

---

### 5.7 Delay definition  

11. **Delay of each train**  

Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment (or destination node) of the chosen path. The final arrival time of train \(t\) is \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The scheduled arrival time is \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}\). The delay variable captures the positive difference:

\[
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{sched}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t},
\qquad
\delta_{t} \;\ge\; 0
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

If early arrival is allowed, the objective will simply ignore negative values because \(\delta_t\) is forced non‑negative.

---

### 5.8 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,p\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
&z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,\ell\\[2pt]
&\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s},\;\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_t\ge 0 &&\forall t
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

## 6. Discussion of the Model  

| Component | What it does | Why it is linear |
|---|---|---|
| **Path‑selection variables \(x_{t,p}\)** | Choose a single feasible route (including the option to use the opposite track). | Binary, summed to 1 (constraint R1). |
| **Occupancy variables \(y_{t,s,k}\)** | Indicate whether a train occupies a concrete segment during a concrete time interval. | Binary, linked to path via (R2). |
| **Speed‑level variables \(z_{t,s,\ell}\)** | Choose one speed level per occupied segment; travel‑time and energy become linear expressions because the speed‑level set is enumerated. | Binary, exactly‑one via (S1). |
| **Time variables \(\tau^{\text{arr}} , \tau^{\text{dep}}\)** | Capture continuous timing; travel‑time added linearly because \(\tau^{\ell}_s\) are constants. | Linear equations (S2, T1‑T3). |
| **Blockage constraints (B1)** | Use big‑M (“if‑then”) logic to forbid occupancy of blocked original track; opposite‑track possibility handled through the binary matrix \(R\). | Only linear inequalities with binary coefficients. |
| **Conflict constraints (C1)** | Guarantees safety (no two trains in same physical piece at the same time). | Simple linear ≤ 1. |
| **Acceleration constraints (A1)** | Pre‑compute allowed speed‑level transitions; exclude forbidden ones by a linear inequality. | Binary variables with big‑M style logic. |
| **Delay definition (D1)** | Introduces a non‑negative variable that measures lateness; linear because the difference of a continuous variable and a constant is linear. | Linear inequality. |
| **Objective** | Weighted linear sum of delay variables and energy terms (energy per segment × binary speed‑level). | Both terms are linear in the decision variables. |

The whole formulation is **mixed‑integer linear**: all non‑linearities in a physical system (division by speed, product of binary with continuous) have been eliminated by *enumeration* (discrete speed levels) and by the usual “big‑M” linearisation technique.  

A commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) can handle instances of realistic size (tens of trains, a few hundred segments, a moderate number of time intervals) after appropriate data preprocessing (generation of feasible paths \(\mathcal{P}_t\), pre‑computation of admissible speed transitions, etc.). The model can be extended with extra terms (e.g., passenger‑crowding penalties, crew‑working‑time limits) by adding further linear constraints and objective coefficients without changing its MILP nature.

response.content:
**MILP for Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management under Partial Segment Blockage**  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of line **segments** (track pieces) between two consecutive stations/control points, indexed by \(s\). |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,K_{\max }\}\) | Discrete **time‑interval indices** (e.g. 1 min each). |
| \(L=\{1,\dots ,L_{\max }\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (constant speed over a segment). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_t\) | Set of feasible **paths** (routes) for train \(t\); each path \(p\) is an ordered list of segments \((s^p_1,\dots ,s^p_{|p|})\). |
| \(\mathcal{B}_s\subseteq K\) | Time intervals in which segment \(s\) is **blocked on the original (right‑hand) track**. |
| \(\mathcal{O}_s\subseteq K\) | Time intervals in which segment \(s\) is **blocked on the opposite (left‑hand) track** (if known). |
| \(S_{\text{station}}\subseteq S\) | Set of segments that correspond to stations (where dwell time is required). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / comment |
|---|---|---|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(v^{\ell}\) | Physical speed (km/h) of speed level \(\ell\). |
| \(\tau^{\ell}_s = \dfrac{L_s}{v^{\ell}}\) | Deterministic travel time (min) to traverse segment \(s\) at speed level \(\ell\). |
| \(e^{\ell}_s\) | Energy consumption (kWh) for segment \(s\) at speed level \(\ell\) (often proportional to \(L_s\)). |
| \(d^{\text{sched}}_{t}\) | Scheduled departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (in minutes). |
| \(a^{\text{sched}}_{t}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (in minutes). |
| \(\underline{D}_t\) | Minimum dwell time at any station for train \(t\) (min). |
| \(M\) | Large constant for “big‑M” linearisation (e.g. \(M=K_{\max}\)). |
| \(\lambda_{\text{delay}}, \lambda_{\text{energy}} >0\) | Weights for the bi‑objective (delay vs. energy). |
| \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if a speed change from \(\ell\) to \(\ell'\) respects acceleration/deceleration limits, 0 otherwise (pre‑computed). |
| \(R_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | 1 if, on the chosen path, train \(t\) uses the **original** track for segment \(s\); 0 if it uses the opposite track. |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| \(x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) chooses path \(p\) (exactly one). |
| \(y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) during interval \(k\). |
| \(z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | Train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(\ell\). |
| \(\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at upstream node of segment \(s\) (min). |
| \(\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from downstream node of segment \(s\) (min). |
| \(\delta_t\ge0\) | continuous | Total delay of train \(t\) (actual final arrival – scheduled). |

All times are expressed in the same unit as the discretisation (minutes).

---

### 4. Model  

#### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\lambda_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t
\;+\;
\lambda_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\ell\in L} e^{\ell}_s \, z_{t,s,\ell}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

The first term penalises passenger/operational delay, the second term penalises total energy consumption.

---

#### 4.2 Path‑selection  

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

\[
y_{t,s,k}\le \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_t}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}\,x_{t,p} 
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K \tag{R2}
\]

(\(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in p\}}=1\) if segment \(s\) belongs to path \(p\), otherwise 0.)

---

#### 4.3 Speed‑level selection  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} z_{t,s,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{S1}
\]

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}= \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}
        +\sum_{\ell\in L}\tau^{\ell}_s\,z_{t,s,\ell}
        \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{S2}
\]

---

#### 4.4 Temporal continuity  

For every pair \((s, s^{+})\) of successive segments on the chosen path of train \(t\) (denote \(s^{+}= \text{succ}_t(s)\)):

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{+}}\ge \tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \text{ with a successor} \tag{T1}
\]

If \(s\) is a station (\(s\in S_{\text{station}}\)):

\[
\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}-\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s}\ge \underline{D}_t\,
      \sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S_{\text{station}} \tag{T2}
\]

Initial departure:

\[
\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_t}= d^{\text{sched}}_{t}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{T3}
\]

where \(s^{\text{orig}}_t\) is the first segment of the selected path.

---

#### 4.5 Blockage handling  

Original‑track blockage forces use of opposite track:

\[
y_{t,s,k}\le M\,(1-R_{t,s}) + M\,(1-\mathbf{1}_{\{k\in\mathcal{B}_s\}})
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K \tag{B1}
\]

If the opposite track is also blocked (\(k\in\mathcal{O}_s\)) an analogous constraint is added with \((1-R_{t,s})\) replaced by \(R_{t,s}\).

---

#### 4.6 Conflict‑avoidance (single‑track occupancy)  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} y_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; k\in K \tag{C1}
\]

(If the line is double‑track with separate directions, the inequality can be relaxed per direction.)

---

#### 4.7 Acceleration limits  

\[
z_{t,s,\ell}+z_{t,s^{+},\ell'}\le 1+ c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; \ell,\ell'\in L \tag{A1}
\]

If a speed transition is infeasible (\(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}=0\)), the inequality forces at most one of the two binary variables to be 1, thus prohibiting the forbidden change.

---

#### 4.8 Delay definition  

Let \(s^{\text{dest}}_t\) be the last segment of the selected path of train \(t\).

\[
\delta_t \ge \tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t}- a^{\text{sched}}_{t},
\qquad
\delta_t \ge 0
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1}
\]

---

#### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,p\\
&y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
&z_{t,s,\ell}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,\ell\\
&\tau^{\text{arr}}_{t,s},\;\tau^{\text{dep}}_{t,s}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
&\delta_t\ge 0 &&\forall t
\end{aligned}
\tag{DOM}
\]

---

### 5. Remarks  

* **Linearisation of speed‑dependent travel time** – by enumerating a finite set of admissible speed levels \(\ell\), the travel time \(\tau^{\ell}_s\) becomes a known constant; the binary variable \(z_{t,s,\ell}\) selects the appropriate constant, keeping the model linear.  
* **Blockage logic** – the binary matrix \(R_{t,s}\) tells whether the train would travel on the original or opposite track for a given path. The big‑M constraint (B1) forces occupancy to be zero on a blocked original track, while allowing the opposite track if it is free.  
* **Conflict‑avoidance** – constraint (C1) guarantees a conflict‑free timetable: at most one train may occupy a physical segment in any time interval.  
* **Acceleration limits** – the pre‑computed matrix \(c^{\text{acc}}_{\ell,\ell'}\) encodes admissible speed‑level transitions; constraint (A1) removes forbidden changes without creating products of variables.  
* **Objective** – the weighted sum of total delay and total energy is linear; additional terms (e.g., passenger‑count penalties, crew‑working‑time limits) can be added similarly.  

The presented formulation is a **complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP) model** for the integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem under partial segment blockages. It can be solved directly with commercial MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
