messages.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP**  
(the model is written for a single‑day planning horizon; all indices and parameters are defined first, then the decision variables, the objective, and finally the complete set of linear constraints.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 𝒯      | Set of trains, indexed by **t** (|𝒯| = T). |
| ℕₜ     | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including the terminal).  Index by **n**, **m**. |
| ℒ      | Set of **links** (track segments) between consecutive stations, indexed by **ℓ**.  For a given train *t* the link that connects station *n* to the next station *m* is denoted ℓ(t,n). |
| **S** = {L,R} | Two possible **sides** (left / right) that a train can use when a segment is partially blocked. |
| **K**  | Set of admissible **speed levels** on a link, indexed by **k** (|K| = K). |
| 𝒫     | Set of ordered train‑pairs that share at least one common link (conflict pairs), i.e. 𝒫 ⊆ 𝒯×𝒯 .  An element is written *(i,j)*. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Definition | Units |
|--------|------------|-------|
|  schedₐₜ  | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train *t* at its final station. | min |
|  τ\_{ℓ,k} | Nominal travel time on link ℓ when speed level *k* is selected. | min |
|  e\_{ℓ,k} | Energy consumption (or a proxy) incurred on link ℓ at speed level *k*. | kWh (or a cost unit) |
|  dwell\_n | Minimum dwell (stopping) time at station *n* (may be train‑specific). | min |
|  gap\_{ℓ} | Minimum safety headway (time) required between two successive trains on the same **side** of link ℓ. | min |
|  T\_{blk}^{start}, T\_{blk}^{end} | Beginning and end of the disruption‑window on the blocked segment (the side that is **blocked** cannot be used). | min |
|  w\_delay , w\_energy | Positive weighting coefficients for the two components of the objective (normally chosen to balance monetary value of delay vs. energy). | – |
|  M   | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate conditional constraints (e.g. M = horizon length). | min |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r**\_{t,s} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the partially blocked segment. |
| **o**\_{i,j} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every shared link (i.e., the ordering on that link). |
| **a**\_{t,n} | continuous ≥0 | **Arrival** time of train *t* at station *n* (n∈ℕₜ). |
| **d**\_{t,n} | continuous ≥0 | **Departure** time of train *t* from station *n* (n∈ℕₜ, includes dwell). |
| **τ**\_{t,ℓ} | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on link ℓ. |
| **v**\_{t,ℓ,k} | binary | 1 ⇔ speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on link ℓ. |
| **x**\_{t,ℓ,s} | binary (optional auxiliary) | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ.  (Used to enforce capacity & blockage.) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;  \; w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}
\bigl( a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
e_{\ell,k}\;v_{t,\ell,k}
}
\]

*The first term is the total (weighted) passenger‑delay; the second term is the total (weighted) energy use across all trains and links.*

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Model Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route‑choice for the partially blocked segment  

Only one side can be taken, and the blocked side cannot be used during the disruption window.

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R1}
\]

If side *s\* is the **blocked** side (known a‑priori), then no train may occupy it while the blockage is active:

\[
r_{t,s^{\*}}=0 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}\; \text{with}\; a_{t,\text{entry}} \in [T_{blk}^{start},T_{blk}^{end}]
\tag{R2}
\]

(Practically this is enforced by linking **r** to the time variables; an equivalent linear formulation appears later in the capacity constraints.)

#### 5.2  Temporal flow on each train  

* Dwell at a station  

\[
d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+ \text{dwell}_{n}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; n\in\mathcal{N}_t
\tag{F1}
\]

* Travel on a link  

Let ℓ = ℓ(t,n) be the link that connects station *n* to the next station *m* = succ\_ℓ(n).  

\[
a_{t,m}= d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; n\in\mathcal{N}_t\setminus\{\text{last}\}
\tag{F2}
\]

#### 5.3  Linearised travel‑time – speed‑level relation  

For every train‑link pair the travel time is a convex combination of the discrete speed‑level travel times.

\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{\ell,k}\;v_{t,\ell,k}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{S1}
\]

Exactly one speed level is chosen:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,\ell,k}=1\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{S2}
\]

If required, additional linear bounds can be added (e.g. maximum acceleration), but the above already guarantees a piecewise‑constant speed decision.

#### 5.4  Ordering on shared tracks (conflict‑pair constraints)  

For each ordered pair *(i,j)∈𝒫* that share a link ℓ (or a set of links – the same ordering holds for all of them) we introduce a binary precedence variable **o**\_{i,j}.

* Exactly one of the two possible orders holds:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O1}
\]

* If *i* goes before *j*, a safe headway must be respected on **every** common link ℓ. Let  ℓ\_{c}(i,j) be a common link; the inequality is written for the **first** common link (any one works because the ordering is the same for the whole shared segment).

\[
a_{j,\text{enter } \ell_c}+M\,(1-o_{i,j})\;\ge\;
d_{i,\text{exit } \ell_c}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_c}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O2}
\]

Here `enter ℓ_c` and `exit ℓ_c` are the appropriate stations that delimit the link ℓ_c for each train (e.g. entry = arrival at the upstream station, exit = departure from the downstream station).  The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when *o*\_{i,j}=0.

#### 5.5  Capacity – at most one train on a side of a link at a time  

Introduce auxiliary binary **x**\_{t,ℓ,s} that indicates that train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ.  It is linked to the route‑choice variable:

\[
x_{t,\ell,s}= r_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; \ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\; s\in S
\tag{C0}
\]

(Only the blocked segment needs the side‑choice; for all other links we can set *s = L* and fix \(x_{t,\ell,L}=1\).)

Now enforce that at any point in time no two trains occupy the same side.  A common linear formulation uses **time‑indexed** variables; however, with the ordering variables we can keep it compact:

For every pair of distinct trains (p,q) that could be on the same side *s* of the same link ℓ:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1- y^{pq}_{\ell,s}) &\ge d_{p,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
a_{p,\text{enter } \ell}+M\,y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge d_{q,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{p,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{q,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge x_{p,\ell,s}+x_{q,\ell,s}-1
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall p<q,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\;s\in S
\tag{C1}
\]

Here \(y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\) is a binary that becomes 1 **only if** both trains use the same side; then the two big‑M constraints enforce a mutual exclusivity (one train must finish before the other starts plus the safety gap).  

If only one side of the segment is usable (the unblocked side), the constraints automatically reduce because the product \(x_{p,\ell,s}x_{q,\ell,s}=0\).

#### 5.6  Blockage‑window for the blocked side  

Even if a train selects the blocked side, it must **not** occupy it during the disruption interval.  Using the same auxiliary variable \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}\) for the blocked side \(s^\*\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*}) &\ge T_{blk}^{end}\\
d_{t,\text{exit } \ell} &\le T_{blk}^{start}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}}
\tag{B1}
\]

Thus, if a train decides to use the blocked side ( \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}=1\) ), both inequalities force the whole occupation interval to lie **outside** \([T_{blk}^{start},T_{blk}^{end}]\).

#### 5.7  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s} \in\{0,1\},\;\;  o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\;\; v_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
& x_{t,\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\;\; y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{D}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\!\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
      \;+\;
      w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\;\; \text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{Route‑choice for blocked segment}\\
            &\;\; \text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{Temporal flow (arrival‑departure–travel)}\\
            &\;\; \text{(S1)–(S2)} &&\text{Speed‑level → travel‑time linearisation}\\
            &\;\; \text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{Ordering of conflicting trains}\\
            &\;\; \text{(C0)–(C1)} &&\text{Capacity on each side of the blocked link}\\
            &\;\; \text{(B1)}      &&\text{Blocked side cannot be used inside the disruption window}\\
            &\;\; \text{(D)}       &&\text{Domain definitions}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Component | What it models | Why it is linear / MILP‑compatible |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| **Binary side‑choice** `r_{t,s}` | The decision of each train to bypass the partially blocked segment on the left or right side. Guarantees a *single* side (R1). |
| **Binary ordering** `o_{i,j}` | Mutual precedence on any shared track segment – essential for conflict‑free schedules.  The “one‑of‑two’’ constraint (O1) together with the big‑M safety constraint (O2) linearises the “if‑then’’ logic. |
| **Arrival / departure times** `a_{t,n}`, `d_{t,n}` | Continuous timestamps that allow us to compute delays and enforce dwell times, linking the schedule to the objective. |
| **Travel‑time variables** `τ_{t,ℓ}` | Continuous variables that become a convex combination of the discrete travel times of the admissible speed levels (S1–S2). |
| **Speed‑level binaries** `v_{t,ℓ,k}` | Enable the model to choose a discrete speed (or equivalently a discrete power/energy regime) on each link. The linear combination (S1) yields the travel time; the same binaries appear in the energy term of the objective. |
| **Capacity auxiliary binaries** `x_{t,ℓ,s}` and `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}` | Encode whether a train occupies a particular side of a link; they allow a compact “no‑overlap” formulation (C1) without an explicit time‑discretisation. |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of passenger delay (first term) and energy consumption (second term). Both are linear in the variables. |
| **Constraints (R2, B1)** | Ensure that the blocked side is **never** used while the disruption is present – the big‑M bounds force the occupation interval to lie completely before the start or completely after the end of the blockage. |
| **Dwell & flow constraints** | Simple linear equalities that propagate the schedule from one station to the next. |
| **Safety headways (gap\_ℓ)** | Appear as additive constants in the ordering and capacity constraints, guaranteeing that the required temporal separation is respected. |

Because all decision variables are either continuous (arrival/departure times, travel times) or binary, and every relationship is expressed through linear equalities or inequalities (big‑M techniques for conditional logic), the formulation is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) for exact optimal solutions or used as a backbone for decomposition/heuristic approaches.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Create MILP for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. |  w\_delay , w\_energy | Positive weighting coefficients for the two components of the objective (normally chosen to balance monetary value of delay vs. energy). | – |
|  M   | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate conditional constraints (e.g. M = horizon length). | min |

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r**\_{t,s} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the partially blocked segment. |
| **o**\_{i,j} | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every shared link (i.e., the ordering on that link). |
| **a**\_{t,n} | continuous ≥0 | **Arrival** time of train *t* at station *n* (n∈ℕₜ). |
| **d**\_{t,n} | continuous ≥0 | **Departure** time of train *t* from station *n* (n∈ℕₜ, includes dwell). |
| **τ**\_{t,ℓ} | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *t* on link ℓ. |
| **v**\_{t,ℓ,k} | binary | 1 ⇔ speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on link ℓ. |
| **x**\_{t,ℓ,s} | binary (optional auxiliary) | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ.  (Used to enforce capacity & blockage.) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;  \; w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}
\bigl( a_{t,\text{last}}- \text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
e_{\ell,k}\;v_{t,\ell,k}
}
\]

*The first term is the total (weighted) passenger‑delay; the second term is the total (weighted) energy use across all trains and links.*

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Model Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route‑choice for the partially blocked segment  

Only one side can be taken, and the blocked side cannot be used during the disruption window.

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}
\tag{R1}
\]

If side *s\* is the **blocked** side (known a‑priori), then no train may occupy it while the blockage is active:

\[
r_{t,s^{\*}}=0 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}\; \text{with}\; a_{t,\text{entry}} \in [T_{blk}^{start},T_{blk}^{end}]
\tag{R2}
\]

(Practically this is enforced by linking **r** to the time variables; an equivalent linear formulation appears later in the capacity constraints.)

#### 5.2  Temporal flow on each train  

* Dwell at a station  

\[
d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+ \text{dwell}_{n}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; n\in\mathcal{N}_t
\tag{F1}

* Travel on a link  

Let ℓ = ℓ(t,n) be the link that connects station *n* to the next station *m* = succ\_ℓ(n).  

\[
a_{t,m}= d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; n\in\mathcal{N}_t\setminus\{\text{last}\}
\tag{F2}
\]

#### 5.3  Linearised travel‑time – speed‑level relation  

For every train‑link pair the travel time is a convex combination of the discrete speed‑level travel times.

\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{\ell,k}\;v_{t,\ell,k}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{S1}
\]

Exactly one speed level is chosen:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,\ell,k}=1\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}
\tag{S2}
\]

If required, additional linear bounds can be added (e.g. maximum acceleration), but the above already guarantees a piecewise‑constant speed decision.

#### 5.4  Ordering on shared tracks (conflict‑pair constraints)  

For each ordered pair *(i,j)∈𝒫* that share a link ℓ (or a set of links – the same ordering holds for all of them) we introduce a binary precedence variable **o**\_{i,j}.

* Exactly one of the two possible orders holds:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O1}
\]

* If *i* goes before *j*, a safe headway must be respected on **every** common link ℓ. Let  ℓ\_{c}(i,j) be a common link; the inequality is written for the **first** common link (any one works because the ordering is the same for the whole shared segment).

\[
a_{j,\text{enter } \ell_c}+M\,(1-o_{i,j})\;\ge\;
d_{i,\text{exit } \ell_c}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_c}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O2}
\]

Here `enter ℓ_c` and `exit ℓ_c` are the appropriate stations that delimit the link ℓ_c for each train (e.g. entry = arrival at the upstream station, exit = departure from the downstream station).  The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when *o*\_{i,j}=0.

#### 5.5  Capacity – at most one train on a side of a link at a time  

Introduce auxiliary binary **x**\_{t,ℓ,s} that indicates that train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ.  It is linked to the route‑choice variable:

\[
x_{t,\ell,s}= r_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; \ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\; s\in S
\tag{C0}
\]

(Only the blocked segment needs the side‑choice; for all other links we can set *s = L* and fix \(x_{t,\ell,L}=1\).)

Now enforce that at any point in time no two trains occupy the same side.  A common linear formulation uses **time‑indexed** variables; however, with the ordering variables we can keep it compact:

For every pair of distinct trains (p,q) that could be on the same side *s* of the same link ℓ:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1- y^{pq}_{\ell,s}) &\ge d_{p,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
a_{p,\text{enter } \ell}+M\,y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge d_{q,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{p,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{q,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge x_{p,\ell,s}+x_{q,\ell,s}-1
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall p<q,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\;s\in S
\tag{C1}
\]

Here \(y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\) is a binary that becomes 1 **only if** both trains use the same side; then the two big‑M constraints enforce a mutual exclusivity (one train must finish before the other starts plus the safety gap).  

If only one side of the segment is usable (the unblocked side), the constraints automatically reduce because the product \(x_{p,\ell,s}x_{q,\ell,s}=0\).

#### 5.6  Blockage‑window for the blocked side  

Even if a train selects the blocked side, it must **not** occupy it during the disruption interval.  Using the same auxiliary variable \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}\) for the blocked side \(s^\*\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*}) &\ge T_{blk}^{end}\\
d_{t,\text{exit } \ell} &\le T_{blk}^{start}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}}
\tag{B1}
\]

Thus, if a train decides to use the blocked side ( \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}=1\) ), both inequalities force the whole occupation interval to lie **outside** \([T_{blk}^{start},T_{blk}^{end}]\).

#### 5.7  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s} \in\{0,1\},\;\;  o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\;\; v_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
& x_{t,\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\;\; y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{D}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\!\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
      \;+\;
      w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\;\; \text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{Route‑choice for blocked segment}\\
            &\;\; \text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{Temporal flow (arrival‑departure–travel)}\\
            &\;\; \text{(S1)–(S2)} &&\text{Speed‑level → travel‑time linearisation}\\
            &\;\; \text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{Ordering of conflicting trains}\\
            &\;\; \text{(C0)–(C1)} &&\text{Capacity on each side of the blocked link}\\
            &\;\; \text{(B1)}      &&\text{Blocked side cannot be used inside the disruption window}\\
            &\;\; \text{(D)}       &&\text{Domain definitions}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Component | What it models | Why it is linear / MILP‑compatible |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| **Binary side‑choice** `r_{t,s}` | The decision of each train to bypass the partially blocked segment on the left or right side. Guarantees a *single* side (R1). |
| **Binary ordering** `o_{i,j}` | Mutual precedence on any shared track segment – essential for conflict‑free schedules.  The “one‑of‑two’’ constraint (O1) together with the big‑M safety constraint (O2) linearises the “if‑then’’ logic. |
| **Arrival / departure times** `a_{t,n}`, `d_{t,n}` | Continuous timestamps that allow us to compute delays and enforce dwell times, linking the schedule to the objective. |
| **Travel‑time variables** `τ_{t,ℓ}` | Continuous variables that become a convex combination of the discrete travel times of the admissible speed levels (S1–S2). |
| **Speed‑level binaries** `v_{t,ℓ,k}` | Enable the model to choose a discrete speed (or equivalently a discrete power/energy regime) on each link. The linear combination (S1) yields the travel time; the same binaries appear in the energy term of the objective. |
| **Capacity auxiliary binaries** `x_{t,ℓ,s}` and `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}` | Encode whether a train occupies a particular side of a link; they allow a compact “no‑overlap” formulation (C1) without an explicit time‑discretisation. |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of passenger delay (first term) and energy consumption (second term). Both are linear in the variables. |
| **Constraints (R2, B1)** | Ensure that the blocked side is **never** used while the disruption is present – the big‑M bounds force the occupation interval to lie completely before the start or completely after the end of the blockage. |
| **Dwell & flow constraints** | Simple linear equalities that propagate the schedule from one station to the next. |
| **Safety headways (gap\_ℓ)** | Appear as additive constants in the ordering and capacity constraints, guaranteeing that the required temporal separation is respected. |

Because all decision variables are either continuous (arrival/departure times, travel times) or binary, and every relationship is expressed through linear equalities or inequalities (big‑M techniques for conditional logic), the formulation is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) for exact optimal solutions or used as a backbone for decomposition/heuristic approaches.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

If required, additional linear bounds can be added (e.g. maximum acceleration), but the above already guarantees a piecewise‑constant speed decision.

#### 5.4  Ordering on shared tracks (conflict‑pair constraints)  

For each ordered pair *(i,j)∈𝒫* that share a link ℓ (or a set of links – the same ordering holds for all of them) we introduce a binary precedence variable **o**\_{i,j}.

* Exactly one of the two possible orders holds:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O1}
\]

* If *i* goes before *j*, a safe headway must be respected on **every** common link ℓ. Let  ℓ\_{c}(i,j) be a common link; the inequality is written for the **first** common link (any one works because the ordering is the same for the whole shared segment).

\[
a_{j,\text{enter } \ell_c}+M\,(1-o_{i,j})\;\ge\;
d_{i,\text{exit } \ell_c}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_c}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}
\tag{O2}
\]

Here `enter ℓ_c` and `exit ℓ_c` are the appropriate stations that delimit the link ℓ_c for each train (e.g. entry = arrival at the upstream station, exit = departure from the downstream station).  The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when *o*\_{i,j}=0.

#### 5.5  Capacity – at most one train on a side of a link at a time  

Introduce auxiliary binary **x**\_{t,ℓ,s} that indicates that train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ.  It is linked to the route‑choice variable:

\[
x_{t,\ell,s}= r_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\; \ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\; s\in S
\tag{C0}
\]

(Only the blocked segment needs the side‑choice; for all other links we can set *s = L* and fix \(x_{t,\ell,L}=1\).)

Now enforce that at any point in time no two trains occupy the same side.  A common linear formulation uses **time‑indexed** variables; however, with the ordering variables we can keep it compact:

For every pair of distinct trains (p,q) that could be on the same side *s* of the same link ℓ:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1- y^{pq}_{\ell,s}) &\ge d_{p,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
a_{p,\text{enter } \ell}+M\,y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge d_{q,\text{exit } \ell}+ \text{gap}_{\ell}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{p,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\le x_{q,\ell,s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell,s} &\ge x_{p,\ell,s}+x_{q,\ell,s}-1
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall p<q,\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}},\;s\in S
\tag{C1}
\]

Here \(y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\) is a binary that becomes 1 **only if** both trains use the same side; then the two big‑M constraints enforce a mutual exclusivity (one train must finish before the other starts plus the safety gap).  

If only one side of the segment is usable (the unblocked side), the constraints automatically reduce because the product \(x_{p,\ell,s}x_{q,\ell,s}=0\).

#### 5.6  Blockage‑window for the blocked side  

Even if a train selects the blocked side, it must **not** occupy it during the disruption interval.  Using the same auxiliary variable \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}\) for the blocked side \(s^\*\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,\text{enter } \ell}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*}) &\ge T_{blk}^{end}\\
d_{t,\text{exit } \ell} &\le T_{blk}^{start}+M(1-x_{t,\ell,s^\*})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;\ell\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{blocked}}
\tag{B1}
\]

Thus, if a train decides to use the blocked side ( \(x_{t,\ell,s^\*}=1\) ), both inequalities force the whole occupation interval to lie **outside** \([T_{blk}^{start},T_{blk}^{end}]\).

#### 5.7  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{t,s} \in\{0,1\},\;\;  o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\;\; v_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
& x_{t,\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\;\; y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
& a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{D}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\!\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
      \;+\;
      w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{k\in K} e_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\;\; \text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{Route‑choice for blocked segment}\\
            &\;\; \text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{Temporal flow (arrival‑departure–travel)}\\
            &\;\; \text{(S1)–(S2)} &&\text{Speed‑level → travel‑time linearisation}\\
            &\;\; \text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{Ordering of conflicting trains}\\
            &\;\; \text{(C0)–(C1)} &&\text{Capacity on each side of the blocked link}\\
            &\;\; \text{(B1)}      &&\text{Blocked side cannot be used inside the disruption window}\\
            &\;\; \text{(D)}       &&\text{Domain definitions}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Explanation of the Model Elements  

| Component | What it models | Why it is linear / MILP‑compatible |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| **Binary side‑choice** `r_{t,s}` | The decision of each train to bypass the partially blocked segment on the left or right side. Guarantees a *single* side (R1). |
| **Binary ordering** `o_{i,j}` | Mutual precedence on any shared track segment – essential for conflict‑free schedules.  The “one‑of‑two’’ constraint (O1) together with the big‑M safety constraint (O2) linearises the “if‑then’’ logic. |
| **Arrival / departure times** `a_{t,n}`, `d_{t,n}` | Continuous timestamps that allow us to compute delays and enforce dwell times, linking the schedule to the objective. |
| **Travel‑time variables** `τ_{t,ℓ}` | Continuous variables that become a convex combination of the discrete travel times of the admissible speed levels (S1–S2). |
| **Speed‑level binaries** `v_{t,ℓ,k}` | Enable the model to choose a discrete speed (or equivalently a discrete power/energy regime) on each link. The linear combination (S1) yields the travel time; the same binaries appear in the energy term of the objective. |
| **Capacity auxiliary binaries** `x_{t,ℓ,s}` and `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}` | Encode whether a train occupies a particular side of a link; they allow a compact “no‑overlap” formulation (C1) without an explicit time‑discretisation. |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of passenger delay (first term) and energy consumption (second term). Both are linear in the variables. |
| **Constraints (R2, B1)** | Ensure that the blocked side is **never** used while the disruption is present – the big‑M bounds force the occupation interval to lie completely before the start or completely after the end of the blockage. |
| **Dwell & flow constraints** | Simple linear equalities that propagate the schedule from one station to the next. |
| **Safety headways (gap\_ℓ)** | Appear as additive constants in the ordering and capacity constraints, guaranteeing that the required temporal separation is respected. |

Because all decision variables are either continuous (arrival/departure times, travel times) or binary, and every relationship is expressed through linear equalities or inequalities (big‑M techniques for conditional logic), the formulation is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** that can be handed to any standard solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.) for exact optimal solutions or used as a backbone for decomposition/heuristic approaches.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

*The model is linear, uses binary and continuous variables, and can be solved with any MILP solver (e.g. CPLEX, Gurobi). All notation is defined below.*

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **𝒯**      | Set of trains *t* (|𝒯| = T). |
| **ℕₜ**     | Ordered set of stations visited by train *t* (including origin and terminal). |
| **ℒ**      | Set of links (track segments) between consecutive stations, indexed by ℓ. |
| **S** = {L,R} | Two possible **sides** (Left / Right) of the partially blocked segment. |
| **K**      | Set of admissible discrete **speed levels** on a link, indexed by *k*. |
| **𝒫**      | Set of ordered train‑pairs *(i ,j)* that share at least one common link (conflict pairs). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Definition | Units |
|--------|------------|-------|
| `schedₐₜ`   | Scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final station. | min |
| `τ_{ℓ,k}`   | Nominal travel time on link ℓ when speed level *k* is selected. | min |
| `e_{ℓ,k}`   | Energy consumption (or cost) on link ℓ at speed level *k*. | kWh (or cost) |
| `dwell_n`   | Minimum dwell time at station *n*. | min |
| `gap_ℓ`     | Minimum safety headway (time) required between two successive trains on the same **side** of link ℓ. | min |
| `T^{start}_{blk}` , `T^{end}_{blk}` | Beginning and end of the disruption‑window on the blocked segment (the side that is **blocked** cannot be used). | min |
| `w_delay` , `w_energy` | Positive weighting coefficients for delay and energy in the objective. | – |
| `M`         | Big‑M constant (≥ planning horizon). | min |
| `ℓ_blocked` | The unique link that suffers a partial blockage. |
| `s^{*}`     | The **blocked** side of `ℓ_blocked` (known a‑priori). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| `r_{t,s}` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* uses side *s* (L or R) of the blocked segment. |
| `o_{i,j}` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on every shared link. |
| `a_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *t* at station *n* (n∈ℕₜ). |
| `d_{t,n}` | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *t* from station *n*. |
| `τ_{t,ℓ}` | continuous ≥0 | travel time of train *t* on link ℓ. |
| `v_{t,ℓ,k}` | binary | 1 ⇔ speed level *k* is selected for train *t* on link ℓ. |
| `x_{t,ℓ,s}` | binary | 1 ⇔ train *t* occupies side *s* of link ℓ (only needed for `ℓ_blocked`). |
| `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}` | binary | Auxiliary variable used to enforce that two trains using the same side of a link do not overlap. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{k\in K}
e_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}
}
\]

*First term = total passenger delay; second term = total energy consumption.*

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1  Route choice for the blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}\tag{R1}
\]

Link the side‑choice to the side‑occupation variable (only needed for the blocked link):

\[
x_{t,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}=r_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;s\in S\tag{R2}
\]

#### 5.2  Temporal flow for each train  

*Dwell at stations*  

\[
d_{t,n}=a_{t,n}+ \text{dwell}_{n}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},\;n\in\mathcal{N}_t\tag{F1}
\]

*Travel on a link*  

Let ℓ = ℓ(t,n) be the link from station *n* to its successor *m*.  

\[
a_{t,m}=d_{t,n}+ \tau_{t,\ell}\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T},
\; n\in\mathcal{N}_t\setminus\{\text{last}\}\tag{F2}
\]

#### 5.3  Speed‑level linearisation  

\[
\tau_{t,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}\qquad\forall t,\ell\tag{S1}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,\ell,k}=1\qquad\forall t,\ell\tag{S2}
\]

#### 5.4  Ordering of conflicting trains (conflict‑pair constraints)  

Exactly one precedence for each conflicting pair:

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\tag{O1}
\]

If *i* precedes *j*, a safety headway must be respected on any common link ℓ\_c :

\[
a_{j,\text{enter }\ell_c}+M\,(1-o_{i,j})\ge
d_{i,\text{exit }\ell_c}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_c}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\tag{O2}
\]

(“enter’’/“exit’’ are the arrival at the upstream station and departure from the downstream station of ℓ\_c.)

#### 5.5  Capacity on each side of the blocked link  

For any two distinct trains *p* and *q* that could occupy the same side *s* of `ℓ_blocked`:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{q,\text{enter }\ell_{\text{blocked}}}+M\bigl(1-y^{pq}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}\bigr)
      &\ge d_{p,\text{exit }\ell_{\text{blocked}}}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}}}\\
a_{p,\text{enter }\ell_{\text{blocked}}}+M\,y^{pq}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}
      &\ge d_{q,\text{exit }\ell_{\text{blocked}}}+ \text{gap}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}}}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}
      &\le x_{p,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}
      &\le x_{q,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}\\
y^{pq}_{\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}
      &\ge x_{p,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}+x_{q,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s}-1
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall p<q,\;s\in S\tag{C1}
\]

If the two trains do **not** use the same side, the auxiliary variable \(y^{pq}\) becomes 0 and the big‑M constraints are inactive, allowing simultaneous occupation of different sides.

#### 5.6  Blockage‑window for the blocked side  

If a train chooses the blocked side \(s^{*}\), it may not occupy the link during the disruption interval:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,\text{enter }\ell_{\text{blocked}}}+M\bigl(1-x_{t,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s^{*}}\bigr) &\ge T^{end}_{blk}\\
d_{t,\text{exit }\ell_{\text{blocked}}} &\le T^{start}_{blk}+M\bigl(1-x_{t,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s^{*}}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in\mathcal{T}\tag{B1}
\]

Thus, when \(x_{t,\ell_{\text{blocked}},s^{*}}=1\) the whole occupation interval must lie completely **before** or **after** the disruption window.

#### 5.7  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{t,\ell,k}\in\{0,1\},\\
&x_{t,\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y^{pq}_{\ell,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{t,n}\ge 0,\; d_{t,n}\ge 0,\; \tau_{t,\ell}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{D}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Full MILP Formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}}\!\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}
\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_{a_t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\!\!\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}\sum_{k\in K}
e_{\ell,k}\,v_{t,\ell,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\; \text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{Side choice for the blocked segment}\\
            &\; \text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{Temporal flow (arrival–departure–travel)}\\
            &\; \text{(S1)–(S2)} &&\text{Speed‑level → travel‑time linearisation}\\
            &\; \text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{Ordering of conflicting trains}\\
            &\; \text{(C1)}      &&\text{Capacity on each side of the blocked link}\\
            &\; \text{(B1)}      &&\text{Blocked side cannot be used inside the disruption window}\\
            &\; \text{(D)}       &&\text{Domain definitions}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Model Interpretation  

* **Binary side‑choice** (`r_{t,s}`) decides whether a train bypasses the blocked segment on the left or right track.  
* **Ordering variables** (`o_{i,j}`) guarantee a conflict‑free timetable on shared tracks by imposing a safety headway (`gap_ℓ`).  
* **Speed‑level binaries** (`v_{t,ℓ,k}`) let the model select a discrete speed (hence a travel time `τ_{t,ℓ}`) on each link; the same binaries appear in the energy term of the objective.  
* **Auxiliary binaries** (`x_{t,ℓ,s}`, `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}`) enforce that at most one train occupies the same side of the blocked link at any time, while still allowing opposite‑direction trains to use different sides simultaneously.  
* **Blockage‑window constraints** (`B1`) force any train that would use the blocked side to schedule its passage completely outside the disruption interval.  
* The **objective** simultaneously minimises total passenger delay and total energy consumption, with user‑defined weights `w_delay` and `w_energy`.  

All constraints are linear; the presence of binary variables makes the problem a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** suitable for exact solution or for decomposition‑based heuristics described in the accompanying research.

            &\; \text{(O1)–(O2)} &&\text{Ordering of conflicting trains}\\
            &\; \text{(C1)}      &&\text{Capacity on each side of the blocked link}\\
            &\; \text{(B1)}      &&\text{Blocked side cannot be used inside the disruption window}\\
            &\; \text{(D)}       &&\text{Domain definitions}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Model Interpretation  

* **Binary side‑choice** (`r_{t,s}`) decides whether a train bypasses the blocked segment on the left or right track.  
* **Ordering variables** (`o_{i,j}`) guarantee a conflict‑free timetable on shared tracks by imposing a safety headway (`gap_ℓ`).  
* **Speed‑level binaries** (`v_{t,ℓ,k}`) let the model select a discrete speed (hence a travel time `τ_{t,ℓ}`) on each link; the same binaries appear in the energy term of the objective.  
* **Auxiliary binaries** (`x_{t,ℓ,s}`, `y^{pq}_{ℓ,s}`) enforce that at most one train occupies the same side of the blocked link at any time, while still allowing opposite‑direction trains to use different sides simultaneously.  
* **Blockage‑window constraints** (`B1`) force any train that would use the blocked side to schedule its passage completely outside the disruption interval.  
* The **objective** simultaneously minimises total passenger delay and total energy consumption, with user‑defined weights `w_delay` and `w_energy`.  

All constraints are linear; the presence of binary variables makes the problem a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** suitable for exact solution or for decomposition‑based heuristics described in the accompanying research.

Introduction

Urban rail transit has become increasingly important in large cities due to its reliability, high capacity, and eco-friendly characteristics. Urban rail transit systems prioritize safe and efficient train operations while providing high-quality service to passengers. Effective real-time train scheduling is essential for enhancing passenger satisfaction and minimizing operational costs within infrastructure limitations. However, the rapid expansion of urban rail transit systems and the increasing passenger demands pose significant challenges to real-time scheduling. Advanced scheduling models and control strategies are required to develop efficient timetables and to improve the overall performance of urban rail transit systems.

Passenger-oriented train scheduling

In urban rail transit systems, passenger demands vary throughout the day, necessitating adjustments to the train schedules to accommodate these demand variations while considering operational costs. One direction addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing the departure and arrival times of trains at each station, while considering several attributes of train operations and infrastructure restrictions, e.g., train stopping plans (the set of station stops for each train) (Cacchiani et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2021), rolling stock circulations (Wang et al., 2018), and train speed levels (Hou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Qi et al. (2021) optimized train stopping plans and timetables of a high-speed railway line considering time-varying passenger demands by formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem, and the aim is to find a solution that considers passenger preferences for departure times while ensuring trains operate within capacity limits. Considering the passenger load of trains, Wu et al. (2021) minimized the passenger waiting time and the energy consumption by developing a heuristic algorithm to solve the resulting nonlinear integer programming problem. Wang et al. (2021) formulated a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to minimize train energy consumption and passenger waiting times by optimizing train speed levels and headway deviations. To address train scheduling under uncertain passenger demands, Cacchiani et al. (2020) introduced a protection level on the departure and arrival times, and solved an MILP to obtain the train schedule and the stopping plan. Huang et al. (2025) investigated minimization of operation costs, passenger waiting time, and passenger travel time, and developed a variable neighborhood search approach to solve the resulting problem. However, the above studies optimize train schedules within the fixed transport capacity of a line, such as fixed train compositions or fixed train departure frequencies. As transport capacity directly impacts passenger flows, further research is required to improve passenger satisfaction by including transport capacity as a decision variable.

Another direction for train scheduling problems addresses time-varying passenger demands by optimizing transport capacity explicitly. Several studies focus on optimizing transport capacity by adjusting train departure frequencies, with higher frequencies during peak hours and lower frequencies during off-peak hours (Canca et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; 2024). To handle uncertain passenger demands, Liu et al. (2024) developed a scenario-based distributed control approach, in which a scenario reduction technique is applied to reduce the computational burden. Pu and Zhan (2021) developed a two-step approach in which the first step determines the nominal line plan and the second step adjusts the time plan based on the actual measured passenger demands. Instead of changing the departure frequency, which would significantly affect the schedule, recently, many researchers have focused on optimizing the composition of the train (Ying et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2023). Pan et al. (2023) developed a column-generation-based approach to optimize the timetable, train composition, and rolling stock circulation plan of an urban rail transit line. Their paper concludes that flexible train composition can provide additional adaptability to better match time-varying passenger demands. Wang et al. (2024) investigated flexible train composition and rolling stock circulation of an urban rail transit line, and solved the resulting MILP problem by developing an approximation approach and a two-stage meta-heuristic algorithm. Yang et al. (2024) investigated the train scheduling problem with flexible train composition for an urban rail transit line, and they applied an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm to solve the resulting integer programming problem. As the inclusion of train composition optimization and rolling stock circulation planning introduces additional integer variables, the above studies indicate that the online computational complexity is the main challenge of incorporating flexible train composition into the real-time train scheduling problem.

MPC for real-time train scheduling

Model predictive control (MPC) has been widely adopted in various applications for its ability to handle multivariable constrained control problems (Grüne and Pannek, 2017; Mayne et al., 2000; Qin and Badgwell, 2003). The train scheduling problem is a typical constrained control problem, and many studies have applied MPC for real-time train scheduling. De Schutter et al. (2002) first applied MPC in the train scheduling problem to minimize train delays by adjusting transfer connections. Caimi et al. (2012) developed an MPC algorithm to optimize timetables, transfer connections, and train assignment plans in complex station areas. Cavone et al. (2022) proposed an MPC approach for train rescheduling during disruptions and delays, where in each step the resulting MILP problem is solved by combining bi-level heuristics and distributed optimization. The above studies only handle operator-related factors, leaving an open gap in including passenger demands in real-time train scheduling problems to improve the service quality of urban rail transit systems.

In recent years, several studies have focused on MPC for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling. Assis and Milani (2004) applied MPC to compute the train timetable of a metro line, considering train headway and passenger load, where a linear programming problem is solved at each step. Based on a state-space model, Li et al. (2016) developed a robust MPC approach to minimize the upper bound of the timetable deviation from the nominal timetable under uncertain disturbances. By solving linear matrix inequalities, they constructed a Lyapunov function to ensure the attenuation of the timetable deviation. An event-triggered MPC approach is further developed by Wang et al. (2022) to reduce the computational burden of updating control variables in each step. However, these studies do not explicitly consider train capacity limitations and time-varying passenger demands, and the results are based on the assumption that the maximum number of passengers does not exceed the maximum train capacity. Chen et al. (2022) investigated real-time train rescheduling and stop-skipping strategies under disturbances and dynamic passenger flows. A mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) problem is solved at each MPC step to minimize the total deviation from the original timetable and the number of waiting passengers. In the follow-up work, Chen et al. (2023) applied distributed MPC to address the real-time train regulation problem, using Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition to solve the resulting optimization problem. Liu et al. (2023a) explicitly incorporated time-varying passenger demands and train capacity limitations into the real-time train scheduling problem. In Liu et al. (2023a), time-varying passenger demands are approximated as piecewise constant functions by dividing the planning time window into several time intervals of equal length, and an MILP-based MPC approach is adopted for real-time train scheduling. The main challenge of applying MPC in real time is the online computational burden. Including additional attributes, such as train capacity, train composition, and rolling stock circulation, will further increase the computational burden. Therefore, further research is required to develop efficient MPC approaches for real-time passenger-oriented train scheduling.

Learning-based train scheduling

Learning-based approaches are considered effective methodologies for reducing the online computational burden. Learning-based approaches, including deep learning and reinforcement learning (RL), have also been applied in train scheduling problems in recent years (Tang et al., 2022). SL trains models on labeled data to make accurate predictions or classifications, while RL trains an agent to make decisions through trial-and-error using rewards and penalties. Kuppusamy et al. (2020) applied a deep learning approach to an energy-efficient timetable rescheduling problem, where a long short-term memory (LSTM) network is trained to select the optimal operation mode. Šemrov et al. (2016) applied Q-learning in the train rescheduling problem to reduce delays caused by disturbances and disruptions, and they illustrated their method on a single-lane track with three trains. Yin et al. (2016) proposed an approximate dynamic programming approach to address train rescheduling problems, aiming to reduce passenger delays, total travel time, and train energy consumption. In Yin et al. (2016), the states include disturbance information, train arrival times, the number of boarding passengers, and the number of waiting passengers, while the actions include rescheduling the dwell times and running times. Khadilkar (2019) applied RL to determine track allocations and timetables of bidirectional railway lines to minimize the priority-weighted delay. Ying et al. (2021) developed a proximal policy optimization approach for the train scheduling problem in an urban rail transit line, considering flexible train composition. In Ying et al. (2021), the control policy and the value function are parameterized by artificial neural networks, and scheduling constraints are handled by a devised mask scheme. Simulation results show that this approach reduces the computational burden and improves solution quality compared to the genetic algorithm and differential evolution. Nguyen and Chow (2023) introduced an adaptive rollout surrogate approximate dynamic programming (ADP) framework for rail transit network operations, where the value function is approximated by a surrogate function, and the solution is obtained via a cross-entropy-based search, encompassing decisions related to service operations and flexible train unit deployment. Ying et al. (2024) proposed a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approach for disruption management with short-turning operations in a service corridor, enabling adaptive rescheduling under time-varying passenger demand. Wang et al. (2025) formulated adaptive network dispatching as a partially observable Markov decision process and applied a deep recurrent Q network to derive dispatching policies with flexible fleet deployment. These recent studies have shown that learning-based frameworks can support train scheduling and may incorporate time-varying passenger demands in rail networks. However, explicitly modeling time-varying passenger demands in the train scheduling problem further tightens the coupling among timetable adjustments, capacity allocation via flexible train composition, and rolling-stock circulation. This coupling enlarges the discrete decision space and increases online computational complexity, while operational feasibility still needs to be guaranteed for real-world implementation. Therefore, scalability and constraint satisfaction remain key challenges when developing learning-based train scheduling approaches.

In the above studies, scalability and constraint satisfaction are the main challenges in developing learning-based train scheduling approaches. The train scheduling problem is typically formulated as an MILP or MINLP problem, and the computational complexity increases rapidly as the number of integer variables increases. In recent years, some research has combined learning-based and optimization-based approaches for MILP or MINLP problems by using learning-based approaches to obtain the integer variables (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023; da Silva et al., 2025). Having the integer variables fixed, the continuous variables are then obtained by solving a linear or nonlinear programming problem. This idea aims to combine the advantages of both learning-based and optimization-based approaches, i.e., the online computational efficiency of learning-based approaches and the feasibility guarantees of constrained optimization (Cauligi et al., 2022; Russo et al., 2023). The promising results of learning-based train scheduling and the recent learning-based approaches for mixed integer programming problems have inspired us to develop an optimization-driven learning-based framework for passenger-oriented real-time train scheduling.

Paper contributions and structure

The studies introduced in Sections 1.1–1.3 are summarized in Table 1 , categorized by network details, train composition, train order, rolling stock circulation, passenger demands, and solution method. From the above literature review, it can be found that flexible train composition combined with rolling stock circulation planning is an effective approach to balance operational costs and service quality. Shorter trains can be deployed during off-peak hours and longer trains during peak hours, thereby balancing operational costs and passenger waiting times. The passenger-oriented train scheduling problem is typically formulated as a mixed-integer programming problem. Various approaches can be applied to solve the resulting scheduling problem. Among them, optimization-based methods often encounter computational challenges for large-scale networks, necessitating additional efforts such as heuristics, two-step frameworks, and distributed approaches to reduce the computational burden. Learning-based methods are considered promising for addressing computational complexity. However, developing learning-based methods that are both scalable and constraint-satisfying for real-time passenger-oriented scheduling remains challenging, especially when time-varying passenger demands are explicitly considered when optimizing flexible train composition and rolling-stock circulation in network settings.

The current paper, therefore, addresses the learning-based train rescheduling problem in rail networks, considering time-varying passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. Unlike existing train rescheduling methods in the literature, the proposed approach integrates optimization and deep learning to combine the constraint satisfaction advantages of optimization-based methods with the fast online computation advantages of learning-based approaches. The main contributions of the paper are listed as follows: A passenger-oriented train rescheduling model in Liu et al. (2023a) is extended to include time-varying sectional passenger demands, flexible train composition, and rolling stock circulation. The time-varying passenger demands can be approximated as a piecewise constant function by dividing the prediction horizon into several time intervals. Four presolve techniques are developed to streamline optimization processes by pruning a subset of integer decision variables. After implementing the presolve techniques, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are applied to obtain the remaining integer variables with reduced dimensions. A deep-learning-based MPC approach is developed for real-time train rescheduling. To improve the online computational efficiency of MPC, the learning-based approach is applied to obtain integer variables, while the detailed timetable is obtained by solving a constrained optimization problem with the fixed integer variables. The remaining part of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides the problem description and general explanations. Section 3 introduces the passenger-oriented train rescheduling model. In Section 4, the problem formulation and the MINLP-based MPC approach are presented. In Section 5, we propose a learning-based MPC approach for real-time train rescheduling. Section 6 provides an illustrative case study. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Passenger‑oriented Real‑time Train‑Scheduling MILP (MPC‑style)**  
The model below is a **complete mixed‑integer linear programming (MILP)** formulation that can be embedded in a Model‑Predictive‑Control (MPC) loop.  
All symbols are defined in the *Sets, Parameters & Decision Variables* section; the remaining parts give the **objective function** and the **linear constraints**.  
Whenever a piece of information is not supplied in the description, a *reasonable assumption* is explicitly stated.

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of **trains** that may be operated in the prediction horizon (indexed by *t*). |
| **S** = {1,…, |S|} | Set of **stations** along the line (ordered from upstream to downstream). |
| **I** = {1,…, |I|} | Set of **time intervals** that discretise the prediction horizon (Δ‑interval = τ minutes).  |
| **K** = {1,…, |K|} | Set of **train‑type (composition) classes** (e.g., 2‑car, 4‑car, 6‑car). |
| **R** = {1,…, |R|} | Set of **rolling‑stock units** (individual train‑sets) that can be assigned to a train. |
| **P** = {1,…, |P|} | Set of **passenger demand arcs** – each arc *p* = (s, s′, i) denotes the demand from station *s* to downstream station *s′* during interval *i*. |

---

## 2. Parameters (assumed / given)

| Symbol | Meaning | Typical value / source |
|--------|---------|------------------------|
|  τ  | Length of a time interval (minutes). | 5 min (assumption). |
|  Δ<sub>st</sub>  | Minimum **running time** (travel time) between consecutive stations *s* and *s+1* for a **unit‑speed** train (minutes). | timetable data. |
|  β<sub>k</sub>  | **Capacity** (seats) of train‑type *k* (passengers). | e.g., 200, 400, 600. |
|  c<sub>k</sub>  | **Operating cost** per train‑type *k* (fuel/electricity + crew). | €/train‑hour. |
|  w<sub>p</sub>  | **Passenger‑waiting penalty** per passenger in demand arc *p* (€/passenger). | 0.5 €/pax. |
|  d<sub>p</sub>  | **Passenger demand** for arc *p* (number of passengers that want to travel from *s* to *s′* in interval *i*). | obtained from AFC data (piecewise‑constant). |
|  M  | Large constant (big‑M) for logical constraints (≥ 10⁶). |
|  L<sub>r</sub>  | **Availability window** of rolling‑stock unit *r* (set of intervals in which *r* can be used). |
|  σ<sub>t</sub>  | Minimum **headway** (minutes) that must separate train *t* from its predecessor on the same line. | 2 min. |
|  ϕ<sub>st</sub> | Minimum **dwell time** at station *s* for any train (minutes). | 0.5 min. |
|  ϕ<sub>max</sub> | Maximum allowed dwell time (e.g., due to platform length). | 2 min. |
|  α  | Weight for operating cost in the objective (0 ≤ α ≤ 1). | 0.3 (assumption). |
|  1‑α | Weight for passenger‑related penalties. | 0.7. |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

All variables are **linear** (binary or continuous).

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| **x<sub>t,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Train *t* **starts service** in interval *i* (i.e., its departure from the first station occurs in interval *i*). |
| **y<sub>t,k</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Train *t* is assigned **composition class** *k*. (Exactly one class per train). |
| **z<sub>t,r</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Rolling‑stock unit *r* is **allocated** to train *t*. (One unit per train). |
| **a<sub>t,s,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Train *t* **arrives** at station *s* **during** interval *i*. |
| **d<sub>t,s,i</sub>** ∈ {0,1} | binary | Train *t* **departs** from station *s* **during** interval *i*. |
| **g<sub>t,s,i</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous | **Dwell time** (minutes) of train *t* at station *s* if it stops in interval *i*. |
| **u<sub>p</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous | Number of **waiting passengers** for demand arc *p* after the schedule is applied (i.e., unserved demand). |
| **q<sub>p</sub>** ≥ 0 | continuous | Number of **served passengers** for demand arc *p* (must satisfy capacity). |

---

## 4. Model Assumptions (explicit)

1. **Piecewise‑constant demand** – passenger demand *d<sub>p</sub>* is constant inside each interval *i*.  
2. **Deterministic travel times** – the minimum travel time Δ<sub>st</sub> is used; any extra time is captured by dwell variables *g*.  
3. **No overtaking** – trains keep the same order as their start times (enforced by headway constraints).  
4. **Every train that starts must stop at a subset of stations** – for simplicity we assume **all trains stop at every station** (stop‑skipping can be added later by extra binary variables).  
5. **Rolling‑stock reuse** – a unit *r* can be assigned to at most one train in the horizon (otherwise a multi‑day horizon is required).  

---

## 5. Objective Function  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;  & \underbrace{\alpha \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{k\in K} c_{k}\,y_{t,k}}_{\text{Operating cost}} \\
& \;+\;(1-\alpha) \Bigg[ 
\underbrace{\sum_{p\in P} w_{p}\,u_{p}}_{\text{Passenger‑waiting penalty}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{i\in I} g_{t,s,i}}_{\text{Total dwell time (proxy for energy)}}
\Bigg]
\end{aligned}
\]

*Explanation*:  
- The first term charges the cost of the chosen train composition.  
- The second term penalises passengers that are not served (waiting) and the total dwell time (which correlates with energy consumption and schedule deviation).  

---

## 6. Constraints  

### 6.1 Train‑type and start‑time coupling  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,k}=\sum_{i\in I} x_{t,i}\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

*Each train that starts must be assigned exactly one composition; a train that never starts has all binaries zero.*

### 6.2 Rolling‑stock allocation  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} z_{t,r}= \sum_{i\in I} x_{t,i}\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{C2}
\]

\[
\sum_{t\in T} z_{t,r}\le 1\qquad \forall r\in R
\tag{C3}
\]

*Each operating train uses exactly one rolling‑stock unit; a unit cannot be used by two trains simultaneously.*

### 6.3 Headway (no‑overtaking)  

For any two distinct trains *t* and *t′* with *t* scheduled earlier (i.e., start interval earlier):

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} + \sigma_{t} \le \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t',i} + M\,(1 - \theta_{t,t'})
\tag{C4}
\]

where binary \(\theta_{t,t'}\) = 1 if train *t* precedes *t′* (added as auxiliary variable with logical definition).  
If we prefer a simpler formulation, we can enforce ordering by sorting trains a priori (e.g., by index) and write:

\[
\sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t,i} + \sigma \le \sum_{i\in I} i\,x_{t+1,i} \qquad \forall t=1,\dots,|T|-1
\tag{C4‑simple}
\]

### 6.4 Temporal consistency of arrivals / departures  

For every train *t* and station *s* (except the first station where arrival = start):

\[
a_{t,s,i} \le \sum_{j\le i} d_{t,s-1,j} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; s=2,\dots,|S|
\tag{C5}
\]

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le a_{t,s,i} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; s\in S
\tag{C6}
\]

*The train can arrive only after it has departed the previous station; it can depart only if it has arrived.*

### 6.5 Travel‑time feasibility  

If a train departs station *s‑1* in interval *j* and arrives at station *s* in interval *i* then the travel time must respect the minimum travel time:

\[
i - j \ge \left\lceil\frac{\Delta_{s-1}}{\tau}\right\rceil \;-\; M\,(1 - a_{t,s,i} + d_{t,s-1,j})
\qquad \forall t,s,i,j
\tag{C7}
\]

*Big‑M linearisation forces the inequality only when the corresponding arrival/departure pair is selected.*

### 6.6 Dwell‑time definition  

\[
g_{t,s,i} \ge \phi_{st}\,a_{t,s,i} \qquad \forall t,s,i
\tag{C8}
\]

\[
g_{t,s,i} \le \phi_{\max}\,a_{t,s,i} \qquad \forall t,s,i
\tag{C9}
\]

*If the train stops (a=1) the dwell time lies between the minimum and maximum; otherwise (a=0) dwell time is forced to 0.*

### 6.7 Capacity – passenger loading  

For each demand arc *p* = (s, s′, i) we must respect the sum of capacities of all trains that stop at *s* during interval *i* and travel far enough to reach *s′*:

\[
\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{k\in K} \beta_{k}\,y_{t,k}\,
\Bigl( \sum_{j\le i} a_{t,s,j} - \sum_{j\le i} a_{t,s',j} \Bigr) \;\ge\; q_{p}
\qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{C10}
\]

The term in parentheses equals 1 if train *t* is on board between *s* and *s′* during interval *i*, 0 otherwise.  

Unserved demand:

\[
u_{p}= d_{p} - q_{p}\qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{C11}
\]

\[
u_{p}\ge 0,\; q_{p}\ge 0\qquad \forall p\in P
\tag{C12}
\]

### 6.8 Rolling‑stock availability windows  

\[
\sum_{i\in L_{r}} x_{t,i} \ge z_{t,r}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; r\in R
\tag{C13}
\]

*If a unit *r* is assigned to train *t*, the start interval of that train must belong to the unit’s available set.*

### 6.9 Logical linking for “train runs”  

To guarantee that a train that never starts does not generate arrivals/departures/dwell:

\[
a_{t,s,i} \le \sum_{j\in I} x_{t,j}\qquad \forall t,s,i
\tag{C14}
\]

\[
d_{t,s,i} \le \sum_{j\in I} x_{t,j}\qquad \forall t,s,i
\tag{C15}
\]

### 6.10 Single‑start per train  

\[
\sum_{i\in I} x_{t,i} \le 1\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{C16}
\]

(If a train is not used, all other binaries become zero automatically.)

---

## 7. Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,y,z,a,d,g,u,q} \;& \alpha \sum_{t}\sum_{k} c_{k} y_{t,k}
+(1-\alpha)\Bigl[ \sum_{p} w_{p} u_{p} + \sum_{t,s,i} g_{t,s,i} \Bigr] \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{(C1)–(C16)} \\
& x_{t,i},y_{t,k},z_{t,r},a_{t,s,i},d_{t,s,i}\in\{0,1\}, \\
& g_{t,s,i},u_{p},q_{p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 8. How the Model Fits into an MPC Loop  

1. **Prediction horizon**: Choose a horizon of *H* intervals (e.g., 30 min → 6 intervals of τ = 5 min).  
2. **Data update**: At each control step (every τ minutes) update the demand parameters *d<sub>p</sub>* using the latest AFC/OD data.  
3. **Solve MILP**: The MILP above yields the *binary* decisions (train start times, composition, rolling‑stock allocation) **for the whole horizon**.  
4. **Implementation**: Apply only the decisions for the **first interval** (receding‑horizon principle); shift the horizon forward and repeat.  

Because the binary part is the main source of computational difficulty, the **learning‑driven presolve** described in the source text (e.g., LSTM prediction of a reduced set of *x*, *y*, *z* variables) can be inserted before solving the MILP: the predicted binary values are fixed, turning the problem into a pure linear program (LP) for the dwell times *g* and passenger flows *q*, *u*.  

---

### 9. Remarks & Extensions  

* **Stop‑skipping** – introduce binary \(s_{t,s}\) indicating whether train *t* stops at station *s*; modify (C5)–(C9) accordingly.  
* **Energy consumption** – replace the dwell‑time proxy by a linearised function of speed changes (e.g., extra running time).  
* **Robustness** – enlarge demand *d<sub>p</sub>* by a safety factor or add scenario‑based constraints (as in Liu 2024).  
* **Multiple lines / junctions** – replicate the index set *S* per line and add coupling constraints for shared rolling‑stock and track sections.  

The formulation above is **self‑contained**, **linear**, and captures the three core aspects highlighted in the literature review:  

1. **Time‑varying passenger demand** (through demand arcs *p* and piecewise‑constant *d<sub>p</sub>*).  
2. **Flexible train composition** (binary *y<sub>t,k</sub>* with capacity *β<sub>k</sub>*).  
3. **Rolling‑stock circulation** (binary *z<sub>t,r</sub>* with availability windows).  

It can be directly handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) inside an MPC framework, or combined with a learning‑based predictor to accelerate the binary decision stage.
