Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave – an integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under a track‑disruption.  
All symbols are defined first, then the **decision variables**, the **objective function**, and finally the **constraints** (with a short comment that explains the role of each group).  
The model is written in a textbook‑style algebraic form; any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP …) can read it directly after a trivial translation into the solver’s own syntax.

---

## 1. Sets and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**                | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S**                | Set of track sides (normally *S = {L,R}* for left/right). |
| **K**                | Set of track sections (or “track cells”) that a train traverses, indexed by *k* (ordered along the route). |
| **B**                | Set of train pairs \((i,j)\) that can potentially conflict (i.e. share a section‑side). |
| **Δmin\_{i,k}**       | Minimum dwell time of train *i* at the end of section *k*. |
| **L\_{k}**           | Length of section *k*. |
| **v\_max, v\_min**   | Global speed limits (km/h). |
| **a\_up, a\_down**   | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h per minute). |
| **c\_speed**         | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per (km/h)²·minute). |
| **M**                | “Big‑M’’ constant – a number larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶ min). |
| **T\_blk**           | Disruption time window \([t^{start},t^{end}]\). |
| **SideBlocked\_{k}** | Side of section *k* that is **blocked** during the disruption (∈ S ∪ {∅} if no block). |
| **PreRout\_{i,k}**    | Original side (L/R) that train *i* would use on section *k* before the disruption. |
| **w\_delay**         | Weight on total delay in the objective. |
| **w\_energy**        | Weight on total energy consumption in the objective. |
| **θ\_{i,k}(v)**       | Travel time of train *i* through section *k* when it uses speed *v* (normally *θ = L\_k / v*).  
  For a linear MILP we linearise this by piece‑wise constant speed‑level variables (see §2). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| **r\_{i,s}**   | binary | = 1 if train *i* uses side *s* ( L or R ) on **all** sections that are still reachable after rerouting; otherwise 0. |
| **o\_{i,j}**   | binary | = 1 if train *i* passes **before** train *j* on a common side/section, 0 otherwise (pairwise ordering). |
| **a\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at the **beginning** of section *k* (i.e. when it enters the section). |
| **d\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from the **end** of section *k* (i.e. when it leaves the section). |
| **v\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Chosen average speed of train *i* on section *k*. (bounded by *v\_min* and *v\_max*). |
| **p\_{i,k}**   | binary | Speed‑level indicator used for linearisation of the quadratic energy term (see below). Typically a set of levels  ℓ = 1…L; p\_{i,k,ℓ}=1 ⇔ speed v\_{i,k}=v\_ℓ. For brevity we keep a single *v\_{i,k}* and later replace \(v_{i,k}^2\) by a linear approximation. |

*Note:* The model can be made **purely linear** by (i) discretising the admissible speed range into a small set of levels (e.g. 3‑5 levels) and (ii) using a linear expression for energy, i.e.  

\[
E = \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K} \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} c\_{\text{speed},\ell}\; p_{i,k,\ell}\; \theta_{i,k,\ell},
\]  

where \(c_{\text{speed},\ell}=c\_{\text{speed}}\,v_\ell^{2}\) and \(\theta_{i,k,\ell}=L_k/v_\ell\).  
Below we write the MILP with *v\_{i,k}* as a continuous variable and later replace the quadratic term with its linearised counterpart.

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,|K|} - a_{i,|K|}^{\text{orig}}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger‑delay}} \;
+\; \underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K} c_{\text{speed}}\;v_{i,k}^{2}\;\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

*Explanation*  

* **Delay term** – the difference between the actual arrival at the *last* section of the train’s itinerary \((a_{i,|K|})\) and the originally planned arrival \(a_{i,|K|}^{\text{orig}}\).  
* **Energy term** – for every section the energy is proportional to the squared speed (a well‑known approximation for aerodynamic drag) multiplied by the travel time on that section. Because the product \(v^{2}\cdot \theta = v^{2}\cdot L_k/v = L_k\,v\) is still nonlinear, we linearise it in the implementation (see the “speed‑level” linearisation).  

Both components are weighted by user‑chosen importance coefficients \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\).

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice and side‑availability  

1. **Exactly one side per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T .
   \]

2. **Blocked side cannot be chosen during disruption**  

   \[
   r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in T,\; \forall k\in K\;\text{with}\;SideBlocked_{k}=s .
   \]

   (If a section’s blocked side is “∅” (no block) the constraint is inactive.)

3. **Link side choice to the binary occupancy on each section**  

   Introduce a binary occupancy variable  

   \[
   y_{i,k,s}\in\{0,1\} \quad\text{(train i uses side s on section k)} .
   \]

   Then  

   \[
   y_{i,k,s}\le r_{i,s} \qquad\forall i,k,s .
   \]

   (If a train chooses side s, it may occupy it on all sections; otherwise it cannot.)

### 4.2 Temporal‑flow (arrival–departure)  

4. **Travel‑time relation (linearised)**  

   \[
   a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+ \theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})  \qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K\setminus\{|K|\}.
   \]

   Using the piece‑wise linear speed levels, \(\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})\) becomes a linear combination of the \(\theta_{i,k,\ell}\) with the binary level variables \(p_{i,k,\ell}\).

5. **Dwell‑time (minimum stop) at stations**  

   \[
   d_{i,k}\ge a_{i,k}+ \Delta^{\min}_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in K_{\text{station}} .
   \]

### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance on a common side  

For every pair of trains that may occupy the same side of the same section we use the classic “big‑M ordering”:

6. **Order definition**  

   \[
   o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B .
   \]

   (Exactly one of the two trains passes first.)

7. **No‑overlap on the same side**  

   If both trains use side *s* on section *k* (i.e. \(y_{i,k,s}=y_{j,k,s}=1\)), then  

   \[
   a_{j,k} \ge d_{i,k} - M\,(1-o_{i,j}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\;k\in K,\;s\in S .
   \]

   Similarly,  

   \[
   a_{i,k} \ge d_{j,k} - M\,(1-o_{j,i}) .
   \]

   The big‑M term de‑activates the inequality when the ordering variable indicates the opposite order.

### 4.4 Speed‑related physical limits  

8. **Speed bounds**  

   \[
   v_{\min}\le v_{i,k}\le v_{\max} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

9. **Acceleration / deceleration limits between successive sections**  

   \[
   v_{i,k+1}-v_{i,k}\le a_{\uparrow}\,\Delta t_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

   \[
   v_{i,k}-v_{i,k+1}\le a_{\downarrow}\,\Delta t_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

   where \(\Delta t_{i,k}=d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\) (the actual dwell + travel time on section *k*). If you prefer a simpler linear bound, you can directly bound the difference between successive speeds with a constant:  

   \[
   -a_{\downarrow}\le v_{i,k+1}-v_{i,k}\le a_{\uparrow}.
   \]

### 4.5 Flow‑conservation for rerouting (optional)  

If a train may switch side only at a predefined “junction” set \(J\subset K\):

10. **Side‑switch only at junctions**  

    \[
    y_{i,k,s}=y_{i,k-1,s} \qquad\forall i,\;k\notin J,\;s\in S .
    \]

    (Side can change only when the index belongs to the junction set.)

### 4.6 Transitivity of the ordering (to avoid cycles)  

11. **Transitivity constraints** (only needed if the model size is moderate; otherwise a subtour‑elimination‐type cut is added lazily)

    \[
    o_{i,j}+o_{j,l}-o_{i,l}\le 1 \qquad\forall i,j,l\in T .
    \]

### 4.7 Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

If we keep *v\_{i,k}* continuous, introduce an auxiliary variable  

\[
e_{i,k}=v_{i,k}^{2}
\]

and enforce a **piece‑wise linear** approximation:

12. **Convex hull of the quadratic function**  

   Choose a set of break‑points \(\{(v^{\ell}, (v^{\ell})^{2})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\).  
   Let \(\lambda_{i,k,\ell}\) be the convex‑combination weights (continuous, ≥0, sum to 1). Then  

   \[
   v_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   e_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} (v^{\ell})^{2}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   \sum_{\ell}\lambda_{i,k,\ell}=1 .
   \]

   The energy part of the objective becomes linear in *e\_{i,k}* :

   \[
   \text{Energy}=w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i,k} c_{\text{speed}}\, e_{i,k}\,\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k}) .
   \]

   Because \(\theta_{i,k}(v)=L_k/v\) is also nonlinear, we replace it by the pre‑computed travel‑time for each breakpoint:

   \[
   \theta_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} \frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell}.
   \]

   The product \(e_{i,k}\theta_{i,k}\) is still bilinear; a common alternative is to **directly model energy as**  

   \[
   \text{Energy}= \sum_{i,k,\ell} c_{\text{speed}}\; (v^{\ell})^{2}\; \frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}} \; \lambda_{i,k,\ell}
               =\sum_{i,k,\ell} c_{\text{speed}}\; L_k \; v^{\ell}\; \lambda_{i,k,\ell},
   \]

   which is **purely linear**. Hence, in the final linear MILP we use the speed‑level variables \(p_{i,k,\ell}\) (the same as \(\lambda\) above) and the objective term

   \[
   w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
          \bigl(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\bigr)\; p_{i,k,\ell}.
   \]

   The constraints linking \(v_{i,k}\) to the level variables are  

   \[
   v_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}\,p_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   \sum_{\ell} p_{i,k,\ell}=1\qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

---

## 5. Full Linear MILP (compact form)

Putting everything together, the **final linear model** reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,|K|}-a^{\text{orig}}_{i,|K|}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
       \bigl(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\bigr)\,p_{i,k,\ell}  \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\qquad
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1                                    &&\forall i\\
&\qquad
r_{i,s}=0 \;\; \text{if }SideBlocked_{k}=s                &&\forall i,k,s\\[2pt]
&\qquad
y_{i,k,s}\le r_{i,s}                                      &&\forall i,k,s\\[2pt]
&\qquad
a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+ \sum_{\ell}\frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}}\,p_{i,k,\ell}
                                                            &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
d_{i,k}\ge a_{i,k}+ \Delta^{\min}_{i,k}                     &&\forall i,k\in K_{\text{station}}\\[2pt]
&\qquad
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1                                          &&\forall (i,j)\in B\\
&\qquad
a_{j,k}\ge d_{i,k}-M(1-o_{i,j}) \;\; \forall (i,j)\in B,\;k,s
      \text{ with }y_{i,k,s}=y_{j,k,s}=1                &&\text{(big‑M)}\\[2pt]
&\qquad
v_{\min}\le \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k,\ell}\le v_{\max}   &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
-\;a_{\downarrow}\le \Bigl(\sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k+1,\ell}
            -\sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k,\ell}\Bigr)\le a_{\uparrow}
                                                            &&\forall i,k\\[2pt]
&\qquad
y_{i,k,s}=y_{i,k-1,s} \;\; \forall i,\;k\notin J,\;s\in S   &&\text{(side‑switch only at junction)}\\
&\qquad
\sum_{\ell} p_{i,k,\ell}=1                                 &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
p_{i,k,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,k,s},\; r_{i,s},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\} \\
&\qquad
a_{i,k},d_{i,k}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; binary variables appear only in the side choice, ordering, and speed‑level decisions. The model therefore belongs to the **MILP** class and can be handed to any branch‑and‑bound solver.

---

## 6. What each part does (plain‑English recap)

| Block | What it enforces |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Route‑choice** | Every train must decide once and for all whether it will stay on the left or right side of the track. The side that is blocked by the disruption cannot be chosen. |
| **Timing flow** | Arrival → travel (travel time depends on the speed level) → departure, with a mandatory minimum dwell at stations. |
| **Conflict‑avoidance** | If two trains would occupy the same side of the same section, a binary ordering variable forces one to finish before the other enters (big‑M formulation). |
| **Speed limits & dynamics** | Keeps the chosen speed inside physical limits and respects acceleration/deceleration capabilities between consecutive sections. |
| **Side‑switch rule** (optional) | Allows a train to change from left to right only at predefined junctions, guaranteeing a feasible track topology. |
| **Transitivity** | Guarantees that the pairwise order variables do not create cycles (i.e. the ordering is a partial order). |
| **Energy linearisation** | Replaces the non‑linear \(v^{2}\) term by a set of discrete speed levels; the coefficient \(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\) exactly corresponds to the energy cost of travelling section *k* with speed level *ℓ*. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay (difference between actual and planned arrival) and the total energy consumption of all trains. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, K, S, B*, compute the original arrival times \(a^{\text{orig}}_{i,|K|}\), define the disruption window *T\_blk* and the blocked side per section. Choose a small number of speed levels (e.g. 3: 40 km/h, 60 km/h, 80 km/h) and compute the corresponding travel‑time and energy coefficients.  
2. **Parameter tuning** – Set the weights *w\_delay* and *w\_energy* according to the operator’s policy (e.g. prioritize punctuality).  
3. **Implementation** – Encode the variables and constraints in the modelling language of your favourite solver (Python‑PuLP, Gurobi‑Py, AMPL, Julia‑JuMP, …).  
4. **Solve** – Run the MILP solver; the result gives for each train the chosen side (*r*), the speed level on every section (*p*), and the exact arrival/departure schedule (*a*,*d*).  

The presented MILP is fully self‑contained, linear, and captures the essential interactions between **routing**, **conflict resolution**, **speed management**, **disruption handling**, and the **trade‑off between delay and energy** you asked for.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main decisions described in the request  

* **Route choice** – which side of a track segment a train may use while a disruption blocks one side.  
* **Temporal ordering** – which train passes a shared resource (a side of a segment or a station platform) first, to avoid collisions.  
* **Speed management** – selection of a discrete speed level for every train on every section of track, which influences travel time and the energy cost.

The model is written in the **standard MILP form** (linear objective, linear constraints, binary and continuous variables).  Wherever a non‑linear term would appear (e.g. the quadratic energy term) we replace it by a **linearisation with auxiliary continuous variables** and a set of “big‑M’’ constraints.  All sets, parameters and variables are defined first; then the objective function; finally the constraints are grouped by theme.  After the formulation a short narrative explains every piece.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *i, j* |
| **S**   | Set of sides of a two‑track segment (normally *S={L,R}*), indexed by *s* |
| **K\_i**| Ordered set of **track sections** traversed by train *i* (including stations).  Index *k* runs from 1 to |K\_i|. |
| **V**   | Finite set of admissible speed levels (e.g.  V={v¹,…,v^P}), indexed by *p* |
| **Δ**   | Set of unordered train pairs that ever share a side (potential conflict pairs). |

Additional derived sets  

* **K\_i⁺ = {k | k = 1,…,|K\_i|−1 }** – sections that have a *next* section.  
* **K\_i⁻ = {k | k = 2,…,|K\_i| }** – sections that have a *previous* section.

---

## 2️⃣  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **L\_{i,k}** | Length of section *k* for train *i* (km). |
| **τ\_{i,k}^{min}**, **τ\_{i,k}^{max}** | Minimum / maximum travel time that can be obtained on section *k* for train *i* (seconds).  They are derived from the speed limits and acceleration limits. |
| **d\_{i,k}^{min}** | Minimum dwell (station stop) time for train *i* on section *k* (seconds).  Zero if the section is not a station. |
| **c\_{p}** | Energy coefficient for speed level *p* (kWh · s⁻¹).  The original quadratic term *c\*v²* is pre‑computed for each discrete speed level. |
| **M\_{i,j}** | Large positive constant (big‑M) used to linearise ordering constraints.  Typically set larger than the maximum possible schedule horizon (e.g. 10⁶ s). |
| **B\_{s,k}** | Binary flag = 1 if side *s* of the physical segment that contains section *k* is **blocked** (disruption), 0 otherwise. |
| **w\_{delay}**, **w\_{energy}** | Positive weights determining the relative importance of total delay vs. energy consumption in the objective. |
| **T₀\_{i}** | Planned (baseline) arrival time of train *i* at the first node of its route (seconds). |
| **β\_{i,k}** | Minimum admissible speed level on section *k* for train *i* (index in V).  (e.g. due to curvature). |
| **α\_{i,k}** | Maximum admissible speed level on section *k* for train *i* (index in V). |

---

## 3️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r\_{i,s}** | binary | 1 if train *i* uses side *s* on every section of its (original) route; 0 otherwise.  For rerouting we allow a train to switch side at most once – see flow constraints. |
| **o\_{i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *i* is scheduled **after** train *j* on a common side (i.e. *i* passes the conflict point later).  For each conflicting pair *(i,j)∈Δ* we have *o\_{i,j}+o\_{j,i}=1*. |
| **a\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at the **beginning** of section *k*. |
| **d\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from the **end** of section *k* (i.e. after any dwell). |
| **v\_{i,k,p}** | binary | 1 if train *i* travels on section *k* with speed level *p∈V*.  For each *(i,k)* exactly one speed level is chosen: ∑\_{p∈V} v\_{i,k,p}=1. |
| **τ\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *i* on section *k* (seconds).  It will be linked to the chosen speed level. |
| **E** | continuous ≥0 | Total (linearised) energy consumption, to be minimised in the objective. |
| **Δa\_{i}** | continuous ≥0 | Total delay of train *i* (difference between actual arrival at its final node and the planned arrival).  Used for the objective. |

---

## 4️⃣  Linearisation of the Energy Term  

The *real* energy for a section would be  

\[
\text{energy}_{i,k}=c\;v_{i,k}^{2}\;\tau_{i,k} .
\]

Because we restrict **v** to a finite set *V* we pre‑compute a constant **c\_p** for each speed level *p* that already contains the factor *v_{p}^{2}*.  Then we can write

\[
\text{energy}_{i,k}= \sum_{p\in V} c_{p}\; \tau_{i,k}\; v_{i,k,p}.
\]

The product of a continuous variable (τ) and a binary variable (v) is linear because τ can be bounded by known min/max travel times for that speed level:

\[
\tau_{i,k}^{\min}(p)\,v_{i,k,p} \le \tau_{i,k} \le \tau_{i,k}^{\max}(p)\,v_{i,k,p},
\quad\forall p\in V .
\]

Summing for all *p* gives the exact value of τ when exactly one binary *v\_{i,k,p}=1*.

The total energy is then

\[
E \;=\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K_i}\sum_{p\in V} c_{p}\,\tau_{i,k}\,v_{i,k,p}.
\]

Because all products involve a binary variable, the expression is linear.

---

## 5️⃣  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \;  w_{delay}\; \sum_{i\in T}\Delta a_i \;+\; w_{energy}\;E
}
\]

*The first term penalises the sum of all train delays; the second term penalises the total energy consumption.*

---

## 6️⃣  Constraints  

### 6.1  Route‑choice and disruption  

1. **Side feasibility:** a train cannot be assigned to a blocked side  

\[
r_{i,s}\; \le\; 1- B_{s,k}\qquad \forall i\in T,\; \forall k\in K_i,\; \forall s\in S .
\]

(If any section *k* belonging to train *i* lies on a blocked side *s*, the RHS becomes 0, forcing *r\_{i,s}=0*.)

2. **Exactly one side is used (original network has two sides).**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T .
\]

If a train is rerouted, the model can allow a **side‑change** at a pre‑defined “switch node’’ – this can be handled by duplicate binary variables; for brevity we keep the simple formulation above.

---

### 6.2  Temporal dynamics (travel‑time linking)  

3. **Travel‑time definition (linked to speed level).** For every *(i,k)*  

\[
\tau_{i,k}= \sum_{p\in V}\tau^{p}_{i,k}\;v_{i,k,p},
\qquad 
\text{with } \tau^{p}_{i,k}= \frac{L_{i,k}}{v_{p}} .
\]

Because *v\_{i,k,p}* is binary, the equation is linear.

4. **Sequencing of arrival / departure across sections**  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ \tau_{i,k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+}.
\]

5. **Dwell time (minimum stop at stations).**  

\[
d_{i,k}\; \ge\; a_{i,k}+ d^{\min}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

If a section is not a station, set \(d^{\min}_{i,k}=0\).

6. **Delay definition** – let *f\_i* be the index of the final section for train *i*.  

\[
\Delta a_i \; \ge\; a_{i,f_i} - T^{0}_{i}\qquad\forall i\in T .
\]

(If the schedule is already later than the baseline, the difference is the delay; otherwise the constraint is inactive because Δa_i is non‑negative.)

---

### 6.3  Conflict‑resolution ordering  

Consider any unordered pair *(i,j)∈Δ* that may occupy the **same side** *s* of a segment at the same time. Let *C(i,j)* be the **conflict point** (the beginning of the overlapping section). We enforce a classic big‑M ordering:

7. **Mutual exclusion (big‑M):**  

\[
a_{i,c} \; \ge\; d_{j,c} \;-\; M_{i,j}\,o_{j,i}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,
\]  

\[
a_{j,c} \; \ge\; d_{i,c} \;-\; M_{i,j}\,o_{i,j}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,
\]

where *c* denotes the **entry node** of the common side.  

8. **Binary ordering relationship:**  

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta .
\]

9. **Side‑compatibility:** the ordering constraints only apply when both trains are on the same side:  

\[
o_{i,j}\; \le\; r_{i,s}+r_{j,s} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,\; s\in S .
\]

If the trains use different sides, the RHS ≤1 makes the ordering variable forced to 0, de‑activating the big‑M constraints.

---

### 6.4  Speed‑level feasibility  

10. **Exactly one speed per section**  

\[
\sum_{p\in V} v_{i,k,p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

11. **Speed‑range (respect vehicle‑specific limits).**  

\[
\beta_{i,k}\; \le\; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p}\; \le\; \alpha_{i,k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

(If *V* is ordered, the left‑hand side can be expressed with binary “interval’’ variables; the compact formulation above works when *p* is numeric.)

12. **Acceleration / deceleration limits** – between two consecutive sections the selected speed levels must respect a maximum change Δv\_{max}.  

Let *Δp* be the numeric speed difference between two levels. Then

\[
\sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k+1,p} \; - \; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p}
\;\le\; \Delta v^{\max}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+},
\]

\[
\sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p} \; - \; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k+1,p}
\;\le\; \Delta v^{\max}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+}.
\]

These are linear because each sum is a weighted combination of binaries.

---

### 6.5  Transitivity of ordering (optional but improves LP‑relaxation)  

13. **If i after j and j after ℓ, then i after ℓ**  

\[
o_{i,\ell} \; \ge\; o_{i,j}+o_{j,\ell}-1
\qquad\forall i,j,\ell\in T \text{ distinct, that share a side}.
\]

---

### 6.6  Big‑M values  

All big‑M constants are chosen conservatively:

* \(M_{i,j}= \text{Horizon}= \max_{i}(\text{latest possible arrival})\) – e.g. 10⁶ s.  
* In the speed‑change constraints, Δv\_{max} is computed from the physical acceleration limit multiplied by the minimum travel time of the section.

---

## 7️⃣  Summary of the Model  

| Component | Decision variables | Main constraints | Physical meaning |
|-----------|--------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Route choice** | *r\_{i,s}* (binary) | side feasibility (1), exactly‑one‑side (2) | Determines which side of a two‑track segment each train may occupy respecting the disruption. |
| **Temporal ordering** | *o\_{i,j}* (binary) | mutual exclusion (7‑9), ordering sum (8) | Guarantees that two trains never occupy the same side at the same time; decides who goes first. |
| **Timing** | *a\_{i,k}, d\_{i,k}* (continuous) | sequencing (4‑5), delay definition (6) | Propagates arrivals/departures along the itinerary, enforces dwell times and records delays. |
| **Speed management** | *v\_{i,k,p}* (binary), *τ\_{i,k}* (continuous), *E* (continuous) | speed‑choice (10‑12), travel‑time linking (3), energy linearisation (see §4) | Selects a discrete speed level for each section, controls travel time, and measures energy use. |
| **Physical limits** | – | acceleration limits (12), speed bounds (11) | Guarantees that chosen speeds are feasible for the train and the infrastructure. |
| **Objective** | – | – | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay (∑Δa\_i) and total energy (E). |

The model is **linear** (all products involve at most one binary factor), hence solvable with any commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.).  By tuning the weights *w\_{delay}* and *w\_{energy}* the planner can explore the trade‑off between keeping passengers on time and limiting fuel/electricity consumption while respecting disruption‑induced side closures, safety‑critical conflict avoidance, and physical speed limits.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP. Variables: binary route choice r_{i,s} for train i using side s of segment during disruption, binary order o_{i,j} for conflict resolution, continuous arrival times a_{i,k}, departure times d_{i,k}, speed levels v_{i,k} per track section. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption (energy = sum_i sum_k c_speed * v_{i,k}^2 * travel_time). Constraints: sequential timing a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+travel_time_{i,k}(v), dwell time min, binary ordering ensures no two trains occupy same side at same time, disruption window prohibits use of blocked side, route choice linking to binary side, speed limits bounds, acceleration/deceleration limits linking successive v, flow conservation for rerouting, total order transitivity, and big-M for ordering constraints.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave – an integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem under a track‑disruption.  
All symbols are defined first, then the **decision variables**, the **objective function**, and finally the **constraints** (with a short comment that explains the role of each group).  
The model is written in a textbook‑style algebraic form; any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP …) can read it directly after a trivial translation into the solver’s own syntax.

---

## 1. Sets and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**                | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S**                | Set of track sides (normally *S = {L,R}* for left/right). |
| **K**                | Set of track sections (or “track cells”) that a train traverses, indexed by *k* (ordered along the route). |
| **B**                | Set of train pairs \((i,j)\) that can potentially conflict (i.e. share a section‑side). |
| **Δmin\_{i,k}**       | Minimum dwell time of train *i* at the end of section *k*. |
| **L\_{k}**           | Length of section *k*. |
| **v\_max, v\_min**   | Global speed limits (km/h). |
| **a\_up, a\_down**   | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h per minute). |
| **c\_speed**         | Energy‑cost coefficient (e.g. kWh per (km/h)²·minute). |
| **M**                | “Big‑M’’ constant – a number larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶ min). |
| **T\_blk**           | Disruption time window \([t^{start},t^{end}]\). |
| **SideBlocked\_{k}** | Side of section *k* that is **blocked** during the disruption (∈ S ∪ {∅} if no block). |
| **PreRout\_{i,k}**    | Original side (L/R) that train *i* would use on section *k* before the disruption. |
| **w\_delay**         | Weight on total delay in the objective. |
| **w\_energy**        | Weight on total energy consumption in the objective. |
| **θ\_{i,k}(v)**       | Travel time of train *i* through section *k* when it uses speed *v* (normally *θ = L\_k / v*).  
  For a linear MILP we linearise this by piece‑wise constant speed‑level variables (see §2). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| **r\_{i,s}**   | binary | = 1 if train *i* uses side *s* ( L or R ) on **all** sections that are still reachable after rerouting; otherwise 0. |
| **o\_{i,j}**   | binary | = 1 if train *i* passes **before** train *j* on a common side/section, 0 otherwise (pairwise ordering). |
| **a\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at the **beginning** of section *k* (i.e. when it enters the section). |
| **d\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from the **end** of section *k* (i.e. when it leaves the section). |
| **v\_{i,k}**   | continuous, ≥0 | Chosen average speed of train *i* on section *k*. (bounded by *v\_min* and *v\_max*). |
| **p\_{i,k}**   | binary | Speed‑level indicator used for linearisation of the quadratic energy term (see below). Typically a set of levels  ℓ = 1…L; p\_{i,k,ℓ}=1 ⇔ speed v\_{i,k}=v\_ℓ. For brevity we keep a single *v\_{i,k}* and later replace \(v_{i,k}^2\) by a linear approximation. |

*Note:* The model can be made **purely linear** by (i) discretising the admissible speed range into a small set of levels (e.g. 3‑5 levels) and (ii) using a linear expression for energy, i.e.  

\[
E = \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K} \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} c\_{\text{speed},\ell}\; p_{i,k,\ell}\; \theta_{i,k,\ell},
\]  

where \(c_{\text{speed},\ell}=c\_{\text{speed}}\,v_\ell^{2}\) and \(\theta_{i,k,\ell}=L_k/v_\ell\).  
Below we write the MILP with *v\_{i,k}* as a continuous variable and later replace the quadratic term with its linearised counterpart.

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,|K|} - a_{i,|K|}^{\text{orig}}\bigr)}_{\text{total passenger‑delay}} \;
+\; \underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K} c_{\text{speed}}\;v_{i,k}^{2}\;\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})}_{\text{energy consumption}} .
\]

*Explanation*  

* **Delay term** – the difference between the actual arrival at the *last* section of the train’s itinerary \((a_{i,|K|})\) and the originally planned arrival \(a_{i,|K|}^{\text{orig}}\).  
* **Energy term** – for every section the energy is proportional to the squared speed (a well‑known approximation for aerodynamic drag) multiplied by the travel time on that section. Because the product \(v^{2}\cdot \theta = v^{2}\cdot L_k/v = L_k\,v\) is still nonlinear, we linearise it in the implementation (see the “speed‑level” linearisation).  

Both components are weighted by user‑chosen importance coefficients \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\).

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice and side‑availability  

1. **Exactly one side per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T .
   \]

2. **Blocked side cannot be chosen during disruption**  

   \[
   r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in T,\; \forall k\in K\;\text{with}\;SideBlocked_{k}=s .
   \]

   (If a section’s blocked side is “∅” (no block) the constraint is inactive.)

3. **Link side choice to the binary occupancy on each section**  

   Introduce a binary occupancy variable  

   \[
   y_{i,k,s}\in\{0,1\} \quad\text{(train i uses side s on section k)} .
   \]

   Then  

   \[
   y_{i,k,s}\le r_{i,s} \qquad\forall i,k,s .
   \]

   (If a train chooses side s, it may occupy it on all sections; otherwise it cannot.)

### 4.2 Temporal‑flow (arrival–departure)  

4. **Travel‑time relation (linearised)**  

   \[
   a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+ \theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})  \qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K\setminus\{|K|\}.
   \]

   Using the piece‑wise linear speed levels, \(\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k})\) becomes a linear combination of the \(\theta_{i,k,\ell}\) with the binary level variables \(p_{i,k,\ell}\).

5. **Dwell‑time (minimum stop) at stations**  

   \[
   d_{i,k}\ge a_{i,k}+ \Delta^{\min}_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in K_{\text{station}} .
   \]

### 4.3 Conflict‑avoidance on a common side  

For every pair of trains that may occupy the same side of the same section we use the classic “big‑M ordering”:

6. **Order definition**  

   \[
   o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B .
   \]

   (Exactly one of the two trains passes first.)

7. **No‑overlap on the same side**  

   If both trains use side *s* on section *k* (i.e. \(y_{i,k,s}=y_{j,k,s}=1\)), then  

   \[
   a_{j,k} \ge d_{i,k} - M\,(1-o_{i,j}) \qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\;k\in K,\;s\in S .
   \]

   Similarly,  

   \[
   a_{i,k} \ge d_{j,k} - M\,(1-o_{j,i}) .
   \]

   The big‑M term de‑activates the inequality when the ordering variable indicates the opposite order.

### 4.4 Speed‑related physical limits  

8. **Speed bounds**  

   \[
   v_{\min}\le v_{i,k}\le v_{\max} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

9. **Acceleration / deceleration limits between successive sections**  

   \[
   v_{i,k+1}-v_{i,k}\le a_{\uparrow}\,\Delta t_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

   \[
   v_{i,k}-v_{i,k+1}\le a_{\downarrow}\,\Delta t_{i,k} \qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

   where \(\Delta t_{i,k}=d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\) (the actual dwell + travel time on section *k*). If you prefer a simpler linear bound, you can directly bound the difference between successive speeds with a constant:  

   \[
   -a_{\downarrow}\le v_{i,k+1}-v_{i,k}\le a_{\uparrow}.
   \]

### 4.5 Flow‑conservation for rerouting (optional)  

If a train may switch side only at a predefined “junction” set \(J\subset K\):

10. **Side‑switch only at junctions**  

    \[
    y_{i,k,s}=y_{i,k-1,s} \qquad\forall i,\;k\notin J,\;s\in S .
    \]

    (Side can change only when the index belongs to the junction set.)

### 4.6 Transitivity of the ordering (to avoid cycles)  

11. **Transitivity constraints** (only needed if the model size is moderate; otherwise a subtour‑elimination‐type cut is added lazily)

    \[
    o_{i,j}+o_{j,l}-o_{i,l}\le 1 \qquad\forall i,j,l\in T .
    \]

### 4.7 Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

If we keep *v\_{i,k}* continuous, introduce an auxiliary variable  

\[
e_{i,k}=v_{i,k}^{2}
\]

and enforce a **piece‑wise linear** approximation:

12. **Convex hull of the quadratic function**  

   Choose a set of break‑points \(\{(v^{\ell}, (v^{\ell})^{2})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\).  
   Let \(\lambda_{i,k,\ell}\) be the convex‑combination weights (continuous, ≥0, sum to 1). Then  

   \[
   v_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   e_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} (v^{\ell})^{2}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   \sum_{\ell}\lambda_{i,k,\ell}=1 .
   \]

   The energy part of the objective becomes linear in *e\_{i,k}* :

   \[
   \text{Energy}=w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i,k} c_{\text{speed}}\, e_{i,k}\,\theta_{i,k}(v_{i,k}) .
   \]

   Because \(\theta_{i,k}(v)=L_k/v\) is also nonlinear, we replace it by the pre‑computed travel‑time for each breakpoint:

   \[
   \theta_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} \frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}}\,\lambda_{i,k,\ell}.
   \]

   The product \(e_{i,k}\theta_{i,k}\) is still bilinear; a common alternative is to **directly model energy as**  

   \[
   \text{Energy}= \sum_{i,k,\ell} c_{\text{speed}}\; (v^{\ell})^{2}\; \frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}} \; \lambda_{i,k,\ell}
               =\sum_{i,k,\ell} c_{\text{speed}}\; L_k \; v^{\ell}\; \lambda_{i,k,\ell},
   \]

   which is **purely linear**. Hence, in the final linear MILP we use the speed‑level variables \(p_{i,k,\ell}\) (the same as \(\lambda\) above) and the objective term

   \[
   w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
          \bigl(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\bigr)\; p_{i,k,\ell}.
   \]

   The constraints linking \(v_{i,k}\) to the level variables are  

   \[
   v_{i,k}= \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}\,p_{i,k,\ell},\qquad
   \sum_{\ell} p_{i,k,\ell}=1\qquad\forall i,k .
   \]

---

## 5. Full Linear MILP (compact form)

Putting everything together, the **final linear model** reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in T}\bigl(a_{i,|K|}-a^{\text{orig}}_{i,|K|}\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
       \bigl(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\bigr)\,p_{i,k,\ell}  \\[4pt]
\text{s.t.}&\qquad
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1                                    &&\forall i\\
&\qquad
r_{i,s}=0 \;\; \text{if }SideBlocked_{k}=s                &&\forall i,k,s\\[2pt]
&\qquad
y_{i,k,s}\le r_{i,s}                                      &&\forall i,k,s\\[2pt]
&\qquad
a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+ \sum_{\ell}\frac{L_k}{v^{\ell}}\,p_{i,k,\ell}
                                                            &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
d_{i,k}\ge a_{i,k}+ \Delta^{\min}_{i,k}                     &&\forall i,k\in K_{\text{station}}\\[2pt]
&\qquad
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1                                          &&\forall (i,j)\in B\\
&\qquad
a_{j,k}\ge d_{i,k}-M(1-o_{i,j}) \;\; \forall (i,j)\in B,\;k,s
      \text{ with }y_{i,k,s}=y_{j,k,s}=1                &&\text{(big‑M)}\\[2pt]
&\qquad
v_{\min}\le \sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k,\ell}\le v_{\max}   &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
-\;a_{\downarrow}\le \Bigl(\sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k+1,\ell}
            -\sum_{\ell} v^{\ell}p_{i,k,\ell}\Bigr)\le a_{\uparrow}
                                                            &&\forall i,k\\[2pt]
&\qquad
y_{i,k,s}=y_{i,k-1,s} \;\; \forall i,\;k\notin J,\;s\in S   &&\text{(side‑switch only at junction)}\\
&\qquad
\sum_{\ell} p_{i,k,\ell}=1                                 &&\forall i,k\\
&\qquad
p_{i,k,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,k,s},\; r_{i,s},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\} \\
&\qquad
a_{i,k},d_{i,k}\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; binary variables appear only in the side choice, ordering, and speed‑level decisions. The model therefore belongs to the **MILP** class and can be handed to any branch‑and‑bound solver.

---

## 6. What each part does (plain‑English recap)

| Block | What it enforces |
|-------|-------------------|
| **Route‑choice** | Every train must decide once and for all whether it will stay on the left or right side of the track. The side that is blocked by the disruption cannot be chosen. |
| **Timing flow** | Arrival → travel (travel time depends on the speed level) → departure, with a mandatory minimum dwell at stations. |
| **Conflict‑avoidance** | If two trains would occupy the same side of the same section, a binary ordering variable forces one to finish before the other enters (big‑M formulation). |
| **Speed limits & dynamics** | Keeps the chosen speed inside physical limits and respects acceleration/deceleration capabilities between consecutive sections. |
| **Side‑switch rule** (optional) | Allows a train to change from left to right only at predefined junctions, guaranteeing a feasible track topology. |
| **Transitivity** | Guarantees that the pairwise order variables do not create cycles (i.e. the ordering is a partial order). |
| **Energy linearisation** | Replaces the non‑linear \(v^{2}\) term by a set of discrete speed levels; the coefficient \(c_{\text{speed}}\,L_k\,v^{\ell}\) exactly corresponds to the energy cost of travelling section *k* with speed level *ℓ*. |
| **Objective** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay (difference between actual and planned arrival) and the total energy consumption of all trains. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, K, S, B*, compute the original arrival times \(a^{\text{orig}}_{i,|K|}\), define the disruption window *T\_blk* and the blocked side per section. Choose a small number of speed levels (e.g. 3: 40 km/h, 60 km/h, 80 km/h) and compute the corresponding travel‑time and energy coefficients.  
2. **Parameter tuning** – Set the weights *w\_delay* and *w\_energy* according to the operator’s policy (e.g. prioritize punctuality).  
3. **Implementation** – Encode the variables and constraints in the modelling language of your favourite solver (Python‑PuLP, Gurobi‑Py, AMPL, Julia‑JuMP, …).  
4. **Solve** – Run the MILP solver; the result gives for each train the chosen side (*r*), the speed level on every section (*p*), and the exact arrival/departure schedule (*a*,*d*).  

The presented MILP is fully self‑contained, linear, and captures the essential interactions between **routing**, **conflict resolution**, **speed management**, **disruption handling**, and the **trade‑off between delay and energy** you asked for.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP. Variables: binary route choice r_{i,s} for train i using side s of segment during disruption, binary order o_{i,j} for conflict resolution, continuous arrival times a_{i,k}, departure times d_{i,k}, speed levels v_{i,k} per track section. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption (energy = sum_i sum_k c_speed * v_{i,k}^2 * travel_time). Constraints: sequential timing a_{i,k+1}=d_{i,k}+travel_time_{i,k}(v), dwell time min, binary ordering ensures no two trains occupy same side at same time, disruption window prohibits use of blocked side, route choice linking to binary side, speed limits bounds, acceleration/deceleration limits linking successive v, flow conservation for rerouting, total order transitivity, and big-M for ordering constraints.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main decisions described in the request  

* **Route choice** – which side of a track segment a train may use while a disruption blocks one side.  
* **Temporal ordering** – which train passes a shared resource (a side of a segment or a station platform) first, to avoid collisions.  
* **Speed management** – selection of a discrete speed level for every train on every section of track, which influences travel time and the energy cost.

The model is written in the **standard MILP form** (linear objective, linear constraints, binary and continuous variables).  Wherever a non‑linear term would appear (e.g. the quadratic energy term) we replace it by a **linearisation with auxiliary continuous variables** and a set of “big‑M’’ constraints.  All sets, parameters and variables are defined first; then the objective function; finally the constraints are grouped by theme.  After the formulation a short narrative explains every piece.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**   | Set of trains, indexed by *i, j* |
| **S**   | Set of sides of a two‑track segment (normally *S={L,R}*), indexed by *s* |
| **K\_i**| Ordered set of **track sections** traversed by train *i* (including stations).  Index *k* runs from 1 to |K\_i|. |
| **V**   | Finite set of admissible speed levels (e.g.  V={v¹,…,v^P}), indexed by *p* |
| **Δ**   | Set of unordered train pairs that ever share a side (potential conflict pairs). |

Additional derived sets  

* **K\_i⁺ = {k | k = 1,…,|K\_i|−1 }** – sections that have a *next* section.  
* **K\_i⁻ = {k | k = 2,…,|K\_i| }** – sections that have a *previous* section.

---

## 2️⃣  Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **L\_{i,k}** | Length of section *k* for train *i* (km). |
| **τ\_{i,k}^{min}**, **τ\_{i,k}^{max}** | Minimum / maximum travel time that can be obtained on section *k* for train *i* (seconds).  They are derived from the speed limits and acceleration limits. |
| **d\_{i,k}^{min}** | Minimum dwell (station stop) time for train *i* on section *k* (seconds).  Zero if the section is not a station. |
| **c\_{p}** | Energy coefficient for speed level *p* (kWh · s⁻¹).  The original quadratic term *c\*v²* is pre‑computed for each discrete speed level. |
| **M\_{i,j}** | Large positive constant (big‑M) used to linearise ordering constraints.  Typically set larger than the maximum possible schedule horizon (e.g. 10⁶ s). |
| **B\_{s,k}** | Binary flag = 1 if side *s* of the physical segment that contains section *k* is **blocked** (disruption), 0 otherwise. |
| **w\_{delay}**, **w\_{energy}** | Positive weights determining the relative importance of total delay vs. energy consumption in the objective. |
| **T₀\_{i}** | Planned (baseline) arrival time of train *i* at the first node of its route (seconds). |
| **β\_{i,k}** | Minimum admissible speed level on section *k* for train *i* (index in V).  (e.g. due to curvature). |
| **α\_{i,k}** | Maximum admissible speed level on section *k* for train *i* (index in V). |

---

## 3️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **r\_{i,s}** | binary | 1 if train *i* uses side *s* on every section of its (original) route; 0 otherwise.  For rerouting we allow a train to switch side at most once – see flow constraints. |
| **o\_{i,j}** | binary | 1 if train *i* is scheduled **after** train *j* on a common side (i.e. *i* passes the conflict point later).  For each conflicting pair *(i,j)∈Δ* we have *o\_{i,j}+o\_{j,i}=1*. |
| **a\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at the **beginning** of section *k*. |
| **d\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from the **end** of section *k* (i.e. after any dwell). |
| **v\_{i,k,p}** | binary | 1 if train *i* travels on section *k* with speed level *p∈V*.  For each *(i,k)* exactly one speed level is chosen: ∑\_{p∈V} v\_{i,k,p}=1. |
| **τ\_{i,k}** | continuous ≥0 | Actual travel time of train *i* on section *k* (seconds).  It will be linked to the chosen speed level. |
| **E** | continuous ≥0 | Total (linearised) energy consumption, to be minimised in the objective. |
| **Δa\_{i}** | continuous ≥0 | Total delay of train *i* (difference between actual arrival at its final node and the planned arrival).  Used for the objective. |

---

## 4️⃣  Linearisation of the Energy Term  

The *real* energy for a section would be  

\[
\text{energy}_{i,k}=c\;v_{i,k}^{2}\;\tau_{i,k} .
\]

Because we restrict **v** to a finite set *V* we pre‑compute a constant **c\_p** for each speed level *p* that already contains the factor *v_{p}^{2}*.  Then we can write

\[
\text{energy}_{i,k}= \sum_{p\in V} c_{p}\; \tau_{i,k}\; v_{i,k,p}.
\]

The product of a continuous variable (τ) and a binary variable (v) is linear because τ can be bounded by known min/max travel times for that speed level:

\[
\tau_{i,k}^{\min}(p)\,v_{i,k,p} \le \tau_{i,k} \le \tau_{i,k}^{\max}(p)\,v_{i,k,p},
\quad\forall p\in V .
\]

Summing for all *p* gives the exact value of τ when exactly one binary *v\_{i,k,p}=1*.

The total energy is then

\[
E \;=\;\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K_i}\sum_{p\in V} c_{p}\,\tau_{i,k}\,v_{i,k,p}.
\]

Because all products involve a binary variable, the expression is linear.

---

## 5️⃣  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \;  w_{delay}\; \sum_{i\in T}\Delta a_i \;+\; w_{energy}\;E
}
\]

*The first term penalises the sum of all train delays; the second term penalises the total energy consumption.*

---

## 6️⃣  Constraints  

### 6.1  Route‑choice and disruption  

1. **Side feasibility:** a train cannot be assigned to a blocked side  

\[
r_{i,s}\; \le\; 1- B_{s,k}\qquad \forall i\in T,\; \forall k\in K_i,\; \forall s\in S .
\]

(If any section *k* belonging to train *i* lies on a blocked side *s*, the RHS becomes 0, forcing *r\_{i,s}=0*.)

2. **Exactly one side is used (original network has two sides).**  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T .
\]

If a train is rerouted, the model can allow a **side‑change** at a pre‑defined “switch node’’ – this can be handled by duplicate binary variables; for brevity we keep the simple formulation above.

---

### 6.2  Temporal dynamics (travel‑time linking)  

3. **Travel‑time definition (linked to speed level).** For every *(i,k)*  

\[
\tau_{i,k}= \sum_{p\in V}\tau^{p}_{i,k}\;v_{i,k,p},
\qquad 
\text{with } \tau^{p}_{i,k}= \frac{L_{i,k}}{v_{p}} .
\]

Because *v\_{i,k,p}* is binary, the equation is linear.

4. **Sequencing of arrival / departure across sections**  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ \tau_{i,k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+}.
\]

5. **Dwell time (minimum stop at stations).**  

\[
d_{i,k}\; \ge\; a_{i,k}+ d^{\min}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

If a section is not a station, set \(d^{\min}_{i,k}=0\).

6. **Delay definition** – let *f\_i* be the index of the final section for train *i*.  

\[
\Delta a_i \; \ge\; a_{i,f_i} - T^{0}_{i}\qquad\forall i\in T .
\]

(If the schedule is already later than the baseline, the difference is the delay; otherwise the constraint is inactive because Δa_i is non‑negative.)

---

### 6.3  Conflict‑resolution ordering  

Consider any unordered pair *(i,j)∈Δ* that may occupy the **same side** *s* of a segment at the same time. Let *C(i,j)* be the **conflict point** (the beginning of the overlapping section). We enforce a classic big‑M ordering:

7. **Mutual exclusion (big‑M):**  

\[
a_{i,c} \; \ge\; d_{j,c} \;-\; M_{i,j}\,o_{j,i}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,
\]  

\[
a_{j,c} \; \ge\; d_{i,c} \;-\; M_{i,j}\,o_{i,j}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,
\]

where *c* denotes the **entry node** of the common side.  

8. **Binary ordering relationship:**  

\[
o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta .
\]

9. **Side‑compatibility:** the ordering constraints only apply when both trains are on the same side:  

\[
o_{i,j}\; \le\; r_{i,s}+r_{j,s} \qquad\forall (i,j)\in\Delta,\; s\in S .
\]

If the trains use different sides, the RHS ≤1 makes the ordering variable forced to 0, de‑activating the big‑M constraints.

---

### 6.4  Speed‑level feasibility  

10. **Exactly one speed per section**  

\[
\sum_{p\in V} v_{i,k,p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

11. **Speed‑range (respect vehicle‑specific limits).**  

\[
\beta_{i,k}\; \le\; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p}\; \le\; \alpha_{i,k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i .
\]

(If *V* is ordered, the left‑hand side can be expressed with binary “interval’’ variables; the compact formulation above works when *p* is numeric.)

12. **Acceleration / deceleration limits** – between two consecutive sections the selected speed levels must respect a maximum change Δv\_{max}.  

Let *Δp* be the numeric speed difference between two levels. Then

\[
\sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k+1,p} \; - \; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p}
\;\le\; \Delta v^{\max}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+},
\]

\[
\sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k,p} \; - \; \sum_{p\in V} p\;v_{i,k+1,p}
\;\le\; \Delta v^{\max}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;k\in K_i^{+}.
\]

These are linear because each sum is a weighted combination of binaries.

---

### 6.5  Transitivity of ordering (optional but improves LP‑relaxation)  

13. **If i after j and j after ℓ, then i after ℓ**  

\[
o_{i,\ell} \; \ge\; o_{i,j}+o_{j,\ell}-1
\qquad\forall i,j,\ell\in T \text{ distinct, that share a side}.
\]

---

### 6.6  Big‑M values  

All big‑M constants are chosen conservatively:

* \(M_{i,j}= \text{Horizon}= \max_{i}(\text{latest possible arrival})\) – e.g. 10⁶ s.  
* In the speed‑change constraints, Δv\_{max} is computed from the physical acceleration limit multiplied by the minimum travel time of the section.

---

## 7️⃣  Summary of the Model  

| Component | Decision variables | Main constraints | Physical meaning |
|-----------|--------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **Route choice** | *r\_{i,s}* (binary) | side feasibility (1), exactly‑one‑side (2) | Determines which side of a two‑track segment each train may occupy respecting the disruption. |
| **Temporal ordering** | *o\_{i,j}* (binary) | mutual exclusion (7‑9), ordering sum (8) | Guarantees that two trains never occupy the same side at the same time; decides who goes first. |
| **Timing** | *a\_{i,k}, d\_{i,k}* (continuous) | sequencing (4‑5), delay definition (6) | Propagates arrivals/departures along the itinerary, enforces dwell times and records delays. |
| **Speed management** | *v\_{i,k,p}* (binary), *τ\_{i,k}* (continuous), *E* (continuous) | speed‑choice (10‑12), travel‑time linking (3), energy linearisation (see §4) | Selects a discrete speed level for each section, controls travel time, and measures energy use. |
| **Physical limits** | – | acceleration limits (12), speed bounds (11) | Guarantees that chosen speeds are feasible for the train and the infrastructure. |
| **Objective** | – | – | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay (∑Δa\_i) and total energy (E). |

The model is **linear** (all products involve at most one binary factor), hence solvable with any commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, etc.).  By tuning the weights *w\_{delay}* and *w\_{energy}* the planner can explore the trade‑off between keeping passengers on time and limiting fuel/electricity consumption while respecting disruption‑induced side closures, safety‑critical conflict avoidance, and physical speed limits.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
