messages.content:
Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** when a subset of track segments is partially blocked.  
The model simultaneously decides **(i)** a routing (which train uses which alternative segment), **(ii)** the order in which trains occupy a single‑track segment, **(iii)** the departure/arrival times of every train at every node, and **(iv)** the speed at which a train traverses each free‑flow segment.  

The objective is a **weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and the energy consumed by all trains**.  
All constraints are linear (or linearised) so that a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress…) can solve the model directly.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| 𝑇 = {t} | Set of trains (|𝑇| = N). |
| 𝑁 = {i} | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points). |
| 𝐸 ⊆ 𝑁×𝑁 | Set of directed track **segments** (i,j). |
| 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ ⊆ 𝐸 | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (partial blockage). |
| 𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾ = 𝐸 \ 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | Free (unblocked) segments. |
| 𝐾ᵢⱼ ⊆ 𝐸  | Set of **alternative** segments that can be used to replace a blocked segment (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ (detour arcs). |
| 𝑆 = {s} | Set of **speed‑levels** (piecewise‑linear speed‑energy approximation). |
| 𝑇𝑚 = {τ} | Discrete time‑points (τ = 0,…,Tmax/Δτ). |
| 𝑂 = { (t₁,t₂,i,j) } | Ordered pairs of trains that may share a **single‑track** segment (i,j)∈𝐸 (i.e. they cannot occupy the segment simultaneously). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝐿ᵢⱼ   | Physical length of segment (i,j) | km |
| 𝑣̅ᵢⱼ  | Nominal speed limit on (i,j) (maximum admissible speed) | km/h |
| 𝑎⁺ , 𝑎⁻ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | km/h² |
| 𝑇ᵣᵉᵍ,𝑇ᵈᵉᵖ | Desired **release** (departure) and **arrival** times at the origin/destination of train t (timetable) | h |
| 𝑤ᴰ , 𝑤ᴱ | Scalar weights for delay and energy in the objective | – |
| 𝑑ᵢⱼˢ | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑level s on segment (i,j) (linearised) | kWh/km |
| 𝑣ˢ   | Speed value associated with speed‑level s (mid‑point of the piece) | km/h |
| 𝑀   | Large constant (big‑M) for linking constraints | – |
| 𝑈ᵢⱼ   | Capacity of a **single‑track** segment (i,j) – 1 train at a time | – |
| 𝑝ᵗᵢⱼ | Planned (original) travel time on (i,j) for train t (from timetable) | h |
| 𝑟ᵗᵢⱼ | Binary indicator =1 if train t is **required** to use segment (i,j) in the original schedule (routing‑requirement) | – |
| 𝑏ᵢⱼᵏ | Blockage time‑window on segment (i,j) (start, end) – only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | (h,h) |
| 𝜏ᵗᵢ   | Minimum dwell time of train t at node i (e.g., station dwell) | h |
| 𝑈ᵗ   | Set of admissible **paths** for train t (pre‑computed simple paths from origin to destination). Each path p∈𝑈ᵗ is a sequence of arcs.  |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| 𝑥ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) (routing decision). |
| 𝑦ᵗᵢⱼˢ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) **with speed level** *s* (only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾). |
| 𝑧ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **enters** segment (i,j) (used for ordering constraints). |
| 𝑤ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **leaves** segment (i,j). |
| 𝑇ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at node *i*. |
| 𝑑ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from node *i* (≥ 𝑇ᵗᵢ + dwell). |
| 𝛿ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment (i,j). |
| 𝑈ᵗ  (binary) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses a **detour** for a blocked segment (i.e., chooses an alternative arc from 𝐾ᵢⱼ). |
| 𝜋ᵗᵢⱼᵏ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the *k*‑th alternative arc to replace blocked (i,j). |
| 𝑂ᵗ₁ₜ₂ᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable: 1 if train *t₁* traverses (i,j) **before** train *t₂* (used only when (i,j) is single‑track). |
| 𝑙ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at destination and scheduled arrival). |
| 𝑒ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Energy** consumed by train *t* (sum over arcs and speed‑levels). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{ \; w^{D}\;\sum_{t\in T}  l^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{ \; w^{E}\;\sum_{t\in T}  e^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

where  

*Delay*  

\[
l^{t}= \; T^{t}_{\text{dest}} \;-\; T^{t}_{\text{sched\_arr}}
\]

*Energy* (linear piecewise approximation)  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S}\; d^{s}_{ij}\;  L_{ij}\; y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

\(d^{s}_{ij}\) is the energy coefficient (kWh per km) for speed level *s* on segment (i,j).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing (flow conservation)

For every train *t* and node *i* (except origin *oₜ* and destination *dₜ*)  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E} x^{t}_{ij} \;-\; \sum_{j:(j,i)\in E} x^{t}_{ji}=0
\]

Origin and destination  

\[
\sum_{j:(o_t,j)\in E} x^{t}_{o_t j}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j:(j,d_t)\in E} x^{t}_{j d_t}=1
\]

### 5.2 Mandatory arcs (original schedule)

If a segment is **required** for train *t* (e.g., because the original timetable uses it and no detour is defined), enforce  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}\; \ge\; r^{t}_{ij}\qquad \forall (i,j)\in E
\]

### 5.3 Detour / Blockage handling  

For every blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ and train *t* that would have used it (rᵗᵢⱼ = 1)  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}+ \sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}=1
\]

Only one alternative may be selected  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}\le 1
\]

If an alternative *k* is chosen, the corresponding arc must be traversed  

\[
\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le x^{t}_{i'_{k} j'_{k}}\qquad\forall k\in K_{ij}
\]

### 5.4 Speed‑level linking  

A speed level can be selected only if the arc is used  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}= x^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

Only one speed level per traversed arc  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}\le 1\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

### 5.5 Travel‑time definition (speed = distance / speed)

For a free‑flow segment (i,j)∈Eᶠ  

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}= \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}}\; y^{t}_{ij s}\quad\forall s\in S
\]

Because the model must stay linear, we use the big‑M linearisation:

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} - M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]
\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\le\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} + M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]

Only the selected speed‑level will bind the travel‑time.

### 5.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (between consecutive arcs)

If train *t* leaves node *i* at time \(d^{t}_{i}\) and enters next arc (i,j), the departure speed cannot exceed the admissible speed of the next arc plus the acceleration capability. Using the speed‑level representation, a simple linear bound is

\[
v^{s_{next}} \;-\; v^{s_{prev}} \;\le\; a^{+}\,\Delta\tau \quad\text{or}\quad
v^{s_{prev}} \;-\; v^{s_{next}} \;\le\; a^{-}\,\Delta\tau
\]

These are enforced through auxiliary binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels (standard “big‑M” linearisation). For brevity they are omitted here but can be added as:

\[
v^{s_{next}} - v^{s_{prev}} \le a^{+}\,\Delta\tau + M(2-y^{t}_{i j s_{prev}}-y^{t}_{j k s_{next}})
\]

and analogous for deceleration.

### 5.7 Time‑propagation (timetable feasibility)

For every traversed arc (i,j) and train *t*  

\[
T^{t}_{j} \;\ge\; d^{t}_{i} \;+\; \delta^{t}_{ij} \;-\; M\,(1-x^{t}_{ij})
\]

Departure after arrival + dwell  

\[
d^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; T^{t}_{i} \;+\; \tau^{t}_{i} \qquad\forall i
\]

Origin release window  

\[
T^{t}_{o_t} \;\ge\; T^{\text{reg}}_{t} \qquad\text{(release time from timetable)} 
\]

Destination delay definition  

\[
l^{t}= T^{t}_{d_t} - T^{\text{sched\_arr}}_{t}
\]

### 5.8 Blockage time‑window (cannot occupy blocked segment during its closure)

For a blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ with closure interval \([B^{\text{start}}_{ij}, B^{\text{end}}_{ij}]\)  

\[
T^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; B^{\text{end}}_{ij}\quad\text{or}\quad
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \;\le\; B^{\text{start}}_{ij}
\]

Linearised with binary variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\) that decides “before” or “after”:

\[
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \le B^{\text{start}}_{ij} + M b^{t}_{ij}
\]
\[
T^{t}_{i} \ge B^{\text{end}}_{ij} - M (1-b^{t}_{ij})
\]
\[
b^{t}_{ij} \in \{0,1\}
\]

### 5.9 Single‑track capacity & ordering (no overtaking)

For each single‑track segment (i,j)∈E (capacity =1) and each ordered pair of trains \((t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}\) :

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \;\ge\; d^{t_{1}}_{i} + \delta^{t_{1}}_{ij} - M\,(1-O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij})
\]

\[
O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij} + O^{t_{2}t_{1}}_{ij}=1 \qquad\forall (t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}
\]

Only one of the two orders can be chosen, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the segment simultaneously.

### 5.10 No‑overtaking within the same path (optional)

If the infrastructure forces a strict order of trains on a corridor, we can add:

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \ge d^{t_{1}}_{i} \quad\text{whenever}\; r^{t_{1}}_{i j}=r^{t_{2}}_{i j}=1 \text{ and } t_{1}\text{ precedes }t_{2}\text{ in schedule}
\]

### 5.11 Energy calculation (already linear)

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}} \sum_{s\in S} d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\, y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

### 5.12 Variable domains  

\[
x^{t}_{ij},y^{t}_{ij s},z^{t}_{ij},w^{t}_{ij},\pi^{t}_{ij k},O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij},b^{t}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}
\]

\[
T^{t}_{i}, d^{t}_{i},\delta^{t}_{ij},l^{t},e^{t}\ge 0
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on Linearisation  

* **Travel‑time = distance / speed** is non‑linear. By pre‑defining a *finite* set of speed levels **S** and associating each level with a constant speed \(v^{s}\) and an energy coefficient \(d^{s}_{ij}\), the relationship becomes linear once the binary variable \(y^{t}_{ij s}\) selects the level.  
* **Acceleration / deceleration** constraints are also linearised with big‑M and binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels.  
* **Blockage‑avoidance** uses a binary “before/after” decision variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\).  
* **Ordering on single‑track** uses binary variables \(O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\) to enforce a strict sequence.  

All non‑linearities are therefore replaced by standard MILP constructs (binary variables + big‑M).

---

## 7.  Complete MILP Model  

Putting everything together, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{D}\sum_{t\in T} l^{t} \;+\; w^{E}\sum_{t\in T} e^{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(routing flow)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}\\
&\text{(origin/destination)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(mandatory arcs)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\
&\text{(detour for blocked arcs)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{b}\\
&\text{(speed‑level linking)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}\\
&\text{(travel‑time = distance / speed)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{f},\; s\in S\\
&\text{(acceleration / deceleration)} && \forall\text{consecutive arcs}\\
&\text{(time propagation)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\
&\text{(dwell time)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\\
&\text{(blockage window)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{b}\\
&\text{(single‑track ordering)} && \forall (i,j)\in E,\;(t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}\\
&\text{(delay definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(energy definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(binary / non‑negative domains)} && \text{as listed above.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### How the model works  

1. **Routing** decides which arcs (including detours for blocked segments) each train will use.  
2. **Speed‑level variables** choose a feasible speed on every free‑flow segment, respecting acceleration limits and linking travel time to speed.  
3. **Time‑propagation** computes arrival/departure times from the selected travel times, guaranteeing that no train enters a blocked segment during its closure.  
4. **Ordering variables** enforce that a single‑track segment is occupied by at most one train at any instant and that overtaking is prohibited.  
5. **Delay** is measured as the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the scheduled arrival.  
6. **Energy** is the sum of linearised energy consumption over all traversed arcs, weighted by the chosen speed level.  

The resulting MILP can be fed directly to any state‑of‑the‑art solver. By adjusting the weight parameters \(w^{D}\) and \(w^{E}\) the railway operator can explore the trade‑off between punctuality (delay) and sustainability (energy).

response.content:
Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** when a subset of track segments is partially blocked.  
The model simultaneously decides **(i)** a routing (which train uses which alternative segment), **(ii)** the order in which trains occupy a single‑track segment, **(iii)** the departure/arrival times of every train at every node, and **(iv)** the speed at which a train traverses each free‑flow segment.  

The objective is a **weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and the energy consumed by all trains**.  
All constraints are linear (or linearised) so that a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress…) can solve the model directly.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| 𝑇 = {t} | Set of trains (|𝑇| = N). |
| 𝑁 = {i} | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points). |
| 𝐸 ⊆ 𝑁×𝑁 | Set of directed track **segments** (i,j). |
| 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ ⊆ 𝐸 | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (partial blockage). |
| 𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾ = 𝐸 \ 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | Free (unblocked) segments. |
| 𝐾ᵢⱼ ⊆ 𝐸  | Set of **alternative** segments that can be used to replace a blocked segment (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ (detour arcs). |
| 𝑆 = {s} | Set of **speed‑levels** (piecewise‑linear speed‑energy approximation). |
| 𝑇𝑚 = {τ} | Discrete time‑points (τ = 0,…,Tmax/Δτ). |
| 𝑂 = { (t₁,t₂,i,j) } | Ordered pairs of trains that may share a **single‑track** segment (i,j)∈𝐸 (i.e. they cannot occupy the segment simultaneously). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝐿ᵢⱼ   | Physical length of segment (i,j) | km |
| 𝑣̅ᵢⱼ  | Nominal speed limit on (i,j) (maximum admissible speed) | km/h |
| 𝑎⁺ , 𝑎⁻ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | km/h² |
| 𝑇ᵣᵉᵍ,𝑇ᵈᵉᵖ | Desired **release** (departure) and **arrival** times at the origin/destination of train t (timetable) | h |
| 𝑤ᴰ , 𝑤ᴱ | Scalar weights for delay and energy in the objective | – |
| 𝑑ᵢⱼˢ | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑level s on segment (i,j) (linearised) | kWh/km |
| 𝑣ˢ   | Speed value associated with speed‑level s (mid‑point of the piece) | km/h |
| 𝑀   | Large constant (big‑M) for linking constraints | – |
| 𝑈ᵢⱼ   | Capacity of a **single‑track** segment (i,j) – 1 train at a time | – |
| 𝑝ᵗᵢⱼ | Planned (original) travel time on (i,j) for train t (from timetable) | h |
| 𝑟ᵗᵢⱼ | Binary indicator =1 if train t is **required** to use segment (i,j) in the original schedule (routing‑requirement) | – |
| 𝑏ᵢⱼᵏ | Blockage time‑window on segment (i,j) (start, end) – only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | (h,h) |
| 𝜏ᵗᵢ   | Minimum dwell time of train t at node i (e.g., station dwell) | h |
| 𝑈ᵗ   | Set of admissible **paths** for train t (pre‑computed simple paths from origin to destination). Each path p∈𝑈ᵗ is a sequence of arcs.  |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| 𝑥ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) (routing decision). |
| 𝑦ᵗᵢⱼˢ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) **with speed level** *s* (only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾). |
| 𝑧ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **enters** segment (i,j) (used for ordering constraints). |
| 𝑤ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **leaves** segment (i,j). |
| 𝑇ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at node *i*. |
| 𝑑ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from node *i* (≥ 𝑇ᵗᵢ + dwell). |
| 𝛿ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment (i,j). |
| 𝑈ᵗ  (binary) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses a **detour** for a blocked segment (i.e., chooses an alternative arc from 𝐾ᵢⱼ). |
| 𝜋ᵗᵢⱼᵏ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the *k*‑th alternative arc to replace blocked (i,j). |
| 𝑂ᵗ₁ₜ₂ᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable: 1 if train *t₁* traverses (i,j) **before** train *t₂* (used only when (i,j) is single‑track). |
| 𝑙ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at destination and scheduled arrival). |
| 𝑒ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Energy** consumed by train *t* (sum over arcs and speed‑levels). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{ \; w^{D}\;\sum_{t\in T}  l^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{ \; w^{E}\;\sum_{t\in T}  e^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

where  

*Delay*  

\[
l^{t}= \; T^{t}_{\text{dest}} \;-\; T^{t}_{\text{sched\_arr}}
\]

*Energy* (linear piecewise approximation)  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S}\; d^{s}_{ij}\;  L_{ij}\; y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

\(d^{s}_{ij}\) is the energy coefficient (kWh per km) for speed level *s* on segment (i,j).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing (flow conservation)

For every train *t* and node *i* (except origin *oₜ* and destination *dₜ*)  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E} x^{t}_{ij} \;-\; \sum_{j:(j,i)\in E} x^{t}_{ji}=0
\]

Origin and destination  

\[
\sum_{j:(o_t,j)\in E} x^{t}_{o_t j}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j:(j,d_t)\in E} x^{t}_{j d_t}=1
\]

### 5.2 Mandatory arcs (original schedule)

If a segment is **required** for train *t* (e.g., because the original timetable uses it and no detour is defined), enforce  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}\; \ge\; r^{t}_{ij}\qquad \forall (i,j)\in E
\]

### 5.3 Detour / Blockage handling  

For every blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ and train *t* that would have used it (rᵗᵢⱼ = 1)  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}+ \sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}=1
\]

Only one alternative may be selected  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}\le 1
\]

If an alternative *k* is chosen, the corresponding arc must be traversed  

\[
\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le x^{t}_{i'_{k} j'_{k}}\qquad\forall k\in K_{ij}
\]

### 5.4 Speed‑level linking  

A speed level can be selected only if the arc is used  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}= x^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

Only one speed level per traversed arc  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}\le 1\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

### 5.5 Travel‑time definition (speed = distance / speed)

For a free‑flow segment (i,j)∈Eᶠ  

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}= \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}}\; y^{t}_{ij s}\quad\forall s\in S
\]

Because the model must stay linear, we use the big‑M linearisation:

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} - M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]
\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\le\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} + M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]

Only the selected speed‑level will bind the travel‑time.

### 5.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (between consecutive arcs)

If train *t* leaves node *i* at time \(d^{t}_{i}\) and enters next arc (i,j), the departure speed cannot exceed the admissible speed of the next arc plus the acceleration capability. Using the speed‑level representation, a simple linear bound is

\[
v^{s_{next}} \;-\; v^{s_{prev}} \;\le\; a^{+}\,\Delta\tau \quad\text{or}\quad
v^{s_{prev}} \;-\; v^{s_{next}} \;\le\; a^{-}\,\Delta\tau
\]

These are enforced through auxiliary binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels (standard “big‑M” linearisation). For brevity they are omitted here but can be added as:

\[
v^{s_{next}} - v^{s_{prev}} \le a^{+}\,\Delta\tau + M(2-y^{t}_{i j s_{prev}}-y^{t}_{j k s_{next}})
\]

and analogous for deceleration.

### 5.7 Time‑propagation (timetable feasibility)

For every traversed arc (i,j) and train *t*  

\[
T^{t}_{j} \;\ge\; d^{t}_{i} \;+\; \delta^{t}_{ij} \;-\; M\,(1-x^{t}_{ij})
\]

Departure after arrival + dwell  

\[
d^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; T^{t}_{i} \;+\; \tau^{t}_{i} \qquad\forall i
\]

Origin release window  

\[
T^{t}_{o_t} \;\ge\; T^{\text{reg}}_{t} \qquad\text{(release time from timetable)} 
\]

Destination delay definition  

\[
l^{t}= T^{t}_{d_t} - T^{\text{sched\_arr}}_{t}
\]

### 5.8 Blockage time‑window (cannot occupy blocked segment during its closure)

For a blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ with closure interval \([B^{\text{start}}_{ij}, B^{\text{end}}_{ij}]\)  

\[
T^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; B^{\text{end}}_{ij}\quad\text{or}\quad
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \;\le\; B^{\text{start}}_{ij}
\]

Linearised with binary variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\) that decides “before” or “after”:

\[
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \le B^{\text{start}}_{ij} + M b^{t}_{ij}
\]
\[
T^{t}_{i} \ge B^{\text{end}}_{ij} - M (1-b^{t}_{ij})
\]
\[
b^{t}_{ij} \in \{0,1\}
\]

### 5.9 Single‑track capacity & ordering (no overtaking)

For each single‑track segment (i,j)∈E (capacity =1) and each ordered pair of trains \((t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}\) :

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \;\ge\; d^{t_{1}}_{i} + \delta^{t_{1}}_{ij} - M\,(1-O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij})
\]

\[
O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij} + O^{t_{2}t_{1}}_{ij}=1 \qquad\forall (t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}
\]

Only one of the two orders can be chosen, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the segment simultaneously.

### 5.10 No‑overtaking within the same path (optional)

If the infrastructure forces a strict order of trains on a corridor, we can add:

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \ge d^{t_{1}}_{i} \quad\text{whenever}\; r^{t_{1}}_{i j}=r^{t_{2}}_{i j}=1 \text{ and } t_{1}\text{ precedes }t_{2}\text{ in schedule}
\]

### 5.11 Energy calculation (already linear)

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}} \sum_{s\in S} d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\, y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

### 5.12 Variable domains  

\[
x^{t}_{ij},y^{t}_{ij s},z^{t}_{ij},w^{t}_{ij},\pi^{t}_{ij k},O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij},b^{t}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}
\]

\[
T^{t}_{i}, d^{t}_{i},\delta^{t}_{ij},l^{t},e^{t}\ge 0
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on Linearisation  

* **Travel‑time = distance / speed** is non‑linear. By pre‑defining a *finite* set of speed levels **S** and associating each level with a constant speed \(v^{s}\) and an energy coefficient \(d^{s}_{ij}\), the relationship becomes linear once the binary variable \(y^{t}_{ij s}\) selects the level.  
* **Acceleration / deceleration** constraints are also linearised with big‑M and binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels.  
* **Blockage‑avoidance** uses a binary “before/after” decision variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\).  
* **Ordering on single‑track** uses binary variables \(O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\) to enforce a strict sequence.  

All non‑linearities are therefore replaced by standard MILP constructs (binary variables + big‑M).

---

## 7.  Complete MILP Model  

Putting everything together, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{D}\sum_{t\in T} l^{t} \;+\; w^{E}\sum_{t\in T} e^{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(routing flow)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}\\

&\text{(mandatory arcs)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\

&\text{(travel‑time = distance / speed)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{f},\; s\in S\\

&\text{(time propagation)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\
&\text{(dwell time)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\\
&\text{(blockage window)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{b}\\

&\text{(delay definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(energy definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(binary / non‑negative domains)} && \text{as listed above.}

\]

2. **Speed‑level variables** choose a feasible speed on every free‑flow segment, respecting acceleration limits and linking travel time to speed.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** when a subset of track segments is partially blocked.  
The model simultaneously decides **(i)** a routing (which train uses which alternative segment), **(ii)** the order in which trains occupy a single‑track segment, **(iii)** the departure/arrival times of every train at every node, and **(iv)** the speed at which a train traverses each free‑flow segment.  

The objective is a **weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and the energy consumed by all trains**.  
All constraints are linear (or linearised) so that a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress…) can solve the model directly.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| 𝑇 = {t} | Set of trains (|𝑇| = N). |
| 𝑁 = {i} | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points). |
| 𝐸 ⊆ 𝑁×𝑁 | Set of directed track **segments** (i,j). |
| 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ ⊆ 𝐸 | Sub‑set of **blocked** segments (partial blockage). |
| 𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾ = 𝐸 \ 𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | Free (unblocked) segments. |
| 𝐾ᵢⱼ ⊆ 𝐸  | Set of **alternative** segments that can be used to replace a blocked segment (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ (detour arcs). |
| 𝑆 = {s} | Set of **speed‑levels** (piecewise‑linear speed‑energy approximation). |
| 𝑇𝑚 = {τ} | Discrete time‑points (τ = 0,…,Tmax/Δτ). |
| 𝑂 = { (t₁,t₂,i,j) } | Ordered pairs of trains that may share a **single‑track** segment (i,j)∈𝐸 (i.e. they cannot occupy the segment simultaneously). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| 𝐿ᵢⱼ   | Physical length of segment (i,j) | km |
| 𝑣̅ᵢⱼ  | Nominal speed limit on (i,j) (maximum admissible speed) | km/h |
| 𝑎⁺ , 𝑎⁻ | Max acceleration / deceleration (positive numbers) | km/h² |
| 𝑇ᵣᵉᵍ,𝑇ᵈᵉᵖ | Desired **release** (departure) and **arrival** times at the origin/destination of train t (timetable) | h |
| 𝑤ᴰ , 𝑤ᴱ | Scalar weights for delay and energy in the objective | – |
| 𝑑ᵢⱼˢ | Energy consumption coefficient for speed‑level s on segment (i,j) (linearised) | kWh/km |
| 𝑣ˢ   | Speed value associated with speed‑level s (mid‑point of the piece) | km/h |
| 𝑀   | Large constant (big‑M) for linking constraints | – |
| 𝑈ᵢⱼ   | Capacity of a **single‑track** segment (i,j) – 1 train at a time | – |
| 𝑝ᵗᵢⱼ | Planned (original) travel time on (i,j) for train t (from timetable) | h |
| 𝑟ᵗᵢⱼ | Binary indicator =1 if train t is **required** to use segment (i,j) in the original schedule (routing‑requirement) | – |
| 𝑏ᵢⱼᵏ | Blockage time‑window on segment (i,j) (start, end) – only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᵇ⁾ | (h,h) |
| 𝜏ᵗᵢ   | Minimum dwell time of train t at node i (e.g., station dwell) | h |
| 𝑈ᵗ   | Set of admissible **paths** for train t (pre‑computed simple paths from origin to destination). Each path p∈𝑈ᵗ is a sequence of arcs.  |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| 𝑥ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) (routing decision). |
| 𝑦ᵗᵢⱼˢ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment (i,j) **with speed level** *s* (only for (i,j)∈𝐸⁽ᶠ⁾). |
| 𝑧ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **enters** segment (i,j) (used for ordering constraints). |
| 𝑤ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **leaves** segment (i,j). |
| 𝑇ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at node *i*. |
| 𝑑ᵗᵢ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from node *i* (≥ 𝑇ᵗᵢ + dwell). |
| 𝛿ᵗᵢⱼ ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment (i,j). |
| 𝑈ᵗ  (binary) | binary | 1 if train *t* uses a **detour** for a blocked segment (i.e., chooses an alternative arc from 𝐾ᵢⱼ). |
| 𝜋ᵗᵢⱼᵏ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* uses the *k*‑th alternative arc to replace blocked (i,j). |
| 𝑂ᵗ₁ₜ₂ᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | Ordering variable: 1 if train *t₁* traverses (i,j) **before** train *t₂* (used only when (i,j) is single‑track). |
| 𝑙ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Delay** of train *t* (difference between actual arrival at destination and scheduled arrival). |
| 𝑒ᵗ  ∈ ℝ₊ | continuous | **Energy** consumed by train *t* (sum over arcs and speed‑levels). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \;  \underbrace{ \; w^{D}\;\sum_{t\in T}  l^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted delay}} \;+\;
\underbrace{ \; w^{E}\;\sum_{t\in T}  e^{t}\; }_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\]

where  

*Delay*  

\[
l^{t}= \; T^{t}_{\text{dest}} \;-\; T^{t}_{\text{sched\_arr}}
\]

*Energy* (linear piecewise approximation)  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S}\; d^{s}_{ij}\;  L_{ij}\; y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

\(d^{s}_{ij}\) is the energy coefficient (kWh per km) for speed level *s* on segment (i,j).

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Routing (flow conservation)

For every train *t* and node *i* (except origin *oₜ* and destination *dₜ*)  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E} x^{t}_{ij} \;-\; \sum_{j:(j,i)\in E} x^{t}_{ji}=0
\]

Origin and destination  

\[
\sum_{j:(o_t,j)\in E} x^{t}_{o_t j}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j:(j,d_t)\in E} x^{t}_{j d_t}=1
\]

### 5.2 Mandatory arcs (original schedule)

If a segment is **required** for train *t* (e.g., because the original timetable uses it and no detour is defined), enforce  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}\; \ge\; r^{t}_{ij}\qquad \forall (i,j)\in E
\]

### 5.3 Detour / Blockage handling  

For every blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ and train *t* that would have used it (rᵗᵢⱼ = 1)  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}+ \sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}=1
\]

Only one alternative may be selected  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{ij}} \pi^{t}_{ij k}\le 1
\]

If an alternative *k* is chosen, the corresponding arc must be traversed  

\[
\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le x^{t}_{i'_{k} j'_{k}}\qquad\forall k\in K_{ij}
\]

### 5.4 Speed‑level linking  

A speed level can be selected only if the arc is used  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}= x^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

Only one speed level per traversed arc  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} y^{t}_{ij s}\le 1\qquad\forall (i,j)\in E^{f},\; \forall t
\]

### 5.5 Travel‑time definition (speed = distance / speed)

For a free‑flow segment (i,j)∈Eᶠ  

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}= \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}}\; y^{t}_{ij s}\quad\forall s\in S
\]

Because the model must stay linear, we use the big‑M linearisation:

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} - M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]
\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\le\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}} + M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]

Only the selected speed‑level will bind the travel‑time.

### 5.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits (between consecutive arcs)

If train *t* leaves node *i* at time \(d^{t}_{i}\) and enters next arc (i,j), the departure speed cannot exceed the admissible speed of the next arc plus the acceleration capability. Using the speed‑level representation, a simple linear bound is

\[
v^{s_{next}} \;-\; v^{s_{prev}} \;\le\; a^{+}\,\Delta\tau \quad\text{or}\quad
v^{s_{prev}} \;-\; v^{s_{next}} \;\le\; a^{-}\,\Delta\tau
\]

These are enforced through auxiliary binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels (standard “big‑M” linearisation). For brevity they are omitted here but can be added as:

\[
v^{s_{next}} - v^{s_{prev}} \le a^{+}\,\Delta\tau + M(2-y^{t}_{i j s_{prev}}-y^{t}_{j k s_{next}})
\]

and analogous for deceleration.

### 5.7 Time‑propagation (timetable feasibility)

For every traversed arc (i,j) and train *t*  

\[
T^{t}_{j} \;\ge\; d^{t}_{i} \;+\; \delta^{t}_{ij} \;-\; M\,(1-x^{t}_{ij})
\]

Departure after arrival + dwell  

\[
d^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; T^{t}_{i} \;+\; \tau^{t}_{i} \qquad\forall i
\]

Origin release window  

\[
T^{t}_{o_t} \;\ge\; T^{\text{reg}}_{t} \qquad\text{(release time from timetable)} 
\]

Destination delay definition  

\[
l^{t}= T^{t}_{d_t} - T^{\text{sched\_arr}}_{t}
\]

### 5.8 Blockage time‑window (cannot occupy blocked segment during its closure)

For a blocked segment (i,j)∈Eᵇ with closure interval \([B^{\text{start}}_{ij}, B^{\text{end}}_{ij}]\)  

\[
T^{t}_{i} \;\ge\; B^{\text{end}}_{ij}\quad\text{or}\quad
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \;\le\; B^{\text{start}}_{ij}
\]

Linearised with binary variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\) that decides “before” or “after”:

\[
T^{t}_{i} + \delta^{t}_{ij} \le B^{\text{start}}_{ij} + M b^{t}_{ij}
\]
\[
T^{t}_{i} \ge B^{\text{end}}_{ij} - M (1-b^{t}_{ij})
\]
\[
b^{t}_{ij} \in \{0,1\}
\]

### 5.9 Single‑track capacity & ordering (no overtaking)

For each single‑track segment (i,j)∈E (capacity =1) and each ordered pair of trains \((t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}\) :

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \;\ge\; d^{t_{1}}_{i} + \delta^{t_{1}}_{ij} - M\,(1-O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij})
\]

\[
O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij} + O^{t_{2}t_{1}}_{ij}=1 \qquad\forall (t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}
\]

Only one of the two orders can be chosen, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the segment simultaneously.

### 5.10 No‑overtaking within the same path (optional)

If the infrastructure forces a strict order of trains on a corridor, we can add:

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i} \ge d^{t_{1}}_{i} \quad\text{whenever}\; r^{t_{1}}_{i j}=r^{t_{2}}_{i j}=1 \text{ and } t_{1}\text{ precedes }t_{2}\text{ in schedule}
\]

### 5.11 Energy calculation (already linear)

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}} \sum_{s\in S} d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\, y^{t}_{ij s}
\]

### 5.12 Variable domains  

\[
x^{t}_{ij},y^{t}_{ij s},z^{t}_{ij},w^{t}_{ij},\pi^{t}_{ij k},O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij},b^{t}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}
\]

\[
T^{t}_{i}, d^{t}_{i},\delta^{t}_{ij},l^{t},e^{t}\ge 0
\]

---

## 6.  Remarks on Linearisation  

* **Travel‑time = distance / speed** is non‑linear. By pre‑defining a *finite* set of speed levels **S** and associating each level with a constant speed \(v^{s}\) and an energy coefficient \(d^{s}_{ij}\), the relationship becomes linear once the binary variable \(y^{t}_{ij s}\) selects the level.  
* **Acceleration / deceleration** constraints are also linearised with big‑M and binary variables that activate the appropriate inequality for the selected speed levels.  
* **Blockage‑avoidance** uses a binary “before/after” decision variable \(b^{t}_{ij}\).  
* **Ordering on single‑track** uses binary variables \(O^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\) to enforce a strict sequence.  

All non‑linearities are therefore replaced by standard MILP constructs (binary variables + big‑M).

---

## 7.  Complete MILP Model  

Putting everything together, the model reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{D}\sum_{t\in T} l^{t} \;+\; w^{E}\sum_{t\in T} e^{t} \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(routing flow)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}\\
&\text{(origin/destination)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(mandatory arcs)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\
&\text{(detour for blocked arcs)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{b}\\
&\text{(speed‑level linking)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}\\
&\text{(travel‑time = distance / speed)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{f},\; s\in S\\
&\text{(acceleration / deceleration)} && \forall\text{consecutive arcs}\\
&\text{(time propagation)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E\\
&\text{(dwell time)} && \forall t\in T,\; i\in N\\
&\text{(blockage window)} && \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E^{b}\\
&\text{(single‑track ordering)} && \forall (i,j)\in E,\;(t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}\\
&\text{(delay definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(energy definition)} && \forall t\in T\\
&\text{(binary / non‑negative domains)} && \text{as listed above.}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### How the model works  

1. **Routing** decides which arcs (including detours for blocked segments) each train will use.  
2. **Speed‑level variables** choose a feasible speed on every free‑flow segment, respecting acceleration limits and linking travel time to speed.  
3. **Time‑propagation** computes arrival/departure times from the selected travel times, guaranteeing that no train enters a blocked segment during its closure.  
4. **Ordering variables** enforce that a single‑track segment is occupied by at most one train at any instant and that overtaking is prohibited.  
5. **Delay** is measured as the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the scheduled arrival.  
6. **Energy** is the sum of linearised energy consumption over all traversed arcs, weighted by the chosen speed level.  

The resulting MILP can be fed directly to any state‑of‑the‑art solver. By adjusting the weight parameters \(w^{D}\) and \(w^{E}\) the railway operator can explore the trade‑off between punctuality (delay) and sustainability (energy).

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) under Partial Segment Blockage**  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = { t } | Trains (|T| = N) |
| **N** = { i } | Network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points) |
| **E** ⊆ N×N | Directed track segments (i , j) |
| **Eᵇ** ⊆ E | Segments that are **partially blocked** during a disruption |
| **Eᶠ** = E \ Eᵇ | Free (unblocked) segments |
| **Kᵢⱼ** ⊆ E | Set of **alternative** arcs that can replace a blocked segment (i , j) ∈ Eᵇ (detour arcs) |
| **S** = { s } | Discrete speed‑levels (piece‑wise linear speed‑energy approximation) |
| **Oᵢⱼ** | Ordered pairs of trains that may share a **single‑track** segment (i , j) (capacity = 1) |
| **τ** ∈ {0,…,Tmax/Δτ} | Discrete time points (used only for big‑M linearisation) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Lᵢⱼ   | Length of segment (i , j) | km |
| v̄ᵢⱼ  | Speed limit on (i , j) | km h⁻¹ |
| a⁺ , a⁻ | Max acceleration / deceleration | km h⁻² |
| Tᵣᵉᵍᵗ , Tᵈᵉᵖᵗ | Desired release (departure) and scheduled arrival times of train t at its origin/destination | h |
| wᴰ , wᴱ | Weights for delay and energy in the objective | – |
| dᵢⱼˢ | Energy coefficient (kWh km⁻¹) for speed‑level s on segment (i , j) | kWh km⁻¹ |
| vˢ   | Representative speed of level s (mid‑point) | km h⁻¹ |
| M     | Large constant for big‑M linearisation | – |
| Uᵢⱼ   | Capacity of a single‑track segment (i , j) – 1 train at a time | – |
| rᵗᵢⱼ | =1 if train t **must** use (i , j) in the original schedule, 0 otherwise | – |
| Bᵢⱼˢᵗ , Bᵢⱼᵉᵗ | Start / end of the blockage time window on (i , j) ∈ Eᵇ | h |
| τᵗᵢ | Minimum dwell time of train t at node i (e.g., station dwell) | h |
| Pᵗ   | Pre‑computed feasible paths for train t (each path is a sequence of arcs) | – |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| xᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t traverses segment (i , j) (routing) |
| yᵗᵢⱼˢ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t traverses (i , j) **with speed level** s (only for (i , j)∈Eᶠ) |
| πᵗᵢⱼᵏ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t uses alternative arc k ∈ Kᵢⱼ to replace blocked (i , j) |
| Tᵗᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train t at node i |
| Dᵗᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train t from node i (≥ Tᵗᵢ + τᵗᵢ) |
| δᵗᵢⱼ ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train t on segment (i , j) |
| bᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t passes **after** the blockage window on (i , j) |
| oᵗ₁ₜ₂ᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t₁ traverses (i , j) before train t₂ (single‑track ordering) |
| lᵗ ≥ 0 | continuous | Delay of train t (actual arrival – scheduled arrival at destination) |
| eᵗ ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumed by train t |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min \; w^{D}\;\sum_{t\in T} l^{t}\;+\;w^{E}\;\sum_{t\in T} e^{t}
\]

where  

*Delay* \(l^{t}= T^{t}_{\text{dest}}-T^{\text{sched}}_{\text{dest},t}\)  

*Energy* \(e^{t}= \displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S}\; d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\,y^{t}_{ij s}\)

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing (flow conservation)  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x^{t}_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in E}x^{t}_{ji}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\;i\in N\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}
\]

\[
\sum_{j:(o_t,j)\in E}x^{t}_{o_tj}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j:(j,d_t)\in E}x^{t}_{jd_t}=1\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 5.2 Mandatory arcs (original schedule)  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; r^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
\]

#### 5.3 Blockage handling (detour or before/after)  

For every blocked arc (i , j)∈Eᵇ and train t that would have used it (rᵗᵢⱼ=1):

\[
x^{t}_{ij}+ \sum_{k\in K_{ij}}\pi^{t}_{ij k}=1
\]

Only one alternative may be selected  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{ij}}\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le 1
\]

If alternative k is chosen, the corresponding physical arc must be traversed  

\[
\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le x^{t}_{i'_{k}j'_{k}}\qquad\forall k\in K_{ij}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed‑level linking  

\[
\sum_{s\in S}y^{t}_{ij s}=x^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}
\]

Only one speed level per traversed free‑flow arc  

\[
\sum_{s\in S}y^{t}_{ij s}\le 1\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}
\]

#### 5.5 Travel‑time from speed level (linearised)  

For each free‑flow arc (i , j)∈Eᶠ, train t and speed level s:

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}}-M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]

\[
\delta^{t}_{ij}\;\le\; \frac{L_{ij}}{v^{s}}+M\,(1-y^{t}_{ij s})\qquad\forall s\in S
\]

Thus the selected speed level fixes the travel time.

#### 5.6 Acceleration / deceleration limits  

If train t leaves arc (i , j) with speed level s and enters the next arc (j , k) with level s′:

\[
v^{s'}-v^{s}\le a^{+}\,\Delta\tau+M\bigl(2-y^{t}_{ij s}-y^{t}_{jk s'}\bigr)
\]

\[
v^{s}-v^{s'}\le a^{-}\,\Delta\tau+M\bigl(2-y^{t}_{ij s}-y^{t}_{jk s'}\bigr)
\]

(Δτ is a chosen time granularity, e.g., 1 min.)

#### 5.7 Time propagation (timetable feasibility)  

\[
T^{t}_{j}\;\ge\; D^{t}_{i}+ \delta^{t}_{ij}-M\,(1-x^{t}_{ij})\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E
\]

\[
D^{t}_{i}\;\ge\; T^{t}_{i}+ \tau^{t}_{i}\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N
\]

Origin release window  

\[
T^{t}_{o_t}\;\ge\; T^{\text{reg}}_{t}\qquad\forall t
\]

#### 5.8 Blockage time‑window (cannot occupy during closure)  

For each blocked arc (i , j)∈Eᵇ:

\[
T^{t}_{i}+ \delta^{t}_{ij}\le B^{\text{start}}_{ij}+M\,b^{t}_{ij}
\]

\[
T^{t}_{i}\ge B^{\text{end}}_{ij}-M\,(1-b^{t}_{ij})
\]

\(b^{t}_{ij}=1\) ⇒ train passes **after** the blockage; \(b^{t}_{ij}=0\) ⇒ passes **before**.

#### 5.9 Single‑track capacity & ordering  

For every single‑track segment (i , j) (capacity =1) and each ordered pair (t₁ , t₂)∈Oᵢⱼ :

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i}\;\ge\; D^{t_{1}}_{i}+ \delta^{t_{1}}_{ij}-M\,(1-o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij})
\]

\[
o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}+o^{t_{2}t_{1}}_{ij}=1\qquad\forall (t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}
\]

Thus exactly one ordering is chosen and the two trains never occupy the segment simultaneously.

#### 5.10 Delay definition  

\[
l^{t}= T^{t}_{d_t}-T^{\text{sched}}_{d_t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 5.11 Energy definition (already linear)  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S} d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\,y^{t}_{ij s}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 5.12 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x^{t}_{ij},\,y^{t}_{ij s},\,\pi^{t}_{ij k},\,b^{t}_{ij},\,o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\\
&T^{t}_{i},\,D^{t}_{i},\,\delta^{t}_{ij},\,l^{t},\,e^{t}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6.  Model Summary  

The MILP simultaneously decides  

* **Routing / detouring** (variables \(x^{t}_{ij},\pi^{t}_{ij k}\)) to avoid blocked segments,  
* **Speed level** on each free‑flow arc (variables \(y^{t}_{ij s}\)) respecting acceleration limits,  
* **Arrival / departure times** (variables \(T^{t}_{i}, D^{t}_{i}\)) that satisfy travel‑time, dwell, and blockage‑window constraints,  
* **Ordering** on single‑track sections (variables \(o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\)) to guarantee conflict‑free use of shared resources,  

while minimising a weighted sum of **total passenger delay** and **energy consumption**.  

All non‑linear relations (speed‑time, acceleration, blockage‑avoidance, ordering) are linearised with binary variables and big‑M constants, yielding a pure MILP that can be solved with any commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  

By adjusting the weights \(w^{D}\) and \(w^{E}\) the railway operator can explore the trade‑off between punctuality and sustainability.

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = { t } | Trains (|T| = N) |
| **N** = { i } | Network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points) |

| **Eᵇ** ⊆ E | Segments that are **partially blocked** during a disruption |
| **Eᶠ** = E \ Eᵇ | Free (unblocked) segments |
| **Kᵢⱼ** ⊆ E | Set of **alternative** arcs that can replace a blocked segment (i , j) ∈ Eᵇ (detour arcs) |
| **S** = { s } | Discrete speed‑levels (piece‑wise linear speed‑energy approximation) |
| **Oᵢⱼ** | Ordered pairs of trains that may share a **single‑track** segment (i , j) (capacity = 1) |
| **τ** ∈ {0,…,Tmax/Δτ} | Discrete time points (used only for big‑M linearisation) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| Lᵢⱼ   | Length of segment (i , j) | km |
| v̄ᵢⱼ  | Speed limit on (i , j) | km h⁻¹ |
| a⁺ , a⁻ | Max acceleration / deceleration | km h⁻² |
| Tᵣᵉᵍᵗ , Tᵈᵉᵖᵗ | Desired release (departure) and scheduled arrival times of train t at its origin/destination | h |
| wᴰ , wᴱ | Weights for delay and energy in the objective | – |
| dᵢⱼˢ | Energy coefficient (kWh km⁻¹) for speed‑level s on segment (i , j) | kWh km⁻¹ |
| vˢ   | Representative speed of level s (mid‑point) | km h⁻¹ |
| M     | Large constant for big‑M linearisation | – |

| τᵗᵢ | Minimum dwell time of train t at node i (e.g., station dwell) | h |
| Pᵗ   | Pre‑computed feasible paths for train t (each path is a sequence of arcs) | – |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| xᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t traverses segment (i , j) (routing) |
| yᵗᵢⱼˢ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t traverses (i , j) **with speed level** s (only for (i , j)∈Eᶠ) |
| πᵗᵢⱼᵏ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t uses alternative arc k ∈ Kᵢⱼ to replace blocked (i , j) |
| Tᵗᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train t at node i |
| Dᵗᵢ ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train t from node i (≥ Tᵗᵢ + τᵗᵢ) |
| δᵗᵢⱼ ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train t on segment (i , j) |
| bᵗᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t passes **after** the blockage window on (i , j) |
| oᵗ₁ₜ₂ᵢⱼ ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 ⇔ train t₁ traverses (i , j) before train t₂ (single‑track ordering) |
| lᵗ ≥ 0 | continuous | Delay of train t (actual arrival – scheduled arrival at destination) |
| eᵗ ≥ 0 | continuous | Energy consumed by train t |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min \; w^{D}\;\sum_{t\in T} l^{t}\;+\;w^{E}\;\sum_{t\in T} e^{t}
\]

where  

*Delay* \(l^{t}= T^{t}_{\text{dest}}-T^{\text{sched}}_{\text{dest},t}\)  

*Energy* \(e^{t}= \displaystyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S}\; d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\,y^{t}_{ij s}\)

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing (flow conservation)  

\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x^{t}_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in E}x^{t}_{ji}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\;i\in N\setminus\{o_t,d_t\}
\]

\[
\sum_{j:(o_t,j)\in E}x^{t}_{o_tj}=1,\qquad
\sum_{j:(j,d_t)\in E}x^{t}_{jd_t}=1\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 5.2 Mandatory arcs (original schedule)  

\[
x^{t}_{ij}\;\ge\; r^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
\]

#### 5.3 Blockage handling (detour or before/after)

\[
x^{t}_{ij}+ \sum_{k\in K_{ij}}\pi^{t}_{ij k}=1
\]

Only one alternative may be selected  

\[
\sum_{k\in K_{ij}}\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le 1
\]

If alternative k is chosen, the corresponding physical arc must be traversed  

\[
\pi^{t}_{ij k}\le x^{t}_{i'_{k}j'_{k}}\qquad\forall k\in K_{ij}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed‑level linking  

\[
\sum_{s\in S}y^{t}_{ij s}=x^{t}_{ij}\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}
\]

Only one speed level per traversed free‑flow arc  

\[
\sum_{s\in S}y^{t}_{ij s}\le 1\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E^{f}
\]

\[

\]

\[
v^{s}-v^{s'}\le a^{-}\,\Delta\tau+M\bigl(2-y^{t}_{ij s}-y^{t}_{jk s'}\bigr)
\]

(Δτ is a chosen time granularity, e.g., 1 min.)

#### 5.7 Time propagation (timetable feasibility)  

\[
T^{t}_{j}\;\ge\; D^{t}_{i}+ \delta^{t}_{ij}-M\,(1-x^{t}_{ij})\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E
\]

\[
D^{t}_{i}\;\ge\; T^{t}_{i}+ \tau^{t}_{i}\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N
\]

\[
T^{t}_{o_t}\;\ge\; T^{\text{reg}}_{t}\qquad\forall t

\[
T^{t_{2}}_{i}\;\ge\; D^{t_{1}}_{i}+ \delta^{t_{1}}_{ij}-M\,(1-o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij})
\]

\[
o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}+o^{t_{2}t_{1}}_{ij}=1\qquad\forall (t_{1},t_{2})\in O_{ij}
\]

#### 5.10 Delay definition  

\[
l^{t}= T^{t}_{d_t}-T^{\text{sched}}_{d_t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

#### 5.11 Energy definition (already linear)  

\[
e^{t}= \sum_{(i,j)\in E^{f}}\;\sum_{s\in S} d^{s}_{ij}\,L_{ij}\,y^{t}_{ij s}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x^{t}_{ij},\,y^{t}_{ij s},\,\pi^{t}_{ij k},\,b^{t}_{ij},\,o^{t_{1}t_{2}}_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\\
&T^{t}_{i},\,D^{t}_{i},\,\delta^{t}_{ij},\,l^{t},\,e^{t}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6.  Model Summary  

The MILP simultaneously decides  

* **Routing / detouring** (variables \(x^{t}_{ij},\pi^{t}_{ij k}\)) to avoid blocked segments,  
* **Speed level** on each free‑flow arc (variables \(y^{t}_{ij s}\)) respecting acceleration limits,

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
