Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the key decisions required for **integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management** when a **partial segment of the line is blocked** (e.g., due to an incident, maintenance work or a broken rail).  

The model is written in a **canonical linear‐programming form** (variables, objective, linear constraints).  After the formulation each component is explained so that you can see how the description maps onto the mathematics.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets, Parameters and Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(\\mathcal{T}=\\{1,\dots,T\\}\\) | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| \\(\\mathcal{S}=\\{1,\dots,S\\}\\) | Set of **track segments** (the line is divided into elementary sections). |
| \\(\\mathcal{K}=\\{1,\dots,K\\}\\) | Set of admissible **speed‑profile choices** for a train on a segment (e.g., “full speed”, “reduced speed”, “stop”). |
| \\(\\mathcal{R}=\\{r_1,\dots,r_R\\}\\) | Set of **feasible routes** (ordered list of segments) that a train may follow from its origin to its destination.  For each train \\(i\\) we denote the admissible routes by \\(\\mathcal{R}_i\\subseteq\\mathcal{R}\\). |
| \\(\\mathcal{B}\\subseteq \\mathcal{S}\\) | Subset of segments that are **blocked** during a known disruption window \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\\). |
| \\(\\delta_{i,r,s}\\) | 1 if segment \\(s\\) belongs to route \\(r\\) for train \\(i\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(L_{s}\\) | Length (km) of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(v^{\max}_{k}\\) | Speed (km/h) associated with speed‑profile choice \\(k\\).  (All \\(v^{\max}_{k}\\) are constants.) |
| \\(a^{\max},d^{\max}\\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h²) that can be applied when switching between speed profiles. |
| \\(t^{\text{sched}}_{i}\\) | Planned (pre‑disruption) departure time of train \\(i\\) from its origin. |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Positive weights for the two components of the objective (delay vs. energy). |
| \\(E_{i,k}\\) | Energy cost (e.g. kWh) incurred by train \\(i\\) when it runs on a segment with speed profile \\(k\\).  Typically proportional to \\(L_s\) and \\(v_k\\). |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g., \\(M = 10^6\\) minutes). |
| \\(\\epsilon\\) | Minimum head‑way (in minutes) required between two trains occupying the same segment (safety margin). |

---

## 2️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \\(x_{i,r}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) uses route \\(r\\in\\mathcal{R}_i\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed‑profile \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Arrival time** (in minutes) of train \\(i\\) at the **up‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Departure time** of train \\(i\\) from the **down‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(Δ_i\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(i\\) (difference between actual departure from origin and scheduled departure). |
| \\(z_{i,s}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) **occupies** segment \\(s\\) (any speed) – useful for capacity/conflict constraints. |

*All other variables that appear below are linear expressions of these variables.*

---

## 3️⃣  Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption**:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} Δ_i \;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}  E_{i,k}\; y_{i,s,k}
}
\]

* The first term penalises the sum of all train delays.  
* The second term adds the energy cost of the selected speed profiles.

Both terms are linear because \\(Δ_i\\) and \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) are decision variables.

---

## 4️⃣  Core Linear Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice feasibility  

\[
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i} x_{i,r}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T}\tag{R1}
\]

Every train selects **exactly one** feasible route.

### 4.2 Linking route, segment, and speed‑profile variables  

\[
y_{i,s,k}\le \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}\delta_{i,r,s}\,x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,s,k\tag{R2}
\]

If a route that does **not** contain segment \\(s\\) is chosen, the binary \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) must be 0.  
Conversely, when a route contains \\(s\\), we may pick *any* speed profile; the model will later decide which one to activate.

### 4.3 Occupancy indicator  

\[
z_{i,s}\;=\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i,s\tag{R3}
\]

A train occupies a segment if it traverses it with **some** speed profile.

### 4.4 Delay definition  

\[
Δ_i \; \ge\; a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}} - t^{\text{sched}}_{i} \qquad\forall i\tag{R4}
\]

where \\(s^{\text{orig}}\\) is the (virtual) segment that represents the train’s origin node.  Because \\(a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}}\\) is the actual departure time, the difference is the delay.  (If you prefer a tight equality you can add a “≤” version together, but “≥” is sufficient for minimisation.)

### 4.5 Travel‑time (kinematic) constraints  

If train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed profile \\(k\\), the **minimum travel time** across that segment is

\[
\frac{L_{s}}{v_k}\quad (\text{minutes if }v_k\text{ in km/min})
\]

Let \\(τ_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\\) be a pre‑computed constant.  Then:

\[
d_{i,s} \; \ge\; a_{i,s} + \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} τ_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i,s\tag{R5}
\]

The departure from the downstream node cannot be earlier than arrival + travel time.

### 4.6 Successive‑segment linking (continuity)  

For any two **consecutive** segments \\(s\\) and \\(s'\\) on the same route, the arrival at the next segment equals the departure from the previous one:

\[
a_{i,s'} \; \ge\; d_{i,s} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{i,s})\qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on a route}\tag{R6}
\]

If the train does **not** occupy segment \\(s\\) (\\(z_{i,s}=0\\)), the big‑M deactivates the constraint.

### 4.7 Single‑track capacity (one train at a time)  

For every segment \\(s\\) we must ensure that at any moment only **one train** occupies it (single‑track).  This is expressed with a disjunctive “ordering” constraint using binary order variables \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\in\{0,1\}\\) that decide who passes first:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i',s} &\ge d_{i,s} + \epsilon - M\,θ_{i,i',s} \qquad\forall i\neq i',\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R7a}\\
a_{i,s}  &\ge d_{i',s} + \epsilon - M\,(1-θ_{i,i',s}) \qquad\forall i\neq i',\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R7b}\\
θ_{i,i',s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

Only one of the two inequalities is active (the one with the smaller right‑hand side), guaranteeing a **head‑way of at least \\(\\epsilon\\)** minutes.

*If the line is double‑track for some segments, you can replace (R7) by a capacity limit:*
\[
\sum_{i} z_{i,s}\le C_s\qquad \forall s,
\]
where \\(C_s\\) is the number of parallel tracks (normally 1).  

### 4.8 Conflict‑avoidance for the **blocked** window  

If a segment \\(s\\) is blocked during the interval \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\\), no train may occupy it then:

\[
a_{i,s} \;\ge\; t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \quad\text{or}\quad d_{i,s} \;\le\; t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\,(1-z_{i,s})\qquad\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{B}\tag{R8}
\]

A common linearisation uses a binary “use‑or‑avoid” variable, but the big‑M form above forces the whole traversal to lie **outside** the blocked interval.

### 4.9 Acceleration / deceleration limits when changing speed profile  

If a train changes from speed profile \\(k\\) on segment \\(s\\) to profile \\(k'\\) on the next segment \\(s'\\), the time difference between departure from \\(s\\) and arrival at \\(s'\\) must respect the maximum acceleration/deceleration.  A compact linear formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{i,s} + \frac{v_{k'}-v_{k}}{a^{\max}} &\le a_{i,s'} + M\,(2-y_{i,s,k} - y_{i,s',k'}) \qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')\\
d_{i,s} + \frac{v_{k}-v_{k'}}{d^{\max}} &\le a_{i,s'} + M\,(2-y_{i,s,k} - y_{i,s',k'}) \qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')
\end{aligned}
\]

Only when both binary variables are 1 does the inequality become active; otherwise the big‑M disables it.  The fractions are constants (pre‑computed).  

### 4.10 Routing feasibility (origin/destination)  

For each train we must enforce that the chosen route starts at its origin node and ends at its destination node.  This can be modelled by fixing the binary variables for the first and last segment of each admissible route, e.g.:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s^{\text{orig}},k}=x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\text{ with origin }s^{\text{orig}}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s^{\text{dest}},k}=x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\text{ with destination }s^{\text{dest}}
\]

(Only the route actually selected will activate the corresponding segment‑occupancy variables.)

---

## 5️⃣  Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} Δ_i
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}E_{i,k}\, y_{i,s,k}    \\
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i} x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\in\mathcal{T} &&\text{(R1)}\\[2mm]
& y_{i,s,k}\le\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}\delta_{i,r,s}\,x_{i,r} &&\forall i,s,k &&\text{(R2)}\\[2mm]
& z_{i,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s &&\text{(R3)}\\[2mm]
& Δ_i \ge a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}} - t^{\text{sched}}_{i} &&\forall i &&\text{(R4)}\\[2mm]
& d_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s} + \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} τ_{s,k}\, y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s &&\text{(R5)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} - M\,(1-z_{i,s}) &&\forall i,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive} &&\text{(R6)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i',s} \ge d_{i,s} + \epsilon - M\,θ_{i,i',s} &&\forall i\neq i',\; s &&\text{(R7a)}\\
& a_{i,s}  \ge d_{i',s} + \epsilon - M\,(1-θ_{i,i',s}) &&\forall i\neq i',\; s &&\text{(R7b)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i,s} \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-z_{i,s})\; \text{or}\;
  d_{i,s} \le t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-z_{i,s}) &&\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{B} &&\text{(R8)}\\[2mm]
&\text{Acceleration limits (R9)} &&\forall i,\;(s,s'),k,k'\\[2mm]
&\text{Origin/Destination linking (R10)} &&\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\\[2mm]
& x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\ y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\ z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\ θ_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},Δ_i \ge 0 \qquad &&\forall i,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** in the decision variables; the only integer components are the binary variables.

---

## 6️⃣  How Each Modelling Element Relates to the Description  

| Description element | MILP component |
|---------------------|----------------|
| **Binary route‑choice** | \\(x_{i,r}\\) (R1) and the linking (R2) |
| **Arrival / departure times** | \\(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\\) with travel‑time (R5) and continuity (R6) |
| **Speed‑segment selection** | \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) (binary) – tells which speed profile is used on each traversed segment |
| **Weighted sum of delay & energy** | Objective term \\(w^{\text{delay}}\sum Δ_i + w^{\text{energy}}\sum E_{i,k} y_{i,s,k}\\) |
| **Time feasibility** | (R5)‑(R6) ensure enough time for distance at chosen speed; acceleration limits (R9) |
| **Single‑track capacity** | Ordering binaries \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\) enforce at most one train on a segment at any moment (R7) |
| **Conflict‑avoidance** | Same as capacity; also the head‑way ε |
| **Kinematics (speed‑profile) constraints** | (R5) travel time, (R9) acceleration/deceleration limits |
| **Routing feasibility** | (R1) route‑choice, (R10) origin/destination anchoring |
| **Disruption‑window blockages** | (R8) forces any traversal of a blocked segment to be outside the blockage interval |

---

## 7️⃣  Practical Remarks  

* **Big‑M selection** – Choose \\(M\\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., a few hours expressed in minutes).  
* **Pre‑computation** – The constants \\(τ_{s,k}=L_s/v_k\\) and \\(E_{i,k}\\) can be computed before solving.  
* **Scalability** – If the network has many trains, the pairwise ordering variables \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\) become large (\\(O(T^2 S)\\)).  In practice you can replace them with a **time‑indexed** formulation or a **capacity‑based** (≤C) formulation when multiple parallel tracks exist.  
* **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with additional linear terms (e.g., crew cost, passenger‑time penalties, platform‑occupancy constraints) without changing its MILP nature.

---

**Result:** The formulation above is a *complete, linear mixed‑integer programming model* that captures train‑rescheduling together with speed‑management when part of the line is blocked.  All elements of the problem statement appear as variables, a linear objective, and a set of linear constraints, ready to be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model** that captures the three inter‑related sub‑problems mentioned in the description:

* **(i) Route‑choice** – a train may be rerouted around a blocked segment.  
* **(ii) Timetabling** – arrival / departure times must respect travelling‑time, head‑way and single‑track capacity.  
* **(iii) Speed‑management** – for every line segment a train can select one of a small set of admissible speed‑levels (each level is a discrete “speed‑profile” with a known energy cost and travel‑time).

The model is **linear**; all non‑linear relationships (e.g., kinetic‑energy formulas) have been pre‑computed for the discrete speed‑levels so that they appear as constant coefficients.  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| **N** = {1,…, |N|} | Set of *nodes* (stations, junctions, block terminals). |
| **S** ⊂ N×N | Set of *track segments* (directed arcs) that connect two nodes.  An arc is written **s = (i, j)**. |
| **K** = {1,…, |K|} | Set of admissible *speed‑levels* (or speed‑profiles).  For a given segment **s** the feasible speed‑levels are denoted **K_s ⊆ K**. |
| **B ⊆ S** | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** during a disruption window.  For each blocked segment **b∈B** we know the blockage start **τ_b^start** and end **τ_b^end** and the length of the blocked sub‑segment (e.g., one‑third of the total length). |
| **R_i** | Set of *alternative routes* (ordered node‑lists) that train *i* may use to travel from its origin to its destination.  Each route **r∈R_i** is a sequence of arcs **s∈S**. |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **x_{i,r}** | binary | =1 if train *i* uses route *r ∈ R_i*, 0 otherwise. |
| **a_{i,n}** | continuous ≥0 | **arrival time** of train *i* at node *n* (only defined if *n* belongs to the chosen route). |
| **d_{i,n}** | continuous ≥0 | **departure time** of train *i* from node *n*. |
| **y_{i,s,k}** | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* with speed‑level *k∈K_s*.  (Only one k can be chosen per traversed segment.) |
| **z_{i,s}** | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* at all (used for capacity constraints). |
| **Δ_i** | continuous ≥0 | **total delay** of train *i* with respect to its scheduled (planned) arrival at its final destination. |
| **E_i** | continuous ≥0 | **energy consumption** of train *i* (sum of the energy of the selected speed‑levels). |

---

## 3. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **O_i**, **D_i** | Origin node and destination node of train *i*. |
| **T_i^{plan}** | Planned (un‑disrupted) arrival time of train *i* at its destination. |
| **L_s** | Physical length of segment *s*. |
| **t_{s,k}** | Travel time needed to cover segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (pre‑computed as  `L_s / v_k`). |
| **e_{s,k}** | Energy consumption incurred on segment *s* with speed‑level *k* (pre‑computed, e.g., kWh). |
| **h_{i}** | Minimum **head‑way** (service‑time) that train *i* must respect at every station (dwell + safety). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible schedule time (e.g., 10⁶ minutes). |
| **γ**, **β** | Weighting coefficients in the objective:  γ for total delay, β for total energy. |
| **C_s** | Capacity of segment *s*: for a single‑track line **C_s = 1** (only one train at a time). |
| **τ_b^{start}**, **τ_b^{end}** | Start and end times of the disruption window on blocked segment *b∈B*. |
| **α_{b}** | Fraction of segment *b* that is blocked (0 < α_b < 1).  The un‑blocked length is (1‑α_b)·L_b; travel for the blocked part must be avoided or traversed at a reduced speed‑level (modelled via special speed‑levels in K_b). |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\gamma\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_i}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; 
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{i\in T}E_i}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_i = a_{i,\text{dest}(i)} - T_i^{plan}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

\[
E_i = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k}\;y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

The objective is a **weighted sum**; the decision maker can tune γ and β to reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

### 4.2 Routing constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**

\[
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage**  

For every segment *s* that belongs to a route *r* we define a parameter  

\[
\delta_{s}^{r}= \begin{cases}
1 &\text{if segment }s\text{ is part of route }r\\
0 &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

Then  

\[
z_{i,s}= \sum_{r\in R_i}\delta_{s}^{r}\;x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;s\in S
\]

Thus **z_{i,s}=1** iff the selected route for train *i* contains segment *s*.

3. **Exactly one speed‑level per traversed segment**

\[
\sum_{k\in K_s} y_{i,s,k}= z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;s\in S
\]

If train *i* does not traverse *s* (z_{i,s}=0) then all y‑variables for that segment are forced to 0.

---

### 4.3 Time‑feasibility (travel‑time)  

For every train *i* and every segment *s=(u,v)∈S* that it traverses:

\[
a_{i,v}\; \ge\; d_{i,u} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k} \qquad\forall i\in T,\;s=(u,v)\in S
\]

The departure time from the upstream node plus the travelled time (chosen speed‑level) gives a lower bound on the arrival at the downstream node.

---

### 4.4 Dwell / service time at stations  

For every train *i* and every node *n* that belongs to its route (including origin and destination):

\[
d_{i,n}\; \ge\; a_{i,n}+h_i\;-\;M\;(1-\underbrace{z_{i,s^{in}}}_{\text{train visits }n})\qquad\forall i\in T,\; n\in N
\]

where *s^{in}* is the incoming segment to node *n* on the selected route (if a train never visits *n*, the big‑M term de‑activates the constraint).

---

### 4.5 Single‑track capacity (conflict avoidance)  

Because each segment can be occupied by **at most one train at a time**, we introduce *ordering* binary variables:

\[
\theta_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i<i',\; s\in S
\]

Interpretation:  

*θ_{i,i',s}=1* ⇔ train *i* passes segment *s* **before** train *i'*.

The standard disjunctive (big‑M) formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i',\text{end}(s)} \;&\ge\; d_{i,\text{start}(s)} + \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} \;-\; M\;(1-\theta_{i,i',s})\\
a_{i,\text{end}(s)} \;&\ge\; d_{i',\text{start}(s)} + \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i',s,k} \;-\; M\;\theta_{i,i',s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<i',\; s\in S
\]

Additionally we must enforce that the ordering variables are only relevant when **both** trains actually use the segment:

\[
\theta_{i,i',s} \le z_{i,s},\qquad \theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i',s}\qquad\forall i<i',\,s\in S
\]

If either train does not occupy *s*, the binary may be forced to 0 by the above constraints, and the big‑M terms relax the time inequalities.

---

### 4.6 Blockage (partial segment) constraints  

For each blocked segment *b∈B* we must guarantee that **no train occupies the blocked sub‑length during the disruption window**. There are two common ways; we adopt the “speed‑level” approach, i.e., we provide a *special low‑speed* level *k_b^{slow}* that respects the reduced available length (1‑α_b)·L_b and whose travel time is pre‑computed accordingly. The model then forces any train that traverses *b* during the window to use that level.

1. **Identify if a train uses the blocked segment during the window**

Introduce binary **w_{i,b}**:

\[
w_{i,b}\; \ge\; a_{i,\text{end}(b)} \;-\; \tau_b^{start}\;-\;M\;(1-z_{i,b}) \quad\text{(lower bound)} 
\]

\[
w_{i,b}\; \ge\; \tau_b^{end}\;-\; a_{i,\text{start}(b)}\;-\;M\;(1-z_{i,b}) \quad\text{(upper bound)}
\]

A more compact big‑M formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{start}(b)} &\ge \tau_b^{end} - M(1-w_{i,b})\\
a_{i,\text{end}(b)}   &\le \tau_b^{start} + M(1-w_{i,b})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B
\]

Thus **w_{i,b}=1** only if the train’s presence on *b* overlaps the disruption window.

2. **Force a “slow” speed‑level when overlap occurs**

Let **k_b^{slow}∈K_b** denote the admissible speed‑level for the (1‑α_b) un‑blocked part. Then:

\[
y_{i,b,k_b^{slow}} \;\ge\; w_{i,b}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B
\]

and for all **other** speed‑levels *k≠k_b^{slow}* on the blocked segment:

\[
y_{i,b,k} \;\le\; 1-w_{i,b}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B,\;k\in K_b\setminus\{k_b^{slow}\}
\]

If a train does **not** overlap the window (w_{i,b}=0) it may select any admissible speed‑level; if it does overlap, the only feasible choice is the reduced‑speed level.

---

### 4.7 Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_i \;=\; a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

If early arrival is allowed and should not be penalised, we add:

\[
\Delta_i \ge 0,\qquad
\Delta_i \ge a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan}
\]

The first inequality already forces non‑negativity; the second links Δ to the actual arrival.

---

### 4.8 Energy accumulation  

\[
E_i \;=\; \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

Because each *y* is binary and each train traverses each segment at most once, this sum correctly aggregates the energy of the chosen speed‑levels.

---

### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\qquad y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\qquad z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&\theta_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad w_{i,b}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,n}\ge 0,\; d_{i,n}\ge 0,\; \Delta_i\ge 0,\; E_i\ge 0 \quad\forall i,n.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Component | What it Represents | How it is Enforced in the MILP |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Route choice** | Each train may follow any of its pre‑computed alternative routes (e.g., detours around a blockage). | Binary variables *x_{i,r}* (one per route). Constraint (1) forces exactly one route per train; linking constraints (2) translate the chosen route into segment‑usage binaries *z_{i,s}* . |
| **Speed‑profile selection** | For every traversed segment, a discrete speed level is chosen; each level has a known travel time *t_{s,k}* and energy cost *e_{s,k}*. | Binary *y_{i,s,k}* with (3) guaranteeing exactly one speed level per traversed segment. Travel‑time and energy terms are linear because *t_{s,k}* and *e_{s,k}* are constants. |
| **Timetable (arrival/departure times)** | Actual times at each node must respect travel times (according to the selected speed), dwell times, and head‑way/single‑track capacity. | Constraints (4)–(5) link arrivals/departures with travel‑time. Dwell is imposed by (5). Capacity/conflict avoidance uses ordering binaries *θ* and big‑M constraints (6). |
| **Partial‑segment blockage** | A fraction α of a segment is unavailable during a known time window; only trains that cross during that window must adopt a lower‑speed level (or be rerouted). | Overlap binaries *w_{i,b}* detect whether a train is on a blocked segment during the window (7). Then (8) forces the “slow” speed level *k_b^{slow}* for overlapped trains, while prohibiting all other levels. |
| **Delay** | Deviation of the actual arrival at the destination from the planned (pre‑disruption) arrival. | Δ_i defined by (9) and appears in the objective with weight γ. |
| **Energy consumption** | Sum of the energy of all chosen speed levels on all traversed segments. | E_i defined by (10) and appears in the objective with weight β. |
| **Objective** | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay (punctuality) and total energy (environmental cost). | Equation (0). By changing γ/β the planner can prioritize one goal over the other. |
| **Capacity (single‑track)** | No two trains may occupy the same segment at the same instant. | Binary ordering variables *θ_{i,i',s}* together with (6) guarantee a temporal order for any pair of trains sharing a segment, respecting the segment’s capacity C_s=1. |
| **Feasibility bounds** | Ensure all variables stay within realistic ranges (times ≥0, binary on/off). | Variable domain declarations (11). |

---

## 6. Remarks on Practical Use  

1. **Pre‑processing** – The sets *R_i* (alternative routes) and *K_s* (allowed speed‑levels per segment) are usually generated by a *routing* or *speed‑profiling* preprocessing step. The travel‑time *t_{s,k}* and energy *e_{s,k}* are computed (e.g., from a physics‑based model) **once** and then fed as data to the MILP.  

2. **Big‑M selection** – *M* must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 24 h ≈ 1440 min). A tighter *M* improves solver performance.  

3. **Scalability** – The number of ordering binaries *θ* is O(|T|²·|S|). For large instances a **time‑window** (conflict‑graph) reduction, or a *continuous‑time* “time‑indexed” formulation, may be used to keep the model tractable.  

4. **Extensions** – Additional realistic aspects can be added without breaking linearity:  
   * Train‑specific energy tariffs (different β per train).  
   * Penalties for excessive speed‑level changes (add binary variables for “speed‑switch”).  
   * Minimum/maximum dwell times at particular stations (replace constant *h_i* by station‑specific bounds).  

---

### 7. Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&\gamma\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_i \;+\; \beta\sum_{i\in T}E_i\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }\\
&\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\in T\\
&z_{i,s}= \sum_{r\in R_i}\delta_{s}^{r}\,x_{i,r} &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\\
&\sum_{k\in K_s} y_{i,s,k}=z_{i,s} &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\\
&a_{i,v} \ge d_{i,u}+ \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i\in T,\;(u,v)=s\in S\\
&d_{i,n} \ge a_{i,n}+h_i &&\forall i\in T,\; n\in N\text{ visited by }i\\
&\Delta_i \ge a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan} &&\forall i\in T\\
&E_i = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i\in T\\
&\text{(capacity)}\;\;
\begin{cases}
a_{i',\text{end}(s)} \ge d_{i,\text{start}(s)}+\sum_k t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k}-M(1-\theta_{i,i',s})\\[2pt]
a_{i,\text{end}(s)} \ge d_{i',\text{start}(s)}+\sum_k t_{s,k} y_{i',s,k}-M\theta_{i,i',s}
\end{cases}\\
&\theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i,s},\;\theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i',s} &&\forall i<i',\;s\in S\\
&\text{(blocked segment)}\;
\begin{aligned}
&a_{i,\text{start}(b)} \ge \tau_b^{end} - M(1-w_{i,b})\\
&a_{i,\text{end}(b)}   \le \tau_b^{start} + M(1-w_{i,b})
\end{aligned}
&&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B\\
&y_{i,b,k_b^{slow}} \ge w_{i,b} &&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B\\
&y_{i,b,k} \le 1-w_{i,b} &&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B,\;k\neq k_b^{slow}\\
&\text{domain constraints (binary / non‑negative)}\\[4pt]
\end{aligned}
\]

All symbols are defined in Sections 1‑5. This model can be handed directly to a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). By solving it, the planner obtains for every train:

* the **route** (via the *x* variables),  
* the **departure/arrival schedule** (via *a* and *d*),  
* the **speed‑profile** on each segment (via *y*),  

that together give the **minimum weighted sum of total delay and energy** while respecting the partial blockage, single‑track capacity, and all physical/operational constraints.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the key decisions required for **integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management** when a **partial segment of the line is blocked** (e.g., due to an incident, maintenance work or a broken rail).  

The model is written in a **canonical linear‐programming form** (variables, objective, linear constraints).  After the formulation each component is explained so that you can see how the description maps onto the mathematics.

---

## 1️⃣  Sets, Parameters and Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(\\mathcal{T}=\\{1,\dots,T\\}\\) | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| \\(\\mathcal{S}=\\{1,\dots,S\\}\\) | Set of **track segments** (the line is divided into elementary sections). |
| \\(\\mathcal{K}=\\{1,\dots,K\\}\\) | Set of admissible **speed‑profile choices** for a train on a segment (e.g., “full speed”, “reduced speed”, “stop”). |
| \\(\\mathcal{R}=\\{r_1,\dots,r_R\\}\\) | Set of **feasible routes** (ordered list of segments) that a train may follow from its origin to its destination.  For each train \\(i\\) we denote the admissible routes by \\(\\mathcal{R}_i\\subseteq\\mathcal{R}\\). |
| \\(\\mathcal{B}\\subseteq \\mathcal{S}\\) | Subset of segments that are **blocked** during a known disruption window \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\\). |
| \\(\\delta_{i,r,s}\\) | 1 if segment \\(s\\) belongs to route \\(r\\) for train \\(i\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(L_{s}\\) | Length (km) of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(v^{\max}_{k}\\) | Speed (km/h) associated with speed‑profile choice \\(k\\).  (All \\(v^{\max}_{k}\\) are constants.) |
| \\(a^{\max},d^{\max}\\) | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km/h²) that can be applied when switching between speed profiles. |
| \\(t^{\text{sched}}_{i}\\) | Planned (pre‑disruption) departure time of train \\(i\\) from its origin. |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Positive weights for the two components of the objective (delay vs. energy). |
| \\(E_{i,k}\\) | Energy cost (e.g. kWh) incurred by train \\(i\\) when it runs on a segment with speed profile \\(k\\).  Typically proportional to \\(L_s\) and \\(v_k\\). |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g., \\(M = 10^6\\) minutes). |
| \\(\\epsilon\\) | Minimum head‑way (in minutes) required between two trains occupying the same segment (safety margin). |

---

## 2️⃣  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| \\(x_{i,r}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) uses route \\(r\\in\\mathcal{R}_i\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed‑profile \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Arrival time** (in minutes) of train \\(i\\) at the **up‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | **Departure time** of train \\(i\\) from the **down‑stream** node of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(Δ_i\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(i\\) (difference between actual departure from origin and scheduled departure). |
| \\(z_{i,s}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) **occupies** segment \\(s\\) (any speed) – useful for capacity/conflict constraints. |

*All other variables that appear below are linear expressions of these variables.*

---

## 3️⃣  Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption**:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} Δ_i \;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\;\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}  E_{i,k}\; y_{i,s,k}
}
\]

* The first term penalises the sum of all train delays.  
* The second term adds the energy cost of the selected speed profiles.

Both terms are linear because \\(Δ_i\\) and \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) are decision variables.

---

## 4️⃣  Core Linear Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice feasibility  

\[
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i} x_{i,r}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{T}\tag{R1}
\]

Every train selects **exactly one** feasible route.

### 4.2 Linking route, segment, and speed‑profile variables  

\[
y_{i,s,k}\le \sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}\delta_{i,r,s}\,x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,s,k\tag{R2}
\]

If a route that does **not** contain segment \\(s\\) is chosen, the binary \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) must be 0.  
Conversely, when a route contains \\(s\\), we may pick *any* speed profile; the model will later decide which one to activate.

### 4.3 Occupancy indicator  

\[
z_{i,s}\;=\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i,s\tag{R3}
\]

A train occupies a segment if it traverses it with **some** speed profile.

### 4.4 Delay definition  

\[
Δ_i \; \ge\; a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}} - t^{\text{sched}}_{i} \qquad\forall i\tag{R4}
\]

where \\(s^{\text{orig}}\\) is the (virtual) segment that represents the train’s origin node.  Because \\(a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}}\\) is the actual departure time, the difference is the delay.  (If you prefer a tight equality you can add a “≤” version together, but “≥” is sufficient for minimisation.)

### 4.5 Travel‑time (kinematic) constraints  

If train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) with speed profile \\(k\\), the **minimum travel time** across that segment is

\[
\frac{L_{s}}{v_k}\quad (\text{minutes if }v_k\text{ in km/min})
\]

Let \\(τ_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\\) be a pre‑computed constant.  Then:

\[
d_{i,s} \; \ge\; a_{i,s} + \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} τ_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i,s\tag{R5}
\]

The departure from the downstream node cannot be earlier than arrival + travel time.

### 4.6 Successive‑segment linking (continuity)  

For any two **consecutive** segments \\(s\\) and \\(s'\\) on the same route, the arrival at the next segment equals the departure from the previous one:

\[
a_{i,s'} \; \ge\; d_{i,s} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{i,s})\qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on a route}\tag{R6}
\]

If the train does **not** occupy segment \\(s\\) (\\(z_{i,s}=0\\)), the big‑M deactivates the constraint.

### 4.7 Single‑track capacity (one train at a time)  

For every segment \\(s\\) we must ensure that at any moment only **one train** occupies it (single‑track).  This is expressed with a disjunctive “ordering” constraint using binary order variables \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\in\{0,1\}\\) that decide who passes first:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i',s} &\ge d_{i,s} + \epsilon - M\,θ_{i,i',s} \qquad\forall i\neq i',\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R7a}\\
a_{i,s}  &\ge d_{i',s} + \epsilon - M\,(1-θ_{i,i',s}) \qquad\forall i\neq i',\; s\in\mathcal{S} \tag{R7b}\\
θ_{i,i',s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

Only one of the two inequalities is active (the one with the smaller right‑hand side), guaranteeing a **head‑way of at least \\(\\epsilon\\)** minutes.

*If the line is double‑track for some segments, you can replace (R7) by a capacity limit:*
\[
\sum_{i} z_{i,s}\le C_s\qquad \forall s,
\]
where \\(C_s\\) is the number of parallel tracks (normally 1).  

### 4.8 Conflict‑avoidance for the **blocked** window  

If a segment \\(s\\) is blocked during the interval \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\\), no train may occupy it then:

\[
a_{i,s} \;\ge\; t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\,(1-z_{i,s}) \quad\text{or}\quad d_{i,s} \;\le\; t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\,(1-z_{i,s})\qquad\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{B}\tag{R8}
\]

A common linearisation uses a binary “use‑or‑avoid” variable, but the big‑M form above forces the whole traversal to lie **outside** the blocked interval.

### 4.9 Acceleration / deceleration limits when changing speed profile  

If a train changes from speed profile \\(k\\) on segment \\(s\\) to profile \\(k'\\) on the next segment \\(s'\\), the time difference between departure from \\(s\\) and arrival at \\(s'\\) must respect the maximum acceleration/deceleration.  A compact linear formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{i,s} + \frac{v_{k'}-v_{k}}{a^{\max}} &\le a_{i,s'} + M\,(2-y_{i,s,k} - y_{i,s',k'}) \qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')\\
d_{i,s} + \frac{v_{k}-v_{k'}}{d^{\max}} &\le a_{i,s'} + M\,(2-y_{i,s,k} - y_{i,s',k'}) \qquad\forall i,\; (s,s')
\end{aligned}
\]

Only when both binary variables are 1 does the inequality become active; otherwise the big‑M disables it.  The fractions are constants (pre‑computed).  

### 4.10 Routing feasibility (origin/destination)  

For each train we must enforce that the chosen route starts at its origin node and ends at its destination node.  This can be modelled by fixing the binary variables for the first and last segment of each admissible route, e.g.:

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s^{\text{orig}},k}=x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\text{ with origin }s^{\text{orig}}
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s^{\text{dest}},k}=x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\text{ with destination }s^{\text{dest}}
\]

(Only the route actually selected will activate the corresponding segment‑occupancy variables.)

---

## 5️⃣  Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} Δ_i
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}E_{i,k}\, y_{i,s,k}    \\
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i} x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\in\mathcal{T} &&\text{(R1)}\\[2mm]
& y_{i,s,k}\le\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}\delta_{i,r,s}\,x_{i,r} &&\forall i,s,k &&\text{(R2)}\\[2mm]
& z_{i,s}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s &&\text{(R3)}\\[2mm]
& Δ_i \ge a_{i,s^{\text{orig}}} - t^{\text{sched}}_{i} &&\forall i &&\text{(R4)}\\[2mm]
& d_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s} + \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} τ_{s,k}\, y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s &&\text{(R5)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} - M\,(1-z_{i,s}) &&\forall i,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive} &&\text{(R6)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i',s} \ge d_{i,s} + \epsilon - M\,θ_{i,i',s} &&\forall i\neq i',\; s &&\text{(R7a)}\\
& a_{i,s}  \ge d_{i',s} + \epsilon - M\,(1-θ_{i,i',s}) &&\forall i\neq i',\; s &&\text{(R7b)}\\[2mm]
& a_{i,s} \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-z_{i,s})\; \text{or}\;
  d_{i,s} \le t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-z_{i,s}) &&\forall i,\; s\in\mathcal{B} &&\text{(R8)}\\[2mm]
&\text{Acceleration limits (R9)} &&\forall i,\;(s,s'),k,k'\\[2mm]
&\text{Origin/Destination linking (R10)} &&\forall i,r\in\mathcal{R}_i\\[2mm]
& x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\ y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\ z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\ θ_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},Δ_i \ge 0 \qquad &&\forall i,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear** in the decision variables; the only integer components are the binary variables.

---

## 6️⃣  How Each Modelling Element Relates to the Description  

| Description element | MILP component |
|---------------------|----------------|
| **Binary route‑choice** | \\(x_{i,r}\\) (R1) and the linking (R2) |
| **Arrival / departure times** | \\(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\\) with travel‑time (R5) and continuity (R6) |
| **Speed‑segment selection** | \\(y_{i,s,k}\\) (binary) – tells which speed profile is used on each traversed segment |
| **Weighted sum of delay & energy** | Objective term \\(w^{\text{delay}}\sum Δ_i + w^{\text{energy}}\sum E_{i,k} y_{i,s,k}\\) |
| **Time feasibility** | (R5)‑(R6) ensure enough time for distance at chosen speed; acceleration limits (R9) |
| **Single‑track capacity** | Ordering binaries \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\) enforce at most one train on a segment at any moment (R7) |
| **Conflict‑avoidance** | Same as capacity; also the head‑way ε |
| **Kinematics (speed‑profile) constraints** | (R5) travel time, (R9) acceleration/deceleration limits |
| **Routing feasibility** | (R1) route‑choice, (R10) origin/destination anchoring |
| **Disruption‑window blockages** | (R8) forces any traversal of a blocked segment to be outside the blockage interval |

---

## 7️⃣  Practical Remarks  

* **Big‑M selection** – Choose \\(M\\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., a few hours expressed in minutes).  
* **Pre‑computation** – The constants \\(τ_{s,k}=L_s/v_k\\) and \\(E_{i,k}\\) can be computed before solving.  
* **Scalability** – If the network has many trains, the pairwise ordering variables \\(θ_{i,i',s}\\) become large (\\(O(T^2 S)\\)).  In practice you can replace them with a **time‑indexed** formulation or a **capacity‑based** (≤C) formulation when multiple parallel tracks exist.  
* **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with additional linear terms (e.g., crew cost, passenger‑time penalties, platform‑occupancy constraints) without changing its MILP nature.

---

**Result:** The formulation above is a *complete, linear mixed‑integer programming model* that captures train‑rescheduling together with speed‑management when part of the line is blocked.  All elements of the problem statement appear as variables, a linear objective, and a set of linear constraints, ready to be handed to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management MILP for partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, arrival/departure times, speed segment selection. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, single track capacity, conflict avoidance, speed-profile kinematics, routing feasibility, disruption window blockages.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model** that captures the three inter‑related sub‑problems mentioned in the description:

* **(i) Route‑choice** – a train may be rerouted around a blocked segment.  
* **(ii) Timetabling** – arrival / departure times must respect travelling‑time, head‑way and single‑track capacity.  
* **(iii) Speed‑management** – for every line segment a train can select one of a small set of admissible speed‑levels (each level is a discrete “speed‑profile” with a known energy cost and travel‑time).

The model is **linear**; all non‑linear relationships (e.g., kinetic‑energy formulas) have been pre‑computed for the discrete speed‑levels so that they appear as constant coefficients.  

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** = {1,…, |T|} | Set of trains that have to be scheduled. |
| **N** = {1,…, |N|} | Set of *nodes* (stations, junctions, block terminals). |
| **S** ⊂ N×N | Set of *track segments* (directed arcs) that connect two nodes.  An arc is written **s = (i, j)**. |
| **K** = {1,…, |K|} | Set of admissible *speed‑levels* (or speed‑profiles).  For a given segment **s** the feasible speed‑levels are denoted **K_s ⊆ K**. |
| **B ⊆ S** | Subset of segments that are **partially blocked** during a disruption window.  For each blocked segment **b∈B** we know the blockage start **τ_b^start** and end **τ_b^end** and the length of the blocked sub‑segment (e.g., one‑third of the total length). |
| **R_i** | Set of *alternative routes* (ordered node‑lists) that train *i* may use to travel from its origin to its destination.  Each route **r∈R_i** is a sequence of arcs **s∈S**. |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|----------|
| **x_{i,r}** | binary | =1 if train *i* uses route *r ∈ R_i*, 0 otherwise. |
| **a_{i,n}** | continuous ≥0 | **arrival time** of train *i* at node *n* (only defined if *n* belongs to the chosen route). |
| **d_{i,n}** | continuous ≥0 | **departure time** of train *i* from node *n*. |
| **y_{i,s,k}** | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* with speed‑level *k∈K_s*.  (Only one k can be chosen per traversed segment.) |
| **z_{i,s}** | binary | =1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* at all (used for capacity constraints). |
| **Δ_i** | continuous ≥0 | **total delay** of train *i* with respect to its scheduled (planned) arrival at its final destination. |
| **E_i** | continuous ≥0 | **energy consumption** of train *i* (sum of the energy of the selected speed‑levels). |

---

## 3. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **O_i**, **D_i** | Origin node and destination node of train *i*. |
| **T_i^{plan}** | Planned (un‑disrupted) arrival time of train *i* at its destination. |
| **L_s** | Physical length of segment *s*. |
| **t_{s,k}** | Travel time needed to cover segment *s* when speed‑level *k* is used (pre‑computed as  `L_s / v_k`). |
| **e_{s,k}** | Energy consumption incurred on segment *s* with speed‑level *k* (pre‑computed, e.g., kWh). |
| **h_{i}** | Minimum **head‑way** (service‑time) that train *i* must respect at every station (dwell + safety). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible schedule time (e.g., 10⁶ minutes). |
| **γ**, **β** | Weighting coefficients in the objective:  γ for total delay, β for total energy. |
| **C_s** | Capacity of segment *s*: for a single‑track line **C_s = 1** (only one train at a time). |
| **τ_b^{start}**, **τ_b^{end}** | Start and end times of the disruption window on blocked segment *b∈B*. |
| **α_{b}** | Fraction of segment *b* that is blocked (0 < α_b < 1).  The un‑blocked length is (1‑α_b)·L_b; travel for the blocked part must be avoided or traversed at a reduced speed‑level (modelled via special speed‑levels in K_b). |

---

## 4. Model Formulation  

### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min \; \underbrace{\gamma\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_i}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; 
\underbrace{\beta\sum_{i\in T}E_i}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

where  

\[
\Delta_i = a_{i,\text{dest}(i)} - T_i^{plan}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

\[
E_i = \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k}\;y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

The objective is a **weighted sum**; the decision maker can tune γ and β to reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

### 4.2 Routing constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**

\[
\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage**  

For every segment *s* that belongs to a route *r* we define a parameter  

\[
\delta_{s}^{r}= \begin{cases}
1 &\text{if segment }s\text{ is part of route }r\\
0 &\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

Then  

\[
z_{i,s}= \sum_{r\in R_i}\delta_{s}^{r}\;x_{i,r}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;s\in S
\]

Thus **z_{i,s}=1** iff the selected route for train *i* contains segment *s*.

3. **Exactly one speed‑level per traversed segment**

\[
\sum_{k\in K_s} y_{i,s,k}= z_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;s\in S
\]

If train *i* does not traverse *s* (z_{i,s}=0) then all y‑variables for that segment are forced to 0.

---

### 4.3 Time‑feasibility (travel‑time)  

For every train *i* and every segment *s=(u,v)∈S* that it traverses:

\[
a_{i,v}\; \ge\; d_{i,u} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k} \qquad\forall i\in T,\;s=(u,v)\in S
\]

The departure time from the upstream node plus the travelled time (chosen speed‑level) gives a lower bound on the arrival at the downstream node.

---

### 4.4 Dwell / service time at stations  

For every train *i* and every node *n* that belongs to its route (including origin and destination):

\[
d_{i,n}\; \ge\; a_{i,n}+h_i\;-\;M\;(1-\underbrace{z_{i,s^{in}}}_{\text{train visits }n})\qquad\forall i\in T,\; n\in N
\]

where *s^{in}* is the incoming segment to node *n* on the selected route (if a train never visits *n*, the big‑M term de‑activates the constraint).

---

### 4.5 Single‑track capacity (conflict avoidance)  

Because each segment can be occupied by **at most one train at a time**, we introduce *ordering* binary variables:

\[
\theta_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\}\qquad\forall i<i',\; s\in S
\]

Interpretation:  

*θ_{i,i',s}=1* ⇔ train *i* passes segment *s* **before** train *i'*.

The standard disjunctive (big‑M) formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i',\text{end}(s)} \;&\ge\; d_{i,\text{start}(s)} + \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} \;-\; M\;(1-\theta_{i,i',s})\\
a_{i,\text{end}(s)} \;&\ge\; d_{i',\text{start}(s)} + \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i',s,k} \;-\; M\;\theta_{i,i',s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<i',\; s\in S
\]

Additionally we must enforce that the ordering variables are only relevant when **both** trains actually use the segment:

\[
\theta_{i,i',s} \le z_{i,s},\qquad \theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i',s}\qquad\forall i<i',\,s\in S
\]

If either train does not occupy *s*, the binary may be forced to 0 by the above constraints, and the big‑M terms relax the time inequalities.

---

### 4.6 Blockage (partial segment) constraints  

For each blocked segment *b∈B* we must guarantee that **no train occupies the blocked sub‑length during the disruption window**. There are two common ways; we adopt the “speed‑level” approach, i.e., we provide a *special low‑speed* level *k_b^{slow}* that respects the reduced available length (1‑α_b)·L_b and whose travel time is pre‑computed accordingly. The model then forces any train that traverses *b* during the window to use that level.

1. **Identify if a train uses the blocked segment during the window**

Introduce binary **w_{i,b}**:

\[
w_{i,b}\; \ge\; a_{i,\text{end}(b)} \;-\; \tau_b^{start}\;-\;M\;(1-z_{i,b}) \quad\text{(lower bound)} 
\]

\[
w_{i,b}\; \ge\; \tau_b^{end}\;-\; a_{i,\text{start}(b)}\;-\;M\;(1-z_{i,b}) \quad\text{(upper bound)}
\]

A more compact big‑M formulation is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{start}(b)} &\ge \tau_b^{end} - M(1-w_{i,b})\\
a_{i,\text{end}(b)}   &\le \tau_b^{start} + M(1-w_{i,b})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B
\]

Thus **w_{i,b}=1** only if the train’s presence on *b* overlaps the disruption window.

2. **Force a “slow” speed‑level when overlap occurs**

Let **k_b^{slow}∈K_b** denote the admissible speed‑level for the (1‑α_b) un‑blocked part. Then:

\[
y_{i,b,k_b^{slow}} \;\ge\; w_{i,b}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B
\]

and for all **other** speed‑levels *k≠k_b^{slow}* on the blocked segment:

\[
y_{i,b,k} \;\le\; 1-w_{i,b}\qquad\forall i\in T,\; b\in B,\;k\in K_b\setminus\{k_b^{slow}\}
\]

If a train does **not** overlap the window (w_{i,b}=0) it may select any admissible speed‑level; if it does overlap, the only feasible choice is the reduced‑speed level.

---

### 4.7 Delay definition  

\[
\Delta_i \;=\; a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

If early arrival is allowed and should not be penalised, we add:

\[
\Delta_i \ge 0,\qquad
\Delta_i \ge a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan}
\]

The first inequality already forces non‑negativity; the second links Δ to the actual arrival.

---

### 4.8 Energy accumulation  

\[
E_i \;=\; \sum_{s\in S}\;\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k}\; y_{i,s,k}\qquad\forall i\in T
\]

Because each *y* is binary and each train traverses each segment at most once, this sum correctly aggregates the energy of the chosen speed‑levels.

---

### 4.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{i,r}\in\{0,1\},\qquad y_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\qquad z_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\\
&\theta_{i,i',s}\in\{0,1\},\qquad w_{i,b}\in\{0,1\},\\
&a_{i,n}\ge 0,\; d_{i,n}\ge 0,\; \Delta_i\ge 0,\; E_i\ge 0 \quad\forall i,n.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 5. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Component | What it Represents | How it is Enforced in the MILP |
|-----------|-------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Route choice** | Each train may follow any of its pre‑computed alternative routes (e.g., detours around a blockage). | Binary variables *x_{i,r}* (one per route). Constraint (1) forces exactly one route per train; linking constraints (2) translate the chosen route into segment‑usage binaries *z_{i,s}* . |
| **Speed‑profile selection** | For every traversed segment, a discrete speed level is chosen; each level has a known travel time *t_{s,k}* and energy cost *e_{s,k}*. | Binary *y_{i,s,k}* with (3) guaranteeing exactly one speed level per traversed segment. Travel‑time and energy terms are linear because *t_{s,k}* and *e_{s,k}* are constants. |
| **Timetable (arrival/departure times)** | Actual times at each node must respect travel times (according to the selected speed), dwell times, and head‑way/single‑track capacity. | Constraints (4)–(5) link arrivals/departures with travel‑time. Dwell is imposed by (5). Capacity/conflict avoidance uses ordering binaries *θ* and big‑M constraints (6). |
| **Partial‑segment blockage** | A fraction α of a segment is unavailable during a known time window; only trains that cross during that window must adopt a lower‑speed level (or be rerouted). | Overlap binaries *w_{i,b}* detect whether a train is on a blocked segment during the window (7). Then (8) forces the “slow” speed level *k_b^{slow}* for overlapped trains, while prohibiting all other levels. |
| **Delay** | Deviation of the actual arrival at the destination from the planned (pre‑disruption) arrival. | Δ_i defined by (9) and appears in the objective with weight γ. |
| **Energy consumption** | Sum of the energy of all chosen speed levels on all traversed segments. | E_i defined by (10) and appears in the objective with weight β. |
| **Objective** | Minimise a weighted sum of total delay (punctuality) and total energy (environmental cost). | Equation (0). By changing γ/β the planner can prioritize one goal over the other. |
| **Capacity (single‑track)** | No two trains may occupy the same segment at the same instant. | Binary ordering variables *θ_{i,i',s}* together with (6) guarantee a temporal order for any pair of trains sharing a segment, respecting the segment’s capacity C_s=1. |
| **Feasibility bounds** | Ensure all variables stay within realistic ranges (times ≥0, binary on/off). | Variable domain declarations (11). |

---

## 6. Remarks on Practical Use  

1. **Pre‑processing** – The sets *R_i* (alternative routes) and *K_s* (allowed speed‑levels per segment) are usually generated by a *routing* or *speed‑profiling* preprocessing step. The travel‑time *t_{s,k}* and energy *e_{s,k}* are computed (e.g., from a physics‑based model) **once** and then fed as data to the MILP.  

2. **Big‑M selection** – *M* must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 24 h ≈ 1440 min). A tighter *M* improves solver performance.  

3. **Scalability** – The number of ordering binaries *θ* is O(|T|²·|S|). For large instances a **time‑window** (conflict‑graph) reduction, or a *continuous‑time* “time‑indexed” formulation, may be used to keep the model tractable.  

4. **Extensions** – Additional realistic aspects can be added without breaking linearity:  
   * Train‑specific energy tariffs (different β per train).  
   * Penalties for excessive speed‑level changes (add binary variables for “speed‑switch”).  
   * Minimum/maximum dwell times at particular stations (replace constant *h_i* by station‑specific bounds).  

---

### 7. Full MILP Summary  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&\gamma\sum_{i\in T}\Delta_i \;+\; \beta\sum_{i\in T}E_i\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }\\
&\sum_{r\in R_i} x_{i,r}=1 &&\forall i\in T\\
&z_{i,s}= \sum_{r\in R_i}\delta_{s}^{r}\,x_{i,r} &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\\
&\sum_{k\in K_s} y_{i,s,k}=z_{i,s} &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\\
&a_{i,v} \ge d_{i,u}+ \sum_{k\in K_s} t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i\in T,\;(u,v)=s\in S\\
&d_{i,n} \ge a_{i,n}+h_i &&\forall i\in T,\; n\in N\text{ visited by }i\\
&\Delta_i \ge a_{i,D_i} - T_i^{plan} &&\forall i\in T\\
&E_i = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K_s} e_{s,k} y_{i,s,k} &&\forall i\in T\\
&\text{(capacity)}\;\;
\begin{cases}
a_{i',\text{end}(s)} \ge d_{i,\text{start}(s)}+\sum_k t_{s,k} y_{i,s,k}-M(1-\theta_{i,i',s})\\[2pt]
a_{i,\text{end}(s)} \ge d_{i',\text{start}(s)}+\sum_k t_{s,k} y_{i',s,k}-M\theta_{i,i',s}
\end{cases}\\
&\theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i,s},\;\theta_{i,i',s}\le z_{i',s} &&\forall i<i',\;s\in S\\
&\text{(blocked segment)}\;
\begin{aligned}
&a_{i,\text{start}(b)} \ge \tau_b^{end} - M(1-w_{i,b})\\
&a_{i,\text{end}(b)}   \le \tau_b^{start} + M(1-w_{i,b})
\end{aligned}
&&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B\\
&y_{i,b,k_b^{slow}} \ge w_{i,b} &&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B\\
&y_{i,b,k} \le 1-w_{i,b} &&\forall i\in T,\;b\in B,\;k\neq k_b^{slow}\\
&\text{domain constraints (binary / non‑negative)}\\[4pt]
\end{aligned}
\]

All symbols are defined in Sections 1‑5. This model can be handed directly to a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …). By solving it, the planner obtains for every train:

* the **route** (via the *x* variables),  
* the **departure/arrival schedule** (via *a* and *d*),  
* the **speed‑profile** on each segment (via *y*),  

that together give the **minimum weighted sum of total delay and energy** while respecting the partial blockage, single‑track capacity, and all physical/operational constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
