messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request: * **routing** – choose for every train whether it stays on its original track or is diverted to the opposite (reverse) track when a segment is partially blocked; * **timing** – decide the departure and arrival times of each train on every network segment; * **speed management** – select a discrete speed level for each train‑segment pair (the speed level determines both travel time and energy consumption). The model is written in a **linear** form (all constraints are linear, the only non‑linearities are replaced by binary‑selection variables and big‑M constructions). All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly, followed by a short explanation of each block. --- ## 1. Notation ### Index sets | Symbol | Meaning | |--------|---------| | \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\) | | \\(S\\) | Set of network **segments** (track sections) indexed by \\(s\\) | | \\(R\\) | Set of **routes** (directions) for a segment: \\(R=\{o,p\}\\) where
• \\(o\\) = original direction (as originally planned)
• \\(p\\) = opposite direction (the “reverse” track) | | \\(V\\) | Set of discrete **speed levels**, indexed by \\(v\\) (e.g. \\(v=1,\dots,V_{\max}\\)) | | \\(K\\) | Set of **time periods** (discrete horizon), indexed by \\(k\\) – used for conflict‑avoidance constraints | ### Parameters | Symbol | Description | |--------|-------------| | \\(d_{s}\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\) (km) | | \\(v^{\max}_{s,r}\\) | Maximum admissible speed on segment \\(s\\) when travelled in direction \\(r\\) (km/h) | | \\(v^{\min}_{s,r}\\) | Minimum admissible speed (usually a safety lower bound) | | \\(e_{s,v}\\) | Energy consumption (MJ) when a train traverses segment \\(s\\) at speed level \\(v\\). (Assumed linear in speed level) | | \\(T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r}\\) | Blockage time window on side \\(r\\) of segment \\(s\\): \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{start}},\,t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{end}}]\\) | | \\(t^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\\) | Planned (original) arrival time of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream** end of segment \\(s\\) (if no disruption) | | \\(w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\\) | Minimum dwell (stop) time of train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) (e.g. for passenger boarding) | | \\(M\\) | A sufficiently large constant (big‑M) – see constraints (5) | | \\(\alpha, \beta\\) | Positive weighting coefficients in the objective (delay vs. energy) | | \\(\Delta\\) | Length of a time‑period in the discrete horizon (e.g. 1 min). All times are expressed in the same unit. | ### Derived data * Travel time on segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(v\\): \[ \tau_{s,v}= \frac{d_{s}}{v_{v}} \qquad\text{(in the same time unit as } \Delta\text{)}. \] * For each train‑segment pair we also know the **original direction** (the direction it was scheduled to travel). Denote it \\(r^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\in R\\). --- ## 2. Decision variables | Variable | Type | Meaning | |----------|------|---------| | \\(x^{r}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) traverses segment \\(s\\) in direction \\(r\\) (\\(r=o\) original, \\(r=p\) opposite). | | \\(y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\}\\) | binary | 1 if speed level \\(v\\) is chosen for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\). | | \\(a_{t,s}\ge 0\\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \\(t\\) at the **down‑stream** end of segment \\(s\\). | | \\(d_{t,s}\ge 0\\) | continuous | Departure time of train \\(t\\) from the **up‑stream** end of segment \\(s\\). | | \\(z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) occupies segment \\(s\\) (in any direction) during time‑period \\(k\\). | | \\(E\\ge 0\\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of the whole schedule (used in the objective). | *Note*: The **up‑stream** end of a segment is the entry point for the chosen direction; the **down‑stream** end is the exit point. For a train travelling in the opposite direction the “up‑stream” and “down‑stream” ends are swapped, but the same variables are used – the routing binary \\(x^{r}_{t,s}\\) tells the model which orientation applies. --- ## 3. Objective function \[ \boxed{ \min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; \beta\;E } \] * The first term sums, for every train, the **difference** between its actual arrival time at the last (destination) segment (denoted \\(a_{t,\text{last}}\\)) and the originally planned arrival time. This is the total system delay. * The second term is the total energy consumption (see constraint (8) for its definition). * Weights \\(\alpha, \beta\\) allow the decision‑maker to trade off punctuality against energy usage. --- ## 4. Constraints ### 4.1 Routing – exactly one direction per segment \[ \sum_{r\in R} x^{r}_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{1} \] If a segment is **blocked** on one side, the corresponding binary will be forced to zero (see 4.4). ### 4.2 Speed‑level selection – exactly one speed per segment \[ \sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{2} \] ### 4.3 Time feasibility (travel‑time equation) The travel time on a segment equals the travel time associated with the selected speed level: \[ a_{t,s}= d_{t,s}+ \sum_{v\in V}\tau_{s,v}\;y_{t,s,v} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{3} \] The **departure** from the upstream end of a segment is the arrival at the downstream end of the preceding segment plus any required dwell time: \[ d_{t,s}= a_{t,s^{-}}+ w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s^{-}} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; s^{-}\text{ predecessor of }s. \tag{4} \] For the first segment of a train’s path we set \[ d_{t,s^{\text{first}}}= t^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{first}}}. \tag{4a} \] ### 4.4 Blockage – forbidden use of the blocked side If segment \\(s\\) is blocked on side \\(r\\) during interval \\([t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{start}},\,t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{end}}]\\), then any train that would occupy that side must be scheduled **outside** that window. This is enforced by linking the routing binary to the occupation‑binary variables (see 4.5) and by a simple time‑window exclusion: \[ z_{t,s,k}\le 1- x^{r}_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; r\in R,\; k\in K \text{ with } k\Delta\in T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r}. \tag{5} \] If the side is blocked, the right‑hand side becomes zero, forcing \\(z_{t,s,k}=0\\) for all periods inside the blockage. The routing binary can still be 1 only if the train uses the *other* side. ### 4.5 Occupancy‑binary linking (big‑M) We need to know whether a train occupies a segment during a particular time period. Let \[ L_{t,s}= d_{t,s} \qquad\text{(entry time)} ,\qquad U_{t,s}= a_{t,s} \qquad\text{(exit time)} . \] Using a big‑M we linearise the “train \\(t\\) is on segment \\(s\\) at period \\(k\\)” condition: \[ \begin{aligned} L_{t,s} &\le k\Delta + M\,(1-z_{t,s,k}) ,\\ U_{t,s} &\ge (k+1)\Delta - M\,(1-z_{t,s,k}) . \end{aligned} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K. \tag{6} \] If \\(z_{t,s,k}=1\\) the two inequalities force the interval \\([L_{t,s},U_{t,s}]\\) to contain the whole period \\([k\Delta,(k+1)\Delta)\\); if \\(z_{t,s,k}=0\\) the constraints are relaxed by the large constant \\(M\\). ### 4.6 Bidirectional conflict – at most one train on a shared segment For every segment and every time period the sum of occupancy binaries (over all trains, irrespective of direction) cannot exceed one: \[ \sum_{t\in T} z_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\; k\in K. \tag{7} \] If a segment is **double‑tracked** (two independent tracks) the model would contain a separate index for each track; here we assume a *single* physical track per segment, so the conflict must be avoided. ### 4.7 Speed limits – the selected speed must respect min / max for the chosen direction We link the speed‑level binary to the routing binary using a big‑M formulation: \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\ge v^{\min}_{s,r}\;x^{r}_{t,s} ,\\ \sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\le v^{\max}_{s,r}\;x^{r}_{t,s} , \end{aligned} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; r\in R. \tag{8} \] Because exactly one direction is selected (by (1)) and exactly one speed level (by (2)), the left‑hand side reduces to the **actual speed** of the train on that segment, which is forced to lie inside the admissible interval for the chosen direction. ### 4.8 Energy accounting Total energy is the sum of the per‑segment, per‑speed‑level contributions: \[ E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\;y_{t,s,v}. \tag{9} \] Because each \\(y_{t,s,v}\\) is binary and only one speed level is selected (2), this expression is linear. ### 4.9 Dwell‑time windows (optional lower/upper bounds) If a train must stay at a station for at least a given dwell time, we already have (4). If an **upper** bound \\(\bar w_{t,s}\\) also exists, add: \[ a_{t,s} - d_{t,s} \le \bar w_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S. \tag{10} \] ### 4.10 Non‑negativity / binary domains \[ \begin{aligned} &x^{r}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\},\\ &a_{t,s}\ge 0,\; d_{t,s}\ge 0,\; E\ge 0 . \end{aligned} \qquad\forall t,s,r,v,k. \tag{11} \] --- ## 5. Model summary Putting everything together, the MILP reads: \[ \begin{aligned} \min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr) +\beta\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\;y_{t,s,v} \\[4pt] \text{s.t. } & \sum_{r\in R} x^{r}_{t,s}=1 &&\forall t,s \quad\text{(1)}\\ &\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}=1 &&\forall t,s \quad\text{(2)}\\ &a_{t,s}= d_{t,s}+ \sum_{v\in V}\tau_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v} &&\forall t,s \quad\text{(3)}\\ &d_{t,s}= a_{t,s^{-}}+ w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s^{-}} &&\forall t,s\neq s^{\text{first}} \quad\text{(4)}\\ &d_{t,s^{\text{first}}}= t^{\text{orig}}_{t,s^{\text{first}}} &&\forall t \quad\text{(4a)}\\ &z_{t,s,k}\le 1- x^{r}_{t,s} \qquad \forall t,s,r,k\text{ with }k\Delta\in T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r} &&\text{(5)}\\ &L_{t,s}\le k\Delta + M(1-z_{t,s,k}),\; U_{t,s}\ge (k+1)\Delta - M(1-z_{t,s,k}) &&\forall t,s,k \quad\text{(6)}\\ &\sum_{t\in T} z_{t,s,k}\le 1 &&\forall s,k \quad\text{(7)}\\ &\sum_{v\in V} v_{v}y_{t,s,v}\ge v^{\min}_{s,r}x^{r}_{t,s}, \;\; \sum_{v\in V} v_{v}y_{t,s,v}\le v^{\max}_{s,r}x^{r}_{t,s} &&\forall t,s,r \quad\text{(8)}\\ &E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}y_{t,s,v} &&\text{(9)}\\ &a_{t,s}-d_{t,s}\le \bar w_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \quad\text{(10)}\\ &x^{r}_{t,s},y_{t,s,v},z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}, \; a_{t,s},d_{t,s},E\ge 0 &&\forall t,s,r,v,k \quad\text{(11)} . \end{aligned} \] All constraints are **linear**; the only source of integrality is the binary variables that encode routing, speed‑level choice and time‑slot occupation. The big‑M constant \\(M\\) must be chosen larger than the maximum possible travel time of any train on any segment (e.g. the horizon length). --- ## 6. Explanation of each component | Block | What it does | Why it is needed | |-------|--------------|------------------| | **Variables** | Binary routing \\(x\\), binary speed choice \\(y\\), continuous times \\(d,a\\), occupancy binaries \\(z\\), total energy \\(E\\). | Captures the three decision layers (route, speed, schedule) while keeping the model linear. | | **Objective** | Weighted sum of total delay and total energy. | Decision‑maker can prioritize punctuality (large \\(\alpha\\)) or sustainability (large \\(\beta\\)). | | **(1) Routing** | Forces each train‑segment pair to use exactly one direction. | Guarantees a feasible physical path; the opposite direction is only allowed when the original side is blocked. | | **(2) Speed selection** | Exactly one discrete speed level per train‑segment. | Guarantees a deterministic travel time and energy consumption. | | **(3) Travel‑time equation** | Links chosen speed level to arrival time. | Ensures that the timetable respects physics (distance/speed). | | **(4) Dwell‑time** | Propagates arrival of a segment to the departure of the next, adding mandatory stop times. | Models realistic station stops and minimum lay‑over. | | **(5) Blockage exclusion** | Prevents a train from occupying a side that is blocked during its blockage window. | Implements the partial‑segment blockage condition. | | **(6) Occupancy‑binary linking** | Determines whether a train is on a segment during a discrete time slot. | Needed for conflict constraints; the big‑M linearises the logical “if‑then”. | | **(7) Bidirectional conflict** | At most one train on a segment in any time slot. | Guarantees safety on a single‑track section (no head‑on collisions). | | **(8) Speed limits** | Enforces min/max admissible speed for the selected direction. | Guarantees compliance with track geometry, signalling and safety limits. | | **(9) Energy accounting** | Computes total energy as the sum of per‑segment, per‑speed contributions. | Provides the term that appears in the objective. | | **(10) Upper dwell bound (optional)** | Limits maximum station dwell. | Useful when timetable windows are tight. | | **(11) Domain definitions** | Declares binaries and non‑negativity. | Completes the MILP formulation. | --- ## 7. How to use the model 1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets \\(T,S,R,V,K\\) and fill all parameters (segment lengths, speed‑level list \\(v_v\\), energy per speed, blockage windows, original schedule times, dwell times, speed limits). 2. **Choose a horizon** – The discrete periods \\(K\\) must be fine enough to capture the smallest travel time of any speed level (e.g. 1 min). 3. **Select big‑M** – A safe value is the total horizon length (e.g. \\(M = |K|\Delta\\)). 4. **Solve** – Feed the model to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). The solution provides: * For each train‑segment the chosen direction \\(x^{r}_{t,s}\\); * The selected speed level \\(y_{t,s,v}\\) → travel time and energy; * The exact departure/arrival times \\(d_{t,s},a_{t,s}\\) that respect blockage and conflict constraints. 5. **Post‑processing** – Translate the binary variables back into a human‑readable timetable (e.g. Gantt chart) and compute the achieved total delay and energy. --- ### Remarks & possible extensions * **Multiple tracks** – If a segment has two independent tracks, replace the conflict constraint (7) by a per‑track version, or add a track index to the occupancy variable. * **Dynamic blockage** – The model already allows arbitrary time windows per side; multiple disjoint windows can be modelled by adding extra binary variables per window. * **Robustness** – To hedge against uncertainty in travel times, one can introduce a “budget‑of‑uncertainty” on the travel‑time parameters \\(\tau_{s,v}\\) and keep the formulation linear (robust MILP). * **Passenger‑level objectives** – Additional weighted terms (e.g. number of missed connections) can be added without changing the core structure. The formulation above satisfies the request: it is a **complete linear MILP** that simultaneously decides routing, scheduling and speed profile for trains under a partially blocked track segment, while minimizing a weighted combination of delay and energy consumption.

function.description: Generate an MILP for the described problem, or revise it after feedback.
function.name: or_operator

description.description: The problem description, plus any feedback on a previous model.

response.content:
**Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\) |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments, indexed by \(s\) |
| \(R=\{o,p\}\) | Directions on a segment: \(o\) = original side, \(p\) = opposite side |
| \(V\) | Discrete speed levels, indexed by \(v\) |
| \(K\) | Discrete time periods of the planning horizon, indexed by \(k\) |
| \(\text{Pred}(s)\) | Predecessor segment of \(s\) on the train’s path (empty for the first segment) |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(d_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km) |
| \(v_v\) | Speed value of level \(v\) (km/h) |
| \(\tau_{s,v}= \dfrac{d_s}{v_v}\) | Travel time on \(s\) with speed level \(v\) (in the same unit as \(\Delta\)) |
| \(e_{s,v}\) | Energy consumption (MJ) when traversing \(s\) at speed level \(v\) |
| \(v^{\min}_{s,r},\;v^{\max}_{s,r}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on side \(r\) of segment \(s\) |
| \(T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r}=[t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{s,r,\text{end}}]\) | Blockage interval on side \(r\) of segment \(s\) |
| \(t^{\text{orig}}_{t,s}\) | Planned arrival time of train \(t\) at the upstream end of segment \(s\) (no disruption) |
| \(w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,s}\) | Minimum dwell time of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) |
| \(\bar w_{t,s}\) | Optional maximum dwell time (if required) |
| \(\Delta\) | Length of one discrete time period (e.g. 1 min) |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than the planning horizon |
| \(\alpha,\beta>0\) | Weights for delay and energy in the objective |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x^{r}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses side \(r\) of segment \(s\) |
| \(y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if speed level \(v\) is chosen for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the downstream end of segment \(s\) |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from the upstream end of segment \(s\) |
| \(z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) during period \(k\) |
| \(E\ge0\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of the schedule |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\,E}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

The first term sums the difference between actual and originally planned arrival times at the final segment of each train (system‑wide delay). The second term is the total energy (defined in constraint (9)).

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side per segment  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x^{r}_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{1}
\]

#### 5.2 Speed‑level selection – exactly one speed per segment  

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{2}
\]

#### 5.3 Travel‑time relation  

\[
a_{t,s}= d_{t,s}+ \sum_{v\in V}\tau_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{3}
\]

#### 5.4 Dwell and propagation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,s}&= a_{t,\text{Pred}(s)}+ w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,\text{Pred}(s)} &&\forall t\in T,\; s\neq\text{first}(t)\\
d_{t,\text{first}(t)}&= t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{first}(t)} &&\forall t\in T
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]

#### 5.5 Blockage – forbidden occupation of blocked side  

\[
z_{t,s,k}\le 1- x^{r}_{t,s}
\qquad
\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;r\in R,\;k\in K \text{ with } k\Delta\in T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r} \tag{5}
\]

If side \(r\) is blocked during period \(k\), the RHS becomes 0, forcing \(z_{t,s,k}=0\).

#### 5.6 Occupancy‑binary linking (big‑M)  

Let \(L_{t,s}=d_{t,s}\) (enter time) and \(U_{t,s}=a_{t,s}\) (exit time).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{t,s} &\le k\Delta + M\,(1-z_{t,s,k})\\
U_{t,s} &\ge (k+1)\Delta - M\,(1-z_{t,s,k})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;k\in K \tag{6}
\]

#### 5.3 Conflict – at most one train on a segment per period  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} z_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\;k\in K \tag{7}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed limits per chosen side  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\ge v^{\min}_{s,r}\,x^{r}_{t,s}\\
\sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\le v^{\max}_{s,r}\,x^{r}_{t,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;r\in R \tag{8}
\]

Because exactly one \(x^{r}_{t,s}\) and one \(y_{t,s,v}\) are 1, the left‑hand side equals the actual speed, which must lie inside the admissible interval for the selected side.

#### 5.5 Energy accounting  

\[
E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v} \tag{9}
\]

#### 5.6 Optional upper dwell bound  

\[
a_{t,s}-d_{t,s}\le \bar w_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{10}
\]

#### 5.7 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x^{r}_{t,s},\;y_{t,s,v},\;z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,s},\;d_{t,s},\;E\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,s,r,v,k \tag{11}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(1)}\!-\!\text{(11)}\;\text{as listed above.}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries that encode routing, speed level, and segment occupation. The model simultaneously decides:

* **Routing** – whether a train uses the original side or the opposite side of each segment (necessary when a side is blocked).  
* **Timing** – exact departure/arrival times that respect dwell requirements, blockage windows, and conflict‑avoidance on the single track.  
* **Speed management** – selection of a discrete speed level per segment, linking travel time and energy consumption.

---

### 7. How to use  

1. **Data preparation** – Build sets \(T,S,V,K\) and fill all parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, energy per speed, blockage intervals, original timetable, dwell times, speed limits).  
2. **Choose horizon** – Set \(\Delta\) and the number of periods \(|K|\) fine enough to capture the smallest travel time.  
3. **Select big‑M** – Any value larger than the total planning horizon (e.g., \(M = |K|\Delta\)).  
4. **Solve** – Feed the model to a MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …). The solution yields the binary routing/speed decisions and the continuous times \(d_{t,s},a_{t,s}\).  
5. **Post‑process** – Translate binaries into a readable timetable, compute total delay and energy, and verify that no conflict or blockage violation occurs.

---

### 8. Remarks  

* The formulation can be extended to **multiple parallel tracks** by adding a track index to \(z_{t,s,k}\) and relaxing constraint (7) per track.  
* **Robustness** against uncertain travel times can be added by a budget‑of‑uncertainty on \(\tau_{s,v}\) while keeping linearity.  
* Additional service‑level objectives (e.g., missed connections) can be incorporated as extra linear terms in the objective without changing the core structure.

The model above satisfies the request: it is a **complete linear MILP** that integrates train rescheduling, routing, and speed management under partial segment blockages, while minimizing a weighted combination of total delay and energy consumption.

---

### 1. Sets

| \(\Delta\) | Length of one discrete time period (e.g. 1 min) |
| \(M\) | Large constant (big‑M) larger than the planning horizon |
| \(\alpha,\beta>0\) | Weights for delay and energy in the objective |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x^{r}_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses side \(r\) of segment \(s\) |
| \(y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if speed level \(v\) is chosen for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the downstream end of segment \(s\) |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from the upstream end of segment \(s\) |
| \(z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) during period \(k\) |
| \(E\ge0\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of the schedule |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{\alpha\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\,E}_{\text{total energy}}
\]

The first term sums the difference between actual and originally planned arrival times at the final segment of each train (system‑wide delay). The second term is the total energy (defined in constraint (9)).

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Routing – exactly one side per segment  

\[
\sum_{r\in R} x^{r}_{t,s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{1}
\]

#### 5.2 Speed‑level selection – exactly one speed per segment  

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{2}
\]

#### 5.3 Travel‑time relation  

\[
a_{t,s}= d_{t,s}+ \sum_{v\in V}\tau_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v} \qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{3}
\]

#### 5.4 Dwell and propagation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{t,s}&= a_{t,\text{Pred}(s)}+ w^{\text{dwell}}_{t,\text{Pred}(s)} &&\forall t\in T,\; s\neq\text{first}(t)\\
d_{t,\text{first}(t)}&= t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{first}(t)} &&\forall t\in T
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]

#### 5.5 Blockage – forbidden occupation of blocked side  

\[
z_{t,s,k}\le 1- x^{r}_{t,s}
\qquad
\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;r\in R,\;k\in K \text{ with } k\Delta\in T^{\text{blk}}_{s,r} \tag{5}
\]

If side \(r\) is blocked during period \(k\), the RHS becomes 0, forcing \(z_{t,s,k}=0\).

#### 5.6 Occupancy‑binary linking (big‑M)  

Let \(L_{t,s}=d_{t,s}\) (enter time) and \(U_{t,s}=a_{t,s}\) (exit time).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{t,s} &\le k\Delta + M\,(1-z_{t,s,k})\\
U_{t,s} &\ge (k+1)\Delta - M\,(1-z_{t,s,k})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;k\in K \tag{6}
\]

#### 5.3 Conflict – at most one train on a segment per period  

\[
\sum_{t\in T} z_{t,s,k}\le 1 \qquad\forall s\in S,\;k\in K \tag{7}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed limits per chosen side  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\ge v^{\min}_{s,r}\,x^{r}_{t,s}\\
\sum_{v\in V} v_{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &\le v^{\max}_{s,r}\,x^{r}_{t,s}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;r\in R \tag{8}
\]

Because exactly one \(x^{r}_{t,s}\) and one \(y_{t,s,v}\) are 1, the left‑hand side equals the actual speed, which must lie inside the admissible interval for the selected side.

#### 5.5 Energy accounting  

\[
E = \sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v} \tag{9}
\]

#### 5.6 Optional upper dwell bound  

\[
a_{t,s}-d_{t,s}\le \bar w_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\;s\in S \tag{10}
\]

#### 5.7 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x^{r}_{t,s},\;y_{t,s,v},\;z_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,s},\;d_{t,s},\;E\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall t,s,r,v,k \tag{11}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}}-t^{\text{orig}}_{t,\text{last}}\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_{s,v}\,y_{t,s,v}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(1)}\!-\!\text{(11)}\;\text{as listed above.}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries that encode routing, speed level, and segment occupation. The model simultaneously decides:

* **Routing** – whether a train uses the original side or the opposite side of each segment (necessary when a side is blocked).  
* **Timing** – exact departure/arrival times that respect dwell requirements, blockage windows, and conflict‑avoidance on the single track.  
* **Speed management** – selection of a discrete speed level per segment, linking travel time and energy consumption.

---

### 7. How to use  

1. **Data preparation** – Build sets \(T,S,V,K\) and fill all parameters (segment lengths, speed levels, energy per speed, blockage intervals, original timetable, dwell times, speed limits).  
2. **Choose horizon** – Set \(\Delta\) and the number of periods \(|K|\) fine enough to capture the smallest travel time.  
3. **Select big‑M** – Any value larger than the total planning horizon (e.g., \(M = |K|\Delta\)).  
4. **Solve** – Feed the model to a MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …). The solution yields the binary routing/speed decisions and the continuous times \(d_{t,s},a_{t,s}\).  
5. **Post‑process** – Translate binaries into a readable timetable, compute total delay and energy, and verify that no conflict or blockage violation occurs.

---

### 8. Remarks  

* The formulation can be extended to **multiple parallel tracks** by adding a track index to \(z_{t,s,k}\) and relaxing constraint (7) per track.  
* **Robustness** against uncertain travel times can be added by a budget‑of‑uncertainty on \(\tau_{s,v}\) while keeping linearity.  
* Additional service‑level objectives (e.g., missed connections) can be incorporated as extra linear terms in the objective without changing the core structure.

The model above satisfies the request: it is a **complete linear MILP** that integrates train rescheduling, routing, and speed management under partial segment blockages, while minimizing a weighted combination of total delay and energy consumption.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) – MILP Formulation**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures the description you gave:

* binary route‑choice variables, continuous departure/arrival times, binary speed‑level selections for each time‑interval, a weighted objective that penalises total delay and total energy, and all the required operational constraints (flow, time‑windows, partial segment blockage, bidirectional headway, and a linearised speed‑profile‑travel‑time relationship).  

The model is written for a **single planning horizon** \([0,T]\) that is discretised into a set of small time‑intervals \(\mathcal{H}=\{1,\dots ,H\}\) (e.g., 1‑minute slots).  
All indices and sets are defined first, followed by the decision variables, the objective function and the constraints.  After the mathematical statement a short narrative explains every component.

---

## 1. Sets, Parameters and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal{I}\) | Set of trains \(i=1,\dots ,N\). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_i\) | Set of admissible routes (paths) for train \(i\). Each route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\) is an ordered list of track‑segments \((e)\). |
| \(\mathcal{E}\) | Set of track‑segments \(e=1,\dots ,E\). |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of discrete speed‑levels \(k=1,\dots ,K\) (e.g., “slow”, “medium”, “fast”). |
| \(\mathcal{H}\) | Set of planning time‑intervals (slots) \(h=1,\dots ,H\). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{H}\) | Pairs \((e,h)\) that are **blocked** (or partially blocked) during interval \(h\).  If \((e,h)\in\mathcal{B}\) the segment cannot be used (or capacity is reduced – see below). |
| \(\mathcal{C}_e\) | Set of trains that can travel on segment \(e\) (direction‑specific). |
| \(\underline{d}_i,\ \overline{d}_i\) | Earliest and latest admissible departure time for train \(i\). |
| \(\underline{a}_i,\ \overline{a}_i\) | Earliest and latest admissible arrival time for train \(i\). |
| \(\tau_{e,k}\) | **Deterministic travel time** (in minutes) to traverse segment \(e\) when speed‑level \(k\) is chosen (pre‑computed from physics). |
| \(\eta_{e,k}\) | Energy consumption (in kWh) for traversing segment \(e\) at speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weights used in the objective (decision‑maker’s preference). |
| \(\Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}\) | Minimum headway time (in slots) required between two trains moving in opposite directions on segment \(e\). |
| \(M\) | A large constant (big‑M) used for logical linking. |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(r_{i,p}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(d_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Planned departure time of train \(i\) (in minutes from horizon start). |
| \(a_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Planned arrival time of train \(i\). |
| \(x_{i,e,h}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) occupies segment \(e\) during time‑slot \(h\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(s_{i,e,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(e\) with speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(\delta_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay of train \(i\) w.r.t. its planned (reference) timetable (used in the objective). |
| \(e_{i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumption of train \(i\) (used in the objective). |

*All variables are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries.*

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \delta_i \;+\;
w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} e_i
}
\]

*Explanation*  

* **Delay term** – \(\delta_i = d_i - d_i^{\text{ref}}\) (or \(a_i - a_i^{\text{ref}}\)) where the reference departure/arrival times are known data. The model drives the solution toward the smallest possible total delay.  
* **Energy term** – The total energy of a train equals the sum of the energy contributions of each segment–speed pair (see the linearisation constraint below). The weight lets the planner balance punctuality against energy efficiency.

Both parts are linear because \(\delta_i\) and \(e_i\) will be expressed linearly in the constraints that follow.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice and flow conservation  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i} r_{i,p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}
   \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage** – for each train‑segment pair, the binary occupancy variables can be active only if the selected route contains that segment. Let \(\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\) be 1 if segment \(e\) belongs to route \(p\). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} x_{i,e,h} \;\le\; 
   \Bigl(\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\; r_{i,p}\Bigr)\; H
   \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{R2}
   \]

   The right‑hand side is either 0 (route does not contain \(e\)) or \(H\) (large enough to allow occupancy).

### 4.2 Time‑window constraints  

3. **Departure and arrival windows**  
   \[
   \underline{d}_i \le d_i \le \overline{d}_i \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T1}
   \]
   \[
   \underline{a}_i \le a_i \le \overline{a}_i \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T2}
   \]

4. **Delay definition (relative to reference departure)**  

   If a reference departure time \(d_i^{\text{ref}}\) is given:  

   \[
   \delta_i \;=\; d_i - d_i^{\text{ref}} \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T3}
   \]

   (If the reference is an arrival time, use a similar equation with \(a_i\).)

### 4.3 Segment‑occupancy timing (travel‑time linking)  

5. **Each segment must be traversed exactly once, at exactly one speed level**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} s_{i,e,k}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\; r_{i,p}
   \qquad\forall i,\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{S1}
   \]

6. **Travel‑time of a segment equals the selected speed‑level travel time**  

   The total number of occupied slots on segment \(e\) for train \(i\) must match the travel time \(\tau_{e,k}\) (converted to slots). Let \(\sigma\) be the length of a slot (e.g., 1 min). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} x_{i,e,h}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k} / \sigma
   \qquad\forall i,\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{S2}
   \]

   Because \(\tau_{e,k}\) is an integer multiple of the slot length in most practical discretisations, the right‑hand side is integral; otherwise a rounding variable can be added (omitted here for clarity).

7. **Temporal consistency – linking departure/arrival to segment occupancy**  

   Let \(\text{pred}_e(p)\) denote the predecessor segment of \(e\) in route \(p\) (or “origin” for the first segment). Define a big‑M formulation that forces the start of occupancy on the first segment to be the departure time, and the start on any following segment to be after the finish of the previous one.

   For each train \(i\), each segment \(e\) belonging to a selected route \(p\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\;
      \bigl(d_i - M\,(1-r_{i,p})\bigr) && \text{if } e\text{ is first segment of }p,\\[2mm]
   &\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\;
      \Bigl(\sum_{h'\in\mathcal{H}} h' \, x_{i,\text{pred}_e(p),h'}\Bigr)
      + \frac{\tau_{\text{pred}_e(p),k_{\text{pred}}}}{\sigma}
      - M\,(1-r_{i,p}),
      &&\forall e\neq\text{first}(p)
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{S3}
   \]

   The term \(M(1-r_{i,p})\) relaxes the constraint when route \(p\) is not chosen.

### 4.4 Blockage (partial segment unavailability)  

8. **Do not occupy a blocked segment in a blocked time‑slot**  

   \[
   x_{i,e,h}=0 \qquad\forall i,\; (e,h)\in\mathcal{B}
   \tag{B1}
   \]

   If a segment is only **partially** blocked (e.g., reduced capacity to one train per direction), the model can be extended with a capacity parameter, but the current binary formulation enforces complete exclusion.

### 4.5 Bidirectional conflict (headway)  

9. **Headway between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment**  

   For every unordered pair of trains \((i,j)\) that may meet on segment \(e\) traveling in opposite directions (i.e., \(i\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\uparrow}\), \(j\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\downarrow}\)):

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{j,e,h} + \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}
   \; \; \text{or} \;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{j,e,h}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} + \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}
   \tag{H1}
   \]

   This “either‑or” logical condition can be linearised with additional binaries \(z_{ij}^e\) :

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &\sum_{h} h\,x_{i,e,h} \;-\; \sum_{h} h\,x_{j,e,h} \;\ge\; \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}} \;-\; M(1-z_{ij}^e)\\
   &\sum_{h} h\,x_{j,e,h} \;-\; \sum_{h} h\,x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\; \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}} \;-\; M z_{ij}^e\\
   &z_{ij}^e\in\{0,1\}
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{H2}
   \]

   Exactly one of the two headway orders holds, guaranteeing a safe separation.

### 4.6 Energy‑consumption linearisation  

10. **Compute total energy of each train**  

   \[
   e_i = \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \eta_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k}
   \qquad\forall i
   \tag{E1}
   \]

   This is already linear because \(s_{i,e,k}\) are binaries.

### 4.7 Linking delay to arrival (optional)  

If a reference arrival time \(a_i^{\text{ref}}\) is used instead of departure:

\[
\delta_i = a_i - a_i^{\text{ref}} \qquad\forall i
\tag{A1}
\]

If both departure and arrival have to be consistent with the traversed travel times, an extra constraint ensures that:

\[
a_i = d_i + \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k} / \sigma
\qquad\forall i
\tag{A2}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the complete mixed‑integer linear program is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \delta_i
        + w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} e_i  \\[2mm]
\text{s.t.}&\; \text{(R1)}\!-\!\text{(R2)} &&\text{route choice / flow} \\
            &\; \text{(T1)}\!-\!\text{(T3)} &&\text{time windows and delay definition}\\
            &\; \text{(S1)}\!-\!\text{(S3)} &&\text{segment‑speed linking and temporal consistency}\\
            &\; \text{(B1)}                &&\text{blockage avoidance}\\
            &\; \text{(H1)}\!-\!\text{(H2)} &&\text{bidirectional headway}\\
            &\; \text{(E1)}                &&\text{energy linearisation}\\
            &\; \text{(A1)}\!-\!\text{(A2)} &&\text{optional arrival‑delay definition}\\
            &\; d_i,\; a_i,\; \delta_i,\; e_i \ge 0 \\
            &\; r_{i,p},\; x_{i,e,h},\; s_{i,e,k},\; z_{ij}^e \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All symbols are as defined above. The model is **linear** (objective and constraints are linear in the decision variables) and contains **binary** variables for route selection, segment occupation, speed level, and head‑way ordering—hence it is a Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP).

---

## 6. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** –  
   * Compute for each segment‑speed pair \((e,k)\) the travel time \(\tau_{e,k}\) (using \( \tau_{e,k}= \frac{\text{length}_e}{v_k}\) rounded to the nearest slot).  
   * Compute energy \(\eta_{e,k}\) (e.g., from a resistance‑and‑traction model).  
   * Identify blocked segment‑time pairs \(\mathcal{B}\) from the incident information.  
   * Set the headway \(\Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}\) according to signalling rules.  

2. **Choose weights** –  
   * If punctuality is paramount, set \(w_{\text{delay}}\) large relative to \(w_{\text{energy}}\); otherwise increase the energy weight.  

3. **Solve** –  
   * Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The problem size grows with \(|\mathcal{I}|\times|\mathcal{E}|\times|\mathcal{H}|\); for very large horizons a rolling‑horizon or decomposition approach may be required.  

4. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * \(r_{i,p}=1\) tells you which route each train will take.  
   * \(d_i\) and \(a_i\) give the scheduled start/finish times (and \(\delta_i\) the delay).  
   * \(s_{i,e,k}=1\) tells you the speed level on each traversed segment – from which a concrete speed profile can be derived.  
   * \(x_{i,e,h}=1\) provides a *track‑occupation timetable* that respects blockages and headway constraints.  

---

### Bottom line  

The formulation above captures **all the elements you requested**:

* **Binary route‑choice** \(r_{i,p}\) and **binary speed‑level** selections \(s_{i,e,k}\).  
* **Continuous departure/arrival times** \(d_i, a_i\) and derived **delay variables** \(\delta_i\).  
* A **weighted linear objective** that simultaneously minimises total delay and total energy.  
* **Flow, time‑window, blockage, bidirectional headway, speed‑profile feasibility** and **energy‑consumption linearisation** constraints—all expressed linearly, thus delivering a proper MILP that can be handed to any standard solver.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) formulation** for the *Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) with partial segment blockage*.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, and finally every set of constraints together with a short explanation of its purpose.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains (indexed by *i*) |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of track segments (indexed by *ℓ*) |
| **K** = {1,…,|K|} | Set of admissible speed‑level choices (indexed by *k*) |
| **Δt** | Length of the discrete planning horizon (e.g., 1 min) |
| **τ** = {0,Δt,2Δt,…,H} | Discrete time points (indexed by *t*) |
| **L_i ⊂ S** | Ordered list of segments travelled by train *i* (its route) |
| **len_ℓ** | Physical length of segment ℓ (km) |
| **v_k** | Speed associated with speed level *k* (km/h) – linearised to the discretised interval Δt (i.e., distance covered in one time step) |
| **e_k** | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed level *k* (kWh/km).  
  (Linearised so that total energy on a segment is linear in the binary speed‑level variables) |
| **c_i^d,  c_i^a** | Desired/ scheduled departure and arrival times for train *i* (minutes) |
| **w_d, w_e** | Scalars weighting delay vs. energy in the objective (user‑chosen) |
| **B_ℓ(t)** | 0/1 parameter → 1 if segment ℓ is **blocked** (unavailable) at time *t*, 0 otherwise (partial blockage) |
| **h_min** | Minimum head‑way (in minutes) required between two trains moving in opposite directions on the same segment (safety) |
| **M** | A “big‑M” constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., H) |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| **r\_{i,t}** | binary | 1 if train *i* departs (starts moving) at the beginning of time interval *t*, 0 otherwise |
| **d_i** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *i* (minutes) |
| **a_i** | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (minutes) |
| **x\_{i,ℓ,t}** | binary | 1 if train *i* **occupies** segment ℓ during time interval *t*, 0 otherwise |
| **s\_{i,ℓ,k}** | binary | 1 if train *i* traverses segment ℓ using speed level *k* (i.e., travels the whole segment ℓ at speed *v_k*), 0 otherwise |
| **y_i** | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train *i*:  y_i = d_i – c_i^d + (a_i – c_i^a)  (both departure‑ and arrival‑delay are summed) |
| **E_i** | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumed by train *i* on its whole path |

---

## 2. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  \;  w_d \sum_{i\in T} y_i \;+\;  w_e \sum_{i\in T} E_i
}
\]

*The first term penalises total train‑delay (departure + arrival).  
The second term penalises the total energy consumption (linear in the speed‑level choices). The weights *w_d* and *w_e* let the planner express the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy.*

---

## 3. Constraints  

### 3.1 Departure and arrival times – linking to binary departure decision  

1. **Departure time definition**  
   \[
   d_i \;=\; \sum_{t\in\tau} t \; r_{i,t} \qquad  \forall i\in T
   \]
   *Exactly one departure instant must be chosen.*

2. **Exactly one departure instant**  
   \[
   \sum_{t\in\tau} r_{i,t}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
   \]

3. **Arrival time definition** (arrival occurs when the train leaves its last segment)  
   Let ℓ\_{last}(i) be the last segment of train *i*.  
   \[
   a_i \;=\; \sum_{t\in\tau} t \; x_{i,\ell_{\text{last}(i)},t}
   \qquad\forall i\in T
   \]

### 3.2 Flow‑conservation on each segment (train must continue from one segment to the next)  

For every train *i* and for every interior segment ℓ∈L_i (except the first and last):

\[
\sum_{t\in\tau} x_{i,\ell,t} \;=\; \sum_{t\in\tau} x_{i,\ell',t} \qquad 
\text{where } \ell' \text{ is the predecessor of } \ell \text{ in } L_i.
\]

Alternatively expressed with a “time‑shift”:

\[
x_{i,\ell,t} \;\le\; \sum_{t' \le t} x_{i,\ell',t'} \quad
\forall i,\; \ell\in L_i\setminus\{\ell_{1}(i)\},\; t\in\tau.
\]

The first segment is activated by the departure decision:

\[
x_{i,\ell_{1}(i),t} \; \ge\; r_{i,t} \quad \forall i,\; t\in\tau.
\]

### 3.3 Time‑window (service‑level) constraints  

Departure must not be earlier than the scheduled departure:

\[
d_i \; \ge\; c_i^d \qquad \forall i\in T .
\]

Arrival must be at least the scheduled arrival (otherwise a negative delay would be counted, which we forbid):

\[
a_i \; \ge\; c_i^a \qquad \forall i\in T .
\]

### 3.4 Blockage availability (partial segment blockage)  

If a segment ℓ is blocked at time *t*, no train may occupy it:

\[
x_{i,\ell,t} \; \le\; 1 - B_{\ell}(t) \qquad \forall i\in T,\; \ell\in S,\; t\in\tau .
\]

### 3.5 Head‑way / conflict avoidance for opposite‑direction trains  

Let **opp(i,ℓ)** be the set of trains travelling on segment ℓ in the opposite direction to train *i*.  
For any pair *(i,j)∈T×T* with *j∈opp(i,ℓ)* we enforce a minimum separation *h_min* (in time steps). Using big‑M:

\[
\sum_{t'=t}^{t+h_{\min }/\Delta t} x_{i,\ell,t'} \;+\; \sum_{t'=t}^{t+h_{\min }/\Delta t} x_{j,\ell,t'} \;\le\; 1 \qquad
\forall \ell\in S,\; t\in\tau .
\]

This forbids simultaneous (or too close) occupation of the same segment by opposite‑moving trains.

### 3.6 Speed‑profile feasibility – linking segment occupation to a speed level  

For each train *i* and each segment ℓ∈L_i we must choose **exactly one speed level** when the train traverses the segment:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} s_{i,\ell,k}\;=\; \sum_{t\in\tau} x_{i,\ell,t} \qquad \forall i,\; \ell\in L_i .
\]

The travel time required to cross segment ℓ at speed level *k* is

\[
\theta_{\ell,k}= \frac{ \text{len}_\ell }{v_k } \quad\text{(in minutes)} .
\]

Because time is discretised, we model the relationship with a “time‑window” linking the start‑time of the segment to its finish‑time. Let *t_{i,\ell}^{\text{start}}* be the first time step where \(x_{i,\ell,t}=1\); we can linearise it with an auxiliary variable \(z_{i,\ell,t}\) (binary) that indicates that the segment starts at *t*.  

**Start‑time definition**

\[
z_{i,\ell,t}\; \le\; x_{i,\ell,t} \qquad \forall i,\ell,t
\]

\[
z_{i,\ell,t}\; \le\; 1- x_{i,\ell,t-1} \qquad \forall i,\ell,t>0
\]

\[
\sum_{t\in\tau} z_{i,\ell,t}= \sum_{t\in\tau} x_{i,\ell,t} \qquad \forall i,\ell
\]

Now enforce that if speed level *k* is chosen, the segment must be occupied for exactly \(\lceil\theta_{\ell,k}/\Delta t\rceil\) consecutive time steps:

Let \(L_{\ell,k}= \big\lceil \theta_{\ell,k}/\Delta t\big\rceil\).

\[
\sum_{t'=t}^{t+L_{\ell,k}-1} x_{i,\ell,t'}\; \ge\; L_{\ell,k}\; s_{i,\ell,k}\;-\; M\,(1-z_{i,\ell,t})\qquad
\forall i,\ell,k,t\in\tau.
\]

The big‑M term deactivates the constraint when the segment does **not** start at *t* (i.e., \(z_{i,\ell,t}=0\)). Together with the equality \(\sum_k s_{i,\ell,k}= \sum_t x_{i,\ell,t}\) this guarantees a feasible, linear‑time‑consistent speed profile.

### 3.7 Energy consumption – linearisation  

Energy on a segment ℓ for train *i* equals distance × energy‑per‑km of the selected speed level:

\[
E_i = \sum_{\ell\in L_i}\;\sum_{k\in K}  \big( e_k \,\text{len}_\ell \big) \; s_{i,\ell,k}
\qquad \forall i\in T .
\]

Because *e_k* and *len_ℓ* are data, the right‑hand side is linear in the binary variables \(s_{i,\ell,k}\).

### 3.8 Definition of total delay *y_i*  

\[
y_i \;=\; (d_i - c_i^{d}) \;+\; (a_i - c_i^{a}) \qquad \forall i\in T .
\]

Optionally, to force non‑negativity explicitly (already ensured by the time‑window constraints):

\[
y_i \;\ge\; 0 \qquad \forall i\in T .
\]

---

## 4. Summary of the model  

| Component | What it guarantees |
|-----------|--------------------|
| **Variables** | Binary route‑choice / departure / segment‑occupancy / speed‑level decisions, continuous times & energy. |
| **Objective** | Weighted minimisation of total train delay and total energy consumption. |
| **Departure / Arrival constraints** | Exactly one departure instant, arrival defined by last occupied segment, respecting scheduled windows. |
| **Flow‑conservation** | Trains follow a coherent sequence of segments from origin to destination. |
| **Blockage constraints** | No train may occupy a segment when it is blocked (partial blockage model). |
| **Head‑way / conflict constraints** | Safety separation between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment. |
| **Speed‑profile constraints** | Choice of a single speed level per segment, with the required number of time steps consistent with the physical travel time. |
| **Energy linearisation** | Energy consumption is a linear function of the chosen speed levels. |
| **Delay definition** | Captures both departure and arrival tardiness. |

All constraints are linear (or can be written as linear inequalities with a big‑M constant). The model is therefore a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** that can be handed to any modern solver (e.g., CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) to obtain an optimal integrated schedule and speed plan that respects partial blockages, safety head‑ways, and service‑time windows while minimising a trade‑off between punctuality and energy use.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP) – MILP Formulation**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures the description you gave:

* binary route‑choice variables, continuous departure/arrival times, binary speed‑level selections for each time‑interval, a weighted objective that penalises total delay and total energy, and all the required operational constraints (flow, time‑windows, partial segment blockage, bidirectional headway, and a linearised speed‑profile‑travel‑time relationship).  

The model is written for a **single planning horizon** \([0,T]\) that is discretised into a set of small time‑intervals \(\mathcal{H}=\{1,\dots ,H\}\) (e.g., 1‑minute slots).  
All indices and sets are defined first, followed by the decision variables, the objective function and the constraints.  After the mathematical statement a short narrative explains every component.

---

## 1. Sets, Parameters and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(\mathcal{I}\) | Set of trains \(i=1,\dots ,N\). |
| \(\mathcal{P}_i\) | Set of admissible routes (paths) for train \(i\). Each route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\) is an ordered list of track‑segments \((e)\). |
| \(\mathcal{E}\) | Set of track‑segments \(e=1,\dots ,E\). |
| \(\mathcal{K}\) | Set of discrete speed‑levels \(k=1,\dots ,K\) (e.g., “slow”, “medium”, “fast”). |
| \(\mathcal{H}\) | Set of planning time‑intervals (slots) \(h=1,\dots ,H\). |
| \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{H}\) | Pairs \((e,h)\) that are **blocked** (or partially blocked) during interval \(h\).  If \((e,h)\in\mathcal{B}\) the segment cannot be used (or capacity is reduced – see below). |
| \(\mathcal{C}_e\) | Set of trains that can travel on segment \(e\) (direction‑specific). |
| \(\underline{d}_i,\ \overline{d}_i\) | Earliest and latest admissible departure time for train \(i\). |
| \(\underline{a}_i,\ \overline{a}_i\) | Earliest and latest admissible arrival time for train \(i\). |
| \(\tau_{e,k}\) | **Deterministic travel time** (in minutes) to traverse segment \(e\) when speed‑level \(k\) is chosen (pre‑computed from physics). |
| \(\eta_{e,k}\) | Energy consumption (in kWh) for traversing segment \(e\) at speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(w_{\text{delay}}, w_{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weights used in the objective (decision‑maker’s preference). |
| \(\Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}\) | Minimum headway time (in slots) required between two trains moving in opposite directions on segment \(e\). |
| \(M\) | A large constant (big‑M) used for logical linking. |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(r_{i,p}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) uses route \(p\in\mathcal{P}_i\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(d_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Planned departure time of train \(i\) (in minutes from horizon start). |
| \(a_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Planned arrival time of train \(i\). |
| \(x_{i,e,h}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) occupies segment \(e\) during time‑slot \(h\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(s_{i,e,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(i\) traverses segment \(e\) with speed‑level \(k\). |
| \(\delta_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Delay of train \(i\) w.r.t. its planned (reference) timetable (used in the objective). |
| \(e_{i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy consumption of train \(i\) (used in the objective). |

*All variables are linear; the only integer variables are the binaries.*

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \delta_i \;+\;
w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} e_i
}
\]

*Explanation*  

* **Delay term** – \(\delta_i = d_i - d_i^{\text{ref}}\) (or \(a_i - a_i^{\text{ref}}\)) where the reference departure/arrival times are known data. The model drives the solution toward the smallest possible total delay.  
* **Energy term** – The total energy of a train equals the sum of the energy contributions of each segment–speed pair (see the linearisation constraint below). The weight lets the planner balance punctuality against energy efficiency.

Both parts are linear because \(\delta_i\) and \(e_i\) will be expressed linearly in the constraints that follow.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice and flow conservation  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
   \[
   \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i} r_{i,p}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}
   \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment usage** – for each train‑segment pair, the binary occupancy variables can be active only if the selected route contains that segment. Let \(\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\) be 1 if segment \(e\) belongs to route \(p\). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} x_{i,e,h} \;\le\; 
   \Bigl(\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\; r_{i,p}\Bigr)\; H
   \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{R2}
   \]

   The right‑hand side is either 0 (route does not contain \(e\)) or \(H\) (large enough to allow occupancy).

### 4.2 Time‑window constraints  

3. **Departure and arrival windows**  
   \[
   \underline{d}_i \le d_i \le \overline{d}_i \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T1}
   \]
   \[
   \underline{a}_i \le a_i \le \overline{a}_i \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T2}
   \]

4. **Delay definition (relative to reference departure)**  

   If a reference departure time \(d_i^{\text{ref}}\) is given:  

   \[
   \delta_i \;=\; d_i - d_i^{\text{ref}} \qquad\forall i
   \tag{T3}
   \]

   (If the reference is an arrival time, use a similar equation with \(a_i\).)

### 4.3 Segment‑occupancy timing (travel‑time linking)  

5. **Each segment must be traversed exactly once, at exactly one speed level**  

   \[
   \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} s_{i,e,k}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_i}\mathbb{1}_{e\in p}\; r_{i,p}
   \qquad\forall i,\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{S1}
   \]

6. **Travel‑time of a segment equals the selected speed‑level travel time**  

   The total number of occupied slots on segment \(e\) for train \(i\) must match the travel time \(\tau_{e,k}\) (converted to slots). Let \(\sigma\) be the length of a slot (e.g., 1 min). Then  

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} x_{i,e,h}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k} / \sigma
   \qquad\forall i,\; e\in\mathcal{E}
   \tag{S2}
   \]

   Because \(\tau_{e,k}\) is an integer multiple of the slot length in most practical discretisations, the right‑hand side is integral; otherwise a rounding variable can be added (omitted here for clarity).

7. **Temporal consistency – linking departure/arrival to segment occupancy**  

   Let \(\text{pred}_e(p)\) denote the predecessor segment of \(e\) in route \(p\) (or “origin” for the first segment). Define a big‑M formulation that forces the start of occupancy on the first segment to be the departure time, and the start on any following segment to be after the finish of the previous one.

   For each train \(i\), each segment \(e\) belonging to a selected route \(p\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\;
      \bigl(d_i - M\,(1-r_{i,p})\bigr) && \text{if } e\text{ is first segment of }p,\\[2mm]
   &\sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\;
      \Bigl(\sum_{h'\in\mathcal{H}} h' \, x_{i,\text{pred}_e(p),h'}\Bigr)
      + \frac{\tau_{\text{pred}_e(p),k_{\text{pred}}}}{\sigma}
      - M\,(1-r_{i,p}),
      &&\forall e\neq\text{first}(p)
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{S3}
   \]

   The term \(M(1-r_{i,p})\) relaxes the constraint when route \(p\) is not chosen.

### 4.4 Blockage (partial segment unavailability)  

8. **Do not occupy a blocked segment in a blocked time‑slot**  

   \[
   x_{i,e,h}=0 \qquad\forall i,\; (e,h)\in\mathcal{B}
   \tag{B1}
   \]

   If a segment is only **partially** blocked (e.g., reduced capacity to one train per direction), the model can be extended with a capacity parameter, but the current binary formulation enforces complete exclusion.

### 4.5 Bidirectional conflict (headway)  

9. **Headway between opposite‑direction trains on the same segment**  

   For every unordered pair of trains \((i,j)\) that may meet on segment \(e\) traveling in opposite directions (i.e., \(i\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\uparrow}\), \(j\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\downarrow}\)):

   \[
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{j,e,h} + \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}
   \; \; \text{or} \;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{j,e,h}
   \;\ge\;
   \sum_{h\in\mathcal{H}} h \, x_{i,e,h} + \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}
   \tag{H1}
   \]

   This “either‑or” logical condition can be linearised with additional binaries \(z_{ij}^e\) :

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &\sum_{h} h\,x_{i,e,h} \;-\; \sum_{h} h\,x_{j,e,h} \;\ge\; \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}} \;-\; M(1-z_{ij}^e)\\
   &\sum_{h} h\,x_{j,e,h} \;-\; \sum_{h} h\,x_{i,e,h} \;\ge\; \Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}} \;-\; M z_{ij}^e\\
   &z_{ij}^e\in\{0,1\}
   \end{aligned}
   \tag{H2}
   \]

   Exactly one of the two headway orders holds, guaranteeing a safe separation.

### 4.6 Energy‑consumption linearisation  

10. **Compute total energy of each train**  

   \[
   e_i = \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \eta_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k}
   \qquad\forall i
   \tag{E1}
   \]

   This is already linear because \(s_{i,e,k}\) are binaries.

### 4.7 Linking delay to arrival (optional)  

If a reference arrival time \(a_i^{\text{ref}}\) is used instead of departure:

\[
\delta_i = a_i - a_i^{\text{ref}} \qquad\forall i
\tag{A1}
\]

If both departure and arrival have to be consistent with the traversed travel times, an extra constraint ensures that:

\[
a_i = d_i + \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \tau_{e,k}\; s_{i,e,k} / \sigma
\qquad\forall i
\tag{A2}
\]

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the complete mixed‑integer linear program is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w_{\text{delay}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \delta_i
        + w_{\text{energy}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} e_i  \\[2mm]
\text{s.t.}&\; \text{(R1)}\!-\!\text{(R2)} &&\text{route choice / flow} \\
            &\; \text{(T1)}\!-\!\text{(T3)} &&\text{time windows and delay definition}\\
            &\; \text{(S1)}\!-\!\text{(S3)} &&\text{segment‑speed linking and temporal consistency}\\
            &\; \text{(B1)}                &&\text{blockage avoidance}\\
            &\; \text{(H1)}\!-\!\text{(H2)} &&\text{bidirectional headway}\\
            &\; \text{(E1)}                &&\text{energy linearisation}\\
            &\; \text{(A1)}\!-\!\text{(A2)} &&\text{optional arrival‑delay definition}\\
            &\; d_i,\; a_i,\; \delta_i,\; e_i \ge 0 \\
            &\; r_{i,p},\; x_{i,e,h},\; s_{i,e,k},\; z_{ij}^e \in \{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\]

All symbols are as defined above. The model is **linear** (objective and constraints are linear in the decision variables) and contains **binary** variables for route selection, segment occupation, speed level, and head‑way ordering—hence it is a Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP).

---

## 6. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** –  
   * Compute for each segment‑speed pair \((e,k)\) the travel time \(\tau_{e,k}\) (using \( \tau_{e,k}= \frac{\text{length}_e}{v_k}\) rounded to the nearest slot).  
   * Compute energy \(\eta_{e,k}\) (e.g., from a resistance‑and‑traction model).  
   * Identify blocked segment‑time pairs \(\mathcal{B}\) from the incident information.  
   * Set the headway \(\Delta_{e}^{\text{headway}}\) according to signalling rules.  

2. **Choose weights** –  
   * If punctuality is paramount, set \(w_{\text{delay}}\) large relative to \(w_{\text{energy}}\); otherwise increase the energy weight.  

3. **Solve** –  
   * Feed the MILP to a commercial solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or an open‑source one (CBC, SCIP). The problem size grows with \(|\mathcal{I}|\times|\mathcal{E}|\times|\mathcal{H}|\); for very large horizons a rolling‑horizon or decomposition approach may be required.  

4. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * \(r_{i,p}=1\) tells you which route each train will take.  
   * \(d_i\) and \(a_i\) give the scheduled start/finish times (and \(\delta_i\) the delay).  
   * \(s_{i,e,k}=1\) tells you the speed level on each traversed segment – from which a concrete speed profile can be derived.  
   * \(x_{i,e,h}=1\) provides a *track‑occupation timetable* that respects blockages and headway constraints.  

---

### Bottom line  

The formulation above captures **all the elements you requested**:

* **Binary route‑choice** \(r_{i,p}\) and **binary speed‑level** selections \(s_{i,e,k}\).  
* **Continuous departure/arrival times** \(d_i, a_i\) and derived **delay variables** \(\delta_i\).  
* A **weighted linear objective** that simultaneously minimises total delay and total energy.  
* **Flow, time‑window, blockage, bidirectional headway, speed‑profile feasibility** and **energy‑consumption linearisation** constraints—all expressed linearly, thus delivering a proper MILP that can be handed to any standard solver.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) with partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice r_{i,t}, departure time d_i, arrival time a_i, speed level s_{i,k} for time intervals. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption.
