**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (Partial Segment Blockage)**  

---

### 1. Sets, parameters & notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, *i* ∈ I (|I| = N) |
| **S** = {1,2} | Track‑side set (1 = normal side, 2 = detour side) |
| **K** | Set of stations (ordered). For each train *i* the visited stations are \(K_i\). |
| **K\_i^{in}**, **K\_i^{out}** | Entry / exit stations of the disrupted segment for train *i* |
| **dist\_{i,k}** | Distance of section *k* for train *i* (km) |
| **sched\_{i,last}** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (min) |
| **α,β** | Energy coefficients (α > 0, β ≥ 0) – instantaneous power \(P = αv^{2}+βv\) |
| **v\_{min}, v\_{max}** | Minimum / maximum admissible speed (km/min) |
| **dwell\_{min}, dwell\_{max}** | Minimum / maximum dwell time at any station (min) |
| **Δ\_{safe}** | Minimum safety headway between successive trains on the same track (min) |
| **T\_{start}, T\_{end}** | Blockage interval on side 1 (min) |
| **M** | Big‑M constant (e.g. 10 000) |
| **w\_d, w\_e** | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |
| **M\_c** | Penalty for cancelling a train (large) |
| **π\_{i,k}** | Set of break‑points for piece‑wise linearisation of \(αv^{2}+βv\) on section *(i,k)*; each breakpoint *p* has speed \(v^{p}\) and energy coefficient \(c^{p}=α(v^{p})^{2}+βv^{p}\) |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| \(r_{i,s}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* while crossing the disrupted segment |
| \(o_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on a shared track segment |
| \(a_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k* |
| \(d_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k* |
| \(t_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on section *k* (from *k* to next station) |
| \(v_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on section *k* |
| \(\theta_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Reciprocal speed, \(\theta_{i,k}=1/v_{i,k}\) (used for linearisation) |
| \(z^{p}_{i,k}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ speed on section *(i,k)* lies in piece *p* of the piece‑wise linear energy approximation |
| \(e_{i,k}\) | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption on section *(i,k)* |
| \(y_i\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is cancelled |
| \(u_i\) | continuous ≥0 | Delay of train *i*: \(u_i = a_{i,last} - \text{sched}_{i,last}\) (forced 0 if cancelled) |
| \(b_i\) | binary | Disjunction selector for blockage avoidance (see (7)) |

---

### 3. Linearised energy term  

For each section *(i,k)* the quadratic energy \(αv^{2}+βv\) is approximated by a convex piece‑wise linear function:

\[
e_{i,k}= \sum_{p\inπ_{i,k}} c^{p}\,t_{i,k}\,z^{p}_{i,k},
\qquad
\sum_{p\inπ_{i,k}} z^{p}_{i,k}=1 \;\; \forall i,k .
\]

Because \(t_{i,k}\) is continuous and \(z^{p}_{i,k}\) binary, the product is linear.

---

### 4. MILP formulation  

#### 4.1 Objective  

\[
\min\;
w_{d}\sum_{i\in I} u_i
\;+\;
w_{e}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{k\in K_i} e_{i,k}
\;+\;
M_{c}\sum_{i\in I} y_i .
\]

#### 4.2 Constraints  

1. **Route‑choice (exactly one side)**  
   \[
   \sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad \forall i\in I \text{ that cross the disrupted segment}. \tag{1}
   \]

2. **Precedence on a shared track segment** (for every ordered pair \((i,j)\) sharing a segment, set \(\mathcal{P}\)):  
   \[
   d_{i,\text{exit}} + \Delta_{\text{safe}} \le a_{j,\text{entry}} + M(1-o_{i,j}) \qquad \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}, \tag{2}
   \]
   \[
   d_{j,\text{exit}} + \Delta_{\text{safe}} \le a_{i,\text{entry}} + M\,o_{i,j} \qquad \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}. \tag{2b}
   \]
   Exactly one ordering holds:
   \[
   o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 \qquad \forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}. \tag{8}
   \]

3. **Time‑flow (arrival‑departure‑travel consistency)**  
   \[
   a_{i,k}= d_{i,k-1}+ t_{i,k-1} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k\in K_i\setminus\{k_{\text{first}}\}. \tag{3}
   \]

4. **Travel‑time – speed coupling (linearised)**  
   \[
   \theta_{i,k}\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}},\qquad
   \theta_{i,k}\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}}, \qquad
   t_{i,k}= \text{dist}_{i,k}\,\theta_{i,k} \qquad \forall i,k . \tag{4‑lin}
   \]

5. **Speed bounds**  
   \[
   v_{\min}\le v_{i,k}\le v_{\max} \qquad \forall i,k . \tag{5}
   \]

6. **Dwell‑time limits**  
   \[
   dwell_{\min}\le d_{i,k}-a_{i,k}\le dwell_{\max} \qquad \forall i\in I,\; k\in K_i . \tag{6}
   \]

7. **Blockage‑avoidance (side 1 blocked)** – disjunction linearised with binary \(b_i\):  
   \[
   a_{i,K_i^{in}} \ge T_{\text{end}} - M(1-b_i), \tag{7a}
   \]
   \[
   d_{i,K_i^{out}} \le T_{\text{start}} + M\,b_i, \tag{7b}
   \]
   \[
   b_i \le r_{i,1},\qquad 1-b_i \le r_{i,1}. \tag{7c}
   \]

   If the train chooses side 2 (\(r_{i,1}=0\)) the constraints become non‑binding.

8. **Cancellation handling** (de‑activate all timing constraints when cancelled):  
   \[
   u_i \le M(1-y_i),\qquad
   a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,k},v_{i,k}\le M(1-y_i) \quad \forall k. \tag{9}
   \]

9. **Delay definition**  
   \[
   u_i = a_{i,\text{last}} - \text{sched}_{i,\text{last}} \qquad \forall i\in I . \tag{10}
   \]

10. **Energy definition** (already linearised, see Section 3).  

11. **Domain restrictions**  
   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   &a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,k},\theta_{i,k},e_{i,k},u_i \ge 0,\\
   &v_{i,k}\ge 0,\\
   &r_{i,s},o_{i,j},z^{p}_{i,k},y_i,b_i \in \{0,1\}.
   \end{aligned} \tag{11}
   \]

---

### 5. Model summary  

| Component | Linear MILP element |
|-----------|--------------------|
| **Variables** | Binary route choice \(r\), binary precedence \(o\), binary cancellation \(y\), binary piece‑selection \(z\); continuous times \(a,d\), travel times \(t\), speeds \(v\), reciprocal speeds \(\theta\), energy \(e\), delay \(u\). |
| **Objective** | Weighted sum of total passenger delay, total energy consumption (piece‑wise linearised quadratic term), and cancellation penalties. |
| **Constraints** | 1) Exactly one side per train; 2) Mutual precedence on shared tracks; 3) Flow of arrivals/departures; 4) Travel‑time ↔ speed coupling (linearised reciprocal); 5) Speed limits; 6) Dwell‑time windows; 7) Blockage avoidance for the closed side; 8) Linearisation of order binaries; 9) Optional cancellation; 10) Delay definition; 11) Variable domains. |

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy and reciprocal speed) are replaced by standard linear approximations, making the formulation directly solvable by any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).  

The model simultaneously decides **(i)** which side each train uses (rerouting), **(ii)** the order of trains on shared tracks (conflict resolution), **(iii)** feasible arrival/departure times (rescheduling), and **(iv)** speed profiles that respect physical limits and minimise energy, while respecting the blockage time window and allowing optional train cancellation.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

| \\( \alpha_{e,k},\; \beta_{e,k}\\) | Linear energy coefficients for segment \\(e\\) and direction \\(k\\) (energy = \\(\alpha v + \beta\\)) |
| \\( w^{\text{delay}},\; w^{\text{energy}} \\) | Positive weights used in the weighted sum objective |
| \\( M\\) | A large constant (big‑M) – chosen larger than any feasible time value (e.g. 10⁶ s) |
| \\( \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,s}\\) | Planned (unperturbed) arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) (used for delay calculation) |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|--------------|
| \\(x_{i,e,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(e\\) in direction \\(k\\) (original = \\(k=O\\), opposite = \\(k=R\\)). |
| \\(y_{i,j,e}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) passes *before* train \\(j\\) on segment \\(e\\) (used only for pairs in \\( \mathcal{C}\\)). |
| \\(a_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(s\\). |
| \\(v_{i,e,k}\\) | continuous | Speed chosen by train \\(i\\) on segment \\(e\\) when travelling in direction \\(k\\). (If \\(x_{i,e,k}=0\\) the variable is forced to 0). |
| \\(t_{i,e}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train \\(i\\) on segment \\(e\\). |
| \\(E_{i}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train \\(i\\). |
| \\(\Delta_{i}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(i\\) (difference between actual arrival at final station and planned arrival). |

---

## 3. Linearisation of the *travel‑time* relation  

The physical relation is  

\[
t_{i,e}= \frac{L_{e}}{v_{i,e}} .
\]

Because the denominator is a variable, we replace it with a set of *piece‑wise linear* (or big‑M) constraints.  
A simple, exact linearisation for a bounded speed interval is the **epigraph formulation**:

Introduce an auxiliary binary variable \\(z_{i,e,k}\\) that selects a speed *break‑point* (or use a set of pre‑defined speed levels). For brevity we present the compact big‑M version that works when the speed range is narrow (typical for high‑speed lines):

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,e} &\ge \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max }_{e,k}} \; -\; M\;(1-x_{i,e,k}) &&\forall i,e,k,\\
t_{i,e} &\le \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\min }_{e,k}} \; +\; M\;(1-x_{i,e,k}) &&\forall i,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

If a tighter linear approximation is needed, replace the two inequalities by a set of **SOS‑2** or *multiple* break‑points; the formulation below assumes the simple bounds are sufficient for the MILP.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}} \underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Delta_{i}}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}} \underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_{i}}_{\text{total energy}} .
\]

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑choice feasibility  

*Exactly one direction is selected for each train on every segment it must traverse.*

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{i,e,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T},\; \forall e\in\mathcal{E}_{i},
\]

where \\(\mathcal{E}_{i}\\) is the set of segments belonging to train \\(i\\)’s itinerary (derived from the timetable).  
If the train does **not** need a segment (e.g., it terminates earlier) the corresponding \(x\) variables are fixed to 0.

### 5.2 Flow conservation through stations  

For each train, departure from station \\(s\\) equals arrival plus dwell time, and the arrival at the next station follows from travel time:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{i,s} &= a_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1,\\
a_{i,s+1} &= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,(s,s+1)} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \\(\tau_{i,s}\\) is the *actual* dwell time at station \\(s\\) for train \\(i\\).  

### 5.3 Dwell‑time bounds  

\[
d^{\min }_{s}\le \tau_{i,s}\le d^{\max }_{s}
\qquad\forall i,\; s=1,\dots,S-1.
\]

(For the origin station \\(s=0\\) and the final station \\(S\\) the dwell time can be set to 0.)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

If a train uses direction \\(k\\) on segment \\(e\\) its speed must respect the admissible interval; otherwise it must be 0.

\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{\min }_{e,k}\; x_{i,e,k} \;\le\; v_{i,e,k} \;\le\; v^{\max }_{e,k}\; x_{i,e,k}
\qquad\forall i,e,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

The *effective* speed on segment \\(e\\) for train \\(i\\) is  

\[
v_{i,e}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} v_{i,e,k}.
\]

### 5.5 Energy consumption (linear)  

Energy on each segment is linear in speed:

\[
E_{i}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{i}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \bigl(\alpha_{e,k}\, v_{i,e,k}+ \beta_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}\bigr) .
\]

(The term \( \beta_{i,e,k} x_{i,e,k}\) accounts for a fixed component that depends only on the fact the segment is traversed.)

### 5.6 Delay calculation  

Delay of train \\(i\\) is the difference between its actual arrival at the final station \\(S\\) and the planned arrival:

\[
\Delta_{i}= a_{i,S} - \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,S} \qquad \forall i .
\]

(If early arrival is allowed, a non‑negativity constraint on \\(\Delta_i\\) already forces the model to treat early arrivals as zero delay.)

### 5.7 Safety head‑way between any two trains on the **same** track  

For every unordered pair \\((i,j)\\in\mathcal{W}\\) that share at least one segment, enforce that at any common segment one train leaves *before* the other arrives by at least the prescribed head‑way. Using the ordering binary \\(y_{i,j,e}\\) only for pairs that conflict on a **blocked** segment (see 5.8), for the general head‑way we write:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} &\ge d_{i,s} + h_{i,j} \;-\; M\bigl(1 - \theta_{i,j,s}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; \forall s,\\
a_{i,s} &\ge d_{j,s} + h_{i,j} \;-\; M\bigl(\theta_{i,j,s}\bigr)          &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; \forall s,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \\(\theta_{i,j,s}\\) is a binary variable that decides which train is ahead on segment \\(s\\).  
If only one shared segment exists, the index \\(s\\) can be omitted.

### 5.8  Bidirectional conflict avoidance on the *blocked* segment  

Let the blocked segment be \\(e^{*}\\). For every unordered pair of trains \\((i,j)\\) that both need to use this segment (i.e. \\((i,j,e^{*})\in\mathcal{C}\\)), introduce a binary ordering variable \\( y_{i,j,e^{*}}\\) such that

* \(y_{i,j,e^{*}} = 1\) ⇒ train \\(i\\) passes before train \\(j\\) on the blocked segment,
* \(y_{i,j,e^{*}} = 0\) ⇒ the opposite order.

The head‑way constraints become

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,\text{up}(e^{*})} &\ge d_{i,\text{down}(e^{*})} + h_{i,j}
 \;-\; M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,e^{*}}\bigr) ,
\\
a_{i,\text{up}(e^{*})} &\ge d_{j,\text{down}(e^{*})} + h_{i,j}
 \;-\; M\bigl(y_{i,j,e^{*}}\bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Here, ``down’’ is the station at the **entry** side of the segment for the considered travel direction, and ``up’’ the **exit** side.  
Additionally we enforce consistency between the ordering variables:

\[
y_{i,j,e^{*}} + y_{j,i,e^{*}} = 1 \qquad \forall (i,j,e^{*})\in\mathcal{C}.
\]

If more than two trains may occupy the same blocked segment (rare for high‑speed lines), a *pairwise* ordering model together with transitivity constraints can be added, but the pairwise formulation above is sufficient for the usual case of two competing trains.

### 5.9  Linking speed to travel time (big‑M version)  

Using the linear bounds described in 5.3 we already have a range for \\(t_{i,e}\\). To make the model tighter we may add an exact linear relationship by **discretising** the admissible speed set into \\(P\\) candidate speed levels \\(v^{p}_{e,k}\\) (e.g., 300, 320, 340 km/h). Introduce binaries \\(u^{p}_{i,e,k}\\) with  

\[
\sum_{p=1}^{P} u^{p}_{i,e,k}= x_{i,e,k}, \qquad 
v_{i,e,k}= \sum_{p} v^{p}_{e,k}\, u^{p}_{i,e,k},
\qquad
t_{i,e}= \sum_{p} \frac{L_{e}}{v^{p}_{e,k}} \, u^{p}_{i,e,k}.
\]

All terms stay linear; the model size grows only moderately because the number of speed levels per segment is small (3‑5).

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\; w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Delta_{i}
   \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_{i}  &&\text{(objective)} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
& \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{i,e,k}=1 &&\forall i,\;e\in\mathcal{E}_{i} \tag{R1}\\
& d_{i,s}= a_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1 \tag{R2}\\
& a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,(s,s+1)} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1 \tag{R3}\\
& d^{\min }_{s}\le \tau_{i,s}\le d^{\max }_{s} &&\forall i,\; s=1,\dots,S-1 \tag{R4}\\
& v^{\min }_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}\le v_{i,e,k}\le v^{\max }_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R5}\\
& t_{i,e}\ge \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max }_{e,k}} - M(1-x_{i,e,k})
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R6a}\\
& t_{i,e}\le \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\min }_{e,k}} + M(1-x_{i,e,k})
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R6b}\\
& E_{i}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{i}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
        \bigl(\alpha_{e,k} v_{i,e,k}+ \beta_{e,k} x_{i,e,k}\bigr)
   &&\forall i \tag{R7}\\
& \Delta_{i}= a_{i,S} - \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,S}
   &&\forall i \tag{R8}\\
& a_{j,\text{up}(e)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(e)}+h_{i,j}
   -M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,e}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9a}\\
& a_{i,\text{up}(e)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(e)}+h_{i,j}
   -M y_{i,j,e} &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9b}\\
& y_{i,j,e}+y_{j,i,e}=1 &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9c}\\
& a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+h_{i,j} - M(1-\theta_{i,j,s}) &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; s\\
& a_{i,s}\ge d_{j,s}+h_{i,j} - M\theta_{i,j,s} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; s \tag{R10}\\
& x_{i,e,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,j,e}\in\{0,1\},\; \theta_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},\tau_{i,s}, t_{i,e}, v_{i,e,k}, E_{i},\Delta_{i}\ge 0 &&\forall\text{continuous}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Block | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-------|--------------|------------------|
| **Binary route‑choice \\(x_{i,e,k}\\)** | Selects the direction (original vs opposite) for each train on every segment. | Guarantees a feasible physical route and activates the correct speed bounds. |
| **Flow‑conservation (R2–R3)** | Links arrivals, departures, dwell times and travel times along the train’s path. | Enforces a realistic timetable structure. |
| **Speed limits (R5)** | Bounds the continuous speed variable by the admissible interval of the chosen direction. | Prevents illegal speeds and couples binary direction to continuous speed. |
| **Travel‑time linearisation (R6)** | Provides a linear envelope for the non‑linear relation *time = length / speed* using big‑M. | Keeps the model MILP‑compatible while still representing the physics. |
| **Energy model (R7)** | Linear function of speed (coefficients \\(\alpha, \beta\\)). | Allows the objective to penalise high speeds (energy cost). |
| **Delay definition (R8)** | Computes the lateness of the train at its final destination. | Part of the weighted objective. |
| **Head‑way constraints (R9, R10)** | Guarantees a minimum safety time between successive trains on the *same* track segment; ordering binaries decide which train goes first. | Avoids collisions, respects signalling rules, and especially handles the blocked segment where opposite directions may meet. |
| **Ordering consistency (R9c)** | For each conflicting pair exactly one of the two possible orders is selected. | Guarantees a well‑defined schedule on the disputed segment. |
| **Binary ordering variables \\(y_{i,j,e}\\)** | Explicitly model which train passes first on a segment where bidirectional traffic is possible (especially the blocked segment). | Enables the MILP to decide the optimal sequence, which directly influences delay and energy. |
| **Weighted objective** | Minimises a linear combination of total delay and total energy consumption. | Allows the planner to trade‑off punctuality against sustainability. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Populate all sets and parameters (segment lengths, speed limits, head‑way times, planned arrivals, energy coefficients).  
2. **Choose \(M\)** – Set \(M\) larger than any feasible time (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s).  
3. **Optional speed discretisation** – If a tighter representation of the \(t = L/v\) curve is desired, replace the big‑M bounds (R6) with the SOS‑2/price‑break‑point formulation shown in Section 5.9.  
4. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, HiGHS) MILP solver.  
5. **Post‑processing** – Extract the optimal routes (values of \(x_{i,e,k}\)), speeds (\(v_{i,e,k}\)), and the resulting timetable (\(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)).  

The formulation above is **complete and linear** and can be directly implemented in a modelling language such as AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, or OPL. It captures all the elements you listed: route choice, ordering on conflicting segments, continuous timing and speed decisions, safety head‑ways, dwell‑time limits, speed limits, a linearised energy model, and a weighted objective that balances punctuality with energy consumption.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave.  
The formulation is written in a compact mathematical notation, followed by a plain‑English explanation of every set, variable, objective term and constraint family.

---

## 1. Index sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \mathcal{T} =\{1,\dots ,T\}\) | Set of trains to be scheduled |
| \( \mathcal{S} =\{1,\dots ,S\}\) | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train) |
| \( \mathcal{E}= \{(i,j) \mid i,j\in \mathcal{S}, i\neq j\}\) | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) between two successive stations |
| \( \mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}} \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) | Segments that belong to the **original** (planned) track direction |
| \( \mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}} \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) | Segments that belong to the **opposite** (reversed) direction – used when a train is rerouted |
| \( \mathcal{K}_{e} \subseteq \mathcal{T}\) | Trains that may travel on segment \(e\) (all trains whose origin‑dest path contains \(e\)) |
| \( \mathcal{C} \subseteq \{(t,t')\mid t<t'\}\) | Set of *conflicting* train pairs; i.e. two trains that could occupy the same physical track piece at the same time (including bidirectional conflicts caused by the partial blockage) |

---

## 2. Data (parameters)  

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment \(e\) |
| \(\underline v_{e},\ \overline v_{e}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(e\) (km h\(^{-1}\)) |
| \(\underline d_{s},\ \overline d_{s}\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station \(s\) (minutes) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}\) | Safety head‑way (minimum time gap) required between any two trains travelling on the **same** direction of segment \(e\) (minutes) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}\) | Minimum time gap that must be respected on a **shared** (bidirectional) segment during the disruption window (minutes) |
| \(E^{\text{base}}_{t}\) | Planned (baseline) arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (without any disruption) |
| \(\alpha_{e},\ \beta_{e}\) | Linear energy coefficients for segment \(e\) (energy = \(\alpha_{e} v_{e}+ \beta_{e}\)  kWh per km) |
| \(w^{\text{delay}},\ w^{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weighting factors used in the bi‑objective linear combination (chosen by the planner) |
| \(T^{\text{start}}_{t},\ T^{\text{end}}_{t}\) | Earliest possible start‑time (departure from the first station) and latest allowed arrival‑time at the last station for train \(t\) ‑ these bounds embed timetable limits and the disruption window |

All parameters are assumed to be known a‑priori (e.g. from the timetable, from the blockage information, from the train performance curves).

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows its **original** route direction; 0 if it uses the opposite (detour) direction. |
| \(y_{tt',e} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | Ordering variable for a **conflicting pair** \((t,t')\in\mathcal{C}\) on segment \(e\): \(y_{tt',e}=1\) means train \(t\) passes *before* train \(t'\) on \(e\); otherwise \(t'\) passes first. |
| \(a_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,e} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Chosen speed** of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (km h\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(\theta_{t,e}\ge 0\) | continuous | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (minutes). |
| \(E_{t}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Total energy** consumed by train \(t\) (kWh). |

---

## 4. Linear relationships that link variables  

### 4.1 Route‑choice linking  
A train can travel a segment only if the chosen direction permits it:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,e} &\le \overline v_{e}\, \bigl(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
               + (1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}}) \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}\bigr) &&\forall t,\;e\\
v_{t,e} &\ge \underline v_{e}\, \bigl(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
               + (1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}}) \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}\bigr) &&\forall t,\;e
\end{aligned}
\]

(\(\mathbf 1_{\cdot}\) is the indicator function; it equals 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.)  
If a segment belongs to the *non‑selected* direction, the right‑hand side becomes zero, forcing \(v_{t,e}=0\) (i.e. the train never uses that segment).

### 4.2 Travel‑time definition (linearised)

\[
\theta_{t,e} = \frac{L_{e}}{v_{t,e}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
L_{e} = v_{t,e}\,\theta_{t,e}.
\]

The product \(v_{t,e}\theta_{t,e}\) is bilinear, but it can be **linearised** with standard big‑M / piecewise‑linear approximation.  
For simplicity we present the *exact* relation and note that in an actual MILP it must be replaced by a set of linear constraints (e.g. using a break‑point discretisation of the admissible speed interval).  

Assume we have a discretisation \(v_{e}^{(k)}\), \(k=1,\dots,K_{e}\) and binary selection variables \(\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}\) (with \(\sum_{k}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}=1\)). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,e}        &= \sum_{k} v_{e}^{(k)} \lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}\\
\theta_{t,e}   &= \sum_{k} \frac{L_{e}}{v_{e}^{(k)}} \lambda_{t,e}^{(k)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model written below uses the compact notation \(\theta_{t,e}=L_{e}/v_{t,e}\) with the understanding that a linearization is applied.

### 4.3 Flow conservation at stations  

For every train \(t\) and every **intermediate** station \(s\) (i.e. not the first or last),

\[
d_{t,s} + \theta_{t,(s,s^+)} = a_{t,s^+},
\]

where \((s,s^+)\) denotes the outgoing segment from \(s\) on the chosen route (similarly for the incoming segment \((s^-,s)\)).  

At the origin station \(s^{\text{orig}}_{t}\),

\[
a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_{t}} = T^{\text{start}}_{t},
\]

and at the final station \(s^{\text{dest}}_{t}\),

\[
d_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}} = a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}} + \theta_{t,(s^{\text{dest}}_{t-1},s^{\text{dest}}_{t})}.
\]

### 4.4 Dwell‑time bounds  

\[
\underline d_{s}\le d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le \overline d_{s}\qquad \forall t,\;s\in\mathcal{S}.
\]

(For the origin and destination stations, the lower bound can be set to zero.)

### 4.5 Safety headway (same‑direction)  

If two trains travel **the same direction** on the same physical segment \(e\) (i.e. both are using the original direction or both the opposite direction),

\[
a_{t',\,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
\qquad\forall e,\;t,t'\in\mathcal{K}_{e},\; t\neq t'.
\]

The above is enforced only when the ordering variable indicates that \(t\) is ahead of \(t'\). A compact big‑M formulation using the ordering \(y_{tt',e}\) is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
 - M\,(1-y_{tt',e})\\
a_{t,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
 - M\,y_{tt',e},
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\text{sameDir}} .
\]

\(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g. larger than the planning horizon).

### 4.6 Bidirectional conflict avoidance (blocked segment)  

For any segment \(e\) that becomes **single‑track** because of the partial blockage, and any pair of trains \((t,t')\) that would use opposite directions on that segment, we impose:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
 - M\,(1-y_{tt',e})\\
a_{t,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
 - M\,y_{tt',e},
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\text{oppDir}} .
\]

The binary \(y_{tt',e}\) decides which train gets the “first‑through” right on the contested piece.

### 4.7 Energy consumption linearisation  

For each train \(t\),

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}  L_{e}\bigl(\alpha_{e}\,v_{t,e}+ \beta_{e}\bigr) .
\]

Because \(v_{t,e}\) is already linear (or expressed through the piecewise‑linear \(\lambda\) variables), the energy term is linear as well.

### 4.8 Total delay  

The delay of train \(t\) is measured against its baseline arrival time at the final destination:

\[
\text{delay}_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\quad\forall t.
\]

---

## 5. Objective function  

The planner wants a **weighted sum** of the two performance criteria:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} E_{t}
}
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

## 6. Full MILP model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t}\bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\bigr)
+ w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t}\sum_{e} L_{e}\bigl(\alpha_{e}v_{t,e}+ \beta_{e}\bigr)                                                  \\
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(i)   Route‑choice speed bounds}      && \underline v_{e}\,z_{t,e}\le v_{t,e}\le\overline v_{e}\,z_{t,e}
                                &&\forall t,e                                   \\
&\text{with } z_{t,e}= x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
                +(1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}})\mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}                                                \\
\text{(ii)  Travel‑time linearisation}      && v_{t,e}= \sum_{k} v_{e}^{(k)}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}                       &&\forall t,e\\
& && \theta_{t,e}= \sum_{k} \frac{L_{e}}{v_{e}^{(k)}}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}                                   &&\forall t,e\\
& && \sum_{k}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)} = z_{t,e}                                                               &&\forall t,e\\[2mm]
\text{(iii) Flow conservation}               && d_{t,s}+ \theta_{t,(s,s^+)} = a_{t,s^+}                                 &&\forall t,\; s\neq s^{\text{dest}}_t\\
\text{(iv)  Dwell‑time bounds}                && \underline d_{s}\le d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le \overline d_{s}                &&\forall t,s\\
\text{(v)   Headway (same direction)}         && a_{t',\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
                                                -M(1-y_{tt',e})                                                     &&\forall e,\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{sameDir}}_e\\
& && a_{t,\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
                                                -M\,y_{tt',e}                                                        &&\forall e,\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{sameDir}}_e\\[2mm]
\text{(vi)  Bidirectional conflict (blocked)}&& a_{t',\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
                                                -M(1-y_{tt',e})                                                     &&\forall e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{oppDir}}_e\\
& && a_{t,\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
                                                -M\,y_{tt',e}                                                        &&\forall e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{oppDir}}_e\\[2mm]
\text{(vii)  Ordering consistency}            && y_{tt',e}+y_{t't,e}=1 \qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C},\;e     &&\text{(binary choice)}\\
\text{(viii) Time windows}                   && T^{\text{start}}_{t}\le a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_{t}} \le T^{\text{end}}_{t}   &&\forall t\\
\text{(ix)   Variable domains}              && x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{tt',e}\in\{0,1\},\;
                                         a,d,\theta,v\ge 0.                                                      \\
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. What each component does (plain‑English)

1. **Binary route‑choice \(x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\).**  
   Decides whether train *t* stays on its planned track (value = 1) or detours on the opposite track (value = 0). All subsequent speed‑and‑time variables are forced to zero on segments that belong to the non‑selected direction.

2. **Ordering binaries \(y_{tt',e}\).**  
   Resolve conflicts on any segment that can be used by two trains at the same time (either because they run the same direction or because a blockage forces a single‑track operation). Setting \(y_{tt',e}=1\) means *t* obtains the “first‑through” right on that segment; the big‑M constraints then impose the appropriate head‑way or conflict‑gap.

3. **Arrival/Departure times \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\).**  
   Capture the exact schedule at every station. Flow‑conservation constraints tie successive stations together through the travel time on the intervening segment.

4. **Speeds \(v_{t,e}\) and travel times \(\theta_{t,e}\).**  
   The model chooses a speed for each train‑segment pair inside the admissible interval. Travel time is the segment length divided by the chosen speed (linearised with a piecewise‑constant speed set). Faster speeds reduce travel time (hence delay) but increase the linear energy term.

5. **Energy consumption \(E_{t}\).**  
   A simple linear approximation of the real physics: on each kilometre, energy ≈ \(a\cdot v + b\). Summing over all travelled kilometres yields the total energy for each train, which appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{energy}}\).

6. **Objective (weighted sum).**  
   - The first term adds all **delays** (difference between realised arrival at the destination and the baseline timetable).  
   - The second term adds all **energy consumptions**.  
   By adjusting the scalar weights the planner can emphasise punctuality, sustainability, or a compromise between them.

7. **Safety constraints.**  
   - **Head‑way** ensures a minimum time gap between successive trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical track piece.  
   - **Bidirectional conflict** ensures that, on a segment that has become single‑track because of the blockage, opposite‑direction trains respect a larger gap (or the same gap if the operator chooses so). The ordering binaries guarantee that only one of the two possible orderings is active.

8. **Dwell‑time bounds.**  
   Guarantees that each train stays at a platform long enough for passengers to board/alight but not longer than the platform’s capacity or timetable limits.

9. **Speed‑limit constraints.**  
   The chosen speed must stay inside the legal minimum and maximum for each segment; this also implicitly respects the physical capability of the high‑speed train.

10. **Time‑window constraints.**  
    Enforce that the first departure cannot be earlier than the disruption‑aware earliest start, and that the final arrival cannot exceed a latest‑allowed time (e.g., due to crew working‑time regulations).

---

## 8. How to solve  

The model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** once the bilinear term \(L_{e}=v_{t,e}\theta_{t,e}\) is replaced by a piecewise‑linear approximation (the \(\lambda\)‑variables above). It can be handed to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, GLPK, etc.).  
Typical solution sizes for a medium‑sized high‑speed corridor (≈ 30‑50 trains, ≈ 100 segments) are well within the capability of modern solvers; the main computational effort lies in the combinatorial ordering variables \(y_{tt',e}\), but the formulation is *compact* (no need for time‑expanded networks).

---

**In summary**, the presented MILP simultaneously chooses:

* the **route direction** for each train,  
* the **speed level** on every travelled segment,  
* the **exact timing** at every station, and  
* the **conflict ordering** on shared track pieces,

while minimising a weighted combination of **total delay** and **energy consumption** and respecting all safety, operational and physical constraints of a high‑speed railway under a partial blockage.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) for high-speed railway under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice (original or opposite track), binary ordering for conflicting trains, continuous arrival/departure times at stations, continuous speed levels per track segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and total energy consumption. Constraints: (1) each train must choose a feasible route; (2) flow conservation of train through stations; (3) time feasibility linking speeds to travel times (t = length / speed); (4) safety headway constraints between any two trains on same track segment (arrival time difference >= headway); (5) bidirectional conflict avoidance on shared track during disruption window; (6) dwell time bounds; (7) speed limits per segment; (8) binary ordering variables enforce which train passes first on a conflicting segment; (9) energy consumption linearized as a function of speed (e.g., energy = a*speed + b).

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)**  
*High‑speed railway with a partially‑blocked segment*  

Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, followed by the constraints grouped by their logical meaning.  
The model is *linear* (the only non‑linear terms – travel time = length/speed – have been linearised by introducing auxiliary variables and big‑M techniques).  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Data

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\( \mathcal{T}= \{1,\dots,T\}\\) | Set of trains |
| \\( \mathcal{S}= \{0,1,\dots,S\}\\) | Ordered list of stations (station 0 = origin, station \\(S\\) = final destination) |
| \\( \mathcal{E}= \{(s,s+1) \mid s=0,\dots,S-1\}\\) | Track **segments** between consecutive stations |
| \\( \mathcal{K}= \{1,\dots,K\}\\) | Set of *track‑direction* alternatives for each segment (normally two: original direction “O” and opposite direction “R”) |
| \\( \mathcal{C}\subseteq \mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{E}\\) | Set of *conflicting* train‑segment triples where two trains cannot occupy the same segment at the same time (includes the blocked segment) |
| \\( \mathcal{W}\subseteq \mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}\\) | Set of unordered train pairs that share at least one segment (head‑way constraints) |
| \\( L_{e}\\) | Physical length of segment \\(e\\) (km) |
| \\( v^{\min }_{e,k},\;v^{\max }_{e,k}\\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \\(e\\) when travelled in direction \\(k\\) (km/h) |
| \\( h_{i,j}\\) | Minimum safety head‑way time that must separate the *departure* of train \\(i\\) and the *arrival* of train \\(j\\) on a common segment (seconds) |
| \\( d^{\min }_{s},\;d^{\max }_{s}\\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station \\(s\\) (seconds) |
| \\( \alpha_{e,k},\; \beta_{e,k}\\) | Linear energy coefficients for segment \\(e\\) and direction \\(k\\) (energy = \\(\alpha v + \beta\\)) |
| \\( w^{\text{delay}},\; w^{\text{energy}} \\) | Positive weights used in the weighted sum objective |
| \\( M\\) | A large constant (big‑M) – chosen larger than any feasible time value (e.g. 10⁶ s) |
| \\( \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,s}\\) | Planned (unperturbed) arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) (used for delay calculation) |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|--------------|
| \\(x_{i,e,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) traverses segment \\(e\\) in direction \\(k\\) (original = \\(k=O\\), opposite = \\(k=R\\)). |
| \\(y_{i,j,e}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(i\\) passes *before* train \\(j\\) on segment \\(e\\) (used only for pairs in \\( \mathcal{C}\\)). |
| \\(a_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{i,s}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(s\\). |
| \\(v_{i,e,k}\\) | continuous | Speed chosen by train \\(i\\) on segment \\(e\\) when travelling in direction \\(k\\). (If \\(x_{i,e,k}=0\\) the variable is forced to 0). |
| \\(t_{i,e}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train \\(i\\) on segment \\(e\\). |
| \\(E_{i}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total energy consumption of train \\(i\\). |
| \\(\Delta_{i}\\) | continuous, ≥0 | Total delay of train \\(i\\) (difference between actual arrival at final station and planned arrival). |

---

## 3. Linearisation of the *travel‑time* relation  

The physical relation is  

\[
t_{i,e}= \frac{L_{e}}{v_{i,e}} .
\]

Because the denominator is a variable, we replace it with a set of *piece‑wise linear* (or big‑M) constraints.  
A simple, exact linearisation for a bounded speed interval is the **epigraph formulation**:

Introduce an auxiliary binary variable \\(z_{i,e,k}\\) that selects a speed *break‑point* (or use a set of pre‑defined speed levels). For brevity we present the compact big‑M version that works when the speed range is narrow (typical for high‑speed lines):

\[
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,e} &\ge \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max }_{e,k}} \; -\; M\;(1-x_{i,e,k}) &&\forall i,e,k,\\
t_{i,e} &\le \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\min }_{e,k}} \; +\; M\;(1-x_{i,e,k}) &&\forall i,e,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

If a tighter linear approximation is needed, replace the two inequalities by a set of **SOS‑2** or *multiple* break‑points; the formulation below assumes the simple bounds are sufficient for the MILP.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}} \underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Delta_{i}}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}} \underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_{i}}_{\text{total energy}} .
\]

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑choice feasibility  

*Exactly one direction is selected for each train on every segment it must traverse.*

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{i,e,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in\mathcal{T},\; \forall e\in\mathcal{E}_{i},
\]

where \\(\mathcal{E}_{i}\\) is the set of segments belonging to train \\(i\\)’s itinerary (derived from the timetable).  
If the train does **not** need a segment (e.g., it terminates earlier) the corresponding \(x\) variables are fixed to 0.

### 5.2 Flow conservation through stations  

For each train, departure from station \\(s\\) equals arrival plus dwell time, and the arrival at the next station follows from travel time:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{i,s} &= a_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1,\\
a_{i,s+1} &= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,(s,s+1)} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \\(\tau_{i,s}\\) is the *actual* dwell time at station \\(s\\) for train \\(i\\).  

### 5.3 Dwell‑time bounds  

\[
d^{\min }_{s}\le \tau_{i,s}\le d^{\max }_{s}
\qquad\forall i,\; s=1,\dots,S-1.
\]

(For the origin station \\(s=0\\) and the final station \\(S\\) the dwell time can be set to 0.)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

If a train uses direction \\(k\\) on segment \\(e\\) its speed must respect the admissible interval; otherwise it must be 0.

\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{\min }_{e,k}\; x_{i,e,k} \;\le\; v_{i,e,k} \;\le\; v^{\max }_{e,k}\; x_{i,e,k}
\qquad\forall i,e,k .
\end{aligned}
\]

The *effective* speed on segment \\(e\\) for train \\(i\\) is  

\[
v_{i,e}= \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} v_{i,e,k}.
\]

### 5.5 Energy consumption (linear)  

Energy on each segment is linear in speed:

\[
E_{i}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{i}} \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} \bigl(\alpha_{e,k}\, v_{i,e,k}+ \beta_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}\bigr) .
\]

(The term \( \beta_{i,e,k} x_{i,e,k}\) accounts for a fixed component that depends only on the fact the segment is traversed.)

### 5.6 Delay calculation  

Delay of train \\(i\\) is the difference between its actual arrival at the final station \\(S\\) and the planned arrival:

\[
\Delta_{i}= a_{i,S} - \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,S} \qquad \forall i .
\]

(If early arrival is allowed, a non‑negativity constraint on \\(\Delta_i\\) already forces the model to treat early arrivals as zero delay.)

### 5.7 Safety head‑way between any two trains on the **same** track  

For every unordered pair \\((i,j)\\in\mathcal{W}\\) that share at least one segment, enforce that at any common segment one train leaves *before* the other arrives by at least the prescribed head‑way. Using the ordering binary \\(y_{i,j,e}\\) only for pairs that conflict on a **blocked** segment (see 5.8), for the general head‑way we write:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,s} &\ge d_{i,s} + h_{i,j} \;-\; M\bigl(1 - \theta_{i,j,s}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; \forall s,\\
a_{i,s} &\ge d_{j,s} + h_{i,j} \;-\; M\bigl(\theta_{i,j,s}\bigr)          &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; \forall s,
\end{aligned}
\]

where \\(\theta_{i,j,s}\\) is a binary variable that decides which train is ahead on segment \\(s\\).  
If only one shared segment exists, the index \\(s\\) can be omitted.

### 5.8  Bidirectional conflict avoidance on the *blocked* segment  

Let the blocked segment be \\(e^{*}\\). For every unordered pair of trains \\((i,j)\\) that both need to use this segment (i.e. \\((i,j,e^{*})\in\mathcal{C}\\)), introduce a binary ordering variable \\( y_{i,j,e^{*}}\\) such that

* \(y_{i,j,e^{*}} = 1\) ⇒ train \\(i\\) passes before train \\(j\\) on the blocked segment,
* \(y_{i,j,e^{*}} = 0\) ⇒ the opposite order.

The head‑way constraints become

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{j,\text{up}(e^{*})} &\ge d_{i,\text{down}(e^{*})} + h_{i,j}
 \;-\; M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,e^{*}}\bigr) ,
\\
a_{i,\text{up}(e^{*})} &\ge d_{j,\text{down}(e^{*})} + h_{i,j}
 \;-\; M\bigl(y_{i,j,e^{*}}\bigr) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Here, ``down’’ is the station at the **entry** side of the segment for the considered travel direction, and ``up’’ the **exit** side.  
Additionally we enforce consistency between the ordering variables:

\[
y_{i,j,e^{*}} + y_{j,i,e^{*}} = 1 \qquad \forall (i,j,e^{*})\in\mathcal{C}.
\]

If more than two trains may occupy the same blocked segment (rare for high‑speed lines), a *pairwise* ordering model together with transitivity constraints can be added, but the pairwise formulation above is sufficient for the usual case of two competing trains.

### 5.9  Linking speed to travel time (big‑M version)  

Using the linear bounds described in 5.3 we already have a range for \\(t_{i,e}\\). To make the model tighter we may add an exact linear relationship by **discretising** the admissible speed set into \\(P\\) candidate speed levels \\(v^{p}_{e,k}\\) (e.g., 300, 320, 340 km/h). Introduce binaries \\(u^{p}_{i,e,k}\\) with  

\[
\sum_{p=1}^{P} u^{p}_{i,e,k}= x_{i,e,k}, \qquad 
v_{i,e,k}= \sum_{p} v^{p}_{e,k}\, u^{p}_{i,e,k},
\qquad
t_{i,e}= \sum_{p} \frac{L_{e}}{v^{p}_{e,k}} \, u^{p}_{i,e,k}.
\]

All terms stay linear; the model size grows only moderately because the number of speed levels per segment is small (3‑5).

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\; w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} \Delta_{i}
   \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}} E_{i}  &&\text{(objective)} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
& \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}} x_{i,e,k}=1 &&\forall i,\;e\in\mathcal{E}_{i} \tag{R1}\\
& d_{i,s}= a_{i,s}+ \tau_{i,s} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1 \tag{R2}\\
& a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,(s,s+1)} &&\forall i,\; s=0,\dots,S-1 \tag{R3}\\
& d^{\min }_{s}\le \tau_{i,s}\le d^{\max }_{s} &&\forall i,\; s=1,\dots,S-1 \tag{R4}\\
& v^{\min }_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}\le v_{i,e,k}\le v^{\max }_{e,k}\, x_{i,e,k}
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R5}\\
& t_{i,e}\ge \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max }_{e,k}} - M(1-x_{i,e,k})
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R6a}\\
& t_{i,e}\le \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\min }_{e,k}} + M(1-x_{i,e,k})
   &&\forall i,e,k \tag{R6b}\\
& E_{i}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{i}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}
        \bigl(\alpha_{e,k} v_{i,e,k}+ \beta_{e,k} x_{i,e,k}\bigr)
   &&\forall i \tag{R7}\\
& \Delta_{i}= a_{i,S} - \overline{t}^{\text{plan}}_{i,S}
   &&\forall i \tag{R8}\\
& a_{j,\text{up}(e)}\ge d_{i,\text{down}(e)}+h_{i,j}
   -M\bigl(1-y_{i,j,e}\bigr) &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9a}\\
& a_{i,\text{up}(e)}\ge d_{j,\text{down}(e)}+h_{i,j}
   -M y_{i,j,e} &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9b}\\
& y_{i,j,e}+y_{j,i,e}=1 &&\forall (i,j,e)\in\mathcal{C} \tag{R9c}\\
& a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+h_{i,j} - M(1-\theta_{i,j,s}) &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; s\\
& a_{i,s}\ge d_{j,s}+h_{i,j} - M\theta_{i,j,s} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{W},\; s \tag{R10}\\
& x_{i,e,k}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,j,e}\in\{0,1\},\; \theta_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},\tau_{i,s}, t_{i,e}, v_{i,e,k}, E_{i},\Delta_{i}\ge 0 &&\forall\text{continuous}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Block | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-------|--------------|------------------|
| **Binary route‑choice \\(x_{i,e,k}\\)** | Selects the direction (original vs opposite) for each train on every segment. | Guarantees a feasible physical route and activates the correct speed bounds. |
| **Flow‑conservation (R2–R3)** | Links arrivals, departures, dwell times and travel times along the train’s path. | Enforces a realistic timetable structure. |
| **Speed limits (R5)** | Bounds the continuous speed variable by the admissible interval of the chosen direction. | Prevents illegal speeds and couples binary direction to continuous speed. |
| **Travel‑time linearisation (R6)** | Provides a linear envelope for the non‑linear relation *time = length / speed* using big‑M. | Keeps the model MILP‑compatible while still representing the physics. |
| **Energy model (R7)** | Linear function of speed (coefficients \\(\alpha, \beta\\)). | Allows the objective to penalise high speeds (energy cost). |
| **Delay definition (R8)** | Computes the lateness of the train at its final destination. | Part of the weighted objective. |
| **Head‑way constraints (R9, R10)** | Guarantees a minimum safety time between successive trains on the *same* track segment; ordering binaries decide which train goes first. | Avoids collisions, respects signalling rules, and especially handles the blocked segment where opposite directions may meet. |
| **Ordering consistency (R9c)** | For each conflicting pair exactly one of the two possible orders is selected. | Guarantees a well‑defined schedule on the disputed segment. |
| **Binary ordering variables \\(y_{i,j,e}\\)** | Explicitly model which train passes first on a segment where bidirectional traffic is possible (especially the blocked segment). | Enables the MILP to decide the optimal sequence, which directly influences delay and energy. |
| **Weighted objective** | Minimises a linear combination of total delay and total energy consumption. | Allows the planner to trade‑off punctuality against sustainability. |

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Populate all sets and parameters (segment lengths, speed limits, head‑way times, planned arrivals, energy coefficients).  
2. **Choose \(M\)** – Set \(M\) larger than any feasible time (e.g., \(M = 10^5\) s).  
3. **Optional speed discretisation** – If a tighter representation of the \(t = L/v\) curve is desired, replace the big‑M bounds (R6) with the SOS‑2/price‑break‑point formulation shown in Section 5.9.  
4. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (CBC, HiGHS) MILP solver.  
5. **Post‑processing** – Extract the optimal routes (values of \(x_{i,e,k}\)), speeds (\(v_{i,e,k}\)), and the resulting timetable (\(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)).  

The formulation above is **complete and linear** and can be directly implemented in a modelling language such as AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, or OPL. It captures all the elements you listed: route choice, ordering on conflicting segments, continuous timing and speed decisions, safety head‑ways, dwell‑time limits, speed limits, a linearised energy model, and a weighted objective that balances punctuality with energy consumption.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave.  
The formulation is written in a compact mathematical notation, followed by a plain‑English explanation of every set, variable, objective term and constraint family.

---

## 1. Index sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \( \mathcal{T} =\{1,\dots ,T\}\) | Set of trains to be scheduled |
| \( \mathcal{S} =\{1,\dots ,S\}\) | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train) |
| \( \mathcal{E}= \{(i,j) \mid i,j\in \mathcal{S}, i\neq j\}\) | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) between two successive stations |
| \( \mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}} \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) | Segments that belong to the **original** (planned) track direction |
| \( \mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}} \subseteq \mathcal{E}\) | Segments that belong to the **opposite** (reversed) direction – used when a train is rerouted |
| \( \mathcal{K}_{e} \subseteq \mathcal{T}\) | Trains that may travel on segment \(e\) (all trains whose origin‑dest path contains \(e\)) |
| \( \mathcal{C} \subseteq \{(t,t')\mid t<t'\}\) | Set of *conflicting* train pairs; i.e. two trains that could occupy the same physical track piece at the same time (including bidirectional conflicts caused by the partial blockage) |

---

## 2. Data (parameters)  

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| \(L_{e}\) | Length (km) of segment \(e\) |
| \(\underline v_{e},\ \overline v_{e}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(e\) (km h\(^{-1}\)) |
| \(\underline d_{s},\ \overline d_{s}\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time at station \(s\) (minutes) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}\) | Safety head‑way (minimum time gap) required between any two trains travelling on the **same** direction of segment \(e\) (minutes) |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}\) | Minimum time gap that must be respected on a **shared** (bidirectional) segment during the disruption window (minutes) |
| \(E^{\text{base}}_{t}\) | Planned (baseline) arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (without any disruption) |
| \(\alpha_{e},\ \beta_{e}\) | Linear energy coefficients for segment \(e\) (energy = \(\alpha_{e} v_{e}+ \beta_{e}\)  kWh per km) |
| \(w^{\text{delay}},\ w^{\text{energy}}\) | Positive weighting factors used in the bi‑objective linear combination (chosen by the planner) |
| \(T^{\text{start}}_{t},\ T^{\text{end}}_{t}\) | Earliest possible start‑time (departure from the first station) and latest allowed arrival‑time at the last station for train \(t\) ‑ these bounds embed timetable limits and the disruption window |

All parameters are assumed to be known a‑priori (e.g. from the timetable, from the blockage information, from the train performance curves).

---

## 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows its **original** route direction; 0 if it uses the opposite (detour) direction. |
| \(y_{tt',e} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | Ordering variable for a **conflicting pair** \((t,t')\in\mathcal{C}\) on segment \(e\): \(y_{tt',e}=1\) means train \(t\) passes *before* train \(t'\) on \(e\); otherwise \(t'\) passes first. |
| \(a_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | Arrival time of train \(t\) at station \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | Departure time of train \(t\) from station \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,e} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Chosen speed** of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (km h\(^{-1}\)). |
| \(\theta_{t,e}\ge 0\) | continuous | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(e\) (minutes). |
| \(E_{t}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Total energy** consumed by train \(t\) (kWh). |

---

## 4. Linear relationships that link variables  

### 4.1 Route‑choice linking  
A train can travel a segment only if the chosen direction permits it:

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,e} &\le \overline v_{e}\, \bigl(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
               + (1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}}) \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}\bigr) &&\forall t,\;e\\
v_{t,e} &\ge \underline v_{e}\, \bigl(x_{t}^{\text{orig}} \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
               + (1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}}) \mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}\bigr) &&\forall t,\;e
\end{aligned}
\]

(\(\mathbf 1_{\cdot}\) is the indicator function; it equals 1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise.)  
If a segment belongs to the *non‑selected* direction, the right‑hand side becomes zero, forcing \(v_{t,e}=0\) (i.e. the train never uses that segment).

### 4.2 Travel‑time definition (linearised)

\[
\theta_{t,e} = \frac{L_{e}}{v_{t,e}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
L_{e} = v_{t,e}\,\theta_{t,e}.
\]

The product \(v_{t,e}\theta_{t,e}\) is bilinear, but it can be **linearised** with standard big‑M / piecewise‑linear approximation.  
For simplicity we present the *exact* relation and note that in an actual MILP it must be replaced by a set of linear constraints (e.g. using a break‑point discretisation of the admissible speed interval).  

Assume we have a discretisation \(v_{e}^{(k)}\), \(k=1,\dots,K_{e}\) and binary selection variables \(\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}\) (with \(\sum_{k}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}=1\)). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{t,e}        &= \sum_{k} v_{e}^{(k)} \lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}\\
\theta_{t,e}   &= \sum_{k} \frac{L_{e}}{v_{e}^{(k)}} \lambda_{t,e}^{(k)} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model written below uses the compact notation \(\theta_{t,e}=L_{e}/v_{t,e}\) with the understanding that a linearization is applied.

### 4.3 Flow conservation at stations  

For every train \(t\) and every **intermediate** station \(s\) (i.e. not the first or last),

\[
d_{t,s} + \theta_{t,(s,s^+)} = a_{t,s^+},
\]

where \((s,s^+)\) denotes the outgoing segment from \(s\) on the chosen route (similarly for the incoming segment \((s^-,s)\)).  

At the origin station \(s^{\text{orig}}_{t}\),

\[
a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_{t}} = T^{\text{start}}_{t},
\]

and at the final station \(s^{\text{dest}}_{t}\),

\[
d_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}} = a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}} + \theta_{t,(s^{\text{dest}}_{t-1},s^{\text{dest}}_{t})}.
\]

### 4.4 Dwell‑time bounds  

\[
\underline d_{s}\le d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le \overline d_{s}\qquad \forall t,\;s\in\mathcal{S}.
\]

(For the origin and destination stations, the lower bound can be set to zero.)

### 4.5 Safety headway (same‑direction)  

If two trains travel **the same direction** on the same physical segment \(e\) (i.e. both are using the original direction or both the opposite direction),

\[
a_{t',\,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
\qquad\forall e,\;t,t'\in\mathcal{K}_{e},\; t\neq t'.
\]

The above is enforced only when the ordering variable indicates that \(t\) is ahead of \(t'\). A compact big‑M formulation using the ordering \(y_{tt',e}\) is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
 - M\,(1-y_{tt',e})\\
a_{t,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
 - M\,y_{tt',e},
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\text{sameDir}} .
\]

\(M\) is a sufficiently large constant (e.g. larger than the planning horizon).

### 4.6 Bidirectional conflict avoidance (blocked segment)  

For any segment \(e\) that becomes **single‑track** because of the partial blockage, and any pair of trains \((t,t')\) that would use opposite directions on that segment, we impose:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
 - M\,(1-y_{tt',e})\\
a_{t,\text{exit}(e)} - d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} &\ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
 - M\,y_{tt',e},
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C}_e^{\text{oppDir}} .
\]

The binary \(y_{tt',e}\) decides which train gets the “first‑through” right on the contested piece.

### 4.7 Energy consumption linearisation  

For each train \(t\),

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}  L_{e}\bigl(\alpha_{e}\,v_{t,e}+ \beta_{e}\bigr) .
\]

Because \(v_{t,e}\) is already linear (or expressed through the piecewise‑linear \(\lambda\) variables), the energy term is linear as well.

### 4.8 Total delay  

The delay of train \(t\) is measured against its baseline arrival time at the final destination:

\[
\text{delay}_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\quad\forall t.
\]

---

## 5. Objective function  

The planner wants a **weighted sum** of the two performance criteria:

\[
\boxed{
\min \; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\bigr)
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}} E_{t}
}
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

## 6. Full MILP model (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;&
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t}\bigl(a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_{t}}-E^{\text{base}}_{t}\bigr)
+ w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t}\sum_{e} L_{e}\bigl(\alpha_{e}v_{t,e}+ \beta_{e}\bigr)                                                  \\
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(i)   Route‑choice speed bounds}      && \underline v_{e}\,z_{t,e}\le v_{t,e}\le\overline v_{e}\,z_{t,e}
                                &&\forall t,e                                   \\
&\text{with } z_{t,e}= x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{orig}}}
                +(1-x_{t}^{\text{orig}})\mathbf 1_{e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{opp}}}                                                \\
\text{(ii)  Travel‑time linearisation}      && v_{t,e}= \sum_{k} v_{e}^{(k)}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}                       &&\forall t,e\\
& && \theta_{t,e}= \sum_{k} \frac{L_{e}}{v_{e}^{(k)}}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)}                                   &&\forall t,e\\
& && \sum_{k}\lambda_{t,e}^{(k)} = z_{t,e}                                                               &&\forall t,e\\[2mm]
\text{(iii) Flow conservation}               && d_{t,s}+ \theta_{t,(s,s^+)} = a_{t,s^+}                                 &&\forall t,\; s\neq s^{\text{dest}}_t\\
\text{(iv)  Dwell‑time bounds}                && \underline d_{s}\le d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\le \overline d_{s}                &&\forall t,s\\
\text{(v)   Headway (same direction)}         && a_{t',\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
                                                -M(1-y_{tt',e})                                                     &&\forall e,\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{sameDir}}_e\\
& && a_{t,\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{headway}}_{e}
                                                -M\,y_{tt',e}                                                        &&\forall e,\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{sameDir}}_e\\[2mm]
\text{(vi)  Bidirectional conflict (blocked)}&& a_{t',\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t,\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
                                                -M(1-y_{tt',e})                                                     &&\forall e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{oppDir}}_e\\
& && a_{t,\text{exit}(e)}- d_{t',\text{enter}(e)} \ge \Delta^{\text{conflict}}_{e}
                                                -M\,y_{tt',e}                                                        &&\forall e\in\mathcal{E}^{\text{blocked}},\;(t,t')\in\mathcal{C}^{\text{oppDir}}_e\\[2mm]
\text{(vii)  Ordering consistency}            && y_{tt',e}+y_{t't,e}=1 \qquad\forall (t,t')\in\mathcal{C},\;e     &&\text{(binary choice)}\\
\text{(viii) Time windows}                   && T^{\text{start}}_{t}\le a_{t,s^{\text{orig}}_{t}} \le T^{\text{end}}_{t}   &&\forall t\\
\text{(ix)   Variable domains}              && x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{tt',e}\in\{0,1\},\;
                                         a,d,\theta,v\ge 0.                                                      \\
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. What each component does (plain‑English)

1. **Binary route‑choice \(x_{t}^{\text{orig}}\).**  
   Decides whether train *t* stays on its planned track (value = 1) or detours on the opposite track (value = 0). All subsequent speed‑and‑time variables are forced to zero on segments that belong to the non‑selected direction.

2. **Ordering binaries \(y_{tt',e}\).**  
   Resolve conflicts on any segment that can be used by two trains at the same time (either because they run the same direction or because a blockage forces a single‑track operation). Setting \(y_{tt',e}=1\) means *t* obtains the “first‑through” right on that segment; the big‑M constraints then impose the appropriate head‑way or conflict‑gap.

3. **Arrival/Departure times \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\).**  
   Capture the exact schedule at every station. Flow‑conservation constraints tie successive stations together through the travel time on the intervening segment.

4. **Speeds \(v_{t,e}\) and travel times \(\theta_{t,e}\).**  
   The model chooses a speed for each train‑segment pair inside the admissible interval. Travel time is the segment length divided by the chosen speed (linearised with a piecewise‑constant speed set). Faster speeds reduce travel time (hence delay) but increase the linear energy term.

5. **Energy consumption \(E_{t}\).**  
   A simple linear approximation of the real physics: on each kilometre, energy ≈ \(a\cdot v + b\). Summing over all travelled kilometres yields the total energy for each train, which appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{energy}}\).

6. **Objective (weighted sum).**  
   - The first term adds all **delays** (difference between realised arrival at the destination and the baseline timetable).  
   - The second term adds all **energy consumptions**.  
   By adjusting the scalar weights the planner can emphasise punctuality, sustainability, or a compromise between them.

7. **Safety constraints.**  
   - **Head‑way** ensures a minimum time gap between successive trains travelling in the same direction on the same physical track piece.  
   - **Bidirectional conflict** ensures that, on a segment that has become single‑track because of the blockage, opposite‑direction trains respect a larger gap (or the same gap if the operator chooses so). The ordering binaries guarantee that only one of the two possible orderings is active.

8. **Dwell‑time bounds.**  
   Guarantees that each train stays at a platform long enough for passengers to board/alight but not longer than the platform’s capacity or timetable limits.

9. **Speed‑limit constraints.**  
   The chosen speed must stay inside the legal minimum and maximum for each segment; this also implicitly respects the physical capability of the high‑speed train.

10. **Time‑window constraints.**  
    Enforce that the first departure cannot be earlier than the disruption‑aware earliest start, and that the final arrival cannot exceed a latest‑allowed time (e.g., due to crew working‑time regulations).

---

## 8. How to solve  

The model is a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program (MILP)** once the bilinear term \(L_{e}=v_{t,e}\theta_{t,e}\) is replaced by a piecewise‑linear approximation (the \(\lambda\)‑variables above). It can be handed to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, GLPK, etc.).  
Typical solution sizes for a medium‑sized high‑speed corridor (≈ 30‑50 trains, ≈ 100 segments) are well within the capability of modern solvers; the main computational effort lies in the combinatorial ordering variables \(y_{tt',e}\), but the formulation is *compact* (no need for time‑expanded networks).

---

**In summary**, the presented MILP simultaneously chooses:

* the **route direction** for each train,  
* the **speed level** on every travelled segment,  
* the **exact timing** at every station, and  
* the **conflict ordering** on shared track pieces,

while minimising a weighted combination of **total delay** and **energy consumption** and respecting all safety, operational and physical constraints of a high‑speed railway under a partial blockage.
