Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave – an integrated train‑rescheduling and speed‑management problem when a part of the line is blocked.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, and finally every set of constraints.  The model is written in a **compact linear‑algebraic form** that can be copied directly into a solver such as CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, or an open‑source MILP engine.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Set of trains (each train is indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Set of line **segments** (ordered from upstream to downstream). |
| \(K=\{1,\dots ,|K|\}\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (e.g., 1 = low, 2 = medium, 3 = high). |
| \(B\subseteq S\) | Sub‑set of **blocked segments** (the portion of the line that is unavailable for a given time window). |
| \(P_t\subseteq S\) | Set of **feasible routes** (ordered list of segments) that train \(t\) may use.  For a simple line, \(P_t=S\); for a network with switches, each route is a different ordered subset of segments. |
| \(R_t=\{1,\dots ,|R_t|\}\) | Index set of the **candidate routes** for train \(t\).  For each \(r\in R_t\) we denote the ordered list of segments on that route by \(\text{seg}(t,r)=\bigl(s_{t,r,1},\dots ,s_{t,r,|s_{t,r}|}\bigr)\). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at the **up‑stream end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from the **down‑stream end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(v_{t,s,k}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(e_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Total delay** of train \(t\) with respect to its scheduled (baseline) arrival at its final destination. |
| \(c_{t}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | **Energy consumption** of train \(t\) (linearised as a weighted sum of speed‑level usage). |

*Auxiliary linearisation variables (optional but often convenient):*  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(\delta_{t,s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) actually traverses segment \(s\) (i.e., the segment belongs to the chosen route). |
| \(\theta_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (used to link arrival/departure). |

---

## 3. Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). |
| \(\tau_{k}\) | Travel time per km for speed level \(k\) (h/km).  (Thus the travel time on segment \(s\) at speed \(k\) is \(\tau_k L_s\)). |
| \(\epsilon_{k}\) | Energy consumption per km for speed level \(k\) (kWh/km). |
| \(T^{\text{sched}}_{t}\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (baseline, no blockage). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g., horizon length). |
| \(\alpha,\beta\) | Positive weighting coefficients for delay and energy in the objective (chosen by the planner). |
| \(t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{start}}, t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{end}}\) | Start and end of the blockage time window on blocked segment \(s\in B\). |
| \(p_{t,s}^{\text{min}}, p_{t,s}^{\text{max}}\) | Minimum / maximum permissible dwell (or traversal) time for train \(t\) on segment \(s\) (e.g., due to safety or signalling). |
| \(C^{\text{track}}\) | Capacity of a segment (normally 1 train at a time; can be >1 for double‑track). |
| \(R_{t,r}\) | 1 if route \(r\) for train \(t\) is **compatible** with the blockage (i.e., does not contain a blocked segment during its blocked interval); 0 otherwise.  This can be pre‑computed. |

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; Z \;=\; \alpha \sum_{t\in T} e_{t} \;+\; \beta \sum_{t\in T} c_{t}
}
\]

*Interpretation* – we minimise a weighted sum of **total delay** (first term) and **energy consumption** (second term).  By changing \(\alpha,\beta\) the planner can stress punctuality or sustainability.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑choice and continuity  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑usage indicator**  

\[
\delta_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in \text{seg}(t,r)} x_{t,r}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{R2}
\]

Thus \(\delta_{t,s}=1\) iff the selected route contains segment \(s\).

3. **Speed‑level can be chosen only on traversed segments**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= \delta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{R3}
\]

4. **Each traversed segment gets exactly one speed level**  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= \delta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{R4}
\]

(identical to R3 – written for clarity).

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility (travel‑time linking)

5.1 **Travel time on a segment equals the selected speed‑level travel time**  

\[
\theta_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{k}\,L_s \, v_{t,s,k}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{T1}
\]

5.2 **Departure = arrival + travel time** (only if the segment is traversed)  

\[
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \theta_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{T2}
\]

5.3 **Link successive segments on the chosen route**  
Let \(s_{t,r,\ell}\) be the \(\ell\)-th segment on route \(r\) for train \(t\). For every train and every pair of consecutive segments on its selected route:

\[
a_{t,s_{t,r,\ell+1}} \;\ge\; d_{t,s_{t,r,\ell}} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{t,r})
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t,\; \ell=1,\dots,|s_{t,r}|-1
\tag{T3}
\]

If route \(r\) is not chosen (\(x_{t,r}=0\)), the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.

5.4 **Dwell‑time (or minimum/maximum traversal) bounds**  

\[
p_{t,s}^{\text{min}} \,\delta_{t,s}\;\le\; \theta_{t,s}\;\le\; p_{t,s}^{\text{max}} \,\delta_{t,s}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{T4}
\]

### 5.3 Blockage (partial segment unavailability)

6.1 **No train may occupy a blocked segment during its blocked window**  

For each blocked segment \(s\in B\) we enforce a **time‑window exclusion** using a classic disjunctive (big‑M) formulation. Introduce binary variable \(z_{t,s}\) = 1 if train \(t\) passes *before* the blockage, 0 otherwise.

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s} &\le t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{start}} + M\,z_{t,s} \\
d_{t,s} &\ge t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{end}} - M\,(1-z_{t,s}) \\
z_{t,s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{B1}
\]

If \(\delta_{t,s}=0\) (train does not use the segment) the constraints are redundant; we can multiply the left‑hand sides by \(\delta_{t,s}\) or simply rely on the fact that \(a_{t,s},d_{t,s}\) are never used elsewhere.

6.2 **Pre‑filter infeasible routes** (optional, but speeds up the model)  

\[
x_{t,r}\le R_{t,r}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t
\tag{B2}
\]

where \(R_{t,r}=0\) if route \(r\) contains a blocked segment during its blocked interval.

### 5.4 Bidirectional conflict (single‑track sections)

If a segment is single‑track, at most one train may occupy it at any time. A classic **pairwise ordering** formulation is used.

Introduce binary variable \(y_{t,t',s}\) = 1 if train \(t\) passes segment \(s\) **before** train \(t'\); otherwise 0. For every unordered pair \(\{t,t'\}\) with \(t<t'\) and for every segment \(s\) that can be traversed by both trains (\(\delta_{t,s}= \delta_{t',s}=1\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\,(1-y_{t,t',s}) \\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} - M\,y_{t,t',s} \\
y_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\}
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall s\in S,\; t<t',\; t,t'\in T
\tag{C1}
\]

If the segment has capacity \(C^{\text{track}} >1\) the pairwise formulation can be replaced by a **cumulative** or **interval‑based** formulation; the above is the simplest linear version.

### 5.5 Delay calculation  

The **total delay** of train \(t\) is the difference between its actual arrival at the last segment of its route and the scheduled arrival:

\[
e_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{last}}_{t}} - T^{\text{sched}}_{t} \qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{D1}
\]

where \(s^{\text{last}}_{t}\) denotes the downstream end of the final segment on the selected route. Because \(a_{t,\cdot}\) is defined for every segment, we can write this with a big‑M linking to the route choice:

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\Bigl( a_{t,s_{t,r,|s_{t,r}|}} - T^{\text{sched}}_{t}\Bigr) x_{t,r}
\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{D2}
\]

and enforce \(e_{t}\ge 0\).

### 5.6 Energy consumption  

Energy on a segment is linear in the chosen speed level:

\[
c_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} \epsilon_{k}\,L_s \, v_{t,s,k}
\qquad \forall t\in T
\tag{E1}
\]

(If a train does not traverse a segment, \(\delta_{t,s}=0\) forces all \(v_{t,s,k}=0\).)

### 5.7 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{t,r} &\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t\\
v_{t,s,k} &\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; k\in K\\
\delta_{t,s} &\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S\\
z_{t,s},\,y_{t,t',s} &\in\{0,1\} &&\text{as defined above}\\
a_{t,s},\,d_{t,s},\,\theta_{t,s},\,e_{t},\,c_{t} &\ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\tag{V}
\]

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T} e_{t} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T} c_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\in T \tag{R1}\\
&\delta_{t,s}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\; s\in \text{seg}(t,r)} x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R2}\\
&\sum_{k\in K} v_{t,s,k}= \delta_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \tag{R3}\\
&\theta_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K} \tau_{k}L_s v_{t,s,k} &&\forall t,s \tag{T1}\\
&d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \theta_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \tag{T2}\\
& a_{t,s_{t,r,\ell+1}} \ge d_{t,s_{t,r,\ell}} - M(1-x_{t,r}) &&\forall t,r,\ell \tag{T3}\\
& p^{\min}_{t,s}\,\delta_{t,s}\le \theta_{t,s}\le p^{\max}_{t,s}\,\delta_{t,s} &&\forall t,s \tag{T4}\\
& a_{t,s} \le t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{start}} + M z_{t,s} &&\forall t, s\in B \tag{B1a}\\
& d_{t,s} \ge t^{\text{block}}_{s,\text{end}} - M (1-z_{t,s}) &&\forall t, s\in B \tag{B1b}\\
& x_{t,r}\le R_{t,r} &&\forall t,r \tag{B2}\\
& a_{t',s} \ge d_{t,s} - M(1-y_{t,t',s}) &&\forall s,\; t<t' \tag{C1a}\\
& a_{t,s}  \ge d_{t',s} - M y_{t,t',s} &&\forall s,\; t<t' \tag{C1b}\\
& e_{t}= \sum_{r\in R_t}\bigl(a_{t,s_{t,r,|s_{t,r}|}}-T^{\text{sched}}_{t}\bigr) x_{t,r} &&\forall t \tag{D2}\\
& c_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} \epsilon_{k}L_s v_{t,s,k} &&\forall t \tag{E1}\\
& \text{Domain constraints } (V). &
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 7. How the Model Works (Explanation)

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **Route‑choice (R1‑R3)** | Guarantees each train selects exactly one feasible path and that the binary variables \(v_{t,s,k}\) are only active on the segments belonging to that path. |
| **Speed‑profile (T1‑T4)** | Links the chosen speed level to a deterministic travel time on each segment, and enforces any minimum/maximum dwell or traversal times. |
| **Temporal continuity (T2‑T3)** | Guarantees that the departure from a segment equals its arrival plus travel time, and that the arrival at the next segment cannot be earlier than the previous departure (no “teleportation”). |
| **Blockage handling (B1‑B2)** | Uses a big‑M disjunction to force a train either to finish the segment before the blockage starts or to start after the blockage ends. Infeasible routes that would have to cross the blocked segment during the blocked window are eliminated by the pre‑computed parameter \(R_{t,r}\). |
| **Bidirectional conflict (C1)** | For single‑track sections, the pairwise ordering variables \(y_{t,t',s}\) ensure that two trains never occupy the same segment at the same time. The formulation can be extended to multi‑track capacity by a cumulative constraint. |
| **Delay calculation (D2)** | Computes the lateness of each train with respect to its original schedule; the model can penalise this lateness in the objective. |
| **Energy calculation (E1)** | Energy is a linear function of the selected speed levels (higher speed → higher \(\epsilon_k\)). This term is also part of the objective. |
| **Objective** | By minimising \(\alpha\sum e_t + \beta\sum c_t\) the planner trades off punctuality against energy consumption. Changing the weights lets you explore different operating policies (e.g., “on‑time” vs “green”). |

---

### 8. Practical Tips for Implementation  

1. **Big‑M sizing** – Choose \(M\) as the planning horizon (e.g., total schedule length) rather than an arbitrarily huge number; this improves numerical stability.  
2. **Pre‑processing** – Remove routes that intersect a blocked segment during its blocked interval (set \(R_{t,r}=0\)). This dramatically reduces the number of binary variables.  
3. **Symmetry breaking** – If many trains are identical, add a small ordering constraint (e.g., \(x_{t,1}\ge x_{t+1,1}\)) to avoid symmetric solutions.  
4. **Strengthening the conflict constraints** – For dense traffic, the pairwise formulation can become large (\(O(|T|^2|S|)\)). In that case, replace it with a **time‑indexed** or **cumulative** formulation (e.g., using a resource‑capacity variable).  
5. **Solver settings** – Because the model is mixed‑integer but linear, modern branch‑and‑bound solvers solve it efficiently for realistic network sizes (tens of trains, a few dozen segments).  

---

**In summary**, the MILP above captures every element you asked for: binary route‑choice, arrival/departure times, speed‑level decisions, a weighted objective of delay + energy, and all the necessary feasibility, blockage, and conflict constraints.  Plug the model into any MILP solver, feed the data (segment lengths, speed‑level parameters, blockage windows, schedules, etc.), and you will obtain an optimal rescheduling and speed‑profile that respects the partial segment blockage while balancing punctuality and energy use.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave:  

*‑ a railway network that may contain a partially blocked segment,  
*‑ each train can choose one of several admissible routes,  
*‑ the schedule (arrival / departure times) and the speed level that is used on every traversed segment are decision variables,  
*‑ the objective is a weighted sum of total passenger‑delay and of the energy that the trains consume,  
*‑ all the usual feasibility, capacity, conflict‑avoidance and speed‑profile linking constraints are included.*

The model is written in a **compact, linear** form (no products of variables).  Wherever a product would appear (e.g. “speed × time”), we introduce auxiliary continuous variables and linear linking constraints so that the whole formulation stays MILP‑compatible.

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(N\) | Set of network nodes (stations, junctions, block‑entry/exit points). |
| \(E\subseteq N\times N\) | Set of directed track segments (arcs).  An arc \((i,j)\) goes from node \(i\) to node \(j\). |
| \(R_t\) | Set of admissible **routes** for train \(t\).  A route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of arcs \((i,j)\). |
| \(S\) | Set of discrete speed levels that can be selected on any arc (e.g. \(S=\{1,2,3,4\}\) corresponding to 30, 60, 90, 120 km/h). |
| \(B\subseteq E\) | Sub‑set of arcs that belong to the **partially blocked segment** (the segment where a blockage may occur). |
| \(C\subseteq E\) | Set of arcs that are **bidirectional** (two trains may travel in opposite directions on the same physical track). |

For each arc \((i,j)\in E\) we denote:

* \(L_{ij}\) – physical length of the arc (km).  
* \(d_{ij}^s\) – travel time (hours) required to traverse arc \((i,j)\) when speed level \(s\in S\) is used (i.e. \(d_{ij}^s = L_{ij}/v_s\) where \(v_s\) is the speed in km/h).  
* \(e_{ij}^s\) – energy consumption (MJ) incurred when traversing \((i,j)\) at speed level \(s\).  These data are assumed known from a pre‑computed lookup table.

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(a_{t,i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \(d_{t,i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \(y_{t,ij}^s\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) **with speed level** \(s\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(z_{t,ij}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) at **any** speed (i.e. the arc is used). |
| \(\Delta_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) with respect to its scheduled (baseline) arrival time at its destination. |
| \(E_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumed by train \(t\). |

Auxiliary variables that keep the model linear:

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(\theta_{t,ij}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from the appropriate \(d_{ij}^s\)). |
| \(\varepsilon_{t,ij}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Energy spent by train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from the appropriate \(e_{ij}^s\)). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \;\; \alpha \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t}_{\text{total passenger delay}} \;+\; \beta \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}E_t}_{\text{total energy consumption}}
\]

* \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\) are user‑defined weights that reflect the relative importance of punctuality versus energy efficiency.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Route‑choice and continuity  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{R1}
   \]

2. **Link route choice to arc‑usage** – an arc is used iff it belongs to the selected route  

   \[
   z_{t,ij}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\;(i,j)\in r} x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{R2}
   \]

3. **Link arc‑usage to speed‑level selection** – exactly one speed level is chosen on a used arc  

   \[
   \sum_{s\in S} y_{t,ij}^s = z_{t,ij} \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{R3}
   \]

### 4.2 Time‑feasibility on each arc  

4. **Travel‑time definition** (linear selection from the discrete set)  

   \[
   \theta_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} d_{ij}^s \, y_{t,ij}^s \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{T1}
   \]

5. **Energy definition**  

   \[
   \varepsilon_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} e_{ij}^s \, y_{t,ij}^s \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{T2}
   \]

6. **Flow of time along a route** – departure from the tail node plus travel time equals arrival at the head node  

   \[
   a_{t,j} \ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-z_{t,ij}) \qquad \forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{T3}
   \]

   \(M\) is a big‑M constant larger than any feasible schedule horizon (e.g. 24 h).  
   The “\(\ge\)” direction allows for optional waiting at intermediate stations.

7. **Minimum dwell time at stations** (if a node is a station)  

   \[
   d_{t,i} \ge a_{t,i} + \tau_i^{\min}\,z_{t,ij} \qquad \forall t\in T,\;i\in N_{\text{st}},\;(i,j)\in E
   \tag{T4}
   \]

   where \(\tau_i^{\min}\) is the required minimum stop time at station \(i\).

### 4.3 Delay calculation  

8. **Delay at the destination node**  

   Let \(dest(t)\) be the destination node of train \(t\) (known from the route data) and let \(\bar a_{t, dest(t)}\) be the scheduled (baseline) arrival time.  

   \[
   \Delta_t \ge a_{t, dest(t)} - \bar a_{t, dest(t)} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{D1}
   \]

   (If early arrival is allowed, the RHS can be truncated at zero.)

### 4.4 Energy aggregation  

9. **Total energy per train**  

   \[
   E_t = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\varepsilon_{t,ij} \qquad \forall t\in T
   \tag{E1}
   \]

### 4.5 Blockage occupancy (partial segment)  

The blocked segment is a set of arcs \(B\).  A **capacity** of 1 train at a time is assumed (the blockage can host at most one train).  

10. **No‑overlap on blocked arcs** – classic disjunctive (big‑M) formulation  

   For every pair of distinct trains \((t,t')\) and for every arc \((i,j)\in B\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   a_{t',i} \;\; &\ge\; d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1 - w_{tt',ij}) \\
   a_{t,i} \;\; &\ge\; d_{t',i} + \theta_{t',ij} - M\,(w_{tt',ij})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad \forall (i,j)\in B,\; t<t'
   \tag{B1}
   \]

   where \(w_{tt',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first.  The constraints are activated only if both trains actually use the arc (\(z_{t,ij}=z_{t',ij}=1\)).  To enforce that, we add:

   \[
   w_{tt',ij} \le z_{t,ij},\qquad w_{tt',ij} \le 1- z_{t',ij} \quad\text{(and symmetric)} 
   \tag{B2}
   \]

   A simpler alternative (if the number of trains is modest) is to use a **time‑window** variable:

   \[
   d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} \le a_{t',i} + M\,(1 - u_{tt',ij}) \\
   d_{t',i} + \theta_{t',ij} \le a_{t,i} + M\,(u_{tt',ij})
   \]

   with binary \(u_{tt',ij}\).  Either formulation guarantees that two trains never occupy the same blocked arc at overlapping times.

### 4.6 Bidirectional conflict on shared tracks  

For arcs that are physically the same track but modelled as two opposite directed arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) (set \(C\)), we must prevent head‑on collisions.

11. **Head‑on avoidance** – for each unordered pair \(\{(i,j),(j,i)\}\in C\) and each pair of trains \(t\neq t'\):

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   a_{t',j} &\ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1 - u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij})\\
   a_{t,i} &\ge d_{t',j} + \theta_{t',ji} - M\,(u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij})
   \end{aligned}
   \qquad \forall (i,j)\in C,\; t<t'
   \tag{H1}
   \]

   where \(u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij}\in\{0,1\}\) decides which train passes first.  The constraints are only relevant when both directed arcs are used, i.e.:

   \[
   u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij} \le z_{t,ij},\qquad u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij} \le 1- z_{t',ij}
   \tag{H2}
   \]

### 4.7 Logical consistency  

12. **Link arrival / departure to arc usage** – a train cannot have a departure time from a node unless it actually leaves the node on some outgoing arc:

   \[
   d_{t,i} \ge a_{t,i} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; i\in N
   \tag{L1}
   \]

   (If a train terminates at node \(i\), the model forces \(z_{t,ij}=0\) for all outgoing arcs, so the inequality is harmless.)

13. **Non‑negativity of travel‑time variables**  

   \[
   \theta_{t,ij} \ge 0,\;\; \varepsilon_{t,ij}\ge 0 \qquad \forall t,i,j
   \tag{L2}
   \]

---

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route choice and speed‑level linking} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T4)} &&\text{time feasibility and dwell constraints} \\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{delay definition} \\
&\text{(E1)} &&\text{energy aggregation} \\
&\text{(B1)–(B2)} &&\text{partial‑segment blockage occupancy} \\
&\text{(H1)–(H2)} &&\text{bidirectional (head‑on) conflict avoidance} \\
&\text{(L1)–(L2)} &&\text{basic logical bounds} \\
& x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,ij}^s\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,ij}\in\{0,1\},\;
w_{tt',ij},u_{tt',ij},u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{t,i}, d_{t,i}, \theta_{t,ij}, \varepsilon_{t,ij},
\Delta_t, E_t \ge 0 \qquad \forall t,i,j.
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries that encode route choice, speed‑level selection, and the ordering decisions required for conflict resolution on the blocked segment and on bidirectional tracks.  Consequently the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** that can be handed to any modern MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – for every arc compute the travel‑time table \(\{d_{ij}^s\}_{s\in S}\) and the corresponding energy table \(\{e_{ij}^s\}_{s\in S}\).  Provide the baseline arrival times \(\bar a_{t, dest(t)}\) and the minimum dwell times \(\tau_i^{\min}\).  

2. **Parameter tuning** – choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to reflect the railway operator’s policy (e.g. \(\alpha=1\) €/min of delay, \(\beta=0.01\) €/MJ).  

3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to a solver.  The optimal solution gives:  

   * the selected route for each train (\(x_{t,r}=1\)),  
   * the exact arrival/departure schedule (\(a_{t,i}, d_{t,i}\)),  
   * the speed level on each traversed segment (\(y_{t,ij}^s=1\)),  
   * the resulting total delay and energy consumption.  

4. **Interpretation** – the binary ordering variables (\(w_{tt',ij}, u^{\text{head}}_{tt',ij}\)) directly tell the planner which train should be given priority on the blocked segment or on a bidirectional track, providing actionable dispatching rules.

---

**That completes the MILP formulation** for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partially blocked segment, together with an explanation of each component.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Segment Blockage)**  

The model below captures every element described in the prompt: binary route‑choice, arrival/departure times, speed‑level decisions on each traversed segment, a weighted objective that balances total delay and energy consumption, and all necessary feasibility, blockage‑avoidance and bidirectional‑conflict constraints.  All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, so the formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** ready for CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Trains (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Discrete speed levels (e.g. low, medium, high). |
| \(E\subseteq N\times N\) | Directed track **segments** (arcs) \((i,j)\) from node \(i\) to node \(j\). |
| \(R_t\) | Feasible **routes** for train \(t\); a route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of arcs. |
| \(B\subseteq E\) | Set of arcs belonging to the **partially blocked segment**. |
| \(C\subseteq E\) | Set of arcs that are **bidirectional** (two opposite arcs share the same physical track). |

For each arc \((i,j)\in E\) we know:

* \(L_{ij}\) – length (km).  
* \(d_{ij}^s\) – travel time (h) when speed level \(s\) is used (pre‑computed from \(L_{ij}\) and speed \(v_s\)).  
* \(e_{ij}^s\) – energy consumption (kWh) for speed level \(s\).  

---

### 2. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\). |
| \(z_{t,ij}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) (any speed). |
| \(y_{t,ij}^s\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) **with speed level** \(s\). |
| \(a_{t,i}\) | \(\ge0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \(d_{t,i}\) | \(\ge0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \(\theta_{t,ij}\) | \(\ge0\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from \(d_{ij}^s\)). |
| \(\varepsilon_{t,ij}\) | \(\ge0\) | Energy spent by train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from \(e_{ij}^s\)). |
| \(\Delta_t\) | \(\ge0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) w.r.t. its scheduled arrival at its destination. |
| \(E_t\) | \(\ge0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\). |
| \(w_{tt',ij}\) | binary | Ordering on a **blocked** arc \((i,j)\in B\): 1 if train \(t\) passes before train \(t'\). |
| \(u_{tt',ij}\) | binary | Ordering on a **bidirectional** arc \((i,j)\in C\): 1 if train \(t\) passes before train \(t'\). |

---

### 3. Parameters  

* \(\alpha>0\) – weight of total delay in the objective.  
* \(\beta>0\) – weight of total energy in the objective.  
* \(\bar a_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) – scheduled (baseline) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination node.  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (e.g. horizon length, 24 h).  

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\min\; \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t }
\]

The planner can tune \(\alpha,\beta\) to emphasise punctuality or energy efficiency.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route choice & speed‑level linking  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc usage from route choice**  
\[
z_{t,ij}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\;(i,j)\in r} x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{R2}
\]

3. **Exactly one speed level on a used arc**  
\[
\sum_{s\in S} y_{t,ij}^s = z_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.2 Travel‑time & energy selection  

4. **Travel‑time definition**  
\[
\theta_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} d_{ij}^s\, y_{t,ij}^s
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j) \tag{T1}
\]

5. **Energy definition**  
\[
\varepsilon_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} e_{ij}^s\, y_{t,ij}^s
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j) \tag{T2}
\]

#### 5.3 Temporal continuity along a route  

6. **Flow of time** (departure from tail + travel = arrival at head)  
\[
a_{t,j} \ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-z_{t,ij})
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{T3}
\]

7. **Minimum dwell at stations** (if node \(i\) is a station, \(\tau_i^{\min}\) is the required stop)  
\[
d_{t,i} \ge a_{t,i} + \tau_i^{\min}\,z_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N_{\text{st}},\;(i,j)\in E \tag{T4}
\]

#### 5.4 Delay and energy aggregation  

8. **Delay at destination**  
\[
\Delta_t \ge a_{t,\text{dest}(t)} - \bar a_{t}^{\text{dest}}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1}
\]

9. **Total energy per train**  
\[
E_t = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\varepsilon_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1}
\]

#### 5.5 Partial‑segment blockage (no overlap)  

For every blocked arc \((i,j)\in B\) and every unordered pair of trains \(t<t'\):

10. **Ordering on blocked arc**  
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',i} &\ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-w_{tt',ij})\\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',i} + \theta_{t',ij} - M\,w_{tt',ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\; t<t' \tag{B1}
\]

The constraints are active only when both trains actually use the arc; this is enforced by  

\[
w_{tt',ij}\le z_{t,ij},\qquad w_{tt',ij}\le 1- z_{t',ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\; t<t' \tag{B2}
\]

(If a train does not traverse the blocked arc, the corresponding \(z\) is 0 and the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.)

#### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance)  

For each pair of opposite arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) belonging to the same physical track (\((i,j)\in C\)) and each unordered pair of trains \(t<t'\):

11. **Ordering on bidirectional track**  
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',j} &\ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-u_{tt',ij})\\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',j} + \theta_{t',ji} - M\,u_{tt',ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in C,\; t<t' \tag{H1}
\]

Again, the ordering variable is only relevant when both directed arcs are used:

\[
u_{tt',ij}\le z_{t,ij},\qquad u_{tt',ij}\le 1- z_{t',ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in C,\; t<t' \tag{H2}
\]

#### 5.7 Logical consistency  

12. **Departure cannot precede arrival**  
\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N \tag{L1}
\]

13. **Variable domains**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r},\,z_{t,ij},\,y_{t,ij}^s,\,w_{tt',ij},\,u_{tt',ij}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,i},\,d_{t,i},\,\theta_{t,ij},\,\varepsilon_{t,ij},\,\Delta_t,\,E_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{V}
\]

---

### 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route choice \& speed‑level linking}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T4)} &&\text{travel‑time, energy, and temporal flow}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{delay definition}\\
&\text{(E1)} &&\text{energy aggregation}\\
&\text{(B1)–(B2)} &&\text{no‑overlap on blocked arcs}\\
&\text{(H1)–(H2)} &&\text{head‑on avoidance on bidirectional tracks}\\
&\text{(L1)} &&\text{basic time ordering}\\
&\text{(V)} &&\text{binary / non‑negative domains.}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries that encode route selection, speed‑level choice, and the ordering decisions required for conflict resolution.  Consequently the formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program**.

---

### 7. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – compute \(d_{ij}^s\) and \(e_{ij}^s\) for every arc and speed level; list all feasible routes \(R_t\) for each train; provide the baseline arrival times \(\bar a_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) and minimum dwell times \(\tau_i^{\min}\).  
2. **Set weights** – choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to reflect the operator’s trade‑off between punctuality and energy consumption.  
3. **Solve** – feed the MILP to any modern MILP solver.  The optimal solution yields:  

   * the selected route for each train (\(x_{t,r}=1\)),  
   * the exact arrival/departure schedule (\(a_{t,i},d_{t,i}\)),  
   * the speed level on each traversed segment (\(y_{t,ij}^s=1\)),  
   * the total delay \(\Delta_t\) and energy \(E_t\).  

4. **Interpret ordering variables** – \(w_{tt',ij}\) tells which train should be given priority on a blocked segment, while \(u_{tt',ij}\) resolves head‑on conflicts on bidirectional tracks, providing concrete dispatching rules for the controller.

---

**The model above is a complete, linear MILP that simultaneously reschedules trains, selects executable speed profiles, respects partial‑segment blockages, resolves bidirectional conflicts, and minimises a weighted sum of delay and energy consumption.**

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (Partial‑Segment Blockage)**  

The model below captures every element described in the prompt: binary route‑choice, arrival/departure times, speed‑level decisions on each traversed segment, a weighted objective that balances total delay and energy consumption, and all necessary feasibility, blockage‑avoidance and bidirectional‑conflict constraints.  All constraints are linear; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, so the formulation is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)** ready for CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …  

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T=\{1,\dots ,|T|\}\) | Trains (indexed by \(t\)). |
| \(S=\{1,\dots ,|S|\}\) | Discrete speed levels (e.g. low, medium, high). |
| \(E\subseteq N\times N\) | Directed track **segments** (arcs) \((i,j)\) from node \(i\) to node \(j\). |
| \(R_t\) | Feasible **routes** for train \(t\); a route \(r\in R_t\) is an ordered list of arcs. |
| \(B\subseteq E\) | Set of arcs belonging to the **partially blocked segment**. |
| \(C\subseteq E\) | Set of arcs that are **bidirectional** (two opposite arcs share the same physical track). |

For each arc \((i,j)\in E\) we know:

* \(L_{ij}\) – length (km).  
* \(d_{ij}^s\) – travel time (h) when speed level \(s\) is used (pre‑computed from \(L_{ij}\) and speed \(v_s\)).  
* \(e_{ij}^s\) – energy consumption (kWh) for speed level \(s\).  

---

### 2. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) follows route \(r\in R_t\). |
| \(z_{t,ij}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) (any speed). |
| \(y_{t,ij}^s\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses arc \((i,j)\) **with speed level** \(s\). |
| \(a_{t,i}\) | \(\ge0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at node \(i\). |
| \(d_{t,i}\) | \(\ge0\) | Departure time of train \(t\) from node \(i\). |
| \(\theta_{t,ij}\) | \(\ge0\) | Travel time of train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from \(d_{ij}^s\)). |
| \(\varepsilon_{t,ij}\) | \(\ge0\) | Energy spent by train \(t\) on arc \((i,j)\) (selected from \(e_{ij}^s\)). |
| \(\Delta_t\) | \(\ge0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) w.r.t. its scheduled arrival at its destination. |
| \(E_t\) | \(\ge0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\). |
| \(w_{tt',ij}\) | binary | Ordering on a **blocked** arc \((i,j)\in B\): 1 if train \(t\) passes before train \(t'\). |
| \(u_{tt',ij}\) | binary | Ordering on a **bidirectional** arc \((i,j)\in C\): 1 if train \(t\) passes before train \(t'\). |

---

### 3. Parameters  

* \(\alpha>0\) – weight of total delay in the objective.  
* \(\beta>0\) – weight of total energy in the objective.  
* \(\bar a_{t}^{\text{dest}}\) – scheduled (baseline) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination node.  
* \(M\) – a sufficiently large constant (e.g. horizon length, 24 h).  

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\min\; \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t }
\]

The planner can tune \(\alpha,\beta\) to emphasise punctuality or energy efficiency.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route choice & speed‑level linking  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  
\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{R1}
\]

2. **Arc usage from route choice**  
\[
z_{t,ij}= \sum_{r\in R_t:\;(i,j)\in r} x_{t,r}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{R2}
\]

3. **Exactly one speed level on a used arc**  
\[
\sum_{s\in S} y_{t,ij}^s = z_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.2 Travel‑time & energy selection  

4. **Travel‑time definition**  
\[
\theta_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} d_{ij}^s\, y_{t,ij}^s
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j) \tag{T1}
\]

5. **Energy definition**  
\[
\varepsilon_{t,ij}= \sum_{s\in S} e_{ij}^s\, y_{t,ij}^s
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j) \tag{T2}
\]

#### 5.3 Temporal continuity along a route  

6. **Flow of time** (departure from tail + travel = arrival at head)  
\[
a_{t,j} \ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-z_{t,ij})
\qquad\forall t,\;(i,j)\in E \tag{T3}
\]

7. **Minimum dwell at stations** (if node \(i\) is a station, \(\tau_i^{\min}\) is the required stop)  
\[
d_{t,i} \ge a_{t,i} + \tau_i^{\min}\,z_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N_{\text{st}},\;(i,j)\in E \tag{T4}
\]

#### 5.4 Delay and energy aggregation  

8. **Delay at destination**  
\[
\Delta_t \ge a_{t,\text{dest}(t)} - \bar a_{t}^{\text{dest}}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{D1}
\]

9. **Total energy per train**  
\[
E_t = \sum_{(i,j)\in E}\varepsilon_{t,ij}
\qquad\forall t\in T \tag{E1}
\]

#### 5.5 Partial‑segment blockage (no overlap)  

For every blocked arc \((i,j)\in B\) and every unordered pair of trains \(t<t'\):

10. **Ordering on blocked arc**  
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',i} &\ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-w_{tt',ij})\\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',i} + \theta_{t',ij} - M\,w_{tt',ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\; t<t' \tag{B1}
\]

The constraints are active only when both trains actually use the arc; this is enforced by  

\[
w_{tt',ij}\le z_{t,ij},\qquad w_{tt',ij}\le 1- z_{t',ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in B,\; t<t' \tag{B2}
\]

(If a train does not traverse the blocked arc, the corresponding \(z\) is 0 and the big‑M term relaxes the constraint.)

#### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (head‑on avoidance)  

For each pair of opposite arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) belonging to the same physical track (\((i,j)\in C\)) and each unordered pair of trains \(t<t'\):

11. **Ordering on bidirectional track**  
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',j} &\ge d_{t,i} + \theta_{t,ij} - M\,(1-u_{tt',ij})\\
a_{t,i}   &\ge d_{t',j} + \theta_{t',ji} - M\,u_{tt',ij}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in C,\; t<t' \tag{H1}
\]

Again, the ordering variable is only relevant when both directed arcs are used:

\[
u_{tt',ij}\le z_{t,ij},\qquad u_{tt',ij}\le 1- z_{t',ij}
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in C,\; t<t' \tag{H2}
\]

#### 5.7 Logical consistency  

12. **Departure cannot precede arrival**  
\[
d_{t,i}\ge a_{t,i}\qquad\forall t,\;i\in N \tag{L1}
\]

13. **Variable domains**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r},\,z_{t,ij},\,y_{t,ij}^s,\,w_{tt',ij},\,u_{tt',ij}\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{t,i},\,d_{t,i},\,\theta_{t,ij},\,\varepsilon_{t,ij},\,\Delta_t,\,E_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{V}
\]

---

### 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T}\Delta_t \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R3)} &&\text{route choice \& speed‑level linking}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T4)} &&\text{travel‑time, energy, and temporal flow}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{delay definition}\\
&\text{(E1)} &&\text{energy aggregation}\\
&\text{(B1)–(B2)} &&\text{no‑overlap on blocked arcs}\\
&\text{(H1)–(H2)} &&\text{head‑on avoidance on bidirectional tracks}\\
&\text{(L1)} &&\text{basic time ordering}\\
&\text{(V)} &&\text{binary / non‑negative domains.}
\end{aligned}

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP) – Full Linear Formulation**  

The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a partial‑segment blockage forces a high‑speed railway operator to (i) **retime** arrivals/departures, (ii) **reorder / reroute** trains that share the blocked track, and (iii) **choose feasible speed profiles** for every train‑run segment.  

All notation, sets, parameters and decision variables are defined first, followed by the objective function and the complete set of linear constraints. Where data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are explicitly stated (marked **Assumption**).

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning (Assumption) |
|--------|----------------------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run during the planning horizon (including those that may be cancelled). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including the origin and terminal of each train). |
| **E** ⊆ S×S | Set of directed track‑segments (edges) connecting two successive stations.  An edge *e = (i,j)* represents the line between station *i* and *j*. |
| **B ⊆ E** | Sub‑set of edges that are **blocked** (partial‑segment blockage). |
| **K** = {1,…,K} | Set of **speed‑profile types** that can be assigned to a train on a given edge (e.g., “fast”, “medium”, “slow”).  Each type k is characterised by a constant average speed *v_k* and a constant energy consumption rate *e_k* (Assumption). |
| **Δ** = {0,1,…,Δ_max} | Discrete time‑grid (in minutes) used to linearise continuous time.  All event times are forced to lie on this grid (Assumption). |
| **P** = {1,…,P} | Set of **pre‑computed feasible plans** for each train (see Section 4.2).  A plan *p* for train *t* specifies a complete sequence of (edge, speed‑type, departure‑time, arrival‑time) tuples that respects physical limits and the blockage window.  Plans are generated offline by a speed‑profile sub‑problem (Assumption). |

### Basic Parameters  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| *a_t* , *b_t* | Original (planned) **departure** and **arrival** times of train *t* at its origin and terminal (minutes from horizon start). |
| *τ_e* | Nominal travel time on edge *e* when travelling at the design speed *v_design* (minutes). |
| *L_e* | Length of edge *e* (km). |
| *v_k* | Average speed associated with speed‑type *k* (km/min). |
| *c_k* | Energy consumption per kilometre for speed‑type *k* (kWh/km). |
| *M* | A large constant (big‑M) used for logical constraints (e.g., 10⁶). |
| *T_start*, *T_end* | Beginning and end of the planning horizon (minutes). |
| *Δ_block_start*, *Δ_block_end* | Start and end of the blockage time window on every blocked edge *e∈B* (minutes). |
| *γ* | Weighting factor for the energy‑minimisation term (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1). |
| *β* | Penalty weight for train cancellation (high value to discourage cancellations). |
| *θ* | Maximum allowed dwell time at any station (minutes). |
| *ρ* | Minimum headway (time separation) required between two trains travelling in the **same direction** on the same edge (minutes). |
| *σ* | Minimum headway required between two trains travelling in **opposite directions** on a shared single‑track edge (minutes). |
| *π_t* | Priority level of train *t* (higher → more important, used in weighted tardiness). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| *x_{t,p}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if **plan p** is selected for train *t*, 0 otherwise. |
| *y_t* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* is **cancelled**, 0 otherwise. |
| *d_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Departure time** of train *t* from station *i* (if *i* is the origin of *t* or a intermediate stop). |
| *a_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Arrival time** of train *t* at station *i*. |
| *z_{t,e,k}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses edge *e* with speed‑type *k* (implied by the selected plan). |
| *c_{t,e}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Entry time** of train *t* onto edge *e* (i.e., departure from upstream station). |
| *h_{t,e}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Exit time** of train *t* from edge *e* (i.e., arrival at downstream station). |
| *w_{t,i}* ∈ Δ | integer | **Dwell time** of train *t* at station *i* (≥ 0). |
| *δ_{t,t',e}^{dir}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on edge *e* in the **same direction** (dir = “same”), 0 otherwise. |
| *δ_{t,t',e}^{opp}* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if trains *t* and *t'* conflict on edge *e* in **opposite directions** (dir = “opp”), 0 otherwise. |

*Auxiliary variables* (used only in linearisation):  

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|--------|
| *Δ_{t,t',e}* = *c_{t',e} – h_{t,e}* | Time gap between the entry of *t'* and exit of *t* on edge *e*. |
| *Δ'_{t,t',e}* = *c_{t,e} – h_{t',e}* | Symmetric gap. |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

The planner seeks a **trade‑off between service quality (tardiness / cancellations) and energy consumption**. A weighted sum formulation is used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \; & \underbrace{\gamma \; \sum_{t\in T}\;\sum_{p\in P_t}\; \Bigl( \sum_{e\in E}\sum_{k\in K} c_k \, L_e \, z_{t,e,k} \Bigr) \; x_{t,p}}_{\text{(1) Energy consumption}} \\
& \;+\; (1-\gamma)\; \Bigl[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( \pi_t \, \max\{0,\, a_{t,\text{dest}}-b_t\}\bigr)}_{\text{(2) Weighted tardiness}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} y_t}_{\text{(3) Cancellation penalty}} \Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

*Explanation*  

* (1) Energy: For each selected plan, the total energy equals the sum over all traversed edges of (energy‑rate × length). Because *z_{t,e,k}* is 1 only for the speed‑type used on edge *e*, the term is linear.  
* (2) Tardiness: Arrival at the destination station *dest(t)* is *a_{t,dest}*. The original scheduled arrival is *b_t*. Positive lateness is penalised proportionally to the train’s priority *π_t*. Early arrivals are not penalised (they can be absorbed by dwell time).  
* (3) Cancellation: A large penalty *β* discourages unnecessary cancellations but allows them when infeasibility would otherwise occur.

The weight *γ* (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1) lets the decision‑maker emphasise energy vs. service quality.

---

## 4. Constraints  

### 4.1 Plan‑selection consistency  

1. **Exactly one plan (or cancellation) per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P_t} x_{t,p} + y_t = 1 \qquad \forall t\in T. \tag{C1}
\]

2. **Link plan variables to edge‑speed variables**  

For each train *t* and each edge *e* that appears in plan *p* with speed‑type *k* (denoted by indicator *α_{t,p,e,k}* = 1 if plan *p* uses (e,k), 0 otherwise):

\[
z_{t,e,k} = \sum_{p\in P_t} \alpha_{t,p,e,k}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; e\in E,\; k\in K. \tag{C2}
\]

3. **Derive entry/exit times from selected plan**  

If plan *p* specifies entry time *c_{t,p,e}* and exit time *h_{t,p,e}* on edge *e* (pre‑computed), then:

\[
c_{t,e} = \sum_{p\in P_t} c_{t,p,e}\; x_{t,p}, \qquad
h_{t,e} = \sum_{p\in P_t} h_{t,p,e}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t, e. \tag{C3}
\]

Similarly for station arrival/departure times:

\[
a_{t,i} = \sum_{p\in P_t} a_{t,p,i}\; x_{t,p}, \qquad
d_{t,i} = \sum_{p\in P_t} d_{t,p,i}\; x_{t,p} \qquad \forall t, i\in S_t. \tag{C4}
\]

*(Here \(S_t\) denotes the ordered set of stations visited by train *t* in any feasible plan.)*  

If a train is cancelled (*y_t = 1*), all its timing variables are forced to a dummy value (e.g., 0) using big‑M constraints, which are omitted for brevity.

### 4.2 Physical feasibility of speed profiles  

4. **Travel‑time consistency on each edge**  

\[
h_{t,e} - c_{t,e} = \frac{L_e}{v_k} \; z_{t,e,k} \qquad \forall t, e, k\in K. \tag{C5}
\]

Because each edge is traversed with exactly one speed‑type (by (C2)), the RHS reduces to the appropriate travel time.

5. **Dwell‑time definition**  

For each intermediate station *i* (i.e., not origin or terminal of *t*):

\[
w_{t,i} = d_{t,i} - a_{t,i} \qquad \forall t, i\in S_t\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{dest}\}. \tag{C6}
\]

6. **Maximum dwell‑time bound**  

\[
0 \le w_{t,i} \le \theta \qquad \forall t,i\in S_t\setminus\{\text{origin},\text{dest}\}. \tag{C7}
\]

### 4.3 Blockage‑window feasibility  

For every blocked edge *e∈B* and every train that traverses it (i.e., *z_{t,e,k}=1*) the entry must lie **outside** the blockage interval:

\[
c_{t,e} \le \Delta_{\text{block\_start}} \;+\; M\,(1 - z_{t,e,k}) \quad \text{or} \quad
c_{t,e} \ge \Delta_{\text{block\_end}} \;-\; M\,(1 - z_{t,e,k}) \qquad \forall t, e\in B, k. \tag{C8}
\]

The logical “or” is linearised by introducing a binary *b_{t,e}* that selects which side of the window is used:

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{t,e} &\le \Delta_{\text{block\_start}} + M\,b_{t,e} ,\\
c_{t,e} &\ge \Delta_{\text{block\_end}} - M\,(1-b_{t,e}),\\
b_{t,e} &\in\{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

### 4.4 Conflict‑avoidance on shared tracks  

The network contains **bidirectional single‑track sections** (edges where trains travelling in opposite directions must not occupy the track simultaneously). Two families of headway constraints are required.

#### 4.4.1 Same‑direction headway  

For any pair of distinct trains *t ≠ t'* that use the same edge *e* in the **same direction** (i.e., both travel from *i*→*j*), we enforce a minimum separation *ρ*:

\[
c_{t',e} \ge h_{t,e} + \rho \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}}\bigr) \qquad \forall t<t', e\in E. \tag{C9}
\]

The binary *δ_{t,t',e}^{same}* is forced to 1 when both trains actually occupy the edge:

\[
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \le \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k}, \qquad
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \le \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k}, \qquad
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{same}} \ge \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k} + \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k} -1. \tag{C10}
\]

If either train does not use the edge, *δ* becomes 0 and the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

#### 4.4.2 Opposite‑direction headway (single‑track)  

For edges that are **single‑track** (set *U ⊆ E*), we must guarantee that trains travelling in opposite directions do not overlap. Let *dir(t,e)* denote the direction of train *t* on edge *e* (0 = forward, 1 = reverse). For any pair *(t,t')* with opposite directions on *e∈U*:

\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{t',e} &\ge h_{t,e} + \sigma \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}}\bigr),\\
c_{t,e} &\ge h_{t',e} + \sigma \;-\; M\bigl(1-\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}}\bigr),\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\le \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k},\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\le \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k},\\
\delta_{t,t',e}^{\text{opp}} &\ge \sum_{k} z_{t,e,k} + \sum_{k} z_{t',e,k} -1.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall t<t', e\in U. \tag{C11}
\]

The binary *δ^{opp}* becomes 1 only when both trains occupy the same single‑track edge, activating the mutual‑exclusion constraints.

### 4.5 Temporal bounds  

All event times must lie inside the planning horizon:

\[
T_{\text{start}} \le a_{t,i}, d_{t,i}, c_{t,e}, h_{t,e} \le T_{\text{end}} \qquad \forall t,i,e. \tag{C12}
\]

### 4.6 Logical linking of arrival / departure  

For each train *t* and each consecutive pair of stations *(i,j)* on its route:

\[
c_{t,(i,j)} = d_{t,i}, \qquad
a_{t,j} = h_{t,(i,j)}. \tag{C13}
\]

Thus the departure from the upstream station equals the entry onto the connecting edge, and the arrival at the downstream station equals the exit from that edge.

### 4.7 Cancellation handling (optional but useful)  

If a train is cancelled, all its timing variables are forced to a dummy value (e.g., *T_end+1*) and no conflicts are generated:

\[
c_{t,e} \ge T_{\text{end}}+1 - M y_t,\qquad
h_{t,e} \le T_{\text{end}} + M y_t,\qquad
\forall t,e. \tag{C14}
\]

Similarly for station times. This ensures that cancelled trains do not interfere with any headway constraints (the big‑M term deactivates them).

## 5. Summary of the MILP  

Putting everything together, the **TRSMP MILP** is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \text{(objective (1)–(3))} \\
\text{s.t. } & \text{Plan selection (C1)–(C4)}\\
& \text{Physical feasibility (C5)–(C7)}\\
& \text{Blockage avoidance (C8)}\\
& \text{Conflict‑avoidance (C9)–(C11)}\\
& \text{Temporal bounds (C12)–(C13)}\\
& \text{Cancellation logic (C14)}\\
& x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_t\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,e,k}\in\{0,1\},\; \delta^{\cdot}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{t,i},d_{t,i},c_{t,e},h_{t,e},w_{t,i}\in\Delta .
\end{aligned}
\]

The model is **purely linear**: all products involve a binary variable and a continuous (or integer) variable, which can be linearised with standard big‑M techniques.  

---

## 6. Remarks & Modeling Assumptions  

| # | Assumption | Rationale |
|---|------------|-----------|
| A1 | Time is discretised on a uniform minute grid Δ (Δ = {0,…,Δ_max}). | Guarantees integrality of all timing variables and enables linearisation of “max” tardiness. |
| A2 | A small finite set *K* of speed‑profile types (fast/medium/slow) is pre‑computed. | Real high‑speed trains can follow a limited number of admissible acceleration/deceleration patterns; each type is represented by a constant average speed *v_k* and energy rate *c_k*. |
| A3 | Feasible **train‑plans** *p∈P_t* are generated offline by solving a deterministic speed‑profile sub‑problem for each train under the blockage window. | This reduces the coupling between speed‑profile selection and timetable decisions to a binary plan‑selection problem, preserving linearity. |
| A4 | Energy consumption on an edge is approximated by *c_k·L_e* (average power × travel distance). | Detailed traction‑regeneration curves are non‑linear; the linear approximation is standard in high‑level railway optimisation. |
| A5 | Headway values ρ (same direction) and σ (opposite direction) are constant for all edges of the same type. | In practice, headways are dictated by signalling and safety standards and can be treated as uniform within a corridor. |
| A6 | Blockage affects the whole edge for the whole interval [Δ_block_start, Δ_block_end]; trains may either pass before the start or after the end (no partial occupancy). | Simplifies the logical “outside‑window” constraint while still representing the essential operational restriction. |
| A7 | Cancellation is allowed but heavily penalised (β large). | Provides a feasibility fallback when the disruption is too severe; the penalty ensures cancellations only occur when unavoidable. |
| A8 | All trains travel at a constant average speed on a chosen edge (no intra‑edge speed changes). | Guarantees linear travel‑time relation (C5). More detailed intra‑edge acceleration can be embedded by refining the set *K* or by splitting edges. |

---

## 7. Potential Extensions (outside the core MILP)  

* **Energy‑recovery**: introduce a negative coefficient for braking phases on descending gradients.  
* **Passenger‑level objective**: add a weighted sum of passenger‑minutes lost, using load factors per train.  
* **Robustness**: replace deterministic blockage times by intervals and enforce feasibility for all realizations (robust MILP).  
* **Dynamic re‑routing**: allow a train to switch from its nominal route to an alternative parallel line; this is modelled by adding extra edges and corresponding plan variables.  

---

**The formulation above constitutes a complete, linear, mixed‑integer model for the *Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)* under partial‑segment blockages, integrating timetable adjustments, bidirectional conflict resolution, and energy‑aware speed‑profile selection.**

A plan *p* for train *t* specifies a complete sequence of (edge, speed‑type, departure‑time, arrival‑time) tuples that respects physical limits and the blockage window. \[

& \;+\; (1-\gamma)\; \Bigl[ \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} \bigl( \pi_t \, \max\{0,\, a_{t,\text{dest}}-b_t\}\bigr)}_{\text{(2) Weighted tardiness}} \;+\; \underbrace{\beta \sum_{t\in T} y_t}_{\text{(3) Cancellation penalty}} \Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

* (1) Energy: For each selected plan, the total energy equals the sum over all traversed edges of (energy‑rate × length). Because *z_{t,e,k}* is 1 only for the speed‑type used on edge *e*, the term is linear.

| A1 | Time is discretised on a uniform minute grid Δ (Δ = {0,…,Δ_max}). | Guarantees integrality of all timing variables and enables linearisation of “max” tardiness. |
| A2 | A small finite set *K* of speed‑profile types (fast/medium/slow) is pre‑computed. | Real high‑speed trains can follow a limited number of admissible acceleration/deceleration patterns; each type is represented by a constant average speed *v_k* and energy rate *c_k*. |
| A3 | Feasible **train‑plans** *p∈P_t* are generated offline by solving a deterministic speed‑profile sub‑problem for each train under the blockage window. | This reduces the coupling between speed‑profile selection and timetable decisions to a binary plan‑selection problem, preserving linearity. |
| A4 | Energy consumption on an edge is approximated by *c_k·L_e* (average power × travel distance). | Detailed traction‑regeneration curves are non‑linear; the linear approximation is standard in high‑level railway optimisation. |
| A5 | Headway values ρ (same direction) and σ (opposite direction) are constant for all edges of the same type. | In practice, headways are dictated by signalling and safety standards and can be treated as uniform within a corridor. |
| A6 | Blockage affects the whole edge for the whole interval [Δ_block_start, Δ_block_end]; trains may either pass before the start or after the end (no partial occupancy). | Simplifies the logical “outside‑window” constraint while still representing the essential operational restriction. |
| A7 | Cancellation is allowed but heavily penalised (β large). | Provides a feasibility fallback when the disruption is too severe; the penalty ensures cancellations only occur when unavoidable. |
| A8 | All trains travel at a constant average speed on a chosen edge (no intra‑edge speed changes). | Guarantees linear travel‑time relation (C5). More detailed intra‑edge acceleration can be embedded by refining the set *K* or by splitting edges. |

---

## 7. Potential Extensions (outside the core MILP)  

* **Energy‑recovery**: introduce a negative coefficient for braking phases on descending gradients.  
* **Passenger‑level objective**: add a weighted sum of passenger‑minutes lost, using load factors per train.  
* **Robustness**: replace deterministic blockage times by intervals and enforce feasibility for all realizations (robust MILP).  
* **Dynamic re‑routing**: allow a train to switch from its nominal route to an alternative parallel line; this is modelled by adding extra edges and corresponding plan variables.  

---

**The formulation above constitutes a complete, linear, mixed‑integer model for the *Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)* under partial‑segment blockages, integrating timetable adjustments, bidirectional conflict resolution, and energy‑aware speed‑profile selection.**

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
