Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main decisions mentioned in the description  

* **route choice** (binary variables – which line/track a train will use),  
* **departure / arrival times** (continuous variables – when a train enters and leaves each track segment), and  
* **speed level** on each segment (continuous variables – average speed chosen from a small discrete set, linearised with binary “speed‑level” variables).

The model is written in a **compact, linear** form that can be fed directly to a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  After the formulation you will find a short **explanation of each set, parameter, variable and constraint**.

---

## 1. Index sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments (or “blocks”), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(R\) | Set of admissible routes for a train. A route is an ordered list of segments; we denote by \(R_{t}\subseteq R\) the routes that train \(t\) may use. |
| \(V\) | Set of admissible speed levels (e.g., \(V=\{v^{1},v^{2},v^{3}\}\) = low, medium, high). |
| \(D\) | Set of directions on a segment, \(D=\{+,-\}\) (forward / backward). |

For a given route \(r\in R_{t}\) we write \(\text{seg}(r)=\{s_{1}^{r},s_{2}^{r},\dots ,s_{|r|}^{r}\}\) – the ordered list of segments traversed by that route.

---

## 2. Parameters (data)

| Symbol | Description | Typical units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| \(L_{s}\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). | km |
| \(B_{s}\subseteq T\) | Set of trains that **must** pass through segment \(s\) (i.e., the segment belongs to at least one feasible route of the train). | – |
| \(P_{s}\in\{0,1\}\) | Blockage indicator: 1 if segment \(s\) is partially blocked during the planning horizon, 0 otherwise. | – |
| \(\underline{v}_{s},\overline{v}_{s}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(s\) (km/h). | km/h |
| \(\tau^{\text{min}}_{t},\tau^{\text{max}}_{t}\) | Earliest possible departure time and latest allowed arrival time for train \(t\) (minutes from a reference). | min |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g., 1 € per minute). | – |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total energy consumption (e.g., 0.01 € per kWh). | – |
| \(c^{v}\) | Energy coefficient for speed level \(v\) (kWh per km). Usually \(c^{v}=a\,v^{2}+b\) linearised; we treat it as a constant for each discrete level. | kWh/km |
| \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\) | Maximum extra travel time that can be incurred on a blocked segment \(s\) (minutes). | min |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g., \(M=10^{5}\)). | – |
| \(g_{s}^{d}\) | Direction of traffic allowed on segment \(s\) for direction \(d\) (1 if allowed, 0 otherwise). | – |

---

## 3. Decision variables

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in R_{t}\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(v\in V\). |
| \(\delta_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Delay** of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) relative to the nominal (free‑flow) travel time. |
| \(E_{t}\ge 0\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |
| \(z_{t,s}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) in direction \(d\) (used for bidirectional conflict). |

*Note*: Because speed levels are discrete, the actual speed on a segment is a linear combination  
\(\displaystyle v_{t,s}= \sum_{v\in V} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\) (used only for reporting; the model never needs the product).

---

## 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t}\bigr)^{+}}_{\text{total delay (minutes)}}
\;+\;
\beta\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{total energy (kWh)}}
}
\]

*Explanation*  

* The term \((a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t})^{+}\) is the **positive part** of the difference between the actual arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (the arrival time at the last segment of the chosen route) and the latest allowed arrival time. In a linear MILP we linearise the positive part with an auxiliary variable \(D_{t}\ge0\) and constraints  

  \[
  D_{t}\ge a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t},\qquad D_{t}\ge 0 .
  \]

  Then the delay contribution becomes \(\alpha\sum_{t} D_{t}\).

* The energy term is simply the sum of the per‑train energy variables \(E_{t}\) multiplied by the weight \(\beta\).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_{t}} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T .
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑level variables** – a segment (or speed‑level) can be active only if the route that contains it is selected. For every train \(t\) and segment \(s\):

   \[
   a_{t,s}\le M\;\sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r},
   \qquad
   d_{t,s}\le M\;\sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}.
   \]

   The same idea is used for the speed‑level binaries:

   \[
   y_{t,s}^{v}\le \sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall v\in V .
   \]

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility along a chosen route  

For a train that uses route \(r\) the departure time from a segment must be the arrival time at the next segment plus the travel time on the current segment.

Let  

\[
\theta_{s}^{v}= \frac{L_{s}}{v}\times 60 \quad\text{(travel time in minutes if speed level }v\text{ is used).}
\]

Then for every train \(t\), every segment \(s\) that belongs to a route \(r\) of that train, and every speed level \(v\):

\[
d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \theta_{s}^{v}\; y_{t,s}^{v} - M\bigl(1-\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\bigr) .
\]

The **arrival time at the next segment** equals the departure time of the current segment:

\[
a_{t,s'}\ge d_{t,s}\quad\text{for every consecutive pair }(s,s')\text{ in the chosen route}.
\]

### 5.3 Blockage (partial segment) constraints  

If a segment \(s\) is blocked (\(P_{s}=1\)), the travel time may increase but not beyond a prescribed extra time \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\).

\[
d_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \theta_{s}^{v} y_{t,s}^{v}+ \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\;P_{s}\qquad\forall t,s,v .
\]

Equivalently, we can bound the **delay variable** \(\delta_{t,s}\):

\[
\delta_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}-\sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v},
\qquad
0\le \delta_{t,s}\le \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s} P_{s}.
\]

### 5.4 Speed‑level feasibility  

Only one speed level can be chosen on a segment that the train actually traverses:

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s}^{v}= \sum_{r\ni s} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s .
\]

The chosen speed must respect the segment’s admissible interval:

\[
\underline{v}_{s}\;\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\le \sum_{v\in V} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\le \overline{v}_{s}\;\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}.
\]

Because the set \(V\) is small, the above two linear constraints are sufficient (they are automatically satisfied when a single \(y_{t,s}^{v}=1\) is selected).

### 5.5 Energy‑calculation constraints  

Energy on a segment is the product of length and the energy coefficient of the selected speed level:

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} c^{v}\,L_{s}\; y_{t,s}^{v}\qquad\forall t .
\]

(If a train does not use a segment, all \(y_{t,s}^{v}=0\) and the term contributes nothing.)

### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (single‑track) constraints  

Two trains cannot occupy the same segment **in opposite directions** at overlapping times. We use the binary occupancy variables \(z_{t,s}^{d}\) (1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) in direction \(d\)).  

First, link occupancy to route choice and direction:

\[
z_{t,s}^{d}\le \sum_{r\ni s,\; \text{dir}(r,s)=d} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s,d .
\]

Second, enforce a **time‑ordering** for any pair of trains that would conflict:

For every unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t\neq t'\), for every segment \(s\) and direction pair \((d,-d)\):

\[
a_{t',s}\ge d_{t,s} - M\bigl(1- z_{t,s}^{d} - z_{t',s}^{-d}\bigr) \quad\text{or}\quad
a_{t,s}\ge d_{t',s} - M\bigl(1- z_{t,s}^{d} - z_{t',s}^{-d}\bigr).
\]

In practice we linearise the “either‑or’’ by introducing an auxiliary binary \(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\) :

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\bigl(1-\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} - M\bigl(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\in\{0,1\},\\
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\le z_{t,s}^{d},\qquad
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} \le z_{t',s}^{-d}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If both trains try to use the segment in opposite directions, \(\omega\) forces one of the two ordering constraints to be active, guaranteeing non‑overlap.

### 5.7 Departure‑/arrival‑time windows  

Each train must start no earlier than its earliest release time and must finish no later than its latest allowed arrival (the latter is already captured by the delay variable, but we also keep a hard upper bound if desired):

\[
a_{t,s_{0}}\ge \tau^{\text{min}}_{t}\qquad\forall t,
\]
\[
a_{t,\text{last}(t)}\le \tau^{\text{max}}_{t}+D_{t}\qquad\forall t,
\]
where \(s_{0}\) is the first segment of the selected route.

### 5.8 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}^{d}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t,s},E_{t},D_{t}\ge 0 .
\]

---

## 6. Full linear MILP (compact form)

Putting everything together, the model can be written as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_{t} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_{t}} x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\in T \tag{R1}\\
& a_{t,s}\le M\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R2}\\
& d_{t,s}\le M\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R3}\\
& y_{t,s}^{v}\le \sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s,v \tag{R4}\\
& \sum_{v} y_{t,s}^{v}= \sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R5}\\
& d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t,s \tag{T1}\\
& a_{t,s'}\ge d_{t,s} &&\forall t,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive in chosen route} \tag{T2}\\
& \delta_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}-\sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t,s \tag{B1}\\
& 0\le \delta_{t,s}\le \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}P_{s} &&\forall t,s \tag{B2}\\
& \underline{v}_{s}\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\le \sum_{v} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\le \overline{v}_{s}\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{V1}\\
& E_{t}= \sum_{s}\sum_{v} c^{v}L_{s} y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t \tag{E1}\\
& D_{t}\ge a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t},\; D_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t \tag{D1}\\
& a_{t,s_{0}}\ge \tau^{\text{min}}_{t} &&\forall t \tag{W1}\\
& z_{t,s}^{d}\le \sum_{r\ni s,\; \text{dir}(r,s)=d}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s,d \tag{C1}\\
& a_{t',s}\ge d_{t,s} - M(1-\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}) &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C2}\\
& a_{t,s}\ge d_{t',s} - M\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C3}\\
& \omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\le z_{t,s}^{d},\; \omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\le z_{t',s}^{-d} &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C4}\\
& x_{t,r},y_{t,s}^{v},z_{t,s}^{d},\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\in\{0,1\} &&\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t,s},E_{t},D_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (product of binary and continuous) have been eliminated by the standard “big‑M’’ technique or by using auxiliary binary variables.

---

## 7. How each part of the description is reflected  

| Description element | Model component |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Binary route‑choice** | \(x_{t,r}\) with (R1) – exactly one route per train. |
| **Departure / arrival times** | \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) with (T1)–(T2) linking them along the chosen route and respecting earliest‑release windows (W1). |
| **Speed levels per segment** | \(y_{t,s}^{v}\) with (R4)–(R5) and (V1) – one speed level per traversed segment, speed bounds, and travel‑time contribution \(\theta_{s}^{v}\). |
| **Objective: weighted sum of total delay and energy** | Objective \(\alpha\sum D_{t} + \beta\sum E_{t}\). Delay \(D_{t}\) is the positive part of final‑arrival lateness; energy \(E_{t}\) is computed in (E1). |
| **Time feasibility** | (T1)–(T2) guarantee that a train cannot leave a segment before it has arrived and that travel times follow the selected speed. |
| **Block occupancy** | (B1)–(B2) limit the extra travel time on blocked segments (\(P_{s}=1\)). |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | Occupancy binaries \(z_{t,s}^{d}\) and ordering constraints (C1)–(C4) ensure that two trains travelling opposite directions on the same single‑track segment never overlap in time. |
| **Speed‑profile feasibility** | (V1) forces the chosen speed to lie inside the admissible interval; (R5) forces exactly one speed level per used segment. |
| **Energy calculation** | (E1) sums the per‑segment energy contributions (length × coefficient of the selected speed level). |

---

### Ready‑to‑use  

*Copy‑paste* the compact formulation (section 6) into any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …).  
Replace the generic sets \(R_{t}\) and the “big‑M’’ value with problem‑specific numbers (e.g., \(M = 10^{4}\) minutes is usually safe).  
All data (segment lengths, blockage flags, speed‑level coefficients, etc.) are supplied through the parameter tables.

The resulting MILP will give you:

* the **optimal route** for each train,  
* the **exact departure/arrival schedule** on every segment,  
* the **speed level** to be used on each segment,  

while **minimising a weighted combination of total delay and total energy consumption** and respecting all operational constraints imposed by partial blockages and bidirectional single‑track sections.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives)  
* **Speed‑management** (which discrete speed level is used on each track segment)  
* **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window)

The model is written in a **canonical linear‑programming style** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints).  After the formulation each component is explained in plain English so that the reader can see how the mathematics implements the operational logic.

---

## 1.  Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of *track segments* (ordered from origin to destination), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(R_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\) (each route is a sequence of segments).  A route \(r\in R_t\) is represented by the ordered list \(\{s_{r,1},\dots ,s_{r,|r|}\}\). |
| \(V\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (discrete), indexed by \(v\).  Speed level \(v\) corresponds to a constant speed \(v\) (km/h) and a known energy‑consumption rate \(e_v\) (kWh per km). |
| \(B\) | Set of **blocked sub‑segments** (partial blockages).  Each element \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b_s^{\text{start}},b_s^{\text{end}},\tau_b^{\text{start}},\tau_b^{\text{end}})\) meaning that on segment \(s\) the sub‑interval \([b_s^{\text{start}},b_s^{\text{end}}]\) (in metres from the segment start) is unavailable during the time window \([\tau_b^{\text{start}},\tau_b^{\text{end}}]\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters (data)

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (metres). |
| \(d_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (scheduled) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). |
| \(a_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (scheduled) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (minutes). |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}\) | Weight (cost) per minute of train delay (e.g. € / min). |
| \(w^{\text{energy}}\) | Weight (cost) per kWh of energy consumption (e.g. € / kWh). |
| \(e_v\) | Energy consumption rate for speed level \(v\) (kWh per kilometre). |
| \(v\) | Physical speed value for level \(v\) (metres per minute). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{headway}}\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment (minutes). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\) | Minimum separation time for opposite‑direction trains on a single‑track segment (minutes). |
| \(\beta_{t,s}\) | Binary indicator =1 if segment \(s\) belongs to at least one feasible route for train \(t\) (used to prune infeasible arcs). |

---

## 3.  Decision variables

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) is assigned to route \(r\in R_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(d_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\) (if \(s\) is on the chosen route). |
| \(c_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure (exit) time of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s,v}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(v\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(\delta_{t,b}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **passes through** blocked sub‑segment \(b\); 0 otherwise (used to forbid the conflict). |
| \(z_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \(s\) (same direction); 0 otherwise. |
| \(w_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) and train \(t'\) travel **opposite** directions on segment \(s\) and \(t\) passes first; 0 otherwise. |
| \(D_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(E_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |

---

## 4.  Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \; 
\underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T} D_t}_{\text{Delay cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T} E_t}_{\text{Energy cost}}
}
\]

The model therefore seeks a schedule that **balances punctuality (delay) against energy usage**.

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link segment‑level variables to the chosen route**  

For every train‑segment pair we force the binary speed‑level variables to be zero unless the segment belongs to the selected route:

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v} \le \sum_{r\in R_t} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

where \(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\) is 1 if segment \(s\) appears in route \(r\), 0 otherwise.

### 5.2 Timing feasibility on a chosen route  

3. **Departure from origin**  

\[
d_t = d_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

4. **Arrival at first segment** (if the route starts with segment \(s_1\))  

\[
a_{t,s_1} = d_t \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s_1 = \text{first segment of the selected route}
\]

5. **Travel time on a segment** – linearised using the big‑M and the binary speed‑level variable  

\[
c_{t,s} \; \ge \; a_{t,s} \; + \; \frac{L_s}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; v\in V
\]

Because exactly one \(y_{t,s,v}\) can be 1 (see later), the RHS reduces to the travel time at the chosen speed.

6. **Continuity between consecutive segments**  

If segment \(s'\) follows \(s\) on the selected route, the arrival at \(s'\) equals the departure from \(s\):

\[
a_{t,s'} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route}
\]

(If the route skips a segment, the corresponding \(y\) variables are forced to 0, making the constraint redundant.)

7. **Arrival at final destination**  

\[
a_{t,\text{dest}} \; \le \; a_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(Alternative: enforce \(c_{t,\text{last}} \le a_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t\).)

### 5.3 Speed‑level selection  

8. **Exactly one speed level per traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}= \sum_{r\in R_t} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If the segment is not on the chosen route the RHS is 0, forcing all \(y\)’s to 0; otherwise exactly one speed level is chosen.

### 5.4 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy per segment**  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_v \, \frac{L_s}{1000}\; y_{t,s,v} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(The factor \(L_s/1000\) converts metres to kilometres.)

### 5.5 Head‑way and conflict avoidance (same direction)  

10. **Ordering binary \(z\)** – for any two trains that share a segment in the same direction  

\[
a_{t',s} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{headway}} - M\,(1-z_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \; \ge \; c_{t',s} + \Delta^{\text{headway}} - M\,z_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

The two constraints together force **one** of the two possible orderings and guarantee the required head‑way.

### 5.6 Opposite‑direction conflict (single‑track)  

11. **Ordering binary \(w\)** – for trains travelling opposite directions on the same segment  

\[
a_{t',s} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,(1-w_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \; \ge \; c_{t',s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,w_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

Only one of the two orderings can be active; the other is forced by the big‑M.

### 5.7 Partial‑segment blockage  

12. **Blockage feasibility** – a train may not occupy a blocked sub‑segment during its forbidden time window.  
For each blocked sub‑segment \(b=(s,b^{\text{start}},b^{\text{end}},\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}})\) we introduce a binary \(\delta_{t,b}\) that is 1 if train \(t\) *passes through* the blocked part. The following linear constraints forbid that situation:

\[
a_{t,s} + \frac{b^{\text{start}}}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \; \ge \; \tau^{\text{end}} \; - \; M\,(1-\delta_{t,b}) \qquad \forall t,s,v,b\text{ with }s=b_s
\]

\[
c_{t,s} - \frac{L_s-b^{\text{end}}}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \; \le \; \tau^{\text{start}} \; + \; M\,(1-\delta_{t,b}) \qquad \forall t,s,v,b\text{ with }s=b_s
\]

If \(\delta_{t,b}=1\) the two inequalities force the train’s entry‑time at the start of the blocked sub‑segment to be **after** the blockage ends and its exit‑time to be **before** the blockage starts – an impossibility, thus \(\delta_{t,b}\) must be forced to 0.  
To keep the model linear we simply set:

\[
\delta_{t,b}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; b\in B
\]

and the above two constraints become **hard exclusion** constraints (the big‑M term disappears). In practice one can keep \(\delta_{t,b}\) as a modelling aid for “if‑then’’ logic, but the final MILP can drop it and keep the two big‑M constraints directly.

### 5.8 Delay definition  

13. **Delay as difference between actual and scheduled arrival at destination**  

\[
D_t = a_{t,\text{dest}} - a_t^{\text{orig}} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(If the model also allows early arrival, one may replace by \(D_t \ge a_{t,\text{dest}}-a_t^{\text{orig}}\) and keep \(D_t\ge 0\).)

### 5.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t\\
&y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; v\in V\\
&z_{t,t',s},w_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\neq t',\; s\in S\\
&d_t, a_{t,s}, c_{t,s}, D_t, E_t \ge 0, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  How the model works – plain‑language explanation  

| Component | What it does | How the math implements it |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------------|
| **Route choice** | Each train may be rerouted (e.g., to avoid a blocked segment). | Binary variable \(x_{t,r}\) picks exactly one route per train (constraint 1). All downstream variables (arrival times, speed choices) are only allowed on the selected route (constraints 2 & 8). |
| **Departure/arrival timing** | Trains may be delayed at the origin; subsequent times follow from travel times on each segment. | \(d_t\) is the actual departure (origin delay = \(D_t\)). Arrival at a segment equals the departure from the previous one (constraint 6). Travel time on a segment is length divided by the chosen speed (constraint 5). |
| **Speed‑level selection** | For each traversed segment a discrete speed (e.g., 30, 50, 80 km/h) is chosen, influencing travel time and energy use. | Binary \(y_{t,s,v}\) selects exactly one speed per segment (constraint 8). The travel‑time equation (5) uses the selected speed, and the energy equation (9) multiplies the speed‑specific energy rate by the distance. |
| **Delay objective** | Minimise the sum of weighted minutes that trains are late. | Delay variable \(D_t\) is defined as the difference between actual and scheduled arrival (13) and appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{delay}}\). |
| **Energy objective** | Minimise the sum of weighted energy consumption (or trade‑off with delay). | Energy per train \(E_t\) is computed from the chosen speeds (9) and appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{energy}}\). |
| **Head‑way / conflict avoidance** | Trains travelling in the same direction must keep a safe time gap; opposite‑direction trains on a single‑track must not meet. | Ordering binaries \(z_{t,t',s}\) and \(w_{t,t',s}\) enforce that on any shared segment one train finishes before the other starts, plus the required safety gap (constraints 10‑11). |
| **Partial segment blockage** | A portion of a segment is unavailable for a known time window (e.g., due to maintenance). | For each blocked sub‑segment we force the train’s entry‑time to be after the blockage ends and its exit‑time to be before the blockage starts (constraints 12). The big‑M formulation makes the constraint active only when the train actually uses that segment. |
| **Feasibility** | All times must be non‑negative and respect physical limits. | Variable domains (5.9) and the big‑M constant \(M\) guarantee a bounded feasible region. |

---

## 7.  Remarks for implementation  

1. **Big‑M size** – Choose \(M\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 min). A tighter \(M\) improves solver performance.  
2. **Linearisation of product \(y_{t,s,v}\cdot \frac{L_s}{v}\)** – Because exactly one \(y\) is 1, the term can be written as a sum of separate linear constraints (as done in (5)).  
3. **Symmetry reduction** – If many trains share identical data, one can aggregate identical routes or pre‑compute feasible speed‑segment pairs to keep the model size manageable.  
4. **Scalability** – The number of binary ordering variables \(z_{t,t',s}\) and \(w_{t,t',s}\) grows quadratically with the number of trains. In practice one adds them only for pairs that can physically conflict (e.g., same line, overlapping time windows).  
5. **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with platform‑capacity constraints, crew‑working‑time limits, or stochastic blockage durations by adding additional binary variables and scenario‑based constraints.

---

### Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t} D_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t}E_t \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{v} y_{t,s,v}\le\sum_{r}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&d_t = d_t^{\text{orig}}+D_t &&\forall t\\
& a_{t,s'}\ge c_{t,s} &&\forall t,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive on chosen route}\\
&c_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\sum_{v} y_{t,s,v}= \sum_{r}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&E_t = \sum_{s}\sum_{v} e_v\frac{L_s}{1000}y_{t,s,v} &&\forall t\\
&a_{t',s}\ge c_{t,s}+ \Delta^{\text{headway}}-M(1-z_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,s}\ge c_{t',s}+ \Delta^{\text{headway}}-M z_{t,t',s} &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t',s}\ge c_{t,s}+ \Delta^{\text{conflict}}-M(1-w_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,s}\ge c_{t',s}+ \Delta^{\text{conflict}}-M w_{t,t',s} &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,\text{dest}}-a_t^{\text{orig}} = D_t &&\forall t\\
&\text{(blockage constraints 12)}\\
&x_{t,r},y_{t,s,v},z_{t,t',s},w_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\\
&d_t,a_{t,s},c_{t,s},D_t,E_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable and a constant) and therefore can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  By adjusting the weights \(w^{\text{delay}}\) and \(w^{\text{energy}}\) the railway operator can explore the trade‑off between punctuality and energy efficiency while respecting the physical constraints imposed by partial blockages, safety head‑ways, and speed‑profile feasibility.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-profile feasibility, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main decisions mentioned in the description  

* **route choice** (binary variables – which line/track a train will use),  
* **departure / arrival times** (continuous variables – when a train enters and leaves each track segment), and  
* **speed level** on each segment (continuous variables – average speed chosen from a small discrete set, linearised with binary “speed‑level” variables).

The model is written in a **compact, linear** form that can be fed directly to a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  After the formulation you will find a short **explanation of each set, parameter, variable and constraint**.

---

## 1. Index sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of track segments (or “blocks”), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(R\) | Set of admissible routes for a train. A route is an ordered list of segments; we denote by \(R_{t}\subseteq R\) the routes that train \(t\) may use. |
| \(V\) | Set of admissible speed levels (e.g., \(V=\{v^{1},v^{2},v^{3}\}\) = low, medium, high). |
| \(D\) | Set of directions on a segment, \(D=\{+,-\}\) (forward / backward). |

For a given route \(r\in R_{t}\) we write \(\text{seg}(r)=\{s_{1}^{r},s_{2}^{r},\dots ,s_{|r|}^{r}\}\) – the ordered list of segments traversed by that route.

---

## 2. Parameters (data)

| Symbol | Description | Typical units |
|--------|-------------|---------------|
| \(L_{s}\) | Length of segment \(s\) (km). | km |
| \(B_{s}\subseteq T\) | Set of trains that **must** pass through segment \(s\) (i.e., the segment belongs to at least one feasible route of the train). | – |
| \(P_{s}\in\{0,1\}\) | Blockage indicator: 1 if segment \(s\) is partially blocked during the planning horizon, 0 otherwise. | – |
| \(\underline{v}_{s},\overline{v}_{s}\) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on segment \(s\) (km/h). | km/h |
| \(\tau^{\text{min}}_{t},\tau^{\text{max}}_{t}\) | Earliest possible departure time and latest allowed arrival time for train \(t\) (minutes from a reference). | min |
| \(\alpha\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g., 1 € per minute). | – |
| \(\beta\) | Weight for total energy consumption (e.g., 0.01 € per kWh). | – |
| \(c^{v}\) | Energy coefficient for speed level \(v\) (kWh per km). Usually \(c^{v}=a\,v^{2}+b\) linearised; we treat it as a constant for each discrete level. | kWh/km |
| \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\) | Maximum extra travel time that can be incurred on a blocked segment \(s\) (minutes). | min |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary variable is 0 (e.g., \(M=10^{5}\)). | – |
| \(g_{s}^{d}\) | Direction of traffic allowed on segment \(s\) for direction \(d\) (1 if allowed, 0 otherwise). | – |

---

## 3. Decision variables

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) uses route \(r\in R_{t}\). |
| \(a_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\). |
| \(d_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(v\in V\). |
| \(\delta_{t,s}\ge 0\) | continuous | **Delay** of train \(t\) on segment \(s\) relative to the nominal (free‑flow) travel time. |
| \(E_{t}\ge 0\) | continuous | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |
| \(z_{t,s}^{d}\in\{0,1\}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) in direction \(d\) (used for bidirectional conflict). |

*Note*: Because speed levels are discrete, the actual speed on a segment is a linear combination  
\(\displaystyle v_{t,s}= \sum_{v\in V} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\) (used only for reporting; the model never needs the product).

---

## 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\; \alpha\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t}\bigr)^{+}}_{\text{total delay (minutes)}}
\;+\;
\beta\;\underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}E_{t}}_{\text{total energy (kWh)}}
}
\]

*Explanation*  

* The term \((a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t})^{+}\) is the **positive part** of the difference between the actual arrival time of train \(t\) at its final destination (the arrival time at the last segment of the chosen route) and the latest allowed arrival time. In a linear MILP we linearise the positive part with an auxiliary variable \(D_{t}\ge0\) and constraints  

  \[
  D_{t}\ge a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t},\qquad D_{t}\ge 0 .
  \]

  Then the delay contribution becomes \(\alpha\sum_{t} D_{t}\).

* The energy term is simply the sum of the per‑train energy variables \(E_{t}\) multiplied by the weight \(\beta\).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

   \[
   \sum_{r\in R_{t}} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T .
   \]

2. **Link route choice to segment‑level variables** – a segment (or speed‑level) can be active only if the route that contains it is selected. For every train \(t\) and segment \(s\):

   \[
   a_{t,s}\le M\;\sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r},
   \qquad
   d_{t,s}\le M\;\sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}.
   \]

   The same idea is used for the speed‑level binaries:

   \[
   y_{t,s}^{v}\le \sum_{r\in R_{t}: s\in \text{seg}(r)} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall v\in V .
   \]

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility along a chosen route  

For a train that uses route \(r\) the departure time from a segment must be the arrival time at the next segment plus the travel time on the current segment.

Let  

\[
\theta_{s}^{v}= \frac{L_{s}}{v}\times 60 \quad\text{(travel time in minutes if speed level }v\text{ is used).}
\]

Then for every train \(t\), every segment \(s\) that belongs to a route \(r\) of that train, and every speed level \(v\):

\[
d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \theta_{s}^{v}\; y_{t,s}^{v} - M\bigl(1-\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\bigr) .
\]

The **arrival time at the next segment** equals the departure time of the current segment:

\[
a_{t,s'}\ge d_{t,s}\quad\text{for every consecutive pair }(s,s')\text{ in the chosen route}.
\]

### 5.3 Blockage (partial segment) constraints  

If a segment \(s\) is blocked (\(P_{s}=1\)), the travel time may increase but not beyond a prescribed extra time \(\Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\).

\[
d_{t,s}\le a_{t,s}+ \theta_{s}^{v} y_{t,s}^{v}+ \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}\;P_{s}\qquad\forall t,s,v .
\]

Equivalently, we can bound the **delay variable** \(\delta_{t,s}\):

\[
\delta_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}-\sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v},
\qquad
0\le \delta_{t,s}\le \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s} P_{s}.
\]

### 5.4 Speed‑level feasibility  

Only one speed level can be chosen on a segment that the train actually traverses:

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s}^{v}= \sum_{r\ni s} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s .
\]

The chosen speed must respect the segment’s admissible interval:

\[
\underline{v}_{s}\;\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\le \sum_{v\in V} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\le \overline{v}_{s}\;\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}.
\]

Because the set \(V\) is small, the above two linear constraints are sufficient (they are automatically satisfied when a single \(y_{t,s}^{v}=1\) is selected).

### 5.5 Energy‑calculation constraints  

Energy on a segment is the product of length and the energy coefficient of the selected speed level:

\[
E_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} c^{v}\,L_{s}\; y_{t,s}^{v}\qquad\forall t .
\]

(If a train does not use a segment, all \(y_{t,s}^{v}=0\) and the term contributes nothing.)

### 5.6 Bidirectional conflict (single‑track) constraints  

Two trains cannot occupy the same segment **in opposite directions** at overlapping times. We use the binary occupancy variables \(z_{t,s}^{d}\) (1 if train \(t\) occupies segment \(s\) in direction \(d\)).  

First, link occupancy to route choice and direction:

\[
z_{t,s}^{d}\le \sum_{r\ni s,\; \text{dir}(r,s)=d} x_{t,r}\qquad\forall t,s,d .
\]

Second, enforce a **time‑ordering** for any pair of trains that would conflict:

For every unordered pair \((t,t')\) with \(t\neq t'\), for every segment \(s\) and direction pair \((d,-d)\):

\[
a_{t',s}\ge d_{t,s} - M\bigl(1- z_{t,s}^{d} - z_{t',s}^{-d}\bigr) \quad\text{or}\quad
a_{t,s}\ge d_{t',s} - M\bigl(1- z_{t,s}^{d} - z_{t',s}^{-d}\bigr).
\]

In practice we linearise the “either‑or’’ by introducing an auxiliary binary \(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\) :

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t',s} &\ge d_{t,s} - M\bigl(1-\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
a_{t,s}  &\ge d_{t',s} - M\bigl(\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\bigr),\\
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\in\{0,1\},\\
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &\le z_{t,s}^{d},\qquad
\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} \le z_{t',s}^{-d}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If both trains try to use the segment in opposite directions, \(\omega\) forces one of the two ordering constraints to be active, guaranteeing non‑overlap.

### 5.7 Departure‑/arrival‑time windows  

Each train must start no earlier than its earliest release time and must finish no later than its latest allowed arrival (the latter is already captured by the delay variable, but we also keep a hard upper bound if desired):

\[
a_{t,s_{0}}\ge \tau^{\text{min}}_{t}\qquad\forall t,
\]
\[
a_{t,\text{last}(t)}\le \tau^{\text{max}}_{t}+D_{t}\qquad\forall t,
\]
where \(s_{0}\) is the first segment of the selected route.

### 5.8 Non‑negativity / binary domains  

\[
x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}^{v}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{t,s}^{d}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t,s},E_{t},D_{t}\ge 0 .
\]

---

## 6. Full linear MILP (compact form)

Putting everything together, the model can be written as:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \alpha\sum_{t\in T} D_{t} \;+\; \beta\sum_{t\in T}E_{t} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_{t}} x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\in T \tag{R1}\\
& a_{t,s}\le M\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R2}\\
& d_{t,s}\le M\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R3}\\
& y_{t,s}^{v}\le \sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s,v \tag{R4}\\
& \sum_{v} y_{t,s}^{v}= \sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{R5}\\
& d_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t,s \tag{T1}\\
& a_{t,s'}\ge d_{t,s} &&\forall t,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive in chosen route} \tag{T2}\\
& \delta_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}-\sum_{v}\theta_{s}^{v}y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t,s \tag{B1}\\
& 0\le \delta_{t,s}\le \Delta^{\text{blk}}_{s}P_{s} &&\forall t,s \tag{B2}\\
& \underline{v}_{s}\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r}\le \sum_{v} v\,y_{t,s}^{v}\le \overline{v}_{s}\sum_{r\ni s}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s \tag{V1}\\
& E_{t}= \sum_{s}\sum_{v} c^{v}L_{s} y_{t,s}^{v} &&\forall t \tag{E1}\\
& D_{t}\ge a_{t,\text{last}(t)}-\tau^{\text{max}}_{t},\; D_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t \tag{D1}\\
& a_{t,s_{0}}\ge \tau^{\text{min}}_{t} &&\forall t \tag{W1}\\
& z_{t,s}^{d}\le \sum_{r\ni s,\; \text{dir}(r,s)=d}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s,d \tag{C1}\\
& a_{t',s}\ge d_{t,s} - M(1-\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}) &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C2}\\
& a_{t,s}\ge d_{t',s} - M\omega_{t,t',s}^{d} &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C3}\\
& \omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\le z_{t,s}^{d},\; \omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\le z_{t',s}^{-d} &&\forall t<t',s,d \tag{C4}\\
& x_{t,r},y_{t,s}^{v},z_{t,s}^{d},\omega_{t,t',s}^{d}\in\{0,1\} &&\\
& a_{t,s},d_{t,s},\delta_{t,s},E_{t},D_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities that could appear (product of binary and continuous) have been eliminated by the standard “big‑M’’ technique or by using auxiliary binary variables.

---

## 7. How each part of the description is reflected  

| Description element | Model component |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Binary route‑choice** | \(x_{t,r}\) with (R1) – exactly one route per train. |
| **Departure / arrival times** | \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) with (T1)–(T2) linking them along the chosen route and respecting earliest‑release windows (W1). |
| **Speed levels per segment** | \(y_{t,s}^{v}\) with (R4)–(R5) and (V1) – one speed level per traversed segment, speed bounds, and travel‑time contribution \(\theta_{s}^{v}\). |
| **Objective: weighted sum of total delay and energy** | Objective \(\alpha\sum D_{t} + \beta\sum E_{t}\). Delay \(D_{t}\) is the positive part of final‑arrival lateness; energy \(E_{t}\) is computed in (E1). |
| **Time feasibility** | (T1)–(T2) guarantee that a train cannot leave a segment before it has arrived and that travel times follow the selected speed. |
| **Block occupancy** | (B1)–(B2) limit the extra travel time on blocked segments (\(P_{s}=1\)). |
| **Bidirectional conflict** | Occupancy binaries \(z_{t,s}^{d}\) and ordering constraints (C1)–(C4) ensure that two trains travelling opposite directions on the same single‑track segment never overlap in time. |
| **Speed‑profile feasibility** | (V1) forces the chosen speed to lie inside the admissible interval; (R5) forces exactly one speed level per used segment. |
| **Energy calculation** | (E1) sums the per‑segment energy contributions (length × coefficient of the selected speed level). |

---

### Ready‑to‑use  

*Copy‑paste* the compact formulation (section 6) into any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, …).  
Replace the generic sets \(R_{t}\) and the “big‑M’’ value with problem‑specific numbers (e.g., \(M = 10^{4}\) minutes is usually safe).  
All data (segment lengths, blockage flags, speed‑level coefficients, etc.) are supplied through the parameter tables.

The resulting MILP will give you:

* the **optimal route** for each train,  
* the **exact departure/arrival schedule** on every segment,  
* the **speed level** to be used on each segment,  

while **minimising a weighted combination of total delay and total energy consumption** and respecting all operational constraints imposed by partial blockages and bidirectional single‑track sections.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice, departure/arrival times, speed levels per segment. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: time feasibility, block occupancy, bidirectional conflict, speed-profile feasibility, energy calculation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the prompt:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which train runs on which route, when it departs/arrives)  
* **Speed‑management** (which discrete speed level is used on each track segment)  
* **Partial segment blockage** (a portion of a track segment is unavailable for a given time window)

The model is written in a **canonical linear‑programming style** (sets, parameters, decision variables, objective, constraints).  After the formulation each component is explained in plain English so that the reader can see how the mathematics implements the operational logic.

---

## 1.  Sets

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \(T\) | Set of trains, indexed by \(t\). |
| \(S\) | Set of *track segments* (ordered from origin to destination), indexed by \(s\). |
| \(R_t\) | Set of feasible **routes** for train \(t\) (each route is a sequence of segments).  A route \(r\in R_t\) is represented by the ordered list \(\{s_{r,1},\dots ,s_{r,|r|}\}\). |
| \(V\) | Set of admissible **speed levels** (discrete), indexed by \(v\).  Speed level \(v\) corresponds to a constant speed \(v\) (km/h) and a known energy‑consumption rate \(e_v\) (kWh per km). |
| \(B\) | Set of **blocked sub‑segments** (partial blockages).  Each element \(b\in B\) is a tuple \((s,b_s^{\text{start}},b_s^{\text{end}},\tau_b^{\text{start}},\tau_b^{\text{end}})\) meaning that on segment \(s\) the sub‑interval \([b_s^{\text{start}},b_s^{\text{end}}]\) (in metres from the segment start) is unavailable during the time window \([\tau_b^{\text{start}},\tau_b^{\text{end}}]\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters (data)

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| \(L_s\) | Length of segment \(s\) (metres). |
| \(d_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (scheduled) departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). |
| \(a_t^{\text{orig}}\) | Planned (scheduled) arrival time of train \(t\) at its destination (minutes). |
| \(w^{\text{delay}}\) | Weight (cost) per minute of train delay (e.g. € / min). |
| \(w^{\text{energy}}\) | Weight (cost) per kWh of energy consumption (e.g. € / kWh). |
| \(e_v\) | Energy consumption rate for speed level \(v\) (kWh per kilometre). |
| \(v\) | Physical speed value for level \(v\) (metres per minute). |
| \(M\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{headway}}\) | Minimum head‑way time required between two trains travelling in the same direction on the same segment (minutes). |
| \(\Delta^{\text{conflict}}\) | Minimum separation time for opposite‑direction trains on a single‑track segment (minutes). |
| \(\beta_{t,s}\) | Binary indicator =1 if segment \(s\) belongs to at least one feasible route for train \(t\) (used to prune infeasible arcs). |

---

## 3.  Decision variables

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,r}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) is assigned to route \(r\in R_t\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(d_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Actual departure time of train \(t\) from its origin (minutes). |
| \(a_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(t\) at the **beginning** of segment \(s\) (if \(s\) is on the chosen route). |
| \(c_{t,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Departure (exit) time of train \(t\) from the **end** of segment \(s\). |
| \(y_{t,s,v}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) traverses segment \(s\) with speed level \(v\); 0 otherwise. |
| \(\delta_{t,b}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) **passes through** blocked sub‑segment \(b\); 0 otherwise (used to forbid the conflict). |
| \(z_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) precedes train \(t'\) on segment \(s\) (same direction); 0 otherwise. |
| \(w_{t,t',s}\) | binary | 1 if train \(t\) and train \(t'\) travel **opposite** directions on segment \(s\) and \(t\) passes first; 0 otherwise. |
| \(D_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total delay of train \(t\) (minutes). |
| \(E_t\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(t\) (kWh). |

---

## 4.  Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \; 
\underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T} D_t}_{\text{Delay cost}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T} E_t}_{\text{Energy cost}}
}
\]

The model therefore seeks a schedule that **balances punctuality (delay) against energy usage**.

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{r\in R_t} x_{t,r}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Link segment‑level variables to the chosen route**  

For every train‑segment pair we force the binary speed‑level variables to be zero unless the segment belongs to the selected route:

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v} \le \sum_{r\in R_t} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

where \(\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\) is 1 if segment \(s\) appears in route \(r\), 0 otherwise.

### 5.2 Timing feasibility on a chosen route  

3. **Departure from origin**  

\[
d_t = d_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

4. **Arrival at first segment** (if the route starts with segment \(s_1\))  

\[
a_{t,s_1} = d_t \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s_1 = \text{first segment of the selected route}
\]

5. **Travel time on a segment** – linearised using the big‑M and the binary speed‑level variable  

\[
c_{t,s} \; \ge \; a_{t,s} \; + \; \frac{L_s}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; v\in V
\]

Because exactly one \(y_{t,s,v}\) can be 1 (see later), the RHS reduces to the travel time at the chosen speed.

6. **Continuity between consecutive segments**  

If segment \(s'\) follows \(s\) on the selected route, the arrival at \(s'\) equals the departure from \(s\):

\[
a_{t,s'} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive on the chosen route}
\]

(If the route skips a segment, the corresponding \(y\) variables are forced to 0, making the constraint redundant.)

7. **Arrival at final destination**  

\[
a_{t,\text{dest}} \; \le \; a_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(Alternative: enforce \(c_{t,\text{last}} \le a_t^{\text{orig}} + D_t\).)

### 5.3 Speed‑level selection  

8. **Exactly one speed level per traversed segment**  

\[
\sum_{v\in V} y_{t,s,v}= \sum_{r\in R_t} \mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}\,x_{t,r} \qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If the segment is not on the chosen route the RHS is 0, forcing all \(y\)’s to 0; otherwise exactly one speed level is chosen.

### 5.4 Energy calculation  

9. **Energy per segment**  

\[
E_t = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{v\in V} e_v \, \frac{L_s}{1000}\; y_{t,s,v} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(The factor \(L_s/1000\) converts metres to kilometres.)

### 5.5 Head‑way and conflict avoidance (same direction)  

10. **Ordering binary \(z\)** – for any two trains that share a segment in the same direction  

\[
a_{t',s} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{headway}} - M\,(1-z_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \; \ge \; c_{t',s} + \Delta^{\text{headway}} - M\,z_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

The two constraints together force **one** of the two possible orderings and guarantee the required head‑way.

### 5.6 Opposite‑direction conflict (single‑track)  

11. **Ordering binary \(w\)** – for trains travelling opposite directions on the same segment  

\[
a_{t',s} \; \ge \; c_{t,s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,(1-w_{t,t',s}) \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \; \ge \; c_{t',s} + \Delta^{\text{conflict}} - M\,w_{t,t',s} \qquad \forall t\neq t',\; s\in S
\]

Only one of the two orderings can be active; the other is forced by the big‑M.

### 5.7 Partial‑segment blockage  

12. **Blockage feasibility** – a train may not occupy a blocked sub‑segment during its forbidden time window.  
For each blocked sub‑segment \(b=(s,b^{\text{start}},b^{\text{end}},\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}})\) we introduce a binary \(\delta_{t,b}\) that is 1 if train \(t\) *passes through* the blocked part. The following linear constraints forbid that situation:

\[
a_{t,s} + \frac{b^{\text{start}}}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \; \ge \; \tau^{\text{end}} \; - \; M\,(1-\delta_{t,b}) \qquad \forall t,s,v,b\text{ with }s=b_s
\]

\[
c_{t,s} - \frac{L_s-b^{\text{end}}}{v}\; y_{t,s,v} \; \le \; \tau^{\text{start}} \; + \; M\,(1-\delta_{t,b}) \qquad \forall t,s,v,b\text{ with }s=b_s
\]

If \(\delta_{t,b}=1\) the two inequalities force the train’s entry‑time at the start of the blocked sub‑segment to be **after** the blockage ends and its exit‑time to be **before** the blockage starts – an impossibility, thus \(\delta_{t,b}\) must be forced to 0.  
To keep the model linear we simply set:

\[
\delta_{t,b}=0 \qquad \forall t\in T,\; b\in B
\]

and the above two constraints become **hard exclusion** constraints (the big‑M term disappears). In practice one can keep \(\delta_{t,b}\) as a modelling aid for “if‑then’’ logic, but the final MILP can drop it and keep the two big‑M constraints directly.

### 5.8 Delay definition  

13. **Delay as difference between actual and scheduled arrival at destination**  

\[
D_t = a_{t,\text{dest}} - a_t^{\text{orig}} \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

(If the model also allows early arrival, one may replace by \(D_t \ge a_{t,\text{dest}}-a_t^{\text{orig}}\) and keep \(D_t\ge 0\).)

### 5.9 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t,r}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; r\in R_t\\
&y_{t,s,v}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S,\; v\in V\\
&z_{t,t',s},w_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\neq t',\; s\in S\\
&d_t, a_{t,s}, c_{t,s}, D_t, E_t \ge 0, &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  How the model works – plain‑language explanation  

| Component | What it does | How the math implements it |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------------|
| **Route choice** | Each train may be rerouted (e.g., to avoid a blocked segment). | Binary variable \(x_{t,r}\) picks exactly one route per train (constraint 1). All downstream variables (arrival times, speed choices) are only allowed on the selected route (constraints 2 & 8). |
| **Departure/arrival timing** | Trains may be delayed at the origin; subsequent times follow from travel times on each segment. | \(d_t\) is the actual departure (origin delay = \(D_t\)). Arrival at a segment equals the departure from the previous one (constraint 6). Travel time on a segment is length divided by the chosen speed (constraint 5). |
| **Speed‑level selection** | For each traversed segment a discrete speed (e.g., 30, 50, 80 km/h) is chosen, influencing travel time and energy use. | Binary \(y_{t,s,v}\) selects exactly one speed per segment (constraint 8). The travel‑time equation (5) uses the selected speed, and the energy equation (9) multiplies the speed‑specific energy rate by the distance. |
| **Delay objective** | Minimise the sum of weighted minutes that trains are late. | Delay variable \(D_t\) is defined as the difference between actual and scheduled arrival (13) and appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{delay}}\). |
| **Energy objective** | Minimise the sum of weighted energy consumption (or trade‑off with delay). | Energy per train \(E_t\) is computed from the chosen speeds (9) and appears in the objective with weight \(w^{\text{energy}}\). |
| **Head‑way / conflict avoidance** | Trains travelling in the same direction must keep a safe time gap; opposite‑direction trains on a single‑track must not meet. | Ordering binaries \(z_{t,t',s}\) and \(w_{t,t',s}\) enforce that on any shared segment one train finishes before the other starts, plus the required safety gap (constraints 10‑11). |
| **Partial segment blockage** | A portion of a segment is unavailable for a known time window (e.g., due to maintenance). | For each blocked sub‑segment we force the train’s entry‑time to be after the blockage ends and its exit‑time to be before the blockage starts (constraints 12). The big‑M formulation makes the constraint active only when the train actually uses that segment. |
| **Feasibility** | All times must be non‑negative and respect physical limits. | Variable domains (5.9) and the big‑M constant \(M\) guarantee a bounded feasible region. |

---

## 7.  Remarks for implementation  

1. **Big‑M size** – Choose \(M\) larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 10 000 min). A tighter \(M\) improves solver performance.  
2. **Linearisation of product \(y_{t,s,v}\cdot \frac{L_s}{v}\)** – Because exactly one \(y\) is 1, the term can be written as a sum of separate linear constraints (as done in (5)).  
3. **Symmetry reduction** – If many trains share identical data, one can aggregate identical routes or pre‑compute feasible speed‑segment pairs to keep the model size manageable.  
4. **Scalability** – The number of binary ordering variables \(z_{t,t',s}\) and \(w_{t,t',s}\) grows quadratically with the number of trains. In practice one adds them only for pairs that can physically conflict (e.g., same line, overlapping time windows).  
5. **Extensions** – The model can be enriched with platform‑capacity constraints, crew‑working‑time limits, or stochastic blockage durations by adding additional binary variables and scenario‑based constraints.

---

### Full MILP statement (compact)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t} D_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t}E_t \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{r\in R_t}x_{t,r}=1 &&\forall t\\
&\sum_{v} y_{t,s,v}\le\sum_{r}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&d_t = d_t^{\text{orig}}+D_t &&\forall t\\
& a_{t,s'}\ge c_{t,s} &&\forall t,\;(s,s')\text{ consecutive on chosen route}\\
&c_{t,s}\ge a_{t,s}+ \frac{L_s}{v}\,y_{t,s,v} &&\forall t,s,v\\
&\sum_{v} y_{t,s,v}= \sum_{r}\mathbf{1}_{\{s\in r\}}x_{t,r} &&\forall t,s\\
&E_t = \sum_{s}\sum_{v} e_v\frac{L_s}{1000}y_{t,s,v} &&\forall t\\
&a_{t',s}\ge c_{t,s}+ \Delta^{\text{headway}}-M(1-z_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,s}\ge c_{t',s}+ \Delta^{\text{headway}}-M z_{t,t',s} &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t',s}\ge c_{t,s}+ \Delta^{\text{conflict}}-M(1-w_{t,t',s}) &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,s}\ge c_{t',s}+ \Delta^{\text{conflict}}-M w_{t,t',s} &&\forall t\neq t',s\\
&a_{t,\text{dest}}-a_t^{\text{orig}} = D_t &&\forall t\\
&\text{(blockage constraints 12)}\\
&x_{t,r},y_{t,s,v},z_{t,t',s},w_{t,t',s}\in\{0,1\}\\
&d_t,a_{t,s},c_{t,s},D_t,E_t\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

This formulation is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable and a constant) and therefore can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …).  By adjusting the weights \(w^{\text{delay}}\) and \(w^{\text{energy}}\) the railway operator can explore the trade‑off between punctuality and energy efficiency while respecting the physical constraints imposed by partial blockages, safety head‑ways, and speed‑profile feasibility.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
