Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

| Symbol | Meaning |

| **B ⊂ S** | Side that is *blocked* on the critical segment (e.g. **B = {L}**). |

| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **Δ<sub>safe</sub>** | Minimum safety headway between two consecutive trains on the same side of a segment (minutes). |
| **γ<sub>i</sub>** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (allows priority). |
| **w<sub>delay</sub>, w<sub>energy</sub>** | Global weights that balance the two parts of the objective. |
| **π<sub>seg</sub>** | Set of linearisation break‑points for speed (see § 4). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r<sub>i,s</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* on the *blocked* segment; exactly one side must be chosen. |
| **o<sub>i,j,seg</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on side *s* of *seg* (only defined when both trains use the same side). |
| **a<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k*. |
| **d<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **t<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **v<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **c<sub>i</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is **canceled** (optional). When *c<sub>i</sub>=1* all its times are forced to zero (big‑M). |
| **e<sub>i,seg,p</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Portion of speed *v<sub>i,seg</sub>* allocated to linearisation piece *p* (see § 4). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\Bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}- \text{sched}_i\Bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\Bigl(\alpha\,v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta\,v_{i,seg}\Bigr)}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
\]

*The first term penalises the deviation of the actual arrival at the final station from the scheduled arrival.  
The second term is a convex quadratic energy model; it will be linearised in § 4 so that the whole formulation stays MILP.*

---

## 4. Linearisation of the Quadratic Energy Term  

Because a pure quadratic term is not allowed in a MILP, we replace  

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}
\]

by a **piece‑wise linear** approximation over a set of break‑points \(\pi_{seg}=\{p_1,p_2,\dots,p_P\}\) (e.g. 0, v<sub>min</sub>, v<sub>max</sub>).  

Introduce auxiliary variables \(e_{i,seg,p}\) that represent the *fraction* of speed contributed by each segment of the piecewise function.

1. **Reconstruction of speed**

\[
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p}\qquad\forall i,seg
\]

2. **Convex combination constraints**

\[
\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \lambda_{p}=1,\qquad 
\lambda_{p}\ge 0\quad\text{(these are implicit in the definition of }e_{i,seg,p}\text{).}
\]

3. **Linear energy expression**

Let \(\phi_{p}\) be the value of the quadratic function at break‑point \(p\) (i.e. \(\phi_{p}= \alpha p^{2}+ \beta p\)). Then

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}\;\; \approx\;\; \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \phi_{p}\; e_{i,seg,p}
\]

Because each \(e_{i,seg,p}\) is bounded by the length of the interval between two consecutive break‑points, the approximation is exact if the break‑points are dense enough.  

All constraints that involve the energy term in the objective are now linear.

---

## 5. Model Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑choice on the blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

If side *s* is blocked, we force all trains to avoid it:

\[
r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in B \tag{R2}
\]

(If the blockage is temporary, the time‑window constraints below will be used instead; R2 is a “hard” blockage.)

### 5.2 Flow conservation at stations  

For every train *i* and every interior station *k* (i.e. not the first one):

\[
d_{i,k}= a_{i,k}+ \text{dwell}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{first}\} \tag{F1}
\]

Travel from station *k* to the next station *k+1* passes through a segment *seg(i,k)* (the segment that connects the two stations).  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,\,\text{seg}(i,k)} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{last}\} \tag{F2}
\]

### 5.3 Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship  

\[
t_{i,seg}= \frac{\text{len}_{seg}}{v_{i,seg}} \qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T1}
\]

Because the division is non‑linear, we linearise it with a **big‑M / reciprocal** technique (or use a set of linear constraints derived from a piecewise linear approximation of \(1/v\)).  
A common linearisation uses the following for each segment *seg*:

Introduce auxiliary variable \(u_{i,seg}=1/v_{i,seg}\). Then

\[
t_{i,seg}= \text{len}_{seg}\; u_{i,seg} \tag{T2}
\]

and enforce the reciprocal relationship by the McCormick envelopes (valid because \(v_{i,seg}\) is bounded):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} - \frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}(v_{i,seg}-v_{\min}) &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} - \frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}(v_{i,seg}-v_{\max}) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\]

(If a tighter linearisation is required, a piecewise linear approximation of \(1/v\) can be used analogously to § 4.)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\; \le\; v_{i,seg}\; \le\; v_{\max}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{S1}
\]

### 5.5 Capacity / ordering on a shared side  

Consider any **pair of distinct trains** \((i,j)\) that use the **same side** *s* of the **same segment** *seg*.  
Define a binary ordering variable \(o_{i,j,seg}\) (only needed when the side is the same).  

The “enter” time of a train on a segment is the departure time from the upstream station:

\[
\text{enter}_{i,seg}= d_{i,\,\text{up}(seg)} \qquad\forall i,seg
\]

The “exit” time is the arrival at the downstream station:

\[
\text{exit}_{i,seg}= a_{i,\,\text{down}(seg)} \qquad\forall i,seg
\]

Capacity (no overlap) is enforced by the classic big‑M formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{exit}_{i,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{j,seg}+ M\;(1-o_{i,j,seg}) \\
\text{exit}_{j,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{i,seg}+ M\;o_{i,j,seg}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; \forall s\in S \text{ with } r_{i,s}=r_{j,s}=1 \tag{C1}
\]

The “big‑M” term de‑activates the inequality when the corresponding ordering variable is 0.

### 5.6 Ordering‑consistency (mutual exclusivity)  

\[
o_{i,j,seg}+o_{j,i,seg}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg \text{ where both trains share a side} \tag{C2}
\]

If one of the trains does **not** use the side (i.e. \(r_{i,s}=0\) or \(r_{j,s}=0\)), the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0 by the following linking constraints:

\[
o_{i,j,seg} \le r_{i,s},\qquad 
o_{i,j,seg} \le r_{j,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C3}
\]

### 5.7 Disruption‑window (no‑occupancy of blocked side)  

If the blockage is **temporary**, a train may still be assigned to the blocked side *provided* it does not occupy the segment during the window \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\).

Let \(\text{enter}_{i,blk}\) and \(\text{exit}_{i,blk}\) be the entry/exit times on the blocked side (same definitions as above). Then:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i,blk} &\ge T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\;(1-r_{i,B}) \\
\text{exit}_{i,blk}  &\le T_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\;(1-r_{i,B})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in I \tag{D1}
\]

If \(r_{i,B}=0\) the constraints are relaxed (big‑M). If \(r_{i,B}=1\) they force the whole passage to lie **outside** the disruption window.

### 5.8 Optional cancellation  

If a train is cancelled (\(c_i=1\)) all its timing variables are forced to zero (or to a dummy value) and the energy term disappears:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
d_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
t_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg\\
v_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\tag{CAN}
\]

The objective can be extended with a penalty term \(\rho_i c_i\) if cancellations are to be discouraged (not required in the statement, but shown for completeness).

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}
\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \phi_{p}\; e_{i,seg,p} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice on blocked segment} \\
&\text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{flow conservation at stations} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{travel‑time ↔ speed (linearised)} \\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{speed limits} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{capacity / ordering on shared side} \\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{no‑occupancy of blocked side during disruption window} \\
&\text{(CAN)} &&\text{optional cancellation} \\
&\text{(piecewise reconstruction)}\;
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(piecewise convexity)}\;
\sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p}= v_{i,seg} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(binary domain)}\;
r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,seg}\in\{0,1\},\; c_i\in\{0,1\} \\
&\text{(continuous domain)}\;
a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,seg},v_{i,seg},e_{i,seg,p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy term and division) have been replaced by standard MILP linearisation techniques (piecewise linear approximation and McCormick envelopes).  

---

## 7. How the Model Works – Short Narrative  

1. **Route choice** (`r_{i,s}`) forces every train to decide which side of the blocked segment it will use. The blocked side can be forbidden completely (hard blockage) or only during a time window (`D1`).  

2. **Timing variables** (`a`, `d`, `t`) describe the exact schedule of each train. Flow constraints (`F1`, `F2`) guarantee that a train’s departure from a station equals its arrival plus the mandatory dwell, and that the arrival at the next station equals the departure plus the travel time on the connecting segment.  

3. **Speed–time coupling** (`T1`/`T2`) links the travel time on a segment to the average speed. The linearised reciprocal formulation keeps the model MILP‑compatible.  

4. **Capacity** is handled by binary ordering variables (`o_{i,j,seg}`). For any two trains that share the same side of a segment, exactly one must be scheduled first (`C2`). The big‑M constraints (`C1`) enforce a safety headway (`Δ_safe`) between the exit of the first train and the entry of the second.  

5. **Disruption window** (`D1`) guarantees that no train occupies the blocked side while the incident is active. If a train is forced onto the opposite side (`r_{i,blocked}=0`), the constraint is automatically satisfied.  

6. **Energy** is minimised through the weighted sum of a piecewise linear approximation of the convex function \(\alpha v^{2}+ \beta v\). The auxiliary variables `e_{i,seg,p}` make the term linear while preserving a good approximation of the true energy curve.  

7. **Objective** balances two competing goals: (i) keep trains as close as possible to their original timetable (delay term) and (ii) run them at speeds that minimise energy consumption. The weights `w_delay` and `w_energy` allow the planner to stress one objective more than the other.  

8. **Optional cancellation** (`c_i`) provides a safety valve: if a feasible schedule cannot be found for a train, the model may set `c_i=1` (paying a large penalty if desired) and remove the train from the network.  

---

### Ready‑to‑Use  

The formulation above can be copied into a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
All that remains is to:

* Populate the sets **I**, **SEG**, **K(i)**, the parameters (segment lengths, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, big‑M value).  
* Choose a suitable number of break‑points for the speed‑energy piecewise linearisation (the finer the mesh, the more accurate the energy estimate).  
* Solve the MILP with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.  

The optimal solution will give, for every train, the side it should use on the blocked segment, the exact departure/arrival times at every station, the speed to adopt on each segment, and the ordering of trains on shared tracks – all while minimising a weighted combination of delay and energy consumption.

Assumptions: linearization of speed-energy via piecewise linear segments, big-M constants M. Provide full MILP equations.

\[

a_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
d_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
t_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg\\
v_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\tag{CAN}
\]

The objective can be extended with a penalty term \(\rho_i c_i\) if cancellations are to be discouraged (not required in the statement, but shown for completeness).

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}
\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \phi_{p}\; e_{i,seg,p} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice on blocked segment} \\
&\text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{flow conservation at stations} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{travel‑time ↔ speed (linearised)} \\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{speed limits} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{capacity / ordering on shared side} \\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{no‑occupancy of blocked side during disruption window} \\
&\text{(CAN)} &&\text{optional cancellation} \\
&\text{(piecewise reconstruction)}\;
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(piecewise convexity)}\;
\sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p}= v_{i,seg} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(binary domain)}\;
r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,seg}\in\{0,1\},\; c_i\in\{0,1\} \\
&\text{(continuous domain)}\;
a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,seg},v_{i,seg},e_{i,seg,p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy term and division) have been replaced by standard MILP linearisation techniques (piecewise linear approximation and McCormick envelopes).  

---

## 7. How the Model Works – Short Narrative  

1. **Route choice** (`r_{i,s}`) forces every train to decide which side of the blocked segment it will use. The blocked side can be forbidden completely (hard blockage) or only during a time window (`D1`).  

2. **Timing variables** (`a`, `d`, `t`) describe the exact schedule of each train. Flow constraints (`F1`, `F2`) guarantee that a train’s departure from a station equals its arrival plus the mandatory dwell, and that the arrival at the next station equals the departure plus the travel time on the connecting segment.  

3. **Speed–time coupling** (`T1`/`T2`) links the travel time on a segment to the average speed. The linearised reciprocal formulation keeps the model MILP‑compatible.  

4. **Capacity** is handled by binary ordering variables (`o_{i,j,seg}`). For any two trains that share the same side of a segment, exactly one must be scheduled first (`C2`). The big‑M constraints (`C1`) enforce a safety headway (`Δ_safe`) between the exit of the first train and the entry of the second.  

5. **Disruption window** (`D1`) guarantees that no train occupies the blocked side while the incident is active. If a train is forced onto the opposite side (`r_{i,blocked}=0`), the constraint is automatically satisfied.  

6. **Energy** is minimised through the weighted sum of a piecewise linear approximation of the convex function \(\alpha v^{2}+ \beta v\). The auxiliary variables `e_{i,seg,p}` make the term linear while preserving a good approximation of the true energy curve.  

7. **Objective** balances two competing goals: (i) keep trains as close as possible to their original timetable (delay term) and (ii) run them at speeds that minimise energy consumption. The weights `w_delay` and `w_energy` allow the planner to stress one objective more than the other.  

8. **Optional cancellation** (`c_i`) provides a safety valve: if a feasible schedule cannot be found for a train, the model may set `c_i=1` (paying a large penalty if desired) and remove the train from the network.  

---

### Ready‑to‑Use  

The formulation above can be copied into a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
All that remains is to:

* Populate the sets **I**, **SEG**, **K(i)**, the parameters (segment lengths, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, big‑M value).  
* Choose a suitable number of break‑points for the speed‑energy piecewise linearisation (the finer the mesh, the more accurate the energy estimate).  
* Solve the MILP with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.  

The optimal solution will give, for every train, the side it should use on the blocked segment, the exact departure/arrival times at every station, the speed to adopt on each segment, and the ordering of trains on shared tracks – all while minimising a weighted combination of delay and energy consumption.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP**  
*(partial segment blockage – one of the two parallel tracks of a segment is blocked for a known time window)*  

Below a **complete, linear** mixed‑integer model is presented.  
All symbols are defined first, then the objective function, and finally every set of constraints together with a short explanation of its role.  
The model is written in a *compact* algebraic form that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress) after expanding the index sets.

---

## 1. Sets and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* |
| **K(i)** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including the origin and the final destination).  Index *k* ∈ K(i). |
| **S = {L,R}** | Two parallel sides (Left / Right) of a segment that may be blocked. |
| **B ⊂ S** | Side that is *blocked* on the critical segment (e.g. **B = {L}**). |
| **SEG** | Set of track segments (including the blocked one).  Index *seg*. |
| **len<sub>seg</sub>** | Physical length of segment *seg* (km). |
| **sched<sub>i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “on‑time” reference). |
| **dwell<sub>i,k</sub>** | Minimum dwell time required at station *k* for train *i* (minutes). |
| **v<sub>min</sub>, v<sub>max</sub>** | Global lower / upper speed limits (km/min). |
| **α, β** | Energy‑cost coefficients (α > 0, β ≥ 0).  Energy on a segment is approximated by α v² + β v. |
| **T<sub>start</sub>, T<sub>end</sub>** | Start / end of the disruption window on the blocked side (minutes from the planning horizon origin). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **Δ<sub>safe</sub>** | Minimum safety headway between two consecutive trains on the same side of a segment (minutes). |
| **γ<sub>i</sub>** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (allows priority). |
| **w<sub>delay</sub>, w<sub>energy</sub>** | Global weights that balance the two parts of the objective. |
| **π<sub>seg</sub>** | Set of linearisation break‑points for speed (see § 4). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r<sub>i,s</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* on the *blocked* segment; exactly one side must be chosen. |
| **o<sub>i,j,seg</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on side *s* of *seg* (only defined when both trains use the same side). |
| **a<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k*. |
| **d<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **t<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **v<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **c<sub>i</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is **canceled** (optional). When *c<sub>i</sub>=1* all its times are forced to zero (big‑M). |
| **e<sub>i,seg,p</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Portion of speed *v<sub>i,seg</sub>* allocated to linearisation piece *p* (see § 4). |

---

## 3. Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\Bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}- \text{sched}_i\Bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\Bigl(\alpha\,v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta\,v_{i,seg}\Bigr)}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
\]

*The first term penalises the deviation of the actual arrival at the final station from the scheduled arrival.  
The second term is a convex quadratic energy model; it will be linearised in § 4 so that the whole formulation stays MILP.*

---

## 4. Linearisation of the Quadratic Energy Term  

Because a pure quadratic term is not allowed in a MILP, we replace  

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}
\]

by a **piece‑wise linear** approximation over a set of break‑points \(\pi_{seg}=\{p_1,p_2,\dots,p_P\}\) (e.g. 0, v<sub>min</sub>, v<sub>max</sub>).  

Introduce auxiliary variables \(e_{i,seg,p}\) that represent the *fraction* of speed contributed by each segment of the piecewise function.

1. **Reconstruction of speed**

\[
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p}\qquad\forall i,seg
\]

2. **Convex combination constraints**

\[
\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \lambda_{p}=1,\qquad 
\lambda_{p}\ge 0\quad\text{(these are implicit in the definition of }e_{i,seg,p}\text{).}
\]

3. **Linear energy expression**

Let \(\phi_{p}\) be the value of the quadratic function at break‑point \(p\) (i.e. \(\phi_{p}= \alpha p^{2}+ \beta p\)). Then

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}\;\; \approx\;\; \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \phi_{p}\; e_{i,seg,p}
\]

Because each \(e_{i,seg,p}\) is bounded by the length of the interval between two consecutive break‑points, the approximation is exact if the break‑points are dense enough.  

All constraints that involve the energy term in the objective are now linear.

---

## 5. Model Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑choice on the blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

If side *s* is blocked, we force all trains to avoid it:

\[
r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in B \tag{R2}
\]

(If the blockage is temporary, the time‑window constraints below will be used instead; R2 is a “hard” blockage.)

### 5.2 Flow conservation at stations  

For every train *i* and every interior station *k* (i.e. not the first one):

\[
d_{i,k}= a_{i,k}+ \text{dwell}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{first}\} \tag{F1}
\]

Travel from station *k* to the next station *k+1* passes through a segment *seg(i,k)* (the segment that connects the two stations).  

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,\,\text{seg}(i,k)} \qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{last}\} \tag{F2}
\]

### 5.3 Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship  

\[
t_{i,seg}= \frac{\text{len}_{seg}}{v_{i,seg}} \qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T1}
\]

Because the division is non‑linear, we linearise it with a **big‑M / reciprocal** technique (or use a set of linear constraints derived from a piecewise linear approximation of \(1/v\)).  
A common linearisation uses the following for each segment *seg*:

Introduce auxiliary variable \(u_{i,seg}=1/v_{i,seg}\). Then

\[
t_{i,seg}= \text{len}_{seg}\; u_{i,seg} \tag{T2}
\]

and enforce the reciprocal relationship by the McCormick envelopes (valid because \(v_{i,seg}\) is bounded):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} - \frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}(v_{i,seg}-v_{\min}) &&\forall i,seg\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} - \frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}(v_{i,seg}-v_{\max}) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\]

(If a tighter linearisation is required, a piecewise linear approximation of \(1/v\) can be used analogously to § 4.)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\; \le\; v_{i,seg}\; \le\; v_{\max}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{S1}
\]

### 5.5 Capacity / ordering on a shared side  

Consider any **pair of distinct trains** \((i,j)\) that use the **same side** *s* of the **same segment** *seg*.  
Define a binary ordering variable \(o_{i,j,seg}\) (only needed when the side is the same).  

The “enter” time of a train on a segment is the departure time from the upstream station:

\[
\text{enter}_{i,seg}= d_{i,\,\text{up}(seg)} \qquad\forall i,seg
\]

The “exit” time is the arrival at the downstream station:

\[
\text{exit}_{i,seg}= a_{i,\,\text{down}(seg)} \qquad\forall i,seg
\]

Capacity (no overlap) is enforced by the classic big‑M formulation:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{exit}_{i,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{j,seg}+ M\;(1-o_{i,j,seg}) \\
\text{exit}_{j,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{i,seg}+ M\;o_{i,j,seg}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; \forall s\in S \text{ with } r_{i,s}=r_{j,s}=1 \tag{C1}
\]

The “big‑M” term de‑activates the inequality when the corresponding ordering variable is 0.

### 5.6 Ordering‑consistency (mutual exclusivity)  

\[
o_{i,j,seg}+o_{j,i,seg}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg \text{ where both trains share a side} \tag{C2}
\]

If one of the trains does **not** use the side (i.e. \(r_{i,s}=0\) or \(r_{j,s}=0\)), the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0 by the following linking constraints:

\[
o_{i,j,seg} \le r_{i,s},\qquad 
o_{i,j,seg} \le r_{j,s} \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C3}
\]

### 5.7 Disruption‑window (no‑occupancy of blocked side)  

If the blockage is **temporary**, a train may still be assigned to the blocked side *provided* it does not occupy the segment during the window \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\).

Let \(\text{enter}_{i,blk}\) and \(\text{exit}_{i,blk}\) be the entry/exit times on the blocked side (same definitions as above). Then:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i,blk} &\ge T_{\text{end}} \;-\; M\;(1-r_{i,B}) \\
\text{exit}_{i,blk}  &\le T_{\text{start}} \;+\; M\;(1-r_{i,B})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in I \tag{D1}
\]

If \(r_{i,B}=0\) the constraints are relaxed (big‑M). If \(r_{i,B}=1\) they force the whole passage to lie **outside** the disruption window.

### 5.8 Optional cancellation  

If a train is cancelled (\(c_i=1\)) all its timing variables are forced to zero (or to a dummy value) and the energy term disappears:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
d_{i,k} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
t_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg\\
v_{i,seg} &\le M\;(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\tag{CAN}
\]

The objective can be extended with a penalty term \(\rho_i c_i\) if cancellations are to be discouraged (not required in the statement, but shown for completeness).

---

## 6. Full MILP Statement  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}
\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} \phi_{p}\; e_{i,seg,p} \\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice on blocked segment} \\
&\text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{flow conservation at stations} \\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{travel‑time ↔ speed (linearised)} \\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{speed limits} \\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{capacity / ordering on shared side} \\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{no‑occupancy of blocked side during disruption window} \\
&\text{(CAN)} &&\text{optional cancellation} \\
&\text{(piecewise reconstruction)}\;
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(piecewise convexity)}\;
\sum_{p} e_{i,seg,p}= v_{i,seg} &&\forall i,seg \\
&\text{(binary domain)}\;
r_{i,s}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,seg}\in\{0,1\},\; c_i\in\{0,1\} \\
&\text{(continuous domain)}\;
a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,seg},v_{i,seg},e_{i,seg,p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy term and division) have been replaced by standard MILP linearisation techniques (piecewise linear approximation and McCormick envelopes).  

---

## 7. How the Model Works – Short Narrative  

1. **Route choice** (`r_{i,s}`) forces every train to decide which side of the blocked segment it will use. The blocked side can be forbidden completely (hard blockage) or only during a time window (`D1`).  

2. **Timing variables** (`a`, `d`, `t`) describe the exact schedule of each train. Flow constraints (`F1`, `F2`) guarantee that a train’s departure from a station equals its arrival plus the mandatory dwell, and that the arrival at the next station equals the departure plus the travel time on the connecting segment.  

3. **Speed–time coupling** (`T1`/`T2`) links the travel time on a segment to the average speed. The linearised reciprocal formulation keeps the model MILP‑compatible.  

4. **Capacity** is handled by binary ordering variables (`o_{i,j,seg}`). For any two trains that share the same side of a segment, exactly one must be scheduled first (`C2`). The big‑M constraints (`C1`) enforce a safety headway (`Δ_safe`) between the exit of the first train and the entry of the second.  

5. **Disruption window** (`D1`) guarantees that no train occupies the blocked side while the incident is active. If a train is forced onto the opposite side (`r_{i,blocked}=0`), the constraint is automatically satisfied.  

6. **Energy** is minimised through the weighted sum of a piecewise linear approximation of the convex function \(\alpha v^{2}+ \beta v\). The auxiliary variables `e_{i,seg,p}` make the term linear while preserving a good approximation of the true energy curve.  

7. **Objective** balances two competing goals: (i) keep trains as close as possible to their original timetable (delay term) and (ii) run them at speeds that minimise energy consumption. The weights `w_delay` and `w_energy` allow the planner to stress one objective more than the other.  

8. **Optional cancellation** (`c_i`) provides a safety valve: if a feasible schedule cannot be found for a train, the model may set `c_i=1` (paying a large penalty if desired) and remove the train from the network.  

---

### Ready‑to‑Use  

The formulation above can be copied into a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
All that remains is to:

* Populate the sets **I**, **SEG**, **K(i)**, the parameters (segment lengths, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, big‑M value).  
* Choose a suitable number of break‑points for the speed‑energy piecewise linearisation (the finer the mesh, the more accurate the energy estimate).  
* Solve the MILP with any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.  

The optimal solution will give, for every train, the side it should use on the blocked segment, the exact departure/arrival times at every station, the speed to adopt on each segment, and the ordering of trains on shared tracks – all while minimising a weighted combination of delay and energy consumption.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP**  
*(Partial segment blockage – one of the two parallel tracks of a segment is blocked for a known time window)*  

---

### 1. Sets and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* |
| **K(i)** | Ordered list of stations visited by train *i* (including origin and destination). Index *k* ∈ K(i). |
| **S = {L,R}** | Two parallel sides (Left / Right) of a segment that may be blocked. |
| **B ⊂ S** | Side that is *blocked* on the critical segment (e.g. **B = {L}**). |
| **SEG** | Set of track segments (including the blocked one). Index *seg*. |
| **len<sub>seg</sub>** | Physical length of segment *seg* (km). |
| **sched<sub>i</sub>** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “on‑time’’ reference). |
| **dwell<sub>i,k</sub>** | Minimum dwell time required at station *k* for train *i* (minutes). |
| **v<sub>min</sub>, v<sub>max</sub>** | Global lower / upper speed limits (km /min). |
| **α, β** | Energy‑cost coefficients (α > 0, β ≥ 0). Energy on a segment is approximated by α v² + β v. |
| **T<sub>start</sub>, T<sub>end</sub>** | Start / end of the disruption window on the blocked side (minutes from the planning horizon origin). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **Δ<sub>safe</sub>** | Minimum safety headway between two consecutive trains on the same side of a segment (minutes). |
| **γ<sub>i</sub>** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (allows priority). |
| **w<sub>delay</sub>, w<sub>energy</sub>** | Global weights that balance the two parts of the objective. |
| **π<sub>seg</sub>** | Set of linearisation break‑points for speed (see § 4). |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **r<sub>i,s</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses side *s* on the blocked segment (exactly one side must be chosen). |
| **o<sub>i,j,seg</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* precedes train *j* on the same side of segment *seg*. |
| **a<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *k*. |
| **d<sub>i,k</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *k*. |
| **t<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **v<sub>i,seg</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment *seg*. |
| **c<sub>i</sub>** | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is cancelled (optional). |
| **e<sub>i,seg,p</sub>** | continuous ≥0 | Portion of speed *v<sub>i,seg</sub>* allocated to linearisation piece *p* (see § 4). |

---

### 3. Objective function  

\[
\min\;
w_{\text{delay}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\;\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\;\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\;e_{i,seg,p}
\]

*First term*: weighted total delay (arrival at final station vs. scheduled).  
*Second term*: linearised energy consumption; \(\phi_{p}= \alpha p^{2}+ \beta p\) is the energy value at break‑point *p*.

---

### 4. Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

1. **Reconstruction of speed**  

\[
v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p}\qquad\forall i,seg
\]

2. **Convex‑combination bounds**  

\[
0\le e_{i,seg,p}\le p_{\text{next}}-p_{\text{prev}}\qquad\forall i,seg,\;p\in\pi_{seg}
\]

(If the break‑points are dense the approximation is tight.)

3. **Linear energy expression**  

\[
\alpha v_{i,seg}^{2}+ \beta v_{i,seg}\;\approx\;\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\;e_{i,seg,p}
\]

All terms in the objective are now linear.

---

### 5. Model constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑choice on the blocked segment  

\[
\sum_{s\in S} r_{i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

If side *s* is blocked permanently:  

\[
r_{i,s}=0 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in B \tag{R2}
\]

(If the blockage is only temporary, use the time‑window constraints in § 5.6.)

#### 5.2 Flow conservation at stations  

\[
d_{i,k}= a_{i,k}+ \text{dwell}_{i,k}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{first}\} \tag{F1}
\]

\[
a_{i,k+1}= d_{i,k}+ t_{i,\text{seg}(i,k)}\qquad\forall i,\;k\in K(i)\setminus\{\text{last}\} \tag{F2}
\]

where **seg(i,k)** is the segment linking station *k* to *k+1* for train *i*.

#### 5.3 Travel‑time ↔ speed relationship (linearised)  

Introduce auxiliary variable \(u_{i,seg}=1/v_{i,seg}\).  

\[
t_{i,seg}= \text{len}_{seg}\; u_{i,seg}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T1}
\]

McCormick envelopes (valid because \(v_{min}\le v_{i,seg}\le v_{max}\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}} \\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}} \\
u_{i,seg} &\ge \frac{1}{v_{\max}}-\frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}\bigl(v_{i,seg}-v_{\min}\bigr)\\
u_{i,seg} &\le \frac{1}{v_{\min}}-\frac{1}{v_{\max}v_{\min}}\bigl(v_{i,seg}-v_{\max}\bigr)
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{T2}
\]

#### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\le v_{i,seg}\le v_{\max}\qquad\forall i,seg \tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.5 Capacity / ordering on a shared side  

For any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that use the **same side** *s* of the **same segment** *seg* define:

\[
\text{enter}_{i,seg}= d_{i,\text{up}(seg)},\qquad
\text{exit}_{i,seg}= a_{i,\text{down}(seg)}
\]

Big‑M ordering constraints:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{exit}_{i,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{j,seg}+ M\,(1-o_{i,j,seg})\\
\text{exit}_{j,seg}+ \Delta_{\text{safe}} &\le \text{enter}_{i,seg}+ M\,o_{i,j,seg}
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C1}
\]

Mutual exclusivity:

\[
o_{i,j,seg}+o_{j,i,seg}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg \tag{C2}
\]

Linking to side‑choice:

\[
o_{i,j,seg}\le r_{i,s},\qquad o_{i,j,seg}\le r_{j,s}\qquad\forall i<j,\; \forall seg,\; s\in S \tag{C3}
\]

If a train does not use side *s*, the corresponding ordering variables are forced to 0.

#### 5.6 Disruption‑window (temporary blockage)  

If the blockage is only active during \([T_{\text{start}},T_{\text{end}}]\) and a train *i* is assigned to the blocked side (*r<sub>i,B</sub>=1*), its passage must lie outside the window:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{enter}_{i,blk} &\ge T_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-r_{i,B})\\
\text{exit}_{i,blk}  &\le T_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-r_{i,B})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i\in I \tag{D1}
\]

If the blockage is permanent, (R2) already forces \(r_{i,B}=0\).

#### 5.7 Optional cancellation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,k} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
d_{i,k} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,k\\
t_{i,seg} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg\\
v_{i,seg} &\le M\,(1-c_i) &&\forall i,seg
\end{aligned}
\tag{CAN}
\]

(If cancellations are to be penalised, add \(\sum_i \rho_i c_i\) to the objective.)

---

### 6. Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&
w_{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in I}\gamma_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)
\;+\;
w_{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{seg\in SEG}\sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}}\phi_{p}\,e_{i,seg,p}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&
\text{(R1)–(R2)} &&\text{route choice on blocked segment}\\
&\text{(F1)–(F2)} &&\text{flow conservation at stations}\\
&\text{(T1)–(T2)} &&\text{travel‑time ↔ speed (linearised)}\\
&\text{(S1)} &&\text{speed limits}\\
&\text{(C1)–(C3)} &&\text{capacity / ordering on shared side}\\
&\text{(D1)} &&\text{no‑occupancy of blocked side during disruption window}\\
&\text{(CAN)} &&\text{optional cancellation}\\
&v_{i,seg}= \sum_{p\in\pi_{seg}} e_{i,seg,p} &&\forall i,seg\\
&0\le e_{i,seg,p}\le p_{\text{next}}-p_{\text{prev}} &&\forall i,seg,p\\
&r_{i,s},o_{i,j,seg},c_i\in\{0,1\}\\
&a_{i,k},d_{i,k},t_{i,seg},v_{i,seg},e_{i,seg,p}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearities (quadratic energy and division) have been replaced by standard MILP linearisation techniques (piecewise linear approximation and McCormick envelopes).  

---

### 7. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – fill the sets *I*, *SEG*, *K(i)*, the parameters (segment lengths, dwell times, scheduled arrivals, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, big‑M, safety headway).  
2. **Linearisation granularity** – choose a set of speed break‑points *π<sub>seg</sub>* (e.g., 0, v<sub>min</sub>, mid‑point, v<sub>max</sub>) to obtain the desired trade‑off between model size and energy‑approximation accuracy.  
3. **Solve** – feed the formulation to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, etc.).  
4. **Result interpretation** – the optimal solution provides for each train:  
   * which side of the blocked segment to use (`r_{i,s}`),  
   * exact arrival/departure times at every station (`a_{i,k}`, `d_{i,k}`),  
   * average speed on each segment (`v_{i,seg}`),  
   * ordering of trains on shared tracks (`o_{i,j,seg}`),  
   * and, if allowed, a cancellation decision (`c_i`).  

The solution simultaneously minimises total delay and energy consumption while guaranteeing a conflict‑free timetable that respects the disruption, bidirectional track capacity, speed limits, and safety headways.

Introduction

With millions of passenger trips on an average day, railway networks play a big role in the European mobility system. In the European Union, the railway infrastructure and the railway operations are mandated by law to be managed separately. In the Netherlands, ProRail is responsible for managing the railway network infrastructure and Netherlands Railways (NS) is the main passenger railway operator. One of the tasks of the railway operator is the planning of individual train units, or rolling stock. A rolling stock schedule specifies which rolling stock units operate which trips in the timetable. Disruptions on the railway network, such as a missing rolling stock unit in a train trip or a complete blockage of a railway track as a result of an accident or a train breakdown, require the rolling stock plan to be updated. The rescheduling measures that pertain to the (availability of the) railway infrastructure, i.e., the changes in the rolling stock assignments, are created by rolling stock dispatchers who work for the railway operator, after which local infrastructure dispatchers who work for the infrastructure manager are tasked with performing the suggested rolling stock movements.

We focus our research on the rescheduling of rolling stock units in the case of disruptions in the railway system. It is necessary that the rolling stock is efficiently operated and utilized to maintain a good balance between the service to passengers and the incurred operational costs. Unavailability of rolling stock influences passenger satisfaction, as passengers possibly have to stand or even wait for the next train in case not enough capacity is available. An efficient rescheduling process reduces such problems and also reduces the number of trains that are needed as a buffer to catch disrupted train services, leading to a reduction in the capital costs for the train operator. It is also beneficial if the adjusted plan is similar to the original plan, as this requires fewer rolling stock movements during the night to get each rolling stock unit to its starting position for the next day. Additionally, an advantage for both passengers and crew members is that they are familiar with the original plan and may prefer the rolling stock units to be operated as originally planned.

Currently, the rescheduling of rolling stock after disruptions is mostly done by hand. As a result, railway planners manually try to find an updated rolling stock allocation without the use of any mathematical methods or solvers. This can largely be attributed to the difficulty of the problem. For a rolling stock plan to work in practice, feasible train compositions need to be assigned to each train trip, the associated shunting movements need to be executable and shunting drivers need to be available for all shunting movements. Past papers have often tackled these problems separately, meaning that there are practical requirements that are not considered in their solution approaches. One of these requirements is the availability of railway tracks for the shunting movements to take place. To the best of our knowledge, no previous research has focused on ensuring feasibility of a rolling stock schedule with regard to this aspect. In practice, this is an important part of rolling stock rescheduling; if the rolling stock movements are not possible due to unavailability of the railway tracks, the entire plan could fall apart and could need to be adjusted.

We introduce two solution approaches which ensure that all shunting movements are feasible with respect to the available infrastructure: an exact algorithm and an iterative heuristic. The basis for our methods is the composition model by Fioole et al. (2006), which outputs a rolling stock circulation for the passenger train timetable. To check whether each of the suggested trips and shunting movements can be performed, we implement an infrastructure model which is based on the model by Van Aken et al. (2017) for solving the Train Timetable Adjustment Problem, which aims at finding an alternative timetable that minimizes the deviation from the original timetable in terms of the incurred delays and cancellations of train services. Our tailored version of this model represents every shunting movement as an event that takes place on a specific track at a specific station and outputs whether a shunting movement is possible and whether other trains need to be delayed to make the shunting movement possible. Although delaying other trains is typically not preferred, a short delay could open up the necessary windows for performing additional shunting movements. We therefore include the option of delaying other trains by at most a few minutes in our framework and assume that such short delays are resolved by the buffers that are present in the timetable for the remainder of the affected train lines.

Our exact approach resembles a Combinatorial Benders’ approach in line with Codato and Fischetti (2004). It alternates between the composition model, which suggests shunting movements, and the infrastructure model, which checks whether each combination of shunting movements can be performed. The infrastructure model then returns cuts that prohibit combinations of shunting movements, which violate the railway infrastructure availability constraints, from being performed simultaneously. A drawback of the exact approach is the underlying assumption that the creation of a new rolling stock plan and the performance of the shunting movements are carried out simultaneously by one and the same entity, which conflicts with the separation of the railway tasks as mandated by European laws. * \\(\alpha_2\\) medium (avoid unnecessary shunting).

\[

If event \\(k\\) is delayed, its occupied time interval shifts by \\(d_k\\). The binary variable \\(v_{kp}\\) must reflect the new slot usage:

\[

\]

(This ensures that each movement is attached to exactly one RSU.)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \text{(weighted sum of objectives)}\\
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4.1)–(4.8) } \\

\]

1. **Time discretisation** (set \\(Q\\)) is assumed fine enough (e.g., 1 min) to capture all conflicts.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
