response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** on a high‑speed railway with a partially blocked segment.  
The model is written in the classic “sets‑parameters‑variables‑objective‑constraints’’ style, and every term that appears in the objective or in a constraint is explained thereafter.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (or “nodes’’) on the network, indexed by *s* (ordered along each route). |
| **K** | Set of feasible **routes** that a train may take, indexed by *k*. A route is a sequence of stations (or track‑segments). |
| **B** | Set of **blocked track‑segments** (or “blocked sections’’) caused by an incident, indexed by *b*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible **speed levels**, indexed by *ℓ* (e.g., ℓ = 1 … L, where ℓ = 1 = lowest speed, ℓ = L = maximum speed). |
| **E** | Set of **track‑segments** (or “edges’’) between consecutive stations, indexed by *e*. Each segment *e* belongs to a unique ordered pair of stations (s, s′). |
| **C(e)** | Set of trains that may use segment *e* (i.e., those whose chosen route contains *e*). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| **\( \hat a_{i} \)** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “plan’’). | minutes |
| **\( \hat d_{i,s} \)** | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s* (used for dwell‑time windows). | minutes |
| **\( \underline{d}_{i,s},\ \overline{d}_{i,s} \)** | Minimum / maximum allowable dwell time at station *s* for train *i*. | minutes |
| **\( L_{e} \)** | Length of segment *e* (km). | km |
| **\( v^{\max}_{\ell} \)** | Physical speed (km/h) associated with speed level ℓ. | km/h |
| **\( a^{\max}_{\ell},\ a^{\min}_{\ell} \)** | Maximum / minimum admissible acceleration (or deceleration) when changing to speed level ℓ (km/h²). | km/h² |
| **\( M \)** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary is 0 (e.g., 10⁶). | minutes·km/h etc. |
| **\( \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}},\ \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} \)** | Start and end of the time window in which blocked segment *b* is unavailable. | minutes |
| **\( e_{\ell} \)** | Energy consumption rate (e.g., kWh per km) when travelling at speed level ℓ. | kWh/km |
| **\( w^{\text{delay}}_{i} \)** | Weight of train *i*’s delay in the objective (may reflect passenger importance). | – |
| **\( w^{\text{energy}} \)** | Global weight for total energy consumption. | – |
| **\( \text{Cap}_{e} \)** | Capacity of segment *e* (maximum number of trains that may occupy it simultaneously, usually 1 for a single‑track, >1 for double‑track). | trains |

*Derived parameters*  

- Travel time if speed level ℓ is used on segment *e*:  

\[
\theta_{e,\ell}= \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max}_{\ell}} \times 60 \qquad (\text{minutes})
\]

- Minimum travel time allowed by acceleration/deceleration limits (optional, can be pre‑computed and stored as \(\underline{t}_{e,\ell}\)).  

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| **\( r_{i,k} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* follows route *k*; 0 otherwise. |
| **\( o_{i,j} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on any shared segment; 0 otherwise. (Only defined for unordered pairs \((i,j)\) that may share a segment.) |
| **\( a_{i,s} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| **\( d_{i,s} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| **\( t_{i,e} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *e* (if *e* belongs to the chosen route). |
| **\( v_{i,e,\ell} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* travels on segment *e* with speed level ℓ; 0 otherwise. (Only one ℓ can be chosen per (i,e)). |
| **\( y_{i,b} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* traverses blocked segment *b* **after** the blockage window; 0 otherwise (used to enforce avoidance). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\Bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_{i}\Bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\,
\sum_{i\in T}\;\sum_{e\in E}\;\sum_{\ell\in L}
e_{\ell}\,L_{e}\,v_{i,e,\ell}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}}
\]

*Explanation*  

- **Delay term**: \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (the last station on the selected route). The difference from the scheduled arrival \(\hat a_i\) is the train’s delay.  
- **Energy term**: Energy consumption on a segment is the product of the energy‑rate of the chosen speed level, the segment length, and the binary indicator that selects that speed level.

Both parts are linear because the speed‑level choice is binary.

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

Each train must select exactly one feasible route.

### 5.2 Linking route to segment‑level variables  

For every train *i* and segment *e*:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K:\,e\in \text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; e\in E
\tag{R2}
\]

If the chosen route contains segment *e*, exactly one speed level must be selected; otherwise all \(v_{i,e,\ell}=0\).

### 5.3 Travel‑time definition  

\[
t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L} \theta_{e,\ell}\, v_{i,e,\ell}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; e\in E
\tag{R3}
\]

Because \(\theta_{e,\ell}\) is the deterministic travel time for level ℓ, this equation linearly maps the binary speed‑level choice to the continuous travel time.

### 5.4 Time‑propagation along a route  

Let the ordered list of stations on the selected route of train *i* be  
\(s_{i}^{0}, s_{i}^{1},\dots , s_{i}^{p_i}\) (with \(s_{i}^{0}\) the origin and \(s_{i}^{p_i}\) the destination).  
For each consecutive pair \((s_{i}^{q}, s_{i}^{q+1})\) let the connecting segment be \(e_{i}^{q}\).

\[
a_{i,s_{i}^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_{i}^{q}} + t_{i,e_{i}^{q}}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1
\tag{R4}
\]

### 5.5 Dwell‑time (minimum / maximum)  

\[
\underline{d}_{i,s}\;\le\; d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\;\le\; \overline{d}_{i,s}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; s\in S\ \text{that belong to the chosen route}
\tag{R5}
\]

### 5.6 Blocked‑segment avoidance  

If segment *e* belongs to a blocked segment *b* (i.e., *e*∈*b*), the train must either finish the segment **before** the blockage starts or **after** it ends. Using binary \(y_{i,b}\) to decide the “after’’ case:

\[
a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} + t_{i,b} \;\le\; \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} \;+\; M\; y_{i,b}
\tag{R6a}
\]

\[
a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} \;\ge\; \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} \;-\; M\;(1-y_{i,b})
\tag{R6b}
\]

where \(a_{i,\text{enter}(b)}\) is the arrival time at the **up‑stream** station of blocked segment *b* (the same for all trains that traverse *b*). The two constraints together force the train to respect the blockage window.

### 5.7 Precedence on a shared segment (big‑M)  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that may occupy the same segment *e* (i.e., both routes contain *e*). Introduce ordering binary \(o_{i,j}\) (1 if *i* precedes *j*). Let  

- \(a^{\text{out}}_{i,e}\) = departure time of train *i* from the downstream station of *e* (i.e., \(d_{i,\text{down}(e)}\)).  
- \(a^{\text{in}}_{j,e}\) = arrival time of train *j* at the upstream station of *e* (i.e., \(a_{j,\text{up}(e)}\)).

Then:

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} \;+\; \epsilon \;\le\; a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} \;+\; M\,(1-o_{i,j})
\tag{R7a}
\]

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} \;+\; \epsilon \;\le\; a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} \;+\; M\;o_{i,j}
\tag{R7b}
\]

where \(\epsilon>0\) is a safety head‑way (e.g., 0.5 min). Exactly one of the two constraints is active, enforcing a non‑overtaking order on the shared track.

### 5.8 Capacity of a segment  

For each segment *e* and any time instant the number of trains occupying *e* must not exceed its capacity. A linear formulation uses **time‑indexed** binary occupancy variables, but to keep the model compact we can enforce a **pairwise** capacity of 1 (single‑track) using the ordering constraints (R7). For double‑track (capacity = 2) we would need a set‑partitioning or a time‑discretization; a simple linear surrogate is:

\[
\sum_{i\in C(e)} \bigl( v_{i,e,\ell}\bigr) \;\le\; \text{Cap}_{e}
\qquad \forall e\in E
\tag{R8}
\]

Because each train can be on *e* at most once (binary speed‑level), this ensures that at any moment no more than the allowed number of trains are scheduled on that segment. (If a finer temporal capacity is required, a time‑slice formulation can be added – omitted here for brevity.)

### 5.9 Speed‑level feasibility (optional acceleration limit)  

If the model must respect that a train cannot instantaneously jump from speed level ℓ₁ on segment *e₁* to ℓ₂ on the next segment *e₂*, we can linearise a simple bound:

\[
v_{i,e_{i}^{q},\ell_2} \;\le\; v_{i,e_{i}^{q-1},\ell_1} \;+\; A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}
\qquad \forall i,\; q,\; \ell_1,\ell_2
\tag{R9}
\]

where \(A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\) is a pre‑computed binary constant equal to 1 if the acceleration/deceleration required to go from ℓ₁ to ℓ₂ is admissible, 0 otherwise. This keeps the model linear.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity and binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{i,e,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k,e,\ell,i\neq j,b\\
& a_{i,s}\ge 0,\; d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; t_{i,e}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,e
\end{aligned}
\tag{R10}
\]

---

## 6.  Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}L_{e}\,v_{i,e,\ell}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\in T \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}\\
& t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell}\,v_{i,e,\ell}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}\\
& a_{i,s_{i}^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_{i}^{q}} + t_{i,e_{i}^{q}}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}\\
& \underline{d}_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline{d}_{i,s}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ on route}(i) \tag{R5}\\
& a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} + t_{i,b} \le \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} + M y_{i,b}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; b\in B\text{ traversed by }i \tag{R6a}\\
& a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} \ge \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} - M(1-y_{i,b})
   &&\forall i\in T,\; b\in B\text{ traversed by }i \tag{R6b}\\
& a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} + \epsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} + M(1-o_{i,j})
   &&\forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P},\; e\in E_{ij} \tag{R7a}\\
& a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} + \epsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} + M o_{i,j}
   &&\forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P},\; e\in E_{ij} \tag{R7b}\\
& \sum_{i\in C(e)}\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell} \le \text{Cap}_{e}
   &&\forall e\in E \tag{R8}\\
& v_{i,e_{i}^{q},\ell_2} \le v_{i,e_{i}^{q-1},\ell_1}+A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}
   &&\forall i,\; q,\; \ell_1,\ell_2 \tag{R9}\\
& r_{i,k},v_{i,e,\ell},o_{i,j},y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\}
   &&\forall i,k,e,\ell,i\neq j,b\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,e}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,e
\end{aligned}}
\]

---

## 7.  Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the real system |
|--------|---------------------------------|
| **Binary route‑choice \(r_{i,k}\)** | Forces each train to pick one feasible path (e.g., a detour around the blocked section). |
| **Binary speed‑level \(v_{i,e,\ell}\)** | Selects a discrete operating speed on each traversed segment; this directly determines travel time and energy use. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the schedule that we are adjusting; they are linked by travel times and dwell‑time constraints. |
| **Ordering binaries \(o_{i,j}\)** | Resolve conflicts on any segment that can be used by more than one train. The big‑M constraints guarantee that either *i* finishes before *j* enters, or vice‑versa. |
| **Blockage‑avoidance binaries \(y_{i,b}\)** | Decide whether a train crosses a blocked segment before the incident starts or after it ends; the big‑M formulation enforces the appropriate time window. |
| **Weighted objective** | Balances two operational goals: (i) keeping trains as close as possible to their planned arrival times (customer service) and (ii) limiting energy consumption (environmental/economic cost). |
| **Capacity constraints** | Guarantee that the physical infrastructure (single‑track, double‑track, etc.) is not overloaded. |
| **Acceleration feasibility (R9)** | Optional but realistic: a train cannot instantly jump from a very low to a very high speed; the constraint uses a pre‑computed feasibility matrix. |
| **Dwell‑time limits** | Enforce minimum service time at stations (for passenger boarding) and maximum allowed waiting (to avoid excessive delays). |

---

## 8.  How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, K, S, E, B, L* and compute all parameters (segment lengths, speed‑level travel times \(\theta_{e,\ell}\), blockage windows, scheduled times, etc.).  
2. **Modeling environment** – The formulation is linear; it can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) using a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
3. **Solution** – The solver returns the optimal binary decisions (route choice, speed levels, train ordering) and the corresponding schedule (arrival/departure times).  
4. **Interpretation** – From the solution we obtain:  
   * Which detour each train takes (if any).  
   * The exact speed level on every segment (hence the energy profile).  
   * The revised timetable that respects the blockage and avoids conflicts.  

---

### Remarks & Possible Extensions  

* **Time‑discretised capacity** – If a more accurate capacity model is required (e.g., a double‑track where two trains may be on the same segment at the same time but not at the same instant), introduce a set of time‑intervals *τ* and binary occupancy variables \(z_{i,e,τ}\).  
* **Robustness** – The model can be turned into a robust MILP by adding uncertainty sets on travel times or blockage durations and by using worst‑case or chance‑constrained formulations.  
* **Multiple blockages** – The same structure works for several blocked segments; each gets its own \(y_{i,b}\) and window parameters.  
* **Passenger‑weighting** – The delay weight \(w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\) can be made proportional to train occupancy or revenue to prioritize high‑value services.  

---

**In summary**, the MILP above captures all the ingredients you listed: binary route selection, binary ordering on shared tracks, binary speed‑level choice, avoidance of a partially blocked segment, propagation of arrival/departure times, dwell‑time limits, capacity limits, and a bi‑objective (weighted delay + energy) that is linearized through binary variables. Solving it yields a feasible, conflict‑free, energy‑efficient rescheduled timetable for the high‑speed railway.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

Below is a *complete, linear* mixed‑integer programming model that captures all the elements mentioned in the description.  
The model is written in a compact, index‑set notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
All variables, parameters, the objective function and every constraint are explained after the formulation.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| \\(\mathcal I\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(i\\) |
| \\(\mathcal K_i\\) | Feasible route alternatives for train \\(i\\) (each route is a sequence of track‑segments) |
| \\(\mathcal S\\) | Set of stations (or “nodes”) that can be visited, indexed by \\(s\\) |
| \\(\mathcal P\\) | Set of track‑segments (or “links”) between two consecutive stations, indexed by \\(p\\) |
| \\(\mathcal V\\) | Discrete speed levels that can be selected, indexed by \\(v\\) (e.g. 0 = stop, 1 = low, …, V = max) |
| \\(\mathcal I_{p}\\) | Sub‑set of trains that may use segment \\(p\\) (derived from the routes) |
| \\(\mathcal B\\) | Set of *blocked* segments (partial blockage). For each \\(p\in\mathcal B\\) a time window \\([B^{\text{start}}_p,\;B^{\text{end}}_p]\\) is given. |
| \\(\mathcal L_i\\) | Last station visited by train \\(i\\) (its destination). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Units |
|--------|-------------|-------|
| \\( \hat a_{i,s} \\) | Scheduled arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) (baseline timetable) | [min] |
| \\( \hat d_{i,s} \\) | Scheduled departure time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) | [min] |
| \\( \alpha_{i,s} \\) | Minimum dwell time at station \\(s\\) for train \\(i\\) | [min] |
| \\( \beta_{i,s} \\) | Maximum dwell time at station \\(s\\) for train \\(i\\) | [min] |
| \\( L_{p} \\) | Physical length of segment \\(p\\) | [km] |
| \\( v^{\max}_v \\) | Physical speed corresponding to speed level \\(v\\) | [km/h] |
| \\( a^{\max}_i \\) | Maximum acceleration (positive) for train \\(i\\) | [km/h²] |
| \\( d^{\max}_i \\) | Maximum deceleration (positive) for train \\(i\\) | [km/h²] |
| \\( e_v \\) | Energy consumption rate (per unit time) when travelling with speed level \\(v\\) | [kWh/h] |
| \\( M \\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min) |
| \\( w^{\text{delay}}_i \\) | Weight for delay of train \\(i\\) in the objective | – |
| \\( w^{\text{energy}}_i \\) | Weight for energy of train \\(i\\) in the objective | – |
| \\( C_p \\) | Capacity (maximum number of trains simultaneously on segment \\(p\\)) – usually 1 for a single‑track line | – |
| \\( \gamma_{i,k,p} \\) | 1 if route \\(k\\) of train \\(i\\) uses segment \\(p\\), 0 otherwise (data‑derived) | – |
| \\( \sigma_{i,k,s} \\) | 1 if route \\(k\\) of train \\(i\\) visits station \\(s\\), 0 otherwise | – |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| \\( r_{i,k} \\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) chooses route \\(k\\) |
| \\( o_{i,j} \\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) is scheduled **before** train \\(j\\) on any common segment (see §4.3) |
| \\( a_{i,s} \\) | continuous ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train \\(i\\) at station \\(s\\) |
| \\( d_{i,s} \\) | continuous ≥0 | Actual departure time of train \\(i\\) from station \\(s\\) |
| \\( t_{i,p} \\) | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train \\(i\\) on segment \\(p\\) (only defined if \\( \gamma_{i,k,p}=1\\) for the selected route) |
| \\( v_{i,p} \\) | binary for each speed level \\(v\\in\mathcal V\\) | 1 ⇔ train \\(i\\) travels on segment \\(p\\) with speed level \\(v\\) |
| \\( y_{i,p} \\) | continuous | Auxiliary variable equal to \\(v^{\max}_v \, t_{i,p}\\) when speed level \\(v\\) is selected (linearisation – see §4.6) |

*Note*: Because the speed level is discrete, we use a set of binaries \\(v_{i,p}\\) and a linking constraint that forces exactly one speed level on each travelled segment.

---

## 4.  Model  

### 4.1 Objective function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\,
\bigl(a_{i,\;L_i} - \hat a_{i,L_i}\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}
\Bigl(\sum_{v\in\mathcal V} e_v\, v_{i,p}\Bigr)\; t_{i,p}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Both terms are linear because the product \(e_v v_{i,p}\) is a constant coefficient (binary times a constant).  

---

### 4.2 Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I
\tag{R1}
\]

2. **Link route choice to the existence of variables on stations/segments**  

For every station \(s\) and segment \(p\) we “activate’’ the corresponding time variables only if the chosen route visits them:

\[
a_{i,s} \le M\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_i}\sigma_{i,k,s}\, r_{i,k}
\qquad
d_{i,s} \le M\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_i}\sigma_{i,k,s}\, r_{i,k}
\qquad
t_{i,p} \le M\;\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_i}\gamma_{i,k,p}\, r_{i,k}
\tag{R2}
\]

If a route does **not** include the station/segment, the right‑hand side is zero and the corresponding variable is forced to 0 (or can be left free but never used).

---

### 4.3 Blocked‑segment avoidance  

If a segment \(p\) is partially blocked, the train may either **pass before** the blockage starts or **wait until it ends**. Using a binary “skip‑block’’ variable \(b_{i,p}\) (1 ⇔ train passes after the blockage) we obtain:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + t_{i,p} &\le B^{\text{start}}_p + M\,(1-b_{i,p}) &&\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;p\in\mathcal B\\
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} &\ge B^{\text{end}}_p - M\,b_{i,p} &&\forall i\in\mathcal I,\;p\in\mathcal B
\end{aligned}
\tag{B1}
\]

Here \(\text{up}(p)\) denotes the *up‑stream* station of segment \(p\).  
If \(b_{i,p}=0\) the first inequality forces the train to finish the segment **before** the blockage starts; if \(b_{i,p}=1\) the second inequality forces the departure from the upstream station to be **after** the blockage ends.  

The binary \(b_{i,p}\) can be omitted when the modeler prefers a simpler “big‑M” formulation directly on \(t_{i,p}\); the above version keeps the linearity and clarity.

---

### 4.4 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on shared tracks  

For any pair of trains that may occupy the same segment \(p\) (i.e. both have \(\gamma_{i,k,p}=\gamma_{j,k',p}=1\) for the chosen routes) we enforce a **first‑come‑first‑served** order using the ordering binary \(o_{i,j}\) (only needed for unordered pairs, i.e. \(i<j\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + t_{i,p} &\le a_{j,\text{up}(p)} + M\,(1-o_{i,j}) &&\forall i<j,\;p\in\mathcal P\\
a_{j,\text{up}(p)} + t_{j,p} &\le a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + M\;o_{i,j} &&\forall i<j,\;p\in\mathcal P
\end{aligned}
\tag{P1}
\]

The constraints are *activated* only when both trains actually travel on the segment; this can be modelled by multiplying the left‑hand side with the product of the route‑segment binaries, but a common linear trick is to use the following **big‑M activation**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + t_{i,p} &\le a_{j,\text{up}(p)} + M\Bigl(1-o_{i,j} + 2 - \sum_{k}\gamma_{i,k,p} r_{i,k} - \sum_{k'}\gamma_{j,k',p} r_{j,k'}\Bigr)\\
a_{j,\text{up}(p)} + t_{j,p} &\le a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + M\Bigl(o_{i,j} + 2 - \sum_{k}\gamma_{i,k,p} r_{i,k} - \sum_{k'}\gamma_{j,k',p} r_{j,k'}\Bigr)
\end{aligned}
\tag{P2}
\]

If either train does **not** use the segment, the right‑hand side contains a large \(M\) and the constraint becomes non‑binding.

---

### 4.5 Time‑propagation (travel‑time linking)  

For every train \(i\) and every *consecutive* pair of stations \((s,s')\) that belong to the selected route we have:

\[
a_{i,s'} = d_{i,s} + t_{i,p(s,s')} \qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\; (s,s')\in\text{route }k\text{ with }r_{i,k}=1
\tag{T1}
\]

Again we linearise with big‑M activation:

\[
a_{i,s'} \le d_{i,s} + t_{i,p(s,s')} + M\Bigl(1-\sum_{k}\sigma_{i,k,s}\sigma_{i,k,s'} r_{i,k}\Bigr)
\]
\[
a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} + t_{i,p(s,s')} - M\Bigl(1-\sum_{k}\sigma_{i,k,s}\sigma_{i,k,s'} r_{i,k}\Bigr)
\tag{T2}
\]

---

### 4.6 Dwell‑time constraints at stations  

\[
\alpha_{i,s}\;\le\; d_{i,s} - a_{i,s}\;\le\;\beta_{i,s}\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\; s\in\mathcal S
\tag{D1}
\]

If a train does not stop at a station (the route does not contain it) the corresponding binary \(\sigma_{i,k,s}\) forces \(a_{i,s}=d_{i,s}=0\) via (R2).

---

### 4.7 Speed‑level selection and travel‑time bounds  

1. **Exactly one speed level on each travelled segment**  

\[
\sum_{v\in\mathcal V} v_{i,p}= \sum_{k}\gamma_{i,k,p}\, r_{i,k}\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal I,\; p\in\mathcal P
\tag{S1}
\]

The right‑hand side is 1 if the segment belongs to the chosen route, 0 otherwise.

2. **Link speed level to travel time**  

The physical relationship (ignoring acceleration/deceleration for the moment) is  

\[
t_{i,p} \ge \frac{L_{p}}{v^{\max}_v}\; v_{i,p}\qquad\forall i,\;p,\;v\in\mathcal V
\tag{S2}
\]

Because the left‑hand side is the same for all speed levels, we can write a compact version using the auxiliary variable \(y_{i,p}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_{i,p} &= \sum_{v\in\mathcal V} v^{\max}_v \, v_{i,p} &&\forall i,p\\
t_{i,p} &\ge \frac{L_{p}}{y_{i,p}} \quad\text{(non‑linear)} 
\end{aligned}
\]

To keep linearity we replace (S2) by a set of *upper* bounds that are tight for each speed level:

\[
t_{i,p} \le \frac{L_{p}}{v^{\max}_v} + M\,(1-v_{i,p})\qquad\forall i,p,\;v\in\mathcal V
\tag{S3}
\]

Thus, if speed level \(v\) is selected (\(v_{i,p}=1\)) the travel time cannot exceed the minimum physical travel time for that speed; the lower bound is given by (S2) – together they force the travel time to be exactly the physical travel time (or a little larger to allow for acceleration/deceleration).

3. **Acceleration / deceleration limits**  

A simple linear approximation: the change of speed between two consecutive segments cannot exceed the maximum acceleration/deceleration. Let \(s(p)\) be the upstream station of segment \(p\) and \(p^{\text{next}}(i,s)\) the segment that leaves station \(s\) for train \(i\). Define a *speed‑value* variable  

\[
\tilde v_{i,p}= \sum_{v\in\mathcal V} v^{\max}_v \, v_{i,p}
\]

Then for every train \(i\) and every station \(s\) that is internal to its route:

\[
\tilde v_{i,p^{\text{next}}} - \tilde v_{i,p} \le a^{\max}_i \, \Delta t_{i,s}
\]
\[
\tilde v_{i,p} - \tilde v_{i,p^{\text{next}}} \le d^{\max}_i \, \Delta t_{i,s}
\]

where \(\Delta t_{i,s}=d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\) (the dwell time).  
Both inequalities are linear because \(\tilde v\) is a linear combination of binaries.

---

### 4.8 Capacity (track‑section) constraints  

For each segment \(p\) and any time horizon we enforce that at most \(C_p\) trains occupy the segment simultaneously. A classic linear way is to use **time‑window discretisation** (e.g., split the horizon into small intervals \(\tau\)). Let \(z_{i,p,\tau}\) be a binary that equals 1 if train \(i\) occupies segment \(p\) during interval \(\tau\). The occupancy relationship is linearised with big‑M:

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} &\le \tau^{\text{end}}_{\tau} + M\,(1-z_{i,p,\tau})\\
a_{i,\text{up}(p)} + t_{i,p} &\ge \tau^{\text{start}}_{\tau} - M\,(1-z_{i,p,\tau})
\end{aligned}
\qquad\forall i,p,\tau
\]

Then the capacity constraint is  

\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_p} z_{i,p,\tau} \le C_p \qquad\forall p,\tau
\tag{Cap}
\]

If the planner prefers a **continuous‑time** formulation, the precedence constraints (P1) already guarantee that at most one train is on a single‑track segment, so \(C_p=1\) can be omitted.

---

### 4.9 Non‑negativity and binary definitions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{i,k} &\in\{0,1\},\quad o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\quad v_{i,p}\in\{0,1\}\\
a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}, t_{i,p} &\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\tag{B}
\]

---

## 5.  Explanation of Model Elements  

| Part | What it does | Why it is needed |
|------|--------------|------------------|
| **Decision variables** | Choose a route, decide the order on shared tracks, set exact arrival/departure times, pick a speed level for each travelled segment. | Captures both *rescheduling* (when a train runs) and *speed management* (how fast it runs). |
| **Objective** | Minimise a weighted sum of (i) total passenger delay (difference between actual and scheduled arrival at the destination) and (ii) total energy consumption (energy‑rate × travel time). | Reflects the two main performance criteria of high‑speed railways. |
| **Route‑selection constraints (R1‑R2)** | Guarantees each train follows exactly one feasible path and de‑activates variables that do not belong to that path. | Enforces feasibility of the chosen itinerary. |
| **Blocked‑segment avoidance (B1)** | Forces a train to either finish the blocked segment before the blockage starts or to wait until it ends. | Handles partial closures (maintenance, accidents). |
| **Precedence constraints (P1‑P2)** | Implements a first‑come‑first‑served rule on any segment that may be used by more than one train, using binary ordering variables. | Prevents collisions and respects single‑track capacity. |
| **Time‑propagation (T1‑T2)** | Links arrival at the next station to departure from the previous one plus the travel time on the connecting segment. | Guarantees a physically consistent schedule. |
| **Dwell‑time bounds (D1)** | Keeps the stop time at each station within a minimum (for passenger exchange) and a maximum (to avoid excessive idling). | Models realistic station operations. |
| **Speed‑level selection (S1‑S3)** | Forces exactly one discrete speed on each travelled segment and ties the selected speed to the travel time via linear big‑M bounds. | Allows the model to decide whether to run slower (e.g., to avoid a conflict) or at the maximum permissible speed. |
| **Acceleration / deceleration (linearised)** | Limits how quickly the train can change speed between two consecutive segments. | Guarantees that the chosen speed profile is physically attainable. |
| **Capacity constraints (Cap)** | If a segment can host more than one train (e.g., double‑track), a time‑window discretisation limits the simultaneous occupancy to the given capacity. | Extends the model to multi‑track lines or sections with limited overtaking slots. |
| **Binary/continuous domains (B)** | Declares the nature of each variable. | Needed for a MILP solver. |

---

### 6.  How to use the formulation  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets \(\mathcal K_i\) (all admissible routes for each train), the incidence parameters \(\sigma_{i,k,s},\gamma_{i,k,p}\) and the blockage windows \([B^{\text{start}}_p,B^{\text{end}}_p]\).  
2. **Parameter tuning** – Choose the weights \(w^{\text{delay}}_i\) and \(w^{\text{energy}}_i\) according to the operator’s priority (e.g., give a higher weight to delay for passenger‑focused services).  
3. **Big‑M selection** – Set \(M\) larger than the longest possible travel time (e.g., 10 000 min) to avoid numerical issues.  
4. **Solve** – Feed the model to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …). The solution returns the selected route, the exact timetable, the ordering on each shared segment and the speed level for every travelled segment.  
5. **Post‑processing** – Compute the actual delay per train, total energy consumption, and (if needed) a detailed speed profile (by translating the selected speed level \(v_{i,p}\) into a constant speed on segment \(p\)).  

---

### 7.  Full linear model (compact)  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \sum_{i\in\mathcal I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(a_{i,L_i}-\hat a_{i,L_i}\bigr)
      + \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\Bigl(\sum_{v\in\mathcal V} e_v v_{i,p}\Bigr) t_{i,p}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in\mathcal K_i} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,p}\le M\!\sum_{k}\sigma_{i,k,s} r_{i,k}\;,\;
M\!\sum_{k}\gamma_{i,k,p} r_{i,k} &&\forall i,s,p\\
&\text{(blocked segment constraints (B1))}\\
&\text{(precedence constraints (P1)–(P2))}\\
& a_{i,s'} = d_{i,s}+t_{i,p(s,s')} &&\forall i,(s,s')\text{ consecutive on chosen route}\\
& \alpha_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le\beta_{i,s} &&\forall i,s\\
& \sum_{v\in\mathcal V} v_{i,p}= \sum_{k}\gamma_{i,k,p} r_{i,k} &&\forall i,p\\
& t_{i,p}\ge \frac{L_{p}}{v^{\max}_v}\,v_{i,p} &&\forall i,p,v\\
& t_{i,p}\le \frac{L_{p}}{v^{\max}_v}+M(1-v_{i,p}) &&\forall i,p,v\\
&\text{(acc/dec constraints using }\tilde v_{i,p})\\
&\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_p} z_{i,p,\tau}\le C_p &&\forall p,\tau\\
& r_{i,k},o_{i,j},v_{i,p},z_{i,p,\tau}\in\{0,1\}\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,p}\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linear relationships (speed ↔ travel time) have been linearised with big‑M bounds, making the model a **Mixed‑Integer Linear Program** ready for exact optimisation.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the description you gave for the **Integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** on a high‑speed railway with a partially blocked segment.  
The model is written in the classic “sets‑parameters‑variables‑objective‑constraints’’ style, and every term that appears in the objective or in a constraint is explained thereafter.

---

## 1.  Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (or “nodes’’) on the network, indexed by *s* (ordered along each route). |
| **K** | Set of feasible **routes** that a train may take, indexed by *k*. A route is a sequence of stations (or track‑segments). |
| **B** | Set of **blocked track‑segments** (or “blocked sections’’) caused by an incident, indexed by *b*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible **speed levels**, indexed by *ℓ* (e.g., ℓ = 1 … L, where ℓ = 1 = lowest speed, ℓ = L = maximum speed). |
| **E** | Set of **track‑segments** (or “edges’’) between consecutive stations, indexed by *e*. Each segment *e* belongs to a unique ordered pair of stations (s, s′). |
| **C(e)** | Set of trains that may use segment *e* (i.e., those whose chosen route contains *e*). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical unit |
|--------|-------------|--------------|
| **\( \hat a_{i} \)** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (the “plan’’). | minutes |
| **\( \hat d_{i,s} \)** | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s* (used for dwell‑time windows). | minutes |
| **\( \underline{d}_{i,s},\ \overline{d}_{i,s} \)** | Minimum / maximum allowable dwell time at station *s* for train *i*. | minutes |
| **\( L_{e} \)** | Length of segment *e* (km). | km |
| **\( v^{\max}_{\ell} \)** | Physical speed (km/h) associated with speed level ℓ. | km/h |
| **\( a^{\max}_{\ell},\ a^{\min}_{\ell} \)** | Maximum / minimum admissible acceleration (or deceleration) when changing to speed level ℓ (km/h²). | km/h² |
| **\( M \)** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when a binary is 0 (e.g., 10⁶). | minutes·km/h etc. |
| **\( \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}},\ \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} \)** | Start and end of the time window in which blocked segment *b* is unavailable. | minutes |
| **\( e_{\ell} \)** | Energy consumption rate (e.g., kWh per km) when travelling at speed level ℓ. | kWh/km |
| **\( w^{\text{delay}}_{i} \)** | Weight of train *i*’s delay in the objective (may reflect passenger importance). | – |
| **\( w^{\text{energy}} \)** | Global weight for total energy consumption. | – |
| **\( \text{Cap}_{e} \)** | Capacity of segment *e* (maximum number of trains that may occupy it simultaneously, usually 1 for a single‑track, >1 for double‑track). | trains |

*Derived parameters*  

- Travel time if speed level ℓ is used on segment *e*:  

\[
\theta_{e,\ell}= \frac{L_{e}}{v^{\max}_{\ell}} \times 60 \qquad (\text{minutes})
\]

- Minimum travel time allowed by acceleration/deceleration limits (optional, can be pre‑computed and stored as \(\underline{t}_{e,\ell}\)).  

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| **\( r_{i,k} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* follows route *k*; 0 otherwise. |
| **\( o_{i,j} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* **precedes** train *j* on any shared segment; 0 otherwise. (Only defined for unordered pairs \((i,j)\) that may share a segment.) |
| **\( a_{i,s} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| **\( d_{i,s} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| **\( t_{i,e} \)** | Continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *e* (if *e* belongs to the chosen route). |
| **\( v_{i,e,\ell} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* travels on segment *e* with speed level ℓ; 0 otherwise. (Only one ℓ can be chosen per (i,e)). |
| **\( y_{i,b} \)** | Binary | 1 if train *i* traverses blocked segment *b* **after** the blockage window; 0 otherwise (used to enforce avoidance). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min \; 
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\,\Bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_{i}\Bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\,
\sum_{i\in T}\;\sum_{e\in E}\;\sum_{\ell\in L}
e_{\ell}\,L_{e}\,v_{i,e,\ell}}_{\text{Total energy consumption}}
\]

*Explanation*  

- **Delay term**: \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (the last station on the selected route). The difference from the scheduled arrival \(\hat a_i\) is the train’s delay.  
- **Energy term**: Energy consumption on a segment is the product of the energy‑rate of the chosen speed level, the segment length, and the binary indicator that selects that speed level.

Both parts are linear because the speed‑level choice is binary.

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

Each train must select exactly one feasible route.

### 5.2 Linking route to segment‑level variables  

For every train *i* and segment *e*:

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K:\,e\in \text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; e\in E
\tag{R2}
\]

If the chosen route contains segment *e*, exactly one speed level must be selected; otherwise all \(v_{i,e,\ell}=0\).

### 5.3 Travel‑time definition  

\[
t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L} \theta_{e,\ell}\, v_{i,e,\ell}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; e\in E
\tag{R3}
\]

Because \(\theta_{e,\ell}\) is the deterministic travel time for level ℓ, this equation linearly maps the binary speed‑level choice to the continuous travel time.

### 5.4 Time‑propagation along a route  

Let the ordered list of stations on the selected route of train *i* be  
\(s_{i}^{0}, s_{i}^{1},\dots , s_{i}^{p_i}\) (with \(s_{i}^{0}\) the origin and \(s_{i}^{p_i}\) the destination).  
For each consecutive pair \((s_{i}^{q}, s_{i}^{q+1})\) let the connecting segment be \(e_{i}^{q}\).

\[
a_{i,s_{i}^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_{i}^{q}} + t_{i,e_{i}^{q}}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1
\tag{R4}
\]

### 5.5 Dwell‑time (minimum / maximum)  

\[
\underline{d}_{i,s}\;\le\; d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\;\le\; \overline{d}_{i,s}
\qquad \forall i\in T,\; s\in S\ \text{that belong to the chosen route}
\tag{R5}
\]

### 5.6 Blocked‑segment avoidance  

If segment *e* belongs to a blocked segment *b* (i.e., *e*∈*b*), the train must either finish the segment **before** the blockage starts or **after** it ends. Using binary \(y_{i,b}\) to decide the “after’’ case:

\[
a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} + t_{i,b} \;\le\; \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} \;+\; M\; y_{i,b}
\tag{R6a}
\]

\[
a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} \;\ge\; \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} \;-\; M\;(1-y_{i,b})
\tag{R6b}
\]

where \(a_{i,\text{enter}(b)}\) is the arrival time at the **up‑stream** station of blocked segment *b* (the same for all trains that traverse *b*). The two constraints together force the train to respect the blockage window.

### 5.7 Precedence on a shared segment (big‑M)  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that may occupy the same segment *e* (i.e., both routes contain *e*). Introduce ordering binary \(o_{i,j}\) (1 if *i* precedes *j*). Let  

- \(a^{\text{out}}_{i,e}\) = departure time of train *i* from the downstream station of *e* (i.e., \(d_{i,\text{down}(e)}\)).  
- \(a^{\text{in}}_{j,e}\) = arrival time of train *j* at the upstream station of *e* (i.e., \(a_{j,\text{up}(e)}\)).

Then:

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} \;+\; \epsilon \;\le\; a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} \;+\; M\,(1-o_{i,j})
\tag{R7a}
\]

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} \;+\; \epsilon \;\le\; a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} \;+\; M\;o_{i,j}
\tag{R7b}
\]

where \(\epsilon>0\) is a safety head‑way (e.g., 0.5 min). Exactly one of the two constraints is active, enforcing a non‑overtaking order on the shared track.

### 5.8 Capacity of a segment  

For each segment *e* and any time instant the number of trains occupying *e* must not exceed its capacity. A linear formulation uses **time‑indexed** binary occupancy variables, but to keep the model compact we can enforce a **pairwise** capacity of 1 (single‑track) using the ordering constraints (R7). For double‑track (capacity = 2) we would need a set‑partitioning or a time‑discretization; a simple linear surrogate is:

\[
\sum_{i\in C(e)} \bigl( v_{i,e,\ell}\bigr) \;\le\; \text{Cap}_{e}
\qquad \forall e\in E
\tag{R8}
\]

Because each train can be on *e* at most once (binary speed‑level), this ensures that at any moment no more than the allowed number of trains are scheduled on that segment. (If a finer temporal capacity is required, a time‑slice formulation can be added – omitted here for brevity.)

### 5.9 Speed‑level feasibility (optional acceleration limit)  

If the model must respect that a train cannot instantaneously jump from speed level ℓ₁ on segment *e₁* to ℓ₂ on the next segment *e₂*, we can linearise a simple bound:

\[
v_{i,e_{i}^{q},\ell_2} \;\le\; v_{i,e_{i}^{q-1},\ell_1} \;+\; A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}
\qquad \forall i,\; q,\; \ell_1,\ell_2
\tag{R9}
\]

where \(A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\) is a pre‑computed binary constant equal to 1 if the acceleration/deceleration required to go from ℓ₁ to ℓ₂ is admissible, 0 otherwise. This keeps the model linear.

### 5.10 Non‑negativity and binary domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{i,e,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k,e,\ell,i\neq j,b\\
& a_{i,s}\ge 0,\; d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; t_{i,e}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,e
\end{aligned}
\tag{R10}
\]

---

## 6.  Complete MILP Statement  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L} e_{\ell}L_{e}\,v_{i,e,\ell}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\in T \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}\\
& t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell}\,v_{i,e,\ell}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}\\
& a_{i,s_{i}^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_{i}^{q}} + t_{i,e_{i}^{q}}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}\\
& \underline{d}_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline{d}_{i,s}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ on route}(i) \tag{R5}\\
& a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} + t_{i,b} \le \Delta_{b}^{\text{start}} + M y_{i,b}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; b\in B\text{ traversed by }i \tag{R6a}\\
& a_{i,\text{enter}(b)} \ge \Delta_{b}^{\text{end}} - M(1-y_{i,b})
   &&\forall i\in T,\; b\in B\text{ traversed by }i \tag{R6b}\\
& a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} + \epsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} + M(1-o_{i,j})
   &&\forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P},\; e\in E_{ij} \tag{R7a}\\
& a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} + \epsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} + M o_{i,j}
   &&\forall (i,j)\in \mathcal{P},\; e\in E_{ij} \tag{R7b}\\
& \sum_{i\in C(e)}\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell} \le \text{Cap}_{e}
   &&\forall e\in E \tag{R8}\\
& v_{i,e_{i}^{q},\ell_2} \le v_{i,e_{i}^{q-1},\ell_1}+A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}
   &&\forall i,\; q,\; \ell_1,\ell_2 \tag{R9}\\
& r_{i,k},v_{i,e,\ell},o_{i,j},y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\}
   &&\forall i,k,e,\ell,i\neq j,b\\
& a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,e}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s,e
\end{aligned}}
\]

---

## 7.  Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the real system |
|--------|---------------------------------|
| **Binary route‑choice \(r_{i,k}\)** | Forces each train to pick one feasible path (e.g., a detour around the blocked section). |
| **Binary speed‑level \(v_{i,e,\ell}\)** | Selects a discrete operating speed on each traversed segment; this directly determines travel time and energy use. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the schedule that we are adjusting; they are linked by travel times and dwell‑time constraints. |
| **Ordering binaries \(o_{i,j}\)** | Resolve conflicts on any segment that can be used by more than one train. The big‑M constraints guarantee that either *i* finishes before *j* enters, or vice‑versa. |
| **Blockage‑avoidance binaries \(y_{i,b}\)** | Decide whether a train crosses a blocked segment before the incident starts or after it ends; the big‑M formulation enforces the appropriate time window. |
| **Weighted objective** | Balances two operational goals: (i) keeping trains as close as possible to their planned arrival times (customer service) and (ii) limiting energy consumption (environmental/economic cost). |
| **Capacity constraints** | Guarantee that the physical infrastructure (single‑track, double‑track, etc.) is not overloaded. |
| **Acceleration feasibility (R9)** | Optional but realistic: a train cannot instantly jump from a very low to a very high speed; the constraint uses a pre‑computed feasibility matrix. |
| **Dwell‑time limits** | Enforce minimum service time at stations (for passenger boarding) and maximum allowed waiting (to avoid excessive delays). |

---

## 8.  How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets *T, K, S, E, B, L* and compute all parameters (segment lengths, speed‑level travel times \(\theta_{e,\ell}\), blockage windows, scheduled times, etc.).  
2. **Modeling environment** – The formulation is linear; it can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …) using a modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, etc.).  
3. **Solution** – The solver returns the optimal binary decisions (route choice, speed levels, train ordering) and the corresponding schedule (arrival/departure times).  
4. **Interpretation** – From the solution we obtain:  
   * Which detour each train takes (if any).  
   * The exact speed level on every segment (hence the energy profile).  
   * The revised timetable that respects the blockage and avoids conflicts.  

---

### Remarks & Possible Extensions  

* **Time‑discretised capacity** – If a more accurate capacity model is required (e.g., a double‑track where two trains may be on the same segment at the same time but not at the same instant), introduce a set of time‑intervals *τ* and binary occupancy variables \(z_{i,e,τ}\).  
* **Robustness** – The model can be turned into a robust MILP by adding uncertainty sets on travel times or blockage durations and by using worst‑case or chance‑constrained formulations.  
* **Multiple blockages** – The same structure works for several blocked segments; each gets its own \(y_{i,b}\) and window parameters.  
* **Passenger‑weighting** – The delay weight \(w^{\text{delay}}_{i}\) can be made proportional to train occupancy or revenue to prioritize high‑value services.  

---

**In summary**, the MILP above captures all the ingredients you listed: binary route selection, binary ordering on shared tracks, binary speed‑level choice, avoidance of a partially blocked segment, propagation of arrival/departure times, dwell‑time limits, capacity limits, and a bi‑objective (weighted delay + energy) that is linearized through binary variables. Solving it yields a feasible, conflict‑free, energy‑efficient rescheduled timetable for the high‑speed railway.

function.description: Generate several independent MILPs for the described problem.
function.name: or_factory

description.description: A description of the MILP to generate.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below captures the whole problem described in the prompt: a high‑speed railway faces a partial‑segment blockage; trains may be rerouted, reordered and driven with different speed levels; the aim is to obtain a conflict‑free timetable that minimises passenger delay and energy consumption. All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and every constraint are given explicitly and are linear, so the formulation can be handed directly to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (or nodes) on the network, indexed by *s*. |
| **K_i** | Feasible route alternatives for train *i*, indexed by *k* (each route is a sequence of stations/segments). |
| **E** | Set of track‑segments (edges) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *e*. |
| **B** | Set of *blocked* segments (partial blockages), indexed by *b*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *ℓ* (ℓ = 1 … L). |
| **C(e)** | Sub‑set of trains that can travel on segment *e* (derived from the routes). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| \( \hat a_i\) | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (baseline timetable). | min |
| \( \hat d_{i,s}\) | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s*. | min |
| \( \underline d_{i,s},\; \overline d_{i,s}\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time of train *i* at station *s*. | min |
| \( L_e\) | Physical length of segment *e*. | km |
| \( v^{\max}_\ell\) | Physical speed (km/h) belonging to speed level ℓ. | km/h |
| \( \theta_{e,\ell}= \frac{L_e}{v^{\max}_\ell}\times 60\) | Travel time (min) on *e* if speed level ℓ is used. | min |
| \( e_\ell\) | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) for speed level ℓ. | kWh/km |
| \( \Delta^{\text{start}}_b,\; \Delta^{\text{end}}_b\) | Start / end of the time window in which blocked segment *b* is unavailable. | min |
| \( w^{\text{delay}}_i\) | Weight of train *i*’s delay in the objective. | – |
| \( w^{\text{energy}}\) | Global weight for total energy consumption. | – |
| \( \text{Cap}_e\) | Capacity of segment *e* (max. simultaneous trains, usually 1). | trains |
| \( M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | – |
| \( \varepsilon\) | Safety head‑way on a shared segment (e.g. 0.5 min). | min |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \( r_{i,k}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses route *k*. |
| \( o_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on any common segment (i < j). |
| \( a_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| \( d_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| \( t_{i,e}\) | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *e* (if the segment belongs to the chosen route). |
| \( v_{i,e,\ell}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* travels on segment *e* with speed level ℓ. |
| \( y_{i,b}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* traverses blocked segment *b* **after** the blockage window (otherwise 0 – i.e. before the window). |

---

### 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\; &\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_i\,
\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}\\
&\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\,
\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L}
e_\ell\,L_e\,v_{i,e,\ell}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\end{aligned}}
\]

* \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train *i* at its destination (the last station on the selected route).  
* Because the speed‑level choice is binary, the energy term is linear.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route selection  
\[
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Linking route to segment‑level variables  
For every train *i* and segment *e*  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K_i:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}
\]

If the chosen route contains *e*, exactly one speed level must be selected; otherwise all \(v_{i,e,\ell}=0\).

#### 5.3 Travel‑time definition from speed level  
\[
t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell}\,v_{i,e,\ell}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4 Time propagation along a route  

Let the ordered list of stations on the selected route of train *i* be  
\(s_i^{0},s_i^{1},\dots ,s_i^{p_i}\) (origin → destination) and let the connecting segment between \(s_i^{q}\) and \(s_i^{q+1}\) be \(e_i^{q}\).

\[
a_{i,s_i^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_i^{q}} + t_{i,e_i^{q}}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}
\]

#### 5.5 Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\underline d_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline d_{i,s}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ that belong to the chosen route of }i \tag{R5}
\]

#### 5.6 Blocked‑segment avoidance  

For every blocked segment *b* traversed by train *i* (the upstream station of *b* is denoted \(s^{\text{up}}_b\)):

\[
a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}+t_{i,b}\le \Delta^{\text{start}}_b + M\,y_{i,b}
\tag{R6a}
\]

\[
a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}\ge \Delta^{\text{end}}_b - M\,(1-y_{i,b})
\tag{R6b}
\]

If \(y_{i,b}=0\) the train must finish the segment **before** the blockage starts; if \(y_{i,b}=1\) it must start **after** the blockage ends.

#### 5.7 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on shared segments  

Consider any unordered pair \((i,j)\) that can both use segment *e* (i.e. both belong to \(C(e)\)).  
Define  

- \(a^{\text{out}}_{i,e}= d_{i,s^{\text{down}}_e}\) – departure from the downstream station of *e*.  
- \(a^{\text{in}}_{j,e}= a_{j,s^{\text{up}}_e}\) – arrival at the upstream station of *e*.

Then

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} + \varepsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} + M\,(1-o_{i,j})
\tag{R7a}
\]

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} + \varepsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} + M\,o_{i,j}
\tag{R7b}
\]

Exactly one of the two constraints is active, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the same segment simultaneously.

#### 5.8 Segment capacity (optional for multi‑track)  

If a segment may host more than one train (capacity \(\text{Cap}_e>1\)), a simple linear surrogate is

\[
\sum_{i\in C(e)} \sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell} \le \text{Cap}_e
\qquad\forall e\in E \tag{R8}
\]

For a single‑track line \(\text{Cap}_e=1\) and the precedence constraints (R7) already enforce conflict‑free usage.

#### 5.9 (Optional) Acceleration / deceleration feasibility  

Define a binary feasibility matrix \(A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\) that equals 1 if a train can change from speed level \(\ell_1\) on segment *e* to level \(\ell_2\) on the next segment, respecting the maximum acceleration/deceleration of the train. Then for every train *i* and every pair of consecutive segments \((e_i^{q-1},e_i^{q})\):

\[
v_{i,e_i^{q},\ell_2}\le v_{i,e_i^{q-1},\ell_1}+ \bigl(1-A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\bigr)
\qquad\forall \ell_1,\ell_2\in L \tag{R9}
\]

If the matrix entry is 0 the constraint forces the corresponding binary to be 0, thus prohibiting an infeasible speed jump.

#### 5.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{i,e,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{i,s}\ge 0,\; d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; t_{i,e}\ge 0
\qquad\forall i,k,e,\ell,j,b,s
\end{aligned}
\tag{R10}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L}
        e_\ell L_e v_{i,e,\ell} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\in T \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}\\
& t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell} v_{i,e,\ell}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}\\
& a_{i,s_i^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_i^{q}} + t_{i,e_i^{q}}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}\\
& \underline d_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline d_{i,s}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ on route}(i) \tag{R5}\\
& a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}+t_{i,b}\le \Delta^{\text{start}}_b + M y_{i,b}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; b\in B\text{ traversed by }i \tag{R6a}\\

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below captures the whole problem described in the prompt: a high‑speed railway faces a partial‑segment blockage; trains may be rerouted, reordered and driven with different speed levels; the aim is to obtain a conflict‑free timetable that minimises passenger delay and energy consumption. All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and every constraint are given explicitly and are linear, so the formulation can be handed directly to any MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP, …).

---

### 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of stations (or nodes) on the network, indexed by *s*. |
| **K_i** | Feasible route alternatives for train *i*, indexed by *k* (each route is a sequence of stations/segments). |
| **E** | Set of track‑segments (edges) between two consecutive stations, indexed by *e*. |
| **B** | Set of *blocked* segments (partial blockages), indexed by *b*. |
| **L** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *ℓ* (ℓ = 1 … L). |
| **C(e)** | Sub‑set of trains that can travel on segment *e* (derived from the routes). |

---

### 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| \( \hat a_i\) | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final station (baseline timetable). | min |
| \( \hat d_{i,s}\) | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s*. | min |
| \( \underline d_{i,s},\; \overline d_{i,s}\) | Minimum / maximum dwell time of train *i* at station *s*. | min |
| \( L_e\) | Physical length of segment *e*. | km |
| \( v^{\max}_\ell\) | Physical speed (km/h) belonging to speed level ℓ. | km/h |
| \( \theta_{e,\ell}= \frac{L_e}{v^{\max}_\ell}\times 60\) | Travel time (min) on *e* if speed level ℓ is used. | min |
| \( e_\ell\) | Energy consumption rate (kWh per km) for speed level ℓ. | kWh/km |
| \( \Delta^{\text{start}}_b,\; \Delta^{\text{end}}_b\) | Start / end of the time window in which blocked segment *b* is unavailable. | min |
| \( w^{\text{delay}}_i\) | Weight of train *i*’s delay in the objective. | – |
| \( w^{\text{energy}}\) | Global weight for total energy consumption. | – |
| \( \text{Cap}_e\) | Capacity of segment *e* (max. simultaneous trains, usually 1). | trains |
| \( M\) | “Big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). | – |
| \( \varepsilon\) | Safety head‑way on a shared segment (e.g. 0.5 min). | min |

---

### 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|--------|
| \( r_{i,k}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* uses route *k*. |
| \( o_{i,j}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* is scheduled **before** train *j* on any common segment (i < j). |
| \( a_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| \( d_{i,s}\) | continuous ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| \( t_{i,e}\) | continuous ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment *e* (if the segment belongs to the chosen route). |
| \( v_{i,e,\ell}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* travels on segment *e* with speed level ℓ. |
| \( y_{i,b}\) | binary | 1 ⇔ train *i* traverses blocked segment *b* **after** the blockage window (otherwise 0 – i.e. before the window). |

---

### 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\; &\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_i\,
\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}\\
&\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\,
\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L}
e_\ell\,L_e\,v_{i,e,\ell}}_{\text{total weighted energy}}
\end{aligned}}
\]

* \(a_{i,\text{last}}\) is the arrival time of train *i* at its destination (the last station on the selected route).  
* Because the speed‑level choice is binary, the energy term is linear.

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route selection  
\[
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in T \tag{R1}
\]

#### 5.2 Linking route to segment‑level variables  
For every train *i* and segment *e*  

\[
\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k\in K_i:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}
\]

If the chosen route contains *e*, exactly one speed level must be selected; otherwise all \(v_{i,e,\ell}=0\).

#### 5.3 Travel‑time definition from speed level  
\[
t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell}\,v_{i,e,\ell}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}
\]

#### 5.4 Time propagation along a route  

Let the ordered list of stations on the selected route of train *i* be  
\(s_i^{0},s_i^{1},\dots ,s_i^{p_i}\) (origin → destination) and let the connecting segment between \(s_i^{q}\) and \(s_i^{q+1}\) be \(e_i^{q}\).

\[
a_{i,s_i^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_i^{q}} + t_{i,e_i^{q}}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}
\]

#### 5.5 Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\underline d_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline d_{i,s}
\qquad\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ that belong to the chosen route of }i \tag{R5}
\]

#### 5.6 Blocked‑segment avoidance  

For every blocked segment *b* traversed by train *i* (the upstream station of *b* is denoted \(s^{\text{up}}_b\)):

\[
a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}+t_{i,b}\le \Delta^{\text{start}}_b + M\,y_{i,b}
\tag{R6a}
\]

\[
a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}\ge \Delta^{\text{end}}_b - M\,(1-y_{i,b})
\tag{R6b}
\]

If \(y_{i,b}=0\) the train must finish the segment **before** the blockage starts; if \(y_{i,b}=1\) it must start **after** the blockage ends.

#### 5.7 Precedence (conflict‑avoidance) on shared segments  

Consider any unordered pair \((i,j)\) that can both use segment *e* (i.e. both belong to \(C(e)\)).  
Define  

- \(a^{\text{out}}_{i,e}= d_{i,s^{\text{down}}_e}\) – departure from the downstream station of *e*.  
- \(a^{\text{in}}_{j,e}= a_{j,s^{\text{up}}_e}\) – arrival at the upstream station of *e*.

Then

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{i,e} + \varepsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{j,e} + M\,(1-o_{i,j})
\tag{R7a}
\]

\[
a^{\text{out}}_{j,e} + \varepsilon \le a^{\text{in}}_{i,e} + M\,o_{i,j}
\tag{R7b}
\]

Exactly one of the two constraints is active, guaranteeing that the two trains never occupy the same segment simultaneously.

#### 5.8 Segment capacity (optional for multi‑track)  

If a segment may host more than one train (capacity \(\text{Cap}_e>1\)), a simple linear surrogate is

\[
\sum_{i\in C(e)} \sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell} \le \text{Cap}_e
\qquad\forall e\in E \tag{R8}
\]

For a single‑track line \(\text{Cap}_e=1\) and the precedence constraints (R7) already enforce conflict‑free usage.

#### 5.9 (Optional) Acceleration / deceleration feasibility  

Define a binary feasibility matrix \(A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\) that equals 1 if a train can change from speed level \(\ell_1\) on segment *e* to level \(\ell_2\) on the next segment, respecting the maximum acceleration/deceleration of the train. Then for every train *i* and every pair of consecutive segments \((e_i^{q-1},e_i^{q})\):

\[
v_{i,e_i^{q},\ell_2}\le v_{i,e_i^{q-1},\ell_1}+ \bigl(1-A_{\ell_1,\ell_2}\bigr)
\qquad\forall \ell_1,\ell_2\in L \tag{R9}
\]

If the matrix entry is 0 the constraint forces the corresponding binary to be 0, thus prohibiting an infeasible speed jump.

#### 5.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; v_{i,e,\ell}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} \\
& a_{i,s}\ge 0,\; d_{i,s}\ge 0,\; t_{i,e}\ge 0
\qquad\forall i,k,e,\ell,j,b,s
\end{aligned}
\tag{R10}
\]

---

### 6. Complete MILP  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in T} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}}-\hat a_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{\ell\in L}
        e_\ell L_e v_{i,e,\ell} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\sum_{k\in K_i} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\in T \tag{R1}\\
&\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell}= \sum_{k:\,e\in\text{route}(k)} r_{i,k}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R2}\\
& t_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell\in L}\theta_{e,\ell} v_{i,e,\ell}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; e\in E \tag{R3}\\
& a_{i,s_i^{q+1}} = d_{i,s_i^{q}} + t_{i,e_i^{q}}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; q=0,\dots ,p_i-1 \tag{R4}\\
& \underline d_{i,s}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le \overline d_{i,s}
   &&\forall i\in T,\; s\in S\text{ on route}(i) \tag{R5}\\
& a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}+t_{i,b}\le \Delta^{\text{start}}_b + M y_{i,b}

& a_{i,s^{\text{up}}_b}\ge \Delta^{\text{end}}_b - M(1-y_{i,b})

& \sum_{i\in C(e)}\sum_{\ell\in L} v_{i,e,\ell} \le \text{Cap}_e
   &&\forall e\in E \tag{R8}\\
& v_{i,e_i^{q},\ell_2}\le v_{i,e_i^{q-1},\ell_1}+ (1-A_{\ell_1,\ell_2})
   &&\forall i,\; q,\; \ell_1,\ell_2\in L \tag{R9}\\
& r_{i,k},v_{i,e,\ell},o_{i,j},y_{i,b}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,k,e,\ell,j,b\\
