Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

| **K** = {1,…,K} | Set of **discrete speed levels** (indexed by *k*). Level *k* corresponds to a constant speed  \(v_k\)  (km h⁻¹) and a known energy coefficient  \(e_k\)  (kWh per km). |
| **τ** = {1,…,τ_max} | Set of **time‑interval indices** used to discretise the travel on a segment (indexed by *τ*). The length of each interval is Δt (minutes). |
| **B** ⊆ S | Subset of segments that are **blocked** for a known time window \([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\). |
| **O** ⊆ S | Subset of segments that are the **opposite track** (available only when the original is blocked). |
| **N_i** ⊆ S | Ordered list of segments that train *i* must traverse if it follows its **original route** (the “normal” direction). |
| **N_i^{\text{opp}}** ⊆ S | Ordered list of segments for train *i* if it uses the **opposite track** (reverse direction on the blocked segment). |
| **d_{s}** | Physical length of segment *s* (km). |
| **v_{\max}, v_{\min}** | Global maximum/minimum admissible speeds (km h⁻¹). |
| **a_{\max}, a_{\min}** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻²). |
| **h** | Safety headway time (minutes) that must separate two trains on the same segment. |
| **\(\underline{w}_i\)** | Minimum dwell (stop) time of train *i* at any station (minutes). |
| **\(\alpha_i\)** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (e.g. passenger importance). |
| **\(\beta\)** | Global weight of the energy‑consumption part of the objective. |
| **\(\hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s)\)** | **Nominal** (undelayed) arrival time of train *i* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (computed from the timetable). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶ minutes). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_i \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | Route choice of train *i*: 0 = original route, 1 = opposite‑track (detour) when the blocked segment is used. |
| **\(y_{i,s,\tau,k} \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | Speed‑level selection: 1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* during interval *τ* with speed level *k*. |
| **\(a_{i,s} \ge 0\)** | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *i* at the upstream end of segment *s*. |
| **\(d_{i,s} \ge 0\)** | continuous | **Departure time** of train *i* from the downstream end of segment *s* (i.e. after finishing the segment). |
| **\(z_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | **Ordering** on a shared segment *s*: 1 if train *i* passes *s* **before** train *j* (i.e. *i* departs before *j* arrives). Defined only for pairs \((i,j)\) that may use the same segment. |
| **\(E\)** | continuous | Total **energy consumption** (kWh) of all trains (used in the objective). |

---

## 3. Linearised Relations  

### 3.1. Exactly one speed level per interval  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train } i \text{ uses segment } s \text{ during interval } \tau,\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

To enforce the “otherwise’’ case we introduce an auxiliary binary **\(u_{i,s,\tau}\)** that indicates whether train *i* occupies segment *s* in interval *τ*:

\[
u_{i,s,\tau}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k}\qquad\forall i,s,\tau .
\tag{2}
\]

### 3.2. Travel‑time on a segment  

The travel time contributed by interval *τ* is Δt (the discretisation step). Hence the **total travel time** of train *i* on segment *s* is

\[
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s}= \Delta t \sum_{\tau\in\tau} u_{i,s,\tau}.
\tag{3}
\]

Because each interval can be used at most once, (3) is linear.

### 3.3. Speed‑level feasibility (speed limits & acceleration)  

For each speed level *k* we know the corresponding speed \(v_k\). The **minimum** time needed to travel segment *s* at level *k* is \(t_{s,k}= d_s / v_k\). Since we discretise time, we enforce a **lower bound** on the number of intervals that must be selected when a high speed is chosen:

\[
\Delta t \sum_{\tau} u_{i,s,\tau} \;\ge\; \frac{d_s}{v_{\max}} \qquad\forall i,s,
\tag{4a}
\]

\[
\Delta t \sum_{\tau} u_{i,s,\tau} \;\le\; \frac{d_s}{v_{\min}} \qquad\forall i,s.
\tag{4b}
\]

If a more detailed piece‑wise linear acceleration model is required, we can add constraints linking consecutive intervals:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau-1,k}
\le a_{\max}\,\Delta t,
\qquad\forall i,s,\tau>1,
\tag{5}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau-1,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau,k}
\le |a_{\min}|\,\Delta t,
\qquad\forall i,s,\tau>1.
\tag{6}
\]

Both (5) and (6) are linear because the speed variables are binary.

### 3.4. Route‑choice linking  

If the blocked segment *b* ∈ B is traversed, the train must decide whether to stay on the original track (possible only **outside** the blockage window) or to use the opposite track. This is modelled by the binary \(x_i\):

\[
a_{i,b} \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} - M\,(1-x_i),
\tag{7a}
\]

\[
a_{i,b} \le t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} + M\,x_i .
\tag{7b}
\]

Thus, when \(x_i=0\) (original route) the arrival at the blocked segment must be **outside** the blocked window; when \(x_i=1\) the train is forced to use the opposite‑track list \(N_i^{\text{opp}}\) (see next).

### 3.5. Flow conservation (temporal continuity)  

For any train *i* and any two consecutive segments *s* and *s′* on the **chosen** route we must have

\[
a_{i,s'} = d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i \quad\text{if } s' \text{ is the downstream neighbour of } s .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the route depends on \(x_i\), we write (8) for both possibilities and activate the appropriate one with a big‑M:

\[
a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i - M\,x_i,
\qquad
a_{i,s'} \le d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i + M\,x_i,
\quad \forall (s,s')\in N_i .
\tag{9a}
\]

\[
a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i - M\,(1-x_i),
\qquad
a_{i,s'} \le d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i + M\,(1-x_i),
\quad \forall (s,s')\in N_i^{\text{opp}} .
\tag{9b}
\]

Thus only the segment‑pair belonging to the selected route is enforced.

### 3.6. Safety headway on a shared segment  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that may occupy the **same** physical segment *s* (whether original or opposite). The binary ordering variable \(z_{i,j,s}\) decides who goes first:

\[
a_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M\,(1- z_{i,j,s}),
\qquad
a_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\,z_{i,j,s},
\tag{10}
\]

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S \text{ that both use}.
\tag{11}
\]

If a pair never uses the same segment, the corresponding \(z\) variables can be omitted.

### 3.7. Capacity of the opposite track  

The opposite track can host **at most one** train at any instant. Using the interval‑level occupancy variables we write:

\[
\sum_{i\in T} \sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k} \le 1,
\qquad\forall s\in O,\;\forall \tau .
\tag{12}
\]

(If the opposite track is a single‑track line, the same constraint also applies to the original track when it is not blocked.)

### 3.8. Energy consumption  

Energy for a train on a segment is approximated linearly by the chosen speed level:

\[
E = \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau\in\tau}\sum_{k\in K}
e_k \, d_s \, y_{i,s,\tau,k}.
\tag{13}
\]

Because \(d_s\) is constant, (13) is linear.

### 3.9. Delay calculation (used in the objective)  

The **delay** of train *i* at its final destination (last segment \(s^{\text{last}}_i\)) is

\[
\text{delay}_i = a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i} - \hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i) .
\tag{14}
\]

If a penalty for intermediate stations is required, the same expression can be summed over all stations.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption:

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} \alpha_i \,
\bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i} - \hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i)\bigr)}_{\text{Total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \, E}_{\text{Total energy cost}}
}
\tag{15}
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables (the delay term uses the arrival‑time variables, the energy term uses (13)).

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T}\alpha_i\bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i}-\hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i)\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i,s,\tau,k} e_k d_s\, y_{i,s,\tau,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(14)   (all constraints listed above)} \\[2pt]
& x_i\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,s,\tau,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{i,s,\tau}\in\{0,1\},\\
& z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; a_{i,s}\ge0,\; d_{i,s}\ge0,\; E\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the real world |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Binary route choice \(x_i\)** | Decides whether a train detours onto the opposite track when its normal track is blocked. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \(y_{i,s,\tau,k}\)** | Choose a discrete speed (hence a discrete energy consumption) for each train on each segment and each time‑slot. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the exact schedule after rescheduling; they are the primary variables that encode delays. |
| **Ordering binaries \(z_{i,j,s}\)** | Enforce a safe temporal order on any segment that can be occupied by more than one train (headway constraint). |
| **Capacity constraint (12)** | Guarantees that the opposite track (single‑track line) never hosts two trains simultaneously. |
| **Energy expression (13)** | Provides a linear approximation of the physical energy needed, proportional to speed level and distance. |
| **Delay objective (15)** | Penalises late arrivals (weighted by train importance) while also rewarding low‑energy operation. |
| **Flow‑conservation (8–9)** | Guarantees that a train’s departure from one segment becomes the arrival at the next, plus the mandatory dwell time. |
| **Speed‑limit & acceleration constraints (4–6)** | Keep the chosen speed levels feasible with respect to physical limits of the rolling stock. |
| **Blockage‑window constraints (7)** | Prevent a train from entering the blocked segment during the disruption unless it uses the opposite track. |
| **Safety headway (10–11)** | Guarantees a minimum time gap *h* between any two consecutive trains on the same piece of rail. |

---

### Remarks on Practical Use  

* **Discretisation** – The choice of Δt (e.g., 1 min) and the number of speed levels K (e.g., 3–5) determines model size. Typical railway MILPs with a few hundred trains and a few hundred segments are solvable with commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) within minutes.  
* **Big‑M values** – M must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes). Tightening M (using the known latest possible arrival) improves solver performance.  
* **Extensions** – Additional realistic features (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity, variable dwell times) can be added by extra linear constraints without changing the MILP nature.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above provides a **complete linear MILP** that simultaneously decides (i) which route each train should take around a blocked segment, (ii) the order in which trains occupy the shared track, (iii) the exact timing of arrivals/departures, and (iv) the discrete speed level for each train‑segment‑interval, while minimising a weighted combination of total delay and energy consumption. The model respects all operational constraints listed in the problem description.

messages.content: Based on your input, generate a complete, linear MILP with variables, objective function and constraints. Explain the elements of the model.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Formulate a MILP for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under partial segment blockage. Variables: binary for route choice (original or opposite track), binary for train ordering on shared segment, continuous for arrival times at stations, departure times, travel times, and speed levels per time interval. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay and energy consumption. Constraints: (1) each train follows exactly one route; (2) flow conservation of travel times; (3) speed limits and acceleration/deceleration bounds linking travel time to speed level; (4) time-window availability of disrupted segment; (5) no overlap on shared track: for any two trains using same track segment, either train i departs after train j arrives plus safety headway; (6) dwell time minimum; (7) binary ordering variables linking to time precedence; (8) capacity of opposite track limited to one train at a time; (9) total energy consumption calculated as sum over intervals of (force*distance) approximated linearly by speed level. Assumptions: discretize each track segment into equal time intervals, linear energy approximation, safety headway constant, disruption time window given, all trains have same length, acceleration/deceleration linear piecewise approximated.

\qquad

\qquad
a_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\,z_{i,j,s},
\tag{10}
\]

\tag{11}

\[

\]

\[
E = \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau\in\tau}\sum_{k\in K}
e_k \, d_s \, y_{i,s,\tau,k}.
\tag{13}
\]

\tag{15}

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T}\alpha_i\bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i}-\hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i)\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i,s,\tau,k} e_k d_s\, y_{i,s,\tau,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(14)   (all constraints listed above)} \\[2pt]
& x_i\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,s,\tau,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{i,s,\tau}\in\{0,1\},\\
& z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; a_{i,s}\ge0,\; d_{i,s}\ge0,\; E\ge0 .

| Element | What it does in the real world |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Binary route choice \(x_i\)** | Decides whether a train detours onto the opposite track when its normal track is blocked. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \(y_{i,s,\tau,k}\)** | Choose a discrete speed (hence a discrete energy consumption) for each train on each segment and each time‑slot. |

| **Ordering binaries \(z_{i,j,s}\)** | Enforce a safe temporal order on any segment that can be occupied by more than one train (headway constraint). |
| **Capacity constraint (12)** | Guarantees that the opposite track (single‑track line) never hosts two trains simultaneously. |
| **Energy expression (13)** | Provides a linear approximation of the physical energy needed, proportional to speed level and distance. |
| **Delay objective (15)** | Penalises late arrivals (weighted by train importance) while also rewarding low‑energy operation. |
| **Flow‑conservation (8–9)** | Guarantees that a train’s departure from one segment becomes the arrival at the next, plus the mandatory dwell time. |
| **Speed‑limit & acceleration constraints (4–6)** | Keep the chosen speed levels feasible with respect to physical limits of the rolling stock. |
| **Blockage‑window constraints (7)** | Prevent a train from entering the blocked segment during the disruption unless it uses the opposite track. |
| **Safety headway (10–11)** | Guarantees a minimum time gap *h* between any two consecutive trains on the same piece of rail. |

---

### Remarks on Practical Use  

* **Discretisation** – The choice of Δt (e.g., 1 min) and the number of speed levels K (e.g., 3–5) determines model size. Typical railway MILPs with a few hundred trains and a few hundred segments are solvable with commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) within minutes.  
* **Big‑M values** – M must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes). Tightening M (using the known latest possible arrival) improves solver performance.  
* **Extensions** – Additional realistic features (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity, variable dwell times) can be added by extra linear constraints without changing the MILP nature.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above provides a **complete linear MILP** that simultaneously decides (i) which route each train should take around a blocked segment, (ii) the order in which trains occupy the shared track, (iii) the exact timing of arrivals/departures, and (iv) the discrete speed level for each train‑segment‑interval, while minimising a weighted combination of total delay and energy consumption. The model respects all operational constraints listed in the problem description.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

messages.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three‑dimensional decision problem described in the request:

* **Integrated train‑rescheduling** (which route to take, the order of trains on a congested segment, and the exact arrival/departure times);  
* **Speed‑management** (choice of a discrete speed level for every time‑interval on every travelled segment); and  
* **Partial segment blockage** (a time‑window during which the original track is unavailable and the opposite track can be used only with limited capacity).

The model is written in a **compact, linear** form (all constraints are linear, the only non‑linearities that appear in the description – e.g. the product of speed and distance – have been linearised by piece‑wise constant “speed‑level” variables).  

---

## 1. Sets, Indices and Parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains (indexed by *i*). |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of track **segments** (indexed by *s*). Each segment is a physical piece of line between two consecutive stations. |
| **K** = {1,…,K} | Set of **discrete speed levels** (indexed by *k*). Level *k* corresponds to a constant speed  \(v_k\)  (km h⁻¹) and a known energy coefficient  \(e_k\)  (kWh per km). |
| **τ** = {1,…,τ_max} | Set of **time‑interval indices** used to discretise the travel on a segment (indexed by *τ*). The length of each interval is Δt (minutes). |
| **B** ⊆ S | Subset of segments that are **blocked** for a known time window \([t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}},t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}}]\). |
| **O** ⊆ S | Subset of segments that are the **opposite track** (available only when the original is blocked). |
| **N_i** ⊆ S | Ordered list of segments that train *i* must traverse if it follows its **original route** (the “normal” direction). |
| **N_i^{\text{opp}}** ⊆ S | Ordered list of segments for train *i* if it uses the **opposite track** (reverse direction on the blocked segment). |
| **d_{s}** | Physical length of segment *s* (km). |
| **v_{\max}, v_{\min}** | Global maximum/minimum admissible speeds (km h⁻¹). |
| **a_{\max}, a_{\min}** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻²). |
| **h** | Safety headway time (minutes) that must separate two trains on the same segment. |
| **\(\underline{w}_i\)** | Minimum dwell (stop) time of train *i* at any station (minutes). |
| **\(\alpha_i\)** | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (e.g. passenger importance). |
| **\(\beta\)** | Global weight of the energy‑consumption part of the objective. |
| **\(\hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s)\)** | **Nominal** (undelayed) arrival time of train *i* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (computed from the timetable). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10⁶ minutes). |

---

## 2. Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **\(x_i \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | Route choice of train *i*: 0 = original route, 1 = opposite‑track (detour) when the blocked segment is used. |
| **\(y_{i,s,\tau,k} \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | Speed‑level selection: 1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* during interval *τ* with speed level *k*. |
| **\(a_{i,s} \ge 0\)** | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *i* at the upstream end of segment *s*. |
| **\(d_{i,s} \ge 0\)** | continuous | **Departure time** of train *i* from the downstream end of segment *s* (i.e. after finishing the segment). |
| **\(z_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}\)** | binary | **Ordering** on a shared segment *s*: 1 if train *i* passes *s* **before** train *j* (i.e. *i* departs before *j* arrives). Defined only for pairs \((i,j)\) that may use the same segment. |
| **\(E\)** | continuous | Total **energy consumption** (kWh) of all trains (used in the objective). |

---

## 3. Linearised Relations  

### 3.1. Exactly one speed level per interval  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train } i \text{ uses segment } s \text{ during interval } \tau,\\
0 & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

To enforce the “otherwise’’ case we introduce an auxiliary binary **\(u_{i,s,\tau}\)** that indicates whether train *i* occupies segment *s* in interval *τ*:

\[
u_{i,s,\tau}= \sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k}\qquad\forall i,s,\tau .
\tag{2}
\]

### 3.2. Travel‑time on a segment  

The travel time contributed by interval *τ* is Δt (the discretisation step). Hence the **total travel time** of train *i* on segment *s* is

\[
d_{i,s} - a_{i,s}= \Delta t \sum_{\tau\in\tau} u_{i,s,\tau}.
\tag{3}
\]

Because each interval can be used at most once, (3) is linear.

### 3.3. Speed‑level feasibility (speed limits & acceleration)  

For each speed level *k* we know the corresponding speed \(v_k\). The **minimum** time needed to travel segment *s* at level *k* is \(t_{s,k}= d_s / v_k\). Since we discretise time, we enforce a **lower bound** on the number of intervals that must be selected when a high speed is chosen:

\[
\Delta t \sum_{\tau} u_{i,s,\tau} \;\ge\; \frac{d_s}{v_{\max}} \qquad\forall i,s,
\tag{4a}
\]

\[
\Delta t \sum_{\tau} u_{i,s,\tau} \;\le\; \frac{d_s}{v_{\min}} \qquad\forall i,s.
\tag{4b}
\]

If a more detailed piece‑wise linear acceleration model is required, we can add constraints linking consecutive intervals:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau-1,k}
\le a_{\max}\,\Delta t,
\qquad\forall i,s,\tau>1,
\tag{5}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau-1,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\, y_{i,s,\tau,k}
\le |a_{\min}|\,\Delta t,
\qquad\forall i,s,\tau>1.
\tag{6}
\]

Both (5) and (6) are linear because the speed variables are binary.

### 3.4. Route‑choice linking  

If the blocked segment *b* ∈ B is traversed, the train must decide whether to stay on the original track (possible only **outside** the blockage window) or to use the opposite track. This is modelled by the binary \(x_i\):

\[
a_{i,b} \ge t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{start}} - M\,(1-x_i),
\tag{7a}
\]

\[
a_{i,b} \le t^{\text{blk}}_{\text{end}} + M\,x_i .
\tag{7b}
\]

Thus, when \(x_i=0\) (original route) the arrival at the blocked segment must be **outside** the blocked window; when \(x_i=1\) the train is forced to use the opposite‑track list \(N_i^{\text{opp}}\) (see next).

### 3.5. Flow conservation (temporal continuity)  

For any train *i* and any two consecutive segments *s* and *s′* on the **chosen** route we must have

\[
a_{i,s'} = d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i \quad\text{if } s' \text{ is the downstream neighbour of } s .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the route depends on \(x_i\), we write (8) for both possibilities and activate the appropriate one with a big‑M:

\[
a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i - M\,x_i,
\qquad
a_{i,s'} \le d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i + M\,x_i,
\quad \forall (s,s')\in N_i .
\tag{9a}
\]

\[
a_{i,s'} \ge d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i - M\,(1-x_i),
\qquad
a_{i,s'} \le d_{i,s} + \underline{w}_i + M\,(1-x_i),
\quad \forall (s,s')\in N_i^{\text{opp}} .
\tag{9b}
\]

Thus only the segment‑pair belonging to the selected route is enforced.

### 3.6. Safety headway on a shared segment  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that may occupy the **same** physical segment *s* (whether original or opposite). The binary ordering variable \(z_{i,j,s}\) decides who goes first:

\[
a_{j,s} \ge d_{i,s} + h - M\,(1- z_{i,j,s}),
\qquad
a_{i,s} \ge d_{j,s} + h - M\,z_{i,j,s},
\tag{10}
\]

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S \text{ that both use}.
\tag{11}
\]

If a pair never uses the same segment, the corresponding \(z\) variables can be omitted.

### 3.7. Capacity of the opposite track  

The opposite track can host **at most one** train at any instant. Using the interval‑level occupancy variables we write:

\[
\sum_{i\in T} \sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,\tau,k} \le 1,
\qquad\forall s\in O,\;\forall \tau .
\tag{12}
\]

(If the opposite track is a single‑track line, the same constraint also applies to the original track when it is not blocked.)

### 3.8. Energy consumption  

Energy for a train on a segment is approximated linearly by the chosen speed level:

\[
E = \sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{\tau\in\tau}\sum_{k\in K}
e_k \, d_s \, y_{i,s,\tau,k}.
\tag{13}
\]

Because \(d_s\) is constant, (13) is linear.

### 3.9. Delay calculation (used in the objective)  

The **delay** of train *i* at its final destination (last segment \(s^{\text{last}}_i\)) is

\[
\text{delay}_i = a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i} - \hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i) .
\tag{14}
\]

If a penalty for intermediate stations is required, the same expression can be summed over all stations.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

We minimise a **weighted sum** of total passenger delay and total energy consumption:

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T} \alpha_i \,
\bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i} - \hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i)\bigr)}_{\text{Total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta \, E}_{\text{Total energy cost}}
}
\tag{15}
\]

All terms are linear in the decision variables (the delay term uses the arrival‑time variables, the energy term uses (13)).

---

## 5. Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T}\alpha_i\bigl(a_{i,s^{\text{last}}_i}-\hat{t}_{i}^{\text{arr}}(s^{\text{last}}_i)\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i,s,\tau,k} e_k d_s\, y_{i,s,\tau,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(14)   (all constraints listed above)} \\[2pt]
& x_i\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,s,\tau,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{i,s,\tau}\in\{0,1\},\\
& z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; a_{i,s}\ge0,\; d_{i,s}\ge0,\; E\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements  

| Element | What it does in the real world |
|---------|--------------------------------|
| **Binary route choice \(x_i\)** | Decides whether a train detours onto the opposite track when its normal track is blocked. |
| **Speed‑level binaries \(y_{i,s,\tau,k}\)** | Choose a discrete speed (hence a discrete energy consumption) for each train on each segment and each time‑slot. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s}, d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the exact schedule after rescheduling; they are the primary variables that encode delays. |
| **Ordering binaries \(z_{i,j,s}\)** | Enforce a safe temporal order on any segment that can be occupied by more than one train (headway constraint). |
| **Capacity constraint (12)** | Guarantees that the opposite track (single‑track line) never hosts two trains simultaneously. |
| **Energy expression (13)** | Provides a linear approximation of the physical energy needed, proportional to speed level and distance. |
| **Delay objective (15)** | Penalises late arrivals (weighted by train importance) while also rewarding low‑energy operation. |
| **Flow‑conservation (8–9)** | Guarantees that a train’s departure from one segment becomes the arrival at the next, plus the mandatory dwell time. |
| **Speed‑limit & acceleration constraints (4–6)** | Keep the chosen speed levels feasible with respect to physical limits of the rolling stock. |
| **Blockage‑window constraints (7)** | Prevent a train from entering the blocked segment during the disruption unless it uses the opposite track. |
| **Safety headway (10–11)** | Guarantees a minimum time gap *h* between any two consecutive trains on the same piece of rail. |

---

### Remarks on Practical Use  

* **Discretisation** – The choice of Δt (e.g., 1 min) and the number of speed levels K (e.g., 3–5) determines model size. Typical railway MILPs with a few hundred trains and a few hundred segments are solvable with commercial solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi) within minutes.  
* **Big‑M values** – M must be larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes). Tightening M (using the known latest possible arrival) improves solver performance.  
* **Extensions** – Additional realistic features (e.g., crew‑change windows, platform capacity, variable dwell times) can be added by extra linear constraints without changing the MILP nature.  

---

**In summary**, the formulation above provides a **complete linear MILP** that simultaneously decides (i) which route each train should take around a blocked segment, (ii) the order in which trains occupy the shared track, (iii) the exact timing of arrivals/departures, and (iv) the discrete speed level for each train‑segment‑interval, while minimising a weighted combination of total delay and energy consumption. The model respects all operational constraints listed in the problem description.

**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for the integrated Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockages**

---

### 1. Sets, indices and parameters  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | set of trains (index *i*) |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | set of track segments (index *s*) |
| **K** = {1,…,K} | set of discrete speed levels (index *k*) |
| **τ** = {1,…,τmax} | set of time‑interval indices for a segment (index *τ*) |
| **B** ⊆ S | segments that are **blocked** during a known window \([t^{blk}_{start},t^{blk}_{end}]\) |
| **O** ⊆ S | segments that are the **opposite track** (available only when the original is blocked) |
| **N_i** | ordered list of segments of the **original route** of train *i* |
| **N_i^{opp}** | ordered list of segments of the **detour route** (opposite track) of train *i* |
| **d_s** | length of segment *s* (km) |
| **v_k** | speed associated with level *k* (km h⁻¹) |
| **e_k** | energy coefficient of level *k* (kWh per km) |
| **Δt** | length of a discretisation interval (minutes) |
| **v_max , v_min** | global speed limits (km h⁻¹) |
| **a_max , a_min** | max acceleration / deceleration (km h⁻²) |
| **h** | safety headway (minutes) |
| **\underline w_i** | minimum dwell time of train *i* at any station (minutes) |
| **α_i** | weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective |
| **β** | weight of the energy‑consumption part of the objective |
| **\hat t_i^{arr}(s)** | nominal (undelayed) arrival time of train *i* at the upstream end of segment *s* |
| **M** | big‑M constant (≥ any feasible time, e.g. 10⁶) |

---

### 2. Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| **x_i ∈ {0,1}** | binary | route choice of train *i*: 0 = original route, 1 = opposite‑track detour |
| **y_{i,s,τ,k} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | speed‑level selection: 1 if train *i* traverses segment *s* in interval *τ* with speed level *k* |
| **u_{i,s,τ} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | occupancy of train *i* on segment *s* during interval *τ* ( \(u_{i,s,τ}=∑_k y_{i,s,τ,k}\) ) |
| **a_{i,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | arrival time of train *i* at the upstream end of segment *s* |
| **d_{i,s} ≥ 0** | continuous | departure time of train *i* from the downstream end of segment *s* |
| **z_{i,j,s} ∈ {0,1}** | binary | ordering on shared segment *s*: 1 if train *i* passes *s* before train *j* |
| **E ≥ 0** | continuous | total energy consumption (kWh) |

---

### 3. Model constraints  

#### 3.1. Exactly one speed level per occupied interval  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,τ,k}=u_{i,s,τ}\qquad\forall i\in T,\;s\in S,\;τ\in τ .
\tag{1}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,τ,k}\le 1\qquad\forall i,s,τ .
\tag{2}
\]

#### 3.2. Travel time on a segment  

\[
d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}=Δt\sum_{τ\in τ} u_{i,s,τ}\qquad\forall i,s .
\tag{3}
\]

#### 3.3. Speed‑limit and acceleration (piece‑wise linear)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{i,s,τ,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{i,s,τ-1,k}
\le a_{\max}Δt\qquad\forall i,s,τ>1 .
\tag{4}
\]

\[
\sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{i,s,τ-1,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,y_{i,s,τ,k}
\le |a_{\min}|Δt\qquad\forall i,s,τ>1 .
\tag{5}
\]

(If a simpler model is sufficient, constraints (4)–(5) can be omitted and only (3) together with the bounds (6) below are kept.)

\[
Δt\sum_{τ}u_{i,s,τ}\ge \frac{d_s}{v_{\max}},\qquad
Δt\sum_{τ}u_{i,s,τ}\le \frac{d_s}{v_{\min}}
\qquad\forall i,s .
\tag{6}
\]

#### 3.4. Route‑choice and blockage window  

For every blocked segment \(b\in B\):

\[
a_{i,b}\ge t^{blk}_{start}-M(1-x_i),\qquad
a_{i,b}\le t^{blk}_{end}+Mx_i\qquad\forall i .
\tag{7}
\]

Thus, if \(x_i=0\) the train may enter the blocked segment only **outside** the disruption window; if \(x_i=1\) it must use the opposite‑track route.

For any consecutive pair \((s,s')\) on the **original** route \(N_i\):

\[
a_{i,s'}\ge d_{i,s}+ \underline w_i - Mx_i,\qquad
a_{i,s'}\le d_{i,s}+ \underline w_i + Mx_i .
\tag{8a}
\]

For any consecutive pair on the **detour** route \(N_i^{opp}\):

\[
a_{i,s'}\ge d_{i,s}+ \underline w_i - M(1-x_i),\qquad
a_{i,s'}\le d_{i,s}+ \underline w_i + M(1-x_i) .
\tag{8b}
\]

Only the constraints belonging to the chosen route are active.

#### 3.6. Safety headway on a shared segment  

For every unordered pair \((i,j)\) that may use the same segment *s*:

\[
a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+h-M(1-z_{i,j,s}),\qquad
a_{i,s}\ge d_{j,s}+h-Mz_{i,j,s},
\tag{9}
\]

\[
z_{i,j,s}+z_{j,i,s}=1\qquad\forall i<j,\;s\text{ shared}.
\tag{10}
\]

#### 3.7. Capacity of the opposite track (single‑track)  

\[
\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{k\in K} y_{i,s,τ,k}\le 1\qquad\forall s\in O,\;τ\in τ .
\tag{11}
\]

(If the original track is also single‑track when not blocked, the same constraint is added for \(s\notin B\).)

#### 3.8. Energy consumption  

\[
E=\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{τ\in τ}\sum_{k\in K}
e_k\,d_s\,y_{i,s,τ,k}.
\tag{12}
\]

#### 3.9. Delay definition (used in the objective)  

Let \(s_i^{last}\) be the last segment of train *i* (according to the selected route).  

\[
\text{delay}_i = a_{i,s_i^{last}}-\hat t_i^{arr}(s_i^{last})\qquad\forall i .
\tag{13}
\]

---

### 4. Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in T}\alpha_i\,
\bigl(a_{i,s_i^{last}}-\hat t_i^{arr}(s_i^{last})\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\beta\,E}_{\text{total energy cost}}
}
\tag{14}
\]

Both terms are linear in the decision variables.

---

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& \sum_{i\in T}\alpha_i\bigl(a_{i,s_i^{last}}-\hat t_i^{arr}(s_i^{last})\bigr)
      +\beta\sum_{i,s,τ,k} e_k d_s\,y_{i,s,τ,k} \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(1)–(13)   (all constraints listed above)} \\[2pt]
& x_i\in\{0,1\},\; y_{i,s,τ,k}\in\{0,1\},\; u_{i,s,τ}\in\{0,1\},\\
& z_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\; a_{i,s}\ge0,\; d_{i,s}\ge0,\; E\ge0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6. Remarks & modelling assumptions  

* **Discretisation** – Δt (e.g., 1 min) and the number of speed levels K (e.g., 3–5) determine model size; the formulation remains linear for any choice.  
* **Big‑M** – M must be larger than the planning horizon (e.g., 24 h expressed in minutes). Tightening M improves solver performance.  
* **Energy linearisation** – Energy is approximated by a constant coefficient per speed level; this yields a linear term while still capturing the trade‑off between fast (high‑energy) and slow (low‑energy) operation.  
* **Bidirectional conflict** – The ordering variables \(z_{i,j,s}\) together with the headway constraint (9) guarantee a conflict‑free timetable on the shared track, even when trains travel in opposite directions on the opposite track.  
* **Scalability** – The model can be solved directly with commercial MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) for medium‑size instances; for larger instances a decomposition (IP master + train‑plan sub‑problems) can be applied, as described in the source paper.  

---

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

* **Objective** – weighted sum of total delay and total energy.  
* **Constraints** – route‑choice, blockage, flow continuity, speed limits, travel‑time‑speed coupling, dwell‑time, capacity/conflict, energy calculation and linking of arrival/departure times.

The model is fully linear; the quadratic term `v²` in the energy expression is **linearised with a piece‑wise (McCormick) approximation** using auxiliary variables `z[i,s,t]`.  If you have a solver that accepts quadratic objectives you can replace the linearisation by a true quadratic term.

## 1.  Install required packages  

```bash
pip install pulp numpy
```

---

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

"""
MILP model for integrated train rescheduling and speed management
under partial segment blockage.

Author:  <your name>
Date:    2024‑06‑XX
"""

import pulp
import numpy as np

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. INPUT DATA
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Sets ---------------------------------------------------------------
I = ['T1', 'T2', 'T3']                     # trains
S = ['S1', 'S2', 'S3', 'S4']               # track segments
T = list(range(0, 61))                    # time periods (e.g. 0 … 60 minutes)
# For each train i, a list of feasible routes (each route is an ordered list of segments)
R = {
    'T1': {'r1': ['S1', 'S2', 'S3'],
           'r2': ['S1', 'S4', 'S3']},
    'T2': {'r1': ['S2', 'S3'],
           'r2': ['S2', 'S4']},
    'T3': {'r1': ['S3', 'S4'],
           'r2': ['S1', 'S3', 'S4']}
}

# Parameters ---------------------------------------------------------
# scheduled arrival times at the destination (in minutes)
scheduled_arr = {'T1': 30, 'T2': 35, 'T3': 40}

# length of each segment (km)
length = {'S1': 10, 'S2': 8, 'S3': 12, 'S4': 7}

# speed limits (km/min) – same for all trains, can be made train‑specific
v_min = 0.2
v_max = 0.6

# dwell time required at the terminal (minutes)
dwell_time = 2

# blockage windows: for each segment a set of forbidden time periods
# (example: S2 blocked from t=20 to t=30)
blocked = {
    'S1': set(),
    'S2': set(range(20, 31)),
    'S3': set(),
    'S4': set(range(45, 51))
}

# capacity of a segment (1 = single track, >1 for multiple tracks)
capacity = {s: 1 for s in S}

# Energy coefficient α (kWh per (km/min)^2 per minute)
alpha = 0.05

# Weights in the objective
w_delay = 1.0
w_energy = 1.0

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. MODEL DEFINITION
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = pulp.LpProblem("Train_Rescheduling_and_Speed_Management", pulp.LpMinimize)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. VARIABLES
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Route‑selection binary x[i,r]
x = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("x", ((i, r) for i in I for r in R[i]), lowBound=0, upBound=1, cat='Binary')

# Occupancy binary y[i,s,t]  (train i occupies segment s at time t)
y = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("y", ((i, s, t) for i in I for s in S for t in T),
                         lowBound=0, upBound=1, cat='Binary')

# Speed continuous v[i,s,t] (km/min) – defined only when y=1, otherwise forced to 0
v = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("v", ((i, s, t) for i in I for s in S for t in T),
                         lowBound=v_min, upBound=v_max, cat='Continuous')

# Linearisation of v^2 : z[i,s,t] ≈ v[i,s,t]^2
z = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("z", ((i, s, t) for i in I for s in S for t in T),
                         lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')

# Arrival and departure times at the destination (continuous)
a = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("a", I, lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')
d = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("d", I, lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')

# Energy consumption per train (continuous)
e = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("e", I, lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. OBJECTIVE
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

model += ( w_delay * pulp.lpSum( a[i] - scheduled_arr[i] for i in I )
           + w_energy * pulp.lpSum( e[i] for i in I ) ), "Weighted_Total_Delay_+_Energy"

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. CONSTRAINTS
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5.1  Each train selects exactly one feasible route
for i in I:
    model += pulp.lpSum( x[i, r] for r in R[i] ) == 1, f"OneRoute_{i}"

# 5.2  Occupancy only allowed on the chosen route
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        # is segment s part of any feasible route of train i?
        routes_using_s = [r for r in R[i] if s in R[i][r]]
        if routes_using_s:
            model += ( pulp.lpSum( y[i, s, t] for t in T )
                       <= pulp.lpSum( x[i, r] for r in routes_using_s ) * len(T) ), f"OccupancyOnChosenRoute_{i}_{s}"
        else:
            # segment never used → y must be zero
            for t in T:
                model += y[i, s, t] == 0, f"NeverUsed_{i}_{s}_{t}"

# 5.3  Blockage windows: no occupancy when segment is blocked
for s in S:
    for t in blocked[s]:
        for i in I:
            model += y[i, s, t] == 0, f"Blockage_{i}_{s}_{t}"

# 5.4  Capacity / conflict avoidance (single‑track assumption)
for s in S:
    for t in T:
        model += pulp.lpSum( y[i, s, t] for i in I ) <= capacity[s], f"Capacity_{s}_{t}"

# 5.5  Bidirectional conflict – if a segment can be travelled in both directions,
#       the same capacity constraint already enforces mutual exclusion.
#       (If you have explicit direction sets, add an extra constraint here.)

# 5.6  Speed limits – already enforced by variable bounds.
#       Additionally force v = 0 when the segment is not occupied:
M_big = v_max   # because v ≤ v_max, we can use M = v_max
for i in I:

        for t in T:
            model += v[i, s, t] <= M_big * y[i, s, t], f"SpeedZeroIfNotOccupied_ub_{i}_{s}_{t}"

#       length[s] * y[i,s,t] = v[i,s,t]   (because when occupied for one period,
#       distance covered = speed * 1)
#       However a train may stay on a segment for several periods.
#       We enforce that the *total* time spent on a segment equals length / speed.
#       This is linearised with a big‑M formulation:
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        # total time spent on segment s by train i
        total_time = pulp.lpSum( y[i, s, t] for t in T )

        avg_speed = pulp.lpSum( v[i, s, t] for t in T ) / total_time if total_time != 0 else 0
        # Instead of a non‑linear equality we use:
        # length[s] <= v_max * total_time   (feasibility)
        # length[s] >= v_min * total_time   (feasibility)
        # and a tighter equality via a linearised product:
        model += length[s] <= v_max * total_time, f"TravelTimeUpper_{i}_{s}"
        model += length[s] >= v_min * total_time, f"TravelTimeLower_{i}_{s}"

# 5.8  Flow continuity – a train can be on at most one segment at a time
for i in I:
    for t in T:
        model += pulp.lpSum( y[i, s, t] for s in S ) <= 1, f"OneSegmentAtATime_{i}_{t}"

# 5.9  Dwell time at the terminal (arrival = a[i], departure = d[i])
#       The train must occupy the *last* segment of its chosen route for at least dwell_time periods.
#       First we need to identify the terminal segment for each (i,r):
terminal_segment = {}
for i in I:
    terminal_segment[i] = {}
    for r, seglist in R[i].items():
        terminal_segment[i][r] = seglist[-1]

# Enforce dwell time:
for i in I:
    for r in R[i]:
        term = terminal_segment[i][r]
        # Sum of occupancy on terminal segment when route r is chosen
        model += ( pulp.lpSum( y[i, term, t] for t in T )
                   >= dwell_time * x[i, r] ), f"DwellTime_{i}_{r}"

# 5.10  Linking arrival/departure times with occupancy
#       Arrival time a[i] = first time index when train i occupies its terminal segment
#       Departure time d[i] = a[i] + dwell_time
#       Because of discretisation we linearise with big‑M:
M_time = max(T) + 1
for i in I:
    # auxiliary binary indicating whether train i has already arrived by time t
    arrived = pulp.LpVariable.dicts(f"arrived_{i}", T, lowBound=0, upBound=1, cat='Binary')
    for t in T:
        # arrived[t] = 1  ⇒  there exists some τ ≤ t with occupancy on terminal segment

        model += arrived[t] >= pulp.lpSum( y[i, s, tau]
                                          for s in term_segments
                                          for tau in range(0, t+1) ) / len(term_segments) / (t+1), f"ArrivedDef_{i}_{t}"

    model += d[i] == a[i] + dwell_time, f"DepartureTime_{i}"

#       e_i = Σ α * v_{i,s,t}^2 * y_{i,s,t}
#       We approximate v^2 with auxiliary variable z and McCormick envelopes.
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        for t in T:
            # z ≤ v_max * v
            model += z[i, s, t] >= v_min * v[i, s, t], f"McCormick1_{i}_{s}_{t}"
            model += z[i, s, t] >= v[i, s, t] * v_min, f"McCormick2_{i}_{s}_{t}"
            model += z[i, s, t] <= v_max * v[i, s, t], f"McCormick3_{i}_{s}_{t}"
            model += z[i, s, t] <= v[i, s, t] * v_max, f"McCormick4_{i}_{s}_{t}"

            model += z[i, s, t] <= v_max * y[i, s, t], f"ZZeroIfNotOccupied_ub_{i}_{s}_{t}"
            model += z[i, s, t] >= 0, f"ZNonNeg_{i}_{s}_{t}"
