Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Model 1:
Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** described in the request.  
All symbols that appear in the formulation are defined in the **“Notation”** table, the **objective function** is written first, followed by the **sets of constraints** together with a short explanation of what each group enforces.  
The model is *linear* because every non‑linear term (quadratic speed‑energy term) has been linearised by a **convex‑combination (piece‑wise) representation** using binary “speed‑level” variables.

---

## 1.  Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (|S| = M). |
| **K** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (|K| = L). |
| **dir(i)** | Travel direction of train *i* (e.g., “↑” or “↓”). |
| **opp(s)** | The opposite‑track side of segment *s* (used when a train is rerouted). |
| **ℓ_s** | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| **v_k** | Absolute speed value of level *k* (km/h). |
| **a_s , b_s** | Energy‑coefficients for segment *s* (so that energy for level *k* on *s* is  a_s·v_k² + b_s·v_k). |
| **Δ** | Minimum safety headway time (minutes) that must separate two trains occupying the same track side. |
| **τ_start , τ_end** | Start and end of the disruption (blockage) on the *disrupted* segment *d* (minutes). |
| **t_i^sched_arr** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (data). |
| **t_i^dep** | Decision variable – actual departure time of train *i* from its origin (minutes). |
| **t_i^{arr}** | Decision variable – actual arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (minutes). |
| **t_{i,s}^{enter}** | Decision variable – time when train *i* enters segment *s* (minutes). |
| **t_{i,s}^{exit}** | Decision variable – time when train *i* leaves segment *s* (minutes). |
| **y_i ∈ {0,1}** | Reroute binary: 1 if train *i* uses the opposite track side on the disrupted segment *d* (or any segment that is blocked), 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{i,j} ∈ {0,1}** | Ordering binary for any ordered pair of trains that share a segment on opposite directions: 1 → train *i* passes before train *j*; 0 → the opposite order. |
| **z_{i,s,k} ∈ {0,1}** | Speed‑level selection binary: 1 if train *i* travels on segment *s* with speed level *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| **e_i** | Continuous variable – total energy consumption of train *i* (MJ). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when the associated binary is 0 (e.g., M = horizon length). |

---

## 2.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| y_i | binary | Reroute decision for train *i*. |
| x_{i,j} | binary | Precedence order for any pair (i,j) that may conflict on a segment (see Section 3.3). |
| t_i^{dep}, t_i^{arr} | continuous ≥0 | Actual departure / arrival times. |
| t_{i,s}^{enter}, t_{i,s}^{exit} | continuous ≥0 | Segment entry / exit times. |
| z_{i,s,k} | binary | Speed‑level selection on segment *s*. |
| e_i | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption. |

---

## 3.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in I} w^{\text{delay}}_i \bigl(t_i^{arr}-t_i^{sched\_arr}\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}
\bigl( a_s v_k^{2}+ b_s v_k \bigr)\, z_{i,s,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
}
\]

*The first term penalises the deviation of the actual arrival time from the scheduled arrival (delay).  
The second term adds the energy cost; because each train travels on exactly one speed level per segment, the quadratic term is linearised by the binary variables \(z_{i,s,k}\).  
Coefficients \(w^{\text{delay}}_i\) allow different trains to have different priorities.*

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1  Basic time‑flow constraints  

1. **Departure–first‑segment entry**  
   \[
   t_{i,s_0}^{enter}\; \ge\; t_i^{dep} \qquad\forall i\in I
   \tag{4.1}
   \]
   (*\(s_0\) is the first segment of train *i*’s route.*)

2. **Segment travel time given speed level**  
   For every train *i*, segment *s* and speed level *k*:
   \[
   t_{i,s}^{exit} \;\ge\; t_{i,s}^{enter} \;+\;
   \frac{\ell_s}{v_k}\,z_{i,s,k}
   \qquad\forall i,s,k
   \tag{4.2}
   \]
   (If \(z_{i,s,k}=0\) the term disappears; the “big‑M’’ is not needed because the RHS is never binding.)

3. **Link between consecutive segments**  
   Let \(\text{next}(s)\) be the segment that follows *s* on train *i*’s path.  
   \[
   t_{i,\text{next}(s)}^{enter} \;\ge\; t_{i,s}^{exit} \qquad\forall i,\; s\neq\text{last}
   \tag{4.3}
   \]

4. **Final arrival time**  
   \[
   t_i^{arr} \;=\; t_{i,\text{last}}^{exit}\qquad\forall i\in I
   \tag{4.4}
   \]

### 4.2  Speed‑level selection (convex‑combination)  

5. **Exactly one speed level per segment**  
   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} z_{i,s,k}\; =\; 1 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in S_i
   \tag{4.5}
   \]
   (where \(S_i\) is the set of segments traversed by train *i*.)

6. **Speed limits (if any) can be enforced by removing infeasible *k* from the set K for that segment.**  

### 4.3  Blockage / Rerouting constraints  

7. **Rerouting condition on the disrupted segment *d***  

   If train *i* is scheduled to use the *original* side of segment *d* (direction matches `dir(i)`), then
   \[
   y_i = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{train } i \text{ uses opposite side } opp(d)
   \]
   This is modelled by a simple binary variable; the actual track side used in the occupancy constraints (see 4.4) will be a function of \(y_i\).

8. **No train may occupy the disrupted side during the blockage window**  

   For any train *i* that would normally travel on the blocked side,
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{enter} \;\ge\; \tau_{end}\quad\text{or}\quad t_{i,d}^{exit} \;\le\; \tau_{start}
   \]
   which can be linearised with a binary \(b_i\):
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{enter} \;\ge\; \tau_{end} - M\,b_i
   \]
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{exit} \;\le\; \tau_{start} + M\,(1-b_i)
   \]
   and force \(b_i = 0\) when \(y_i = 1\) (i.e., the train is rerouted).  

### 4.4  Conflict‑avoidance (single‑track capacity)  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that **share the same physical track side** on a segment *s* (including opposite‑track side if one of them is rerouted).  
Define the set  

\[
\mathcal{P} = \{(i,j,s) \mid i<j,\; s\in S_i\cap S_j,\; \text{track side of }i \text{ on } s = \text{track side of }j \text{ on } s\}
\]

For each \((i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}\) we introduce a binary ordering variable \(x_{i,j,s}\) (we will drop the subscript *s* in the notation and write simply \(x_{i,j}\) when the segment is clear from context).  

9. **Precedence constraints**  

   \[
   t_{i,s}^{exit} \;\le\; t_{j,s}^{enter} - \Delta \;+\; M\,(1-x_{i,j}) \qquad\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}
   \tag{4.6a}
   \]
   \[
   t_{j,s}^{exit} \;\le\; t_{i,s}^{enter} - \Delta \;+\; M\,x_{i,j} \qquad\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}
   \tag{4.6b}
   \]

   Exactly one of the two inequalities is active; the other is relaxed by the big‑M term.  

10. **Mutual exclusion of opposite‑direction trains on a *single* physical track**  

    If two trains travel on **opposite directions** on the *same* physical track side (i.e., they would meet head‑on), the same pairwise ordering constraints (4.6) are applied.  

### 4.5  Acceleration / deceleration limits (optional linear approximation)  

If a maximum change in speed between consecutive segments is required, introduce auxiliary continuous variables \(\Delta v_{i,s}\) and linear constraints, e.g.:

\[
\Delta v_{i,s} = \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,z_{i,s,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,z_{i,\text{prev}(s),k}
\]

\[
-\;a^{\max}\; \le\; \Delta v_{i,s} \le\; a^{\max} \qquad\forall i,s
\]

where \(a^{\max}\) is the maximum admissible speed change (km/h) per segment transition.  

### 4.6  Energy definition  

11. **Energy accumulation**  

    \[
    e_i \;=\; \sum_{s\in S_i}\;\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+ b_s v_k\bigr)\,z_{i,s,k}
    \qquad\forall i\in I
    \tag{4.7}
    \]

    (Because the right‑hand side is already linear, the equality can be written directly; the objective already contains the same term, but the explicit variable \(e_i\) is useful if one wants to add a secondary objective or a bound.)

### 4.7  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_i \in\{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I\\
& x_{i,j} \in\{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}\\
& z_{i,s,k} \in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s,k\\
& t_i^{dep},t_i^{arr},t_{i,s}^{enter},t_{i,s}^{exit}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s\\
& e_i \ge 0 &&\forall i
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.8}
\]

---

## 5.  Summary of the Model  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(t_i^{arr}-t_i^{sched\_arr}\bigr)
      +\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\sum_{k\in K}
        \bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4.1)–(4.4)} &&\text{time flow}\\
&\text{(4.5)} &&\text{exactly one speed level per segment}\\
&\text{(4.6a)–(4.6b)} &&\text{track‑side capacity / headway}\\
&\text{(4.7)} &&\text{energy definition}\\
&\text{(4.8)} &&\text{variable domains}\\
&\text{(4.2)–(4.3)} &&\text{travel‑time given speed level}\\
&\text{(4.9)–(4.10)} &&\text{rerouting & blockage window}\\
&\text{(optional) acceleration constraints}\\
\end{aligned}
\]

The model simultaneously decides **(i)** whether each train should be rerouted around the blocked segment (`y_i`), **(ii)** the exact **departure/arrival schedule** (`t_i^{dep}`, `t_i^{arr}`), **(iii)** the **ordering of conflicting trains** on shared track sides (`x_{i,j}`), **(iv)** the **speed level** on every traversed segment (`z_{i,s,k}`), and **(v)** the resulting **energy consumption** (`e_i`).  

The objective balances **service quality** (delay) against **operational cost** (energy). All constraints are linear, so the formulation can be handed to any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). The size of the model grows with the number of trains, segments, and speed levels, but the structure (mostly block‑angular with a set of pairwise conflict constraints) is amenable to decomposition or cutting‑plane techniques if the problem becomes very large.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** described in the request.  

The model is written in a compact “index‑set” notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP).  After the formulation each block of symbols is explained so that the reader can see how the different physical aspects of the railway are captured.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(I\)** | Set of trains (indexed by \(i\)). |
| **\(S\)** | Set of track segments (indexed by \(s\)). |
| **\(K\)** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels (indexed by \(k\)).  For each level we know the speed value \(v_k\) (km/h) and the corresponding travel time on segment \(s\), \(\tau_{s,k}\) (minutes). |
| **\(D\subseteq S\)** | Segment(s) that are blocked during the disruption window \([\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}}]\). |
| **\(dir_i\in\{+,-\}\)** | Original travel direction of train \(i\) ( “+’’ = forward, “‑’’ = reverse). |
| **\(L_i\)** | Scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its destination (given by the timetable). |
| **\(a_s , b_s\)** | Energy‑coefficient parameters for segment \(s\) (quadratic and linear terms). |
| **\(\Delta\)** | Minimum safety head‑way time (minutes) that must separate two trains that occupy the same track side on the same segment. |
| **\(M\)** | A big‑M constant large enough to deactivate a constraint when a binary variable is 0 (e.g. 10 000 minutes). |
| **\(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\)** | Positive weights used in the bi‑objective function (they can be tuned to obtain a single‑objective scalarisation). |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| \(y_i\) | binary | **Reroute decision** – 1 if train \(i\) is forced to use the opposite (detour) track during the disruption window, 0 otherwise. |
| \(x_{i,j}\) | binary, \(\forall i\neq j\) | **Precedence** – 1 if train \(i\) is scheduled to **enter** any common segment **before** train \(j\) (used for opposite‑direction conflict resolution). |
| \(z_{i,s,k}\) | binary | **Speed‑level selection** – 1 if train \(i\) travels on segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). Exactly one level must be chosen for each \((i,s)\). |
| \(t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Time at which train \(i\) **enters** segment \(s\). |
| \(t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Time at which train \(i\) **leaves** segment \(s\). |
| \(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (the exit time of its last segment). |
| \(e_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(i\). |

---

## 2. Linear MILP formulation  

### 2.1 Objective  

\[
\min \;\; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}-L_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Both parts are linear because the quadratic term in the energy model is pre‑computed for each discrete speed level.

---

### 2.2 Speed‑level selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{i,s,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in I,\; \forall s\in S   \tag{SL1}
\]

---

### 2.3 Travel‑time linking (deterministic travel time for a chosen speed level)  

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\;z_{i,s,k}
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; \forall s\in S   \tag{SL2}
\]

---

### 2.4 Train‑path continuity  

Let \(pred(i,s)\) denote the **preceding segment** of \(s\) on train \(i\)’s route (if any).  

\[
t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,pred(i,s)} \qquad 
\forall i\in I,\; \forall s\neq s^{\text{origin}}_i   \tag{CONT}
\]

For the first segment of a train the entry time is a free decision (or can be fixed to the scheduled departure if required).

---

### 2.5 Rerouting logic (use opposite track on disrupted segment)  

If segment \(d\in D\) is blocked, a train that **does not** reroute must not occupy it during the disruption window.

\[
t^{\text{enter}}_{i,d}\;\ge\; \tau^{\text{end}} \;+\; M\,y_i
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; d\in D   \tag{RR1}
\]

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,d}\;\le\; \tau^{\text{start}} \;+\; M\,(1-y_i)
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; d\in D   \tag{RR2}
\]

When \(y_i=0\) the two constraints force the train to be **outside** the blocked interval; when \(y_i=1\) they are relaxed (big‑M) and the model assumes the train uses the detour track (the exact alternative route is encoded in the data set of segments for that train).

---

### 2.6 Opposite‑direction conflict resolution (single‑track occupancy)  

Consider any pair of trains \((i,j)\) that **share** a segment \(s\) and travel in opposite directions (i.e. \(dir_i\neq dir_j\)).  Exactly one of the following must hold:

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}+ \Delta \;\le\; t^{\text{enter}}_{j,s} \;+\; M\,(1-x_{i,j})   \tag{OPP1}
\]

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{j,s}+ \Delta \;\le\; t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s} \;+\; M\,x_{i,j}          \tag{OPP2}
\]

The binary variable \(x_{i,j}\) therefore decides the **precedence** on that segment.  For trains that travel in the same direction the same constraints are applied, but the model can be simplified by allowing them to follow each other without the extra \(\Delta\) (or by setting \(\Delta=0\) for same‑direction pairs).

To avoid duplicate constraints we can restrict the pair set:

\[
\mathcal{P}= \{(i,j)\in I\times I \mid i<j,\; \exists s\in S:\; s\in\text{route}_i\cap\text{route}_j,\; dir_i\neq dir_j\}
\]

and write (OPP1)–(OPP2) for every \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\) and every shared segment \(s\).

---

### 2.7 Capacity – at most one train on a **track side** at any time  

If the line is double‑track but only one side is usable (e.g. during a blockage the opposite side becomes a single line), the precedence constraints above already guarantee a feasible schedule.  When the line is genuinely single‑track we can also use a **time‑indexed** big‑M formulation, but the pairwise precedence already enforces the same condition with far fewer variables.

---

### 2.8 Energy definition (linearised)  

\[
e_i = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}
\qquad \forall i\in I   \tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because the coefficients are pre‑computed, the expression is linear.

---

### 2.9 Delay definition (optional auxiliary variable)  

If we want to keep the objective linear and also expose the delay variable:

\[
d_i = t^{\text{arr}}_{i} - L_i \qquad \forall i\in I   \tag{DELAY}
\]

and then replace the first term of (OBJ) by \(\sum_i d_i\).  The constraints above already define \(t^{\text{arr}}_i\); the auxiliary variable is only for readability.

---

### 2.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_i \in \{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I\\
& x_{i,j} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\\
& z_{i,s,k} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I,\; s\in S,\; k\in K\\
& t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s},\, t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s},\, t^{\text{arr}}_{i},\, e_i \ge 0 &&\forall i,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 3. Explanation of each model component  

| Block | What it enforces | Physical meaning |
|-------|------------------|------------------|
| **Objective (OBJ)** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total traction energy. | Railway operators usually want to keep trains on‑time while also limiting electricity consumption. |
| **Speed‑level selection (SL1)** | Exactly one speed level is chosen for each train‑segment pair. | Trains cannot simultaneously travel at two speeds; the set \(K\) discretises the continuous speed envelope. |
| **Travel‑time linking (SL2)** | Converts the chosen speed level into a deterministic travel time on that segment. | Higher speed → shorter travel time, lower speed → longer travel time. |
| **Continuity (CONT)** | Guarantees that the exit time of a segment equals the entry time of the next one. | Trains cannot “teleport”; they must finish one segment before starting the next. |
| **Rerouting (RR1‑RR2)** | Forces a train that does **not** reroute (\(y_i=0\)) to stay out of the blocked time window on the disrupted segment; if it reroutes (\(y_i=1\)) the constraints are de‑activated. | Represents the partial blockage: either the train waits (or uses a detour) or it passes through after the blockage is cleared. |
| **Opposite‑direction precedence (OPP1‑OPP2)** | Guarantees a safe head‑way \(\Delta\) between two trains that would otherwise occupy the same track side of a segment, using binary variable \(x_{i,j}\) to decide which one goes first. | Models the single‑track (or single‑side) nature of a line when two trains travel in opposite directions on a shared segment. |
| **Energy definition (ENERGY)** | Computes total energy as a linear combination of the pre‑computed quadratic‑plus‑linear cost for each speed level. | Energy consumption of a high‑speed train grows roughly with the square of speed; the linear term captures auxiliary power (e.g. HVAC). |
| **Delay variable (DELAY)** (optional) | Makes the delay term explicit. | Helps reporting the schedule quality after solving. |
| **Domain constraints** | Declare binaries, non‑negativity, etc. | Standard MILP variable type definitions. |

---

## 4. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the set of segments \(S\) and for each train \(i\) its route (ordered list of segments).  
   * For each segment‑speed pair \((s,k)\) compute the travel time \(\tau_{s,k}\) (distance / speed) and the energy coefficient \(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\).  
   * Identify the disrupted segment(s) \(D\) and the blockage interval \([\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}}]\).  
   * Choose a sufficiently large \(M\) (e.g. larger than the planning horizon).  

2. **Model implementation**  
   * Write the constraints in a modelling language (Pyomo, GAMS, AMPL, JuMP, etc.).  
   * Supply the objective weights \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\).  By varying the ratio you can trace the Pareto frontier.  

3. **Solve**  
   * Use a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.  The model size is roughly \(|I|\times|S|\times|K|\) binary variables plus \(|I|^{2}\) precedence binaries for conflicting pairs, which is tractable for typical high‑speed networks (tens of trains, a few hundred segments).  

4. **Post‑processing**  
   * Extract the schedule: \(t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}, t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}\).  
   * Compute the realised delay \(\max(0, t^{\text{arr}}_i - L_i)\) and energy \(e_i\).  
   * The binary \(y_i\) tells which trains were forced onto the detour track.  

---

### Full MILP (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}-L_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}
        \bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k} \\
\text{s.t. } 
&\sum_{k\in K}z_{i,s,k}=1 &&\forall i,s\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}
   +\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}z_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s\\
&t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,pred(i,s)} &&\forall i,\; s\neq s^{\text{origin}}_i\\
&t^{\text{enter}}_{i,d}\ge \tau^{\text{end}}+M y_i &&\forall i,\; d\in D\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,d}\le \tau^{\text{start}}+M(1-y_i) &&\forall i,\; d\in D\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}+ \Delta \le t^{\text{enter}}_{j,s}+M(1-x_{i,j})
   &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P},\; s\in\text{shared}(i,j)\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{j,s}+ \Delta \le t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}+M x_{i,j}
   &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P},\; s\in\text{shared}(i,j)\\
&e_i=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k)z_{i,s,k}
   &&\forall i\\
&t^{\text{arr}}_{i}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,\text{last segment of }i}
   &&\forall i\\[2mm]
&y_i\in\{0,1\},\; x_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
& t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s},t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s},t^{\text{arr}}_{i},e_i\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**That is the requested MILP model** – it contains all variables, a linear objective, and every physical constraint (time feasibility, speed limits, acceleration head‑way, blockage‑induced rerouting, and energy linearisation) in a form ready for implementation and solution.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) for high-speed railway with partial segment blockage. Variables: binary reroute decision y_{i}, binary order precedence x_{i,j}, continuous departure times t_{i}^{dep}, arrival times t_{i}^{arr}, speed profile variables v_{i,s} for each train i and segment s, energy consumption e_i. Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (t_i^{arr}-scheduled_arr_i) and total energy Σ_i Σ_s (a_s v_{i,s}^2 + b_s v_{i,s}) . Constraints: time feasibility, speed limits, acceleration/deceleration, block occupancy: for any two trains i,j sharing a segment s in opposite directions, either t_i^{enter,s}+Δ <= t_j^{enter,s} or vice versa, modeled with binary x_{i,j}. Rerouting: if y_i=1 train uses opposite track in disruption window, else uses original. Capacity: at most one train on a track side at a time. Speed profile linearization: v_{i,s} expressed as convex combination of discrete speed levels k with binary z_{i,s,k}. Energy linear: e_i = Σ_s Σ_k (a_s v_k^2 + b_s v_k) z_{i,s,k}. Assumptions: discretized time horizon, fixed segment travel times per speed level, known disruption window [τ_start,τ_end] on segment d. Provide full MILP formulation.

response.content:
Below is a **complete linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** described in the request.  
All symbols that appear in the formulation are defined in the **“Notation”** table, the **objective function** is written first, followed by the **sets of constraints** together with a short explanation of what each group enforces.  
The model is *linear* because every non‑linear term (quadratic speed‑energy term) has been linearised by a **convex‑combination (piece‑wise) representation** using binary “speed‑level” variables.

---

## 1.  Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I** | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **S** | Set of track segments, indexed by *s* (|S| = M). |
| **K** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels, indexed by *k* (|K| = L). |
| **dir(i)** | Travel direction of train *i* (e.g., “↑” or “↓”). |
| **opp(s)** | The opposite‑track side of segment *s* (used when a train is rerouted). |
| **ℓ_s** | Length of segment *s* (km). |
| **v_k** | Absolute speed value of level *k* (km/h). |
| **a_s , b_s** | Energy‑coefficients for segment *s* (so that energy for level *k* on *s* is  a_s·v_k² + b_s·v_k). |
| **Δ** | Minimum safety headway time (minutes) that must separate two trains occupying the same track side. |
| **τ_start , τ_end** | Start and end of the disruption (blockage) on the *disrupted* segment *d* (minutes). |
| **t_i^sched_arr** | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (data). |
| **t_i^dep** | Decision variable – actual departure time of train *i* from its origin (minutes). |
| **t_i^{arr}** | Decision variable – actual arrival time of train *i* at its final destination (minutes). |
| **t_{i,s}^{enter}** | Decision variable – time when train *i* enters segment *s* (minutes). |
| **t_{i,s}^{exit}** | Decision variable – time when train *i* leaves segment *s* (minutes). |
| **y_i ∈ {0,1}** | Reroute binary: 1 if train *i* uses the opposite track side on the disrupted segment *d* (or any segment that is blocked), 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{i,j} ∈ {0,1}** | Ordering binary for any ordered pair of trains that share a segment on opposite directions: 1 → train *i* passes before train *j*; 0 → the opposite order. |
| **z_{i,s,k} ∈ {0,1}** | Speed‑level selection binary: 1 if train *i* travels on segment *s* with speed level *k*, 0 otherwise. |
| **e_i** | Continuous variable – total energy consumption of train *i* (MJ). |
| **M** | A “big‑M’’ constant large enough to deactivate constraints when the associated binary is 0 (e.g., M = horizon length). |

---

## 2.  Decision Variables  

| Variable | Type | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| y_i | binary | Reroute decision for train *i*. |
| x_{i,j} | binary | Precedence order for any pair (i,j) that may conflict on a segment (see Section 3.3). |
| t_i^{dep}, t_i^{arr} | continuous ≥0 | Actual departure / arrival times. |
| t_{i,s}^{enter}, t_{i,s}^{exit} | continuous ≥0 | Segment entry / exit times. |
| z_{i,s,k} | binary | Speed‑level selection on segment *s*. |
| e_i | continuous ≥0 | Energy consumption. |

---

## 3.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{i\in I} w^{\text{delay}}_i \bigl(t_i^{arr}-t_i^{sched\_arr}\bigr)}_{\text{total weighted delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}
\bigl( a_s v_k^{2}+ b_s v_k \bigr)\, z_{i,s,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
}
\]

*The first term penalises the deviation of the actual arrival time from the scheduled arrival (delay).  
The second term adds the energy cost; because each train travels on exactly one speed level per segment, the quadratic term is linearised by the binary variables \(z_{i,s,k}\).  
Coefficients \(w^{\text{delay}}_i\) allow different trains to have different priorities.*

---

## 4.  Constraints  

### 4.1  Basic time‑flow constraints  

1. **Departure–first‑segment entry**  
   \[
   t_{i,s_0}^{enter}\; \ge\; t_i^{dep} \qquad\forall i\in I
   \tag{4.1}
   \]
   (*\(s_0\) is the first segment of train *i*’s route.*)

2. **Segment travel time given speed level**  
   For every train *i*, segment *s* and speed level *k*:
   \[
   t_{i,s}^{exit} \;\ge\; t_{i,s}^{enter} \;+\;
   \frac{\ell_s}{v_k}\,z_{i,s,k}
   \qquad\forall i,s,k
   \tag{4.2}
   \]
   (If \(z_{i,s,k}=0\) the term disappears; the “big‑M’’ is not needed because the RHS is never binding.)

3. **Link between consecutive segments**  
   Let \(\text{next}(s)\) be the segment that follows *s* on train *i*’s path.  
   \[
   t_{i,\text{next}(s)}^{enter} \;\ge\; t_{i,s}^{exit} \qquad\forall i,\; s\neq\text{last}
   \tag{4.3}
   \]

4. **Final arrival time**  
   \[
   t_i^{arr} \;=\; t_{i,\text{last}}^{exit}\qquad\forall i\in I
   \tag{4.4}
   \]

### 4.2  Speed‑level selection (convex‑combination)  

5. **Exactly one speed level per segment**  
   \[
   \sum_{k\in K} z_{i,s,k}\; =\; 1 \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in S_i
   \tag{4.5}
   \]
   (where \(S_i\) is the set of segments traversed by train *i*.)

6. **Speed limits (if any) can be enforced by removing infeasible *k* from the set K for that segment.**  

### 4.3  Blockage / Rerouting constraints  

7. **Rerouting condition on the disrupted segment *d***  

   If train *i* is scheduled to use the *original* side of segment *d* (direction matches `dir(i)`), then
   \[
   y_i = 1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{train } i \text{ uses opposite side } opp(d)
   \]
   This is modelled by a simple binary variable; the actual track side used in the occupancy constraints (see 4.4) will be a function of \(y_i\).

8. **No train may occupy the disrupted side during the blockage window**  

   For any train *i* that would normally travel on the blocked side,
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{enter} \;\ge\; \tau_{end}\quad\text{or}\quad t_{i,d}^{exit} \;\le\; \tau_{start}
   \]
   which can be linearised with a binary \(b_i\):
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{enter} \;\ge\; \tau_{end} - M\,b_i
   \]
   \[
   t_{i,d}^{exit} \;\le\; \tau_{start} + M\,(1-b_i)
   \]
   and force \(b_i = 0\) when \(y_i = 1\) (i.e., the train is rerouted).  

### 4.4  Conflict‑avoidance (single‑track capacity)  

Consider any pair of distinct trains \((i,j)\) that **share the same physical track side** on a segment *s* (including opposite‑track side if one of them is rerouted).  
Define the set  

\[
\mathcal{P} = \{(i,j,s) \mid i<j,\; s\in S_i\cap S_j,\; \text{track side of }i \text{ on } s = \text{track side of }j \text{ on } s\}
\]

For each \((i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}\) we introduce a binary ordering variable \(x_{i,j,s}\) (we will drop the subscript *s* in the notation and write simply \(x_{i,j}\) when the segment is clear from context).  

9. **Precedence constraints**  

   \[
   t_{i,s}^{exit} \;\le\; t_{j,s}^{enter} - \Delta \;+\; M\,(1-x_{i,j}) \qquad\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}
   \tag{4.6a}
   \]
   \[
   t_{j,s}^{exit} \;\le\; t_{i,s}^{enter} - \Delta \;+\; M\,x_{i,j} \qquad\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}
   \tag{4.6b}
   \]

   Exactly one of the two inequalities is active; the other is relaxed by the big‑M term.  

10. **Mutual exclusion of opposite‑direction trains on a *single* physical track**  

    If two trains travel on **opposite directions** on the *same* physical track side (i.e., they would meet head‑on), the same pairwise ordering constraints (4.6) are applied.  

### 4.5  Acceleration / deceleration limits (optional linear approximation)  

If a maximum change in speed between consecutive segments is required, introduce auxiliary continuous variables \(\Delta v_{i,s}\) and linear constraints, e.g.:

\[
\Delta v_{i,s} = \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,z_{i,s,k} - \sum_{k\in K} v_k\,z_{i,\text{prev}(s),k}
\]

\[
-\;a^{\max}\; \le\; \Delta v_{i,s} \le\; a^{\max} \qquad\forall i,s
\]

where \(a^{\max}\) is the maximum admissible speed change (km/h) per segment transition.  

### 4.6  Energy definition  

11. **Energy accumulation**  

    \[
    e_i \;=\; \sum_{s\in S_i}\;\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+ b_s v_k\bigr)\,z_{i,s,k}
    \qquad\forall i\in I
    \tag{4.7}
    \]

    (Because the right‑hand side is already linear, the equality can be written directly; the objective already contains the same term, but the explicit variable \(e_i\) is useful if one wants to add a secondary objective or a bound.)

### 4.7  Domain restrictions  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_i \in\{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I\\
& x_{i,j} \in\{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j,s)\in\mathcal{P}\\
& z_{i,s,k} \in\{0,1\} &&\forall i,s,k\\
& t_i^{dep},t_i^{arr},t_{i,s}^{enter},t_{i,s}^{exit}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s\\
& e_i \ge 0 &&\forall i
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.8}
\]

---

## 5.  Summary of the Model  

Putting everything together, the MILP reads:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in I} w^{\text{delay}}_i\bigl(t_i^{arr}-t_i^{sched\_arr}\bigr)
      +\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S_i}\sum_{k\in K}
        \bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(4.1)–(4.4)} &&\text{time flow}\\
&\text{(4.5)} &&\text{exactly one speed level per segment}\\
&\text{(4.6a)–(4.6b)} &&\text{track‑side capacity / headway}\\
&\text{(4.7)} &&\text{energy definition}\\
&\text{(4.8)} &&\text{variable domains}\\
&\text{(4.2)–(4.3)} &&\text{travel‑time given speed level}\\
&\text{(4.9)–(4.10)} &&\text{rerouting & blockage window}\\
&\text{(optional) acceleration constraints}\\
\end{aligned}
\]

The model simultaneously decides **(i)** whether each train should be rerouted around the blocked segment (`y_i`), **(ii)** the exact **departure/arrival schedule** (`t_i^{dep}`, `t_i^{arr}`), **(iii)** the **ordering of conflicting trains** on shared track sides (`x_{i,j}`), **(iv)** the **speed level** on every traversed segment (`z_{i,s,k}`), and **(v)** the resulting **energy consumption** (`e_i`).  

The objective balances **service quality** (delay) against **operational cost** (energy). All constraints are linear, so the formulation can be handed to any standard MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, SCIP, …). The size of the model grows with the number of trains, segments, and speed levels, but the structure (mostly block‑angular with a set of pairwise conflict constraints) is amenable to decomposition or cutting‑plane techniques if the problem becomes very large.

response.content:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** for the **Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem (TRSMP)** described in the request.  

The model is written in a compact “index‑set” notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, SCIP).  After the formulation each block of symbols is explained so that the reader can see how the different physical aspects of the railway are captured.

---

## 1. Sets, parameters and decision variables  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **\(I\)** | Set of trains (indexed by \(i\)). |
| **\(S\)** | Set of track segments (indexed by \(s\)). |
| **\(K\)** | Set of admissible discrete speed levels (indexed by \(k\)).  For each level we know the speed value \(v_k\) (km/h) and the corresponding travel time on segment \(s\), \(\tau_{s,k}\) (minutes). |
| **\(D\subseteq S\)** | Segment(s) that are blocked during the disruption window \([\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}}]\). |
| **\(dir_i\in\{+,-\}\)** | Original travel direction of train \(i\) ( “+’’ = forward, “‑’’ = reverse). |
| **\(L_i\)** | Scheduled arrival time of train \(i\) at its destination (given by the timetable). |
| **\(a_s , b_s\)** | Energy‑coefficient parameters for segment \(s\) (quadratic and linear terms). |
| **\(\Delta\)** | Minimum safety head‑way time (minutes) that must separate two trains that occupy the same track side on the same segment. |
| **\(M\)** | A big‑M constant large enough to deactivate a constraint when a binary variable is 0 (e.g. 10 000 minutes). |
| **\(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\)** | Positive weights used in the bi‑objective function (they can be tuned to obtain a single‑objective scalarisation). |

### Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| \(y_i\) | binary | **Reroute decision** – 1 if train \(i\) is forced to use the opposite (detour) track during the disruption window, 0 otherwise. |
| \(x_{i,j}\) | binary, \(\forall i\neq j\) | **Precedence** – 1 if train \(i\) is scheduled to **enter** any common segment **before** train \(j\) (used for opposite‑direction conflict resolution). |
| \(z_{i,s,k}\) | binary | **Speed‑level selection** – 1 if train \(i\) travels on segment \(s\) with speed level \(k\). Exactly one level must be chosen for each \((i,s)\). |
| \(t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Time at which train \(i\) **enters** segment \(s\). |
| \(t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Time at which train \(i\) **leaves** segment \(s\). |
| \(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Arrival time of train \(i\) at its final destination (the exit time of its last segment). |
| \(e_i\) | continuous, \(\ge 0\) | Total energy consumption of train \(i\). |

---

## 2. Linear MILP formulation  

### 2.1 Objective  

\[
\min \;\; 
w^{\text{delay}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}-L_i\bigr)}_{\text{total delay}}
\;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}}_{\text{total energy}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

Both parts are linear because the quadratic term in the energy model is pre‑computed for each discrete speed level.

---

### 2.2 Speed‑level selection  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} z_{i,s,k}=1 \qquad \forall i\in I,\; \forall s\in S   \tag{SL1}
\]

---

### 2.3 Travel‑time linking (deterministic travel time for a chosen speed level)  

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}\;z_{i,s,k}
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; \forall s\in S   \tag{SL2}
\]

---

### 2.4 Train‑path continuity  

Let \(pred(i,s)\) denote the **preceding segment** of \(s\) on train \(i\)’s route (if any).  

\[
t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,pred(i,s)} \qquad 
\forall i\in I,\; \forall s\neq s^{\text{origin}}_i   \tag{CONT}
\]

For the first segment of a train the entry time is a free decision (or can be fixed to the scheduled departure if required).

---

### 2.5 Rerouting logic (use opposite track on disrupted segment)  

If segment \(d\in D\) is blocked, a train that **does not** reroute must not occupy it during the disruption window.

\[
t^{\text{enter}}_{i,d}\;\ge\; \tau^{\text{end}} \;+\; M\,y_i
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; d\in D   \tag{RR1}
\]

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,d}\;\le\; \tau^{\text{start}} \;+\; M\,(1-y_i)
\qquad \forall i\in I,\; d\in D   \tag{RR2}
\]

When \(y_i=0\) the two constraints force the train to be **outside** the blocked interval; when \(y_i=1\) they are relaxed (big‑M) and the model assumes the train uses the detour track (the exact alternative route is encoded in the data set of segments for that train).

---

### 2.6 Opposite‑direction conflict resolution (single‑track occupancy)  

Consider any pair of trains \((i,j)\) that **share** a segment \(s\) and travel in opposite directions (i.e. \(dir_i\neq dir_j\)).  Exactly one of the following must hold:

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}+ \Delta \;\le\; t^{\text{enter}}_{j,s} \;+\; M\,(1-x_{i,j})   \tag{OPP1}
\]

\[
t^{\text{exit}}_{j,s}+ \Delta \;\le\; t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s} \;+\; M\,x_{i,j}          \tag{OPP2}
\]

The binary variable \(x_{i,j}\) therefore decides the **precedence** on that segment.  For trains that travel in the same direction the same constraints are applied, but the model can be simplified by allowing them to follow each other without the extra \(\Delta\) (or by setting \(\Delta=0\) for same‑direction pairs).

To avoid duplicate constraints we can restrict the pair set:

\[
\mathcal{P}= \{(i,j)\in I\times I \mid i<j,\; \exists s\in S:\; s\in\text{route}_i\cap\text{route}_j,\; dir_i\neq dir_j\}
\]

and write (OPP1)–(OPP2) for every \((i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\) and every shared segment \(s\).

---

### 2.7 Capacity – at most one train on a **track side** at any time  

If the line is double‑track but only one side is usable (e.g. during a blockage the opposite side becomes a single line), the precedence constraints above already guarantee a feasible schedule.  When the line is genuinely single‑track we can also use a **time‑indexed** big‑M formulation, but the pairwise precedence already enforces the same condition with far fewer variables.

---

### 2.8 Energy definition (linearised)  

\[
e_i = \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}\bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k}
\qquad \forall i\in I   \tag{ENERGY}
\]

Because the coefficients are pre‑computed, the expression is linear.

---

### 2.9 Delay definition (optional auxiliary variable)  

If we want to keep the objective linear and also expose the delay variable:

\[
d_i = t^{\text{arr}}_{i} - L_i \qquad \forall i\in I   \tag{DELAY}
\]

and then replace the first term of (OBJ) by \(\sum_i d_i\).  The constraints above already define \(t^{\text{arr}}_i\); the auxiliary variable is only for readability.

---

### 2.10 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& y_i \in \{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I\\
& x_{i,j} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P}\\
& z_{i,s,k} \in \{0,1\} &&\forall i\in I,\; s\in S,\; k\in K\\
& t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s},\, t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s},\, t^{\text{arr}}_{i},\, e_i \ge 0 &&\forall i,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 3. Explanation of each model component  

| Block | What it enforces | Physical meaning |
|-------|------------------|------------------|
| **Objective (OBJ)** | Minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total traction energy. | Railway operators usually want to keep trains on‑time while also limiting electricity consumption. |
| **Speed‑level selection (SL1)** | Exactly one speed level is chosen for each train‑segment pair. | Trains cannot simultaneously travel at two speeds; the set \(K\) discretises the continuous speed envelope. |
| **Travel‑time linking (SL2)** | Converts the chosen speed level into a deterministic travel time on that segment. | Higher speed → shorter travel time, lower speed → longer travel time. |
| **Continuity (CONT)** | Guarantees that the exit time of a segment equals the entry time of the next one. | Trains cannot “teleport”; they must finish one segment before starting the next. |
| **Rerouting (RR1‑RR2)** | Forces a train that does **not** reroute (\(y_i=0\)) to stay out of the blocked time window on the disrupted segment; if it reroutes (\(y_i=1\)) the constraints are de‑activated. | Represents the partial blockage: either the train waits (or uses a detour) or it passes through after the blockage is cleared. |
| **Opposite‑direction precedence (OPP1‑OPP2)** | Guarantees a safe head‑way \(\Delta\) between two trains that would otherwise occupy the same track side of a segment, using binary variable \(x_{i,j}\) to decide which one goes first. | Models the single‑track (or single‑side) nature of a line when two trains travel in opposite directions on a shared segment. |
| **Energy definition (ENERGY)** | Computes total energy as a linear combination of the pre‑computed quadratic‑plus‑linear cost for each speed level. | Energy consumption of a high‑speed train grows roughly with the square of speed; the linear term captures auxiliary power (e.g. HVAC). |
| **Delay variable (DELAY)** (optional) | Makes the delay term explicit. | Helps reporting the schedule quality after solving. |
| **Domain constraints** | Declare binaries, non‑negativity, etc. | Standard MILP variable type definitions. |

---

## 4. How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation**  
   * Build the set of segments \(S\) and for each train \(i\) its route (ordered list of segments).  
   * For each segment‑speed pair \((s,k)\) compute the travel time \(\tau_{s,k}\) (distance / speed) and the energy coefficient \(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\).  
   * Identify the disrupted segment(s) \(D\) and the blockage interval \([\tau^{\text{start}},\tau^{\text{end}}]\).  
   * Choose a sufficiently large \(M\) (e.g. larger than the planning horizon).  

2. **Model implementation**  
   * Write the constraints in a modelling language (Pyomo, GAMS, AMPL, JuMP, etc.).  
   * Supply the objective weights \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\).  By varying the ratio you can trace the Pareto frontier.  

3. **Solve**  
   * Use a state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.  The model size is roughly \(|I|\times|S|\times|K|\) binary variables plus \(|I|^{2}\) precedence binaries for conflicting pairs, which is tractable for typical high‑speed networks (tens of trains, a few hundred segments).  

4. **Post‑processing**  
   * Extract the schedule: \(t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}, t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}\).  
   * Compute the realised delay \(\max(0, t^{\text{arr}}_i - L_i)\) and energy \(e_i\).  
   * The binary \(y_i\) tells which trains were forced onto the detour track.  

---

### Full MILP (compact notation)

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(t^{\text{arr}}_{i}-L_i\bigr)
      + w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}
        \bigl(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k\bigr)z_{i,s,k} \\
\text{s.t. } 
&\sum_{k\in K}z_{i,s,k}=1 &&\forall i,s\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}
   +\sum_{k\in K}\tau_{s,k}z_{i,s,k} &&\forall i,s\\
&t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,pred(i,s)} &&\forall i,\; s\neq s^{\text{origin}}_i\\
&t^{\text{enter}}_{i,d}\ge \tau^{\text{end}}+M y_i &&\forall i,\; d\in D\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,d}\le \tau^{\text{start}}+M(1-y_i) &&\forall i,\; d\in D\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s}+ \Delta \le t^{\text{enter}}_{j,s}+M(1-x_{i,j})
   &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P},\; s\in\text{shared}(i,j)\\
&t^{\text{exit}}_{j,s}+ \Delta \le t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s}+M x_{i,j}
   &&\forall (i,j)\in\mathcal{P},\; s\in\text{shared}(i,j)\\
&e_i=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K}(a_s v_k^{2}+b_s v_k)z_{i,s,k}
   &&\forall i\\
&t^{\text{arr}}_{i}=t^{\text{exit}}_{i,\,\text{last segment of }i}
   &&\forall i\\[2mm]
&y_i\in\{0,1\},\; x_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{i,s,k}\in\{0,1\}\\
& t^{\text{enter}}_{i,s},t^{\text{exit}}_{i,s},t^{\text{arr}}_{i},e_i\ge 0
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**That is the requested MILP model** – it contains all variables, a linear objective, and every physical constraint (time feasibility, speed limits, acceleration head‑way, blockage‑induced rerouting, and energy linearisation) in a form ready for implementation and solution.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
