Model 1:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main decisions that appear in the description  

* **Rerouting / sequencing** of trains when a part of the line is blocked,  
* **Speed‑profile selection** for every train on every track segment, and  
* **Timing (arrival, departure, dwell) and energy** for each train.

The model is written in a compact, “linear‑programming‑style’’ notation that can be copied directly into a MILP solver (e.g. CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, CBC) after a short data‑pre‑processing step.  After the formulation, each set, parameter, variable and constraint is explained in plain English.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| \\(T\\) | Set of trains, indexed by \\(t\\). |
| \\(S\\) | Set of track **segments** (the line is divided into consecutive segments).  Index \\(s\\). |
| \\(P\\) | Set of **possible routes** that a train may follow while the blockage is present (each route is a sequence of segments).  Index \\(p\\). |
| \\(K\\) | Set of admissible **speed‑levels** (discrete speed choices) that can be used on a segment, indexed by \\(k\\). |
| \\(B\\subseteq S\\) | Sub‑set of segments that are **blocked** (partial blockage). |
| \\(N_t\\) | Ordered list of **successor trains** that share a common segment with train \\(t\\) (used for conflict‑avoidance).  Index \\(n\\in N_t\\). |
| \\(D\\) | Set of **directions** (e.g. 0 = “north‑bound”, 1 = “south‑bound”).  Index \\(d\\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

All parameters are known data (they are computed from the timetable, the infrastructure geometry and the physics of the rolling stock).

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|--------------|
| \\(L_s\\) | Length of segment \\(s\\) (km). |
| \\(v_{k}\\) | Absolute speed (km/h) associated with speed‑level \\(k\\). |
| \\(c_{k}\\) | Energy consumption per kilometre when travelling at speed level \\(k\\) (kWh/km). |
| \\(t^{\text{min}}_{t,s}\\) | Minimum **travel time** for train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) (if it could run at its maximum admissible speed). |
| \\(t^{\text{max}}_{t,s}\\) | Maximum allowed travel time on segment \\(s\\) (e.g. due to speed limits, signalling). |
| \\(d^{\text{dw}}_{t}\\) | Nominal dwell time required at the scheduled stop of train \\(t\\) (minutes). |
| \\(a^{\text{arr}}_{t}\\) | Original (planned) arrival time of train \\(t\\) at the beginning of its route (minutes from a common zero). |
| \\(M\\) | A “big‑M’’ constant larger than any feasible time (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| \\(w^{\text{delay}}\\) | Weight for total delay in the objective (e.g. 1 € per minute). |
| \\(w^{\text{energy}}\\) | Weight for total energy consumption (e.g., 0.1 € per kWh). |
| \\(R_{t,p}\\) | Binary indicator = 1 if route \\(p\\) is **compatible** with train \\(t\\) (e.g., length, direction). |
| \\(B_{s}=1\\) if segment \\(s\\) belongs to the blocked part, otherwise 0. |
| \\(dir_{t}\\) | Direction of train \\(t\\) (0 or 1). |
| \\(conf_{t,n,s}\\) = 1 if trains \\(t\\) and \\(n\\) would occupy the same segment \\(s\\) at the same time when travelling in opposite directions; 0 otherwise. This is pre‑computed from the network topology. |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \\(x_{t,p}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) **uses route** \\(p\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(y_{t,s,k}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) travels on segment \\(s\\) with speed level \\(k\\); 0 otherwise. |
| \\(a_{t,s}\\) | continuous ≥0 | **Arrival time** of train \\(t\\) at the **up‑stream end** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(d_{t,s}\\) | continuous ≥0 | **Departure time** of train \\(t\\) from the **down‑stream end** of segment \\(s\\). |
| \\(u_{t,s}\\) | continuous ≥0 | **Dwell time** of train \\(t\\) on segment \\(s\\) (non‑zero only for stations). |
| \\(e_{t}\\) | continuous ≥0 | **Total energy consumption** of train \\(t\\) over its whole route. |
| \\(z_{t}\\) | continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train \\(t\\) (difference between actual and planned arrival at its final destination). |
| \\(c_{t,n}\\) | binary | 1 if train \\(t\\) **passes before** train \\(n\\) on a shared segment (used for ordering). |

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\min\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T} z_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T} e_{t}}_{\text{Weighted total energy}}
\]

The model simultaneously reduces passenger‑related delay and the energy used by the fleet.  By changing the weights the planner can explore the trade‑off curve.

---

## 5.  Constraints  

### 5.1  Route‑selection constraints  

1. **Exactly one route per train**  

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t,p}=1 \qquad \forall t\in T
\]

2. **Only compatible routes may be chosen**  

\[
x_{t,p}\le R_{t,p}\qquad \forall t\in T,\;p\in P
\]

3. **Link speed‑level variables to the chosen route** – a train can only travel on segments that belong to its selected route.  
Let \\(\mathcal{S}_{p}\\) be the set of segments that compose route \\(p\\). Then  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\; \le\; \sum_{p\in P:\;s\in\mathcal{S}_{p}} x_{t,p}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If a segment does **not** belong to the chosen route, the right‑hand side is 0, forcing the left‑hand side to 0 (i.e. no speed level can be selected).

### 5.2  Speed‑level selection (one speed per traversed segment)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if train }t\text{ traverses }s\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

The “otherwise’’ case is automatically enforced by the previous link‑constraint.

### 5.3  Time‑propagation (kinematics)  

For every traversed segment the departure time equals arrival time plus travel time (which depends on the selected speed level).  

\[
d_{t,s}= a_{t,s}+ \sum_{k\in K}\frac{L_s}{v_{k}}\,y_{t,s,k}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\]

If a segment is not traversed, the corresponding \\(y\\) variables are zero, and the equality collapses to \\(d_{t,s}=a_{t,s}\\) (no effect).

### 5.4  Dwell‑time definition (stations only)  

Let \\(\mathcal{St}_t\\) be the subset of segments where train \\(t\\) must stop (stations).  

\[
u_{t,s}= d_{t,s}-a_{t,s}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{St}_t
\]

The dwell time must respect the minimum required dwell:

\[
u_{t,s}\ge d^{\text{dw}}_{t}\qquad \forall t\in T,\; s\in\mathcal{St}_t
\]

On non‑station segments \\(u_{t,s}=0\\) automatically because the left‑hand side is not defined (or we can add a big‑M constraint that forces it to zero).

### 5.5  Continuity between consecutive segments  

If segment \\(s\\) is followed by segment \\(s'\\) on the same route, the arrival at \\(s'\\) equals the departure from \\(s\\).  

\[
a_{t,s'} = d_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\in\text{Adj}
\]

where **Adj** is the set of ordered adjacent segment pairs belonging to at least one feasible route.

### 5.6  Blockage feasibility  

A train **cannot** occupy a blocked segment unless it has been rerouted around it. This is already enforced by the route‑selection link, but we also add a direct “big‑M’’ version for safety:

\[
\sum_{k\in K} y_{t,s,k}\le 1- B_{s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\]

If \\(B_{s}=1\\) (blocked), the RHS becomes 0, forbidding any speed‑level on that segment.

### 5.7  Bidirectional conflict (single‑track)  

When two trains travel in opposite directions on the same physical track segment, they must not be on it at the same time.  For every unordered pair \\((t,n)\\) that share a segment \\(s\\) in opposite directions we impose a **disjunctive** ordering using binary variable \\(c_{t,n}\\):

\[
a_{t,s} \ge d_{n,s} - M\;c_{t,n}\qquad
a_{n,s} \ge d_{t,s} - M\;(1-c_{t,n}) \qquad\forall s\in S,\; (t,n)\in N_t
\]

If \\(c_{t,n}=1\\) the first inequality is relaxed (big‑M) and the second forces train \\(t\\) to depart after train \\(n\\) has cleared the segment; the opposite occurs when \\(c_{t,n}=0\\).  The binary variable therefore **orders** the two conflicting trains.

### 5.8  Minimum headway on the same direction  

Even when travelling in the same direction, a safety headway \\(h\\) (minutes) must be respected:

\[
a_{t,s} \ge d_{n,s}+h \qquad \forall (t,n)\in N_t^{\text{sameDir}},\; s\in S
\]

where \\(N_t^{\text{sameDir}}\\) is the set of trains that follow train \\(t\\) on the same line.

### 5.9  Delay calculation  

Let \\(s^{\text{dest}}_t\\) be the last segment of train \\(t\\)’s selected route (the destination). The **total delay** is the difference between the actual arrival at the destination and the originally planned arrival:

\[
z_{t}= a_{t,s^{\text{dest}}_t} - a^{\text{arr}}_{t}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

We also enforce non‑negativity (a train cannot finish earlier than the schedule, unless early‑arrival is allowed – in that case the constraint can be removed or changed to a lower bound).

### 5.10  Energy consumption  

Energy on a segment equals the distance times the per‑km energy factor of the chosen speed level. Summing over all traversed segments yields the total energy for the train:

\[
e_{t}= \sum_{s\in S}\sum_{k\in K} L_s\,c_{k}\; y_{t,s,k}\qquad\forall t\in T
\]

Because both \\(L_s\\) and \\(c_k\\) are data, this expression is linear.

### 5.11  Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& x_{t,p}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\;p\in P\\
& y_{t,s,k}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall t\in T,\;s\in S,\;k\in K\\
& c_{t,n}\in\{0,1\}, &&\forall (t,n)\in N_t\\[2pt]
& a_{t,s}\ge 0,\; d_{t,s}\ge 0,\; u_{t,s}\ge 0,\; e_{t}\ge 0,\; z_{t}\ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

---

## 6.  How the Model Works – Narrative Explanation  

1. **Choose a route** (`x_{t,p}`) for each train.  The route must be compatible with the train’s direction and must avoid the blocked segment(s).  Because the route decides which segments are traversed, the binary variables `y_{t,s,k}` are forced to zero on any segment that does not belong to the selected route.

2. **Pick a speed level** (`y_{t,s,k}`) on every traversed segment.  Only one speed level can be active per segment, and the travel time on that segment is the segment length divided by the chosen speed (`v_k`).  This is a linear relationship because the product `L_s/v_k` is a known constant.

3. **Propagate times** (`a_{t,s}`, `d_{t,s}`).  Arrival at the start of a segment plus the travel time (determined by the speed level) yields the departure from the segment.  The departure of a segment becomes the arrival of the next segment, guaranteeing a feasible schedule.

4. **Add dwell times** at stations (`u_{t,s}`).  The model forces a minimum dwell (`d^{dw}_t`) but can allow longer dwell if the optimisation decides that a longer stop reduces downstream conflicts.

5. **Prevent collisions** on the single‑track portion.  For any two trains that would occupy the same physical segment in opposite directions, the binary ordering variable `c_{t,n}` forces one of the two possible temporal orders.  The same‑direction headway constraint (`h`) guarantees a safety gap.

6. **Respect the blockage**.  The big‑M constraint `∑ y_{t,s,k} ≤ 1‑B_s` guarantees that no train can be assigned a speed on a blocked segment.  If a train’s original timetable would have used that segment, the only way to satisfy the model is to pick a different route (`x_{t,p}`) that bypasses the blocked part.

7. **Compute performance measures**.  
   * **Delay** (`z_t`) is the difference between the actual arrival at the final destination and the originally scheduled arrival.  
   * **Energy** (`e_t`) is a linear sum of per‑kilometre energy consumption for the selected speed levels.

8. **Objective**.  The weighted sum of total delay and total energy (`w^{delay}` and `w^{energy}`) is minimized.  By changing the weights the planner can explore “delay‑only”, “energy‑only”, or balanced policies.

---

## 7.  Remarks & Extensions  

| Issue | Possible Extension |
|-------|---------------------|
| **More than one blocked segment** | The set `B` can contain any number of segments; the same big‑M constraint works for each. |
| **Continuous speed** | If a piecewise‑linear speed‑energy relationship is desired, introduce additional speed‑levels (finer discretisation) or use SOS‑2 variables. |
| **Early‑arrival credit** | Replace `z_t = a_{t,dest} - a^{arr}_t` with `z_t ≥ a_{t,dest} - a^{arr}_t` and allow `z_t` to be negative (or introduce a separate early‑arrival variable). |
| **Capacity of stations** | Add constraints that limit the number of trains simultaneously dwelling at a station. |
| **Rolling‑stock constraints** (e.g., only a limited number of locomotives with a given power rating) | Add a global resource balance using additional binary variables linking trains to locomotives. |
| **Robustness to uncertainty** | Replace deterministic travel times with worst‑case bounds and use a robust optimisation formulation. |

---

### Ready‑to‑Use Skeleton (in a solver‑friendly format)

Below is a compact version that can be pasted into a modelling language such as **AMPL**, **GAMS**, or the **Python‑PuLP / Pyomo** API.  Only the data‑generation part (sets, parameters) has to be filled with the real instance.

```ampl
set T;               # trains
set S;               # segments
set P;               # routes
set K;               # speed levels
set D;               # directions {0,1};

param L{S} > 0;                 # length of segment (km)
param v{K} > 0;                 # speed (km/h)
param c{K} >= 0;                # energy per km (kWh/km)
param B{S} binary;              # 1 if segment blocked
param R{T,P} binary;             # route compatibility
param a0{T} >= 0;                # scheduled arrival at origin
param dw{T} >= 0;                # minimum dwell time (min)
param h >= 0;                    # safety headway (min)
param M  > 0;                    # big-M (large number)
param w_delay >= 0, w_energy >= 0;

var x{T,P} binary;               # route choice
var y{T,S,K} binary;              # speed choice
var a{T,S} >= 0;                  # arrival time
var d{T,S} >= 0;                  # departure time
var u{T,S} >= 0;                  # dwell time
var z{T} >= 0;                    # delay
var e{T} >= 0;                    # energy
var cord{T,T} binary;             # ordering for opposite‑direction conflicts

# 1. one route per train
s.t. one_route{t in T}: sum{p in P} x[t,p] = 1;

# 2. route compatibility
s.t. compat_route{t in T, p in P}: x[t,p] <= R[t,p];

# 3. link speed to route (S_p is the set of segments of route p)
#    (pre‑compute a param seg_of_route[p,s] = 1 if s in route p)
param seg_of_route{P,S} binary;
s.t. speed_route_link{t in T, s in S}:
    sum{k in K} y[t,s,k] <= sum{p in P} seg_of_route[p,s] * x[t,p];

# 4. exactly one speed per traversed segment
s.t. one_speed{t in T, s in S}:
    sum{k in K} y[t,s,k] = sum{p in P} seg_of_route[p,s] * x[t,p];

# 5. travel time propagation
s.t. travel_time{t in T, s in S}:
    d[t,s] = a[t,s] + sum{k in K} (L[s]/v[k]) * y[t,s,k];

# 6. continuity between consecutive segments (Adj is a set of ordered pairs)
set Adj within {S,S};
s.t. continuity{t in T, (s1,s2) in Adj}:
    a[t,s2] = d[t,s1];

# 7. dwell time at stations (St[t] is the set of station segments for train t)
set St{T} within S;
s.t. dwell_def{t in T, s in St[t]}:
    u[t,s] = d[t,s] - a[t,s];
s.t. dwell_min{t in T, s in St[t]}:
    u[t,s] >= dw[t];

# 8. blocked segments cannot be used
s.t. blocked{t in T, s in S: B[s]=1}:
    sum{k in K} y[t,s,k] = 0;

# 9. bidirectional conflict ordering (pre‑compute Conf[t,n,s] = 1 if opposite)
param Conf{T,T,S} binary;
s.t. conflict_order{t in T, n in T, s in S: Conf[t,n,s]=1}:
    a[t,s] >= d[n,s] - M*cord[t,n];
s.t. conflict_order_rev{t in T, n in T, s in S: Conf[t,n,s]=1}:
    a[n,s] >= d[t,s] - M*(1-cord[t,n]);

# 10. same‑direction headway (pre‑compute SameDir[t,n,s]=1 if same direction)
param SameDir{T,T,S} binary;
s.t. headway{t in T, n in T, s in S: SameDir[t,n,s]=1}:
    a[t,s] >= d[n,s] + h;

# 11. delay definition (dest[t] is the last segment of the chosen route)
param dest{T} symbolic;   # will be linked to x[t,p] later
s.t. delay_def{t in T}:
    z[t] = a[t,dest[t]] - a0[t];

# 12. energy calculation
s.t. energy_calc{t in T}:
    e[t] = sum{s in S, k in K} L[s]*c[k] * y[t,s,k];

# 13. objective
minimize obj: w_delay*sum{t in T} z[t] + w_energy*sum{t in T} e[t];
```

*All the “pre‑compute’’ parameters (`seg_of_route`, `Adj`, `Conf`, `SameDir`, `dest`) are pure data that can be generated from the network topology, the list of possible detours around the blocked area, and the original timetable.*

---

### Bottom line  

The formulation above is **linear** (all products involve at most one binary variable) and therefore solvable by any state‑of‑the‑art MILP solver.  It simultaneously decides **where each train goes**, **how fast it travels**, and **when it occupies each piece of track**, while respecting the physics of motion, the safety constraints of a single‑track line, and the presence of a partial blockage.  The weighted objective lets the planner trade off passenger delay against energy consumption, which is exactly the balance required for modern, sustainable railway operations.

Model 2:
Below is a **complete, linear mixed‑integer programming (MILP) model** that captures the three main tasks mentioned in the description  

* **(i) Rerouting / re‑ordering** of trains when a part of the line is blocked,  
* **(ii) Speed‑profile selection** for each train on each free segment, and  
* **(iii) Energy‑aware timing** (arrival, departure and dwell)  

The model is written in a **canonical linear form** (objective = linear, all constraints = linear) and therefore can be handed directly to any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, HiGHS, …).  

---

## 1.  Sets, parameters and notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T**  | Set of trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S**  | Set of track segments (including the blocked one).  Segment *s* has a known length  \(L_s\)  (km). |
| **B ⊂ S** | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the part of the line that cannot be used). |
| **F = S \ B** | Set of *free* (usable) segments. |
| **P**  | Set of admissible **speed‑profile levels** on a free segment, indexed by *p*.  Each level has a constant speed  \(v_{p}\) (km/h) and an associated **energy consumption rate**  \(e_{p}\) (kWh per km). |
| **O**  | Set of admissible **orderings** of trains on a given segment (used for head‑way enforcement).  For a pair of trains \((t,t')\) we write  \(o\in O_{tt'}\)  if *t* is scheduled before *t'* on the same segment. |
| **Δ**  | A large constant (big‑M) that is “larger than any feasible time”.  Typical value: 10 000 s. |

### Fixed data (known before solving)

* \(L_s\) – length of segment *s* (km).  
* \(v^{\max}_t\) – maximum admissible speed of train *t* (km/h).  
* \(v^{\min}_t\) – minimum admissible speed of train *t* (km/h).  
* \(d^{\text{min}}_t\) – minimum dwell time required at stations for train *t* (s).  
* \(a^{\text{max}}_t, a^{\text{min}}_t\) – max / min acceleration (km/h²) – used only to guarantee linear feasibility of speed choices (see Section 4).  
* \(E^{\text{ref}}_t\) – reference (baseline) energy consumption of train *t* on its original schedule (kWh).  
* \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) – positive weights for the two components of the objective (chosen by the planner).  

---

## 2.  Decision variables  

| Variable | Type | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| \(x_{t,s,p} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Speed‑profile selection** – 1 if train *t* traverses free segment *s* with speed level *p*, 0 otherwise. |
| \(r_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Reroute indicator** – 1 if train *t* is allowed to use segment *s* (i.e., *s* is not blocked for *t*).  For blocked segments \(s\in B\) we force \(r_{t,s}=0\). |
| \(y_{t,s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Segment‑usage** – 1 if train *t* actually passes through segment *s* (either the original segment or a detour).  For a feasible schedule we will have \(y_{t,s}=r_{t,s}\). |
| \(z_{tt',s} \in \{0,1\}\) | binary | **Ordering** – 1 if train *t* is scheduled **before** train *t'* on segment *s* (only needed when both trains use the same segment). |
| \(a_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Arrival time** of train *t* at the **up‑stream** end of segment *s* (seconds). |
| \(d_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Departure time** of train *t* from the **down‑stream** end of segment *s* (seconds). |
| \(h_{t,s} \ge 0\) | continuous | **Dwell time** of train *t* on segment *s* (seconds).  For pure running segments \(h_{t,s}=0\); for station segments it is ≥ \(d^{\text{min}}_t\). |
| \(\delta_t \ge 0\) | continuous | **Total delay** of train *t* (seconds) with respect to its original schedule. |
| \(\epsilon_t \ge 0\) | continuous | **Extra energy** of train *t* (kWh) with respect to the reference value. |

---

## 3.  Objective function  

\[
\boxed{
\min\;  w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t
}
\]

*The first term penalises total passenger‑or‑operational delay; the second term penalises any increase in energy consumption caused by speed changes or detours.*

---

## 4.  Core constraints  

### 4.1  Speed‑profile consistency  

For every train *t* and every free segment *s* that the train uses, exactly **one** speed level must be chosen:

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t,s,p}= y_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in F
\tag{C1}
\]

If a segment is blocked for the train, the left‑hand side is forced to zero because \(y_{t,s}=0\).

### 4.2  Speed limits  

The chosen speed level must respect the train’s admissible speed interval:

\[
v^{\min}_t \; y_{t,s}\;\le\; \sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,x_{t,s,p}\;\le\; v^{\max}_t \; y_{t,s}
\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in F
\tag{C2}
\]

(Linear because the left‑hand side is a sum of binary variables multiplied by constants.)

### 4.3  Travel‑time calculation  

Travel time on a free segment equals length divided by the selected speed:

\[
d_{t,s} \;-\; a_{t,s} \;=\; \frac{L_s}{\displaystyle\sum_{p\in P} v_{p}\,x_{t,s,p}} \;+\; h_{t,s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in F
\tag{C3}
\]

The denominator is a *piecewise‑constant* expression because only one \(x_{t,s,p}=1\).  To keep the model linear we replace the fraction by a set of **big‑M linearizations**:

Introduce auxiliary continuous variable \(\tau_{t,s}\) (travel time on *s*) and enforce

\[
\tau_{t,s} \ge \frac{L_s}{v_{p}}\,x_{t,s,p}\qquad\forall p\in P,\; \forall t,s
\tag{C3a}
\]

\[
d_{t,s} - a_{t,s} = \tau_{t,s}+h_{t,s}
\tag{C3b}
\]

Because exactly one \(x_{t,s,p}=1\), \(\tau_{t,s}\) will equal the correct travel time.

### 4.4  Dwell‑time lower bound (stations)  

If segment *s* contains a station for train *t* (denoted by a parameter \(\sigma_{t,s}\in\{0,1\}\)) then a minimum dwell is required:

\[
h_{t,s} \;\ge\; d^{\text{min}}_t \, \sigma_{t,s}\qquad\forall t,s
\tag{C4}
\]

If the segment is not a station, \(\sigma_{t,s}=0\) and the constraint is inactive.

### 4.5  Continuity of times along a route  

For every train, the departure time from a segment becomes the arrival time at the next segment (including possible detours).  Let \(\text{next}(s)\) be the downstream neighbour in the **chosen** path (this is a data‑dependent mapping that can be pre‑computed for each feasible detour).  The continuity constraints are:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in S\setminus\{ \text{last segment of }t\}
\tag{C5}
\]

If a train skips a segment (i.e., \(y_{t,s}=0\)), the corresponding arrival/departure variables are irrelevant; we protect them with big‑M:

\[
a_{t,\text{next}(s)} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \;-\; \Delta\bigl(1-y_{t,s}\bigr)
\tag{C5‑M}
\]

### 4.6  Blockage (no‑go) constraints  

A train may **not** occupy a blocked segment:

\[
y_{t,s}=0 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; \forall s\in B
\tag{C6}
\]

If a detour exists, the model must allow the train to skip the blocked part; this is achieved by setting \(y_{t,s}=0\) for the blocked segment and letting the path mapping \(\text{next}(\cdot)\) jump over it.

### 4.7  Conflict (single‑track) constraints  

On any free segment *s* that is **single‑track**, two trains cannot be on it at the same time.  Let \(H_s\) be a binary parameter = 1 if segment *s* is single‑track, otherwise 0.  For every unordered pair \(\{t,t'\}\) with \(t\neq t'\):

\[
a_{t',s} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \;-\; \Delta\bigl(1 - z_{tt',s}\bigr) \qquad\forall t<t',\; \forall s\in F
\tag{C7a}
\]

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; d_{t',s} \;-\; \Delta\bigl(z_{tt',s}\bigr) \qquad\forall t<t',\; \forall s\in F
\tag{C7b}
\]

The binary ordering variable forces **one** of the two inequalities to be active (the one with the smaller big‑M term).  Finally we link the ordering variable to the usage of the segment:

\[
z_{tt',s} \le y_{t,s},\qquad 
z_{tt',s} \le y_{t',s}
\tag{C7c}
\]

If either train does not use the segment, the ordering variable is forced to 0 and the constraints become non‑binding.

### 4.8  Delay definition  

Let \(a^{\text{orig}}_{t}\) be the scheduled arrival time of train *t* at its final destination in the original (unperturbed) timetable.  The total delay is the difference between the actual arrival at the final node (call it segment \(s^{\text{last}}_t\)) and the original arrival:

\[
\delta_t \;=\; a_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \;-\; a^{\text{orig}}_{t} \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{C8}
\]

If early arrival is allowed, we enforce \(\delta_t\ge 0\) (no negative delay) by adding a simple non‑negativity bound.

### 4.9  Energy consumption calculation  

Energy on a free segment is the product of travelled distance and the energy‑rate of the chosen speed level.  Because the rate is constant per kilometre, the total energy for train *t* is linear:

\[
\underbrace{\sum_{s\in F}\;\sum_{p\in P}\; e_{p}\,L_s \, x_{t,s,p}}_{\text{energy on free segments}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{s\in B}\; e^{\text{detour}}_{t,s}\,L_s \, y_{t,s}}_{\text{energy on detour (if any)}} 
\;-\; E^{\text{ref}}_t \;=\; \epsilon_t
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{C9}
\]

* \(e^{\text{detour}}_{t,s}\) is a (possibly higher) energy‑rate that can be pre‑computed for each detour segment (e.g., because the train must climb a gradient).  
* The left‑hand side is linear because each \(x_{t,s,p}\) and \(y_{t,s}\) is binary.

### 4.10  Reroute feasibility (optional)  

If a train is allowed to use a **detour path** that consists of a set of alternative segments \(\mathcal{D}_{t}\subseteq S\), we can enforce that the train either follows its original route or a complete detour, but not a mixture.  Let a binary variable \(\rho_t\) indicate “detour used”.

\[
\sum_{s\in \mathcal{D}_{t}} y_{t,s} = \rho_t \;|\mathcal{D}_{t}|
\qquad
\sum_{s\in \text{original route}_t} y_{t,s}= (1-\rho_t)\;|\text{original route}_t|
\tag{C10}
\]

These constraints guarantee that a train either sticks to the original line ( \(\rho_t=0\) ) or switches completely to the pre‑defined detour ( \(\rho_t=1\) ).

---

## 5.  Full MILP formulation  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}} \sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}} \sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } 
&\text{(C1)–(C10) } &&\forall\; \text{appropriate indices} \\
&x_{t,s,p}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t,s}\in\{0,1\},\; z_{tt',s}\in\{0,1\},\;
r_{t,s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,p,tt'\\
&a_{t,s},d_{t,s},h_{t,s},\tau_{t,s},\delta_t,\epsilon_t \ge 0 &&\forall t,s
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑continuous variables are binaries, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

## 6.  Explanation of each component  

| Component | What it does | Why it is needed for the problem |
|-----------|--------------|---------------------------------|
| **Binary speed‑profile variables** \(x_{t,s,p}\) | Choose exactly one speed level for each train on each free segment. | Allows the optimizer to trade‑off travel time (higher speed) vs. energy (lower speed). |
| **Segment‑usage binaries** \(y_{t,s}\) | Indicate whether a train actually traverses a segment (original or detour). | Enforces blockage (no use of blocked segments) and enables rerouting decisions. |
| **Ordering binaries** \(z_{tt',s}\) | Decide which of two trains goes first on a single‑track segment. | Guarantees conflict‑free occupancy (head‑way) while keeping the model linear (big‑M formulation). |
| **Arrival / departure times** \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) | Capture the schedule of each train along its path. | Needed to compute delays, ensure continuity, and enforce head‑way constraints. |
| **Travel‑time linearization** \(\tau_{t,s}\) | Replace the non‑linear division “length / speed” by a set of linear inequalities. | Keeps the model MILP‑compatible. |
| **Delay variables** \(\delta_t\) | Measure how late each train finishes compared with its original timetable. | Directly appears in the objective, driving the optimizer to minimise passenger impact. |
| **Energy variables** \(\epsilon_t\) | Record extra energy consumption due to speed changes or detours. | Allows the second part of the objective to penalise inefficient schedules. |
| **Blockage constraints** (C6) | Force \(y_{t,s}=0\) on any segment that is physically blocked. | Models the “partial track blockage” situation. |
| **Detour feasibility** (C10, optional) | Guarantees that a train either follows its original route or a pre‑defined alternative path. | Makes the rerouting decision explicit and avoids fragmented routes. |
| **Big‑M constants** \(\Delta\) | Activate/de‑activate constraints depending on binary decisions. | Standard technique to keep the model linear while modelling conditional logic. |
| **Weights** \(w^{\text{delay}}, w^{\text{energy}}\) | Trade‑off between punctuality and energy consumption. | Gives the planner control over the relative importance of the two goals. |

---

## 7.  How to use the model  

1. **Data preparation** – Build the sets **T**, **S**, **F**, **B**, the speed‑profile set **P**, and the parameters (segment lengths, speed limits, energy rates, original timetable, station locations, single‑track flags, detour definitions).  
2. **Select big‑M** – Choose \(\Delta\) larger than any feasible arrival time (e.g., 10 000 s).  
3. **Choose weights** – Decide how much you want to penalise delay vs. energy (e.g., \(w^{\text{delay}}=1\), \(w^{\text{energy}}=0.01\)).  
4. **Feed the MILP** to any commercial or open‑source MILP solver.  
5. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * \(x_{t,s,p}=1\) tells you the speed for each train on each segment.  
   * \(y_{t,s}=1\) tells you the actual path (original or detour).  
   * \(a_{t,s}, d_{t,s}\) give the new schedule, from which you compute \(\delta_t\).  
   * \(\epsilon_t\) gives the extra energy cost.  

The solver will return the schedule that **minimises the weighted sum of total delay and extra energy** while respecting all physical, safety, and operational constraints imposed by the partial blockage of the track.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (partial‑track‑blockage)**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) which route each train will use (original or a detour that bypasses the blocked segment), (ii) the speed level on every traversed segment, and (iii) the exact arrival / departure times.  
It guarantees a conflict‑free timetable on a single‑track line, respects the blocked segment, and minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.

---

### 1. Sets & indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered from upstream to downstream) |
| **B ⊂ S** | Blocked segments (partial blockage) |
| **F = S \ B** | Free (usable) segments |
| **P** | Discrete speed‑levels, indexed by *p* (each level has a constant speed *vₚ* and energy rate *eₚ*) |
| **Dₜ ⊂ S** | Set of segments belonging to the **detour** route for train *t* (empty if no detour exists) |
| **Rₜ ⊂ S** | Set of segments belonging to the **original** route of train *t* |
| **Adj** ⊂ S×S | Ordered pairs *(s,s′)* that are consecutive on a feasible route (original or detour) |
| **Confₜₙₛ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if trains *t* and *n* would occupy the same physical track on segment *s* while travelling in opposite directions (single‑track conflict) |
| **Stₜ ⊂ S** | Segments where train *t* must stop (stations) |

---

### 2. Parameters (data)  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| *Lₛ* | Length of segment *s* (km) |
| *vₚ* | Speed of level *p* (km/h) |
| *eₚ* | Energy consumption per kilometre at level *p* (kWh/km) |
| *aₜ⁰* | Original planned arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (minutes) |
| *dₜᵈʷ* | Minimum dwell time at any station for train *t* (minutes) |
| *h* | Minimum headway between two successive trains on the same direction (minutes) |
| *M* | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000) |
| *wᵈᵉˡᵃʸ*, *wᵉⁿᵉʳɢʸ* | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |
| *σₜₛ* ∈ {0,1} | 1 if segment *s* is a station for train *t*, 0 otherwise |
| *dirₜ* ∈ {0,1} | Direction of train *t* (0 = north‑bound, 1 = south‑bound) |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| *xₜₚₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses **free** segment *s* with speed level *p* |
| *yₜₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **uses** segment *s* (original or detour) |
| *aₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at the upstream end of segment *s* (minutes) |
| *dₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from the downstream end of segment *s* (minutes) |
| *τₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (minutes) |
| *uₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Dwell time of train *t* on segment *s* (minutes) |
| *δₜ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *t* (minutes) |
| *εₜ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Extra energy of train *t* w.r.t. the original schedule (kWh) |
| *cₜₙₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* passes **before** train *n* on segment *s* (conflict‑resolution ordering) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t}
\]

*First term penalises passenger‑or‑operational delay, second term penalises additional energy consumption.*

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑selection  
*Exactly one route (original or detour) is chosen for each train.*

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t} y_{t s} + \sum_{s\in D_t} y_{t s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

If a train has no detour, the second sum is zero and the constraint forces the original route to be used.

#### 5.2 Speed‑level consistency  
*If a segment is used, exactly one speed level is selected.*

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t p s}= y_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F
\tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.3 Travel‑time linearisation  
*Travel time on a free segment equals length divided by the chosen speed.*

\[
\tau_{t s}\;\ge\; \frac{L_s}{v_p}\;x_{t p s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F,\; p\in P
\tag{S2}
\]

\[
d_{t s}=a_{t s}+ \tau_{t s}+u_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F
\tag{S3}
\]

#### 5.4 Dwell‑time at stations  

\[
u_{t s}\ge d^{\text{dw}}_t\,\sigma_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{D1}
\]

If *s* is not a station (σₜₛ=0) the constraint forces *uₜₛ = 0*.

#### 5.5 Time continuity along the chosen path  

For every ordered pair *(s,s′)∈Adj* that belongs to the **selected** route of train *t*:

\[
a_{t s'}\;\ge\; d_{t s}\;-\;M\bigl(1-y_{t s}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in Adj
\tag{C1}
\]

If segment *s* is not used (yₜₛ=0) the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

#### 5.6 Blockage (no‑go)  

\[
y_{t s}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{B1}
\]

Thus a blocked segment can never be traversed.

#### 5.7 Single‑track conflict (opposite directions)  

For every unordered pair of trains *(t,n)* that would meet on segment *s* in opposite directions (Confₜₙₛ=1):

\[
a_{t s}\;\ge\; d_{n s}\;-\;M\bigl(1-c_{t n s}\bigr)
\tag{F1}
\]

\[
a_{n s}\;\ge\; d_{t s}\;-\;M\bigl(c_{t n s}\bigr)
\tag{F2}
\]

\[
c_{t n s}\le y_{t s},\qquad c_{t n s}\le y_{n s}
\tag{F3}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities (F1)–(F2) becomes active, thereby ordering the two trains on the shared single‑track segment.

#### 5.8 Same‑direction headway  

If two trains travel in the same direction on the same segment, a minimum headway *h* must be kept:

\[
a_{t s}\;\ge\; d_{n s}+h\qquad\forall t,n\in T,\; t\neq n,\; s\in F,\; dir_t=dir_n
\tag{H1}
\]

#### 5.9 Delay definition  

Let *sₜ^{last}* be the last segment of the **selected** route of train *t* (either the original terminus or the detour terminus).

\[
\delta_t = a_{t\,s_t^{last}} - a_t^{0}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{DL}
\]

#### 5.10 Energy consumption  

Energy on a free segment is the product of distance and the energy‑rate of the chosen speed level:

\[
\epsilon_t = 
\underbrace{\sum_{s\in F}\sum_{p\in P} e_p\,L_s\,x_{t p s}}_{\text{energy on free segments}}
\;-\;E_t^{\text{orig}}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{EN}
\]

*Eₜ^{orig}* is the baseline energy of train *t* on its original schedule (data).  
If a detour is used, the same expression automatically accounts for the different segment set *Dₜ* because the corresponding *x* variables will be 1 on those segments.

#### 5.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t p s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t s}\in\{0,1\},\; c_{t n s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,n\in T,\; s\in S,\; p\in P\\
&a_{t s}, d_{t s}, \tau_{t s}, u_{t s}, \delta_t, \epsilon_t \ge 0 &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6.  Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1), (S1)–(S3), (D1), (C1), (B1), (F1)–(F3), (H1), (DL), (EN)}\\
& x_{t p s},\,y_{t s},\,c_{t n s}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t s},d_{t s},\tau_{t s},u_{t s},\delta_t,\epsilon_t\ge0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are binaries, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

### 7.  How to use the model  

1. **Prepare data** – Build the sets *T, S, B, P*, the original routes *Rₜ*, any feasible detour routes *Dₜ*, segment lengths *Lₛ*, speed‑level data *(vₚ, eₚ)*, original arrival times *aₜ⁰*, dwell times *dₜᵈʷ*, headway *h*, and the conflict matrix *Confₜₙₛ*.  
2. **Choose big‑M** – Take *M* larger than the longest possible horizon (e.g., 10 000 min).  
3. **Set weights** – Decide the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., *w^{delay}=1*, *w^{energy}=0.01*).  
4. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (HiGHS, CBC) MILP solver.  
5. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * *yₜₛ = 1* tells which route (original or detour) each train follows.  
   * *xₜₚₛ = 1* gives the speed level on each traversed segment (hence the speed profile).  
   * *aₜₛ, dₜₛ* provide the new conflict‑free timetable; *δₜ* is the resulting delay.  
   * *εₜ* is the extra energy consumption.

The solution returned by the solver is a **feasible, conflict‑free rescheduled timetable together with executable speed profiles** that respects the partial track blockage, resolves bidirectional conflicts, and balances delay against energy consumption – exactly the integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management problem described in the introduction.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management MILP (partial‑track‑blockage)**  

The model below simultaneously decides (i) which route each train will use (original or a detour that bypasses the blocked segment), (ii) the speed level on every traversed segment, and (iii) the exact arrival / departure times.  
It guarantees a conflict‑free timetable on a single‑track line, respects the blocked segment, and minimises a weighted sum of total passenger delay and total energy consumption.

---

### 1. Sets & indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **T** | Trains, indexed by *t* |
| **S** | Track segments, indexed by *s* (ordered from upstream to downstream) |
| **B ⊂ S** | Blocked segments (partial blockage) |
| **F = S \ B** | Free (usable) segments |
| **P** | Discrete speed‑levels, indexed by *p* (each level has a constant speed *vₚ* and energy rate *eₚ*) |
| **Dₜ ⊂ S** | Set of segments belonging to the **detour** route for train *t* (empty if no detour exists) |
| **Rₜ ⊂ S** | Set of segments belonging to the **original** route of train *t* |
| **Adj** ⊂ S×S | Ordered pairs *(s,s′)* that are consecutive on a feasible route (original or detour) |
| **Confₜₙₛ** ∈ {0,1} | 1 if trains *t* and *n* would occupy the same physical track on segment *s* while travelling in opposite directions (single‑track conflict) |
| **Stₜ ⊂ S** | Segments where train *t* must stop (stations) |

---

### 2. Parameters (data)  

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| *Lₛ* | Length of segment *s* (km) |
| *vₚ* | Speed of level *p* (km/h) |
| *eₚ* | Energy consumption per kilometre at level *p* (kWh/km) |
| *aₜ⁰* | Original planned arrival time of train *t* at its final destination (minutes) |
| *dₜᵈʷ* | Minimum dwell time at any station for train *t* (minutes) |
| *h* | Minimum headway between two successive trains on the same direction (minutes) |
| *M* | Large constant (big‑M) larger than any feasible time (e.g., 10 000) |
| *wᵈᵉˡᵃʸ*, *wᵉⁿᵉʳɢʸ* | Positive weights for delay and energy in the objective |
| *σₜₛ* ∈ {0,1} | 1 if segment *s* is a station for train *t*, 0 otherwise |
| *dirₜ* ∈ {0,1} | Direction of train *t* (0 = north‑bound, 1 = south‑bound) |

---

### 3. Decision variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| *xₜₚₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* traverses **free** segment *s* with speed level *p* |
| *yₜₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* **uses** segment *s* (original or detour) |
| *aₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Arrival time of train *t* at the upstream end of segment *s* (minutes) |
| *dₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Departure time of train *t* from the downstream end of segment *s* (minutes) |
| *τₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment *s* (minutes) |
| *uₜₛ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Dwell time of train *t* on segment *s* (minutes) |
| *δₜ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Total delay of train *t* (minutes) |
| *εₜ* ≥ 0 | continuous | Extra energy of train *t* w.r.t. the original schedule (kWh) |
| *cₜₙₛ* ∈ {0,1} | binary | 1 if train *t* passes **before** train *n* on segment *s* (conflict‑resolution ordering) |

---

### 4. Objective  

\[
\boxed{\min\;
w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\;
w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t}
\]

*First term penalises passenger‑or‑operational delay, second term penalises additional energy consumption.*

---

### 5. Constraints  

#### 5.1 Route‑selection  
*Exactly one route (original or detour) is chosen for each train.*

\[
\sum_{s\in R_t} y_{t s} + \sum_{s\in D_t} y_{t s}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{R1}
\]

If a train has no detour, the second sum is zero and the constraint forces the original route to be used.

#### 5.2 Speed‑level consistency  
*If a segment is used, exactly one speed level is selected.*

\[
\sum_{p\in P} x_{t p s}= y_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F
\tag{S1}
\]

#### 5.3 Travel‑time linearisation  
*Travel time on a free segment equals length divided by the chosen speed.*

\[
\tau_{t s}\;\ge\; \frac{L_s}{v_p}\;x_{t p s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F,\; p\in P
\tag{S2}
\]

\[
d_{t s}=a_{t s}+ \tau_{t s}+u_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in F
\tag{S3}
\]

#### 5.4 Dwell‑time at stations  

\[
u_{t s}\ge d^{\text{dw}}_t\,\sigma_{t s}\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\tag{D1}
\]

If *s* is not a station (σₜₛ=0) the constraint forces *uₜₛ = 0*.

#### 5.5 Time continuity along the chosen path  

For every ordered pair *(s,s′)∈Adj* that belongs to the **selected** route of train *t*:

\[
a_{t s'}\;\ge\; d_{t s}\;-\;M\bigl(1-y_{t s}\bigr)
\qquad\forall t\in T,\;(s,s')\in Adj
\tag{C1}
\]

If segment *s* is not used (yₜₛ=0) the big‑M term deactivates the constraint.

#### 5.6 Blockage (no‑go)  

\[
y_{t s}=0\qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in B
\tag{B1}
\]

Thus a blocked segment can never be traversed.

#### 5.7 Single‑track conflict (opposite directions)  

For every unordered pair of trains *(t,n)* that would meet on segment *s* in opposite directions (Confₜₙₛ=1):

\[
a_{t s}\;\ge\; d_{n s}\;-\;M\bigl(1-c_{t n s}\bigr)
\tag{F1}
\]

\[
a_{n s}\;\ge\; d_{t s}\;-\;M\bigl(c_{t n s}\bigr)
\tag{F2}
\]

\[
c_{t n s}\le y_{t s},\qquad c_{t n s}\le y_{n s}
\tag{F3}
\]

Exactly one of the two inequalities (F1)–(F2) becomes active, thereby ordering the two trains on the shared single‑track segment.

#### 5.8 Same‑direction headway  

If two trains travel in the same direction on the same segment, a minimum headway *h* must be kept:

\[
a_{t s}\;\ge\; d_{n s}+h\qquad\forall t,n\in T,\; t\neq n,\; s\in F,\; dir_t=dir_n
\tag{H1}
\]

#### 5.9 Delay definition  

Let *sₜ^{last}* be the last segment of the **selected** route of train *t* (either the original terminus or the detour terminus).

\[
\delta_t = a_{t\,s_t^{last}} - a_t^{0}\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{DL}
\]

#### 5.10 Energy consumption  

Energy on a free segment is the product of distance and the energy‑rate of the chosen speed level:

\[
\epsilon_t = 
\underbrace{\sum_{s\in F}\sum_{p\in P} e_p\,L_s\,x_{t p s}}_{\text{energy on free segments}}
\;-\;E_t^{\text{orig}}
\qquad\forall t\in T
\tag{EN}
\]

*Eₜ^{orig}* is the baseline energy of train *t* on its original schedule (data).  
If a detour is used, the same expression automatically accounts for the different segment set *Dₜ* because the corresponding *x* variables will be 1 on those segments.

#### 5.11 Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_{t p s}\in\{0,1\},\; y_{t s}\in\{0,1\},\; c_{t n s}\in\{0,1\} &&\forall t,n\in T,\; s\in S,\; p\in P\\
&a_{t s}, d_{t s}, \tau_{t s}, u_{t s}, \delta_t, \epsilon_t \ge 0 &&\forall t\in T,\; s\in S
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### 6.  Full MILP formulation  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;& w^{\text{delay}}\sum_{t\in T}\delta_t \;+\; w^{\text{energy}}\sum_{t\in T}\epsilon_t \\[2mm]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(R1), (S1)–(S3), (D1), (C1), (B1), (F1)–(F3), (H1), (DL), (EN)}\\
& x_{t p s},\,y_{t s},\,c_{t n s}\in\{0,1\},\;
a_{t s},d_{t s},\tau_{t s},u_{t s},\delta_t,\epsilon_t\ge0
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only integer variables are binaries, therefore the model is a **mixed‑integer linear program (MILP)**.

---

### 7.  How to use the model  

1. **Prepare data** – Build the sets *T, S, B, P*, the original routes *Rₜ*, any feasible detour routes *Dₜ*, segment lengths *Lₛ*, speed‑level data *(vₚ, eₚ)*, original arrival times *aₜ⁰*, dwell times *dₜᵈʷ*, headway *h*, and the conflict matrix *Confₜₙₛ*.  
2. **Choose big‑M** – Take *M* larger than the longest possible horizon (e.g., 10 000 min).  
3. **Set weights** – Decide the relative importance of punctuality vs. energy (e.g., *w^{delay}=1*, *w^{energy}=0.01*).  
4. **Solve** – Feed the MILP to any commercial (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress) or open‑source (HiGHS, CBC) MILP solver.  
5. **Interpret the solution** –  
   * *yₜₛ = 1* tells which route (original or detour) each train follows.  
   * *xₜₚₛ = 1* gives the speed level on each traversed segment (hence the speed profile).  
   * *aₜₛ, dₜₛ* provide the new conflict‑free timetable; *δₜ* is the resulting delay.  
   * *εₜ* is the extra energy consumption.

The solution returned by the solver is a **feasible, conflict‑free rescheduled timetable together with executable speed profiles** that respects the partial track blockage, resolves bidirectional conflicts, and balances delay against energy consumption – exactly the integrated Train‑Rescheduling & Speed‑Management problem described in the introduction.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
