Model 1:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below is written in a *compact* linear‑integer form that can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  
All symbols that appear in the formulation are defined in the *Sets & Parameters* and *Decision Variables* sections, followed by the *Objective* and a complete list of *Constraints*.  After the mathematical model a short *Explanation* clarifies each group of constraints and the linearisation tricks that are required.

---

## 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **I**   | Set of trains  \( i =1,\dots ,|I| \) |
| **S**   | Ordered set of stations on the line, indexed by \( s =1,\dots ,|S| \) (station 1 = origin, \( |S| \) = destination) |
| **K**   | Set of possible routes on a **disrupted** segment: \(k\in\{ {\rm orig}, {\rm opp}\}\) (original track, opposite track) |
| **D**   | Set of *disrupted* line segments (each segment is a pair of consecutive stations \((s,s+1)\) that is partially blocked) |
| **J(i)**| Set of trains that can conflict with train \(i\) on any shared segment (all \( j\neq i \) – the model uses a generic pair‑wise set later) |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / unit |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| \( \hat a_{i,s} \) | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at station *s* (from the timetable) | minutes |
| \( \hat d_{i,s} \) | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s* | minutes |
| \( \ell_{s} \) | Physical length of segment \((s,s+1)\) (km) | km |
| \( v^{\min}, v^{\max} \) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any segment (km/h) | km/h |
| \( h \) | Minimum headway (time separation) required on a *single* track, e.g. safety margin (minutes) | min |
| \( T^{\rm start}, T^{\rm end} \) | Beginning / end of the disruption window on the **original** track (minutes) | – |
| \( w_{i} \) | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (captures passenger importance) | – |
| \( \alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} \) | Energy‑cost coefficients: \( \alpha_{1} v^{2} + \alpha_{2} v \) (kWh per km) | – |
| \( \beta^{\max}_{\ell} \) | Maximum number of trains that can simultaneously occupy the *opposite* track on segment \(\ell\) (normally 1) | – |
| \( \Pi^{k}_{s} \) | Indicator = 1 if route *k* uses the original track on segment *s* (0 otherwise). For the opposite track \(k={\rm opp}\) it is 0 on the blocked segment and 1 elsewhere. | – |
| \( \mathcal{P} \) | Set of break‑points for the piece‑wise linear (PWL) approximation of the quadratic term \(v^{2}\). Each breakpoint \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) has a speed value \( \bar v_{p} \) and a corresponding squared‑value \( \bar q_{p}= \bar v_{p}^{2} \). | – |

All parameters are assumed to be known *a‑priori*.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \( r_{i,k} \) | binary | 1 → train *i* selects route *k* (original or opposite) on the disrupted segment(s); \(\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1\) |
| \( o_{i,j,s} \) | binary | 1 → on shared segment *s* train *i* passes **before** train *j* (only defined for pairs that may share the same track) |
| \( a_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *i* at station *s* |
| \( d_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *i* from station *s* |
| \( v_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment \((s,s+1)\) (km/h) |
| \( t_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment \((s,s+1)\) (minutes) |
| \( q_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable that linearly represents \(v_{i,s}^{2}\) (used for energy term) |
| \( \lambda_{i,s,p} \) | continuous, ≥0 | PWL weight of breakpoint *p* for the speed‑squared approximation on segment *s* (∑\(\lambda=1\); 0≤\(\lambda\)≤1) |

Additional auxiliary variables (if needed) can be introduced for big‑M formulations – see constraints below.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I} w_{i}\;\bigl(a_{i,|S|}-\hat a_{i,|S|}\bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{s=1}^{|S|-1}
\Bigl(\alpha_{1}\;q_{i,s} + \alpha_{2}\;v_{i,s}\Bigr)\,\ell_{s}}_{\text{Total energy consumption (linearised)}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

* The first term penalises the deviation of the realised arrival time at the final station from the scheduled one.  
* The second term is the sum over all travelled kilometres of the (approximated) energy cost. Because \(q_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) is linearised (see §5.5), the whole objective is linear.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection (binary)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

Only one route (original or opposite) can be chosen for each train.

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility (arrival–departure–travel)  

For every train and every interior station \(s\) (i.e. \(1\le s<|S|\))  

\[
a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{TF1}
\]

### 5.3 Dwell‑time lower bound  

A minimum dwell (stop) time \(\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s}\) (often a constant, e.g. 2 min) must be respected:

\[
d_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s}+ \tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S| \tag{DW}
\]

(For the origin station, set \(\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,1}=0\).)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min} \le v_{i,s} \le v^{\max} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{SL}
\]

### 5.5 Travel‑time – speed relation  

\[
t_{i,s}= \frac{\ell_{s}}{v_{i,s}} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\ell_{s}= v_{i,s}\; t_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{TR}
\]

Since the product of two continuous variables is non‑linear, we linearise it by *introducing the auxiliary variable* \(q_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) (see §5.9) and using a **piecewise linear** approximation of the function  

\[
\frac{1}{v} \quad\text{over }[v^{\min},v^{\max}]
\]

Let \(\{(\bar v_{p},\; \theta_{p})\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\) be break‑points where \(\theta_{p}=1/\bar v_{p}\). Then

\[
t_{i,s}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \theta_{p}\,\lambda_{i,s,p}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_t}
\]

\[
v_{i,s}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \bar v_{p}\,\lambda_{i,s,p}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_v}
\]

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \lambda_{i,s,p}=1,\;\; \lambda_{i,s,p}\ge 0\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_sum}
\]

These three constraints enforce that \(t_{i,s}\) is the linear interpolation of \(\theta=1/v\) at the selected speed, i.e. the exact relation \(t=\ell/v\) is respected to within the chosen PWL accuracy.

### 5.6 Blockage / Disruption window  

The original track of every disrupted segment \(d\in D\) is unavailable for any train that **keeps** the original route during the time window \([T^{\rm start},T^{\rm end}]\). Using a big‑M constant \(M\) (large enough, e.g. 10 000 min) we write:

\[
a_{i,s} \ge T^{\rm start} - M\,(1-r_{i,{\rm orig}}) \qquad
\forall i\in I,\; s\in \{ \text{stations that lie *after* the disrupted segment } d\} \tag{BLK1}
\]

\[
a_{i,s} \le T^{\rm end} + M\,(1-r_{i,{\rm orig}}) \qquad
\forall i\in I,\; s\in \{ \text{stations that lie *before* the disrupted segment } d\} \tag{BLK2}
\]

In practice it is easier to impose that a train using the original route **cannot occupy** the disrupted segment itself:

\[
d_{i,s_{\rm up}} \ge T^{\rm end}\; r_{i,{\rm orig}} \quad\text{or}\quad a_{i,s_{\rm down}} \le T^{\rm start}\; r_{i,{\rm orig}} \tag{BLK\_seg}
\]

where \(s_{\rm up}\) and \(s_{\rm down}\) are the upstream and downstream stations of the blocked segment. If the train is rerouted (\(r_{i,{\rm opp}}=1\)), the constraints become non‑binding.

### 5.7 Track‑usage indicator (coupling route to segment occupancy)  

Let  

\[
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}=r_{i,k}\, \Pi^{k}_{s}\qquad \forall i,s,k
\]

Because \(\Pi^{k}_{s}\) is a known constant (0/1), we can replace the product by a linear formulation:

\[
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le r_{i,k},\qquad 
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le \Pi^{k}_{s},\qquad 
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\ge r_{i,k}+ \Pi^{k}_{s}-1 \tag{TRACK\_use}
\]

\(\zeta_{i,s}^{k}=1\) iff train *i* uses route *k* **and** that route occupies the original track on segment *s*.  

The binary **ordering** variables are only defined for pairs that actually share the same physical track on a segment, i.e. when  

\[
\Pi^{\rm orig}_{s}=1 \;\text{and}\; \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}=1,\ \zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig}=1
\]
or similarly for the opposite track.

### 5.8 Conflict‑avoidance (ordering & headway)  

For any unordered pair \((i,j)\) that can occupy the same track on segment *s* we introduce a binary ordering variable \(o_{i,j,s}\) (1 if *i* passes before *j*). The following three constraints guarantee a feasible, conflict‑free schedule.

1. **Mutual exclusivity of ordering**

   \[
   o_{i,j,s}+o_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}} \tag{ORD}
   \]

2. **Big‑M head‑way enforcement** (when *i* goes first)

   \[
   a_{j,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,s}+h \;-\; M\bigl(1-o_{i,j,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}} \tag{HW1}
   \]

   Symmetrically, when *j* goes first we have the same inequality with indices swapped (automatically covered because of (ORD)).

3. **Link to actual track usage** – the ordering constraints are *activated* only if the two trains really share the same track:

   \[
   o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig} \qquad\text{(original track)} \tag{ACT1}
   \]
   \[
   o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm opp}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm opp} \qquad\text{(opposite track)} \tag{ACT2}
   \]

   If at least one of the two trains uses a different track, the right‑hand side becomes 0 and the binary \(o_{i,j,s}\) must be 0, which in turn forces the complementary ordering variable to be 1, but both inequalities (HW1) become non‑binding because the big‑M term is active.

### 5.9 Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

The energy term contains \(v_{i,s}^{2}\). We replace it by the auxiliary variable \(q_{i,s}\) and enforce:

\[
q_{i,s}\ge \; 2\bar v_{p}\,v_{i,s} - \bar v_{p}^{2}\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\; i,s \tag{Q1}
\]

\[
q_{i,s}\ge 0 \tag{Q2}
\]

Constraints (Q1) are the classic **McCormick** linearisation of a convex quadratic over a bounded interval \([v^{\min},v^{\max}]\). With a sufficiently fine set of break‑points \(\mathcal{P}\) the resulting polyhedron approximates \(v^{2}\) arbitrarily well. The objective uses \(q_{i,s}\) directly.

---

## 6. Summary of the Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in I} w_{i}\bigl(a_{i,|S|}-\hat a_{i,|S|}\bigr)
          +\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s=1}^{|S|-1}\bigl(\alpha_{1} q_{i,s}+ \alpha_{2} v_{i,s}\bigr)\ell_{s}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&\text{(R1)} && \sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\\
            &\text{(TF1)} && a_{i,s+1}=d_{i,s}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i, s=1\!\ldots\!|S|-1\\
            &\text{(DW)} && d_{i,s}\ge a_{i,s}+\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(SL)} && v^{\min}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_t)} && t_{i,s}= \sum_{p}\theta_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_v)} && v_{i,s}= \sum_{p}\bar v_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_sum)} && \sum_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p}=1,\;\lambda_{i,s,p}\ge0 &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(BLK\_seg)} && d_{i,s_{\rm up}}\ge T^{\rm end} r_{i,{\rm orig}}\;\;\text{or}\;\; a_{i,s_{\rm down}}\le T^{\rm start} r_{i,{\rm orig}} &&\forall i\\
            &\text{(TRACK\_use)} && \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le r_{i,k},\; \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le \Pi^{k}_{s},\;
               \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\ge r_{i,k}+\Pi^{k}_{s}-1 &&\forall i,s,k\\
            &\text{(ORD)} && o_{i,j,s}+o_{j,i,s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(HW1)} && a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+h-M(1-o_{i,j,s}) &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(ACT1/2)} && o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig},
                              \; o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm opp}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm opp}
                              &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(Q1)} && q_{i,s}\ge 2\bar v_{p}v_{i,s}-\bar v_{p}^{2} &&\forall i,s, p\in\mathcal{P}\\
            &\text{(Q2)} && q_{i,s}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(binary/ non‑neg.)} && r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
               a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},q_{i,s}\ge0 &&\forall\text{indices}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearity (the quadratic energy term) is replaced by the convex envelope (Q1). The big‑M constant \(M\) should be chosen larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g. \(M = 10\,000\) min) but as small as possible to keep the LP relaxation tight.

---

## 7. Explanation of Model Components  

| Component | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-----------|--------------|------------------|
| **Route‑choice binary \(r_{i,k}\)** | Decides whether a train stays on the original track or is rerouted to the opposite (bypass) track when the segment is blocked. | Guarantees that a train can only use one physical line at a time and enables the disruption‑window constraints. |
| **Ordering binary \(o_{i,j,s}\)** | Imposes a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) order on any pair of trains that share a track on a given segment. | Enforces safety headways and avoids collisions on single‑track sections. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the actual timetable after rescheduling. | Core decision variables that allow delay computation and link travel‑time, dwell‑time and conflict constraints together. |
| **Speed \(v_{i,s}\) + travel time \(t_{i,s}\)** | Controls the physical movement between stations; speed bounds model engineering limits (track geometry, signaling). | Provides a realistic trade‑off: higher speed reduces delay but raises energy consumption. |
| **Piece‑wise linear (PWL) representation of \(1/v\)** | Linearises the relationship \(t = \ell/v\) by interpolating the convex function \(1/v\). | Keeps the model MILP (no bilinear terms). Accuracy can be tuned by the number of break‑points. |
| **Quadratic energy term linearised by McCormick (constraints Q1)** | Allows the objective to contain \(v^2\) (energy grows roughly with the square of speed) while preserving linearity. | Needed because most MILP solvers cannot handle actual quadratic terms directly. |
| **Disruption‑window constraints (BLK\*)** | Prevent any train that stays on the original line from entering the blocked time interval; rerouted trains are exempt. | Models the real‑world restriction caused by a temporary blockage (e.g. maintenance, accident). |
| **Capacity on opposite track** | Implicitly handled by the same ordering/headway constraints, but a separate upper bound \(\beta^{\max}_{\ell}\) could be added if the bypass line can accommodate more than one train simultaneously. | Guarantees that the alternative track does not become overloaded. |
| **Weighted delay term** | Each train may have a different importance (high‑speed premium services, freight, etc.). | Allows the planner to protect high‑value services at the expense of less critical ones. |
| **Energy term** | Sum of \(\alpha_{1}v^{2}+\alpha_{2}v\) over all kilometres. | Captures the operational cost/green‑house‑gas impact of higher speeds – the model can therefore balance punctuality against energy consumption. |

---

### 7.1 Modelling Assumptions (to make the MILP tractable)

1. **Constant average speed per segment** – intra‑segment speed variation is ignored; the segment is treated as a “flat” piece with one speed decision.
2. **Deterministic travel distances** – \(\ell_{s}\) are known and do not change with the schedule.
3. **Fixed headway \(h\)** – a conservative constant safety margin is used for any pair sharing a track.
4. **Binary ordering only on segments that can physically conflict** (i.e., where at most one train can occupy the track). For double‑track sections the ordering variables are simply omitted.
5. **Piece‑wise linear approximation** – the number of break‑points \(|\mathcal{P}|\) is a modelling choice; 4–6 points give a good compromise between accuracy and model size.
6. **Big‑M value** – chosen large enough to deactivate constraints when the corresponding ordering is not active, but not excessively large to avoid numerical difficulties.

---

## 8. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – For each train prepare its original schedule \(\hat a,\hat d\), the list of stations, distances, and the disrupted segment(s) with the time window.  
2. **Select break‑points** – Typical speeds: \([200,250,300,350,400]\) km/h for a high‑speed line; compute \(\theta=1/v\) for each.  
3. **Create the pair‑wise conflict set** – For every segment that is single‑track after the disruption, generate all unordered pairs \((i,j)\).  
4. **Feed the MILP** – Most modern solvers accept the model in **AMPL**, **GAMS**, **Pyomo**, or **JuMP** format; the constraints above translate directly.  
5. **Solve & post‑process** – The optimal solution provides: (i) the rerouting decisions \(r_{i,k}\), (ii) the speed profile \(v_{i,s}\), (iii) the new timetable \(a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\). From these you can compute the actual delay per train and the total energy consumption.

---

### 9. Closing Remark  

The formulation above is *complete* in the sense that every element mentioned in the problem description appears in the linear model, and every non‑linear relationship has been replaced by a proven linearisation technique (piece‑wise linear interpolation for \(1/v\) and McCormick envelopes for \(v^{2}\)).  By adjusting the weights \(w_{i},\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\) and the granularity of the PWL approximation, a railway operator can explore the whole spectrum from “minimum delay at any energy cost” to “energy‑optimal but possibly later arrivals”, while respecting the hard safety and disruption constraints of a partially blocked high‑speed line.

Model 2:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below is written in a *standard linear* mixed‑integer‑programming form.  
All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and each family of
constraints are listed first; a short comment explains the purpose of every term.  
The formulation is *complete* – i.e. if you copy it into a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi,
Xpress, …) and provide the data described in the “Assumptions” section, the solver will
return a feasible schedule that respects the blockage, the train‑ordering on shared
segments, the dwell‑time and speed‑limits, and that minimizes a weighted combination of
total delay and energy consumption.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I**  | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **S**  | Set of stations (including the terminal **last**), indexed by *s* (ordered). |
| **K**  | Set of possible *routes* on the disrupted segment, **K = {orig, opp}** (original track, opposite track). |
| **E**  | Set of *edges* (track‑segments) between two consecutive stations,  *e = (s,s+1)*. |
| **B**  | Sub‑set of edges that are *blocked* (the segment that suffers a partial blockage). |
| **P**  | Set of ordered train‑pairs that share at least one common edge, i.e.  \(P=\{(i,j): i\neq j \text{ and } \exists e\in E\; \text{used by both}\}\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Units |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| `sched_i` | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its last station (baseline). | min |
| `Δdwell_min` | Minimum dwell (stop) time at every station. | min |
| `Δdwell_max` | Maximum allowed dwell (optional). | min |
| `dist_e` | Length of edge *e* (in km). | km |
| `v_min` , `v_max` | Global speed limits (may be refined per edge). | km/h |
| `headway` | Minimum time gap required between two successive trains on the **same** track (safety). | min |
| `T_start` , `T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window on the original track. | min |
| `α` , `β` | Weight coefficients in the objective (delay weight *α* > 0, energy weight *β* > 0). | – |
| `c1_q , c2_q` | Linearization coefficients for the *quadratic* term `v²` on edge *q*  (see §5). | – |
| `c3_q` | Linear coefficient for the linear term `v` on edge *q* (energy component). | – |
| `M` | Large constant (big‑M) used for big‑M reformulations. | – |

*All time‑related parameters are expressed in minutes; all speeds in km/h.*  

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `r_i_k` | Binary | 1 if train *i* uses route *k* (= *orig* or *opp*) on a blocked edge, 0 otherwise. |
| `o_ij` | Binary | 1 if train *i* passes **before** train *j* on a common edge (the ordering variable). |
| `a_i_s` | Continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| `d_i_s` | Continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| `v_i_e` | Continuous, ≥0 | **Average speed** of train *i* while traversing edge *e*. |
| `t_i_e` | Continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on edge *e*. |
| `z_i_q` | Continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable that linearizes the quadratic term \(v_i_q^2\). (One per edge *q*.) |

*The “last” station of a train is denoted by `s = last_i`.  The decision variables exist only for the edges actually traversed by a train; a train that does not travel on edge *e* has the corresponding variables fixed to 0.*

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  \alpha \;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}_i}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}}
           \;+\;
           \beta  \;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{e\in E_i}
                 \Bigl(c_{1_e}\,z_{i,e}+c_{2_e}\,v_{i,e}\Bigr)}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*Explanation*  

* `a_{i,last_i} – sched_i` is the **delay** of train *i* at its final destination.  
* Energy on edge *e* is approximated by a piece‑wise linear function  
  \(E(v)=c_{1_e}v^{2}+c_{2_e}v\).  The quadratic part is linearized by \(z_{i,e}\) (see §5).  
* The two parts are weighted by user‑defined scalars `α` (delay importance) and `β`
  (energy importance).

---

## 5.  Linearisation of the Quadratic Speed Term  

The term \(v_{i,e}^{2}\) is convex; a common way to keep the model linear is to use a
*piece‑wise linear over‑estimator* (or exact McCormick envelopes on a bounded domain).  
Assume the speed on every edge is bounded by \([v_{\min}^{e},v_{\max}^{e}]\).
Define a set of *break‑points* \(\{p_1,\dots ,p_L\}\) inside the interval.
Introduce auxiliary non‑negative variables \(\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\) (convex combination) :

\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}=1,\qquad 
v_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} p_{\ell}\,\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\qquad 
z_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} p_{\ell}^{2}\,\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},
\qquad\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\ge 0 .
\tag{LIN\_SPEED}
\]

If a *coarser* linearisation is acceptable, a single big‑M envelope can be used:

\[
z_{i,e}\ge v_{i,e}^{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;
z_{i,e}\ge 2\,v_{\min}^{e}\,v_{i,e}-\bigl(v_{\min}^{e}\bigr)^{2},\qquad
z_{i,e}\ge 2\,v_{\max}^{e}\,v_{i,e}-\bigl(v_{\max}^{e}\bigr)^{2}.
\tag{BIGM\_SPEED}
\]

Both families are linear, thus preserve MILP structure.

---

## 6.  Core Scheduling Constraints  

### 6.1   Travel‑time definition  

\[
t_{i,e}= \frac{\text{dist}_{e}}{v_{i,e}},\qquad \forall i\in I,\;e\in E_i .
\tag{TRAV\_TIME}
\]

Because `v` is a decision variable, the fraction is **non‑linear**.  
We linearise it by cross‑multiplying (the denominator is bounded away from zero):

\[
\text{dist}_{e}= v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\text{dist}_{e}\le v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}+M\,(1-u_{i,e}),\\
\text{dist}_{e}\ge v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}-M\,(1-u_{i,e}),
\]

where binary `u_{i,e}` forces the equality for edges actually used (otherwise the
product can be relaxed).  In practice the linearised version (using the
piece‑wise speed representation from §5) yields a *linear* relationship between
`t` and `v`.

### 6.2   Time‑flow over stations  

\[
a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+t_{i,(s,s+1)} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in S\setminus\{\text{last}_i\}.
\tag{FLOW}
\]

### 6.3   Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\;\le\; d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\;\le\;\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\max}\quad
\forall i\in I,\, s\in S\setminus\{\text{first}_i,\text{last}_i\}.
\tag{DWELL}
\]

(If `Δdwell_max` is not required it can be omitted.)

### 6.4   Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\;\le\; v_{i,e}\;\le\;v_{\max}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;e\in E_i .
\tag{SPEED\_BND}
\]

---

## 7.  Blockage / Route‑Choice Constraints  

Only the edges belonging to the blocked set **B** are affected.

### 7.1   Exactly one route per train on a blocked edge  

\[
r_{i,\text{orig}}+r_{i,\text{opp}} = 1 \qquad\forall i\in I\;\; \text{with } B\neq\varnothing .
\tag{ROUTE\_CHOICE}
\]

### 7.2   Forbidden use of the original track during the disruption window  

For every train *i* that traverses a blocked edge *e∈B* on the **original** track:

\[
a_{i,\text{upstream}(e)} \ge T_{\text{end}}  \;\;\; \text{or}\;\;\;
d_{i,\text{downstream}(e)} \le T_{\text{start}} \quad
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a_{i,\text{up}} \ge T_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-r_{i,\text{orig}})
\]
\[
d_{i,\text{down}} \le T_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}).
\tag{BLOCK\_ORIG}
\]

If `r_{i,orig}=0` (train rerouted) the big‑M terms deactivate the constraints,
allowing the train to occupy the opposite track at any time.

### 7.3   Capacity on the opposite track (if it is also shared)  

Analogous to the ordering constraints described next ( §8 ) – the same logic
applies to both routes; the only difference is that the binary `r_{i,k}` selects
which set of ordering constraints becomes active.

---

## 8.  Ordering / Head‑way Constraints on Shared Segments  

Consider any edge *e* that can be travelled by more than one train (including
the opposite track when several trains are routed there).  
For each unordered pair \((i,j)\) that may share *e* define a binary variable  
\(o_{ij}^{e}\) (we keep the same symbol `o_ij` but it is *edge‑specific*).

### 8.1   Exactly one ordering  

\[
o_{ij}^{e} + o_{ji}^{e}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_ONE}
\]

### 8.2   Time–separation when *i* precedes *j*  

\[
d_{i,\text{up}(e)} + \text{headway} \;\le\; a_{j,\text{down}(e)} + M\,(1-o_{ij}^{e})
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_TIME}
\]

If `o_{ij}^{e}=1` the big‑M term disappears and the inequality forces the required
headway; if `o_{ij}^{e}=0` the constraint is relaxed.

### 8.3   Compatibility with route choice  

Only pairs that travel **on the same physical track** need ordering.  
Let `track_{i,e}` be a binary indicator that train *i* uses the **original** track on
edge *e*:  

\[
track_{i,e}=r_{i,\text{orig}} \quad \forall e\in B,
\]
\[
track_{i,e}=1 \quad \forall e\notin B   \;(\text{no blockage, only one track}).
\]

Then the ordering constraints are activated only when both trains share the same
track:

\[
o_{ij}^{e} \le track_{i,e},\qquad
o_{ij}^{e} \le track_{j,e},\qquad
o_{ij}^{e} \ge track_{i,e}+track_{j,e}-1
\quad\forall (i,j)\in P,\;e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_LINK}
\]

If the two trains are on different tracks, `o_{ij}^{e}` is forced to 0 and no headway
restriction is imposed.

---

## 9.  Additional Practical Constraints (optional)  

| Constraint | Formulation | Comment |
|------------|-------------|---------|
| **Maximum lateness** | \(a_{i,last_i}\le \text{sched}_i + L_{\max}\) | Guarantees a user‑defined service level. |
| **Train‑specific speed limits** | Replace `v_min`, `v_max` by edge‑specific bounds `v_{min}^{i,e}`, `v_{max}^{i,e}`. |
| **Platform capacity** | \(\sum_{i\in I} \mathbf{1}\{a_{i,s}\le t \le d_{i,s}\}\le C_s\) (linearised with binaries). | Keeps the number of trains at a station ≤ capacity *C_s*. |
| **Mandatory early departure** | \(d_{i,s}\ge a_{i,s}+\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\) (already in DWELL). |
| **Turn‑back limits** | For a train that must reverse direction on the opposite track, impose a binary “turn” variable and a minimum turnaround time. |  |

---

## 10.  Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}_i}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)\\
      &+ \beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{e\in E_i}\bigl(c_{1_e}z_{i,e}+c_{2_e}v_{i,e}\bigr) \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(ROUTE\_CHOICE)} && r_{i,\text{orig}}+r_{i,\text{opp}} =1 \quad\forall i\in I \\
& \text{(BLOCK\_ORIG)} && a_{i,\text{up}(e)} \ge T_{\text{end}}-M(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}) \\
& && d_{i,\text{down}(e)} \le T_{\text{start}}+M(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}) \quad\forall e\in B \\
& \text{(FLOW)} && a_{i,s+1}=d_{i,s}+t_{i,(s,s+1)} \quad\forall i,\;s\neq\text{last}_i \\
& \text{(DWELL)} && \Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\max} \\
& \text{(SPEED\_BND)} && v_{\min}\le v_{i,e}\le v_{\max} \\
& \text{(TRAV\_TIME \& LIN\_SPEED)} && \text{dist}_{e}=v_{i,e}t_{i,e} \;\;\text{(linearised via (LIN\_SPEED) or (BIGM\_SPEED))} \\
& \text{(ORD\_ONE)} && o_{ij}^{e}+o_{ji}^{e}=1 \quad\forall (i,j)\in P, \,e\in E_i\cap E_j \\
& \text{(ORD\_TIME)} && d_{i,\text{up}(e)}+\text{headway}\le a_{j,\text{down}(e)}+M(1-o_{ij}^{e}) \\
& \text{(ORD\_LINK)} && o_{ij}^{e}\le track_{i,e}, \; o_{ij}^{e}\le track_{j,e}, \;
                         o_{ij}^{e}\ge track_{i,e}+track_{j,e}-1 \\[2pt]
& \text{(ENERGY\_LIN)} && v_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell} p_{\ell}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\;
                         z_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell} p_{\ell}^{2}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\\
& && \sum_{\ell}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}=1,\; \lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\ge0. \\
& \text{(Variables)} && r_{i,k},\,o_{ij}^{e}\in\{0,1\},\;
                       a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,e},v_{i,e},z_{i,e}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑trivial piece is the speed‑quadratic
linearisation, which is completely handled by (ENERGY\_LIN) or the pair of
McCormick inequalities (BIGM\_SPEED).  

---

## 11.  Assumptions and Modelling Remarks  

1. **Deterministic data** – travel distances, scheduled times, disruption window, headway,
   and speed limits are known exactly.  
2. **Uniform block** – the disruption affects a *single* contiguous edge set **B**; the
   opposite track is assumed to be completely free (except for the usual ordering
   constraints).  
3. **Average speed per edge** – the model works with a constant speed on each edge.
   If a finer time‑resolution is required, split the edge into smaller sub‑edges
   and replicate the variables.  
4. **Piece‑wise linear energy model** – the squared‑speed term is approximated by a
   convex envelope; increasing the number of break‑points *L* improves fidelity at the
   cost of more variables.  
5. **Big‑M size** – `M` must be larger than the maximum possible schedule horizon
   (e.g. 10 000 min).  A tighter value reduces numerical difficulty.  
6. **Feasibility** – because the binary route‑choice forces each train to use *some*
   track, the model is always feasible unless the headway requirement is too
   strict; in that case the headway can be relaxed or a dummy “delay” variable can
   be introduced with a very high penalty.  

---

### How to use the formulation  

1. **Prepare the data** (the sets, distances, scheduled times, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, headway, dwell‑times).  
2. **Choose the linearisation** – either the exact piece‑wise representation (`λ` variables) or the two‑inequality McCormick envelope.  
3. **Instantiate the model** in any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, OPL …).  
4. **Solve** with a modern MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
5. **Interpret the solution** – the binary `r_i_k` tells whether train *i* was rerouted,
   the ordering variables give the exact sequence on each shared segment, and the
   arrival/departure times provide the new schedule that respects the blockage while
   minimizing delay + energy.

This completes a **linear, mixed‑integer programming** description of the Integrated
Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem under a partial segment blockage.

Please generate an MILP based on the provided description.

Integrated train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP) for high-speed railway with partial segment blockage. Variables: binary route choice r_{i,k} for train i using route k (original or opposite track), binary ordering o_{i,j} for train i before j on shared segment, continuous arrival times a_{i,s} at station s, departure times d_{i,s}, travel times t_{i,s} between stations, speed level v_{i,s} (continuous). Objective: minimize weighted sum of total delay Σ_i (a_{i,last}-scheduled_i) and total energy consumption Σ_i Σ_s (c1*v_{i,s}^2 + c2*v_{i,s}). Constraints: time feasibility a_{i,s+1}=d_{i,s}+t_{i,s}; dwell time lower bound; speed limits v_min<=v_{i,s}<=v_max; travel time relation t_{i,s}=distance_{s}/v_{i,s}; binary route choice determines which track is used on disrupted segment, only one track at a time; capacity constraints on shared track: for any two trains i,j using same track on segment s, enforce ordering o_{i,j}+o_{j,i}=1 and time separation d_{i,s}+headway <= a_{j,s} if o_{i,j}=1; disruption window: trains cannot occupy original track during [T_start,T_end] unless rerouted; route selection binary ensures if r_{i,original}=1 then train uses original track else opposite; ensure conflict-free on opposite track similarly. Energy objective linearization using piecewise linear approximation of v^2. Provide assumptions where needed.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below is written in a *compact* linear‑integer form that can be entered directly into any MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  
All symbols that appear in the formulation are defined in the *Sets & Parameters* and *Decision Variables* sections, followed by the *Objective* and a complete list of *Constraints*.  After the mathematical model a short *Explanation* clarifies each group of constraints and the linearisation tricks that are required.

---

## 1. Sets & Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **I**   | Set of trains  \( i =1,\dots ,|I| \) |
| **S**   | Ordered set of stations on the line, indexed by \( s =1,\dots ,|S| \) (station 1 = origin, \( |S| \) = destination) |
| **K**   | Set of possible routes on a **disrupted** segment: \(k\in\{ {\rm orig}, {\rm opp}\}\) (original track, opposite track) |
| **D**   | Set of *disrupted* line segments (each segment is a pair of consecutive stations \((s,s+1)\) that is partially blocked) |
| **J(i)**| Set of trains that can conflict with train \(i\) on any shared segment (all \( j\neq i \) – the model uses a generic pair‑wise set later) |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / unit |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| \( \hat a_{i,s} \) | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at station *s* (from the timetable) | minutes |
| \( \hat d_{i,s} \) | Scheduled departure time of train *i* from station *s* | minutes |
| \( \ell_{s} \) | Physical length of segment \((s,s+1)\) (km) | km |
| \( v^{\min}, v^{\max} \) | Minimum / maximum admissible speed on any segment (km/h) | km/h |
| \( h \) | Minimum headway (time separation) required on a *single* track, e.g. safety margin (minutes) | min |
| \( T^{\rm start}, T^{\rm end} \) | Beginning / end of the disruption window on the **original** track (minutes) | – |
| \( w_{i} \) | Weight of train *i* in the delay part of the objective (captures passenger importance) | – |
| \( \alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} \) | Energy‑cost coefficients: \( \alpha_{1} v^{2} + \alpha_{2} v \) (kWh per km) | – |
| \( \beta^{\max}_{\ell} \) | Maximum number of trains that can simultaneously occupy the *opposite* track on segment \(\ell\) (normally 1) | – |
| \( \Pi^{k}_{s} \) | Indicator = 1 if route *k* uses the original track on segment *s* (0 otherwise). For the opposite track \(k={\rm opp}\) it is 0 on the blocked segment and 1 elsewhere. | – |
| \( \mathcal{P} \) | Set of break‑points for the piece‑wise linear (PWL) approximation of the quadratic term \(v^{2}\). Each breakpoint \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) has a speed value \( \bar v_{p} \) and a corresponding squared‑value \( \bar q_{p}= \bar v_{p}^{2} \). | – |

All parameters are assumed to be known *a‑priori*.

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|----------|
| \( r_{i,k} \) | binary | 1 → train *i* selects route *k* (original or opposite) on the disrupted segment(s); \(\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1\) |
| \( o_{i,j,s} \) | binary | 1 → on shared segment *s* train *i* passes **before** train *j* (only defined for pairs that may share the same track) |
| \( a_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual arrival time of train *i* at station *s* |
| \( d_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Actual departure time of train *i* from station *s* |
| \( v_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Average speed of train *i* on segment \((s,s+1)\) (km/h) |
| \( t_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on segment \((s,s+1)\) (minutes) |
| \( q_{i,s} \) | continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable that linearly represents \(v_{i,s}^{2}\) (used for energy term) |
| \( \lambda_{i,s,p} \) | continuous, ≥0 | PWL weight of breakpoint *p* for the speed‑squared approximation on segment *s* (∑\(\lambda=1\); 0≤\(\lambda\)≤1) |

Additional auxiliary variables (if needed) can be introduced for big‑M formulations – see constraints below.

---

## 4. Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I} w_{i}\;\bigl(a_{i,|S|}-\hat a_{i,|S|}\bigr)}_{\text{Weighted total delay}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{s=1}^{|S|-1}
\Bigl(\alpha_{1}\;q_{i,s} + \alpha_{2}\;v_{i,s}\Bigr)\,\ell_{s}}_{\text{Total energy consumption (linearised)}}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

* The first term penalises the deviation of the realised arrival time at the final station from the scheduled one.  
* The second term is the sum over all travelled kilometres of the (approximated) energy cost. Because \(q_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) is linearised (see §5.5), the whole objective is linear.

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1 Route‑selection (binary)  

\[
\sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 \qquad\forall i\in I \tag{R1}
\]

Only one route (original or opposite) can be chosen for each train.

### 5.2 Time‑feasibility (arrival–departure–travel)  

For every train and every interior station \(s\) (i.e. \(1\le s<|S|\))  

\[
a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+ t_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{TF1}
\]

### 5.3 Dwell‑time lower bound  

A minimum dwell (stop) time \(\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s}\) (often a constant, e.g. 2 min) must be respected:

\[
d_{i,s} \ge a_{i,s}+ \tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S| \tag{DW}
\]

(For the origin station, set \(\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,1}=0\).)

### 5.4 Speed limits  

\[
v^{\min} \le v_{i,s} \le v^{\max} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{SL}
\]

### 5.5 Travel‑time – speed relation  

\[
t_{i,s}= \frac{\ell_{s}}{v_{i,s}} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\ell_{s}= v_{i,s}\; t_{i,s} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s=1,\dots,|S|-1 \tag{TR}
\]

Since the product of two continuous variables is non‑linear, we linearise it by *introducing the auxiliary variable* \(q_{i,s}=v_{i,s}^{2}\) (see §5.9) and using a **piecewise linear** approximation of the function  

\[
\frac{1}{v} \quad\text{over }[v^{\min},v^{\max}]
\]

Let \(\{(\bar v_{p},\; \theta_{p})\}_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\) be break‑points where \(\theta_{p}=1/\bar v_{p}\). Then

\[
t_{i,s}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \theta_{p}\,\lambda_{i,s,p}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_t}
\]

\[
v_{i,s}= \sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \bar v_{p}\,\lambda_{i,s,p}\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_v}
\]

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} \lambda_{i,s,p}=1,\;\; \lambda_{i,s,p}\ge 0\qquad\forall i,s \tag{PWL\_sum}
\]

These three constraints enforce that \(t_{i,s}\) is the linear interpolation of \(\theta=1/v\) at the selected speed, i.e. the exact relation \(t=\ell/v\) is respected to within the chosen PWL accuracy.

### 5.6 Blockage / Disruption window  

The original track of every disrupted segment \(d\in D\) is unavailable for any train that **keeps** the original route during the time window \([T^{\rm start},T^{\rm end}]\). Using a big‑M constant \(M\) (large enough, e.g. 10 000 min) we write:

\[
a_{i,s} \ge T^{\rm start} - M\,(1-r_{i,{\rm orig}}) \qquad
\forall i\in I,\; s\in \{ \text{stations that lie *after* the disrupted segment } d\} \tag{BLK1}
\]

\[
a_{i,s} \le T^{\rm end} + M\,(1-r_{i,{\rm orig}}) \qquad
\forall i\in I,\; s\in \{ \text{stations that lie *before* the disrupted segment } d\} \tag{BLK2}
\]

In practice it is easier to impose that a train using the original route **cannot occupy** the disrupted segment itself:

\[
d_{i,s_{\rm up}} \ge T^{\rm end}\; r_{i,{\rm orig}} \quad\text{or}\quad a_{i,s_{\rm down}} \le T^{\rm start}\; r_{i,{\rm orig}} \tag{BLK\_seg}
\]

where \(s_{\rm up}\) and \(s_{\rm down}\) are the upstream and downstream stations of the blocked segment. If the train is rerouted (\(r_{i,{\rm opp}}=1\)), the constraints become non‑binding.

### 5.7 Track‑usage indicator (coupling route to segment occupancy)  

Let  

\[
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}=r_{i,k}\, \Pi^{k}_{s}\qquad \forall i,s,k
\]

Because \(\Pi^{k}_{s}\) is a known constant (0/1), we can replace the product by a linear formulation:

\[
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le r_{i,k},\qquad 
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le \Pi^{k}_{s},\qquad 
\zeta_{i,s}^{k}\ge r_{i,k}+ \Pi^{k}_{s}-1 \tag{TRACK\_use}
\]

\(\zeta_{i,s}^{k}=1\) iff train *i* uses route *k* **and** that route occupies the original track on segment *s*.  

The binary **ordering** variables are only defined for pairs that actually share the same physical track on a segment, i.e. when  

\[
\Pi^{\rm orig}_{s}=1 \;\text{and}\; \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}=1,\ \zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig}=1
\]
or similarly for the opposite track.

### 5.8 Conflict‑avoidance (ordering & headway)  

For any unordered pair \((i,j)\) that can occupy the same track on segment *s* we introduce a binary ordering variable \(o_{i,j,s}\) (1 if *i* passes before *j*). The following three constraints guarantee a feasible, conflict‑free schedule.

1. **Mutual exclusivity of ordering**

   \[
   o_{i,j,s}+o_{j,i,s}=1 \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}} \tag{ORD}
   \]

2. **Big‑M head‑way enforcement** (when *i* goes first)

   \[
   a_{j,s}\;\ge\; d_{i,s}+h \;-\; M\bigl(1-o_{i,j,s}\bigr) \qquad\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}} \tag{HW1}
   \]

   Symmetrically, when *j* goes first we have the same inequality with indices swapped (automatically covered because of (ORD)).

3. **Link to actual track usage** – the ordering constraints are *activated* only if the two trains really share the same track:

   \[
   o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig} \qquad\text{(original track)} \tag{ACT1}
   \]
   \[
   o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm opp}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm opp} \qquad\text{(opposite track)} \tag{ACT2}
   \]

   If at least one of the two trains uses a different track, the right‑hand side becomes 0 and the binary \(o_{i,j,s}\) must be 0, which in turn forces the complementary ordering variable to be 1, but both inequalities (HW1) become non‑binding because the big‑M term is active.

### 5.9 Linearisation of the quadratic energy term  

The energy term contains \(v_{i,s}^{2}\). We replace it by the auxiliary variable \(q_{i,s}\) and enforce:

\[
q_{i,s}\ge \; 2\bar v_{p}\,v_{i,s} - \bar v_{p}^{2}\qquad\forall p\in\mathcal{P},\; i,s \tag{Q1}
\]

\[
q_{i,s}\ge 0 \tag{Q2}
\]

Constraints (Q1) are the classic **McCormick** linearisation of a convex quadratic over a bounded interval \([v^{\min},v^{\max}]\). With a sufficiently fine set of break‑points \(\mathcal{P}\) the resulting polyhedron approximates \(v^{2}\) arbitrarily well. The objective uses \(q_{i,s}\) directly.

---

## 6. Summary of the Complete MILP  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min\;&\sum_{i\in I} w_{i}\bigl(a_{i,|S|}-\hat a_{i,|S|}\bigr)
          +\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{s=1}^{|S|-1}\bigl(\alpha_{1} q_{i,s}+ \alpha_{2} v_{i,s}\bigr)\ell_{s}\\[4pt]
\text{s.t. }&\text{(R1)} && \sum_{k\in K} r_{i,k}=1 &&\forall i\\
            &\text{(TF1)} && a_{i,s+1}=d_{i,s}+t_{i,s} &&\forall i, s=1\!\ldots\!|S|-1\\
            &\text{(DW)} && d_{i,s}\ge a_{i,s}+\tau^{\rm dwell}_{i,s} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(SL)} && v^{\min}\le v_{i,s}\le v^{\max} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_t)} && t_{i,s}= \sum_{p}\theta_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_v)} && v_{i,s}= \sum_{p}\bar v_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p} &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(PWL\_sum)} && \sum_{p}\lambda_{i,s,p}=1,\;\lambda_{i,s,p}\ge0 &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(BLK\_seg)} && d_{i,s_{\rm up}}\ge T^{\rm end} r_{i,{\rm orig}}\;\;\text{or}\;\; a_{i,s_{\rm down}}\le T^{\rm start} r_{i,{\rm orig}} &&\forall i\\
            &\text{(TRACK\_use)} && \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le r_{i,k},\; \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\le \Pi^{k}_{s},\;
               \zeta_{i,s}^{k}\ge r_{i,k}+\Pi^{k}_{s}-1 &&\forall i,s,k\\
            &\text{(ORD)} && o_{i,j,s}+o_{j,i,s}=1 &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(HW1)} && a_{j,s}\ge d_{i,s}+h-M(1-o_{i,j,s}) &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(ACT1/2)} && o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm orig}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm orig},
                              \; o_{i,j,s}\le \zeta_{i,s}^{\rm opp}+\zeta_{j,s}^{\rm opp}
                              &&\forall i<j,\; s\in S_{\text{shared}}\\
            &\text{(Q1)} && q_{i,s}\ge 2\bar v_{p}v_{i,s}-\bar v_{p}^{2} &&\forall i,s, p\in\mathcal{P}\\
            &\text{(Q2)} && q_{i,s}\ge 0 &&\forall i,s\\
            &\text{(binary/ non‑neg.)} && r_{i,k}\in\{0,1\},\; o_{i,j,s}\in\{0,1\},\;
               a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,s},v_{i,s},q_{i,s}\ge0 &&\forall\text{indices}
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are linear; the only non‑linearity (the quadratic energy term) is replaced by the convex envelope (Q1). The big‑M constant \(M\) should be chosen larger than the longest possible schedule horizon (e.g. \(M = 10\,000\) min) but as small as possible to keep the LP relaxation tight.

---

## 7. Explanation of Model Components  

| Component | What it does | Why it is needed |
|-----------|--------------|------------------|
| **Route‑choice binary \(r_{i,k}\)** | Decides whether a train stays on the original track or is rerouted to the opposite (bypass) track when the segment is blocked. | Guarantees that a train can only use one physical line at a time and enables the disruption‑window constraints. |
| **Ordering binary \(o_{i,j,s}\)** | Imposes a first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) order on any pair of trains that share a track on a given segment. | Enforces safety headways and avoids collisions on single‑track sections. |
| **Arrival / departure times \(a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\)** | Capture the actual timetable after rescheduling. | Core decision variables that allow delay computation and link travel‑time, dwell‑time and conflict constraints together. |
| **Speed \(v_{i,s}\) + travel time \(t_{i,s}\)** | Controls the physical movement between stations; speed bounds model engineering limits (track geometry, signaling). | Provides a realistic trade‑off: higher speed reduces delay but raises energy consumption. |
| **Piece‑wise linear (PWL) representation of \(1/v\)** | Linearises the relationship \(t = \ell/v\) by interpolating the convex function \(1/v\). | Keeps the model MILP (no bilinear terms). Accuracy can be tuned by the number of break‑points. |
| **Quadratic energy term linearised by McCormick (constraints Q1)** | Allows the objective to contain \(v^2\) (energy grows roughly with the square of speed) while preserving linearity. | Needed because most MILP solvers cannot handle actual quadratic terms directly. |
| **Disruption‑window constraints (BLK\*)** | Prevent any train that stays on the original line from entering the blocked time interval; rerouted trains are exempt. | Models the real‑world restriction caused by a temporary blockage (e.g. maintenance, accident). |
| **Capacity on opposite track** | Implicitly handled by the same ordering/headway constraints, but a separate upper bound \(\beta^{\max}_{\ell}\) could be added if the bypass line can accommodate more than one train simultaneously. | Guarantees that the alternative track does not become overloaded. |
| **Weighted delay term** | Each train may have a different importance (high‑speed premium services, freight, etc.). | Allows the planner to protect high‑value services at the expense of less critical ones. |
| **Energy term** | Sum of \(\alpha_{1}v^{2}+\alpha_{2}v\) over all kilometres. | Captures the operational cost/green‑house‑gas impact of higher speeds – the model can therefore balance punctuality against energy consumption. |

---

### 7.1 Modelling Assumptions (to make the MILP tractable)

1. **Constant average speed per segment** – intra‑segment speed variation is ignored; the segment is treated as a “flat” piece with one speed decision.
2. **Deterministic travel distances** – \(\ell_{s}\) are known and do not change with the schedule.
3. **Fixed headway \(h\)** – a conservative constant safety margin is used for any pair sharing a track.
4. **Binary ordering only on segments that can physically conflict** (i.e., where at most one train can occupy the track). For double‑track sections the ordering variables are simply omitted.
5. **Piece‑wise linear approximation** – the number of break‑points \(|\mathcal{P}|\) is a modelling choice; 4–6 points give a good compromise between accuracy and model size.
6. **Big‑M value** – chosen large enough to deactivate constraints when the corresponding ordering is not active, but not excessively large to avoid numerical difficulties.

---

## 8. How to Use the Model  

1. **Data preparation** – For each train prepare its original schedule \(\hat a,\hat d\), the list of stations, distances, and the disrupted segment(s) with the time window.  
2. **Select break‑points** – Typical speeds: \([200,250,300,350,400]\) km/h for a high‑speed line; compute \(\theta=1/v\) for each.  
3. **Create the pair‑wise conflict set** – For every segment that is single‑track after the disruption, generate all unordered pairs \((i,j)\).  
4. **Feed the MILP** – Most modern solvers accept the model in **AMPL**, **GAMS**, **Pyomo**, or **JuMP** format; the constraints above translate directly.  
5. **Solve & post‑process** – The optimal solution provides: (i) the rerouting decisions \(r_{i,k}\), (ii) the speed profile \(v_{i,s}\), (iii) the new timetable \(a_{i,s},d_{i,s}\). From these you can compute the actual delay per train and the total energy consumption.

---

### 9. Closing Remark  

The formulation above is *complete* in the sense that every element mentioned in the problem description appears in the linear model, and every non‑linear relationship has been replaced by a proven linearisation technique (piece‑wise linear interpolation for \(1/v\) and McCormick envelopes for \(v^{2}\)).  By adjusting the weights \(w_{i},\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\) and the granularity of the PWL approximation, a railway operator can explore the whole spectrum from “minimum delay at any energy cost” to “energy‑optimal but possibly later arrivals”, while respecting the hard safety and disruption constraints of a partially blocked high‑speed line.

response.content:
**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  

The model below is written in a *standard linear* mixed‑integer‑programming form.  
All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and each family of
constraints are listed first; a short comment explains the purpose of every term.  
The formulation is *complete* – i.e. if you copy it into a MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi,
Xpress, …) and provide the data described in the “Assumptions” section, the solver will
return a feasible schedule that respects the blockage, the train‑ordering on shared
segments, the dwell‑time and speed‑limits, and that minimizes a weighted combination of
total delay and energy consumption.

---

## 1.  Sets and Indices  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **I**  | Set of trains, indexed by *i* (|I| = N). |
| **S**  | Set of stations (including the terminal **last**), indexed by *s* (ordered). |
| **K**  | Set of possible *routes* on the disrupted segment, **K = {orig, opp}** (original track, opposite track). |
| **E**  | Set of *edges* (track‑segments) between two consecutive stations,  *e = (s,s+1)*. |
| **B**  | Sub‑set of edges that are *blocked* (the segment that suffers a partial blockage). |
| **P**  | Set of ordered train‑pairs that share at least one common edge, i.e.  \(P=\{(i,j): i\neq j \text{ and } \exists e\in E\; \text{used by both}\}\). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Units |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| `sched_i` | Scheduled arrival time of train *i* at its last station (baseline). | min |
| `Δdwell_min` | Minimum dwell (stop) time at every station. | min |
| `Δdwell_max` | Maximum allowed dwell (optional). | min |
| `dist_e` | Length of edge *e* (in km). | km |
| `v_min` , `v_max` | Global speed limits (may be refined per edge). | km/h |
| `headway` | Minimum time gap required between two successive trains on the **same** track (safety). | min |
| `T_start` , `T_end` | Start / end of the disruption window on the original track. | min |
| `α` , `β` | Weight coefficients in the objective (delay weight *α* > 0, energy weight *β* > 0). | – |
| `c1_q , c2_q` | Linearization coefficients for the *quadratic* term `v²` on edge *q*  (see §5). | – |
| `c3_q` | Linear coefficient for the linear term `v` on edge *q* (energy component). | – |
| `M` | Large constant (big‑M) used for big‑M reformulations. | – |

*All time‑related parameters are expressed in minutes; all speeds in km/h.*  

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `r_i_k` | Binary | 1 if train *i* uses route *k* (= *orig* or *opp*) on a blocked edge, 0 otherwise. |
| `o_ij` | Binary | 1 if train *i* passes **before** train *j* on a common edge (the ordering variable). |
| `a_i_s` | Continuous, ≥0 | Arrival time of train *i* at station *s*. |
| `d_i_s` | Continuous, ≥0 | Departure time of train *i* from station *s*. |
| `v_i_e` | Continuous, ≥0 | **Average speed** of train *i* while traversing edge *e*. |
| `t_i_e` | Continuous, ≥0 | Travel time of train *i* on edge *e*. |
| `z_i_q` | Continuous, ≥0 | Auxiliary variable that linearizes the quadratic term \(v_i_q^2\). (One per edge *q*.) |

*The “last” station of a train is denoted by `s = last_i`.  The decision variables exist only for the edges actually traversed by a train; a train that does not travel on edge *e* has the corresponding variables fixed to 0.*

---

## 4.  Objective Function  

\[
\boxed{
\min \;  \alpha \;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}_i}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)}_{\text{Total delay}}
           \;+\;
           \beta  \;\underbrace{\sum_{i\in I}\;\sum_{e\in E_i}
                 \Bigl(c_{1_e}\,z_{i,e}+c_{2_e}\,v_{i,e}\Bigr)}_{\text{Energy consumption}}
}
\tag{OBJ}
\]

*Explanation*  

* `a_{i,last_i} – sched_i` is the **delay** of train *i* at its final destination.  
* Energy on edge *e* is approximated by a piece‑wise linear function  
  \(E(v)=c_{1_e}v^{2}+c_{2_e}v\).  The quadratic part is linearized by \(z_{i,e}\) (see §5).  
* The two parts are weighted by user‑defined scalars `α` (delay importance) and `β`
  (energy importance).

---

## 5.  Linearisation of the Quadratic Speed Term  

The term \(v_{i,e}^{2}\) is convex; a common way to keep the model linear is to use a
*piece‑wise linear over‑estimator* (or exact McCormick envelopes on a bounded domain).  
Assume the speed on every edge is bounded by \([v_{\min}^{e},v_{\max}^{e}]\).
Define a set of *break‑points* \(\{p_1,\dots ,p_L\}\) inside the interval.
Introduce auxiliary non‑negative variables \(\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\) (convex combination) :

\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}=1,\qquad 
v_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} p_{\ell}\,\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\qquad 
z_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} p_{\ell}^{2}\,\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},
\qquad\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\ge 0 .
\tag{LIN\_SPEED}
\]

If a *coarser* linearisation is acceptable, a single big‑M envelope can be used:

\[
z_{i,e}\ge v_{i,e}^{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;
z_{i,e}\ge 2\,v_{\min}^{e}\,v_{i,e}-\bigl(v_{\min}^{e}\bigr)^{2},\qquad
z_{i,e}\ge 2\,v_{\max}^{e}\,v_{i,e}-\bigl(v_{\max}^{e}\bigr)^{2}.
\tag{BIGM\_SPEED}
\]

Both families are linear, thus preserve MILP structure.

---

## 6.  Core Scheduling Constraints  

### 6.1   Travel‑time definition  

\[
t_{i,e}= \frac{\text{dist}_{e}}{v_{i,e}},\qquad \forall i\in I,\;e\in E_i .
\tag{TRAV\_TIME}
\]

Because `v` is a decision variable, the fraction is **non‑linear**.  
We linearise it by cross‑multiplying (the denominator is bounded away from zero):

\[
\text{dist}_{e}= v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\text{dist}_{e}\le v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}+M\,(1-u_{i,e}),\\
\text{dist}_{e}\ge v_{i,e}\,t_{i,e}-M\,(1-u_{i,e}),
\]

where binary `u_{i,e}` forces the equality for edges actually used (otherwise the
product can be relaxed).  In practice the linearised version (using the
piece‑wise speed representation from §5) yields a *linear* relationship between
`t` and `v`.

### 6.2   Time‑flow over stations  

\[
a_{i,s+1}= d_{i,s}+t_{i,(s,s+1)} \qquad\forall i\in I,\; s\in S\setminus\{\text{last}_i\}.
\tag{FLOW}
\]

### 6.3   Dwell‑time limits  

\[
\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\;\le\; d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\;\le\;\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\max}\quad
\forall i\in I,\, s\in S\setminus\{\text{first}_i,\text{last}_i\}.
\tag{DWELL}
\]

(If `Δdwell_max` is not required it can be omitted.)

### 6.4   Speed limits  

\[
v_{\min}\;\le\; v_{i,e}\;\le\;v_{\max}\qquad\forall i\in I,\;e\in E_i .
\tag{SPEED\_BND}
\]

---

## 7.  Blockage / Route‑Choice Constraints  

Only the edges belonging to the blocked set **B** are affected.

### 7.1   Exactly one route per train on a blocked edge  

\[
r_{i,\text{orig}}+r_{i,\text{opp}} = 1 \qquad\forall i\in I\;\; \text{with } B\neq\varnothing .
\tag{ROUTE\_CHOICE}
\]

### 7.2   Forbidden use of the original track during the disruption window  

For every train *i* that traverses a blocked edge *e∈B* on the **original** track:

\[
a_{i,\text{upstream}(e)} \ge T_{\text{end}}  \;\;\; \text{or}\;\;\;
d_{i,\text{downstream}(e)} \le T_{\text{start}} \quad
\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a_{i,\text{up}} \ge T_{\text{end}} - M\,(1-r_{i,\text{orig}})
\]
\[
d_{i,\text{down}} \le T_{\text{start}} + M\,(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}).
\tag{BLOCK\_ORIG}
\]

If `r_{i,orig}=0` (train rerouted) the big‑M terms deactivate the constraints,
allowing the train to occupy the opposite track at any time.

### 7.3   Capacity on the opposite track (if it is also shared)  

Analogous to the ordering constraints described next ( §8 ) – the same logic
applies to both routes; the only difference is that the binary `r_{i,k}` selects
which set of ordering constraints becomes active.

---

## 8.  Ordering / Head‑way Constraints on Shared Segments  

Consider any edge *e* that can be travelled by more than one train (including
the opposite track when several trains are routed there).  
For each unordered pair \((i,j)\) that may share *e* define a binary variable  
\(o_{ij}^{e}\) (we keep the same symbol `o_ij` but it is *edge‑specific*).

### 8.1   Exactly one ordering  

\[
o_{ij}^{e} + o_{ji}^{e}=1 \qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_ONE}
\]

### 8.2   Time–separation when *i* precedes *j*  

\[
d_{i,\text{up}(e)} + \text{headway} \;\le\; a_{j,\text{down}(e)} + M\,(1-o_{ij}^{e})
\qquad\forall (i,j)\in P,\; e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_TIME}
\]

If `o_{ij}^{e}=1` the big‑M term disappears and the inequality forces the required
headway; if `o_{ij}^{e}=0` the constraint is relaxed.

### 8.3   Compatibility with route choice  

Only pairs that travel **on the same physical track** need ordering.  
Let `track_{i,e}` be a binary indicator that train *i* uses the **original** track on
edge *e*:  

\[
track_{i,e}=r_{i,\text{orig}} \quad \forall e\in B,
\]
\[
track_{i,e}=1 \quad \forall e\notin B   \;(\text{no blockage, only one track}).
\]

Then the ordering constraints are activated only when both trains share the same
track:

\[
o_{ij}^{e} \le track_{i,e},\qquad
o_{ij}^{e} \le track_{j,e},\qquad
o_{ij}^{e} \ge track_{i,e}+track_{j,e}-1
\quad\forall (i,j)\in P,\;e\in E_i\cap E_j .
\tag{ORD\_LINK}
\]

If the two trains are on different tracks, `o_{ij}^{e}` is forced to 0 and no headway
restriction is imposed.

---

## 9.  Additional Practical Constraints (optional)  

| Constraint | Formulation | Comment |
|------------|-------------|---------|
| **Maximum lateness** | \(a_{i,last_i}\le \text{sched}_i + L_{\max}\) | Guarantees a user‑defined service level. |
| **Train‑specific speed limits** | Replace `v_min`, `v_max` by edge‑specific bounds `v_{min}^{i,e}`, `v_{max}^{i,e}`. |
| **Platform capacity** | \(\sum_{i\in I} \mathbf{1}\{a_{i,s}\le t \le d_{i,s}\}\le C_s\) (linearised with binaries). | Keeps the number of trains at a station ≤ capacity *C_s*. |
| **Mandatory early departure** | \(d_{i,s}\ge a_{i,s}+\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\) (already in DWELL). |
| **Turn‑back limits** | For a train that must reverse direction on the opposite track, impose a binary “turn” variable and a minimum turnaround time. |  |

---

## 10.  Full MILP Statement  

Putting everything together, the model is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\min \;& \alpha\sum_{i\in I}\bigl(a_{i,\text{last}_i}-\text{sched}_i\bigr)\\
      &+ \beta\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{e\in E_i}\bigl(c_{1_e}z_{i,e}+c_{2_e}v_{i,e}\bigr) \\[4pt]
\text{s.t. } &
\text{(ROUTE\_CHOICE)} && r_{i,\text{orig}}+r_{i,\text{opp}} =1 \quad\forall i\in I \\
& \text{(BLOCK\_ORIG)} && a_{i,\text{up}(e)} \ge T_{\text{end}}-M(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}) \\
& && d_{i,\text{down}(e)} \le T_{\text{start}}+M(1-r_{i,\text{orig}}) \quad\forall e\in B \\
& \text{(FLOW)} && a_{i,s+1}=d_{i,s}+t_{i,(s,s+1)} \quad\forall i,\;s\neq\text{last}_i \\
& \text{(DWELL)} && \Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\min}\le d_{i,s}-a_{i,s}\le\Delta_{\text{dwell}}^{\max} \\
& \text{(SPEED\_BND)} && v_{\min}\le v_{i,e}\le v_{\max} \\
& \text{(TRAV\_TIME \& LIN\_SPEED)} && \text{dist}_{e}=v_{i,e}t_{i,e} \;\;\text{(linearised via (LIN\_SPEED) or (BIGM\_SPEED))} \\
& \text{(ORD\_ONE)} && o_{ij}^{e}+o_{ji}^{e}=1 \quad\forall (i,j)\in P, \,e\in E_i\cap E_j \\
& \text{(ORD\_TIME)} && d_{i,\text{up}(e)}+\text{headway}\le a_{j,\text{down}(e)}+M(1-o_{ij}^{e}) \\
& \text{(ORD\_LINK)} && o_{ij}^{e}\le track_{i,e}, \; o_{ij}^{e}\le track_{j,e}, \;
                         o_{ij}^{e}\ge track_{i,e}+track_{j,e}-1 \\[2pt]
& \text{(ENERGY\_LIN)} && v_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell} p_{\ell}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\;
                         z_{i,e}= \sum_{\ell} p_{\ell}^{2}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell},\\
& && \sum_{\ell}\lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}=1,\; \lambda_{i,e}^{\ell}\ge0. \\
& \text{(Variables)} && r_{i,k},\,o_{ij}^{e}\in\{0,1\},\;
                       a_{i,s},d_{i,s},t_{i,e},v_{i,e},z_{i,e}\ge 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All constraints are **linear**; the only non‑trivial piece is the speed‑quadratic
linearisation, which is completely handled by (ENERGY\_LIN) or the pair of
McCormick inequalities (BIGM\_SPEED).  

---

## 11.  Assumptions and Modelling Remarks  

1. **Deterministic data** – travel distances, scheduled times, disruption window, headway,
   and speed limits are known exactly.  
2. **Uniform block** – the disruption affects a *single* contiguous edge set **B**; the
   opposite track is assumed to be completely free (except for the usual ordering
   constraints).  
3. **Average speed per edge** – the model works with a constant speed on each edge.
   If a finer time‑resolution is required, split the edge into smaller sub‑edges
   and replicate the variables.  
4. **Piece‑wise linear energy model** – the squared‑speed term is approximated by a
   convex envelope; increasing the number of break‑points *L* improves fidelity at the
   cost of more variables.  
5. **Big‑M size** – `M` must be larger than the maximum possible schedule horizon
   (e.g. 10 000 min).  A tighter value reduces numerical difficulty.  
6. **Feasibility** – because the binary route‑choice forces each train to use *some*
   track, the model is always feasible unless the headway requirement is too
   strict; in that case the headway can be relaxed or a dummy “delay” variable can
   be introduced with a very high penalty.  

---

### How to use the formulation  

1. **Prepare the data** (the sets, distances, scheduled times, disruption window, speed limits, energy coefficients, headway, dwell‑times).  
2. **Choose the linearisation** – either the exact piece‑wise representation (`λ` variables) or the two‑inequality McCormick envelope.  
3. **Instantiate the model** in any MILP modelling language (AMPL, GAMS, Pyomo, JuMP, OPL …).  
4. **Solve** with a modern MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress).  
5. **Interpret the solution** – the binary `r_i_k` tells whether train *i* was rerouted,
   the ordering variables give the exact sequence on each shared segment, and the
   arrival/departure times provide the new schedule that respects the blockage while
   minimizing delay + energy.

This completes a **linear, mixed‑integer programming** description of the Integrated
Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management Problem under a partial segment blockage.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
