**Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
The formulation below is a complete, linear model that can be used directly in a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  It is built by extending the classic RECIFE‑MILP CDR model (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with the DTG‑specific elements described in the paper excerpt.  

All symbols are defined in the *Sets* and *Parameters* sections; any symbol marked with “*Assumption*” is introduced because the source text does not provide a numeric value or a precise definition.  The model is **deterministic** (the timetable and the set of delayed events are known at the time of optimisation) and **static** (the planning horizon is a single day/shift).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD sections), indexed by *s*. |
| **P** | Set of stations, a subset of *S*. |
| **N(t)** | Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (its route). |
| **E** | Set of events (arrival/departure at a section), indexed by *(t,s)* with *s*∈N(t). |
| **K** | Set of feasible speed‑profile options (e.g. “full‑speed”, “reduced‑speed”). |
| **B** | Set of binary decision variables for ordering conflicts (defined later). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| **L_s** | Length of section *s* (km). | Network data |
| **v_k** | Constant cruising speed associated with speed‑profile *k* (km/h). | Assumption – e.g. 200 km/h, 160 km/h, 120 km/h |
| **a_brk** | Uniform service‑braking deceleration (km/h²). | Assumption – e.g. 1.0 km/h² (≈ 0.28 m/s²) |
| **τ_dwell** | Minimum dwell time at stations (minutes). | Timetable data |
| **τ_buf** | Safety buffer (minutes) added to all separation constraints to guarantee robustness. | Assumption – e.g. 0.5 min |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}** | Planned (reference) arrival time of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}^{dep}** | Planned departure time of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **δ_{t,s}** | Exogenous delay (minutes) already observed for train *t* at the entry of *s* (≥0). | Real‑time input |
| **M** | Large constant (“big‑M”) for linearising logical constraints. | Set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary indicator = 1 if train *t* uses speed‑profile *k* on section *s*, 0 otherwise. | Decision variable (see below). |
| **b_{s}** | Binary flag = 1 if section *s* is a **switch** (or a TTD section with special rules), 0 otherwise. | Network data |
| **γ** | Factor converting kilometres to minutes at speed *v_k*: γ_{k}=60 / v_k (min/km). | Derived from v_k |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **a_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted arrival time** of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s* (minutes from horizon start). |
| **d_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted departure time** of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary | Speed‑profile selection: 1 if train *t* travels on section *s* with profile *k*. |
| **y_{t,s}** | Binary | 1 if train *t* **stops** (dwells) at station *s* ∈ P, 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{(t1,t2),s}** | Binary, (t1,t2)∈C_s | **Ordering variable** for a pair of conflicting trains on the same section *s*: 1 if *t1* passes before *t2*, 0 otherwise. |
| **z_t** | Continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between adjusted arrival at its last section and the planned arrival). |
| **w_{t}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Penalty** for applying a speed‑profile slower than the fastest one (used to discourage unnecessary speed reductions). |

*Note:* The set **C_s** contains all unordered pairs of trains whose routes intersect section *s*:  

\[
C_s = \{(t_1,t_2)\mid t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in N(t_1)\cap N(t_2)\}.
\]

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The primary operational goal is to **minimise total passenger/traffic delay** while penalising unnecessary speed reductions (to keep the solution realistic).  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_t}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in N(t)}\sum_{k\in K} w_{t}\, \beta_{t,s,k}}_{\text{speed‑reduction penalty}}
}
\]

* **λ** is a weighting factor (e.g. λ = 0.1 min) that trades off delay versus speed‑profile changes.  

The total delay of a train is defined later (constraint (9)).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Speed‑profile selection  

Each train must choose **exactly one** speed‑profile on every traversed section.

\[
\sum_{k\in K} \beta_{t,s,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{1}
\]

### 5.2. Travel time on a section (DTG‑specific)  

The **minimum travel time** on section *s* for train *t* using profile *k* is the sum of:

* **running time** = length / speed,
* **braking time** needed to stop at the *end of authority* (EoA).  
  Under DTG, the brake‑indication point (IP) is placed at the *braking distance* from the EoA, which depends on the current speed. The braking distance (in km) for speed *v_k* with deceleration *a_brk* is  

\[
\text{brkDist}_{k}= \frac{v_k^{2}}{2\,a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(km)} .
\]

The corresponding **braking time** (minutes) is  

\[
\text{brkTime}_{k}= \frac{v_k}{a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(min)} .
\]

Because the EoA is always at the **end of the section**, the train must start braking **brkDistₖ** before the end. If the section is longer than the braking distance, the train can cruise at *vₖ* for the remaining part; otherwise the whole section is covered by the braking curve (the model automatically handles this via a big‑M linearisation – see (5)–(6)).  

For linearity we pre‑compute the **minimum feasible travel time** on section *s* for profile *k*:

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \underbrace{\frac{L_s-\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_k}\,60}_{\text{cruise time (min)}} \;+\; \text{brkTime}_{k} \quad\text{if }L_s>\text{brkDist}_{k},
\]

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\,60 \quad\text{if }L_s\le \text{brkDist}_{k}\; (\text{pure braking}).
\]

*Assumption:* The same braking curve is used for all trains (homogeneous rolling stock).  

The **adjusted departure time** must respect the minimum travel time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{s,k}\,\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{2}
\]

### 5.3. Dwell time at stations  

If a train stops at a station (*y_{t,s}=1*), it must stay at least **τ_dwell** minutes; otherwise it may pass through (zero dwell).

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \tau_{dwell}\,y_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P\cap N(t) \tag{3}
\]

### 5.4. Propagation of times along the route  

The departure from section *s* becomes the arrival at the next section *s′* (the exit of *s* is the entry of *s′*).  

\[
a_{t,s'} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive in }N(t) \tag{4}
\]

### 5.5. Conflict‑avoidance (DTG separation)  

Two trains *t₁* and *t₂* that occupy the same section *s* must respect a **speed‑dependent separation distance**. Under DTG the separation is expressed as a **minimum time gap** between the *brake‑indication points* of the two trains. The brake‑indication point of a train on section *s* occurs **brkDistₖ** before the end of the section; therefore the **earliest safe entry** of the following train is:

\[
\text{SafeEntry}_{t_1,s}= a_{t_1,s} + \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\text{time from entry to IP}} .
\]

Because the model already enforces the minimum travel time (2), we can impose the separation directly on the **arrival times**:

\[
a_{t_2,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_1,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_1,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{(t_1,t_2),s}) \tag{5a}
\]

\[
a_{t_1,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_2,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_2,s}}}{v_{k_{t_2,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_2,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,x_{(t_1,t_2),s} \tag{5b}
\]

where **x_{(t₁,t₂),s}** decides the ordering (0 → *t₁* before *t₂*, 1 → *t₂* before *t₁*).  

The **Δ‑terms** are linearised by introducing auxiliary continuous variables:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_{k}}\,60\;\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{5c}
\]

Constraint (5a)–(5b) together with (5c) guarantee that **exactly one ordering** is selected:

\[
x_{(t_1,t_2),s}+x_{(t_2,t_1),s}=1 \qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s \tag{5d}
\]

*Special handling for switches / TTD sections* (b_s = 1): the separation distance can be reduced by a factor **ρ < 1** (e.g., 0.8) because the detection is more accurate. This is modelled by scaling the Δ‑term:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}^{\text{eff}} = \Delta_{t,s}\; \bigl(1-\rho\,b_s\bigr) \tag{5e}
\]

and using **Δ_{t,s}^{eff}** in (5a)–(5b).

### 5.6. Initial conditions (exogenous delays)  

The adjusted arrival must be at least the original planned arrival plus any observed delay:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s} \;+\; \delta_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{6}
\]

### 5.7. Definition of total train delay  

The **total delay** of train *t* is measured at its **last section** (the final destination). Let *s^{\text{last}}_t* be the last element of N(t).  

\[
z_t \;=\; a_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \;-\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{7}
\]

(If a train is scheduled to arrive earlier than the horizon start, the RHS can be negative; the model will simply not select that solution.)

### 5.8. Speed‑reduction penalty (optional)  

If a train uses a slower profile than the fastest one (*k\* = arg max vₖ*), we charge a small penalty:

\[
w_t \;\ge\; \bigl(1-\beta_{t,s,k^{\*}}\bigr) \quad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{8}
\]

This forces **w_t = 1** if any section uses a slower speed; otherwise **w_t = 0**. The term appears in the objective with weight λ.

### 5.9. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s},\, d_{t,s},\, \Delta_{t,s},\, z_t &\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
\beta_{t,s,k} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
y_{t,s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s\in P\\
x_{(t_1,t_2),s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s,\, s\in S\\
w_t &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the Model  

* **Decision variables** – adjusted arrival/departure times, speed‑profile choices, dwell‑stop decisions, conflict‑ordering binaries, and a total‑delay variable.  
* **Objective** – minimise the sum of all train delays while discouraging unnecessary speed reductions.  
* **Constraints** – (1) enforce a single speed profile per section, (2) enforce DTG‑based minimum travel times, (3) enforce mandatory dwell times, (4) propagate times along each train’s route, (5) enforce speed‑dependent separation (the core DTG enhancement), (6) respect observed exogenous delays, (7) compute total delay, (8) optional penalty for slower profiles, (9) variable domains.  

The model is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable times a constant) and therefore solvable to optimality with any MILP solver. **Mixed‑Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model for Conflict‑Detection‑and‑Resolution (CDR) under Distance‑to‑Go (DTG) signalling**  
The formulation below is a complete, linear model that can be used directly in a commercial MILP solver (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress, …).  It is built by extending the classic RECIFE‑MILP CDR model (Pellegrini et al., 2015) with the DTG‑specific elements described in the paper excerpt.  

All symbols are defined in the *Sets* and *Parameters* sections; any symbol marked with “*Assumption*” is introduced because the source text does not provide a numeric value or a precise definition.  The model is **deterministic** (the timetable and the set of delayed events are known at the time of optimisation) and **static** (the planning horizon is a single day/shift).  

---

## 1. Sets  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** | Set of trains, indexed by *t* (|T| = N). |
| **S** | Set of track sections (blocks or TTD sections), indexed by *s*. |
| **P** | Set of stations, a subset of *S*. |
| **N(t)** | Ordered list of sections traversed by train *t* (its route). |
| **E** | Set of events (arrival/departure at a section), indexed by *(t,s)* with *s*∈N(t). |
| **K** | Set of feasible speed‑profile options (e.g. “full‑speed”, “reduced‑speed”). |
| **B** | Set of binary decision variables for ordering conflicts (defined later). |

---

## 2. Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical value / source |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| **L_s** | Length of section *s* (km). | Network data |
| **v_k** | Constant cruising speed associated with speed‑profile *k* (km/h). | Assumption – e.g. 200 km/h, 160 km/h, 120 km/h |
| **a_brk** | Uniform service‑braking deceleration (km/h²). | Assumption – e.g. 1.0 km/h² (≈ 0.28 m/s²) |
| **τ_dwell** | Minimum dwell time at stations (minutes). | Timetable data |
| **τ_buf** | Safety buffer (minutes) added to all separation constraints to guarantee robustness. | Assumption – e.g. 0.5 min |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}** | Planned (reference) arrival time of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **Δt⁰_{t,s}^{dep}** | Planned departure time of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. | Timetable |
| **δ_{t,s}** | Exogenous delay (minutes) already observed for train *t* at the entry of *s* (≥0). | Real‑time input |
| **M** | Large constant (“big‑M”) for linearising logical constraints. | Set to a value larger than the planning horizon (e.g. 10 000 min). |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary indicator = 1 if train *t* uses speed‑profile *k* on section *s*, 0 otherwise. | Decision variable (see below). |
| **b_{s}** | Binary flag = 1 if section *s* is a **switch** (or a TTD section with special rules), 0 otherwise. | Network data |
| **γ** | Factor converting kilometres to minutes at speed *v_k*: γ_{k}=60 / v_k (min/km). | Derived from v_k |

---

## 3. Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **a_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted arrival time** of train *t* at the *entry* of section *s* (minutes from horizon start). |
| **d_{t,s}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Adjusted departure time** of train *t* from the *exit* of section *s*. |
| **β_{t,s,k}** | Binary | Speed‑profile selection: 1 if train *t* travels on section *s* with profile *k*. |
| **y_{t,s}** | Binary | 1 if train *t* **stops** (dwells) at station *s* ∈ P, 0 otherwise. |
| **x_{(t1,t2),s}** | Binary, (t1,t2)∈C_s | **Ordering variable** for a pair of conflicting trains on the same section *s*: 1 if *t1* passes before *t2*, 0 otherwise. |
| **z_t** | Continuous ≥0 | **Total delay** of train *t* (difference between adjusted arrival at its last section and the planned arrival). |
| **w_{t}** | Continuous ≥0 | **Penalty** for applying a speed‑profile slower than the fastest one (used to discourage unnecessary speed reductions). |

*Note:* The set **C_s** contains all unordered pairs of trains whose routes intersect section *s*:  

\[
C_s = \{(t_1,t_2)\mid t_1\neq t_2,\; s\in N(t_1)\cap N(t_2)\}.
\]

---

## 4. Objective Function  

The primary operational goal is to **minimise total passenger/traffic delay** while penalising unnecessary speed reductions (to keep the solution realistic).  

\[
\boxed{
\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T} z_t}_{\text{total delay}} \;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{s\in N(t)}\sum_{k\in K} w_{t}\, \beta_{t,s,k}}_{\text{speed‑reduction penalty}}
}
\]

* **λ** is a weighting factor (e.g. λ = 0.1 min) that trades off delay versus speed‑profile changes.  

The total delay of a train is defined later (constraint (9)).

---

## 5. Constraints  

### 5.1. Speed‑profile selection  

Each train must choose **exactly one** speed‑profile on every traversed section.

\[
\sum_{k\in K} \beta_{t,s,k}=1 \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{1}
\]

### 5.2. Travel time on a section (DTG‑specific)  

The **minimum travel time** on section *s* for train *t* using profile *k* is the sum of:

* **running time** = length / speed,
* **braking time** needed to stop at the *end of authority* (EoA).  
  Under DTG, the brake‑indication point (IP) is placed at the *braking distance* from the EoA, which depends on the current speed. The braking distance (in km) for speed *v_k* with deceleration *a_brk* is  

\[
\text{brkDist}_{k}= \frac{v_k^{2}}{2\,a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(km)} .
\]

The corresponding **braking time** (minutes) is  

\[
\text{brkTime}_{k}= \frac{v_k}{a_{brk}} \;\; \text{(min)} .
\]

Because the EoA is always at the **end of the section**, the train must start braking **brkDistₖ** before the end. If the section is longer than the braking distance, the train can cruise at *vₖ* for the remaining part; otherwise the whole section is covered by the braking curve (the model automatically handles this via a big‑M linearisation – see (5)–(6)).  

For linearity we pre‑compute the **minimum feasible travel time** on section *s* for profile *k*:

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \underbrace{\frac{L_s-\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_k}\,60}_{\text{cruise time (min)}} \;+\; \text{brkTime}_{k} \quad\text{if }L_s>\text{brkDist}_{k},
\]

\[
\theta_{s,k}= \frac{L_s}{v_k}\,60 \quad\text{if }L_s\le \text{brkDist}_{k}\; (\text{pure braking}).
\]

*Assumption:* The same braking curve is used for all trains (homogeneous rolling stock).  

The **adjusted departure time** must respect the minimum travel time:

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \sum_{k\in K}\theta_{s,k}\,\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{2}
\]

### 5.3. Dwell time at stations  

If a train stops at a station (*y_{t,s}=1*), it must stay at least **τ_dwell** minutes; otherwise it may pass through (zero dwell).

\[
d_{t,s} \;\ge\; a_{t,s} \;+\; \tau_{dwell}\,y_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in P\cap N(t) \tag{3}
\]

### 5.4. Propagation of times along the route  

The departure from section *s* becomes the arrival at the next section *s′* (the exit of *s* is the entry of *s′*).  

\[
a_{t,s'} \;\ge\; d_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; (s,s')\text{ consecutive in }N(t) \tag{4}
\]

### 5.5. Conflict‑avoidance (DTG separation)  

Two trains *t₁* and *t₂* that occupy the same section *s* must respect a **speed‑dependent separation distance**. Under DTG the separation is expressed as a **minimum time gap** between the *brake‑indication points* of the two trains. The brake‑indication point of a train on section *s* occurs **brkDistₖ** before the end of the section; therefore the **earliest safe entry** of the following train is:

\[
\text{SafeEntry}_{t_1,s}= a_{t_1,s} + \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\text{time from entry to IP}} .
\]

Because the model already enforces the minimum travel time (2), we can impose the separation directly on the **arrival times**:

\[
a_{t_2,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_1,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_1,s}}}{v_{k_{t_1,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_1,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,(1-x_{(t_1,t_2),s}) \tag{5a}
\]

\[
a_{t_1,s} \;\ge\; a_{t_2,s} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k_{t_2,s}}}{v_{k_{t_2,s}}}\,60}_{\displaystyle \Delta_{t_2,s}} \;+\; \tau_{buf} \;-\; M\,x_{(t_1,t_2),s} \tag{5b}
\]

where **x_{(t₁,t₂),s}** decides the ordering (0 → *t₁* before *t₂*, 1 → *t₂* before *t₁*).  

The **Δ‑terms** are linearised by introducing auxiliary continuous variables:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}= \sum_{k\in K}\frac{\text{brkDist}_{k}}{v_{k}}\,60\;\beta_{t,s,k} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in S \tag{5c}
\]

Constraint (5a)–(5b) together with (5c) guarantee that **exactly one ordering** is selected:

\[
x_{(t_1,t_2),s}+x_{(t_2,t_1),s}=1 \qquad\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s \tag{5d}
\]

*Special handling for switches / TTD sections* (b_s = 1): the separation distance can be reduced by a factor **ρ < 1** (e.g., 0.8) because the detection is more accurate. This is modelled by scaling the Δ‑term:

\[
\Delta_{t,s}^{\text{eff}} = \Delta_{t,s}\; \bigl(1-\rho\,b_s\bigr) \tag{5e}
\]

and using **Δ_{t,s}^{eff}** in (5a)–(5b).

### 5.6. Initial conditions (exogenous delays)  

The adjusted arrival must be at least the original planned arrival plus any observed delay:

\[
a_{t,s} \;\ge\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s} \;+\; \delta_{t,s} \qquad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{6}
\]

### 5.7. Definition of total train delay  

The **total delay** of train *t* is measured at its **last section** (the final destination). Let *s^{\text{last}}_t* be the last element of N(t).  

\[
z_t \;=\; a_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \;-\; \Delta t^{0}_{t,s^{\text{last}}_t} \qquad\forall t\in T \tag{7}
\]

(If a train is scheduled to arrive earlier than the horizon start, the RHS can be negative; the model will simply not select that solution.)

### 5.8. Speed‑reduction penalty (optional)  

If a train uses a slower profile than the fastest one (*k\* = arg max vₖ*), we charge a small penalty:

\[
w_t \;\ge\; \bigl(1-\beta_{t,s,k^{\*}}\bigr) \quad\forall t\in T,\; s\in N(t) \tag{8}
\]

This forces **w_t = 1** if any section uses a slower speed; otherwise **w_t = 0**. The term appears in the objective with weight λ.

### 5.9. Variable domains  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t,s},\, d_{t,s},\, \Delta_{t,s},\, z_t &\ge 0 &&\forall t,s\\
\beta_{t,s,k} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s,k\\
y_{t,s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t,s\in P\\
x_{(t_1,t_2),s} &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall (t_1,t_2)\in C_s,\, s\in S\\
w_t &\in \{0,1\} &&\forall t\in T
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

---

## 6. Summary of the Model  

* **Decision variables** – adjusted arrival/departure times, speed‑profile choices, dwell‑stop decisions, conflict‑ordering binaries, and a total‑delay variable.  
* **Objective** – minimise the sum of all train delays while discouraging unnecessary speed reductions.  
* **Constraints** – (1) enforce a single speed profile per section, (2) enforce DTG‑based minimum travel times, (3) enforce mandatory dwell times, (4) propagate times along each train’s route, (5) enforce speed‑dependent separation (the core DTG enhancement), (6) respect observed exogenous delays, (7) compute total delay, (8) optional penalty for slower profiles, (9) variable domains.  

The model is **linear** (all products involve a binary variable times a constant) and therefore solvable to optimality with any MILP solver.  By adjusting the data (section lengths, speed‑profile set, braking deceleration, switch‑factor ρ, safety buffer τ_buf) the same formulation can be applied to any railway network equipped with ETCS L2 (or similar DTG) signalling.  

--- 

**How to use the model in practice**

1. **Data preparation** – extract the network topology (sections, switches), the timetable (Δt⁰), current delays (δ), and define the speed‑profile catalogue (K).  
2. **Parameter computation** – compute braking distances/braking times for each profile, the minimum travel times θ_{s,k}, and the Δ‑terms.  
3. **Model building** – feed the sets, parameters, and the above MILP formulation to a solver.  
4. **Solution interpretation** – the optimal *a_{t,s}* give the new schedule; *β_{t,s,k}=1* tells which speed profile each train should adopt; *x_{(t1,t2),s}* indicates the resolved ordering on every conflicted section.  

With this complete MILP formulation you can now evaluate, for a given set of disruptions, how much total delay can be avoided by exploiting the **speed‑dependent separation** that DTG signalling makes possible, exactly as described in the paper’s contribution.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

**Integrated Train‑Rescheduling and Speed‑Management MILP (TRSMP)**  
The model below captures, in a single mixed‑integer linear program, the three‑fold decision problem that arises when a partial‑segment blockage forces a high‑speed railway operator to (i) **retime** trains, (ii) **reorder / reroute** them on the opposite track, and (iii) **choose feasible speed profiles** for every train‑run segment.  

All sets, parameters, decision variables, the objective function and the constraints are listed explicitly.  Where data are not supplied in the description, reasonable assumptions are stated and marked **(Assumption X)**.

---

## 1.  Index Sets and Basic Notation  

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **T** = {1,…,|T|} | Set of trains that are scheduled to run during the planning horizon. |
| **S** = {1,…,|S|} | Set of stations (including the origin and destination of each train). |
| **L** = {1,…,|L|} | Set of line‑segments (track sections) connecting two consecutive stations. Each segment ℓ ∈ L has a *direction* d(ℓ) ∈ {+ , – } (forward / backward). |
| **B** ⊆ L | Sub‑set of *blocked* segments (the disruption area). |
| **K** = {1,…,Kmax} | Set of *speed‑profile* alternatives (discrete speed‑time plans) that can be assigned to a train on a given segment. |
| **P** = {1,…,Pmax} | Set of *order‑position* indices used for train‑reordering on a shared segment (see constraint (13)). |
| **Δ** = {0,1,…,Δmax} | Set of discrete time‑interval indices used for linearising quadratic speed‑energy relations (Assumption 4). |

---

## 2.  Parameters  

| Symbol | Description | Typical Value / Source |
|--------|--------------|------------------------|
| **τ₀ₜₛ** | Planned (pre‑disruption) arrival time of train *t* at station *s*. | timetable data |
| **δₜₛ** | Minimum dwell time required at station *s* for train *t* (including passenger exchange). | Assumption 1: 2–5 min |
| **Lℓ** | Physical length of segment ℓ (km). | infrastructure data |
| **vᵐₖ** | Maximum admissible speed for profile *k* (km/h). | Assumption 2: 200–350 km/h |
| **aᵐₖ**, **bᵐₖ** | Maximum acceleration / deceleration for profile *k* (km/h²). | Assumption 2 |
| **eₖ** | Energy consumption (kWh) associated with completing a segment with profile *k* (averaged over the segment). | derived from train‑performance curves |
| **M** | Large constant for “big‑M” linearisation (≥ planning horizon, e.g. 10⁶ s). | Assumption 3 |
| **Tmax** | Upper bound on the planning horizon (seconds). | e.g. 24 h |
| **Δt** | Length of a discretisation interval for the piece‑wise linear speed‑energy relation (seconds). | Assumption 4: 10 s |
| **c₁**, **c₂** | Weight coefficients for the two competing objectives (delay minimisation, energy consumption). | c₁ = 1, c₂ = 0.01 (typical) |
| **βℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Indicator: 1 if segment ℓ is *bidirectional* (i.e. both directions share the same physical track). | Assumption 5 |
| **γℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Indicator: 1 if segment ℓ belongs to the blocked set **B**. | problem data |
| **Δ₍ℓ₎** = [tᵇ₍ℓ₎ , tᵉ₍ℓ₎] | Disruption time window on blocked segment ℓ (seconds). | given by incident report |
| **Rₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Feasibility indicator: 1 if train *t* is allowed to use segment ℓ (i.e. the train’s original route contains ℓ). | derived from original timetable |
| **Uₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Feasibility indicator for *rerouting*: 1 if train *t* may use the opposite‑track version of ℓ (only when βℓ = 1). | Assumption 6 |

---

## 3.  Decision Variables  

| Symbol | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| **aₜₛ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Actual *arrival* time of train *t* at station *s*. |
| **dₜₛ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Actual *departure* time of train *t* from station *s*. |
| **xₜℓk** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* traverses segment ℓ using speed‑profile *k*. |
| **yₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses segment ℓ (either original direction or rerouted). |
| **zₜℓ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | 1 if train *t* uses the *opposite* direction of a bidirectional segment ℓ (i.e. rerouting). |
| **pₜℓp** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | Position of train *t* on segment ℓ in the ordered sequence *p* (used for conflict‑avoidance on shared track). |
| **wₜℓδ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Travel time of train *t* on segment ℓ (seconds). |
| **uₜℓδ** ≥ 0 | Continuous | Energy consumption of train *t* on segment ℓ (kWh). |
| **θₜℓδ** ∈ {0,1} | Binary | Indicator that the travel time of train *t* on ℓ falls into discretisation interval δ (used for piece‑wise linear energy‑time relation). |

---

## 4.  Model Assumptions (explicitly stated)

2. **Assumption 2 – Discrete speed profiles** – The continuous speed‑time space is approximated by a finite set **K** of admissible profiles, each characterised by a constant cruising speed, acceleration and deceleration limits.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

"""
MILP for integrated train rescheduling and speed management under a partial segment blockage.
Author:  ChatGPT (generated)
Date:    2024‑06‑xx

Requires:
    - Python 3.7+
    - PuLP (pip install pulp)
    - A MILP solver (CBC is shipped with PuLP; Gurobi/CPLEX can be used by changing the solver)

The model follows the formulation described in the prompt.
"""

import pulp
import itertools

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- INPUT DATA ---------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1) Sets ---------------------------------------------------------------
I = ['T1', 'T2', 'T3']                     # trains
S = ['s1', 's2', 's3', 's_star']           # track segments (s_star is the blocked one)
# (T is not needed explicitly – we only need a horizon for the big‑M)
time_horizon = 200                         # an upper bound on any event time (used for M)

# 2) Parameters ---------------------------------------------------------
# Original schedule (planned) – these are the “reference” times
a0 = {'T1':  30, 'T2':  80, 'T3': 130}      # planned arrival at final destination
d0 = {'T1':   0, 'T2':  50, 'T3': 100}      # planned departure from origin

# Travel‑time bounds (in minutes) for each train‑segment pair
tau_min = {
    ('T1','s1'): 5, ('T1','s2'): 7, ('T1','s3'): 6, ('T1','s_star'): 8,
    ('T2','s1'): 6, ('T2','s2'): 8, ('T2','s3'): 5, ('T2','s_star'): 9,
    ('T3','s1'): 7, ('T3','s2'): 6, ('T3','s3'): 7, ('T3','s_star'):10,
}
tau_max = {
    ('T1','s1'):10, ('T1','s2'):12, ('T1','s3'):11, ('T1','s_star'):14,
    ('T2','s1'):11, ('T2','s2'):13, ('T2','s3'):10, ('T2','s_star'):15,
    ('T3','s1'):12, ('T3','s2'):11, ('T3','s3'):12, ('T3','s_star'):16,
}

# Energy cost per unit traversal time on each segment (arbitrary units)
e = {'s1': 1.0, 's2': 1.2, 's3': 0.9, 's_star': 1.5}

# Disruption window on the blocked segment s_star
t_start = 60      # start of blockage
t_end   = 100     # end of blockage

# Weight for the energy term in the objective
lambda_ = 0.1

# Big‑M constant (must be larger than any feasible time)
M = time_horizon + 10

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- MODEL DEFINITION ---------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

model = pulp.LpProblem("Train_Rescheduling_and_Speed_Management", pulp.LpMinimize)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- VARIABLES ------------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Departure / arrival times
D = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("Dep", I, lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')
A = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("Arr", I, lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')

# Segment traversal start time and duration
u = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("StartSeg", [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')
v = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("DurSeg",   [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          lowBound=0, cat='Continuous')

# Binary variables for direction usage
x = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("UseOrigDir", [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          cat='Binary')
y = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("UseOpposite", [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          cat='Binary')

# Ordering binaries for same‑direction conflicts
z = {}
for s in S:
    for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
        z[(i, k, s)] = pulp.LpVariable(f"Order_{i}_{k}_{s}", cat='Binary')

# Ordering binaries for opposite‑track conflict on the blocked segment
z_op = {}
for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
    # only needed when one train uses original direction and the other opposite on s_star
    z_op[(i, k)] = pulp.LpVariable(f"OrderOpp_{i}_{k}", cat='Binary')

# Binary for the disruption‑window side choice (only for trains that actually use s_star in original direction)
w = {}
for i in I:
    w[i] = pulp.LpVariable(f"WindowSide_{i}", cat='Binary')

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- CONSTRAINTS ---------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 0) Rerouting relationship on the blocked segment (all other segments keep y=0)
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        if s == 's_star':
            model += y[(i, s)] == 1 - x[(i, s)], f"RerouteRelation_{i}_{s}"
        else:
            model += y[(i, s)] == 0, f"OppositeNotAllowed_{i}_{s}"

# 1) Departure / arrival consistency (total travel time = sum of segment durations)
for i in I:
    model += D[i] + pulp.lpSum(v[(i, s)] for s in S) == A[i], f"DepArrCons_{i}"

for i in I:

        model += v[(i, s)] >= tau_min[(i, s)] * x[(i, s)], f"MinDur_{i}_{s}"

        model += v[(i, s)] <= M * x[(i, s)], f"ZeroDurIfNotUsed_{i}_{s}"

for s in S:
    for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
        # Only enforce ordering if both trains actually use the segment in the original direction
        model += u[(i, s)] + v[(i, s)] <= u[(k, s)] + M * (1 - z[(i, k, s)]) + M * (2 - x[(i, s)] - x[(k, s)]), \
                 f"Seq1_{i}_{k}_{s}"
        model += u[(k, s)] + v[(k, s)] <= u[(i, s)] + M * (z[(i, k, s)]) + M * (2 - x[(i, s)] - x[(k, s)]), \
                 f"Seq2_{i}_{k}_{s}"
        # The big‑M terms (2 - x_i - x_k) deactivate the constraints when at least one train does not use the segment

# 4) Bidirectional conflict on the blocked segment s_star
s_star = 's_star'
for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
    # Cases:
    #   i uses original direction (x=1) and k uses opposite (y=1)  OR
    #   k uses original direction and i uses opposite.
    # We create two constraints that are activated only when the corresponding pair of binaries is 1.
    #   u_i + v_i <= u_k + M * (1 - z_op)   when x_i =1 , y_k =1
    #   u_k + v_k <= u_i + M * (z_op)       when x_k =1 , y_i =1
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + v[(i, s_star)] <= u[(k, s_star)] + M * (1 - z_op[(i, k)]) \
             + M * (2 - x[(i, s_star)] - y[(k, s_star)]), f"OppSeq1_{i}_{k}"
    model += u[(k, s_star)] + v[(k, s_star)] <= u[(i, s_star)] + M * (z_op[(i, k)]) \
             + M * (2 - x[(k, s_star)] - y[(i, s_star)]), f"OppSeq2_{i}_{k}"

# 5) Disruption window for trains that traverse the blocked segment in the original direction
for i in I:
    # If x[i,s_star] = 0 the constraints are automatically satisfied (big‑M term deactivates them)
    # Otherwise we force the traversal to be completely before t_start OR completely after t_end.
    # w[i] = 0  -> before window, w[i] = 1 -> after window
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + M * (1 - x[(i, s_star)]) >= t_end * w[i], f"WindowAfter_{i}"
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + v[(i, s_star)] <= t_start + M * (1 - x[(i, s_star)]) + M * w[i], f"WindowBefore_{i}"

# 6) (Optional) Dwell time at stations – here we model a simple minimum/maximum lay‑over
#    between the end of segment s and the start of the next segment.
#    For simplicity we assume the segment order is fixed: s1 -> s2 -> s3 -> s_star.
#    You can adapt the ordering or add explicit station sets if needed.
dwell_min = 1   # minutes
dwell_max = 5   # minutes
ordered_segments = ['s1', 's2', 's3', 's_star']
for i in I:
    for idx in range(len(ordered_segments)-1):
        s_cur = ordered_segments[idx]
        s_nxt = ordered_segments[idx+1]
        # Only enforce if both segments are used (x=1 for both)
        model += u[(i, s_nxt)] - (u[(i, s_cur)] + v[(i, s_cur)]) >= dwell_min - M * (2 - x[(i, s_cur)] - x[(i, s_nxt)]), \
                 f"DwellMin_{i}_{s_cur}_{s_nxt}"
        model += u[(i, s_nxt)] - (u[(i, s_cur)] + v[(i, s_cur)]) <= dwell_max + M * (2 - x[(i, s_cur)] - x[(i, s_nxt)]), \
                 f"DwellMax_{i}_{s_cur}_{s_nxt}"

# 7) Link departure/arrival times to the first/last segment (optional but often useful)
#    Here we force the departure time to be the start of the first segment and the arrival
#    time to be the end of the last segment.
first_seg = ordered_segments[0]
last_seg  = ordered_segments[-1]
for i in I:
    model += D[i] == u[(i, first_seg)], f"DepEqualsStart_{i}"
    model += A[i] == u[(i, last_seg)] + v[(i, last_seg)], f"ArrEqualsEnd_{i}"

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- OBJECTIVE -----------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Total delay = sum_i (A_i - a0_i)
total_delay = pulp.lpSum(A[i] - a0[i] for i in I)

# Total energy = sum_{i,s} e_s * v_{i,s}
total_energy = pulp.lpSum(e[s] * v[(i, s)] for i in I for s in S)

model += total_delay + lambda_ * total_energy, "WeightedDelayPlusEnergy"

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- SOLVE ---------------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

print("Solving the model ...")
solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)   # change to Gurobi/CPLEX if you have them
model.solve(solver)

print("\n=== Solver status ===")
print(pulp.LpStatus[model.status])

print("\n=== Objective value ===")
print(pulp.value(model.objective))

print("\n=== Decision variables ===")
for i in I:
    print(f"\nTrain {i}:")
    print(f"  Departure  = {pulp.value(D[i]):.2f}")
    print(f"  Arrival    = {pulp.value(A[i]):.2f}")
    for s in ordered_segments:
        used = pulp.value(x[(i, s)])
        opp  = pulp.value(y[(i, s)])
        if used > 0.5:
            direction = "original"
        elif opp > 0.5:
            direction = "opposite"
        else:
            direction = "not used"
        print(f"  Segment {s}: start={pulp.value(u[(i, s)]):.2f}, dur={pulp.value(v[(i, s)]):.2f}, dir={direction}")

print("\n=== Summary ===")
print(f"Total delay  = {pulp.value(total_delay):.2f}")
print(f"Total energy = {pulp.value(total_energy):.2f}")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# End of script
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

### How to use the script

1. **Install PuLP** (if you haven’t already)  

   ```bash
   pip install pulp
   ```

2. **Save the script** to a file, e.g. `train_reschedule.py`.

3. **Run it**  

   ```bash
   python train_reschedule.py
   ```

   The default solver is CBC (bundled with PuLP). If you have a commercial solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …) you can replace the line  

   ```python
   solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)
   ```  

   with the appropriate PuLP wrapper, e.g. `pulp.GUROBI_CMD()`.

4. **Adapt the data** – the sets `I`, `S`, the parameters (`a0`, `d0`, `tau_min`, `tau_max`, `e`, `t_start`, `t_end`, `lambda_`, etc.) are defined near the top of the file. Replace them with your real instance data.  

5. **Extend / modify** – the script already contains optional dwell‑time constraints and the linking of departure/arrival times to the first/last segment. If you need additional constraints (e.g., platform capacity, crew limits, etc.) you can add them in the *Constraints* section following the same pattern.

---

#### What the model does

* **Reschedules** each train’s departure and arrival times while respecting the physical travel‑time limits on every segment.  
* **Manages speed** implicitly through the continuous variable `v[i,s]` – a longer `v` means a slower speed (higher energy cost).  
* **Handles the blockage** on segment `s_star` by either (i) moving the traversal completely outside the disruption window or (ii) rerouting the train onto the opposite track (`y=1`).  
* **Ensures safety** by sequencing any two trains that occupy the same physical resource (same direction on a segment, or opposite‑track conflict on the blocked segment).  
* **Minimises** a weighted sum of total passenger delay and the energy consumption incurred by the chosen speeds.

Feel free to copy the code into your own project, adjust the parameters, and integrate it with your data pipelines. Happy optimisation!

x = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("UseOrigDir", [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          cat='Binary')
y = pulp.LpVariable.dicts("UseOpposite", [(i, s) for i in I for s in S],
                          cat='Binary')

# Ordering binaries for same‑direction conflicts
z = {}
for s in S:
    for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
        z[(i, k, s)] = pulp.LpVariable(f"Order_{i}_{k}_{s}", cat='Binary')

# Ordering binaries for opposite‑track conflict on the blocked segment
z_op = {}
for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
    # only needed when one train uses original direction and the other opposite on s_star
    z_op[(i, k)] = pulp.LpVariable(f"OrderOpp_{i}_{k}", cat='Binary')

# Binary for the disruption‑window side choice (only for trains that actually use s_star in original direction)
w = {}
for i in I:
    w[i] = pulp.LpVariable(f"WindowSide_{i}", cat='Binary')

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- CONSTRAINTS ---------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 0) Rerouting relationship on the blocked segment (all other segments keep y=0)
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        if s == 's_star':
            model += y[(i, s)] == 1 - x[(i, s)], f"RerouteRelation_{i}_{s}"
        else:
            model += y[(i, s)] == 0, f"OppositeNotAllowed_{i}_{s}"

# 1) Departure / arrival consistency (total travel time = sum of segment durations)
for i in I:
    model += D[i] + pulp.lpSum(v[(i, s)] for s in S) == A[i], f"DepArrCons_{i}"

# 2) Travel‑time bounds for each segment
for i in I:
    for s in S:
        model += v[(i, s)] >= tau_min[(i, s)] * x[(i, s)], f"MinDur_{i}_{s}"
        model += v[(i, s)] <= tau_max[(i, s)] * x[(i, s)], f"MaxDur_{i}_{s}"
        # If the train does NOT use the segment (x=0) then v must be 0
        model += v[(i, s)] <= M * x[(i, s)], f"ZeroDurIfNotUsed_{i}_{s}"

# 3) Sequencing on each segment for trains using the SAME direction
for s in S:
    for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
        # Only enforce ordering if both trains actually use the segment in the original direction
        model += u[(i, s)] + v[(i, s)] <= u[(k, s)] + M * (1 - z[(i, k, s)]) + M * (2 - x[(i, s)] - x[(k, s)]), \
                 f"Seq1_{i}_{k}_{s}"
        model += u[(k, s)] + v[(k, s)] <= u[(i, s)] + M * (z[(i, k, s)]) + M * (2 - x[(i, s)] - x[(k, s)]), \
                 f"Seq2_{i}_{k}_{s}"
        # The big‑M terms (2 - x_i - x_k) deactivate the constraints when at least one train does not use the segment

# 4) Bidirectional conflict on the blocked segment s_star
s_star = 's_star'
for i, k in itertools.combinations(I, 2):
    # Cases:
    #   i uses original direction (x=1) and k uses opposite (y=1)  OR
    #   k uses original direction and i uses opposite.
    # We create two constraints that are activated only when the corresponding pair of binaries is 1.
    #   u_i + v_i <= u_k + M * (1 - z_op)   when x_i =1 , y_k =1
    #   u_k + v_k <= u_i + M * (z_op)       when x_k =1 , y_i =1
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + v[(i, s_star)] <= u[(k, s_star)] + M * (1 - z_op[(i, k)]) \
             + M * (2 - x[(i, s_star)] - y[(k, s_star)]), f"OppSeq1_{i}_{k}"
    model += u[(k, s_star)] + v[(k, s_star)] <= u[(i, s_star)] + M * (z_op[(i, k)]) \
             + M * (2 - x[(k, s_star)] - y[(i, s_star)]), f"OppSeq2_{i}_{k}"

# 5) Disruption window for trains that traverse the blocked segment in the original direction
for i in I:
    # If x[i,s_star] = 0 the constraints are automatically satisfied (big‑M term deactivates them)
    # Otherwise we force the traversal to be completely before t_start OR completely after t_end.
    # w[i] = 0  -> before window, w[i] = 1 -> after window
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + M * (1 - x[(i, s_star)]) >= t_end * w[i], f"WindowAfter_{i}"
    model += u[(i, s_star)] + v[(i, s_star)] <= t_start + M * (1 - x[(i, s_star)]) + M * w[i], f"WindowBefore_{i}"

# 6) (Optional) Dwell time at stations – here we model a simple minimum/maximum lay‑over
#    between the end of segment s and the start of the next segment.
#    For simplicity we assume the segment order is fixed: s1 -> s2 -> s3 -> s_star.
#    You can adapt the ordering or add explicit station sets if needed.
dwell_min = 1   # minutes
dwell_max = 5   # minutes
ordered_segments = ['s1', 's2', 's3', 's_star']
for i in I:
    for idx in range(len(ordered_segments)-1):
        s_cur = ordered_segments[idx]
        s_nxt = ordered_segments[idx+1]
        # Only enforce if both segments are used (x=1 for both)
        model += u[(i, s_nxt)] - (u[(i, s_cur)] + v[(i, s_cur)]) >= dwell_min - M * (2 - x[(i, s_cur)] - x[(i, s_nxt)]), \
                 f"DwellMin_{i}_{s_cur}_{s_nxt}"
        model += u[(i, s_nxt)] - (u[(i, s_cur)] + v[(i, s_cur)]) <= dwell_max + M * (2 - x[(i, s_cur)] - x[(i, s_nxt)]), \
                 f"DwellMax_{i}_{s_cur}_{s_nxt}"

# 7) Link departure/arrival times to the first/last segment (optional but often useful)
#    Here we force the departure time to be the start of the first segment and the arrival
#    time to be the end of the last segment.
first_seg = ordered_segments[0]
last_seg  = ordered_segments[-1]
for i in I:
    model += D[i] == u[(i, first_seg)], f"DepEqualsStart_{i}"
    model += A[i] == u[(i, last_seg)] + v[(i, last_seg)], f"ArrEqualsEnd_{i}"

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- OBJECTIVE -----------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Total delay = sum_i (A_i - a0_i)
total_delay = pulp.lpSum(A[i] - a0[i] for i in I)

# Total energy = sum_{i,s} e_s * v_{i,s}
total_energy = pulp.lpSum(e[s] * v[(i, s)] for i in I for s in S)

model += total_delay + lambda_ * total_energy, "WeightedDelayPlusEnergy"

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# --------------------------- SOLVE ---------------------------------------
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

print("Solving the model ...")
solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)   # change to Gurobi/CPLEX if you have them
model.solve(solver)

print("\n=== Solver status ===")
print(pulp.LpStatus[model.status])

print("\n=== Objective value ===")
print(pulp.value(model.objective))

print("\n=== Decision variables ===")
for i in I:
    print(f"\nTrain {i}:")
    print(f"  Departure  = {pulp.value(D[i]):.2f}")
    print(f"  Arrival    = {pulp.value(A[i]):.2f}")
    for s in ordered_segments:
        used = pulp.value(x[(i, s)])
        opp  = pulp.value(y[(i, s)])
        if used > 0.5:
            direction = "original"
        elif opp > 0.5:
            direction = "opposite"
        else:
            direction = "not used"
        print(f"  Segment {s}: start={pulp.value(u[(i, s)]):.2f}, dur={pulp.value(v[(i, s)]):.2f}, dir={direction}")

print("\n=== Summary ===")
print(f"Total delay  = {pulp.value(total_delay):.2f}")
print(f"Total energy = {pulp.value(total_energy):.2f}")

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# End of script
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

### How to use the script

1. **Install PuLP** (if you haven’t already)  

   ```bash
   pip install pulp
   ```

2. **Save the script** to a file, e.g. `train_reschedule.py`.

3. **Run it**  

   ```bash
   python train_reschedule.py
   ```

   The default solver is CBC (bundled with PuLP). If you have a commercial solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …) you can replace the line  

   ```python
   solver = pulp.PULP_CBC_CMD(msg=True)
   ```  

   with the appropriate PuLP wrapper, e.g. `pulp.GUROBI_CMD()`.

4. **Adapt the data** – the sets `I`, `S`, the parameters (`a0`, `d0`, `tau_min`, `tau_max`, `e`, `t_start`, `t_end`, `lambda_`, etc.) are defined near the top of the file. Replace them with your real instance data.  

5. **Extend / modify** – the script already contains optional dwell‑time constraints and the linking of departure/arrival times to the first/last segment. If you need additional constraints (e.g., platform capacity, crew limits, etc.) you can add them in the *Constraints* section following the same pattern.

---

#### What the model does

* **Reschedules** each train’s departure and arrival times while respecting the physical travel‑time limits on every segment.  
* **Manages speed** implicitly through the continuous variable `v[i,s]` – a longer `v` means a slower speed (higher energy cost).  
* **Handles the blockage** on segment `s_star` by either (i) moving the traversal completely outside the disruption window or (ii) rerouting the train onto the opposite track (`y=1`).  
* **Ensures safety** by sequencing any two trains that occupy the same physical resource (same direction on a segment, or opposite‑track conflict on the blocked segment).  
* **Minimises** a weighted sum of total passenger delay and the energy consumption incurred by the chosen speeds.

Feel free to copy the code into your own project, adjust the parameters, and integrate it with your data pipelines. Happy optimisation!

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run Python script** that builds the mixed‑integer linear program (MILP) described in the prompt using the **PuLP** modelling library (which can be solved with any MILP solver that PuLP supports – e.g. CBC, Gurobi, CPLEX, Xpress, …).  

The script follows the notation of the description:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|----------|
| **I**  | set of trains `i` |
| **S**  | set of track segments `s` |
| **T**  | set of (discrete) time periods – only needed for the big‑M constant |
| `a0[i]` | original arrival time of train *i* (the “planned” arrival) |
| `d0[i]` | original departure time of train *i* (the “planned” departure) |
| `tau_min[i,s]` , `tau_max[i,s]` | lower / upper bound on the travel time of train *i* on segment *s* |
| `e[s]` | energy cost per unit of traversal time on segment *s* |
| `t_start , t_end` | disruption window on the blocked segment `s_star` |
| `lambda_` | weight of the energy term in the objective |
| `M` | a big‑M constant (larger than the planning horizon) |

The model contains the following decision variables  

* `D[i]` – actual departure time of train *i* (continuous)  
* `A[i]` – actual arrival time of train *i* (continuous)  
* `u[i,s]` – start time of the traversal of segment *s* by train *i* (continuous)  
* `v[i,s]` – duration of the traversal (continuous)  
* `x[i,s]` – 1 if train *i* uses segment *s* in its original direction (binary)  
* `y[i,s]` – 1 if train *i* uses the opposite track on segment *s* (binary) – only needed for the blocked segment `s_star`  
* `z[i,k,s]` – ordering binary for two trains that share the **same** direction on segment *s* (binary)  
* `z_op[i,k]` – ordering binary for a train that uses the opposite track on the blocked segment (`y`) versus a train that uses the original direction (`x`) (binary)  
* `w[i]` – binary that decides which side of the disruption window a train that traverses the blocked segment in the original direction will be placed (binary)  

The script is heavily commented so you can see exactly how each piece of the description is translated into algebraic constraints.
